25-OHD: Main circulating form of vitamin D; low levels indicate deficiency and secondary hyperparathyroidism risk.
AAA: Focal infrarenal aortic dilation >3 cm; rupture risk increases sharply above 5.5 cm (men) or 5.0 cm (women). Screened by one-off abdominal ultrasound in men ≥65 who have ever smoked; elective repair (open or EVAR) for large or rapidly expanding aneurysms. Ruptured AAA (sudden back/flank pain, hypotension, pulsatile mass) is a surgical emergency with high mortality.
ABG: Arterial sample measuring pH, pCO₂, pO₂, bicarbonate, and base excess to assess oxygenation, ventilation, and acid–base status simultaneously. Allows precise classification of acid–base disorder (respiratory vs metabolic, degree of compensation); many analysers also report lactate, carboxyhaemoglobin, and methaemoglobin.
ABPI: Ratio of ankle to brachial systolic BP measured by Doppler; <0.9 indicates peripheral arterial disease, <0.4 indicates critical ischaemia, >1.3 suggests vessel calcification.
ACE: Enzyme converting angiotensin I to II; ACE inhibitors (lisinopril, ramipril, enalapril) block this step, reducing BP, afterload, and proteinuria. First-line for HFrEF, post-MI, CKD with proteinuria, and diabetic nephropathy; main side effect is dry cough (10–15% from bradykinin accumulation); rare angioedema - switch to ARB if cough is intolerable.
ACS: Spectrum of acute myocardial ischaemia encompassing unstable angina, NSTEMI (troponin rise, no ST elevation), and STEMI (ST elevation). All require aspirin, anticoagulation, and risk stratification; STEMI and high-risk NSTEMI need urgent revascularisation.
ACTH: Pituitary hormone stimulating adrenal cortisol production; used diagnostically in Synacthen test.
ADH: Posterior pituitary hormone promoting water reabsorption; dysregulation causes SIADH or diabetes insipidus.
ADHD: Neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by persistent inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity impairing function across ≥2 settings; DSM-5 requires symptoms before age 12. First-line pharmacotherapy: stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamines); atomoxetine is a non-stimulant alternative; behavioural therapy is integral, especially in young children.
AED: A medication used to prevent or reduce the frequency of epileptic seizures.
AF: Disorganised atrial electrical activity producing an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm; classified as paroxysmal (<7 days, self-terminating), persistent, or permanent. CHA₂DS₂-VASc score guides anticoagulation (DOAC preferred); rate control with beta-blocker or non-DHP CCB; rhythm control by cardioversion or ablation.
AFP: Tumour marker elevated in hepatocellular carcinoma and germ cell tumours.
Maternal serum AFP is used in prenatal screening for neural tube defects and Down syndrome.
AFib: Disorganised atrial electrical activity producing an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm; raises embolic stroke risk significantly. CHA₂DS₂-VASc score guides anticoagulation; rate control (beta-blocker, digoxin) or rhythm control (cardioversion, antiarrhythmics, catheter ablation) depending on symptoms and duration.
AKI: Abrupt decline in renal function over hours to days: creatinine rise ≥26.5 µmol/L in 48 h, ≥1.5× baseline in 7 days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 h (KDIGO). Ddx: pre-renal - hypovolaemia, sepsis, cardiorenal or hepatorenal syndrome, NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors; intrinsic - acute tubular necrosis is commonest, then glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis, vascular causes; post-renal - bladder outlet obstruction, stones, pelvic malignancy. Mx: treat the cause, restore perfusion, cease nephrotoxins, review every drug for renal dosing, relieve obstruction. Red flags: refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload or uraemic complications mean dialysis.
ALL: Most common childhood malignancy; clonal expansion of immature lymphoblasts causing pancytopenia, bone pain, lymphadenopathy, and CNS involvement. Pre-B ALL (most common) driven by translocations (ETV6-RUNX1, hyperdiploidy); BFM/COG multi-phase protocols achieve >90% cure in children; CNS prophylaxis with intrathecal chemotherapy is essential.
ALP: Enzyme elevated in cholestatic liver disease (bile duct obstruction, PBC, PSC, infiltrative liver disease) and bone disorders (Paget's disease, bone metastases, osteomalacia). To identify the source, check GGT (rises with hepatobiliary ALP, stays normal with bone ALP) and isoenzymes; isolated ALP elevation in a young person may be physiological (bone growth).
ALS: Progressive degeneration of both upper and lower motor neurons causing asymmetric limb weakness, wasting, fasciculations, and hyperreflexia; bulbar involvement causes dysarthria and dysphagia. Riluzole modestly extends survival; multidisciplinary care with NIV (non-invasive ventilation) and PEG feeding improves quality of life; median survival 3–5 years.

Advanced resuscitation protocol addressing shockable (VF/pulseless VT) and non-shockable (PEA/asystole) cardiac arrest rhythms; includes high-quality CPR, defibrillation, IV/IO adrenaline every 3–5 min, and advanced airway management. ALS (ARC/ANZCOR) (American) and ALS (UK/Australia) algorithms share core principles but differ slightly in drug choices and sequencing.
ALT: Transaminase most specific to hepatocyte injury; markedly elevated (>1000 U/L) in acute viral hepatitis, ischaemic hepatitis ('shock liver'), or severe drug-induced liver injury (paracetamol overdose). Mild elevation (<3× ULN) is common in NAFLD - persistently elevated ALT should prompt investigation for chronic liver disease causes.
AML: Clonal proliferation of myeloid blasts (≥20% in bone marrow); presents with cytopenias (anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia), fatigue, bleeding, and infection; Auer rods in blasts are pathognomonic. Prognosis determined by cytogenetics/molecular mutations (FLT3, NPM1, IDH1/2); standard induction is anthracycline + cytarabine ('7+3'); allogeneic HSCT for high-risk disease.
ANA: Autoantibody directed against nuclear antigens; positive in SLE and other connective tissue diseases.
ANCA: Antineutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibody - c-ANCA (PR3, granulomatosis with polyangiitis)
c-ANCA (anti-PR3) is associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's).
p-ANCA (anti-MPO) is associated with microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
APACHE: Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II
ICU prognostic scoring system using 12 acute physiology variables plus age and chronic health; predicts hospital mortality.
APGAR: Scoring system assessing newborn status at 1 and 5 minutes using Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, and Respiration.
APTT: Coagulation test measuring the intrinsic pathway; used to monitor unfractionated heparin therapy.
AR: Backflow through an incompetent aortic valve producing an early diastolic murmur and wide pulse pressure (collapsing/waterhammer pulse); causes include bicuspid aortic valve, rheumatic disease, infective endocarditis, and aortic root dilation (Marfan syndrome). Chronic AR causes LV volume overload; valve replacement indicated when symptomatic, EF <50%, or LV end-systolic diameter >50 mm.
ARB: Blocks AT1 (angiotensin II) receptors; same clinical indications as ACE inhibitors (HFrEF, CKD, hypertension, post-MI) but does not cause cough since bradykinin is unaffected. Never combine with ACE-I (dual RAAS blockade increases hyperkalaemia and renal impairment risk); examples: losartan, valsartan, irbesartan, candesartan.
ARDS: Acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure defined by Berlin criteria: onset within 1 week, bilateral opacities on imaging not fully explained by effusions or cardiac failure, and PaO₂/FiO₂ <300 mmHg (mild <300, moderate <200, severe <100). Managed with lung-protective ventilation (6 mL/kg ideal body weight, PEEP titration) and prone positioning for moderate-severe ARDS; treat the underlying cause (sepsis, aspiration, etc.).
ARM: Deliberate rupture of the fetal membranes using an amnihook to induce or augment labour.
ARNI: Sacubitril/valsartan (Entresto) combines neprilysin inhibition (increases natriuretic peptides, vasodilation, natriuresis) with AT1 receptor blockade; PARADIGM-HF demonstrated reduced CV death and HF hospitalisation vs enalapril in HFrEF. Requires ≥36 h washout from ACE-I before initiation; contraindicated concomitantly with ACE-I to prevent angioedema.
AS: Narrowed aortic valve orifice (severe: AVA <1.0 cm², mean gradient >40 mmHg) producing a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the RUSB radiating to the carotids; classic triad of exertional syncope, angina, and dyspnoea. Age-related calcific degeneration is the commonest cause; treated by SAVR or TAVR when symptomatic or with significant LV dysfunction.

Seronegative spondyloarthropathy characterised by sacroiliitis and axial inflammation; strongly HLA-B27 associated; presents in young males with inflammatory back pain and morning stiffness >1 h improving with exercise. Extra-articular: anterior uveitis, aortic regurgitation, and pulmonary apical fibrosis; NSAIDs first-line, anti-TNF or anti-IL-17 biologics for refractory disease.
ASD: Congenital opening between the atria causing left-to-right shunting; ostium secundum (most common) produces fixed split S2 and a pulmonary flow murmur. Large unrepaired defects cause RV volume overload, AF, and paradoxical embolism; transcatheter or surgical closure recommended when haemodynamically significant.

Neurodevelopmental disorder with social-communication deficits and restricted, repetitive behaviours or interests; DSM-5 spectrum replaces older subtypes (Asperger's, PDD-NOS). Diagnosed by clinical assessment and standardised tools (ADOS, ADI-R); management is multidisciplinary - behavioural therapy, speech therapy, and educational support.
AST: Transaminase elevated in hepatocellular injury; less liver-specific than ALT - also raised in myocardial infarction, rhabdomyolysis, and haemolysis. AST:ALT ratio >2:1 suggests alcoholic liver disease (mitochondrial damage favours AST release); >3:1 is strongly suggestive; isolated elevated AST warrants checking CK and troponin to exclude cardiac or muscle source.
ATN: Commonest cause of intrinsic AKI; ischaemic ATN follows sustained hypoperfusion (sepsis, surgery, hypovolaemia), nephrotoxic ATN from aminoglycosides, contrast agents, or cisplatin. Characterised by muddy brown granular casts on urinalysis and FENA >2%; management is supportive with fluid optimisation and avoidance of further nephrotoxins.
AUB: Any deviation from normal menstrual pattern including heavy, prolonged, or irregular uterine bleeding.
AUC: Pharmacokinetic measure of total drug exposure over time; used in Calvert formula for carboplatin dosing.
AUDIT: WHO 10-item questionnaire screening for hazardous and harmful alcohol use; score ≥8 indicates hazardous drinking.
AVNRT: Most common cause of SVT; reentrant circuit within the AV node produces a rapid regular narrow-complex tachycardia terminated by adenosine or vagal manoeuvres.
AVPU: Simple 4-point scale for rapid neurological assessment: Alert → responds to Voice → responds to Pain → Unresponsive; a 'V' or lower correlates roughly with GCS ≤12.
AVRT: SVT using an accessory pathway (e.g. WPW); can be orthodromic (narrow) or antidromic (wide); avoid AV nodal blockers in antidromic AVRT.
AVSD: Congenital heart defect with combined ASD and VSD sharing a common AV valve; strongly associated with Down syndrome (trisomy 21); complete AVSD requires surgical repair in infancy.
AXR: Plain abdominal radiograph used to identify bowel obstruction, calcification, or free air.
Alvarado: Nine-point clinical score for suspected appendicitis (Migration, Anorexia, Nausea, Tenderness, Rebound, Elevated temp, Leukocytosis, Shift); score ≥7 suggests appendicitis.
BAER: Electrophysiological test assessing the auditory nerve and brainstem pathway; used in neonatal hearing screening.
BB: Class of antihypertensives blocking beta-adrenergic receptors; used in hypertension, heart failure, arrhythmia, and angina.
BGL: AU term for blood glucose concentration; measured at the bedside by glucometry or in the laboratory.
BMI: Weight (kg) divided by height² (m²). Classification: underweight <18.5, normal 18.5–24.9, overweight 25–29.9, obese ≥30 kg/m². Correlates with cardiometabolic risk but does not directly measure body fat distribution; waist circumference complements BMI in assessing visceral adiposity and metabolic risk.
BNP: Vasoactive peptide hormone released by ventricular cardiomyocytes in response to wall stretch and pressure overload; BNP <100 pg/mL effectively excludes heart failure as a cause of acute dyspnoea; >400 pg/mL strongly supports the diagnosis. Elevated by AF, PE, CKD, and sepsis (non-cardiac causes); serial BNP guides HF treatment response.
BP: Pressure exerted by circulating blood on arterial walls; recorded as systolic/diastolic (e.g. 120/80 mmHg). Measured non-invasively by sphygmomanometer or invasively via arterial line; ambulatory BP monitoring (ABPM) and home BP monitoring are more accurate than isolated clinic readings for diagnosing and managing hypertension.
BPD: Pervasive pattern of unstable relationships, affect, and self-image with marked impulsivity, recurrent self-harm/suicidal behaviour, identity disturbance, and fear of abandonment; diagnosed by ≥5 of 9 DSM-5 criteria. Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) is the primary evidence-based treatment; adjunctive low-dose antipsychotics or mood stabilisers may target specific symptoms.
BPH: Non-malignant enlargement of the prostate gland causing lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) including hesitancy, weak stream, nocturia, and incomplete emptying in older men. Managed with alpha-blockers (tamsulosin) for symptom relief and 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride) to reduce gland volume; TURP for refractory cases.
BSI: Infection with viable organisms in the bloodstream, detected by positive blood cultures; may be primary or from a source.
BSL: Australian colloquial term for blood glucose level measured by fingerprick glucometry.
BUN: Measure of urea in the blood; rises in renal impairment, dehydration, high protein intake, or upper GI bleeding. BUN:creatinine ratio >20:1 suggests pre-renal azotaemia or upper GI bleeding; <10:1 suggests intrinsic renal disease; urea is freely filtered but partially reabsorbed, unlike creatinine.
BV: Polymicrobial vaginal dysbiosis (overgrowth of Gardnerella, anaerobes; reduced Lactobacillus) diagnosed by Amsel criteria: 3 of 4 - homogeneous grey-white discharge, vaginal pH >4.5, clue cells on wet mount, positive whiff/amine test. Treat with metronidazole (oral or gel) or clindamycin; recurrence is common; associated with preterm labour and increased STI susceptibility.
CA-125: Tumour marker elevated in ovarian cancer and peritoneal disease; also raised in benign conditions.
CABG: Surgical revascularisation using the left internal mammary artery (LIMA to LAD - best long-term patency) and saphenous vein grafts for severe coronary disease. Preferred over PCI for left main or complex three-vessel disease (high SYNTAX score) and preserved LV function; typically performed via median sternotomy on cardiopulmonary bypass.
CAD: Atherosclerotic narrowing of the coronary arteries leading to stable angina, ACS, or sudden cardiac death; risk factors include hypertension, dyslipidaemia, diabetes, smoking, and family history. Stable disease managed medically (aspirin, statin, nitrates, beta-blocker); significant or unstable disease requires revascularisation by PCI or CABG.
CAGE: Four-question alcohol dependence screening tool (Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener); ≥2 positive responses suggests dependence.
CAP: Pneumonia acquired outside hospital or within 48 h of admission; commonest cause Streptococcus pneumoniae; atypical pathogens include Mycoplasma, Legionella, and Chlamydophila. CURB-65 score (Confusion, Urea >7, RR ≥30, BP <90/60, age ≥65) guides admission; score ≥2 warrants hospital treatment - amoxicillin + macrolide or doxycycline for ambulatory disease.
CAUTI: UTI developing in a patient with an indwelling urinary catheter; most preventable hospital-acquired infection.
CBC: Routine blood test reporting haemoglobin, haematocrit, RBC count, total and differential WBC count (neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils), and platelets. Used to diagnose anaemia (classify by MCV), infection/inflammation (leukocytosis), haematological malignancy, and thrombocytopenia.
CCB: Antihypertensive blocking voltage-gated calcium channels; dihydropyridines (amlodipine) vasodilate, non-dihydropyridines control rate.
CDAI: Clinical index measuring Crohn's disease activity from stool frequency, pain, general wellbeing, and other factors; remission <150.
CDI: Toxin-mediated colitis from Clostridioides difficile following antibiotic use; ranges from mild diarrhoea to toxic megacolon.
CEA: Tumour marker used in colorectal cancer monitoring and staging.
CHA2DS2-VASc: Stroke risk stratification tool in AF: Congestive HF, Hypertension, Age ≥75, Diabetes, Stroke, Vascular disease, Age 65-74, Sex category.
CHF: Heart's inability to maintain adequate cardiac output, causing pulmonary and/or systemic venous congestion. Classified by ejection fraction: HFrEF (EF ≤40%), HFmrEF (41–49%), or HFpEF (≥50%); symptoms include dyspnoea, orthopnoea, and peripheral oedema. BNP/NT-proBNP aids diagnosis; management targets fluid overload, neurohormonal blockade, and underlying aetiology.
CIWA: Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol

10-item scale scoring severity of alcohol withdrawal symptoms (tremor, diaphoresis, anxiety, nausea, seizures, perceptual disturbances); guides benzodiazepine dosing in symptom-triggered detoxification.
CK: Enzyme released from damaged muscle; elevated in rhabdomyolysis, myositis, myocardial infarction, and statin-induced myopathy.
CKD: Progressive irreversible loss of kidney function over ≥3 months; staged G1–G5 by eGFR (≥90 to <15 mL/min/1.73m²) combined with albuminuria categories A1–A3. Leading causes are diabetic nephropathy and hypertensive nephrosclerosis; ACE-I/ARB and BP control slow progression.
CLL: Commonest adult leukaemia in Western countries; indolent clonal CD5+ B-cell accumulation causing lymphocytosis, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly; smudge cells on peripheral smear. Early-stage CLL is managed by watch-and-wait; symptomatic or progressive disease treated with BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib, acalabrutinib) or venetoclax-based regimens.
CML: Myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by the BCR-ABL fusion oncogene from t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome; presents with leukocytosis, splenomegaly, and left shift. TKIs (imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib) achieve deep molecular remission; treatment-free remission (TFR) is possible in patients sustaining deep molecular response for ≥2 years.
CMV: Herpesvirus ubiquitous in the adult population; causes mononucleosis-like illness in immunocompetent hosts but severe disease in immunocompromised patients (transplant recipients, HIV/AIDS): retinitis, pneumonitis, colitis, and encephalitis. Congenital CMV is the commonest non-genetic cause of sensorineural hearing loss. Treatment: IV ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir.
COPD: Progressive, incompletely reversible airflow limitation due to emphysema and/or chronic bronchitis, most often from smoking; defined by post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC < 0.7. Staged by GOLD criteria (I–IV) based on FEV₁; management includes smoking cessation, bronchodilators (SABA, LAMA, LABA), ICS for frequent exacerbators, pulmonary rehabilitation, and long-term oxygen therapy when SpO₂ ≤88%.
COWS: 11-item observer-rated scale measuring opioid withdrawal severity; score guides timing of buprenorphine induction (start when COWS ≥8–12 to avoid precipitated withdrawal).
CPE: Gram-negative bacteria producing carbapenemase enzymes, conferring resistance to carbapenems; requires strict infection control.
CPR: Life-saving intervention combining chest compressions (100–120/min, 5–6 cm depth) and ventilation to maintain perfusion in cardiac arrest. BLS can be performed by lay-responders; ALS adds defibrillation (VF/pVT), IV/IO adrenaline every 3–5 min, and advanced airway management. Minimising interruptions to compressions is the most important determinant of outcome.
CRP: Acute-phase protein synthesised by the liver in response to IL-6; rises within 6–8 h, peaks at 48 h, and has a half-life of ~19 h - allowing serial monitoring of treatment response. Very high CRP (>200 mg/L) is common in bacterial infections and severe inflammatory disease; modest elevation also seen in obesity, smoking, and T2DM.
CRS: Systemic inflammatory response from massive cytokine release; complication of CAR-T cell therapy and bispecific antibodies; treated with tocilizumab (anti-IL-6R) and corticosteroids.
CSF: Fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord; sampled by lumbar puncture to diagnose meningitis and SAH.
CT: Cross-sectional imaging using X-rays and computer reconstruction of Hounsfield-unit attenuation values; superior to plain films for intracranial haemorrhage, abdominal pathology, solid organ injury, and pulmonary embolism (CTPA). Involves ionising radiation; intravenous contrast enhances vascular and solid organ structures but risks nephrotoxicity and contrast reactions.
CTPA: Contrast-enhanced CT of the pulmonary arteries; gold-standard test for suspected PE (sensitivity ~96%, specificity ~98%). Requires IV contrast (risk: AKI, anaphylaxis) and ionising radiation; Wells score + D-dimer should guide pre-test selection to avoid unnecessary imaging; V/Q scan is an alternative in pregnancy or contrast allergy.
CURB-65: Five-point score predicting 30-day mortality in community-acquired pneumonia; score ≥2 suggests hospital admission.
CVA: Sudden focal neurological deficit from cerebral ischaemia (85%) or haemorrhage (15%); NIHSS quantifies severity. Mx: ischaemic - thrombolysis with tenecteplase or alteplase within 4.5 h, endovascular thrombectomy within 24 h in selected large-vessel occlusion; haemorrhagic - blood pressure control, reverse anticoagulation, neurosurgical assessment. Secondary prevention: antiplatelet or anticoagulation by aetiology, statin, blood pressure control; early rehabilitation.
CVC: Catheter placed in a large central vein for medication infusion, haemodynamic monitoring, and CVP measurement.
CXR: Plain radiograph of the thorax used to assess cardiac size, lung fields, and mediastinum.
Child-Pugh: Scoring system for cirrhosis severity and operative risk using bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, and encephalopathy; grades A/B/C.
Cr: End-product of creatine phosphate catabolism in muscle, cleared almost entirely by glomerular filtration; serum creatinine rises as GFR falls. Production is proportional to muscle mass - a 'normal' creatinine may mask significant CKD in sarcopaenic patients; used with age and sex in the CKD-EPI equation to estimate GFR.
Cu-IUD: Non-hormonal intrauterine contraceptive device; also used as emergency contraception within 5 days of unprotected intercourse.
DAS28: Composite score of 28-joint tenderness/swelling counts, CRP/ESR, and patient global assessment to measure RA disease activity.
DCM: Ventricular dilatation with impaired systolic function; causes include idiopathic (genetic sarcomere mutations), viral myocarditis, alcohol, peripartum, and drug toxicity (chemotherapy, anthracyclines). Managed as HFrEF with the four foundational therapies; ICD for EF ≤35% with high sudden-death risk; cardiac transplantation for refractory end-stage disease.
DEXA: Low-dose X-ray scan measuring bone mineral density (BMD) at the lumbar spine and hip; reports T-score (vs young normal) and Z-score (vs age-matched). Criteria: osteoporosis is a T-score of −2.5 or lower; osteopenia −1.0 to −2.5. FRAX tool combines BMD with clinical risk factors to estimate 10-year fracture probability and guide treatment decisions.
DI: Inability to concentrate urine from deficient ADH secretion (central DI - pituitary/hypothalamic injury) or renal resistance to ADH (nephrogenic DI - lithium, hypercalcaemia, CKD). Presents with polyuria >3 L/day and compensatory polydipsia; water deprivation test with desmopressin challenge distinguishes central from nephrogenic. Central DI treated with intranasal desmopressin.
DIC: Pathological systemic coagulation activation causing simultaneous microvascular thrombosis and consumption coagulopathy (bleeding); triggered by sepsis, major trauma, malignancy, obstetric emergencies. Ix: prolonged PT/APTT, low fibrinogen, elevated D-dimer, thrombocytopenia, and schistocytes. Mx: address the trigger; replace clotting factors (FFP, cryoprecipitate) and platelets for active bleeding.
DKA: Triad of hyperglycaemia (>11 mmol/L), ketonaemia/ketonuria, and metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3, bicarbonate <15 mmol/L) from absolute insulin deficiency; typically in T1DM, precipitated by infection or missed doses. Treatment: IV saline resuscitation, fixed-rate IV insulin infusion, close potassium replacement, and addressing the precipitant.
DLCO: Measure of gas exchange efficiency across the alveolar-capillary membrane; reduced in emphysema and fibrosis.
DM: Group of metabolic disorders characterised by chronic hyperglycaemia from defective insulin secretion or action; diagnosed by fasting glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L, random glucose ≥11.1 with symptoms, or HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol. Chronic hyperglycaemia drives microvascular complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) and macrovascular disease.
DMARD: Drugs that reduce inflammation and slow structural damage in inflammatory arthritis; conventional synthetic DMARDs (csDMARDs: methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, leflunomide); biologic DMARDs (bDMARDs: anti-TNF, anti-IL-6, anti-CD20); targeted synthetic DMARDs (tsDMARDs: JAK inhibitors). Treat-to-target (remission/low disease activity) is the standard approach in RA.
DMPA: Long-acting injectable progestogen contraceptive given every 12 weeks; may cause irregular bleeding and reduced bone density.
DNC: Gynaecological procedure involving cervical dilation and uterine curettage; used to manage miscarriage and abnormal bleeding.
DNR: Patient directive (or surrogate decision) declining CPR in the event of cardiopulmonary arrest; does not prohibit other active treatments unless a broader DNAR/DNACPR or goals-of-care plan is in place. Should be documented after informed discussion about prognosis, quality of life, and patient values; terminology varies (DNAR, DNACPR, POLST, MOLST) by jurisdiction.
DOAC: Newer oral anticoagulants directly inhibiting thrombin (dabigatran) or factor Xa (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban).
DRE: Physical examination technique assessing prostate size/texture, rectal masses, anal sphincter tone, and stool character; performed with a lubricated gloved finger.
DRESS: Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms
Severe drug hypersensitivity (2–8 weeks after drug start) with widespread rash, fever, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia and multi-organ dysfunction; mortality ~10%; stop causative drug immediately.
DVT: Thrombus in a deep vein (usually lower limb); risks pulmonary embolism if dislodged. Wells pre-test probability score combined with D-dimer guides investigation; confirmed by compression duplex ultrasound. Treated with anticoagulation (DOAC preferred) for ≥3 months; provoked DVT may warrant shorter courses.
EBUS: Bronchoscopic ultrasound technique for real-time guided biopsy of mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes.
EBV: Herpesvirus causing infectious mononucleosis ('mono'): pharyngitis, cervical lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, fatigue, and atypical lymphocytes. Ix: EBV-specific serology (VCA IgM and IgG, EBNA) is preferred; heterophile antibody tests are insensitive early and in young children. Avoid amoxicillin/ampicillin (causes extensive maculopapular rash); avoid contact sports with splenomegaly. Associations: Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
ECG: 12-lead recording of cardiac electrical activity from skin electrodes; provides rate, rhythm, axis, PR/QRS/QT intervals, ST segments, and T-wave morphology. Essential for diagnosing MI (ST elevation/depression, T-wave changes), arrhythmias, conduction blocks, and electrolyte disturbances (hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia).
ECHO: Ultrasound imaging of the heart to assess structure, function, and valve disease.
ED: Hospital area providing acute, unscheduled care for undifferentiated and emergency presentations; patients triaged by acuity (ATS or ESI scale). Provides initial resuscitation, diagnostic workup, stabilisation, and disposition - admission, observation, or discharge.

Inability to attain or maintain an erection adequate for satisfactory sexual activity; often a marker of underlying cardiovascular disease (shared vascular risk factors). First-line pharmacotherapy: PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil); address underlying causes (diabetes, hypogonadism, medication effects, psychogenic factors).
EDD: Expected delivery date calculated by Naegele's rule (LMP + 280 days/40 weeks) assuming a 28-day cycle; adjusted for cycle length deviations. First-trimester dating ultrasound is more accurate than LMP and takes precedence when there is a discrepancy >5 days; correct EDD is critical for managing post-dates pregnancy and screening result interpretation.
EDH: Arterial blood collection between the skull and dura, classically from middle meningeal artery rupture; lucid interval then rapid deterioration.
EEG: Recording of electrical brain activity used to diagnose epilepsy and encephalopathy.
EF: Fraction of end-diastolic ventricular volume ejected with each beat (normal 55–70%); measured by echocardiography, cardiac MRI, or radionuclide ventriculography. Classification: HFrEF (EF ≤40%), HFmrEF (41–49%), HFpEF (≥50%); EF ≤35% with LBBB defines eligibility for CRT, and EF ≤35% for primary-prevention ICD implantation.
EGD: US term for upper GI endoscopy visualising the oesophagus, stomach, and duodenum.
EKG: 12-lead recording of cardiac electrical activity from skin electrodes (US terminology equivalent to ECG); provides rate, rhythm, axis, PR/QRS/QT intervals, ST segments, and T-wave morphology. Essential for diagnosing MI, arrhythmias, conduction blocks, and electrolyte disturbances.
EMG: Diagnostic test recording electrical activity of muscles to evaluate neuromuscular disease.
EN: Delivery of nutrients directly into the GI tract via NGT or feeding tube; preferred over parenteral nutrition when the gut functions.
EPDS: 10-item self-report questionnaire screening for postnatal depression; score ≥13 indicates likely depression requiring referral.
EPO: Renal hormone stimulating red cell production; synthetic EPO (darbepoetin) treats anaemia of CKD and chemotherapy.
ERCP: Endoscopic procedure combining endoscopy and fluoroscopy to diagnose and treat biliary and pancreatic duct disorders.
ESBL: Bacterial enzyme conferring resistance to most penicillins and cephalosporins; infections often require carbapenem therapy.
ESR: Non-specific inflammation marker measuring how fast erythrocytes settle in a tube of blood; rises slowly over 24–48 h (less responsive than CRP). Markedly elevated ESR (>100 mm/h) is characteristic of giant cell arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, multiple myeloma, and severe infections. Physiologically higher in elderly patients, pregnancy, and anaemia.
ESRD: Stage 5 CKD with eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73m²; uraemic symptoms (nausea, pruritus, fatigue, pericarditis) develop as filtration fails. Options for renal replacement: in-centre or home haemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, or kidney transplantation (superior survival and quality of life when possible).
EUA: Clinical examination performed under general or regional anaesthesia to allow thorough assessment without patient discomfort.
EUC: Alternative AU abbreviation for UEC - the standard renal and electrolyte blood panel.
EUS: Endoscope with integrated ultrasound transducer enabling high-resolution imaging and FNA of periluminal structures.
FBC: Routine blood test reporting haemoglobin, red cell indices, white cell count and differential, and platelets. Called CBC in US sources.
FBE: US name for the full blood count (FBC), which is the term used in Australia; reports haemoglobin, white cell differential and platelets.
FEV1: Volume of air forcefully exhaled in the first second of spirometry; reduced in obstructive lung disease.
FFP: Plasma product containing all clotting factors; used for coagulopathy reversal and massive haemorrhage.
FOB: Microscopic blood in stool; detected by guaiac or immunochemical (FIT) test; positive result requires colonoscopy to exclude colorectal cancer or significant polyps.
FOBT: Stool test detecting blood not visible to the naked eye; immunochemical FOBT (FIT) preferred over guaiac-based tests for colorectal cancer screening in the National Bowel Cancer Screening Programme.
FSH: Pituitary gonadotropin stimulating follicular development in females and spermatogenesis in males.
FT3: Unbound fraction of T3; elevated in hyperthyroidism and thyroid storm.
FT4: Unbound fraction of thyroxine (T4); measured with TSH to assess thyroid function.
FTT: Inadequate weight gain or linear growth in a child relative to age-based norms on standardised growth charts; defined by weight <3rd centile or crossing ≥2 centiles downward. Classified as organic (coeliac disease, CKD, cardiac disease) or non-organic (inadequate caloric intake, psychosocial); evaluation includes dietary history, growth chart review, and targeted investigations based on clinical clues.
FVC: Total volume of air forcefully exhaled after maximum inhalation; reduced in restrictive lung disease.
G-CSF: Cytokine stimulating neutrophil production; used to prevent or treat chemotherapy-induced neutropenia and mobilise stem cells.
G6PD: Most common enzymopathy worldwide; X-linked deficiency of the enzyme protecting RBCs from oxidative stress - triggers (infections, drugs such as primaquine/dapsone/nitrofurantoin, fava beans) cause intravascular haemolysis with Heinz bodies and bite cells on smear. Haemolysis is self-limiting; avoid precipitants; most prevalent in malaria-endemic regions (partial protective effect in heterozygous females).
GAD: Chronic, excessive, uncontrollable worry across multiple domains (work, health, family) for ≥6 months, accompanied by somatic symptoms (muscle tension, poor concentration, sleep disturbance, irritability). CBT is first-line psychological treatment; SSRIs/SNRIs are first-line pharmacotherapy; buspirone and pregabalin are alternatives.
GAD-7: Seven-item self-report tool scoring anxiety symptoms 0-21; scores ≥10 suggest moderate-to-severe anxiety.
GBS: Streptococcus agalactiae - leading cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis; intrapartum penicillin prophylaxis given to colonised mothers.
Acute autoimmune polyneuropathy with ascending flaccid weakness and areflexia, often following Campylobacter or viral infection.
GCS: 15-point score grading consciousness from three domains: Eye opening (4–1), Verbal response (5–1), and Motor response (6–1); GCS ≤8 indicates severe impairment and is the threshold for airway protection by intubation. Note: intubated patients cannot be verbally scored; FOUR score offers an alternative for intubated patients.
GERD: Reflux of gastric contents into the oesophagus causing heartburn, regurgitation, and potential mucosal injury; complications include oesophagitis, stricture, and Barrett's oesophagus (premalignant metaplasia). Managed with lifestyle modification and PPIs; Barrett's requires endoscopic surveillance for progression to adenocarcinoma.
GFR: Volume of plasma filtered by the glomeruli per unit time; the key index of kidney function, normally 90–120 mL/min/1.73m². Clinically estimated from serum creatinine, age, and sex using the CKD-EPI equation (eGFR); two measurements ≥3 months apart are required to establish CKD staging.
GGT: Liver enzyme elevated in cholestasis and particularly sensitive to alcohol use; raised GGT in proportion to ALP supports a hepatobiliary rather than bone origin of the ALP elevation. GGT is induced by enzyme inducers (phenytoin, rifampicin) and is a marker of fatty liver disease alongside elevated ALT.
GI: Pertaining to the digestive tract from mouth to anus, including the oesophagus, stomach, small and large intestine, rectum, and anus, plus accessory organs (liver, pancreas, gallbladder). GI bleeding is classified as upper (above the ligament of Treitz - haematemesis, melaena) or lower (haematochezia).
GIB: Haemorrhage anywhere in the GI tract; upper GIB (haematemesis, melaena) from peptic ulcers, varices, or Mallory-Weiss tears - Blatchford/Rockall score guides urgency of endoscopy. Lower GIB (haematochezia) from diverticular disease, angiodysplasia, or colorectal cancer; colonoscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic.
GLP1: Incretin hormone potentiating insulin secretion and suppressing glucagon; GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide) lower HbA1c, cause significant weight loss, and reduce major cardiovascular events (LEADER, SUSTAIN-6 trials). Weekly injectable or oral semaglutide; main side effects are nausea and vomiting (dose-dependent).
GRACE: Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events Score
Risk stratification score in ACS predicting in-hospital and 6-month mortality from clinical and ECG variables.
GTT: Oral glucose tolerance test measuring glucose response to a standard glucose load; used to diagnose GDM and prediabetes.
Geneva: Revised Geneva score estimating pre-test probability of pulmonary embolism using clinical variables without physician judgement.
H2RA: Histamine H2 receptor blocker reducing gastric acid secretion; largely superseded by PPIs for peptic ulcer disease.
HAP: Pneumonia developing ≥48 h after hospital admission and not incubating at time of admission; pathogens include Gram-negative bacilli (Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, Acinetobacter) and MRSA - often multidrug resistant. Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics guided by local antibiograms; VAP is the most severe subtype occurring in mechanically ventilated patients.
HAS-BLED: Estimates annual major bleeding risk in anticoagulated AF patients; score ≥3 indicates high bleeding risk.
HAV: Faecal-oral picornavirus causing acute, self-limiting hepatitis (incubation 2–6 weeks); presents with jaundice, fatigue, nausea, and right upper quadrant pain; rarely causes fulminant hepatic failure; no chronic carrier state. Treatment is supportive; two-dose vaccination recommended for travellers to endemic areas and high-risk groups.
HBV: Partially double-stranded DNA hepadnavirus; perinatal transmission leads to chronic infection in 90% of exposed infants (vs ~5% in adults). Chronic HBV (HBsAg+ >6 months) drives cirrhosis and HCC; antiviral therapy (tenofovir, entecavir) suppresses HBV DNA, reduces fibrosis progression, and lowers HCC risk. Three-dose vaccination is preventive; HBIG + birth dose for neonates of HBsAg-positive mothers.
HCC: Primary liver malignancy arising most commonly in cirrhosis from HBV, HCV, alcohol, or NASH; surveillance with 6-monthly AFP + liver ultrasound in at-risk patients. Diagnosis confirmed by CT/MRI showing arterial enhancement with portal washout (LI-RADS); treatment depends on tumour stage and liver function: resection, ablation, TACE, SIRT, or systemic therapy (sorafenib/lenvatinib/atezolizumab-bevacizumab).
HCM: Genetic LV hypertrophy (most commonly myosin heavy chain or myosin binding protein C mutations) with asymmetric septal hypertrophy ± dynamic LVOT obstruction; commonest cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes. Obstruction managed with beta-blockers or disopyramide; septal reduction (alcohol ablation or myectomy) for refractory symptoms; ICD for high-risk patients (HCM Risk-SCD score >6%).
HCV: Single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted via blood-to-blood contact (PWID, transfusion pre-1992, needlestick); 75–85% of acute infections become chronic, driving cirrhosis and HCC over decades. Pan-genotypic direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens (sofosbuvir/velpatasvir, glecaprevir/pibrentasvir) achieve >95% sustained virological response (functional cure) in 8–12 weeks.
HEART: Five-domain ED risk score for chest pain (History, ECG, Age, Risk factors, Troponin); stratifies need for early invasive management.
HFpEF: Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction

Heart failure with EF ≥50% driven by diastolic dysfunction and ventricular stiffness; strongly associated with hypertension, AF, obesity, and ageing. Symptoms identical to HFrEF; SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) have demonstrated mortality and hospitalisation benefit; management otherwise focuses on symptom control and comorbidities.
HFrEF: Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction

Heart failure with EF ≤40%; most often from ischaemic or dilated cardiomyopathy; the 'foundational four' therapies (ARNI/ACE-I, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2-i) each independently reduce mortality and HF hospitalisation. CRT reduces mortality in selected patients with LBBB and EF ≤35%; ICD for primary prevention of sudden cardiac death.
HHS: Severe hyperglycaemia (glucose typically >33 mmol/L) with profound dehydration and hyperosmolality (>320 mOsm/kg) but minimal ketosis; occurs in T2DM, precipitated by infection, illness, or missed medications. Treatment: slow IV fluid replacement, low-dose insulin once euvolaemia established, close electrolyte monitoring, and thromboprophylaxis (high VTE risk).
HIV: Retrovirus infecting and depleting CD4 T-cells, leading to progressive immunodeficiency and AIDS (CD4 <200/µL or AIDS-defining illness) if untreated; transmitted sexually, via blood, and vertically. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) suppresses viral load to undetectable, restores immunity, prevents transmission (U=U), and achieves near-normal life expectancy when started early.
HL: B-cell lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells on biopsy; bimodal age incidence (20s and >60s); classic presentation is painless cervical or mediastinal lymphadenopathy with B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss). ABVD or BV-AVD chemotherapy ± radiotherapy achieves >85% 5-year survival; highly curable even at advanced stage.
HLH: Hyperinflammatory syndrome with uncontrolled macrophage activation; HScore guides diagnosis; treat with dexamethasone ± etoposide ± ciclosporin; allogeneic HSCT for familial form.
HPV: DNA virus with >200 genotypes; high-risk types 16 and 18 cause ~70% of cervical cancers and are implicated in oropharyngeal, anal, vulval, vaginal, and penile cancers; low-risk types 6 and 11 cause genital warts. Nonavalent vaccine (Gardasil 9) prevents infection with 9 types; cervical screening (cytology ± HPV co-testing) detects pre-invasive CIN.
HR: Cardiac beats per minute; normal adult resting range 60–100 bpm (well-trained athletes may have resting HR <50 bpm). Tachycardia (>100 bpm) reflects pain, anxiety, fever, hypovolaemia, anaemia, or arrhythmia; bradycardia (<60 bpm) may be physiological or indicate heart block, hypothyroidism, elevated ICP, or drug effect (beta-blockers, digoxin).
HRT: Older term for MHT; oestrogen-based therapy for menopausal symptoms; weigh benefits against breast cancer and VTE risk.
HSV: HSV-1 causes oro-labial herpes and most cases of HSV encephalitis; HSV-2 causes genital herpes - primary episode presents with painful vesicles/ulcers, dysuria, and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Aciclovir/valaciclovir shortens episodes and suppresses recurrences. HSV encephalitis (temporal lobe predilection, fever, altered consciousness) requires urgent IV aciclovir.
HTN: Sustained elevation of arterial blood pressure ≥130/80 mmHg (international guidelines 2017); leading modifiable risk factor for stroke, MI, heart failure, and CKD. Managed with lifestyle modification and antihypertensives (ACE-I/ARB, CCB, thiazide diuretics); secondary causes (renal artery stenosis, phaeochromocytoma, Conn syndrome) should be excluded in young or resistant hypertension.
HUS: Thrombotic microangiopathy triad of MAHA, thrombocytopenia, and AKI; typical (STEC-HUS) follows Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7 diarrhoea in children - avoid antibiotics and antimotility agents. Atypical HUS (complement dysregulation) treated with eculizumab (anti-C5); supportive care (dialysis if needed) for STEC-HUS which usually resolves.
HbA1c: Reflects average blood glucose over approximately 3 months; used to diagnose and monitor diabetes.
Hct: Volume fraction of red blood cells in whole blood; normal adults: men 40–52%, women 36–48%. Falls in anaemia; rises in dehydration (haemoconcentration), polycythaemia vera, or at high altitude. Approximately equals 3× haemoglobin (g/dL); used with Hgb to calculate RBC indices.
Hgb: Iron-containing tetrameric protein in RBCs responsible for oxygen transport; normal levels: men 130–175 g/L, women 115–160 g/L. Anaemia defined as Hgb below the lower limit of normal; oxygen-carrying capacity is determined by Hgb concentration, SpO₂, and the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve.
IBD: Chronic immune-mediated GI inflammation encompassing Crohn's disease (transmural, skip lesions, any GI segment) and ulcerative colitis (mucosal, contiguous from rectum). Management escalates from 5-ASA through corticosteroids, immunomodulators (azathioprine, methotrexate), to biologics (anti-TNF, anti-integrin, anti-IL-12/23) for refractory disease.
IBS: Functional GI disorder diagnosed by Rome IV criteria: recurrent abdominal pain ≥1 day/week over 3 months, related to defaecation or change in stool frequency or form, with no structural cause. Subtypes IBS-C, IBS-D, and IBS-M; managed with dietary changes (low-FODMAP), antispasmodics, and targeted pharmacotherapy (e.g. loperamide, linaclotide).
ICH: Spontaneous bleeding within the brain parenchyma; hypertension is the most common cause in adults.
ICP: Pressure within the cranial vault; elevated ICP causes herniation and requires urgent management.
ICS: Preventer inhaler reducing airway inflammation in asthma; examples include budesonide and fluticasone.
ICU: Hospital area providing the highest level of monitoring and organ support for critically ill patients; includes mechanical ventilation, vasopressors, renal replacement therapy, and invasive haemodynamic monitoring. Criteria: actual or threatened acute organ failure; prognostic scoring systems (APACHE II, SOFA) predict mortality and aid benchmarking.
IDC: Urinary catheter left in situ, i.e. a Foley; monitor for catheter-associated UTI and review the indication daily.
ILD: Heterogeneous group of disorders affecting the lung parenchyma and interstitium, producing a restrictive ventilatory defect and reduced DLCO; classified as idiopathic (IPF, NSIP, DIP), CTD-associated, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, sarcoidosis, or drug/occupational-induced. HRCT is the primary diagnostic modality; BAL and surgical lung biopsy may be needed for classification.
IM: Injection into skeletal muscle; common sites are the deltoid (≤2 mL), vastus lateralis, and ventrogluteal regions. Used for vaccines (offering depot absorption), depot antipsychotics, glucagon, and some analgesics; absorption faster than subcutaneous but slower than IV.
INR: Standardised prothrombin time ratio used to monitor warfarin therapy; therapeutic range is 2.0–3.0 for most indications (2.5–3.5 for mechanical heart valves). Elevated INR increases bleeding risk; reversed with vitamin K for non-urgent, or FFP/PCC for urgent reversal; also used as a marker of hepatic synthetic function in liver disease.
IOL: Medical or mechanical initiation of labour before spontaneous onset; includes cervical ripening and oxytocin infusion.
IPF: Progressive fibrotic ILD of unknown cause; HRCT shows the UIP pattern (basal, subpleural honeycombing ± traction bronchiectasis); bibasilar fine crackles on auscultation. Antifibrotic agents (nintedanib or pirfenidone) slow the rate of FVC decline; lung transplant is the only curative option; median survival 3–5 years from diagnosis.
ITP: Autoimmune destruction of platelets by anti-GP IIb/IIIa antibodies causing isolated thrombocytopenia; acute ITP in children (post-viral, usually self-limiting); chronic ITP in adults requiring treatment. Mx: corticosteroids ± IVIg for rapid response; TPO receptor agonists (eltrombopag, romiplostim) and rituximab for refractory disease; splenectomy remains an option for chronic ITP.
IUD: Long-acting reversible intrauterine contraceptive; copper IUD (non-hormonal, also effective emergency contraception within 5 days) or levonorgestrel IUS (Mirena - reduces menstrual flow, treats dysmenorrhoea). Both types have >99% efficacy; small risk of expulsion, uterine perforation at insertion, and ectopic pregnancy if failure occurs.
IUGR: Condition in which a fetus fails to achieve its growth potential, often due to placental insufficiency.
IV: Administration directly into a vein, allowing rapid drug delivery and precise dose titration; essential for emergency resuscitation, parenteral nutrition, and chemotherapy. Peripheral IV cannulas (IVCs) are standard for short-term access; central venous catheters (CVCs) required for caustic or hyperosmolar infusions, vasopressors, and haemodynamic monitoring.
IVC: Peripheral IV cannula for fluids and medication; site checked each shift for phlebitis and resited per local policy.
IVIG: Pooled human IgG administered IV; mechanisms include Fc receptor blockade, complement modulation, and anti-idiotypic antibodies. Indications: primary immunodeficiency (replacement), Kawasaki disease (prevents coronary artery aneurysms), ITP, GBS, CIDP, and other autoimmune conditions. High-dose IVIG (2 g/kg) provides rapid but temporary immunomodulation (onset 24–48 h, effect wanes after 3–4 weeks).
IVP: Contrast radiograph of the renal collecting system and ureters; largely replaced by CT urogram.
KUB: Plain abdominal radiograph centred on the urinary tract; used to detect renal calculi and assess urinary anatomy.
LA: Cardiac chamber receiving oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins and delivering it through the mitral valve to the LV. LA dilatation reflects chronic mitral disease, AF, or diastolic dysfunction; enlarged LA is an independent stroke risk factor and predisposes to AF.
LABA: Long-acting inhaled bronchodilator used with ICS in asthma and COPD; examples include salmeterol and formoterol.
LAMA: Long-acting inhaled anticholinergic bronchodilator for COPD maintenance; tiotropium (Spiriva) is the prototypical agent.
LBBB: Delayed conduction through the left bundle branch; broad QRS (>120 ms) with broad monophasic R in I/V5-6, deep S in V1, masking ischaemic ST changes. New LBBB with acute chest pain warrants STEMI management (Sgarbossa criteria help identify underlying ischaemia). Chronic LBBB causes dyssynchrony, which may benefit from CRT in HFrEF with EF ≤35%.
LDH: Intracellular enzyme released in cell injury; elevated in haemolysis, lymphoma, and tumour lysis syndrome.
LFT: Panel assessing hepatocellular injury (ALT, AST), cholestasis (ALP, GGT, bilirubin), and synthetic function (albumin, PT/INR). Elevated transaminases indicate hepatocellular damage; raised ALP/GGT with bilirubin suggests cholestasis; low albumin and coagulopathy reflect loss of synthetic function in severe liver disease.
LGA: Birth weight or fetal size above the 90th centile for gestational age, associated with gestational diabetes.
LH: Pituitary gonadotropin triggering ovulation and stimulating gonadal steroid production.
LLETZ: Large Loop Excision of the Transformation Zone
Electrosurgical loop excision of cervical transformation zone for treatment of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN).
LMP: First day of the last normal menstrual period; used to calculate gestational age and estimated date of delivery (Naegele's rule: LMP + 280 days, assuming a 28-day cycle). Accurate LMP is crucial for dating-dependent antenatal screening (nuchal translucency, serum AFP); first-trimester ultrasound is used if LMP is uncertain or discordant by >5–10 days.
LNG-IUS: Hormonal IUD releasing levonorgestrel locally; used for contraception, menorrhagia, and endometriosis management.
LP: Procedure to sample CSF from the subarachnoid space at the lumbar level.
LRTI: Infection of the airways below the larynx encompassing acute bronchitis (usually viral, antibiotics not indicated) and pneumonia (bacterial, requires antibiotics). Severity tools (CURB-65, PSI) guide site of care; empirical antibiotic choice covers the most likely pathogens (amoxicillin for CAP, broader cover for HAP/VAP).
LSCS: Surgical delivery of the fetus through a transverse uterine incision in the lower uterine segment; preferred AU term over 'C-section'.
LV: Main pumping chamber of the heart, ejecting oxygenated blood into the aorta; normal EF 55–70%. LV hypertrophy develops with pressure overload (hypertension, AS); dilatation occurs with volume overload or dilated cardiomyopathy; EF guides HF classification and treatment eligibility for ICD/CRT.
MAC: Non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection causing disseminated disease in advanced HIV; prophylaxis with azithromycin when CD4 <50.
MAOI: Antidepressants inhibiting MAO-A/B; irreversible agents (phenelzine, tranylcypromine) require a strict tyramine-free diet to avoid hypertensive crisis (cheese, red wine, cured meats). Serotonin syndrome can be fatal if combined with SSRIs, pethidine, or tramadol - require ≥14-day washout before switching. Moclobemide (reversible MAOI) has fewer dietary restrictions.
MAP: Average arterial pressure during one cardiac cycle; target ≥65 mmHg in septic shock.
MAS: Potentially fatal hyperinflammatory syndrome (secondary HLH) complicating systemic JIA and other rheumatic diseases; characterised by extreme hyperferritinaemia, cytopenia, and haemophagocytosis on marrow biopsy.
Neonatal respiratory distress from aspiration of meconium-stained amniotic fluid; may cause chemical pneumonitis, airway obstruction, and PPHN.
MCAS: Recurrent episodes of mast cell mediator release (flushing, urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis) with evidence of mast cell activation but without systemic mastocytosis; treated with antihistamines and mast cell stabilisers.
MCS: Microbiology investigation examining a specimen under microscopy, culturing for organisms, and testing antibiotic susceptibility.
MCV: Average volume of a red blood cell; used to classify anaemia as microcytic, normocytic, or macrocytic.
MDD: ≥2 weeks of depressed mood or anhedonia plus ≥5 neurovegetative/cognitive symptoms (SIGECAPS: Sleep, Interest, Guilt, Energy, Concentration, Appetite, Psychomotor, Suicidality). Mx: SSRI or SNRI combined with CBT; ECT reserved for severe, psychotic, or treatment-resistant MDD.
MDR: Resistant to at least one agent in three or more antimicrobial categories; e.g. MDR-TB resistant to isoniazid and rifampicin.
MELD: Score predicting 90-day mortality in cirrhosis and prioritising liver transplant allocation, based on bilirubin, INR, and creatinine.
MEN: Inherited tumour syndromes: MEN1 (3Ps - Parathyroid hyperplasia, Pituitary adenoma, Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour; MEN1 gene); MEN2A (medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma, hyperparathyroidism; RET mutation); MEN2B (MTC, phaeochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus; RET). Genetic testing essential; prophylactic thyroidectomy in RET mutation carriers.
MERS: Severe respiratory illness caused by MERS-CoV, transmitted from dromedary camels; higher mortality (~35%) than SARS.
MEWS: Bedside early-warning score derived from physiological observations; triggers escalation of care when elevated.
MHT: Modern AU preferred term for hormone replacement therapy (HRT) in menopause; manages vasomotor symptoms and reduces osteoporosis risk.
MI: Acute coronary occlusion causing myocardial necrosis; diagnosed by the combination of ischaemic symptoms, ECG changes, and troponin rise. STEMI (ST elevation) requires emergent reperfusion (PCI ≤90 min); NSTEMI managed with anticoagulation, dual antiplatelet therapy, and early coronary angiography in high-risk patients.
MIC: Lowest concentration of an antibiotic that inhibits visible bacterial growth in vitro.
MIS-C: Severe post-COVID hyperinflammatory syndrome in children with features overlapping Kawasaki disease.
MM: Plasma-cell malignancy producing a monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein) and end-organ damage defined by CRAB criteria: hyperCalcaemia, Renal impairment, Anaemia, Bone lytic lesions. Diagnosed by ≥10% clonal plasma cells on marrow biopsy; treated with proteasome inhibitors (bortezomib), IMiDs (lenalidomide), monoclonal antibodies (daratumumab), and autologous HSCT in eligible patients.
MMSE: 30-point bedside cognitive screen assessing orientation, registration, attention, recall, language, and visuospatial function; cut-off of 24/30 suggests cognitive impairment. Has ceiling effects in highly educated patients and does not assess executive function; MoCA is preferred for detecting mild cognitive impairment.
MODS: Progressive failure of ≥2 organ systems in critically ill patients; commonest complication of sepsis, major trauma, and pancreatitis. SOFA score quantifies dysfunction across respiratory, renal, hepatic, cardiovascular, haematological, and neurological domains; mortality increases with the number and severity of failing organs.
MR: Regurgitation through an incompetent mitral valve producing a holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla; causes include MVP (commonest), ischaemic papillary muscle dysfunction, endocarditis, and rheumatic disease. Chronic severe MR causes LA dilation, LV volume overload, and pulmonary hypertension; surgical repair or replacement when symptomatic or when LV function/dimensions deteriorate.
MRA: Aldosterone receptor antagonists (spironolactone - non-selective, causes gynaecomastia; eplerenone - selective, fewer hormonal side effects); each reduces mortality in HFrEF and is used in resistant hypertension and primary hyperaldosteronism. Monitor potassium and renal function closely - risk of dangerous hyperkalaemia, especially in CKD.
MRCP: Non-invasive MRI technique imaging the biliary and pancreatic ducts without contrast or endoscopy.
Member of the Royal College of Physicians
UK postgraduate medical qualification awarded by the Royal College of Physicians after written and clinical examinations.
MRI: Cross-sectional imaging using magnetic fields and radiofrequency pulses; superior soft-tissue contrast with no ionising radiation - the modality of choice for brain, spinal cord, joints, and soft tissues. Gadolinium contrast enhances areas of blood-brain barrier disruption or inflammation; contraindicated with ferromagnetic implants and certain cardiac devices.
MRSA: S. aureus harbouring mecA (encoding PBP2a) conferring resistance to all beta-lactams; CA-MRSA typically causes skin/soft tissue infections (abscesses, furuncles); HA-MRSA causes BSI, pneumonia, and surgical site infections. Treat with vancomycin (BSI/pneumonia), daptomycin, linezolid, or TMP-SMX (skin infections); strict contact precautions to limit spread.
MS: Chronic immune-mediated demyelinating CNS disease with lesions disseminated in time and space; presents with optic neuritis, sensory disturbance, limb weakness, or bladder dysfunction. MRI shows periventricular plaques; CSF oligoclonal bands confirm intrathecal inflammation. Disease-modifying therapies (interferons, natalizumab, ocrelizumab) reduce relapse rate and disability accumulation.

Narrowing of the mitral valve orifice, most often from rheumatic heart disease; causes left atrial dilation, pulmonary hypertension, and AF. Presents with progressive dyspnoea and haemoptysis; severe stenosis (valve area <1.5 cm²) treated by percutaneous balloon commissurotomy (suitable anatomy) or surgical valve replacement.
MSA: Rapidly progressive Parkinsonism-plus: autonomic failure (orthostatic hypotension, urinary dysfunction), cerebellar ataxia ± Parkinsonism; alpha-synuclein inclusions; poor levodopa response.
Mayo: Composite score for ulcerative colitis disease activity combining stool frequency, rectal bleeding, endoscopy, and physician assessment.
MoCA: 30-point cognitive screening tool more sensitive than MMSE for mild cognitive impairment; tests visuospatial, executive function, naming, memory, attention, language, abstraction, and orientation; <26 suggests impairment.
NAFLD: Hepatic steatosis (>5% of hepatocytes) without significant alcohol consumption; closely linked to metabolic syndrome (obesity, T2DM, dyslipidaemia, hypertension); spectrum ranges from simple steatosis to NASH, fibrosis, and cirrhosis. Mainstay of treatment is weight loss (≥7–10% reduces steatosis and inflammation); GLP-1 agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors offer additional benefit.
NASH: Progressive inflammatory form of NAFLD with histological features of steatosis, lobular inflammation, and hepatocyte ballooning (± fibrosis); 15–25% of NAFLD patients have NASH with significant fibrosis risk. Resmetirom (thyroid hormone receptor-β agonist) is the first approved therapy; weight loss and GLP-1 agonists also reduce hepatic inflammation and fibrosis.
NCS: Electrophysiological test measuring speed and amplitude of nerve signals to diagnose peripheral neuropathy.
NEC: Inflammatory necrosis of the neonatal bowel, predominantly in preterm infants; presents with feeding intolerance, abdominal distension, bloody stools, and systemic sepsis; pneumatosis intestinalis on AXR is pathognomonic. Bell stage I–II managed medically (bowel rest, IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics); stage III with perforation requires emergency surgery; mortality is high.
NEWS: Composite physiological score triggering clinical review at threshold scores; standardised across Australian and UK hospitals.
NGT: Tube passed through the nose into the stomach for feeding, medication delivery, or gastric decompression.
NHL: Heterogeneous group of B- or T-cell lymphomas without Reed-Sternberg cells; DLBCL (most common aggressive subtype) treated with R-CHOP; follicular lymphoma (commonest indolent subtype) managed with watch-and-wait or immunochemotherapy for symptomatic/bulky disease. Prognosis varies widely by histological subtype, stage, and molecular features.
NICU: Specialised unit providing intensive care for preterm infants (especially <32 weeks or <1500 g), neonates with congenital anomalies, respiratory distress syndrome, infection, and metabolic disorders. Mx: exogenous surfactant, mechanical ventilation/CPAP, phototherapy for jaundice, parenteral nutrition, and thermoregulation in an incubator.
NIHSS: National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale

15-item standardised neurological assessment scoring consciousness, gaze, visual fields, facial palsy, limb strength, ataxia, sensation, language, dysarthria, and neglect; higher score = greater severity.
NMS: Life-threatening reaction to dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics): hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability, raised CK; stop offending drug, supportive care, dantrolene/bromocriptine.
NOAC: Older term for DOACs; novel (direct) oral anticoagulants not requiring routine INR monitoring.
NPH: Clinical features: gait apraxia ('magnetic gait'), urinary incontinence, and cognitive impairment (Hakim triad); ventriculomegaly with normal CSF pressure; may respond to VP shunt.
Intermediate-acting insulin suspension (isophane); onset 1–2 h, peak 4–12 h, duration 12–18 h; used as basal insulin in twice-daily regimens.
NPO: Nothing by mouth; preoperative fasting guidelines: solids/milk ≥6 h, breast milk ≥4 h, clear fluids ≥2 h before anaesthesia (ANZCA/ASA). Also used for bowel rest (pancreatitis, bowel obstruction) and aspiration risk; enhanced recovery protocols allow clear carbohydrate drinks up to 2 h pre-operatively in uncomplicated cases.
NSAID: Drugs inhibiting cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and/or COX-2) to reduce pain, inflammation, and fever; non-selective NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) inhibit both isoforms causing GI bleeding and renal impairment risk. Avoid in CKD, peptic ulcer disease, heart failure, and the third trimester; selective COX-2 inhibitors (celecoxib) have less GI toxicity but retain cardiovascular risk.
NSTEMI: Acute MI without ST elevation; diagnosed by elevated high-sensitivity troponin with ischaemic symptoms or ECG changes (ST depression, T-wave inversion). Risk stratified by GRACE/TIMI score: high-risk patients proceed to early coronary angiography (≤24 h); antiplatelet therapy and anticoagulation initiated immediately.
NT-proBNP: Inactive fragment of BNP released with ventricular stretch; elevated in heart failure and used for diagnosis and monitoring.
NTD: Congenital malformation from failure of neural tube closure; prevented by periconceptional folic acid supplementation.
NaSSA: Atypical antidepressant increasing noradrenaline and serotonin via presynaptic alpha-2 blockade; mirtazapine is the main example.
OA: Degenerative joint disease characterised by cartilage loss, osteophyte formation, and subchondral bone changes; predominantly affects knees, hips, and distal hand joints (Heberden's DIP nodes, Bouchard's PIP nodes). Risk factors: age, obesity, prior joint injury; managed with weight loss, exercise, physiotherapy, NSAIDs/paracetamol, intra-articular injections, and joint replacement for severe functional impairment.
OCD: Ego-dystonic, intrusive obsessions driving repetitive compulsive behaviours performed to reduce anxiety; interferes significantly with daily functioning. Mx: high-dose SSRI (e.g. fluvoxamine, sertraline) combined with CBT using exposure and response prevention (ERP); clomipramine or augmentation with atypical antipsychotics for refractory cases.
OCP: Combined OCP contains oestrogen plus progestogen and suppresses ovulation; also alters cervical mucus and endometrium. Contraindicated in VTE history, migraine with aura, and heavy smokers >35 years; non-contraceptive benefits include reduced dysmenorrhoea, ovarian cyst prevention, and lower endometrial/ovarian cancer risk.
OGD: Upper GI endoscopy visualising the oesophagus, stomach, and duodenum; also called EGD in US.
Upper GI endoscopy - visualises oesophagus, stomach and duodenum. Called EGD in US sources.
OPG: Panoramic dental radiograph imaging the entire jaw, teeth, and surrounding structures in a single image.
OR: Positively pressurised, HEPA-filtered surgical theatre maintained to reduce infection risk; strict aseptic technique, sterile field, and universal precautions are observed. The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist (sign-in, time-out, sign-out) is performed before every procedure to reduce preventable surgical errors and wrong-site operations.
OSA: Repetitive upper-airway collapse during sleep producing apnoeas and oxygen desaturations; quantified by the Apnoea-Hypopnoea Index (AHI) - mild 5–14, moderate 15–29, severe ≥30 events/hour. Untreated OSA is associated with hypertension, AF, stroke, and metabolic syndrome; CPAP is first-line therapy, mandibular advancement devices for mild-moderate disease.
PAC: Invasive haemodynamic monitoring catheter placed in the pulmonary artery to measure cardiac output and wedge pressure.
PAD: Atherosclerotic narrowing of peripheral (usually lower limb) arteries causing intermittent claudication or critical limb ischaemia (rest pain, ulceration, gangrene); diagnosed by ankle-brachial index (ABI) <0.9. Managed with smoking cessation, antiplatelet therapy, statin, supervised exercise; revascularisation (angioplasty or bypass) for significant symptoms or critical ischaemia.
PAF: AF episodes lasting <7 days that self-terminate; paroxysmal AF carries similar stroke risk to persistent AF and requires anticoagulation if CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2.
PCC: Concentrated clotting factors II, VII, IX, X used for rapid reversal of vitamin K antagonists.
PCI: Catheter-based coronary revascularisation via balloon angioplasty and drug-eluting stent (DES) deployment; primary PCI is first-line reperfusion in STEMI at experienced centres. DES reduces restenosis vs bare-metal stents but requires dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor) for ≥6–12 months to prevent in-stent thrombosis.
PCOS: Hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound (Rotterdam criteria: 2 of 3 required); insulin resistance is common, driving T2DM, dyslipidaemia, and endometrial cancer risk. OCP for cycle regulation and antiandrogen effect; metformin for insulin resistance; clomifene or letrozole for ovulation induction in fertility-seeking patients.
PCT: Serum biomarker elevated in bacterial sepsis; used to guide antibiotic initiation and de-escalation.
PDA: Failure of the ductus arteriosus to close after birth, producing a continuous 'machinery' murmur; more common and clinically significant in preterm infants. Pharmacological closure with indometacin or ibuprofen in neonates; surgical ligation or catheter device closure if pharmacotherapy fails or in older patients.
PDE5i: Class of drugs inhibiting PDE5 to increase cGMP; used for erectile dysfunction and pulmonary arterial hypertension.
PE: Obstruction of the pulmonary vasculature by thrombus; presents with acute dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, or haemoptysis. Wells score + D-dimer guides investigation; CTPA is the gold standard. Massive PE (haemodynamic compromise) treated with systemic thrombolysis; submassive/low-risk PE managed with anticoagulation (DOAC preferred).

New-onset hypertension (BP ≥140/90) after 20 weeks' gestation with proteinuria or end-organ involvement (thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, liver dysfunction, neurological features, pulmonary oedema). Magnesium sulfate prevents eclamptic seizures; antihypertensives (labetalol, hydralazine) control BP; definitive treatment is delivery.
PEA: Cardiac arrest with organised electrical activity but no pulse; reversible causes include the 4Hs and 4Ts (tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thromboembolism).
PEEP: Pressure maintained in the airways at end-expiration during mechanical ventilation to prevent alveolar collapse.
PEG: Endoscopically placed gastrostomy tube for long-term enteral nutrition in patients unable to swallow.
PET: Functional nuclear medicine imaging using positron-emitting radiotracers; FDG-PET maps glucose metabolism - malignant cells (high metabolic demand) are FDG-avid. PET-CT combines metabolic and anatomical data for precise localisation; used for cancer staging, treatment response assessment (especially lymphoma), and identifying occult primary tumours.
PFT: Battery of tests measuring lung volumes, airflow, and gas exchange; spirometry distinguishes obstructive (FEV₁/FVC <0.7, as in COPD and asthma) from restrictive patterns (reduced FVC with normal ratio, as in ILD). DLCO measures alveolar gas transfer; bronchodilator reversibility (>12% and >200 mL FEV₁ increase) supports asthma.
PHQ-9: Nine-item self-report questionnaire scoring depressive symptoms 0-27; scores ≥10 suggest moderate depression.
PICC: Long-term central venous access device inserted through a peripheral arm vein (basilic, cephalic, or brachial) with the tip positioned at the cavoatrial junction; confirmed by CXR. Suitable for prolonged IV antibiotics, chemotherapy, and TPN; lower infection rate than non-tunnelled CVCs but associated with upper limb DVT risk.
PICU: Critical-care unit providing mechanical ventilation, haemodynamic monitoring, and organ support for critically ill children; distinguished from adult ICU by age-specific physiological parameters, equipment sizes, weight-based drug dosing, and psychosocial support. Manages sepsis, respiratory failure, post-operative cardiac surgery, TBI, status epilepticus, and oncological emergencies.
PID: Ascending infection of the upper genital tract causing endometritis, salpingitis, and pelvic peritonitis; commonest organisms are Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness, and uterine tenderness are diagnostic hallmarks; complications: tubo-ovarian abscess, chronic pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy, and infertility. Treat with broad-spectrum antibiotics (doxycycline + metronidazole ± ceftriaxone).
PJP: Opportunistic fungal pneumonia in immunocompromised patients; key AIDS-defining illness prevented by co-trimoxazole prophylaxis.
PK/PD: Combined term describing drug absorption/distribution/metabolism (PK) and its pharmacological effects (PD).
PN: Intravenous delivery of nutrients; TPN denotes total parenteral nutrition via a central venous catheter.
PNA: Infection of the lung parenchyma - bacterial (Strep. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Staph. aureus), viral (influenza, SARS-CoV-2), or atypical (Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydophila). Presents with productive cough, fever, dyspnoea, and consolidation on CXR; CXR or CT confirms diagnosis; antibiotic selection guided by likely pathogen, severity, and local resistance patterns.
PO: Oral administration - the preferred route when GI function is intact; offers convenience and avoids injection-site complications. First-pass hepatic metabolism reduces bioavailability of some drugs; absorption depends on gut motility, pH, and formulation.
POP: Oral contraceptive containing only progestogen; suitable when oestrogen is contraindicated, e.g. during breastfeeding.
POTS: HR rise ≥30 bpm within 10 min of standing without orthostatic hypotension; causes: deconditioning, hyperadrenergic, neuropathic forms; treat with fluid/salt loading, compression, fludrocortisone, beta-blockers, ivabradine.
PPH: Blood loss >500 mL after vaginal delivery (>1000 mL after caesarean); leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide; atony accounts for ~80%. '4 Ts': Tone (atony), Trauma, Tissue (retained placenta/clots), Thrombin (coagulopathy). Management: uterotonic agents (oxytocin, ergometrine, carboprost, misoprostol), then surgical options (Bakri balloon, B-Lynch suture, uterine artery ligation, hysterectomy) if refractory.
PPI: Prodrugs irreversibly blocking the gastric H⁺/K⁺-ATPase (proton pump) in parietal cells, producing near-complete acid suppression; examples include omeprazole, pantoprazole, and esomeprazole. Used for GERD, PUD, H. pylori eradication, and NSAID ulcer prevention; long-term use associated with hypomagnesaemia, B12 deficiency, and increased C. difficile risk.
PPROM: Membrane rupture before 37 weeks and before labour onset; management balances risks of prematurity against infection. Inpatient monitoring; corticosteroids (betamethasone) <34 weeks for fetal lung maturity; erythromycin to prolong the latency period; magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection <32 weeks; delivery typically planned at 34–37 weeks depending on clinical course.
PRN: As-needed dosing instruction allowing discretionary administration when symptoms occur; commonly prescribed for analgesics, antiemetics, anxiolytics, and laxatives. The prescriber specifies dose, minimum interval (e.g. 4–6 hourly PRN), maximum daily dose, and indication; PRN opioids on a continuous infusion require careful monitoring to prevent respiratory depression.
PROM: Rupture of fetal membranes before the onset of labour at any gestational age; at term (≥37 weeks) ~50% of women labour within 12 h - induction recommended at ≥24 h if labour has not begun, to reduce chorioamnionitis risk. GBS prophylaxis and fetal surveillance are indicated.
PSA: Kallikrein-family glycoprotein produced by prostatic epithelium; raised in prostate cancer but also BPH and prostatitis; not cancer-specific. PSA velocity, free-to-total ratio, and PSA density improve specificity; ≥4 ng/mL or rising PSA warrants urology referral; MRI-targeted biopsy detects more clinically significant cancers than systematic biopsy alone.
PSI: Validated tool stratifying CAP patients into risk classes I-V based on demographics, comorbidities, and findings; class >II warrants admission.
PSP: Parkinsonism-plus syndrome: vertical gaze palsy, postural instability with backward falls, frontal dementia, dysarthria; tau pathology; poor response to levodopa.
Pneumothorax without underlying lung disease; typical patient: tall young male; managed by aspiration or intercostal catheter depending on size and symptoms.
PSVT: Sudden-onset regular narrow-complex tachycardia from reentrant or focal atrial/junctional mechanisms; includes AVNRT, AVRT, and focal AT.
PT: Coagulation test measuring activity of the extrinsic and common pathways (factors VII, X, V, II, and fibrinogen); reported as the INR (standardised ratio) for warfarin monitoring. Prolonged PT indicates hepatic synthetic dysfunction, vitamin K deficiency, warfarin therapy, or DIC; PT/INR is integral to Child-Pugh and MELD liver severity scores.
PTH: Hormone from parathyroid glands regulating calcium and phosphate homeostasis.
PTSD: Psychiatric syndrome following exposure to a traumatic event: re-experiencing (intrusions, nightmares), avoidance, negative alterations in cognition/mood, and hyperarousal for ≥1 month. Trauma-focused CBT (EMDR, CPT, PE) is first-line psychological treatment; SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) are first-line pharmacotherapy.
PTT: Coagulation test of the intrinsic and common pathways (factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II, and fibrinogen); used to monitor unfractionated heparin (target aPTT 60–100 s, 1.5–2.5× normal). Isolated prolonged aPTT with normal PT suggests haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency), haemophilia B (IX), or lupus anticoagulant.
PTX: Accumulation of air in the pleural space causing lung collapse; primary spontaneous PTX in tall young men without lung disease; secondary PTX complicates COPD, asthma, or ILD. Tension PTX (tracheal deviation away, absent breath sounds, haemodynamic compromise) is a clinical emergency requiring immediate needle decompression followed by chest tube insertion.
PUD: Mucosal ulceration of the stomach or duodenum; H. pylori (60–70% of gastric, >90% of duodenal ulcers) and NSAIDs are the leading causes; complications include bleeding, perforation, and gastric outlet obstruction. H. pylori eradication (triple therapy: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin × 7–14 days) plus PPI heals most ulcers.
PVC: Ectopic ventricular impulse producing a wide, early QRS without preceding P wave; usually benign in structurally normal hearts. Frequent PVCs (>10–15% of beats) can cause PVC-induced cardiomyopathy; associated with post-MI scar or HCM they carry higher arrhythmic risk. Treated with beta-blockers for symptoms or catheter ablation for high-burden PVCs causing cardiomyopathy.
Plt: Small anucleate cell fragments derived from megakaryocytes; mediate primary haemostasis by adhering to damaged vessel walls and aggregating to form the platelet plug. Normal count 150–400 ×10⁹/L; thrombocytopenia (<150) increases bleeding risk - spontaneous bleeding typically at <20–30 ×10⁹/L; thrombocytosis (>400) may be reactive or due to myeloproliferative disorders.
PsA: Seronegative inflammatory arthritis associated with psoriasis; patterns include oligoarticular, polyarticular, DIP-predominant, axial spondylitis, and arthritis mutilans; dactylitis ('sausage digit') and enthesitis are characteristic. csDMARDs (methotrexate) for mild-moderate disease; bDMARDs (anti-TNF, anti-IL-17, anti-IL-12/23) for active disease with inadequate response.
RA: Symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis with autoantibody positivity (RF, anti-CCP); presents with morning stiffness >1 h, synovitis of small joints (MCP, PIP, wrists), and systemic features. Treat-to-target approach using csDMARDs (methotrexate first-line), escalating to bDMARDs (anti-TNF, anti-IL-6) or tsDMARDs (JAK inhibitors) if remission not achieved.

Right-sided cardiac chamber receiving deoxygenated systemic venous return from the SVC and IVC, then passing blood through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle. Relevant in arrhythmia assessment, central catheter positioning, and structural heart disease evaluation.
