Mx: Mechanical: requires lifelong anticoagulation (warfarin; target INR depends on valve position/type/risk - mitral/MVST INR 3.0; aortic bileaflet low-risk INR 2.5; high-risk 3.0; add aspirin 75 mg); durability 20-30 yr. Bioprosthetic: no anticoagulation required (aspirin only); degeneration/structural valve deterioration within 10-15 yr (earlier in young patients). Thrombosis: acute valve obstruction (haemodynamic instability, ↑gradients on echo) - thrombolytic therapy vs emergent surgery. Endocarditis: early (<60 d - typically S. aureus/CoNS/Gram-negatives from perioperative seeding; surgery usually required); late (>60 d - like native valve IE; streptococci; treat medically first). Ix: Haemolysis: mechanical valves → para-valvular leak → microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA) → ↑LDH, ↓Hb, ↑reticulocytes, ↑schistocytes.

conditions.name: Parapneumonic effusion
conditions.summary: Pleural effusion complicating pneumonia; spectrum from simple (uncomplicated) to complex (complicated, empyema). Parapneumonic effusion occurs in up to 40% of patients hospitalised with pneumonia. Light's criteria: exudate. Simple/uncomplicated: thin, free-flowing, pH >7.2, glucose >2.2 mmol/L, LDH <1000 IU/L - sterile, resolves with antibiotics alone. Complicated (requires drainage): pH <7.2, glucose <2.2 mmol/L, LDH >1000 - or positive Gram stain/culture. Empyema: frank pus, pH <7 (pH most important indicator for drainage). Ix: USS (identifies effusion, loculations, guides drainage); CT (complex/loculated, assess lung re-expansion); pleural fluid analysis (Light's, pH, LDH, glucose, Gram stain, culture, cytology). RAPID score (renal, age, purulence, infection source, dietary factors) for prognosis. Mx: treat pneumonia (appropriate antibiotics); drain if complicated/empyema (small-bore USS-guided chest drain); intrapleural fibrinolytic therapy (alteplase + DNase, 'MIST2 trial' approach - ↑drainage for complex/loculated); VATS decortication if failed/thick peel.

conditions.name: Osteochondritis dissecans
conditions.summary: Focal osteochondral lesion: necrosis of subchondral bone → separation of osteochondral fragment ± loose body formation; mechanism uncertain (repetitive microtrauma, ischaemia, genetic). Most common: knee (medial femoral condyle - lateral aspect, classic); elbow (lateral capitellum - gymnasts, throwing athletes); talus (ankle - lateral > medial). Adolescents/young adults; males > females. Sx: activity-related pain, swelling, clicking, locking (if loose body), reduced ROM. X-ray: subchondral lucency/flattening; MRI (best - extent, stability - T2 bright fluid under lesion = unstable). Stability determines Mx. Mx: stable (intact cartilage): conservative (activity modification/rest, non-weight bearing; 6-12 months) - majority heal in skeletally immature; unstable/failed conservative: surgical - arthroscopic drilling (stable, open physes), fixation of detached fragment (if viable), osteochondral autograft transfer (OATS/mosaicplasty), microfracture.

conditions.name: Thoracic outlet syndrome
conditions.summary: Compression of neurovascular structures (brachial plexus, subclavian artery/vein) in thoracic outlet between first rib, clavicle, and scalene muscles. Types: neurogenic TOS (95% - brachial plexus compression; C8/T1 - ulnar nerve distribution: numbness/tingling ulnar digits and medial arm, weakness/wasting intrinsics); venous TOS (Paget-Schroetter - axillosubclavian vein thrombosis; swollen upper limb after exertion, effort thrombosis); arterial TOS (rarest - subclavian artery compression, often cervical rib → thrombosis/emboli). Causes: cervical rib, abnormal first rib, scalene/subclavian muscle hypertrophy (swimmers, weightlifters), trauma (clavicle fracture), Pancoast tumour. Ix: Adson test, Roos test (EAST - elevated arm stress test); CXR (cervical rib); MRI/MRA; electrophysiology (neurogenic). Mx: physiotherapy (most neurogenic); surgical - first rib resection ± scalenectomy (refractory neurogenic; venous/arterial TOS); anticoagulation/thrombolysis (venous TOS).

conditions.name: Peripheral arterial disease
conditions.summary: Atherosclerotic occlusion of arteries supplying limbs (usually lower). Risk: smoking (strongest), DM, HTN, hyperlipidaemia, age, male. Fontaine/Rutherford classification. Sx: intermittent claudication (reproducible calf/thigh/buttock pain on exertion, relieved by rest); critical limb ischaemia (CLI): rest pain (severe, nocturnal, relieved by hanging leg dependent), ulceration (ischaemic - pale base, punched-out, painful), gangrene; Leriche syndrome (bilateral iliac disease - buttock claudication + erectile dysfunction + absent femoral pulses). ABI (ankle-brachial index): normal 1.0-1.3; PAD <0.9; CLI <0.5; incompressible (calcification, DM) >1.4. Ix: Duplex USS; CT/MR angiography. Sx: Acute limb ischaemia: 6 Ps (Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paraesthesia, Paralysis, Poikilothermia - 'Perishing cold') → urgent revascularisation (embolectomy/thrombolysis, bypass surgery). Mx: Mx chronic PAD: risk factor modification (smoking cessation most important), supervised exercise; antiplatelet (aspirin/clopidogrel); statin; revascularisation (endovascular angioplasty/stenting or bypass) for CLI/disabling claudication.

conditions.name: Vasculitis
conditions.summary: Inflammation and necrosis of blood vessel walls; classified by vessel size. Large vessel: GCA (> 50 yr, temporal artery); Takayasu (young women). Medium vessel: PAN (hepatitis B); Kawasaki disease (children). Small vessel: ANCA-associated - GPA (Wegener, c-ANCA/PR3), MPA (p-ANCA/MPO), EGPA (Churg-Strauss, p-ANCA/MPO + eosinophilia + asthma); immune complex - IgA vasculitis (HSP), cryoglobulinaemic, anti-GBM. General features: systemic illness (fever, weight loss, fatigue), multi-organ involvement (skin - palpable purpura; kidney - glomerulonephritis; lung - haemorrhage; joints; ENT - sinusitis, saddle-nose deformity in GPA; peripheral nerve - mononeuritis multiplex). ANCA (anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody): positive in GPA/MPA/EGPA. Ix: clinical + serology (ANCA, anti-GBM, complement, cryoglobulins) + biopsy (affected organ - kidney, skin, nerve, nasal); angiography (medium vessel). Mx: induction - cyclophosphamide or rituximab (ANCA-associated) + high-dose prednisolone; maintenance - azathioprine/rituximab; plasma exchange (anti-GBM/severe ANCA with pulmonary haemorrhage or AKI); avacopan (C5aR inhibitor - reduces steroid burden in ANCA).

conditions.name: Psoriatic arthritis
conditions.summary: Chronic seronegative inflammatory arthritis associated with psoriasis; RF negative; HLA-B27 association (especially axial). Psoriasis precedes arthritis in 70%, simultaneous 10%, arthritis first 20%. Patterns (Moll & Wright): distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint disease (with nail psoriasis - classic but not most common), asymmetric oligoarthritis (most common - large + small joints), symmetric polyarthritis (resembles RA), axial disease (spondyloarthritis - sacroiliitis, spondylitis), arthritis mutilans (severe osteolysis - 'opera glass' deformity/'telescoping' digits). Nail involvement: pitting, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis. Extra-articular: uveitis, IBD, CVD (increased risk). Ix: CASPAR criteria (clinical + imaging + serology); RF negative (10% seropositive); ↑ESR/CRP; X-ray (pencil-in-cup deformity - DIP; sacroiliitis). Mx: NSAIDs (mild); conventional DMARDs (methotrexate - skin + joints; sulfasalazine, leflunomide); biologics (TNF inhibitors - adalimumab, etanercept; IL-17i - secukinumab, ixekizumab [preferred for axial]; IL-12/23i - ustekinumab); JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, upadacitinib).

conditions.name: Pre-eclampsia
conditions.summary: Hypertensive disorder of pregnancy (≥20 wk): new-onset HTN (≥140/90 mmHg on two occasions ≥4 hr apart) + proteinuria (≥300 mg/24 hr or urine PCR ≥30 mg/mmol) or end-organ dysfunction. Pathophysiology: abnormal trophoblast invasion → impaired spiral artery remodelling → placental ischaemia → ↑antiangiogenic factors (sFlt-1 → ↓PlGF) → systemic endothelial dysfunction. Complications: HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets - serious variant), eclampsia (tonic-clonic seizures - medical emergency), abruption, fetal growth restriction (IUGR), prematurity, maternal stroke/organ failure. Risk: nulliparity, ↑BMI, pre-existing HTN/renal/autoimmune disease, multiple pregnancy, PCOS, SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome, previous pre-eclampsia. sFlt-1/PlGF ratio (predicts/rules out pre-eclampsia in 1-4 wk). Mx: anti-hypertensives (labetalol, nifedipine, methyldopa; avoid ACEi/ARBs - teratogenic); magnesium sulphate (eclampsia prevention - MgSO4 4 g IV then infusion; also for seizure treatment; antidote: calcium gluconate IV); delivery (definitive cure); aspirin 75-150 mg daily from 12 wk (prophylaxis for high-risk).

conditions.name: Placenta praevia
conditions.summary: Placental implantation overlying or partially covering internal cervical os. Major: placenta completely covers os. Minor: partially covers or leading edge within 20 mm of os. Incidence: 1 in 200 pregnancies. Risk: previous CS (× 4 with 1 previous CS; up to × 22 with ≥4 CS - increasing risk with each); previous uterine surgery, multiparity, IVF, multiple pregnancy. Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS): abnormal invasion of placenta into myometrium (accreta), past myometrium (increta), through serosa (percreta - risk uterine rupture/bladder invasion) - increasing with placenta praevia + prior CS. Sx: painless bright red vaginal bleeding (antepartum haemorrhage - APH) in 2nd/3rd trimester; DO NOT perform vaginal examination (risk of catastrophic haemorrhage). Ix (US): transvaginal USS (best for localisation - safe if performed by trained clinician). Mx: major praevia: elective CS at 36-37 wk; minor: individualise; PAS: multidisciplinary team planned CS (senior obstetrician, urology, interventional radiology for balloon occlusion of iliac arteries, cell salvage); consultant anaesthetist; ICU; consent for hysterectomy.

conditions.name: Abruption
conditions.summary: Premature separation of normally situated placenta from uterine wall before delivery; leading cause of perinatal mortality in developed countries. Risk: maternal HTN/pre-eclampsia (most significant), trauma (domestic violence - screen), smoking, cocaine/amphetamines, prior abruption (× 10 recurrence), PROM, multiple pregnancy, uterine anomalies, advanced maternal age. Sx: sudden onset abdominal/uterine pain (constant, not colicky - distinguishes from labour), vaginal bleeding (may be concealed - large but no external bleeding), uterine hypertonicity/contractions (board-like rigidity), fetal distress (CTG abnormalities → stillbirth). Grades: 0 (incidental post-delivery), 1 (mild), 2 (moderate), 3 (severe - fetal death, DIC). Ix: clinical (USS unreliable for acute diagnosis - may be normal even with large abruption); USS (retroplacental haematoma if present). Coagulation screen (DIC). Mx: stabilise mother; resuscitate (IV access, FBC, group + cross-match, coagulation); fetal monitoring (CTG); expedite delivery (urgent CS if fetal compromise or maternal instability; vaginal delivery if mild, stable, remote from term) - delivery is definitive treatment; manage DIC.

conditions.name: Group B Streptococcus
conditions.summary: Streptococcus agalactiae (GBS); most common cause of neonatal bacterial sepsis and meningitis in developed countries. Maternal genital colonisation in 20-30% of women. Sx: Early-onset disease (EOD, <7 d of life): sepsis (most common), pneumonia, meningitis; high mortality; transmitted intrapartum. Late-onset disease (LOD, 7 d to 3 months): more often meningitis; community-acquired. Maternal risk factors for EOD: GBS bacteriuria in current pregnancy, previous infant with GBS disease, intrapartum fever, preterm labour <37 wk, prolonged rupture of membranes >18 hr. Mx (prevention): intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP - penicillin IV first-line) given during labour if risk factors; universal culture-based screening at 35-37 wk (US/Canada approach) vs risk-based (UK/Australia approach). Ix: Dx neonatal: blood culture + CSF if meningitis suspected. Mx: IV benzylpenicillin (first-line for GBS; ampicillin alternative; clindamycin for penicillin allergy - check sensitivities).

conditions.name: Chronic fatigue syndrome
conditions.summary: Complex multisystem illness; hallmark: post-exertional malaise (PEM) - worsening of symptoms after physical/cognitive exertion disproportionate to effort, with delayed onset (12-48 hr) and slow recovery (days-weeks). Core symptoms: debilitating fatigue (≥6 months, substantial impairment), PEM, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive impairment ('brain fog' - concentration, memory, processing speed), orthostatic intolerance (POTS, orthostatic hypotension). Other: pain (muscle, joint, headache), immune symptoms (sore throat, tender lymph nodes), sensory hypersensitivity. NICE 2021 criteria: debilitating fatigue + PEM + unrefreshing sleep + cognitive impairment or orthostatic intolerance. Post-viral trigger (EBV, COVID-19 → Long COVID, enterovirus); unclear pathophysiology (mitochondrial dysfunction, immune dysregulation, neuroinflammation, autonomic dysfunction - hypotheses). Ix: clinical (exclude other causes); no biomarker. Mx: management (not cure): energy management/pacing (stay within 'energy envelope' - PEM avoidance; not graded exercise which ↑PEM - withdrawn from NICE 2021 guidelines); sleep hygiene; orthostatic management (hydration, compression, fludrocortisone, beta-blockers); symptom management (pain, sleep - low-dose amitriptyline, duloxetine); psychological support (CBT for some - not curative, helps coping strategies); LC-BC rintatolimod (limited evidence).

conditions.name: Fibromuscular dysplasia
conditions.summary: Non-inflammatory, non-atherosclerotic disease of medium-sized arteries affecting mainly women (90%). Arterial involvement: renal (most common - renovascular hypertension), carotid/vertebral (headache, pulsatile tinnitus, cervical bruit, stroke/TIA, cervical artery dissection), mesenteric, coronary. Pathology: medial fibroplasia (most common - 'string of beads' on angiography); intimal fibroplasia; adventitial. Sx: renal - young/middle-aged woman with resistant hypertension (renal artery stenosis); renovascular HTN; renal infarction. Carotid - headache, Horner, stroke, TIA; spontaneous carotid/vertebral artery dissection; pulsatile tinnitus (cervical bruit). Carotid angiography: 'string of beads' (alternating stenoses and aneurysms). Ix: CTA (noninvasive - best overview); conventional angiography (gold standard + allows treatment). Mx: renal FMD: percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA - first-line, excellent results; no stenting unless angioplasty fails - higher complication rate); carotid FMD: antiplatelet (aspirin); PTA for significant stenosis; aneurysm: surveillance ± endovascular.

conditions.name: Systemic mastocytosis
conditions.summary: Clonal mast cell disorder; pathological mast cell accumulation in organs. KIT D816V mutation (>95%). Cutaneous mastocytosis (most common in children - urticaria pigmentosa, solitary mastocytoma); systemic mastocytosis (SM - adults): SM-indolent (ISM), SM with associated haematological neoplasm (SM-AHN - e.g., SM with CMML), aggressive SM (ASM), mast cell leukaemia (MCL). Sx: mediator release (histamine, tryptase, prostaglandins): urticaria/flushing (Darier sign - skin stroking → urticarial wheal), GI (diarrhoea, peptic ulceration), anaphylaxis (spontaneous or triggered by insect stings, drugs, NSAIDS, alcohol - often recurrent, 'idiopathic' anaphylaxis), bone pain (osteoporosis/osteosclerosis); organomegaly (liver, spleen, lymphadenopathy - advanced disease). Serum tryptase (↑>20 ng/mL + clinical features). Ix: skin + bone marrow biopsy (SM criteria: mast cell aggregates >15, atypical/spindle-shaped, CD117/KIT+, CD25+/CD2+ - aberrant, KIT D816V); WHO 2022 criteria. Mx: mediator symptoms - H1 + H2 antihistamines, sodium cromoglicate, omeprazole; anaphylaxis: adrenaline auto-injector (all SM patients); advanced SM: midostaurin (KIT inhibitor - first approved for SM; avapritinib - highly potent KIT D816V inhibitor, preferred for advanced SM); allogenic HSCT (last resort).

conditions.name: Pilonidal sinus
conditions.summary: Acquired sinus/cyst in natal cleft (intergluteal sulcus); predominantly young adult males (3:1 M:F), hairy/obese, sedentary (drivers - originally 'jeep disease' WW2). Pathogenesis: loose hairs penetrate skin → foreign body reaction → chronic granuloma/sinus. Sx: midline pits/openings in natal cleft; acute pilonidal abscess (painful, fluctuant, erythematous); chronic pilonidal sinus (recurrent discharge, pain, chronic infection). Ix: clinical. Mx: acute abscess: incision and drainage (I&D) lateral to midline; chronic: definitive surgery required - excision (elliptical excision ± primary closure off-midline = Karydakis or Bascom procedure; midline closure has high recurrence); fibrin glue/phenol injection (small sinuses); laser epilation (adjunct); postoperative hair removal; wound care (no midline closure - higher recurrence).

conditions.name: Perianal abscess
conditions.summary: Perianal suppuration from blocked anal gland (cryptoglandular origin - most common, 90%); located according to anatomical space: perianal (most common - superficial), ischiorectal, intersphincteric, supralevatoric, horseshoe. Organisms: faecal flora (E. coli, Bacteroides, Enterococcus). Sx: painful tender perianal swelling, fever, systemic sepsis (deep spaces). Fistula in ano (40-50% develop after abscess): persistent track between anal canal/rectum and perianal skin; Parks classification (intersphincteric most common, trans-sphincteric, suprasphincteric, extrasphincteric). Ix: clinical; MRI pelvis (complex/deep abscess - gold standard for fistula mapping); EUA (examination under anaesthesia). Mx: drainage (surgical I&D - never aspirate alone; no antibiotics without drainage); fistula: fistulotomy (if safe for continence - intersphincteric, low trans-sphincteric); seton (draining or cutting) for complex/high fistulae; fistula plug, LIFT (ligation of intersphincteric fistula tract), rectal advancement flap (complex); biologic therapy (anti-TNF - Crohn fistula).

conditions.name: Acute liver failure
conditions.summary: Rapid development of liver failure in person without pre-existing liver disease; massive hepatocyte necrosis + encephalopathy + coagulopathy within 26 wk of jaundice onset. Hyperacute (<7 d): paracetamol toxicity - best prognosis despite severe coagulopathy. Acute (7-21 d): hepatitis A, hepatitis E (pregnancy - mortality 20%), idiosyncratic drug reactions. Subacute (22-26 wk): seronegative hepatitis, Wilson disease - worst prognosis. Other causes: AFLP (acute fatty liver of pregnancy), Budd-Chiari, ischaemic hepatitis ('shock liver'), HSV, parvovirus, leptospirosis. Complications: encephalopathy (grade I-IV: asterixis → confusion → coma), cerebral oedema (grade III-IV - intracranial HTN, Cushing response, herniation - major cause of death), coagulopathy + bleeding (↑PT/INR; variceal bleeding; NOT corrected before procedures unless active bleeding - INR predicts risk, not absolute haemostasis), AKI (hepatorenal/ATN), sepsis, hypoglycaemia, ARDS. Ix: King's College criteria (KCC - for transplant listing: paracetamol: pH <7.3, or PT>100 + creatinine >300 + grade III-IV encephalopathy; non-paracetamol: PT>100, or any 3 of age <10/>40, non-A-non-B/drug/Wilson, jaundice to encephalopathy >7 d, PT>50, bilirubin >300). Mx: ICU; N-acetylcysteine (paracetamol + non-paracetamol ALF - some benefit); liver transplantation (if KCC met); mannitol (cerebral oedema); broad-spectrum antibiotics; tight glucose control; avoid sedation.

conditions.name: Drug-induced liver injury
conditions.summary: Liver damage caused by drugs, herbal/dietary supplements (HDSS), or toxins. Most common cause of acute liver failure in Western world (50%+ of ALF). Two mechanisms: intrinsic (dose-dependent, predictable - paracetamol NAPQI); idiosyncratic (dose-independent, unpredictable - immune-mediated or metabolic). Hepatocellular pattern (↑ALT dominant), cholestatic (↑ALP dominant), or mixed. Common culprits: statins (hepatocellular, usually mild, dose-dependent), antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate - most common cause of cholestatic DILI; isoniazid - hepatocellular, serious), NSAIDs, anticonvulsants (phenytoin, valproate - serious risk), HRT/OCP (cholestatic), antifungals (ketoconazole - rarely used now), herbal supplements (pyrrolizidine alkaloids, kava, Jamaican bush tea, weight loss supplements, anabolic steroids, black cohosh). Ix: exclusion of other causes; RUCAM/CIOMS causality assessment; liver biopsy rarely needed (pattern/chronology helps); drug timeline. Mx: stop causative drug (essential); supportive; N-acetylcysteine (paracetamol/consider non-specific ALF); steroids (immune-mediated/cholestatic DILI - limited evidence); ursodeoxycholic acid (cholestatic); transplant (ALF).

conditions.name: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state
conditions.summary: Life-threatening complication of T2DM; profound hyperglycaemia (glucose >30 mmol/L), hyperosmolality (>320 mOsm/kg), severe dehydration, minimal/no ketosis (residual insulin prevents lipolysis). Precipitants: infection (most common - UTI, pneumonia), MI, stroke, medications (steroids, thiazides, antipsychotics), new-onset T2DM, non-adherence. Pathophysiology: relative insulin deficiency → hyperglycaemia → osmotic diuresis → massive fluid loss (5-10 L) → haemoconcentration + ↑osmolality → impaired consciousness. Contrast with DKA: no/minimal ketones, higher glucose, more extreme dehydration, often older patient. Sx: gradual onset over days; polyuria, polydipsia, weakness, altered consciousness (stupor/coma when osmolality >340), focal neurological signs/seizures. Complications: thromboembolism (↑↑risk - prophylactic LMWH; DVT/PE/cerebral sinus thrombosis), cerebral oedema (rare, usually from rapid correction), rhabdomyolysis. Ix: glucose >30, osmolality >320, pH >7.3, HCO3 >15, minimal/no ketonuria. Mx: IV fluid resuscitation (0.9% NaCl, slower than DKA - aim to replace deficit over 24-48 hr); insulin infusion (start only after fluid resuscitation - risk of rapid glucose drop and cerebral oedema); monitor glucose/osmolality hourly; LMWH; treat precipitant; gradual correction (osmolality fall <3-4 mOsm/kg/hr).

conditions.name: Portal hypertension
conditions.summary: ↑portal venous pressure (>10 mmHg; clinically significant ≥10 mmHg; variceal haemorrhage risk ≥12 mmHg). Causes: prehepatic (portal/splenic vein thrombosis), intrahepatic (cirrhosis - most common; sinusoidal - most; presinusoidal - schistosomiasis, PBC), posthepatic (Budd-Chiari syndrome, right heart failure, IVC obstruction). Pathophysiology: portal resistance + ↑splanchnic blood flow → portosystemic shunting. Complications: oesophageal/gastric varices (bleed: haematemesis, melena - highest mortality risk), ascites (sodium retention, hypoalbuminaemia), spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), hepatic encephalopathy (ammonia + systemic inflammation), hepatorenal syndrome (HRS), splenomegaly + hypersplenism (thrombocytopenia, leucopenia). Ix: hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG - gold standard; >10 = clinically significant); USS Doppler (portal flow, spleen, ascites); endoscopy (varices); fibroscan/elastography (cirrhosis assessment). Mx: non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol/carvedilol - ↓portal pressure; primary and secondary prophylaxis of variceal bleed); band ligation (EVL - varices; acute bleed + secondary prophylaxis); terlipressin + antibiotics (acute variceal haemorrhage); TIPSS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt - refractory bleeding/ascites); liver transplantation.

conditions.name: Lynch syndrome
conditions.summary: Most common hereditary colorectal cancer syndrome (2-4% of all CRC); autosomal dominant defect in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes: MLH1, MSH2 (most common), MSH6, PMS2; microsatellite instability (MSI-H) hallmark. ↑risk: colorectal (40-80% lifetime), endometrial (25-60% - second most common), ovarian, gastric, urinary tract (urothelial), small bowel, biliary, pancreatic, brain (Turcot variant - glioblastoma), sebaceous skin tumours (Muir-Torre variant). CRC in Lynch: right-sided predominance, poorly differentiated, mucinous, early age (mean 40-50 yr), better prognosis than sporadic. Amsterdam II criteria (clinical dx) and revised Bethesda guidelines (guide tumour testing). Ix: tumour MMR immunohistochemistry (IHC - loss of MMR protein staining); MSI testing; germline genetic testing. Ix: colonoscopy every 1-2 yr from 25 yr (or 5 yr before youngest affected relative); annual endometrial sampling/USS; consider prophylactic hysterectomy + BSO after childbearing. Mx: subtotal colectomy preferred (high metachronous risk); immunotherapy (pembrolizumab, nivolumab - MSI-H CRC: excellent response).

conditions.name: Familial adenomatous polyposis
conditions.summary: Autosomal dominant APC gene mutation (chr 5q21); >100 colonic adenomatous polyps (classic FAP - hundreds to thousands); 100% lifetime CRC risk if untreated (average age 40 yr). Attenuated FAP (AFAP): <100 polyps, later onset, same gene. Extracolonic: duodenal/periampullary polyps + cancer (Spigelman classification - major cause of post-colectomy death), desmoid tumours (mesenteric/abdominal wall - often post-surgery; locally aggressive, not metastatic), CHRPE (congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium - benign but marker), osteomas (jaw), epidermoid cysts, supernumerary teeth, thyroid cancer, medulloblastoma (Turcot). Gardner syndrome = FAP + osteomas + soft tissue tumours (historical eponym, same gene). Ix: germline APC testing; flexible sigmoidoscopy + genetic testing from age 10-12. Mx: prophylactic colectomy (ileorectal anastomosis or proctocolectomy + IPAA; timing depends on polyp burden - usually late teens); endoscopic surveillance duodenum; sulindac/celecoxib (NSAIDs - ↓polyp burden; not curative).

conditions.name: Duchenne muscular dystrophy
conditions.summary: X-linked recessive dystrophinopathy; frameshift/deletion mutations in DMD gene (Xp21) → absent dystrophin → progressive sarcolemmal fragility → muscle necrosis. Most common childhood muscular dystrophy (1:3500 male births). Sx: proximal muscle weakness apparent 2-5 yr (toe walking, waddling gait, difficulty climbing stairs, Gowers sign - child uses arms to push up from floor), calf pseudohypertrophy (fatty infiltration), cardiomyopathy (dilated - by late teens, leading cause of death in modern era), respiratory muscle weakness (progressive hypoventilation → respiratory failure - major cause of death), intellectual disability (30%; non-progressive - dystrophin in brain). Loss of ambulation: typically 12 yr without treatment. ↑↑CK (10-100× normal). Ix: genetic testing (deletion/duplication panel; sequencing); muscle biopsy (absent dystrophin on IHC) - less often needed with genetic testing. Mx: corticosteroids (deflazacort preferred, prednisolone - slow progression, preserve ambulation 2-3 yr, ↓scoliosis); ACE-i/beta-blocker (cardiomyopathy); NIV (non-invasive ventilation - respiratory failure); ataluren (premature stop codon - <15% of patients); exon-skipping (eteplirsen, golodirsen - exon 51/53 skipping - small benefit); gene therapy (trials); MDT care.

conditions.name: Myotonic dystrophy
conditions.summary: Most common adult muscular dystrophy; autosomal dominant CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion in DMPK gene (19q13); repeat length correlates with severity (anticipation - worsens each generation). Multisystem disorder. Myotonia: inability to relax after muscle contraction (handshake release difficulty, percussion myotonia of thenar eminence); distal > proximal weakness (footdrop, wrist drop); facial weakness (hatchet face - wasting of temporalis/masseter/sternocleidomastoid); ptosis; dysarthria. Systemic: cardiac conduction defects (AV block, BBB, atrial arrhythmias - sudden cardiac death risk; annual ECG mandatory), respiratory failure (diaphragm + intercostal weakness + hypersomnia), cognitive/behavioural (executive dysfunction, hypersomnia - severe), cataracts (posterior subcapsular - universal), endocrine (testicular atrophy, insulin resistance, hypothyroidism), GI (dysphagia, constipation, pseudo-obstruction). Congenital DM1 (maternal inheritance - severe): neonatal hypotonia, respiratory failure, intellectual disability. Ix: genetic testing (CTG repeat count); EMG (myotonic discharge - dive-bomber sound). Mx: no disease-modifying therapy; mexiletine (myotonia); pacing/ICD (cardiac); NIV; MDT.

conditions.name: Organophosphate poisoning
conditions.summary: Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase (AChE) → accumulation of acetylcholine at muscarinic and nicotinic synapses + CNS. Sources: pesticides (agricultural - global leading cause of deliberate self-poisoning), nerve agents (VX, sarin, tabun - chemical warfare). Toxidrome - SLUDGE/DUMBELS (muscarinic): Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defaecation, GI cramping, Emesis; Bradycardia, Bronchoconstriction + Bronchorrhoea (life-threatening), miosis (pinpoint pupils - classic), sweating; nicotinic: muscle fasciculations → weakness → paralysis (respiratory failure - primary cause of death); CNS: anxiety, seizures, coma. QTc prolongation. Ix (severity): intermediate syndrome (24-96 hr after acute poisoning - proximal limb weakness, respiratory failure). Ix: clinical (SLUDGE + miosis + exposure); plasma cholinesterase (↓- not specific); RBC cholinesterase (more specific). Mx: decontamination (remove clothing, copious water; avoid self-contamination); atropine (muscarinic - titrate until secretions dry; large doses required, 2-4 mg IV then infusion); pralidoxime (2-PAM - reactivates AChE if given early, before 'ageing' of bond occurs - within 24-48 hr); diazepam (seizures); mechanical ventilation (respiratory failure); avoid morphine/succinylcholine.

conditions.name: Methanol poisoning
conditions.summary: Methanol (wood alcohol) ingested as ethanol substitute or inadvertent contamination of illicit spirits. Toxic metabolites: formic acid (from formaldehyde via ADH and ALDH) - inhibits cytochrome oxidase → cellular asphyxia, specifically optic nerve and basal ganglia. Latent period: 12-24 hr (while metabolism proceeds; concurrent ethanol delays symptoms). Sx: initial inebriation (mild), then latent period, then: metabolic acidosis (high-AG - formic acid), visual disturbances (blurred vision, central scotomata, 'snowfield' vision, optic disc hyperaemia → blindness - permanent), headache, nausea, abdominal pain; severe: seizures, coma, cardiovascular collapse. Characteristic: visual disturbance + severe high-AG metabolic acidosis with osmolal gap (↑measured − calculated osmolality - methanol in blood). Ix: serum methanol level (>6 mmol/L toxic); formate level; high-AG acidosis + elevated osmolal gap; fundoscopy (optic disc oedema). Mx: fomepizole (4-methylpyrazole - ADH inhibitor, first-line; inhibits methanol metabolism); ethanol (IV/oral - ADH competitor, alternative if fomepizole unavailable); haemodialysis (removes methanol + formate, corrects acidosis - if methanol >15 mmol/L, severe acidosis, visual symptoms); folinic acid (leucovorin - enhances formate metabolism); sodium bicarbonate.

conditions.name: Toxic megacolon
conditions.summary: Life-threatening non-obstructive colonic dilation (transverse colon >6 cm or caecum >9 cm) with systemic toxicity. Most common in severe UC (most common underlying cause), Crohn colitis, C. difficile colitis (pseudomembranous), less commonly CMV colitis, ischaemic colitis, amoebic colitis. Pathophysiology: transmural inflammation → disruption of enteric nervous system → colonic smooth muscle paralysis → dilation → ↑risk of perforation → faecal peritonitis + death. Precipitants: antidiarrhoeals (loperamide, opioids - avoid in severe colitis), anticholinergics, colonoscopy, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, barium enema. Sx: profuse bloody diarrhoea → sudden reduction in frequency (ileus), abdominal distension + tenderness, fever >38°C, ↑HR >120, WBC >10.5, anaemia; perforation: peritonism, septic shock. Ix: AXR (transverse colon >6 cm; haustral loss; 'thumb-printing'); daily AXR monitoring; CT abdomen (perforation, extent). Mx: NBM + NG decompression; IV corticosteroids (UC - hydrocortisone 100 mg QID); IV ciclosporin (if steroids fail at 72 hr - bridges to colectomy or remission); infliximab (alternative rescue); broad-spectrum antibiotics; IV fluids + electrolyte replacement; avoid triggers; serial AXR; surgical review (emergency subtotal colectomy + ileostomy if: perforation, no improvement 48-72 hr, clinical deterioration).

conditions.name: DiGeorge syndrome
conditions.summary: Most common chromosomal microdeletion syndrome (1:2000-4000); 22q11.2 deletion → defective third and fourth pharyngeal pouch development (CATCH-22 mnemonic: Cardiac defects, Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcaemia + 22). Cardiac: conotruncal defects - tetralogy of Fallot (most common CHD), interrupted aortic arch, truncus arteriosus, VSD; most life-threatening. Immunodeficiency: T-cell deficiency (thymic hypoplasia - spectrum from mild to complete absence; partial DiGeorge most common - mild; complete DiGeorge - severe T-cell deficiency, susceptibility to opportunistic infections, autoimmunity); usually improves with age. Hypocalcaemia: ↓PTH (hypoparathyroidism) → neonatal hypocalcaemia (tetany, seizures - present early); improves but may recur. Dysmorphic features: low-set ears, micrognathia, hypertelorism, broad nasal bridge, long face, small mouth. Other: cleft palate/velopharyngeal insufficiency (nasal speech), feeding difficulties, developmental delay/intellectual disability (VIQ>PIQ), psychiatric disorders (schizophrenia risk 30% in adulthood - most important complication in adults), renal anomalies. Ix: FISH (fluorescence in-situ hybridisation) or chromosomal microarray (CMA - preferred, detects all deletions). Mx: calcium + vitamin D (hypocalcaemia); thymic transplant (complete DiGeorge - rare); treat CHD surgically; speech therapy; neurodevelopmental support; psychiatric monitoring.

conditions.name: Severe combined immunodeficiency
conditions.summary: Heterogeneous group of primary immunodeficiencies with profound deficiency of T + B (and often NK) cells; most severe primary immunodeficiency - fatal without treatment. Most common forms: X-linked SCID (γ-chain/IL2RG mutation - 45%; T-NK-B+ phenotype); ADA deficiency (adenosine deaminase - autosomal recessive - T-B-NK-; toxic metabolite accumulation); RAG1/2 deficiency (T-B-NK+); other forms (Jak3, IL-7Rα, CD45, Artemis). Sx: present 3-6 months (maternal antibodies wane); recurrent/severe infections (opportunistic - PCP, CMV, candida; bacterial - Staphylococcus, Pseudomonas; viral - RSV, parainfluenza - fatal); failure to thrive; diarrhoea; absent thymic shadow on CXR; absent tonsils/lymphadenopathy (no lymphoid tissue); Omenn syndrome (SCID variant: erythroderma, alopecia, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly - oligoclonal T-cell expansion). NB: BCG vaccination contraindicated (fatal disseminated BCG); live vaccines contraindicated; irradiated CMV-negative blood products (prevent transfusion-associated GvHD). Ix: newborn screening (TREC assay - T-cell receptor excision circles; now routine in many countries); lymphocyte count + subsets; absent T-cell proliferation; genetic testing. Mx: haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT - curative; best outcomes HLA-matched sibling donor + early transplant); gene therapy (ADA-SCID - strimvelis - EMA approved; X-linked SCID - trials); enzyme replacement (ADA-SCID - pegademase - bridging); PCP prophylaxis + IVIG until immune reconstitution.

conditions.name: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
conditions.summary: X-linked recessive primary immunodeficiency; WAS gene mutation (Xp11.23) → deficient WASp (Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein) → defective actin cytoskeleton polymerisation in haematopoietic cells. Classic triad: thrombocytopenia (small platelets - microthrombocytopenia, pathognomonic; severe bleeding - intracranial haemorrhage), eczema (atopic; early onset; often severe), recurrent infections (combined T + B cell + NK cell dysfunction + impaired phagocyte chemotaxis: bacterial otitis media, pneumonia; opportunistic - PCP, herpesvirus; autoimmune complications). Autoimmunity: haemolytic anaemia, IBD, arthritis, vasculitis, nephritis - 40-70%. Malignancy: lymphoma (EBV-driven; lymphoproliferative disease) - ↑risk with age. X-linked thrombocytopenia (XLT): milder allelic variant - thrombocytopenia ± eczema, minimal immunodeficiency. Ix: WASp expression (flow cytometry - absent/reduced); WAS gene sequencing; FBC (thrombocytopenia, small platelets - MPV <7 fL). Mx: HSCT (curative - ideally before onset of autoimmunity/malignancy; MUD acceptable); gene therapy (lentiviral WAS gene - clinical trials showing promise); IVIG; anti-infective prophylaxis; splenectomy (↑platelet count - temporary, ↑infection risk); avoid live vaccines pre-transplant.

conditions.name: Tuberous sclerosis
conditions.summary: Autosomal dominant multisystem disorder; TSC1 (hamartin, chr 9) or TSC2 (tuberin, chr 16) mutations → loss of mTOR pathway inhibition → hamartoma formation in multiple organs; TSC2 mutations more severe. Diagnostic features - major: cortical tubers (seizure focus; calcified subependymal nodules/SEGA), subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA - grows, can cause hydrocephalus; requires monitoring/treatment), cardiac rhabdomyoma (neonates - most common cardiac tumour in children; regress spontaneously), pulmonary LAM (lymphangioleiomyomatosis - females; cystic lung destruction; dyspnoea/pneumothorax), renal angiomyolipomas (AML - most common renal manifestation; bleed if >4 cm), facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum - pathognomonic; butterfly distribution; red papules on nose/cheeks), shagreen patches, ungual fibromas, hypomelanotic macules (ash-leaf spots - Wood's lamp, earliest skin sign). Neuropsychiatric: epilepsy (90% - often infantile spasms/West syndrome in infancy; severe refractory), intellectual disability (50%), autism (50%), TAND (TSC-associated neuropsychiatric disorders). Ix: clinical criteria (major/minor features) ± genetic testing; brain MRI; renal USS; ECG/echo. Mx: mTOR inhibitors (everolimus - SEGAs, AML, LAM, refractory epilepsy; rapamycin); vigabatrin (infantile spasms in TSC - first-line); embolisation/resection (bleeding AML); MDT.

conditions.name: Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome
conditions.summary: Autosomal dominant tumour suppressor syndrome; VHL gene mutation (chr 3p25) → loss of HIF-1α degradation → ↑VEGF/angiogenic factors → vascular tumours. Type 1 (no phaeochromocytoma) vs Type 2 (with phaeochromocytoma: 2A no RCC, 2B with RCC, 2C phaeochromocytoma only). Manifestations: CNS haemangioblastomas (cerebellum most common - ataxia, ↑ICP; spinal cord; retina - retinal angiomas/haemangioblastomas - earliest manifestation, bilateral, leads to blindness if untreated), renal cell carcinoma (clear cell - bilateral, multifocal; major cause of death; screen + resect when >3 cm), phaeochromocytoma (often bilateral, extra-adrenal, ↑dopaminergic - headache, sweating, HTN), pancreatic cysts + neuroendocrine tumours (PNETs), endolymphatic sac tumours (hearing loss), epididymal cystadenomas. Ix: germline VHL sequencing; annual surveillance MRI brain/spine, abdominal MRI/CT, retinal examination, urinary metanephrines. Mx: surveillance programme (detect early lesions); CNS haemangioblastoma: surgery/stereotactic radiosurgery when symptomatic; RCC: nephron-sparing surgery (bilateral risk); phaeochromocytoma: surgical resection (alpha-blockade first); belzutifan (HIF-2α inhibitor - US-approved for VHL-associated tumours: RCC, haemangioblastoma, PNET - significant advance); laser/cryotherapy (retinal lesions).

conditions.name: Osteogenesis imperfecta
conditions.summary: Heterogeneous group of heritable connective tissue disorders; defects in type I collagen synthesis/processing (COL1A1/COL1A2 mutations - autosomal dominant, types I-IV; rarer recessive forms). Hallmark: ↑bone fragility → multiple fractures with minimal/no trauma. Type I (mildest, most common): blue sclerae, mild-moderate fragility, hearing loss, no dental abnormalities (osteogenesis imperfecta without dentinogenesis imperfecta - OI type I); Type II (lethal perinatal): in utero fractures, pulmonary hypoplasia, stillbirth/early death; Type III (most severe surviving): progressive deforming - 'popcorn' epiphyses, very short stature, wheelchair-dependent, severe scoliosis, dentinogenesis imperfecta; Type IV (moderate): white sclerae, variable severity. Clinical features: blue/grey sclerae (collagen-thin), dentinogenesis imperfecta (opalescent, fragile teeth), hearing loss (conductive/sensorineural - otosclerosis), short stature, scoliosis, loose joints, easy bruising. Ix: clinical; X-ray (↓bone density, wormian bones - skull); DEXA; collagen biochemistry + molecular genetics (COL1A1/2 sequencing). Mx: bisphosphonates (pamidronate IV or oral - ↑bone density, ↓fracture rate; most evidence in childhood); denosumab (anti-RANKL - emerging); growth hormone (some types); surgical - intramedullary rodding (long bones - correct deformity/stabilise); MDT (physiotherapy, OT, orthopaedics, audiology, dentistry).

conditions.name: Complex regional pain syndrome
conditions.summary: Chronic neuropathic pain disorder characterised by disproportionate pain, sensory, autonomic, trophic, and motor changes; usually following limb injury or surgery (CRPS type I - no identifiable nerve injury; CRPS type II/causalgia - identifiable nerve lesion). Most common in distal extremities (wrist/hand after Colles fracture; foot/ankle). Pathophysiology: peripheral and central sensitisation + sympathetic dysfunction + neuroinflammation. Budapest criteria (Dx): ongoing pain disproportionate to inciting event; ≥1 symptom in 3 of 4 categories AND ≥1 sign in 2 of 4 categories: sensory (allodynia, hyperalgesia), vasomotor (skin colour/temperature asymmetry), sudomotor/oedema, motor/trophic. Sx: allodynia (light touch → pain), oedema, asymmetric skin temperature/colour changes, abnormal sweating, motor dysfunction (weakness, tremor, dystonia), trophic changes (nail/hair/skin changes). Ix: clinical (Budapest criteria); bone scan (↑uptake - diffuse periarticular); no single confirmatory test. Mx: graded motor imagery + mirror therapy (most evidence); multidisciplinary pain programme (physiotherapy, psychology, OT, pain medicine); pharmacotherapy: amitriptyline/gabapentin (neuropathic pain); bisphosphonates (↓pain); short-course corticosteroids (acute warm phase); sympathetic nerve blocks (limited evidence); spinal cord stimulation (refractory); ketamine infusion (severe).

conditions.name: Mucormycosis
conditions.summary: Rapidly progressive angioinvasive infection by Mucorales order fungi (Rhizopus, Mucor, Rhizomucor, Lichtheimia - broad aseptate hyphae with right-angle branching); opportunistic - high mortality (40-80%). Risk: uncontrolled DM + DKA (most common - iron-rich acidic environment favours growth; spores germinate), haematological malignancy + neutropenia, stem cell/solid organ transplant, deferoxamine therapy (iron chelate = substrate), prolonged corticosteroids. COVID-associated mucormycosis (CAM): surge in India 2021 - steroid use + DM + high environmental fungal load. Forms: rhinocerebral/rhino-orbital-cerebral (ROCM - most common: sinusitis → orbital cellulitis → black necrotic eschar/palate - pathognomonic, proptosis, vision loss, intracranial extension), pulmonary, cutaneous (post-trauma), disseminated, GI. Hallmark: angioinvasion → vascular thrombosis → tissue infarction → black necrosis. Ix: histology (broad aseptate hyphae at 90°, GMS stain; tissue biopsy); CT/MRI (sinus, orbit, brain - extent); culture. Mx: liposomal amphotericin B (first-line - IV; high dose; renal protective); surgical debridement (aggressive - remove all necrotic tissue; key to outcome); control predisposing condition (glycaemic control); stepdown: isavuconazole or posaconazole (oral - after clinical response); combination antifungal controversial.

conditions.name: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
conditions.summary: Iatrogenic complication of ovarian stimulation (usually IVF/ART); exaggerated ovarian response → ↑VEGF secretion → ↑capillary permeability → fluid shifts from intravascular to third spaces. Risk: PCOS, low BMI, young age, prior OHSS, high AFC (antral follicle count), high AMH, excessive follicular response (many follicles >12, oestradiol >3000 pmol/L on trigger day), use of hCG trigger (vs GnRH agonist trigger). Early OHSS (<9 d after trigger - hCG-driven): oocyte retrieval period. Late OHSS (≥10 d - pregnancy-driven hCG): worse, especially if conception occurs. Ix (severity): mild (abdominal discomfort, bloating, nausea, ovarian enlargement <8 cm - manage outpatient); moderate (USS ascites, symptoms, ovarian 8-12 cm); severe (tense ascites, oliguria, haematocrit >45%, hepatic dysfunction, hypoalbuminaemia, ovarian >12 cm); critical (massive ascites, AKI, VTE, ARDS, cardiac tamponade). Thromboembolism: major risk (hypercoagulable state - heparin prophylaxis). Ix: clinical + USS (ascites, ovarian size). Mx: most mild - outpatient monitoring, fluid/analgesia; moderate-severe: hospitalisation, IV crystalloid (albumin if hypoalbuminaemia), drainage of ascites (paracentesis ± pleural), LMWH; avoid hCG (use GnRH agonist trigger as prevention - freeze all embryos; cabergoline reduces VEGF); rarely cycle cancellation.

conditions.name: Gestational trophoblastic disease
conditions.summary: Spectrum of tumours arising from trophoblastic tissue: hydatidiform mole (complete or partial), invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblastic tumour (PSTT), epithelioid trophoblastic tumour. Complete mole (CHM): diploid (46,XX or 46,XY - both paternal origin, empty ovum + 1-2 spermatozoa); no fetal tissue; grape-like villi; higher malignant transformation risk (~15-20%). Partial mole (PHM): triploid (69,XXX/XXY/XYY - biparental); some fetal tissue; lower malignant transformation risk (~0.5-1%). Sx: exaggerated pregnancy sx (↑↑↑hCG - hyperemesis), vaginal bleeding (1st trimester - most common), large-for-dates uterus, pre-eclampsia before 20 wk (pathognomonic if present), theca-lutein cysts (bilateral, large - from ↑↑hCG). Ix: USS ('snowstorm' appearance - CHM; fetal parts + abnormal placenta - PHM); serum hCG (markedly elevated). Mx: uterine evacuation (suction curettage - NOT sharp curettage); avoid Syntocinon during evacuation (↑trophoblast embolism risk); hCG surveillance until normal (weekly until normal, then monthly × 6 mo CHM / 3 mo PHM); no pregnancy during surveillance. Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN - persistent/rising hCG post-evacuation, invasive mole, choriocarcinoma): highly chemosensitive - methotrexate (low-risk) or EMA-CO (actinomycin-D + etoposide + methotrexate + cyclophosphamide + vincristine - high-risk); near-100% cure.

conditions.name: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
conditions.summary: Rare but life-threatening liver disease unique to pregnancy (1:7000-20000); typically 3rd trimester (28-40 wk) or postpartum. Pathophysiology: autosomal recessive LCHAD deficiency (long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase) in fetus → accumulation of long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl metabolites from fetoplacental unit → maternal hepatocyte fatty acid oxidation impairment → microvesicular hepatic steatosis (Reye-type). Sx: non-specific onset - nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain (RUQ/epigastric), jaundice, headache; progresses to acute liver failure - encephalopathy, coagulopathy (DIC - life-threatening, massive haemorrhage especially PPH), hypoglycaemia (severe, dangerous), AKI, pancreatitis, ARDS. Swansea criteria (≥6 of 14 features): vomiting, abdominal pain, polyuria/polydipsia, encephalopathy, ↑bilirubin, ↑uric acid (characteristic), ↑WBC, ascites/USS changes, ↑transaminases, ↑creatinine, ↑PT, ↓glucose, microvesicular steatosis on biopsy, DIC. Overlap with severe pre-eclampsia/HELLP. Ix: clinical + Swansea criteria; USS/CT (hyperechoic liver - fatty); liver biopsy (microvesicular steatosis - rarely needed with clinical criteria). Mx: immediate delivery (definitive - regardless of gestation; condition does not improve until delivery); ICU; correct hypoglycaemia + coagulopathy + AKI; maternal outcome good with prompt delivery; neonatal LCHAD testing.

conditions.name: IgG4-related disease
conditions.summary: Fibroinflammatory immune-mediated condition characterised by tissue infiltration with IgG4-positive plasma cells + storiform (cartwheel) fibrosis + obliterative phlebitis → organ swelling/fibrosis. Single or multi-organ involvement. Manifestations: type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP-1 - most common: pancreatic head mass mimicking pancreatic cancer; obstructive jaundice; responds dramatically to steroids - key differentiator from cancer), sclerosing cholangitis (biliary strictures), salivary gland enlargement (Mikulicz disease - parotid, submandibular), orbital pseudotumour (proptosis, diplopia), retroperitoneal fibrosis (ureteric obstruction → hydronephrosis), Riedel thyroiditis, aortitis, interstitial nephritis, pachymeningitis, lung (interstitial pneumonitis/pseudotumours). Males > females; middle-aged/elderly; often multisite. ↑serum IgG4 (>1.35 g/L - sensitive but not specific; normal in 30%). Ix: tissue biopsy (IgG4+ plasma cells >10/hpf + storiform fibrosis + obliterative phlebitis - histological criteria most reliable); IgG4 levels; imaging (CT/MRI); HISORt criteria (pancreas). Mx: corticosteroids (prednisolone - dramatic, often rapid response; most patients respond; first-line); rituximab (refractory/steroid-intolerant; anti-CD20; highly effective); maintenance azathioprine/MMF (prevent relapse); relapse common (30-50%) on steroid taper.

conditions.name: Acute intermittent porphyria
conditions.summary: Most common acute hepatic porphyria; autosomal dominant deficiency of hydroxymethylbilane synthase (HMBS/PBG deaminase) → accumulation of ALA + PBG (porphyrin precursors - neurotoxic). Attacks triggered by: drugs (P450 inducers - rifampicin, AEDs, OCP; barbiturates; sulfonamides; griseofulvin), fasting/caloric restriction, alcohol, infection, hormonal fluctuations (premenstrual - more common in women). Sx - neurovisceral: severe abdominal pain (colicky - most common symptom; no peritonism; severe, mimics surgical emergency), autonomic dysfunction (tachycardia, hypertension, constipation, urinary retention), peripheral neuropathy (predominantly motor - ascending weakness, can mimic GBS - rarely quadriplegia, respiratory failure), psychiatric (anxiety, confusion, psychosis, seizures - AEDs can worsen!), SIADH (hyponatraemia - dilutional, common). Urine: dark (port-wine) on standing (ALA/PBG oxidise to porphyrins). Ix: urine PBG (Watson-Schwartz test, quantitative - markedly ↑ during attack; normal between attacks - 24-hr urine); serum ALA; stool porphyrins; genetic testing (HMBS). Mx: attack - high-dose IV glucose/dextrose (suppresses ALA-synthase) + haem arginate (normosang - IV, most effective - suppresses ALA-synthase, resolves attack; give early); avoid precipitants; givosiran (siRNA targeting ALAS1 - licensed for recurrent attacks; ↓ALA production); seizures: gabapentin/levetiracetam (NOT phenytoin/valproate).

conditions.name: Reye syndrome
conditions.summary: Rare but severe non-inflammatory encephalopathy + hepatopathy in children; typically following viral illness (influenza B, varicella) + aspirin use. Pathophysiology: mitochondrial dysfunction → impaired beta-oxidation → microvesicular hepatic steatosis + cerebral oedema; aspirin metabolites (salicylates) impair mitochondrial function in genetically susceptible children. Now very rare since aspirin contraindicated in children <16. Sx: prodromal viral illness → 3-5 days later: profuse vomiting, encephalopathy (combative confusion → stupor → coma), hepatomegaly (no jaundice - distinguishes from viral hepatitis); no fever at encephalopathic stage. Ix: ↑↑transaminases (AST/ALT), ↑NH3 (ammonia - drives encephalopathy), ↑PT (coagulopathy), hypoglycaemia (severe in infants), normal bilirubin. Staging (Lovejoy): I (vomiting/lethargy) → V (seizures/flaccidity). Ix: clinical + biochemical; liver biopsy (microvesicular steatosis - panlobular; mitochondrial pleomorphism on EM - definitive but rarely done). Ddx: inborn errors of metabolism (MCAD, OTC deficiency, fatty acid oxidation disorders - screen), viral hepatitis, toxic ingestion. Mx: supportive - correct hypoglycaemia (IV dextrose), manage cerebral oedema (mannitol, ICP monitoring, elevate head), correct coagulopathy (FFP, vitamin K); ICU; no specific antidote; mortality ~20% with modern ICU care.

conditions.name: Gas gangrene
conditions.summary: Rapidly progressive, life-threatening necrotising infection of muscle; Clostridium perfringens (type A - most common; also C. novyi, C. septicum - associated with GI/haematological malignancy - spontaneous gas gangrene without wound). Pathophysiology: exotoxins (alpha-toxin - lecithinase/phospholipase C; theta-toxin/perfringolysin - haemolysin) → vascular destruction, haemolysis, myonecrosis, systemic toxaemia; gas production (hydrogen + CO2) from fermentation → subcutaneous/fascial crepitus. Trauma/wound contamination (soil, faecal matter), post-surgical, battlefield injuries, compound fractures; spontaneous (haematogenous - malignancy, immunocompromise). Sx: sudden, severe, disproportionate pain at wound site; rapid progression; bronze/bronze-green skin discolouration → haemorrhagic bullae → necrosis; wound: serosanguinous discharge, sweet/mousy odour; crepitus on palpation (gas); fever, tachycardia → septic shock; cardiovascular collapse + death within hours. Ix: clinical emergency; plain X-ray/CT (gas in soft tissues - tracking along fascial planes); Gram stain (large Gram-positive rods, no spores visible); blood cultures. Mx: emergency surgical debridement (wide excision of all infected tissue - amputation if necessary; life-saving; delay = death); high-dose IV benzylpenicillin + clindamycin (anti-toxin effect - inhibits toxin production); hyperbaric oxygen (adjunct - limited availability); no role for waiting; antitoxin unavailable commercially.

conditions.name: Ludwig angina
conditions.summary: Rapidly progressive bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces (bilateral - distinguishes from other odontogenic infections); most commonly odontogenic (mandibular 2nd/3rd molar - periapical abscess/periodontitis); rarely salivary gland infection, floor of mouth trauma. Pathogen: mixed oral flora (streptococci, staphylococci, anaerobes - Bacteroides, Peptostreptococcus). Pathophysiology: infection spreads along fascial planes → floor of mouth elevation + tongue displacement posterosuperiorly → airway compromise; deep neck space spread → descending mediastinitis (most feared complication). Sx: trismus (jaw stiffness - from pterygoid involvement), odynophagia/dysphagia, drooling (unable to swallow), brawny (woody - indurated, non-fluctuant - key feature; little pus) bilateral submandibular swelling; elevated/displaced tongue; stridor (late - impending airway obstruction), muffled 'hot potato' voice, fever, systemic toxicity. Complications: airway obstruction (primary life threat - tongue/floor displacement obstructs oropharynx), aspiration, descending mediastinitis, pericarditis, empyema, sepsis, necrotising fasciitis. Ix: clinical; CT neck (extent, gas, airway assessment); USS (differentiate cellulitis vs abscess). Mx: AIRWAY FIRST (awake fibreoptic intubation preferred - conventional laryngoscopy hazardous; early call to senior anaesthetist + ENT; tracheostomy if oral intubation fails); IV antibiotics (co-amoxiclav ± metronidazole; tazobactam-piperacillin in severe); surgical drainage (I&D - especially if frank abscess or non-responsive to IV antibiotics); ICU.

conditions.name: Retropharyngeal abscess
conditions.summary: Suppurative infection of retropharyngeal space (between posterior pharyngeal wall and prevertebral fascia); most common in children <5 yr (lymph nodes in this space regress by age 5; posterior cervical lymphadenitis from upper respiratory tract infection/otitis media); adults: trauma (posterior pharyngeal perforation - fish bone, endoscopy, intubation), vertebral osteomyelitis, direct spread. Organisms: Group A Streptococcus (GAS), Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA), oral anaerobes. Sx: neck pain + stiffness, fever, dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling, muffled 'hot potato' voice, hyperextension of neck (classic paediatric posture - extends neck to relieve pressure), stridor (late - impending airway obstruction), systemic toxicity, trismus. Complications: airway obstruction (most urgent), aspiration pneumonia, spread to parapharyngeal/danger space (→ mediastinum - descending mediastinitis, highest mortality), Lemierre syndrome (thrombophlebitis of internal jugular - Fusobacterium necrophorum). Ix: lateral soft-tissue neck X-ray (widened prevertebral soft tissue - >7 mm at C2, >14 mm at C6 in adults; air in soft tissues); CT neck with contrast (gold standard - differentiates phlegmon from abscess; identifies complications). Mx: airway management (priority - intubation/tracheostomy); IV antibiotics (ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin; MRSA cover if risk factors); surgical drainage (trans-oral or external approach - if abscess on CT, no improvement on antibiotics, airway compromise).

conditions.name: Cholangiocarcinoma
conditions.summary: Malignant tumour of bile duct epithelium (cholangiocytes). Location: intrahepatic (20% - rising incidence), perihilar/Klatskin (50-60% - most common; bifurcation of common hepatic duct; Bismuth-Corlette classification), distal extrahepatic (20-30%). Risk: PSC (primary sclerosing cholangitis - most important in West; 10-15% lifetime risk; annual USS + CA 19-9 surveillance), liver fluke (Clonorchis sinensis, Opisthorchis viverrini - Southeast Asia), choledochal cysts, HBV/HCV, congenital hepatic fibrosis, Caroli disease, Lynch syndrome, obesity. Often presents late - poor prognosis (median survival <12 months for advanced). Sx: Klatskin/distal: painless obstructive jaundice (dark urine, pale stools, pruritus - most common), weight loss, RUQ pain; intrahepatic: often asymptomatic until large (abdominal pain/mass). Ix: MRI/MRCP (biliary anatomy, tumour extent - preferred); CT CAP (staging); brush cytology + ERCP (biliary stricture biopsy - low sensitivity); FISH (fluorescence in-situ hybridisation on brush cytology - better); CA 19-9 + CEA (↑, not diagnostic alone); PET-CT. Mx: resectable: surgical resection (hepaticojejunostomy - perihilar; Whipple - distal; hepatic resection - intrahepatic) + regional lymphadenectomy; perihilar: pre-operative biliary drainage (if obstructive jaundice + surgery planned); adjuvant capecitabine (BILCAP trial); unresectable/advanced: gemcitabine + cisplatin + durvalumab (first-line - TOPAZ-1); liver transplantation (highly selected perihilar CCA in PSC - Mayo protocol).

conditions.name: Kaposi sarcoma
conditions.summary: Vascular tumour caused by Human Herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8/KSHV); spindle cell proliferation of lymphoendothelial origin. Four clinical variants: epidemic/AIDS-associated KS (most common worldwide - CD4 <200, multi-focal, aggressive, visceral); classic KS (elderly Mediterranean/Eastern European men - indolent, skin only, lower limbs); endemic/African KS (sub-Saharan Africa - HHV-8 endemic; aggressive, lymphadenopathic form in children); iatrogenic/transplant-related KS (immunosuppression → reactivation - improves with IS reduction). Sx: violaceous/purple-red skin patches/plaques/nodules (non-tender, non-blanchable) - typically lower extremities/face/genitalia in AIDS-KS; lymphoedema; visceral: GI (haemorrhage, malabsorption), pulmonary (dyspnoea, haemoptysis - poor prognosis), oral (palate - pathognomonic location). Ix: skin biopsy (spindle cells + vascular channels + haemosiderin + plasma cells; HHV-8 IHC+); HHV-8 serology; endoscopy/bronchoscopy (visceral). CD4/HIV viral load (AIDS-KS). Mx: AIDS-KS: ART (antiretroviral therapy - essential, reverses immune suppression; cutaneous KS may regress); immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS-KS - worsening on starting ART); liposomal doxorubicin or paclitaxel (systemic chemotherapy - visceral/rapidly progressive); radiotherapy/intralesional vinblastine (localised skin); transplant-KS: reduce/switch immunosuppression (everolimus/sirolimus - mTOR inhibitors; anti-tumour effect).

conditions.name: Chronic granulomatous disease
conditions.summary: Primary immunodeficiency; defective NADPH oxidase (phagocyte oxidase) → failure to generate reactive oxygen species (oxidative burst) → inability to kill catalase-positive organisms. X-linked (CYBB - gp91phox; ~65% of cases; males only) or autosomal recessive (p22phox, p47phox, p67phox, p40phox). Susceptibility: catalase-positive organisms (break down own H2O2, preventing bactericidal killing): Staphylococcus aureus (most common - skin, lung, liver abscesses), Aspergillus spp (most common fungal pathogen - pulmonary aspergillosis, most common cause of death), Serratia marcescens, Nocardia, Burkholderia cepacia complex, Chromobacterium violaceum. Sx: recurrent deep-seated bacterial + fungal infections (lymphadenitis, skin/liver/brain abscesses, osteomyelitis, pneumonia, perianal abscesses); granuloma formation (GI - colitis resembling Crohn; GU - obstructive uropathy, bladder granulomas); failure to thrive; IBD-like colitis (common complication). Female carriers (X-linked): SLE-like illness, mouth ulcers. Ix: DHR (dihydrorhodamine) flow cytometry - failure of neutrophil oxidative burst (gold standard; replaced NBT test); genetic testing. Mx: lifelong prophylaxis (co-trimoxazole + itraconazole); IFN-gamma (adjunct - enhances residual oxidase activity); aggressive management of infections; HSCT (curative - best before end-organ damage); gene therapy (trials, gp91phox lentiviral vector).

conditions.name: Haemolytic disease of fetus and newborn
conditions.summary: Maternal IgG alloantibodies cross placenta → haemolysis of fetal/neonatal red cells. Most important antibodies: anti-D (RhD incompatibility - historically most common cause of severe HDFN; now largely prevented by anti-D prophylaxis), anti-K (Kell - most common non-ABO/non-Rh cause of severe HDFN; suppresses erythropoiesis + haemolysis), anti-c, anti-E, anti-Jka; ABO incompatibility (maternal O + fetal A/B - most common but usually mild; naturally occurring IgG anti-A/B - can occur in first pregnancy). Pathophysiology: maternal sensitisation (previous pregnancy, transfusion, feto-maternal haemorrhage) → IgG → crosses placenta in subsequent pregnancy → fetal haemolysis → anaemia + erythropoiesis stimulation → hepatosplenomegaly + extramedullary haematopoiesis → hydrops fetalis (severe - generalised oedema, ascites, pleural effusion, pericardial effusion) → fetal death. Neonatal: jaundice (unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia - hours after birth; exchange transfusion/phototherapy), kernicterus (bilirubin neurotoxicity - basal ganglia), anaemia, thrombocytopenia. Ix: antenatal: maternal blood group + antibody screen; titre (if anti-D ≥1:16 - monitor closely); middle cerebral artery Doppler (MCA-PSV - non-invasive measure of fetal anaemia; >1.5 MoM → fetal blood sampling/intrauterine transfusion); fetal blood sampling (cordocentesis). Mx: anti-D prophylaxis (RhD-negative women - IM anti-D at 28 wk + within 72 hr of sensitising events - most effective prevention); intrauterine transfusion (IUT - fetal anaemia MCA-PSV >1.5 MoM; into umbilical vein); neonatal: phototherapy, exchange transfusion (for severe jaundice/risk of kernicterus), IVIG, top-up transfusion.
