conditions.name: Neonatal abstinence syndrome
conditions.summary: Postnatal drug withdrawal syndrome in neonates exposed in utero to opioids (most common - heroin, methadone, buprenorphine, prescription opioids) or other substances (benzodiazepines, alcohol, SSRIs, barbiturates, cannabis). Opioids: maternal use → fetal dependency → withdrawal after birth (opioid receptor downregulation). Onset depends on drug half-life: heroin (short-acting) → 24-48 hr; methadone (long-acting) → 2-5 d; buprenorphine (variable) → 36-60 hr. Duration: weeks. Sx (Finnegan scoring system): CNS excitability (high-pitched cry, tremors, irritability, poor sleep, seizures), autonomic instability (sweating, mottling, fever, yawning, sneezing, nasal stuffiness), GI dysfunction (poor feeding, vomiting, diarrhoea, poor weight gain), respiratory (tachypnoea, nasal flaring). Complications: poor weight gain, aspiration, seizures, hypothermia. Ix: Finnegan Neonatal Abstinence Scoring System (FNASS) or modified FNASS - scores ≥8 for 3 consecutive assessments or ≥12 on 2 assessments → pharmacological treatment. Ix: maternal and neonatal urine/meconium toxicology (meconium best - reflects 2nd/3rd trimester exposure). Mx: non-pharmacological (first-line: quiet low-stimulation environment, skin-to-skin, swaddling, small frequent feeds - breastfeeding beneficial if no drug use/HIV); pharmacological: oral morphine solution (first-line for opioid NAS; wean slowly over weeks); phenobarbitone (adjunct for polysubstance/refractory); clonidine (adjunct).

conditions.name: Intraventricular haemorrhage
conditions.summary: Bleeding originating from the fragile, highly vascularised germinal matrix (subependymal region, involutes by 34 wk) → into lateral ventricles ± cerebral parenchyma; predominantly affects premature neonates (<32 wk, <1500 g). Pathophysiology: germinal matrix capillaries lack pericytes + actin → vulnerable to fluctuations in cerebral blood flow (hypoxia, hypercarbia, pneumothorax, rapid fluid bolus, RDS, surfactant treatment - early). Grading (Papile): I (germinal matrix haemorrhage only), II (IVH without ventricular dilation), III (IVH with ventricular dilation), IV (periventricular haemorrhagic infarction - PVHI, not true IVH extension - venous infarct; worst prognosis). Sx: most IVH (grade I-II) asymptomatic; severe (grade III-IV): bulging fontanelle, falling haematocrit, seizures, apnoea, bradycardia, hypotension, deterioration. Post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus: periventricular leukomalacia (PVL - white matter injury). Ix: cranial USS (routine screening in all <32 wk at 7-10 d, 28-30 d; grades bleed well; serial monitoring for hydrocephalus). Mx: no specific treatment for acute IVH; prevention: antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone - ↓risk, most effective prevention); indometacin prophylaxis (↓IVH rate - neonatal); avoid large fluid boluses; careful ventilation; post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus: serial LP or ventricular access device (Ommaya reservoir) → VP shunt.

conditions.name: Duodenal atresia
conditions.summary: Congenital complete or partial obstruction of duodenum from failure of recanalisation (8-10 wk gestation); most common level: D2 (2nd part, ampullary or periampullary - 85%). Strong association: Down syndrome (30% of duodenal atresia; conversely, ~5-8% of Down syndrome have duodenal atresia - important to screen), other GI anomalies (malrotation, annular pancreas - wraps around D2, less common intrinsic cause), cardiac defects, VACTERL association. Sx: polyhydramnios (failed fetal swallowing detected antenatally by USS). Postnatal: bilious (if obstruction below Papilla of Vater - 85%) or non-bilious (if pre-ampullary) vomiting from first feed, absent/minimal abdominal distension (proximal obstruction), dehydration. Ix: AXR - 'double-bubble' sign (gastric bubble + dilated proximal duodenum; no distal gas - complete atresia); USS (antenatal - polyhydramnios + double-bubble). Ix: AXR; UGI contrast (if diagnosis uncertain - webbing/stenosis); echo (cardiac anomalies); karyotype (Down syndrome). Mx: surgical - duodenoduodenostomy (diamond-shaped anastomosis - gold standard; excellent outcomes) after initial resuscitation + NG decompression; results excellent (survival >90%); check for other anomalies (VACTERL).

conditions.name: Tracheo-oesophageal fistula
conditions.summary: Congenital anomaly of oesophageal/tracheal development; 1 in 3000-5000 births. Gross classification: Type C most common (87%) - proximal oesophageal atresia (OA) + distal tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF - lower oesophageal segment connects to trachea via fistula → air in stomach; gastric acid reflux → lungs). Type A (8%): OA only, no fistula. Type H (4%): TEF without OA (H-type - fistula only; presents late with recurrent chest infections, choking on feeds). VACTERL association (30-40%): Vertebral, Anorectal, Cardiac (most common associated defect - requires echo), TEF, Renal, Limb (radial aplasia). Polyhydramnios (proximal obstruction). Sx: neonatal diagnosis: excessive salivation + drooling, coughing/choking/cyanosis with first feed, recurrent aspiration pneumonia; Type C: coiling of nasogastric tube in blind-ending oesophageal pouch (AXR - coiled NGT at T3/T4 level, gas in stomach confirming distal TEF). Ix: inability to pass NGT; AXR (NGT position, gas pattern); echo (cardiac); renal USS; spinal X-ray. Mx: surgical repair (oesophageal anastomosis + fistula ligation - primary repair or staged if long-gap; preferably within 24-48 hr of birth); Replogle tube (continuous suction, drains pouch - pre-op); position upright to reduce aspiration; long-term complications: GOR, oesophageal dysmotility, anastomotic stricture, tracheomalacia.

conditions.name: Achondroplasia
conditions.summary: Most common skeletal dysplasia (1:25000); autosomal dominant gain-of-function mutation in FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 - Gly380Arg, >97% of cases; inhibits endochondral ossification → short long bones); ~80% de novo mutations (advanced paternal age). Rhizomelic shortening (proximal limb segments - humerus/femur shorter than distal), short stature (average adult height 124-131 cm), macrocephaly (large head), frontal bossing, midface hypoplasia, trident hand (inability to appose middle/ring fingers), lumbar lordosis, thoracolumbar gibbus (kyphosis), genu varum (bowing knees). Neurological complications: foramen magnum stenosis (cervicomedullary junction compression - apnoea/sudden death in infants - sleep study essential; surgical decompression if severe), spinal stenosis (adults - neurogenic claudication, lower limb weakness, urinary/faecal incontinence - majority of adults affected to some degree). Hydrocephalus (ventricular dilation - usually communicating; CSF drainage monitoring). Intelligence: normal. Otitis media (recurrent), hearing loss. Ix: clinical; X-ray (shortened long bones, champagne glass pelvis, chevron/inverted V appearance distal femoral growth plate, narrowing L1-L5 interpedicular distance - spinal stenosis); FGFR3 mutation testing (molecular). Mx: vosoritide (C-type natriuretic peptide analogue - licensed 2021; ↑height velocity; does not treat complications); growth hormone (limited benefit); surgical decompression (foramen magnum, spinal stenosis); limb lengthening (controversial); MDT.

conditions.name: Gaucher disease
conditions.summary: Most common lysosomal storage disorder; autosomal recessive deficiency of glucocerebrosidase (GBA gene) → accumulation of glucocerebroside (glucosylceramide) in macrophages → 'Gaucher cells' (engorged macrophages with crinkled tissue-paper cytoplasm) infiltrate organs. Type 1 (non-neuronopathic - 95%): hepatosplenomegaly (splenomegaly most prominent - often massive; hypersplenism → cytopenias - thrombocytopenia most common → bleeding), bone disease (bone pain, bone crises - acute severe pain + fever, avascular necrosis - femoral head most common, pathological fractures, Erlenmeyer flask deformity of distal femur on X-ray), anaemia, fatigue; no CNS disease; Ashkenazi Jewish predominance (N370S mutation). Type 2 (acute neuronopathic): infantile onset, rapidly progressive CNS + visceral; fatal by 2-3 yr. Type 3 (chronic neuronopathic): juvenile/adult; slower CNS progression + visceral. Associated: ↑risk Parkinson disease (GBA heterozygotes - most common genetic risk factor for Parkinson). Ix: leukocyte glucocerebrosidase enzyme assay (diagnostic); glucosylsphingosine (lyso-Gb1 - biomarker); chitotriosidase + CCL18 (monitoring); GBA sequencing; bone marrow biopsy (Gaucher cells). Mx: enzyme replacement therapy (ERT - imiglucerase, velaglucerase, taliglucerase - IV biweekly; standard of care for type 1; improves visceral/haematological, stabilises bone; no CNS effect); substrate reduction therapy (SRT - miglustat, eliglustat - oral; type 1 alternative; eliglustat preferred).

conditions.name: Tay-Sachs disease
conditions.summary: Autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder; HEXA gene mutation → deficiency of hexosaminidase A → GM2 ganglioside accumulation in neurons → progressive neuronal destruction. Ashkenazi Jewish population (carrier frequency 1:30 vs 1:300 general population). Classic infantile form (most severe): normal development until 3-6 months → progressive neurodegeneration - motor weakness (floppy, loss of milestones), exaggerated startle response (hyperacusis - sound-triggered myoclonus; early), cherry-red spot on macula (ganglioside-laden ganglion cells of retina with central fovea appearing red against pale surroundings - present in all infantile; pathognomonic), progressive blindness, seizures, dementia, macrocephaly (brain enlargement from storage), progressive spasticity/decerebrate posturing → vegetative state → death by 3-5 yr; no hepatosplenomegaly (unlike Gaucher/Niemann-Pick). Juvenile form: slower progression, onset 2-10 yr, surviving into teens. Adult/late-onset form: psychiatric symptoms (psychosis, mood disorder), spinocerebellar degeneration, lower motor neuron disease (resembles SMA/ALS). Ix: serum/leukocyte hex A enzyme assay; HEXA mutation analysis. Prenatal: CVS or amniocentesis. Mx: no disease-modifying therapy for infantile/juvenile; supportive/palliative (seizure management, nutritional support, respiratory support); gene therapy (trials).

conditions.name: Niemann-Pick disease
conditions.summary: Heterogeneous group of autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorders. Types A and B: SMPD1 gene mutation → acid sphingomyelinase deficiency → sphingomyelin accumulation in macrophages/neurons. Type A (classic infantile neuronopathic - Ashkenazi Jewish): hepatosplenomegaly (early; massive), cherry-red macula (50%), progressive neurodegeneration (hypotonia, progressive intellectual regression, seizures), death by 3 yr. Type B (chronic non-neuronopathic): hepatosplenomegaly, pulmonary infiltrates, bone marrow infiltration, no neurological involvement, survival to adulthood. Type C (NPC - NPC1/NPC2 mutations; cholesterol trafficking defect - sphingomyelinase normal): progressive neurological disease at any age - vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (VSGP - pathognomonic; inability to move eyes up/down on command; preserved reflex), cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, cognitive decline/dementia, seizures, gelastic cataplexy (sudden laughter-triggered loss of tone), psychiatric manifestations (psychosis); visceral: hepatosplenomegaly (less prominent). Ix: enzyme assay (acid sphingomyelinase - types A/B); NPC1/NPC2 gene sequencing; filipin staining (fibroblasts - cholesterol accumulation - NPC); oxysterols/plasma 7-ketocholesterol (NPC biomarker). Mx: types A/B: no disease-modifying therapy; B: olipudase alfa (ERT - approved 2022); NPC: miglustat (substrate reduction therapy - ↓GM2 accumulation, slows neurological progression); arimoclomol (NPC - Phase 3 trials).

conditions.name: Pompe disease
conditions.summary: Autosomal recessive deficiency of acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA - acid maltase; lysosomal enzyme) → glycogen accumulates in lysosomes of all organs, predominantly muscle. GAA gene (chr 17q25). Classic infantile-onset Pompe disease (IOPD): severe (<1% enzyme activity); presents within weeks of birth - rapidly progressive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (massive; main cause of death - cardiorespiratory failure by 2 yr untreated), profound hypotonia ('floppy baby'), respiratory insufficiency, feeding difficulties, macroglossia, hepatomegaly; Ix (ECG): massive QRS voltages + short PR. Late-onset Pompe disease (LOPD): residual enzyme activity; wide age range (1 yr to 70 yr); progressive proximal myopathy (limb-girdle pattern, scapular winging, Gowers sign), respiratory muscle weakness (diaphragm predominantly - nocturnal hypoventilation, daytime somnolence, unexplained respiratory failure), often no cardiomyopathy; wheelchair and ventilator dependence. Newborn screening (GAA activity) increasingly available. Ix: dried blood spot or leukocyte acid alpha-glucosidase assay (≤1% = classic IOPD; 1-40% = LOPD range); urine Glc4 (tetrasaccharide - biomarker); GAA gene sequencing; muscle biopsy (vacuolar myopathy with lysosomal glycogen - PAS+). Mx: enzyme replacement therapy (ERT - alglucosidase alfa, cipaglucosidase alfa - IV biweekly; dramatically improves survival in IOPD; stabilises/slows LOPD); avalglucosidase alfa + miglustat (next-generation ERT + chaperone - superior to alglucosidase in trials); ventilatory support (NIV); cardiac management (IOPD).

conditions.name: McArdle disease
conditions.summary: Autosomal recessive deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase (myophosphorylase; PYGM gene) → muscle unable to break down glycogen → glycogen accumulates in muscle; blocked energy supply during aerobic exercise (glycolysis blocked). Most common glycogenosis affecting skeletal muscle. Sx: exercise intolerance - fixed pattern: muscular pain + cramps on initiation of moderate/intense exercise (within first 10-15 min); 'second wind' phenomenon (classic - patient feels sudden improvement in exercise tolerance after ~10 min; hepatic glycogenolysis + fatty acid oxidation compensate as primary fuels); myoglobinuria (burgundy/dark urine - rhabdomyolysis after strenuous exercise - risk of AKI); fixed muscle weakness (older patients - progressive proximal weakness, late); no fatigue at rest. Forearm ischaemic exercise test (FIET): no rise in venous lactate (blocked glycolysis) but normal ammonia rise (distinguishes from AMP deaminase deficiency where ammonia also fails to rise). ↑CK (elevated at baseline - always↑ in McArdle); myoglobinuria on exercise. Ix: non-ischaemic forearm exercise test (NIFET - ammonia rise without lactate rise); muscle biopsy (PAS stain - ↑glycogen; absent myophosphorylase activity histochemically); PYGM gene sequencing (W797* mutation - most common in Northern Europe). Mx: no definitive therapy; aerobic exercise training (↑capacity for activity - most beneficial; start slowly); pre-exercise glucose/sucrose (exogenous glucose bypasses block; helps if taken 5 min before exercise); avoid intense sustained exercise (rhabdomyolysis prevention); vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate - cofactor; limited evidence); low-intensity aerobic lifestyle.

conditions.name: Rickets
conditions.summary: Failure of mineralisation of growing bone and cartilage in children due to deficiency of calcium, phosphate, or vitamin D; contrast with osteomalacia (same process in adults). Nutritional rickets (most common globally): inadequate vitamin D (↓sun exposure + ↓dietary - exclusive breastfeeding with no supplementation; dark skin, covered skin), calcium deficiency (Africa - calcium-deficient rickets with normal vitamin D), phosphate-deficiency rickets (rare). Metabolic: X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets (XLH - PHEX mutation → FGF23 → phosphate wasting - most common heritable rickets; X-linked dominant); vitamin D-dependent rickets (VDDR type I: CYP27B1 - 1α-hydroxylase deficiency; VDDR type II: VDR mutation). Clinical features: bony deformities - genu varum (bow legs) or genu valgum (knock knees), rachitic rosary (costochondral junction expansion - 'beads'), Harrison sulcus (horizontal groove at diaphragm insertion), craniotabes (softened skull - pingpong ball on palpation), frontal bossing, delayed fontanelle closure, dental delay; muscle weakness + hypotonia; pathological fractures (Looser zones on X-ray), growth retardation; hypocalcaemia symptoms (tetany, seizures, carpopedal spasm - especially nutritional). Ix: ↓25-OH vitamin D (nutritional), ↓phosphate (XLH), ↑ALP, ↑PTH; X-ray (cupped/frayed/widened metaphyses - wrist - pathognomonic; growth plate widening). Mx: nutritional - vitamin D3 + calcium supplementation; XLH: phosphate + alfacalcidol + burosumab (anti-FGF23 monoclonal - licensed for XLH; superior outcomes).

conditions.name: Osteomalacia
conditions.summary: Defective mineralisation of osteoid (unmineralised bone matrix) in adults (after growth plates closed); equivalent of rickets in adults. Causes: vitamin D deficiency (↓sunlight, malabsorption - coeliac, Crohn, post-gastrectomy; chronic liver/renal disease - impaired hydroxylation), phosphate deficiency (renal phosphate wasting - XLH, oncogenic osteomalacia - FGF23-producing tumours, usually small mesenchymal), renal tubular acidosis, drug-induced (anticonvulsants - induce CYP450 → ↑vitamin D catabolism; aluminium toxicity in CKD - blocks mineralisation), hypophosphataemia. Sx: diffuse bone pain (dull, aching - axial skeleton: back, ribs, hips - often misdiagnosed as fibromyalgia/arthritis), muscle weakness (proximal myopathy - difficulty rising from chair, waddling gait), tenderness on bone palpation, pathological fractures (Looser zones - pseudofractures: bilateral symmetrical radiolucent bands perpendicular to cortex - pubic rami, femoral neck, lateral scapulae, ribs - pathognomonic). Minimal/no trauma fractures; ↓bone density on DEXA. Ix: ↓25-OH vitamin D (<25 nmol/L usually symptomatic), ↑PTH, ↑ALP, ↓/normal calcium, ↓phosphate (if XLH/FGF23-mediated); X-ray (Looser zones); bone biopsy (excess unmineralised osteoid - gold standard but rarely needed). Mx: vitamin D3 (high-dose supplementation, e.g., 50000 IU weekly) + calcium; treat underlying cause (malabsorption, renal, hepatic); XLH/oncogenic: phosphate + alfacalcidol ± burosumab; treat vitamin D deficiency rickets prophylactically.

conditions.name: Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia
conditions.summary: Autosomal dominant vascular dysplasia; loss-of-function mutations in TGF-β signalling pathway genes: ENG (endoglin - HHT1; ↑pulmonary/cerebral AVM risk), ACVRL1 (ALK1 - HHT2; ↑hepatic AVM risk), SMAD4 (combined HHT + juvenile polyposis), GDF2; defective angiogenesis → fragile telangiectases + AVMs. Curaçao diagnostic criteria (≥3 = definite HHT): epistaxis (recurrent, spontaneous - most common and earliest manifestation; affects 90%+), mucocutaneous telangiectases (lips, fingers, tongue, nasal mucosa - multiple, characteristic), visceral AVMs/telangiectases (pulmonary - right-to-left shunt → hypoxaemia, paradoxical embolism/stroke, haemoptysis; hepatic - high-output cardiac failure, portal hypertension, biliary disease; GI - bleeding, iron-deficiency anaemia; cerebral/spinal - haemorrhage, seizures), family history (first-degree relative). Complications: iron-deficiency anaemia (recurrent epistaxis + GI bleeding - most common complication), pulmonary AVM (30-50% - paradoxical embolism → stroke/brain abscess in young person with no cardiac shunt), cerebral AVM (10-25% - intracerebral haemorrhage). Ix: Curaçao criteria ± genetic testing; CT chest (pulmonary AVMs); MRI brain; contrast echocardiography (bubble study - intracardiac/pulmonary shunt). Mx: nasal - tranexamic acid, humidification, laser/argon photocoagulation, septal dermoplasty, bevacizumab (anti-VEGF - systemic or intranasal); pulmonary AVMs: transcatheter embolisation (if feeding vessel >3 mm - prevents stroke); cerebral AVMs: neurosurgery/radiosurgery; IV iron/blood transfusion; iron supplementation.

conditions.name: Primary ciliary dyskinesia
conditions.summary: Autosomal recessive disorder of ciliary structure/function due to mutations in genes encoding axonemal proteins (dynein arms - DNAI1, DNAI2, DNAH5, DNAH11 - most common; outer dynein arm defect on EM). Defective mucociliary clearance → chronic sino-pulmonary disease. Kartagener syndrome (50% of PCD): situs inversus (complete organ lateralisation including dextrocardia) + sinusitis + bronchiectasis - because ciliary motility is required to establish left-right asymmetry in embryogenesis (nodal cilia → random lateralisation; 50% situs inversus totalis, 50% situs solitus). Sx: neonatal respiratory distress (term infant - from birth); chronic wet cough (from infancy - productive, daily); recurrent otitis media (conductive hearing loss - glue ear from poor Eustachian tube clearance), chronic sinusitis, nasal polyps; bronchiectasis (progressive - CT chest); male infertility (immotile sperm - absent dynein arms; sperm flagellum = modified cilium); female infertility (ectopic pregnancy - fallopian tube cilia); situs inversus (random lateralisation in 50%). Ix: nasal nitric oxide (nNO - low <77 nL/min - sensitive screening; nNO not specific, also ↓in CF); high-speed video microscopy (nasal brushings - ciliary beat frequency + waveform pattern - diagnostic); transmission EM (axoneme ultrastructure - dynein arm defects); genetic testing. Mx: chest physiotherapy (airway clearance - lifelong, daily); antibiotics (early, aggressive - respiratory exacerbations, long-term prophylactic); hearing aids; grommets (controversial); surveillance CT; fertility assistance (IVF/ICSI).

conditions.name: Tularaemia
conditions.summary: Zoonotic infection by Francisella tularensis (Category A bioterrorism agent - highly infectious, aerosol transmission). Reservoir: wild rabbits, hares, rodents, ticks (Dermacentor, Amblyomma - most common vector in USA), deer flies. Transmission: tick/insect bite (most common), contact with infected animals (hunters - skinning, direct contact), ingestion (contaminated water), inhalation (mowing grass, bioterrorism). Clinical forms: ulceroglandular (most common - 75%): painful skin ulcer + regional lymphadenopathy (tender, fluctuant, may suppurate) at inoculation site - tick/insect bite; glandular (lymphadenopathy without ulcer); oculoglandular (conjunctivitis - Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome - direct inoculation to eye); oropharyngeal (ingestion - pharyngitis, cervical lymphadenopathy); pneumonic (inhalation - most severe; primary or secondary - community-acquired pneumonia pattern, high mortality if untreated, bioterrorism concern); typhoidal (septicaemic - no localising findings, severe systemic illness). Systemic: fever, headache, myalgia. Ix: serology (agglutination/ELISA - ↑titre ×4 between acute/convalescent or single high titre ≥160); culture (BSL3 facility - warn lab); PCR (ulcer/lymph node aspirate). Mx: streptomycin (gold standard - intramuscular); gentamicin (alternative - IV, equally effective); doxycycline (oral - mild/moderate, ↑relapse rate); ciprofloxacin (oral - reasonable alternative, good CNS penetration); post-exposure prophylaxis (doxycycline or ciprofloxacin × 14 d).

conditions.name: Norovirus
conditions.summary: Most common cause of epidemic viral gastroenteritis worldwide; non-enveloped single-stranded RNA virus (Caliciviridae); highly contagious (infectious dose ~10-100 viral particles). Faecal-oral transmission; vomit-mediated aerosol (efficient). Outbreaks: cruise ships, hospitals, care homes, schools, restaurants (foodborne - oysters/shellfish especially). No immunity: multiple serotypes + rapid antigenic variation → reinfection common. Sx: abrupt onset (12-48 hr incubation) profuse vomiting + watery non-bloody diarrhoea, nausea, abdominal cramps, low-grade fever, myalgia; sudden onset distinguishes norovirus from most other GE. Duration: 24-72 hr self-limiting; stool shedding continues 2-3 wk. Ix (severity): usually mild-moderate; dehydration especially dangerous in elderly/infants/immunocompromised. Ix: clinical; stool RT-PCR (gold standard - very sensitive; nucleic acid amplification); stool EM (historically). No routine blood tests needed in typical cases. Mx: supportive (oral/IV rehydration); no antiviral; no antibiotic; infection control (contact + vomit droplet precautions - key for outbreak control; 70% alcohol less effective than bleach - hypochlorite solution; hand washing with soap more effective than alcohol gel in outbreak). Isolation of symptomatic patients; exclusion from food handling/healthcare for 48 hr after last symptom.

conditions.name: Rotavirus
conditions.summary: Leading cause of severe dehydrating gastroenteritis in children <5 yr globally; non-enveloped double-stranded RNA virus (Reoviridae); highly contagious. Faecal-oral; peaks in winter (temperate climates - 'winter diarrhoea'). Previously leading cause of diarrhoeal death in children; now vaccine-preventable. Sx: abrupt onset vomiting + profuse watery diarrhoea (up to 10-20 stools/day - non-bloody), fever; duration 3-8 d; dehydration major risk (isonatraemic in most); vomiting often precedes diarrhoea (distinguishes from bacterial GE where diarrhoea predominant). Ix (severity): ranges from asymptomatic to severe dehydration requiring IV fluids/hospitalisation. Ix: stool rapid antigen test (EIA - point-of-care, widely used); stool RT-PCR (more sensitive); EM; routine bloods unremarkable unless severe dehydration. Mx: oral rehydration solution (ORS - first-line for mild-moderate dehydration; WHO-ORS low osmolarity; small, frequent sips); IV fluids (Ringer's lactate or 0.9% NaCl - moderate-severe dehydration or unable to tolerate ORS); zinc supplementation (low-income settings - ↓duration); no antiemetics routinely (ondansetron reduces vomiting, facilitates ORS); no antibiotic. Vaccine (primary prevention): RV1 (Rotarix - 2 doses) or RV5 (RotaTeq - 3 doses); oral; markedly ↓hospitalisations (globally recommended by WHO).

conditions.name: Fournier gangrene
conditions.summary: Rapidly progressive polymicrobial necrotising fasciitis of the perineum, genitalia, and perianal region; urological/colorectal emergency with mortality 20-40%. Predominantly males (male:female 10:1) but also females (labia, perineum). Risk: DM (most common - 50-70%; hyperglycaemia impairs immune function), obesity, immunocompromise (malignancy, HIV, steroids, cirrhosis), local trauma (perineal/urethral injury, recent surgery, insect bite, urethral catheter), urological pathology (urethral stricture, periurethral abscess), anorectal infection, Bartholin gland abscess. Microbiology: synergistic polymicrobial (aerobic + anaerobic organisms - E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Bacteroides, streptococci, Clostridium, Staphylococcus); aerobe-anaerobe synergy drives rapid fascial destruction + gas production. Sx: severe perineal/scrotal pain + swelling + erythema → rapid progression to crepitus (subcutaneous gas - gas-producing organisms), skin discolouration (dusky purple → black necrosis), foul odour (putrid), systemic sepsis (fever, tachycardia, shock). Ix: clinical emergency; CT (gas in fascial planes - tracks along deep fascial planes of perineum, thigh, abdominal wall; extent of disease; CT faster/more sensitive than X-ray); wound swab + blood cultures. Mx: EMERGENCY surgical debridement (wide excision of all necrotic tissue - extend until viable bleeding tissue; often multiple return trips to theatre; may require orchiectomy if testicular involvement - usually spared as testes have separate blood supply); broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam + metronidazole + vancomycin ± carbapenem for immunocompromised); ICU; glycaemic control; hyperbaric oxygen (adjunct - limited evidence); wound care + reconstruction (VAC dressing, split-skin grafting).

conditions.name: Bacterial tracheitis
conditions.summary: Acute bacterial infection of trachea with exudative pseudomembrane formation; rare but life-threatening cause of upper airway obstruction in children (6 months to 8 yr, peak 3-5 yr); Staphylococcus aureus most common (including MRSA - community-acquired); also Streptococcus, H. influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis; often superinfection following viral croup (parainfluenza). Sx: prodromal viral URTI (few days) → acute deterioration with high fever (>39°C), toxic appearance (systemically unwell - unlike viral croup), barking cough, stridor (initially inspiratory - later biphasic with tracheal obstruction), severe respiratory distress, inability to manage secretions, drooling (less than epiglottitis), no positional preference (unlike epiglottitis - prefers sitting). Differentiation from viral croup: toxaemia, high fever, older age, failure to respond to nebulised adrenaline. Differentiation from epiglottitis: younger age, barking cough, less drooling (but considerable overlap). Ix: CXR (subglottic narrowing + irregularity; 'steeple sign' as in croup; pseudomembranous debris in trachea - sometimes visible); lateral neck X-ray (subglottic narrowing, tracheal irregularity); direct laryngoscopy/bronchoscopy under GA (diagnostic - membrane extraction + airway securing; copious purulent secretions + membrane in trachea). Mx: AIRWAY (secure in theatre under GA - intubation almost always required; nasal intubation preferred; frequent ETT suctioning - membrane occludes); IV antibiotics (antistaphylococcal - cloxacillin/flucloxacillin ± vancomycin if MRSA risk; ceftriaxone often used initially); ICU; helium-oxygen (heliox - temporising measure); corticosteroids (limited evidence); usually requires 3-10 days intubation.

conditions.name: Foreign body aspiration
conditions.summary: Inhalation of solid foreign body into airway; bimodal distribution: young children (1-3 yr - most common; reach/put objects in mouth; no back teeth to chew; immature swallowing reflex) and elderly (impaired swallowing, poor dentition, reduced cough reflex). Commonly aspirated: peanuts/nuts (most common - organic, swell + cause intense inflammation), small toys, popcorn, coins, dental materials (elderly). Location: right main bronchus (most common - more vertical, wider, higher flow than left). Acute event: sudden-onset choking, coughing, gagging, cyanosis (laryngeal/tracheal - immediate complete obstruction); may be witnessed. Delayed/missed: recurrent/persistent wheeze (unilateral), stridor, pneumonia (recurrent in same lobe - classic indicator of FB), chronic cough, atelectasis (check valve mechanism: air enters but cannot leave → obstructive emphysema; or total block → collapse); asymptomatic interval (hours to weeks) after initial choking episode - classical history. Ix: CXR (radio-opaque FBs - minority; air trapping/obstructive emphysema on expiratory/lateral decubitus films; lobar collapse; mediastinal shift); CT chest (radio-lucent FBs, bronchiectasis, complications); FBC (infection). Mx: acute complete obstruction (witnessed): back blows + abdominal thrusts (Heimlich - >1 yr; chest thrusts <1 yr); rigid bronchoscopy (diagnostic + therapeutic - gold standard for known/suspected FBA; flexible bronchoscope in experienced hands); thoracotomy (failed bronchoscopy); avoid blind finger sweeps; no corticosteroids routinely.

conditions.name: Hypospadias
conditions.summary: Congenital anomaly of male urethra; urethral meatus opens on ventral (underside) of penis proximal to normal tip position; 1 in 150-300 male births; most common urological anomaly in males. Embryology: failure of fusion of urethral folds (8-16 wk gestation). Location: distal/glanular (50% - mild), penile shaft (30%), penoscrotal/scrotal/perineal (20% - severe). Three components (not always all present): ectopic urethral meatus (proximal), chordee (ventral penile curvature - fibrous band, prevents erection), hooded prepuce (incomplete foreskin - dorsal only; absent ventrally). Associated anomalies: undescended testis (9%), inguinal hernia; major structural anomalies uncommon unless severe/hypospadias with cryptorchidism → DSD (disorders of sexual development) workup. Complications if untreated: abnormal stream (downward), inability to void standing, sexual dysfunction (chordee), infertility (penoscrotal). Ix: clinical examination (newborn check); USS/karyotype (if severe/ambiguous genitalia). Mx: surgical repair (hypospadias repair - 'HYPE': urethroplasty + chordee correction; optimal timing 6-18 months; distal: single-stage MAGPI/TIP; proximal: staged procedures); avoid circumcision (prepuce used for repair); success rates >90%; complications: fistula (most common), meatal stenosis, urethral stricture, diverticulum, recurrent curvature.

conditions.name: Cryptorchidism
conditions.summary: Failure of one or both testes to descend into the scrotum; most common genital anomaly in males (3% term, 30% premature infants; most descend spontaneously - 1% at 1 yr). Location: inguinal canal (most common - 70%); intraabdominal (20%); ectopic (superficial inguinal pouch, femoral, perineal - 10%); retractile testis (not true UDT - cremasteric reflex, can be manipulated to scrotum). Bilateral: associated with hypogonadism, DSD, chromosomal anomaly. Risk factors: prematurity, low birth weight, family history, gestational DM, maternal oestrogen exposure. Complications: malignancy (testicular germ cell tumour - ↑risk × 4-8 in cryptorchidism; intraabdominal worst; orchidopexy before age 2 may ↓risk - still ↑vs normal); infertility (impaired spermatogenesis from ↑testicular temperature; bilateral cryptorchidism major risk); testicular torsion (↑risk in UDT); psychological (body image). Ix: clinical examination (by 3 months); USS (inguinal); MRI/laparoscopy (impalpable testis). Mx: hormonal (hCG or GnRH - limited evidence, occasional spontaneous descent, not routine guideline); surgical orchidopexy (standard of care: if not descended by 6 months, operate at 6-18 months; inguinal: Fowler-Stephens for intraabdominal; single-stage/two-stage laparoscopic for high UDT); impalpable testis: laparoscopy (diagnostic + therapeutic - orchiectomy if atrophic nubbin, orchidopexy if viable).

conditions.name: Varicocele
conditions.summary: Abnormal dilation of pampiniform plexus of veins in spermatic cord; analogous to lower limb varicose veins; 15% of general male population; 35-40% of men presenting with infertility (most common correctable cause of male infertility). Left sided predominance (90% left; 10% bilateral; isolated right-side varicocele → retroperitoneal mass until proven otherwise - impairs left gonadal vein drainage into left renal vein at right angle). Pathophysiology: reflux in internal spermatic vein (incompetent/absent valves) → venous hypertension → ↑testicular temperature → impaired spermatogenesis + ↑oxidative stress → sperm motility/morphology/count defects; ↓testosterone (Leydig cell dysfunction). Sx: scrotal heaviness/dull ache (worse with prolonged standing/exercise); 'bag of worms' appearance on inspection (grade III); most asymptomatic. Ix (grading): I (palpable only on Valsalva); II (palpable at rest); III (visible through scrotum). Ix: clinical examination (supine then standing + Valsalva); USS Doppler (confirms reflux; subclinical); semen analysis (oligospermia, asthenospermia, abnormal morphology - OAT syndrome). Mx: observation if asymptomatic + normal semen analysis; surgical ligation (open - Palomo/inguinal or subinguinal microscopic varicocelectomy) or percutaneous embolisation (radiological) - for: symptomatic, abnormal semen analysis, testicular growth retardation in adolescents; evidence for ↑pregnancy rates after varicocelectomy (meta-analysis supporting treatment for infertility); microsurgical varicocelectomy (lowest complication/recurrence rate).

conditions.name: Scurvy
conditions.summary: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency; vitamin C essential cofactor for prolyl/lysyl hydroxylases (collagen synthesis) → defective collagen → connective tissue breakdown; also essential for iron absorption + antioxidant defence. Populations at risk: elderly, alcoholics, food insecurity, limited diet (no fresh fruit/vegetables - classic: sailors before citrus rations), infants fed unfortified formula, psychiatric conditions (restricted eating). Sx appear after 1-3 months deficiency. Classic features: perifollicular haemorrhages (corkscrew hairs - coiled hairs surrounded by petechiae around follicles - pathognomonic), gum disease (perifollicular bleeding → inflamed/bleeding gums → tooth loss - only in adults with teeth), purpura + ecchymoses (poor collagen → vessel fragility), poor wound healing, haemarthrosis, subperiosteal haemorrhage (children - periosteal elevation), anaemia (iron-deficiency + megaloblastic from impaired iron absorption + folate metabolism), hyperkeratosis, dry skin; 'Woody leg' (subperiosteal haemorrhage - extremely painful - children); weakness, fatigue (general). Children: irritability, pain on handling, pseudoparalysis (pain prevents movement - looks like paralysis), frog-leg posture (least painful), subperiosteal bleeding (scorbutic rosary - costochondral junction - distinct from rachitic rosary). Ix: clinical (plasma vitamin C level - confirm); X-ray (children - Trummerfeld zone, Pelkan spurs, Frankel line, ground-glass metaphyses). Mx: vitamin C replacement (1000 mg/d × 1 month, then maintenance - rapid symptom resolution within days-weeks).

conditions.name: Pellagra
conditions.summary: Niacin (vitamin B3/nicotinic acid) deficiency - niacin or its precursor tryptophan; niacin essential for NAD+/NADP+ (cellular energy metabolism/redox reactions). Causes: dietary (maize-based diets without alkali processing - nixtamalisation releases bound niacin; maize also low in tryptophan); Hartnup disease (tryptophan malabsorption - congenital amino acid transport defect); carcinoid syndrome (tryptophan diverted to serotonin synthesis); isoniazid therapy (interferes with B6/niacin metabolism); alcoholism; malabsorption (Crohn, coeliac). Classic triad: '4 Ds' - Dermatitis, Diarrhoea, Dementia (+ Death if untreated). Dermatitis: bilaterally symmetrical photosensitive dermatitis on sun-exposed areas (Casal necklace - collar-like rash around neck; dorsum of hands/'gloves'; Casal necklace is pathognomonic); initial erythema/blistering → hyperpigmentation/thickening → desquamation; mucous membrane involvement (angular stomatitis, glossitis, scarlet tongue). GI: diarrhoea (secretory, may be bloody), nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain; mucosal atrophy. Neuropsychiatric: depression, anxiety, confusion, psychosis, dementia; peripheral neuropathy; aggressive behaviour (historic). Ix: clinical (triad + exposure/risk); urinary N-methylnicotinamide (↓); plasma niacin (unreliable); therapeutic trial. Mx: nicotinamide (preferred form - less flushing than nicotinic acid) supplementation; dietary niacin; treat underlying cause.

conditions.name: Carotid artery stenosis
conditions.summary: Atherosclerotic narrowing of internal carotid artery (ICA) - most commonly at bifurcation of common carotid artery. Major risk factor for ischaemic stroke + TIA (carotid emboli account for ~15-20% of ischaemic strokes). Risk factors: same as atherosclerosis (hypertension most important, smoking, hyperlipidaemia, DM, age, male sex). Sx: may be asymptomatic (detected on USS); symptomatic: TIA or ipsilateral hemisphere stroke (contralateral hemiparesis/hemisensory loss, ipsilateral monocular blindness - amaurosis fugax - classic; aphasia if dominant hemisphere); carotid bruit (auscultation - unreliable marker, present in ~40% significant stenosis). Classification: asymptomatic vs symptomatic; severity by % stenosis (NASCET criteria). Ix: carotid duplex USS (first-line screening); CTA or MRA (further evaluation, operative planning); conventional angiography (gold standard, reserved for equivocal cases). Mx: medical (all patients): antiplatelet (aspirin + clopidogrel short-term post-TIA/stroke; single antiplatelet long-term), high-intensity statin (plaque stabilisation), ACE-i/ARB, risk factor modification (smoking cessation critical). Symptomatic carotid stenosis 50-99% (NASCET): carotid endarterectomy (CEA - gold standard surgical; benefit greatest 70-99%; operate within 2 wk of TIA/minor stroke - highest early recurrence risk); carotid artery stenting (CAS - comparable to CEA in high surgical risk; ↑early stroke risk, ↓MI risk vs CEA). Asymptomatic 60-99%: CEA benefit modest (ACST trial); careful patient selection; medical therapy improving.

conditions.name: Moyamoya disease
conditions.summary: Progressive occlusive cerebrovascular disease affecting bilateral internal carotid arteries (supraclinoid ICA) and proximal MCA/ACA with compensatory collateral vessel development (fragile, lenticulostriate/thalamoperforator collaterals - 'puff of smoke' appearance on angiography - Japanese 'moyamoya'). Primary (idiopathic): strong East Asian predominance (Japan, Korea, China - 10× higher than West); bimodal age distribution (children 5-10 yr, adults 30-40 yr). Secondary (moyamoya syndrome): sickle cell disease (most common cause in West), neurofibromatosis type 1, Down syndrome, prior cranial irradiation, thyroid disease, giant cell arteritis. RNF213 (gene - susceptibility variant in East Asians). Sx: children: ischaemic strokes/TIAs (triggered by hyperventilation - crying, exercise, wind instruments - hypocapnia → vasoconstriction of already compromised vessels); progressive cognitive decline, seizures. Adults: more commonly haemorrhagic stroke (rupture of fragile collaterals). Ix: MRI/MRA (arterial narrowing + 'puff of smoke' collaterals); conventional angiography (gold standard - shows extent + collaterals); perfusion imaging (acetazolamide challenge SPECT/PET - assess cerebrovascular reserve). Mx: surgical revascularisation (gold standard for symptomatic - indirect: EDAS encephaloduroarteriosynangiosis; direct: STA-MCA bypass; combination); antiplatelet therapy (medical management only); no proven role for anticoagulation; treat underlying condition.

conditions.name: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection
conditions.summary: Non-atherosclerotic, non-traumatic, non-iatrogenic dissection of coronary artery wall → intramural haematoma → true lumen compression → ischaemia/MI; accounts for ~4% of ACS overall but ~35% of ACS in women <50 yr - important cause of MI in young women. Pathophysiology: disruption of intimal-medial plane (Type 1: intimal tear visible; Type 2: intramural haematoma without visible tear - most common; Type 3: focal stenosis on angiography, subtle). Peripartum SCAD: most serious peripartum cardiac emergency (days to weeks post-partum). Predisposing conditions: fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD - most common associated condition in non-peripartum SCAD; 50-86%), extreme physical/emotional stress triggers (isometric exercise - weightlifting; labour), connective tissue disease (Marfan, EDS), inflammatory conditions, multiparity. Sx: Atypical MI profile: young woman, no conventional risk factors, severe chest pain. Coronary angiogram: multi-vessel involvement (30%); LAD most commonly affected; dual lumen appearance (Type 1) or long segment smooth narrowing (Type 2). Mx: conservative management preferred (most heal spontaneously; PCI technically difficult + may extend dissection); antiplatelet (aspirin - standard); beta-blockers (↓arterial shear stress - recommended); ACEI; avoid P2Y12 inhibitors if possible (dual antiplatelet ↑bleeding); PCI (if ongoing ischaemia/haemodynamic compromise - high complication rate); CABG (multivessel/main stem); exercise restriction (avoid high-intensity); cardiac rehabilitation; psychological support (high PTSD rate); cardiac MRI (follow-up).

conditions.name: Acute limb ischaemia
conditions.summary: Sudden decrease in limb perfusion threatening viability; surgical emergency - 'time is tissue'. Causes: embolism (50% - most commonly cardiac origin: AFib mural thrombus, post-MI LV thrombus, prosthetic valve, IE, atrial myxoma; peripheral emboli lodge at bifurcations - femoral bifurcation most common), thrombosis in situ (atherosclerotic plaque rupture/thrombosis - pre-existing PAD; graft/stent thrombosis), dissection, trauma, popliteal aneurysm thrombosis, compartment syndrome. 6 Ps: Pain (sudden severe rest pain, unrelenting), Pallor, Pulselessness (absent Doppler signal), Paraesthesia (numbness - indicates sensory nerve ischaemia), Paralysis (motor loss - severe ischaemia; worst prognostic sign), Poikilothermia (cold limb). Rutherford classification: I (viable - sensorimotor intact); IIa (marginally threatened - paraesthesia, Doppler signals present); IIb (immediately threatened - paralysis, no Doppler); III (irreversible - irreversible muscle damage/nerve loss - amputation inevitable). Ix: clinical + hand-held Doppler; CT angiography (confirms level of occlusion, plans intervention); ABI <0.5 (unreliable in ALI - clinical assessment primary). Mx: IV heparin immediately (all cases - prevents propagation); urgent revascularisation (Rutherford IIa-IIb): embolectomy (Fogarty catheter - embolism, within 6 hr); catheter-directed thrombolysis (thrombosis in situ, graft occlusion); surgical bypass; fasciotomy (compartment syndrome - all cases after prolonged ischaemia); Rutherford III: primary amputation; post-reperfusion: monitor for reperfusion injury (hyperkalaemia, myoglobinuria - AKI).

conditions.name: Transposition of great arteries
conditions.summary: Ventriculoarterial discordance: aorta arises from right ventricle; pulmonary artery arises from left ventricle → two parallel circulations (systemic + pulmonary run in parallel not in series) → severe cyanosis from birth. Most common cyanotic congenital heart disease presenting as neonatal emergency; second most common CHD overall. Associations: maternal DM (strongest), male sex. D-TGA (dextro, complete transposition): aorta is anterior + rightward of PA. Physiology: deoxygenated blood → RV → aorta → body; oxygenated → LV → PA → lungs - no mixing → progressive hypoxaemia → death without intervention. Survival depends on mixing: PFO/ASD, VSD (30-40%), PDA (maintained by prostaglandins). Sx: cyanosis from birth (severe, progressive); tachypnoea; no murmur (unless VSD); 'egg on a string'/'egg on its side' appearance on CXR (narrow mediastinum from AP vessel relationship + cardiomegaly + ↑pulmonary vascularity). Ix: antenatal USS (4-chamber view + outflow tracts - detected prenatally in 50%); neonatal echo (confirms anatomy, rules out VSD, coronary anatomy); pulse oximetry (hypoxaemia). Mx: prostaglandin E1 (PGE1 - IV infusion immediately to maintain PDA + mixing - bridge to surgery); balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind procedure - catheter, enlarges PFO → ↑mixing → temporising); arterial switch operation (Jatene procedure - definitive; within first 2 wk of life; reconnects great arteries to correct ventricles + reimplants coronaries; excellent long-term outcomes).

conditions.name: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome
conditions.summary: Spectrum of congenital cardiac anomalies with severe hypoplasia/atresia of left-sided structures: aortic atresia/stenosis, mitral atresia/stenosis, hypoplastic LV and ascending aorta; most common cause of cardiac death in first week of life. Physiology: entire cardiac output maintained by right ventricle (single ventricle physiology) through PDA → parallel circulations (aorta + PA perfused by RV via PDA); systemic perfusion dependent on PDA (ductus-dependent systemic circulation). Sx: deterioration on PDA closure (day 2-7 of life): shock, cyanosis, respiratory distress, metabolic acidosis, absent femoral pulses. Occasionally detected antenatally (echo - absent/small LV). Ix: antenatal: anomaly scan 20 wk + fetal echo; postnatal: echo (diagnostic); CXR (cardiomegaly, ↑pulmonary vascularity). Mx: prostaglandin E1 (immediate - maintain PDA); staged surgical palliation (3 operations): Stage 1 - Norwood procedure (neonatal: creates neo-aorta from native PA + ascending aorta, systemic-pulmonary shunt); Stage 2 - bidirectional Glenn/hemi-Fontan (3-6 months: SVC anastomosed to PA - passive pulmonary flow); Stage 3 - Fontan completion (2-4 yr: IVC → PA, total cavopulmonary connection - complete passive pulmonary flow); OR cardiac transplantation (alternative to Norwood); outcomes improving (50-70% survival to adulthood with staged repair); Fontan circulation complications: protein-losing enteropathy, plastic bronchitis, thromboembolism, arrhythmias, FALD (Fontan-associated liver disease), progressive heart failure.

conditions.name: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of newborn
conditions.summary: Failure of normal postnatal decrease in pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) → right-to-left shunting through PDA and/or PFO → hypoxaemia disproportionate to lung disease severity. Normal transition: at birth, oxygenation + lung expansion → ↓PVR → ↑pulmonary blood flow; in PPHN: PVR remains elevated → shunting of deoxygenated blood into systemic circulation. Causes: idiopathic; associated with parenchymal lung disease (meconium aspiration syndrome - most common; RDS, pneumonia, congenital diaphragmatic hernia); maladaptive (antenatal NSAID/SSRI - prenatal PDA closure; perinatal asphyxia); developmental (CDH - pulmonary hypoplasia, underdeveloped vasculature; ↑PVR congenitally). Sx: term/near-term neonate; severe hypoxaemia (SaO2 <85%); pre-ductal vs post-ductal SpO2 difference >10% (right hand vs lower limb - right-to-left shunt at PDA); labile hypoxaemia (rapid swings with minimal stimulation); tachypnoea; RV strain on echo. Ix: echocardiography (confirms shunting direction + PVR elevation + RV function; rules out structural CHD - must exclude ductal-dependent lesions before starting O2); pre/post-ductal SpO2 gradient. Mx: optimise ventilation (target PaCO2 40-45, pH 7.35-7.45 - avoid hyperventilation/alkalosis; currently low-tidal-volume ventilation + high PEEP); inhaled nitric oxide (iNO - selective pulmonary vasodilator; US-approved for PPHN in >34 wk; 20 ppm; reduces need for ECMO); ECMO (extracorporeal membrane oxygenation - refractory PPHN; bridge to recovery); treat underlying cause (meconium aspiration - surfactant); sildenafil (chronic/post-iNO weaning); avoid alkalinisation (↓cerebral perfusion).

conditions.name: Amniotic fluid embolism
conditions.summary: Catastrophic, unpredictable obstetric emergency; amniotic fluid/fetal cells/debris enter maternal circulation → biphasic: initial acute pulmonary hypertension + RV failure + hypoxia (minutes), then cardiovascular collapse + DIC (within 30-60 min - haemorrhage from consumptive coagulopathy). Incidence 1-12 per 100000 deliveries; mortality historically 60-80% (improving with modern ICU care - now ~20-40%); leading cause of maternal death in developed countries. Risk factors: advanced maternal age, multiparity, uterine hyperstimulation, instrumental/operative delivery, placenta praevia/abruption, amniocentesis (rare); often no identifiable risk factor. Pathophysiology: not simple mechanical obstruction - immune-mediated anaphylactoid response to fetal antigens (hence 'anaphylactoid syndrome of pregnancy' - preferred term); mast cell degranulation + complement activation. Sx: sudden cardiovascular collapse + respiratory failure + altered consciousness during labour/delivery/immediately postpartum; profound DIC (massive haemorrhage - dominant feature); seizures; fetal distress. Ix: clinical exclusion (no specific test - diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out PE, haemorrhage, eclampsia, anaphylaxis); complement, tryptase, zinc coproporphyrin (not validated). Mx: immediate resuscitation (CPR; secure airway; 100% O2; left lateral decubitus); delivery of fetus (emergency CS if cardiac arrest - perimortem CS within 4-5 min); massive transfusion protocol (FFP, RBCs, platelets, cryoprecipitate - DIC); vasopressors; ECMO (refractory); right heart failure management (pulmonary vasodilators - epoprostenol, iNO); no antidote; supportive ICU.

conditions.name: Brown-Sequard syndrome
conditions.summary: Incomplete spinal cord injury from hemisection of cord; classically penetrating trauma (knife/bullet wound) but also demyelination (MS - most common cause of incomplete Brown-Sequard), tumour, disc herniation, haematoma, radiation myelopathy. Pathophysiology: ipsilateral motor tracts (corticospinal - descend, cross in medulla) + ipsilateral dorsal columns (ascend, cross in medulla) interrupted; contralateral spinothalamic tract (crosses within 1-2 segments of entry) interrupted. Classic syndrome: ipsilateral (same side as lesion): spastic paralysis (UMN - corticospinal tract), loss of proprioception + vibration + fine touch (dorsal column); contralateral (opposite side, 1-2 levels below lesion): loss of pain + temperature (spinothalamic tract); ipsilateral LMN signs at level of lesion (anterior horn + nerve root). Sx: unilateral arm/leg weakness with crossed sensory loss = classic presentation; Brown-Sequard-plus syndrome (incomplete - contralateral weakness with ipsilateral pain/temp loss - mild degrees of the full syndrome; most common in clinical practice). Ix: MRI spine (lesion, extent); CT spine (if acute trauma - fracture/dislocation). Mx: treat underlying cause (neurosurgical for tumour/disc, steroids for MS relapse, anticoagulation for haematoma); high-dose methylprednisolone (acute traumatic injury - NASCIS trials - benefit modest, controversial; still used in many centres); physiotherapy; bladder/bowel management; prognosis: better than complete cord injury - majority of patients regain ambulatory function.

conditions.name: Central cord syndrome
conditions.summary: Most common incomplete spinal cord injury (50% of incomplete injuries); predominantly affects older patients with cervical spondylosis subjected to hyperextension injury (fall, RTC - forced hyperextension of degenerate cervical spine compresses cord between osteophytes anteriorly + infolded ligamentum flavum posteriorly); also younger patients with disc herniation. Anatomy: corticospinal tract somatotopy - cervical fibres run centrally, sacral peripherally → central damage preferentially affects upper limb (arm > hand >> leg); spinothalamic (anterolateral) partially spared. Syndrome: greater weakness in ARMS > legs (upper limb worst affected - hand/grip weakness most prominent), variable sensory loss below level, bladder dysfunction (urinary retention - most common; detrusor areflexia), sacral sparing (preserved perianal sensation/anal tone ± some voluntary motor function - indicates incomplete injury + better prognosis). Complete loss of hand function (fine motor) in severe cases. Hyperaesthesia/dysaesthesia at level of injury. Ix: MRI cervical spine (urgently - cord oedema/signal change, disc herniation, spondylosis, canal diameter); CT (bone/osteophyte). Mx: immobilise/spine precautions acutely; manage hypotension (↑spinal cord perfusion pressure; MAP ≥85-90 mmHg - vasopressors if needed); steroids (controversial, avoid in penetrating injury); surgical decompression (timing debated: early <24 hr for worsening; elderly spondylotic - timing individualised); rehabilitation (most improve - walking usually recovers before arm function; hand function slowest/most incomplete recovery).

conditions.name: Anterior cord syndrome
conditions.summary: Incomplete spinal cord injury involving anterior two-thirds of cord (anterior spinal artery territory); affects corticospinal tracts (motor) + spinothalamic tracts (pain/temperature) bilaterally; SPARES posterior columns (proprioception, vibration, light touch - intact). Causes: anterior spinal artery occlusion (infarction - aortic surgery, aortic dissection, thromboembolism, hypotension), large central disc herniation, severe hyperflexion injury, tumour/abscess, vasculitis. Sx: bilateral motor paralysis (upper and lower motor neuron - flaccid acutely, then spastic) below level of lesion; bilateral loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic); PRESERVED position sense/vibration/light touch (posterior columns - key distinguishing feature); bladder/bowel dysfunction (neurogenic). Prognosis: worst of incomplete cord syndromes (only ~10-20% recover useful motor function); preserved proprioception suggests relatively intact cord - better prognosis overall vs anterior cord. Ix: MRI spine (diffusion-weighted imaging - DWI; cord infarct appears as 'owl eye' pattern T2 signal - bilateral anterior horn + corticospinal involvement); CT angiography (vascular cause). Mx: treat underlying cause (aortic repair/stenting; thrombectomy; antibiotics for abscess); spinal cord ischaemia: spinal fluid drainage (CSF drainage - lowers pressure around cord, improves perfusion - used perioperatively for thoracoabdominal aortic surgery); MAP augmentation (vasopressors - MAP >80 mmHg); antiplatelet/anticoagulation (embolic); rehabilitation; poor functional prognosis but bladder/bowel management + skin care essential.

conditions.name: Hangman's fracture
conditions.summary: Bilateral fractures through the pedicles (posterior arch) of C2 (axis) with variable C2-C3 disc disruption and subluxation; most common mechanism: hyperextension + axial load (motor vehicle collision - dashboard impact, dive into shallow water, judicial hanging - original eponym from sudden arrest with ligamentous disruption). Levine-Edwards classification: Type I (<3 mm displacement, <11° angulation - stable; ligamentous and disc intact); Type II (>3 mm displacement or >11° angulation - most common; C2-C3 disc disrupted, ↑instability); Type IIa (angulated without anterior displacement - flexion-distraction); Type III (displacement + facet dislocation - most unstable). Paradox of hangman's fracture: severe-appearing fracture often with minimal neurological deficit because the fracture itself decompresses the canal (bilateral pedicle fracture expands canal diameter). Sx: neck pain, may have no neurological deficit (most cases - fracture widens canal); severe cases: quadriparesis; associated C-spine/skull base injury. Ix: CT cervical spine (gold standard - visualises fracture, displacement, angulation); MRI (ligamentous/disc injury, cord signal). Mx: Type I: cervical collar immobilisation (rigid, 8-12 wk); Type II: halo brace (definitive for most; external immobilisation); Type IIa: traction contraindicated (worsens angulation) - halo brace in extension; Type III: surgical stabilisation (C2-3 fusion); most heal without surgery; neurological deficit rare.

conditions.name: Diffuse axonal injury
conditions.summary: Traumatic brain injury from rotational acceleration-deceleration forces → shear strain → widespread axonal disruption throughout brain white matter (corpus callosum, corticospinal tracts, dorsolateral brainstem, grey-white matter interface); leading cause of post-traumatic coma + persistent vegetative state. Not a focal injury - microscopic/ultrastructural damage to axons → cytoskeletal disruption → axonal swelling (retraction balls) → secondary axotomy (Wallerian degeneration - hours-days later). Causes: MVA (most common), falls, assaults, shaking (non-accidental injury - infants). Grading (Adams): Grade I (lobar white matter - corpus callosum); Grade II (+ corpus callosum); Grade III (+ dorsolateral brainstem - worst prognosis). Sx: immediate loss of consciousness at moment of impact (no lucid interval - distinguishes from extradural haematoma); prolonged coma; vegetative state; Glasgow Coma Scale often severely impaired from outset; posturing (decorticate/decerebrate). CT often relatively normal or shows only petechial haemorrhages (microhaemorrhages) - misleadingly normal CT in severe TBI → suspect DAI. MRI (especially SWI - susceptibility weighted imaging; DWI): haemorrhagic foci at grey-white interface + corpus callosum + brainstem + basal ganglia; superior to CT for DAI detection. Mx: ICP management (intracranial pressure monitoring - goal <20 mmHg; MAP >70 mmHg; head elevation 30°; osmotherapy - mannitol/hypertonic saline; surgical decompressive craniectomy - refractory ICP); neuroprotective ventilation; targeted temperature management (controversial); rehabilitation (prolonged - major functional disability common); prognosis: grade III - severe disability/vegetative state common; outcomes difficult to predict early.

conditions.name: Hypophosphataemia
conditions.summary: Serum phosphate <0.8 mmol/L; severe <0.32 mmol/L. Causes: refeeding syndrome (most clinically critical - severe hypophosphataemia on resuming feeding after starvation; insulin surge → intracellular phosphate shift → dangerous depletion: cardiac arrhythmias, respiratory failure, rhabdomyolysis, haemolysis, seizures, encephalopathy; monitor + supplement before/during refeeding); DKA treatment (insulin → intracellular shift); antacid use (aluminium/magnesium hydroxide binds phosphate); malabsorption; primary hyperparathyroidism (↑PTH → ↑phosphaturia); X-linked hypophosphataemia (PHEX/FGF23 - renal phosphate wasting → rickets/osteomalacia); oncogenic osteomalacia (FGF23-secreting tumours - tumour-induced osteomalacia); vitamin D deficiency. Sx: mild-moderate asymptomatic; severe (<0.32): muscle weakness (proximal), respiratory failure (diaphragm weakness - may require ventilation), haemolytic anaemia (RBC fragility), platelet dysfunction, rhabdomyolysis, confusion/seizures/coma (neuropsychiatric), cardiomyopathy/heart failure, immune dysfunction. Ix: serum phosphate; urine phosphate (TRP, FEPi - distinguish renal vs non-renal loss); 25-OH vitamin D; PTH; FGF23 (if XLH/OOM suspected). Mx: oral phosphate supplements (mild-moderate; GI upset limits tolerance); IV sodium/potassium phosphate (severe/symptomatic; monitor calcium - hypocalcaemia risk); treat underlying cause; XLH: phosphate + alfacalcidol + burosumab.

conditions.name: Hyperphosphataemia
conditions.summary: Serum phosphate >1.45 mmol/L. Causes: reduced excretion (CKD - most common; GFR <30 → progressive hyperphosphataemia; hypoparathyroidism - ↓PTH → ↓phosphaturia); increased intake/absorption (excess supplementation; enema/laxative abuse - sodium phosphate); transcellular shift (rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis syndrome, haemolysis, DKA treatment - cellular phosphate release). Pathophysiology: ↑phosphate + ↓calcium (phosphate chelates Ca2+) → secondary hyperparathyroidism (CKD: ↑PTH attempting to correct phosphate/calcium - → renal osteodystrophy); calcification: metastatic calcification (calcium-phosphate product >5 mmol²/L² → soft tissue, vascular, coronary, valvular calcification - ↑cardiovascular mortality in CKD); calciphylaxis (calcification of small vessels → skin necrosis - severe CKD complication). Sx: hypocalcaemia symptoms (tetany, perioral tingling, seizures - especially hypoparathyroidism); pruritus (calcium-phosphate deposits in skin - CKD); extraskeletal calcification; band keratopathy (calcium phosphate in cornea); vascular calcification → ↑CVD. Ix: serum phosphate; calcium; PTH; renal function; urine phosphate (hypoparathyroidism vs renal cause). Mx: CKD: phosphate-restricted diet (limit dairy, processed foods); phosphate binders (calcium carbonate/acetate - cheap; sevelamer - preferred in ↑Ca or calcification; lanthanum carbonate; sucroferric oxyhydroxide); dialysis (removes phosphate); treat secondary HPT; hypoparathyroidism: dietary restriction + calcium carbonate; tumour lysis/rhabdo: hydration + dialysis.

conditions.name: Lactic acidosis
conditions.summary: Metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate (>5 mmol/L) + pH <7.35. Lactate: product of anaerobic glycolysis; cleared by liver/kidneys. Type A (tissue hypoperfusion/hypoxia - most common, most serious): septic shock, cardiogenic shock, hypovolaemic shock, mesenteric ischaemia, carbon monoxide poisoning, severe anaemia, cardiac arrest - impaired O2 delivery → anaerobic metabolism → excess lactate. Type B (no overt tissue hypoperfusion): drugs (metformin - accumulates in renal failure → inhibits complex I; NRTIs - inhibit mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma - HIV therapy; propofol infusion syndrome; linezolid; cyanide - inhibits complex IV), liver failure (↓clearance + ↓gluconeogenesis), thiamine deficiency (B1 - cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase; starvation/alcoholism → type B lactic acidosis - give IV thiamine before glucose in alcoholics), malignancy (Warburg effect - aerobic glycolysis in cancer cells; haematological malignancy especially - lymphoma/leukaemia), inborn errors of metabolism (mitochondrial disease, pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency). Ix: arterial/venous lactate (venous reasonable); ABG (pH, HCO3, AG); high-AG metabolic acidosis; exclude DKA. Mx: treat underlying cause (Type A: restore perfusion - fluid, vasopressors, source control); thiamine (all Type B if cause unclear - IV before glucose); withhold metformin (if AKI/contrast/surgery); bicarbonate (controversial, reserved for severe acidosis pH <7.1/HCO3 <6 - may transiently worsen intracellular acidosis); haemodialysis (metformin-associated, refractory).

conditions.name: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome
conditions.summary: Rare cause of upper GI obstruction; compression of third part of duodenum (D3/horizontal duodenum) between superior mesenteric artery (SMA) anteriorly and aorta posteriorly → reduced aortomesenteric angle/distance (normal angle 38-65°; SMA syndrome <25°; normal distance 10-28 mm; SMA syndrome <8 mm). Predisposing factors: rapid/excessive weight loss (↓retroperitoneal/mesenteric fat - most common trigger; anorexia nervosa, post-surgical, burns, malabsorption, TPN weaning, catabolic illness), immobilisation (body cast - 'cast syndrome'), scoliosis surgery (Harrington rod correction - ↑trunk length → ↑SMA stretch), very thin/asthenic body habitus. Sx: chronic intermittent: post-prandial epigastric pain, nausea, bilious vomiting, early satiety, weight loss, relief in left lateral/prone position (reduces duodenal compression); acute: acute high duodenal obstruction (vomiting, distension - less common. Mimics: gastroparesis, peptic ulcer, eating disorders (anorexia nervosa commonly confused with - may co-exist). Ix: CT abdomen (aortomesenteric angle + distance - diagnostic criteria; dilated stomach + duodenum proximal to obstruction; abrupt cut-off at SMA); upper GI contrast study (duodenal 'to and fro' peristalsis; holds at SMA level; relief in prone position); UGI endoscopy (exclude mucosal lesion). Mx: nutritional rehabilitation (weight gain first - conservative; NGJ/NJ tube bypassing obstruction + PN; high-calorie diet; positional manoeuvres - left lateral decubitus, prone, knee-chest position after meals); surgical (Ladd procedure or duodenojejunostomy - if conservative fails).

conditions.name: Primary myelofibrosis
conditions.summary: MPN with bone marrow fibrosis, extramedullary haematopoiesis (massive splenomegaly), and leukoerythroblastic film (tear-drop poikilocytes, nucleated RBCs, immature granulocytes). Mutations: JAK2 V617F (45%), CALR (25%), MPL (5%). Sx: massive splenomegaly, constitutional symptoms (B-symptoms), anaemia. Ix: BM biopsy (fibrosis grade MF-0→3), JAK2/CALR/MPL testing, DIPSS-plus (prognostic score). Mx: ruxolitinib (JAK1/2 inhibitor - ↓spleen volume + symptoms - COMFORT trials; all risk groups), allogeneic HSCT (only cure - high/very-high risk), transfusions, ESAs, danazol; median survival 3–7 years by risk.

conditions.name: Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
conditions.summary: IgG autoantibody-mediated haemolytic anaemia (antibodies optimally active at 37°C - 'warm'). Causes: idiopathic (50%), secondary (SLE, CLL, lymphoma, drugs - methyldopa, penicillin, fludarabine). Sx: anaemia symptoms, jaundice, splenomegaly; blood film (spherocytes, polychromasia, reticulocytosis). Ix: direct Coombs test (DAT positive - IgG +/- C3), indirect Coombs (serum autoantibody), reticulocyte count, ↑LDH, ↑unconjugated bilirubin, ↓haptoglobin. Mx: corticosteroids 1st-line (prednisolone 1 mg/kg - response in 70–80%); rituximab (2nd-line - superior to azathioprine - RAIHA trial); splenectomy (3rd-line); IVIg (acute severe); folate supplementation; avoid cold.

conditions.name: Haemophilia A
conditions.summary: X-linked recessive bleeding disorder (factor VIII deficiency; males affected, females carriers). Ix (severity): severe (<1% FVIII), moderate (1–5%), mild (6–40%). Sx: haemarthroses (knees, ankles, elbows - joint destruction), muscle haematomas, intracranial haemorrhage (most dangerous), prolonged bleeding after trauma/surgery. Ix: ↑APTT (normal PT, TT, platelet count), ↓FVIII activity, FVIII inhibitor assay (development in 25% of severe after treatment - major complication). Mx: FVIII concentrate (recombinant preferred - on-demand or prophylaxis); emicizumab (anti-FVIII mimetic bispecific antibody - HAVEN trials - 1st-line prophylaxis, bridges VIII structure; SC weekly/biweekly/monthly - game-changer); DDAVP (mild disease - ↑FVIII/vWF release); inhibitors - bypass agents (rFVIIa, FEIBA) or fitusiran.

conditions.name: Autoinflammatory diseases
conditions.summary: Monogenic disorders of innate immunity causing recurrent fever and inflammation without autoantibodies (distinct from autoimmune). Key diseases: Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF - MEFV mutation; most common hereditary periodic fever; autosomal recessive; Mediterranean/Middle Eastern; episodic fever + serositis + arthritis + erysipelas-like skin; amyloidosis if untreated; colchicine - highly effective, treats and prevents amyloid). TRAPS (TNF receptor-associated periodic syndrome - TNFRSF1A; longer attacks >1 week; myalgia, periorbital oedema, migratory rash; etanercept/canakinumab). CAPS (cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome - NLRP3; cold-triggered; urticaria-like rash; canakinumab highly effective). HIDS (hyper-IgD syndrome - MVK; IgD elevation). PFAPA (periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, adenitis - most common in children; not monogenic; tonsillectomy curative). Ix: genetic panel, SAA (acute-phase; ↑in attacks). Mx: colchicine (FMF), IL-1 inhibitors (anakinra, canakinumab - CAPS, TRAPS, FMF refractory).

conditions.name: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1
conditions.summary: Autosomal dominant tumour syndrome (MEN1 tumour suppressor gene - menin). Classic triad: pituitary adenoma (prolactinoma most common - 60%), parathyroid hyperplasia (primary hyperparathyroidism - 90%; first to present and most penetrant), pancreatic/duodenal NETs (gastrinoma - ZES most common; insulinoma 2nd; VIPoma, glucagonoma). Mnemonic: '3 Ps' - Pituitary, Parathyroid, Pancreatic. Genetics: germline MEN1 mutation + somatic 'second hit' (Knudson two-hit hypothesis). Sx: hypercalcaemia (parathyroid), ZES (peptic ulcers), hypoglycaemia (insulinoma), acromegaly/Cushing/prolactinaemia (pituitary), adrenal adenomas (non-functioning usually), carcinoid tumours (thymic/bronchial). Ix: annual surveillance (calcium, PTH, prolactin, IGF-1, fasting gastrin, chromogranin A, MRI/EUS), genetic testing all family members. Mx: parathyroidectomy (subtotal), somatostatin analogues (gastrinoma), PPIs (ZES), surgery (insulinoma), dopamine agonists/surgery (prolactinoma).

conditions.name: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2
conditions.summary: Autosomal dominant syndrome (RET proto-oncogene mutations). MEN2A (Sipple): medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC - 95%; calcitonin-secreting C-cells; amyloid deposition; diarrhoea from calcitonin) + phaeochromocytoma (50%) + hyperparathyroidism (20%). MEN2B: MTC (early onset - prophylactic thyroidectomy in infancy) + phaeochromocytoma + mucosal neuromas (tongue, lips - Marfanoid habitus, eyelid neuromas) - NO hyperparathyroidism. FMTC (familial MTC only - MEN2A variant with no other features). RET codon determines aggressiveness (highest risk - C634, M918 → thyroidectomy in 1st year of life). Ix: genetic testing (RET mutation), calcitonin (MTC), 24-h urinary catecholamines/metanephrines (phaeochromocytoma - screen before thyroid surgery), calcium/PTH. Mx: prophylactic thyroidectomy (timing by RET codon risk category), phaeochromocytoma removal before thyroid surgery (α-block then β-block pre-operatively - crucial); cabozantinib/vandetanib (metastatic MTC).

conditions.name: Hungry bone syndrome
conditions.summary: Severe, prolonged hypocalcaemia following parathyroidectomy (or other treatment of hyperparathyroidism) as demineralised bone rapidly incorporates calcium. Pathophysiology: longstanding PTH-driven bone resorption → large calcium deficit in bone; when PTH removed → bone 'hungers' for calcium → profound hypocalcaemia (may also involve Mg, PO4). Risk factors: severe preoperative hypercalcaemia, large gland weight, high ALP (marker of bone remodelling), vitamin D deficiency. Sx: symptomatic hypocalcaemia (paraesthesiae, carpopedal spasm, Chvostek's sign, Trousseau's sign, tetany, seizures, QTc prolongation), often within hours of surgery. Mx: aggressive IV calcium gluconate (continuous infusion often needed for days-weeks); oral calcium + active vitamin D (calcitriol - dose may be very high); magnesium replacement; phosphate monitoring (may fall too - hungry bone consumes PO4). Duration: days to weeks; distinguishes from primary hypoparathyroidism (which is permanent).

conditions.name: Cavernous sinus thrombosis
conditions.summary: Septic or aseptic thrombosis of cavernous sinuses (paired venous sinuses flanking sella turcica). Septic: most common cause - facial infections (furuncles, carbuncles - 'dangerous triangle' of face), sinusitis (sphenoidal/ethmoidal), dental infections, orbital cellulitis; Staphylococcus aureus most common pathogen. Structures at risk: CN III, IV, V1, V2, VI (in sinus wall), internal carotid artery (in sinus). Sx: periorbital oedema/proptosis (chemosis, conjunctival oedema), ophthalmoplegia (painful - CN VI palsy earliest - abducens runs freely in sinus lumen), CN V1/V2 sensory loss, fever and systemic toxicity; bilateral involvement pathognomonic. Ix: MRI (filling defect) + MRV (superior; gadolinium - absent/irregular filling), CT (may show enlarged cavernous sinus). Mx: high-dose IV antibiotics (anti-staphylococcal - vancomycin + ceftriaxone + metronidazole to cover polymicrobial); anticoagulation (controversial - generally recommended for septic CST); surgical drainage if sinus source. High mortality/morbidity without treatment.

conditions.name: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
conditions.summary: Thrombosis of cerebral venous sinuses or cortical veins → venous infarction/haemorrhage. Causes: hypercoagulable states (OCP - most common modifiable risk factor; pregnancy/puerperium, thrombophilias), infection (otitis media/mastoiditis → sigmoid sinus thrombosis - Lemierre syndrome variant), malignancy, dehydration. Sx: headache (most common - progressively worsening, thunderclap in SAH-like presentations), focal deficit, seizures, ↑ICP (papilloedema, VI cranial nerve palsy), venous infarction (haemorrhagic - parasagittal). Ix: MRI/MRV (filling defect - 'empty delta' sign on contrast CT - superior sagittal sinus; venous infarcts), D-dimer (if negative makes CVST unlikely). Mx: anticoagulation (LMWH then warfarin - even if haemorrhagic infarction - reduces propagation and death), endovascular thrombolysis (clinical deterioration despite anticoagulation), acetazolamide (↑ICP), treat underlying cause. Duration: anticoagulate 3–6 months (provoked) to 12 months (unprovoked) to lifelong (thrombophilia).
