conditions.name: Watershed infarct
conditions.summary: Ischaemic stroke at junctions between major cerebral artery territories (border zones), caused by systemic hypoperfusion rather than focal vascular occlusion. Cortical watershed: junction ACA/MCA (parasagittal - proximal arm/leg weakness in 'man in a barrel' distribution) and MCA/PCA (posterior parietal - visual symptoms, hemianopia). Internal watershed: between deep perforators and cortical branches (internal capsule/corona radiata - capsular warning syndrome). Causes: cardiac arrest, severe hypotension, carotid stenosis (critical - ↓distal perfusion pressure), hyperviscosity. Ix (MRI): string of pearls' pattern of infarcts in DWI along watershed territories. Mx: optimise cerebral perfusion (cautious BP management - avoid aggressive BP lowering acutely); treat underlying cause (cardiac arrest resuscitation, carotid revascularisation); same secondary prevention as other ischaemic strokes.

conditions.name: Locked-in syndrome
conditions.summary: Catastrophic brainstem injury preserving consciousness while abolishing voluntary movement. Pathology: bilateral ventral pons infarction (basilar artery occlusion most common - thrombosis or embolism) → bilateral corticospinal + corticobulbar tract destruction; reticular activating system preserved (consciousness intact). Classic: complete paralysis of all voluntary muscles except vertical eye movements and blinking (corticospinal/corticobulbar destroyed; CN III/IV nuclei spared in dorsal midbrain). Communication: eye blink codes (vertical movement) - QWERTY spelling, eye-tracking devices. Ix: clinical recognition; MRI (pontine infarction); EEG (normal - consciousness preserved - distinguish from coma). Mx: communication aids (AAC devices, eye-tracking), supportive care, VTE prophylaxis, enteral nutrition (PEG); tracheostomy (ventilator-dependent initially). Prognosis: variable - some partial recovery possible if haemodynamically treated rapidly (basilar artery occlusion - endovascular thrombectomy within window).

conditions.name: Prion disease
conditions.summary: Fatal neurodegenerative diseases caused by misfolded prion proteins (PrPSc) propagating conformational change in normal PrPc. Types: Sporadic CJD (sCJD - most common, 85%; rapidly progressive dementia + myoclonus + cerebellar ataxia; EEG periodic sharp wave complexes; CSF 14-3-3 protein; MRI DWI cortical ribboning + caudate/putamen signal). Ix: Variant CJD (vCJD - UK BSE epidemic; younger patients; psychiatric prodrome + ataxia then dementia; 'pulvinar sign' on MRI). Familial (PRNP mutation - FFI, GSS). Iatrogenic (cadaveric GH, dura mater grafts). Ix: brain biopsy (gold standard - prion plaques), MRI DWI (cortical ribboning, basal ganglia), EEG, CSF RT-QuIC (seed amplification assay - highly sensitive for sCJD), CSF 14-3-3. Mx: No treatment (uniformly fatal within months); infection control (autoclave decontamination - standard sterilisation insufficient for prions; CJD patients need dedicated surgical instruments).

conditions.name: Pyoderma gangrenosum
conditions.summary: Neutrophilic dermatosis causing rapidly expanding painful ulcers with violaceous undermined edges. Associated with IBD (Crohn's, UC), RA, haematological malignancy. Pathergy: lesions worsen with trauma. Ix: Biopsy is non-specific; diagnosis clinical/exclusion. Mx: high-dose systemic corticosteroids (1st-line); ciclosporin; infliximab (especially IBD-related); wound care with non-adherent dressings.

conditions.name: Melasma
conditions.summary: Acquired symmetrical hyperpigmentation of sun-exposed skin (cheeks, forehead, upper lip). Triggers: UV exposure, pregnancy, combined OCP, thyroid disease. Pathogenesis: excess melanin production by melanocytes. Mx: strict photoprotection (SPF50+, physical barriers - most important); hydroquinone (bleaching agent, 1st-line); azelaic acid, kojic acid, retinoids; chemical peels; laser (risk of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation).

conditions.name: Epistaxis
conditions.summary: Nasal haemorrhage; 90% anterior (Kiesselbach plexus - Little's area on nasal septum), 10% posterior (more severe, often elderly/hypertensive). Anterior epistaxis: direct pressure, nasal packing, silver nitrate cautery. Mx: Posterior epistaxis: posterior packing, balloon catheter; embolisation or surgery if refractory. Causes: trauma, dry mucosa, anticoagulants, thrombocytopaenia, hypertension, hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT).

conditions.name: Eosinophilic oesophagitis
conditions.summary: Chronic immune-mediated oesophageal disease characterised by eosinophilic infiltration (≥15 eos/HPF on biopsy). Sx: adults - dysphagia, food bolus obstruction; children - feeding difficulties, failure to thrive, abdominal pain. Triggers: food antigens (milk, wheat, egg, soy, nuts, seafood) + aeroallergens. PPI-responsive EoE subset exists. Mx: proton pump inhibitors (high-dose - 1st-line), swallowed (not inhaled) topical steroids (budesonide/fluticasone slurry), 6-food elimination diet; oesophageal dilatation for strictures.

conditions.name: Organising pneumonia
conditions.summary: Interstitial lung disease with intraluminal buds of granulation tissue (Masson bodies) in alveoli and bronchioles. Cryptogenic (COP) or secondary (infection, drugs, CTD, radiation). Sx: subacute illness (4–8 weeks) with cough, dyspnoea, fever, malaise; bilateral patchy alveolar consolidation on CT (often peripheral/peribronchial - 'reversed halo'/atoll sign). Ix: BAL with CD4/CD8 reversal, biopsy if uncertain. Mx: systemic corticosteroids (high-dose prednisolone) → dramatic response in 1–2 weeks; relapses on steroid taper common.

conditions.name: Silicosis
conditions.summary: Occupational lung disease from crystalline silica inhalation (mining, quarrying, sandblasting, construction). Types: chronic (>10 years exposure), accelerated (5–10 years), acute (intense short-term exposure - rapidly fatal). Pathology: silicotic nodules (concentric 'onion-skin' whorled collagen) → progressive massive fibrosis. Complications: ↑risk of pulmonary TB (silica impairs macrophage killing), lung cancer, systemic sclerosis, COPD. Ix: occupational history + CT (upper-lobe nodules, eggshell calcification of lymph nodes). No disease-modifying therapy; prevent with dust control.

conditions.name: Asbestosis
conditions.summary: Diffuse interstitial pulmonary fibrosis from inhalation of asbestos fibres (amphibole > chrysotile). Latency period 20–40 years. Sx: progressive dyspnoea, bibasal crackles, clubbing. CT: bilateral subpleural lower-lobe fibrosis (similar to UIP); asbestos bodies on BAL. Complications: mesothelioma (especially pleural, peritoneal - fibrous/amphibole types), pleural plaques (hyaline), lung cancer (especially in smokers). Ix: occupational history + imaging; no disease-modifying therapy.

conditions.name: Cold autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
conditions.summary: IgM autoantibody (cold agglutinins) activating complement at <37°C → intravascular haemolysis (C5b-9 MAC). Primary (idiopathic/chronic) or secondary (Mycoplasma pneumoniae - anti-I antibody; EBV - anti-i; CLL/lymphoma). Sx: acrocyanosis/Raynaud in cold; haemoglobinuria; anaemia worse in winter. Laboratory: DAT positive for C3d only; agglutination on blood film (clumping); cold agglutinin titre. Mx: keep warm (most important), treat underlying cause; rituximab; sutimlimab (anti-C1s) for primary cold agglutinin disease.

conditions.name: Pernicious anaemia
conditions.summary: Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells → ↓intrinsic factor (IF) → ↓cobalamin (B12) absorption. Antibodies: anti-parietal cell (90%), anti-IF (60% - more specific). Sx: macrocytic anaemia, glossitis, subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (posterior columns + lateral corticospinal tracts → dorsal column loss, then UMN signs), peripheral neuropathy, mild cognitive impairment. Mx: IM hydroxocobalamin (1 mg 3× weekly × 2 weeks, then every 3 months lifelong); or high-dose oral B12 (1000 µg daily) if no neurological involvement. Monitor: ↑risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.

conditions.name: Diabetic nephropathy
conditions.summary: Leading cause of end-stage renal disease (ESRD) worldwide; microvascular complication of DM. Pathology: glomerular basement membrane thickening, mesangial expansion, Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules (pathognomonic), arteriolar hyalinosis. Ix (staging): by ACR (albuminuria) and eGFR. Early: microalbuminuria (30–300 mg/g) with hyperfiltration; Late: macroalbuminuria, declining GFR. Mx: strict glycaemic control (target HbA1c ≤53 mmol/mol), BP control (ACEi/ARB - reduce proteinuria, slow progression), SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin - ↓progression - DAPA-CKD, CREDENCE), finerenone; refer nephrology when eGFR <30 or rapid decline.

conditions.name: Hypertensive nephropathy
conditions.summary: Chronic kidney disease secondary to sustained hypertension causing renal arteriolar changes → ischaemic nephron loss. Pathology: hyaline arteriolosclerosis (benign), hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis (malignant hypertension - 'onion skin' lesions). Sx: slowly progressive CKD in long-standing HTN; often minimal proteinuria (<1 g/d, non-nephrotic), bland urinary sediment. Mx: strict BP control (target <130/80 mmHg - SPRINT trial); ACEi/ARB preferred (↓intraglomerular pressure + proteinuria).

conditions.name: Systemic sclerosis
conditions.summary: Autoimmune connective tissue disease characterised by vasculopathy, fibrosis and immune activation. Subtypes: Limited (lcSSc/CREST): Calcinosis, Raynaud, oEsophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia; anti-centromere Ab; slower progression. Diffuse (dcSSc): widespread skin thickening, rapid progression; anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70) Ab; ↑risk ILD and renal crisis. Mx: Organs: Raynaud (first in 90%), ILD (leading cause of death), PAH, scleroderma renal crisis (ARF + malignant HTN - use ACEi even in pregnancy). Mx: organ-specific; methotrexate/MMF for skin/ILD; bosentan/sildenafil for PAH; ACEi for renal crisis.

conditions.name: ANCA-associated vasculitis
conditions.summary: Small-vessel vasculitis associated with antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA). Subtypes: GPA (granulomatosis with polyangiitis): c-ANCA/PR3 - ENT (saddle-nose, sinus), lungs (haemoptysis, cavities), renal (pauci-immune GN). MPA (microscopic polyangiitis): p-ANCA/MPO - pulmonary-renal syndrome. EGPA (eosinophilic GPA/Churg-Strauss): p-ANCA/MPO - asthma, eosinophilia, neuropathy, cardiac. Ix: ANCA serology, biopsy (pauci-immune crescentic GN). Mx: induction - rituximab or cyclophosphamide + high-dose glucocorticoids; maintenance - azathioprine or rituximab.

conditions.name: Korsakoff syndrome
conditions.summary: Chronic amnestic syndrome caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency; typically follows Wernicke encephalopathy (Wernicke-Korsakoff spectrum). Sx: severe anterograde amnesia (cannot form new memories), variable retrograde amnesia, confabulation (unconscious fabrication of memories without intent to deceive), apathy, relatively preserved procedural memory. Causes: chronic alcohol misuse, malabsorption, prolonged vomiting, hyperemesis gravidarum. Mx: high-dose IV thiamine (Wernicke prevention/treatment); Korsakoff changes often irreversible.

conditions.name: Central pontine myelinolysis
conditions.summary: Osmotic demyelination of the pons (and sometimes extrapontine regions) caused by too-rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia. Pathophysiology: chronic hyponatraemia → CNS osmotic adaptation; rapid correction → osmotic gradient → oligodendrocyte apoptosis → demyelination. Sx: 2–6 days after correction: dysarthria, dysphagia, behavioural change, then quadriplegia, pseudobulbar palsy, locked-in syndrome. Mx (prevention): correct sodium at ≤8–10 mmol/L per 24 h (maximum). No proven treatment; supportive care.

conditions.name: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome
conditions.summary: Neurological disorder of autoregulation failure: failure of cerebrovascular autoregulation → hyperperfusion → vasogenic oedema, predominantly in posterior white matter. Causes: hypertensive emergency, eclampsia, immunosuppressants (tacrolimus, ciclosporin), sepsis, TTP. Sx: headache, seizures (often first sign), visual disturbance (cortical blindness), encephalopathy, focal neurological deficits. Ix (MRI): bilateral parieto-occipital T2/FLAIR white matter changes. Mx: BP control (IV labetalol/nicardipine), remove precipitant; usually reversible within days-weeks.

conditions.name: Cryptococcosis
conditions.summary: Fungal infection by Cryptococcus neoformans (immunocompromised - HIV CD4 <100, transplant) or C. gattii (immunocompetent, Pacific NW/tropical regions). Sx: subacute meningitis (weeks of headache, fever, meningism - may be absent); raised ICP → papilloedema, CN palsies, herniation. CSF: India ink (+), cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) serum/CSF (95% sensitive), low glucose, elevated protein. Mx: induction - IV liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine × 2 weeks; consolidation - fluconazole 400 mg × 8 weeks; maintenance - fluconazole 200 mg lifelong in HIV. ICP management: serial LPs or drain.

conditions.name: Nocardiosis
conditions.summary: Opportunistic infection by aerobic filamentous Nocardia spp. (N. asteroides complex most common). Risk: immunosuppression (high-dose steroids, solid organ transplant, HIV), lung disease (alveolar proteinosis). Sx: Pulmonary (most common) - subacute pneumonia with cavitation mimicking TB; Disseminated - can spread to brain (cerebral abscess - 'abscess without surrounding oedema'), skin. Ix: modified acid-fast stain (weakly positive), culture (slow growing, 1–2 weeks). Mx: TMP-SMX (sulfamethoxazole) 1st-line; imipenem + amikacin for severe/CNS; prolonged therapy (6–12 months; 12 months for CNS).

conditions.name: Schizoaffective disorder
conditions.summary: Psychotic disorder with concurrent substantial mood (major depressive or bipolar) symptoms. Sx: DSM-5: psychotic features present ≥2 weeks without concurrent mood episode; mood episodes present for majority of total illness duration. Subtypes: depressive type (MDD periods); bipolar type (manic/mixed periods). Mx: antipsychotics (mainstay - SGA: risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine); mood stabilisers (lithium, valproate) or antidepressants depending on subtype; psychosocial rehabilitation. Prognosis: better than schizophrenia, worse than pure mood disorders.

conditions.name: Delusional disorder
conditions.summary: Persistent non-bizarre delusions (plausible scenarios) in absence of schizophrenia, mood disorder, or substance use. Subtypes: erotomanic (persecutor loves patient), grandiose, jealous (Othello syndrome), persecutory (most common), somatic (delusional parasitosis), mixed. Auditory hallucinations absent or minor. Insight absent. Mx: difficult to treat - antipsychotics (pimozide - especially for somatic subtype); CBT; consider safety (persecutory → risk to others). Prognosis: often chronic; social functioning may be relatively preserved.

conditions.name: REM sleep behaviour disorder
conditions.summary: Parasomnia characterised by loss of normal muscle atonia during REM sleep → acting out vivid/violent dreams (punching, kicking, shouting - injuring self or bed partner). Ix: polysomnography (REM without atonia). Idiopathic RBD is a prodrome: >80% develop synucleinopathy (Parkinson's disease, Lewy body dementia, MSA) within 10-15 years. Mx: melatonin (2–6 mg, safest) or clonazepam (0.5–2 mg at bedtime); safety modifications (bed rails, floor mat).

conditions.name: Small bowel obstruction
conditions.summary: Mechanical obstruction of small intestine causing proximal distension, failure to pass flatus/stool, nausea, vomiting. Causes: adhesions (most common - prior surgery), hernias (inguinal, femoral, obturator), malignancy, Crohn's stricture, volvulus, intussusception. Ix: AXR (dilated loops, air-fluid levels, 'stepladder' pattern); CT (most accurate - identifies cause, ischaemia). Mx: NPO, NG decompression, IV fluids (Hartmann's), urinary catheter; surgical - emergency laparotomy if signs of strangulation (peritonism, fever, leucocytosis) or failure to resolve.

conditions.name: Ogilvie syndrome
conditions.summary: Acute massive non-mechanical dilatation of the colon (typically right and transverse colon) in acutely ill/post-operative patients. Aetiology: autonomic imbalance (↑parasympathetic tone to distal colon, ↓proximal sympathetic tone). Risk: post-operative, ICU, opioids, metabolic derangements. Ix: AXR/CT: massively dilated colon with no mechanical obstruction. Risk of perforation when caecal diameter >12 cm. Mx: treat precipitant, stop constipating drugs; neostigmine (2 mg IV - rapid pharmacological decompression; bradycardia risk); colonoscopic decompression; surgery if fails.

conditions.name: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome
conditions.summary: Leading cause of neonatal mortality in preterm infants; caused by surfactant deficiency → atelectasis → diffuse alveolar damage. Risk: prematurity (inversely proportional to gestational age), maternal diabetes, male sex, second twin. Sx: grunting (PEEP effect), nasal flaring, subcostal/intercostal recession, cyanosis from birth or within hours; worsens at 48 h then improves. Ix (CXR): ground-glass opacification, air bronchograms, reduced lung volumes. Mx: antenatal corticosteroids (if <34 weeks - ↓incidence by 50%); surfactant replacement (intratracheal - Curosurf, Calfactant); CPAP; mechanical ventilation; O2 supplementation.

conditions.name: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia
conditions.summary: Chronic lung disease in premature infants requiring respiratory support/supplemental O2 at 36 weeks corrected gestational age. New BPD: dysregulated lung development (arrested alveolarisation) rather than just injury from ventilation (old definition). Risk factors: extreme prematurity, prolonged ventilation, O2 toxicity, infection, PDA. Sx: ongoing O2 requirement, pulmonary hypertension, recurrent respiratory infections. Mx: lung-protective ventilation (minimal tidal volumes, gentle permissive hypercapnia), surfactant, caffeine (↓apnoeas, ↓BPD - first-line), post-natal corticosteroids (carefully - risk of cerebral palsy).

conditions.name: Kernicterus
conditions.summary: Neurological damage from unconjugated bilirubin deposition in basal ganglia, hippocampus and cerebellum; occurs when bilirubin crosses BBB (especially in preterm, haemolytic disease, hypoalbuminaemia). Acute: hypertonia, opisthotonus, high-pitched cry, seizures. Chronic (classic kernicterus tetrad): choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, hearing loss (sensorineural), vertical gaze palsy, enamel dysplasia. Mx: PREVENT with phototherapy (light converts unconjugated bilirubin to water-soluble isomers); exchange transfusion for severe cases (bilirubin >500 µmol/L in term infant or rapidly rising).

conditions.name: Mastocytosis
conditions.summary: Clonal proliferation of mast cells in skin and/or other organs (bone marrow, liver, spleen, GI tract). Cutaneous (urticaria pigmentosa): orange-brown macules/papules - Darier sign (urticaria on rubbing). Systemic: D findings (SM serum tryptase >20 µg/L, KIT D816V mutation in marrow, atypical CD25+ mast cells on biopsy, organomegaly). Sx: mast cell mediator symptoms - flushing, urticaria, anaphylaxis, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, osteoporosis. Mx: antihistamines (H1+H2), cromolyn, adrenaline auto-injector; avoidance of triggers (NSAIDs, alcohol, opioids); cytoreductive therapy (midostaurin - KIT inhibitor) for advanced SM.

conditions.name: Hereditary angioedema
conditions.summary: Rare autosomal dominant disease causing recurrent attacks of bradykinin-mediated subcutaneous and mucosal oedema (not histamine-mediated). Types: Type I (↓C1-INH level); Type II (dysfunctional C1-INH - normal or ↑level); Type III (normal C1-INH - factor XII mutation, often oestrogen-dependent). Ix: Laboratory: ↓C4 (best screening test, low even between attacks), ↓C1-INH level/function. Sx: Attacks: non-pitting oedema face/extremities/GI (severe abdominal pain)/larynx (life-threatening). Mx: acute - C1-INH concentrate (Berinert, Ruconest), icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist), ecallantide; prophylaxis: tranexamic acid, danazol, lanadelumab (anti-kallikrein).

conditions.name: POEMS syndrome
conditions.summary: Rare plasma cell dyscrasia: Polyneuropathy, Organomegaly, Endocrinopathy, Monoclonal protein (usually IgG or IgA lambda), Skin changes. Additional features: papilloedema, oedema/effusions, sclerotic bone lesions, thrombocytosis/polycythaemia, Castleman disease. Pathogenesis: VEGF overproduction from plasma cells. Ix: monoclonal protein (lambda > kappa) + osteosclerotic lesion + neuropathy. Mx: radiation for isolated sclerotic lesion; systemic chemotherapy + autologous HSCT for widespread disease; prognosis variable.

conditions.name: Castleman disease
conditions.summary: Rare lymph node disorder. Mx: Unicentric (UCD): solitary enlarged LN mass; usually mediastinum; often hyaline-vascular subtype; curative surgical resection. Sx: Multicentric (MCD): systemic disease with multiple LN enlargement, splenomegaly, fever, weight loss, cytopenias; iMCD (idiopathic - IL-6 driven) or HHV-8/KSHV-associated MCD (in HIV/immunocompromised). Mx: UCD - surgical excision; iMCD - siltuximab (anti-IL-6 mAb); HHV-8 MCD - rituximab ± chemotherapy. Note: associated with Kaposi sarcoma in HHV-8 MCD.

conditions.name: Hypereosinophilic syndrome
conditions.summary: Peripheral blood eosinophilia (>1.5×10⁹/L for >1 month) with end-organ damage (cardiac - Loeffler endocarditis, eosinophilic endomyocardial fibrosis; skin; nervous system; lungs). Causes: primary (FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion → imatinib-sensitive), lymphocytic variant (TH2 clone), idiopathic. Cardiac: eosinophilic infiltration → necrosis → fibrosis → restrictive CMP → mural thrombi. Ix: exclude secondary causes (atopy, parasites, drugs, malignancy). Mx: molecular (FIP1L1-PDGFRA+) → imatinib; others → prednisolone ± hydroxycarbamide/mepolizumab.

conditions.name: VIPoma
conditions.summary: Rare pancreatic NET secreting vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP). Sx: profuse watery diarrhoea (>3 L/day) + hypokalaemia + achlorhydria (WDHA/Verner-Morrison syndrome). VIP causes intestinal secretion, glycogenolysis, vasodilation. Ix: serum VIP (>200 pg/mL), CT/MRI (large pancreatic tumour, often body/tail), SRS or Ga-68 DOTATATE PET. Mx: octreotide/lanreotide (somatostatin analogues - ↓VIP, ↓secretion); curative surgical resection; streptozocin/everolimus for unresectable.

conditions.name: Glucagonoma
conditions.summary: Rare pancreatic alpha-cell NET secreting glucagon. Sx: necrolytic migratory erythema (pathognomonic - painful, crusting, migratory rash, most often perigenital and lower extremities), diabetes mellitus, weight loss, anaemia, thromboembolism, hypoaminoacidaemia. Ix: elevated serum glucagon (>500 pg/mL), CT/MRI (large tumour, often tail of pancreas, frequently metastatic at diagnosis). Mx: surgical resection (curative if resectable); octreotide (somatostatin analogues for symptoms and possible anti-tumour); chemotherapy for metastatic.

conditions.name: Somatostatinoma
conditions.summary: Very rare NET secreting somatostatin; usually in pancreas or duodenum. Clinical (somatostatinoma triad): diabetes mellitus (↓insulin secretion), steatorrhoea/cholelithiasis (↓pancreatic/biliary secretion), achlorhydria (↓gastric acid). Often discovered incidentally or presents with abdominal pain/mass; metastases common at presentation. Ix: elevated plasma somatostatin, CT/MRI, SRS. Mx: surgical resection; somatostatin analogues for symptoms; chemotherapy for metastatic disease.

conditions.name: Medullary thyroid carcinoma
conditions.summary: Malignant tumour of thyroid parafollicular C-cells → secretes calcitonin (tumour marker). Hereditary (25%): MEN2A (RET C634 mutations), MEN2B (RET M918T - most aggressive), familial MTC. Sporadic (75%): RET mutations less common. Sx: thyroid nodule ± cervical lymphadenopathy; calcitonin elevation; diarrhoea (high calcitonin). Genetics: all patients should have RET germline testing. Mx: total thyroidectomy + central lymph node dissection; vandetanib or cabozantinib (RET/VEGFR/MET inhibitors) for advanced disease; selpercatinib (RET-selective) preferred if RET-mutated.

conditions.name: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma
conditions.summary: Most aggressive thyroid malignancy; almost universally fatal (median survival 3–5 months). Sx: Rapidly enlarging neck mass causing tracheal compression (stridor), dysphagia, hoarseness. Pathology: completely undifferentiated large cells; TP53 mutations common; often arises in pre-existing differentiated thyroid cancer. BRAF V600E mutation in ~50%. Mx: combination chemoradiation (doxorubicin + cisplatin + radiotherapy); BRAF-mutated ATC → dabrafenib + trametinib (ROAR study - significant disease control rate); clinical trial preferred.

conditions.name: Paraganglioma
conditions.summary: Neuroendocrine tumour arising from paraganglia (extra-adrenal chromaffin tissue). Functional: catecholamine-secreting (treated like phaeochromocytoma - alpha-blockade first, then beta-blockade pre-op). Non-functional: typically head-neck paragangliomas (carotid body, jugular-tympanic, vagal). Genetics: >35% hereditary (SDH mutations - SDHA, SDHB most common; SDHB associated with ↑malignancy; also VHL, RET, NF1, MAX). Mx: surgical resection; alpha-blockade pre-operatively for functional; lutetium DOTATATE PRRT or MIBG for metastatic.

conditions.name: Adrenocortical carcinoma
conditions.summary: Rare but aggressive malignancy of adrenal cortex. Often presents large at diagnosis. Functional (60%): Cushing syndrome (most common - cortisol hypersecretion), virilisation (androgens), Conn syndrome (aldosterone). Non-functional: incidental adrenal mass on imaging. Ix: unilateral adrenal mass >4–6 cm, heterogeneous, irregular margins, ↑Hounsfield units on CT wash-out study. Mx: surgical resection (curative only if complete); mitotane (adrenolytic - adjuvant after R0 resection or for advanced); etoposide, doxorubicin, cisplatin (EDP) + mitotane for metastatic.

conditions.name: Rabies
conditions.summary: Invariably fatal zoonotic viral encephalitis (Lyssavirus). Transmission: infected animal bites (dogs most common globally; bats in Australia - ABLV - Australian bat lyssavirus). Incubation: days to months (proportional to distance from brain). Sx: prodrome (pain/paraesthesia at bite site) → encephalitic (hydrophobia - hypersalivation, pharyngeal spasm, aerophobia) or paralytic form → coma → death. Mx (prevention): ESSENTIAL - post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP): wound wash (20 min), rabies immunoglobulin into wound (if unvaccinated), rabies vaccine × 4 doses. Fatal if symptomatic.

conditions.name: Diphtheria
conditions.summary: Toxin-mediated disease from Corynebacterium diphtheriae (exotoxin inhibits EF-2 via ADP-ribosylation → halts protein synthesis). Sx: pharyngeal - grey-white pseudomembrane (tonsils, pharynx - bleeds when removed), 'bull neck' (cervical LN + soft tissue oedema), stridor/airway obstruction; systemic toxin - myocarditis (most fatal complication - heart block, cardiac failure), neuropathy (CN palsies, peripheral). Mx: diphtheria antitoxin (urgently - neutralises circulating toxin); benzylpenicillin or azithromycin; airway management; vaccination (DTP) is preventive.

conditions.name: Toxic epidermal necrolysis
conditions.summary: Severe mucocutaneous drug reaction with epidermal detachment >30% BSA (SJS <10%, SJS-TEN overlap 10–30%). Pathogenesis: drug-specific CD8+ T-cell-mediated keratinocyte apoptosis (FasL pathway); commonest culprits: allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, sulfonamides, NSAIDs, nevirapine. Sx: fever → macular rash → widespread blistering, Nikolsky sign, mucosal erosions (eyes, mouth, genitalia). Mortality ~30–50% in TEN. SCORTEN score predicts mortality. Mx: immediate drug cessation (most important); burns/ICU care; ophthalmology (prevent ocular sequelae); ciclosporin or IVIG (debated; no RCT).

conditions.name: Actinomycosis
conditions.summary: Chronic granulomatous infection by Actinomyces spp. (anaerobic gram-positive filamentous bacteria; normal oral/GI flora). Forms: cervicofacial ('lumpy jaw' - most common, following dental trauma/extraction), thoracic (mimics malignancy - chest wall mass/sinus), abdominal (ileocaecal - following appendicitis/surgery), pelvic (associated with IUD use - actinomycosis in Pap smear finding). Characteristic: sulphur granules (yellow) in discharge; crosses fascial planes. Mx: penicillin (high-dose for prolonged period - 6–12 months); drainage of abscesses.

conditions.name: Acute psychosis
conditions.summary: De novo onset of psychotic symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganised thinking/behaviour) lasting ≥1 day but not attributable to a pre-existing psychotic disorder, substance or medical cause. Brief psychotic disorder: <1 month duration, often precipitated by stress. Ix: First-episode psychosis (FEP): assessment critical - exclude organic causes (brain MRI, EEG, metabolic screen, substance screen, anti-NMDAR antibodies). Duration of untreated psychosis (DUP) directly predicts outcome. Mx: antipsychotic (preferably olanzapine, risperidone, or quetiapine - low-dose initially); family involvement; early psychosis intervention programme.

conditions.name: Neonatal sepsis
conditions.summary: Systemic bacterial infection in neonates. Early-onset (<72 h): maternal organisms (GBS, E. coli, Listeria, Klebsiella); vertical transmission. Late-onset (≥72 h – 28 days): nosocomial organisms (Staphylococcus epidermidis, Staphylococcus aureus, Candida) or GBS. Sx: temperature instability (hypo- or hyperthermia), apnoea, poor feeding, bulging fontanelle, seizures, hepatosplenomegaly, petechiae. Ix: FBC, CRP, blood culture (gold standard), LP (if stable), urine culture. Mx: empiric IV ampicillin + gentamicin (EOS); broaden for LOS if CONS/Staph likely (add vancomycin). GBS prevention: intrapartum penicillin prophylaxis.

conditions.name: Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy
conditions.summary: Neonatal brain injury from peri-partum hypoxia-ischaemia. Staging (Sarnat): Mild (hyperalertness, poor feeding, irritability - usually resolves), Moderate (seizures, hypotonia, weakness, MRI abnormalities - variable outcome), Severe (coma, multi-organ failure, seizures - poor prognosis). Pathophysiology: primary energy failure → reperfusion → secondary energy failure (6–24 h later - therapeutic window). Mx: therapeutic hypothermia (core temp 33–34°C for 72 h - reduces death/disability if initiated <6 h of age in ≥36 week gestation infants); seizure control (phenobarbitone); supportive.

conditions.name: Retinopathy of prematurity
conditions.summary: Proliferative retinal vasculopathy in premature infants from abnormal retinal angiogenesis; oxygen use is a major risk factor. Risk: gestational age <32 weeks and/or birthweight <1500 g. Ix (staging): 5 zones and 3+ stages (1-5); plus disease (arterial tortuosity + venous dilation - indicates severity). Stage 4–5 and/or plus disease → risk of retinal detachment and blindness. Ix: dilated fundus exam at 31 weeks corrected gestation or 4 weeks post-natal. Mx: laser photocoagulation (peripheral retina ablation) or bevacizumab injection (intravitreal anti-VEGF); surgery for detachments.
utd: acute management of Retinopathy of prematurity

conditions.name: Fat embolism syndrome
conditions.summary: Embolic complication of long bone/pelvis fractures (especially femur, tibia), orthopaedic surgery, or liposuction. Mechanism: mechanical (fat globules enter venous circulation) + biochemical (free fatty acids → endothelial injury). Triad (Gurd's criteria): respiratory (hypoxaemia, ARDS - most important), neurological (confusion, agitation, seizures), dermatological (petechiae - axilla, conjunctiva, oral mucosa - pathognomonic but transient). Onset: 24–72 h post-injury. Mx: supportive (O2, ventilation); prophylactic early fracture fixation ↓risk.
utd: acute management of Fat embolism syndrome

conditions.name: Peritonitis
conditions.summary: Inflammation of peritoneum. Primary (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis - SBP): in ascites/cirrhosis (see SBP). Secondary: from bowel perforation, anastomotic leak, abdominal trauma. Sx: rigid board-like abdomen, rebound/guarding, generalised tenderness, absent bowel sounds, fever, haemodynamic compromise. Ix: AXR/CT (free air), WBC, lactate, blood cultures. Mx: surgical emergency - laparotomy (perforation repair/resection), lavage, drain; IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem for faecal peritonitis); HDU/ICU; bowel rest.

conditions.name: Cholangitis
conditions.summary: Bacterial infection of biliary tree from biliary obstruction. Causes: choledocholithiasis (most common), biliary stricture, malignancy, post-ERCP. Charcot's triad: right upper quadrant pain + fever/rigors + jaundice. Reynolds' pentad (severe): Charcot's triad + hypotension + confusion. Ix: elevated bilirubin/ALP/GGT, WBC, blood cultures (gram-negative bacteraemia - E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus). Mx: IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam); urgent biliary drainage (ERCP with stone extraction/stenting - within 24–48 h for moderate, immediate for severe); cholecystectomy after recovery.

conditions.name: Pancreatic pseudocyst
conditions.summary: Fluid collection with fibrous wall (no epithelial lining) developing 4+ weeks after acute pancreatitis or pancreatic trauma. Aetiology: pancreatic ductal disruption → enzyme-rich fluid collection → walled off. Sx: persistent abdominal pain, early satiety, palpable epigastric mass; may be asymptomatic. Complications: infection (→ infected pseudocyst), rupture, haemorrhage, compression of adjacent structures. Ix: CT or MRI (well-defined, round, homogeneous fluid density, thick wall). Mx: small/asymptomatic → watchful waiting; symptomatic/large → endoscopic drainage (EUS-guided) or percutaneous/surgical.

conditions.name: Scleritis
conditions.summary: Inflammation of the sclera - typically more severe than episcleritis. Sx: severe, deep, boring eye pain (often radiating to head/jaw), tenderness on palpation, scleral oedema and violaceous discolouration, ↓vision (posterior). Associated with autoimmune diseases: RA (most common systemic association - necrotising scleritis = scleromalacia perforans), GPA, SLE, PAN, IBD. Complications: perforation (necrotising), vision loss. Mx: oral NSAIDs (mild); systemic corticosteroids (moderate-severe); immunosuppressives for resistant/systemic disease.

conditions.name: Central retinal vein occlusion
conditions.summary: Occlusion of retinal vein causing retinal haemorrhage. Sx: CRVO: sudden painless vision loss; fundus - diffuse flame haemorrhages in all 4 quadrants, disc oedema, tortuous dilated veins ('stormy sunset' appearance), cotton-wool spots. BRVO: sectoral (wedge-shaped) haemorrhages. Risk factors: HTN (most important), hyperlipidaemia, DM, glaucoma, thrombophilia. Complications: macular oedema (main cause of visual loss), neovascular glaucoma (CRVO). Mx: anti-VEGF injections (macular oedema); laser photocoagulation (neovascularisation); treat risk factors.

conditions.name: Eaton-Lambert syndrome
conditions.summary: Presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder caused by antibodies against voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC-Ab) → ↓ACh release. Associations: paraneoplastic (60% - SCLC most common) or autoimmune (40%). Sx: proximal limb weakness (especially hip flexors), autonomic dysfunction (dry mouth, constipation, impotence), areflexia with post-exercise facilitation (reflexes temporarily improve after brief exercise - opposite to MG). EMG: low CMAP amplitude increasing with high-frequency stimulation (↑facilitation). Mx: 3,4-diaminopyridine (↑ACh release - 1st-line for symptoms); immunosuppression (prednisolone, azathioprine); treat underlying malignancy.

conditions.name: Myasthenic crisis
conditions.summary: Life-threatening exacerbation of myasthenia gravis with respiratory muscle failure → need for ventilatory support. Mx: Precipitants: infection (most common), medications (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium, beta-blockers, neuromuscular blockers, general anaesthesia), tapering immunosuppression, surgery. Cholinergic crisis (excess neostigmine): muscarinic excess (SLUDGE + bradycardia) - distinguish by edrophonium test (improves myasthenic crisis, worsens cholinergic). Mx: ICU; ventilatory support (early intubation); IVIG or plasmapheresis (equivalent efficacy); continue or resume pyridostigmine; avoid precipitants.

conditions.name: Stress cardiomyopathy
conditions.summary: Transient left ventricular dysfunction (apical ballooning) triggered by emotional or physical stress. Predominantly affects post-menopausal women (90%). Mimics ACS: chest pain, ST elevation (diffuse, anterior), elevated troponin, but coronary angiography shows no significant CAD. Ix (echo): characteristic apical ballooning with preserved or hypercontractile base. Pathogenesis: catecholamine surge → microvascular spasm + direct myocardial toxicity. Mx: supportive (ACEi, beta-blockers, diuretics if HF); LV thrombus (anticoagulate); usually complete recovery in 4–8 weeks; mortality <5%.

conditions.name: Papilloedema
conditions.summary: Optic disc swelling from raised intracranial pressure (ICP). Bilateral (unlike other causes of disc swelling). Causes: raised ICP from any cause (brain tumour, hydrocephalus, IIH, venous sinus thrombosis, meningitis). Sx: blurred disc margins, absent venous pulsation, disc hyperaemia, peripapillary flame haemorrhages, visual obscurations. Sx: often headache (especially morning), nausea; visual field loss (enlarged blind spot, then inferior nasal field). Mx: treat underlying cause; IIH → weight loss, acetazolamide; LP shunting or optic nerve sheath fenestration for vision threat.

conditions.name: Mpox
conditions.summary: Zoonotic Orthopoxvirus infection (related to smallpox, vaccinia). Transmission: direct contact (skin lesions, respiratory droplets, sexual contact - clade IIb 2022 outbreak). Incubation: 5–21 days. Sx: prodrome (fever, lymphadenopathy - more prominent than smallpox) → distinctive rash (centrifugal, progresses from macule→papule→vesicle→pustule→crust, all at same stage - unique). Genital/perianal lesions common in 2022 outbreak (MSM predominantly). Ix: PCR from lesion swab. Mx: supportive; tecovirimat (TPOXX - antivirals for smallpox/mpox); vaccination (JYNNEOS - modified vaccinia Ankara - 2-dose non-replicating vaccine; ring vaccination).

conditions.name: Strongyloidiasis
conditions.summary: Intestinal nematode infection (Strongyloides stercoralis) with unique autoinfection cycle (persists for decades). Endemic: tropical/subtropical regions; Australian Indigenous communities. Immunocompetent: asymptomatic or mild GI symptoms (diarrhoea, abdominal pain), urticarial rash (larva currens - rapidly migrating urticarial track). Immunocompromised: hyperinfection syndrome (↑larval burden) or disseminated disease (larvae in all organs) → gram-negative bacteraemia (larvae carry gut bacteria), meningitis, ARDS - high mortality. Ix: stool microscopy (larva - low sensitivity, multiple samples), serology (ELISA), Baermann concentration. Mx: ivermectin (1st-line) or albendazole; screen before immunosuppression in endemic areas.

conditions.name: Felty syndrome
conditions.summary: Triad of seropositive RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia; rare complication of long-standing RA. Pathogenesis: likely immune complex-mediated splenic sequestration and bone marrow suppression; anti-neutrophil antibodies. Sx: severe RA (nodules, vasculitis), massive splenomegaly, recurrent bacterial infections (due to neutropenia - portal of entry often skin ulcers). Ix: ANC <1.5×10⁹/L, RF strongly positive (>95%), anti-CCP. Mx: DMARDs (methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine); G-CSF for severe neutropenia; splenectomy for refractory cytopenias; rituximab.

conditions.name: TORCH infections
conditions.summary: Acronym for congenital/perinatal infections: Toxoplasmosis, Other (syphilis, VZV, parvovirus B19, HIV, Zika), Rubella, CMV (most common), Herpes simplex. Sx: Common features: IUGR, microcephaly/hydrocephalus, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, chorioretinitis. CMV (most common): periventricular calcifications, sensorineural hearing loss, mild-severe neurodevelopmental delay. Mx: Toxoplasmosis: periventricular calcifications + hydrocephalus + chorioretinitis triad; treat with pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin. Sx: Rubella: cataracts, CHD (PDA, pulmonary artery stenosis), sensorineural deafness, blueberry muffin rash. Ix: maternal/infant serology, PCR, ophthalmology, neuroimaging.

conditions.name: Sudden infant death syndrome
conditions.summary: Sudden, unexplained death of an infant <1 year after thorough investigation (autopsy, death scene investigation, medical history review). Peak: 2–4 months. Risk factors: prone sleeping (major modifiable risk - 'Back to Sleep' campaign ↓SIDS by 50%), soft bedding, overheating, parental smoking, bed-sharing (especially with alcohol), prematurity, male sex. Protective factors: supine sleeping, breastfeeding, pacifier use, room sharing (not bed-sharing). Pathophysiology: triple risk model - vulnerable infant + critical developmental period + exogenous stressor (prone sleeping, hypoxia). Investigation: must exclude NAI, metabolic disease, infection.

conditions.name: Post-operative ileus
conditions.summary: Transient inhibition of GI motility following surgery; universal after abdominal surgery, also after non-abdominal procedures. Pathophysiology: neurogenic (sympathetic activation), inflammatory (operative manipulation → prostaglandins, cytokines), pharmacological (opioids). Sx: distension, nausea, failure to pass flatus/stool; persists 3–5 days typically. Distinguish from mechanical obstruction (CT). Mx: limit opioids (ERAS protocols - multimodal analgesia), early mobilisation, early oral intake, chewing gum, alvimopan (peripherally acting μ-antagonist), NG tube if vomiting.

conditions.name: Wallenberg syndrome
conditions.summary: Stroke syndrome from PICA or vertebral artery occlusion → lateral medullary infarction. Sx: Classic features: ipsilateral - facial numbness (CN5), Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), ataxia, dysphagia/hoarseness (CN9/10); contralateral - limb spinothalamic sensory loss. Crossed sensory loss: ipsilateral face + contralateral body (spinothalamic tract). Nystagmus, hiccups (classic), vertigo. Swallowing difficulty may require NG feed initially. Mx: antiplatelet/anticoagulation for stroke; speech pathology for dysphagia.

conditions.name: Carotid artery dissection
conditions.summary: Tear in carotid artery wall → intramural haematoma → arterial occlusion or thromboembolism. Causes: spontaneous (young adults, connective tissue disorders - Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos), trauma (neck manipulation, sports, motor vehicle). Sx: neck pain/headache (anterior neck) + Horner syndrome (partial - ptosis + miosis; anhidrosis less common as superior cervical ganglion spared) + stroke/TIA (embolic, same-side); pulsatile tinnitus. Ix: MRI/MRA (string sign, flame-shaped occlusion, mural haematoma) or CTA. Mx: antiplatelet or anticoagulation (both acceptable - CADISS trial); acute large stroke → thrombectomy.

conditions.name: Vertebral artery dissection
conditions.summary: Tear in vertebral artery wall → posterior circulation stroke (often Wallenberg or cerebellar). Causes: spontaneous, trauma (neck manipulation, chiropractic - rare), connective tissue disease. Sx: posterior neck/occipital pain + Wallenberg syndrome or cerebellar stroke (ataxia, vertigo, diplopia). Ix: MRI/MRA or CTA. Mx: antiplatelet or anticoagulation; endovascular if haemodynamically significant.

conditions.name: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis
conditions.summary: Acute flaccid muscle weakness with profound hypokalaemia in hyperthyroid patients; predominantly Asian/Pacific Islander men. Pathophysiology: excess thyroid hormone sensitises Na-K-ATPase to catecholamines + insulin → massive intracellular K shift → acute hypokalaemia → membrane hyperpolarisation → muscle inexcitability. Triggers: carbohydrate-rich meals, exercise, alcohol. Sx: proximal limb weakness, areflexia, normal consciousness; may affect respiratory muscles. Mx: IV potassium chloride (cautiously - serum K rebounds); propranolol (↓Na-K-ATPase activity - very effective); treat hyperthyroidism (prevents recurrence).

conditions.name: Anthrax
conditions.summary: Bacterial infection by Bacillus anthracis (gram-positive spore-forming rod); spores highly stable in environment. Forms: cutaneous (most common - painless black eschar 'malignant pustule'; good prognosis with treatment), inhalation (bioterrorism concern - widened mediastinum on CXR from haemorrhagic mediastinitis; very high mortality), gastrointestinal (contaminated meat), injection. Pathogenesis: anthrax toxins (LF + EF + PA) → cellular death and immune evasion. Mx: ciprofloxacin or doxycycline + protein synthesis inhibitor; antitoxin for severe disease. Reportable disease.

conditions.name: Plague
conditions.summary: Zoonotic infection from Yersinia pestis (gram-negative coccobacillus); transmitted by flea bites from infected rodents. Forms: bubonic (most common - painful lymph node swelling 'buboes' in inguinal/axillary/cervical region, fever, rigors); pneumonic (secondary or primary - highly contagious person-to-person via respiratory droplets; rapidly fatal pneumonia); septicaemic. Historical: Black Death pandemic. Mx: streptomycin or gentamicin (1st-line); doxycycline or ciprofloxacin (alternatives). Notifiable disease; strict isolation for pneumonic plague.

conditions.name: Typhus
conditions.summary: Vector-borne Rickettsial diseases: Epidemic typhus (R. prowazekii - body louse; historically decimated armies); Murine typhus (R. typhi - rat flea); Scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi - chigger mites, endemic north Queensland/NT/Pacific Islands). Sx: fever, headache, myalgia + characteristic eschar (painless black necrotic lesion at bite site - pathognomonic of scrub typhus and some spotted fevers) + maculopapular rash (spreading from trunk). Weil-Felix agglutination test (historical). Ix: serology, PCR. Mx: doxycycline (treatment of choice for all rickettsial diseases); chloramphenicol (alternative in pregnancy).

conditions.name: Cryptosporidiosis
conditions.summary: Diarrhoeal illness from Cryptosporidium parvum/hominis (protozoan). Transmission: faecal-oral (waterborne - resistant to chlorination), person-to-person, animal contact. Immunocompetent: self-limiting profuse watery diarrhoea (1–2 weeks); may cause large outbreaks (Milwaukee 1993 - 400,000 cases). Immunocompromised (HIV CD4 <100): severe, protracted, cholera-like watery diarrhoea; biliary cryptosporidiosis (sclerosing cholangitis-like). Ix: stool PCR or acid-fast stain (oocysts). Mx: nitazoxanide (modest benefit in immunocompetent); immune restoration (ART) essential in HIV.

conditions.name: Hydatid disease
conditions.summary: Helminthic infection by Echinococcus granulosus (dog tapeworm); sheep/cattle are intermediate hosts. Highly prevalent in sheep-raising areas (central Australia, outback communities). Larvae form slowly expanding cysts predominantly in liver (70%) and lung (20%); other organs occasionally. Sx: often asymptomatic for years; hepatomegaly/mass, chest mass, allergic reaction if cyst ruptures (anaphylaxis, dissemination). Ix: serology (ELISA), USS/CT (daughter cysts - 'water lily sign', sand-like contents). Mx: PAIR (Puncture-Aspiration-Injection-Reaspiration) for accessible cysts with mebendazole/albendazole cover; surgery for complicated cysts; avoid aspiration without cover (anaphylaxis/seeding risk).

conditions.name: Neurocysticercosis
conditions.summary: CNS infection by Taenia solium larvae (pork tapeworm cysticerci); most common cause of adult-onset epilepsy in endemic regions (Latin America, South Asia, sub-Saharan Africa). Transmission: faecal-oral (ingestion of T. solium eggs from contaminated water/food - NOT from eating pork; pork transmits the adult tapeworm). Sx: seizures (most common presentation), headache, focal deficits, hydrocephalus (periventricular cysts), meningitis (racemose form - subarachnoid). Ix: MRI (viable cysts with scolex, ring-enhancing degenerating cysts, calcified cysts), serology. Mx: albendazole + praziquantel (antiparasitic) + steroids (↓inflammatory reaction) + antiepileptics.

conditions.name: Hypothermia
conditions.summary: Core temperature <35°C. Ix (grading): mild (32–35°C - shivering, tachycardia, confusion), moderate (28–32°C - no shivering, bradycardia, arrhythmias, stupor), severe (<28°C - VF/asystole, apnoea, coma, apparent death). Causes: environmental (cold exposure/immersion), alcohol, drugs, hypothyroidism, hypoadrenalism, hypoglycaemia, sepsis. Ix (ECG): Osborn (J) waves (pathognomonic - positive deflection at J-point, most prominent in V3-V6). Mx: 'No one is dead until warm and dead'; active rewarming (warm blankets, warmed IV fluids, thoracic irrigation, ECMO/ECLS for severe - allows cardiac bypass while rewarming); correct electrolytes; stabilise VF with ECMO rather than repeated defibrillation in severe hypothermia.

conditions.name: Altitude sickness
conditions.summary: Illness from rapid ascent to altitude due to hypoxia and ↓atmospheric pressure. Sx: AMS: headache + at least one of: fatigue, dizziness, GI symptoms, insomnia; occurs >2500 m typically. Mx: HACE (life-threatening): AMS + ataxia + altered consciousness → cerebral oedema; treat with immediate descent, dexamethasone, supplemental O2, Gamow bag. HAPE (most fatal): non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema; ↑pulmonary vascular resistance → hypoxia → oedema; treat with immediate descent, O2, nifedipine, phosphodiesterase inhibitors; dexamethasone adjunct. Mx (prevention): gradual ascent (<500 m/day above 3000 m), acetazolamide prophylaxis (inhibits carbonic anhydrase → ↑ventilation → ↑SpO2).

conditions.name: Decompression sickness
conditions.summary: Disorder from dissolved nitrogen coming out of solution when pressure decreases rapidly (diving ascent, altitude exposure). Nitrogen bubbles form in tissues/blood. Sx: Type I: mild - joint pain ('the bends'), skin marbling, lymphoedema. Type II: serious - neurological (spinal cord most common - paraplegia/paraesthesia), pulmonary ('chokes' - pleuritic pain, dyspnoea), cerebral, inner ear (vertigo, hearing loss). Mx: 100% O2 immediately (↓nitrogen bubble size), rehydration; definitive - hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) therapy (re-compression → dissolves bubbles, enhanced wound healing). Mx (prevention): ascent rate, safety stops, decompression tables.

conditions.name: Bowel adhesions
conditions.summary: Fibrous bands forming between bowel loops/abdominal structures after peritoneal injury. Causes: most commonly post-surgical (80% - laparotomy, appendicectomy, gynaecological surgery), also peritonitis, endometriosis, IBD, radiation. Sx: can be asymptomatic, acute SBO (abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, obstipation), or chronic recurrent episodes. Ix: clinical + AXR (air-fluid levels) or CT abdomen (CT preferred - shows transition point, loop dilatation). Mx: conservative (IV fluids, NGT decompression) for partial obstruction; surgery (adhesiolysis) for complete/failed conservative. Complications: recurrent SBO, bowel strangulation/ischaemia, female infertility (peritubal adhesions). Note: most common cause of SBO in developed countries (~75%).

conditions.name: Hemifacial spasm
conditions.summary: Involuntary twitching/contraction of muscles on one side of face. Causes: most commonly vascular compression of facial nerve (CN VII) at root entry zone (AICA or PICA most common); rarely facial nerve tumour, MS, Bell's palsy sequelae. Sx: begins with orbicularis oculi twitching → spreads to ipsilateral cheek/mouth/platysma; initially intermittent, becomes continuous; distinctive synchronous co-contraction. Ix: clinical; MRI brain/MRA (vascular loop at CPA); EMG (lateral spread response - pathognomonic). Mx: botulinum toxin injections (1st-line - very effective; 3-4 monthly injections); microvascular decompression (MVD) of facial nerve (definitive surgical cure - 90% success). Note: benign essential blepharospasm is bilateral (different diagnosis); starts in eye then spreads.

conditions.name: Filariasis
conditions.summary: Parasitic infection by filarial nematodes transmitted by mosquitoes. Types: lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti - most common; Brugia malayi/timori) → lymphoedema/elephantiasis; loiasis (Loa loa - eye worm; West/Central Africa); onchocerciasis (river blindness - Onchocerca volvulus). Epidemiology: endemic tropics/subtropics; 120 million infected worldwide. Sx: acute → fever, lymphangitis, lymphadenitis; chronic → lymphoedema (progressive; arms, legs, genitalia - elephantiasis; hydrocele); tropical pulmonary eosinophilia. Ix: microfilariae on nocturnal blood smear (10pm–2am); antigen tests (circulating filarial antigen); serology; ultrasound (dancing worm sign - live adult worms in lymphatics). Mx: diethylcarbamazine (DEC; also ivermectin/albendazole). Note: WHO Global Programme to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis (mass drug administration - DEC + albendazole or ivermectin + albendazole).

conditions.name: Transient tachypnoea of the newborn
conditions.summary: Benign self-limiting respiratory distress from delayed clearance of foetal lung fluid. Pathophysiology: foetal lung fluid normally cleared via labour (catecholamine surge → ↑Na+ channels, also chest compression); delayed clearance → ↓lung compliance → ↑respiratory work. Risk factors: elective Caesarean section (no labour → ↓catecholamine surge), precipitate labour, maternal diabetes/asthma, male sex, prematurity. Sx: tachypnoea (>60/min), mild respiratory distress, oxygen requirement; onset within hours of birth; resolves within 12-72 hours. Ix (CXR): prominent perihilar streaking (vascular congestion), fluid in fissures, hyperinflation. Mx: supportive (supplemental oxygen, monitoring); most resolve within 48-72 hours. Note: Caesarean without labour increases TTN risk 3-4× - discuss elective CS timing (37+ weeks gestation); distinct from RDS (premature surfactant deficiency).

conditions.name: Medullary sponge kidney
conditions.summary: Congenital renal tubular malformation with cystic dilatation of collecting tubules in renal medulla. Pathophysiology: cystic/sponge-like dilatation of papillary collecting ducts → urinary stasis → calcium deposition + calculi formation. Sx: usually incidental; recurrent nephrolithiasis (calcium oxalate/phosphate); recurrent UTIs; haematuria; incomplete distal RTA (20%); risk of hypercalciuria + nephrocalcinosis. Ix: CT urogram (classic 'paintbrush' appearance of ectatic tubules filling with contrast in medullary papillae; calcifications). Mx: high fluid intake (2-2.5 L/day); thiazide diuretics (hypercalciuria); citrate supplementation (if low urinary citrate/RTA); treat stones as they occur. Note: associated with hemihypertrophy, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome; generally benign prognosis - rarely leads to CKD unless recurrent infection/obstruction.

conditions.name: Liddle syndrome
conditions.summary: Rare autosomal dominant channelopathy causing early-onset severe hypertension with hypokalaemia. Pathophysiology: gain-of-function mutation in β or γ subunit of epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) in collecting duct → ENaC constitutively open → ↑Na+ reabsorption → ↑BP, ↓K+, ↓aldosterone (suppressed by ECF expansion). Sx: severe hypertension in young patients; hypokalaemia; metabolic alkalosis; low plasma renin + low aldosterone (cf. primary hyperaldosteronism: low renin but HIGH aldosterone). Ix: genetic testing (SCNN1B/SCNN1G mutations); aldosterone:renin ratio (low aldosterone and low renin). Mx: ENaC blockers (triamterene or amiloride - block ENaC directly; do NOT respond to spironolactone); low sodium diet; NOT spironolactone. Note: distinguishing from primary hyperaldosteronism critical - Liddle's has LOW aldosterone + responds only to ENaC blockers, not spironolactone.

conditions.name: Buerger disease
conditions.summary: Non-atherosclerotic, segmental, inflammatory occlusive disease of small-medium vessels of limbs. Pathophysiology: inflammatory thrombosis of small/medium arteries + veins of distal extremities; strongly linked to tobacco use (all forms including smokeless tobacco). Epidemiology: young men (<45 years); smokers (virtually never occurs in non-smokers); more prevalent in Middle East, Asia. Sx: claudication (calf, foot, arch); rest pain, ischaemic ulceration/gangrene of digits; Raynaud's phenomenon; migratory superficial thrombophlebitis. Ix: clinical + angiography (corkscrew collateral vessels - pathognomonic); exclude atherosclerosis; exclude hypercoagulable states. Mx: SMOKING CESSATION (most critical - disease remits with cessation; progresses with continued smoking); wound care; iloprost IV (for critical ischaemia); amputation if advanced gangrene. Note: tobacco use is sine qua non - complete cessation is only effective treatment; even electronic cigarettes/smokeless tobacco maintain the disease.

aliases: facial port-wine stain with brain angioma
conditions.name: Sturge-Weber syndrome
conditions.summary: Rare congenital neurocutaneous syndrome (phakomatosis) caused by somatic GNAQ mutation. Features (triad): port-wine stain (naevus flammeus) in V1 distribution (forehead ± eyelid), leptomeningeal angiomata (ipsilateral - causing seizures, progressive neurological deficit), glaucoma (ipsilateral - congenital angle anomaly). Pathophysiology: somatic GNAQ c.548G>A mutation → aberrant vascular development. Sx: seizures (90% - contralateral to facial stain; onset typically first year; often refractory), developmental delay/intellectual disability, contralateral hemiplegia, glaucoma. Ix: MRI brain with gadolinium (leptomeningeal enhancement, cortical calcification - 'tram-track' calcification on CT), ophthalmology assessment. Mx: anticonvulsants; aspirin (low-dose - ↓stroke-like episodes); laser treatment for port-wine stain; glaucoma management. Note: port-wine stain in V1 distribution → always ophthalmology review (glaucoma) + consider MRI; not all port-wine stains indicate SWS.

conditions.name: Fibrous dysplasia
conditions.summary: Benign skeletal disorder with replacement of normal bone by fibro-osseous tissue. Pathophysiology: somatic GNAS1 mutation → constitutively active Gsα → ↑cAMP → abnormal osteoblast differentiation → fibrous tissue replaces medullary bone → structural weakness. Types: monostotic (one bone - most common; 70-80%); polyostotic (multiple bones; ±McCune-Albright syndrome with café-au-lait spots + endocrinopathy). Sx: bone pain, deformity (leg - 'shepherd's crook' deformity of proximal femur), pathological fractures; incidental XR finding. XR: 'ground-glass' appearance, endosteal scalloping, cortical thinning. Mx: bisphosphonates (pamidronate/zoledronic acid - reduce pain + ↑bone density); surgical stabilisation for weight-bearing bones at fracture risk. Complications: malignant transformation (rare - <1%; usually fibrosarcoma). Note: associated with McCune-Albright syndrome (polyostotic FD + café-au-lait + precocious puberty ± other endocrinopathies).

conditions.name: Pseudoxanthoma elasticum
conditions.summary: Rare autosomal recessive connective tissue disorder affecting elastic fibres. Pathophysiology: ABCC6 mutation → defective cellular export of ATP → ↓pyrophosphate (mineralisation inhibitor) → progressive calcification and fragmentation of elastic fibres in skin, eyes, cardiovascular system. Sx: skin (yellowish papules in flexural areas - 'plucked chicken skin'; neck, axillae, antecubital fossa; skin laxity); eyes (angioid streaks on fundus - breaks in Bruch's membrane; visual loss from CNV); cardiovascular (premature atherosclerosis, claudication, angina, stroke, GI haemorrhage). Ix: skin biopsy (calcified elastic fibres - von Kossa stain); genetic testing (ABCC6). Mx: no disease-modifying treatment; ophthalmology monitoring (anti-VEGF for CNV); cardiovascular risk reduction. Note: angioid streaks are pathognomonic of PXE (also seen in Paget disease, sickle cell, Ehlers-Danlos, haemochromatosis); physical trauma may trigger CNV.

conditions.name: McCune-Albright syndrome
conditions.summary: Sporadic syndrome from somatic GNAS1 mutation causing triad of polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, café-au-lait spots, and peripheral precocious puberty. Pathophysiology: postzygotic somatic GNAS1 mutation → constitutive Gsα activation → ↑cAMP in affected tissues → autonomous hormone hypersecretion. Sx: (1) polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (bone - shepherd's crook deformity, fractures, pain); (2) café-au-lait spots (large, jagged 'coast of Maine' border - cf. NF1's smooth 'coast of California'); (3) GnRH-independent precocious puberty (girls > boys; ovarian cysts → early menses, breast development, advanced bone age). Additional endocrinopathies: hyperthyroidism, GH excess, Cushing syndrome, hyperprolactinaemia, FGF23-mediated hypophosphataemia. Ix: clinical triad; GNAS1 sequencing. Mx: treat each endocrinopathy individually; bisphosphonates for bone disease; aromatase inhibitors for precocious puberty.

conditions.name: Bowen's disease
conditions.summary: Intraepidermal squamous cell carcinoma in situ. Pathophysiology: full-thickness epidermal dysplasia without dermal invasion; risk factors: UV exposure (chronic), HPV (16/18 - especially penile/vulval/periungual), arsenic exposure, immunosuppression. Sx: well-demarcated, erythematous scaly plaque (can be pink or pigmented); chronic, slow-growing; may bleed or develop crusting; any sun-exposed site; erythroplasia of Queyrat = glans penis involvement (bright red, moist plaque). Ix: clinical ± dermoscopy; skin biopsy (full-thickness keratinocyte atypia, mitoses; intact BM on histology - no invasion). Mx: topical 5-fluorouracil (5% cream - 12 weeks), imiquimod (5% cream), photodynamic therapy (PDT - preferred for large/field), curettage + electrodesiccation, cryotherapy, surgical excision. Note: ~3-8% risk of progression to invasive SCC - particularly in immunosuppressed; treat all lesions.

conditions.name: Granuloma annulare
conditions.summary: Benign dermatosis characterised by ring-shaped dermal papules with central clearing. Pathophysiology: granulomatous inflammation with palisading histiocytes around central degenerate collagen; aetiology unknown - possibly T-cell mediated delayed hypersensitivity; associations with diabetes (generalised form), thyroid disease, dyslipidaemia, HIV. Sx: asymptomatic annular ring of papules (often misdiagnosed as ringworm - no scale/fungal cause); dorsal hands/feet/ankles (localised); generalised form - widespread (stronger DM association); self-limiting in 50% within 2 years. Ix: clinical; biopsy if uncertain (palisading granulomas - histiocytes + degenerate collagen core). Mx: often none (resolves spontaneously); intralesional/topical corticosteroids; cryotherapy; for generalised: hydroxychloroquine, dapsone, phototherapy. Note: check HbA1c (DM association especially with generalised GA); distinguish from tinea corporis (which has scale and positive KOH).

conditions.name: Chilblains
conditions.summary: Localised inflammatory skin response to cold, damp conditions. Pathophysiology: repeated cold/damp exposure → abnormal vasomotor response → vasoconstriction followed by reactive vasodilatation → oedema, inflammation. Sx: painful/itchy purple-red lesions on toes/fingers/heels/nose/ears; worse in winter; develop hours after cold exposure; localised swelling, blistering in severe cases. Types: idiopathic (most common); lupus pernio (chilblain lupus - from systemic lupus); COVID-19 associated (COVID toes - acrocyanosis/erythema on toes); familial chilblain lupus (TREX1 mutation). Ix: clinical; consider ANA/ENA if lupus suspected; skin biopsy shows perivascular lymphocytic inflammation. Mx: keep extremities warm; avoid cold/damp; vasodilators (nifedipine 5-20 mg TDS - for recurrent cases); topical corticosteroids for inflammation. Note: distinguish from lupus pernio (chilblain lupus) - associated with SLE, positive ANA - test ANA in persistent or atypical cases.

conditions.name: Cerebral cavernous malformation
conditions.summary: Vascular lesion - clusters of enlarged, thin-walled blood-filled sinusoidal spaces without normal intervening brain parenchyma. Pathophysiology: sporadic (80%) or familial (autosomal dominant - CCM1/KRIT1, CCM2, CCM3 gene mutations); prone to repeated small haemorrhages. Sx: incidental (25%); seizures (most common symptom - 50%); focal neurological deficit (depends on location); headache; recurrent haemorrhage. Ix (MRI): 'popcorn' or 'mulberry' appearance with haemosiderin rim (blood breakdown products - mixed signal core; dark rim on T2/GRE - haemosiderin); gradient echo sequences sensitive. Mx: observation if asymptomatic or incidental; anticonvulsants for seizures; neurosurgical resection (accessible lesions + recurrent haemorrhage or drug-refractory seizures). Note: 'popcorn lesion' on MRI (T2) = cavernoma until proven otherwise; avoid anticoagulation if possible; screen family members if familial form (CCM1-3 genes).

conditions.name: Hemiballismus
conditions.summary: Involuntary, violent, flinging movements of one limb. Pathophysiology: most commonly subthalamic nucleus (STN) lesion (usually lacunar infarct - STN injury → ↓STN output → ↑GPe activity → ↓GPi inhibition → thalamus disinhibited → involuntary movement); also hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (bilateral ballismus). Causes: ischaemic stroke (STN lacunar infarct - most common), hyperglycaemia (HHS/HBG - classically bilateral), haemorrhage, tumour, lupus, drug-induced. Sx: sudden onset violent, flinging, large-amplitude involuntary movements affecting arm > leg; exhausting; consciousness preserved. Mx: treat underlying cause (glucose for hyperglycaemia → often resolves within days); dopamine-depleting agents (tetrabenazine) or dopamine receptor blockers (haloperidol, olanzapine); often self-limiting with stroke. Note: bilateral hemiballismus → think hyperglycaemia (check BGL immediately); MRI STN for unilateral to identify underlying cause.

conditions.name: Body dysmorphic disorder
conditions.summary: OCD-spectrum disorder characterised by preoccupation with perceived defect(s) in physical appearance. Pathophysiology: excessive focus on perceived flaw (often invisible/minimal to others); OCD-spectrum (similar serotonergic mechanisms); abnormal visual processing (enhanced local processing); high comorbidity with MDD, social anxiety, OCD. Sx: preoccupation (hours daily); repetitive behaviours (mirror checking, skin picking, camouflaging); seeks cosmetic procedures (never satisfied); often housebound; high suicidality. Common areas: skin, hair, nose, genitalia, muscle (muscle dysmorphia - mostly men). Ix: DSM-5 criteria; BDDQ screening tool. Mx: CBT (ERP - exposure + response prevention); SSRIs (high doses - fluoxetine 60-80 mg; fluvoxamine); combined CBT + SSRI for moderate/severe. Note: cosmetic surgery is contraindicated (does not help - symptoms transfer to another body part); suicidality assessment essential.

conditions.name: Microscopic colitis
conditions.summary: Inflammatory bowel disease characterised by chronic, non-bloody, watery diarrhoea with normal endoscopy but abnormal histology. Epidemiology: middle-aged to elderly; female predominance; strongly associated with NSAIDs, PPIs, SSRIs, olmesartan, ranitidine (causal association). Types: collagenous colitis (thickened subepithelial collagen band >10 μm) and lymphocytic colitis (↑intraepithelial lymphocytes >20/100 epithelial cells). Sx: profuse, watery, non-bloody diarrhoea (chronic or recurrent - 4-9 stools/day); nocturnal diarrhoea (distinguishes from IBS); weight loss; normal colonoscopy (diagnosis only on biopsy). Ix: colonoscopy with biopsies (random biopsies throughout colon - right colon preferred; must biopsy even if mucosa looks normal). Mx: stop causative medications (NSAIDs, PPIs, SSRIs - may resolve); budesonide (1st-line - 9 mg/day × 6-8 weeks); bismuth subsalicylate; loperamide. Note: NSAIDs/PPIs most important drugs to stop; budesonide 1st-line but relapse on cessation common - may need maintenance.

conditions.name: Intestinal lymphangiectasia
conditions.summary: Disorder of intestinal lymphatics causing protein-losing enteropathy. Types: primary (congenital - Waldmann disease - dilated submucosal/subserosal lymphatics); secondary (obstructed lymphatics - malignancy, constrictive pericarditis, Whipple disease, retroperitoneal fibrosis). Sx: protein-losing enteropathy → hypoalbuminaemia → peripheral oedema, ascites, pleural effusion; fat malabsorption → steatorrhoea, fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies; lymphopenia (lymphocyte loss into gut) → ↑infection susceptibility; chylous ascites. Ix: ↓albumin + ↓lymphocytes + ↓immunoglobulins; stool α1-antitrypsin (elevated - protein-losing enteropathy marker); endoscopy (white-tipped villi - 'snowflake' appearance); biopsy (dilated lacteals). Mx: low-fat diet + medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs bypass lymphatics - absorbed directly to portal system); treat underlying cause (secondary); octreotide (↓chyle leakage); rapamycin (primary cases). Note: lymphopenia despite normal WBC → think protein-losing enteropathy; MCT diet is cornerstone of management.

conditions.name: Eosinophilic gastritis
conditions.summary: GI disorder characterised by eosinophil-rich inflammation of gastric and/or intestinal mucosa. Pathophysiology: Th2-mediated eosinophilic infiltration; often overlaps with eosinophilic oesophagitis (EoE) and food allergy; atopic background common. Types: mucosal (most common - nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, protein-losing enteropathy), muscular (obstructive symptoms - gastric outlet obstruction), serosal (eosinophilic ascites). Sx: nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, postprandial fullness, weight loss; peripheral eosinophilia (50%); may have concurrent atopy/food allergy. Ix: upper endoscopy with biopsies (≥30 eosinophils/HPF in gastric biopsy); exclude parasites, IBD, coeliac disease, drugs, lymphoma. Mx: food elimination diet (6-food/elemental diet); corticosteroids (prednisolone 20-40 mg/day → taper); PPIs; montelukast; dupilumab (emerging evidence). Note: often overlaps with EoE - consider concurrent conditions; food allergy evaluation important.

conditions.name: Myofascial pain syndrome
conditions.summary: Chronic pain condition characterised by trigger points in muscle and associated referred pain. Pathophysiology: 'trigger points' (hyperirritable nodules within taut muscle bands) → localised and referred pain; sensitisation of peripheral + central nervous system; distinct from fibromyalgia (central sensitisation without trigger points). Common sites: trapezius, SCM, levator scapulae, suboccipitals, gluteal muscles. Sx: localised muscle pain with trigger points (palpable nodules - reproduce pain on pressure); referred pain pattern (characteristic for each muscle - e.g., SCM trigger → headache; trapezius → neck/shoulder pain); restricted range of motion. Ix: clinical (trigger point examination - local twitch response, jump sign, referred pain); no specific lab tests. Mx: trigger point injections (dry needling or lidocaine injection); physical therapy (stretching, massage, spray-and-stretch technique); analgesics (NSAIDs, TCAs); address perpetuating factors (posture, ergonomics). Note: distinguish from fibromyalgia (widespread vs localised; presence of trigger points); trigger point injections: evidence moderate but clinically useful.

conditions.name: Capgras syndrome
conditions.summary: Delusional misidentification syndrome - belief that familiar person has been replaced by identical impostor. Pathophysiology: proposed disconnect between face recognition (temporal/occipital - normal visual recognition) and emotional response (limbic system - no familiar emotional response) → brain concludes 'this can't be the real person'. Aetiology: neurodegenerative (DLB, Alzheimer's, PD-dementia - most common underlying cause), psychotic disorders (schizophrenia), TBI, metabolic. Sx: patient correctly identifies person's physical appearance but believes they are an impostor; may become distressed, defensive, aggressive towards 'impostor'. Ix: clinical neuropsychiatric assessment; neuroimaging (underlying cause). Mx: treat underlying condition; antipsychotics; education for carers; reduce confrontation. Note: Capgras = familiar person replaced by impostor; Fregoli = strangers are actually known people in disguise; commonest in DLB - screen for parkinsonism features.

conditions.name: Cotard syndrome
conditions.summary: Rare neuropsychiatric syndrome characterised by nihilistic delusions - belief that one is dead, does not exist, or has lost organs. Pathophysiology: similar disconnection to Capgras but involving all stimuli → patient feels no emotional response to any sensory input → concludes they must be dead or non-existent. Spectrum: denial of existence of body parts, believing they are dead, denying bodily needs, immortality delusion ('I cannot die because I am already dead'). Aetiology: severe depression (most common), bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, dementia, drugs (aciclovir in renal failure → Cotard-like state). Sx: nihilistic delusions; severe depression; self-neglect (refuses food); malnutrition; occasional self-harm. Mx: treat underlying condition; ECT (electroconvulsive therapy - often effective especially with depression); antidepressants + antipsychotics; olanzapine. Note: ECT often dramatically effective; aciclovir/valaciclovir in renal impairment → neurotoxic → Cotard-like presentation - check renal function, dose-adjust antiviral therapy.

conditions.name: SAPHO syndrome
conditions.summary: Rare inflammatory disorder combining osteoarticular and skin manifestations. Acronym: Synovitis, Acne, Pustulosis, Hyperostosis, Osteitis. Pathophysiology: possibly autoinflammatory (innate immune dysregulation → inflammatory bone/skin changes); association with Cutibacterium acnes; spectrum with CRMO (chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis) in children. Sx: osteoarticular (anterior chest wall - sternoclavicular joint, manubriosternal joint - swelling/tenderness; spine - osteitis; peripheral arthritis); skin (palmoplantar pustulosis - most common 75%; severe acne, psoriasis). Bone scan: 'bull's head sign' - ↑uptake at manubriosternal + sternoclavicular joints. Ix: clinical; MRI (bone marrow oedema → osteitis); bone scan. Mx: NSAIDs (1st-line); bisphosphonates (pamidronate/zoledronate - bone involvement); DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine); TNF-α inhibitors (refractory). Note: anterior chest wall pain + palmoplantar pustulosis = SAPHO until proven otherwise; bone scan critical for diagnosis.

conditions.name: Kikuchi disease
conditions.summary: Rare, self-limiting, benign lymphadenopathy syndrome predominantly affecting young Asian women. Pathophysiology: aetiology unknown; proposed viral triggers (HHV-6, EBV, parvovirus B19); immune-mediated histiocytic necrotising lymphadenitis; strong association with SLE. Epidemiology: young females (20s-30s); higher prevalence in Asia but worldwide. Sx: tender cervical lymphadenopathy (posterior cervical - characteristic); constitutional symptoms (fever 38-40°C, fatigue, night sweats); rash (less common); no pharyngitis or hepatosplenomegaly. Ix: lymph node biopsy (essential - necrotising histiocytic lymphadenitis without neutrophils; distinguishes from lymphoma, TB, SLE); blood counts (↓WBC - leukopenia common); ANA (20-25% have positive ANA - risk of subsequent SLE). Mx: self-limiting (90% resolve within 1-4 months); analgesics; NSAIDs; short-course corticosteroids for severe/prolonged cases. Note: malignant lymphoma must be excluded (biopsy essential); screen for SLE (ANA, anti-dsDNA) at presentation and follow-up - evolves to SLE in 5%.

conditions.name: VEXAS syndrome
conditions.summary: Recently discovered (2020) haematoinflammatory syndrome from somatic UBA1 mutation in haematopoietic stem cells. Pathophysiology: somatic (not germline) mutation of UBA1 (X-linked - affects males predominantly; females rarely) → dysfunctional ubiquitylation → innate immune dysregulation → autoinflammation + cytopenia. Sx: adult-onset severe autoinflammatory disease (typically men >50 years); recurrent fever; inflammatory skin lesions (neutrophilic - similar to Sweet syndrome); pulmonary infiltrates; chondritis; DVT/PE; cytopenia (MDS-like; bone marrow shows vacuolisation in myeloid/erythroid precursors). Ix: bone marrow biopsy (vacuoles in precursors - pathognomonic); UBA1 somatic mutation (blood or BM - next-generation sequencing); associated MDS or plasma cell dyscrasia in 25-50%. Mx: no established treatment; corticosteroids (high doses required); JAK inhibitors (ruxolitinib); azacitidine (if associated MDS); allogeneic SCT (curative potential). Note: consider VEXAS in any man >50 with steroid-dependent multisystem autoinflammation + cytopenia; estimated prevalence 1/13,000 males in USA.

conditions.name: Undifferentiated connective tissue disease
conditions.summary: Autoimmune syndrome with features of connective tissue disease not meeting criteria for any defined condition. Epidemiology: mostly young/middle-aged women; common in rheumatology practice (20-25% of autoimmune referrals); 25-30% eventually evolve to defined CTD (SLE, SS, SSc, MCTD). Sx: arthralgia/arthritis, Raynaud's phenomenon, fatigue, photosensitivity; positive ANA (typically ANA ≥1:160); may have low-titre specific antibodies (anti-Ro, anti-La, anti-U1-RNP). Ix: positive ANA + clinical features but does not meet classification criteria for SLE/SS/SSc/MCTD/RA/PM-DM; exclude ANA-positive normal variants. Mx: hydroxychloroquine (most patients - treats symptoms, may prevent evolution to definite CTD); NSAIDs (musculoskeletal); sun protection; low-dose prednisolone if needed. Note: ~30% evolve to defined CTD (usually within 5 years); predictors of evolution: anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, anti-Scl-70, haematological involvement; annual review and repeat ANA/ENA panel.
