conditions.name: Spinal epidural abscess
conditions.summary: Purulent infection in the epidural space of the spinal canal - neurosurgical emergency. Epidemiology: increasing incidence (IV drug use, diabetes, immunosuppression, spinal procedures). Causative organisms: Staphylococcus aureus (60-70% - most common; MRSA increasingly); Streptococcus; gram-negatives (IV drug users, diabetics); TB (Pott's disease). Risk factors: IVDU, diabetes, spinal procedures/instrumentation, immunosuppression, adjacent infection (discitis, vertebral osteomyelitis), bacteraemia. Presentation (triad): fever, back/neck pain, neurological deficits (weakness, sensory loss, sphincter dysfunction - late finding → paralysis if untreated); triad rarely all present simultaneously. Ix: MRI spine with gadolinium (investigation of choice - rim-enhancing epidural collection); blood cultures + CRP/ESR. Mx: surgical decompression + drainage (emergency - if neurological deficit or large collection); IV antibiotics (anti-Staph ± broad cover - 6-8 weeks; MRSA: vancomycin); percutaneous aspiration for culture if no deficit. Note: neurological deficit → emergency surgery within hours; antibiotics alone only if no deficit + no surgical candidate; blood cultures before antibiotics.

conditions.name: Cervical myelopathy
conditions.summary: Progressive spinal cord dysfunction from chronic cervical cord compression. Pathophysiology: degenerative changes (disc herniation, osteophyte formation, ligament hypertrophy - especially OPLL) → progressive cervical cord compression → demyelination, cord atrophy. Sx: insidious onset; gait disturbance (broad-based, unsteady - often 1st symptom); hand dysfunction (loss of dexterity - 'clumsy hands', can't button shirts); sensory disturbance (numbness/tingling - hands); upper motor neurone signs (hyperreflexia, Babinski - lower limb); Lhermitte's sign (electric shock on neck flexion); sphincter dysfunction (late). Ix: MRI cervical spine (spinal cord compression + signal change within cord - T2 hyperintensity = myelomalacia; poor prognostic sign); clinical assessment (mJOA scale). Mx: surgical decompression (anterior cervical discectomy/fusion - ACDF; or posterior laminoplasty) - for moderate/severe myelopathy or progressive; conservative for mild. Note: early decompression prevents irreversible cord damage - refer promptly; cord signal change on MRI (T2 hyperintensity) = poor prognostic factor; natural history is stepwise deterioration.

conditions.name: Brachial plexopathy
conditions.summary: Disorder affecting brachial plexus (C5-T1 nerve network). Types: traumatic (traction injury - birth palsy, motorcycle/contact sport trauma; Erb's palsy - upper trunk C5-6 - 'waiter's tip'; Klumpke's palsy - lower trunk C8-T1 - claw hand); Parsonage-Turner syndrome (neuralgic amyotrophy - idiopathic inflammatory; sudden severe shoulder pain → weakness/atrophy; often post-viral/vaccination); neoplastic (Pancoast tumour, breast/lung metastases - lower trunk → Horner's syndrome); radiation-induced (breast/Hodgkin radiotherapy - delayed months-years). Sx: shoulder pain, arm weakness, sensory loss; Horner's syndrome (T1 disruption - ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis); phrenic nerve palsy (C3-5 - ipsilateral hemidiaphragm paralysis). Ix: clinical + EMG/NCS; MRI brachial plexus (neoplastic/structural); CXR/CT chest (Pancoast). Mx: Parsonage-Turner - analgesia (NSAIDs, opioids, gabapentin), physio; traumatic - urgent surgical repair for root avulsions; neoplastic - treat underlying malignancy. Note: Parsonage-Turner: sudden severe shoulder pain → weakness → partial recovery over months; Pancoast tumour: lower plexus (C8-T1) + Horner's = suspect apex lung cancer.

conditions.name: Phantom limb pain
conditions.summary: Painful sensation perceived in amputated or deafferented limb. Pathophysiology: central sensitisation (cortical reorganisation - somatosensory cortex maps adjacent limb representations to amputated zone); peripheral mechanisms (neuroma formation at stump, ectopic discharges from severed nerves); maladaptive neuroplasticity. Sx: pain perceived in absent limb (burning, shooting, cramping - variable quality); onset weeks-months post-amputation; distinct from stump pain (residual limb pain from local wound/neuroma - non-referred); phantom sensation (non-painful perception of absent limb - very common 80%). Mx: first-line (mirror therapy - visual feedback treats cortical maladaptive reorganisation; gabapentin/pregabalin; TCAs - amitriptyline); second-line (SNRIs - duloxetine; NMDA antagonists - ketamine infusion, memantine); neuromodulation (spinal cord stimulation, transcranial magnetic stimulation); graded motor imagery. Note: mirror therapy (Ramachandran's mirror box) - effective, non-pharmacological, cheap; pain persisting >6 months despite treatment → specialist pain management.

conditions.name: Glossopharyngeal neuralgia
conditions.summary: Rare cranial neuralgia involving CN IX (glossopharyngeal) and occasionally CN X (vagus). Pathophysiology: most commonly vascular compression of CN IX at root entry zone (similar to trigeminal neuralgia); rarely CPA tumour, elongated styloid process (Eagle's syndrome), oropharyngeal tumour. Sx: sudden, severe, electric shock-like pain in throat/tonsillar fossa/tongue base/ear; triggered by swallowing, talking, coughing, yawning; may radiate to ear; cardiac syncope (vagal triggers from CN X overlap - cardioinhibitory form → bradycardia/asystole → syncope; rare but life-threatening). Ix: clinical; MRI brain/posterior fossa (vascular loop, CPA lesion); ECG monitoring during attack (document cardiac effects). Mx: carbamazepine (1st-line - same as trigeminal neuralgia); oxcarbazepine; gabapentin; microvascular decompression of CN IX (surgical - effective if vascular compression); glossopharyngeal block. Note: cardiac syncope complication - pacemaker if severe cardioinhibitory type; rare but severe episodes can cause VF → death; distinguish from trigeminal neuralgia (tongue/throat vs face).

conditions.name: Occipital neuralgia
conditions.summary: Neuropathic pain syndrome from greater/lesser/third occipital nerve dysfunction. Pathophysiology: compression, injury, or inflammation of occipital nerves (C2-C3 roots) → aching, burning, or throbbing pain in occipital/suboccipital region; may be idiopathic or secondary to cervical OA, trauma, muscular entrapment, C1-C2 pathology. Sx: unilateral (more common) or bilateral; constant dull ache with superimposed lancinating/electric shocks; starts in subocciput → radiates to vertex/forehead/retro-orbital; scalp hypersensitivity/allodynia over occiput; tenderness at nerve exit points (occipital notch). Ix: clinical + response to occipital nerve block (diagnostic and therapeutic); MRI if secondary cause suspected. Mx: conservative (NSAIDs, muscle relaxants, local heat); occipital nerve block (local anaesthetic ± corticosteroid - diagnostic + therapeutic); carbamazepine, gabapentin; botulinum toxin injections; rarely pulsed radiofrequency or surgical decompression. Note: tender point at greater occipital notch (halfway between mastoid and C7 spinous process) → diagnostic clue; distinguish from migraine (not lancinating; occipital trigger; scalp allodynia).

conditions.name: Sézary syndrome
conditions.summary: Aggressive leukaemic variant of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL); triad of erythroderma + lymphadenopathy + circulating neoplastic T-cells (Sézary cells). Pathophysiology: CD4+ T-cell malignancy; Sézary cells (cerebriform nuclei) ≥1,000/mm³ in peripheral blood. Sx: generalised erythroderma (intense pruritus - often debilitating), lymphadenopathy, Sézary cells in blood, leonine facies, palmoplantar keratoderma, nail dystrophy, ectropion, alopecia. Ix: skin biopsy (epidermotropism, Pautrier microabscesses); peripheral blood flow cytometry (CD4+/CD7− or CD4+/CD26− clone); T-cell receptor gene rearrangement; PET-CT staging. Mx: systemic (extracorporeal photopheresis - ECP, first-line for erythrodermic CTCL; mogamulizumab, brentuximab vedotin, romidepsin; alemtuzumab for refractory); allogeneic SCT in eligible patients; skin-directed + systemic combined. Note: prognosis poor (median OS 2-4 yr); distinguish from Mycosis fungoides (patch/plaque stage → no leukaemia); erythroderma with pruritus in older adult → exclude Sézary syndrome.

conditions.name: Primary CNS lymphoma
conditions.summary: Rare extra-nodal B-cell NHL (DLBCL - diffuse large B-cell lymphoma) confined to CNS; no systemic lymphoma. Risk factors: immunosuppression (HIV/AIDS - EBV driven; transplant recipients), but majority are immunocompetent. Sx: focal neurological deficits (most common), cognitive decline, personality change, raised ICP (headache, vomiting), seizures (less common than other brain tumours); in HIV: multifocal ring-enhancing lesions (confused with toxoplasmosis). Ix: MRI brain - homogeneously enhancing periventricular/deep white matter mass (basal ganglia, corpus callosum); CSF cytology (positive in 25% - malignant B-cells), vitreoretinal biopsy; brain biopsy (stereotactic - gold standard; avoid steroids before biopsy - profound response obscures diagnosis 'biopsy-negative lymphoma'). Mx: high-dose methotrexate (HD-MTX)-based chemotherapy (cornerstone - crosses BBB); rituximab; whole-brain radiotherapy (WBR - effective but neurotoxic in elderly); autologous SCT consolidation (younger patients); in HIV: ART + HD-MTX. Note: steroid-induced 'ghost tumour' - dramatic regression on steroids but biopsy becomes non-diagnostic; avoid steroids until biopsy planned; median OS 2-5 yr with treatment.

conditions.name: Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma
conditions.summary: Aggressive peripheral T-cell lymphoma (PTCL); second most common PTCL subtype. Pathophysiology: neoplastic follicular helper T-cells (TFH cells - CD4+CXCL13+PD-1+); arises from germinal centre T-cells; IDH2/DNMT3A/TET2 mutations common. Sx: advanced-stage disease typical; constitutional B symptoms (fever, sweats, weight loss); generalised lymphadenopathy; hepatosplenomegaly; skin rash (macular - immune-mediated); ascites, pleural effusions; polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia; autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. Ix: lymph node biopsy (polymorphous infiltrate, arborising high endothelial venules, follicular dendritic cell meshworks, TFH immunophenotype - CD4+CD10+CXCL13+PD-1+); EBV-positive B-cells within tumour; BM biopsy + PET-CT staging. Mx: CHOP or CHOP-like (anthracycline-based); brentuximab vedotin + CHP (for CD30+ PTCL); romidepsin; autologous SCT consolidation in first remission (eligible patients). Note: prognosis poor (5-yr OS ~35%); frequent relapses; EBV-associated B-cell proliferations can develop → EBV-positive DLBCL.

conditions.name: Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma
conditions.summary: Aggressive EBV-associated lymphoma with NK-cell or cytotoxic T-cell phenotype; predilection for nasal cavity/nasopharynx. Epidemiology: Asia and Latin America > Western populations; EBV universally present (clonal episomal EBV in tumour cells). Nasal type: most common - midfacial destruction ('lethal midline granuloma' - destructive ulceration of nose/palate/sinuses); perforated nasal septum, proptosis (orbital extension). Extranasal type: skin, GI tract, testes - worse prognosis. Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) complication. Ix: biopsy (angioinvasion/angiodestruction - necrosis, coagulative; NK-cell markers: CD56+, CD3ε+; cytotoxic granules: TIA-1/granzyme B; EBV-EBER ISH+); PET-CT staging. Mx: non-anthracycline-based (P-GEMOX - cisplatin, gemcitabine, oxaliplatin; or AspaMetDex - L-asparaginase, methotrexate, dexamethasone); concurrent RT for nasal-type localised disease; L-asparaginase-containing regimens most effective. Note: resistance to anthracyclines (P-glycoprotein expression); EBV DNA (plasma) monitors disease; prognosis poor for disseminated disease.

conditions.name: Primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma
conditions.summary: Distinct DLBCL subtype arising from thymic B-cells; young adults, female predominance. Pathophysiology: JAK2 amplification (chromosome 9p24.1); PDL1/PDL2 overexpression (immune evasion); related to nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma (overlapping features - 'grey zone' lymphoma). Sx: anterior mediastinal mass (rapid growth) → SVC syndrome, dyspnoea, chest pain, cough; local invasion (pericardium, lung, pleura, chest wall); rarely extranodal at diagnosis. Ix: biopsy (compartmentalising sclerosis, medium-large B-cells - CD20+CD30+CD15−; PDL1 overexpression); PET-CT staging; differentiate from Hodgkin lymphoma (grey zone challenging). Mx: dose-adjusted EPOCH-R (etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin + rituximab - first-line; avoids RT in complete responders); or R-CHOP then mediastinal RT; pembrolizumab (checkpoint inhibitor - exploits PDL1 overexpression; approved for R/R). Note: consolidation RT debated (significant long-term toxicity: coronary artery disease, second malignancies, breast cancer in young women); PET-CR after induction → RT may be omitted; excellent prognosis in responders (5-yr OS ~80%).

conditions.name: Hairy cell leukaemia
conditions.summary: Rare mature B-cell malignancy; characteristic 'hairy' cytoplasmic projections. Pathophysiology: BRAF V600E mutation (present in >95% - diagnostic). Epidemiology: middle-aged males; rare. Sx: massive splenomegaly (often presenting complaint), pancytopenia (anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia - recurrent infections); monocytopenia (characteristic); lymphadenopathy uncommon (spleen infiltrated). Complications: recurrent infections (especially atypical mycobacteria - Mycobacterium avium complex, aspergillosis); vasculitis, polyarteritis nodosa. Ix: peripheral blood (hairy cells - villous lymphocytes; TRAP [tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase] stain+); BM biopsy (dry tap - reticulin fibrosis; characteristic infiltrate); flow cytometry (CD19+CD20+CD22+CD11c+CD25+CD103+CD123+ - TRAP+). Mx: cladribine (2-chlorodeoxyadenosine - purine analogue; single course → 85% CR); pentostatin (alternative purine analogue); BRAF inhibitors (vemurafenib - for relapsed/refractory or upfront treatment under investigation); rituximab combinations. Note: excellent prognosis with purine analogues; BRAF V600E = diagnostic; monocytopenia = distinguishing feature of HCL (low monocytes despite infection).

conditions.name: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma
conditions.summary: Indolent B-cell lymphoma arising from marginal zone B-cells of spleen; often presents with massive splenomegaly. Pathophysiology: del(7q) in ~40%; NOTCH2 mutations; association with hepatitis C virus (HCV - screen all patients). Sx: splenomegaly (often massive, symptomatic - abdominal discomfort, early satiety); lymphocytosis with villous lymphocytes in blood; autoimmune cytopenias (AIHA, ITP); minimal peripheral lymphadenopathy. Ix: splenectomy (histology - gold standard; nodular marginal zone pattern); peripheral blood flow cytometry (CD20+IgM+CD5−CD10−CD23−CD103−; villous lymphocytes); BM trephine; exclude HCV (hepatitis C serology). Mx: watch-and-wait (indolent course; asymptomatic); HCV treatment (for HCV+ - antiviral therapy alone can induce lymphoma remission); splenectomy (symptomatic splenomegaly - rapid cytoreduction + diagnostic); rituximab (single agent or R-chemo for HCV-negative or refractory); prognosis good (median OS 10+ yr). Note: HCV association critical - treat HCV first; del(7q) associated with worse prognosis; transformation to DLBCL in ~10%.

aliases: giant cell tumour of tendon sheath
conditions.name: Pigmented villonodular synovitis
conditions.summary: Locally aggressive benign synovial proliferative disorder; now termed tenosynovial giant cell tumour (TGCT). Pathophysiology: CSF1 gene translocation → CSF1 overexpression → monocyte/macrophage recruitment → synovial proliferation; haemosiderin deposition (brown discolouration - 'villonodular'). Types: diffuse TGCT (previously PVNS - entire joint, locally aggressive); localised TGCT (previously giant cell tumour of tendon sheath - discrete nodule, hand/foot). Sites: knee most common (diffuse); hand/wrist (localised). Sx: knee - chronic pain, swelling (haemarthrosis - serosanguinous aspirate), stiffness, locked joint (loose body); insidious onset; age 20-50 yr. Ix: MRI (characteristic - low signal on T1 and T2 from haemosiderin; blooming artefact on GRE/SWI - diagnostic; irregular synovial masses); synovial biopsy (histology - mononuclear cells, multinucleated giant cells, haemosiderin, xanthoma cells). Mx: surgical synovectomy (complete - reduces recurrence; arthroscopic for localised; open/combined for diffuse); pexidartinib (CSF1R inhibitor - US-approved for diffuse TGCT; significant liver toxicity - REMS programme); radiotherapy (adjuvant - for recurrent/unresectable). Note: recurrence common after incomplete synovectomy (diffuse TGCT); pexidartinib available in Australia via TGA - specialist use only.

conditions.name: Superficial siderosis
conditions.summary: Haemosiderin deposition in CNS leptomeninges and subpial tissues from chronic or recurrent subarachnoid bleeding. Pathophysiology: repeated microhaemorrhages → haemoglobin breakdown → haemosiderin deposits on pial surface → iron-mediated neurotoxicity (free radicals) → progressive neurodegeneration, especially cochlear nerve (VIII), cerebellum, cerebral cortex. Causes: spinal dural defect/tear (most common - CSF-venous fistula, post-surgical/traumatic), intradural tumour (ependymoma, schwannoma), vascular malformation, unknown (idiopathic). Classical triad: sensorineural hearing loss (bilateral, progressive - CN VIII most vulnerable), cerebellar ataxia (progressive), myelopathy (pyramidal signs). Ix (MRI): T2*/SWI - hypointense 'coating' of pial surfaces (brain surface, cranial nerves, cerebellum, spinal cord). Ix: MRI (characteristic T2* signal - 'rim of hemosiderin'); CSF (xanthochromia - chronic; siderophages; elevated ferritin); search for bleeding source (spinal MRI - dural defect). Mx: identify and treat bleeding source (surgical repair of dural defect - stops progression); chelation therapy (deferoxamine - limited evidence); supportive (hearing aids, rehabilitation). Note: progressive and often irreversible once symptomatic; early identification of source critical; now increasingly recognised cause - spinal dural CSF-venous fistula most common treatable cause.

conditions.name: Seborrhoeic keratosis
conditions.summary: Common benign epidermal tumour; clonal keratinocyte proliferation. Pathophysiology: FGFR3 and PIK3CA mutations in sporadic lesions; somatic. Epidemiology: extremely common; increases with age (>50 yr); sun-exposed and non-exposed sites; multiple lesions typical. Sx: well-demarcated, 'stuck-on' appearance; brown-black colour variation; warty/greasy surface; comedone-like openings (horn cysts on dermoscopy); painless; trunk, face, limbs. Sign of Leser-Trélat: sudden eruption of multiple SKs = rare paraneoplastic sign (GI malignancy - stomach, colon). Ix: clinical (dermoscopy - comedo-like openings, milia-like cysts, gyri/sulci pattern, sharply demarcated border); biopsy if melanoma excluded. Mx: reassurance (benign); removal for cosmesis or irritation (cryotherapy, curettage, electrocautery, laser). Note: no malignant potential; dermoscopy differentiates from melanoma (comedo openings - not melanoma); new rapid-onset multiple SKs → consider paraneoplastic workup.

conditions.name: Dermatofibroma
conditions.summary: Common benign dermal fibrohistiocytic tumour; spindle cell proliferation in dermis. Aetiology: unknown; possible reactive (insect bite, minor trauma - common history); some considered true neoplasms. Sx: firm, slightly raised or depressed, red-brown papule/nodule (4-10 mm); lower limbs (especially anterior shin) most common; dimple sign (Fitzpatrick sign - pinching = central dimpling as tumour tethered to dermis); mildly itchy; solitary typical; stable or slowly grow. Ix: clinical (dimple sign + dermoscopy - central white scar-like patch, peripheral pigment network); biopsy if atypical (distinguish from DFSP - dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans). Mx: none required; excision if symptomatic, large, or diagnostic uncertainty. Note: dimple/Fitzpatrick sign distinguishes from DFSP (DFSP protrudes on pinching - grows outward - locally aggressive); multiple DFs (>15) associated with SLE, HIV, myasthenia gravis.

conditions.name: Keloid
conditions.summary: Abnormal fibroproliferative scar tissue extending beyond original wound margins (keloid) or confined within wound (hypertrophic scar). Pathophysiology: dysregulated wound healing - excessive fibroblast activity, collagen deposition (predominantly type III → remodelled to type I); TGF-β overexpression; keloids: invade surrounding tissue, don't regress; hypertrophic scars: confined, may spontaneously regress. Risk factors: dark skin (Black, Asian, Hispanic - 15-20× risk vs fair skin); sites (sternum, shoulders, earlobes, mandible - 'high-tension' areas); genetics (family history); young adults; prior keloid. Sx: keloid - firm, rubbery, shiny plaque/nodule extending beyond wound; pruritus, pain, tenderness; earlobes (piercings - common), chest, shoulders; hypertrophic - raised red scar confined to wound; resolves over 1-2 yr. Mx: intralesional corticosteroid injection (triamcinolone - first-line; repeat at 4-6 wk); silicone gel sheets (prevention + treatment); pressure therapy; cryotherapy (effective for small keloids); excision (risk of recurrence - combine with adjuvant: steroid injection, RT); laser therapy; 5-fluorouracil (intralesional); low-dose superficial radiotherapy (post-excision - recalcitrant keloids). Note: keloid ≠ hypertrophic scar (grows beyond wound vs stays within); recurrence after excision alone very high (~50-100%) - always combine with adjuvant therapy.

conditions.name: Telogen effluvium
conditions.summary: Diffuse hair shedding from excessive premature shift of hair follicles from anagen (growth) to telogen (resting) phase. Pathophysiology: trigger → synchronised follicle shift to telogen → mass shedding 2-3 months after trigger; normally <15% follicles in telogen - TE: >25%. Acute causes: childbirth (most common - postpartum TE, 2-3 months post-delivery), febrile illness (COVID-19, influenza), major surgery, acute psychological stress, crash dieting, iron deficiency. Chronic causes: hypothyroidism, iron deficiency, malnutrition, medications (retinoids, anticoagulants, lithium, beta-blockers, OCP cessation). Sx: diffuse shedding (positive pull test - >6 hairs per pull), diffuse thinning (non-scarring - follicles intact), hair part widening; 100-300 hairs/day shed (normal <100); scalp not inflamed. Ix: clinical; FBC, iron studies, TFTs, ferritin, zinc (exclude underlying cause); scalp biopsy if uncertain (telogen:anagen ratio >25%); trichoscopy (empty follicles, decreased density). Mx: treat underlying cause; reassurance (self-limiting - regrowth within 6-12 months acute TE); iron supplementation (if deficient); nutritional optimisation. Note: spontaneous recovery within 6 months if trigger removed; distinguish from androgenetic alopecia (patterned, male/female pattern - miniaturisation on biopsy).

conditions.name: Androgenetic alopecia
conditions.summary: Commonest form of hair loss; androgen-dependent progressive follicular miniaturisation. Pathophysiology: genetically determined sensitivity to DHT (dihydrotestosterone - converted from testosterone by 5α-reductase in follicles) → follicle miniaturisation → shorter, finer vellus hairs; HLA-related predisposition. Males (Hamilton-Norwood): frontotemporal recession + vertex balding → confluence; Females (Ludwig): diffuse crown thinning (central part widening) - frontal hairline preserved (FPHL). Sx: males - temple recession + crown thinning; females - widening central part, crown thinning, preserved frontal hairline. Ix: clinical (pattern distribution); trichoscopy (follicular miniaturisation - variable hair shaft diameters, perifollicular pigmentation); biopsy if uncertain (miniaturised follicles, telogen:anagen >1). Mx: males - finasteride (5α-reductase inhibitor - 1 mg daily, effective; SE: sexual dysfunction, post-finasteride syndrome - rare but persistent); females - minoxidil topical (2% - first-line for women); both sexes - minoxidil topical/oral; low-level laser therapy; hair transplant (FUE - follicular unit extraction). Note: finasteride contraindicated in pregnancy/women of childbearing potential; dutasteride more potent than finasteride; treatment must be lifelong to maintain benefit.

conditions.name: Livedoid vasculopathy
conditions.summary: Occlusive vasculopathy of dermal vessels (NOT true vasculitis); painful lower leg ulceration with characteristic atrophie blanche scarring. Pathophysiology: thrombotic occlusion of superficial dermal vessels → ischaemia → ulceration → stellate white scars (atrophie blanche); association with thrombophilias (factor V Leiden, prothrombin mutation, antiphospholipid syndrome, hyperhomocysteinaemia) in ~50% and autoimmune disease (SLE, Sjögren's). Sx: recurrent, painful ulcers (lower legs, especially ankles); livedo reticularis (net-like mottling); atrophie blanche scars (porcelain-white stellate scars with telangiectasia - pathognomonic); summer exacerbation; young-middle-aged women. Ix: clinical + skin biopsy (hyaline thrombi in dermal vessels, fibrin deposition - no leucocytoclastic vasculitis); thrombophilia screen; ANA, APLA. Mx: anticoagulation (low-dose aspirin, low molecular weight heparin, warfarin, rivaroxaban - antiplatelet/anticoagulant); pentoxifylline, dipyridamole; hyperbaric oxygen; avoid venous stasis; vasodilators. Note: not a true vasculitis (no inflammation - occlusive); atrophie blanche = stellate white scar = pathognomonic; screen for thrombophilia in all patients; painful ulcers may be confused with pyoderma gangrenosum (PG - neutrophilic, pathergy positive).

conditions.name: Necrobiosis lipoidica
conditions.summary: Granulomatous dermopathy; strongly associated with diabetes mellitus. Pathophysiology: unknown; microangiopathy and collagen degeneration; possible immune-mediated mechanism; associated with T1DM most commonly (0.3-1%), T2DM less so; can precede diabetes diagnosis. Sx: bilateral pretibial plaques (lower legs - classic site); yellow-brown waxy plaques with telangiectasia; central atrophy + ulceration (prone to recurrent ulceration - traumatic); violaceous border; well-demarcated; slow progression. Ix: clinical; biopsy (full-thickness dermal granulomas - 'tier-like' arrangement, necrobiotic collagen, palisading histiocytes, plasma cells, telangiectasia). Mx: topical/intralesional corticosteroids (triamcinolone - ulcerated → avoid systemic steroids); tacrolimus; fumaric acid esters; anti-TNF (infliximab, adalimumab - severe); PUVA; wound care for ulcers; diabetic control (glycaemic control does not consistently alter NL course). Note: ulceration complicates ~35% (injury prone pretibial location); distinguish from pretibial myxoedema (hypothyroid, non-pitting oedema); association with diabetes - check glucose; glycaemic control doesn't reliably improve NL.

conditions.name: Hailey-Hailey disease
conditions.summary: Rare autosomal dominant blistering skin disorder from acantholysis. Pathophysiology: ATP2C1 mutation → defective Golgi Ca2+/Mn2+ pump (hSPCA1) → impaired intracellular calcium signalling → desmoglein processing failure → acantholysis (loss of keratinocyte cohesion) in superficial epidermis. Sx: recurrent erosions/crusted plaques in flexures (axillae, groins, inframammary, neck - friction + moisture areas); macerated, malodorous erosions; flares triggered by friction, heat, sweating, UV, infection (Candida, HSV, Staphylococcus); painful; onset 2nd-3rd decade; worsens in summer; blistering resolves over weeks → leaves hyper/hypopigmentation. Ix: skin biopsy (acantholysis in all epidermal layers - 'dilapidated brick wall'; no DIF [direct immunofluorescence] deposition - differentiates from pemphigus); ATP2C1 sequencing. Mx: avoid triggers (friction, heat, moisture control); antibacterial/antifungal cover (Staph/Candida); topical tacrolimus (non-steroidal maintenance); botulinum toxin (axillary - reduces sweating - effective); topical/oral antibiotics; laser ablation (CO2 laser); surgical dermabrasion (recalcitrant); retinoids. Note: confused with pemphigus vulgaris (DIF negative, acantholysis ALL layers, familial - ATP2C1); botulinum toxin for axillary disease - reduces sweating, reduces flares.

conditions.name: Pityriasis rubra pilaris
conditions.summary: Papulosquamous disorder characterised by salmon-orange erythroderma, follicular keratosis, and palmoplantar keratoderma. Classification (Griffiths): Type I (adult classical - 55%; cephalocaudal spread, islands of sparing, palm/sole orange hyperkeratosis; good prognosis - resolves 3 yr); Type III (juvenile classical - similar to Type I in children); Type II (adult atypical - chronic, ichthyosiform, alopecia); Type V (atypical juvenile - familial, CARD14 mutation - chronic; associated with CARD14-related papulosquamous eruption). Pathophysiology: idiopathic in most; CARD14 mutations (familial, Type V); association with HIV, internal malignancy (paraneoplastic PRP). Sx: follicular keratotic papules coalescing → orange-red scaly plaques with islands of normal skin (pathognomonic in Type I); palmoplantar orangey hyperkeratosis (PPK); cephalocaudal progression → erythroderma. Ix: clinical + biopsy (follicular plugging, alternating orthokeratosis/parakeratosis - 'chessboard pattern' on pathology). Mx: retinoids (acitretin - systemic - mainstay); methotrexate; cyclosporin; biologics (ustekinumab, TNF inhibitors - for refractory); PUVA. Note: 'islands of sparing' = pathognomonic (areas of normal skin within erythroderma); distinguish from psoriasis (islands of sparing, orange colour, follicular papules); Type I spontaneously remits; CARD14 mutation in familial.

conditions.name: Pityriasis lichenoides chronica
conditions.summary: Spectrum of T-cell-mediated papulosquamous disorders from acute ulceronecrotic (PLEVA) to chronic (PLC) forms. Pathophysiology: clonal CD8+ T-cell reaction (atypical T-cells in skin); some consider spectrum between inflammatory dermatosis and lymphoma (rare progression to lymphoma - MF/LyP); association with infections (parvovirus B19, EBV, HIV, Toxoplasma). PLC: chronic, scaling papules and plaques (months-years); trunk, proximal limbs; hyperpigmented/hypopigmented macules post-resolution; minimal symptoms; waxes and wanes. PLEVA (acute): abrupt onset; erythematous papulovesicles → haemorrhagic crusting → necrotic punched-out ulcers; systemic symptoms (fever - Mucha-Habermann disease - severe variant with fever, ulcers). Ix: biopsy (wedge-shaped T-cell infiltrate, epidermal spongiosis, lymphocyte exocytosis - CD8+ predominant; lichenoid pattern). Mx: tetracyclines (doxycycline - first-line - anti-inflammatory); NB-UVB phototherapy; methotrexate (PLEVA/severe PLC); topical steroids; observation (PLC often self-limiting). Note: risk of lymphoma transformation low but real (monitor for persistent clonal disease); distinguish from LyP (lymphomatoid papulosis - recurring, self-healing papules - CD30+; higher lymphoma risk).

conditions.name: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy
conditions.summary: Cholestatic liver disorder unique to pregnancy; associated with adverse perinatal outcomes. Pathophysiology: genetic predisposition (ABCB4, ABCB11, ATP8B1 - bile salt transporter mutations) + oestrogen/progesterone triggers → impaired bile acid transport → bile acid accumulation in maternal serum; bile acids cross placenta → fetal cardiac arrhythmia + placental dysfunction. Sx: pruritus (intense, characteristic - palms/soles, worse at night, no primary skin lesion - excoriation marks only), onset 2nd-3rd trimester; resolves within 2-4 wk postpartum; jaundice in <10%; dark urine, pale stools (cholestatic). Complications: stillbirth (association - risk increases with bile acids >40 μmol/L; sudden fetal death - mechanism unclear - cardiac arrhythmia likely), preterm birth (often iatrogenic), meconium-stained liquor, fetal distress, neonatal RDS. Ix: serum bile acids (>10 μmol/L - diagnostic; >40 μmol/L = high risk; measure fasting); ↑ALT/AST (mild-moderate); ↑bilirubin (variable); ↑GGT; exclude other causes (hepatitis, biliary obstruction, AFLP - acute fatty liver of pregnancy). Mx: ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA - mainstay; reduces bile acids, pruritus, improves LFTs; benefit on fetal outcomes debated - PITCH trial no mortality benefit but improves pruritus); early delivery (36-37 wk if bile acids >40 μmol/L; 38-39 wk if milder; individualised); fetal monitoring (CTG - though limitations for predicting sudden death). Note: recurs in future pregnancies (~60-70%); avoid OCP/progesterone-only pill in history of ICP; notify patient re: family members (inherited); bile acids >40 μmol/L = high-risk threshold for active delivery planning.

conditions.name: Vulvodynia
conditions.summary: Chronic vulvar pain without identifiable cause; multifactorial aetiology. Types: localised (vestibulodynia - most common - pain at vulvar vestibule, provoked by touch/penetration - dyspareunia, tampon insertion pain); generalised (unprovoked - constant aching/burning). Pathophysiology: peripheral sensitisation (increased vulvar nerve density - C-fibres); central sensitisation; pelvic floor hypertonicity; psychosocial factors (anxiety, depression, sexual dysfunction, relationship distress); prior genital trauma/surgery; hormonal changes (low oestrogen - atrophic changes). Diagnosis of exclusion: exclude infection (candida, herpes, STIs), dermatoses (lichen sclerosus, LP - biopsy if uncertain), neurological cause. Ix: cotton-swab test (Q-tip test - map pain on vestibule - allodynia); vulvoscopy; biopsy (only if lesion present - rule out dermatosis). Mx: multidisciplinary (pelvic floor physiotherapy - first-line; psychological/psychosexual therapy; topical lignocaine/lidocaine; low-dose TCAs [amitriptyline]/SNRIs [duloxetine]; gabapentin; vestibulectomy [surgical - for localised refractory vestibulodynia - 80% success]; hormonal: local oestrogen/testosterone cream). Note: frequently misdiagnosed as recurrent candidiasis or dismissed; pelvic floor physiotherapy essential component; vestibulectomy reserved for refractory localised vestibulodynia with demonstrated allodynia on Q-tip test.

conditions.name: Lichen sclerosus
conditions.summary: Chronic inflammatory skin disease causing atrophy, sclerosis, and architectural distortion; predominantly anogenital. Pathophysiology: autoimmune (Th1-mediated); HLA association; associated with other autoimmune disease (thyroid disease, vitiligo, RA - 20%); dysregulated autoantibodies to ECM-1 and BP180. Sites: vulva (most common in females - ~90% anogenital), glans penis/prepuce (balanitis xerotica obliterans - BXO, in males), anal, extragenital (wrists, upper back, neck - less common). Sx: females - intense pruritus (vulvar), pale white atrophic plaques ('white crinkled cigarette paper' appearance), figure-of-8 distribution (vulva + perianal), loss of labia minora architecture (resorption), clitoral hood fusion/phimosis; dyspareunia, dysuria, fissuring; males - BXO - white plaques glans/prepuce → phimosis → urinary obstruction. Complications: vulvar squamous cell carcinoma (SCC - 2-5% lifetime risk; closely linked to differentiated vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia [dVIN]); urinary/sexual dysfunction. Ix: clinical + biopsy (basal layer vacuolation, sclerosis - homogenised collagen, lichenoid infiltrate). Mx: ultra-potent topical corticosteroid (clobetasol propionate 0.05% - first-line; reduces symptoms + risks of SCC if used consistently; lifelong maintenance likely needed); tacrolimus (alternative steroid-sparing); regular surveillance (vulvoscopy annually - for VIN/SCC). Note: lifelong treatment required; annual surveillance essential (SCC risk); male BXO → circumcision + meatal dilatation if urinary obstruction; LS ≠ lichen planus (LS: pale, atrophic, figure-8; LP: violaceous, Wickham striae, erosive).

conditions.name: Lichen simplex chronicus
conditions.summary: Thickened lichenified skin from chronic scratching/rubbing cycle. Pathophysiology: itch-scratch cycle → epidermal hyperplasia (acanthosis, hypergranulosis) + lichenification (skin thickening with accentuated skin markings); may be primary (idiopathic itch) or secondary (superimposed on atopic eczema, contact dermatitis, psoriasis, lichen sclerosus). Sites: easily accessible areas - nape of neck (posterior), lower leg (shin), anogenital (vulva, scrotum - see vulvodynia overlap), ankle, forearm, scalp. Sx: intensely pruritic, well-demarcated, thickened, hyperpigmented plaques; exaggerated skin markings (lichenification); scratch marks/excoriations; psychological stress often exacerbating. Ix: clinical; biopsy if uncertain (psoriasiform hyperplasia, hypergranulosis, fibrosis - no diagnostic features). Mx: break the itch-scratch cycle - potent topical corticosteroids (occlusion enhances penetration); tacrolimus/pimecrolimus; sedating antihistamines (chlorphenamine - reduce nocturnal scratching); doxepin; psychotherapy (habit reversal, CBT); intralesional triamcinolone (refractory); address underlying skin condition. Note: often associated with anxiety/OCD spectrum; address psychological triggers; distinguish from psoriasis (silvery scale, Koebner, extensor distribution), plaque eczema (atopy history, family history).

conditions.name: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause
conditions.summary: Chronic, progressive hypoestrogenic changes affecting genitourinary tissues; replaced term 'atrophic vaginitis'. Pathophysiology: declining oestrogen (menopause, lactation, GNRH analogues, aromatase inhibitors, anti-oestrogens) → vaginal/vulvar epithelial atrophy + loss of glycogen → alkaline pH → dysbiosis (loss of lactobacilli) → symptoms; affects vulva, vagina, urethra, bladder. Sx: vaginal dryness, dyspareunia (superficial - most bothersome), vaginal discharge (watery/yellow), post-coital bleeding, vulvar pruritus/burning; urinary: frequency, urgency, recurrent UTIs, dysuria, urge incontinence; NOT associated with hot flushes (unlike vasomotor sx). Ix: clinical; pH >5 (vaginal pH >5 = atrophic); maturation index (VM - preponderance of parabasal cells); speculum (pale, smooth - loss of rugae, petechiae, friability). Mx: first-line - local/topical oestrogen (vaginal oestrogen - cream [Ovestin/Premarin], pessary, ring - highly effective, minimal systemic absorption - safe in most women including breast cancer survivors with caution); lubricants/moisturisers (non-hormonal - water-based lubricants for dyspareunia; hyaluronic acid moisturisers); systemic HRT (if systemic vasomotor sx also present); ospemifene (oral SERM - alternative if topical not tolerated); prasterone (vaginal DHEA). Note: GSM ≠ menopausal hot flushes (different mechanism - doesn't improve without treatment; hot flushes may resolve spontaneously); unlike vasomotor symptoms, GSM doesn't improve spontaneously - worsens without treatment; local oestrogen very safe - does not significantly raise serum oestrogen.

conditions.name: Cervical ectropion
conditions.summary: Eversion of columnar endocervical epithelium onto ectocervix (squamocolumnar junction visible on ectocervix); normal anatomical variant in many women. Pathophysiology: oestrogen-dependent - columnar epithelium 'rolls out'; physiological in: adolescents, pregnancy (most extensive), OCP users; regression after menopause (columnar epithelium recedes into endocervical canal). Sx: asymptomatic (most common - incidental finding on speculum exam); symptoms: post-coital bleeding (contact bleeding - common presenting complaint), excess vaginal discharge (cervical mucus from columnar cells); dyspareunia (less common); NO pain typically. Ix: speculum examination (salmon-pink/reddish area around os - granular/velvety - normal columnar mucosa); colposcopy (if atypical - acetic acid: no acetowhitening in ectropion; rule out CIN/cervical cancer); Pap smear/HPV test (routine cervical screening - not diagnostic for ectropion). Mx: most asymptomatic - reassurance (physiological); symptomatic post-coital bleeding - ablation (cryotherapy, cold coagulation - destroys columnar epithelium → squamous metaplasia); treat concurrent cervicitis (STI screen if discharge - gonorrhoea, chlamydia). Note: reassure patient - not cancer, not an 'erosion' (avoid term); post-coital bleeding always requires cervical smear + colposcopy to exclude CIN/cervical cancer before attributing to ectropion.

conditions.name: Uterine polyp
conditions.summary: Localised overgrowth of endometrial glands and stroma projecting into uterine cavity. Epidemiology: common (25% of women with abnormal uterine bleeding); perimenopausal women most affected; incidence increases with age; obesity, tamoxifen use, unopposed oestrogen are risk factors. Sx: abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) - intermenstrual bleeding most common (post-coital bleeding, heavy periods, postmenopausal bleeding - all warrant investigation); may be asymptomatic (incidental on USS). Complications: rarely malignant (~1-2% - endometrial carcinoma arising in polyp; higher with: postmenopausal bleeding, size >1.5 cm, obesity, tamoxifen use, diabetes). Ix: transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS - hyperechoic endometrial lesion ± colour Doppler single feeding vessel - 'pedicle artery sign'); saline infusion sonohysterography (SIS - best non-invasive); hysteroscopy (gold standard - direct visualisation + directed biopsy). Mx: hysteroscopic polypectomy (gold standard - resection + histology mandatory to exclude malignancy); watchful waiting (asymptomatic, small, premenopausal - may spontaneously regress); levonorgestrel IUD (reduces recurrence in premenopausal). Note: tamoxifen (breast cancer adjuvant) → uterine polyps + endometrial hyperplasia/cancer (stimulates endometrial oestrogen receptors); any postmenopausal bleeding → refer for investigation; hysteroscopic removal + histology required in all symptomatic.

conditions.name: Parametritis
conditions.summary: Infection/inflammation of parametrium (pelvic connective tissue lateral to uterus). Pathophysiology: spread from endometrium (endometritis) → parametrial connective tissue (broad ligament, cardinal ligaments) → cellulitis → abscess (if untreated). Causes: puerperal infection (post-partum/post-caesarean - most common context), post-abortion infection (post-procedural), PID extension (ascending genital tract infection). Organisms: polymicrobial (Group A Streptococcus, E. coli, Bacteroides - anaerobes, Group B Strep). Sx: fever (often high - 39-40°C), lower abdominal/pelvic pain, uterine tenderness (boggy), parametrial tenderness (on vaginal examination - 'board-like' parametrium laterally), tachycardia; risk of extension → pelvic/broad ligament abscess → sepsis, ileus. Ix: clinical + investigations (FBC - leucocytosis; CRP elevated; blood cultures; endocervical/high vaginal swab; USS pelvis - rule out abscess, though CT/MRI more sensitive for parametrial extension). Mx: IV antibiotics (broad-spectrum - IV ampicillin-sulbactam; or IV clindamycin + gentamicin - covers anaerobes + gram-negatives; continue IV until afebrile 24-48 h → oral step-down); drainage if abscess; surgical drainage if refractory. Note: distinguish from simple endometritis (uterine tenderness only - earlier stage - antibiotics resolve) vs parametritis (lateral extension - more serious - risk of abscess); postpartum fever + lateral parametrial tenderness = parametritis until proven otherwise.

conditions.name: Periprocedural bridging anticoagulation
conditions.summary: Decisions on holding/resuming anticoagulation around surgery or procedures. Risk-stratify thromboembolism risk vs procedural bleed risk. Mx: high thrombotic risk (mechanical mitral valve, recent VTE, AF + CHA2DS2-VASc ≥7 or recent stroke) → bridge with LMWH/UFH; low risk → simply hold. DOACs generally don't need bridging (short half-life). Resume post-op once haemostasis secured.

conditions.name: Statin-associated muscle symptoms
conditions.summary: Spectrum from myalgia (CK normal) to rare rhabdomyolysis. Mx: Most 'intolerance' is non-specific muscle symptoms; true statin-induced myopathy uncommon. Mx: hold statin, recheck CK, reintroduce same/alternative statin at lower dose or alternate-day dosing. Persistent: ezetimibe, bempedoic acid, PCSK9 inhibitor. Ix: Distinguish from immune-mediated necrotising myopathy (anti-HMGCR antibodies, persists after stopping).
utd: alternatives to statins lipid lowering therapy

conditions.name: Cardiac risk stratification
conditions.summary: Pre-operative assessment of perioperative MACE risk for non-cardiac surgery. Mx: Tools: RCRI (6 factors: high-risk surgery, IHD, HF, CVA, insulin-treated DM, Cr >2.0); NSQIP MICA. Functional capacity (METs ≥4 = good). Stress testing only if it would change management. Mx: Continue β-blockers/aspirin/statins; hold ACE-i morning of surgery (controversial).
utd: evaluation of cardiac risk prior to noncardiac surgery
revised cardiac risk index noncardiac surgery
perioperative beta blocker therapy noncardiac surgery

conditions.name: Refeeding syndrome
conditions.summary: Metabolic disturbance after reintroducing nutrition to malnourished/starved patient. Insulin surge → intracellular shift of phosphate, K, Mg → severe hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, thiamine deficiency. Sx: arrhythmia, HF, respiratory failure, encephalopathy, Wernicke. Mx: identify high-risk pre-feed; start at ≤10 kcal/kg/day, advance slowly over 4-7 days; replace electrolytes proactively; thiamine 200-300 mg IV before/with carbs.

conditions.name: Adult immunisation
conditions.summary: Routine adult vaccinations. Annual: influenza. One-off / boosters: Tdap (every 10 y), MMR (catch-up), varicella, HPV (≤26 y, shared decision 27-45), zoster (RZV ≥50 y), pneumococcal (PCV20 or PCV15+PPSV23 ≥65 y or comorbid), COVID. Ix: Special groups: meningococcal (asplenia, complement deficiency, college dorms), Hep B (DM, CKD, MSM, healthcare). Travel + occupational additions as indicated.

conditions.name: Driving and seizures
conditions.summary: Seizure-free interval requirements before driving vary by jurisdiction (commonly 6-12 mo for private; longer for commercial/HGV). Provoked seizure with reversible cause may have shorter ban. Doctors have a duty to counsel + (in some jurisdictions) report. Document discussion. Aircraft/diving/heavy machinery rules differ. Patient should self-report to licensing authority.
utd: driving restrictions for patients with seizures epilepsy

conditions.name: Approach to anaemia
conditions.summary: Stepwise workup of anaemia. Ix: Classify by MCV: microcytic (iron deficiency, thalassaemia, anaemia of chronic disease, sideroblastic), normocytic (acute blood loss, haemolysis, ACD, CKD, marrow failure), macrocytic (B12/folate, alcohol, hypothyroidism, MDS, drugs). Reticulocyte count: ↑ = haemolysis/blood loss, ↓ = production failure. Ix: Iron studies, B12/folate, TFTs, peripheral smear, BM biopsy if unexplained.
utd: approach to the adult with anemia

conditions.name: Polypharmacy and deprescribing
conditions.summary: Concurrent use of ≥5 medications, common in older adults. Risks: ADRs, interactions, falls, cognitive impairment, non-adherence, prescribing cascade. Ix: Tools: Beers Criteria, STOPP/START, Medication Appropriateness Index. Approach: medication reconciliation at every transition, deprescribe one drug at a time, monitor for withdrawal effects. High-yield candidates: anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, PPIs (long-term), antipsychotics for BPSD.
utd: beers criteria potentially inappropriate medication use older adults

descriptive.name: Macule
descriptive.summary: Flat, circumscribed change in skin colour, under 1 cm, with no elevation or depression - visible but not palpable. Note: a flat lesion 1 cm or larger is a patch.

descriptive.name: Patch
descriptive.summary: Flat, circumscribed colour change 1 cm or larger. The large-lesion counterpart of a macule; vitiligo and melasma are typical examples.

descriptive.name: Papule
descriptive.summary: Solid, raised lesion under 1 cm. Palpable elevation is what separates it from a macule. Note: a raised solid lesion 1 cm or larger is a plaque if flat-topped and broad, or a nodule if deep and rounded.

descriptive.name: Plaque
descriptive.summary: Raised, flat-topped lesion 1 cm or larger - broader than it is deep. Classically psoriasis. Formed either de novo or by papules coalescing.

descriptive.name: Nodule
descriptive.summary: Solid, palpable lesion 1 cm or larger extending into the dermis or subcutis - deeper than it is wide, which is the distinction from a plaque. Erythema nodosum and rheumatoid nodules are typical.

descriptive.name: Vesicle
descriptive.summary: Fluid-filled blister under 1 cm. Herpes simplex, varicella and acute eczema are typical. Note: 1 cm or larger is a bulla.

descriptive.name: Bulla
descriptive.summary: Fluid-filled blister 1 cm or larger. Bullous pemphigoid, pemphigus vulgaris and burns. Note: in respiratory medicine the same word means an air-filled emphysematous space in lung.

descriptive.name: Pustule
descriptive.summary: Circumscribed lesion containing purulent material. Not necessarily infected - the pus of acne and of pustular psoriasis is sterile inflammatory exudate.

descriptive.name: Wheal
descriptive.summary: Transient, oedematous, raised lesion from dermal fluid extravasation, typically pruritic and resolving within 24 hours. The lesion of urticaria. Note: individual wheals lasting beyond 24 hours or leaving bruising suggests urticarial vasculitis.

descriptive.name: Cyst
descriptive.summary: Epithelium-lined cavity containing fluid or semi-solid material. Palpably fluctuant, which distinguishes it from a nodule.

descriptive.name: Comedone
descriptive.summary: Plugged pilosebaceous follicle - the primary lesion of acne, and the lesion that defines it as acne. Types: closed (whitehead) where the follicular opening is covered, so contents stay pale; open (blackhead) where the opening is dilated and the plug darkens through melanin oxidation, not dirt. Note: comedonal acne responds to topical retinoids, which act on the plug itself; benzoyl peroxide and antibiotics target the inflammatory component instead.

descriptive.name: Scale
descriptive.summary: Visible accumulation or shedding of stratum corneum from abnormal keratinisation or increased epidermal turnover. Note: desquamation specifically means sheet-like shedding, as after scarlet fever, toxic shock syndrome or a burn.

descriptive.name: Crust
descriptive.summary: Dried serum, blood or pus on the skin surface - a scab. Golden or honey-coloured crust is characteristic of impetigo.

descriptive.name: Excoriation
descriptive.summary: Linear or punctate erosion produced by scratching. Note: its presence is objective evidence of pruritus, which is useful when itch is being reported rather than observed.

descriptive.name: Lichenification
descriptive.summary: Thickened skin with accentuated surface markings, caused by chronic rubbing or scratching. Indicates a process running for weeks to months - chronic atopic dermatitis, lichen simplex chronicus.

descriptive.name: Erosion
descriptive.summary: Loss of epidermis only, with the basement membrane intact. Heals without scarring, which is the clinically useful distinction from an ulcer.

descriptive.name: Ulcer
descriptive.summary: Full-thickness loss of epidermis extending into dermis or deeper. Heals with scarring. Note: whether a lesion ulcerates is often the pivotal discriminator - erythema nodosum does not ulcerate, which separates it from nodular vasculitis.

descriptive.name: Fissure
descriptive.summary: Linear split through epidermis into dermis, typically in thickened or dehydrated skin over a flexural or weight-bearing site. Painful and slow to heal.

descriptive.name: Epidermal atrophy
descriptive.summary: Thinning of the skin from loss of tissue substance. Epidermal atrophy gives translucent, finely wrinkled skin; dermal atrophy gives a depression. Note: the commonest cause in practice is potent topical corticosteroid, particularly on the face or flexures.

descriptive.name: Induration
descriptive.summary: Abnormal firmness of the skin and subcutis on palpation, from inflammatory infiltrate, oedema or fibrosis. Note: it is a palpated sign, not a visual one - the measured diameter in tuberculin skin testing is of induration, not of erythema.

descriptive.name: Xerosis
descriptive.summary: Abnormally dry skin, with a rough or scaly surface and often fine fissuring. Common in the elderly, in atopic dermatitis, and with hypothyroidism or chronic kidney disease. A leading cause of pruritus with no primary rash.

descriptive.name: Hyperkeratosis
descriptive.summary: Thickening of the stratum corneum. Orthokeratotic when the cells are anucleate; parakeratotic when nuclei are retained, as in psoriasis, indicating accelerated epidermal turnover.

descriptive.name: Acanthosis
descriptive.summary: Thickening of the epidermal stratum spinosum. Note: distinct from acanthosis nigricans, which is a clinical pattern of velvety hyperpigmented flexural skin associated with insulin resistance and, less often, internal malignancy.

descriptive.name: Spongiosis
descriptive.summary: Intercellular oedema within the epidermis, separating keratinocytes so the tissue looks sponge-like. The histological hallmark of eczematous dermatitis.

descriptive.name: Erythema
descriptive.summary: Redness from dilatation of dermal blood vessels. Blanches on pressure - the single most useful bedside test, because it separates erythema from extravasated blood. Note: non-blanching redness is purpura and demands a different differential entirely, including meningococcal sepsis.

descriptive.name: Violaceous
descriptive.summary: Violet or purple-tinged discolouration. Suggests a deeper or more established vascular process than bright erythema. Note: characteristic of the Gottron papules and heliotrope eruption of dermatomyositis, and of lichen planus.

descriptive.name: Telangiectasia
descriptive.summary: Permanently dilated small superficial vessels, visible as fine red linear or web-like threads. Blanch on pressure and refill immediately. Causes: rosacea, chronic sun damage, topical corticosteroid, systemic sclerosis, hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, chronic liver disease.

descriptive.name: Poikiloderma
descriptive.summary: A composite sign, not a single change: hyperpigmentation plus hypopigmentation plus telangiectasia plus epidermal atrophy, together in one area. Note: photodistributed poikiloderma is a recognised sign of dermatomyositis - the shawl sign over the upper back, the V sign over the anterior neck, and the Holster sign on the lateral thigh. Also seen in mycosis fungoides and after chronic radiation.

descriptive.name: Hyperpigmentation
descriptive.summary: Increased skin pigmentation, from more melanin or from deposition of another pigment. Causes: post-inflammatory change (commonest), melasma, Addison disease, haemochromatosis, amiodarone, minocycline.

descriptive.name: Hypopigmentation
descriptive.summary: Reduced skin pigmentation with some melanin remaining. Note: complete absence of pigment is depigmentation, as in vitiligo, and the distinction matters - hypopigmentation is usually post-inflammatory and reversible.

descriptive.name: Purpura
descriptive.summary: Extravasation of blood into skin or mucosa, producing discolouration that does not blanch on pressure. Types: by size, petechiae under 3 mm, purpura 3 mm to 1 cm, ecchymoses larger. By mechanism, palpable purpura implies vessel-wall inflammation. Causes: thrombocytopenia, platelet dysfunction, vasculitis, meningococcaemia, senile or corticosteroid purpura, scurvy. Red flags: palpable purpura, or purpura with fever, warrants urgent assessment - vasculitis and meningococcal sepsis both present this way.

descriptive.name: Petechiae
descriptive.summary: Pinpoint non-blanching haemorrhages under 3 mm. Typically reflect a platelet problem - low count or poor function - rather than a coagulation-factor deficiency, which tends to bleed into joints and muscle instead.

descriptive.name: Ecchymosis
descriptive.summary: Extravasated blood larger than 1 cm - a bruise. Colour evolves through red to purple, then green and yellow as haemoglobin is broken down, which allows rough ageing of the injury.

descriptive.name: Livedo reticularis
descriptive.summary: Net-like or lacy violaceous mottling from sluggish flow in the dermal venous plexus. Note: benign and cold-induced when it resolves on warming (cutis marmorata); persistent or broken-ringed livedo racemosa suggests antiphospholipid syndrome, vasculitis or cholesterol embolism.

descriptive.name: Myalgia
descriptive.summary: Muscle pain. A symptom the patient reports, carrying no implication of muscle damage on its own. Note: myalgia with weakness and a raised creatine kinase suggests myositis; myalgia with normal strength and normal CK is far more often viral, drug-related (statins) or part of a chronic pain syndrome.

descriptive.name: Arthralgia
descriptive.summary: Joint pain without objective signs of inflammation. Note: the contrast with arthritis is deliberate and worth preserving in your own writing - arthritis requires swelling, warmth, erythema or effusion on examination. Many rheumatological criteria sets score the two differently.

descriptive.name: Myositis
descriptive.summary: Inflammation of skeletal muscle, producing proximal weakness with a raised creatine kinase. Types: dermatomyositis, polymyositis, immune-mediated necrotising myopathy, inclusion body myositis (distal and asymmetric, and characteristically treatment-resistant).

descriptive.name: Panniculitis
descriptive.summary: Inflammation of subcutaneous fat, presenting as tender deep nodules. Classification: septal, where inflammation tracks the fibrous septa - erythema nodosum is the archetype; or lobular, involving the fat lobule itself. Whether vasculitis is present subdivides each.

descriptive.name: Pathognomonic
descriptive.summary: A finding whose presence establishes the diagnosis on its own - specificity approaching 100 percent. Note: this says nothing about sensitivity, and genuinely pathognomonic signs are rare and usually uncommon, so absence is close to worthless. Gottron papules in dermatomyositis and Koplik spots in measles are real examples; most signs called pathognomonic in teaching are merely highly suggestive.

descriptive.name: Constitutional symptoms
descriptive.summary: Systemic, non-localising symptoms: fever, night sweats, unintentional weight loss, fatigue, anorexia and malaise. Note: B symptoms is the narrower lymphoma-staging term - fever above 38 degrees, drenching night sweats, or loss of more than 10 percent body weight over six months - and it changes the stage suffix, so it is not a synonym.

descriptive.name: Malaise
descriptive.summary: A generalised sense of being unwell, without localisation. Non-specific but not meaningless: new persistent malaise in an older patient warrants a broad rather than a narrow work-up.

descriptive.name: Prodrome
descriptive.summary: Early non-specific symptoms preceding the characteristic features of an illness. Note: often the only phase in which intervention still changes the course - antivirals in herpes zoster, triptans in migraine.

descriptive.name: Insidious onset
descriptive.summary: Gradual onset over weeks to months, without a point the patient can identify as the start. Contrasts with acute onset, which is often datable to the hour, and distinguishing the two frequently narrows the differential more than any single sign.

descriptive.name: Proximal
descriptive.summary: Nearer the trunk. Note: proximal weakness has a specific bedside meaning - difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs, or reaching above the head, i.e. hip and shoulder girdle. It points to myopathy, whereas distal weakness points to neuropathy.

descriptive.name: Symmetrical
descriptive.summary: Affecting both sides of the body comparably. Note: symmetry is often the discriminating feature rather than a descriptive aside - symmetrical small-joint arthritis suggests rheumatoid arthritis, asymmetrical large-joint suggests spondyloarthritis; symmetrical proximal weakness suggests myositis.

descriptive.name: Haematemesis
descriptive.summary: Vomiting blood, indicating bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz. Bright red suggests brisk bleeding; coffee-ground appearance suggests blood altered by gastric acid and therefore slower or stopped.

descriptive.name: Melaena
descriptive.summary: Black, tarry, offensively-smelling stool from digested blood - usually an upper gastrointestinal source, and requiring only about 50 mL of blood. Note: iron and bismuth darken stool without the tarry texture or the characteristic smell, and this is a common source of false alarm.

descriptive.name: Haematochezia
descriptive.summary: Fresh blood passed per rectum, usually a lower gastrointestinal source. Note: a brisk upper GI bleed can present this way, so haematochezia with haemodynamic instability should not be assumed to be lower-tract.

descriptive.name: Normocytic anaemia
descriptive.summary: Anaemia with a normal mean cell volume, roughly 80 to 100 fL. Causes: anaemia of chronic disease or inflammation (commonest), acute blood loss before the marrow responds, chronic kidney disease, marrow failure, haemolysis, mixed deficiency where a low and a high MCV cancel out. Note: the reticulocyte count splits this quickly - low means underproduction, high means loss or destruction.

descriptive.name: Microcytic anaemia
descriptive.summary: Anaemia with MCV below about 80 fL. Causes: iron deficiency (commonest by a wide margin), thalassaemia, anaemia of chronic disease, sideroblastic anaemia, lead poisoning. Note: iron studies distinguish iron deficiency from thalassaemia trait; a normal or high ferritin with microcytosis and a normal red cell count is not iron deficiency.

descriptive.name: Macrocytic anaemia
descriptive.summary: Anaemia with MCV above about 100 fL. Types: megaloblastic, from B12 or folate deficiency or antifolate drugs, with hypersegmented neutrophils; and non-megaloblastic, from alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, myelodysplasia or reticulocytosis.

descriptive.name: Reactive thrombocytosis
descriptive.summary: Platelet count above the reference range as an acute-phase response rather than a marrow disorder. Causes: infection, inflammation, tissue injury or surgery, iron deficiency, malignancy, post-splenectomy. Note: distinguished from essential thrombocythaemia, which is clonal and carries genuine thrombotic risk; reactive thrombocytosis rarely does and needs no specific treatment.

descriptive.name: Leukocytosis
descriptive.summary: Raised total white cell count. Note: the differential carries the information, not the total - neutrophilia suggests bacterial infection, inflammation or corticosteroid effect; lymphocytosis suggests viral infection or chronic lymphocytic leukaemia; eosinophilia suggests atopy, parasites or drug reaction.

descriptive.name: Left shift
descriptive.summary: Increased circulating immature neutrophils, chiefly band forms, reflecting accelerated marrow release. Supports significant bacterial infection or another strong inflammatory stimulus.

descriptive.name: Acute phase reactant
descriptive.summary: Plasma protein whose concentration shifts substantially with inflammation, driven largely by IL-6. Types: positive reactants rise - CRP, ferritin, fibrinogen, haptoglobin, complement; negative reactants fall - albumin, transferrin. Note: this is why ferritin is unreliable for iron status during inflammation, and why albumin drops in illness without malnutrition.

drug_summaries.amiodarone: Class III antiarrhythmic that in practice blocks all four Vaughan Williams classes. MOA: prolongs repolarisation by potassium channel blockade, with sodium channel, beta and calcium channel effects on top. Indications: shock-refractory VF and pulseless VT; haemodynamically stable VT; rhythm control in atrial fibrillation, including where structural heart disease rules out flecainide. Half-life 50 to 100 days with an enormous volume of distribution, so it needs loading, and both its effect and its toxicity persist for months after the last dose. SE: the molecule is 37% iodine by weight, so thyroid disease is common in both directions - hypothyroidism is usually managed with thyroxine while continuing the drug, whereas thyrotoxicosis splits into iodine-induced type 1 and a destructive thyroiditis type 2 treated with corticosteroid. Also pulmonary toxicity and fibrosis, presenting as dry cough and exertional dyspnoea; hepatitis; near-universal corneal microdeposits; a slate-grey photosensitive skin discolouration; optic and peripheral neuropathy; bradycardia. Interactions: roughly doubles digoxin levels and markedly potentiates warfarin, so both doses come down when amiodarone starts; raises statin myopathy risk. Monitoring: TFTs and LFTs at baseline and six-monthly, chest imaging at baseline and if symptomatic, ECG.
drug_summaries.aripiprazole: Atypical antipsychotic and dopamine system stabiliser. MOA: D2 PARTIAL agonist, so it behaves as an antagonist where dopamine is high and an agonist where it is low, with 5-HT2A antagonism and 5-HT1A partial agonism alongside. Indications: schizophrenia; bipolar mania; adjunct in major depression; irritability in autism; Tourette syndrome. SE: akathisia is the signature effect and the reason patients stop it - an inner restlessness that reads as anxiety or agitation, is often answered with a dose increase, and gets worse when it is. Treat by reducing the dose, and propranolol helps. Nausea, insomnia and headache early on. Red flags: impulse control disorders - pathological gambling, hypersexuality, compulsive shopping and binge eating - carry a TGA warning and resolve on withdrawal. Patients almost never volunteer them, so ask directly at review. Note: metabolically the most favourable of the atypicals and close to prolactin-sparing, which is what earns it a place despite the akathisia. Because it is a partial agonist, switching to it abruptly from a full antagonist can precipitate rebound psychosis and agitation - cross-taper.
drug_summaries.aspirin: Antiplatelet at low dose, NSAID at high dose. MOA: irreversibly acetylates COX-1, so thromboxane A2 production is gone for that platelet's whole 7 to 10 day life while nucleated endothelium simply makes more enzyme - that asymmetry is the entire basis of low-dose selectivity, and it is why the effect outlasts the drug. Indications: acute coronary syndrome, loading dose then daily; secondary prevention after MI, ischaemic stroke or in peripheral arterial disease; dual antiplatelet therapy after stenting; low dose nocte from early pregnancy for pre-eclampsia prophylaxis in women at high risk. Not routine for primary prevention - the bleeding cost outweighs the benefit in most people. SE: gastric erosion and upper GI bleeding, dyspepsia, bronchospasm in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, which runs with asthma and nasal polyps; tinnitus at high dose. CI: children and adolescents with a viral illness, because of Reye syndrome; active bleeding; third trimester. Note: salicylate overdose gives a respiratory alkalosis and a metabolic acidosis together, with tinnitus, hyperventilation and hyperthermia. Because inhibition is irreversible, stopping it days before surgery does not restore platelet function immediately.
drug_summaries.beclometasone: Inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) - a preventer, not a reliever. MOA: beclometasone dipropionate is a prodrug, hydrolysed in airway tissue to active 17-BMP; glucocorticoid receptor binding suppresses NF-kB driven transcription, reducing airway eosinophilic inflammation and bronchial hyperresponsiveness over days to weeks. It does nothing acutely. Indications: asthma preventer therapy in adults and children. Dose: the extrafine HFA formulation (about 1.1 micrometre particles) deposits far better in small airways and is roughly twice as potent as the older CFC product, so its dose bands are about half those of budesonide - read the Australian Asthma Handbook table rather than converting between ICS by eye, because that error runs in both directions. SE: oral candidiasis and dysphonia, both largely preventable by rinsing and spitting after use and by a spacer; at high dose and long duration, adrenal suppression, reduced bone mineral density, cataract, glaucoma, and a small reduction in growth velocity in children that is mostly recovered. Note: Australian practice for mild asthma has moved away from short-acting beta agonist alone toward as-needed ICS-formoterol, and beclometasone monotherapy is not a maintenance-and-reliever product - if a patient is using it that way, the regimen is wrong rather than the dose.
drug_summaries.carbamazepine: Anticonvulsant, mood stabiliser and first-line drug for trigeminal neuralgia. MOA: use-dependent blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels, reducing high-frequency repetitive firing. Indications: focal seizures; trigeminal neuralgia; bipolar disorder second line. CI: absence and myoclonic seizures and generalised epilepsies such as JME, which it aggravates - prescribing it for an undifferentiated generalised epilepsy makes the patient worse. Screening: test HLA-B*1502 before starting in patients of Han Chinese, Thai, Malay or other South-East Asian ancestry - the allele carries a large increase in SJS and TEN risk. SE: rash in 5 to 10%, DRESS, dose-related hyponatraemia from SIADH that is worse in the elderly, benign leucopenia commonly and aplastic anaemia rarely, neural tube defects in pregnancy. Interactions: a potent CYP3A4, 2C9 and UGT inducer - lowers combined oral contraceptives to the point of contraceptive failure, and lowers warfarin, the DOACs, lamotrigine and quetiapine. It also induces its own metabolism over two to four weeks, so a dose that worked initially stops working. FBC, LFTs and sodium at baseline and periodically.
drug_summaries.ceftriaxone: Third-generation cephalosporin. MOA: beta lactam binding penicillin-binding proteins to block cell wall cross-linking. Indications: community-acquired pneumonia requiring admission; pyelonephritis; bacterial meningitis, where it crosses inflamed meninges well and is given with dexamethasone in adults; gonorrhoea as a single IM dose; septic arthritis and cellulitis with atypical risk; empirical cover in sepsis of unknown source. Note: once-daily dosing and biliary as well as renal excretion, so no dose adjustment in renal impairment - which together with the long half-life is why it suits home and outpatient parenteral therapy. CI: neonates, in whom it displaces bilirubin from albumin and risks kernicterus, and it must never be co-administered with calcium-containing fluids in that group. SE: rash, diarrhoea including C. difficile, biliary sludging that can mimic cholecystitis, and rarely haemolysis. Red flags: it does not cover Pseudomonas, Listeria or MRSA - so meningitis in the elderly, pregnant or immunosuppressed needs benzylpenicillin added for Listeria, and cross-reactivity with penicillin allergy is real but much lower than the traditional 10% figure.
drug_summaries.clozapine: Atypical antipsychotic (dibenzodiazepine) and the only agent with proven superiority in treatment-resistant schizophrenia. MOA: low-affinity, rapidly dissociating D2 antagonism plus 5-HT2A, D4, H1, M1 and alpha-1 blockade - the loose D2 binding is why it causes almost no EPS and no hyperprolactinaemia. Indications: treatment-resistant schizophrenia after two adequate antipsychotic trials; persistent suicidality in schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder; psychosis in Parkinson disease. Monitoring: FBC at baseline, WEEKLY for 18 weeks, then every 28 days for as long as the drug continues, through a mandatory monitoring service. Amber is neutrophils 1.5 to 2.0 or WCC 3.0 to 3.5 and means twice-weekly counts; red is neutrophils below 1.5 or WCC below 3.0 and means cease immediately with no rechallenge. Troponin and CRP at baseline and weekly for the first four weeks. SE: agranulocytosis, highest between weeks 6 and 18; myocarditis, peaking in weeks 2 to 3; dose-related seizures above about 600 mg daily; the worst metabolic burden of any antipsychotic; constipation progressing to ileus, which kills more patients than agranulocytosis does and warrants prophylactic aperients; hypersalivation, sedation, postural hypotension and tachycardia on titration. Note: a CYP1A2 substrate, so stopping smoking removes an inducer and levels can nearly double within days - a patient admitted to a smoke-free ward is the classic presentation. A break of over 48 hours requires full retitration.
drug_summaries.diazepam: Long-acting benzodiazepine. MOA: positive allosteric modulation at the GABA-A benzodiazepine site, increasing the FREQUENCY of chloride channel opening - it needs GABA already present, which is why it has a ceiling that barbiturates do not. Indications: alcohol withdrawal, symptom-triggered; status epilepticus; muscle spasm and spasticity; short-term severe anxiety. Half-life is long and its active metabolites longer still, so it accumulates - a single dose is short-acting because the drug redistributes out of the brain, not because it has left the body. In alcohol withdrawal that long tail is a feature, since the drug self-tapers; in an older patient or in liver disease it is the problem, and oxazepam or lorazepam are the ones to reach for because they are only glucuronidated. SE: sedation, anterograde amnesia, falls and hip fractures in the elderly, respiratory depression when combined with opioids or alcohol, paradoxical disinhibition, and tolerance and dependence within weeks of regular use. Note: never stop abruptly after regular use - withdrawal causes seizures and delirium. Flumazenil is rarely the right answer and precipitates seizures in a dependent or mixed overdose.
drug_summaries.doxycycline: Tetracycline. MOA: binds the 30S subunit and blocks aminoacyl-tRNA docking; bacteriostatic, with broad activity including the intracellular organisms that beta lactams cannot reach. Indications: atypical and community-acquired pneumonia; chlamydia and pelvic inflammatory disease; Q fever, rickettsial infection, leptospirosis, melioidosis eradication and Lyme disease; acne and rosacea; malaria prophylaxis; COPD exacerbation. SE: photosensitivity, which matters in Australia and needs saying out loud; pill-induced oesophagitis, so take it upright with a full glass of water and not at bedtime; nausea; candidiasis; benign intracranial hypertension. CI: pregnancy, breastfeeding and children under eight, because it chelates calcium in developing bone and teeth and causes permanent discolouration. Interactions: absorption is blocked by calcium, iron, magnesium and antacids, so separate them by at least two hours - a genuinely common reason for apparent treatment failure. Note: unlike other tetracyclines it is safe in renal impairment, being cleared largely through the gut.
drug_summaries.estradiol: Oestrogen (17-beta-estradiol), identical to the principal premenopausal ovarian oestrogen. MOA: agonist at nuclear oestrogen receptors alpha and beta; restores hypothalamic-pituitary feedback and reverses target-tissue atrophy. Indications: menopausal hormone therapy for vasomotor and genitourinary symptoms; premature ovarian insufficiency and hypogonadism, where it is replacement rather than treatment and continues to the average age of menopause; feminising gender-affirming hormone therapy. Route: transdermal patch or gel is preferred - it bypasses first-pass metabolism, so it does not raise VTE risk the way oral oestrogen does, and it is the clear choice with obesity, migraine or thrombotic risk. CI: oestrogen-dependent malignancy, undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, active VTE or arterial thrombosis, active liver disease. SE: breast tenderness, nausea, headache, breakthrough bleeding. Note: an intact uterus mandates a progestogen, because unopposed oestrogen causes endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma - micronised progesterone nightly, or cyclically for 12 to 14 days a month if a withdrawal bleed is acceptable. Australian notes: `estradiol` is the current Australian Approved Name, filed by the TGA as a minor spelling change; wards and exam papers still write oestradiol, and both resolve.
drug_summaries.furosemide: Loop diuretic. MOA: inhibits NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, abolishing the medullary concentrating gradient and producing the most potent natriuresis available. In acute pulmonary oedema it also venodilates within minutes, before any diuresis, which is why the patient improves before the catheter bag fills. Indications: acute pulmonary oedema; congestion in chronic heart failure; oedema in nephrotic syndrome and cirrhosis; hypercalcaemia once the patient is volume-replete. Dose: oral bioavailability is about half and highly variable, so the IV dose is roughly half the oral one. The drug only works from inside the tubular lumen, reached by active secretion, so anything competing for that transporter - NSAIDs in particular - or a low albumin blunts the response. That is most of what is meant by diuretic resistance. SE: hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyponatraemia, metabolic alkalosis, hyperuricaemia and gout, hypovolaemia and prerenal AKI, hyperglycaemia, and ototoxicity with rapid IV administration, high doses or concurrent aminoglycosides. Monitoring: electrolytes, renal function, daily weight and fluid balance.
drug_summaries.gentamicin: Aminoglycoside, active against aerobic Gram negatives including Pseudomonas, and synergistic with a beta lactam against enterococci and staphylococci. MOA: irreversibly binds the 30S ribosomal subunit causing misreading; uptake is oxygen-dependent, hence no anaerobic activity, and impaired in the acidic environment of an abscess. Concentration-dependent killing with a long post-antibiotic effect, which is the rationale for once-daily dosing. Indications: severe Gram-negative sepsis, usually empirically and for a short course; pyelonephritis; surgical prophylaxis; infective endocarditis in combination. Dose: on lean or adjusted body weight, with renal function and levels guiding subsequent doses - a trough that has not fallen means the drug has not cleared, not that the dose was small. SE: nephrotoxicity, typically non-oliguric and usually reversible; ototoxicity, both cochlear and vestibular, which is NOT reversible and is the reason short courses are the rule; rarely neuromuscular blockade. Note: risk rises with duration, concurrent loop diuretics, vancomycin, contrast and pre-existing renal impairment. Beyond 48 to 72 hours, the question is whether it can stop rather than what the next dose is.
drug_summaries.haloperidol: High-potency typical antipsychotic (butyrophenone). MOA: potent D2 antagonism, and the four dopamine pathways explain the whole side-effect profile - mesolimbic blockade is the antipsychotic effect, nigrostriatal blockade the extrapyramidal effects, tuberoinfundibular blockade the prolactin rise. Indications: schizophrenia; acute behavioural disturbance; short-term in hyperactive delirium at the lowest dose; Tourette; intractable nausea in palliative care. CI: Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies, where sensitivity reactions can be severe and prolonged.
