SE: acute dystonia within hours to days, reversed with benzatropine; akathisia, an inner restlessness that is repeatedly mistaken for worsening agitation and treated by raising the dose, which makes it worse; drug-induced parkinsonism over weeks; tardive dyskinesia over months to years, which may not reverse. Hyperprolactinaemia gives galactorrhoea and reduced bone density. Red flags: dose-related QT prolongation, worst with the IV route - check the ECG and correct potassium and magnesium. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is fever, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability and a raised CK, and it is a stop-the-drug emergency. Note: antipsychotics raise mortality and stroke risk in dementia.
drug_summaries.heparin: Unfractionated heparin, an indirect parenteral anticoagulant. MOA: binds antithrombin and accelerates it roughly a thousandfold against thrombin (IIa) and factor Xa. Inhibiting thrombin needs the long saccharide chain to bridge both molecules, which is the structural reason UFH inhibits IIa and Xa about equally while the shorter low molecular weight heparins are far more Xa-selective. Indications: where anticoagulation may need to be switched off quickly or renal function is poor - the half-life is about an hour and it is not renally cleared, so it is preferred in severe renal impairment, around surgery and in the unstable patient. Monitoring: APTT ratio or anti-Xa on an infusion. LMWH needs no routine monitoring, which is most of why it displaced UFH. SE: bleeding; heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, an immune-mediated PROTHROMBOTIC platelet fall around day 5 to 10 that must not be treated with platelet transfusion and requires stopping all heparin including flushes; osteoporosis with prolonged use; hyperkalaemia from aldosterone suppression. Note: protamine reverses UFH fully and LMWH only partially.
drug_summaries.hydrocortisone: Short-acting glucocorticoid, and the reference against which the others are measured. MOA: binds both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid receptors - the substantial mineralocorticoid activity is precisely why it is the REPLACEMENT steroid rather than an anti-inflammatory one. 20 mg hydrocortisone is equivalent to 5 mg prednisolone. Indications: adrenal insufficiency, given in divided doses with the larger dose on waking to approximate the diurnal rhythm; adrenal crisis, as a bolus followed by regular dosing alongside aggressive fluid resuscitation; severe asthma; as an adjunct after adrenaline in anaphylaxis, where it does nothing acutely and must never delay or replace the adrenaline; topically in eczema. Note: in suspected adrenal crisis, treat first and confirm later - but hydrocortisone cross-reacts in the cortisol assay and dexamethasone does not, so if the diagnosis genuinely has to be established, dexamethasone is the steroid to give. Every patient on replacement needs sick-day rules, a steroid card and an emergency ampoule at home: double the dose for a febrile illness, and give it parenterally if vomiting.
drug_summaries.insulin: Anabolic peptide hormone, given as replacement in type 1 diabetes and as escalation in type 2. MOA: insulin receptor tyrosine kinase drives GLUT4 to the membrane in muscle and fat, suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis, and switches off lipolysis and ketogenesis - the last is why its absence gives ketoacidosis and why a type 1 patient never stops basal insulin, even when not eating. Types: rapid-acting analogues (aspart, lispro) act within about 15 minutes and cover a meal; short-acting neutral insulin is slower; intermediate isophane sits between; long-acting analogues (glargine, degludec) are near-peakless basal cover. Indications: all type 1 diabetes; type 2 when other agents fail or during acute illness, steroids, surgery or pregnancy; DKA and hyperosmolar states as an infusion; hyperkalaemia, with glucose. SE: hypoglycaemia, the dose-limiting toxicity - autonomic warning symptoms are blunted by beta blockers and lost in hypoglycaemia unawareness; weight gain; lipohypertrophy at unrotated injection sites, which makes absorption erratic and is worth palpating for when control looks inexplicably unstable. Note: sick-day rules run opposite to intuition - during intercurrent illness insulin requirements RISE, so basal insulin continues even if the patient is not eating, with increased monitoring and ketone testing.
drug_summaries.lamotrigine: Anticonvulsant and bipolar maintenance agent. MOA: use-dependent blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels, reducing presynaptic glutamate release. Indications: focal and generalised seizures including absence and Lennox-Gastaut; bipolar maintenance, where it prevents DEPRESSIVE relapse specifically and does not treat acute mania. Dose: about 10% of patients get a rash and roughly 1 in 1,000 get SJS or TEN, and the risk is driven almost entirely by starting dose and titration speed - so 25 mg daily for two weeks, 50 mg for two weeks, then fortnightly increases. Any rash means stop and review, not watch and wait. Interactions: this is the examinable part. Valproate inhibits glucuronidation and roughly doubles lamotrigine levels, so the starting dose is halved. Carbamazepine, phenytoin and phenobarbital induce it and the dose roughly doubles. Oestrogen-containing contraceptives induce it too, dropping levels by about half, with a rebound rise in the hormone-free week. Clearance rises sharply through pregnancy. SE: rash, headache, diplopia, insomnia, tremor; rarely aseptic meningitis and haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Note: with levetiracetam, one of the two preferred antiepileptics in pregnancy. After a break of more than five days, retitrate from the beginning.
drug_summaries.lithium: Mood stabiliser, and the only psychotropic with a replicated anti-suicide effect independent of its mood effect. MOA: inhibits inositol monophosphatase, depleting the phosphoinositide pool, and inhibits GSK-3. Indications: acute mania; bipolar maintenance, where it remains first line and prevents BOTH poles; augmentation in treatment-resistant depression. Monitoring: not metabolised - cleared renally and handled like sodium, which is the origin of every interaction it has. Trough level 12 hours post-dose, weekly until stable then three-monthly; maintenance 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L; eGFR, calcium and TFTs six-monthly. SE: fine tremor, polyuria and polydipsia from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, weight gain, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, chronic interstitial nephritis. Interactions: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and ARBs, and thiazides all cut renal clearance and raise the level, as do dehydration, vomiting, diarrhoea and a low-salt diet. Red flags: above 1.5 mmol/L expect coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, vomiting, confusion and myoclonus; above 2.5 is life-threatening. Stop, rehydrate, dialyse if severe. Prescribe by brand - Australian modified-release and immediate-release lithium carbonate are not bioequivalent.
drug_summaries.mercaptamine (cysteamine): Aminothiol cystine-depleting agent for nephropathic cystinosis. MOA: the free thiol reacts with intralysosomal cystine to form a mixed disulfide that leaves through an intact transporter, bypassing the defective CTNS carrier and lowering lysosomal cystine load. Indications: nephropathic cystinosis - started as early as possible and continued for life, delaying progression from Fanconi syndrome to end-stage kidney disease; ophthalmic drops separately for corneal crystals, because systemic drug does not reach the avascular cornea. Monitoring: leukocyte cystine about 6 hours post-dose, titrated to target. SE: a penetrating sulfurous breath and body odour from excreted metabolites, which is the dominant adherence problem and not a trivial one socially; nausea and vomiting; skin striae. Red flags: `mercaptamine` and `mercaptopurine` are a look-alike, sound-alike pair with a standing TGA safety advisory - one treats cystinosis, the other leukaemia and IBD, and a reported swap left an infant pancytopenic. Australian notes: the Approved Name is the whole dual-labelled string, and it is one of a handful the TGA has no plan to shorten, precisely because the bracket keeps the pair apart.
drug_summaries.metformin: Biguanide, and first-line pharmacotherapy in type 2 diabetes. MOA: activates AMP-activated protein kinase, suppressing hepatic gluconeogenesis and improving peripheral insulin sensitivity. It does not stimulate insulin secretion, which is why it does not cause hypoglycaemia on its own and does not cause weight gain. Indications: type 2 diabetes, alone or with anything else; polycystic ovary syndrome, for cycle regularity and ovulation; attenuating antipsychotic-associated weight gain. SE: nausea, diarrhoea and abdominal discomfort, which are the usual reason people stop - start low, take it with food, and switch to the extended-release form rather than abandoning the drug. Long-term use lowers vitamin B12, so check it if there is anaemia or a peripheral neuropathy. Red flags: lactic acidosis is rare but has high mortality, and it happens when metformin accumulates in renal impairment or when tissue hypoxia is already present. Withhold during any acute illness with dehydration, vomiting, sepsis or hypoperfusion, and around iodinated contrast and surgery. Renal: reduce the dose as eGFR falls and stop below about 30.
drug_summaries.methotrexate: Antifolate, and the anchor DMARD in rheumatoid arthritis. MOA: inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, but the low-dose anti-inflammatory effect is mostly adenosine-mediated rather than antiproliferative - hence a DMARD dose a hundredth of the oncology dose. Indications: rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis, psoriasis, IBD; ectopic pregnancy and gestational trophoblastic disease; high dose in ALL and lymphoma. Dose: WEEKLY, and this is the most dangerous prescribing error in the drug book - daily dosing causes fatal pancytopenia and mucositis, and it happens through transcription rather than ignorance. Name the day on the script. Co-prescribe folic acid on a different day. SE: nausea, mucositis, hepatotoxicity, myelosuppression, alopecia, and an idiosyncratic pneumonitis that can appear at any point as dry cough and breathlessness. Interactions: trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole are also antifolates and the combination causes pancytopenia; NSAIDs and PPIs reduce renal clearance. CI: pregnancy, significant renal impairment, active infection, significant liver disease. Monitoring: FBC, LFTs and renal function at baseline, then fortnightly to monthly for the first three months and three-monthly after. Rescue is folinic acid, not folic acid.
drug_summaries.metronidazole: Nitroimidazole antimicrobial covering anaerobes and protozoa. MOA: reduced by anaerobic organisms to a nitro radical that fragments DNA - so it is selectively activated only where there is no oxygen, which is also why it has no aerobic activity at all. Indications: intra-abdominal and pelvic sepsis, in combination for Gram-negative and enterococcal cover; Clostridioides difficile colitis; dental and other anaerobic abscesses; aspiration pneumonia; bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis; amoebiasis and giardiasis; part of Helicobacter pylori eradication. SE: metallic taste, nausea, and with prolonged courses a peripheral neuropathy that may not fully recover - the practical consequence is that duration matters more than dose. Rarely encephalopathy and cerebellar toxicity. Interactions: a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol - flushing, vomiting, tachycardia - so warn the patient during treatment and for a day or two after. It also potentiates warfarin. Note: excellent oral bioavailability, so there is rarely a reason to keep it intravenous once the patient is absorbing.
drug_summaries.naloxone: Competitive opioid receptor antagonist. MOA: displaces opioids at the mu receptor with higher affinity and no intrinsic activity. Indications: opioid-induced respiratory depression. The target is adequate ventilation, NOT full consciousness - titrate in small increments, because a large bolus in a dependent patient precipitates acute withdrawal, agitation and vomiting into an unprotected airway, and occasionally flash pulmonary oedema. Half-life is shorter than that of most opioids, and far shorter than methadone, slow-release oxycodone or a fentanyl patch - so the patient who wakes up can re-sedate an hour later, and either needs prolonged observation or an infusion. Discharging them after a single dose is the classic error. Route: IV, IM or intranasal; the take-home intranasal product is available without prescription in Australia and is a reasonable thing to offer anyone on high-dose opioids or with a history of overdose. Note: it does nothing for a non-opioid cause, so an unimproved conscious state after adequate naloxone is a reason to look elsewhere rather than to give more.
drug_summaries.olanzapine: Atypical antipsychotic (thienobenzodiazepine). MOA: D2 and 5-HT2A antagonism with substantial M1, H1 and alpha-1 blockade. Indications: schizophrenia; acute mania and bipolar maintenance; acute behavioural disturbance by IM injection; adjunct in treatment-resistant depression; also well evidenced for chemotherapy-induced nausea and for appetite in palliative care. SE: the largest weight gain and metabolic burden of any antipsychotic except clozapine, with insulin resistance and dyslipidaemia that appear within months; sedation; anticholinergic dry mouth and constipation; postural hypotension. EPS and prolactin rise are modest at usual doses. Monitoring: weight and waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose or HbA1c and lipids at baseline, at three months and then at least yearly. Metabolic monitoring after a first episode is the intervention most often skipped and most often regretted. Note: IM olanzapine given close to a parenteral benzodiazepine risks excessive sedation and cardiorespiratory depression - separate them by at least an hour. Weight gain is a leading reason young patients stop antipsychotics, so raise it before it happens; metformin has reasonable evidence for attenuating it.
drug_summaries.phenobarbital: Barbiturate antiepileptic, the oldest anticonvulsant still in routine use. MOA: binds GABA-A and prolongs the DURATION of chloride channel opening - benzodiazepines increase the frequency, which is why barbiturates keep working without GABA present and depress respiration where benzodiazepines plateau. Indications: neonatal seizures, still first line worldwide on parenteral availability, cost and a long safety record; refractory status epilepticus after a benzodiazepine and a second-line agent. Half-life 80 to 100 hours, so once daily and a fortnight to steady state. SE: sedation and cognitive blunting, paradoxical hyperactivity in children, tolerance and dependence, respiratory depression on rapid IV loading, osteomalacia with chronic use. Interactions: potent inducer of CYP3A4, 2C9 and glucuronidation - lowers combined oral contraceptives to the point of contraceptive failure, and lowers warfarin, the DOACs and most co-prescribed antiepileptics. CI: acute porphyria, severe respiratory insufficiency. Note: never stop abruptly - withdrawal precipitates seizures and a delirium closer to alcohol withdrawal. `phenobarbital` is the Australian Approved Name; the sole-name transition from phenobarbital (phenobarbitone) closed on 30 April 2026.
drug_summaries.prednisolone: Intermediate-acting glucocorticoid and the default oral corticosteroid in Australian practice. MOA: glucocorticoid receptor agonist, about four times the potency of hydrocortisone with much less mineralocorticoid effect; already active, unlike prednisone, which needs hepatic conversion - so prednisolone is the one to use in liver disease. 5 mg prednisolone is equivalent to 20 mg hydrocortisone. Indications: asthma and COPD exacerbations; acute gout; polymyalgia rheumatica and giant cell arteritis, where visual symptoms mean high dose now, not after biopsy; IBD flares. SE: hyperglycaemia, which will unmask or destabilise diabetes; weight gain and Cushingoid change; hypertension; osteoporosis and avascular necrosis; myopathy; cataract and glaucoma; thin skin and bruising; insomnia and mood change up to frank steroid psychosis; infection risk, including reactivation of tuberculosis and strongyloides. Note: a course under three weeks can usually stop outright, but longer or repeated courses suppress the HPA axis and must be tapered - and that patient then needs sick-day rules, because an intercurrent illness on a suppressed axis is an adrenal crisis. Consider bone protection at 7.5 mg for three months, and PJP prophylaxis at 20 mg for four weeks.
drug_summaries.quetiapine: Atypical antipsychotic (dibenzothiazepine) whose pharmacology changes with dose - which is the whole point of the drug. MOA: D2 and 5-HT2A antagonism with very fast D2 dissociation; potent H1 blockade gives sedation and alpha-1 blockade gives postural drop; the active metabolite norquetiapine is a noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor and 5-HT2C antagonist, which is where the antidepressant effect comes from. Dose: below about 50 mg the effect is essentially antihistamine sedation with no antipsychotic action at all; 150 to 300 mg is the antidepressant range; 400 to 800 mg is needed for schizophrenia. Indications: schizophrenia; acute mania; bipolar DEPRESSION, where it is one of very few agents with real evidence; adjunct in major depression. SE: sedation, postural hypotension during titration, weight gain and metabolic syndrome, dry mouth, QT prolongation. EPS and prolactin elevation are minimal, which with clozapine makes it one of the two usable antipsychotics in Parkinson disease. Note: low-dose quetiapine is widely prescribed as a hypnotic. It has no good evidence in that role, carries the full metabolic risk, is not subsidised for it, and is diverted in custodial and inpatient settings - recognising the inappropriate indication is worth more marks than reciting the receptor profile.
drug_summaries.risperidone: Atypical antipsychotic (benzisoxazole). MOA: D2 plus 5-HT2A antagonism; the 5-HT2A blockade is what buys the reduced EPS, and it stops buying it above about 6 mg daily, at which point risperidone behaves like a typical. Indications: schizophrenia; bipolar mania; short-term for behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia, the only antipsychotic with an Australian indication for it and one limited to a few weeks; irritability in autism. SE: the highest prolactin elevation of any atypical, which matters clinically rather than as a number - galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, sexual dysfunction and reduced bone density are common reasons young patients stop taking it and do not say why. Dose-related EPS, moderate weight gain, postural hypotension during titration. Note: its active metabolite is paliperidone, cleared renally, so renal impairment demands a dose reduction where hepatic impairment matters less. The fortnightly long-acting injection does not reach therapeutic levels for about three weeks and needs oral cover over that gap - stopping the tablets on the day of the first injection is a relapse waiting to happen.
drug_summaries.sertraline: SSRI, and a reasonable default first-line antidepressant. MOA: blocks the serotonin transporter, raising synaptic 5-HT; the receptor change takes weeks, which is why the effect does and the side effects do not. Indications: major depression, generalised anxiety, panic disorder, OCD, PTSD, social anxiety. SE: nausea and loose stools in the first week or two, usually transient; sexual dysfunction, which is common, persistent and under-reported unless asked about directly; insomnia or sedation; hyponatraemia from SIADH, particularly in older patients in the first weeks; increased bleeding risk, compounded by NSAIDs or anticoagulants. Note: minimal CYP inhibition makes it the SSRI of choice with polypharmacy, after myocardial infarction, and in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Anxiety can worsen in the first week, so start low and warn the patient, or they will stop on day three. Red flags: review within one to two weeks in patients under 25, in whom suicidal ideation may increase early. Serotonin syndrome with MAOIs, tramadol, linezolid or triptans is agitation, clonus, hyperreflexia and hyperthermia. Taper on stopping.
drug_summaries.sodium valproate: Broad-spectrum anticonvulsant and mood stabiliser. MOA: raises GABA by inhibiting GABA transaminase and inducing GAD, blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, and blocks T-type calcium channels - the last is why it works in absence seizures where carbamazepine makes them worse. Indications: absence seizures, juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and generalised tonic-clonic seizures, all first line; acute mania and bipolar maintenance; migraine prophylaxis. SE: weight gain, tremor, alopecia, polycystic ovarian morphology, thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction, idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, and hyperammonaemic encephalopathy that occurs with entirely normal LFTs and responds to carnitine. Interactions: an enzyme INHIBITOR, unlike most older antiepileptics - it raises lamotrigine, phenobarbital and the active carbamazepine epoxide. CI: pregnancy and women or girls of childbearing potential unless every alternative has failed; known or suspected mitochondrial disease, where POLG variants make fatal liver failure far more likely; urea cycle disorders. Red flags: the most teratogenic antiepileptic in use - major congenital malformation in about 10%, and neurodevelopmental impairment or autism in a much larger fraction of exposed children. The TGA carries a boxed warning; prescribing to a woman of childbearing potential requires a documented discussion and effective contraception, and this is specifically examined.
drug_summaries.spironolactone: Potassium-sparing diuretic and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist. MOA: competitive MR blockade in the collecting duct reduces sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion; it also blocks androgen and progesterone receptors, which is simultaneously its main nuisance effect and its therapeutic mechanism in hirsutism. Indications: HFrEF added to standard therapy, with a mortality benefit; resistant hypertension, where it is the fourth-line agent of choice; primary aldosteronism; ascites in cirrhosis, where it is the first-line diuretic and is combined with furosemide in a fixed ratio; acne and hirsutism in women. SE: hyperkalaemia is the dominant risk and it is the one that kills - multiplied by an ACE inhibitor or ARB, NSAIDs, potassium supplements, renal impairment and, easily missed, trimethoprim, which blocks the epithelial sodium channel like amiloride. Gynaecomastia and breast tenderness in men, menstrual irregularity in women. Monitoring: potassium and creatinine at baseline, at about one week and one month, after every dose change, and during any intercurrent illness - withhold it in acute illness with vomiting, diarrhoea or dehydration. Note: a small creatinine rise on starting is haemodynamic and expected. Eplerenone is the alternative if gynaecomastia is intolerable.
drug_summaries.thiamine: Water-soluble vitamin B1. MOA: as thiamine pyrophosphate it is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase, so deficiency blocks aerobic glucose metabolism in exactly the tissues that cannot use anything else. Stores last only two to three weeks. Indications: Wernicke encephalopathy, established or suspected; prophylaxis in alcohol withdrawal, chronic alcohol use, hyperemesis gravidarum, bariatric surgery, prolonged vomiting or malnutrition; refeeding syndrome; wet and dry beriberi. Red flags: Wernicke is a clinical diagnosis and the classical triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia is present in a minority - so treat on suspicion, because untreated Wernicke becomes Korsakoff amnesia, which does not reverse. Give high-dose PARENTERAL thiamine; oral absorption is saturable and cannot achieve the required levels. Note: give thiamine BEFORE or with glucose in anyone at risk. A glucose load in a thiamine-deplete patient consumes what little cofactor remains and can precipitate the encephalopathy it was meant to treat. This is one of the few genuinely iatrogenic-if-you-get-the-order-wrong interventions on the ward. Anaphylaxis to IV thiamine is very rare and is not a reason to withhold it.
drug_summaries.venlafaxine: SNRI. MOA: serotonin reuptake inhibition at low dose, with noradrenaline reuptake inhibition added only at higher doses - so below about 150 mg daily it is functionally an SSRI, and a patient described as having failed an SNRI at 75 mg has not. Indications: major depression, generalised anxiety, panic disorder, social anxiety, neuropathic pain. SE: dose-related hypertension from the noradrenergic effect, so check blood pressure before and after any dose increase; nausea; sweating; sexual dysfunction. Red flags: the worst discontinuation syndrome of the class, because the half-life is short - dizziness, electric-shock sensations, irritability and flu-like symptoms within a day of a missed dose. Use the extended-release form and taper slowly. It is also more cardiotoxic in overdose than any SSRI, with seizures and arrhythmias, which is worth weighing when suicide risk is part of the presentation. CI: an MAOI within the preceding two weeks; caution in uncontrolled hypertension.
drug_summaries.warfarin: Vitamin K antagonist. MOA: inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, so factors II, VII, IX and X cannot be gamma-carboxylated. Onset follows each factor's half-life, and because protein C goes first there is a transient PROCOAGULANT window - which is why loading without heparin cover risks skin necrosis and why bridging exists. Indications: mechanical heart valves and moderate to severe mitral stenosis with AF, where the DOACs are contraindicated and warfarin remains the only option; antiphospholipid syndrome; VTE and AF where a DOAC is unsuitable. Monitoring: INR, target 2 to 3 for most indications and higher for mechanical valves. Interactions: extensive, and the two directions matter equally. Antibiotics, amiodarone, metronidazole, azole antifungals, cranberry juice and acute alcohol raise the INR; carbamazepine, phenobarbital, rifampicin, St John's wort and a sudden increase in dietary vitamin K lower it. Intercurrent illness alone will move it. Note: reversal depends on bleeding, not on the number - withhold for a high INR without bleeding, oral vitamin K if higher, and for major bleeding give IV vitamin K with prothrombin complex concentrate, since vitamin K alone takes hours.

drugs.summary: Statin. MOA: inhibits HMG-CoA reductase → ↓hepatic cholesterol synthesis, ↑LDL receptors. Indications: hyperlipidaemia, primary/secondary CV prevention. SE: myalgia, ↑LFTs, rhabdomyolysis (rare). CI: pregnancy, active liver disease. Note: CYP3A4 substrate - caution with macrolides, azoles.

Statin (most potent LDL-lowering). MOA: same HMG-CoA reductase inhibition; not CYP3A4 metabolised. Indications: hyperlipidaemia, CV prevention. SE: myalgia, proteinuria (high doses). CI: pregnancy. Note: fewer drug interactions than atorvastatin.

Statin (prodrug). MOA: inhibits HMG-CoA reductase. Indications: hyperlipidaemia, CV prevention. SE: myalgia, ↑LFTs. CI: pregnancy. Note: many CYP3A4 interactions; max 20 mg with amiodarone/amlodipine.
Statin. MOA: inhibits HMG-CoA reductase; not CYP3A4 metabolised. Indications: hyperlipidaemia, CV prevention. SE: myalgia. CI: pregnancy. Note: preferred when drug interactions are a concern.

ACE inhibitor. MOA: blocks angiotensin I→II conversion → ↓aldosterone, ↓afterload. Indications: HTN, HFrEF, post-MI, diabetic nephropathy. SE: dry cough (10%, bradykinin), hyperkalaemia, ↑Cr, angioedema. CI: pregnancy, bilateral RAS, prior angioedema.
ACE inhibitor (prodrug → enalaprilat). MOA: blocks Ang I→II conversion. Indications: HTN, HFrEF. SE: dry cough, hyperkalaemia, angioedema. CI: pregnancy, bilateral RAS.

ACE inhibitor (high tissue affinity). MOA: blocks Ang I→II conversion. Indications: HTN, HFrEF, post-MI; HOPE trial - ↓CV mortality in high-risk patients. SE: dry cough, hyperkalaemia, angioedema. CI: pregnancy.
Long-acting ACE inhibitor (prodrug). MOA: blocks Ang I→II conversion. Indications: HTN, HFrEF, stable CAD (EUROPA trial). SE: dry cough, hyperkalaemia. CI: pregnancy.

Short-acting ACE inhibitor. MOA: blocks Ang I→II conversion; rapid onset. Indications: hypertensive urgency, HTN, HFrEF; renal artery scintigraphy. SE: dry cough, rash, neutropenia (more than other ACEi). CI: pregnancy, bilateral RAS.

ARB. MOA: blocks AT1 receptor → ↓angiotensin II effects; also uricosuric (unique). Indications: HTN, HFrEF, diabetic nephropathy. SE: hyperkalaemia, ↑Cr. CI: pregnancy. Note: use when ACEi cough/angioedema not tolerated.
ARB. MOA: selective AT1 receptor blockade. Indications: HTN, HFrEF (PARADIGM-HF - combined with sacubitril as Entresto), post-MI. SE: hyperkalaemia, ↑Cr. CI: pregnancy.
ARB. MOA: selective AT1 blockade (not a prodrug). Indications: HTN, diabetic nephropathy in T2DM (IDNT trial). SE: hyperkalaemia, ↑Cr. CI: pregnancy.
ARB (longest half-life ~24 h). MOA: AT1 receptor blockade; also PPAR-γ partial agonist. Indications: HTN, CV risk reduction. SE: hyperkalaemia. CI: pregnancy.

ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan). MOA: sacubitril inhibits neprilysin → ↑natriuretic peptides; valsartan blocks AT1. Indications: HFrEF (superior to ACEi - PARADIGM-HF). SE: hypotension, hyperkalaemia, angioedema. Note: wash out ACEi ≥36 h before starting.

Cardioselective β1-blocker. MOA: competitive β1 antagonism → ↓HR, ↓contractility, ↓renin. Indications: HTN, HFrEF (succinate - mortality benefit), post-MI, AFib rate control. SE: bradycardia, fatigue, bronchospasm (high dose). CI: severe asthma, decompensated HF, 2°/3° AV block.

Cardioselective β1-blocker (renally cleared). MOA: β1 antagonism; less lipophilic - fewer CNS effects. Indications: HTN, stable angina. SE: bradycardia, fatigue. CI: decompensated HF. Note: less favoured in HF (no mortality benefit).

Highly cardioselective β1-blocker. MOA: selective β1 antagonism maintained at all doses. Indications: HTN, HFrEF (CIBIS-II - mortality benefit). SE: bradycardia, fatigue. CI: decompensated HF, severe bradycardia.

Non-selective β + α1 blocker. MOA: β1/β2 blockade + α1 vasodilation → ↓afterload. Indications: HFrEF (mortality benefit), HTN, post-MI LV dysfunction. SE: dizziness, fatigue, orthostasis. Note: take with food.

Non-selective β-blocker (β1+β2). MOA: β-blockade → ↓HR, ↑airway resistance (β2), CNS effects (lipophilic). Indications: migraine prophylaxis, essential tremor, performance anxiety, hyperthyroid Sx, portal HTN. SE: bronchospasm, bradycardia. CI: asthma.

Combined non-selective β + α1 blocker. MOA: β-blockade + α1 vasodilation → ↓BP without reflex tachycardia. Indications: hypertensive emergency, HTN in pregnancy. SE: orthostasis, fatigue. Note: safe in pregnancy.

Dihydropyridine CCB. MOA: blocks L-type Ca channels in vascular smooth muscle → vasodilation; minimal cardiac effect. Indications: HTN (isolated systolic), stable angina. SE: ankle oedema, flushing, headache, gingival hyperplasia. Note: long half-life, once daily.

DHP CCB (potent vasodilator). MOA: L-type Ca channel blockade → arterial vasodilation, reflex tachycardia. Indications: HTN, Raynaud's, tocolysis. SE: flushing, ankle oedema, reflex tachycardia. Note: long-acting forms ONLY - immediate-release linked to MI/death.

Non-DHP CCB (phenylalkylamine). MOA: L-type Ca channel blockade in cardiac muscle and SA/AV node → slows conduction. Indications: SVT, AFib rate control, HTN. SE: constipation, bradycardia, negative inotropy. CI: HFrEF, β-blocker combination (severe heart block).

Non-DHP CCB (benzothiazepine). MOA: cardiac and vascular L-type Ca channel blockade; less negative inotrope than verapamil. Indications: AFib/flutter rate control, SVT, HTN, angina. SE: bradycardia, peripheral oedema. CI: HFrEF (EF <40%), severe bradycardia.

Loop diuretic. MOA: inhibits NKCC2 in ascending Loop of Henle → potent natriuresis. Indications: acute pulmonary oedema, HF, ascites, refractory HTN. SE: hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyperuricaemia, ototoxicity (rapid IV), AKI. Note: sulfa cross-reactivity (rare).
Loop diuretic (better oral absorption than furosemide). MOA: inhibits NKCC2 cotransporter. Indications: oedema when furosemide absorption is impaired (gut oedema). SE: same class as furosemide.

Thiazide diuretic. MOA: inhibits NCC in distal tubule → ↓Na reabsorption; ↓renal Ca excretion. Indications: HTN (1st-line), mild oedema, hypercalciuria. SE: ↓K, ↓Na, ↑Ca, ↑uric acid, ↑glucose, ↑lipids. CI: anuria.

Thiazide-like diuretic (additional vasodilatory effect). MOA: inhibits NCC; also direct vascular relaxation. Indications: HTN (SHEP trial - elderly). SE: same class as HCTZ. Note: safer than HCTZ in diabetes.

K-sparing diuretic (aldosterone antagonist/MRA). MOA: competitively blocks mineralocorticoid receptor → ↓Na reabsorption, ↑K; anti-androgenic. Indications: HFrEF (RALES - mortality benefit), resistant HTN, ascites, PCOS, primary aldosteronism. SE: hyperkalaemia, gynaecomastia, ↑Cr.

Selective MRA (no anti-androgenic activity). MOA: selective mineralocorticoid receptor blockade. Indications: HFrEF post-MI (EPHESUS), resistant HTN. SE: hyperkalaemia. Note: less gynaecomastia than spironolactone.

Cardiac glycoside. MOA: inhibits Na-K-ATPase → ↑intracellular Ca (inotropy); ↑vagal tone → slows AV node. Indications: AFib rate control, symptomatic HFrEF (no mortality benefit). SE: nausea, yellow visual halos, arrhythmias, hyperK. Note: narrow TI; toxicity worse with ↓K, ↓Mg, renal failure. Antidote: Fab fragments.

Class III antiarrhythmic (K/Na/Ca/β blocker). MOA: prolongs action potential; iodine-rich → thyroid effects. Indications: VT/VF, AFib/flutter (acute + maintenance). SE: pulmonary fibrosis, hyper- and hypothyroidism, hepatotoxicity, corneal deposits, blue-grey skin. Note: T1/2 ~60 days.

Organic nitrate. MOA: releases NO → ↑cGMP → venodilation → ↓preload; dilates coronary arteries. Indications: acute angina, ACS, pulmonary oedema. SE: headache, hypotension, reflex tachycardia, tolerance. CI: PDE5 inhibitors within 24-48 h, severe AS, RV infarction.

Direct arteriolar vasodilator. MOA: opens KATP channels → arterial smooth muscle relaxation → ↓afterload. Indications: HTN in pregnancy, HFrEF (with isosorbide dinitrate - AHeFT). SE: reflex tachycardia, fluid retention, drug-induced lupus (>200 mg/day).

If-channel (HCN) blocker. MOA: selectively inhibits SA node If channel → ↓HR without affecting contractility or BP. Indications: HFrEF in sinus rhythm with HR ≥70 despite β-blocker. SE: visual phosphenes, bradycardia. CI: AFib, sick sinus syndrome.

Antiplatelet (low dose) / NSAID (high dose). MOA: irreversibly inhibits COX-1/2 → ↓TXA2 → ↓platelet aggregation. Indications: secondary CV prevention, ACS, post-stent (DAPT). SE: GI bleed, tinnitus (high dose), bronchospasm (ASA-sensitive). CI: age <16 y (Reye), active bleeding.

P2Y12 inhibitor (thienopyridine prodrug). MOA: CYP2C19 activation → irreversible P2Y12 ADP receptor blockade. Indications: ACS, post-PCI DAPT, secondary stroke prevention. SE: bleeding. Note: CYP2C19 poor metabolisers have ↓effect; avoid omeprazole.

P2Y12 inhibitor (direct-acting, reversible). MOA: direct P2Y12 blockade - no prodrug conversion. Indications: ACS (superior to clopidogrel - PLATO). SE: dyspnoea, bradycardia, bleeding. Note: twice daily; discontinue 5 days pre-surgery.

P2Y12 inhibitor (thienopyridine; more potent than clopidogrel). MOA: efficient prodrug conversion → potent irreversible P2Y12 blockade. Indications: ACS with PCI. SE: more bleeding than clopidogrel. CI: prior stroke/TIA, age ≥75, weight <60 kg.

Vitamin K antagonist. MOA: inhibits VKOR → blocks γ-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X, protein C/S. Indications: mechanical valves, valvular AFib, VTE, antiphospholipid syndrome. SE: bleeding, teratogenicity. Note: INR target 2-3; many drug/food interactions. Reversal: vitamin K (slow), PCC (urgent).

Direct factor Xa inhibitor (DOAC). MOA: reversibly inhibits free and clot-bound factor Xa → ↓thrombin generation. Indications: non-valvular AFib, VTE treatment/prevention. SE: bleeding. Note: lower bleeding than warfarin (ARISTOTLE). Reversal: andexanet alfa. CI: mechanical valves, severe renal impairment.

Direct factor Xa inhibitor (DOAC), once daily. MOA: reversibly inhibits free and clot-bound factor Xa. Indications: non-valvular AFib, VTE, post-orthopaedic prophylaxis. SE: bleeding. Note: take 15/20 mg dose with food. CI: mechanical valves, antiphospholipid syndrome.

Direct thrombin inhibitor (DOAC). MOA: reversibly inhibits free and fibrin-bound thrombin (factor IIa). Indications: non-valvular AFib, VTE. SE: dyspepsia, bleeding. Reversal: idarucizumab. CI: eGFR <15, mechanical valves.
Direct factor Xa inhibitor (DOAC). MOA: same class as apixaban/rivaroxaban. Indications: non-valvular AFib, VTE. Note: paradoxically worse stroke risk in AFib with CrCl >95 mL/min.

Unfractionated heparin (IV/SC). MOA: binds antithrombin III → ↑inactivation of thrombin (IIa) and Xa. Indications: VTE, ACS, PE, bridging, cardiac surgery. SE: bleeding, HIT (type II - antibody-mediated, day 5-10; ↑thrombosis), osteoporosis. Reversal: protamine. Note: monitor aPTT.

LMWH. MOA: binds antithrombin → preferential anti-Xa activity; predictable pharmacokinetics. Indications: VTE prophylaxis/treatment, ACS, bridging. SE: bleeding, HIT (lower risk than UFH). Note: renally cleared - reduce if eGFR <30; partial reversal with protamine.

tPA (thrombolytic). MOA: converts plasminogen to plasmin → fibrinolysis (clot dissolution). Indications: acute ischaemic stroke (<4.5 h), STEMI (if no PCI), massive PE with haemodynamic instability. SE: intracranial haemorrhage (most feared), systemic bleeding. CI: recent surgery, active bleeding, severe HTN, prior haemorrhagic stroke.

Biguanide, T2DM 1st-line. MOA: activates AMPK → ↓hepatic gluconeogenesis; no insulin secretion stimulation. Indications: T2DM, prediabetes, PCOS. SE: GI upset (take with food), B12 deficiency, lactic acidosis (rare). CI: eGFR <30, hepatic failure. Note: hold 48 h peri-contrast.

2nd-gen sulfonylurea. MOA: closes KATP channels on β-cells → ↑insulin secretion (glucose-independent). Indications: T2DM. SE: hypoglycaemia (esp. with alcohol/renal impairment), weight gain. CI: T1DM, pregnancy, severe renal/hepatic disease.
Short-acting sulfonylurea. MOA: KATP channel closure on pancreatic β-cells → ↑insulin secretion. Indications: T2DM. SE: hypoglycaemia (lower risk than glibenclamide in elderly). CI: T1DM, pregnancy.

Long-acting sulfonylurea (glibenclamide). MOA: KATP channel closure → ↑insulin secretion; active metabolites. Indications: T2DM. SE: prolonged hypoglycaemia (dangerous in elderly - Beers criterion), weight gain. CI: renal impairment, elderly.

DPP-4 inhibitor (gliptin). MOA: inhibits DPP-4 → ↑endogenous GLP-1/GIP → ↑glucose-dependent insulin, ↓glucagon. Indications: T2DM add-on. SE: pancreatitis (rare), arthralgia, nasopharyngitis. Note: dose adjustment in renal impairment.
DPP-4 inhibitor. MOA: ↑incretin (GLP-1/GIP) levels by blocking DPP-4 degradation. Indications: T2DM. Note: biliary excretion - no renal dose adjustment needed.
SGLT2 inhibitor. MOA: same class as empagliflozin - blocks SGLT2 → glucosuria. Indications: T2DM, HFrEF, HFpEF (DELIVER), CKD (DAPA-CKD). SE: urogenital infections, euglycaemic DKA, volume depletion.

SGLT2 inhibitor. MOA: same SGLT2 blockade; also some SGLT1 inhibition. Indications: T2DM, CKD (CREDENCE). SE: urogenital infections, DKA, possible ↑lower limb amputations (CANVAS - monitor foot care). Note: bone fracture risk.

GLP-1 receptor agonist. MOA: stimulates GLP-1R → ↑glucose-dependent insulin, ↓glucagon, ↓gastric emptying, ↑satiety → weight loss. Indications: T2DM (weekly SC or daily oral), obesity (Wegovy). SE: nausea, ↓gastric emptying, pancreatitis, retinopathy progression. CI: personal/family history of MTC, MEN2.

GLP-1 receptor agonist (daily SC). MOA: same GLP-1R mechanism as semaglutide. Indications: T2DM (LEADER - CV benefit), obesity (Saxenda). SE: GI, pancreatitis, thyroid C-cell tumours (animal). CI: MTC/MEN2 history.
GLP-1 receptor agonist (weekly SC). MOA: Fc-linked GLP-1 analogue → ↑insulin, ↓glucagon, ↑satiety. Indications: T2DM (REWIND - CV benefit). SE: GI upset, pancreatitis.

Long-acting basal insulin analogue (~24 h). MOA: forms microprecipitate at physiological pH → slow sustained absorption; binds insulin receptor. Indications: T1DM, T2DM (basal). SE: hypoglycaemia, weight gain. Note: once daily; do not mix with other insulins.

Long-acting basal insulin analogue (~18-24 h). MOA: albumin-binding at injection site → extended absorption. Indications: T1DM, T2DM. SE: hypoglycaemia, weight gain. Note: may require twice-daily dosing.

Rapid-acting insulin analogue. MOA: amino acid substitutions reduce hexamer formation → faster SC absorption; onset 5-15 min, peak 1-2 h. Indications: mealtime insulin in T1/T2DM. SE: hypoglycaemia, weight gain. Note: inject immediately before meals.
Rapid-acting insulin analogue. MOA: same as lispro - reduced self-aggregation → fast absorption; onset 10-20 min. Indications: mealtime insulin. SE: hypoglycaemia, weight gain.

Synthetic T4 (thyroid hormone). MOA: peripherally converted to active T3 → binds nuclear thyroid receptors → regulates metabolism. Indications: hypothyroidism, TSH suppression in thyroid cancer. SE: over-replacement: AFib, osteoporosis; under-replacement: hypothyroid Sx. Note: empty stomach, separate from Ca/Fe; monitor TSH 6 weeks after dose change.

Glucocorticoid (prodrug → prednisolone). MOA: binds GR → ↓inflammatory cytokines, ↓T-cell activity, ↑gluconeogenesis. Indications: asthma, COPD exacerbation, autoimmune disease, IBD, allergic reactions, adrenal insufficiency. SE: hyperglycaemia, HTN, infection, osteoporosis, Cushingoid features, adrenal suppression (taper if >2 weeks). CI: live vaccines.

Active glucocorticoid. MOA: same GR mechanism as prednisone (no hepatic activation needed). Indications: same as prednisone; preferred in liver disease. SE: same class - hyperglycaemia, HTN, osteoporosis, infection.

Glucocorticoid (IV/oral; ~1.25× prednisolone potency). MOA: GR binding → potent anti-inflammatory. Indications: severe inflammation, anaphylaxis, transplant rejection, ARDS, MS relapse. SE: same class as prednisone.

Long-acting glucocorticoid (no mineralocorticoid effect; ~7× prednisolone). MOA: high-affinity GR binding → potent anti-inflammation. Indications: cerebral oedema, COVID-19 (RECOVERY - ↓mortality in ventilated), croup, antiemetic (peri-op), antenatal lung maturity. SE: hyperglycaemia, immunosuppression.

Short-acting glucocorticoid (reference steroid; significant mineralocorticoid effect). MOA: binds GR and MR → anti-inflammatory + Na/K exchange. Indications: adrenal insufficiency (replacement dose), septic shock, severe asthma, anaphylaxis adjunct. SE: same class.

Synthetic mineralocorticoid. MOA: potent aldosterone receptor agonist → ↑Na reabsorption, ↑K excretion. Indications: primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's - with hydrocortisone), orthostatic hypotension. SE: fluid retention, HTN, hypokalaemia.

Aminopenicillin (β-lactam). MOA: binds PBPs → inhibits transpeptidation → bactericidal cell wall disruption. Indications: AOM, sinusitis, strep pharyngitis, dental prophylaxis, H. pylori (triple therapy). SE: maculopapular rash (esp. in EBV), GI, C. diff. CI: penicillin allergy.

Aminopenicillin (IV β-lactam). MOA: PBP binding → cell wall disruption; broader spectrum than benzylpenicillin. Indications: Listeria meningitis (+ gentamicin), Enterococcus IE, GBS prophylaxis. SE: rash, GI, C. diff. CI: penicillin allergy.

Antistaphylococcal penicillin (β-lactamase-resistant). MOA: PBP binding resistant to staphylococcal β-lactamase (not MRSA PBP2a). Indications: MSSA skin/soft tissue, bone/joint infections, MSSA IE/bacteraemia. SE: cholestatic hepatitis (rare, delayed). CI: penicillin allergy. Note: NOT for MRSA.
Antistaphylococcal penicillin (US). MOA: β-lactamase-resistant PBP binding. Indications: MSSA bacteraemia, IE, bone/joint. Note: hepatically metabolised - safe in renal impairment.

Extended-spectrum ureidopenicillin + tazobactam (pip-tazo). MOA: piperacillin inhibits PBPs; tazobactam inhibits β-lactamases → covers Pseudomonas, anaerobes. Indications: hospital-acquired sepsis, febrile neutropenia, complicated IAI/UTI. SE: hypokalaemia, diarrhoea. CI: penicillin allergy.

1st-gen IV cephalosporin. MOA: PBP binding → bactericidal cell wall disruption. Indications: surgical prophylaxis, MSSA bacteraemia, SSTIs. SE: hypersensitivity. Note: preferred over vancomycin for MSSA if tolerated.

3rd-gen cephalosporin. MOA: PBP binding - broad gram-negative spectrum, excellent CSF penetration. Indications: meningitis, gonorrhoea (IM), pyelonephritis, septic arthritis, CAP. SE: biliary sludging, neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia (displaces bilirubin).

4th-gen cephalosporin. MOA: PBP binding; stable to AmpC β-lactamases; covers Pseudomonas. Indications: febrile neutropenia, HAP, complicated UTI. SE: encephalopathy/seizures in renal impairment. Note: neurotoxic if overdosed in renal failure.

Carbapenem (broad-spectrum β-lactam). MOA: binds all PBPs → extremely broad spectrum; stable to most β-lactamases including ESBLs. Indications: severe hospital-acquired/MDR gram-negative infections, meningitis, intra-abdominal sepsis. SE: seizures (lower than imipenem), C. diff.

Carbapenem (once daily; narrower spectrum). MOA: same PBP binding as meropenem. Indications: ESBL-producing organisms, complicated community infections; outpatient parenteral therapy. Note: NO activity against Pseudomonas or Enterococcus.

Monobactam (β-lactam). MOA: binds PBP3 selectively in aerobic gram-negatives only. Indications: gram-negative infections (incl. Pseudomonas) in penicillin/cephalosporin-allergic patients. Note: no gram-positive or anaerobic coverage; low cross-reactivity with penicillins.

Glycopeptide antibiotic. MOA: binds D-Ala-D-Ala peptidoglycan terminus → inhibits transglycosylation → cell wall disruption; IV for systemic, oral (not absorbed) for C. diff. Indications: MRSA, severe gram-positive IE/meningitis, C. diff (oral). SE: red-man syndrome (slow infusion), nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity. Note: AUC/MIC-guided dosing preferred.

Oxazolidinone antibiotic. MOA: binds 23S rRNA of 50S subunit → inhibits 70S ribosome initiation → bacteriostatic (unique target, no cross-resistance). Indications: VRE, MRSA SSTI, complicated infections, MDR-TB. SE: thrombocytopenia (>2 weeks), serotonin syndrome (MAO-A inhibition + SSRIs/MAOIs), peripheral/optic neuropathy. Note: 100% oral bioavailability.

Cyclic lipopeptide. MOA: Ca-dependent membrane insertion → depolarisation → rapid gram-positive cell death. Indications: MRSA bacteraemia, IE, complicated SSTI. SE: myopathy (monitor CK weekly), eosinophilic pneumonitis. Note: inactivated by pulmonary surfactant - NEVER use for pneumonia.

Macrolide antibiotic. MOA: binds 50S ribosomal subunit → inhibits translocation → bacteriostatic; excellent intracellular penetration. Indications: CAP (atypicals), pertussis, Chlamydia. SE: QT prolongation, GI, cholestatic hepatitis. Note: less CYP3A4 inhibition than clarithromycin.

Macrolide antibiotic. MOA: same 50S ribosomal binding as azithromycin. Indications: H. pylori eradication (with amoxicillin + PPI), CAP, MAC. SE: QT prolongation, metallic taste. Note: strong CYP3A4 inhibitor - ↑statins, warfarin, tacrolimus.

Original macrolide. MOA: 50S ribosomal binding → inhibits protein synthesis; also activates motilin receptors (prokinetic, low dose). Indications: atypical pneumonia, gastroparesis (100-250 mg), alternative to penicillin. SE: severe GI (very common), QT prolongation. Note: strong CYP3A4 inhibitor.

Tetracycline antibiotic. MOA: binds 30S ribosomal subunit → blocks aminoacyl-tRNA binding → bacteriostatic. Indications: atypical pneumonia, Lyme, RMSF, chlamydia, acne, malaria prophylaxis. SE: photosensitivity, oesophageal erosion (take upright with water), dental staining/bone (children). CI: pregnancy, age <8 y.

Tetracycline (more lipophilic than doxycycline). MOA: same 30S ribosomal blockade; greater CNS penetration. Indications: acne, MRSA SSTI, RA adjunct. SE: vestibular toxicity (vertigo, ataxia), blue-grey pigmentation, drug-induced lupus. CI: pregnancy, age <8 y.

Fluoroquinolone. MOA: inhibits DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV → prevents DNA replication → bactericidal. Indications: complicated UTI/pyelonephritis, Pseudomonas, travellers' diarrhoea, anthrax. SE: tendonitis/rupture (esp. + steroids), QT prolongation, C. diff, peripheral neuropathy. Note: chelates with antacids/iron.

Respiratory fluoroquinolone. MOA: dual topoisomerase inhibition; better gram-positive/atypical coverage than ciprofloxacin. Indications: CAP, complicated UTI, Pseudomonas (susceptible). SE: same class - QT, tendon rupture, C. diff, neuropathy.

Respiratory fluoroquinolone (anaerobic coverage). MOA: dual topoisomerase inhibition; excellent gram-positive and anaerobic spectrum. Indications: CAP, complicated IAI. SE: strong QT prolongation (avoid in cardiac patients). Note: NOT effective for UTI (low urinary levels).

Folate antagonist (diaminopyrimidine). MOA: inhibits bacterial DHFR → blocks folic acid synthesis → ↓purine/thymidine synthesis. Indications: UTI (alone or as co-trimoxazole). SE: hyperkalaemia (blocks ENaC K excretion), ↑creatinine (blocks tubular secretion - not true GFR drop).

Sulfonamide antibiotic. MOA: inhibits dihydropteroate synthetase → different folate synthesis step than TMP → synergistic bactericidal combination (Bactrim/Septra). Indications: UTI, MRSA SSTI, PCP treatment/prophylaxis, nocardia. SE: rash (SJS in HIV), haemolysis (G6PD deficiency), hyperkalaemia, ↑Cr.

Nitrofuran antibiotic. MOA: reduced by bacterial flavoproteins → reactive intermediates → multi-target damage (DNA, ribosomes, enzymes); multiple resistance mechanisms prevented. Indications: uncomplicated lower UTI (cystitis). SE: pulmonary fibrosis (long-term), peripheral neuropathy, hepatotoxicity. CI: eGFR <30 (↓levels + toxicity), late pregnancy.

Phosphonic acid antibiotic. MOA: inhibits MurA → blocks first step in peptidoglycan precursor synthesis. Indications: single-dose oral uncomplicated cystitis; MDR E. coli/Enterococcus. Note: convenient 3 g single dose; lower cure rate in complicated UTI.

Nitroimidazole antibiotic/antiparasitic. MOA: reduced by microbial ferredoxin → cytotoxic DNA-damaging intermediates; active against anaerobes and protozoa only. Indications: C. diff, BV, trichomoniasis, Giardia, amoebic liver abscess, intra-abdominal anaerobes. SE: metallic taste, peripheral neuropathy (chronic), disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol. CI: 1st trimester (high-dose).

Lincosamide antibiotic. MOA: binds 50S ribosomal subunit (same site as macrolides) → inhibits peptide elongation → bacteriostatic. Indications: MRSA SSTI, anaerobes above diaphragm, dental infections, toxin-producing GABHS (necrotising fasciitis adjunct). SE: HIGHEST C. diff risk of all antibiotics; rash. CI: prior C. diff.

Aminoglycoside antibiotic. MOA: binds 30S ribosomal subunit → mRNA misreading → bactericidal; concentration-dependent + post-antibiotic effect. Indications: gram-positive IE synergy (with β-lactam), severe gram-negative infections. SE: nephrotoxicity (proximal tubular accumulation), ototoxicity (vestibular + cochlear, irreversible), neuromuscular blockade. Note: once-daily extended-interval dosing preferred.

Antitubercular (RIPE regimen). MOA: KatG activates INH → inhibits InhA (enoyl-ACP reductase) → blocks mycolic acid synthesis (M. tb cell wall). Indications: active TB (first-line), latent TB prophylaxis. SE: hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs), peripheral neuropathy (give pyridoxine/B6), drug-induced lupus. Note: slow/fast acetylator status affects toxicity/levels.

Azole antifungal. MOA: inhibits fungal CYP51 (lanosterol 14α-demethylase) → ↓ergosterol synthesis → membrane disruption. Indications: Candida infections (oral, vaginal, oesophageal, candidaemia), cryptococcal meningitis (consolidation). SE: QT prolongation, hepatotoxicity, GI. Note: potent CYP3A4 inhibitor - ↑warfarin, statins, calcineurin inhibitors.

Extended-spectrum triazole. MOA: same CYP51 inhibition as fluconazole with superior Aspergillus coverage. Indications: invasive aspergillosis (1st-line), serious Candida/fusariosis. SE: visual disturbances (photopsia), photosensitivity/skin cancer (long-term), hepatotoxicity, periostitis. Note: non-linear kinetics - monitor levels.

Nucleoside analogue antiviral. MOA: viral TK phosphorylation → active triphosphate inhibits viral DNA polymerase (chain termination); selective for HSV/VZV. Indications: HSV (genital, encephalitis - IV high-dose), VZV/zoster. SE: crystalline nephropathy (hydrate well), neurotoxicity (high-dose IV). Note: renal dose adjustment required.

Acyclovir prodrug (valyl ester). MOA: rapid first-pass → acyclovir (~55% bioavailability vs 15-30%); same DNA polymerase chain termination mechanism. Indications: genital herpes (treatment/suppression), herpes zoster, cold sores. SE: nausea; rare TTP/HUS (high-dose, immunocompromised).

Neuraminidase inhibitor (influenza antiviral). MOA: competitively inhibits influenza neuraminidase → prevents viral release from host cells → limits spread. Indications: influenza A and B (treatment and post-exposure prophylaxis). Note: start within 48 h of symptom onset; most benefit in severe disease/immunocompromised. SE: nausea, vomiting.

Analgesic, antipyretic (mechanism not fully understood). MOA: central COX-2 inhibition + TRPA1 channel inhibition + possible endocannabinoid system modulation; minimal anti-inflammatory. Indications: mild-moderate pain, fever. SE: hepatotoxicity in OD (NAPQI depletes glutathione - antidote: N-acetylcysteine). Note: max 4 g/day; 3 g/day if liver disease/alcohol use.

NSAID (propionic acid). MOA: reversibly inhibits COX-1 and COX-2 → ↓prostaglandins → anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antipyretic; COX-1 → GI/platelet effects. Indications: pain, fever, musculoskeletal inflammation, dysmenorrhoea. SE: GI bleed/ulcer, AKI, ↑CV events, fluid retention. CI: severe HF, eGFR <30, active GI ulcer, 3rd trimester pregnancy.

NSAID (propionic acid, ~12 h half-life). MOA: reversible COX-1/2 inhibition → ↓prostaglandins. Indications: pain, arthritis, dysmenorrhoea. SE: same class as ibuprofen. Note: lowest CV risk among NSAIDs - preferred in patients with CVD risk.

NSAID (preferential COX-2 inhibitor). MOA: COX-2 > COX-1 inhibition; also PPAR-γ activation. Indications: musculoskeletal pain, OA (topical - minimal systemic absorption), dysmenorrhoea. SE: higher CV risk vs naproxen; GI effects.

COX-2 selective NSAID (coxib). MOA: preferentially inhibits inducible COX-2 over constitutive COX-1 → ↓GI toxicity. Indications: OA, RA, acute pain, FAP (familial adenomatous polyposis). SE: ↑CV events, fluid retention. CI: sulfa allergy. Note: lower GI bleed risk than non-selective NSAIDs.

Potent NSAID (pyrrolizine carboxylic acid; IV/IM/oral). MOA: non-selective COX inhibition - opioid-sparing analgesic. Indications: moderate-severe acute/post-op pain. SE: GI bleeding, AKI, platelet inhibition. Note: max 5 days; avoid in elderly and renal impairment.

Weak opioid, antitussive (CYP2D6 prodrug). MOA: CYP2D6 O-demethylation → morphine (~10%) → μ-opioid receptor agonism. Indications: mild-moderate pain, cough suppression. SE: constipation, sedation, respiratory depression. CI: age <12 y, breastfeeding, ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metabolisers.

Weak opioid + SNRI-like (dual mechanism). MOA: μ-opioid agonism (weak; active metabolite O-desmethyltramadol stronger) + serotonin/NA reuptake inhibition. Indications: moderate pain (WHO step 2). SE: lowers seizure threshold, serotonin syndrome (with SSRIs/SNRIs/MAOIs), hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia.

Strong opioid (μ > κ > δ agonist). MOA: opioid receptor activation → ↑K conductance, ↓Ca conductance → hyperpolarisation → ↓pain transmission. Indications: severe acute/chronic pain, dyspnoea (palliative). SE: respiratory depression, constipation (no tolerance), nausea, sedation, urinary retention, miosis. Note: active metabolite M6G accumulates in renal impairment. Antidote: naloxone.

Strong opioid (~2× morphine; no prodrug step). MOA: potent μ-opioid receptor agonism. Indications: moderate-severe pain. SE: constipation, respiratory depression, sedation, euphoria (high abuse potential). Note: OxyContin ER implicated in opioid epidemic.

Strong opioid (~5× morphine). MOA: potent μ-opioid agonism; no active accumulating metabolites. Indications: severe pain; preferred over morphine in renal impairment. SE: respiratory depression, constipation, sedation.

Strong synthetic opioid (~100× morphine; highly lipophilic). MOA: μ-opioid receptor agonism; rapid CNS penetration. Indications: chronic pain (patches), acute pain (IV/buccal), procedural anaesthesia. SE: respiratory depression, chest wall rigidity (high-dose IV). Note: transdermal patches reach steady state in 12-24 h.

Long-acting synthetic opioid. MOA: μ-opioid agonism + NMDA receptor antagonism (reduces tolerance) + serotonin/NA reuptake inhibition. Indications: opioid use disorder (OAT), refractory cancer pain. SE: QT prolongation (torsades risk), complex T1/2 (8-59 h) → accumulation. Note: titrate carefully.

Partial μ-opioid agonist + κ antagonist. MOA: high receptor affinity with partial efficacy → ceiling effect on respiratory depression. Indications: opioid use disorder (Suboxone - with naloxone), chronic/acute pain. SE: nausea; precipitates withdrawal if given to opioid-dependent patients. Note: Suboxone contains naloxone to deter IV misuse.

Competitive opioid antagonist. MOA: rapidly displaces opioids from μ, κ, δ receptors → reverses sedation/respiratory depression. Indications: opioid OD reversal (IV/IM/intranasal 0.4-2 mg; titrate to effect). SE: acute opioid withdrawal (agitation, tachycardia - in dependent patients), pulmonary oedema. Note: short T1/2 (~1 h) - repeat dosing needed for long-acting opioids.

SSRI. MOA: blocks serotonin transporter (SERT) → ↑synaptic 5-HT. Indications: MDD, GAD, panic disorder, OCD, PTSD, social anxiety. SE: GI (initially), sexual dysfunction, hyponatraemia (SIADH - elderly), ↑bleeding risk. Note: preferred in pregnancy/post-MI; minimal drug interactions.

SSRI. MOA: potent SERT blockade; also mild 5-HT2C antagonism. Indications: MDD, OCD, bulimia, PMDD. SE: anxiety/agitation, sexual dysfunction, insomnia. Note: longest T1/2 (~1-4 weeks for norfluoxetine - no taper needed); strong CYP2D6 inhibitor.

SSRI. MOA: selective SERT inhibition. Indications: MDD. SE: dose-dependent QT prolongation (max 20 mg if >60 y, hepatic impairment, or CYP2C19 inhibitor), GI, sexual dysfunction. Note: relatively selective - fewer drug interactions.

SSRI (S-enantiomer of citalopram). MOA: more selective SERT inhibition with allosteric binding site. Indications: MDD, GAD. SE: similar to citalopram but less QT prolongation. Note: well-tolerated; minimal drug interactions.

SSRI (most anticholinergic; shortest T1/2 → worst discontinuation). MOA: SERT inhibition + muscarinic/H1 blockade + weak NET inhibition. Indications: MDD, panic, GAD, PTSD, social anxiety. SE: anticholinergic, weight gain, severe discontinuation syndrome, sexual dysfunction. CI: pregnancy (cardiac defects - Ebstein's).

SNRI. MOA: SERT >> NET inhibition at low doses; NET blockade also at higher doses → dual analgesic mechanism. Indications: MDD, GAD, panic, social anxiety, neuropathic pain. SE: ↑BP (noradrenergic, dose-related), severe discontinuation syndrome, GI.

SNRI (balanced SERT/NET inhibition). MOA: blocks both serotonin and noradrenaline transporters at low doses (unlike venlafaxine). Indications: MDD, GAD, diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia, chronic MSK pain, stress urinary incontinence. SE: nausea, ↑BP, hepatotoxicity (rare). CI: uncontrolled narrow-angle glaucoma.

Atypical antidepressant (NaSSA). MOA: blocks α2 autoreceptors → ↑NE/5-HT release; blocks 5-HT2/3, H1 → antiemetic, sedation. Indications: MDD (especially with insomnia, poor appetite, nausea). SE: weight gain, sedation (paradoxically more at low doses). Note: useful for insomnia/nausea co-morbidity.

NDRI antidepressant. MOA: inhibits noradrenaline and dopamine transporters (NET/DAT); no serotonergic activity. Indications: MDD (no sexual SE or weight gain), smoking cessation, SAD, ADHD (off-label). SE: lowers seizure threshold, insomnia, agitation. CI: bulimia/anorexia, seizure disorder.

TCA (tricyclic antidepressant). MOA: inhibits SERT + NET; blocks M1, H1, α1 receptors; Na channel blockade → cardiac toxicity in OD. Indications: neuropathic pain (low dose), migraine prophylaxis, MDD. SE: anticholinergic, sedation, weight gain, QT prolongation; lethal in OD. CI: recent MI, MAOI use.

TCA (secondary amine; better tolerated than amitriptyline). MOA: selective NET > SERT inhibition; less muscarinic/H1 blockade. Indications: neuropathic pain, MDD. SE: less anticholinergic; still QT prolongation, orthostasis, OD risk.

Mood stabiliser. MOA: inhibits inositol monophosphatase → ↓PI signalling; modulates GSK-3β; alters serotonin/NE neurotransmission; neuroprotective. Indications: bipolar disorder (mania + maintenance), anti-suicide effect, depression augmentation. SE: tremor, weight gain, polyuria (nephrogenic DI), hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism. Note: narrow TI (0.6-1.2 mmol/L); toxicity: ataxia, confusion, seizures.

Anticonvulsant + mood stabiliser (bipolar depression). MOA: blocks voltage-gated Na/Ca channels → ↓glutamate release. Indications: focal/generalised seizures, bipolar (especially depressive phase). SE: SJS/TEN (requires very slow titration over 6+ weeks). Note: dose ↑ with enzyme inducers (carbamazepine), dose ↓ with valproate.

Anticonvulsant + mood stabiliser. MOA: blocks use-dependent Na channels + voltage-gated Ca channels → ↓repetitive neuronal firing. Indications: focal/generalised seizures, trigeminal neuralgia, bipolar. SE: SJS (HLA-B*1502 - screen East Asian patients), agranulocytosis, SIADH/↓Na. Note: strong CYP3A4 inducer (autoinduction).

Anticonvulsant. MOA: blocks voltage-gated Na channels (use-dependent) → ↓sustained neuronal firing; membrane-stabilising. Indications: focal/tonic-clonic seizures, status epilepticus (IV fosphenytoin). SE: gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, cerebellar toxicity (ataxia, nystagmus), SJS. Note: zero-order kinetics → small dose increases cause disproportionate ↑levels.

Anticonvulsant (unique MOA). MOA: binds SV2A (synaptic vesicle protein 2A) → modulates vesicular NT release → ↓excitatory neurotransmission. Indications: focal/generalised seizures, myoclonic epilepsy, status epilepticus adjunct. SE: irritability, mood changes ('Keppra rage'), psychosis (rare). Note: few drug interactions; renally excreted.

Anticonvulsant (multiple mechanisms). MOA: blocks Na channels, augments GABA-A, blocks AMPA/kainate receptors, inhibits carbonic anhydrase. Indications: seizures, migraine prophylaxis, obesity (+ phentermine). SE: cognitive impairment, paraesthesias, kidney stones, weight loss, acute angle-closure glaucoma.

Typical antipsychotic (butyrophenone). MOA: potent D2 receptor antagonism (mesolimbic - antipsychotic; nigrostriatal - EPS; tuberoinfundibular - ↑prolactin). Indications: schizophrenia, acute agitation, delirium (cautious), Tourette. SE: EPS (acute dystonia, akathisia, Parkinsonism), tardive dyskinesia, NMS, QT prolongation.

Atypical antipsychotic (benzisoxazole). MOA: D2 + 5-HT2A antagonism; 5-HT2A blockade reduces EPS and improves negative symptoms. Indications: schizophrenia, bipolar mania, autism-related irritability. SE: hyperprolactinaemia (most among atypicals), EPS at higher doses, metabolic effects.

Atypical antipsychotic (thienobenzodiazepine). MOA: D2 + 5-HT2A/M1/H1/α1 antagonism; broad receptor blockade. Indications: schizophrenia, acute mania, agitation (IM). SE: significant weight gain + metabolic syndrome (↑glucose, ↑lipids), sedation, orthostasis. Note: IM + benzodiazepine → respiratory depression risk.

Atypical antipsychotic (dibenzothiazepine). MOA: D2 + 5-HT2A antagonism + strong H1 blockade (sedation at low doses). Indications: schizophrenia, bipolar mania and depression (unique - depressive phase), MDD adjunct. SE: sedation (H1, low dose), weight gain, metabolic syndrome, orthostasis.

Atypical antipsychotic (D2 partial agonist/stabiliser). MOA: D2 partial agonism (normalises DA - agonist in low DA, antagonist in high DA states); 5-HT2A antagonism + 5-HT1A partial agonism. Indications: schizophrenia, bipolar mania, MDD adjunct, autism, Tourette. SE: akathisia, impulse control disorders. Note: weight-neutral.

Atypical antipsychotic (benzisothiazolyl). MOA: D2 + 5-HT2A antagonism + 5-HT1A partial agonism + NET/SERT inhibition. Indications: schizophrenia, bipolar mania. SE: QT prolongation (most significant - avoid in cardiac patients). Note: take with food (doubles absorption); weight neutral.

Long-acting benzodiazepine. MOA: positive allosteric GABA-A modulation → ↑Cl⁻ influx → neuronal hyperpolarisation. Indications: alcohol withdrawal, status epilepticus, muscle spasm, acute anxiety. SE: sedation, respiratory depression (+ opioids), dependence, falls. CI: acute narrow-angle glaucoma. Note: long-acting active metabolites - avoid in elderly (Beers).

Intermediate-acting benzodiazepine (no active metabolites). MOA: GABA-A facilitation → ↑Cl⁻ influx → CNS depression. Indications: status epilepticus (IV 1st-line), alcohol withdrawal (preferred in liver disease - glucuronidation only), acute anxiety, procedural sedation. SE: sedation, respiratory depression, dependence.

Short-acting benzodiazepine (water-soluble → lipophilic at physiologic pH). MOA: GABA-A facilitation → rapid CNS penetration. Indications: procedural sedation, pre-op anxiolysis, status epilepticus (IM/IN). SE: respiratory depression, anterograde amnesia, paradoxical agitation. Note: fastest IV onset; used IM/IN for status.

Short-acting benzodiazepine (rapid onset → high abuse potential). MOA: potent GABA-A facilitation; fast receptor binding/dissociation. Indications: panic disorder (short-term), acute anxiety. SE: rapid tolerance, severe rebound anxiety, withdrawal seizures, sedation. Note: avoid long-term - high dependence risk.

Long-acting benzodiazepine (potent anticonvulsant). MOA: GABA-A facilitation; high potency at GABA-A receptor. Indications: panic disorder, myoclonic/absence seizures, REM sleep behaviour disorder, akathisia adjunct. SE: sedation, dependence, cognitive impairment.

Z-drug (non-benzodiazepine GABA-A modulator). MOA: selective BZ1 (ω1) GABA-A subtype agonism → more selective sedation than benzos. Indications: short-term insomnia. SE: complex sleep behaviours (sleep-walking/driving), next-day drowsiness, amnesia. CI: severe respiratory failure. Note: avoid with alcohol.

Benzodiazepine receptor antagonist. MOA: competitive antagonist at GABA-A BZ binding site → rapidly reverses BZ sedation/respiratory depression. Indications: BZ OD reversal, post-procedural sedation reversal. SE: seizures (benzo-dependent patients), acute withdrawal. Note: short T1/2 (~1 h) - sedation may recur.

SABA (short-acting β2-agonist). MOA: β2 receptor stimulation → ↑cAMP → bronchial smooth muscle relaxation; also shifts K into cells. Indications: acute asthma/COPD bronchospasm, hyperkalaemia (IV). SE: tremor, tachycardia, hypokalaemia (high dose), hyperglycaemia. Note: onset ~5 min.

LABA (long-acting β2-agonist; ~12 h). MOA: β2 agonism → ↑cAMP → sustained bronchodilation; prolonged receptor binding. Indications: COPD maintenance, asthma (ONLY with ICS - LABA monotherapy ↑ asthma mortality). SE: tremor, tachycardia, paradoxical bronchospasm (rare).

LABA with rapid onset. MOA: same β2/cAMP bronchodilation as salmeterol; faster onset (~3 min). Indications: COPD, asthma maintenance (with ICS); SMART single-inhaler therapy (Symbicort). SE: same class as salmeterol.

LAMA (long-acting muscarinic antagonist). MOA: blocks M3 receptors in bronchial smooth muscle → ↓bronchoconstriction, ↓mucus; slow M3 dissociation → once daily. Indications: COPD maintenance (↓exacerbations), severe asthma add-on. SE: dry mouth, urinary retention, tachycardia, acute closed-angle glaucoma (if eye contact). CI: narrow-angle glaucoma, severe BPH.

SAMA (short-acting muscarinic antagonist). MOA: M3 receptor blockade → bronchodilation; not systemically absorbed. Indications: acute COPD exacerbation (+ SABA), acute severe asthma (add-on). SE: dry mouth, urinary retention, tachycardia. Note: slower onset than SABAs; synergistic combination.

Inhaled corticosteroid (ICS). MOA: binds GR → ↓inflammatory cytokines (IL-4/5/13), ↓mast cell/eosinophil activation → ↓airway inflammation. Indications: asthma controller (cornerstone - ↓exacerbations), COPD with exacerbation history. SE: oral candidiasis (rinse mouth), dysphonia; systemic effects at high dose (cataracts, ↓bone density).

ICS (high first-pass hepatic metabolism → fewer systemic effects). MOA: GR-mediated ↓airway inflammation. Indications: asthma, COPD; oral viscous (eosinophilic oesophagitis), oral capsules (Crohn's). SE: oral candidiasis at high inhaled doses.
ICS. MOA: GR activation → ↓airway inflammation. Indications: asthma. Note: extrafine HFA particles → improved peripheral airway deposition.

Leukotriene receptor antagonist (LTRA). MOA: blocks CysLT1 receptor → ↓airway inflammation/bronchoconstriction (leukotrienes from eosinophils/mast cells). Indications: asthma (especially aspirin-sensitive, exercise-induced), allergic rhinitis. SE: neuropsychiatric effects (depression, suicidality, vivid dreams - boxed warning). Note: alternatives preferred for most patients.

Proton pump inhibitor (PPI). MOA: irreversibly inhibits H⁺/K⁺-ATPase on gastric parietal cells after acid activation → ↓gastric acid. Indications: GORD, peptic ulcer, H. pylori eradication, Zollinger-Ellison, NSAID prophylaxis. SE (long-term): ↓Mg, ↓B12, ↑fracture risk, C. diff risk, AIN. Note: CYP2C19 substrate - ↓clopidogrel efficacy (use pantoprazole instead).
PPI. MOA: same irreversible H⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition. Indications: GORD, peptic ulcer, H. pylori, stress ulcer prophylaxis (IV). Note: fewer CYP2C19 interactions - preferred with clopidogrel.
PPI (S-enantiomer of omeprazole). MOA: same H⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition; slower CYP2C19 metabolism → slightly higher plasma levels. Indications: GORD, erosive oesophagitis, H. pylori.
PPI. MOA: same proton pump inhibition. Indications: GORD, peptic ulcer, H. pylori. Note: available as orally-disintegrating tablet for NG tubes.

H2 receptor antagonist. MOA: competitive H2 blockade on parietal cells → ↓acid (faster onset but less potent than PPIs). Indications: GORD, peptic ulcer. SE: confusion (elderly/renal impairment - CNS penetration). Note: ranitidine withdrawn globally (NDMA contamination).

5-HT3 serotonin receptor antagonist (setron). MOA: blocks 5-HT3 in GI tract and CTZ/NTS → ↓nausea/vomiting signals. Indications: chemotherapy-induced, post-operative, hyperemesis gravidarum. SE: QT prolongation (dose-dependent), headache, constipation. CI: congenital long QT, strong CYP3A4 inhibitors.

D2 antagonist + 5-HT4 agonist (prokinetic antiemetic). MOA: D2 blockade in CTZ → antiemetic; 5-HT4 agonism → ↑gastric motility. Indications: nausea/vomiting, gastroparesis, migraine adjunct. SE: EPS (acute dystonia, akathisia - young patients), tardive dyskinesia (long-term), hyperprolactinaemia. CI: Parkinson's.

Peripheral μ-opioid agonist (antidiarrhoeal; does not cross BBB). MOA: activates enteric μ receptors → ↓gut motility, ↑anal sphincter tone, ↓fluid secretion. Indications: acute/chronic diarrhoea. CI: bloody diarrhoea/dysentery, acute severe colitis (toxic megacolon risk). Note: high-dose abuse → QT prolongation/arrhythmias.

Osmotic laxative (synthetic disaccharide). MOA: osmotic water retention + colonic bacterial metabolism → ↓luminal pH → traps NH4⁺ → ↓blood ammonia. Indications: constipation, hepatic encephalopathy (titrate to 2-3 soft stools/day). SE: bloating, flatulence, cramping. Note: onset 24-48 h.

Osmotic laxative (PEG). MOA: large MW polymer not absorbed → retains water in bowel by osmosis. Indications: chronic constipation, bowel preparation. SE: bloating, cramping, nausea. Note: electrolyte-free; safe in renal impairment.

α1A/1D-selective adrenergic blocker. MOA: selective α1A blockade in prostate/bladder neck → ↓urethral tone → ↑urine flow. Indications: BPH, ureteric calculi (facilitates stone passage). SE: orthostasis (1st dose - less than non-selective), retrograde ejaculation, intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (warn ophthalmologists before cataract surgery).

5α-reductase inhibitor (type 2). MOA: blocks testosterone → DHT conversion → ↓prostate size, ↓scalp DHT. Indications: BPH (↓urinary obstruction, ↓acute retention risk), male-pattern baldness. SE: sexual dysfunction (ED, ↓libido), ↓PSA ~50% (adjust threshold), rare male breast cancer. CI: women of childbearing potential (teratogenic).

PDE5 inhibitor. MOA: ↓PDE5 → ↑cGMP → vascular smooth muscle relaxation → penile/pulmonary vasodilation. Indications: erectile dysfunction, pulmonary arterial hypertension. SE: headache, flushing, dyspepsia, blue-tinged vision (PDE6 cross-inhibition), NAION (rare). CI: nitrates (severe hypotension), riociguat.

PDE5 inhibitor (T1/2 ~36 h - longest). MOA: same cGMP-mediated smooth muscle relaxation as sildenafil. Indications: ED (on-demand or daily low-dose), BPH, PAH. SE: myalgia/back pain (PDE11 cross-inhibition), headache. CI: nitrates, riociguat.

Bisphosphonate (nitrogen-containing). MOA: binds bone hydroxyapatite → osteoclast phagocytosis → inhibits farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase → osteoclast apoptosis → ↓bone resorption. Indications: osteoporosis, Paget disease. SE: oesophagitis (take upright, full glass of water, 30 min before food), osteonecrosis of jaw, atypical femur fractures (long-term).

RANKL inhibitor (monoclonal antibody). MOA: inhibits RANK ligand → ↓osteoclast differentiation/activation → ↓bone resorption. Indications: osteoporosis, bone metastases (Xgeva - higher dose). SE: hypocalcaemia (supplement Ca/D), osteonecrosis of jaw, rebound vertebral fractures if stopped without follow-on therapy.

SERM (selective oestrogen receptor modulator). MOA: oestrogen receptor agonism in bone (↑bone density) + antagonism in breast/uterus (no ↑endometrial cancer). Indications: postmenopausal osteoporosis, breast cancer prevention. SE: hot flushes, ↑VTE risk, leg cramps. CI: current/past VTE, premenopausal.

Xanthine oxidase inhibitor. MOA: inhibits XO → ↓uric acid synthesis (hypoxanthine → xanthine → urate pathway). Indications: gout (urate-lowering), tumour lysis syndrome, uric acid nephrolithiasis. SE: SJS/TEN (screen HLA-B*5801 - East Asian, Korean, Black patients; stop immediately if rash), hypersensitivity syndrome, acute gout flare at initiation. Note: do NOT start during acute gout attack.

Non-purine selective xanthine oxidase inhibitor. MOA: inhibits both oxidised and reduced forms of XO → ↓uric acid synthesis. Indications: gout with allopurinol intolerance/failure. SE: ↑CV mortality vs allopurinol (CARES - regulatory safety warning), acute gout flare, hepatotoxicity.

Anti-gout, anti-inflammatory (tubulin binding). MOA: binds tubulin → ↓microtubule polymerisation → ↓neutrophil/macrophage function → ↓urate crystal phagocytosis, ↓IL-1β. Indications: acute gout, gout prophylaxis, pericarditis (recurrent), FMF, Dressler syndrome. SE: GI (dose-limiting), myopathy, BM suppression (overdose). Note: CYP3A4/P-gp substrate - caution with azithromycin, cyclosporin, statins.

DMARD (antifolate). MOA: inhibits DHFR → ↓THF → ↓purine/thymidine synthesis (anti-proliferative); also ↑adenosine (anti-inflammatory via A2A). Indications: RA (1st-line), psoriasis, IBD, ectopic pregnancy, choriocarcinoma. SE: hepatotoxicity, BM suppression, mucositis, pulmonary fibrosis. Note: always co-prescribe folic acid 5 mg/week. CI: pregnancy, severe renal/hepatic disease.

Antimalarial DMARD. MOA: alkalinises lysosomes → ↓TLR signalling, ↓antigen processing, ↓autoimmune activation; also ↓platelet aggregation. Indications: SLE (↓flares, ↑survival), RA, malaria prophylaxis. SE: retinopathy (cumulative - annual ophthalmology review after 5 years), rare QT prolongation, haemolysis (G6PD deficiency).

Antimetabolite DMARD (thiopurine). MOA: prodrug → 6-MP → 6-thioguanine nucleotides → incorporated into DNA → ↓lymphocyte proliferation. Indications: IBD, RA, autoimmune hepatitis, transplant, SLE. SE: BM suppression (check TPMT before starting), hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, ↑lymphoma risk. CI: allopurinol coadministration (75% dose reduction required).

TNF-α inhibitor (chimeric monoclonal IgG1; IV). MOA: binds soluble and membrane-bound TNF-α → ↓NF-κB, ↓IL-1/6/8 → anti-inflammatory. Indications: Crohn's, UC, RA, psoriasis, ankylosing spondylitis. SE: serious infections (TB reactivation - screen first), infusion reactions, demyelinating disorders, ↑lymphoma. Note: screen for TB and hepatitis B before starting.

TNF-α inhibitor (fully humanised monoclonal IgG1; SC biweekly). MOA: same TNF-α neutralisation as infliximab. Indications: RA, psoriasis/PsA, Crohn's, UC, ankylosing spondylitis, uveitis. SE: same class - infections, TB reactivation, ↑lymphoma. Note: SC self-administration; no infusion reactions.

TNF-α inhibitor (dimeric TNF receptor/IgG1 Fc fusion protein). MOA: binds circulating TNF-α and lymphotoxin-α; different mechanism from monoclonal anti-TNFs. Indications: RA, psoriasis/PsA. Note: lower efficacy for granulomatous disease (Crohn's) than monoclonal TNF inhibitors.

Anti-CD20 monoclonal Ab (chimeric; IV). MOA: binds CD20 on B lymphocytes → ADCC, CDC, apoptosis → ↓B cells for 6-12 months. Indications: B-cell NHL, CLL, RA (anti-TNF failure), ANCA vasculitis, ITP. SE: infusion reactions, hypogammaglobulinaemia, HBV reactivation (screen/prophylax), PML (rare).

IL-6 receptor antagonist (monoclonal Ab; IV or SC). MOA: blocks IL-6 binding to soluble/membrane IL-6R → ↓IL-6-driven acute phase response, T-cell activation. Indications: RA, giant cell arteritis, systemic JIA, cytokine release syndrome (CAR-T, severe COVID-19). SE: serious infections, neutropenia, ↑LFTs, bowel perforation, dyslipidaemia. Note: masks fever/CRP as acute phase markers.

Endogenous catecholamine; 1st-line emergency drug (AU/UK: adrenaline; US: adrenaline). MOA: α1 agonism → peripheral vasoconstriction (↑BP, ↓mucosal oedema); β1 → ↑HR + contractility; β2 → bronchodilation + mast cell stabilisation → reverses all anaphylaxis pathophysiology simultaneously. Indications: anaphylaxis (1st-line - IM 0.3–0.5 mg anterolateral thigh, repeat q5 min); cardiac arrest (IV/IO 1 mg q3–5 min); severe asthma (IM/nebulised); croup (nebulised racemic 0.5%); local anaesthetic additive (↑duration, ↓systemic absorption). SE: tachycardia, hypertension, arrhythmia, anxiety, pallor; tissue necrosis (extravasation). Note: IM deltoid/thigh preferred over SC for anaphylaxis - faster absorption; carry 2 auto-injectors (risk of biphasic reaction).

Competitive muscarinic antagonist. MOA: blocks M1-M5 receptors → ↓parasympathetic effects: ↑HR (M2), ↓secretions, ↓GI motility, mydriasis, ↑urinary retention. Indications: symptomatic bradycardia, organophosphate/nerve agent poisoning, anaesthetic pre-medication. SE: tachycardia, dry mouth, urinary retention, hyperthermia, confusion, mydriasis.

Hyperglycaemic hormone. MOA: binds glucagon receptor → ↑cAMP → hepatic glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis → ↑blood glucose; also β-receptor-independent positive inotropy.
