Indications: severe hypoglycaemia (no IV access), β-blocker/CCB overdose (↑cardiac output). SE: nausea, vomiting, tachycardia. Note: temporary measure; follow with oral/IV glucose.

Antifibrinolytic (lysine analogue). MOA: competitively binds plasminogen lysine sites → ↓plasminogen/plasmin binding to fibrin → ↓fibrinolysis → stabilises clot. Indications: trauma haemorrhage (CRASH-2 - give within 3 h), menorrhagia, PPH, surgical bleeding, hereditary angioedema. SE: nausea, VTE risk (theoretical), seizures (high-dose IV - especially intrathecal).

Fat-soluble vitamin (phytomenadione). MOA: cofactor for VKOR-dependent γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X, protein C/S → enables Ca²⁺ binding/activation. Indications: warfarin reversal (oral ~6-12 h; IV ~4-6 h), neonatal haemorrhagic disease, vitamin K deficiency. Note: slow reversal - use PCC/FFP for urgent anticoagulation reversal.

Endogenous purine antiarrhythmic. MOA: activates A1 adenosine receptors → ↑K conductance, ↓Ca current → transient AV node block. Indications: SVT termination (rapid IV 6 mg → 12 mg; T1/2 ~10 sec). SE: transient chest tightness, flushing, bronchospasm, asystole (seconds - resolves spontaneously). CI: asthma, 2°/3° AV block, Wolff-Parkinson-White. Note: theophylline is antidote (adenosine antagonist).

Class Ic antiarrhythmic. MOA: potent Na channel blockade → ↓conduction velocity throughout myocardium. Indications: AF/flutter and SVT in structurally normal hearts (pill-in-pocket). SE: proarrhythmia (↑mortality post-MI - CAST trial), dizziness, visual disturbances. CI: structural heart disease, CAD, HF, significant LV dysfunction.

Class III antiarrhythmic + non-selective β-blocker. MOA: blocks K channels → ↑action potential duration, ↑QT + β1/β2 antagonism → ↓HR. Indications: AF/VT maintenance (sinus rhythm maintenance). SE: QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, bradycardia. CI: QT >500 ms, hypokalaemia, eGFR <30, asthma.

Class III multi-channel antiarrhythmic (non-iodinated amiodarone analogue). MOA: blocks K, Na, Ca channels + weak β/α blockade; no iodine → ↓thyroid/pulmonary toxicity vs amiodarone. Indications: paroxysmal/persistent AF (sinus rhythm maintenance). SE: ↑SCr (blocks tubular creatinine secretion - not true GFR drop), bradycardia, hepatotoxicity. CI: permanent AF, severe HF (ANDROMEDA - ↑mortality).

Endogenous catecholamine vasopressor (noradrenaline - AU/UK name). MOA: potent α1 + α2 agonism → vasoconstriction (↑SVR) + β1 agonism (↑contractility); net ↑MAP. Indications: septic shock (1st-line vasopressor per surviving sepsis guidelines), haemorrhagic shock. SE: limb/digital ischaemia (extravasation), reflex bradycardia. Note: administer via central line; titrate to MAP ≥65 mmHg.

Endogenous catecholamine (dose-dependent receptor selectivity). MOA: low dose (1-5 mcg/kg/min): D1/D2 → ↑renal perfusion; medium (5-10): β1 → ↑HR/contractility; high (>10): α1 → vasoconstriction. Indications: cardiogenic shock (inotropy), bradycardia (chronotropy). SE: tachyarrhythmia. Note: no proven renal-protective effect at low dose.

Synthetic catecholamine inotrope (β1 >> β2 > α1). MOA: β1 agonism → ↑contractility, ↑CO; β2 component → ↓SVR. Indications: acute decompensated HF (short-term inotropy), cardiogenic shock, stress echocardiography. SE: tachycardia, arrhythmia. Note: tolerance develops with prolonged infusion; titrate to CO/SvO2.

Posterior pituitary hormone (ADH). MOA: V1 receptors → peripheral vasoconstriction (↑SVR); V2 receptors → renal water reabsorption. Indications: septic shock adjunct (0.03 units/min - vasopressin-deficient state), cardiac arrest, central DI. SE: digital/mesenteric ischaemia, hyponatraemia (V2), coronary vasospasm. Note: fixed dose in septic shock - do not titrate.

PDE3 inhibitor (inodilator). MOA: ↑cAMP in cardiac/vascular tissue → positive inotropy + vasodilation without β-receptor stimulation. Indications: acute decompensated HF, RV failure post-cardiac surgery. SE: hypotension (vasodilation), arrhythmia, ↑mortality in chronic HF (PROMISE). Note: useful when β-blockade limits dobutamine response.

Pure α1-adrenergic agonist. MOA: selective α1 agonism → vasoconstriction, ↑SVR → ↑BP; reflex bradycardia (no β activity). Indications: perioperative hypotension preserving HR (useful in tachycardia), hypotension in AFib. SE: tissue necrosis (extravasation), reflex bradycardia, ↑afterload. Note: avoid in HF/severe aortic stenosis.

Cholesterol absorption inhibitor. MOA: inhibits NPC1L1 transporter in intestinal brush border → ↓cholesterol absorption → ↑hepatic LDL receptor expression. Indications: hyperlipidaemia (adjunct to statin or monotherapy if statin-intolerant). SE: GI, ↑LFTs (rare, more with statin combo). Note: modest LDL-lowering (~18-20%), additive with statins.

Fibrate (PPAR-α agonist). MOA: activates PPAR-α → ↑lipoprotein lipase, ↑apoAI/AII, ↓apoC-III → ↓TG 40-50%, ↑HDL, modest ↓LDL. Indications: hypertriglyceridaemia (severe - pancreatitis risk), mixed dyslipidaemia. SE: myopathy (especially + statins), ↑LFTs, ↑SCr (non-renal mechanism). CI: severe renal/hepatic disease.

PCSK9 inhibitor (monoclonal antibody). MOA: inhibits PCSK9 → prevents LDL receptor degradation → ↑hepatic LDL receptor recycling → ↓LDL 50-60%. Indications: familial hypercholesterolaemia, high-CV-risk patients with statin intolerance or inadequate response (FOURIER - ↓CV events). SE: injection site reactions, flu-like symptoms. Note: SC every 2-4 weeks.

Bile acid sequestrant (anion exchange resin; AU/UK spelling of cholestyramine). MOA: binds bile acids in gut → ↑hepatic bile acid synthesis → ↑LDL receptor expression. Indications: hypercholesterolaemia (modest effect), bile acid malabsorption diarrhoea, cholestatic pruritus. SE: constipation, bloating, ↓absorption of fat-soluble vitamins and drugs (warfarin, digoxin - separate by 4 h). Note: difficult to tolerate.

Thionamide antithyroid drug. MOA: prodrug → methimazole; inhibits thyroid peroxidase → blocks organification and coupling of thyroid hormone synthesis. Indications: hyperthyroidism (Graves', toxic nodular goitre). SE: agranulocytosis (0.1-0.5% - stop immediately if sore throat/fever, check FBC), aplasia cutis (1st-trimester teratogenicity - use PTU instead). Note: blocks new synthesis only - takes weeks to reduce T4 levels.

Thionamide antithyroid drug (PTU). MOA: inhibits thyroid peroxidase + blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion (additional effect vs carbimazole). Indications: hyperthyroidism, preferred in 1st trimester pregnancy. SE: agranulocytosis (same risk as carbimazole), hepatotoxicity (rare but potentially fatal). Note: shorter T1/2 → 8-hourly dosing; use in thyroid storm for rapid T4→T3 blockade.

Thiazolidinedione (TZD), insulin sensitiser. MOA: PPAR-γ agonism → ↑insulin sensitivity in adipose/muscle/liver. Indications: T2DM (adjunct/monotherapy). SE: fluid retention/oedema, weight gain, ↑HF exacerbation, macular oedema, ↑fracture risk (women), ↑bladder cancer risk. CI: HF (NYHA III-IV), active bladder cancer.

GLP-1 receptor agonist (exendin-4; twice-daily or weekly SR). MOA: activates GLP-1R → ↑glucose-dependent insulin, ↓glucagon, ↓gastric emptying, ↑satiety → weight loss. Indications: T2DM. SE: nausea, vomiting, pancreatitis. CI: eGFR <30, MEN2/MTC history. Note: original GLP-1 RA; largely replaced by semaglutide.

Intermediate-acting insulin (isophane). MOA: protamine-complexed → delayed SC absorption; onset 1-2 h, peak 4-8 h, duration ~18 h. Indications: T1/T2DM (twice-daily basal, pre-mixed regimens). SE: hypoglycaemia (peak-related), weight gain. Note: must re-suspend before injection; variable absorption.

Ultra-long-acting basal insulin analogue (>42 h). MOA: forms SC hexamer chains → ultra-slow absorption; lower day-to-day variability than glargine. Indications: T1/T2DM basal insulin. SE: hypoglycaemia (lower nocturnal risk vs glargine), weight gain. Note: flexible timing - dose can shift by ≥8 h.

IV nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate (most potent). MOA: inhibits osteoclast farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase → osteoclast apoptosis → ↓bone resorption. Indications: osteoporosis (once-yearly IV - Aclasta), hypercalcaemia of malignancy, Paget disease, bone metastases (monthly - Zometa). SE: acute phase reaction (flu-like 24-48 h post-dose), hypocalcaemia, osteonecrosis of jaw.

Active vitamin D3 (1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol). MOA: binds VDR → ↑intestinal Ca/PO4 absorption, regulates PTH. Indications: renal osteodystrophy (CKD - bypasses renal 1α-hydroxylation), hypoparathyroidism. SE: hypercalcaemia, hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis. Note: monitor Ca, PO4, PTH regularly; distinct from colecalciferol (inactive precursor).

Vitamin D3 - fat-soluble pro-hormone (secosteroid). MOA: absorbed from diet or synthesised in skin (UV-B irradiation of 7-dehydrocholesterol → pre-vitamin D3 → colecalciferol) → hepatic 25-hydroxylation (25[OH]D = calcidiol - main storage + serum marker) → renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation (calcitriol = 1,25[OH]₂D - active form) → calcitriol binds VDR nuclear receptor → ↑intestinal Ca²⁺ + phosphate absorption, ↑renal Ca²⁺ reabsorption, bone mineralisation (at physiological doses); immunomodulatory (VDR in immune cells - ↑Treg, ↓Th17, ↑innate immunity). Indications: vitamin D deficiency/insufficiency (very common - elderly, dark skin, sun-avoidance, malabsorption, CKD; oral supplement 1000-2000 IU/day maintenance; loading 50,000-100,000 IU/week × 6-12 weeks for severe deficiency); osteoporosis (with calcium - reduces fracture risk); osteomalacia/rickets; secondary hyperparathyroidism (CKD - alongside active vitamin D analogues); calcium absorption (co-administration with calcium for bone health). SE: hypercalcaemia (toxicity - at excessive doses [>10,000 IU/day chronic or very high loading] - nausea, polyuria, confusion, nephrocalcinosis, ↑plasma calcium - check 25[OH]D + corrected calcium if concerned); hypercalciuria (kidney stones - high doses + high calcium intake). Note: 25[OH]D target (sufficient: >50 nmol/L, optimal 75-150 nmol/L); recheck 25[OH]D 8-12 weeks after starting supplementation; choose between colecalciferol (D3 = animal-derived, more potent bioavailability) vs ergocalciferol (D2 = plant-derived, similar but D3 preferred for supplementation); active vitamin D (alfacalcidol/calcitriol) required in CKD (impaired 1-alpha-hydroxylation).

Posterior pituitary peptide hormone. MOA: binds oxytocin receptors on myometrium → ↑intracellular Ca → uterine contraction; also promotes milk ejection. Indications: induction/augmentation of labour, PPH prevention (3rd stage management), PPH treatment. SE: uterine hyperstimulation (fetal distress), water intoxication (antidiuretic effect), hypotension (rapid IV bolus). Note: always dilute and infuse - never rapid IV bolus.

Ergot alkaloid uterotonic. MOA: α-adrenergic + serotonin receptor activation → sustained tonic uterine contraction. Indications: PPH (active management - Syntometrine combines ergometrine + oxytocin), incomplete abortion. SE: hypertension (vasoconstriction), nausea, coronary vasospasm. CI: hypertension, pre-eclampsia, cardiac disease.

Synthetic PGE1 analogue. MOA: prostaglandin E receptors → uterine contractions (high dose); also ↓gastric acid (E1 receptors on parietal cells). Indications: PPH prevention/treatment (sublingual - WHO essential medicine in resource-limited settings), cervical ripening, medical abortion (with mifepristone), NSAID gastroprotection. SE: diarrhoea, fever, uterine hyperstimulation. Note: room temperature stable - key advantage.

Central α2-agonist antihypertensive. MOA: converted to α-methylnoradrenaline → α2 agonism in brainstem → ↓sympathetic outflow → ↓BP. Indications: HTN in pregnancy (most safety data - 1st-line in Australia). SE: sedation, fatigue, drug-induced lupus/haemolytic anaemia, positive Coombs test, ↑LFTs. Note: safe at all trimesters; onset 3-6 h.

Broad-spectrum benzimidazole anthelmintic. MOA: binds β-tubulin → ↓microtubule polymerisation → glucose depletion → worm death. Indications: roundworm, hookworm, pinworm, hydatid cyst, neurocysticercosis (+ corticosteroids). SE: GI, ↑LFTs, teratogenic. Note: poor oral bioavailability - take with fatty meal.

Benzimidazole anthelmintic (minimal systemic absorption). MOA: binds tubulin → blocks glucose uptake → helminth death. Indications: pinworm (single 100 mg dose - 1st-line), roundworm, hookworm, whipworm. SE: GI (minimal - poor absorption). Note: repeat dose after 2 weeks for reinfection.

Macrocyclic lactone antiparasitic. MOA: potentiates GABA-gated Cl channels in invertebrates → paralysis/death; selective (mammalian CNS receptors inaccessible). Indications: strongyloidiasis, scabies (oral), onchocerciasis, lymphatic filariasis. SE: Mazzotti reaction (fever, rash - from dying worms in onchocerciasis). CI: CNS disease (↑BBB permeability). Note: co-administration with alcohol ↑CNS SE.

Antiparasitic (Malarone = atovaquone + proguanil). MOA: inhibits mitochondrial electron transport in Plasmodium; proguanil inhibits DHFR synergistically. Indications: malaria treatment and prophylaxis (Malarone), PCP prophylaxis (monotherapy). SE: GI, headache, rash. Note: high bioavailability with fatty food; weekly compliance advantage over mefloquine.

Quinoline-methanol antimalarial. MOA: disrupts haem polymerisation in parasite food vacuole → toxic haem accumulation. Indications: malaria prophylaxis (weekly - resistant regions), treatment. SE: neuropsychiatric effects (nightmares, anxiety, depression, psychosis - boxed warning), bradycardia. CI: depression, anxiety disorder, psychosis, seizures. Note: poor tolerability limits use.

Prodrug of penciclovir (nucleoside analogue antiviral). MOA: viral TK converts to penciclovir triphosphate → inhibits viral DNA polymerase; active against HSV-1/2, VZV. Indications: herpes zoster (↓duration/PHN), recurrent genital herpes. SE: headache, nausea. Note: higher bioavailability than acyclovir (77% vs 15-30%); simpler dosing regimen for zoster.

Nucleoside analogue antiviral (guanosine analogue). MOA: triphosphate inhibits HBV DNA polymerase at 3 steps: priming, reverse transcription, and DNA synthesis → high barrier to resistance. Indications: chronic hepatitis B (1st-line preferred). SE: lactic acidosis (rare - discontinue if suspected). Note: renal dose adjustment; do not stop abruptly (risk of hepatitis flare).

NS5B nucleotide polymerase inhibitor (HCV direct-acting antiviral). MOA: prodrug → triphosphate inhibits NS5B RdRp → stops HCV replication; pangenotypic with velpatasvir (Epclusa). Indications: chronic HCV (cure rates >95% - Epclusa, Harvoni). SE: fatigue, headache; severe bradycardia with amiodarone. Note: 8-12 week courses revolutionised HCV treatment.

Nucleotide prodrug antiviral (broad-spectrum). MOA: adenosine analogue triphosphate inhibits viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase → premature chain termination. Indications: COVID-19 (hospitalised requiring O2 - ACTT-1). SE: bradycardia, hepatotoxicity, infusion reactions. Note: IV over 30-120 min; limited role as COVID therapy evolved.

Triazole antifungal (broader spectrum than fluconazole). MOA: inhibits fungal CYP51 → ↓ergosterol → membrane disruption; active against Aspergillus (fluconazole is not). Indications: onychomycosis, histoplasmosis, aspergillosis (salvage), dermatophytosis. SE: negative inotropy (↑HF risk), hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation. CI: HF, ventricular dysfunction. Note: variable absorption - take with food/acidic drink.

Echinocandin antifungal. MOA: inhibits β-1,3-glucan synthase → disrupts fungal cell wall; fungicidal vs Candida, fungistatic vs Aspergillus. Indications: invasive candidiasis (preferred if haemodynamically unstable or resistant), aspergillosis (salvage). SE: hepatotoxicity, infusion-related histamine release. Note: excellent safety profile; no renal toxicity.

Polyene antifungal. MOA: binds ergosterol in fungal cell membrane → pores → ↑permeability → cell lysis. Indications: invasive aspergillosis, cryptococcal meningitis, mucormycosis (gold standard), severe candidiasis. SE: nephrotoxicity (conventional - severe; AmBisome liposomal markedly ↓this), infusion reactions (fever, rigors). Note: liposomal form (AmBisome) preferred.

Polyene antifungal (not absorbed orally). MOA: binds ergosterol → membrane pores → fungal cell death; no systemic absorption. Indications: oral candidiasis (thrush - swish-and-swallow), oropharyngeal/oesophageal candidiasis, vulvovaginal candidiasis (cream). SE: GI nausea (oral). Note: purely topical/GI action - no systemic antifungal effect.

Allylamine antifungal (fungicidal against dermatophytes). MOA: inhibits squalene epoxidase → ↓ergosterol synthesis + squalene accumulation (toxic). Indications: onychomycosis (fingernails 6 wk, toenails 12 wk), tinea pedis/corporis. SE: hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs), taste disturbance. Note: superior cure rates for onychomycosis vs itraconazole.

Imidazole antifungal (topical). MOA: inhibits fungal CYP51 → ↓ergosterol → membrane integrity disruption. Indications: vulvovaginal candidiasis (cream/pessary), tinea pedis/corporis/cruris, oral thrush (lozenges). SE: local burning/irritation. Note: 1st-line OTC for vaginal thrush; available as single-dose pessary.

Aminopenicillin + β-lactamase inhibitor (amoxicillin/clavulanate). MOA: clavulanate inhibits β-lactamases → expands amoxicillin spectrum to include MSSA, H. influenzae, Moraxella, anaerobes. Indications: AOM (failure), sinusitis, dental infections, animal bites, CAP, complicated UTI. SE: diarrhoea (clavulanate component - very common), cholestatic hepatitis (more than amoxicillin alone). CI: penicillin allergy.

1st-gen oral cephalosporin (Australian/INN spelling of cephalexin). MOA: PBP binding → bactericidal cell wall disruption; primarily gram-positive spectrum. Indications: MSSA/GAS SSTIs, uncomplicated UTI (PBS 1st-line in Australia). SE: GI, rash. Note: same drug as cephalexin (US/international spelling).

2nd-gen cephalosporin (oral and IV). MOA: PBP binding; broader gram-negative coverage than 1st-gen (H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis). Indications: AOM, sinusitis, CAP, early Lyme disease. SE: GI, rash. Note: oral form poorly absorbed - take with food for ↑bioavailability.

3rd-gen cephalosporin with anti-pseudomonal activity. MOA: PBP binding with extended gram-negative spectrum including Pseudomonas. Indications: Pseudomonas infections, febrile neutropenia, melioidosis (Burkholderia pseudomallei - endemic in northern Australia). SE: hypersensitivity, encephalopathy (renal impairment). Note: limited gram-positive coverage.

Carbapenem (combined with cilastatin to prevent renal metabolism). MOA: broadest-spectrum β-lactam; binds all PBPs; stable to most β-lactamases. Indications: severe polymicrobial/MDR gram-negative infections, febrile neutropenia. SE: seizures (↑CNS penetration vs meropenem - dose-related). Note: cilastatin has no antibacterial activity - prevents imipenem renal tubular degradation.

Polymyxin antibiotic (last-resort gram-negative coverage). MOA: detergent-like disruption of outer membrane in gram-negatives → cell death. Indications: carbapenem-resistant gram-negatives (MDR Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, KPC Klebsiella). SE: nephrotoxicity (~50% - dose-limiting), neurotoxicity. Note: loading dose critical; PK/PD complex; use only as last resort.

Gabapentinoid (α2-δ VGCC ligand). MOA: binds α2-δ subunit of voltage-gated Ca channels → ↓Ca influx → ↓NT release (glutamate, substance P) → ↓neuropathic pain. Indications: neuropathic pain (diabetic, PHN), fibromyalgia, GAD, focal seizures. SE: sedation, dizziness, weight gain, oedema, euphoria (abuse potential - AU Schedule 4). Note: avoid abrupt withdrawal; more linear PK than gabapentin.

Gabapentinoid (α2-δ VGCC ligand). MOA: same mechanism as pregabalin - ↓presynaptic NT release. Indications: focal seizures, neuropathic pain (diabetic, PHN), RLS. SE: sedation, dizziness, ataxia, oedema, weight gain. Note: non-linear (saturable) absorption limits high-dose efficacy; avoid abrupt withdrawal.

Dual-mechanism analgesic (opioid + NRI). MOA: μ-opioid receptor agonism + noradrenaline reuptake inhibition (no serotonin activity → lower serotonin syndrome risk vs tramadol). Indications: moderate-severe acute/chronic pain, diabetic neuropathy. SE: constipation, sedation. Note: opioid-sparing due to NRI component.

Synthetic opioid (pethidine/pethidine - UK/AU name). MOA: μ-opioid agonism; metabolised to norpethidine (CNS excitant - seizures in accumulation). Indications: procedural pain; post-op shivering (low-dose IV); falling out of favour. SE: seizures/tremor (norpethidine accumulation in renal impairment), serotonin syndrome (with MAOIs), tachycardia (atropine-like). CI: MAOIs, renal impairment, elderly. Note: largely replaced.

Dissociative anaesthetic. MOA: non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonism → dissociative state; also μ-opioid receptor agonism, Na channel blockade. Indications: procedural sedation (analgesia + sedation simultaneously), induction in haemodynamic instability, refractory pain (infusion), refractory status epilepticus. SE: emergence reactions (hallucinations - co-administer midazolam), ↑BP/HR/ICP/IOP. Note: bronchodilator - safe in asthma; preserves airway reflexes.

Local anaesthetic + class Ib antiarrhythmic (AU/UK name for lidocaine). MOA: blocks voltage-gated Na channels (use-dependent) → ↓nerve conduction and ventricular ectopy. Indications: infiltration/nerve block/epidural/topical LA, VT/VF (IV 2nd-line), PHN (patch). SE: CNS toxicity (perioral tingling → seizures), cardiovascular toxicity (cardiac arrest at toxic levels). Note: max 3 mg/kg (plain), 7 mg/kg (+ adrenaline).

Long-acting amide local anaesthetic (~4-8 h duration). MOA: Na channel blockade → nerve conduction block; high lipid solubility → prolonged binding. Indications: spinal/epidural/regional nerve blocks, wound infiltration. SE: cardiotoxicity (higher risk vs lignocaine - ventricular arrhythmia/arrest). Note: Intralipid antidote for LA systemic toxicity. CI: IV regional anaesthesia (Bier's block).

Long-acting amide local anaesthetic (S-enantiomer; motor-sparing). MOA: Na channel blockade; preferentially blocks sensory > motor fibres at lower concentrations. Indications: epidural analgesia (labour), major nerve blocks, wound infiltration. SE: cardiotoxicity (lower than bupivacaine). Note: preferred for labour epidurals (sensory block with preserved motor function).

Potent non-selective NSAID (indole acetic acid). MOA: inhibits COX-1/2 → ↓prostaglandins. Indications: acute gout (highly effective), ankylosing spondylitis, patent ductus arteriosus closure (neonatal IV). SE: highest GI toxicity among NSAIDs, headache, AKI. Note: limit use to short courses for specific indications.

5-HT1B/1D agonist (1st triptan). MOA: presynaptic 5-HT1D → ↓trigeminal NT release; 5-HT1B on meningeal vessels → vasoconstriction → ↓neurogenic inflammation. Indications: acute migraine (oral 50-100 mg, nasal, SC), cluster headache (SC - most rapid effect). SE: chest tightness/pressure, flushing, tingling. CI: IHD, uncontrolled HTN, basilar/hemiplegic migraine.

5-HT1B/1D agonist (triptan; fastest oral onset). MOA: same trigeminal modulation and vasoconstriction as sumatriptan. Indications: acute migraine (10 mg - ODT available). SE: sedation, chest discomfort. CI: IHD, uncontrolled HTN. Note: reduce dose with propranolol (MAO-A interaction).

5-HT1B/1D agonist (triptan; oral and nasal spray). MOA: same mechanism as sumatriptan; CNS penetration → central trigeminal modulation. Indications: acute migraine (2.5-5 mg oral/nasal). SE: chest tightness, paraesthesias. CI: IHD, basilar migraine, MAOIs within 2 weeks.

5-HT2B/2C antagonist (migraine prophylaxis; tricyclic-like). MOA: blocks 5-HT2 receptors → ↓neurogenic inflammation; also H1/M1/α1 antagonism. Indications: migraine prophylaxis (especially childhood migraine). SE: significant weight gain, sedation - main limitations. Note: older agent; largely replaced by topiramate, propranolol, amitriptyline.

Dopamine precursor (combined with dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor). MOA: crosses BBB → converted to dopamine in striatum; carbidopa (Sinemet) or benserazide (Madopar) prevents peripheral conversion → ↓SE. Indications: Parkinson's disease (most effective symptomatic treatment). SE: motor fluctuations/wearing off, dyskinesias (peak-dose), nausea, impulse control disorders, orthostasis, hallucinations. Note: gold standard; on-off phenomenon with disease progression.

Non-ergot dopamine agonist (D2/D3 selective). MOA: activates D2/D3 receptors in striatum → direct dopaminergic stimulation. Indications: Parkinson's disease (early or levodopa adjunct), RLS. SE: impulse control disorders (gambling, hypersexuality - screen at every visit), orthostasis, somnolence, hallucinations. Note: D3 selectivity may explain ↑impulse control SE.

Non-ergot dopamine agonist (D2/D3). MOA: D2/D3 agonism in striatum → dopaminergic effect. Indications: Parkinson's disease, RLS. SE: impulse control disorders, orthostasis, nausea, somnolence. Note: similar profile to pramipexole.

Non-ergot dopamine agonist (transdermal patch; D3 > D2 > D1). MOA: continuous dopaminergic stimulation via patch → avoids peak/trough effects. Indications: early and advanced Parkinson's disease, RLS. SE: impulse control disorders, application site reactions, somnolence. Note: once-daily patch useful in patients with swallowing difficulty.

Irreversible MAO-B inhibitor (selective). MOA: inhibits MAO-B → ↓striatal dopamine catabolism → ↑dopamine. Indications: Parkinson's disease (monotherapy or adjunct). SE: generally well tolerated; headache, nausea. Note: mild tyramine restriction; avoid pethidine/pethidine and SSRIs (serotonin syndrome risk).

Peripheral COMT inhibitor. MOA: inhibits catechol-O-methyltransferase → ↓peripheral levodopa breakdown → ↑levodopa bioavailability per dose. Indications: Parkinson's - adjunct to levodopa for wearing-off. SE: dyskinesias (↑levodopa effect - may need levodopa dose reduction), diarrhoea, orange urine. Note: Stalevo = levodopa/carbidopa/entacapone combination tablet.

NMDA receptor antagonist (also ↑dopamine release). MOA: blocks NMDA receptors → ↓glutamatergic overactivity; also inhibits dopamine reuptake. Indications: Parkinson's disease (mild early, or adjunct - ↓levodopa-induced dyskinesias), influenza A (resistance widespread). SE: livedo reticularis, ankle oedema, confusion/hallucinations (elderly), insomnia. Note: unique mechanism for treating levodopa-induced dyskinesias.

Reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (AChEI). MOA: inhibits AChE → ↑synaptic acetylcholine → compensates for loss of cholinergic neurons. Indications: Alzheimer's disease (mild-severe - symptomatic, not disease-modifying). SE: GI (nausea, diarrhoea - take at night to ↓this), bradycardia, vivid dreams, syncope. Note: 5 mg/day × 4 weeks → 10 mg/day; modest cognitive benefit.

Pseudo-irreversible AChEI + BuChEI (butyrylcholinesterase inhibitor). MOA: inhibits both AChE and BuChE → ↑acetylcholine in CNS. Indications: Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's dementia (unique - only approved agent for PDD). SE: severe GI (patch formulation markedly ↓this), bradycardia. Note: transdermal patch preferred for tolerability.

Reversible AChEI + nicotinic allosteric modulator. MOA: inhibits AChE → ↑ACh; also allosteric potentiation of nicotinic ACh receptors. Indications: mild-moderate Alzheimer's disease. SE: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, bradycardia. Note: take with food; nicotinic modulation may provide additional benefit.

Uncompetitive NMDA receptor antagonist. MOA: blocks tonically overactive NMDA receptors in AD → ↓excitotoxic glutamate signalling while allowing physiological activation. Indications: moderate-severe Alzheimer's disease (often combined with AChEI). SE: well tolerated - dizziness, constipation, headache. Note: different mechanism from AChEIs; combination is additive.

SSRI + sigma-1 receptor agonist (unique). MOA: SERT blockade + potent sigma-1 receptor agonism (↓inflammation - proposed COVID-19 mechanism). Indications: OCD (1st-line), social anxiety. SE: GI, insomnia, sexual dysfunction. Note: potent CYP1A2/2C19 inhibitor - ↑theophylline, warfarin, clozapine levels significantly.

SNRI (active O-desmethyl metabolite of venlafaxine). MOA: balanced SERT/NET inhibition (active at low doses unlike venlafaxine). Indications: MDD, vasomotor symptoms of menopause. SE: nausea, ↑BP, discontinuation syndrome. Note: minimal hepatic first-pass - useful in hepatic impairment.

Melatonin agonist + 5-HT2C antagonist (atypical antidepressant). MOA: MT1/MT2 agonism → circadian rhythm normalisation; 5-HT2C antagonism → ↑DA/NE in prefrontal cortex. Indications: MDD. SE: hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs at 6 and 12 weeks - mandatory), headache. Note: no sexual SE, no weight gain, no withdrawal syndrome; avoid alcohol.

1st-gen typical antipsychotic (low-potency phenothiazine). MOA: broad receptor blockade - D2 antagonism + H1 (sedation), α1 (hypotension), M1 (anticholinergic). Indications: schizophrenia, acute agitation, intractable hiccups. SE: profound sedation, orthostatic hypotension, anticholinergic effects, EPS (less than haloperidol), tardive dyskinesia, QT prolongation, cholestatic jaundice.

Typical antipsychotic (thioxanthene; D1/D2 antagonist). MOA: potent D1/D2 receptor blockade. Indications: acute psychotic agitation (Clopixol Acuphase - medium-onset, 2-3 days; NOT a standard depot), chronic schizophrenia (Clopixol Depot - monthly IM). SE: EPS, tardive dyskinesia, sedation, hyperprolactinaemia. Note: Acuphase is NOT for long-term use (max 4 injections) - distinct from Depot formulation.

Z-drug cyclopyrrolone (non-benzodiazepine GABA-A modulator). MOA: binds BZ1/BZ2 GABA-A subtypes (less selective than zolpidem) → sedation/hypnosis. Indications: short-term insomnia (max 2-4 weeks). SE: bitter metallic taste (characteristic SE), dependence, next-day drowsiness, rebound insomnia. Note: AU Schedule 4; avoid in elderly.

CNS stimulant (non-amfetamine DAT/NET blocker). MOA: blocks DAT and NET → ↑synaptic DA and NE in PFC and striatum → improved attention/impulse control. Indications: ADHD (1st-line), narcolepsy. SE: appetite suppression, insomnia, ↑HR/BP, growth deceleration (children), tics. CI: symptomatic CVD, hyperthyroidism, current MAOI use.

Amfetamine prodrug (lysine-dexamfetamine). MOA: cleaved by peptidases → d-amfetamine → releases DA/NE from nerve terminals + blocks DAT/NET → ↑synaptic monoamines. Indications: ADHD, moderate-severe BED. SE: appetite suppression, insomnia, ↑BP/HR, potential for abuse (lower than immediate-release). CI: structural cardiac disease, MAOIs.

Partial α4β2 nicotinic ACh receptor agonist. MOA: partial nAChR agonism → ↓nicotine withdrawal/cravings; competitive antagonism blocks nicotine binding → ↓reward. Indications: smoking cessation (most effective pharmacotherapy - Cochrane). SE: neuropsychiatric effects (depression, suicidality - boxed warning; monitor), nausea, vivid dreams. Note: 12-week course; AU PBS-subsidised.

Opioid receptor antagonist (oral/monthly IM). MOA: competitively blocks μ/κ/δ receptors → ↓reward from opioids and alcohol (endorphin blockade). Indications: opioid use disorder (after detox), alcohol use disorder. SE: hepatotoxicity (high dose), precipitates withdrawal if opioid-dependent, nausea. Note: must be opioid-free ≥7-10 days before starting.

Alcohol use disorder treatment. MOA: NMDA modulation + GABA-A enhancement → restores neurochemical balance disrupted by chronic alcohol → ↓cravings. Indications: maintaining abstinence in alcohol use disorder. SE: diarrhoea, nausea. Note: most effective when abstinent at start; renally excreted - CI if eGFR <30.

Aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor (aversion therapy). MOA: inhibits ALDH-2 → acetaldehyde accumulates after alcohol → flushing, nausea, tachycardia (aversive conditioning). Indications: alcohol use disorder (supervised - requires motivated patient). SE: disulfiram-alcohol reaction (cardiovascular collapse with large amounts), hepatotoxicity. CI: CVD, recent alcohol use, metronidazole.

Methylxanthine bronchodilator. MOA: PDE inhibition → ↑cAMP → bronchodilation; adenosine A1/A2 antagonism; anti-inflammatory at low doses. Indications: COPD (add-on - falling out of favour), severe asthma (IV aminophylline). SE: narrow TI - nausea, palpitations, seizures; monitor levels (target 5-15 mg/L). Note: many interactions (CYP1A2 substrate - ↑by macrolides, ciprofloxacin).

PDE4 inhibitor (oral anti-inflammatory; not a bronchodilator). MOA: selective PDE4 inhibition → ↑cAMP in airway immune cells → ↓neutrophilic inflammation in COPD. Indications: severe COPD (FEV1 <50%, chronic bronchitis, ≥2 exacerbations/year - add-on to bronchodilators). SE: diarrhoea, nausea, weight loss, psychiatric effects. Note: no acute bronchodilatory effect.

β2-selective agonist (SABA/tocolytic). MOA: β2 receptor stimulation → ↑cAMP → bronchodilation; also uterine relaxation. Indications: asthma/COPD bronchospasm, preterm labour tocolysis (SC/IV). SE: tachycardia, tremor, hypokalaemia. Note: available as inhaled/oral/SC; inhaled salbutamol generally preferred for asthma.

PPI. MOA: irreversible H⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition → ↓gastric acid. Indications: GORD, peptic ulcer, H. pylori eradication. Note: less CYP2C19 polymorphism variation than omeprazole - more consistent acid suppression across metaboliser subtypes.

Peripheral D2 antagonist (prokinetic antiemetic). MOA: blocks D2 receptors in CTZ (outside BBB) and gastric wall → antiemetic + ↑gastric motility. Indications: nausea/vomiting, gastroparesis. SE: QT prolongation, hyperprolactinaemia. CI: cardiac disease, QT prolongation, hepatic impairment. Note: lower EPS risk than metoclopramide - does not cross BBB well.

Phenothiazine antiemetic (D2 antagonist). MOA: D2 blockade in CTZ → antiemetic; also H1/M1 antagonism. Indications: nausea/vomiting, vestibular vertigo. SE: acute dystonia (especially IM - treat with benztropine), tardive dyskinesia (long-term), sedation. Note: common cause of iatrogenic acute dystonia.

Anticholinergic (scopolamine). MOA: muscarinic antagonism → ↓smooth muscle spasm (Buscopan - peripheral only; no CNS); transdermal → CNS + peripheral → antiemetic. Indications: Buscopan: IBS/bowel spasm, ureteric/biliary colic; Scopoderm patch: motion sickness, PONV. SE: dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation; CNS effects (scopolamine - confusion in elderly). Note: Buscopan does not cross BBB.

NK1 (neurokinin-1) receptor antagonist. MOA: blocks substance P/NK1 in brainstem → ↓delayed emesis. Indications: highly emetogenic CINV (with 5-HT3 antagonist + dexamethasone), PONV. SE: fatigue, constipation, hiccups. Note: moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor - ↑dexamethasone levels (use 50% dex dose); paradoxically ↑warfarin effect via CYP2C9 induction.

Stimulant laxative (diphenylmethane). MOA: direct enteric nervous system stimulation → ↑colonic motor activity + active Cl secretion. Indications: constipation (short-term), bowel preparation. SE: cramping, electrolyte disturbance (overuse). Note: onset 6-12 h oral, 30-60 min rectal; avoid prolonged use.

Stimulant laxative (anthraquinone glycoside). MOA: bacterial conversion to sennosides → myenteric plexus stimulation → ↑peristalsis + ↓colonic water absorption. Indications: constipation, bowel preparation. SE: cramping, electrolyte disturbance (prolonged use), melanosis coli (benign brown discolouration). Note: onset 8-12 h; routinely co-prescribed with opioids.

DMARD (sulfonamide + 5-ASA). MOA: colonic bacteria cleave → 5-ASA (anti-inflammatory in bowel) + sulfapyridine (DMARD effect in joints). Indications: RA, psoriatic arthritis, IBD (UC - 5-ASA component). SE: GI (take with food), BM suppression, rash, hepatotoxicity, reversible oligospermia. Note: check G6PD; co-prescribe folate.

DMARD (DHODH inhibitor). MOA: prodrug → teriflunomide; inhibits DHODH → ↓de novo pyrimidine synthesis → ↓T/B cell proliferation. Indications: RA, psoriatic arthritis. SE: diarrhoea, ↑LFTs (monitor monthly), hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity. CI: pregnancy (long washout required - cholestyramine accelerates elimination). Note: active metabolite T1/2 15-18 days.

Anti-IL-17A monoclonal antibody. MOA: inhibits IL-17A → ↓Th17-driven neutrophilic inflammation in skin/joints. Indications: plaque psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, non-radiographic axSpA. SE: Candida infections (IL-17 has antifungal role), URTI, IBD exacerbation. Note: SC monthly after loading doses.

Anti-IL-12/23 monoclonal antibody (p40 subunit). MOA: blocks shared p40 subunit of IL-12/23 → ↓Th1 (IL-12) and Th17 (IL-23) pathways. Indications: plaque psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn's disease, UC. SE: URTI, injection site reactions, serious infections. Note: IV induction then SC maintenance.

JAK1/3 inhibitor (small molecule). MOA: inhibits JAK1/3 → ↓JAK-STAT cytokine signalling (IL-2, -4, -7, -15, -21). Indications: RA, psoriatic arthritis, UC, ankylosing spondylitis. SE: serious infections (herpes zoster - vaccinate first), MACE, malignancy, DVT/PE (boxed warning). Note: oral; avoid live vaccines.

JAK1/2 inhibitor. MOA: inhibits JAK1/2 → ↓STAT-mediated cytokine transcription. Indications: RA, alopecia areata, COVID-19 (hospitalised - WHO recommendation). SE: serious infections, VTE, MACE, malignancy, ↑lipids. Note: similar safety profile to tofacitinib; renal dose adjustment required.

SERM (selective oestrogen receptor modulator). MOA: competitive ER antagonism in breast (↓proliferation) + agonist in uterus/bone. Indications: HR+ breast cancer (premenopausal adjuvant - 5-10 years). SE: hot flushes, endometrial cancer (↑2-7×), VTE, cataracts. Note: requires CYP2D6 for active metabolite - avoid CYP2D6 inhibitors (paroxetine, fluoxetine).

Non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor. MOA: inhibits aromatase → ↓peripheral oestrogen synthesis; only effective postmenopausally. Indications: HR+ breast cancer (postmenopausal - adjuvant, superior to tamoxifen). SE: arthralgia/myalgia (AIMSS - common), osteoporosis, hot flushes. Note: requires intact postmenopausal status.

Non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor. MOA: same aromatase inhibition as anastrozole → ↓oestrogen in peripheral tissues. Indications: HR+ breast cancer (postmenopausal), ovarian stimulation in infertility (off-label). SE: arthralgia, osteoporosis, hot flushes. Note: same class/effect as anastrozole; also used for ovulation induction.

Alkylating cytotoxic agent (nitrogen mustard). MOA: CYP450-activated → cross-links DNA strands → blocks replication (non-cell-cycle specific). Indications: NHL, breast cancer, lupus nephritis, ANCA vasculitis, ovarian cancer. SE: haemorrhagic cystitis (mesna + hydration required), BM suppression, nausea, alopecia, secondary AML/bladder cancer (long-term). Note: maintain high urine output.

BCR-ABL/c-KIT/PDGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor. MOA: binds inactive ABL kinase domain → ↓CML cell proliferation; also c-KIT inhibition → GIST activity. Indications: CML (1st-line - revolutionised management), c-KIT mutant GIST, Ph+ ALL. SE: oedema (periorbital, pleural), nausea, ↑LFTs, cytopenias, QT prolongation. Note: paradigm shift - targeted therapy replacing chemotherapy for CML.

Osmotic diuretic. MOA: filtered but not reabsorbed → osmotic gradient → ↑urine output; ↑plasma osmolality → draws water from brain → ↓cerebral oedema. Indications: raised ICP (1.25 g/kg IV bolus), AKI prevention (high-risk surgery), acute angle-closure glaucoma. SE: hypovolaemia, ↑osmolar gap, ↓Na, rebound cerebral oedema. Note: administer via filter; monitor serum osmolality.

IV anaesthetic/sedative (short-acting; rapid redistribution). MOA: potentiates GABA-A receptor → CNS depression; also direct GABA-A activation. Indications: induction/maintenance of GA, ICU sedation (short-term). SE: propofol infusion syndrome (high dose/prolonged - metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, cardiac failure), hypotension (vasodilatory), pain on injection. Note: contains soy/egg lipid emulsion.

Depolarising neuromuscular blocker (AU: suxamethonium = succinylcholine). MOA: persistent nAChR activation at NMJ → depolarisation blockade (fasciculations then flaccid paralysis). Indications: RSI (fastest onset/offset of any NMBA - ideal for crash intubation), laryngospasm. SE: hyperkalaemia (↑K 0.5-1 mmol/L normally; life-threatening in burns/crush/denervation >48 h), bradycardia (children), malignant hyperthermia (MH trigger). CI: burns/crush injury >48 h, UMN/LMN lesions, MH susceptibility.

Non-depolarising aminosteroid NMBA. MOA: competitive nAChR antagonism at NMJ → blockade without fasciculations. Indications: RSI at high dose (1.2 mg/kg - comparable onset to suxamethonium), maintenance paralysis in OR/ICU. SE: residual paralysis, tachycardia (vagolytic). Note: key advantage - completely and immediately reversible with sugammadex.

Modified γ-cyclodextrin (selective relaxant binding agent). MOA: encapsulates rocuronium/vecuronium → forms inactive complex → rapid removal from NMJ → reversal within 3 min even from profound blockade. Indications: reversal of rocuronium/vecuronium (any depth). Note: no ceiling effect; expensive; recurrence rare.

2nd-generation H1 antihistamine (active metabolite of hydroxyzine). MOA: peripherally selective H1 inverse agonist → ↓histamine-mediated wheal/flare; low CNS penetration (↓sedation vs 1st-gen). Indications: allergic rhinitis, urticaria, atopic dermatitis. SE: mild sedation (more than fexofenadine), dry mouth. Note: once daily; OTC in Australia.

2nd-generation H1 antihistamine (active metabolite of terfenadine). MOA: peripherally selective H1 inverse agonism; does not cross BBB - virtually non-sedating. Indications: allergic rhinitis, chronic urticaria. SE: minimal sedation, headache. Note: no cardiac risk (unlike terfenadine predecessor); OTC in Australia.

2nd-generation H1 antihistamine. MOA: H1 inverse agonist; minimal CNS penetration → ↓sedation. Indications: allergic rhinitis, urticaria. SE: minimal sedation, headache. Note: OTC; active metabolite desloratadine is a separate product (Aerius/Claramax).

1st-generation phenothiazine antihistamine. MOA: H1 antagonism + D2/muscarinic/α1 blockade → potent sedating antihistamine with antiemetic properties. Indications: allergic conditions, nausea/vomiting (IM/rectal), motion sickness. SE: profound sedation, anticholinergic effects, respiratory depression. CI: children <2 years (fatal respiratory depression risk), coma.

Water-soluble vitamin B1. MOA: cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-KGDH, transketolase → essential for aerobic carbohydrate metabolism in CNS. Indications: Wernicke's encephalopathy (IV high-dose before glucose in alcoholics), Korsakoff's prevention, alcoholic patients, hyperemesis gravidarum. SE: rare anaphylaxis (IV). Note: always give BEFORE glucose in at-risk patients - glucose depletes thiamine → precipitates Wernicke's.

Water-soluble vitamin B6. MOA: cofactor for aminotransferases, GABA synthesis, glycogen phosphorylase; competes with isoniazid-pyridoxal complex. Indications: isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy (prophylaxis 25-50 mg/day), sideroblastic anaemia, pyridoxine-responsive neonatal seizures. SE: sensory peripheral neuropathy (paradoxical - chronic doses >500 mg/day).

Water-soluble vitamin B9. MOA: essential one-carbon donor for purine/thymidylate synthesis, methylation, homocysteine recycling. Indications: NTD prevention (0.5 mg/day pre-conception; 5 mg/day high-risk), megaloblastic anaemia, methotrexate co-prescription (5 mg weekly - ↓mucositis/hepatotoxicity). Note: never give alone in B12 deficiency (masks anaemia → irreversible neurological damage progresses).

Oral iron supplement (Fe2+ - most bioavailable). MOA: provides elemental iron for haemoglobin/myoglobin/enzyme synthesis; absorbed via DMT-1 in duodenum. Indications: iron deficiency anaemia, iron depletion in pregnancy. SE: constipation, dark stools, nausea (take with food to ↓GI SE). Note: absorption ↑ with vitamin C, ↓ with Ca/tea/antacids; separate from levothyroxine by 4 h.

Potent synthetic glucocorticoid (~25× anti-inflammatory potency of cortisol; negligible mineralocorticoid). MOA: GR agonism → ↑surfactant synthesis (SP-A/B/C/D), ↓inflammatory cytokines; crosses placenta efficiently (not inactivated by placental 11β-HSD2 unlike prednisolone). Indications: antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity (2 × 12 mg IM 24 h apart, 24–34 wk - ↓RDS/IVH/NEC); topical inflammatory dermatoses (Betnovate - moderate/potent); cerebral oedema; adrenal crisis. SE: maternal hyperglycaemia (monitor in GDM), fetal adrenal suppression, ↑infection risk. Note: most important antenatal intervention for preterm birth - administer even if delivery imminent.

Narrow-spectrum IV/IM penicillin (penicillin G - AU/UK name). MOA: binds PBP2a → irreversible transpeptidase inhibition → bactericidal cell wall disruption; excellent gram-positive and anaerobic activity, poor gram-negative. Indications: meningococcal disease (empiric pre-hospital 1.2 g IV/IM - give before LP), syphilis (primary/secondary/neurosyphilis - benzathine penicillin IM), GAS infections (pharyngitis, cellulitis), infective endocarditis (Streptococcus viridans), GBS prophylaxis in labour. SE: hypersensitivity (0.01% anaphylaxis), high-dose seizures, hyperkalaemia (K-salt preparation). CI: penicillin allergy. Note: treat meningococcal disease empirically without awaiting LP - do not delay antibiotics.

Oral narrow-spectrum penicillin (penicillin V - acid-stable). MOA: PBP inhibition → bactericidal cell wall disruption; same spectrum as benzylpenicillin but oral formulation. Indications: GAS pharyngitis/tonsillitis (10-day course - 1st-line), rheumatic fever secondary prophylaxis (250 mg bd long-term), mild GAS SSTIs, oral cavity infections. SE: GI upset, hypersensitivity. CI: penicillin allergy. Note: poor gram-negative activity; preferred over amoxicillin for strep throat (narrower spectrum).

3rd-gen cephalosporin (no anti-pseudomonal activity; excellent CNS penetration). MOA: PBP binding → bactericidal cell wall disruption; broad gram-negative coverage, reasonable gram-positive. Indications: bacterial meningitis (+ ampicillin in neonates; + dexamethasone in children/adults), neonatal sepsis, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. SE: hypersensitivity, GI, C. difficile. Note: preferred over ceftriaxone for meningitis in neonates (no bilirubin displacement); hepatically metabolised unlike ceftriaxone.

Aminoglycoside antibiotic (broadest spectrum of class). MOA: binds 30S ribosomal subunit → mRNA misreading → bactericidal; concentration-dependent killing with post-antibiotic effect. Indications: MDR gram-negative infections resistant to gentamicin (modified aminoglycoside resists most inactivating enzymes), serious Pseudomonas/Klebsiella infections, MDR-TB (2nd-line). SE: nephrotoxicity (AKI - monitor trough levels), ototoxicity (irreversible sensorineural hearing loss). Note: once-daily dosing preferred (↓nephrotoxicity); synergistic with β-lactams.

Aminoglycoside antibiotic (superior anti-pseudomonal activity vs gentamicin). MOA: 30S ribosomal binding → bactericidal; same class mechanism as gentamicin with ↑Pseudomonas aeruginosa activity. Indications: Pseudomonas infections (inhaled Tobi for CF lung disease - ↑local concentration, ↓systemic toxicity), gram-negative sepsis. SE: nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity (monitor levels). Note: inhaled formulation allows high lung concentrations with minimal systemic absorption - mainstay of CF maintenance therapy.

Glycylcycline antibiotic (broad-spectrum reserve agent). MOA: binds 30S ribosome with ~5× higher affinity than tetracycline → overcomes efflux/ribosomal protection resistance mechanisms; bacteriostatic. Indications: complicated SSTIs, intra-abdominal infections, MDR gram-negatives (Acinetobacter baumannii, KPC-producing Klebsiella) when alternatives exhausted. SE: severe nausea/vomiting (most common dose-limiting SE), hepatotoxicity, ↑all-cause mortality vs comparators (boxed warning - use only when alternatives inadequate). CI: not recommended for HAP/VAP (insufficient lung levels). Note: not for bacteraemia as primary agent.

Macrocyclic antibiotic (gut-confined, C. diff-specific). MOA: inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase σ-subunit → bactericidal vs C. difficile; minimal systemic absorption - gut-confined activity. Indications: Clostridioides difficile infection (↓recurrence vs vancomycin per SOLO trials - preferred for 1st or subsequent recurrences). SE: GI (minimal, poor absorption). Note: non-inferior initial cure; significant ↓recurrence vs oral vancomycin - particularly valuable in high-recurrence-risk patients; expensive.

AU/UK name for rifampicin (rifamycin antitubercular). MOA: inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase β-subunit → blocks mRNA synthesis. Indications: TB (RIPE regimen - rifampicin/isoniazid/pyrazinamide/ethambutol), leprosy, meningococcal prophylaxis (contacts - 600 mg bd × 2 days), MRSA decolonisation (+ fusidic acid). SE: hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs), orange-red discolouration of secretions/urine/tears (warn patients; stains soft contact lenses), drug interactions (potent CYP3A4/2C9 inducer - ↓OCP, antiretrovirals, warfarin). CI: severe hepatic disease. Note: never use as monotherapy - rapid resistance develops; same drug as rifampicin.

Antimycobacterial agent (TB - 4th drug). MOA: inhibits arabinosyltransferases (EmbABC) → blocks arabinogalactan synthesis in mycobacterial cell wall → disrupts cell wall integrity. Indications: active TB (4th drug in RIPE regimen, used until susceptibility known), MAC complex (with clarithromycin + rifampicin). SE: optic neuritis (dose-dependent - ↓visual acuity, colour discrimination, central scotoma; check Snellen chart baseline and monthly), hyperuricaemia. Note: stop if visual SE develop; avoid in young children unable to report visual symptoms reliably.

Antimycobacterial agent (TB - sterilising phase drug). MOA: prodrug → pyrazinoic acid in acidic milieu of macrophage phagolysosomes → disrupts M. tuberculosis membrane energetics → bactericidal against dormant intracellular bacteria. Indications: active TB (2-month intensive phase - critical for sterilising activity, enabling 6-month short-course treatment). SE: hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs - dose-limiting), hyperuricaemia (gout flares - allopurinol if needed), arthralgia, photosensitivity. Note: responsible for reducing TB treatment from 9 → 6 months.

Class Ia antiarrhythmic. MOA: blocks Na channels (↓conduction velocity, ↑QRS) + K channels (↑refractoriness, ↑QT) → slows all cardiac conduction. Indications: WPW + AFib (drug of choice - slows accessory pathway conduction; adenosine/digoxin/CCBs contraindicated), stable monomorphic VT. SE: lupus-like syndrome (chronic use 30-50% - arthralgia, fever, ANA positive; resolves on stopping), QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, hypotension (IV). CI: SLE, 2°/3° AV block. Note: largely replaced but remains preferred for WPW + AFib.

Class Ib antiarrhythmic (oral lignocaine analogue). MOA: fast Na channel blockade (use-dependent, preferential for ischaemic tissue) → ↓automaticity and conduction in depolarised myocardium; ↓QRS duration. Indications: symptomatic ventricular arrhythmias (VT prevention), myotonia congenita. SE: GI (nausea/vomiting - take with food), CNS (tremor, ataxia, dizziness). Note: narrow therapeutic window; CYP1A2 substrate - interactions with ciprofloxacin, fluvoxamine.

Long-acting oral organic nitrate. MOA: releases NO → ↑cGMP → venodilation (↓preload) + moderate coronary artery dilation; no hepatic first-pass metabolism (unlike isosorbide dinitrate - 100% bioavailability). Indications: stable angina prophylaxis, HFrEF (with hydralazine - especially where ACEi/ARB contraindicated; AHeFT trial benefit in African American patients). SE: headache (NO → cerebral vasodilation - common early, usually resolves), tolerance with continuous use (provide 8-h nitrate-free interval), hypotension. CI: PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil/tadalafil/vardenafil - severe hypotension), severe aortic stenosis, RV infarction.

Direct-acting vasodilator (balanced arteriolar and venodilation). MOA: spontaneous NO release → ↑cGMP → vascular smooth muscle relaxation → ↓preload and afterload rapidly. Indications: hypertensive emergency (IV infusion - titratable, onset seconds), acute decompensated HF with ↑SVR, aortic dissection (with β-blocker). SE: cyanide toxicity (prolonged/high-dose - metabolic acidosis, seizures; treat with sodium thiosulfate/hydroxocobalamin); thiocyanate accumulation (renal failure); reflex tachycardia; hypotension. Note: light-sensitive - wrap infusion in foil; avoid use >72 h or use with thiosulfate.

Selective α1-adrenergic receptor blocker. MOA: competitive α1 blockade in vascular smooth muscle → ↓SVR → ↓BP; in prostate smooth muscle → ↓urethral resistance → ↑urinary flow rate. Indications: BPH (1st-line to improve urinary symptoms), HTN (adjunct - not 1st-line since ALLHAT). SE: 1st-dose postural hypotension (start at night 1 mg), dizziness, palpitations, reflex tachycardia. Note: ALLHAT showed doxazosin inferior to chlorthalidone for CV outcomes in HTN - now adjunct only; valuable for combined HTN + BPH.

Central α2-adrenergic agonist. MOA: α2 agonism in brainstem (locus coeruleus/nucleus tractus solitarius) → ↓sympathetic outflow → ↓HR and ↓BP; also ↓noradrenaline release in CNS (sedation, analgesia). Indications: HTN (2nd/3rd-line; IV for hypertensive emergency), ADHD (Kapvay - adjunct), opioid/nicotine withdrawal (↓sympathetic symptoms), hot flushes (Dixarit), Tourette syndrome. SE: sedation, dry mouth, bradycardia, constipation, rebound hypertension on abrupt withdrawal. Note: taper slowly over 1-2 weeks to avoid rebound HTN.

Loop diuretic (AU/EU: torasemide; US: torasemide). MOA: inhibits NKCC2 cotransporter in thick ascending Loop of Henle → potent natriuresis; better oral bioavailability (~80%) and longer duration (~12 h) than furosemide. Indications: HF oedema, refractory oedema when furosemide absorption impaired (gut oedema), HTN. SE: hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyperuricaemia; ototoxicity (lower than furosemide). Note: TRANSFORM-HF - no mortality difference vs furosemide, but ↑bioavailability may be advantageous in decompensated HF with gut oedema.

K-sparing diuretic (ENaC blocker; not aldosterone-dependent). MOA: directly blocks epithelial Na channels (ENaC) in cortical collecting duct → ↓Na reabsorption → ↑K retention, independent of aldosterone. Indications: oedema (with thiazide/loop to prevent hypokalaemia), Liddle syndrome (monogenic ENaC overactivation - ENaC blockers are specific treatment), primary aldosteronism. SE: hyperkalaemia. CI: hyperkalaemia, eGFR <30. Note: distinct from spironolactone - no anti-androgenic effects; Liddle syndrome responds to amiloride but NOT spironolactone.

Barbiturate antiepileptic (AU/UK: phenobarbitone; US: phenobarbitone). MOA: potentiates GABA-A receptor (↑Cl⁻ conductance duration) + inhibits AMPA/kainate glutamate receptors → broad CNS depression and anticonvulsant effect. Indications: neonatal seizures (IV 1st-line - 20 mg/kg loading dose; WHO essential medicine), status epilepticus (2nd-line IV), focal and generalised tonic-clonic seizures, febrile seizure prophylaxis. SE: sedation/cognitive impairment (children - paradoxical hyperactivity), tolerance and physical dependence, potent CYP inducer (↓OCP, warfarin, other AEDs). CI: porphyria, severe respiratory insufficiency. Note: 1st-line for neonatal seizures globally due to parenteral availability, low cost, established safety.

Succinimide antiepileptic (absence seizure-specific). MOA: selectively blocks T-type (transient low-threshold) voltage-gated Ca channels in thalamic relay neurons → interrupts 3-Hz spike-wave oscillations generating absence seizures. Indications: absence (petit mal) epilepsy - 1st-line (equally effective to valproate but safer in children - NIEHS Childhood Absence Epilepsy trial). SE: GI (nausea/vomiting - take with food, most common reason for discontinuation), headache, drowsiness, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (rare). Note: no activity against other seizure types - if generalised tonic-clonic seizures coexist, add valproate.

Keto-analogue of carbamazepine (AED). MOA: blocks voltage-gated Na channels (active metabolite MHD) → membrane stabilisation → ↓sustained repetitive firing; no CYP auto-induction (unlike carbamazepine). Indications: focal (partial) seizures - mono- or adjunctive; trigeminal neuralgia. SE: hyponatraemia (SIADH - more common than carbamazepine; monitor Na, especially with thiazides), dizziness, diplopia, ataxia, rash (10-fold ↓SJS vs carbamazepine). Note: HLA-B*1502 testing recommended in Han Chinese (SJS risk); fewer drug interactions than carbamazepine.

Tricyclic antidepressant (most serotonergic TCA). MOA: potent SERT + moderate NET inhibition (active metabolite desmethylclomipramine is selective NET inhibitor); also H1/α1/M1 antagonism. Indications: OCD (most effective pharmacotherapy - 1st-line; superior to other TCAs for obsessive-compulsive symptoms), panic disorder, cataplexy. SE: anticholinergic (dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, blurred vision), sedation, weight gain, sexual dysfunction, QT prolongation, seizures (↑risk vs other TCAs), cardiac arrhythmias. CI: recent MI, MAOIs within 14 days, glaucoma. Note: SE profile limits use; reserve for OCD not responding to SSRIs.

Prototypic TCA. MOA: SERT + NET inhibition → ↑synaptic 5-HT and NA; also potent H1/M1/α1 antagonism. Indications: depression (largely superseded by SSRIs), nocturnal enuresis in children (anticholinergic ± central mechanism), panic disorder, chronic pain. SE: anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation), cardiac arrhythmias (quinidine-like Na channel blockade - dangerous in overdose), orthostatic hypotension, sedation, weight gain. CI: MAOIs, post-MI, glaucoma, cardiac conduction disease. Note: enuresis - 1st-line is bedwetting alarm; imipramine 2nd-line (relapse on stopping).

Selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor (non-stimulant ADHD). MOA: selective NET inhibitor → ↑PFC noradrenaline (and dopamine via NET) → ↑executive function, ↓impulsivity; no dopamine transporter activity → no abuse potential. Indications: ADHD (preferred when: stimulant contraindicated, comorbid tic disorder, substance abuse risk, anxiety comorbidity). SE: ↑BP/HR, nausea/GI, headache, insomnia, growth deceleration (children), sexual dysfunction; rare hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs if jaundice). CI: MAOIs, narrow-angle glaucoma, severe CV disease. Note: onset 4-6 weeks (slower than stimulants); not a controlled substance; may worsen suicidal ideation (adolescents - monitor).

Azapirone anxiolytic. MOA: partial 5-HT1A agonist → presynaptic autoreceptor activation → ↓serotonergic tone; also D2 partial agonism; no GABAergic activity. Indications: generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) - non-sedating, non-addictive alternative to benzodiazepines. SE: dizziness, headache, nausea, restlessness - generally well tolerated; no abuse potential. Note: slow onset 2-4 weeks (not effective PRN/acutely); no cross-tolerance with BZDs (cannot replace BZDs abruptly); useful when sedation/dependence risk a concern.

1st-gen antihistamine with anxiolytic properties. MOA: H1 inverse agonism + 5-HT2A/muscarinic blockade → sedation and anxiolysis; rapid oral absorption (onset 30-60 min). Indications: GAD (acute anxiolysis - rapid onset, no dependence risk), pruritus (urticaria, atopic dermatitis), pre-operative sedation, alcohol withdrawal adjunct. SE: sedation (dose-dependent), dry mouth, urinary retention, QT prolongation (high dose). Note: parent compound of cetirizine (active metabolite); useful for PRN anxiety without BZD dependence; avoid in elderly (Beers criterion - anticholinergic).

Ultra-short IV induction agent (imidazole). MOA: GABA-A positive allosteric modulator → rapid CNS depression; minimal cardiovascular depression (haemodynamically stable). Indications: RSI/induction when haemodynamic instability present (trauma, cardiogenic shock, severe valvular disease - preferred over propofol for BP preservation). SE: adrenocortical suppression (inhibits 11β-hydroxylase → ↓cortisol even with single dose - clinically significant in septic shock), myoclonus on induction, pain on injection, ↑PONV. CI: adrenal insufficiency, prolonged infusion (ICU sedation - prohibited), septic shock (some centres). Note: haemodynamic stability is its defining advantage over propofol.

Selective α2-adrenergic agonist (ICU/procedural sedative). MOA: α2 agonism in locus coeruleus → ↓noradrenaline release → sedation and anxiolysis without significant respiratory depression; also ↓sympathetic tone → ↓HR, ↓BP; ↑analgesia via spinal α2 receptors. Indications: ICU sedation (light cooperative sedation - RASS 0 to −2; ↓delirium vs BZDs), procedural sedation, opioid-sparing analgesia, prevention of alcohol withdrawal delirium. SE: bradycardia, hypotension (especially bolus loading), paradoxical hypertension. Note: unique - patients arousable and cooperative; no respiratory depression - can maintain spontaneous breathing.

Non-depolarising aminosteroid NMBA (intermediate duration ~25-40 min). MOA: competitive nAChR antagonism at NMJ → flaccid neuromuscular blockade without fasciculations or depolarisation. Indications: intubation/surgical relaxation, ICU paralysis (ARDS - facilitate ventilation in prone positioning). SE: residual neuromuscular blockade (train-of-four monitoring), ↑HR (minimal - vagolytic effect less than pancuronium). Note: reversible with neostigmine + glycopyrrolate (partial) or sugammadex (complete, any depth); hepatic/biliary excretion.

Reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. MOA: inhibits AChE at NMJ → ↑synaptic acetylcholine → displaces non-depolarising NMBA from nAChR → reversal of neuromuscular blockade. Indications: reversal of non-depolarising NMBAs (always co-administer glycopyrrolate to counteract muscarinic SE), myasthenia gravis (oral pyridostigmine preferred), ileus (pseudo-obstruction - Ogilvie syndrome). SE: bradycardia, bronchoconstriction, hypersalivation, ↑GI motility (all muscarinic - prevented by glycopyrrolate). Note: unreliable at deep blockade (TOF count <2) - sugammadex preferred for profound rocuronium/vecuronium block.

US name for suxamethonium (depolarising NMBA). MOA: persistent nAChR agonism at NMJ → depolarisation blockade (fasciculations then flaccid paralysis); onset 45-60 s, offset 10-15 min (hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase). Indications: RSI (gold standard for fastest intubating conditions), laryngospasm. SE: hyperkalaemia (↑0.5-1 mmol/L normally; dangerous in burns/crush/denervation >48 h), bradycardia (children - pretreat with atropine), malignant hyperthermia trigger. CI: burns/crush injury >48 h, UMN/LMN disease, MH susceptibility, pseudocholinesterase deficiency. Note: same drug as suxamethonium.

5-Aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA; mesalazine - US name). MOA: topical anti-inflammatory in intestinal mucosa → inhibits NF-κB, COX, LOX → ↓prostaglandin and leukotriene synthesis; mechanism not fully elucidated. Indications: UC (mild-moderate - induction and maintenance; rectal enema/suppository for proctitis), Crohn's disease (modest efficacy - less effective than in UC). SE: headache, nausea, mesalazine-induced nephritis (interstitial nephritis - monitor renal function annually), rare paradoxical colitis exacerbation. Note: different formulations release 5-ASA at different gut sites (Asacol: terminal ileum/colon; Pentasa: throughout small bowel + colon; Mezavant: colon - select by disease location).

Non-absorbable rifamycin antibiotic (gut-confined). MOA: inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase; <0.4% systemic absorption → activity confined to GI lumen. Indications: IBS-D (reduces ammonia-producing gut dysbiosis - 550 mg tds × 2 weeks), hepatic encephalopathy secondary prophylaxis (550 mg bd - ↓gut ammonia-producing bacteria; usually + lactulose), traveller's diarrhoea (non-invasive E. coli - 200 mg tds × 3 days). SE: minimal (virtually no systemic absorption); headache, nausea rarely. Note: expensive; HE indication: rifaximin + lactulose combination more effective than lactulose alone.

Nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NtRTI). MOA: intracellularly phosphorylated to TFV-diphosphate → competes with dATP → chain termination of HIV/HBV reverse transcription. Indications: HIV-1 (backbone of combination ART - TDF or TAF + emtricitabine); chronic hepatitis B (1st-line - high barrier to resistance, virological suppression >90%). SE: nephrotoxicity/Fanconi syndrome (TDF > TAF), ↓bone mineral density (TDF > TAF). Note: TAF (tenofovir alafenamide, Vemlidy) → ↑intracellular:plasma ratio → ↓renal/bone toxicity - preferred in renal impairment.

Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI). MOA: intracellularly phosphorylated to 3TC-TP → inhibits HIV/HBV reverse transcriptase by chain termination. Indications: HIV-1 (component of all combination ART regimens), chronic hepatitis B (monotherapy - but low barrier to HBV resistance; YMDD mutation). SE: generally well tolerated - headache, nausea; lactic acidosis (rare class SE). Note: HBV resistance (YMDD mutation) in ~70% at 5 years - tenofovir preferred for HBV monotherapy; lamivudine remains backbone of HIV regimens due to tolerability.

2nd-gen HIV integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI). MOA: binds integrase active site chelating Mg²⁺ → blocks strand transfer of HIV cDNA into host chromatin; exceptionally high barrier to resistance (no resistance mutations in naive patients in major trials). Indications: HIV-1 - recommended 1st-line (Dovato = dolutegravir/lamivudine; Triumeq = dolutegravir/abacavir/lamivudine). SE: insomnia, ↑weight gain, neuropsychiatric effects, ↑SCr (blocks tubular creatinine secretion - not true GFR↓). Note: possible neural tube defect signal in periconceptual use (Botswana data) - counsel women of childbearing potential; preferred INSTI for treatment-naive patients.

Nucleoside analogue antiviral (guanosine analogue). MOA: phosphorylated by viral UL97 kinase (and cellular kinases) → ganciclovir triphosphate preferentially inhibits CMV DNA polymerase → chain termination; 10× more potent vs CMV than acyclovir. Indications: CMV disease in immunocompromised (SOT, HIV/AIDS - IV induction followed by valganciclovir oral maintenance), CMV retinitis, CMV pneumonitis. SE: bone marrow suppression (neutropenia, thrombocytopenia - dose-limiting; monitor FBC weekly), nephrotoxicity, teratogenicity. Note: IV form - valganciclovir oral prodrug preferred when oral route available.

Oral prodrug of ganciclovir (l-valyl ester). MOA: hydrolysed by intestinal and hepatic esterases → ganciclovir (~60% oral bioavailability); same mechanism - UL97-mediated phosphorylation → CMV DNA polymerase inhibition. Indications: CMV retinitis (treatment and maintenance in HIV/AIDS), CMV prophylaxis and pre-emptive therapy in SOT recipients, moderate CMV disease (replaces IV ganciclovir when oral route viable). SE: neutropenia, anaemia, thrombocytopenia (same as ganciclovir; monitor FBC), nephrotoxicity. Note: 900 mg bd equivalent to IV ganciclovir 5 mg/kg bd.

Long-acting somatostatin analogue. MOA: binds SSTR2/5 → ↓GH, TSH, glucagon, insulin, VIP secretion; also inhibits splanchnic blood flow via ↓portal venous pressure. Indications: variceal bleeding (↓portal pressure - adjunct to endoscopic therapy), acromegaly (↓GH/IGF-1), carcinoid syndrome (↓flushing/diarrhoea), VIPoma, thyrotropinoma, dumping syndrome. SE: GI (nausea, steatorrhoea, abdominal cramp), gallstones/biliary sludge (chronic use - bile stasis), bradycardia, hyperglycaemia. Note: LAR (long-acting release - Sandostatin LAR) monthly IM injection for chronic conditions; short-acting SC tds for acute use.

Ergot-derived dopamine D2 agonist (long half-life - twice weekly dosing). MOA: potent D2 agonism on anterior pituitary lactotrophs → ↓prolactin synthesis/secretion and tumour size. Indications: hyperprolactinaemia (prolactinoma - 1st-line, superior to bromocriptine - DOPACOM trial; effective for both macroprolactinoma and microprolactinoma), Parkinson's disease (2nd-line). SE: nausea (less frequent than bromocriptine), postural hypotension, cardiac valvular fibrosis/regurgitation (at Parkinson's doses - <1% at prolactin doses), impulse control disorders (gambling, hypersexuality). Note: twice-weekly dosing improves adherence for prolactinoma.

Recombinant PTH(1-34) analogue (bone-anabolic agent). MOA: pulsatile PTH receptor activation → net bone formation via osteoblast proliferation and activation > osteoclast recruitment (anabolic net balance - opposite of continuous PTH). Indications: severe osteoporosis with fragility fracture (after bisphosphonate failure/intolerance), glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis. SE: nausea, dizziness, leg cramps, transient hypercalcaemia, hypercalciuria. CI: Paget's disease, prior skeletal radiation, bone metastases/malignancy with skeletal involvement, pregnancy, paediatric patients (open epiphyses). Note: SC daily injection; maximum 24-month course; osteosarcoma signal in rats (not confirmed in humans - post-marketing surveillance ongoing).

Platinum-based cytotoxic (alkylating-like). MOA: forms intrastrand and interstrand DNA crosslinks (GG/AG adducts) → blocks replication and transcription → apoptosis; cell-cycle non-specific. Indications: testicular cancer (curative - BEP regimen: bleomycin/etoposide/cisplatin), ovarian, bladder, NSCLC/SCLC, head and neck, oesophageal. SE: nephrotoxicity (dose-limiting - mandatory pre/post-hydration with normal saline; amifostine cytoprotection); severe nausea/vomiting (schedule NK1 + 5-HT3 antagonist + dexamethasone prophylaxis); ototoxicity (irreversible sensorineural hearing loss - audiogram monitoring); peripheral neuropathy; myelosuppression. Note: aggressive IV hydration (1-2 L NS pre + 2 L post) mandatory for every infusion.

Platinum compound (cisplatin analogue with improved tolerability). MOA: same DNA intrastrand crosslinking mechanism as cisplatin → blocks replication. Indications: ovarian cancer (1st-line - carboplatin + paclitaxel: ICON3/OV-10), NSCLC, SCLC, head and neck. SE: myelosuppression (dose-limiting - thrombocytopenia > cisplatin; neutropenia); hypersensitivity (↑with cumulative cycles - 6th cycle onwards); significantly less nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, nausea than cisplatin. Note: dose by AUC using Calvert formula (AUC × [eGFR + 25] = mg dose); no aggressive hydration required.

Taxane cytotoxic (microtubule stabiliser). MOA: binds β-tubulin of assembled microtubule polymers → prevents depolymerisation → mitotic arrest at G2/M checkpoint → apoptosis; cell-cycle specific (M-phase). Indications: ovarian (carboplatin + paclitaxel - 1st-line), breast (early and metastatic), NSCLC, Kaposi sarcoma. SE: peripheral neuropathy (cumulative dose-limiting - sensory > motor), myelosuppression (neutropenia nadir day 8-11), alopecia, arthralgias/myalgias, hypersensitivity (Cremophor EL excipient - premedicate with dexamethasone + diphenhydramine + ranitidine). Note: nab-paclitaxel (Abraxane) - albumin-bound formulation → no Cremophor → ↓hypersensitivity risk, no steroid premedication needed.

Antimetabolite pyrimidine analogue (5-FU). MOA: fluorodeoxyuridine monophosphate (FdUMP) + leucovorin inhibits thymidylate synthase (TS) → ↓dTMP → 'thymineless death'; FUTP incorporation into RNA → ↓protein synthesis. Indications: colorectal cancer (5-FU + leucovorin backbone of FOLFOX/FOLFIRI), breast, gastric/oesophageal, head and neck; topical (Efudix): actinic keratoses, superficial BCC. SE: mucositis, diarrhoea, myelosuppression, hand-foot syndrome (palmar-plantar erythrodysaesthesia - bolus vs infusion different toxicities); DPD deficiency (DPYD variant - severe/fatal toxicity - genotype before prescribing). Note: leucovorin (folinic acid) stabilises FdUMP-TS complex → ↑5-FU efficacy.

Anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody (immune checkpoint inhibitor). MOA: blocks PD-1/PD-L1 and PD-1/PD-L2 interactions → restores tumour-infiltrating T lymphocyte activity → immune-mediated tumour killing. Indications: melanoma (unresectable/metastatic and adjuvant - KEYNOTE-006/054), NSCLC (TPS ≥50% monotherapy or + chemo - KEYNOTE-024/189), TNBC, cervical, endometrial, colorectal (MSI-H/dMMR any solid tumour - KEYNOTE-158), Hodgkin lymphoma, bladder, MSI-H tumours (tumour-agnostic). SE: immune-related AEs (irAEs): pneumonitis, colitis/diarrhoea, hepatitis, endocrinopathies (hypothyroidism most common, T1DM, adrenalitis), dermatitis; treat irAEs with systemic corticosteroids; permanent discontinuation for severe irAEs. Note: response correlates with PD-L1 TPS, TMB-H, and MSI-H/dMMR status.

Anthracycline antineoplastic. MOA: intercalates DNA + inhibits topoisomerase II → DNA strand breaks → replication arrest → apoptosis; also generates reactive oxygen species (cardiotoxicity mechanism). Indications: breast cancer (AC/FAC regimen), NHL/ALL, AML, sarcomas (Ewing's, osteosarcoma), ovarian. SE: cardiotoxicity (cumulative dose-dependent dilated cardiomyopathy - lifetime dose limit ~450-550 mg/m²; baseline and serial ECHO; dexrazoxane cardioprotection ≥300 mg/m²); myelosuppression; mucositis; alopecia; red urine (not haematuria - warn patients); vesicant (extravasation → severe tissue necrosis → treat with dexrazoxane + cold compress). Note: liposomal doxorubicin (Caelyx) - ↓cardiotoxicity and ↓vesicant risk.

Anti-IgE monoclonal antibody. MOA: binds free circulating IgE at FcεRI binding site → prevents IgE/FcεRI interaction on mast cells/basophils → ↓allergic mediator release; also downregulates FcεRI receptor expression. Indications: moderate-severe persistent allergic asthma (uncontrolled on ICS + LABA, total serum IgE 30-700 IU/mL, sensitised to perennial aeroallergen), chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU - 2nd-line). SE: injection site reactions, anaphylaxis (0.1-0.2% - observe 30-60 min post-dose), ↑parasitic infection susceptibility (IgE role in helminth immunity). Note: dose every 2-4 weeks by weight + serum IgE; response assessed at 16 weeks.

Vinca alkaloid (M-phase specific cytotoxic). MOA: binds β-tubulin → inhibits polymerisation → mitotic spindle disruption → metaphase arrest. Indications: ALL (cornerstone of CHOP/CVP regimens), Hodgkin/NHL, Wilms tumour, rhabdomyosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma. SE: peripheral neuropathy (dose-limiting - sensory then motor; footdrop; autonomic: constipation, ileus, urinary retention), SIADH, alopecia. Note: NO myelosuppression (key distinction from other cytotoxics); fatal if given intrathecally - must label 'For IV use only'.

Vinca alkaloid. MOA: same tubulin binding as vincristine → mitotic arrest at M-phase. Indications: Hodgkin lymphoma (ABVD - doxorubicin/bleomycin/vinblastine/dacarbazine), testicular (BEP adjunct), bladder, Kaposi sarcoma. SE: myelosuppression (dose-limiting - unlike vincristine), ↓peripheral neuropathy vs vincristine, alopecia. Note: opposite toxicity profile to vincristine - more BM suppression, less neuropathy.

Glycopeptide cytotoxic antibiotic. MOA: cleaves DNA via ROS generated by bleomycin-Fe²⁺ complex → strand breaks → apoptosis; G2/M arrest. Indications: Hodgkin lymphoma (ABVD - curative), testicular cancer (BEP - curative), squamous cell carcinomas. SE: pulmonary toxicity (dose-limiting - chemical pneumonitis → fibrosis; cumulative dose >400 units; risk ↑ with ↑O2, radiotherapy - use lowest FiO2 peri-op), Raynaud phenomenon, skin pigmentation/thickening. Note: ↓myelosuppression vs other cytotoxics; avoid high FiO2 anaesthesia in prior bleomycin exposure.

Topoisomerase II inhibitor (semisynthetic podophyllotoxin). MOA: stabilises topo II-DNA cleavage complex → DNA double-strand breaks → cell death; S/G2 phase. Indications: testicular cancer (BEP regimen - curative), SCLC (1st-line), AML (induction), NHL, Kaposi sarcoma. SE: myelosuppression (dose-limiting), nausea, alopecia, secondary AML (topo II inhibitor → 11q23 MLL translocations - therapy-related AML 2-10 yr later). Note: IV or oral formulations; schedule-dependent - fractionated dosing ↑efficacy.

Nucleoside analogue antimetabolite. MOA: phosphorylated to dFdCTP → incorporated into DNA → chain termination; also inhibits ribonucleotide reductase → ↓dNTP pools → self-potentiation. Indications: pancreatic adenocarcinoma (1st-line alone or + nab-paclitaxel), NSCLC (+ cisplatin/carboplatin), bladder, ovarian. SE: myelosuppression (thrombocytopenia > neutropenia), flu-like syndrome, pulmonary toxicity, haemolytic uraemic syndrome (rare, cumulative). Note: schedule-dependent; haemolytic uraemic syndrome is rare but life-threatening - check film + LDH.

Oral prodrug of 5-FU. MOA: converted to 5-FU by thymidine phosphorylase (↑in tumour tissue → tumour-selective activation) → same TYMS inhibition as 5-FU. Indications: colorectal cancer (adjuvant and metastatic - equivalent to IV 5-FU), metastatic breast cancer, gastric cancer. SE: hand-foot syndrome (palmar-plantar erythrodysaesthesia - dose-limiting; reduce dose, use emollients), diarrhoea, mucositis (less than IV 5-FU), nausea. Note: check DPYD genotype before prescribing; warfarin interaction (↑INR via CYP2C9 inhibition).

Taxane cytotoxic (microtubule stabiliser). MOA: same β-tubulin binding as paclitaxel → prevents depolymerisation → mitotic arrest; more potent intracellular accumulation than paclitaxel. Indications: breast cancer (adjuvant + metastatic), NSCLC, prostate (castration-resistant), gastric, head and neck. SE: myelosuppression (severe neutropenia - dose-limiting; G-CSF prophylaxis), peripheral oedema/fluid retention (premedicate with dexamethasone × 3 days), neuropathy, alopecia, nail changes, hypersensitivity (less than paclitaxel). Note: premedication with dexamethasone mandatory to ↓fluid retention.

3rd-generation platinum compound. MOA: forms DNA intrastrand crosslinks (similar to cisplatin but different adduct spectrum - bypasses some cisplatin resistance); non-cross-resistant with cisplatin. Indications: colorectal cancer (FOLFOX - oxaliplatin/5-FU/leucovorin - standard adjuvant and 1st-line metastatic). SE: acute cold-triggered neuropathy (laryngopharyngeal dysaesthesia - avoid cold drinks/food; resolves between cycles), cumulative sensory neuropathy (dose-limiting - ≥8 cycles), myelosuppression (moderate), low emetogenicity vs cisplatin. Note: distinct acute vs chronic neurotoxicity profiles; no significant nephrotoxicity.

Topoisomerase I inhibitor (camptothecin analogue). MOA: stabilises topo I-DNA covalent complex → single-strand DNA breaks → replication fork collision → cell death; S-phase specific. Indications: colorectal cancer (FOLFIRI - irinotecan/5-FU/leucovorin - 1st/2nd-line metastatic), SCLC. SE: diarrhoea (early - cholinergic syndrome, treat with atropine; delayed - secretory, treat with loperamide - dose-limiting), neutropenia, alopecia. Note: UGT1A1*28 polymorphism (Gilbert syndrome genotype) → ↓active metabolite (SN-38) glucuronidation → ↑toxicity - reduce dose.

Anti-HER2 monoclonal antibody. MOA: binds HER2 extracellular domain IV → inhibits HER2 signalling → ↓PI3K/Akt proliferation; ADCC (antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity). Indications: HER2-positive breast cancer (early and metastatic - adjuvant 1 year; ↓recurrence 50% - HERA trial), HER2-positive gastric/gastro-oesophageal cancer (+ chemotherapy). SE: cardiotoxicity (↓LVEF, HF - cumulative, usually reversible - check ECHO q3 months; do not combine with anthracyclines concurrently), infusion reactions (1st dose). Note: test HER2 status (IHC 3+ or FISH amplified) before prescribing.

Anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody. MOA: binds VEGF-A → prevents VEGFR binding → inhibits tumour angiogenesis → ↓tumour blood supply/growth.
