Indications: colorectal cancer (1st/2nd-line metastatic + FOLFOX/FOLFIRI), NSCLC (non-squamous), ovarian, renal cell carcinoma, glioblastoma, cervical. SE: hypertension (monitor BP - ACE-i/ARB first-line Mx), proteinuria, impaired wound healing (hold 4-6 wk pre/post-surgery), GI perforation (1-2%), thromboembolism (arterial > venous), haemorrhage, RPLS. CI: recent haemoptysis, squamous histology (pulmonary haemorrhage risk).

Anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody (checkpoint inhibitor). MOA: blocks PD-1/PD-L1 and PD-1/PD-L2 → restores T-cell anti-tumour immunity; similar mechanism to pembrolizumab. Indications: melanoma (+ ipilimumab - CheckMate), NSCLC, renal cell carcinoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, SCLC, head and neck, gastric, HCC, bladder, oesophageal. SE: irAEs (same class as pembrolizumab - pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis, endocrinopathies; treat with steroids). Note: + ipilimumab (dual checkpoint) → superior efficacy but ↑irAE rate; Q2W or Q4W schedules.

Anti-CTLA-4 monoclonal antibody (1st approved checkpoint inhibitor). MOA: blocks CTLA-4 → prevents down-regulation of T-cell activation at priming phase in lymph nodes → ↑tumour immunity. Indications: melanoma (adjuvant and advanced - alone or + nivolumab), RCC (+ nivolumab), CRC (MSI-H + nivolumab), mesothelioma (+ nivolumab). SE: irAEs (more frequent and severe than anti-PD-1 - colitis most common/serious, hepatitis, hypophysitis, dermatitis; ↑with dual checkpoint therapy). Note: toxicity is dose-dependent; 3 mg/kg (melanoma) vs 1 mg/kg (combination).

Proteasome inhibitor (first-in-class). MOA: reversibly inhibits 26S proteasome chymotryptic activity → ↑misfolded proteins → ER stress → ↑NF-κB → apoptosis (plasma cells especially sensitive). Indications: multiple myeloma (1st-line VMP/VRd regimens; relapsed/refractory), mantle cell lymphoma. SE: peripheral neuropathy (dose-limiting - sensory > motor; IV route has less than SC; reduce if ↑grade), thrombocytopenia, reactivation of VZV (prophylactic aciclovir), diarrhoea. Note: SC administration ↓neuropathy vs IV; check antiviral prophylaxis.

Immunomodulatory drug (IMiD; thalidomide analogue). MOA: binds CRBN E3 ligase → degrades Ikaros/Aiolos transcription factors → ↑T/NK cell activity, ↓myeloma cytokines; also anti-angiogenic. Indications: multiple myeloma (maintenance/relapsed; Rd = lenalidomide + dexamethasone), MDS (del(5q) - ↓transfusions), mantle cell lymphoma, follicular lymphoma. SE: myelosuppression (neutropenia - G-CSF if required), VTE (mandatory prophylaxis - aspirin or LMWH), teratogenicity (absolute CI - REMS programme), ↑second primary malignancies. Note: must use REMS programme (iPledge equivalent); check eGFR for dose adjustment.

BTK inhibitor (Bruton's tyrosine kinase). MOA: irreversibly inhibits BTK → blocks BCR signalling → ↓B-cell proliferation/survival; also inhibits ITK in T cells. Indications: CLL/SLL (1st-line - superior to chemoimmunotherapy in elderly/unfit), mantle cell lymphoma, Waldenström, marginal zone lymphoma, chronic GvHD. SE: atrial fibrillation (5-10% - monitor; manage or switch to acalabrutinib), bleeding (antiplatelet effect - hold perioperatively), diarrhoea, hypertension, opportunistic infections. Note: 1st-gen BTK inhibitor; acalabrutinib has ↓AFib risk.

BCL-2 inhibitor. MOA: selectively inhibits anti-apoptotic BCL-2 protein → restores apoptosis in BCL-2-overexpressing tumour cells (CLL, AML have high BCL-2 expression). Indications: CLL (+ obinutuzumab or rituximab - 1st-line; alone - relapsed/refractory), AML (+ azacitidine or decitabine - elderly/unfit - VIALE-A). SE: tumour lysis syndrome (TLS - mandatory risk stratification, ramp-up dosing, hydration, allopurinol, hospitalisation for high-risk; most feared early SE), neutropenia, GI, fatigue. Note: mandatory dose ramp-up schedule (weekly escalation 20→50→100→200→400 mg) to ↓TLS risk.

Oral alkylating agent (imidazotetrazine prodrug). MOA: spontaneously converts to MTIC at physiological pH → methylates O6-guanine and N7-guanine in DNA → DNA damage → apoptosis; crosses BBB. Indications: glioblastoma (concurrent with radiotherapy + maintenance - EORTC/NCIC trial - standard of care), anaplastic astrocytoma. SE: myelosuppression (thrombocytopenia - monitor FBC), nausea, fatigue, PCP pneumonia (prophylaxis with co-trimoxazole during concurrent phase). Note: MGMT promoter methylation → ↓DNA repair → ↑temozolomide sensitivity (predictive biomarker); take on empty stomach.

Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI; carbocyclic nucleoside). MOA: phosphorylated to carbovir-TP → inhibits HIV reverse transcriptase → chain termination. Indications: HIV-1 (combined ART - Triumeq = abacavir/dolutegravir/lamivudine; Epzicom/Kivexa = abacavir/lamivudine). SE: abacavir hypersensitivity reaction (ABC-HSR - 5-8%; fever, rash, GI, respiratory symptoms - FATAL if rechallenged; linked to HLA-B*5701 allele), MI risk (conflicting evidence - avoid in high CV risk). CI: HLA-B*5701 carriers (screen before prescribing - mandatory). Note: SCREEN HLA-B*5701 before any abacavir prescription.

Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI; cytidine analogue). MOA: phosphorylated to FTC-TP → inhibits HIV/HBV reverse transcriptase → chain termination. Indications: HIV (core component of most regimens - Truvada = emtricitabine/TDF; Descovy = emtricitabine/TAF), HBV co-infection, PrEP. SE: well tolerated - headache, nausea, hyperpigmentation of palms/soles (more in darker skin, benign); lactic acidosis (class SE, rare). Note: long intracellular T1/2 allows once-daily dosing; always used in combination.

Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI; 1st-gen). MOA: binds NNRTI binding pocket of HIV-1 RT → non-competitive RT inhibition → conformational change → ↓polymerase activity. Indications: HIV-1 (Atripla = efavirenz/emtricitabine/TDF - once-daily). SE: CNS/neuropsychiatric (vivid dreams, nightmares, dizziness, depression - most common early; take at bedtime; resolves in weeks; K65R mutation rare cause); rash, ↑lipids, teratogenicity (neural tube defects - avoid in 1st trimester). Note: potent CYP3A4 inducer; being replaced by integrase inhibitors.

HIV integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI; 1st-gen). MOA: binds integrase active site + Mg²⁺ → blocks strand transfer of HIV cDNA into host genome. Indications: HIV-1 (alternative to dolutegravir when CNS SE concern or periconception; treatment-experienced). SE: well tolerated - headache, GI, rash; CK elevation/myopathy (rare); lower genetic barrier to resistance than 2nd-gen INSTIs. Note: twice-daily (or once-daily 1200 mg HD formulation); fewer drug interactions than dolutegravir.

HIV protease inhibitor (PI) - used as pharmacokinetic booster. MOA: as PI: cleaves HIV Gag-Pol polyprotein → immature non-infectious virions; as booster: potent CYP3A4 inhibitor → ↑plasma levels of co-administered PIs. Indications: HIV (sub-therapeutic 'boosting dose' 100 mg for darunavir, atazanavir, lopinavir - no longer used as primary PI due to toxicity); Paxlovid: nirmatrelvir + ritonavir for COVID-19. SE: GI intolerance (major - diarrhoea, nausea), metabolic (↑lipids, lipodystrophy), potent drug interactions (CYP3A4 inhibition - ↑many drugs). Note: used almost exclusively as booster, not primary PI.

HIV protease inhibitor (co-formulated with ritonavir as Kaletra). MOA: binds HIV-1 protease active site → prevents polyprotein cleavage → immature non-infectious virions; ritonavir inhibits lopinavir metabolism → ↑lopinavir levels. Indications: HIV-1 treatment (alternative; less preferred due to twice-daily dosing and GI SE); COVID-19 (no proven benefit). SE: GI (diarrhoea, nausea - very common), dyslipidaemia, insulin resistance, QT/PR prolongation, hepatotoxicity. Note: Kaletra = lopinavir 200 mg + ritonavir 50 mg; largely superseded by INSTI-based regimens.

Anti-glutamate agent (ALS-specific). MOA: blocks voltage-gated Na channels + inhibits presynaptic glutamate release → ↓glutamatergic excitotoxicity in motor neurons; only disease-modifying drug for ALS. Indications: amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (motor neuron disease) - extends survival ~3 months (modest but only proven disease modifier pre-edaravone era). SE: nausea, asthenia, ↑LFTs (monitor monthly × 3, then quarterly), neutropenia (rare). Note: start early; continue while benefit-risk favourable; does not reverse existing deficits.

GABA-B agonist (centrally acting muscle relaxant). MOA: activates pre- and postsynaptic GABA-B receptors in spinal cord → ↓excitatory neurotransmitter release → ↓spasticity. Indications: spasticity (MS, spinal cord injury, cerebral palsy - oral; intrathecal pump for severe cases), trigeminal neuralgia (alternative), alcohol withdrawal (off-label). SE: sedation, dizziness, weakness, confusion (elderly), withdrawal syndrome (abrupt cessation → seizures, hallucinations - taper always). Note: intrathecal baclofen pump for refractory spasticity; abrupt withdrawal = medical emergency.

Central α2-adrenergic agonist (muscle relaxant). MOA: α2 agonism in brainstem/spinal cord → ↓facilitation of spinal motor neurons → ↓muscle tone; different mechanism from baclofen. Indications: spasticity (MS, spinal cord injury - acute or chronic), acute muscle spasm. SE: sedation (prominent), dry mouth, hypotension, hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs - rare but serious), dizziness. Note: CYP1A2 substrate - major interactions with ciprofloxacin/fluvoxamine (↑plasma levels dramatically → severe hypotension); avoid with these.

Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) receptor modulator (1st oral MS drug). MOA: phosphorylated to fingolimod-phosphate → functional S1P receptor antagonism (by downregulation) → sequesters lymphocytes in lymph nodes → ↓CNS inflammatory infiltration. Indications: relapsing-remitting MS (moderate-severe - after failure of 1st-line agents, or high disease activity). SE: 1st-dose bradycardia/AV block (requires 6-h cardiac monitoring for 1st dose), macular oedema (ophthalmic review at 3-4 months), lymphopenia, PML (JC virus - rare), hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity. Note: washout required before pregnancy; VZV vaccination before starting.

Anti-α4-integrin monoclonal antibody. MOA: binds α4β1 and α4β7 integrins on lymphocytes → prevents VLA-4/VCAM-1 interaction → blocks lymphocyte trafficking across blood-brain barrier → ↓CNS inflammation. Indications: highly active relapsing-remitting MS (2nd-line or high disease activity), moderate-severe Crohn disease (off-label). SE: PML - progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (JC virus reactivation - risk stratified by JC antibody index; 1:10,000 seronegative, ↑risk with high JCV index + duration + prior IS therapy), infusion reactions, hepatotoxicity. Note: JC antibody testing every 6 months; benefit-risk decision with neurologist.

Fumaric acid ester (oral MS drug). MOA: activates Nrf2 pathway → ↑cytoprotective antioxidant proteins → ↓oxidative stress in CNS; also ↓pro-inflammatory cytokines. Indications: relapsing-remitting MS (1st/2nd-line). SE: flushing (take with food, aspirin 30 min before ↓flushing), GI (nausea, diarrhoea - most common early; improves with food), lymphopenia (monitor lymphocyte count - withhold if <0.5 × 10⁹/L), PML (JC virus - associated with severe prolonged lymphopenia, very rare). Note: delayed-release capsule; start low dose → titrate up to ↓GI SE.

Immunomodulator (synthetic polypeptide - random copolymer). MOA: mimics myelin basic protein → induces T-regulatory cells, shifts Th1 → Th2 response → ↓autoimmune attack on myelin. Indications: relapsing-remitting MS (1st-line - PRISMS-equivalent efficacy; good safety profile). SE: injection site reactions (lipoatrophy, skin necrosis with prolonged use - rotate sites), immediate post-injection reaction (chest tightness, flushing, palpitations - benign, self-limiting <30 min). Note: no lab monitoring required; no hepatotoxicity; pregnancy-compatible; no PML risk; SC daily or 3× weekly (40 mg).

Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody (humanised; selective B-cell depletion). MOA: binds CD20 on B cells → ADCC + complement → B-cell lysis → ↓autoantibody production and antigen presentation to T cells. Indications: relapsing MS (including PPMS - first disease-modifying therapy proven effective in primary progressive MS - ORATORIO trial). SE: infusion reactions (premedicate with corticosteroids + antihistamine), serious infections, ↑breast cancer risk (signal in ORATORIO - mammography recommended), PML (rare), HBV reactivation (screen before). Note: IV every 6 months; B-cell recovery takes 6-12 months; vaccination before starting.

Anti-fibrotic agent (IPF-specific). MOA: mechanism incompletely understood → ↓TGF-β-stimulated collagen synthesis, ↓fibroblast proliferation, ↓inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β). Indications: idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) - ↓disease progression, ↓FVC decline (CAPACITY/ASCEND trials). SE: photosensitivity (avoid sun exposure, use SPF50+), GI (nausea - most common; take with food), dizziness, ↑LFTs. Note: requires 2-week dose titration; combination with nintedanib controversial but used in some centres.

Tyrosine kinase inhibitor (anti-fibrotic). MOA: inhibits PDGFR, FGFR, VEGFR, and FLT3 → ↓fibroblast proliferation/migration/differentiation → ↓lung fibrosis progression. Indications: IPF (↓FVC decline - INPULSIS trial), systemic sclerosis-associated ILD, progressive fibrosing ILD. SE: diarrhoea (most common - loperamide PRN; dose reduction if needed), nausea, hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs monthly × 3 then quarterly), bleeding risk, teratogenicity. Note: take with food; CI in pregnancy (effective contraception mandatory).

Anti-IL-5 monoclonal antibody. MOA: binds IL-5 → ↓eosinophil proliferation/differentiation/survival → ↓blood and tissue eosinophilia → ↓airway inflammation. Indications: severe eosinophilic asthma (uncontrolled on high-dose ICS + LABA, blood eosinophils ≥300/μL), eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), hypereosinophilic syndrome. SE: injection site reactions, URTI, headache, generally well tolerated. Note: SC monthly; blood eosinophil count guides patient selection; ↓oral steroid dependence.

Anti-IL-5 receptor α monoclonal antibody (ADCC-enhanced). MOA: binds IL-5Rα on eosinophils and basophils → ADCC → near-complete eosinophil depletion (vs mepolizumab which only neutralises IL-5 ligand). Indications: severe eosinophilic asthma (≥300 eosinophils/μL), EGPA. SE: injection site reactions, URTI, headache; very rapid eosinophil depletion (near-zero within 24-48 h). Note: SC every 4 weeks × 3 doses (loading), then every 8 weeks (maintenance - less frequent than mepolizumab).

Anti-IL-4Rα monoclonal antibody (blocks IL-4 and IL-13 signalling). MOA: binds shared IL-4Rα subunit → blocks both IL-4 and IL-13 signalling → ↓Th2-driven inflammation, ↓IgE, ↑skin barrier proteins. Indications: atopic dermatitis (moderate-severe - approved all ages; 1st biologic for eczema), severe asthma (type 2 + eosinophilic/allergic), eosinophilic oesophagitis (EOE), CRS with nasal polyps, prurigo nodularis. SE: injection site reactions, conjunctivitis (common in AD - distinctive SE), nasopharyngitis, headache. Note: SC every 2 weeks; most versatile biologic across type 2 inflammatory conditions.

Late Na current inhibitor (anti-anginal). MOA: selectively inhibits late (persistent) INa in cardiac myocytes → ↓intracellular Na accumulation → ↓Na-Ca exchange → ↓intracellular Ca overload → ↓ischaemic diastolic dysfunction; does not affect HR or BP. Indications: stable angina (add-on when β-blocker/CCB inadequate - MERLIN-TIMI 36). SE: dizziness, constipation, nausea, QT prolongation (modest). CI: hepatic impairment (CYP3A4/CYP2D6 metabolism). Note: unique haemodynamic profile - add to existing therapy without BP/HR effect.

Selective indirect factor Xa inhibitor (synthetic pentasaccharide). MOA: binds antithrombin III → specific conformational change → selective inhibition of factor Xa only (unlike LMWH which also inhibits IIa). Indications: VTE prophylaxis (orthopaedic surgery), PE/DVT treatment, ACS (NSTEMI - OASIS-5: ↓bleeding vs enoxaparin). SE: bleeding; no HIT (does not bind PF4 - no HIT risk). CI: eGFR <30 (renally cleared). Note: no reversal agent (protamine does NOT work); cannot use as UFH alternative for HIT patient (theoretically safe but insufficient evidence).

Direct thrombin inhibitor (DTI; bivalent - binds thrombin active site + exosite 1). MOA: directly inhibits thrombin independent of antithrombin → inhibits both free and fibrin-bound thrombin. Indications: PCI (anticoagulation during procedure - ↓bleeding vs heparin + GPI), HIT with thrombosis (alternative to argatroban). SE: bleeding; thrombosis (short T1/2 means rapid offset - bridging important). Note: renally cleared; monitor ACT during PCI; suitable for HIT patients needing PCI.

Direct thrombin inhibitor (hepatically cleared). MOA: directly inhibits thrombin (free and fibrin-bound) by binding catalytic site; reversible competitive inhibition. Indications: HIT (type II) - anticoagulation when heparin contraindicated; PCI in HIT patients. SE: bleeding, ↑INR (argatroban itself prolongs PT - complicates warfarin transition monitoring). Note: hepatically metabolised - preferred in renal failure (vs bivalirudin); monitor aPTT; switching to warfarin complex (use chromogenic anti-Xa assay for warfarin monitoring).

Synthetic ADH analogue (V2 receptor selective). MOA: V2 receptor agonism → ↑AQP2 → ↑renal water reabsorption (antidiuretic); V2 also → ↑vWF/FVIII release from endothelium (haemostatic effect). Indications: central DI (hyposecretion - not nephrogenic), nocturnal enuresis (children - intranasal/oral), mild haemophilia A/type 1 VWD (↑FVIII + vWF), nocturia, bleeding from uraemia. SE: hyponatraemia (serious - restrict fluid intake; risk ↑with elderly, polydipsia, SSRI use), headache, flushing. Note: no tachyphylaxis with intermittent use; fluid restriction mandatory.

Preferential COX-2 inhibitor (oxicam NSAID). MOA: preferentially (not selectively) inhibits COX-2 > COX-1 at therapeutic doses → ↓PG synthesis → analgesia/anti-inflammatory. Indications: OA, RA, ankylosing spondylitis. SE: GI (less than non-selective NSAIDs but still significant), fluid retention, AKI, CV risk. Note: once-daily dosing; ↓GI risk vs traditional NSAIDs but not celecoxib-equivalent; use with PPI if GI risk.

Highly selective COX-2 inhibitor (coxib). MOA: highly selective COX-2 inhibition → ↓prostaglandin E2 → anti-inflammatory/analgesic without COX-1 inhibition (↓GI effects). Indications: OA, RA, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gout (90 mg - very effective), perioperative pain, chronic musculoskeletal pain. SE: ↑CV risk (↑MI, stroke - class effect of coxibs), fluid retention, hypertension, AKI (minimal GI risk). CI: CV disease, hypertension. Note: not approved in US (US FDA concerns - approved in >80 other countries).

Ergot-derived dopamine D2 agonist. MOA: D2 agonism on pituitary lactotrophs → ↓prolactin secretion; D2 agonism in striatum → dopaminergic benefit in PD. Indications: hyperprolactinaemia (older alternative to cabergoline - more SE, more frequent dosing), Parkinson disease (older agent), acromegaly (adjunct), type 2 DM (Cycloset - improves glycaemic control via CNS mechanism). SE: severe GI (nausea, vomiting - start low, take with food; major reason cabergoline preferred), postural hypotension, headache, Raynaud, pulmonary fibrosis (high-dose chronic use). Note: cabergoline is preferred for prolactinoma due to efficacy and tolerability.

Androgen hormone (replacement). MOA: binds androgen receptor → promotes male secondary sex characteristics, spermatogenesis, muscle/bone anabolism, erythropoiesis. Indications: male hypogonadism (primary - Klinefelter; secondary - pituitary; late-onset hypogonadism - if symptomatic + confirmed low testosterone), transgender men (gender-affirming hormone therapy), delayed puberty, male breast cancer (palliative). SE: erythrocytosis (monitor Hct - phlebotomy if >54%), ↑LFTs, acne, mood changes, testicular atrophy, infertility, ↑BPH symptoms, polycythaemia. CI: prostate cancer, breast cancer, severe polycythaemia. Note: injectable (IM/SC), transdermal, or buccal; check PSA, Hct before and during.

Synthetic progestogen (17α-hydroxy-progesterone derivative). MOA: progesterone receptor agonism → endometrial decidualisation, ↓LH surge → contraception/anti-proliferative effect on endometrium. Indications: contraception (Depo-Provera IM - 150 mg q12 wk), endometrial protection (combined HRT), endometriosis, endometrial cancer (palliative), abnormal uterine bleeding. SE: irregular bleeding (most common early), amenorrhoea (Depo), weight gain, ↓BMD (Depo - reversible), mood changes, delayed return of fertility after Depo (up to 18 months). Note: Depo-Provera - fertility can take 12-18 months to return; not recommended >2 years without DEXA.

Progesterone receptor antagonist (anti-progestogen; RU-486). MOA: competitive PR antagonism → ↓progesterone action → decidual breakdown, ↑myometrial sensitivity to prostaglandins, cervical softening; also antiglucocorticoid. Indications: medical abortion (mifepristone + misoprostol - up to 10 weeks; 95%+ efficacy); cervical ripening (pre-surgical termination), Cushing syndrome (refractory - COSTAR trial), uterine fibroid treatment (low-dose). SE: incomplete abortion (2-5% - surgical completion), heavy bleeding, nausea, abdominal pain; prolonged amenorrhoea (rare). Note: used with misoprostol 24-48 h later for abortion; follow-up to confirm complete.

Synthetic PGE2 analogue. MOA: prostaglandin E2 receptor activation → cervical ripening (↑collagenase → ↓cervical rigidity), uterine contractions at high doses; also bronchospasm. Indications: cervical ripening prior to induction of labour (Cervidil vaginal insert - slow-release; Prostin E2 gel), induction in IUFD/termination. SE: uterine hyperstimulation (tachysystole - must be in hospital with CTG monitoring; remove Cervidil insert if occurs), GI, fever. CI: previous uterine scar (relative CI - ↑rupture risk), active herpes, obstetric emergency. Note: can be removed if hyperstimulation (Cervidil insert advantage).

Selective progesterone receptor modulator (SPRM). MOA: competitive PR antagonism → inhibits/delays ovulation (even after LH surge - key advantage over levonorgestrel), ↓endometrial receptivity; also ↓fibroid growth. Indications: emergency contraception (EllaOne - within 120 h; superior to levonorgestrel up to 72 h and equivalent up to 120 h - ella trial), uterine fibroids (Esmya 5 mg - pre-operative/intermittent). SE: headache, nausea, abdominal pain, delayed menstruation; hepatotoxicity (Esmya 5 mg - rare, serious, EU suspended). Note: less effective if BMI >35; avoid in pregnancy; Esmya suspended in EU due to hepatotoxicity signal.

Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor. MOA: inhibits carbonic anhydrase (CA) → ↓HCO3 reabsorption in proximal tubule → metabolic acidosis → ↑respiratory drive; ocular: ↓aqueous humour production → ↓IOP. Indications: altitude sickness prophylaxis/treatment (Mx before ascent), glaucoma (↓IOP - adjunct), idiopathic intracranial hypertension (↓CSF production), metabolic alkalosis (refractory), periodic paralysis, absence seizures (rarely). SE: metabolic acidosis (paraesthesias, lethargy), hypokalaemia, nephrolithiasis (Ca phosphate stones), sulfonamide hypersensitivity (cross-reaction). Note: start 24-48 h before altitude ascent; continue 2 days at altitude.

Gut-selective anti-integrin monoclonal antibody. MOA: binds α4β7 integrin on gut-homing lymphocytes → blocks MAdCAM-1 interaction → prevents lymphocyte trafficking into gut mucosa; gut-selective (unlike natalizumab which also blocks CNS homing). Indications: UC (moderate-severe - induction and maintenance; 1st biologic option), Crohn disease (2nd-line - after anti-TNF failure; maintenance superior to induction). SE: URTI, nasopharyngitis, arthralgia, headache; ↓systemic immunosuppression vs anti-TNFs (↓serious infection risk). Note: no PML risk due to gut selectivity; IV infusion.

Anti-TNF-α monoclonal antibody (fully human; monthly SC). MOA: binds both soluble and transmembrane TNF-α → ↓TNF-mediated inflammation. Indications: RA (MTX-inadequate responder), psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, non-radiographic axSpA, UC (SC - PURSUIT trial). SE: serious infections (TB reactivation - screen with IGRA/TST), injection site reactions, demyelination, HF exacerbation, lymphoma risk (class). Note: monthly SC dosing (vs biweekly for adalimumab) - adherence advantage; screen for TB, HBV, HCV before starting.

Calcimimetic (positive allosteric CaSR modulator). MOA: binds calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) on parathyroid chief cells → ↑CaSR sensitivity to extracellular Ca → ↓PTH secretion without raising serum Ca. Indications: secondary hyperparathyroidism in CKD on dialysis, primary hyperparathyroidism (inoperable/refused surgery), parathyroid carcinoma. SE: hypocalcaemia (monitor - most common; take with food), nausea/GI, headache. Note: does NOT increase Ca (unlike vitamin D analogues/calcium carbonate phosphate binders); lowers PTH, Ca, and phosphate.

Non-calcium phosphate binder (polymer). MOA: binds dietary phosphate in GI tract via ion exchange → ↓intestinal phosphate absorption → ↓serum phosphate (without adding Ca or aluminium load). Indications: hyperphosphataemia in CKD (dialysis and pre-dialysis). SE: GI (constipation, nausea, dyspepsia), ↓absorption of some drugs (separate by 1-2 h), metabolic acidosis (Renagel - chloride counterion; Renvela carbonate formulation is neutral). Note: Renvela (sevelamer carbonate) preferred over Renagel (sevelamer HCl) - avoids metabolic acidosis.

Atypical antipsychotic (benzisothiazol). MOA: D2 + 5-HT2A antagonism (core atypical mechanism) + potent 5-HT7 antagonism (antidepressant effect) + partial 5-HT1A agonism; minimal H1/M1 → ↓metabolic SE. Indications: schizophrenia (1st-line in some guidelines), bipolar depression (1st-line approved; unique - most atypicals not specifically approved for bipolar depression). SE: akathisia, somnolence, nausea; ↓weight gain/metabolic effects vs olanzapine/quetiapine; must take with food (≥350 kcal - ↑absorption 2-3×). Note: once daily with food; ↓metabolic burden makes it preferred in metabolically at-risk patients.

Active metabolite of risperidone (9-OH-risperidone). MOA: D2 + 5-HT2A antagonism; renally excreted (no hepatic metabolism - advantage over risperidone in liver disease). Indications: schizophrenia (oral; monthly IM Xeplion - Invega Sustenna; 3-monthly Trinza), schizoaffective disorder. SE: EPS, hyperprolactinaemia, QT prolongation, weight gain, sedation; less metabolic SE vs olanzapine. Note: extended-release once-daily oral; most well-established long-acting injectable for schizophrenia (monthly and 3-monthly formulations).

Dopamine D2/D3 partial agonist + 5-HT1A partial agonist + 5-HT2A antagonist (serotonin-dopamine activity modulator; SDAM). MOA: partial D2 agonism (lower intrinsic activity than aripiprazole) → ↓dopaminergic fluctuation; 5-HT1A partial agonism + 5-HT2A antagonism → ↑antidepressant effect. Indications: schizophrenia, adjunctive treatment MDD (with antidepressants), agitation in Alzheimer disease (US-approved 2023). SE: weight gain (more than aripiprazole), akathisia (less than aripiprazole), somnolence. Note: lower akathisia risk than aripiprazole due to lower D2 intrinsic activity.

High-potency typical antipsychotic (piperazine phenothiazine). MOA: potent D2 receptor antagonism → ↓dopaminergic transmission. Indications: schizophrenia (oral + depot injection: fluphenazine decanoate - Modecate - monthly/biweekly IM). SE: EPS (high rate - dystonia, parkinsonism, akathisia), tardive dyskinesia (chronic), hyperprolactinaemia, QT prolongation; ↓sedation and anticholinergic than low-potency typicals (chlorpromazine). Note: Modecate (decanoate) is one of the longest-established long-acting injectables; important for adherence.

5th-gen cephalosporin (MRSA-active β-lactam). MOA: binds PBP2a (the modified penicillin-binding protein that confers methicillin resistance) + standard PBPs → bactericidal cell wall disruption; only β-lactam approved for MRSA. Indications: community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), complicated SSTI including MRSA. SE: hypersensitivity, GI, Coombs-positive haemolytic anaemia (rare, monitor). Note: only β-lactam with true MRSA activity; important alternative for MRSA skin infections when IV needed.

Broad-spectrum antibiotic (reserve/topical). MOA: binds 50S ribosomal subunit (23S rRNA) → inhibits peptidyl transferase → bacteriostatic (bactericidal vs Haemophilus, Streptococcus). Indications: bacterial meningitis (penicillin-allergic patients - historical; now rarely used systemically), typhoid fever (not 1st-line), Rocky Mountain spotted fever (if doxycycline CI - pregnancy), topical: bacterial conjunctivitis, eye drops (Chlorsig - common OTC AU). SE: aplastic anaemia (idiosyncratic - 1:25,000-40,000 - fatal; reason systemic use nearly abandoned), reversible BM suppression (dose-dependent), grey baby syndrome (neonates - ↓glucuronyl transferase → accumulation). Note: topical formulations have negligible systemic absorption; systemic use only when alternatives absent.

Steroid-like antibiotic (topical/systemic). MOA: inhibits elongation factor G (EF-G) → blocks ribosomal translocation → ↓protein synthesis; excellent staphylococcal activity. Indications: MSSA skin/soft tissue infections (topical Fucidin cream - impetigo, infected eczema), MSSA osteomyelitis + bone infections (oral/IV - always combine to prevent resistance), MRSA decolonisation (with rifampicin). SE: GI (oral), hepatotoxicity (systemic), resistance emergence (rapid if monotherapy). Note: never use alone (systemic) - resistance emerges within days; always combine with another antistaphylococcal agent.

EGFR TKI (1st gen). MOA: reversibly inhibits EGFR (HER1) tyrosine kinase → ↓RAS/MAPK and PI3K/AKT signalling → ↓proliferation. Indications: EGFR-mutant NSCLC (exon 19 del, L858R - 1st-line before osimertinib era), pancreatic cancer (modest benefit - Erlotinib + gemcitabine). SE: acneiform rash (correlates with response - treat with topical clindamycin/doxycycline), diarrhoea, interstitial lung disease (rare, serious), hepatotoxicity. Note: now largely superseded by osimertinib in NSCLC but still used in pancreatic cancer.

EGFR TKI (1st gen). MOA: reversible EGFR TK inhibition → ↓proliferation/survival. Indications: EGFR-mutant NSCLC (1st-line, now largely superseded by osimertinib). SE: rash, diarrhoea, ↑LFTs, ILD. Note: landmark IPASS trial established EGFR mutation as predictive biomarker; osimertinib preferred now (fewer resistance mutations).

3rd-gen EGFR TKI (CNS-penetrant, T790M-active). MOA: irreversibly inhibits mutant EGFR (exon 19 del, L858R, T790M resistance mutation) while sparing wild-type EGFR → ↓rash vs 1st-gen TKIs. Indications: EGFR-mutant NSCLC 1st-line (FLAURA trial - superior PFS vs 1st-gen), T790M-acquired resistance, adjuvant after resection (ADAURA trial). SE: ↓rash/diarrhoea vs 1st-gen, QTc prolongation, cardiomyopathy (rare), ILD. Note: best CNS penetration of EGFR TKIs - preferred when brain metastases.

ALK/ROS1/MET inhibitor (1st gen). MOA: inhibits ALK fusion oncoproteins (EML4-ALK) and ROS1/MET → ↓tumour cell proliferation. Indications: ALK-positive NSCLC (1st-line - now largely replaced by alectinib), ROS1-rearranged NSCLC. SE: visual disturbances (bright lights/flashes - distinctive SE), GI, oedema, bradycardia, ↑LFTs, QTc. Note: vision changes occur in ~60% - distinctive; alectinib preferred (better CNS penetration, less toxicity - ALEX trial).

ALK inhibitor (2nd gen; CNS-penetrant). MOA: highly selective ALK inhibition → overcomes crizotinib resistance mutations; excellent CNS penetration (P-gp substrate - but efflux limited). Indications: ALK-positive NSCLC (1st-line - ALEX trial: superior PFS vs crizotinib, ↓CNS progression). SE: myalgia, constipation, oedema, photosensitivity, bradycardia; ↓ visual/GI SE vs crizotinib. Note: now standard 1st-line for ALK+ NSCLC - superior CNS efficacy crucial as brain metastases common.

BRAF V600E inhibitor. MOA: selectively inhibits BRAF V600E kinase → ↓MEK/ERK signalling → ↓proliferation in BRAF-mutant tumours. Indications: BRAF V600E/K-mutant melanoma (1st-line - BRIM-3 trial; now combined with cobimetinib), BRAF V600E+ NSCLC, thyroid cancer. SE: cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (paradoxical MAPK activation in RAS-mutant cells - monitor skin 3-monthly), rash, photosensitivity, arthralgia, QTc. Note: always combine with MEK inhibitor (cobimetinib) to delay resistance and ↓SCC.

BRAF V600E/K inhibitor (used with trametinib). MOA: selective BRAF V600 inhibition → ↓MEK/ERK. Indications: BRAF V600E/K melanoma (combined with trametinib - COMBI-v trial), BRAF-mutant NSCLC and thyroid cancer (with trametinib). SE: pyrexia (distinctive - more common than vemurafenib; treat with dose interruption/paracetamol), SCC (less than monotherapy), hyperglycaemia. Note: dabrafenib + trametinib now standard BRAF-mutant melanoma; pyrexia characteristic SE.

Multi-kinase inhibitor (BRAF/VEGFR/PDGFR/RAF). MOA: inhibits BRAF, VEGFR-2/3, PDGFR-β, RAF-1 → ↓angiogenesis + ↓tumour proliferation. Indications: hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC - 1st-line; SHARP trial - first systemic agent to show OS benefit in HCC), renal cell carcinoma, thyroid cancer (radioiodine-refractory). SE: hand-foot skin reaction (HFSR - palmar-plantar erythrodysaesthesia; dose-limiting), diarrhoea, hypertension, bleeding, fatigue. Note: HFSR is characteristic and dose-limiting - manage with urea cream and dose reduction.

Multi-target TKI (VEGFR/PDGFR/KIT/FLT3). MOA: inhibits VEGFR 1-3, PDGFR, KIT, FLT3, RET → ↓angiogenesis + direct anti-tumour. Indications: renal cell carcinoma (1st-line clear-cell - SUN 1011 trial), GIST (imatinib-resistant), pancreatic NETs. SE: fatigue, diarrhoea, HFSR, hypertension, hypothyroidism (monitor TSH), yellow skin discolouration (metabolite), mucositis, myelosuppression. Note: hypothyroidism in ~14% - check TSH routinely; yellow skin from drug metabolite - reassure.

mTOR inhibitor (rapamycin analogue). MOA: binds FKBP12 → inhibits mTORC1 → ↓protein synthesis, ↓cell cycle progression, ↓angiogenesis (↓HIF-1α/VEGF). Indications: renal cell carcinoma (post-VEGFR-TKI failure), breast cancer (ER+ HER2-neg with exemestane - BOLERO-2), pancreatic NETs, tuberous sclerosis (subependymal giant-cell astrocytoma, pulmonary LAM), transplant immunosuppression (Certican - with reduced tacrolimus). SE: stomatitis (mTOR-specific - use mouthwash, not antifungals unless Candida confirmed), non-infectious pneumonitis (↓dose/steroid), hyperglycaemia, immunosuppression. Note: mTOR stomatitis responds to steroid (prednisolone) mouthwash - not antifungal.

Selective oestrogen receptor degrader (SERD). MOA: binds ER with high affinity → receptor degradation (unlike tamoxifen/AIs which inhibit - fulvestrant eliminates the receptor) → complete oestrogen blockade; no agonist activity. Indications: ER+/HER2-neg advanced breast cancer post-AI failure (or 1st-line with ribociclib/palbociclib - MONARCH-3), endometrial cancer. SE: injection site reactions (IM gluteal), hot flushes, joint pain. Note: IM injection (500 mg monthly) - patient must be seen monthly; no cross-resistance with tamoxifen.

CDK4/6 inhibitor. MOA: inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6 → prevents Rb phosphorylation → G1/S cell cycle arrest → ↓proliferation synergistic with endocrine therapy. Indications: ER+/HER2-neg advanced breast cancer (1st-line with letrozole - PALOMA-2; 2nd-line with fulvestrant - PALOMA-3). SE: neutropaenia (most common - monitor FBC; manageable, rarely febrile), fatigue, alopecia (less than chemotherapy), diarrhoea. Note: oral capsules; neutropaenia requires FBC monitoring - dose modifications common.

CDK4/6 inhibitor. MOA: same CDK4/6 → Rb → G1 arrest mechanism as palbociclib. Indications: ER+/HER2-neg advanced breast cancer (with AI or fulvestrant - MONALEESA trials - first CDK4/6 inhibitor to show OS benefit). SE: neutropaenia, QTc prolongation (monitor ECG - more than palbociclib), ↑LFTs. Note: QTc monitoring required before and during treatment - significant differentiator from palbociclib.

CDK4/6 inhibitor (more selective CDK4 > CDK6). MOA: CDK4 predominant inhibition → G1 arrest; continuous dosing (unlike palbociclib/ribociclib which have 1-week-off cycles). Indications: ER+/HER2-neg advanced breast cancer (MONARCH-2/3 trials), adjuvant after resection (monarchE - ↓distant recurrence in high-risk). SE: diarrhoea (more than other CDK4/6i - prophylactic loperamide), neutropaenia (less than others), VTE. Note: diarrhoea in ~80% - start loperamide early; continuous dosing schedule.

PARP inhibitor. MOA: inhibits PARP-1/2 → prevents single-strand DNA break repair → replication fork collapse → DSBs → catastrophic in BRCA1/2-mutant cells (defective HR) → synthetic lethality. Indications: BRCA1/2-mutant advanced breast cancer (HER2-neg, germline - OlympiAD), BRCA-mutant ovarian cancer (maintenance - SOLO-1/2), BRCA-mutant prostate cancer (PROfound), pancreatic cancer (maintenance after platinum). SE: nausea (most common), fatigue, anaemia, neutropaenia, MDS/AML (rare but serious). Note: synthetic lethality concept - only effective in BRCA-mutant context; test germline BRCA before prescribing.

PARP inhibitor (oral; once daily). MOA: PARP-1/2 inhibition → synthetic lethality (most effective in BRCA/HRD context; some activity in HRD-negative). Indications: recurrent ovarian cancer maintenance (NOVA trial - regardless of BRCA status; greatest benefit in BRCA-mutant/HRD-positive), 1st-line ovarian maintenance (PRIMA trial). SE: thrombocytopaenia (more than olaparib - monitor platelet count), anaemia, hypertension, nausea. Note: individual starting dose based on weight/platelet count to ↓thrombocytopaenia.

Anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody (myeloma). MOA: binds CD38 (highly expressed on myeloma cells) → multiple mechanisms: CDC, ADCC, ADCP, apoptosis, immunomodulation (↓CD38+ Treg/Breg → ↑T-cell activity). Indications: multiple myeloma (relapsed/refractory - POLLUX/CASTOR; now 1st-line in transplant-eligible and ineligible - MAIA/CASSIOPEIA). SE: infusion reactions (1st infusion - ↓if pre-medicate with corticosteroid/antihistamine/paracetamol; ↓with SC formulation), infections, neutropaenia, haemolytic anaemia (interference with blood typing - inform transfusion lab). Note: interferes with indirect antiglobulin test/blood crossmatch - must notify blood bank.

Hypomethylating agent (DNA methyltransferase inhibitor). MOA: incorporates into DNA → inhibits DNA methyltransferase → ↓methylation → re-expression of silenced tumour suppressor genes; also cytotoxic via RNA incorporation. Indications: myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS - 1st-line for intermediate/high-risk - SAKK trial; ↑OS vs conventional care), AML (unfit for intensive chemotherapy - QUAZAR maintenance), CMML. SE: injection site reactions (SC route), myelosuppression (nadir day 14-21), nausea, ↑LFTs. Note: response may take 4-6 cycles - persist through early progression; now oral formulation (Onureg) for AML maintenance.

All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA; differentiation agent). MOA: binds RAR-α (retinoic acid receptor) → differentiation of promyelocytes into granulocytes; in APL, t(15;17) PML-RARα fusion → ATRA disrupts fusion → promyelocyte differentiation. Indications: acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL) - ATRA + arsenic trioxide (ATO) is curative standard of care (>90% cure rate). SE: differentiation syndrome (DS - formerly ATRA syndrome; fever, respiratory distress, oedema, effusions, weight gain - treat with dexamethasone immediately), pseudotumour cerebri (children - ↑ICP), teratogenic. Note: ATRA syndrome is potentially fatal - suspect in any APL patient with respiratory distress on ATRA; start dexamethasone empirically.

Heavy metal anticancer agent (APL). MOA: induces apoptosis and differentiation of APL cells via multiple mechanisms; degrades PML-RARα fusion protein (complementary to ATRA). Indications: acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL) - combined with ATRA (standard curative regimen - APL0406 trial, >90% cure); relapsed/refractory APL. SE: QTc prolongation (serious - monitor ECG, avoid drugs that prolong QT, correct K+/Mg2+), differentiation syndrome (like ATRA), peripheral neuropathy, hyperglycaemia. Note: QTc monitoring essential; ATRA + ATO now preferred over ATRA + chemotherapy for standard-risk APL.

Anti-HER2 monoclonal antibody (dimerisation inhibitor). MOA: binds HER2 domain II (different epitope from trastuzumab) → blocks HER2-HER3 dimerisation → ↓PI3K/AKT/MAPK signalling; synergistic with trastuzumab. Indications: HER2+ metastatic breast cancer (1st-line with trastuzumab + docetaxel - CLEOPATRA trial: ↑OS ~16 months vs T+D), neoadjuvant and adjuvant HER2+ breast cancer (APHINITY). SE: diarrhoea (most common), alopecia, nausea, neutropaenia; cardiac toxicity (monitor LVEF - similar to trastuzumab). Note: dual HER2 blockade (trastuzumab + pertuzumab + taxane) is standard 1st-line metastatic HER2+ regimen.

Anti-PD-L1 monoclonal antibody (ICI). MOA: binds PD-L1 on tumour/immune cells → blocks PD-L1:PD-1 and PD-L1:B7-1 interactions → restores T-cell anti-tumour immunity. Indications: NSCLC (high PD-L1, or with bevacizumab+chemotherapy - IMpower trials), urothelial carcinoma (post-platinum), small-cell lung cancer (with carbo+etoposide - IMpower133), HCC (with bevacizumab - IMbrave150). SE: immune-related AEs (irAEs) - pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis, endocrinopathies (similar class to nivolumab/pembrolizumab). Note: anti-PD-L1 (not anti-PD-1) - theoretical difference from nivolumab/pembrolizumab but similar clinical SE profile.

Anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody (chimeric). MOA: binds EGFR extracellular domain → blocks ligand binding → ↓RAS/MAPK and PI3K/AKT signalling + ADCC. Indications: RAS/RAF wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer (1st-line with FOLFOX/FOLFIRI - CRYSTAL/OPUS; only effective in RAS wild-type), squamous HNSCC (with platinum-based chemotherapy or radiotherapy - EXTREME trial). SE: acneiform rash (correlates with response - biomarker of efficacy), hypomagnesaemia (monitor Mg - distinctive electrolyte SE), infusion reactions, diarrhoea. Note: RAS mutation testing mandatory before use - RAS-mutant CRC has no benefit.

Hypomethylating agent (DNA methyltransferase inhibitor; deoxynucleoside analogue). MOA: incorporates into DNA → irreversibly inhibits DNMT → ↓DNA methylation → re-expression of tumour suppressor genes; more potent demethylation than azacitidine (DNA-only, no RNA incorporation). Indications: MDS (intermediate/high-risk - alternative to azacitidine), AML (unfit for intensive therapy). SE: myelosuppression (nadir day 14-21), nausea, fatigue, injection site. Note: decitabine vs azacitidine - comparable efficacy; decitabine IV only (vs azacitidine SC/IV).

Thrombopoietin receptor agonist (TPO-RA; non-peptide, oral). MOA: binds transmembrane domain of TPO receptor (c-Mpl) → receptor activation → ↑megakaryocyte proliferation/differentiation → ↑platelet production. Indications: immune thrombocytopaenia (ITP - 2nd-line after corticosteroids/IVIG fail - RAISE trial), aplastic anaemia (with immunosuppressive therapy - ELT + CsA + ATG - significant response improvement), hepatitis C-related thrombocytopaenia (pre-antiviral). SE: hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs regularly), thrombosis (↑platelet count → VTE; portal vein thrombosis in liver disease), cataracts (long-term), bone marrow reticulin fibrosis. Note: target platelet count ≥50 × 10⁹/L - do not over-correct; hepatotoxicity requires LFT monitoring every 2 weeks.

TPO receptor agonist (peptibody; SC injection). MOA: binds and activates TPO receptor → ↑megakaryopoiesis → ↑platelet count. Indications: ITP (2nd-line after corticosteroids/IVIG - EXTEND/ITP0602 trials), used when splenectomy contraindicated. SE: headache, arthralgia, thrombosis (if over-corrected), bone marrow reticulin fibrosis (monitor). Note: SC injection; similar efficacy to eltrombopag - choice based on patient preference (oral vs injection), cost, specific CI.

G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor; recombinant human). MOA: binds G-CSF receptor → ↑neutrophil progenitor proliferation/differentiation + ↑neutrophil survival and function → ↑neutrophil count. Indications: chemotherapy-induced neutropaenia (↓febrile neutropaenia duration/severity), neutropaenia in haematological malignancies, stem cell mobilisation (high-dose for collection), congenital neutropaenia. SE: bone pain (most common - treat with paracetamol/NSAIDs), splenomegaly (rupture risk - rare), ↑LDH/alkaline phosphatase. Note: primary G-CSF prophylaxis with high-risk chemotherapy regimens (≥20% febrile neutropaenia risk); bone pain responds to paracetamol.

Erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (ESA; recombinant erythropoietin). MOA: binds EPO receptor on erythroid progenitors → ↑proliferation/differentiation → ↑RBC production. Indications: anaemia of CKD (pre-dialysis and dialysis - ↓transfusion requirement; target Hb 100-115 g/L), chemotherapy-induced anaemia (controversial - ↑thrombosis), anaemia of prematurity (EPO in preterm). SE: hypertension (most common - related to ↑Hct), thrombosis (VTE, vascular access), pure red cell aplasia (rare - anti-EPO antibodies; more common with SC injection in non-dialysis CKD), headache. Note: target Hb 100-115 g/L in CKD - higher targets ↑stroke/CV events (CHOIR/TREAT trials); subcutaneous preferred for dialysis but SC associated with PRCA in non-dialysis.

T-cell co-stimulation blocker (CTLA-4-Ig fusion protein). MOA: binds CD80/CD86 on APCs → blocks CD28:CD80/86 co-stimulation signal required for T-cell activation → selective T-cell suppression without broad immunosuppression. Indications: RA (MTX-inadequate responder - ACR 20/50/70 responses; SC or IV), JIA, psoriatic arthritis (moderate-severe). SE: URTI, nasopharyngitis, headache, serious infections (less than anti-TNF - possible advantage in patients with recurrent infections). Note: preferred in seropositive RA (RF/ACPA+) - better response prediction; ↓infection risk vs anti-TNFs may benefit at-risk patients.

Anti-BLyS (BAFF) monoclonal antibody (SLE-specific). MOA: binds soluble BLyS (B-lymphocyte stimulator/BAFF) → ↓B-cell survival and maturation → ↓autoantibody production; targets BLyS-dependent B-cell subsets. Indications: SLE (active - anti-dsDNA+, low complement - BLISS-52/BLISS-76; only biologic with RCT evidence for SLE; also approved for lupus nephritis). SE: nausea, diarrhoea, infections (URTI, UTI), psychiatric effects (depression, anxiety - discontinue if suicidal ideation), infusion/injection reactions. Note: 1st biologic approved specifically for SLE; most benefit in serologically active disease (↑anti-dsDNA, ↓C3/C4).

Anti-IL-17A monoclonal antibody. MOA: neutralises IL-17A → ↓keratinocyte activation, ↓neutrophil recruitment, ↓inflammatory cytokines at psoriatic plaque/joint. Indications: moderate-severe plaque psoriasis (UNCOVER trials - superior skin clearance vs adalimumab; high PASI 90/100 rates), psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, nr-axSpA. SE: injection site reactions, URTI, candidiasis (oral/vaginal - IL-17 important for mucosal Candida immunity), IBD exacerbation (rare - CI in active IBD). Note: PASI 90 response >50% - among highest skin clearance of all biologics; CI in IBD.

Anti-IL-23 monoclonal antibody (IL-23p19 subunit inhibitor). MOA: selectively blocks IL-23 (p19 subunit) → ↓Th17 cell activation → ↓IL-17A/F → ↓downstream psoriatic inflammation; spares IL-12 (shared p40 with IL-23). Indications: moderate-severe plaque psoriasis (VOYAGE trials), psoriatic arthritis (DISCOVER trials). SE: injection site reactions, URTI, tinea (↓fungal mucosal immunity - less than IL-17 inhibitors), nasopharyngitis. Note: every-8-week SC dosing after loading (q4w ×2 then q8w); less fungal infection risk than IL-17 inhibitors.

Anti-IL-23 monoclonal antibody (IL-23p19). MOA: IL-23 p19 inhibition → ↓Th17 differentiation → ↓IL-17 cascade → ↓psoriatic inflammation. Indications: moderate-severe plaque psoriasis (UltIMMa-1/2 - highest PASI 90 rates ≈75%), Crohn disease (ADVANCE/MOTIVATE - induction + FORTIFY maintenance), psoriatic arthritis. SE: URTI, injection site reactions, ↑triglycerides. Note: 150 mg SC q12 weeks for psoriasis (most infrequent dosing among biologics); highly effective in Crohn disease.

Anti-VEGF-A Fab fragment (intravitreal). MOA: neutralises all VEGF-A isoforms → ↓neovascularisation + ↓vascular permeability in retina/choroid. Indications: neovascular (wet) AMD (monthly intravitreal - MARINA/ANCHOR trials; standard of care), diabetic macular oedema (DMO), retinal vein occlusion (RVO). SE: intravitreal injection: endophthalmitis (rare - strict aseptic technique), vitreous haemorrhage, retinal detachment, ↑IOP (transient). Note: monthly injections initially then PRN; similar efficacy to bevacizumab (CATT trial) but far more expensive - bevacizumab often used off-label for cost reasons.

VEGF trap (fusion protein; intravitreal). MOA: recombinant fusion protein (VEGFR1+VEGFR2 extracellular domains + IgG Fc) → binds VEGF-A, VEGF-B, PlGF with higher affinity than natural receptors → ↓neovascularisation. Indications: wet AMD (q8w after loading - VIEW trials; non-inferior to ranibizumab, less frequent injections), DMO, RVO, myopic CNV. SE: same intravitreal injection risks as ranibizumab. Note: 2 mg q8w (after loading) vs ranibizumab monthly - important adherence advantage; also available as 8 mg high-dose q12-16w (Eylea HD - PHOTON trial).

Prostaglandin F2α analogue (topical ophthalmic). MOA: FP receptor agonism → ↑uveoscleral outflow → ↓IOP (~25-35%); once-daily evening dosing. Indications: open-angle glaucoma (1st-line topical), ocular hypertension. SE: iris colour change (brown pigmentation - permanent; more in hazel/green eyes), periorbital fat atrophy (sunken appearance), hypertrichosis (eyelash growth - longer/darker/thicker), conjunctival hyperaemia. Note: most effective topical glaucoma drop; evening dosing maximises effect; iris colour change is irreversible - counsel.

Prostamide/prostaglandin F analogue (topical). MOA: FP receptor agonism + prostamide receptor → ↑uveoscleral + trabecular outflow → ↓IOP (similar to latanoprost). Indications: open-angle glaucoma/ocular hypertension (1st-line), eyelash hypotrichosis (Latisse - cosmetic use). SE: iris pigmentation change, eyelash growth (lash growth marketed as Latisse), periorbital fat atrophy, conjunctival hyperaemia. Note: Latisse uses cosmetic application for eyelash growth; same drug as glaucoma drops.

Topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (ophthalmic). MOA: inhibits carbonic anhydrase II in ciliary epithelium → ↓HCO3 formation → ↓aqueous humour production → ↓IOP (~17-23%). Indications: open-angle glaucoma/ocular hypertension (adjunctive - less effective than prostaglandin analogues; often combined with timolol as Cosopt). SE: local stinging/burning, bitter taste, superficial punctate keratitis. Note: topical CA inhibitor avoids systemic SE of oral acetazolamide (metabolic acidosis/stones); Cosopt (dorzolamide + timolol) fixed combination reduces drop number.

α2-adrenergic agonist (topical ophthalmic). MOA: α2 agonism → ↓aqueous humour production + ↑uveoscleral outflow → ↓IOP; also neuroprotective (α2 in retinal ganglion cells). Indications: open-angle glaucoma/ocular hypertension (2nd/3rd-line adjunct; sometimes 1st-line when β-blockers/prostaglandins CI). SE: eye redness, allergic conjunctivitis (up to 20% - switch drug), dry mouth, fatigue; CNS depression in infants (CI in children <2 years). Note: CI under 2 years (profound CNS depression - fatigue/bradycardia); ocular allergy common (20% within 1 year).

Non-selective β-blocker (topical ophthalmic). MOA: β1/β2 blockade of ciliary epithelium β receptors → ↓cAMP → ↓aqueous humour production → ↓IOP (~20-25%). Indications: open-angle glaucoma/ocular hypertension (1st-line; often as fixed-combination Cosopt or Combigan). SE: systemic absorption → bronchospasm (CI in asthma/COPD), bradycardia, heart block, masked hypoglycaemia; local: dry eye, stinging. CI: asthma (absolute), severe COPD, 2nd/3rd-degree AV block, cardiogenic shock. Note: systemic SE from topical drops - nasolacrimal occlusion (press inner canthus 1 min) reduces systemic absorption.

Antimuscarinic (OAB; non-selective). MOA: blocks M3 muscarinic receptors in bladder detrusor → ↓involuntary contractions → ↑bladder capacity. Indications: overactive bladder (OAB) - urge incontinence, frequency, urgency; also childhood bladder instability. SE: dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention, cognitive impairment (crosses BBB - highest anticholinergic burden of OAB drugs; problematic in elderly), confusion. Note: avoid in elderly (Beers criteria - high anticholinergic burden); transdermal patch or newer agents (solifenacin, mirabegron) preferred in older patients.

Selective M3 muscarinic antagonist (OAB). MOA: M3-selective antagonism → ↓detrusor contractions with ↓non-bladder anticholinergic SE vs oxybutynin. Indications: OAB (urge incontinence, urgency, frequency). SE: dry mouth (M3 in salivary glands - most common), constipation; less cognitive impairment/confusion than oxybutynin (↓BBB penetration). Note: once-daily oral; better tolerated than oxybutynin in elderly - preferred anticholinergic for OAB when mirabegron not suitable.

β3-adrenergic receptor agonist (OAB - non-anticholinergic). MOA: β3 agonism in bladder detrusor → smooth muscle relaxation → ↑bladder capacity/storage without anticholinergic mechanism. Indications: OAB (urge incontinence, frequency, urgency) - preferred in elderly (no anticholinergic SE), can combine with anticholinergic (SYNERGY trial - additive effect). SE: hypertension (monitor BP), tachycardia, nasopharyngitis, UTI; no cognitive impairment, no dry mouth. Note: mechanism advantage in elderly - no anticholinergic cognitive burden; can combine with solifenacin for additive benefit.

Quinoline alkaloid (antimalarial/nocturnal cramps). MOA: accumulates in acidic food vacuole of plasmodium → inhibits haem polymerisation → toxic free haem accumulates → parasite death; also skeletal muscle relaxant. Indications: severe falciparum malaria (IV quinine → oral; now largely replaced by IV artesunate for severe malaria), uncomplicated malaria (combination), nocturnal leg cramps (oral - controversial, narrow therapeutic window). SE: cinchonism (tinnitus, hearing loss, visual disturbance, headache, nausea - dose-dependent), hypoglycaemia (↑insulin secretion), hypotension (IV rapid infusion), QT prolongation, haemolytic anaemia (G6PD). Note: for severe malaria in settings where artesunate unavailable; QTc monitoring required IV.

Artemisinin derivative (antimalarial; most potent anti-malarial). MOA: endoperoxide bridge → reactive oxygen intermediates → alkylation of haem/parasite proteins → rapid parasite killing; kills all asexual stages. Indications: severe falciparum malaria (IV artesunate - 1st-line globally per WHO; SEAQUAMAT/AQUAMAT trials: ↓mortality vs IV quinine), cerebral malaria, severe vivax malaria, hyperparasitaemia. SE: haemolysis (delayed post-artesunate haemolytic anaemia - occurs weeks after treatment, especially in returning travellers - monitor FBC). Note: fastest acting antimalarial - clears parasitaemia rapidly; delayed haemolysis can occur weeks later - patient education important.

8-aminoquinoline antimalarial (radical cure). MOA: active metabolites → oxidative stress in parasite → kills hepatic hypnozoites (P. vivax/ovale dormant liver forms) and gametocytes. Indications: radical cure of P. vivax and P. ovale (prevent relapse - must follow chloroquine/ACT with 14-day primaquine course), malaria transmission blocking (kills gametocytes). SE: haemolytic anaemia in G6PD deficiency (dose-dependent oxidative haemolysis - absolute requirement for G6PD testing before use), methaemoglobinaemia, GI. CI: G6PD deficiency (severe haemolysis), pregnancy (G6PD status of fetus unknown). Note: G6PD testing MANDATORY before prescribing - can cause life-threatening haemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients.

Antihelminthic (broad-spectrum cestode/trematode). MOA: increases cell membrane permeability to Ca2+ in parasites → muscular contraction → paralysis → disruption of tegument → immune killing; also vacuolisation of tegument. Indications: schistosomiasis (2 doses), cestode infections (tapeworms - Taenia, Diphyllobothrium, Hymenolepis), clonorchiasis, opisthorchiasis, cysticercosis (with dexamethasone to reduce inflammation). SE: GI (nausea, abdominal pain), headache, dizziness; paradoxical seizures in neurocysticercosis (↑inflammation on cyst death - must co-administer steroids). Note: add dexamethasone for neurocysticercosis and for heavy Taenia infections - reduce inflammatory response to dying parasites.

Broad-spectrum antiprotozoal/antihelminthic (thiazolide). MOA: inhibits pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PFOR) → disrupts anaerobic electron transfer in anaerobic organisms; also antiviral mechanisms. Indications: Cryptosporidium and Giardia gastroenteritis (1st-line for cryptosporidiosis - only approved treatment; Giardia alternative), C. difficile (adjunct), norovirus, rotavirus. SE: GI (nausea, abdominal pain), headache, urine discolouration (yellow-green - drug metabolite - reassure). Note: only effective treatment for cryptosporidiosis; especially important in immunocompromised; urine discolouration is harmless.

Hydrophilic bile acid (hepatoprotective; choleretic). MOA: displaces toxic hydrophobic bile acids → ↓bile acid pool toxicity; ↑biliary HCO3 secretion → ↓bile acidity; also ↓hepatocyte apoptosis and immunomodulation. Indications: primary biliary cholangitis (PBC - 13-15 mg/kg/day; ↓progression, ↓LFTs - UDCA-PBC trials; 1st-line), gallstone dissolution (small cholesterol stones - takes 6-24 months; poor results for calcified stones), cholestasis of pregnancy (↓pruritus + ↓adverse outcomes - PITCHES trial debated). SE: diarrhoea, nausea; rare hepatotoxicity paradoxically in biliary obstruction. Note: for PBC response assessment use Paris criteria (ALP <3× ULN, AST <2× ULN, bilirubin normal after 1 year); non-responders need add-on (obeticholic acid).

Topical retinoid (3rd gen; receptor-selective). MOA: selectively binds RAR-β/γ → normalises keratinocyte differentiation and proliferation → ↓hyperkeratosis, ↓psoriatic plaque. Indications: plaque psoriasis (topical - effective for well-demarcated plaques), acne (gel), photoageing. SE: local irritation (erythema, peeling, burning - use moisturiser; apply every other day if irritation), photosensitivity, teratogenic (Category X - avoid in pregnancy). Note: most potent topical retinoid; irritation limits use (start 0.05%, advance to 0.1% as tolerated).

Vitamin D3 analogue (topical psoriasis). MOA: binds VDR → ↓keratinocyte proliferation, ↑differentiation, ↓inflammatory cytokines (IL-2, IL-6, TNF); complementary to steroids. Indications: plaque psoriasis (topical - often combined with betamethasone as Daivobet/Enstilar - superior to either alone). SE: skin irritation, perilesional hypopigmentation; systemic hypercalcaemia (if >100 g/week). Note: often used in combination with betamethasone dipropionate (Daivobet foam - Enstilar - very effective combination); face/flexures avoid (irritation).

Complex mixture of hydrocarbons (antipsoriatric). MOA: reduces epidermal proliferation and ↓scale; anti-inflammatory and antipruritic via unclear mechanism (aryl hydrocarbon receptor activation). Indications: plaque psoriasis (scalp - shampoo; body - cream/lotion), atopic eczema, seborrhoeic dermatitis. SE: malodour, skin staining (clothes/bath - warn patients), photosensitisation (UV light after application - avoid sun exposure), folliculitis. Note: old but effective therapy - useful for scalp psoriasis, safe in pregnancy; avoid in extensive/flexural/facial psoriasis (irritation).

Calcineurin inhibitor (topical and systemic). MOA: binds FKBP12 → inhibits calcineurin → ↓NFAT dephosphorylation → ↓IL-2 and T-cell activation. Indications: Topical (Protopic 0.03%/0.1%): atopic dermatitis (moderate-severe - steroid-sparing; face/flexures/eyelids where steroids risk atrophy; 2nd-line). Systemic (Prograf): organ transplantation (kidney, liver, heart - standard immunosuppression), GvHD. SE: Topical: burning/stinging (transient, resolves after 1 week), ↑infection risk (no skin atrophy - advantage); boxed warning: theoretical lymphoma risk (unproven). Systemic: nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, hypertension, hyperglycaemia. Note: topical tacrolimus: excellent for sensitive areas where topical steroids cause atrophy (face, eyelids, genitals).

SGLT2 inhibitor (gliflozin). MOA: inhibits SGLT2 in proximal tubule → ↓glucose reabsorption → glucosuria + natriuresis + osmotic diuresis → ↓BP, ↓weight; also: haemodynamic benefits (↓pre/afterload), ketone utilisation. Indications: T2DM (glucose-lowering - 2nd-line after metformin), CVD risk reduction (EMPA-REG OUTCOME - ↓CV death/HHF), HFrEF (EMPEROR-Reduced - ↓HHF/CV death), HFpEF (EMPEROR-Preserved - ↓HHF), CKD (EMPA-KIDNEY). SE: genital mycotic infections (most common - especially women; candida, balanitis), UTI, DKA (euglycaemic - rare; stop before surgery/fasting), Fournier's gangrene (rare), hypotension. CI: eGFR <20 (glucose-lowering), T1DM. Note: euglycaemic DKA - ketone/pH abnormality with near-normal glucose; ↑risk in fasting/illness - sick day rules essential.

Angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI). MOA: valsartan (ARB) blocks AT1R; sacubitril inhibits neprilysin → ↓degradation of natriuretic peptides (BNP, ANP) → ↑natriuresis, ↑vasodilation, ↓cardiac remodelling. Indications: HFrEF (EF ≤40% - PARADIGM-HF trial: 20% ↓CV death/HHF vs enalapril; replaces ACEi/ARB in stable HFrEF). SE: hypotension (common, especially 1st dose), hyperkalaemia, angioedema (cannot combine with ACEi - 36-hour washout required). CI: concomitant ACEi (angioedema risk), eGFR <30, bilateral renal artery stenosis, pregnancy. Note: 36-hour washout after stopping ACEi before starting - angioedema risk; strongly recommended in guidelines for all eligible HFrEF patients.

Angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB; high AT1R affinity). MOA: insurmountable AT1R antagonism → ↓angiotensin II effects (vasoconstriction, aldosterone, remodelling). Indications: hypertension, HFrEF (CHARM-Alternative/Added - ↓HHF/CV death), HFpEF (CHARM-Preserved - modest benefit). SE: hyperkalaemia, AKI (renal artery stenosis), hypotension; no dry cough (unlike ACEi). Note: preferred ARB for HF (strong trial data - CHARM); highest AT1R affinity of ARBs.

Potassium binder (non-absorbed polymer; oral). MOA: exchanges Ca2+ for K+ in colon → ↑faecal K+ excretion → ↓serum potassium; works in distal colon (different site from sodium zirconium cyclosilicate). Indications: hyperkalaemia (chronic - especially in CKD, HF, RAAS inhibitor use - allows continuation of RAAS inhibitors). SE: hypomagnesaemia (exchanges Mg2+ as well - monitor Mg), constipation, GI. Note: take 3 hours apart from other medications (binds drugs); not for acute hyperkalaemia (slow onset ~7 hours).

Potassium binder (inorganic crystal; oral). MOA: non-absorbed microporous crystal → traps K+ in GI tract (exchanged for H+/Na+) → ↓GI K+ absorption. Indications: hyperkalaemia (acute and chronic - more rapid onset than patiromer - 1 hour; acute hyperkalaemia treatment option before definitive therapy). SE: oedema (sodium-containing - cautious in HF/fluid overload), hyponatraemia (rare). Note: faster onset than patiromer (~1 hour) - can be used for acute hyperkalaemia as bridge; sodium content may worsen oedema in HF.

Atypical antipsychotic (dibenzodiazepine; gold standard for treatment-resistant schizophrenia). MOA: low-affinity D2 antagonism + D4/D1/5-HT2A/H1/M1/α1 antagonism; loose D2 binding → ↓EPS; high M1 antagonism → anticholinergic SE. Indications: treatment-resistant schizophrenia (only antipsychotic proven superior - CUtLASS/TRIAD; after ≥2 antipsychotics fail), suicidality in schizophrenia/schizoaffective (InterSePT trial), refractory bipolar disorder. SE: agranulocytosis (1-2% - life-threatening; mandatory ANC monitoring - weekly ×26 weeks, then fortnightly ×26 weeks, then monthly; withhold if ANC <1.5, stop if <0.5), myocarditis (first 6-8 weeks - monitor for symptoms; troponin/ECG if symptoms), seizures (dose-related - ↑risk >600 mg/day), metabolic syndrome (significant weight gain, DM, dyslipidaemia), hypersalivation (nocturnal - hyoscine hydrobromide patch helpful), constipation (can cause ileus), sedation. Note: MANDATORY ANC monitoring - delayed recognition of agranulocytosis is fatal; myocarditis monitoring first 4 weeks; highest metabolic risk of all antipsychotics.

Atypical antipsychotic (substituted benzamide; D2/D3 selective). MOA: selective D2/D3 antagonism (no H1/M1/5-HT affinity - cleaner profile); at low doses (<300 mg): preferentially blocks presynaptic D2/D3 → ↑dopamine release (↓negative symptoms); at high doses: postsynaptic D2 blockade (↓positive symptoms). Indications: schizophrenia (positive and negative symptoms - negative symptom improvement distinguishes it from typical antipsychotics), acute psychosis, amisulpride is available in AU/Europe but not US. SE: EPS (moderate risk - less than typicals), hyperprolactinaemia (D2-selective → most potent hyperprolactinaemia of atypicals), QTc prolongation, weight gain (less than olanzapine). Note: low-dose (50-300 mg) specifically targets negative symptoms - unique property; QTc monitoring important.

Antiepileptic (slow inactivation Na channel modulator). MOA: selectively enhances slow (not fast) inactivation of voltage-gated Na channels → reduces availability of channels during sustained repetitive firing; also CRMP-2 binding. Indications: focal onset seizures (adjunctive - CREST-1/2 trials), generalised tonic-clonic seizures (2nd-line adjunct), status epilepticus (IV loading - emerging role). SE: dizziness, diplopia, ataxia (dose-related - at start or dose increase), nausea, PR interval prolongation (cardiac - CI in 2nd/3rd-degree block). Note: PR prolongation - ECG before starting if cardiac risk; well-tolerated once dose stabilised; IV formulation useful for acute seizures.

AMPA receptor antagonist (antiepileptic). MOA: first-in-class non-competitive AMPA glutamate receptor antagonist → ↓excitatory neurotransmission. Indications: focal onset seizures (adjunctive - PIII trials), generalised tonic-clonic seizures (adjunctive). SE: dizziness, somnolence, fatigue, irritability/hostility/aggression (psychiatric SE - distinctive class effect; can be severe - monitor; ↑risk in patients with psychiatric history), weight gain. Note: psychiatric SE (aggression) is distinctive and serious - monitor behaviour changes; once-daily dosing (long T1/2 ~105 h).

Antiepileptic (SV2A ligand; analogue of levetiracetam). MOA: binds synaptic vesicle protein 2A (SV2A) with 15-20× higher affinity than levetiracetam → ↓exocytosis of neurotransmitters from presynaptic terminals. Indications: focal onset seizures (adjunctive - PIII trials; also monotherapy in some regions), as alternative when levetiracetam intolerable. SE: somnolence, dizziness, psychiatric (irritability, depression - less than levetiracetam), headache; ↓psychiatric SE vs levetiracetam - key differentiator. Note: can switch from levetiracetam overnight; fewer behavioural SE than levetiracetam - useful when levetiracetam causes irritability.

2nd-gen BCR-ABL TKI (also inhibits SRC, KIT, PDGFR). MOA: binds BCR-ABL in open/closed conformation → overcomes most imatinib resistance mutations (except T315I). Indications: CML (all phases after imatinib failure or 1st-line), Ph+ ALL. SE: pleural effusion (distinctive - 20-35%; ↓with dose reduction/diuretic), pulmonary arterial hypertension (rare but serious - monitor), myelosuppression, QTc. Note: pleural effusion is most characteristic SE - stop drug, diurese, restart at lower dose.

2nd-gen BCR-ABL TKI (more selective than imatinib). MOA: binds BCR-ABL active site with higher affinity than imatinib; overcomes most resistance mutations. Indications: CML (chronic phase 1st-line or after imatinib failure). SE: QTc prolongation (monitor ECG; avoid QT-prolonging drugs), hyperglycaemia, hyperbilirubinaemia, peripheral arterial occlusive disease (PAOD - long-term; monitor ABI). Note: must be taken fasted (food ↑absorption → toxicity); PAOD risk increases with duration.

3rd-gen BCR-ABL TKI (only agent active against T315I gatekeeper mutation). MOA: binds BCR-ABL including T315I mutation (not covered by 1st/2nd gen TKIs). Indications: CML/Ph+ ALL with T315I mutation or resistant to ≥2 prior TKIs. SE: arterial occlusion (MI, stroke, PAD - serious class-defining risk; ↑CV risk factors → higher risk), hypertension, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis. Note: highest CV toxicity of all BCR-ABL TKIs - use only when T315I confirmed or no alternatives; monitor and aggressively manage CV risk.

Selective VEGFR 1-3 TKI (2nd-line RCC). MOA: highly selective VEGFR 1-3 inhibition → potent anti-angiogenic. Indications: renal cell carcinoma (2nd-line after sunitinib/cytokine failure - AXIS trial; also 1st-line with pembrolizumab - KEYNOTE-426). SE: hypertension (high rate - ↑BP ↑response; manage aggressively), diarrhoea, fatigue, HFSR, hypothyroidism, proteinuria. Note: hypertension correlates with efficacy - treat to target rather than dose-reduce for HTN alone.

Multi-kinase TKI (VEGFR/MET/AXL/RET). MOA: inhibits VEGFR 2, MET, AXL, RET → anti-angiogenic + anti-tumour via MET/AXL (resistance pathways). Indications: RCC (1st-line with nivolumab - CheckMate 9ER; 2nd-line after VEGFR - METEOR trial), HCC (2nd-line after sorafenib - CELESTIAL), thyroid cancer (MTC - Cometriq), differentiated thyroid (radioiodine-refractory). SE: HFSR, diarrhoea, hypertension, weight loss, mucositis, hypothyroidism. Note: dual VEGFR + MET inhibition overcomes MET-driven resistance to VEGFR-only agents.

Multi-kinase TKI (VEGFR/PDGFR/FGFR/KIT/RET/RAF). MOA: broad kinase inhibition → anti-angiogenic + anti-tumour stromal/proliferative effects. Indications: metastatic colorectal cancer (3rd-line after oxaliplatin/irinotecan - CORRECT trial), GIST (3rd-line), HCC (2nd-line after sorafenib - RESORCE trial). SE: HFSR (dose-limiting - palmar-plantar erythrodysaesthesia - prophylactic urea cream), fatigue, diarrhoea, hypertension, hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs - fatal cases). Note: HFSR management critical - start at 80 mg, titrate; monitor LFTs weeks 1-2.

Multi-kinase TKI (VEGFR 1-3, FGFR 1-4, PDGFR-α, KIT, RET). MOA: broad kinase inhibition → potent anti-angiogenic. Indications: thyroid cancer (radioiodine-refractory differentiated - SELECT trial), HCC (1st-line with pembrolizumab - LEAP-002/KEYNOTE-524; non-inferior to sorafenib - REFLECT), RCC (1st-line with pembrolizumab - CLEAR trial), endometrial carcinoma (with pembrolizumab - KEYNOTE-775). SE: hypertension (very common - 70%+), HFSR, diarrhoea, weight loss, proteinuria, hepatotoxicity, QTc. Note: combination lenvatinib + pembrolizumab active across multiple tumour types - emerging as broad-spectrum IO/TKI backbone.

TRK inhibitor (tumour-agnostic; 1st-in-class). MOA: highly selective TRKA/B/C inhibition → blocks NTRK fusion-driven signalling. Indications: any solid tumour with NTRK gene fusion (tumour-agnostic approval - NAVIGATE/SCOUT basket trials; ~75% ORR regardless of histology). SE: dizziness, fatigue, nausea, ↑LFTs; CNS effects (dizziness/paraesthesia). Note: first truly tumour-agnostic TKI - test for NTRK fusion (RNA-based preferred) in any solid tumour; CNS-penetrant.

3rd-gen ALK/ROS1 TKI (CNS-penetrant; broadest resistance coverage). MOA: inhibits ALK + all major resistance mutations including G1202R (not covered by 2nd-gen); potent CNS penetration (P-gp substrate avoided). Indications: ALK+ NSCLC (1st-line - CROWN trial: superior PFS vs crizotinib; all subsequent lines after 1st/2nd-gen TKI failure). SE: hypercholesterolaemia (very common - monitor lipids; statin if needed), oedema, weight gain, cognitive effects/mood changes (CNS penetration), peripheral neuropathy. Note: hypercholesterolaemia in >80% - routine lipid monitoring; CNS effects unique to this agent (mood changes, word-finding difficulty).

Anti-PD-L1 monoclonal antibody (ICI). MOA: blocks PD-L1 → restores T-cell cytotoxicity. Indications: unresectable stage III NSCLC after concurrent chemoradiation (PACIFIC trial - standard of care; ↑PFS/OS), extensive-stage SCLC (with chemotherapy - CASPIAN), biliary tract cancer (with gemcitabine/cisplatin - TOPAZ-1), HCC. SE: immune-related AEs (pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis, endocrinopathies), particularly pneumonitis post-radiation (overlap with radiation pneumonitis - monitor). Note: PACIFIC trial established durvalumab as consolidation after chemoradiation for stage III - major paradigm shift.

Anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody (ICI). MOA: PD-1 blockade → restored T-cell anti-tumour immunity. Indications: advanced cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC - 1st approval; EMPOWER-CSCC trials), basal cell carcinoma (after hedgehog inhibitor failure), NSCLC (1st-line high PD-L1 - EMPOWER-Lung 1). SE: irAEs - fatigue, rash, hepatitis, colitis, pneumonitis; immune toxicity profile similar to other anti-PD-1 agents. Note: cSCC and BCC - cemiplimab changed standard of care for these skin cancers in advanced/metastatic setting.

Anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody (ICI). MOA: PD-1 blockade → T-cell reactivation. Indications: dMMR/MSI-H recurrent/advanced endometrial cancer (GARNET trial - high ORR ~40% in previously treated), dMMR solid tumours (tumour-agnostic). SE: irAEs - fatigue, anaemia, nausea, hepatitis, colitis; endocrine toxicity. Note: high activity in dMMR/MSI-H tumours; rectal cancer complete clinical response in small dMMR cohort (NEJM 2022 - landmark result).

IMiD (immunomodulatory; teratogen). MOA: binds cereblon (CRBN) E3 ubiquitin ligase → degradation of Ikaros/Aiolos transcription factors → ↓myeloma cell growth + ↑T/NK cell activity; anti-angiogenic. Indications: multiple myeloma (combination - MPT or VTd; largely replaced by lenalidomide/pomalidomide in resource-rich settings), erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL), graft-vs-host disease. SE: teratogenicity (absolute CI in pregnancy - phocomelia; strict REMS programme), DVT/PE (mandatory anticoagulation prophylaxis), peripheral neuropathy (dose-limiting; cumulative - irreversible), sedation, constipation. Note: MANDATORY teratogenicity programme (THALOMID REMS) - monthly pregnancy tests, 2 forms contraception, male contraception.

3rd-gen IMiD (lenalidomide/thalidomide resistant myeloma). MOA: cereblon binding → Ikaros/Aiolos degradation (10-100× more potent than thalidomide); ↓myeloma proliferation + ↑immune activation. Indications: relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (after lenalidomide and bortezomib failure - MM-003/MM-010 trials), Kaposi sarcoma (refractory). SE: myelosuppression (neutropaenia most common), DVT/PE (anticoagulation mandatory), peripheral neuropathy (less than thalidomide), teratogenicity (REMS required). Note: REMS programme required (teratogenicity); most active IMiD in lenalidomide-refractory myeloma.

2nd-gen proteasome inhibitor (irreversible; epoxyketone). MOA: irreversibly inhibits 20S proteasome chymotrypsin-like activity → ↑misfolded protein accumulation → myeloma cell apoptosis; more selective than bortezomib (↓peripheral neuropathy). Indications: relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (ASPIRE/ENDEAVOR trials - with lenalidomide/dexamethasone or dexamethasone alone; superior to bortezomib - ENDEAVOR). SE: cardiac toxicity (↑BP, HF, MI - screen LVEF before; distinctive vs bortezomib), dyspnoea, anaemia; ↓peripheral neuropathy vs bortezomib. Note: cardiac monitoring required (ECHO/ECG before) - carfilzomib cardiac events are class-differentiating; IV twice weekly.

Oral proteasome inhibitor (boronate; 1st oral). MOA: reversible 20S proteasome inhibition (same mechanism as bortezomib, oral bioavailability). Indications: relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (with lenalidomide + dexamethasone - TOURMALINE-MM1 trial - 1st all-oral triplet for myeloma). SE: GI (diarrhoea, nausea/vomiting, constipation), rash, peripheral neuropathy (less than bortezomib), thrombocytopaenia. Note: once-weekly oral dosing - major convenience advantage vs IV/SC bortezomib/carfilzomib; enables fully oral myeloma regimen.

Anti-SLAMF7 (CS1/CRACC) monoclonal antibody (myeloma). MOA: binds SLAMF7 on myeloma cells + NK cells → ADCC + direct NK cell activation → dual anti-myeloma mechanism. Indications: relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (with lenalidomide/dexamethasone - ELOQUENT-2; or with pomalidomide/dexamethasone - ELOQUENT-3). SE: infusion reactions (pre-medicate), fatigue, diarrhoea, infections. Note: unique mechanism - activates NK cells (not just myeloma cytotoxicity); no single-agent activity, requires combination.

Anti-CD30 antibody-drug conjugate (ADC; CD30-targeted MMAE delivery). MOA: binds CD30 → internalisation → MMAE release → microtubule disruption → apoptosis; CD30 expressed on Reed-Sternberg cells (HL) and ALCL. Indications: relapsed/refractory Hodgkin lymphoma (after ASCT - AETHERA; or as consolidation post-ASCT), CD30+ T-cell lymphoma (ECHELON-2 - with chemo 1st-line PTCL), systemic ALCL. SE: peripheral neuropathy (MMAE-driven - dose-limiting; monitor), neutropaenia, infusion reactions, PML (rare). Note: peripheral neuropathy is dose-limiting and cumulative - dose reduction/discontinuation may be needed.

Antifibrinolytic (lysine analogue). MOA: competitively inhibits plasminogen activation → ↓fibrinolysis → clot stabilisation. Indications: hyperfibrinolysis states (DIC, post-thrombolysis, cardiac surgery, haematuria from urological procedures), haemophilia (adjunct). SE: thrombosis (if used in DIC without addressing cause), nausea, GI, hypotension (IV rapid infusion). Note: alternative to tranexamic acid; tranexamic acid now preferred in most settings (better data); aminocaproic acid CI if thrombosis risk outweighs bleeding.

Heparin reversal agent (positively charged protein). MOA: strongly basic protein binds negatively charged heparin → electrostatic neutralisation → inactive heparin-protamine complex. Indications: UFH reversal (post-cardiac surgery, overdose - 1 mg per 100 units UFH); partial LMWH reversal (protamine reverses ~60% anti-Xa activity of LMWH). SE: severe hypotension (rapid injection - give slowly over 10 min), bradycardia, pulmonary hypertension, anaphylaxis (fish allergy risk, prior vasectomy). Note: does NOT reverse fondaparinux or DOACs; only partial LMWH reversal; anaphylaxis risk in fish allergy.

Vitamin K1 (phylloquinone; AU/UK name). MOA: cofactor for hepatic gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C/S → required for functional coagulation. Indications: warfarin reversal (oral 1-5 mg ↓INR within 24-48 h; IV if INR >10 or bleeding - faster but anaphylaxis risk), vitamin K deficiency (↑INR, newborn haemorrhagic disease - ALL neonates receive IM 1 mg at birth), haemorrhagic disease of the newborn prophylaxis. SE: anaphylaxis (IV route - give slowly; SC/IM preferred if possible), hypersensitivity, flushing. Note: warfarin reversal - oral phytomenadione preferred unless severe bleeding (then IV + PCC); IV carries anaphylaxis risk.

Vitamin B12 form (hydroxocobalamin; preferred over cyanocobalamin for parenteral use). MOA: converted to active cobalamin coenzymes (methylcobalamin → methionine synthesis; adenosylcobalamin → odd-chain FA metabolism); Cyanokit: binds cyanide → cyanocobalamin → excreted in urine.
