Indications: B12 deficiency (IM - pernicious anaemia, vegan diet, gastrectomy, terminal ileal disease - Schilling test), cyanide poisoning antidote (Cyanokit - IV 5 g over 15 min; first-line in France/UK/AU). SE: skin/urine discolouration (red-pink from drug - transient), acne (IM), anaphylaxis (rare). Note: cyanide antidote dosing very different from B12 replacement; Cyanokit is 5 g IV - do not confuse with B12 doses.

Long-acting ESA (erythropoiesis-stimulating agent; hyperglycosylated EPO analogue). MOA: same EPO receptor agonism as epoetin but T1/2 ~25 h (vs ~8 h) → less frequent dosing (weekly or q2w). Indications: anaemia of CKD (pre-dialysis and dialysis - target Hb 100-115 g/L), chemotherapy-induced anaemia (same cautions as epoetin re: ↑thrombosis). SE: hypertension, thrombosis, PRCA (rare), headache. Note: every-2-3-week dosing possible - advantage over epoetin; same efficacy and same target Hb ceiling (>115 g/L ↑CV events).

IV iron (high-dose formulation). MOA: macromolecular iron complex → releases iron in reticuloendothelial system → replenishes ferritin stores, supports erythropoiesis; single large dose possible (up to 1000 mg over 15 min). Indications: iron deficiency anaemia (oral intolerant, IBD, CKD, post-partum, pre-operative - single infusion advantage). SE: hypophosphataemia (significant - 40-75% with repeat doses; resolves spontaneously; risk of osteomalacia with repeated courses), hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis rare - less than iron dextran), flushing, nausea. Note: hypophosphataemia is characteristic and common - monitor phosphate; significant issue with repeated dosing; choose iron isomaltoside if hypophosphataemia risk.

IV iron (intermediate-dose; well-established safety). MOA: iron sucrose complex releases iron slowly in reticuloendothelium → stores replenishment. Indications: iron deficiency in CKD (dialysis - standard IV iron; safe, established; 100-200 mg per session), IBD, post-partum. SE: hypersensitivity (rare; lower risk than iron dextran), hypotension, GI; minimal hypophosphataemia (unlike ferric carboxymaltose). Note: standard IV iron in dialysis units; requires multiple doses (200 mg per session); considered very safe in dialysis setting.

Oral iron chelator (tridentate; once daily). MOA: binds Fe3+ with high affinity (2:1 ratio) → iron-chelator complex excreted in faeces (minor urinary). Indications: chronic iron overload from transfusions (β-thalassaemia, MDS, sickle cell, aplastic anaemia - EPIC/ESCALATOR trials), haemochromatosis (2nd-line to phlebotomy). SE: renal toxicity (↑Cr, Fanconi - monitor creatinine; dose-reduce/stop if ↑Cr), GI (nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhoea - Jadenu film coat ↓GI SE), rash, hearing/visual disturbance. Note: monitor Cr monthly; Jadenu (new formulation) fewer GI SE; hold during febrile illness.

Parenteral iron/aluminium chelator (siderophore; deferoxamine - US name). MOA: hexadentate chelator binds free Fe3+ and Al3+ → ferrioxamine complex excreted renally. Indications: acute iron overdose (IV/IM - STAT if symptomatic poisoning; 'vin rosé' urine confirms chelation), chronic iron overload (SC infusion - largely replaced by oral deferasirox), aluminium overload (dialysis patients), desferrioxamine test for aluminium toxicity. SE: hypotension (rapid IV), neurotoxicity (high-dose), yersinia infection risk (iron chelates provide substrate for Yersinia - ↑infection), pulmonary toxicity. Note: 'vin rosé'/pink-orange urine confirms active iron chelation in overdose; Yersinia enterocolitica septicaemia is a rare but serious complication.

Novel anti-TB (diarylquinoline; ATP synthase inhibitor). MOA: selectively inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase (subunit c) → disrupts energy metabolism → bactericidal (active against dormant and replicating TB; distinct from all prior TB drugs). Indications: MDR-TB (multidrug-resistant - part of BPaL or BPaLC regimens; WHO-endorsed; STREAM/ZeNix/TB-PRACTECAL trials). SE: QTc prolongation (significant - mandatory ECG monitoring; avoid concurrent QT-prolonging drugs), hepatotoxicity, nausea. Note: transformative for MDR-TB - first new TB drug in 50+ years; QTc monitoring mandatory; usually prescribed only by specialist TB units.

Novel anti-TB (nitroimidazole; mycobacterial cell wall inhibitor). MOA: pro-drug reduced by mycobacterial enzymes → reactive species → inhibit mycolic acid synthesis → cell wall disruption; active against non-replicating TB. Indications: MDR-TB (combination - when other agents unavailable or failed; WHO-endorsed). SE: QTc prolongation (monitor ECG), nausea, vomiting, dizziness, hypoalbuminaemia (↑QTc risk - correct albumin). Note: usually combined with bedaquiline in BPaL+ regimens; both prolong QTc - close monitoring essential.

Rifamycin antibiotic (rifabutin; less CYP induction than rifampicin). MOA: inhibits mycobacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (β-subunit) → ↓transcription. Indications: MAC prophylaxis/treatment in HIV (preferred over rifampicin - less drug-drug interactions with ARVs), TB treatment in HIV patients on PI/INSTI (rifabutin used instead of rifampicin - less CYP induction → better ARV levels). SE: uveitis (orange-red discolouration of urine/tears/saliva - like rifampicin; uveitis - dose-related), neutropaenia, rash. Note: key advantage over rifampicin - significantly less CYP3A4 induction → compatible with PIs/INSTIs in HIV/TB co-infection.

Anti-leprosy/anti-TB drug (phenazine). MOA: binds preferentially to mycobacterial DNA → ↓replication; also anti-inflammatory properties (↓neutrophil/lymphocyte migration). Indications: leprosy (multibacillary - with rifampicin and dapsone; WHO MDT regimen), MDR-TB (part of longer regimens). SE: skin discolouration (pink-red-brown - dose-dependent; affects 75-100% of patients; permanent during treatment, slowly reversible on stopping - warn patient), GI, enteropathy (crystalline deposits), ichthyosis. Note: skin discolouration is universal and distressing - counsel thoroughly before starting; persists months after stopping.

Extended-spectrum triazole antifungal. MOA: inhibits ergosterol synthesis (lanosterol 14α-demethylase) → fungistatic; broadest azole spectrum including Aspergillus, Fusarium, Zygomycetes (mucormycosis). Indications: prophylaxis of invasive fungal infections in high-risk neutropaenic/GVHD patients (POEM trial - superior to fluconazole/itraconazole), refractory aspergillosis/mucormycosis, refractory candidiasis. SE: nausea (suspension form - ↓with new tablet/IV formulation), ↑LFTs, QTc, drug interactions (CYP3A4). Note: broadest azole spectrum - only azole with activity against mucormycosis (Rhizopus, Mucor); delayed-release tablet has better bioavailability than suspension.

Echinocandin antifungal (IV; once daily). MOA: inhibits β-1,3-glucan synthase → disrupts fungal cell wall synthesis; fungicidal vs Candida, fungistatic vs Aspergillus. Indications: invasive candidiasis (including candidaemia - 1st-line with caspofungin/micafungin; non-inferior to fluconazole - ERAXIS trial), oesophageal candidiasis. SE: histamine-like infusion reactions (slow infusion rate), ↑LFTs, hypokalaemia. Note: minimal hepatic metabolism (unique among echinocandins - no dose adjustment in liver disease); no significant drug interactions.

Extended-spectrum triazole (isavuconazonium sulfate pro-drug). MOA: ergosterol synthesis inhibition; similar spectrum to voriconazole plus Mucorales activity. Indications: invasive aspergillosis (non-inferior to voriconazole - SECURE trial; fewer visual SE), mucormycosis (salvage - activity against Mucorales unlike voriconazole), rare moulds. SE: nausea, headache, ↑LFTs; ↓SE than voriconazole (no visual disturbances, no phototoxicity, no fluoride-bone toxicity); QTc shortening (not prolongation - distinctive). Note: preferred over voriconazole in many centres due to better tolerability; note QTc shortening (not prolongation) - avoid in congenital short QT syndrome.

SARS-CoV-2 protease inhibitor (co-packaged with ritonavir as Paxlovid). MOA: inhibits SARS-CoV-2 main protease (3CLpro/Mpro) → prevents polyprotein processing → ↓viral replication; ritonavir boosts nirmatrelvir plasma levels via CYP3A4 inhibition. Indications: mild-moderate COVID-19 in high-risk patients (within 5 days of symptom onset - EPIC-HR: 89% ↓hospitalisation/death vs placebo; TGA-approved in AU). SE: dysgeusia (metallic/bitter taste - distinctive and very common), diarrhoea, hypertension; significant drug-drug interactions (via ritonavir CYP3A4 inhibition - check all medications before prescribing). Note: DDIs are major issue - ritonavir component inhibits CYP3A4 → ↑levels of statins, immunosuppressants, anticoagulants, etc.; check interactions before every prescription.

SARS-CoV-2 RNA polymerase inhibitor (nucleoside analogue pro-drug). MOA: pro-drug converted to NHC → incorporated into viral RNA → lethal mutagenesis (↑error rate → viral extinction). Indications: mild-moderate COVID-19 in high-risk (within 5 days - MOVe-OUT: ~30% ↓hospitalisation; less effective than Paxlovid; 2nd-line option). SE: nausea, diarrhoea, dizziness; theoretical mutagenicity concern (CI in pregnancy, breastfeeding, children). CI: pregnancy, breastfeeding. Note: inferior to Paxlovid but fewer drug interactions - alternative when Paxlovid DDIs are unmanageable; avoid in pregnancy (mutagenicity).

Cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor (influenza; novel mechanism). MOA: inhibits influenza cap-snatching endonuclease (PA subunit of RNA polymerase) → ↓viral mRNA synthesis; novel mechanism distinct from neuraminidase inhibitors; single-dose treatment. Indications: uncomplicated influenza A/B (within 48 h - CAPSTONE-1/2 trials; single oral dose; effective against oseltamivir-resistant strains), influenza prophylaxis (single dose post-exposure). SE: diarrhoea, bronchitis, nausea; resistance can emerge (PA I38X mutations). Note: single-dose convenience advantage over 5-day oseltamivir; active against oseltamivir-resistant influenza - important for outbreak management.

Pyrophosphate analogue antiviral (IV). MOA: directly inhibits viral DNA polymerase and reverse transcriptase at pyrophosphate binding site (not phosphorylated - no kinase activation needed → active against aciclovir-resistant HSV/VZV and ganciclovir-resistant CMV). Indications: ganciclovir-resistant CMV (retinitis/disease in HIV/transplant), aciclovir-resistant HSV/VZV, CMV alternative. SE: nephrotoxicity (most significant - must aggressively hydrate with each infusion; monitor Cr and electrolytes daily), electrolyte disturbances (hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypophosphataemia - chelates divalent cations; genital ulceration - direct contact effect), seizures (electrolyte abnormalities). Note: renal toxicity requires mandatory saline pre/co-hydration with EVERY infusion; monitor electrolytes daily.

Nucleotide analogue antiviral (cytosine; IV). MOA: phosphorylated to cidofovir diphosphate → competitive inhibitor of viral DNA polymerase; long intracellular T1/2 → weekly/biweekly dosing. Indications: CMV retinitis in HIV (weekly × 2, then biweekly - with probenecid), aciclovir/ganciclovir-resistant HSV/CMV, adenovirus (off-label). SE: nephrotoxicity (dose-limiting and severe - MANDATORY probenecid + IV hydration with every dose; proteinuria → stop if ↑Cr 0.4 above baseline), neutropaenia, iritis/uveitis (instil pilocarpine drops). Note: probenecid and IV saline are MANDATORY with every dose (reduces renal tubular secretion of cidofovir); possibly most nephrotoxic antiviral in use.

CMV terminase complex inhibitor (novel mechanism). MOA: inhibits CMV terminase (UL56 subunit) → prevents viral DNA packaging/cleavage → ↓CMV replication; no cross-resistance with ganciclovir (different target). Indications: CMV prophylaxis in CMV-seropositive allogeneic HSCT recipients (PROTECT trial - 61% ↓clinically significant CMV infection vs placebo), prophylaxis in kidney transplant (high-risk D+/R-). SE: GI (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea), oedema, tachycardia; drug interactions (CYP3A4 - check cyclosporin, tacrolimus levels). Note: significantly fewer marrow toxicity than ganciclovir - no neutropaenia; allows CMV prophylaxis in early post-HSCT period when GCV toxicity problematic.

CMV UL97 kinase inhibitor (oral; novel target vs ganciclovir). MOA: inhibits CMV UL97 kinase (different site from ganciclovir) → ↓viral DNA replication and nuclear egress; active against ganciclovir/foscarnet/cidofovir-resistant CMV (different mechanism). Indications: refractory/resistant CMV infection in transplant recipients (SOLSTICE trial - superior to investigator-assigned therapy vs ganciclovir-/foscarnet-/cidofovir-resistant CMV). SE: taste disturbance (dysgeusia - very common, dose-dependent but tolerable), nausea, diarrhoea; antagonises ganciclovir (cannot co-administer - UL97 is needed to phosphorylate ganciclovir). Note: cannot use with ganciclovir/valganciclovir (pharmacological antagonism - maribavir blocks UL97 which activates GCV).

INSTI (integrase strand transfer inhibitor; component of Biktarvy). MOA: inhibits HIV integrase → prevents integration of viral DNA into host genome; high genetic barrier to resistance. Indications: HIV-1 (as Biktarvy = bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir AF - 1st-line preferred regimen in most guidelines; once daily, no pharmacokinetic booster needed). SE: nausea, headache, diarrhoea; ↑creatinine (tenofovir AF component - tubular secretion inhibition; not true GFR decline), ↑weight (INSTI class effect). Note: Biktarvy is single-tablet, once-daily, no booster, high resistance barrier - most commonly prescribed initial HIV regimen globally.

HIV protease inhibitor (PI; 2nd-gen). MOA: inhibits HIV aspartyl protease → prevents polyprotein cleavage → immature, non-infectious virions; must be boosted (ritonavir or cobicistat). Indications: HIV-1 treatment-experienced (darunavir/ritonavir or darunavir/cobicistat - Prezcobix; also in Symtuza with FTC/TAF); preferred PI in treatment-experienced due to high resistance barrier (DRV/r); also used as 1st-line in some guidelines. SE: GI (diarrhoea, nausea), rash (sulfonamide moiety - avoid in sulfa allergy), hepatotoxicity, lipodystrophy (class), dyslipidaemia. Note: requires boosting (ritonavir 100 mg or cobicistat); highest resistance barrier among PIs - useful in heavily treatment-experienced.

NNRTI (2nd-gen; rilpivirine). MOA: non-competitive HIV reverse transcriptase inhibitor (binds allosteric hydrophobic pocket; different binding from 1st-gen NNRTIs → ↓cross-resistance to efavirenz). Indications: HIV-1 (treatment-naive with VL <100,000 and CD4 >200 - ECHO/THRIVE; in combination: Odefsey = RPV/FTC/TAF or Juluca = RPV/dolutegravir - 1st 2-drug regimen). SE: rash, depressive symptoms (less than efavirenz - ↓CNS SE), QTc (less than saquinavir), ↑LFTs; requires food for absorption (must take with meal ≥390 kcal). Note: Juluca (rilpivirine + dolutegravir) = first approved 2-drug complete regimen - maintenance therapy for virologically suppressed patients.

CCR5 antagonist (entry inhibitor). MOA: binds CCR5 co-receptor on CD4 T-cells → conformational change → prevents HIV gp120 binding → ↓viral entry; only active against CCR5-tropic (R5) HIV (not CXCR4-tropic). Indications: CCR5-tropic HIV-1 (treatment-experienced - MOTIVATE trials; requires tropism testing before use). SE: hepatotoxicity (severe - monitor; systemic allergic reaction may precede), URTI, cough, dizziness, abdominal pain, ↑CV events (concern - not confirmed). Note: tropism testing MANDATORY before prescribing (Trofile assay or genotypic testing); inactive against CXCR4-tropic or dual-tropic HIV - tropism shifts on treatment.

Long-acting INSTI (injectable; cabotegravir + rilpivirine = Cabenuva). MOA: HIV integrase inhibition; long-acting injectable formulation allows monthly or bimonthly dosing. Indications: HIV treatment (virologically suppressed - Cabenuva monthly or bimonthly IM injection; ATLAS/FLAIR/ATLAS-2M trials - non-inferior to daily oral); HIV PrEP (Apretude - bimonthly IM injection; superior to daily oral tenofovir/emtricitabine - HPTN 083/084). SE: injection site reactions (most common - pain/induration at gluteal injection), pyrexia, fatigue; weight gain (INSTI class). Note: bimonthly injectable PrEP (Apretude) dramatically improves PrEP adherence - major advance for populations where daily oral adherence is challenging.

Anti-CGRP receptor monoclonal antibody (migraine prevention; monthly SC). MOA: blocks CGRP receptor → ↓nociceptive signalling in trigeminal pathways; only mAb targeting CGRP receptor (others target CGRP ligand). Indications: episodic and chronic migraine prevention (STRIVE/ARISE trials - ≥50% ↓migraine days in ~43-50% of patients; monthly SC auto-injector). SE: constipation (most common - distinctive, may be severe; related to CGRP block in gut), injection site reactions, hypertension (rare). Note: constipation is characteristic SE - CGRP regulates colonic motility; switch to fremanezumab/galcanezumab if constipation problematic.

Anti-CGRP monoclonal antibody (monthly or quarterly SC). MOA: binds CGRP ligand (both α and β isoforms) → ↓CGRP signalling. Indications: episodic and chronic migraine prevention (HALO trials; monthly 225 mg or quarterly 675 mg - only quarterly option among CGRP mAbs). SE: injection site reactions, constipation (less than erenumab). Note: only CGRP mAb with quarterly dosing option - adherence advantage for some patients.

Anti-CGRP monoclonal antibody (monthly SC). MOA: binds CGRP ligand → ↓trigeminal nociception. Indications: episodic and chronic migraine prevention (EVOLVE-1/2 and REGAIN trials), cluster headache (episodic - CONQUER/REHEARSE; only CGRP mAb approved for cluster headache). SE: injection site reactions, constipation. Note: only CGRP mAb with evidence for cluster headache; requires 3× monthly loading dose for cluster.

CGRP receptor antagonist (gepant; oral; acute + preventive). MOA: small-molecule CGRP receptor blocker → ↓trigeminal nociception; unlike triptans - no vasoconstriction. Indications: acute migraine treatment (orally disintegrating tablet - BARBARIAN trial) AND preventive (every other day - first drug approved for both acute and prevention). SE: nausea, UTI, hepatotoxicity (rare - monitor LFTs); no vasoconstriction → safer in CV disease than triptans. Note: dual indication (acute + preventive) is unique; no vasoconstriction - can use when triptans contraindicated (CV disease).

5-HT1F agonist (ditan; acute migraine; no vasoconstriction). MOA: selective 5-HT1F receptor agonism → inhibits CGRP release from trigeminal neurons without vasoconstriction (5-HT1F not expressed in vascular smooth muscle; triptans activate 5-HT1B → vasoconstriction). Indications: acute migraine with or without aura (SAMURAI/SPARTAN trials - especially when triptans CI due to CVD). SE: dizziness (most common - dose-limiting), somnolence, paraesthesia; CNS effects require no driving/machinery for 8 h after dose (Schedule V in US). Note: no vasoconstriction - safe in cardiovascular disease where triptans contraindicated; significant CNS SE (dizziness, sedation) limits use.

CFTR potentiator (1st CFTR modulator approved). MOA: binds mutant CFTR protein → keeps channel open longer (↑channel gating) → ↑Cl transport; only effective for gating mutations (G551D most common). Indications: cystic fibrosis with CFTR gating mutations (G551D and others - STRIVE/ENVISION trials; ~4% of CF patients). SE: ↑LFTs (monitor every 3 months), headache, URTI, rash; transient nasal congestion. Note: first disease-modifying CF treatment; only ~4% of patients have eligible mutations (now combined with elexacaftor/tezacaftor as Trikafta for F508del - much larger population).

Triple CFTR modulator combination (corrector × 2 + potentiator; transformative CF therapy). MOA: elexacaftor + tezacaftor (correctors) → correct F508del CFTR protein folding/trafficking → get protein to cell surface; ivacaftor (potentiator) → keep channel open → substantially ↑Cl transport; synergistic triple mechanism. Indications: CF with ≥1 F508del allele (AU TGA approved; ~90% of CF patients - VX-445 trials: ↑FEV1 ~14%, ↑sweat Cl ↓63 mmol/L, ↑BMI, ↓exacerbations, ↓IV antibiotics). SE: ↑LFTs (monitor; withhold if >5×ULN), rash, headache, rhinorrhoea; cataracts (paediatric - annual ophthalmology review). Note: most transformative CF treatment - dramatically changes disease trajectory; most patients now achieve near-normal lung function if started early; paediatric ophthalmology monitoring for cataracts.

Calcium sensitiser + K-ATP channel opener (inodilator). MOA: binds cardiac troponin C → ↑calcium sensitivity of myofilaments → ↑contractility without ↑intracellular Ca (↓arrhythmia risk); also opens K-ATP channels in vascular smooth muscle → vasodilation. Indications: acute decompensated HF (short-term - LIDO/RUSSLAN trials; particularly useful in cardiogenic shock when inotropes + vasodilation needed; dobutamine-resistant), cardiac surgery (pre-/post-op). SE: hypotension (vasodilation), headache, hypokalaemia, atrial fibrillation, PVCs. Note: unique mechanism - ↑contractility without ↑myocardial O2 demand (vs dobutamine); active metabolite OR-1896 extends haemodynamic effects for weeks.

Non-selective β1/β2 agonist (AU/UK: isoprenaline; US: isoprenaline). MOA: pure β-agonist (no α activity) → β1: ↑HR, ↑contractility; β2: peripheral vasodilation + bronchodilation → ↑CO + ↓SVR. Indications: symptomatic bradycardia (refractory to atropine - bridge to pacing), AV block (temporary pacing bridge), torsades de pointes (bradycardia-dependent - ↑HR → ↓QT interval + suppress TdP), bronchospasm (historical - now replaced by salbutamol), Brugada syndrome (acute arrhythmia suppression). SE: tachyarrhythmia (↑HR → ↑O2 demand), angina (↑MVO2 in CAD), hypotension (β2 vasodilation). Note: used for TdP - ↑HR shortens QT interval; DO NOT use in ischaemic bradycardia (↑O2 demand worsens ischaemia).

V2 receptor antagonist (vaptan; aquaretic). MOA: selectively blocks V2 receptors in renal collecting duct → ↓AQP2 insertion → ↑free water excretion (aquaresis - electrolyte-free water loss unlike loop diuretics which lose NaCl). Indications: hyponatraemia (euvolaemic/hypervolaemic - SIADH, HF, cirrhosis - SALT-1/SALT-2; corrects Na without fluid restriction; 30 mg/day), ADPKD (Jinarc - slows cyst growth - TEMPO 3:4 trial; specialist use only). SE: aquaresis (thirst, polyuria, dry mouth - initiate in-hospital for SIADH), osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS - overly rapid Na correction; strict correction rate ≤8-10 mmol/L per 24 h), hepatotoxicity (ADPKD dose - Jinarc; monitor LFTs). Note: must be initiated in-hospital for SIADH (Na rises rapidly; ODS risk if overcorrected); avoid fluid restriction while taking (drink to thirst).

Non-selective α-blocker (α1/α2 antagonist; short-acting IV). MOA: competitive blockade of α1/α2 adrenergic receptors → peripheral vasodilation + ↓BP; α2 blockade → ↑NE release (reflex tachycardia). Indications: phaeochromocytoma (hypertensive crisis - IV; peri-operative BP control; diagnostic test historically), hypertensive emergency from catecholamine excess (cocaine, tyramine, clonidine withdrawal), local dental anaesthetic vasoconstriction reversal (OraVerse - infiltration). SE: hypotension (profound - have pressor available), reflex tachycardia, arrhythmia. Note: peri-operative phaeochromocytoma management - phentolamine IV bolus for hypertensive surges (phenoxybenzamine used for pre-op oral alpha blockade).

Long-acting somatostatin analogue (depot). MOA: binds somatostatin receptors (SSTR2 > SSTR5) → ↓GH/IGF-1 secretion, ↓tumour blood flow/secretion. Indications: acromegaly (monthly SC depot - non-inferior to octreotide LAR - PRIMARYS trial; 1st-line medical if surgery not possible), gastroenteropancreatic NETs (monthly depot - CLARINET trial: ↑PFS in midgut and pancreatic NETs), carcinoid syndrome. SE: GI (diarrhoea, nausea, flatulence, abdominal cramps), gallstones (↓gallbladder motility - monitor with USS), hyperglycaemia, injection site reactions. Note: monthly deep SC injection - patient or nurse administered; auto-gel formulation easy to administer.

Multi-receptor somatostatin analogue (pan-receptor; higher SSTR5 affinity). MOA: binds SSTR1/2/3/5 (higher SSTR5 affinity than octreotide/lanreotide → activity in ACTH-secreting tumours that express SSTR5). Indications: Cushing disease (pituitary - not controlled by surgery; CSOM230 trial - ↓UFC in ~26%; LAR monthly injection for Cushing disease), acromegaly (LAR if octreotide/lanreotide inadequate). SE: hyperglycaemia (significant and distinctive - 73% of patients; worse than other somatostatin analogues due to SSTR5 inhibition of insulin; requires close monitoring and often anti-diabetic treatment), GI, bradycardia, gallstones. Note: hyperglycaemia is major SE - near-universal; requires diabetes monitoring and management before and during treatment.

GH receptor antagonist (pegylated GH analogue; acromegaly). MOA: competitive GH receptor blocker (no agonist activity) → ↓IGF-1 without affecting GH; normalises IGF-1 in >90% (most effective at IGF-1 normalisation). Indications: acromegaly (inadequate response to surgery + somatostatin analogues; once-daily SC injection - ACROSTUDY). SE: ↑LFTs (monitor - usually transient; HOLD if >3×ULN), injection site reactions, tumour growth (GH rises - does not suppress pituitary tumour; monitor MRI 6-monthly). Note: normalises IGF-1 in >90% - most effective medical therapy for IGF-1 normalisation; GH levels RISE (normal response - do not use GH to monitor response, use IGF-1).

Non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA). MOA: highly selective, non-steroidal MR blocker → ↓aldosterone-driven inflammation/fibrosis in kidney and heart (different binding from spironolactone/eplerenone - ↓off-target SE). Indications: CKD with type 2 diabetes (FIDELIO-DKD + FIGARO-DKD: ↓progression of CKD and ↓CV events - reduces both renal and CV outcomes beyond SGLT2i + RAS blockade). SE: hyperkalaemia (monitor - risk ↑with CKD; avoid if K+ >5.0), hypotension; ↓gynaecomastia/sexual dysfunction vs spironolactone (non-steroidal). Note: first MRA with evidence in diabetic CKD specifically; complements SGLT2i/ACEi/ARB triple strategy in CKD-DM.

D3/D2 partial agonist (dopamine-serotonin activity modulator; high D3 selectivity). MOA: partial D3 > D2 agonism (highest D3 affinity of any antipsychotic - D3 receptors ↑in limbic areas → negative symptom/cognitive benefit) + 5-HT2A antagonism. Indications: schizophrenia (positive and negative symptoms - CANTU/CARIPRAZINE trials; negative symptoms may respond better than other atypicals), bipolar I mania, bipolar depression (CADENCE-BD trial - US-approved). SE: akathisia (most common - higher rate than aripiprazole due to D3 selectivity), somnolence, EPS, nausea. Note: highest D3 selectivity among antipsychotics - theoretical advantage for negative symptoms; akathisia risk requires monitoring.

Inverse agonist at 5-HT2A/2C receptors (atypical antipsychotic; no D2 antagonism). MOA: inverse agonist (not antagonist) at 5-HT2A receptors → ↓psychosis without dopamine blockade → no EPS/tardive dyskinesia, no worsening of PD motor symptoms. Indications: hallucinations/delusions associated with Parkinson disease psychosis (PDP - HARMONY trial - only approved treatment for PDP; does not worsen motor features). SE: QTc prolongation (monitor ECG), peripheral oedema, confusion, hallucinations (paradoxical). Note: only antipsychotic specifically approved for Parkinson disease psychosis - critical because other antipsychotics worsen motor symptoms; QTc monitoring required.

Farnesoid X receptor (FXR) agonist (bile acid analogue). MOA: FXR agonism → ↓bile acid synthesis + ↑bile acid transport/excretion → ↓hepatic lipotoxicity + anti-fibrotic/anti-inflammatory effects. Indications: primary biliary cholangitis (PBC - 2nd-line add-on to UDCA non-responders - POISE trial: ↓ALP, ↓bilirubin); NASH/MAFLD (under investigation - REGENERATE trial - ↓fibrosis; not yet approved for NASH in AU). SE: pruritus (severe - dose-limiting; most common reason for discontinuation; ↓bile acid synthesis → ↑itching paradoxically), hepatic decompensation (avoid in Child B/C), hypercholesterolaemia (FXR inhibits CYP7A1 → ↓bile acid conversion of cholesterol). Note: pruritus management critical - start lowest dose (5 mg), titrate slowly; avoid in decompensated cirrhosis.

Chloride channel activator (ClC-2 activator; chronic constipation). MOA: selectively activates CLC-2 chloride channels on intestinal epithelium → ↑luminal Cl secretion → ↑water flux into bowel lumen → ↑stool softness/frequency. Indications: chronic idiopathic constipation (CIC), IBS-C (irritable bowel syndrome with constipation - women ≥18 years), opioid-induced constipation (with non-cancer pain). SE: nausea (most common - take with food; ↓dose for IBS-C), diarrhoea, headache, dyspnoea (transient, within 1 h of first dose - ↓with subsequent doses). Note: take with food and water to ↓nausea; transient dyspnoea on first dose is a recognised phenomenon - warn patients.

Guanylate cyclase-C agonist (secretagogue; IBS-C and CIC). MOA: binds guanylate cyclase-C on intestinal epithelium → ↑cGMP → ↑Cl/HCO3 secretion (luminal) + ↓pain signalling (↑cGMP in afferent pain fibres). Indications: IBS with constipation (IBS-C - LIBER8 trial), chronic idiopathic constipation (CIC), opioid-induced constipation. SE: diarrhoea (most common and dose-limiting; ↑with food - take 30 min before breakfast), abdominal pain. CI: children <6 (boxed warning - intestinal obstruction deaths in paediatric animal studies). Note: take on empty stomach 30-60 min before first meal; diarrhoea management - dose reduction or temporary hold.

Sucrose octasulfate-aluminium complex (mucosal protectant). MOA: polymerises in acidic pH → binds to ulcer base (positively charged proteins in necrotic ulcer tissue) → physical barrier against acid/pepsin/bile; also ↑prostaglandin synthesis, ↑bicarbonate secretion, ↑mucus. Indications: peptic ulcer disease (acute healing; stress ulcer prophylaxis in ICU - comparable to PPI in PEPTIC trial for most patients), radiation proctitis, oesophagitis. SE: constipation (most common - aluminium content), ↓absorption of other drugs (separate by 2 h - binds warfarin, fluoroquinolones, phenytoin, digoxin), aluminium accumulation (↑in renal failure). Note: separate from other drugs by ≥2 h - significantly ↓absorption of many medications; preferred stress ulcer prophylaxis in some settings (↓C. diff risk vs PPIs).

Peripheral µ-opioid receptor antagonist (PAMORA; oral; opioid-induced constipation). MOA: PEGylated naloxol → restricted CNS penetration (P-gp substrate) → selectively blocks peripheral µ receptors in GI tract without reversing central analgesia. Indications: opioid-induced constipation (OIC) in non-cancer pain (KODIAC trials - ↑spontaneous bowel movements vs placebo; 1st-line OIC in chronic pain). SE: abdominal pain (most common - opioid withdrawal-like GI effects; ↓with dose reduction), nausea, diarrhoea, headache; opioid withdrawal if blood-brain barrier compromised (CNS tumour, trauma). Note: take 1 h before or 2 h after first meal; avoid if GI obstruction; discontinue other laxatives before starting.

Anti-IL-13 monoclonal antibody (atopic dermatitis biologic). MOA: neutralises IL-13 → ↓Th2-driven skin inflammation, ↓IgE, ↑skin barrier function; more selective than dupilumab (IL-13 only, not IL-4/IL-13). Indications: moderate-severe atopic dermatitis (ECZTRA trials - ↓EASI 75 response ~38% vs 12% placebo; SC biweekly). SE: conjunctivitis (less than dupilumab - IL-4R not blocked → ↓conjunctival Th2 suppression), URTI, injection site reactions. Note: ↓conjunctivitis rate vs dupilumab - potential advantage for patients with dupilumab-associated eye disease; biweekly SC, then monthly after good response.

Partial µ/κ opioid receptor agonist + δ antagonist (alcohol dependence). MOA: µ-receptor partial agonism → ↓dopamine reward from alcohol; κ agonism → ↓craving; δ antagonism - combined modulation of reward pathways. Indications: alcohol dependence (as-needed dosing before anticipated drinking - ESENSE trials - ↓heavy drinking days; ↓total alcohol consumption; not abstinence-focused). SE: nausea, dizziness, insomnia, headache (mostly transient - on-demand dosing ↓SE vs daily naltrexone). Note: taken as-needed 1-2 h before anticipated drinking (not daily) - novel harm-reduction approach; different from naltrexone (fixed daily dose); EU-approved but availability varies.

Fibric acid derivative. MOA: activates PPAR-α → ↑LPL activity → ↓TG, ↑HDL; ↓VLDL synthesis. Indications: hypertriglyceridaemia, mixed dyslipidaemia. SE: GI upset, cholelithiasis, myopathy (↑risk with statins - avoid combination). Note: avoid with repaglinide (↑hypoglycaemia) and statins (rhabdomyolysis).
Fibric acid derivative. MOA: PPAR-α activation → ↓TG, ↑HDL. Indications: hypertriglyceridaemia, mixed dyslipidaemia. SE: GI, myopathy, cholestasis. Note: renally cleared - dose reduce in CKD.

Bile acid sequestrant (2nd-gen). MOA: binds bile acids in GI tract → ↓enterohepatic circulation → ↑LDL receptors. Indications: hypercholesterolaemia (add-on), T2DM (modest HbA1c lowering), cholestatic pruritus. SE: constipation, bloating; does not absorb systemically. Note: separates drug absorption - take other meds 1-4 h before.
Statin (shorter-acting). MOA: inhibits HMG-CoA reductase. Indications: hyperlipidaemia. SE: myalgia, ↑LFTs. Note: fewer CYP3A4 interactions (metabolised mainly by CYP2C9).

Statin. MOA: inhibits HMG-CoA reductase; not CYP3A4 metabolised (minimal interaction profile). Indications: hyperlipidaemia. SE: myalgia. Note: can be used in CYP3A4-complex patients; generally once daily, low dose.

Sulfonylurea (first-gen; glibenclamide is the Australian/INN term; glibenclamide in US). MOA: closes KATP channels on pancreatic β-cells → ↑insulin secretion independent of glucose. Indications: T2DM. SE: prolonged hypoglycaemia (active metabolites, especially in elderly/renal impairment), weight gain. Note: Beers criterion - avoid in elderly; gliclazide preferred in Australia.

Meglitinide (prandial glucose regulator). MOA: closes KATP channels on β-cells (different binding site to sulfonylureas) → rapid, short-duration insulin release. Indications: T2DM. SE: hypoglycaemia (shorter duration than SUs), weight gain. Note: taken immediately before meals; useful for irregular meal schedule. Avoid with gemfibrozil (↑drug levels).

Alpha-glucosidase inhibitor. MOA: competitively inhibits intestinal α-glucosidase → delays carbohydrate digestion/absorption → blunts postprandial glucose spike. Indications: T2DM (modest HbA1c reduction ~0.5%). SE: flatulence, diarrhoea, bloating (fermentation of unabsorbed carbs). Note: no systemic absorption; hypoglycaemia from other agents must be treated with glucose (not sucrose).

DPP-4 inhibitor. MOA: inhibits DPP-4 → ↑GLP-1/GIP → ↑glucose-dependent insulin secretion, ↓glucagon. Indications: T2DM add-on (available in Australia; twice daily). SE: nasopharyngitis, dizziness, rare hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs). Note: dose halved in renal impairment.

DPP-4 inhibitor. MOA: same incretin enhancement as other gliptins. Indications: T2DM. SE: nasopharyngitis; possible ↑HF hospitalisation (SAVOR-TIMI - heart failure caution). Note: dose reduce in renal impairment.
DPP-4 inhibitor. MOA: DPP-4 inhibition → ↑GLP-1/GIP. Indications: T2DM. SE: nasopharyngitis, pancreatitis (rare). Note: renal dose adjustment required.

SGLT2 inhibitor. MOA: blocks SGLT2 in proximal tubule → glucosuria, natriuresis. Indications: T2DM. SE: urogenital infections, euglycaemic DKA, volume depletion. Note: hold peri-operatively; evidence base smaller than empagliflozin/dapagliflozin.

GIP/GLP-1 dual receptor agonist. MOA: activates both GIP and GLP-1 receptors → ↑insulin secretion, ↓glucagon, ↓gastric emptying, ↑satiety → potent weight loss (SURMOUNT trials, ~22.5% weight loss). Indications: T2DM, obesity. SE: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea; pancreatitis, thyroid C-cell tumours (animal). CI: MTC/MEN2 personal/family history.

MAO-B inhibitor. MOA: irreversible selective inhibition of MAO-B → ↓dopamine degradation → ↑striatal dopamine. Indications: Parkinson's disease (adjunct to levodopa or early monotherapy). SE: insomnia, nausea, tyramine interactions (at standard doses: selective for MAO-B - low tyramine risk). Note: amfetamine metabolites; drug interactions with serotonergic agents.

1,5-benzodiazepine anticonvulsant. MOA: positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A receptor (chloride channel) → CNS inhibition. Indications: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, adjunctive epilepsy. SE: sedation, tolerance, ataxia, dependence. Note: less sedating than 1,4-benzodiazepines; CYP2C19 induction reduces efficacy.

Sulfonamide-based anticonvulsant. MOA: blocks voltage-gated Na and T-type Ca channels; weak carbonic anhydrase inhibition. Indications: focal and generalised epilepsy (adjunctive), Parkinson's (adjunct). SE: anorexia, weight loss, cognitive dulling, kidney stones (carbonic anhydrase), oligohidrosis (children). CI: sulfonamide allergy.

Endogenous sleep hormone (synthetic supplement). MOA: agonist at MT1/MT2 receptors in SCN → phase-shifts circadian rhythm; promotes sleep onset. Indications: primary insomnia (age >55 - Circadin PR), jet lag, delayed sleep phase disorder, insomnia in autism spectrum/ADHD children (Slenyto). SE: headache, dizziness, next-day somnolence. Note: not a sedative - chronobiotic effect.

Histamine analogue. MOA: weak H1 agonist + H3 antagonist → ↑cochlear blood flow; ↓firing in vestibular nuclei. Indications: Ménière disease (vertigo, tinnitus, hearing loss), vestibular vertigo. SE: GI upset, headache. CI: phaeochromocytoma (theoretical). Note: must be taken long-term (months) to assess benefit; evidence modest.

1st-gen sedating antihistamine (Australian/British term: chlorphenamine; US: chlorpheniramine). MOA: competitive H1 receptor antagonism → ↓histamine-mediated itch, rhinorrhoea, urticaria; significant anticholinergic and CNS sedating effect. Indications: allergic rhinitis, urticaria, anaphylaxis adjunct, pruritus. SE: sedation, antimuscarinic effects, urinary retention. Note: impairs driving; risk of paradoxical excitation in children.

1st-gen sedating antihistamine. MOA: H1 receptor blockade; significant anticholinergic effects; crosses BBB. Indications: allergic reactions, motion sickness, short-term insomnia, dystonia (IV). SE: sedation, dry mouth, urinary retention, confusion (elderly - Beers criterion). Note: OTC sleep aid; avoid in elderly.

Topical alpha-2 adrenergic agonist (nasal decongestant). MOA: vasoconstriction of nasal mucosa vessels → ↓oedema/congestion. Indications: nasal congestion (≤3–5 days only). SE: rebound rhinitis medicamentosa (rhinitis medicamentosa) with prolonged use. CI: MAOIs, hypertensive emergency. Note: strictly limit to 3-5 days to prevent rebound.

Very potent (Class 1) topical corticosteroid. MOA: high-affinity GR binding → ↓inflammatory cytokines, ↓skin inflammation. Indications: severe psoriasis, lichen planus, discoid lupus, alopecia areata; short-term use only. SE: skin atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, adrenal suppression (extensive use), acneiform eruption. Note: avoid face/flexures/children unless specialist-directed.

Moderate-potent (Class III) topical corticosteroid / medium-potency nasal spray. MOA: GR binding → anti-inflammatory. Indications: atopic dermatitis (skin), allergic rhinitis (nasal spray - once daily), nasal polyps. SE: topical: skin atrophy, telangiectasia (with prolonged use); nasal: epistaxis, nasal dryness. Note: well-tolerated for maintenance.

Intermediate-acting synthetic glucocorticoid (IM, intralesional, intraarticular, topical). MOA: GR agonism → anti-inflammatory, immunosuppressive. Indications: intra-articular injection (OA, RA flares), intralesional keloids/psoriatic plaques, topical eczema. SE: post-injection steroid flare (first 24 h), cartilage damage with repeated intra-articular use, adrenal suppression, osteonecrosis.

Topical antibiotic (pseudomonic acid). MOA: inhibits bacterial isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase → ↓protein synthesis; bactericidal against gram-positives. Indications: MSSA impetigo, infected wounds/eczema, MRSA nasal decolonisation (eradication protocol). SE: local irritation, contact dermatitis. Note: avoid intranasal liquid formulation in kidneys/liver disease patients (polyethylene glycol base).

Imidazole antifungal (topical and systemic - systemic largely replaced). MOA: inhibits CYP51 (lanosterol 14α-demethylase) → ↓ergosterol synthesis → fungal membrane disruption. Indications: topical - seborrhoeic dermatitis, pityriasis versicolor, tinea; systemic - refractory fungal infections, Cushing syndrome (adrenal steroidogenesis inhibitor). SE: topical: irritation; systemic: hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation, adrenal suppression.

Imidazole antifungal (topical/buccal). MOA: inhibits fungal CYP51 → ↓ergosterol → membrane disruption. Indications: oral candidiasis (buccal gel), vaginal candidiasis, tinea infections, nappy rash. SE: local irritation; oral gel: systemic absorption sufficient to ↑INR with warfarin - warfarin interaction important. Note: oral gel not to be swallowed by infants (choking risk).

5-HT3 antagonist antiemetic. MOA: selectively blocks 5-HT3 receptors in CTZ and vagal afferents → ↓emesis. Indications: chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV), post-operative nausea and vomiting. SE: headache, constipation, QT prolongation. Note: available as IV, oral, and transdermal patch (Sancuso) for CINV.

2nd-gen 5-HT3 antagonist antiemetic (longer half-life, higher receptor affinity). MOA: 5-HT3 receptor blockade in CTZ and GI vagal afferents. Indications: CINV (single pre-chemotherapy dose; superior to 1st-gen for delayed CINV). SE: headache, constipation. Note: preferred for moderately to highly emetogenic chemotherapy (with dexamethasone and NK1 antagonist).

Leukotriene receptor antagonist (LTRA). MOA: competitive CysLT1 receptor antagonist → ↓bronchoconstriction, mucosal oedema, eosinophilic inflammation. Indications: mild persistent asthma (maintenance), aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease. SE: headache, GI; rare Churg-Strauss (often steroid-dose reduction unmasking). Note: less used than montelukast; CYP2C9 inhibitor (↑warfarin).

Inhaled corticosteroid (prodrug → des-ciclesonide). MOA: activated in lung by airway esterases → local GR binding → ↓airway inflammation; minimal oropharyngeal deposition. Indications: persistent asthma. SE: lower rates of oropharyngeal candidiasis than older ICS (due to small particle size and prodrug activation). Note: once daily dosing; low systemic bioavailability.

Anti-TSLP monoclonal antibody. MOA: blocks TSLP (thymic stromal lymphopoietin) → inhibits upstream allergen/irritant signalling → ↓eosinophil and mast cell activation. Indications: severe uncontrolled asthma (add-on maintenance) - effective across all phenotypes including non-eosinophilic. SE: pharyngitis, arthralgia, injection site reactions. Note: monthly SC injection; broader than anti-IL-5 agents (works regardless of eosinophil count).

Long-acting non-depolarising neuromuscular blocking agent. MOA: competitive nicotinic ACh receptor blockade at NMJ → muscle paralysis. Indications: ICU sedation/ventilation, prolonged surgical paralysis. SE: vagolysis → tachycardia and HTN (unlike other NMBAs - vagolysis is class-specific to pancuronium). Reversal: neostigmine + atropine or sugammadex. Note: avoid in renal failure (active metabolite accumulates).

Ultra-short-acting opioid (context-insensitive). MOA: μ-opioid receptor agonist → analgesia; metabolism by plasma and tissue esterases → predictable offset regardless of infusion duration. Indications: intraoperative analgesia (TIVA, cardiac surgery), procedural sedation. SE: apnoea, bradycardia, chest rigidity (high dose), acute opioid tolerance with prolonged infusion. Note: must have adequate alternative analgesia before discontinuation.

Short-acting opioid. MOA: μ-opioid agonist; faster onset and shorter duration than fentanyl. Indications: induction/supplement to anaesthesia for short procedures. SE: apnoea, bradycardia, rigidity. Note: CYP3A4 substrate - prolonged effect with CYP3A4 inhibitors.

Highly potent opioid (~10× fentanyl). MOA: μ-opioid agonist; high lipophilicity → rapid CNS penetration. Indications: cardiac surgery and neuroanaesthesia (high-dose opioid technique), epidural analgesia in labour/postoperative. SE: apnoea, bradycardia, chest wall rigidity. Note: intranasal sufentanil used for procedural pain.

Dual endothelin receptor antagonist (ERA). MOA: blocks ET-A and ET-B receptors → ↓vasoconstriction and vascular remodelling in pulmonary vasculature. Indications: pulmonary arterial hypertension (WHO FC II-III), digital ulcers in systemic sclerosis. SE: hepatotoxicity (monthly LFTs), teratogenicity (strict REMS), fluid retention, ↓haemoglobin. Note: CYP3A4 inducer - reduces many drug levels (warfarin, statins, hormonal contraception).

Selective ET-A endothelin receptor antagonist. MOA: ET-A blockade → ↓pulmonary vasoconstriction; lower hepatotoxicity than bosentan (no ET-B blockade). Indications: pulmonary arterial hypertension. SE: peripheral oedema, headache, teratogenicity. Note: monthly pregnancy tests required; once daily.

Dual ERA (bosentan successor; higher receptor affinity, tissue penetration). MOA: blocks ET-A/ET-B → ↓vascular remodelling (SERAPHIN trial - ↓morbidity/mortality in PAH). Indications: PAH. SE: anaemia, hepatotoxicity (lower than bosentan), teratogenicity, nasopharyngitis. Note: once daily; preferred ERA.

Antiplatelet agent and phosphodiesterase inhibitor. MOA: inhibits phosphodiesterase → ↑cAMP/cGMP → ↑prostacyclin (vasodilation); inhibits adenosine reuptake → ↑adenosine (coronary vasodilation). Indications: secondary stroke/TIA prevention (with aspirin - ESPS-2 trial; combined as Asasantin SR); cardiac stress testing (pharmacological vasodilator). SE: headache, dizziness, GI, ↑bleeding.

Thrombolytic (modified tPA, single IV bolus). MOA: fibrin-specific plasminogen activator → fibrinolysis; longer half-life than alteplase, more fibrin-specific, bolus dosing. Indications: STEMI (weight-based single IV bolus; comparable to alteplase - ASSENT-2). SE: intracranial haemorrhage, systemic bleeding. CI: same as alteplase.

Thrombolytic (bacterial-derived, non-fibrin specific). MOA: forms complex with plasminogen → plasmin → systemic fibrinolysis. Indications: STEMI (if alteplase/tenecteplase unavailable), DVT/PE. SE: allergic reactions (prior streptokinase → antibodies → anaphylaxis), ICH, bleeding. Note: once-only use (antibodies formed); alteplase preferred in most settings.

Glycopeptide antibiotic (similar to vancomycin). MOA: binds D-Ala-D-Ala terminus → inhibits cell wall synthesis. Indications: MRSA/gram-positive infections, endocarditis, osteomyelitis; once-daily dosing (long half-life) allows outpatient parenteral therapy. SE: nephrotoxicity (less than vancomycin), ototoxicity, thrombocytopenia. Note: preferred in Australia for OPAT; trough-guided dosing.

IL-1 receptor antagonist (recombinant). MOA: competitively blocks IL-1α and IL-1β signalling → ↓systemic inflammation. Indications: RA (second-line), sJIA, adult-onset Still disease, CAPS (cryopyrin-associated), neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease, HLH. SE: injection site reactions (very common), neutropenia, infections. Note: daily SC; less potent for RA than anti-TNF.

JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor. MOA: blocks Janus kinase signalling → ↓pro-inflammatory cytokines; reduces MF-associated splenomegaly. Indications: myelofibrosis, polycythaemia vera (2nd-line), graft-versus-host disease (acute and chronic). SE: thrombocytopenia, anaemia, infections (opportunistic - PCP prophylaxis needed), weight gain, lipid changes. Note: do not stop abruptly (disease flare/cytokine storm).

PDE4 inhibitor (small molecule immunomodulator). MOA: inhibits phosphodiesterase 4 → ↑cAMP → ↓TNF, IL-17, IL-23 → ↓inflammation. Indications: psoriasis (moderate-severe), psoriatic arthritis (oral; no monitoring needed vs biologics), oral ulcers in Behçet. SE: diarrhoea, nausea (often improves), weight loss, depression risk. Note: no immunosuppression monitoring required; gradual dose titration to minimise GI.

Pegylated G-CSF (once-per-cycle). MOA: PEGylation prolongs half-life of filgrastim → single SC injection per chemotherapy cycle vs daily filgrastim → stimulates neutrophil precursor proliferation and maturation. Indications: primary/secondary prophylaxis of febrile neutropenia in myelosuppressive chemotherapy. SE: bone pain (NSAID-responsive), splenomegaly, rare splenic rupture. Note: do not give 14 days before or 24 h after cytotoxic chemotherapy.

Calcineurin inhibitor (CNI). MOA: binds cyclophilin → cyclophilin-ciclosporin complex inhibits calcineurin → ↓IL-2 transcription → ↓T-cell activation. Indications: transplant rejection prophylaxis, nephrotic syndrome, psoriasis, RA, atopic dermatitis. SE: nephrotoxicity (dose-dependent, reversible vs chronic interstitial fibrosis), HTN, hirsutism, gingival hyperplasia, tremor, hyperkalaemia, ↑lipids, neurotoxicity. Note: narrow TI; many CYP3A4 interactions; trough-level monitoring essential.

Selective purine synthesis inhibitor (prodrug → mycophenolic acid). MOA: inhibits IMPDH → ↓guanosine nucleotide synthesis → ↓T- and B-lymphocyte proliferation. Indications: organ transplant rejection prophylaxis (with tacrolimus/ciclosporin), lupus nephritis, ANCA vasculitis maintenance. SE: GI (diarrhoea, nausea - dose-limiting), leucopenia, opportunistic infections, teratogenicity. CI: pregnancy (Category X).

mTOR inhibitor (macrolide; not a CNI). MOA: binds FKBP12 → mTOR inhibition → ↓T-cell cycle progression (G1→S arrest). Indications: renal transplant rejection prophylaxis, LAM (lymphangioleiomyomatosis), tuberous sclerosis complex. SE: hyperlipidaemia, impaired wound healing, thrombocytopenia, myelosuppression, impaired renal function, proteinuria, interstitial pneumonitis. Note: synergistic with CNIs but additive nephrotoxicity.

IL-2 receptor (CD25) monoclonal antibody. MOA: blocks IL-2Rα (CD25) on activated T-cells → ↓T-cell proliferation; induction agent for transplant. Indications: acute organ rejection prophylaxis (induction therapy - 2 doses peri-transplant). SE: generally well tolerated; hypersensitivity (rare).

Alkylating agent. MOA: bifunctional alkylation of DNA → cross-links guanine residues → DNA strand breaks → cell death. Indications: CLL (first-line in elderly/unfit), Waldenström macroglobulinaemia, low-grade NHL, nephrotic syndrome (membranous). SE: myelosuppression, nausea, secondary AML, infertility, pulmonary fibrosis. Note: oral agent; gentle myelosuppression - suitable for elderly.

Nitrogen mustard alkylating agent. MOA: bifunctional DNA alkylation → cross-links → apoptosis. Indications: multiple myeloma (high-dose conditioning before ASCT; low-dose oral palliative), ovarian cancer, AL amyloidosis. SE: severe myelosuppression (dose-limiting), nausea, mucositis (high-dose), secondary AML, infertility.

Bifunctional alkylating agent. MOA: DNA alkylation/cross-linking → myeloablation. Indications: conditioning for HSCT (myeloablative regimens - Bu/Cy); CML (historical, now imatinib preferred). SE: myelosuppression, seizures (prophylactic phenytoin/levetiracetam required with high-dose IV), hepatotoxicity/VOD, pulmonary fibrosis, hyperpigmentation.

Purine analogue. MOA: fludarabine monophosphate (F-AMP) inhibits DNA polymerase α, ribonucleotide reductase, DNA ligase → ↓DNA synthesis; active in non-dividing lymphocytes. Indications: CLL (1st-line in young fit patients, e.g. FCR regimen), low-grade NHL, Waldenström, conditioning HSCT. SE: profound T-lymphocyte immunosuppression (PCP prophylaxis essential; irradiated blood products mandatory to prevent TA-GvHD), myelosuppression, autoimmune haemolysis.

Purine analogue (chloro-substituted deoxyadenosine). MOA: incorporated into DNA → strand breaks; also inhibits adenosine deaminase in lymphocytes → lymphocyte-selective cytotoxicity. Indications: hairy cell leukaemia (1st-line - single course, high remission); MS (oral Mavenclad - annual short courses of immune reconstitution therapy). SE: prolonged lymphopenia (months), opportunistic infections, teratogenicity.

Topoisomerase I inhibitor. MOA: stabilises topoisomerase I–DNA cleavage complex → permanent single-strand DNA breaks → cell death (S-phase specific). Indications: relapsed/refractory SCLC, ovarian cancer (2nd-line), relapsed cervical cancer. SE: severe myelosuppression (neutropenia, thrombocytopenia dose-limiting), nausea, alopecia.

Semi-synthetic vinca alkaloid. MOA: binds tubulin → inhibits spindle formation → M-phase arrest → apoptosis; relatively selective for mitotic vs axonal tubulin. Indications: NSCLC (1st-line with platinum), breast cancer. SE: neutropenia (dose-limiting), neuropathy (less than vincristine), constipation, phlebitis (inject via fast-running IV). Note: available IV and oral.

Synthetic progestogen (19-nortestosterone derivative). MOA: progestogen receptor agonism → ↓FSH/LH (in higher doses), decidualisation of endometrium; weak androgenic activity. Indications: dysfunctional uterine bleeding, endometriosis, amenorrhoea, period postponement, progestogen-only mini-pill (Micronor/Noriday). SE: irregular bleeding, headache, nausea, acne (androgenic). Note: contraindicated in breast cancer, VTE, severe liver disease.

Micronised or gel progesterone. MOA: natural progestogen → ↓endometrial proliferation, maintains decidua, ↓uterine contractility. Indications: luteal phase support in IVF, threatened miscarriage, menopause HRT (progesterone combined with oestrogen), rescue therapy in preterm labour risk (Crinone gel 8% vaginal). SE: drowsiness (oral route - take at night), bloating, breast tenderness. Note: micronised progesterone - lower thromboembolic risk than synthetic progestogens.

Progestogen. MOA: high-dose progestogen → stimulates appetite (mechanism unclear, possibly antagonises glucocorticoid receptors in hypothalamus). Indications: cancer/AIDS-related cachexia and anorexia (palliative); endometrial carcinoma. SE: weight gain, fluid retention, DVT (↑thrombosis risk), adrenal suppression (high doses). Note: Beers criterion - avoid in elderly for appetite stimulation.

Progestogen (active metabolite of desogestrel). MOA: ↓FSH/LH → ↓ovulation (primary), cervical mucus thickening. Indications: subdermal implant contraception (Nexplanon - 68 mg rod, effective 3 years). SE: irregular/absent menstruation (most common), headache, acne. Note: most effective form of contraception (<1 in 2000 over 3 years); no need to remember; safe during breastfeeding.

Synthetic progestogen (most widely used globally). MOA: LNG-IUS (Mirena) → local endometrial suppression, cervical mucus thickening, anovulation in some; emergency contraception - ↑progesterone → ↓LH surge → ↓ovulation. Indications: LNG-IUS (5-year LARC, menorrhagia, endometriosis), combined OCP, progestogen-only pill, emergency contraception. SE: irregular bleeding initially (settles → amenorrhoea in 20% at 1 year with IUS), headache, weight change.

Selective oestrogen receptor modulator (SERM). MOA: ER antagonism at hypothalamus/pituitary → ↓negative feedback → ↑GnRH → ↑FSH/LH → ovulation induction. Indications: anovulatory infertility (PCOS 1st-line), oligomenorrhoea. SE: hot flushes, multiple pregnancy (10% twins), OHSS (ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome - less than gonadotrophins), visual disturbances (rare), anti-oestrogenic on endometrium. Note: 5-day course early in cycle; monitor with USS.

5α-reductase inhibitor (types I + II - dual inhibitor vs finasteride which is type II only). MOA: blocks conversion of testosterone → DHT → ↓prostate volume. Indications: BPH (especially large prostate), AGA (hair loss). SE: decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, ejaculatory dysfunction, gynaecomastia, teratogenicity. Note: PSA halved with long-term use - adjust interpretation; 3-6 months for full benefit.

Organic nitrate. MOA: releases NO → ↑cGMP → venodilation → ↓preload; ± coronary vasodilation. Indications: stable angina (prophylaxis), HFrEF (with hydralazine in patients intolerant of ACEI/ARB - AHeFT). SE: headache, hypotension, reflex tachycardia, tolerance (avoid nitrate-free interval). Note: distinguish from isosorbide mononitrate (active metabolite; once-daily dosing).

Alpha-1 adrenergic blocker. MOA: selective alpha-1 blockade → peripheral vasodilation → ↓BP; ↓urethral resistance. Indications: PTSD nightmares (Prazosin 1–10 mg), phaeochromocytoma pre-operative (with beta-blocker), BPH (less used). SE: first-dose hypotension (take at bedtime), orthostasis, nasal congestion.

Long-acting alpha-1 blocker. MOA: alpha-1 receptor blockade → ↓prostate smooth muscle tone + peripheral vasodilation. Indications: BPH (symptom relief), HTN. SE: first-dose hypotension, dizziness, fatigue, orthostasis.

Selective alpha-1A/1D blocker (uroselectivity). MOA: blocks subtype alpha-1A (predominant in prostate) → ↓LUTS with minimal hypotension. Indications: BPH. SE: dizziness, orthostasis (less than terazosin), intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS) - inform surgeon before cataract surgery.

Thiazide-like diuretic (longer-acting than HCTZ). MOA: inhibits NCC in distal tubule; ↑urinary Ca reabsorption (hypercalciuric nephropathy). Indications: HTN (superior to HCTZ for CV outcomes - ALLHAT), heart failure, diabetes insipidus (nephrogenic). SE: hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperuricaemia, glucose intolerance, hypercalcaemia.

Thiazide-like diuretic. MOA: inhibits NCC in distal tubule; also has some proximal tubule action. Indications: diuretic-resistant oedema (synergistic with loop diuretics in decompensated HF/resistant oedema). SE: profound electrolyte disturbances when combined with furosemide - close monitoring of K, Na, Mg essential.

PDE5 inhibitor. MOA: selective inhibition of PDE5 → ↑cGMP in penile smooth muscle → vasodilation → erection. Indications: erectile dysfunction. SE: headache, flushing, nasal congestion; hypotension with nitrates. CI: nitrates, riociguat, recent CV event.

PDE5 inhibitor (faster onset, more selective than sildenafil). MOA: inhibits PDE5 → ↑cGMP → penile smooth muscle relaxation. Indications: erectile dysfunction. SE: headache, flushing; less visual disturbance than sildenafil (less PDE6 inhibition). Note: onset 15 min.

Prostaglandin E1. MOA: binds prostaglandin receptors → smooth muscle relaxation → vasodilation; relaxes internal urethral sphincter. Indications: erectile dysfunction (intracavernosal injection or intraurethral pellet - MUSE), patent ductus arteriosus maintenance in neonates with duct-dependent CHD (IV Prostin VR). SE: penile pain, priapism, urethral burning (MUSE); hypotension, apnoea (IV neonatal use).

Calcium supplement and antacid. MOA: releases Ca²⁺ ions (requires acid for absorption - take with food); also acts as antacid (neutralises HCl). Indications: hypocalcaemia, osteoporosis prevention (with vitamin D), hyperphosphataemia in CKD (phosphate binder), dyspepsia. SE: constipation, hypercalcaemia (high doses), milk-alkali syndrome. Note: calcium citrate better absorbed in achlorhydria/PPI use.

Magnesium salt (IV and oral). MOA: Mg²⁺ is cofactor for >300 enzymatic reactions; blocks NMDA receptors (anticonvulsant); blocks neuromuscular junction; vasodilation. Indications: eclampsia/pre-eclampsia (seizure prophylaxis/treatment - first-line), torsades de pointes (IV bolus), hypomagnesaemia, severe asthma (↓intracellular bronchospasm), foetal lung maturity + neuroprotection (preterm, 24–30 weeks - IV). SE: loss of DTRs (first sign of toxicity), respiratory depression, cardiac arrest. Antidote: calcium gluconate.

Potassium salt for replacement. MOA: replenishes intracellular K⁺ deficit. Indications: hypokalaemia (from diuretics, vomiting, diarrhoea, alkalosis), hypokalaemic periodic paralysis. SE: IV → cardiac arrest if given too rapidly (strict maximum rate ≤20 mmol/h in monitored setting); oral → GI irritation. Note: always correct Mg before K (hypomagnesaemia causes refractory hypokalaemia).

H2-receptor antagonist (1st-gen). MOA: competitive H2 receptor blockade on parietal cells → ↓gastric acid secretion. Indications: GORD, PUD (now largely replaced by PPIs). SE: anti-androgenic effects (gynaecomastia, impotence - unique among H2RAs), inhibits CYP450 (warfarin, phenytoin interactions), confusion in elderly. Note: largely superseded; occasionally used for urticaria.

Bismuth compound (antidiarrhoeal, cytoprotective). MOA: antibacterial (bismuth ions), antidiarrhoeal (salicylate inhibits prostaglandins → ↓secretory diarrhoea), cytoprotective (stimulates mucus). Indications: acute diarrhoea (travellers' diarrhoea), H. pylori eradication (quadruple therapy), dyspepsia. SE: black stools and tongue (harmless bismuth sulfide), tinnitus (salicylate toxicity at high doses). CI: children <12 y (Reye risk from salicylate component), aspirin allergy.

Anti-IL-1β monoclonal antibody. MOA: fully human IgG1 antibody binds IL-1β → ↓systemic inflammation. Indications: CAPS (cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes), systemic JIA, adult-onset Still disease, gout flares (refractory), FMF, HIDS. SE: infections (especially pneumonia), injection site reactions, neutropenia. Note: single SC injection; very long half-life (~26 days); anti-IL-1 alternatives: anakinra (daily SC), rilonacept.

Selective JAK1 inhibitor. MOA: JAK1 blockade → ↓IL-6, IL-4, IL-13, IL-2 signalling → ↓inflammation. Indications: RA, PsA, AS, atopic dermatitis (very effective), IBD (UC, Crohn's). SE: infections (URTI, herpes zoster), VTE, MACE (especially with CV risk factors - class effect JAK inhibitors), malignancy risk, lipid changes, cytopenias. CI: active infection, severe hepatic impairment.

Selective JAK1 inhibitor. MOA: JAK1-selective blockade → ↓inflammatory cytokine signalling. Indications: RA (moderate-severe), UC. SE: infections, ↑LDL, possible ↓sperm count (notable finding in trials - counsel men); VTE. Note: once daily; more JAK1-selective than older JAK inhibitors.

Anti-IL-17 receptor A monoclonal antibody. MOA: blocks IL-17RA → ↓all IL-17 signalling (IL-17A, F, C, E) → ↓skin inflammation. Indications: moderate-severe plaque psoriasis. SE: injection site reactions, nasopharyngitis, arthralgia; suicidal ideation (black-box warning, REMS program in US). Note: rapid and complete skin clearance (PASI-90/100 rates among highest); avoid in active IBD.

TYK2 inhibitor (allosteric regulatory domain inhibitor - not JAK1/2/3). MOA: selectively binds TYK2 pseudokinase domain → ↓IL-12, IL-23, type I interferon signalling. Indications: moderate-severe plaque psoriasis. SE: URTI, headache; lower infection/VTE risk signal than JAK inhibitors (TYK2 selectivity). Note: once daily oral; superior to apremilast in trials.

CYP17A1 inhibitor. MOA: irreversibly inhibits CYP17A1 → ↓androgen synthesis in testes, adrenal glands and tumour → ↓testosterone/DHT → prostate cancer cell death. Indications: metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC); high-risk metastatic castration-sensitive PCa (LATITUDE trial - with ADT). SE: mineralocorticoid excess (HTN, hypokalaemia, fluid retention - requires concurrent prednisone), hepatotoxicity. Note: take on empty stomach (fatty food massively ↑absorption - standard tablet); Yonsa micronised formulation can be taken with food.

Androgen receptor signalling inhibitor (ARSI). MOA: blocks androgen binding to AR, ↓AR nuclear translocation, ↓AR coactivator recruitment → ↓AR target gene expression. Indications: mCRPC, high-risk metastatic castration-sensitive PCa (ARCHES trial). SE: fatigue, hot flushes, HTN, seizures (rare - lowers seizure threshold), posterior leukoencephalopathy. Note: no steroid required (unlike abiraterone); strong CYP3A4 inducer.

PARP inhibitor. MOA: inhibits PARP-1/2 → blocks DNA single-strand break repair → synthetic lethality in BRCA1/2-mutated (and HRD) tumour cells. Indications: BRCA-mutated ovarian cancer (treatment and maintenance), prostate cancer (BRCA1/2). SE: myelosuppression (anaemia most common), nausea, elevated liver enzymes, MDS/AML risk (secondary). Note: oral twice daily; similar class to olaparib/niraparib.

HER2-directed antibody-drug conjugate (ADC). MOA: anti-HER2 mAb (trastuzumab) linked to topoisomerase I inhibitor (DXd payload via cleavable tetrapeptide linker) → targeted cytotoxicity; bystander killing effect (membrane-permeable payload). Indications: HER2-positive breast cancer (2nd-line after T-DM1 - DESTINY-Breast04 showed activity even in HER2-low), HER2-mutant NSCLC, HER2-positive gastric/GEJ cancer. SE: nausea, fatigue, myelosuppression; interstitial lung disease (ILD - potentially fatal - monitor with low threshold for holding dose).

Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonist. MOA: binds nAChRs → ↑dopamine release from mesolimbic system (reward); replacement therapy prevents withdrawal symptoms. Indications: smoking cessation (NRT - patches, gum, lozenge, inhaler, nasal spray). SE: nausea, local irritation; patch: skin irritation, vivid dreams. Note: NRT most effective when combined with pharmacotherapy (varenicline ± NRT, or bupropion); all forms significantly safer than smoking.

Partial nicotinic receptor agonist (plant-derived; structurally related to varenicline). MOA: partial nAChR agonism → ↓withdrawal symptoms + ↓reward from smoking. Indications: smoking cessation (available in NZ/Eastern Europe; used in primary care in Australia where varenicline unavailable). SE: GI (nausea, vomiting), insomnia; better tolerated than varenicline for some. Note: 25-day course; evidence base growing - comparable efficacy to varenicline.

Intermediate-acting non-depolarising neuromuscular blocking agent (one of 10 isomers of atracurium). MOA: competitive nicotinic ACh receptor blockade at NMJ. Indications: ICU ventilation (preferred in multi-organ failure), anaesthesia. SE: minimal cardiovascular effects (no histamine release, no vagolysis - unlike atracurium). Metabolism: Hofmann elimination + ester hydrolysis - organ-independent → SAFE in liver and renal failure. Note: drug of choice for NMB in ICU.

Quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic. MOA: competitive M-receptor antagonism (does not cross BBB - no CNS effects; quaternary charge limits CNS penetration). Indications: anaesthesia premedication (antisialogogue, vagolysis with neostigmine reversal), hyperhidrosis, COPD (inhaled as LAMA), drooling in children with cerebral palsy. SE: dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, tachycardia; no CNS effects (unlike atropine).

Prodrug of tenofovir (TAF - tenofovir alafenamide fumarate). MOA: phosphorylated intracellularly → tenofovir diphosphate → inhibits HBV/HIV reverse transcriptase. Indications: chronic hepatitis B (Vemlidy), HIV (Descovy - in combination with emtricitabine). SE: less nephrotoxicity and bone density loss than tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) due to intracellular targeting; nausea, headache.

NS3/4A protease inhibitor (Maviret = glecaprevir/pibrentasvir fixed-dose combination). MOA: inhibits HCV NS3/4A serine protease → prevents polyprotein cleavage → ↓viral replication. Indications: HCV all genotypes (pan-genotypic) - 8 weeks treatment for treatment-naïve, non-cirrhotic patients (all genotypes). SE: headache, fatigue, nausea; ↑hepatic decompensation in advanced cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B/C - use alternative). Note: abbreviation GLE/PIB; preferred regimen due to short duration and pan-genotypic activity.

NS5A inhibitor (combined with glecaprevir as Maviret). MOA: inhibits HCV NS5A protein → blocks replication complex assembly, RNA replication, viral assembly. Indications: combined pan-genotypic HCV treatment (see glecaprevir). SE: same as glecaprevir combination. Note: not given alone - always as fixed-dose combination glecaprevir/pibrentasvir.

NS5A inhibitor. MOA: inhibits HCV NS5A → blocks viral RNA replication and virion assembly; pan-genotypic activity (strongest for genotypes 1, 3). Indications: chronic HCV (genotype 3 with sofosbuvir - particularly in patients with decompensated cirrhosis or on dialysis). SE: headache, fatigue, nausea; bradycardia when combined with amiodarone (serious cardiac warning). Note: less commonly used now (largely replaced by glecaprevir/pibrentasvir and sofosbuvir/velpatasvir).

Anticonvulsant. MOA: irreversible inhibitor of GABA transaminase → ↑GABAergic inhibition. Indications: infantile spasms (West syndrome - 1st-line with hormonal therapy), refractory focal epilepsy. SE: Visual field defects (bilateral, concentric, permanent - present in up to 40%; baseline and serial visual field testing mandatory), sedation, weight gain. Note: use limited by visual toxicity; preferred for infantile spasms despite this risk.

Barbiturate anticonvulsant (metabolised to phenobarbitone and PEMA). MOA: enhances GABA-A receptor function + blocks Na/Ca channels. Indications: focal and generalised epilepsy; essential tremor (often preferred over propranolol). SE: sedation, ataxia, nausea, folate deficiency, osteoporosis, tolerance. Note: phenobarbitone is the primary active metabolite - same drug class; CYP3A4 inducer.

Phytocannabinoid (non-psychoactive). MOA: not fully elucidated - modulates TRPV channels, GPR55, adenosine uptake inhibition; not CB1/CB2 receptor agonism. Indications: Dravet syndrome and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (Epidiolex - approved for ≥2 years); Sativex (CBD+THC) for MS spasticity. SE: somnolence, diarrhoea, ↑LFTs (monitor with valproate - pharmacokinetic interaction); teratogenicity unknown. Note: CYP3A4/CYP2C9 inhibitor - ↑drug levels including clobazam.

13-cis-retinoic acid (Vitamin A derivative). MOA: normalises follicular keratinisation, ↓sebaceous gland size, ↓Propionibacterium acnes, anti-inflammatory. Indications: severe nodular/cystic acne, acne unresponsive to antibiotics. SE: teratogenicity (Category X - mandatory contraception and monthly pregnancy testing via Pregnancy Prevention Programme), cheilitis (very common - lip balm essential), dry eyes, hypertriglyceridaemia, ↑LFTs, myalgia, IBD association (debated), depression/suicide (black-box warning - monitor mood). Note: 4–6 month course; often curative.

3rd-gen topical retinoid. MOA: selective RAR-β/γ agonism → normalises follicular keratinisation → ↓comedone formation; anti-inflammatory. Indications: acne vulgaris (1st-line for non-inflammatory + inflammatory lesions), available OTC in lower concentrations. SE: irritation, erythema, peeling (usually improves with time); avoid in pregnancy. Note: less irritating than tretinoin; 3–4 months for maximum benefit; Epiduo combines adapalene + benzoyl peroxide.

Topical antibacterial/keratolytic. MOA: releases free radical oxygen → ↓Cutibacterium acnes (no resistance) + mild keratolysis; ↓sebum lipase. Indications: mild-moderate acne vulgaris (1st-line; OTC). SE: local irritation, bleaching of hair/fabrics/clothing (warn patients). Note: no bacterial resistance (unlike antibiotics); often combined with clindamycin or adapalene for synergistic effect.

Synthetic steroid with oestrogenic, progestogenic and androgenic activity (tissue-specific). MOA: metabolised to compounds acting on oestrogen, progesterone and androgen receptors. Indications: menopausal symptoms (especially women >2 years post-menopause), osteoporosis prevention; no need for separate progestogen. SE: ↑endometrial stimulation (CI in postmenopausal bleeding until investigated), breast cancer risk (LIBERATE trial - avoid after breast cancer), stroke. Note: not for use <2 years post-menopause (uterine stimulation risk).

SERM (selective oestrogen receptor modulator). MOA: tissue-selective ER agonist (vaginal tissue) / partial antagonist (breast) - treats genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM) without stimulating breast. Indications: moderate-severe dyspareunia from GSM (oral alternative to vaginal oestrogen). SE: hot flushes, vaginal discharge, VTE. Note: no breast cancer risk (theoretical advantage); oral once daily; CI in breast cancer.

Pan-HDAC (histone deacetylase) inhibitor. MOA: inhibits class I/II/IV HDACs → ↑acetylation of histones → ↑chromatin relaxation → ↑tumour suppressor gene expression + pro-apoptotic proteins. Indications: multiple myeloma (3rd-line, with bortezomib + dexamethasone). SE: severe diarrhoea (take anti-diarrhoeal prophylaxis), cardiac arrhythmias (QT prolongation, atrial fibrillation), thrombocytopenia, fatigue.

HDAC inhibitor (hydroxamic acid class). MOA: inhibits class I/II HDACs → epigenetic reprogramming → growth arrest and apoptosis of tumour cells. Indications: cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL) - refractory. SE: fatigue, nausea, diarrhoea, thrombocytopenia, PE/DVT risk, QT prolongation. Note: oral, once daily.

Anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody. MOA: binds CD38 on multiple myeloma cells → direct apoptosis + immune-mediated mechanisms (ADCC, CDC, ADCP). Indications: relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (with pomalidomide + dexamethasone, or carfilzomib + dexamethasone). SE: infusion reactions (premedicate), respiratory infections, neutropenia. Note: similar class to daratumumab; interferes with indirect antiglobulin testing (blood bank notification required).

BCMA-directed antibody-drug conjugate. MOA: anti-BCMA (B-cell maturation antigen) antibody linked to MMAF (monomethyl auristatin F - microtubule inhibitor) → targeted cytotoxicity in myeloma cells. Indications: relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (≥4 prior lines). SE: keratopathy (corneal epithelial changes - 70% incidence; requires ophthalmology review every 3 weeks - REMS programme), infusion reactions, thrombocytopenia. Note: currently under conditional/restricted use due to keratopathy.

Radiolabelled somatostatin analogue (PRRT - peptide receptor radionuclide therapy). MOA: binds somatostatin receptor type 2 (SSTR2) on NET cells → internalised → beta radiation from Lu-177 → DNA damage → cell death. Indications: somatostatin receptor-positive gastroenteropancreatic NETs (GEP-NETs), midgut NETs (NETTER-1 trial - significant PFS benefit). SE: nausea (pre-treatment amino acids mitigate renal uptake), haematotoxicity (thrombocytopenia), renal toxicity (nephroprotection with amino acids). Note: highly targeted therapy.

Alpha-emitting radionuclide. MOA: mimics calcium → bone-seeking alpha emitter → deposits in bone metastases → short-range, high-energy alpha radiation → DNA double-strand breaks in bone metastasis. Indications: castration-resistant prostate cancer with symptomatic bone metastases (no known visceral metastases - ALSYMPCA trial - ↓mortality). SE: nausea, diarrhoea, bone marrow suppression. Note: do NOT use with abiraterone + prednisone (↑fractures - ERA 223 trial).

Halichondrin B analogue (microtubule inhibitor). MOA: non-taxane mechanism - binds tubulin at plus ends → sequestration of tubulin → inhibits microtubule polymerisation → mitotic block (distinct binding site from taxanes/vinca alkaloids). Indications: metastatic breast cancer (≥2 prior chemotherapy regimens including anthracycline and taxane), liposarcoma. SE: neutropenia (dose-limiting), peripheral neuropathy, fatigue, QT prolongation.

Carbapenem (lower seizure risk than imipenem). MOA: broad-spectrum PBP binding; stable to most β-lactamases including ESBLs and KPCs. Indications: complicated UTI, complicated IAI, HAP/VAP. SE: headache, nausea, diarrhoea, C. diff; thrombocytopenia.

Prodrug of mecillinam (amdinocillin). MOA: mecillinam selectively binds PBP2 → impairs cell shape maintenance (spheroplast formation) → bactericidal against gram-negatives. Indications: uncomplicated lower UTI (oral; excellent E. coli coverage; no cross-resistance with other beta-lactams; excellent option in ESBL UTI). SE: nausea, GI; oral formulation well tolerated. Note: carnitine deficiency if prolonged use.

Alkalinising agent and buffer. MOA: provides HCO3⁻ → buffers H⁺ → raises pH. Indications: metabolic acidosis (severe - pH <7.1, bicarb <10 in specific contexts), hyperkalaemia (shifts K intracellularly), tricyclic antidepressant overdose (↑pH → ↓TCA cardiac toxicity → QRS narrowing), sodium channel blocker toxicity (flecainide, brugada), urinary alkalinisation (ASA overdose, myoglobinuria). SE: ↑Na (hypernatraemia), alkalosis, paradoxical intracellular acidosis (ICU). Note: IV use in emergency; not for uncomplicated lactic acidosis.

Ion exchange resin (sodium polystyrene sulfonate). MOA: exchanges Na⁺ for K⁺ in gut lumen → ↑faecal K⁺ excretion. Indications: hyperkalaemia (management; less urgent than IV calcium or insulin-dextrose - used to prevent recurrence). SE: constipation, ↓Mg, intestinal necrosis (caution in post-operative bowel, avoid concomitant sorbitol). Note: takes hours-days to work - not for emergency correction; patiromer and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (newer K-binders) are better tolerated.

Irreversible non-selective alpha-adrenergic blocker. MOA: covalently binds alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptors → prolonged vasodilation. Indications: phaeochromocytoma pre-operative blockade (gold standard - alpha-1 blockade must precede beta-blockade to prevent hypertensive crisis). SE: orthostatic hypotension, reflex tachycardia, nasal congestion, inhibition of ejaculation. Note: start weeks before adrenalectomy; titrate with target SBP <130 mmHg supine and some mild orthostasis.

Pegylated interferon alpha (2a or 2b). MOA: activates JAK-STAT pathway → induces antiviral proteins, immunomodulation (↑NK cell activity, ↑CD8 T-cells), antiproliferative effects. Indications: chronic hepatitis B (peginterferon alfa-2a - 48-week course; induces immune control, seroconversion), hairy cell leukaemia, essential thrombocythaemia (in pregnancy). SE: flu-like symptoms (universal, especially first injection), depression (screen carefully), thyroid dysfunction, cytopenias, retinopathy, injection site reactions. Note: use declined significantly for HCV since DAAs.

Butyrophenone antipsychotic (D2 antagonist). MOA: high-affinity D2 blockade → antipsychotic and antiemetic; some alpha-1 blockade → sedation. Indications: PONV (IV/IM - highly effective, low dose), acute agitation (emergency sedation - 'chemical restraint'), acute nausea. SE: QT prolongation (black-box warning in US - ECG monitoring; risk overestimated at clinical doses ≤1.25 mg); extrapyramidal reactions; hypotension. Note: highly effective antiemetic for refractory nausea (migraineurs); renaissance at low doses.

Mid-potency typical antipsychotic (phenothiazine, piperazine side chain). MOA: D2 receptor antagonism + histamine H1, alpha-1, muscarinic blockade. Indications: schizophrenia (CATIE trial - comparable efficacy to SGAs with lower metabolic effects), nausea/vomiting. SE: EPS (less than haloperidol), tardive dyskinesia, hyperprolactinaemia, sedation. Note: often preferred for patients at risk of metabolic syndrome.

Folinic acid (reduced, active form of folate; calcium salt). MOA: provides 5-formyl-THF → bypasses DHFR (blocked by methotrexate) → rescues normal cells from MTX toxicity; also enhances 5-FU activity (stabilises thymidylate synthase inhibition). Indications: high-dose methotrexate rescue (given 24 h after MTX, continued until serum MTX <0.05 µmol/L); 5-FU potentiation (colorectal cancer - FOLFOX, FOLFIRI regimens). SE: minimal; may precipitate seizures in methotrexate-overdosed patients.

Essential trace element supplement. MOA: cofactor for >300 enzymes (carbonic anhydrase, DNA/RNA polymerases, alcohol dehydrogenase); wound healing, immune function, taste/smell (anosmia from deficiency). Indications: zinc deficiency (poor diet, diarrhoea, malabsorption, alcoholism - acrodermatitis enteropathica), Wilson disease (maintenance after chelation - zinc ↓GI copper absorption), post-COVID anosmia (some evidence).
