SE: nausea (take with food), copper deficiency (excess zinc → ↑metallothionein → ↓Cu absorption → cytopenias). Note: zinc lozenges for common cold - modest evidence.

Broad-spectrum anticonvulsant and mood stabiliser. MOA: ↑GABA (↓GABA transaminase, ↑GAD), blocks voltage-gated Na channels, blocks T-type Ca channels. Indications: absence seizures (1st-line), juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME - 1st-line), generalised tonic-clonic seizures; mania (acute and prevention); migraine prophylaxis. SE: weight gain, tremor, alopecia, polycystic ovaries, hyperammonaemia (confusion - carnitine supplementation), teratogenicity (highest risk - spina bifida, neurodevelopmental disorders - avoid in women of childbearing age unless essential; VALPROATE PRECAUTION Programme). CI: pregnancy, women of childbearing potential unless no alternatives.
Australian/British spelling of estradiol (17β-oestradiol). Identical drug and pharmacology. See estradiol entry. Preferred spelling in Australian prescribing.

3rd-generation progestogen; active metabolite etonogestrel. MOA: ovarian suppression (unique among POPs - reliably inhibits ovulation even with 12-h missed dose window) + cervical mucus thickening. Indications: progestogen-only pill (Cerazette - 75 µg/day) - suitable when oestrogen CI (migraine with aura, VTE risk, breastfeeding). SE: irregular bleeding (most common reason for discontinuation), headache, mood changes. Note: 12-hour missed dose window vs 3-hour for other POPs.

Novel progestogen with antimineralocorticoid and antiandrogenic activity. MOA: progestogen receptor agonism + aldosterone receptor antagonism (→ ↑natriuresis, ↓fluid retention) + mild androgen receptor antagonism. Indications: combined OCP (with ethinyl oestradiol); PMDD (Yaz); moderate acne. SE: hyperkalaemia risk (antimineralocorticoid - caution in renal/hepatic/adrenal disease; avoid with ACEi/ARBs/spironolactone); VTE (class effect OCPs).

4th-generation progestogen (strong progestogenic, anti-androgenic, moderate anti-oestrogenic). MOA: suppresses ovarian oestrogen synthesis → ↓endometrial implant growth; also direct anti-proliferative effect on endometrium. Indications: endometriosis (Visanne 2 mg/day - as effective as GnRH analogues but oral, less SE). SE: irregular bleeding, headache, mood changes, initial oestrogen-withdrawal symptoms. Note: lacks androgenic activity; does not cause the hypoestrogenic bone loss of GnRH analogues.

Oral GnRH antagonist (non-peptide). MOA: competitive GnRH receptor antagonism → ↓FSH/LH → ↓ovarian oestrogen production (dose-dependent partial or complete suppression). Indications: endometriosis-associated pain, uterine fibroids (with add-back therapy). SE: hot flushes, mood changes, headache; bone density loss (reversible with add-back oestrogen); ↑liver enzymes. Note: unlike GnRH agonists - immediate onset (no initial flare), oral, partial-full suppression dosing options.

Oral GnRH receptor antagonist. MOA: competitive GnRH receptor blockade → rapid ↓LH/FSH → testosterone/oestradiol suppression within 1 week (vs 4 weeks for GnRH agonists). Indications: advanced prostate cancer (Orgovyx - superior cardiovascular safety vs leuprolide - HERO trial), uterine fibroids (Ryeqo - with add-back therapy). SE: hot flushes, sexual dysfunction (prostate cancer setting), bone density loss. Note: oral once-daily; immediate onset/offset (useful before surgery).

Long-acting injectable testosterone ester (IM - 1000 mg/4 mL; 10–14 week interval). MOA: exogenous testosterone → androgen receptor activation → maintenance of male secondary sexual characteristics, spermatogenesis, haematopoiesis. Indications: male hypogonadism, gender-affirming therapy (FtM). SE: erythrocytosis (monitor haematocrit), acne, mood changes, testicular atrophy, ↓spermatogenesis, ↑cardiovascular risk. Note: Reandron - very long injection interval (3-monthly); safest formulation (no supraphysiological peaks).

Oral immunomodulator (active metabolite of leflunomide). MOA: inhibits DHODH (dihydroorotate dehydrogenase) → ↓pyrimidine synthesis → selectively reduces rapidly dividing lymphocytes. Indications: relapsing-remitting MS (moderate efficacy; once-daily oral). SE: alopecia (usually transient), GI, ↑LFTs, teratogenicity (Category X - accelerated elimination with cholestyramine). Note: very long half-life (>8 months without washout); accelerated elimination protocol required before pregnancy.

Selective S1P1/5 receptor modulator. MOA: functional sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor antagonism → lymphocyte sequestration in lymph nodes → ↓autoreactive lymphocytes in CNS. Indications: secondary progressive MS (EXPAND trial - ↓disability progression in active SPMS); relapsing forms of MS. SE: bradycardia/AV block (1st-dose - 6-hour monitoring required; less than fingolimod), macular oedema (ophthalmology pre-treatment), infections, PML risk. Note: CYP2C9 genotyping required (affects maximum tolerated dose).

Selective S1P1/5 receptor modulator. MOA: same S1P receptor mechanism as siponimod → lymphocyte sequestration. Indications: relapsing-remitting MS, moderately-severely active UC. SE: bradycardia (less than fingolimod - no first-dose monitoring usually required if HR normal), ↑BP, headache, cardiac monitoring pre-treatment (assess HR, ECG, BP). Note: no first-dose monitoring required in most patients; 14-day washout before MAOIs.

Fully human anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody (subcutaneous). MOA: binds distinct epitope on CD20 (more membrane-proximal than rituximab) → B-cell depletion via ADCC and CDC. Indications: relapsing forms of MS (monthly SC injection - patient self-administered after initial loading doses; ASCLEPIOS trials). SE: injection site reactions, infections (↑URTIs, UTIs), neutropenia, PML risk. Note: SC route enables home administration vs IV ocrelizumab.

Anti-CD52 monoclonal antibody (reconstitution therapy). MOA: depletes CD52+ T and B lymphocytes → profound but transient immunodepletion → immune reconstitution (altered immune repertoire). Indications: relapsing-remitting MS (CARE-MS - highly effective; given as 2 annual courses only). SE: infusion reactions (antihistamine/steroids premedication), autoimmune complications (ITP, thyroid disease, anti-GBM nephritis - monitor for 4 years post-infusion; monthly urinalysis, TFTs, blood counts). Note: REMS programme due to serious SE profile; reserved for high-efficacy use.

MAO-B inhibitor + sodium channel blocker (dual mechanism). MOA: selective reversible MAO-B inhibition → ↑dopamine; + state-dependent inhibition of voltage-gated Na channels → ↓glutamate release. Indications: Parkinson's disease (add-on to levodopa - reduces off-time, unlike rasagiline which is monotherapy or adjunct). SE: dyskinesia (may worsen with add-on), insomnia, nausea; hypertensive crisis with tyramine at high doses.

COMT inhibitor (3rd-gen; once-daily; peripheral-only). MOA: inhibits COMT → ↓levodopa degradation → ↑levodopa levels and duration of action → ↓OFF time. Indications: Parkinson's disease (adjunct to levodopa/carbidopa) - fewer gastrointestinal SE than entacapone; once-daily dosing. SE: dyskinesia, nausea, dry mouth, constipation; hepatotoxicity (less than tolcapone - no liver monitoring required). Note: taken at bedtime (separate from levodopa dose).

Free radical scavenger (methylphenylpyrazolone). MOA: scavenges reactive oxygen species and peroxynitrite → ↓oxidative stress-mediated neuronal death. Indications: ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis) - slows functional decline (Phase 3 Japanese trial in selected early ALS patients). SE: bruising, gait disturbance, headache; IV formulation. Note: modest effect size; oral suspension now available (easier administration); requires ALS functional rating scale to select appropriate candidates.

Antisense oligonucleotide (ASO). MOA: binds pre-mRNA of SMN2 gene → promotes exon 7 inclusion → ↑functional SMN protein production (compensates for absent SMN1 gene). Indications: spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) - intrathecal injection; significant motor improvement in infantile-onset SMA. SE: thrombocytopenia, coagulation abnormalities, proteinuria, back pain. Note: intrathecal; loading doses then every 4 months; transformed natural history of SMA; now competing with risdiplam (oral) and onasemnogene (gene therapy).

Skeletal muscle relaxant acting peripherally. MOA: blocks ryanodine receptor (RyR1) in sarcoplasmic reticulum → ↓calcium release → ↓muscle contraction (not CNS-mediated). Indications: malignant hyperthermia (IV - life-saving emergency treatment; 2.5 mg/kg bolus, repeat every 5 min, max 10 mg/kg), neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), spasticity (chronic oral - cerebral palsy, MS, spinal cord injury). SE: generalised weakness (may ↓swallowing/breathing), hepatotoxicity (chronic oral use, especially women >35 y).

Halogenated volatile inhalational anaesthetic. MOA: enhances GABA-A receptor function + inhibits NMDA receptors → dose-dependent CNS depression → anaesthesia. Indications: induction and maintenance of general anaesthesia (paediatric - excellent for mask induction, pleasant smell, rapid onset/offset). SE: postoperative nausea (less than halothane), compound A formation (theoretical renal concern at low flow - clinically not significant), MH trigger (rare - dantrolene treatment). Note: MAC 2.05%; short emergence.

Halogenated volatile anaesthetic. MOA: GABA-A enhancement + NMDA inhibition + K+ channel activation → anaesthesia. Indications: maintenance of general anaesthesia; also used for refractory status epilepticus (ICU). SE: pungent odour (difficult mask induction), coronary steal (debated), mild ↑ICP. Note: MAC 1.15%; coronary vasodilator - use cautiously in unstable angina.

Inorganic gas anaesthetic/analgesic. MOA: inhibits NMDA receptors → analgesia + mild sedation; also ↑endogenous opioid release. Indications: analgesia (Entonox 50% N2O:O2 - labour pain, procedural analgesia, wound care), anaesthesia supplement (reduces MAC of volatile agents, allows lower concentrations). SE: diffusion hypoxia (give O2 after discontinuation), B12 inactivation (irreversible oxidation of cobalt in methionine synthase - risk with prolonged exposure or B12 deficiency - avoid in B12-deficient patients), pressure expansion of gas-filled spaces (pneumothorax, bowel obstruction - CI). Note: rapid onset/offset; patients can remain conscious and cooperative.

Intermediate-acting non-depolarising NMBA. MOA: competitive nicotinic ACh receptor blockade at NMJ → paralysis. Metabolism: Hofmann elimination + ester hydrolysis - organ-independent (safer in hepatic/renal failure than pancuronium). SE: histamine release (hypotension, bronchospasm at rapid IV bolus - less than suxamethonium), laudanosine accumulation (potentially seizure-inducing at very high doses in ICU - less concern with cisatracurium). Reversal: neostigmine + atropine or sugammadex.

Ultra-short-acting barbiturate IV induction agent (thiopentone - Australian/British spelling). MOA: GABA-A receptor allosteric agonist → rapid loss of consciousness (one arm-brain circulation); ↓cerebral metabolism. Indications: rapid sequence induction (largely replaced by propofol), raised ICP (↓CBF and CMRO2), status epilepticus (refractory). SE: respiratory depression/apnoea (injection), hypotension, bronchospasm, tissue necrosis (intra-arterial injection - severe). Note: classified as a controlled drug; not available in all countries; unavailable in Australia since 2011 for most uses.

Levorotatory enantiomer of bupivacaine (L-bupivacaine). MOA: blocks voltage-gated Na channels → ↓neuronal conduction; long-acting local anaesthetic. Indications: epidural analgesia (obstetric, surgical), nerve block (brachial plexus, femoral). SE: less cardiotoxicity than racemic bupivacaine (cardiac Na channel - levo preferentially unbinds more rapidly). Note: preferred over racemic bupivacaine for epidurals; similar efficacy.

GHB (gamma-hydroxybutyrate) sodium salt - Schedule 8 controlled substance. MOA: GHB receptor agonist + GABA-B receptor agonist → strong sedation, ↑slow-wave sleep, ↓delta sleep fragmentation. Indications: narcolepsy with cataplexy (most effective treatment for both EDS and cataplexy - taken twice nightly due to short half-life); idiopathic hypersomnia. SE: nausea, dizziness, CNS depression, respiratory depression (dangerous with alcohol/CNS depressants - boxed warning), enuresis, sleepwalking, abuse potential. Note: REMS programme; restricted distribution.

Wakefulness-promoting agent (eugeroic). MOA: selective dopamine transporter inhibitor → ↑synaptic dopamine; secondary effects on noradrenaline, orexin, histamine. Indications: narcolepsy (EDS), shift work sleep disorder, obstructive sleep apnoea adjunct (EDS only - does not treat apnoea), MS fatigue, cancer-related fatigue (off-label). SE: headache, nausea, insomnia, tachycardia; ↓efficacy of hormonal contraceptives (CYP3A4 induction - alternative contraception needed). Note: Schedule 4 controlled drug; less abuse potential than amphetamines.

Intranasal S-enantiomer of ketamine. MOA: NMDA receptor antagonist → rapid antidepressant effect (within hours-days; glutamate modulation + downstream AMPA signalling → BDNF release). Indications: treatment-resistant depression (TRD - with oral antidepressant) and MDD with acute suicidal ideation (supervised clinic administration). SE: dissociation, dizziness, nausea, sedation (2-hour post-dose monitoring required in clinic); abuse potential; ↑BP. Note: administered in clinic (nurse-observed); only REMS-approved intranasal nasal spray for depression.

Long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA). MOA: once-daily M3 receptor blockade in airways → sustained bronchodilation → ↓bronchoconstriction, ↓mucus secretion. Indications: COPD maintenance (alone: Incruse; combined with vilanterol LABA: Anoro; combined with vilanterol + fluticasone ICS: Trelegy). SE: dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, paradoxical bronchospasm, tachycardia. Note: once daily; part of GOLD-recommended combination inhalers.

LAMA (long-acting muscarinic antagonist). MOA: twice-daily M3 receptor blockade → bronchodilation. Indications: COPD maintenance. SE: dry mouth, UTI, nasopharyngitis. Note: twice-daily dosing (vs once-daily for tiotropium, umeclidinium); unique BRETARIS multi-dose dry powder inhaler.

Dabigatran-specific reversal agent (humanised monoclonal antibody fragment - Fab). MOA: binds dabigatran with 350× greater affinity than thrombin → neutralises anticoagulant effect within minutes. Indications: emergency reversal of dabigatran in life-threatening/uncontrolled bleeding or urgent surgery (REVERSE-AD trial). SE: generally well tolerated; transient hypokalaemia; theoretical ↑thrombosis risk after reversal (anticoagulate when haemostatically stable). Note: single 5 g IV dose (2× 2.5 g infusions); effect immediate.

Factor Xa decoy protein (reversal agent for factor Xa inhibitors - rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban). MOA: recombinant modified factor Xa (catalytically inactive) → acts as decoy → binds and sequesters apixaban/rivaroxaban → restores Xa activity. Indications: reversal of apixaban or rivaroxaban for life-threatening bleeding (ANNEXA-4). SE: arterial/venous thrombotic events (18% in ANNEXA-4), infusion reactions. Note: given as IV bolus + infusion; 4-Factor PCC (prothrombin complex concentrate) is used when andexanet alfa is unavailable.

Recombinant activated factor VII. MOA: at site of tissue injury → binds tissue factor → activates extrinsic pathway → ↑thrombin generation → haemostasis (pharmacological: also activates factor X independent of tissue factor at high concentrations). Indications: haemophilia A/B with inhibitors (bypassing agent), factor VII deficiency, Glanzmann thrombasthenia. Off-label: massive haemorrhage (uncontrolled trauma/surgical bleeding as last resort). SE: arterial thrombosis (MI, stroke - especially in non-haemophilia use), VTE.

4-Factor PCC containing factors II, VII, IX, X + protein C/S (Beriplex) or 3-factor (II, IX, X). MOA: replaces vitamin K-dependent clotting factors → rapidly corrects INR (within minutes). Indications: urgent reversal of warfarin (life-threatening bleeding, emergency surgery); reversal of factor Xa inhibitors (when andexanet not available). Dosing: weight- and INR-based. SE: thrombosis (arterial and venous), anaphylaxis, heparin-induced reactions. Note: faster and more reliable than FFP for warfarin reversal.

2nd-generation oxazolidinone antibiotic. MOA: same 23S rRNA 50S ribosomal subunit binding as linezolid → protein synthesis inhibition. Indications: acute bacterial SSTI (including MRSA); 6-day once-daily course. SE: less myelosuppression than linezolid (shorter course, lower drug exposure); nausea, headache; serotonin syndrome risk (MAO-A inhibition). Note: once daily; shorter treatment duration than linezolid.

Amdinocillin (Australian/British: mecillinam). MOA: selectively binds PBP2 → impairs lateral cell wall synthesis → spheroplast formation → bactericidal for gram-negatives. Indications: gram-negative UTI (including ESBL-producing E. coli - pivmecillinam is oral prodrug). SE: GI; long-term - carnitine deficiency. Note: parenteral formulation; pivmecillinam is the oral prodrug used for oral treatment.

Topical calcineurin inhibitor (macrolactam). MOA: binds macrophilin-12 → inhibits calcineurin → ↓IL-2 and other inflammatory cytokine transcription → suppresses T-cell activation in skin. Indications: mild-moderate atopic dermatitis (face, eyelids, skin folds where topical steroids are problematic). SE: local burning/stinging (first few days), ↑risk of skin infections, photosensitivity; theoretical malignancy risk (black-box warning - no proven increase at clinical use). Note: steroid-sparing; less effective than potent steroids but useful for sensitive skin areas.

N-acetylcysteine (NAC). MOA: paracetamol overdose - replenishes hepatic glutathione stores → safely conjugates NAPQI metabolite; mucolytic - cleaves disulfide bonds in mucus glycoproteins → ↓viscosity. Indications: paracetamol overdose (IV - within 8 h of ingestion is most effective; continue even if >8 h; Rumack-Matthew nomogram guides treatment); mucolytic (inhaled for CF, bronchiectasis), contrast nephropathy prophylaxis (oral - debated evidence). SE: anaphylactoid reactions to IV formulation (urticaria, bronchospasm - treat with antihistamines + slow infusion; rarely severe).

Taxane cytotoxic (2nd-gen; overcomes docetaxel resistance). MOA: binds and stabilises β-tubulin of assembled microtubules → prevents depolymerisation → mitotic arrest → apoptosis; low P-gp affinity → overcomes docetaxel resistance. Indications: metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) after docetaxel failure (TROPIC trial); cabazitaxel + carboplatin for BRCA-mutated mCRPC. SE: myelosuppression (neutropaenia - G-CSF prophylaxis mandatory in ≥65 years or high-risk), diarrhoea, fatigue, nausea, peripheral neuropathy, haematuria. Note: always administer G-CSF prophylaxis; inferior to enzalutamide/abiraterone post-docetaxel unless prior enzalutamide/abi treatment.

Multi-kinase TKI (VEGFR 1-3, PDGFR-α/β, KIT). MOA: inhibits VEGFR 1-3, PDGFR-α/β, FGFR1/3, KIT → anti-angiogenic + anti-proliferative. Indications: renal cell carcinoma (1st-line - COMPARZ: non-inferior to sunitinib but different toxicity), advanced soft tissue sarcoma (2nd-line - PALETTE trial). SE: hepatotoxicity (LFT elevation - monitor; fatal cases; boxed warning), hypertension, diarrhoea, hair colour change (depigmentation - distinctive), HFSR, fatigue. Note: hair colour change (blanching) characteristic but not harmful; hepatotoxicity boxed warning - LFTs every 4 weeks × 4 months.

RET/VEGFR/EGFR TKI. MOA: inhibits RET kinase (including M918T mutation), VEGFR 2-3, EGFR → anti-tumour (RET) + anti-angiogenic (VEGFR). Indications: medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) - unresectable locally advanced or metastatic (ZETA trial). SE: QTc prolongation (boxed warning - monitor ECG; risk of TdP - CYP3A4 interactions critical), diarrhoea, rash, HFSR, hypertension, photosensitivity. Note: REMS programme (QTc monitoring) - QTc >500 ms: hold/dose-reduce; avoid QT-prolonging drugs and CYP3A4 inducers.

Selective RET kinase inhibitor. MOA: highly selective RET inhibition (including gatekeeper mutations) → ↓RET-driven signalling; also covers RET fusions. Indications: RET-altered NSCLC (fusion - LIBRETTO-001; superior to chemotherapy), RET-mutant medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), RET fusion-positive thyroid cancer (differentiated). SE: hypertension, oedema, dry mouth, diarrhoea, fatigue, ↑LFTs, QTc, hyponatraemia. Note: RET-specific (vs vandetanib/cabozantinib with broader kinase inhibition); better tolerated; test for RET alteration (fusion or mutation) before use.

Selective RET inhibitor. MOA: potent, selective RET inhibition → blocks RET fusion/mutation-driven oncogenic signalling. Indications: RET-altered NSCLC (fusion), RET-mutant MTC (ARROW trial). SE: hypertension, constipation, fatigue, oedema, neutropaenia, ↑LFTs, interstitial lung disease. Note: similar class to selpercatinib; both represent 1st-generation selective RET inhibitors; ILD risk - hold for new pulmonary symptoms.

Highly selective HER2 TKI (oral). MOA: selectively inhibits HER2 kinase domain (minimal EGFR binding → ↓skin/GI toxicity vs lapatinib/neratinib); CNS-penetrant. Indications: HER2+ metastatic breast cancer (with trastuzumab + capecitabine - HER2CLIMB trial; significant OS benefit including brain metastases). SE: diarrhoea (most common - antidiarrhoeals required), hepatotoxicity (↑LFTs - monitor), nausea, fatigue, rash. Note: HER2CLIMB demonstrated intracranial activity → now preferred for HER2+ breast cancer with brain metastases; ↓EGFR-mediated toxicity vs lapatinib.

Irreversible pan-HER TKI (HER1/2/4). MOA: covalently binds to EGFR, HER2, HER4 catalytic domain → irreversible inhibition; unlike lapatinib (reversible). Indications: extended adjuvant therapy for HER2+ breast cancer after trastuzumab-based therapy (ExteNET trial - ↓distance recurrence), advanced HER2+ breast cancer. SE: diarrhoea (severe in >95% - prophylactic loperamide mandatory from day 1 of treatment; distinctive class-defining toxicity), nausea, abdominal cramps, hepatotoxicity. Note: diarrhoea prophylaxis essential - loperamide must be started with day 1; dose-titration approach reduces diarrhoea.

Dual HER1/HER2 TKI (reversible; oral). MOA: reversibly inhibits EGFR + HER2 kinase domains → ↓HER2/EGFR-driven downstream signalling (RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT). Indications: HER2+ metastatic breast cancer (with capecitabine after anthracycline/taxane/trastuzumab failure; or with letrozole in HR+/HER2+). SE: diarrhoea (common but less severe than neratinib), rash, hepatotoxicity (↑LFTs - monitor), QTc prolongation, fatigue. Note: largely replaced by tucatinib/neratinib in HER2+ breast; ↓CNS penetration vs tucatinib; still used in resource-limited settings.

Irreversible pan-HER TKI (ErbB family). MOA: covalently inhibits EGFR (including uncommon mutations), HER2, HER4 kinases → blocks all ErbB signalling. Indications: EGFR-mutant NSCLC (exon 19 del / L858R - LUX-Lung 3/6; also uncommon EGFR mutations - Gly719X, Leu861Gln, Ser768Ile - high response rates). SE: diarrhoea (very common - prophylaxis as needed), rash/acneiform, paronychia, dry skin, mucositis, ↑LFTs. Note: superior to chemotherapy for EGFR-uncommon mutations; osimertinib preferred for common EGFR mutations due to CNS penetration and T790M coverage.

2nd-gen ALK TKI with CNS activity. MOA: inhibits ALK + ALK resistance mutations (including G1202R, I1171) and EGFR with exon 19 deletions/L858R; good CNS penetration. Indications: ALK+ NSCLC (1st-line - ALTA-1L: superior PFS vs crizotinib; superior CNS intracranial response rate). SE: early-onset pulmonary events (dyspnoea, hypoxia - within first 7 days; use 7-day dose escalation), rash, hypertension, bradycardia, lipase/amylase elevation. Note: mandatory 7-day lead-in at 90 mg/day to ↓early pulmonary events; monitor for ILD in first week.

TRK/ROS1/ALK inhibitor (CNS-penetrant). MOA: inhibits TRKA/B/C, ROS1, ALK + CNS-penetrant. Indications: NTRK fusion-positive solid tumours (tumour-agnostic - basket trial), ROS1-rearranged NSCLC. SE: fatigue, constipation, dysgeusia, oedema, dizziness, cognitive effects (CNS penetration), bradycardia, QTc. Note: better CNS activity than larotrectinib; both are 1st-line for NTRK+ tumours; CNS activity important as NTRK fusion tumours often metastasise to brain.

Selective MET TKI. MOA: highly selective MET kinase inhibition → ↓MET-driven proliferation, survival, invasion. Indications: MET exon 14 skipping mutation NSCLC (VISION trial). SE: oedema (most common - peripheral, pleural, ascites), nausea, hypoalbuminaemia, ↑creatinine, hepatotoxicity. Note: oedema very common - diuretics often needed; MET ex14 skipping found in 3-4% NSCLC; test by tissue or liquid biopsy.

Selective MET TKI. MOA: selective MET kinase inhibition → blocks MET exon 14 skipping mutation-driven oncogenesis. Indications: MET exon 14 skipping NSCLC (GEOMETRY mono-1 trial - ORR 68% in treatment-naive). SE: oedema, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, ↑creatinine, ILD, hepatotoxicity. Note: ILD risk (potentially fatal) - hold for new pulmonary symptoms; same target as tepotinib; both active in MET ex14 NSCLC.

MEK 1/2 inhibitor. MOA: allosteric MEK 1/2 inhibition → ↓RAF/MEK/ERK signalling downstream of RAS. Indications: neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) with symptomatic, inoperable plexiform neurofibromas (SPRINT trial - 1st systemic therapy for NF1-PN). SE: diarrhoea, nausea/vomiting, rash (acneiform), paronychia, oedema, ↑CK. Note: first approved systemic therapy for NF1 plexiform neurofibromas; paediatric approval (2+ years); distinct from other MEK inhibitors used in BRAF-mutant melanoma.

MEK 1/2 inhibitor (used with encorafenib). MOA: selective MEK 1/2 inhibition → ↓ERK signalling in BRAF-mutant tumours. Indications: BRAF V600E/K-mutant unresectable or metastatic melanoma (with encorafenib - MEKTOVI+BRAFTOVI; COLUMBUS trial). SE: retinal toxicity (serous retinopathy - visual disturbances; distinctive), CK elevation + rhabdomyolysis, oedema, DVT/PE, cardiac toxicity (↓EF), rash. Note: retinal toxicity distinctive to MEK inhibitor class; combination encorafenib + binimetinib: superior outcome vs vemurafenib alone; monthly ophthalmology monitoring.

MEK 1 inhibitor (used with vemurafenib). MOA: allosteric MEK 1 inhibition → ↓ERK phosphorylation in BRAF V600-mutant tumours. Indications: BRAF V600E/K-mutant unresectable/metastatic melanoma (with vemurafenib - BRIM-7/coBRIM trials; now standard). SE: diarrhoea, photosensitivity, retinal toxicity (↓visual acuity - ophthalmology check; similar to binimetinib), CK elevation, hepatotoxicity, skin toxicity. Note: always used with BRAF inhibitor (vemurafenib); retinal toxicity: monthly ophthalmology monitoring.

MEK 1/2 inhibitor (used with dabrafenib). MOA: allosteric MEK 1/2 inhibition → ↓ERK signalling; with dabrafenib provides dual blockade of BRAF-MEK pathway. Indications: BRAF V600E/K-mutant melanoma (with dabrafenib - COMBI-v/COMBI-d; standard of care), BRAF-mutant NSCLC (with dabrafenib), thyroid cancer, low-grade serous ovarian cancer. SE: pyrexia (with dabrafenib - more common than vemurafenib; manage with dose interruption), retinal toxicity (RPE detachment - ophthalmology monitoring), cardiomyopathy (↓LVEF - ECHO before), rash, oedema, GI. Note: retinal toxicity (RPE detachment, RPED) - monthly ophthalmology check; pyrexia management essential - paracetamol ± corticosteroids for severe cases.

Antifolate antimetabolite (multi-enzyme inhibitor). MOA: inhibits DHFR, TS, GARFT → disrupts folate-dependent one-carbon transfer → ↓nucleotide synthesis → cell death; additive with cisplatin/carboplatin. Indications: non-squamous NSCLC (1st-line with carboplatin/platinum ± pembrolizumab; maintenance after platinum doublet), malignant pleural mesothelioma (with cisplatin - standard of care). SE: myelosuppression (neutropaenia - nadir day 8-14), mucositis, rash, fatigue, renal toxicity. Note: MANDATORY folic acid (400-1000 μg daily) + vitamin B12 (1000 μg IM every 9 weeks) supplementation → ↓myelosuppression/mucositis; not for squamous NSCLC (TS overexpressed).

Nitrosourea alkylating agent (crosses BBB). MOA: bifunctional alkylation → interstrand/intrastrand DNA crosslinks → inhibits DNA/RNA synthesis + repair; lipophilic → CNS penetration. Indications: glioblastoma multiforme (systemic + intracranial wafers - Gliadel wafers implanted at resection), primary/recurrent CNS lymphoma (BCVP/BEAM conditioning regimens), multiple myeloma, Hodgkin lymphoma. SE: myelosuppression (delayed - nadir day 28-42; profound thrombocytopaenia), pulmonary fibrosis (cumulative dose-limiting → baseline/annual PFTs; dose limit ~1400 mg/m²), hepatotoxicity, secondary leukaemia. Note: delayed myelosuppression (6 weeks) - do not re-treat until counts recover; cumulative pulmonary toxicity - stop if DLCO <70% predicted.

Alkylating agent (triazene). MOA: non-cell-cycle specific; metabolised to methylating agent MTIC → alkylates DNA at N7/O6 of guanine → DNA damage → apoptosis. Indications: Hodgkin lymphoma (ABVD regimen - doxorubicin/bleomycin/vinblastine/dacarbazine; standard 1st-line), metastatic melanoma (historical - largely replaced by immunotherapy/targeted), soft tissue sarcomas, carcinoid. SE: severe nausea/vomiting (acute - prophylactic 5-HT3 + NK1 antagonists essential), myelosuppression, flu-like syndrome (fever, myalgia - days 7-10), photosensitivity (avoid direct sun exposure). Note: photosensitivity - SPF50+, cover up for 2 days after infusion; N/V one of most emetogenic drugs - ensure optimal prophylaxis.

Ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor (oral cytotoxic). MOA: inhibits ribonucleotide reductase → ↓dNTP pools → DNA synthesis arrest in S-phase; also ↑foetal haemoglobin (HbF) induction in sickle cell. Indications: sickle cell anaemia (↑HbF → ↓sickling frequency/severity - pivotal MSH trial), essential thrombocythaemia (1st-line cytoreduction), polycythaemia vera (2nd-line after venesection/aspirin), CMML. SE: myelosuppression (dose-limiting - FBC weekly initially, then monthly), macrocytosis (MCV rises - benign, predictable), leg ulcers (chronic use - particularly in sickle cell patients; distinctive), skin/nail hyperpigmentation, secondary leukaemia (long-term). Note: leg ulcers with long-term use - examine feet regularly; ↑MCV expected and harmless; teratogenic (contraception required).

PARP inhibitor (most potent PARP-trapping agent). MOA: inhibits PARP-1/2 + traps PARP on DNA single-strand breaks → cannot be removed → replication fork collapse → DSBs → synthetic lethality in BRCA1/2-deficient cells (more potent PARP-trapping than olaparib/niraparib). Indications: germline BRCA1/2-mutant HER2-negative locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer (EMBRACA trial - superior PFS vs chemotherapy). SE: myelosuppression (anaemia and thrombocytopaenia more common vs other PARPis - dose modification often required), fatigue, nausea, MDS/AML risk. Note: potent PARP-trapping → more myelosuppression than olaparib; anaemia may require transfusion; germline BRCA1/2 testing required before prescribing.

Multi-kinase inhibitor (FLT3/KIT/PKC). MOA: inhibits FLT3 (including ITD and TKD mutations), KIT, PDGFR, VEGFR, PKC → ↓proliferation in FLT3-mutant AML. Indications: AML with FLT3 mutation (combined with standard 7+3 induction/consolidation - RATIFY trial; first approved FLT3 inhibitor), aggressive systemic mastocytosis (SM - inhibits KIT D816V), mast cell leukaemia. SE: nausea/vomiting (prophylaxis required - take with food), myelosuppression, fever, mucositis, QTc. Note: must take with food to reduce GI toxicity; given with standard AML chemotherapy during induction and consolidation.

Selective FLT3 inhibitor (ITD + TKD mutations). MOA: inhibits FLT3-ITD, FLT3-TKD, AXL → ↓leukaemic cell proliferation in FLT3-mutant AML. Indications: relapsed/refractory FLT3-mutant AML (ADMIRAL trial - superior OS vs salvage chemotherapy). SE: myalgia, arthralgia, ↑LFTs, oedema, differentiation syndrome (fever, dyspnoea, oedema - rare), posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES). Note: differentiation syndrome risk - monitor for fever + dyspnoea in first 5 weeks; manage with dexamethasone; FLT3 mutation PCR/NGS testing required.

IDH2 inhibitor. MOA: inhibits mutant IDH2 → blocks conversion of α-KG to 2-HG (oncometabolite) → ↓histone hypermethylation → ↑differentiation of myeloid blasts. Indications: relapsed/refractory AML with IDH2 mutation (ORR 40%). SE: differentiation syndrome (fever, dyspnoea, pulmonary infiltrates, weight gain - potentially fatal; high-dose dexamethasone required; distinctive IDH inhibitor class toxicity), indirect bilirubin elevation (benign - Gilbert-like mechanism), nausea. Note: differentiation syndrome in 12% - onset weeks 1-5; dexamethasone 10 mg BD for any new respiratory symptoms; IDH2 testing required.

IDH1 inhibitor. MOA: inhibits mutant IDH1 → ↓2-HG oncometabolite → ↑AML blast differentiation. Indications: AML with IDH1 mutation (relapsed/refractory; 1st-line unfit + azacitidine - AGILE trial), biliary tract cancer with IDH1 mutation (1st-line maintenance after gemcitabine/cisplatin - ClarIDHy trial). SE: differentiation syndrome (same as enasidenib - fever, dyspnoea; 3% risk; monitor/treat with dexamethasone), QTc prolongation (monitor ECG), nausea, fatigue. Note: QTc monitoring mandatory; first approved IDH1-targeted therapy; also active in cholangiocarcinoma.

Dual BCR-ABL/SRC TKI (2nd-gen CML). MOA: inhibits BCR-ABL kinase + SRC family kinases; minimal inhibition of KIT/PDGFR. Indications: CML (1st-line - BFORE trial: superior molecular response vs imatinib; 2nd-line after imatinib/dasatinib/nilotinib failure). SE: diarrhoea (very common - most common grade 3; loperamide PRN; may improve with time), hepatotoxicity (↑LFTs - monitor monthly × 3), rash, myelosuppression. Note: diarrhoea very common but often manageable; ↓cardiac/pulmonary toxicity vs dasatinib; ↓hyperglycaemia vs nilotinib.

STAMP inhibitor (Specifically Targeting the ABL Myristoyl Pocket - 3rd-gen CML). MOA: binds myristoyl pocket of BCR-ABL kinase → allosteric inhibition → ↓ABL activity; mechanistically distinct from ATP-competitive TKIs → active against T315I mutation (at higher dose). Indications: CML-CP after ≥2 TKIs (ASCEMBL trial: superior MMR vs bosutinib); T315I-mutant CML. SE: arterial occlusive events (↑BP, peripheral arterial disease - monitor cardiovascular), pancreatitis, myelosuppression. Note: first-in-class myristoyl pocket inhibitor; active in T315I at 200 mg BD dose.

Anti-CCR4 monoclonal antibody (defucosylated - enhanced ADCC). MOA: binds CCR4 on T-regulatory and malignant T-cells → ADCC → depletion of CCR4+ tumour cells. Indications: relapsed/refractory CTCL (mycosis fungoides, Sézary syndrome - MAVORIC trial: superior PFS vs vorinostat), PTCL. SE: infusion reactions (Grade 3-4 - premedicate; distinctive rash pattern), skin reactions (immune-related rash - distinct from disease), diarrhoea, infections. Note: skin reactions can mimic disease progression - careful assessment; if patient proceeds to HSCT, prolonged drug washout needed (6+ weeks).

Cyclic peptide HDAC inhibitor (class I selective). MOA: prodrug reduced to active thiol form → inhibits class I HDAC (1, 2, 3, 8) → ↑histone acetylation → ↑tumour suppressor gene expression → apoptosis. Indications: CTCL (mycosis fungoides, Sézary syndrome - relapsed/refractory), PTCL (2nd-line). SE: cardiac toxicity (QTc prolongation, ST/T wave changes - ECG monitoring; arrhythmia risk with hypoK+ or hypoMg²+), myelosuppression, nausea, fatigue. Note: correct K+ and Mg²+ before each dose - electrolyte abnormalities amplify QTc risk; IV infusion over 4 hours.

Pan-HDAC inhibitor (hydroxamic acid class). MOA: inhibits class I/II HDACs → ↑histone/non-histone acetylation → ↑tumour suppressor expression + ↓oncogene expression → apoptosis. Indications: relapsed/refractory PTCL (BELIEF trial). SE: nausea, vomiting (prophylaxis required), myelosuppression (thrombocytopaenia), hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs; dose-reduce for UGT1A1*28 homozygotes - poor metabolisers), QTc. Note: dose reduction required for UGT1A1*28 homozygotes (Gilbert syndrome equivalent metaboliser status); IV infusion.

2nd-gen purine nucleoside analogue antimetabolite. MOA: phosphorylated to 5'-triphosphate → inhibits ribonucleotide reductase → ↓dNTPs; also incorporated into DNA → chain termination; resistant to deamination. Indications: relapsed/refractory ALL (paediatric - ≥1 prior regimen; also salvage in adult ALL). SE: severe myelosuppression, systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS - fever, tachycardia, hypotension - ↑cytokine release; manage with dexamethasone), hepatotoxicity, capillary leak syndrome. Note: SIRS/capillary leak syndrome risk - prophylactic dexamethasone often given concurrently; paediatric-labelled drug.

T-cell-specific purine analogue antimetabolite. MOA: prodrug of 9-β-D-arabinofuranosylguanine (ara-G) → selectively accumulates in T-cells → phosphorylated to ara-GTP → incorporated into DNA → chain termination → apoptosis preferentially in T-ALL. Indications: relapsed/refractory T-cell ALL/lymphoblastic lymphoma (T-ALL/LBL - ≥2 prior regimens). SE: severe neurotoxicity (dose-limiting - peripheral neuropathy, somnolence, seizures, paraesthesia - CNS monitoring critical; distinctive for this agent), myelosuppression. Note: neurological assessment before each cycle - any Grade 2+ neurotoxicity: hold drug; risk is cumulative.

PEGylated L-asparaginase enzyme. MOA: depletes serum asparagine (L-asparagine essential for ALL blasts which lack asparagine synthetase - normal cells can synthesise it) → ↓leukaemic cell protein synthesis → apoptosis; PEGylated → ↑half-life vs native L-asparaginase. Indications: ALL (induction and consolidation - standard-of-care in paediatric and young adult ALL protocols; preferred over native asparaginase). SE: hypersensitivity (grade ≥2 in ~10%; switch to Erwinia asparaginase if significant reaction), pancreatitis (10-15% - abdominal pain + ↑lipase; hold if significant), coagulopathy (↓fibrinogen/antithrombin → VTE or bleeding), hepatotoxicity, hyperglycaemia. Note: pancreatitis: check amylase/lipase if abdominal symptoms - hold drug; IM route preferred over IV to ↓anaphylaxis.

Type II anti-CD20 humanised monoclonal antibody (glycoengineered - ↑ADCC). MOA: binds CD20 on B-cells → direct cell death (type II mechanism - ↑direct cell death + ↑ADCC via glycoengineered Fc region); ↑NK cell recruitment vs rituximab. Indications: CLL (1st-line with chlorambucil - CLL11 trial; or with venetoclax - CLL14 trial), follicular lymphoma (1st-line with chemotherapy - GALLIUM trial; maintenance). SE: infusion reactions (more severe than rituximab - premedicate; split 1st infusion over 2 days), tumour lysis syndrome (risk-stratify; prophylaxis), hepatitis B reactivation (screen before), neutropaenia. Note: more potent than rituximab (glycoengineering) - increased ADCC; CLL14 trial: obinutuzumab + venetoclax fixed-duration improved PFS vs chlorambucil-based.

Anti-PD-L1 human monoclonal antibody. MOA: binds PD-L1 → blocks PD-L1:PD-1 interaction → ↑T-cell activation; also retains Fc-mediated ADCC (unlike atezolizumab/durvalumab) → dual mechanism. Indications: Merkel cell carcinoma (1st-line and maintenance - JAVELIN Merkel 200), urothelial carcinoma (1st-line maintenance after platinum - JAVELIN Bladder 100 trial). SE: infusion reactions (common - premedicate with antihistamine + paracetamol for first 4 infusions), immune-related AEs (pneumonitis, hepatitis, endocrinopathy), fatigue. Note: mandatory premedication for first 4 infusions; Merkel cell carcinoma - avelumab is 1st approved therapy; urothelial maintenance regardless of PD-L1 status.

Anti-CD79b ADC (antibody-drug conjugate). MOA: anti-CD79b mAb conjugated to MMAE (monomethyl auristatin E; microtubule inhibitor) → targets CD79b on B-cells → internalised → MMAE released → mitotic arrest → apoptosis. Indications: relapsed/refractory DLBCL (with bendamustine + rituximab - GO29365 trial); 1st-line DLBCL (with R-CHP - POLARIX trial - superior PFS vs R-CHOP). SE: peripheral neuropathy (cumulative - sensory; similar to other MMAE-conjugates; dose delay/reduction), myelosuppression, fatigue, diarrhoea, infusion reactions. Note: CD79b expressed on most mature B-cell lymphomas; POLARIX trial positions pola-R-CHP as new 1st-line option for DLBCL.

Nucleoside analogue antiviral (broad-spectrum). MOA: phosphorylated to 5'-triphosphate → inhibits viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase + inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH) → ↓GTP pools; also immunomodulatory. Indications: chronic HCV (oral - with peginterferon alfa or sofosbuvir-based regimens; now largely replaced by DAA combinations), RSV bronchiolitis (inhaled - aerosolised; high-risk neonates/infants), haemorrhagic fevers (Lassa fever, hantavirus - IV). SE: haemolytic anaemia (dose-limiting - haemoglobin monitoring; Hb-guided dose reduction), teratogenicity (absolute CI in pregnancy; 2 forms contraception for 6 months after), fatigue, rash, cough. Note: haemolytic anaemia predictable - check Hb every 2 weeks; male partners must also use contraception for 6 months post-treatment.

Inhaled neuraminidase inhibitor (influenza A + B). MOA: competitive inhibitor of influenza neuraminidase → prevents cleavage of sialic acid → ↓viral release from infected cells → ↓spread. Indications: treatment of influenza A/B (within 48 hours of symptom onset; ↓duration by ~1 day), prophylaxis in outbreak settings. SE: bronchospasm (clinically significant in asthmatics/COPD - boxed warning; keep bronchodilator at hand), cough, headache. Note: inhaled route - CI in severe asthma/COPD (bronchospasm risk); oseltamivir oral preferred for most; zanamivir IV available for critically ill (compassionate use).

IV neuraminidase inhibitor (influenza A + B). MOA: competitive neuraminidase inhibition → ↓viral spread; IV route enables use in patients unable to take oral/inhaled medications. Indications: acute uncomplicated influenza (IV - within 48 hours; useful in hospitalised patients, ICU, patients with dysphagia or intubated). SE: diarrhoea (most common), nausea, neutropaenia, neuropsychiatric events (rare). Note: only IV neuraminidase inhibitor - useful for critically ill or those who cannot tolerate oral/inhaled; single-dose regimen (600 mg IV over 15-30 min).

NS5A inhibitor (HCV DAA - used as fixed-dose combination with sofosbuvir). MOA: inhibits HCV NS5A protein → blocks viral RNA replication and assembly. Indications: chronic HCV genotype 1, 4, 5, 6 (with sofosbuvir - Harvoni; 8-12 weeks; cure rates >95%). SE: headache, fatigue, nausea, diarrhoea. Note: always combined with sofosbuvir (Harvoni fixed-dose tablet - 90 mg ledipasvir/400 mg sofosbuvir); avoid antacids/PPIs within 4 hours (↓absorption); check NS5A resistance testing for cirrhotic genotype 1a patients.

NS5A inhibitor (HCV DAA - used with grazoprevir). MOA: inhibits HCV NS5A protein → ↓viral RNA replication. Indications: chronic HCV genotype 1, 4 (with grazoprevir - Zepatier; 12-16 weeks; cure rates >90-95%). SE: headache, fatigue, nausea; rarely elevated LFTs. Note: always combined with grazoprevir (Zepatier fixed-dose tablet - 50 mg elbasvir/100 mg grazoprevir); check NS5A resistance-associated substitutions before initiating genotype 1a treatment - determines if 12 vs 16 weeks + ribavirin needed.

NS3/4A protease inhibitor (HCV DAA - used with elbasvir). MOA: inhibits HCV NS3/4A serine protease → ↓viral polyprotein processing → viral replication halted. Indications: chronic HCV genotype 1, 4 (with elbasvir - Zepatier). SE: headache, fatigue; hepatotoxicity (uncommon but monitor LFTs). Note: combined with elbasvir (Zepatier); significant drug interactions (CYP3A4 substrate - avoid CYP3A4 inhibitors/inducers); CI with OATP1B1/3 inhibitors.

Antifungal pyrimidine analogue (always used in combination). MOA: taken up by fungi via cytosine permease → deaminated to 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) → inhibits thymidylate synthetase → ↓DNA synthesis; also inhibits RNA synthesis; synergistic with amphotericin B. Indications: cryptococcal meningitis (with liposomal amphotericin B - standard induction therapy per WHO guidelines; flucytosine critical for CNS clearance), candidal meningitis. SE: myelosuppression (bone marrow suppression - FBC monitoring; dose-limit if renal impairment), GI toxicity (nausea, diarrhoea, hepatotoxicity). Note: NEVER use as monotherapy - rapid resistance development; renal impairment → ↑flucytosine exposure → ↑toxicity - dose-adjust for eGFR.

Antifungal (dermatophyte-specific; oral). MOA: binds tubulin → disrupts mitotic spindle in dividing fungal cells → deposits in keratin precursor cells → incorporated into new skin/hair/nails → renders them resistant to dermatophyte infection as they grow out. Indications: dermatophyte infections (tinea capitis - 1st-line oral for scalp; tinea unguium - largely replaced by terbinafine). SE: GI (nausea - take with fatty food to ↑absorption), headache, photosensitivity, teratogenicity (CI in pregnancy), disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol (rare). Note: fatty meal doubles absorption; long course for tinea capitis (6-12 weeks) - compliance important; largely replaced by terbinafine/itraconazole for nail/body/groin tinea; still 1st-line for tinea capitis.

Oral alkylphosphocholine antileishmanial. MOA: interferes with phospholipid metabolism + cell signalling pathways → membrane disruption → apoptosis-like death in Leishmania. Indications: visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar - oral alternative to parenteral amphotericin B/antimonials), cutaneous/mucosal leishmaniasis, primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM - Naegleria fowleri - off-label but CDC recommended). SE: GI (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea - common; take with food), hepatotoxicity (↑LFTs - monitor), nephrotoxicity, teratogenicity (strict CI in pregnancy - 3 months post-treatment contraception). Note: only oral treatment for visceral leishmaniasis; teratogenicity - 3 months post-treatment contraception for all patients; GI side effects: take with meals.

Anti-TROP-2 ADC (antibody-drug conjugate). MOA: anti-TROP-2 mAb conjugated to SN-38 (active irinotecan metabolite - topoisomerase I inhibitor) via hydrolysable linker → targets TROP-2-expressing tumour cells → internalised → SN-38 released → DNA single-strand breaks → apoptosis; bystander effect (SN-38 diffuses to surrounding cells). Indications: unresectable locally advanced/metastatic TNBC (after 2+ prior therapies - ASCENT trial), urothelial carcinoma (after platinum + PD-1/PD-L1 - TROPiCS-04), HR+ HER2-negative breast cancer (TROPiCS-02). SE: diarrhoea (grade 3-4 - very common; loperamide prophylaxis mandatory; early-onset diarrhoea UGT1A1-related), neutropaenia (G-CSF for grade 4), nausea/vomiting, alopecia. Note: UGT1A1*28 homozygotes → ↑SN-38 exposure → ↑neutropaenia/diarrhoea - consider dose reduction; bystander effect increases efficacy in heterogeneous tumours; loperamide with each dose.

Anti-FRα ADC (folate receptor alpha). MOA: anti-FRα mAb conjugated to DM4 (maytansinoid; microtubule inhibitor) → targets FRα-expressing tumour cells → internalised → DM4 released → mitotic arrest → apoptosis. Indications: platinum-resistant epithelial ovarian cancer (FRα-positive - MIRASOL trial: superior PFS and OS vs chemotherapy in medium/high FRα expression). SE: ocular toxicity (keratopathy - blurred vision, dry eyes, photophobia; corneal epithelial changes - ophthalmology monitoring before + every 2 months; dose-modify if ≥Grade 2), peripheral neuropathy, diarrhoea, fatigue, nausea. Note: FRα testing required before prescribing; ocular toxicity is class-defining ADC toxicity - prophylactic lubricating eye drops mandatory; slit-lamp exam at baseline and with each cycle.

Anti-CD22 ADC. MOA: anti-CD22 mAb conjugated to calicheamicin (DNA-strand breaking; highly potent) via hydrolysable linker → targets CD22 on B-cells → internalised → calicheamicin released → DNA double-strand breaks → apoptosis. Indications: relapsed/refractory B-cell ALL (CD22+; INO-VATE trial - superior remission rate and survival vs chemotherapy; allows ~50% proceed to HSCT). SE: hepatic veno-occlusive disease/sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (VOD/SOS - most feared; particularly post-HSCT; cumulative dose-related; fatal cases; use ursodiol prophylaxis pre-HSCT), neutropaenia, thrombocytopenia, infusion reactions. Note: VOD/SOS risk - monitor LFTs/bilirubin closely; ursodiol prophylaxis pre- and post-HSCT; HSCT conditioning regimen modification needed (avoid busulfan-based); fractionated dosing schedule (D1/8/15 per cycle) to ↓VOD risk vs single large dose.

Anti-CD33 ADC. MOA: anti-CD33 mAb conjugated to calicheamicin (highly potent DNA cleaving agent) → targets CD33 on AML blasts → internalised → calicheamicin released → DNA damage → apoptosis. Indications: CD33+ AML (de novo - with daunorubicin/cytarabine 7+3 - ALFA-0701 trial; favourable/intermediate risk patients; also relapsed/refractory AML). SE: hepatic VOD/SOS (veno-occlusive disease - serious/fatal; cumulative risk; monitor LFTs; do not proceed to HSCT within 2 months if possible), severe myelosuppression (prolonged), infusion reactions (premedicate), mucositis. Note: CD33 testing required; fractionated low-dose regimen (D1/4/7 of induction) ↓VOD risk vs original high-dose single dose (recalled 2010, re-approved 2017); favourable/intermediate cytogenetics - maximum benefit.

CD19×CD3 bispecific T-cell engager (BiTE). MOA: bispecific antibody linking CD19 (on B-cells/ALL blasts) and CD3 (on T-cells) → forms immunological synapse → polyclonal T-cell cytotoxicity against CD19+ target cells; nanomolar potency. Indications: relapsed/refractory B-cell ALL (Philadelphia chromosome-negative - TOWER trial; or Ph+ with TKI failure), B-cell ALL in MRD+ remission (eradicates minimal residual disease - BLAST trial), frontline in older adults (ECOG E1910). SE: cytokine release syndrome (CRS - fever, hypotension, hypoxia - Grade 3-4 in ~10%; tocilizumab/dexamethasone; dexamethasone pre-medication), neurological toxicity (encephalopathy, seizures, aphasia - Grade 3-4 in ~10-15%; hold drug if Grade 3+), infections, cytopaenias. Note: continuous IV infusion (4-week cycle); dexamethasone premedication before each cycle; CRS and neurotoxicity - early recognition and management critical.

CD20×CD3 bispecific antibody (fixed-duration; IV). MOA: bivalent CD20 × monovalent CD3 → binds 2 CD20 epitopes simultaneously → higher avidity → activates T-cell cytotoxicity; given as fixed-duration (12 cycles). Indications: relapsed/refractory DLBCL (≥2 prior lines - STARGLO trial; fixed 12-cycle duration; ORR ~35-40%). SE: cytokine release syndrome (CRS - obinutuzumab pretreatment (cycle 1 Day 1 gating dose) reduces CRS risk; grade 3-4 CRS in ~3-4%), neurotoxicity (ICANS - immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity), infections, cytopaenias. Note: obinutuzumab pretreatment (given 7 days before first glofitamab) - reduces CRS severity; fixed duration (12 cycles) - allows treatment-free period; grade by ASTCT criteria for CRS/ICANS.

CD20×CD3 bispecific antibody (fixed-duration). MOA: bivalent CD20 × monovalent CD3 → T-cell-mediated killing of CD20+ B-cells; fixed-duration therapy (8 cycles - stop-and-go approach). Indications: relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma (≥2 prior lines - CELESTIMO trial; ORR ~80%, CR ~60% - impressive in heavily pretreated FL). SE: cytokine release syndrome (CRS - step-up dosing cycle 1; grade 3-4 CRS ~1%), ICANS (neurotoxicity - rare), infections (prolonged B-cell aplasia), cytopaenias. Note: step-up dosing in cycle 1 (fractionated small/medium/full doses across 3 weeks) dramatically reduces CRS; outpatient administration from cycle 3; fixed duration; impressive remission rates in FL.

CD20×CD3 bispecific antibody (subcutaneous; fixed-duration). MOA: CD20×CD3 bispecific → activates T-cells to kill CD20+ B-cells via immunological synapse; subcutaneous administration allows outpatient treatment. Indications: relapsed/refractory DLBCL (≥2 prior lines - EPCORE NHL-1 trial), follicular lymphoma (r/r - EPCORE NHL-2). SE: CRS (subcutaneous route → ↓severity vs IV bispecifics; step-up dosing; grade 3-4 in ~2-3%), ICANS (rare), injection site reactions, infections. Note: subcutaneous administration - major advantage for outpatient care; step-up dosing (priming 0.16 mg → intermediate 0.8 mg → full dose 48 mg) over first month.

BCMA×CD3 bispecific antibody (subcutaneous; first-in-class for myeloma). MOA: BCMA (B-cell maturation antigen) × CD3 bispecific → redirects T-cells to kill BCMA-expressing myeloma cells; subcutaneous. Indications: relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (≥4 prior lines including proteasome inhibitor, IMiD, anti-CD38 - MajesTEC-1 trial; ORR ~63%). SE: CRS (step-up dosing - first 2 injections hospitalised; grade 3-4 in ~1%), ICANS (rare), infections (↑risk - B-cell aplasia, hypogammaglobulinaemia; IVIG prophylaxis; PCP and herpes prophylaxis mandatory), cytopaenias. Note: mandatory step-up dosing (0.06 → 0.3 → 1.5 mg/kg) with hospitalisation for first 2 doses; IVIG monitoring and replacement essential; infection prophylaxis mandatory (PCP trimethoprim, aciclovir, antifungal); BCMA universal in myeloma - no specific testing required.

XPO1 (exportin 1) inhibitor - first-in-class SINE (selective inhibitor of nuclear export). MOA: blocks XPO1 nuclear export protein → traps tumour suppressor proteins (p53, PP2A, RB1, FOXO) in nucleus → ↑tumour suppressor activity → apoptosis; also blocks NF-κB mRNA export → ↓myeloma cell survival. Indications: relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (with dexamethasone ± bortezomib - STORM/BOSTON trials), relapsed/refractory DLBCL (penta-refractory - ORR ~29%). SE: profound nausea/vomiting (very common - prophylaxis essential - ondansetron + dexamethasone + metoclopramide before each dose), profound fatigue (dose-limiting), anorexia/weight loss, thrombocytopenia, hyponatraemia (SIADH-like - monitor Na+). Note: nausea prophylaxis critical - multiple antiemetics mandatory; dose twice weekly (myeloma); Na+ monitoring required.

IDH1 inhibitor (selective; newer generation). MOA: selectively inhibits mutant IDH1 (R132H/C/G/L/S mutations) → ↓2-HG oncometabolite production → ↑differentiation of leukaemic blasts; complementary binding site to ivosidenib. Indications: relapsed/refractory AML with IDH1 mutation (≥1 prior therapy - Study 2102-HEM-101 trial; ORR ~35%). SE: differentiation syndrome (fever, dyspnoea, weight gain - 10-15%; high-dose dexamethasone required; distinctive IDH inhibitor class toxicity; monitor first 5 weeks), QTc prolongation, ↑LFTs, GI, fatigue. Note: differentiation syndrome management: any new respiratory symptoms in first 5 weeks → dexamethasone 10 mg BD; IDH1 testing required; may be used sequentially after ivosidenib resistance.

Selective FLT3-ITD inhibitor (2nd-gen; highly selective). MOA: selectively inhibits FLT3-ITD kinase (minimal activity against FLT3-TKD); ↓proliferation and survival in FLT3-ITD mutant AML cells; type II kinase inhibitor. Indications: AML with FLT3-ITD mutation (1st-line with standard chemotherapy induction/consolidation + maintenance - QuANTUM-First trial; superior OS vs placebo). SE: QTc prolongation (boxed warning - monitor ECG at baseline and during treatment; dose-modify for QTc >480 ms; avoid QTc-prolonging drugs), myelosuppression, differentiation syndrome (rare), fatigue, nausea. Note: QTc monitoring mandatory (ECG at baseline, day 15 of cycle 1, then monthly); FLT3-ITD specific (not FLT3-TKD) - test specifically for ITD mutation; maintenance therapy for 3 years post-consolidation.

Anti-CTLA-4 monoclonal antibody (IgG2; used with durvalumab). MOA: blocks CTLA-4 → disinhibits T-cell priming in lymph nodes → ↑CD8+ T-cell activation; synergistic with PD-L1 blockade (durvalumab). Indications: unresectable HCC (with durvalumab - HIMALAYA trial - STRIDE regimen: single priming dose + durvalumab monthly; superior OS vs sorafenib in some populations), NSCLC (with durvalumab + chemotherapy - POSEIDON trial). SE: immune-related AEs (combined CTLA-4+PD-L1 blockade - colitis/diarrhoea, hepatitis, endocrinopathy, pneumonitis, rash - higher rate than PD-1 alone). Note: STRIDE regimen (single 300 mg tremelimumab priming dose then durvalumab monthly) - single dose strategy minimises cumulative CTLA-4 irAEs while maintaining immunostimulatory effect; different from ipilimumab (used as ongoing treatment).

BRAF V600E/K inhibitor (used with binimetinib; longer BRAF residence time). MOA: selective BRAF V600 inhibition → ↓MEK/ERK signalling; long dissociation half-life from BRAF → ↓paradoxical MEK activation (vs vemurafenib/dabrafenib). Indications: BRAF V600E/K-mutant unresectable/metastatic melanoma (with binimetinib - COLUMBUS trial - superior PFS vs vemurafenib), BRAF V600E-mutant colorectal cancer (with cetuximab - BEACON trial: superior OS vs FOLFOX after 1+ prior). SE: joint pain, fatigue, nausea, HFSR (less than vemurafenib/dabrafenib), photosensitivity, hepatotoxicity, QTc. Note: unique advantage in BRAF-mutant CRC (encorafenib + cetuximab - BEACON trial - 1st targeted therapy to show OS benefit in BRAF V600E CRC); vemurafenib does not have CRC indication; longer BRAF residence time may explain better therapeutic index.

KRAS G12C inhibitor (first-in-class; covalent). MOA: irreversibly and covalently binds KRAS G12C mutant protein (locked in GDP-bound inactive state) → prevents GTP loading → ↓RAS-driven signalling (MAPK, PI3K); KRAS G12C historically considered 'undruggable'. Indications: KRAS G12C-mutant NSCLC (previously treated - CodeBreaK 100 trial; ORR ~37%), KRAS G12C CRC (less active; ongoing trials). SE: diarrhoea, nausea, fatigue, musculoskeletal pain, hepatotoxicity (↑LFTs - monitor monthly). Note: KRAS G12C testing required - does NOT cover G12D/G12V/other mutations; first drug to target 'undruggable' KRAS; rapidly followed by adagrasib; resistance emerges via secondary KRAS mutations or bypass pathways.

KRAS G12C inhibitor (covalent; improved CNS penetration vs sotorasib). MOA: irreversibly binds KRAS G12C in GDP-bound state → ↓oncogenic RAS signalling; longer half-life (24h vs sotorasib ~6h) → once-daily vs BID dosing; CNS-penetrant. Indications: KRAS G12C-mutant NSCLC (previously treated - KRYSTAL-1 trial; ORR ~43%), KRAS G12C CRC (with cetuximab - KRYSTAL-10 trial). SE: diarrhoea, nausea, fatigue, hepatotoxicity, QTc prolongation (ECG monitoring required), vomiting. Note: CNS penetration advantage vs sotorasib - activity against brain metastases; once-daily dosing; QTc monitoring required; KRAS G12C-specific (not other KRAS mutations).

RNA polymerase II inhibitor (alkylating; synthetic trabectedin analogue). MOA: binds DNA minor groove → covalently adducts → blocks elongating RNA Pol II → stalled transcription complexes → DNA damage response → apoptosis; also depletes tumour-associated macrophages. Indications: relapsed/refractory small cell lung cancer (SCLC) after platinum-based chemotherapy (PM301 trial; ORR ~35% platinum-sensitive, ~22% platinum-resistant). SE: myelosuppression (neutropaenia - most common; G-CSF PRN; nadir day 15), nausea, fatigue, elevated LFTs, peripheral neuropathy. Note: G-CSF recommended prophylactically; hepatic metabolism - dose-adjust for hepatic impairment; active in SCLC where options are very limited post-platinum.

DNA minor groove alkylating agent (from marine organism Ecteinascidia turbinata). MOA: binds DNA minor groove → covalently alkylates N2 of guanine → impairs transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair (TC-NER) → DNA strand breaks → apoptosis; also dysregulates tumour microenvironment (macrophage modulation). Indications: soft tissue sarcoma (liposarcoma, leiomyosarcoma - 2nd-line after anthracycline/ifosfamide - ET743 STS trial), relapsed platinum-sensitive ovarian cancer (with pegylated liposomal doxorubicin - OVA-301 trial). SE: hepatotoxicity (ALT/AST elevation - very common; transient; monitor LFTs; dose-reduction if persistent; rarely fatal), myelosuppression (neutropaenia - nadir day 15), nausea, rhabdomyolysis (rare but serious - ↑CK monitoring), fatigue. Note: LFT monitoring before each cycle mandatory - hepatotoxicity most distinctive SE; liposarcoma/leiomyosarcoma preferred histologies; 24-hour continuous IV infusion.

EGFR/MET bispecific antibody. MOA: binds EGFR + MET extracellular domains simultaneously → ADCC + ADCP + receptor degradation → active in EGFR exon 20 insertion mutations (not covered by standard EGFR TKIs). Indications: NSCLC with EGFR exon 20 insertion mutations (after platinum - CHRYSALIS trial; 1st-line with lazertinib - MARIPOSA trial). SE: EGFR-related (rash - very common - acneiform; paronychia; mucositis), MET-related (oedema), infusion reactions (very common - premedicate; split first infusion; grade 3-4 ~3%); hypoalbuminaemia. Note: EGFR exon 20 insertions (~2% of NSCLC) - not responsive to standard EGFR TKIs (osimertinib, erlotinib); amivantamab and mobocertinib are 1st approved agents; test for EGFR exon 20 insertion specifically; rash management: prophylactic moisturiser, doxycycline.

EGFR exon 20 insertion TKI (first approved oral agent for EGFR exon 20 insertions). MOA: selectively inhibits EGFR exon 20 insertion mutants (not wild-type EGFR or common mutations) → ↓EGFR signalling in exon 20 insertion-driven NSCLC. Indications: NSCLC with EGFR exon 20 insertion mutations (previously treated with platinum - EXCLAIM trial; ORR ~28%). SE: diarrhoea (very common - grade 3 in ~20%; prophylactic loperamide; dose modification often required), rash (EGFR-related acneiform), mucositis, paronychia, ↑LFTs, QTc (ECG monitoring). Note: diarrhoea management critical - loperamide PRN from day 1; EGFR exon 20 insertion testing required (specific mutation detection, not covered by standard EGFR panel); competition with amivantamab for this indication.

Antifolate antimetabolite (high-affinity DHFR inhibitor). MOA: enters cells via RFC-1 (reduced folate carrier) with ~10× higher affinity than methotrexate → inhibits DHFR → depletes tetrahydrofolate → ↓purine/thymidylate synthesis → cell death; high preference for RFC-1-overexpressing T-cells. Indications: relapsed/refractory PTCL (PROPEL trial - ORR ~29%; 1st drug approved specifically for PTCL). SE: mucositis (grade 3-4 - dose-limiting; prophylactic folic acid 1.0-1.25 mg daily + vitamin B12 1000 μg IM every 8-10 weeks mandatory), myelosuppression (thrombocytopenia), skin reactions, hepatotoxicity. Note: folic acid + vitamin B12 supplementation MANDATORY before and during treatment - ↓mucositis; check homocysteine levels (↑ suggests inadequate folate status - delay treatment); similar supplementation paradigm to pemetrexed.

CD19-targeted CAR-T cell therapy (4-1BB costimulatory; autologous). MOA: patient's T-cells genetically engineered ex vivo with anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) → expanded → infused back → CAR-T cells proliferate in vivo → recognise CD19 on B-cells/ALL blasts → cytolysis → sustained remission (with CAR-T persistence). Indications: B-cell ALL in children/young adults ≤25 years (relapsed/refractory - ELIANA trial; CR 81%); relapsed/refractory DLBCL (adults - JULIET trial; 40% CR; ≥2 prior lines). SE: cytokine release syndrome (CRS - fever, hypotension, hypoxia; grade 3-4 in 22%; tocilizumab 1st-line), ICANS (immune effector cell neurotoxicity - encephalopathy, seizures; dexamethasone), prolonged cytopaenias, B-cell aplasia (requires IVIG), infection. Note: REMS programme; specialist CAR-T centres only; hospitalisation for ≥4 weeks monitoring; 4-1BB domain → longer T-cell persistence vs CD28 (axicabtagene).

CD19-targeted CAR-T cell therapy (CD28 costimulatory; autologous). MOA: autologous T-cells engineered with anti-CD19 CAR (CD28 costimulatory domain → rapid expansion, early responses) → infused back → recognise and kill CD19+ B-cells. Indications: relapsed/refractory DLBCL (≥2 prior lines - ZUMA-1 trial; ORR 72%, CR 51%; 1st-line in high-risk relapsed/refractory - ZUMA-7 trial superior to ASCT), follicular lymphoma (r/r - ZUMA-5), marginal zone lymphoma (r/r). SE: CRS (grade 3-4 in 11-13%; tocilizumab; often more rapid/severe than tisagenlecleucel due to CD28 domain → faster expansion), ICANS (grade 3-4 in 28% - higher than tisagenlecleucel; dexamethasone), prolonged cytopaenias, B-cell aplasia. Note: CD28 costimulatory domain → ↑early expansion + CRS/neurotoxicity vs tisagenlecleucel (4-1BB); ZUMA-7: superior to ASCT - paradigm shift for 2nd-line DLBCL.

CD19-targeted CAR-T cell therapy (4-1BB costimulatory; defined CD4:CD8 ratio; autologous). MOA: autologous CAR-T with defined CD4:CD8 T-cell ratio (1:1) → CD19+ B-cell killing; defined ratio → ↓variability in response and toxicity vs undefined CD4:CD8 ratio products. Indications: relapsed/refractory DLBCL (≥2 prior lines - TRANSCEND trial; ORR 73%, CR 53%); 2nd-line DLBCL (TRANSFORM trial). SE: CRS (grade 3-4 in 4% - lower than axicabtagene/tisagenlecleucel; likely due to 4-1BB + defined ratio), ICANS (grade 3-4 in ~10%), infections, B-cell aplasia. Note: defined CD4:CD8 ratio product → may explain lower CRS/neurotoxicity rates; 4-1BB domain → longer T-cell persistence; currently manufactured at defined ratio (vs unselected T-cell products).

BCMA-targeted CAR-T cell therapy (two anti-BCMA VHH domains - nanobody; 4-1BB costimulatory; autologous). MOA: autologous T-cells with biparatopic anti-BCMA nanobody CAR → dual BCMA binding → high avidity → myeloma cell cytolysis; two different BCMA epitopes → ↓antigen escape. Indications: relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (≥4 prior lines including PI, IMiD, anti-CD38 - CARTITUDE-1 trial; ORR ~98%, CR ~83% - highest response rates seen with any myeloma therapy). SE: CRS (grade 3-4 in ~4%), ICANS (rare), cytopenia (prolonged), infections (B-cell aplasia/hypogammaglobulinaemia → IVIG; prophylaxis mandatory), movement/neurocognitive adverse events (MACE - Parkinsonism, delayed neurotoxicity - rare, may be delayed months post-infusion). Note: MACE (movement and neurocognitive adverse events) - distinctive late-onset neurotoxicity seen with anti-BCMA CAR-Ts; responses are very deep but manufacturing takes 4-6 weeks.

BCMA-targeted CAR-T cell therapy (single-domain anti-BCMA; CD28+4-1BB dual costimulatory; autologous). MOA: autologous T-cells with anti-BCMA CAR (single BCMA-binding domain; dual costimulatory) → BCMA-targeted myeloma cell lysis. Indications: relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (≥4 prior lines including PI, IMiD, anti-CD38 - KarMMa trial; ORR ~72%, CR ~28%; 1st approved anti-BCMA CAR-T for myeloma). SE: CRS (grade 3-4 in 5%), ICANS (rare), cytopaenias (prolonged), infections, MACE (movement and neurocognitive events - less reported than ciltacabtagene). Note: 1st approved BCMA CAR-T (March 2021); lower response rates than ciltacabtagene (KarMMa vs CARTITUDE-1 differences in patient selection); similar safety profile to ciltacabtagene.

Transthyretin (TTR) stabiliser - first approved therapy for ATTR cardiomyopathy. MOA: binds TTR tetramer at T4 (thyroxine) binding sites → stabilises native tetrameric conformation → ↓dissociation into monomers → ↓amyloid fibril formation and deposition in heart/peripheral nerves. Indications: wild-type or hereditary TTR amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM - ATTR-ACT trial; ↓mortality + ↓hospitalisation; significant survival benefit). SE: generally well tolerated; GI (mild nausea, diarrhoea); urinary tract infections; falls. Note: ATTR-CM diagnosis requires nuclear scintigraphy (pyrophosphate/DPD scan - grade 2-3 uptake diagnostic without biopsy if no monoclonal protein); tafamidis does not affect established amyloid deposits - early treatment essential; two formulations: 20 mg free acid (Vyndaqel) or 61 mg (Vyndamax - bioequivalent to 80 mg Vyndaqel).

RNA interference siRNA (lipid nanoparticle delivery) - first approved siRNA therapy. MOA: siRNA targeting TTR mRNA → RISC complex → mRNA cleavage → ↓TTR protein synthesis in liver → ↓circulating misfolded TTR → ↓amyloid deposition in peripheral nerves/heart. Indications: hereditary TTR (hATTR) amyloidosis with polyneuropathy (APOLLO trial - ↓polyneuropathy progression + ↑quality of life). SE: infusion reactions (premedication with corticosteroid + antihistamine + paracetamol required), peripheral oedema, vitamin A deficiency (TTR is vitamin A transporter → ↓TTR → ↓vitamin A - supplement 2500 IU daily), hypotension. Note: lipid nanoparticle delivery enables IV siRNA; vitamin A supplementation mandatory (2500 IU/day); premedication before each infusion; given every 3 weeks IV.

RNA interference siRNA (GalNAc-conjugated; subcutaneous) - 2nd-gen TTR siRNA. MOA: GalNAc-conjugated siRNA → liver-targeted delivery via ASGPR receptor → TTR mRNA silencing → ↓circulating misfolded TTR → ↓amyloid deposition; SC administration every 3 months (vs patisiran IV q3 weeks). Indications: hereditary TTR amyloidosis with polyneuropathy (HELIOS-A trial - superior to external placebo; comparable/superior to patisiran). SE: injection site reactions (SC route), myalgia, arthralgia, dizziness, peripheral oedema, vitamin A deficiency. Note: major advantage over patisiran - once-quarterly SC injection vs every-3-week IV infusion; no premedication required; GalNAc conjugation enables liver-targeted subcutaneous delivery; vitamin A supplementation mandatory.

CFTR corrector (next-generation; component of triple combination elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor). MOA: elexacaftor binds CFTR protein at a different site than lumacaftor/tezacaftor → ↑processing and trafficking of misfolded F508del CFTR from ER to cell surface; combined with tezacaftor (corrector) + ivacaftor (potentiator) → synergistic rescue of CFTR function. Indications: cystic fibrosis with ≥1 F508del allele (age ≥2 years - AURORA/BEACON trials; ↑FEV1 ~14% absolute vs placebo; ↓pulmonary exacerbations ~63%; ↓sweat chloride; improved BMI; transformative benefit). SE: hepatotoxicity (↑LFTs - monitor; discontinue if >5× ULN or jaundice), respiratory adverse events, rash, cataracts (paediatric monitoring), neuropsychiatric (mood disorders). Note: Trikafta (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor) is the most transformative CF therapy to date - applicable to ~90% of CF patients (all with ≥1 F508del allele); ophthalmology monitoring for cataracts in paediatric patients.

CFTR corrector (1st-gen; combination with ivacaftor). MOA: corrects folding and trafficking of F508del CFTR from ER to cell surface → ↑cell surface CFTR expression; ivacaftor then potentiates surface CFTR → ↑chloride transport (combined modest benefit; largely superseded by elexacaftor-containing Trikafta). Indications: CF with F508del homozygous (≥2 years - TRAFFIC/TRANSPORT trials; ↑FEV1 ~3-4% absolute; ↓exacerbations ~39%). SE: respiratory symptoms on initiation (dyspnoea, chest tightness - first 8 weeks; dose escalation), hepatotoxicity (↑LFTs), drug interactions (potent CYP3A inducer - ↓immunosuppressants, hormonal contraceptives, azoles), hypertension. Note: potent CYP3A4 inducer - ↓ivacaftor levels → requires higher ivacaftor doses; largely superseded by Trikafta (Kaftrio); still used when Trikafta unavailable.

CFTR corrector (2nd-gen; combination with ivacaftor or component of Trikafta). MOA: corrects F508del CFTR protein folding and trafficking to cell surface → ↑CFTR expression; superior to lumacaftor (↓drug interactions - weaker CYP3A induction; better tolerability); combined with ivacaftor in Symdeko or with elexacaftor+ivacaftor in Trikafta. Indications: CF with F508del homozygous or F508del + specific mutations; also component of Trikafta (elexacaftor+tezacaftor+ivacaftor). SE: hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs), nausea, headache; mild CYP3A induction (↓drug interactions vs lumacaftor). Note: Symdeko largely superseded by Trikafta (Kaftrio) - used for patients not eligible for triple combination; component of Trikafta's superior efficacy via triple mechanism.

PEGylated recombinant uricase (Candida utilis). MOA: converts uric acid → allantoin (soluble, easily excreted) → rapidly ↓serum urate to <1 mg/dL (normal limit ~6.8 mg/dL); humans lack functional uricase. Indications: chronic refractory tophaceous gout (failed standard therapy - allopurinol/febuxostat; IV infusion every 2 weeks). SE: infusion reactions (anaphylaxis/severe - premedicate; monitor for 1 hour post-infusion), gout flares (paradoxical - prophylaxis with colchicine/NSAIDs mandatory), loss of response (anti-drug antibodies - ADAs; if serum urate >6 mg/dL pre-infusion → likely ADA → hold drug - infusing with loss of response dramatically ↑infusion reaction risk). Note: ADA monitoring critical - check serum urate before EVERY infusion; if pre-dose UA >6 mg/dL → hold drug; with methotrexate co-therapy → ↓ADA formation → ↑sustained response (MIRROR trial).

Recombinant urate oxidase enzyme (Aspergillus flavus). MOA: converts uric acid → allantoin → ↓serum urate very rapidly (within hours); most powerful urate-lowering agent available. Indications: tumour lysis syndrome (TLS) prevention and treatment in haematological malignancies (high-risk ALL, aggressive lymphoma - prophylaxis before chemotherapy + treatment of established TLS; single doses often sufficient). SE: hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis - premedicate; observe post-infusion), haemolysis (G6PD-deficient patients - absolute contraindication; H2O2 produced by allantoin pathway → haemolysis → methemoglobinaemia), methaemoglobinaemia. Note: G6PD screening MANDATORY before administration (severe haemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients - contraindicated); blood samples for uric acid must be placed on ice immediately (continues enzymatic conversion ex vivo → false low UA reading); single doses often adequate for established TLS.

Dual IL-17A/IL-17F inhibitor (monoclonal antibody). MOA: binds both IL-17A and IL-17F → blocks both cytokines' effects on keratinocytes/fibroblasts → broader inhibition than IL-17A-only inhibitors (secukinumab/ixekizumab); IL-17F contributes to psoriatic inflammation alongside IL-17A. Indications: moderate-severe plaque psoriasis (BE VIVID/BE SURE trials - PASI 90 in ~90% at 16 weeks; superior to secukinumab and ustekinumab in head-to-head), psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis. SE: URTI, nasopharyngitis, oropharyngeal candidiasis (higher rate than IL-17A-only inhibitors due to dual IL-17A+F blockade → ↑mucosal candidiasis), diarrhoea, IBD flare risk. Note: oropharyngeal candidiasis higher than secukinumab - antifungal management if persistent; superior PASI 90/100 rates in head-to-head trials; caution in IBD (IL-17 pathway important in gut).

Anti-IL-36 receptor monoclonal antibody - first-in-class for GPP. MOA: binds IL-36 receptor → blocks IL-36α/β/γ signalling → ↓neutrophilic skin inflammation in generalised pustular psoriasis (GPP - distinct from plaque psoriasis; IL-36 pathway is dominant in GPP pathogenesis). Indications: generalised pustular psoriasis (GPP) - acute flares (Effisayil-1 trial: rapid pustule clearance within 1 week in 54% vs 6% placebo; IV for acute flares), GPP flare prevention (subcutaneous maintenance - Effisayil-2 trial). SE: infections (↑risk - similar to other biologics), infusion reactions, GI, URTI. Note: GPP is distinct from plaque psoriasis - triggered by infections, medications, pregnancy, stress; IL-36 pathway (not IL-17/IL-23) drives GPP; spesolimab is 1st specific GPP therapy; rapid IV treatment for acute GPP flares.

JAK1 inhibitor (selective; oral - atopic dermatitis). MOA: selectively inhibits JAK1 → ↓Th2 cytokine signalling (IL-4, IL-13, IL-31 - key cytokines in AD) + ↓type I IFN signalling; oral administration. Indications: moderate-severe atopic dermatitis (JADE-COMPARE/MONO trials; EASI-75 ~70% at week 12; superior to dupilumab on some itch endpoints in JADE-COMPARE). SE: nausea (especially early treatment - take with food), headache, ↑herpes simplex/zoster reactivation (VZV prophylaxis for high-risk), acne, thrombocytopenia (dose-dependent - monitor platelets), nasopharyngitis; thromboembolism risk (class warning). Note: JAK inhibitor class warning (boxed warning) - VTE, MACE, malignancy, serious infection - compared to TNF inhibitors in RA patients (ORAL Surveillance); dose-dependent thrombocytopenia requires platelet monitoring.

Topical PDE4 inhibitor (phosphodiesterase type 4; boron-containing; non-steroidal). MOA: inhibits PDE4 → ↑cAMP → ↓inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-12, IL-23, IL-4, IL-13) → ↓T-cell activation + keratinocyte inflammation. Indications: mild-moderate atopic dermatitis (≥2 years; CrisADe CORE1/2 trials; steroid-sparing; safe for face/sensitive areas - no steroid-related side effects). SE: application site pain/burning (common - especially on broken skin; most common reason for discontinuation; usually transient). Note: non-steroidal → no skin atrophy, striae - safe for face, eyelids, skin folds long-term; less effective than moderate/potent topical steroids but safer for chronic/sensitive area use; burning on application - most common complaint; BID application to affected areas.

Topical aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) agonist - novel non-steroidal MOA. MOA: activates AhR → ↑skin barrier proteins (filaggrin, loricrin) + ↑skin microbiome diversity → ↓Th2/Th17 inflammation; unique mechanism distinct from steroids, calcineurin inhibitors, PDE4 inhibitors. Indications: plaque psoriasis (adults - PSOARING trials), atopic dermatitis (adults/children ≥2 years - ADORING trials). SE: folliculitis (most common - distinctive for tapinarof; often staphylococcal; treat with antibiotics; dose-dependent), contact dermatitis (uncommon), application site reactions. Note: folliculitis is class-defining SE - bacterial culture if severe; unique AhR mechanism → ↑skin barrier + ↓inflammation; steroid-free, no age restriction concerns; 'remission duration' seen in some patients after stopping.

Anti-IL-5 monoclonal antibody (IgG4/κ; IV; weight-based dosing). MOA: binds IL-5 → ↓eosinophil maturation/recruitment/activation/survival → ↓blood and tissue eosinophilia. Indications: severe eosinophilic asthma (blood eosinophils ≥400/μL; maintenance add-on - BREATH/COSMOS/ZONDA trials; ↓exacerbations ~59%; ↑FEV1). SE: anaphylaxis (risk - REMS programme in USA; observe 20 min post-infusion), musculoskeletal pain, ↑CK. Note: IV administration only (vs mepolizumab SC); weight-based dosing (3 mg/kg IV q4 weeks - body weight matters); anaphylaxis risk higher than other anti-IL-5 agents - observation required post-infusion; comparable efficacy to mepolizumab/benralizumab.

Anti-IL-23p19 monoclonal antibody. MOA: binds the p19 subunit of IL-23 → ↓Th17 cell differentiation/activation → ↓IL-17A production → ↓downstream keratinocyte inflammation (same target as guselkumab/risankizumab). Indications: moderate-severe plaque psoriasis (reSURFACE1/2 trials - PASI 75 ~64-66% at week 28). SE: URTI, injection site reactions, diarrhoea, back pain; rarely IBD flare (class concern). Note: same IL-23p19 target as guselkumab and risankizumab; every-4-week dosing; choose based on patient preference, access, cost; PASI 90 rates lower than risankizumab in indirect comparisons.

Anti-IL-23p19 monoclonal antibody (IV induction then SC maintenance). MOA: binds IL-23p19 subunit → ↓Th17-mediated intestinal inflammation (IL-23 critical driver of UC/CD). Indications: moderate-severe ulcerative colitis (LUCENT-1/2 trials - clinical remission ~24.2% vs 13.3% placebo at week 12 induction; durable maintenance remission). SE: URTI, injection site reactions, nasopharyngitis.
