Note: IL-23p19 inhibitors have demonstrated efficacy in both psoriasis and IBD (vs IL-17 inhibitors which can worsen IBD); IV loading dose × 12 weeks then SC maintenance (every 4 weeks).

HIV capsid inhibitor - first-in-class, multi-mechanism. MOA: binds HIV-1 capsid protein (CA) → inhibits multiple steps of viral life cycle: nuclear import, capsid assembly, viral reverse transcription, viral RNA translation; first-in-class mechanism. Indications: HIV-1 (treatment-experienced patients with multidrug-resistant HIV - CAPELLA trial; also PrEP - PURPOSE-1/2 trials showing near-100% prevention efficacy in biannual SC injection). SE: injection site reactions (nodules/induration - common; mostly mild; subcutaneous injection; resolves over weeks), nausea, hepatotoxicity (↑LFTs - monitor). Note: long-acting SC injection every 6 months (twice yearly) - unprecedented adherence advantage for both HIV treatment and PrEP; PURPOSE-1 trial in cisgender women showed ~100% prevention efficacy; no cross-resistance with current ARTs due to novel capsid target.

HIV gp120 attachment inhibitor (prodrug of temsavir) - first-in-class. MOA: prodrug hydrolysed to temsavir → binds gp120 on HIV envelope → prevents CD4 receptor attachment → ↓viral entry into T-cells; unique mechanism (no cross-resistance with CCR5 antagonists, other ARTs). Indications: HIV-1 (heavily treatment-experienced adults with multidrug-resistant HIV where otherwise limited options - BRIGHTE trial; combined with other ARTs). SE: nausea, diarrhoea, headache, ↑LFTs; QTc prolongation (monitor if QTc prolonging drugs used concurrently). Note: pre-attachment mechanism (vs enfuvirtide which blocks fusion, vs maraviroc which blocks CCR5); no cross-resistance with other drug classes; option for MDR HIV when standard regimens exhausted.

Anti-CD4 post-attachment HIV inhibitor (humanised monoclonal antibody; IgG4). MOA: binds CD4 receptor on T-cells (domain 2 of CD4 - not the HIV binding domain 1) → blocks post-attachment conformational changes needed for viral fusion → ↓HIV entry without blocking CD4-MHC-II interactions (preserves immune function). Indications: HIV-1 (multidrug-resistant HIV in heavily treatment-experienced adults - TMB-301 trial; IV infusion every 2 weeks). SE: dizziness, nausea, rash, diarrhoea, immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). Note: IV administration q2 weeks; unique CD4 binding site preserves T-cell immunological function; mechanism is distinct from all other drug classes → active against pan-resistant HIV; needs to be combined with other ARTs.

siRNA targeting PCSK9 mRNA in hepatocytes. MOA: small interfering RNA directed against PCSK9 mRNA → RNAi-mediated mRNA silencing → ↓PCSK9 protein → ↑LDL-receptor recycling → ↓LDL-C (~50%). Indications: ASCVD (atherosclerotic CVD) or heterozygous FH - adjunct to diet + max-tolerated statin. SE: injection site reactions (erythema, pain), URTI, nasopharyngitis. Note: twice-yearly SC injection (after initial + 3-month loading doses - then every 6 months); durable mRNA silencing; major adherence advantage; combine with statins/ezetimibe; no myopathy risk (hepatocyte-targeted).

ATP-citrate lyase (ACL) inhibitor - upstream of HMG-CoA reductase. MOA: prodrug activated by ACSVL1 (only in liver, not skeletal muscle) → inhibits ACL → ↓de novo cholesterol synthesis → upregulates LDL-R → ↓LDL-C (~18-28%). Indications: hypercholesterolaemia - adjunct to diet ± max statin/ezetimibe; statin-intolerant patients (CLEAR-Outcomes trial - ↓CV events). SE: gout/hyperuricaemia (clinically significant - monitor uric acid), tendon rupture (rare), ↑uric acid; ↑simvastatin exposure (use simvastatin ≤20 mg). Note: liver-selective prodrug → minimal myopathy (not activated in muscle - unlike statins); CLEAR-Outcomes: significant CV benefit in statin-intolerant patients; available as monotherapy (Nexletol) or fixed combination with ezetimibe (Nexlizet).

Highly purified omega-3 EPA (eicosapentaenoic acid ethyl ester). MOA: ↓triglycerides + pleiotropic anti-inflammatory/membrane-stabilising effects (mechanism of CV benefit beyond TG reduction unclear). Indications: elevated TG (≥1.5 mmol/L) + established CVD or DM with additional risk factors - on statin therapy (REDUCE-IT trial: 4g/day → 25% relative ↓MACE). SE: AF (↑risk - monitor), bleeding, peripheral oedema, constipation. Note: REDUCE-IT used mineral oil placebo (controversial - may have inflated benefit); EPA only (no DHA - different from standard fish oil); 4g/day (2g BD with meals); approved for high-TG + high-CV risk; PBS-listed in Australia.

2nd-generation covalent BTK (Bruton's tyrosine kinase) inhibitor - more BTK-selective than ibrutinib. MOA: irreversible covalent binding to BTK Cys481 → ↓BCR signalling → ↓CLL/B-cell survival. Indications: CLL (1st-line - ELEVATE-TN; R/R - ASCEND), MCL (R/R). SE: headache (common, caffeine helps - transient), diarrhoea, neutropenia, infections, bruising; lower AF/hypertension/bleeding vs ibrutinib. Note: ELEVATE-RR - non-inferior to ibrutinib with significantly lower AF; preferred over ibrutinib for cardiac/bleeding risk patients; twice-daily dosing; cannot use with proton pump inhibitors (pH-dependent absorption - separate by 2h or use H2-blockers).

2nd-generation covalent BTK inhibitor - high BTK selectivity, complete/sustained BTK occupancy, minimal off-target kinase inhibition. MOA: irreversible covalent BTK Cys481 binding → ↓BCR signalling. Indications: CLL (ALPINE trial - superior PFS + lower AF vs ibrutinib; SEQUOIA - 1st-line), MCL (R/R), WM (Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia - ASPEN), MZL. SE: neutropenia, infections, bruising/haemorrhage; AF/atrial flutter (lower than ibrutinib); hypertension. Note: ALPINE trial - significantly lower AF risk vs ibrutinib + superior PFS in CLL; twice-daily dosing; preferred BTKi for Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia (ASPEN trial).

Non-covalent (reversible) BTK inhibitor - first-in-class. MOA: reversibly binds BTK without covalent Cys481 bond → active against BTK C481S point mutation (resistance mechanism for covalent BTKi ibrutinib/acalabrutinib/zanubrutinib). Indications: R/R CLL (after ≥2 prior therapies including covalent BTKi - BRUIN trial); R/R MCL (after ≥2 prior therapies). SE: diarrhoea, fatigue, neutropenia, contusion, infections; lower bleeding + AF than covalent BTKi (theoretical). Note: designed for post-covalent BTKi resistance (C481S mutation = 75% of covalent BTKi resistance); once-daily dosing; provides CLL treatment options after ibrutinib/acalabrutinib/zanubrutinib failure.

PI3Kδ (phosphoinositide 3-kinase delta) inhibitor. MOA: δ-isoform highly expressed in B- and T-lymphocytes; PI3Kδ inhibition → ↓BCR/CD40/CXCR signalling → ↓CLL cell survival/migration. Indications: R/R CLL (with rituximab), R/R FL (after ≥2 prior therapies). SE: diarrhoea/colitis (severe immune-mediated - dose-limiting), pneumonitis (immune-mediated), hepatotoxicity (↑LFTs - monitor), serious infections (PJP, CMV - co-trimoxazole prophylaxis required), intestinal perforation. Note: significant immune-mediated toxicity limits use; PJP prophylaxis mandatory; LFT monitoring frequently; largely superseded by BTKi and newer PI3K inhibitors due to toxicity profile; falling out of favour.

IV PI3Kα/δ inhibitor (pan-class I, primarily α+δ). MOA: IV intermittent dosing → ↓GI/hepatic toxicity vs oral PI3K inhibitors. Indications: R/R FL (after ≥2 prior therapies). SE: hyperglycaemia (acute, transient - peaks 5-8h post-infusion - PI3Kα in β-cells/liver; monitor BSL before each dose), hypertension (acute, infusion-related - PI3Kα; monitor BP), diarrhoea (less than oral PI3K inhibitors), infections, pneumonitis. Note: IV intermittent dosing reduces GI/liver toxicity vs oral PI3Kδ inhibitors (idelalisib); hyperglycaemia and hypertension transient (resolve 4h post-infusion); diabetics may need insulin dose adjustment on infusion days.

Modified activin receptor type IIB-Fc (ActRIIB-Fc) fusion protein - TGF-β superfamily ligand trap. MOA: traps GDF11, activin B, other TGF-β ligands → ↓Smad2/3 signalling → promotes late-stage erythropoiesis (erythroid maturation - differentiation of basophilic/polychromatic erythroblasts). Indications: anaemia in MDS with ring sideroblasts (MDS-RS - MEDALIST trial); transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia (BELIEVE trial); myelofibrosis-associated anaemia (INDEPENDENCE trial - with ruxolitinib). SE: fatigue, diarrhoea, nausea, hypertension (↑Hb), thrombosis, headache, bone pain. CI: pregnancy. Note: NOT an ESA (different MOA - late erythropoiesis maturation); SC injection every 3 weeks; SF3B1 mutation most predictive of MDS response; BELIEVE: ↓transfusion burden in beta-thalassaemia.

First-in-class telomerase inhibitor (RNA template competitive inhibitor). MOA: binds hTERT RNA template component → inhibits telomerase → prevents telomere elongation → selective killing of cells with high telomerase activity (haematological malignancies). Indications: transfusion-dependent low-to-intermediate-1 risk MDS (relapsed/refractory after ESA - IMerge trial - US-approved June 2024); myelofibrosis (clinical studies). SE: cytopenias (thrombocytopenia, neutropenia - dose-limiting), fatigue, nausea, ↑LFTs, infusion reactions. Note: IV infusion every 4 weeks; first clinical telomerase inhibitor; prolonged responses possible in MDS; molecular remissions (TET2, DNMT3A clones) observed in responders.

Oral non-peptide thrombopoietin receptor agonist (TPO-RA). MOA: activates TPO-R (c-Mpl) on megakaryocytes → ↑platelet production. Indications: thrombocytopenia in chronic liver disease (CLD) prior to elective procedures (ADAPT-1/2 - avoids platelet transfusion); ITP. SE: portal vein thrombosis (rare - monitor in cirrhosis), thromboembolic events (especially if count overshoots), headache. Note: 5-day oral course (starting 10-13 days pre-procedure for CLD); oral (advantage over romiplostim - SC); unlike eltrombopag - no food/divalent cation interaction; avoid target platelet count >200×10⁹/L (thrombosis risk).

Oral non-peptide TPO receptor agonist (small molecule, binds transmembrane domain of TPO-R). Indications: thrombocytopenia in CLD prior to elective procedures (L-PLUS 1/2 trials - avoids platelet transfusion). SE: thromboembolic events, portal vein thrombosis. Note: 7-day course starting 9 days before procedure; like avatrombopag - short-course pre-procedural TPO-RA specifically for CLD (vs eltrombopag/romiplostim - longer term for ITP/AA); avoid target count >50×10⁹/L pre-procedure.

Selective oral prostacyclin IP receptor agonist (non-prostanoid - avoids EP₁/EP₃ receptor effects). MOA: stimulates IP receptor → ↑cAMP → pulmonary vasodilation + antiproliferation; active metabolite (ACT-333679) ~37× more potent than selexipag. Indications: PAH (WHO Group 1 - GRIPHON trial: largest PAH RCT, significant ↓morbidity/mortality composite added on background ERA ± PDE5i therapy). SE: headache, diarrhoea, nausea, jaw pain, flushing, arthralgia, myalgia (prostacyclin class - titrate slowly over weeks). Note: oral twice-daily (advantage over SC/IV prostacyclins); individual tolerated dose titration (start low, increase weekly); GRIPHON - morbidity/mortality benefit in triple combination.

Stable prostacyclin analogue. MOA: prostacyclin receptor agonist → pulmonary vasodilation + antiproliferation + antiplatelet. Routes: SC infusion (Remodulin - portable pump), IV infusion, inhaled (Tyvaso - 4× daily, Tyvaso DPI - dry powder), oral (Orenitram - twice or 3× daily). Indications: PAH (all WHO FC groups); multiple RCTs (TRIUMPH-1 inhaled, FREEDOM oral). SE: SC - injection site pain/reactions (dose-limiting), headache, diarrhoea, flushing, jaw pain, nausea; pump site infection. Note: SC route avoids central venous access (vs IV epoprostenol); inhaled/oral routes most patient-friendly; never abruptly discontinue (rebound PAH - life-threatening); dose titration over months.

Stable synthetic prostacyclin analogue. MOA: prostacyclin receptor agonist → vasodilation + antiplatelet + antiproliferative. Routes: inhaled (Ventavis - 6-9 inhalations/day, 5-20 mcg each); IV (Ilomedine - infusion for Raynaud's/scleroderma). Indications: PAH (WHO FC III/IV - inhaled); Raynaud's phenomenon + scleroderma digital ulcers (IV course - 5-day infusions in Australia). SE: cough, headache, flushing, jaw pain, hypotension, syncope; bronchospasm in reactive airways disease. Note: inhaled requires frequent dosing (6-9× daily - adherence challenge); IV course used in scleroderma digital ulcers (Ilomedine 5-day hospital infusions - Australian practice); combination with ERA/PDE5i in PAH.

Soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) stimulator. MOA: directly stimulates sGC (NO-independent) AND sensitises sGC to endogenous NO → ↑cGMP → vasodilation + antiproliferation (dual mechanism - unique vs PDE5 inhibitors which prevent cGMP breakdown). Indications: PAH (WHO Group 1 - PATENT-1); CTEPH (non-operable or persistent post-PTE - CHEST-1 - FIRST drug approved for CTEPH). SE: hypotension (systemic), dizziness, headache, nausea, diarrhoea, haemoptysis. CI: pregnancy (teratogenic - REMS programme - strict contraception); concurrent PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil/tadalafil - severe hypotension - CONTRAINDICATED). Note: CTEPH use unique (only medical therapy approved for post-surgical/inoperable CTEPH); cannot combine with PDE5i (different MOA but additive cGMP effect = dangerous hypotension).

Activin receptor type IIA-Fc (ActRIIA-Fc) fusion protein - ligand trap for TGF-β superfamily members. MOA: traps activin A, GDF11, and related ligands → ↓aberrant vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation in pulmonary vasculature (anti-remodelling - distinct mechanism from all vasodilatory PAH therapies). Indications: PAH (WHO Group 1, FC II-III, on background PAH therapy - STELLAR trial: significant ↑6MWD, ↓PVR, 84% ↓morbidity/mortality vs placebo; HYPERION trial). SE: haemoglobin increase (↑Hb - erythropoietic effect - monitor Hct), telangiectasias, epistaxis, dizziness, thrombocytopenia, hypertension. Note: STELLAR - landmark PAH trial; first PAH therapy targeting vascular remodelling (not vasodilation); SC injection every 3 weeks; haemoglobin monitoring critical (↑Hb → haemoconcentration → thrombosis risk if excessive).

Ultra-long-acting β₂ agonist (ULABA) - 24-hour duration. MOA: β₂-adrenoceptor agonism → bronchodilation; 24-hour half-life → once-daily dosing (vs salmeterol/formoterol - twice daily). Indications: COPD maintenance bronchodilation (NOT approved for asthma - LABA for COPD); often combined with glycopyrronium/aclidinium (LAMA+LABA fixed-dose combinations - Ultibro). SE: headache, nasopharyngitis, muscle cramps; post-inhalation cough/bark (characteristic 5-15s cough - non-adverse, self-resolving). Note: first once-daily LABA for COPD; superior bronchodilation vs twice-daily LABAs; combined with LAMA (glycopyrronium - Ultibro Breezhaler) in dual bronchodilator COPD therapy; characteristic bark cough does not indicate adverse reaction.

First bispecific antibody in ophthalmology - dual VEGF-A + Ang-2 inhibitor. MOA: blocks VEGF-A (anti-angiogenesis/anti-permeability) AND angiopoietin-2 (Ang-2 - destabilises vessels, promotes vascular leakage via Tie-2 receptor); dual inhibition → vessel stabilisation + ↓neovascularisation + ↓macular oedema. Indications: neovascular (wet) AMD (nAMD - TENAYA/LUCERNE trials); diabetic macular oedema (DME - YOSEMITE/RHINE trials); up to 16-weekly dosing in sustained responders. SE: endophthalmitis (<0.1% per injection), intraocular inflammation, elevated IOP, retinal detachment (intravitreal injection complications). Note: dual mechanism may allow less frequent dosing vs anti-VEGF monotherapy; ~45% of patients maintained 16-weekly interval; intravitreal injection every 4-8-16 weeks as tolerated.

Single-chain antibody fragment (scFv) anti-VEGF-A - smallest anti-VEGF molecule (26 kDa). MOA: anti-VEGF-A; small size → higher molar concentration per dose + potentially longer duration in vitreous. Indications: neovascular (wet) AMD; DME. SE: intraocular inflammation (IOI) - retinal vasculitis (clinically significant - ~3.3% in HAWK/HARRIER trials; some cases with retinal arterial/venous occlusion - serious safety signal); endophthalmitis, retinal detachment. Note: IOI/retinal vasculitis safety signal higher than other anti-VEGFs - monitor for eye pain/redness/vision change post-injection; potential 12-weekly dosing; post-marketing pharmacovigilance confirmed vasculitis risk; some ophthalmologists limit use due to this.

Bradykinin B₂ receptor antagonist (synthetic decapeptide). MOA: selective competitive B₂ receptor blockade → inhibits bradykinin-mediated vasodilation and vascular permeability (bradykinin = primary mediator of HAE attacks - produced via kallikrein-kinin system in C1-INH deficiency). Indications: acute attacks of hereditary angioedema (HAE types I, II, III - C1-INH deficiency; acquired angioedema due to C1-INH deficiency). Route: SC self-injection (30 mg). SE: injection site reactions (erythema, oedema, burning - common), headache, nausea. Note: SC self-injection → early at-home treatment; response within 30-60 min; does not prevent attacks (prophylaxis = lanadelumab or berotralstat); C1-INH replacement preferred for severe laryngeal attacks in some guidelines; patient self-administration after training.

Fully human anti-plasma kallikrein monoclonal antibody (IgG1). MOA: inhibits plasma kallikrein → ↓bradykinin production → prevents HAE attacks (plasma kallikrein cleaves high-molecular-weight kininogen → bradykinin). Indications: prophylaxis of HAE attacks (HAE types I/II) ≥12 yr - HELP/HELP-OLE: 300 mg q2 weeks → ~87% ↓attack rate; well-controlled patients may extend to q4 weeks. Route: SC injection every 2-4 weeks. SE: injection site reactions, headache, dizziness, myalgia. Note: superior to danazol/tranexamic acid for HAE prophylaxis; does not replace rescue therapy for acute attacks (icatibant or C1-INH for breakthroughs); plasma kallikrein target (upstream of bradykinin); SC self-injection training required.

Oral plasma kallikrein inhibitor (small molecule) - first oral targeted HAE prophylaxis. MOA: inhibits plasma kallikrein (like lanadelumab but orally bioavailable) → ↓bradykinin generation → ↓HAE attack frequency (APeX-2 trial: 150 mg daily → ~44% ↓attack rate). Indications: prophylaxis of HAE attacks (HAE types I/II). SE: abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhoea, dyspepsia, vomiting, headache; CYP3A4/P-gp substrate (drug interactions - check comedications). Note: first oral targeted HAE prophylaxis (convenient vs SC lanadelumab; IV C1-INH); lower efficacy than lanadelumab but oral once-daily dosing; CYP3A4 interactions - avoid strong inhibitors/inducers; does not replace acute attack rescue therapy.

Non-selective dopamine D1/D2/D3 receptor agonist. Routes: SC injection pen (APO-go/Dacepton - acute use), SC continuous infusion pump (advanced PD), sublingual wafer (Kynmobi). MOA: direct dopaminergic agonism → rapid motor 'on' response (onset 15-20 min SC). Indications: Parkinson's disease - rescue therapy for unpredictable OFF episodes; advanced PD SC pump (continuous infusion for motor fluctuations/dyskinesias refractory to oral therapy). SE: nausea/vomiting (pre-treat domperidone 72h before initiation - NOT metoclopramide which crosses BBB); SC injection site nodules/necrosis (pump); hypotension/syncope; neuropsychiatric (hallucinations, impulse control); haemolytic anaemia; QTc prolongation. Note: domperidone pre-treatment ESSENTIAL (metoclopramide worsens PD - crosses BBB); SC pump for advanced PD with motor fluctuations; rapid onset ideal for unpredictable OFF episodes; NOT confused with aversion therapy (obsolete historical use).

Novel anti-seizure medication with dual mechanism. MOA: (1) preferential inhibition of persistent (late) Na+ current (distinct from fast-inactivation block - unique site vs other Na+ channel blockers); (2) positive allosteric modulation of GABAA receptors at a distinct non-benzodiazepine site. Indications: focal (partial) onset seizures in adults - adjunctive therapy (REDUCE-1/2 trials: up to 55% seizure-free rate in drug-resistant focal epilepsy - highest reported for adjunctive AED). SE: dizziness, somnolence, diplopia, fatigue, nausea; DRESS (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms - SLOW titration MANDATORY over 12-26 weeks - every 2 weeks increases - prevents DRESS); QTc shortening (dose-dependent - unique). Note: highest seizure-free rate of any adjunctive AED in refractory focal epilepsy trials; slow titration critical - prevents DRESS; QTc shortening (opposite of most drugs - caution if on QTc-shortening agents); TGA approved in Australia.

GABA transporter-1 (GAT-1) inhibitor. MOA: inhibits GAT-1 (neuronal/glial GABA reuptake transporter) → ↑synaptic GABA → enhanced GABAA-mediated inhibition. Indications: adjunctive treatment of focal (partial) seizures (≥12 yr). SE: dizziness, asthenia, nervousness, tremor, diarrhoea; seizure exacerbation (paradoxical - especially in non-epileptic conditions or as monotherapy); new-onset seizures/status epilepticus (reported with off-label use). Note: take with food (↓peak levels → fewer CNS SE); avoid in generalised epilepsy (may worsen absence); paradoxical seizures reported with off-label use (anxiety disorders); not used as monotherapy; limited use (more SE-prone than newer AEDs).

Dual orexin receptor antagonist (DORA - blocks OX1R + OX2R). MOA: orexin (hypocretin) promotes wakefulness - DORA blocks both orexin receptors → reduces wake drive → promotes sleep without direct sedation; preserves sleep architecture (natural REM + slow-wave sleep). Indications: insomnia disorder in adults (difficulty with sleep onset and/or sleep maintenance). SE: somnolence (dose-dependent), headache, abnormal dreams; sleep paralysis, hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations (rare); complex sleep behaviours (sleepwalking - class effect). CI: narcolepsy (orexin deficiency - DORA would worsen). Note: no rebound insomnia on discontinuation; Schedule IV controlled substance (US); less next-morning residual sedation vs suvorexant at comparable doses; lower abuse potential than benzodiazepines/Z-drugs; preferred in elderly (daytime function preserved).

Dual orexin receptor antagonist (DORA - OX1R + OX2R blocker) - first approved DORA (US 2014). MOA: blocks orexin receptors → reduces wakefulness signal → promotes sleep onset and maintenance. Indications: insomnia disorder (sleep onset + sleep maintenance difficulties) in adults. SE: somnolence (dose-related - next-morning), headache, abnormal dreams; sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations, cataplexy-like symptoms (rare); complex sleep behaviours (parasomnias). CI: narcolepsy. Note: Schedule IV; 10-20 mg doses; higher doses more effective but more next-day somnolence; class of DORA also includes lemborexant (slightly better next-day profile) and daridorexant; superior to placebo, generally well tolerated vs BZDs.

Dual orexin receptor antagonist (DORA - OX1R + OX2R). MOA: blocks orexin receptors → promotes sleep (same DORA class as suvorexant, lemborexant). Indications: insomnia disorder in adults - AMBIEN trials (25 mg and 50 mg doses). SE: somnolence, headache, fatigue; complex sleep behaviours (rare). CI: narcolepsy. Note: newest approved DORA (US/EU 2022); proprietary evidence suggests improved next-day functioning vs suvorexant at 25/50 mg; Schedule IV; 25 mg or 50 mg tablets; class effect shared with suvorexant and lemborexant - all appropriate for insomnia disorder in adults.

Highly selective 5-HT₄ receptor agonist (benzofurancarboxamide class). MOA: activates 5-HT₄ receptors in colonic enteric neurons → ↑acetylcholine release → prokinetic → ↑colonic motor propulsive activity. Indications: chronic idiopathic constipation (adults) unresponsive to ≥2 laxatives; constipation-predominant IBS (limited evidence). SE: headache (most common - 24h after first dose, transient - usually resolves after 1-2 days), nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, flatulence; NO significant cardiac effects. Note: 5-HT₄ selectivity (vs cisapride - non-selective, hERG block → QT prolongation → withdrawn); safe cardiac profile; 1-2 mg daily; trial 4 weeks to assess response; available in Australia (Resotran).

Mixed opioid receptor modulator. MOA: μ-opioid receptor agonist + δ-opioid receptor antagonist + κ-opioid receptor agonist → ↓intestinal hypermotility + ↓visceral hypersensitivity; δ-antagonism mitigates constipating + anxiogenic effects of μ-agonism; minimal systemic absorption. Indications: IBS with diarrhoea (IBS-D) - ACCORD trials. SE: constipation, nausea, abdominal pain; pancreatitis (sphincter of Oddi spasm - especially without gallbladder). CI: absence of gallbladder (↑↑pancreatitis risk - absolute CI), alcohol use disorder, biliary obstruction, hepatic impairment, chronic constipation. Note: ABSOLUTE CI in patients without gallbladder (sphincter of Oddi dysfunction → pancreatitis); screen for prior cholecystectomy before prescribing; limited availability/PBS listing in Australia.

Synthetic amylin analogue (modified human IAPP - islet amyloid polypeptide - prevents aggregation of native amylin). MOA: activates amylin receptors (area postrema + hypothalamus) → ↓postprandial glucagon, ↑satiety (↓food intake), delays gastric emptying → ↓postprandial glucose excursions. Indications: adjunct to mealtime insulin in T1DM; T2DM on mealtime insulin (SC injection immediately before each meal). SE: nausea/vomiting (dose-limiting - most common; titrate slowly); hypoglycaemia (requires mealtime insulin dose reduction 30-50% at initiation - ↑hypoglycaemia risk with insulin); injection site reactions. Note: reduce mealtime insulin 30-50% when starting (↑hypoglycaemia risk); nausea improves with slow titration; weight loss benefit; 3× daily SC before meals; not widely PBS-listed in Australia - private prescription; only amylin analogue available clinically.

Anti-type I interferon receptor subunit 1 (IFNAR1) monoclonal antibody (IgG1κ). MOA: blocks type I IFN receptor → ↓type I IFN signalling → suppresses interferon gene signature (IFN-high SLE patients respond better); SLE pathogenesis involves type I IFN overactivation. Indications: moderate-to-severe SLE with positive autoantibodies on standard therapy (HCQ ± immunosuppressants - TULIP-1/2 trials: BICLA response, ↓flares, corticosteroid-sparing). SE: URTI, herpes zoster (↓antiviral immunity - vaccinate Shingrix before starting - recombinant zoster vaccine), injection site reactions, infusion reactions. Note: IV infusion every 4 weeks; first anti-IFN therapy for SLE; IFN-high patients respond better (IFN gene signature test); reduce corticosteroids as SLE controlled; Shingrix vaccination BEFORE starting (live vaccines must be given ≥4 weeks before, or delay after last dose ≥4 weeks).

Anti-sclerostin monoclonal antibody (IgG2). MOA: sclerostin inhibits Wnt signalling → ↓osteoblast differentiation; romosozumab → ↓sclerostin → ↑Wnt → ↑bone formation + ↓bone resorption (dual anabolic + antiresorptive - unique mechanism). Indications: postmenopausal osteoporosis (high fracture risk - ≥1 vertebral fracture, T-score ≤−2.5, failed/intolerant to other agents - ARCH trial: superior fracture risk reduction vs alendronate). SE: injection site reactions, arthralgia, headache; ↑MACE (MI, stroke - boxed warning - numerically higher vs alendronate in ARCH). CI: recent MI or stroke within 12 months (absolute). Note: 12-month treatment course only (210 mg SC monthly × 12 doses - then mandatory switch to antiresorptive bisphosphonate to maintain gains); CI recent MI/stroke; TGA approved in Australia; significant vertebral fracture risk ↓ (~70%); follow with antiresorptive (alendronate or denosumab).

Anti-IL-6Rα monoclonal antibody (fully human IgG1). MOA: blocks IL-6 receptor α-subunit (both membrane-bound + soluble forms - same target as tocilizumab) → ↓IL-6-mediated JAK-STAT signalling → anti-inflammatory. Indications: moderate-to-severe RA (inadequate response to ≥1 DMARD - MONARCH trial: sarilumab monotherapy superior to adalimumab monotherapy in some outcomes). SE: neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, ↑LDL/HDL (class effect), ↑LFTs, URTI, herpes zoster; GI perforation (rare - history of diverticulitis). Note: SC injection every 2 weeks (200 mg); same IL-6R class as tocilizumab; monotherapy option in MTX-intolerant RA; available as monotherapy or combined with MTX; TGA approved in Australia.

Selective S1P receptor modulator (S1P₁/₄/₅ - avoids S1P₂/₃). MOA: S1P₁ agonism → functional antagonism (internalisation) → sequesters lymphocytes in secondary lymphoid organs → ↓gut-homing lymphocytes → ↓intestinal inflammation. Indications: moderately-to-severely active UC (inadequate response to conventional/biologic therapy - ELEVATE trials - 2 mg daily). SE: bradycardia + AV block (first dose - cardiovascular monitoring required: ECG pre-dose; monitor 4-6h after first dose if high cardiac risk); nasopharyngitis, pyrexia; lymphopenia; macular oedema (ophthalmic assessment pre-treatment in at-risk patients); pulmonary effects (rare). CI: recent MI/stroke/decompensated HF/severe arrhythmias; active infections; pregnancy (teratogenic). Note: UC indication (vs ozanimod - UC+MS; siponimod - MS); first-dose cardiac monitoring required; live vaccines contraindicated (at least 4 weeks before); no first-dose monitoring needed if low cardiac risk (check guidelines); check baseline cardiac status + ophthalmology.

β-Lactamase-stable carboxypenicillin. MOA: inhibits PBP3/PBP2 (like other β-lactams) but 6α-methoxy group confers stability to most plasmid-encoded β-lactamases (TEM, SHV, CTX-M ESBLs, AmpC) - NOT stable to metallo-β-lactamases (NDM) or carbapenemases (KPC, OXA-48). Indications: ESBL- and AmpC-producing gram-negative infections - UTI, bacteraemia, biliary/hepatobiliary infections (Klebsiella, E.coli, Enterobacter) - carbapenem-sparing agent. SE: GI upset, rash, injection site reactions, hypersensitivity (penicillin class). Note: NOT for carbapenem-resistant organisms (doesn't cover carbapenemases); NOT for Pseudomonas aeruginosa; IV administration; limited distribution (Belgium, UK - used as carbapenem-sparing for ESBL/AmpC infections to preserve carbapenem reserve); available in Australia via TGA Special Access Scheme.

Combination β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor: ceftazidime + avibactam (non-β-lactam diazabicyclooctane BLI). MOA: avibactam inhibits class A (KPC), class C (AmpC), class D (OXA-48) β-lactamases (NOT class B metallo-β-lactamases - NDM/VIM/IMP) → restores ceftazidime activity against carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CPE). Indications: KPC/OXA-48-producing CPE (UTI, HAP/VAP, IAI, bacteraemia); MDR Pseudomonas aeruginosa. SE: nausea, diarrhoea, headache, ↑LFTs; neurotoxicity (high doses + renal impairment - encephalopathy, seizures). Note: does NOT cover NDM-producing organisms (add aztreonam - ceftazidime-avibactam + aztreonam for NDM); renally cleared - dose adjust in AKI; resistance emerging (KPC mutations); hospital formulary use (specialist antimicrobial stewardship).

Novel cephalosporin/BLI combination: ceftolozane + tazobactam. MOA: ceftolozane binds PBP3 + PBP1b in Pseudomonas aeruginosa with high affinity → active against MDR strains (porin mutations, efflux overexpression, even some chromosomal AmpC); tazobactam inhibits TEM/SHV/CTX-M ESBLs. Indications: MDR Pseudomonas aeruginosa (HAP/VAP, complicated UTI, complicated IAI with metronidazole); NOT for carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales. SE: headache, nausea, diarrhoea, fever, ↑LFTs. Note: primarily for MDR Pseudomonas (no carbapenemase coverage - unlike ceftazidime-avibactam); PBP3-binding critical; sensitivity testing required before use; cannot use for CPE (use ceftazidime-avibactam for CPE); available in Australia (hospital formulary).

Siderophore cephalosporin (catechol-conjugated). MOA: catechol siderophore hijacks bacterial iron transport (TonB-dependent active uptake) → highly concentrated inside bacteria → inhibits PBP3 → bactericidal; stable to all 4 β-lactamase classes including metallo-β-lactamases (NDM, VIM, IMP) and all carbapenemases. Indications: carbapenem-resistant gram-negative infections (CRE, MDR Pseudomonas - CRPA, carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii - CRAB) where no alternatives exist - CREDIBLE-CR, APEKS-NP. SE: nausea, diarrhoea, ↑LFTs, hypokalaemia, candidiasis, fever. Note: unique siderophore mechanism overcomes all resistance including MBL; CREDIBLE-CR - numerically higher mortality vs best available care in Acinetobacter (interpret carefully - very sick patients); reserved for truly untreatable MDR gram-negatives; specialist antimicrobial stewardship prescription.

Aminomethylcycline tetracycline (next-generation tetracycline). MOA: binds 30S ribosomal subunit (like tetracycline) but 9-aminomethyl modification overcomes tet pump efflux + ribosomal protection resistance → broad activity including MRSA, macrolide-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae, atypicals. Indications: CAP (community-acquired bacterial pneumonia - OPTIC trial); ABSSSI (OASIS trial); atypicals (Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila). SE: nausea/vomiting (IV especially - pre-medicate with antiemetics; oral better tolerated), diarrhoea, photosensitivity, ↑LFTs; avoid in pregnancy (tetracycline class - dentition/bone). Note: IV + oral (switch therapy); oral once daily (fasted); no dose adjustment in renal/mild-moderate hepatic impairment; alternative to fluoroquinolones for CAP (MRSA + atypical coverage); TGA registration status in Australia - check current availability.

Lipoglycopeptide antibiotic (3rd-generation glycopeptide) - single-dose IV. MOA: triple mechanism - (1) inhibits peptidoglycan cross-linking (like vancomycin); (2) inhibits transglycosylation (unique); (3) membrane disruption; bactericidal; active against VRE, VRSA; half-life >100 hours. Indications: ABSSSI (acute bacterial skin/skin structure infections) - gram-positive (MRSA, streptococci, VRE) - single 1200 mg IV infusion. SE: phlebitis (IV), nausea, headache; falsely elevated PT/APTT/INR for ~5 days (lipid component interferes with coagulation assays - use anti-Xa or thrombin time instead; do NOT withhold anticoagulation based on fake coagulation result). Note: single-dose treatment → outpatient/day hospital use; APTT/PT/INR unreliable for 5 days post-dose (major drug interaction issue - alternative monitoring if anticoagulated); avoids hospitalisation.

Lipoglycopeptide antibiotic (2nd-generation glycopeptide) - once-weekly dosing. MOA: inhibits peptidoglycan synthesis at late stage (D-Ala-D-Ala) + membrane anchoring; long half-life (8-10 days). Indications: ABSSSI (gram-positive - MRSA, streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus); osteomyelitis (off-label - step-down consolidation); endocarditis (off-label - completing IV courses). SE: nausea, diarrhoea, headache, ↑LFTs; infusion reactions (Red Man-like - less than vancomycin); phlebitis. Note: once-weekly or two-dose regimen (1500 mg × 1 OR 1000 mg + 500 mg × 1 week apart) → early hospital discharge + outpatient completion (OPAT); accumulates in bone → osteomyelitis step-down data emerging; cost is significant; excellent gram-positive coverage including MRSA.

Human IgG1 monoclonal antibody targeting Clostridioides difficile toxin B. MOA: neutralises C.diff toxin B → prevents toxin binding to intestinal epithelium → ↓recurrence (does not kill C.diff - combine with antibiotic course). Indications: prevention of recurrent CDI in high-risk patients (age ≥65, severe CDI, immunocompromised, hypervirulent strain - ribotype 027, history of prior CDI - MODIFY I/II trials). Route: single IV infusion (10 mg/kg × 1) during standard antibiotic treatment. SE: cardiac failure exacerbation (↑risk in pre-existing CHF - caution/avoid); infusion reactions; headache, nausea, dizziness. Note: single dose only (given during antibiotic course - not a treatment for active CDI - for RECURRENCE prevention); NOT a replacement for antibiotics; cost-effectiveness debated; best reserved for high-recurrence-risk patients (elderly, multiple prior CDI, immunosuppressed).

First systemic pleuromutilin antibiotic (novel class in humans). MOA: binds 50S ribosomal subunit at peptidyl transferase centre (PTC) in unique 3D configuration → inhibits bacterial protein synthesis; no cross-resistance with existing antibiotics (binds distinct PTC site vs linezolid/chloramphenicol). Indications: CAP (community-acquired bacterial pneumonia - LEAP 1/2 trials); activity against S.pneumoniae, H.influenzae, atypicals (Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila), MRSA. SE: nausea, diarrhoea, ↑LFTs (hepatotoxicity); QTc prolongation (CYP3A4 substrate - avoid CYP3A4 inhibitors + QT-prolonging drugs); hypokalaemia. Note: IV + oral formulations; QTc monitoring required in at-risk patients; crosses BBB - potential CNS infections utility (investigational); novel class - no existing resistance in human pathogens at approval; alternative to fluoroquinolones for CAP.

8-Aminoquinoline antimalarial - long-acting analogue of primaquine. MOA: oxidative mechanism (requires G6PD activity for radical generation); active against P.vivax liver-stage hypnozoites (prevents relapse) + blood-stage parasites (broad multi-stage activity). Indications: radical cure of P.vivax malaria (eliminates hypnozoites → prevents relapse - DETECTIVE trial: single 300 mg dose non-inferior to 14-day primaquine); TGA approved 2019 (Kodatef) in Australia; also prophylaxis (Krintafel). SE: haemolytic anaemia (G6PD deficiency - severe/life-threatening - G6PD TESTING MANDATORY), methaemoglobinaemia, nausea, headache; psychiatric effects (anxiety, depression, psychosis - class 8-aminoquinoline effect). CI: G6PD deficiency (absolute), pregnancy, breastfeeding (until infant G6PD confirmed). Note: SINGLE DOSE (major advantage over 14-day primaquine - major adherence improvement); G6PD testing mandatory before prescribing; first new anti-relapse drug in 60 years; most imported P.vivax in Australia from PNG/SE Asia.

Arylaminoalcohol antimalarial - only used in combination with artemether. MOA: inhibits haem detoxification → accumulation of toxic haem in parasite → parasite death; preferentially active against trophozoite stage. Indications: uncomplicated P.falciparum malaria (as artemether-lumefantrine fixed-dose combination - Coartem/Riamet - 6 doses over 3 days; WHO recommended first-line ACT). SE: headache, dizziness, QTc prolongation (monitor - all antimalarials), nausea, abdominal pain, sleep disturbance, arthralgia/myalgia; hepatotoxicity (rare). Note: ONLY in combination with artemether (never alone - short artemether half-life → lumefantrine provides tail coverage and prevents resistance); MUST take with fatty meal (fat-soluble - bioavailability ↑4-5× with fat; counsel patients explicitly); globally most widely used ACT (artemether-lumefantrine).

Autologous lentiviral gene therapy - adds functional βA-T87Q-globin gene into patient's haematopoietic stem cells. MOA: ex vivo transduction of mobilised HSCs with lentiviral vector encoding βA-T87Q-globin gene → re-infusion after myeloablative conditioning → restored/new HbAT87Q production → ↓/eliminates red cell transfusion dependence. Indications: transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia (TDT) in patients ≥12 yr without matched sibling donor (HGB-207/HGB-212: ~89% transfusion-independent at 2 yr). Process: G-CSF+plerixafor HSC mobilisation → lentiviral transduction → busulfan myeloablative conditioning → one-time IV infusion. SE: myeloablation-related (mucositis, alopecia, cytopenias, infection, VOD/SOS - sinusoidal obstruction syndrome - busulfan); engraftment delays; insertional oncogenesis (theoretical - lentiviral; not yet observed in TDT). Note: one-time treatment → potentially curative; US-approved 2022; very high cost; specialised gene therapy centres only; alternative to allogeneic HSCT without needing matched sibling donor.

Dual ETA endothelin receptor + AT1 angiotensin II receptor antagonist (ERA + ARB combined). MOA: combined ETAR and AT1R blockade → ↓proteinuria + ↓glomerular hypertension in IgA nephropathy; endothelin contributes to podocyte injury + glomerular scarring in IgAN (PROTECT trial). Indications: IgA nephropathy (proteinuria ≥1 g/day despite optimised RASi - US-approved 2023; TGA status - check). SE: hypotension, hyperkalaemia, peripheral oedema; hepatotoxicity (REMS - LFT monitoring); anaemia. CI: pregnancy (REMS - teratogenic - dual contraception + monthly pregnancy tests); concurrent ACEi/ARB. Note: first non-immunosuppressive therapy approved specifically for IgAN; reduces proteinuria ~41% (vs ACEi ~9% - PROTECT 110-week data); endothelin + AT1 dual blockade provides superior proteinuria reduction vs ARB alone; hepatotoxicity monitoring required; consider if proteinuria persists despite maximal RASi optimisation.

Highly selective TTR (transthyretin) tetramer stabiliser. MOA: binds T4 (thyroxine) binding sites on TTR tetramer → stabilises native tetrameric structure → prevents misfolding/disaggregation → ↓amyloid fibril formation in ATTR amyloidosis; >99% TTR stabilisation (more potent than tafamidis - ~68% stabilisation). Indications: ATTR cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM - both wild-type and hereditary - ATTRibute-CM trial: significant ↓all-cause mortality + ↓CV hospitalisation; US-approved 2024). SE: nausea, constipation, arthralgia; generally well tolerated; no hepatotoxicity signal. Note: more potent TTR stabiliser than tafamidis; ATTRibute-CM trial positive outcomes similar to ATTR-ACT (tafamidis) - may supersede tafamidis in ATTR-CM; once-daily oral; also has ATTR-PN data (AG10-201 trial for polyneuropathy); head-to-head vs tafamidis pending.

2'-O-MOE antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) targeting TTR mRNA. MOA: hybridises to TTR mRNA → RNase H cleavage → ↓hepatic TTR protein production by ~80% → ↓amyloid substrate. Indications: hereditary ATTR polyneuropathy (hATTR-PN - NEURO-TTRansform trial) - SC injection weekly. SE: thrombocytopenia (serious - potentially fatal - REMS programme; platelet monitoring every 2 weeks mandatory), glomerulonephritis (renal monitoring required), injection site reactions, vitamin A deficiency (TTR is retinol-binding protein - ↓TTR → ↓vitamin A delivery → supplement). Note: weekly SC injection; platelet count monitoring every 2 weeks (REMS); vitamin A supplementation required; compare to eplontersen (monthly GalNAc-conjugated ASO - potentially less platelet risk) and patisiran (IV siRNA); REMS programme in US.

Next-generation GalNAc-conjugated ASO targeting TTR mRNA (LICA - ligand-conjugated ASO technology). MOA: GalNAc conjugation → hepatocyte ASGR receptor-mediated uptake → RNase H-mediated TTR mRNA cleavage → ↓TTR protein (~80%) at lower dose + less frequent dosing vs inotersen; monthly SC injection (vs weekly inotersen). Indications: hATTR polyneuropathy (hATTR-PN - NEURO-TTRansform trial). SE: thrombocytopenia (class ASO - GalNAc delivery may reduce systemic ASO exposure → potentially lower platelet risk vs inotersen), injection site reactions, vitamin A deficiency, renal effects. Note: monthly SC injection (vs weekly inotersen - improved adherence); GalNAc liver-targeted delivery → higher liver selectivity + lower systemic ASO exposure; still requires vitamin A supplementation + platelet/renal monitoring; evolution of inotersen platform; compare to patisiran (IV siRNA - monthly) and vutrisiran (GalNAc siRNA - quarterly).

Intrathecal ASO targeting SOD1 (superoxide dismutase 1) mRNA. MOA: intrathecal injection → CSF distribution → hybridises to SOD1 mRNA in motor neurons → RNase H cleavage → ↓mutant SOD1 protein (toxic gain-of-function) → slows ALS progression in SOD1-ALS. Indications: ALS with SOD1 gene mutation - VALOR trial (accelerated US approval 2023 based on NfL biomarker reduction; trend to slower functional decline). Route: intrathecal injection every 28 days (after 3 loading doses every 2 weeks). SE: myelitis/meningitis (immune-mediated spinal cord/meningeal inflammation - serious; CSF pleocytosis), headache (post-LP), falls, peripheral oedema. Note: first approved SOD1-ALS therapy; intrathecal (repeat LP every 4 weeks - requires procedure); SOD1 mutations ~2% of ALS (hereditary); neurofilament light chain (NfL) ↓ as biomarker of response (accelerated approval); CSF monitoring for pleocytosis; compassionate use in Australia.

Oral SMN2 pre-mRNA splicing modifier (small molecule). MOA: promotes SMN2 exon 7 inclusion → ↑full-length SMN2 mRNA → ↑functional SMN protein (compensating for absent/defective SMN1); systemic distribution (CNS + peripheral motor neurons - addresses all SMA-affected tissues). Indications: SMA (spinal muscular atrophy) types 1, 2, 3 (paediatric and adult - FIREFISH type 1; SUNFISH types 2-3; JEWELFISH pre-treated types 2-3). Route: oral liquid once daily. SE: well tolerated overall; photosensitivity (riboflavin in formulation - unrelated to drug itself); possible reproductive toxicity (contraception advised - women of childbearing potential); limited long-term safety data. Note: oral once-daily (vs nusinersen - intrathecal; onasemnogene - IV gene therapy); systemic CNS + peripheral distribution (nusinersen CNS-only via IT - risdiplam covers peripheral nerve/muscle too); adults with SMA benefit; photosensitivity counselling; growing evidence for later-onset/milder SMA.

Anti-IL-6Rα monoclonal antibody (humanised IgG2 - SMART-Ig technology for prolonged half-life). MOA: blocks IL-6 receptor α-subunit → ↓IL-6 signalling → ↓neuroinflammation; IL-6 drives astrocyte activation + AQP4-IgG seropositive attacks in NMOSD (neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder). Indications: NMOSD (AQP4-IgG seropositive - SAkuraStar [monotherapy] + SAkuraSky [add-on] trials: ↓annualised relapse rate 55-79%). Route: SC injection loading then every 4 weeks. SE: URTI, headache, arthralgia, ↑lipids, neutropenia; infection risk; hypersensitivity. Note: approved for AQP4-seropositive NMOSD (rare autoimmune demyelinating CNS disease - distinct from MS); NMOSD now has multiple approved therapies (satralizumab SC monthly, inebilizumab IV 6-monthly, eculizumab IV 2-weekly, ublituximab IV 6-monthly); satralizumab IL-6R target (distinct mechanism from anti-CD19 inebilizumab and anti-C5 eculizumab).

Anti-CD19 monoclonal antibody (humanised IgG1 - afucosylated for enhanced ADCC). MOA: depletes CD19+ B-cells (broader than anti-CD20 - includes plasmablasts + some plasma cells that express CD19 but not CD20) → ↓AQP4-IgG producing B-cells → prevents NMOSD attacks. Indications: NMOSD (AQP4-IgG seropositive - N-MOmentum trial: 73% ↓attack risk vs placebo; some benefit in AQP4-seronegative). Route: IV infusion 300 mg × 2 (Day 1 + Day 15 loading) then every 6 months. SE: UTI, nasopharyngitis, arthralgia, headache, infusion reactions; B-cell depletion (↑infection risk - avoid live vaccines, PJP prophylaxis in some protocols); hypogammaglobulinaemia (monitor Ig levels). Note: anti-CD19 provides broader B-cell depletion vs anti-CD20 (rituximab) - includes plasmablasts and plasma cells; NMOSD indication; convenient 6-monthly infusion; AQP4-IgG seropositive patients respond best; distinct mechanism from satralizumab (IL-6R) and eculizumab (C5).

Anti-amyloid β protofibril monoclonal antibody (IgG1). MOA: selectively binds soluble Aβ protofibrils (oligomers and small aggregates - thought to be most toxic species) → promotes clearance → ↓amyloid plaque burden; biweekly IV infusion. Indications: early Alzheimer's disease (MCI or mild dementia due to AD confirmed by amyloid PET/CSF - CLARITY-AD trial: 27% ↓CDR-SB decline at 18 months; US-approved 2023). SE: ARIA (amyloid-related imaging abnormalities) - ARIA-E (oedema/effusion) and ARIA-H (microhaemorrhages/haemosiderosis) - monitored by MRI; symptomatic ARIA: headache, confusion, focal deficits; infusion reactions; APOE ε4 carriers at higher ARIA risk. Note: APOE ε4 homozygotes - substantially higher ARIA risk (may be contraindicated); MRI monitoring protocol mandatory; symptomatic ARIA → pause/stop; costs and access significant barriers; trial in confirmed amyloid-positive patients only (amyloid PET or CSF Aβ42/tau ratio).

Anti-amyloid β plaque monoclonal antibody (IgG1 targeting N-terminal pyroglutamate form of Aβ - found only in plaques). MOA: targets deposited Aβ plaques → plaque removal → slows neurodegeneration; IV infusion every 4 weeks; treatment may stop once amyloid cleared (titrated to amyloid burden - unique). Indications: early symptomatic AD (MCI or mild dementia, amyloid and tau confirmed - TRAILBLAZER-ALZ2 trial: 35% ↓CDR-SB decline at 18 months in low/medium tau subgroup - US-approved 2024). SE: ARIA-E (oedema) and ARIA-H (microhaemorrhages) - higher rate than lecanemab; infusion reactions; headache; APOE ε4 homozygotes at markedly ↑risk. Note: quarterly infusions (vs biweekly lecanemab - potential adherence advantage); treatment can stop when amyloid cleared (confirmed on PET - unique 'stop when done' approach); APOE ε4 genotyping essential; MRI monitoring required; choose between lecanemab and donanemab based on ARIA risk, convenience, and availability.

Anti-CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide) monoclonal antibody - IV quarterly. MOA: binds CGRP ligand → blocks CGRP receptor signalling → ↓meningeal vasodilation and sensitisation involved in migraine. Indications: preventive treatment of migraine (PROMISE-1/2 trials: 30 mg IV → significant migraine day reduction; rapid onset within 24h of first infusion - unique among anti-CGRP mAbs). Route: IV infusion 100 mg or 300 mg every 3 months (quarterly). SE: hypersensitivity/infusion reactions (most common; mostly mild), nasopharyngitis, fatigue, constipation. Note: IV administration (vs SC fremanezumab/galcanezumab/erenumab - monthly or quarterly SC); fastest onset (24h post-infusion - useful if needing rapid migraine control); quarterly dosing; no interaction with standard migraine medications; class contraindication: cardiovascular disease caution (CGRP role in vasodilation).

Oral CGRP receptor antagonist (gepant class) - preventive migraine. MOA: blocks CGRP receptor → ↓meningeal vasodilation and peripheral/central sensitisation involved in migraine generation. Indications: preventive treatment of episodic and chronic migraine (ADVANCE, ELEVATE, PROGRESS trials - significant ↓monthly migraine days). SE: nausea, constipation, fatigue; liver enzyme elevations (rare); weight loss. Note: oral once-daily preventive therapy (vs SC anti-CGRP mAbs - monthly/quarterly); gepant class includes: atogepant (prevention), ubrogepant (acute), rimegepant (both - already present); no cardiovascular limitations of triptans → can be used in triptan-contraindicated patients; CYP3A4 interactions.

Oral CGRP receptor antagonist (gepant) - acute migraine. MOA: blocks CGRP receptor → ↓meningeal neurogenic inflammation and vasodilation during acute migraine attack; does not cause vasoconstriction (unlike triptans). Indications: acute treatment of migraine (ACHIEVE-1/2 trials - significantly ↑pain freedom and symptom relief at 2h vs placebo). SE: nausea, somnolence, dry mouth; elevated LFTs (rare). Note: no contraindication in cardiovascular disease (unlike triptans - vasoconstriction); can be used when triptans fail or contraindicated; gepant class; take at onset of migraine; second dose 2h later if insufficient response; CYP3A4 - avoid strong inhibitors/inducers; available in Australia (TGA approved).

Intranasal CGRP receptor antagonist (gepant) - acute migraine. MOA: blocks CGRP receptor via nasal mucosal absorption → rapid systemic exposure → ↓migraine-related vasodilation and sensitisation. Indications: acute migraine treatment (COURAGE trials - 10 mg intranasal spray: 24% pain freedom at 2h vs 15% placebo - US-approved 2023). Route: intranasal spray (10 mg single dose - repeat permitted after 4h). SE: nasal discomfort, dysgeusia (bitter taste - class gepant effect), nausea. Note: intranasal route - useful in migraine with vomiting (when oral impractical); faster onset than oral gepants (similar to intranasal triptans); unique route in gepant class; avoid strong CYP3A4 inhibitors; alternative to intranasal triptans in cardiovascular disease.

Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody (chimeric IgG1 - glycoengineered for enhanced ADCC). MOA: depletes CD20+ B-cells → ↓inflammatory B-cell activity in MS; glycoengineering (lower fucosylation) → enhanced natural killer cell-mediated ADCC → more potent B-cell depletion than rituximab at similar doses. Indications: relapsing forms of MS (CIS, RRMS, active SPMS - ULTIMATE I/II trials vs teriflunomide - significant ↓ARR + no evidence of disease activity). Route: IV infusion 150 mg over 1h × 2 (week 0 + week 2 loading) → then 450 mg over 1h every 6 months. SE: infusion reactions (premedicate: methylprednisolone + antihistamine + paracetamol), URTI, headache; B-cell depletion (↑infection risk, avoid live vaccines); PML risk (JC virus - monitor). Note: rapid 1-hour infusion (vs ocrelizumab - 3.5h; rituximab - 4-8h - glycoengineering allows lower dose); every-6-months dosing; similar efficacy class to ocrelizumab; check JC virus antibody status before starting.

Oral fumarate prodrug - improved GI tolerability vs dimethyl fumarate. MOA: prodrug hydrolysed to monomethyl fumarate (active metabolite - same as DMF) → activates Nrf2 pathway → antioxidant + immunomodulatory → ↓inflammatory T-cell activity in MS. Indications: relapsing forms of MS (CIS, RRMS, active SPMS - bioequivalent to dimethyl fumarate - EVOLVE-MS-1/2 trials - superior GI tolerability). SE: GI (flushing, nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal pain - significantly less than dimethyl fumarate - EVOLVE-MS-2: 34% vs 49% GI tolerability events); lymphopenia (monitor). Note: same active metabolite as dimethyl fumarate (MMF) but different ester - improved GI tolerability (key reason to prefer vs DMF); twice-daily oral; take with food (↓flushing + GI); switch from DMF to diroximel without washout; lymphocyte count monitoring (withhold if severe lymphopenia <0.5×10⁹/L persistent >6 months → PML risk assessment).

Immediate-release oral monomethyl fumarate (MMF) - active metabolite of dimethyl fumarate and diroximel fumarate. MOA: directly activates Nrf2 pathway (hydroxycarboxylic acid receptor 2 - HCAR2) → antioxidant + ↓NF-κB + ↓inflammatory T-cells in MS; avoids hepatic first-pass metabolism to produce MMF (unlike DMF prodrug). Indications: relapsing forms of MS (EVOLVE-MS trials - bioequivalent to DMF; RRMS maintenance). SE: flushing, GI effects (similar to or potentially less than DMF due to direct MMF form - dose-related); lymphopenia. Note: 190 mg twice daily (vs DMF 240 mg BD - different dose); rationale: direct MMF bypasses monomethyl fumarate production step → potentially more predictable pharmacokinetics; not widely used vs diroximel fumarate (the preferred improved-GI-tolerability fumarate); lymphocyte monitoring required.

Potassium (K⁺) channel blocker (voltage-gated K⁺ channels - Kv1.x family) - MS walking improvement. MOA: K⁺ channel blockade → prolongs action potential → improves conduction in demyelinated axons → ↑motor function (walking speed/endurance) in MS patients with walking impairment. Indications: improvement of walking in adults with MS who have demonstrated walking disability (RRMS, PPMS, SPMS - Timed 25-Foot Walk responder trials). SE: UTI (most common), insomnia, dizziness, headache, balance disturbance, nausea; SEIZURE (dose-dependent - narrow therapeutic index - CI in epilepsy). CI: epilepsy/seizure history (absolute), renal impairment (eGFR <50 - renally cleared → ↑seizure risk). Note: only drug approved specifically for walking improvement in MS (not disease-modifying - symptomatic only); 10 mg BD (sustained release); responder testing recommended (Timed 25-FW ↑ of ≥20% at 2 doses = responder - continue; no improvement → stop); also called dalfampridine (US) / fampridine (Australia).

Serotonin-releasing agent (low-dose antiepileptic formulation) - distinct from high-dose anorectic use. MOA: releases serotonin (5-HT) from presynaptic terminals + weak 5-HT2C agonist + σ1 receptor modulation → activates inhibitory interneurons and serotonergic circuits → ↓seizure frequency; mechanism in Dravet syndrome partially unclear. Indications: Dravet syndrome (SCN1A mutation or equivalent - STUDIO trial: 60-80% responder rate - significant seizure reduction combined with clobazam; Lennox-Gastaut syndrome [LGS] - CONSTELATION). SE: decreased appetite/weight, diarrhoea, fatigue, somnolence; potential valvulopathy/pulmonary hypertension (cardiac echocardiography monitoring mandatory - at low doses used in Fintepla this risk appears low but requires surveillance - REMS programme). Note: contraindicated in obesity treatment (high-dose fenfluramine history - cardiac valvulopathy; current low-dose Fintepla formulation requires regular echo monitoring); combined with clobazam for Dravet; TGA-approved in Australia; not for use as weight-loss drug.

Third-generation antiseizure medication - GABAergic and pharmacokinetic mechanisms. MOA: (1) positive GABAA receptor allosteric modulator (distinct site from benzodiazepines); (2) inhibits GABA reuptake; (3) CYP enzyme inhibition → ↑valproate + clobazam + norclobazam levels (pharmacokinetic potentiation - most clinically relevant). Indications: Dravet syndrome (adjunctive with clobazam + valproate - STICLO trials; EU/TGA licensed specifically for SCN1A-confirmed Dravet) - significant seizure reduction in this intractable epilepsy syndrome. SE: somnolence, ataxia, diplopia, nausea, anorexia, weight loss; pharmacokinetic interactions (↑clobazam/valproate levels - dose reduce). Note: pharmacokinetic interaction is clinically exploited (↑clobazam → ↑active metabolite norclobazam → potentiation); given with food (sprinkled in food - oral sachets/capsules); specific Dravet syndrome indication - not used broadly outside this; monitor LFTs and FBC (valproate-combination monitoring); always in combination with clobazam + valproate.

Triazole anti-seizure medication - Na⁺ channel modulator. MOA: sodium channel modulator (prolongs inactivation state - reduces rapid repetitive firing) - different binding site from carbamazepine/phenytoin; also may reduce glutamate release. Indications: adjunctive treatment of seizures associated with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS - particularly tonic and atonic/drop attacks - LGS trial: 33% ↓drop attack frequency). SE: somnolence, dizziness, headache, diplopia, nausea, vomiting; QTc shortening (dose-dependent - caution in familial short QT, Na channel agents); appetite/weight ↓. CI: familial short QT syndrome. Note: specific LGS indication (tonic/atonic 'drop attacks' - helps with most refractory aspect of LGS); QTc shortening (opposite direction to most drugs - screen for short QT); titrate over weeks; restricted use in Australian PBS - LGS indication only.

3rd-generation sodium channel blocker (voltage-gated Na⁺ channels) - prodrug of S-licarbazepine. MOA: prodrug (acetate) → rapid hydrolysis to S-licarbazepine (active) → selective slow-inactivation state Na⁺ channel binding → reduces high-frequency neuronal firing; more selective for slow-inactivated state than carbamazepine (fewer off-target effects). Indications: focal (partial) onset seizures - adjunctive or monotherapy in adults (ELAN trials). SE: dizziness, somnolence, diplopia, abnormal coordination, nausea, headache; hyponatraemia (Na⁺ channel class - less than carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine - 3rd gen improvement); ↑LFTs. Note: once-daily dosing (vs oxcarbazepine twice daily - adherence advantage); less hyponatraemia than oxcarbazepine and carbamazepine; once-daily S-licarbazepine enantiomer (vs oxcarbazepine - racemic licarbazepine prodrug); fewer drug interactions than carbamazepine (less CYP induction); available in Australia.

Adenosine A2A receptor antagonist - adjunct for Parkinson's disease OFF episodes. MOA: A2A receptors on striatal indirect pathway neurons modulate motor output; A2A antagonism → ↓indirect pathway overactivity → ↑dopaminergic tone in motor circuits without direct dopamine → reduces OFF time. Indications: adjunct to levodopa/carbidopa in adults with PD experiencing OFF episodes (KYOWA studies; US-approved 2019 - Japan extensively used since 2013). SE: dyskinesia (↑risk with levodopa - most common), dizziness, constipation, hallucinations, nausea; ↑LFTs. Note: non-dopaminergic mechanism (adenosinergic - novel adjunct); reduces daily OFF time by ~0.5-1h; does not worsen motor complications as much as increasing levodopa; xanthine derivative (related to caffeine - A1/A2A antagonism of caffeine may explain epidemiological association between coffee consumption and lower PD risk).

Synthetic amino acid - direct noradrenaline precursor. MOA: converted to noradrenaline (noradrenaline) by DOPA decarboxylase in peripheral sympathetic neurons → ↑peripheral vasomotor tone → ↑blood pressure on standing → ↓neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (NOH). Indications: symptomatic neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (NOH) in PD, MSA (multiple system atrophy), PAF (pure autonomic failure), non-diabetic autonomic neuropathy - STOPP trials. SE: headache, dizziness, nausea, hypertension (supine hypertension - elevate head of bed 30°); worsening CHF (avoid). CI: severe supine hypertension, CHF. Note: NOH treatment (unlike midodrine - alpha agonist; droxidopa acts centrally and peripherally by converting to noradrenaline); avoid supine hypertension - measure lying BP; encourage head elevation; take dose timing to avoid supine hypertension at night (last dose by 5pm); only for neurogenic OH (not all OH).

Adeno-associated virus 9 (AAV9) gene therapy delivering functional SMN1 gene. MOA: recombinant AAV9 vector containing codon-optimised human SMN1 cDNA under ubiquitous promoter → one-time IV infusion → AAV transduces motor neurons (AAV9 crosses BBB) → sustained SMN protein expression → prevents/reverses motor neuron degeneration in SMA. Indications: SMA (spinal muscular atrophy) in children ≤2 yr - SMA type 1 (symptomatic) and pre-symptomatic (newborn screening detected SMA - SMN2 copies 1-3). STR1VE/SPR1NT trials. SE: elevated LFTs (hepatotoxicity - prednisolone prophylaxis course required); thrombocytopenia; fever; vomiting; respiratory failure (transient - hospital monitoring); anti-AAV9 antibodies (baseline titre must be below threshold - retesting if exposed previously). Note: ONE-TIME IV infusion → sustained SMN protein → significant motor milestone achievement; very high cost (~$2.1-4 million AUD); PBS listed in Australia under strict criteria; prednisolone cover for hepatotoxicity (3 months); anti-AAV9 antibody testing mandatory pre-treatment; weight limit in some jurisdictions.

Highly selective VMAT2 (vesicular monoamine transporter 2) inhibitor. MOA: depletes monoamine storage in presynaptic vesicles → ↓dopamine release from striatal terminals → ↓dopaminergic overactivity driving repetitive involuntary movements of tardive dyskinesia. Indications: tardive dyskinesia (TD) in adults on antipsychotics (KINECT 3/4 trials - significant ↓AIMS score). SE: somnolence (most common - dose-related), QTc prolongation (dose-related - use caution with QT-prolonging drugs), akathisia (rare), depression (boxed warning - ↑risk of depression/suicidal ideation in HD - watch for), parkinsonism (dopamine depletion). Note: VMAT2 inhibitor class (tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine) for hyperkinesias; valbenazine = highly selective VMAT2 (no MAO inhibition + no CYP2D6 concerns - unlike tetrabenazine); once-daily dosing (40 mg → 80 mg - titrate); preferred first-line TD therapy; do NOT stop antipsychotic abruptly if TD develops (worsens).

Deuterium-substituted tetrabenazine - VMAT2 inhibitor. MOA: same as tetrabenazine (VMAT2 inhibition → ↓presynaptic dopamine storage/release) but deuterium substitution slows CYP2D6 metabolism → longer half-life → smoother drug levels → twice-daily dosing (vs tetrabenazine 3× daily) + lower peak-trough variability → fewer adverse effects. Indications: tardive dyskinesia (AIM-TD - AIMS score improvement); Huntington's chorea (HD - FIRST-HD trial). SE: somnolence, diarrhoea, depression (boxed warning - monitor; ↑depression/suicidal ideation in HD - not contraindicated but close monitoring); QTc prolongation; akathisia, parkinsonism. CI: active depression with suicidal ideation, hepatic impairment, concomitant MAO-inhibitors. Note: twice-daily dosing (vs tetrabenazine 3×/day) - smoother CYP2D6 metabolism via deuterium substitution; used for both TD and Huntington's chorea; genotype CYP2D6 (poor metabolisers → ↑exposure - dose cap); less depression risk than tetrabenazine in practice.

VMAT2 (vesicular monoamine transporter 2) inhibitor - original hyperkinesia treatment. MOA: reversible VMAT2 inhibition → depletes presynaptic monoamine vesicles → ↓dopamine, serotonin, noradrenaline → ↓dopaminergic overactivity in striatum → ↓hyperkinetic movements (chorea, dystonia, tardive dyskinesia). Indications: Huntington's chorea (chorea - moderate-severe); hemiballismus; tardive dyskinesia/tardive dystonia. SE: somnolence (dose-limiting), depression (including suicidal ideation - boxed warning - frequent monitoring; CI in untreated depression), akathisia, parkinsonism (dopamine depletion), QTc prolongation. CI: depression with suicidal ideation (absolute), hepatic impairment, concomitant MAO-inhibitors. Note: original VMAT2 inhibitor (tetrabenazine → largely replaced by deutetrabenazine [less depression risk, twice-daily] and valbenazine for TD); CYP2D6 metabolism → genotyping recommended; 3× daily dosing; boxed warning depression warning critical; still used in Huntington's chorea where PBS-listed in Australia.

Anti-IL-13 monoclonal antibody (high-affinity IgG4 - blocks IL-13 receptor signalling). MOA: binds IL-13 → prevents IL-13 receptor type II signalling → ↓type 2 inflammation, ↓TSLP production, ↓IgE, ↑skin barrier function; IL-13 is key driver of Th2/eosinophilic inflammation in atopic dermatitis (AD). Indications: moderate-severe atopic dermatitis (adults - ADhere trials: significant EASI-75 and IGA response; SC every 2 weeks × 16 weeks → responders to monthly maintenance). SE: conjunctivitis, injection site reactions, URTI, herpes virus infections; injection site pain. Note: IL-13 selective (vs dupilumab - anti-IL-4Rα - blocks both IL-4 and IL-13); lebrikizumab and tralokinumab are IL-13 specific vs dupilumab (IL-4 + IL-13); TGA approved in Australia; monthly maintenance after induction in responders; compare to tralokinumab (same target - anti-IL-13 - similar efficacy).

Anti-IL-31 receptor A (IL-31Rα) monoclonal antibody. MOA: IL-31 is key mediator of itch (pruritus) in atopic dermatitis and prurigo nodularis - binds IL-31Rα → blocks IL-31 signalling in sensory neurons and skin cells → ↓neuroinflammation and itch perception; also reduces skin inflammation. Indications: moderate-severe atopic dermatitis (AD - ARCADIA trials); prurigo nodularis (PN - OLYMPIA trials - significant nodule reduction and itch). SE: injection site reactions, URTI, nausea, headache, atopic dermatitis exacerbation (transient). Note: primarily targets the itch mechanism (IL-31 is the major 'itch cytokine' in AD/PN) - dual anti-itch and anti-inflammatory effects; SC every 4 weeks; prurigo nodularis indication - TGA-approved in Australia; different target from dupilumab (IL-4Rα) - can be combined or used alternatively; rapid itch relief within weeks.

Peripheral κ-opioid receptor agonist (selective, peripherally restricted - does not cross BBB). MOA: activates κ-opioid receptors on peripheral sensory neurons and immune cells (itch-mediating C-fibres in skin and viscera) → ↓neuronal itch signalling + ↓immune-mediated pruritus; peripherally restricted (avoids CNS kappa effects - dysphoria, psychotomimetic). Indications: moderate-to-severe chronic kidney disease-associated pruritus (CKD-aP) in adults on haemodialysis - KALM-1/2 trials: 40-50% of patients achieved ≥3-point NRS itch reduction; IV at each haemodialysis session (3× weekly). SE: diarrhoea, dizziness, nausea, mental status changes (rare - peripherally restricted but minimal CNS effects possible), gait disturbance. Note: IV at haemodialysis (3× weekly); first in class for CKD-aP; peripheral restriction avoids kappa CNS side effects (dysphoria, sedation, hallucinations of central kappa agonists); licensed in Australia; oral formulation under investigation (for non-dialysis CKD pruritus).

Humanised anti-GD2 monoclonal antibody (IgG1). MOA: binds GD2 (ganglioside - overexpressed on neuroblastoma cells + CNS tissue) → ADCC, CDC, ADCP → tumour cell killing; central nervous system penetration (humanised - crosses blood-brain barrier better than chimeric dinutuximab). Indications: R/R high-risk neuroblastoma in bone and/or bone marrow in partial response/complete response/minor response to prior therapy - US FDA accelerated approval 2020; paediatric use. Route: IV + SC (combined regimen). SE: infusion pain (severe - premedicate: morphine/gabapentin, antihistamine, ketamine - GD2 expressed on pain fibres → pain with infusion); fever; vomiting; hypotension; urticaria; capillary leak syndrome. Note: premedication for pain is essential and complex (GD2 expression on C-fibres → intense pain with anti-GD2 antibodies - protocol adherence critical); limited to specialist paediatric oncology centres; combined with GM-CSF and IL-2 (same schedule as dinutuximab approaches - check institutional protocol).

Chimeric anti-GD2 monoclonal antibody (IgG1 - ch14.18) - targeting ganglioside GD2 on neuroblastoma. MOA: GD2-directed ADCC + CDC → neuroblastoma cell death; combined with cytokines (GM-CSF, IL-2) to enhance efficacy. Indications: high-risk neuroblastoma (paediatric - consolidation after high-dose chemotherapy + ASCT - COG ANBL0032 trial: ↑OS from 46% to 66% vs standard; US-approved 2015; dinutuximab beta [Quarziba] for relapse/refractory). SE: severe infusion pain (GD2 on C-fibres - IV morphine required during infusion - dose-limiting; complex multi-drug premedication protocol), fever, vomiting, capillary leak, urticaria, hypotension, neurotoxicity; peripheral neuropathy. Note: complex premedication protocol (morphine + gabapentin/pregabalin + antihistamine + corticosteroid - institutional protocol); given over 10h continuous IV with nurse monitoring for pain/anaphylaxis; specialist paediatric oncology only; combined with GM-CSF + IL-2 ± 13-cis-retinoic acid.

Anti-IL-33 monoclonal antibody. MOA: binds IL-33 → prevents binding to ST2 receptor → ↓type 2/eosinophilic airway inflammation; IL-33 released by damaged epithelium → triggers mast cells, eosinophils, ILC2s → asthma exacerbations + eosinophilic inflammation. Indications: moderate-severe asthma - SOLSTICE trial (high T2 inflammation - blood eosinophils ≥300/μL OR FeNO ≥25ppb: significant ↓exacerbation rate); also under investigation for COVID-19 respiratory illness and other T2-mediated conditions. SE: URTI, headache, injection site reactions; well tolerated overall. Note: IL-33 target (vs tezepelumab - anti-TSLP [upstream of IL-33]; mepolizumab/benralizumab - anti-IL-5; dupilumab - IL-4/13); SC injection every 4 weeks; regulatory status - check TGA approval status in Australia as this drug was in late-stage trials at knowledge cutoff.

Next-generation type II pan-RAF inhibitor (oral, brain-penetrant). MOA: inhibits RAF kinase family (BRAF, CRAF, Class 1/2/3 mutants) including BRAF V600E/non-V600E and RAS-mutant RAF dimers; type II binding mode → active against paradox activation-resistant tumours; penetrates blood-brain barrier (important for CNS tumours). Indications: BRAF V600E-mutated recurrent/refractory paediatric low-grade glioma (LGG) - FIREFLY-1 trial: ORR 67%; US-approved 2024; weekly oral dosing (once weekly). SE: elevated CPK (myopathy), hair colour change (graying/depigmentation - class RAF inhibitor effect), photosensitivity, fatigue, diarrhoea, QTc prolongation. Note: once-weekly oral dosing (unique - adherence advantage in paediatric oncology); brain-penetrant (designed for CNS tumours); BRAF V600E mutation testing required; paediatric LGG is most common paediatric brain tumour - BRAF alterations in ~50%; compare to dabrafenib-trametinib (BRAF+MEK combination - standard for BRAF V600E adult melanoma - also used in paediatric LGG).

Cardiac myosin ATPase inhibitor (allosteric) - first-in-class for obstructive HCM. MOA: inhibits cardiac myosin ATPase → ↓number of myosin-actin cross-bridges in super-relaxed state → ↓contractility → relieves LVOT obstruction (reduces hypercontractility rather than causing ischaemia/negative inotropy from other drugs). Indications: symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HOCM - EXPLORER-HCM trial: significant ↓LVOT gradient, ↑exercise capacity, ↓NT-proBNP, ↑NYHA class). SE: systolic dysfunction (excessive myosin inhibition → reversible ↓LVEF - hold if LVEF <50%; REMS programme - mandatory LVEF monitoring by echo); dizziness, syncope; heart failure exacerbation. Note: REMS programme (Camzyos REMS - mandatory echo monitoring at baseline, 4, 8, 12 weeks, then every 12 weeks - safety critical); stop if LVEF <50% → restart at lower dose when recovered; CYP2C19 substrate (moderate) + inhibitor interactions; alternative to septal reduction therapy (alcohol ablation/myectomy); oral daily.

Next-generation cardiac myosin inhibitor (similar class to mavacamten). MOA: selectively inhibits cardiac myosin ATPase → ↓myosin cross-bridge formation → ↓LVOT obstruction without excessive negative inotropy; potentially faster offset kinetics than mavacamten (shorter t½). Indications: obstructive HCM (SEQUOIA-HCM trial - US-approved 2024 - significant ↓LVOT gradient and improvement in exercise capacity, NT-proBNP, symptoms). SE: LVEF reduction (monitor by echo - mandatory LVEF monitoring protocol as per SEQUOIA REMS; hold if LVEF <50%), dizziness, fatigue. Note: SEQUOIA-HCM was positive (similar endpoint improvements to EXPLORER-HCM for mavacamten); faster elimination than mavacamten (shorter washout - potentially useful if need rapid drug removal, e.g. before procedures); echo monitoring mandatory; CYP2C19 interaction profile - check vs mavacamten; oral daily.

Soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) stimulator - for HFrEF. MOA: directly stimulates sGC AND sensitises sGC to low endogenous NO → ↑cGMP → systemic and pulmonary vasodilation + ↓afterload + anti-fibrotic effects in cardiac myocytes; targets the impaired NO-sGC-cGMP pathway in HF. Indications: symptomatic HFrEF (LVEF <45%) in high-risk patients recently hospitalised for worsening HF or requiring IV diuretics (VICTORIA trial: 10% ↓composite HF death/HF hospitalisation vs placebo - significant; ARR 4.2%; moderate benefit). SE: hypotension (most common - monitor BP), anaemia (possible); well tolerated overall. CI: pregnancy (REMS required - teratogenic), concurrent PDE5 inhibitors (additive hypotension - same caution as riociguat). Note: indicated for HIGH-RISK HFrEF (recently hospitalised/worsening) - NOT for all HFrEF; different from riociguat (which is for PAH and CTEPH - NOT for LV dysfunction); complements standard HFrEF therapy (ARNI/ACEi + β-blocker + MRA + SGLT2i); oral once-daily with food.

Dual PDE3/PDE4 inhibitor - inhaled nebulisation - COPD. MOA: PDE3 inhibition → ↑cAMP → bronchodilation + ↓mast cell mediator release; PDE4 inhibition → ↑cAMP → anti-inflammatory (↓neutrophil/macrophage activation); dual bronchodilator + anti-inflammatory by single inhaled agent; inhaled route reduces systemic PDE4 side effects (nausea/GI - the limiting effect of oral roflumilast). Indications: COPD maintenance (ENHANCE-1/2 trials: added to LAMA, LABA, or LAMA+LABA - significant lung function improvement; US-approved 2024 - nebulised). SE: diarrhoea, nausea (oral PDE4 class effects - reduced with inhaled; mild), URTI, headache. Note: only dual PDE3/PDE4 inhaled agent (vs oral roflumilast - PDE4 only; vs nebulised bronchodilators - no anti-inflammatory component); nebulised twice daily (add-on to existing COPD regimens - LAMA ± LABA); combined mechanism may fill gap between bronchodilation and anti-inflammatory therapy in COPD.

MC4R (melanocortin-4 receptor) agonist - targeted monogenic/syndromic obesity therapy. MOA: activates MC4R in hypothalamus → ↑satiety signalling → ↓hunger + ↑metabolic rate; MC4R pathway is disrupted in POMC/PCSK1/LEP/LEPR deficiency and in Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS) - setmelanotide restores downstream signalling. Indications: monogenic obesity due to POMC/PCSK1/LEPR deficiency (RHYTHM-2/3 trials - significant weight loss ~20-25% from baseline); Bardet-Biedl syndrome (RHYTHM-3 trial). SE: hyperpigmentation (melanocortin skin effect - MC1R stimulation → ↑melanin - common, cosmetically significant, reversible on dose reduction), injection site reactions, nausea, spontaneous erections (MC4R central), depression. CI: do not use without confirmed genetic diagnosis (pathway mutation). Note: genotype-guided therapy (sequence POMC, LEPR, PCSK1 - confirm LOF mutation before prescribing); dramatic weight loss in truly MC4R-deficient patients; ineffective without underlying genetic deficiency; orphan drug with restricted access; SC daily injection.

Highly selective β3-adrenoceptor agonist (OAB therapy). MOA: activates β3-AR on detrusor smooth muscle → ↑cAMP → detrusor relaxation + ↑bladder capacity → ↓urgency, ↓frequency, ↓urgency incontinence episodes; more selective for β3-AR than mirabegron → potentially fewer cardiac/BP effects. Indications: overactive bladder (OAB) with urge incontinence, urgency, frequency (EMPOWUR trial vs placebo; also vs tolterodine). SE: headache, URTI, nasopharyngitis; minimal cardiac effects (β3 selectivity - vs mirabegron which has some β1 effects → BP/HR changes); constipation. Note: β3-AR selectivity provides cardiovascular safety advantage vs less-selective β3-agonists; once-daily oral (75 mg); does not require dose adjustment in renal/hepatic impairment (unlike mirabegron); alternative to antimuscarinic OAB therapy (avoid dry mouth, cognition, constipation); can be combined with antimuscarinics; TGA approved in Australia.

Selective S1P₁ receptor modulator (high S1P₁ selectivity - minimal S1P₃/S1P₄ activity vs fingolimod). MOA: S1P₁ agonism → functional receptor internalisation on lymphocytes → sequestration of lymphocytes in secondary lymphoid organs → ↓autoreactive T- and B-cell trafficking to CNS. Indications: relapsing-remitting MS (OPTIMUM trial - superior to teriflunomide on ARR and brain volume loss at 2 years). SE: first-dose bradycardia/AV block (mandatory 4-6h cardiac monitoring on Day 1 - ECG required; titration schedule over 14 days to minimise); macular oedema (ophthalmology pre-treatment assessment in at-risk patients); ↑LFTs; hypertension; URTI; herpes zoster reactivation. CI: recent MI/stroke/decompensated HF/advanced AV block, active infections, pregnancy. Note: first-dose cardiac monitoring mandatory (clinic observation - arrange as day procedure); 14-day titration schedule to reduce first-dose cardiac effects; once-daily oral tablet; selective S1P₁ (theoretically less bradycardia/AV block vs non-selective fingolimod - though still requires monitoring); available in Australia (PBS listed for RRMS).

Synthetic corticosteroid (oxazoline derivative of prednisolone) - preferred for Duchenne muscular dystrophy. MOA: glucocorticoid receptor agonist → anti-inflammatory + immunosuppression + stabilises muscle membrane function (mechanism in DMD partially unclear - reduces inflammation, fibrosis, immune cell infiltration in dystrophic muscle); ↓mineralocorticoid effects vs equivalent prednisolone → less weight gain + comparable anti-inflammatory potency.
