Indications: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) - slows disease progression (ambulatory maintenance, delays loss of respiratory function); also general corticosteroid uses. SE: weight gain (less than prednisolone - key advantage in DMD), growth retardation, Cushing's features, osteoporosis (supplemental Ca/vitamin D), cataracts (↑risk vs prednisolone - monitor), mood changes. Note: preferred over prednisolone in DMD (less weight gain - CINRG DMD natural history; cataracts possibly higher - monitor); 0.9 mg/kg/day equivalent to 0.75 mg/kg/day prednisolone; daily or intermittent dosing (10/10 days on/off regimen also studied); PBS-listed in Australia for DMD.

Dissociative corticosteroid (steroidal anti-inflammatory) - modified ring-A structure. MOA: glucocorticoid receptor transrepression (GR-TR - anti-inflammatory via NF-κB suppression) WITHOUT significant transcriptional transactivation (GR-TA) → anti-inflammatory effects with markedly ↓glucocorticoid-typical adverse effects (bone loss, growth suppression, insulin resistance, adrenal suppression); designed specifically for Duchenne muscular dystrophy to avoid steroid side effects. Indications: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (CLIMB-DMD/VISION-DMD trials: similar functional benefit to prednisone, significantly ↓bone turnover markers + growth suppression + insulin resistance). SE: fever (non-specific immune effect), nausea, hiccups, behaviour changes; significantly less weight gain, growth suppression, and bone effects than standard corticosteroids. Note: US-approved 2023 (Agamree); dissociative steroid - selectively anti-inflammatory without anabolic/metabolic/bone effects; once-daily oral liquid (mg/kg dosing); significant advance for long-term DMD corticosteroid use in children; TGA status in Australia - check current availability.

Read-through agent for premature stop codons (PTC) - first disease-modifying therapy for nonsense mutation Duchenne MD. MOA: promotes ribosomal read-through of premature stop codon (UGA/UAA/UAG) in mRNA → ↓premature translation termination → partial restoration of full-length dystrophin protein (in nmDMD - nonsense mutation DMD) - mechanism involves aminoglycoside-related PTC read-through by small molecule. Indications: nonsense mutation Duchenne muscular dystrophy (nmDMD) in ambulatory patients ≥2 yr - EU/EMA conditional approval; ongoing confirmatory trials (STRIDE trial); not US-approved (US trials did not meet primary endpoints - ongoing controversy). SE: nausea, vomiting, headache, abdominal pain; potential renal toxicity (monitor creatinine - rare); generally well tolerated. Note: EU conditional approval (EMA) - remains controversial (ACT DMD trial did not meet primary endpoint; ongoing use under conditional approval in Europe); not US-approved; nonsense mutation testing (NGS) required to confirm patient eligibility (only ~10-15% of DMD have nonsense mutations - vs exon-skipping candidates - ~13% skippable exons); TGA approved in Australia.

Recombinant human interferon beta - immunomodulatory MS disease-modifying therapy. MOA: inhibits proinflammatory cytokine production, ↑regulatory T-cells, ↓T-cell activation, ↓trafficking across blood-brain barrier; type I interferon pathway. Indications: relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS - MSCRG/PRISMS trials - classic first-line DMT); CIS (clinically isolated syndrome). Routes: Avonex - IM once weekly (30 mcg); Rebif - SC 3× weekly (22 or 44 mcg). SE: flu-like symptoms (fever, myalgia, headache - on injection days; paracetamol ± NSAIDs for 24h pre/post; reduce over months), injection site reactions (SC - lipodystrophy), liver function abnormalities (monitor LFTs), leucopenia; depression; thyroid disease. Note: neutralising antibodies may develop (more common with SC/Rebif vs IM/Avonex - reduce efficacy - test if apparent failure); flu-like symptoms reduce with time; pre-medication with paracetamol/ibuprofen at injection time; now largely replaced by higher-efficacy DMTs but still widely used; no risk of PML; PBS-listed in Australia.

Anti-ANGPTL3 (angiopoietin-like 3) monoclonal antibody (IgG4). MOA: inhibits ANGPTL3 → ↓lipoprotein lipase (LPL) and endothelial lipase inhibition → ↑LPL activity → ↑VLDL and chylomicron clearance + ↓LDL (LDL-receptor-independent mechanism - active even in homozygous FH patients with no LDL-R function). Indications: homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (HoFH - ELIPSE-HoFH trial: ~47% ↓LDL-C even in LDL-receptor-null patients - unprecedented for LDL-R independent mechanism). Route: IV infusion every 4 weeks. SE: nasopharyngitis, influenza, dizziness, rhinorrhoea; injection/infusion site reactions; ↓TG (expected on-target). Note: unique LDL-R-independent mechanism - only drug that lowers LDL in LDL-receptor null HoFH (PCSK9 inhibitors require at least some LDL-R function; statins upregulate LDL-R - ineffective in null HoFH); IV q4 weekly; TGA approved in Australia for HoFH.

Antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) targeting APOC3 (apolipoprotein C-III) mRNA. MOA: 2'-O-methoxyethyl ASO → reduces hepatic APOC3 mRNA → ↓apoC-III protein → ↓inhibition of lipoprotein lipase (LPL) → ↑triglyceride-rich lipoprotein clearance → ↓↓TG (often >70-80%); also ↓VLDL and remnant lipoproteins. Indications: familial chylomicronaemia syndrome (FCS - genetic LPL deficiency or APOC3 overexpression - severe hypertriglyceridaemia TG >10 mmol/L - APPROACH trial; EU conditional approval; Australian special access). SE: injection site reactions, thrombocytopenia (serious - platelet monitoring mandatory - monthly - significant safety signal), influenza-like illness. Note: thrombocytopenia safety concern - monthly platelet monitoring required; FCS is an ultra-rare disease (LPL deficiency → severe pancreatitis risk from chylomicronaemia); effective when other treatments fail; available in Australia via SAS; compare to olipasiran/inclisiran (siRNA - APOCIII siRNA ARO-APOC3 - investigational).

Once-daily GLP-1 receptor agonist (short-acting). MOA: activates GLP-1 receptor → ↑glucose-dependent insulin secretion, ↓glucagon, delays gastric emptying; short-acting (exendin-4 based - half-life ~3h; once-daily due to binding properties). Indications: T2DM - adjunct to insulin or oral agents (ELIXA trial - CV neutral in post-ACS population); once-daily SC injection. SE: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea (GLP-1 class - most common), headache, hypoglycaemia (with SU/insulin). Note: short-acting profile (once-daily prandial focus - mainly delays gastric emptying → ↓postprandial hyperglycaemia; compare to long-acting once-weekly agents - semaglutide/dulaglutide which have greater fasting glucose effects); part of iGlarLixi (insulin glargine + lixisenatide - Soliqua - fixed-ratio combination); ELIXA: CV neutral (not superior like semaglutide/liraglutide).

3rd-generation sulfonylurea (SU). MOA: binds SUR1 subunit of KATP channels in β-cells → ↑Ca²⁺ influx → ↑insulin secretion (glucose-independent); also some insulin-sensitising effects (↑GLUT4 translocation) - distinct from earlier generation SUs. Indications: T2DM - monotherapy or combination (most commonly with metformin ± other agents); once-daily dosing. SE: hypoglycaemia (dose-limiting; less weight gain vs glibenclamide - 3rd gen advantage), weight gain, nausea; photosensitivity. CI: T1DM, renal impairment (↑hypoglycaemia risk), hepatic failure, pregnancy. Note: once-daily dosing (vs glipizide twice-daily; vs glibenclamide - more hypoglycaemia risk); lower hypoglycaemia risk than glibenclamide (glimepiride - more β-cell selective); PBS-listed in Australia (3rd preferred after metformin ± SGLT2i/GLP-1 in guidelines - use with caution due to hypoglycaemia/weight).

Meglitinide/phenylalanine derivative - prandial insulin secretagogue. MOA: binds SUR1 subunit of KATP channels on β-cells → ↑insulin secretion; faster onset and shorter duration than sulfonylureas → prandial glucose control with ↓inter-meal hypoglycaemia risk; glucose-dependent amplification. Indications: T2DM - prandial glucose control (monotherapy or combination with metformin); taken immediately before each main meal. SE: hypoglycaemia (dose-related, prandial - less than long-acting SUs), weight gain, URTI; rare liver enzyme elevation. Note: take 1-30 min before meals (skip if meal skipped - avoid hypoglycaemia); similar class to repaglinide (also meglitinide - longer action); useful in patients with irregular meal patterns; rarely used currently (overshadowed by DPP4i/SGLT2i/GLP-1 RA with better profiles); PBS-listed in Australia.

PTHrP (parathyroid hormone-related protein) analogue - anabolic osteoporosis agent. MOA: binds PTH1R with selectivity for RG conformation → ↑osteoblast activity + ↑bone formation (anabolic) with less resorption stimulation than teriparatide (which equally stimulates resorption via PTH1R/J conformation); SC daily injection. Indications: postmenopausal osteoporosis (high fracture risk - ACTIVE trial: 43% ↓vertebral fracture, 70% ↓non-vertebral fracture vs placebo; superior to teriparatide on non-vertebral fractures - ATOM trial). SE: hypercalcaemia/hypercalciuria (transient - less than teriparatide), nausea, dizziness, palpitations, injection site reactions; theoretical osteosarcoma risk (boxed warning - bone tumour in rat models at high doses - similar to teriparatide; cumulative lifetime use limit 24 months). CI: Paget's disease, prior skeletal radiation, open growth plates (child/adolescent), prior osteosarcoma. Note: 24-month lifetime limit (combined teriparatide + abaloparatide use); follow with antiresorptive (denosumab/bisphosphonate); not yet TGA-approved in Australia - check current registration status.

Oral nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate (3rd generation). MOA: binds hydroxyapatite at bone resorption surfaces → taken up by osteoclasts → inhibits farnesyl diphosphate synthase (FDPS - enzyme in mevalonate/cholesterol pathway in osteoclasts) → ↓osteoclast function/survival → ↓bone resorption. Indications: postmenopausal osteoporosis (HIP/VERT trials - ↓vertebral and non-vertebral fractures); corticosteroid-induced osteoporosis; male osteoporosis; Paget's disease of bone; prevention of glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis. Dosing: 5 mg daily, 35 mg weekly, 150 mg monthly. SE: oesophagitis/oesophageal ulceration (upper GI - take with full glass water, remain upright 30 min - oral bisphosphonate class), musculoskeletal pain, hypocalcaemia, osteonecrosis of the jaw (rare - dental hygiene; higher risk with cancer/IV bisphosphonate), atypical femoral fracture (AFF - long-term). Note: take fasting + full glass water + upright 30 min; take at least 30 min before food/other medications; calcium/vitamin D supplementation with therapy; drug holiday after 5 years of oral bisphosphonate use in low-risk patients.

Oral/IV nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate. MOA: farnesyl diphosphate synthase inhibition in osteoclasts → ↓bone resorption (same class as alendronate/risedronate). Indications: postmenopausal osteoporosis (BONE trial - significant ↓vertebral fractures); prevention of skeletal events in breast cancer bone metastases (IV). Dosing: oral 150 mg once monthly; IV 3 mg every 3 months (if oral not tolerated). SE: oral - oesophagitis, dyspepsia (must take correctly); IV - flu-like reaction (acute phase reaction - fever, myalgia, headache - 24-72h after first dose; ↓with subsequent doses); osteonecrosis of jaw, AFF (bisphosphonate class). Note: monthly oral dosing (convenience over daily/weekly); IV quarterly (for patients unable to tolerate oral route); similar class to alendronate/risedronate; PBS-listed in Australia; take oral dose first thing in morning on fasting stomach with full glass water + upright 60 min (stricter than alendronate 30 min).

GnRH agonist (gonadorelin analogue - decapeptide superagonist). MOA: initial stimulation of GnRH receptors (flare - ↑LH, FSH, testosterone/oestrogen - 1-2 weeks) → continuous receptor stimulation → receptor downregulation → ↓GnRH receptor expression → pituitary desensitisation → ↓LH, FSH → ↓testosterone (castration levels) in males, ↓oestrogen in females. Indications: prostate cancer (hormone-sensitive - androgen deprivation therapy [ADT]; combined with AR antagonist for combined androgen blockade); breast cancer (premenopausal HR+ disease); endometriosis; uterine fibroids; central precocious puberty. Depot formulations: 1-month, 3-month, 6-month SC/IM depot. SE: testosterone flare (initial - anti-androgen cover required first 4 weeks in prostate cancer with bony metastases - risk of cord compression); hot flushes, loss of libido, erectile dysfunction, weight gain, osteoporosis (long-term ADT), metabolic syndrome; depression. Note: flare risk (initial testosterone ↑ → tumour progression - anti-androgen [bicalutamide] ≥4 weeks before/during depot initiation in metastatic prostate cancer); GnRH antagonist (degarelix) avoids flare; PBS-listed in Australia for multiple indications.

GnRH agonist - subcutaneous depot implant. MOA: superagonist of GnRH receptor → initial flare (↑LH/FSH/sex hormones) → downregulation → medical castration (↓testosterone in males; ↓oestrogen in females); monthly (3.6 mg) or 3-monthly (10.8 mg) SC abdominal implant. Indications: prostate cancer (ADT - hormone-sensitive and CRPC with hormone-sensitive component); breast cancer (premenopausal HR+); endometriosis; uterine fibroids; adjunct in IVF (ovarian hyperstimulation control). SE: hot flushes, sweating, decreased libido, sexual dysfunction, osteoporosis, metabolic syndrome; initial testosterone flare (same as leuprorelin - anti-androgen cover); headache; mood changes. Note: subcutaneous implant device (inserted with trocar - abdomen - monthly or 3-monthly); similar profile to leuprorelin; testosterone flare management same principles; commonly used with bicalutamide (combined androgen blockade - CAB - in prostate cancer); PBS-listed in Australia.

GnRH receptor antagonist (decapeptide - non-peptide). MOA: competitive GnRH receptor antagonist → immediate suppression of LH and FSH → rapid ↓testosterone to castration levels (within 3 days - no initial flare); no testosterone surge seen with agonists (agonists: initial stimulation before downregulation = flare risk). Indications: hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (ADT - alternative to GnRH agonists when flare is a concern - cord compression, urinary obstruction, renal failure from metastases). SE: injection site reactions (hot, red, painful - most common - SC loading dose 240 mg then monthly 80 mg), hot flushes, weight gain, osteoporosis, fatigue; ↑LFTs. Note: advantages over GnRH agonists: (1) NO testosterone flare (no anti-androgen cover needed); (2) faster testosterone suppression; (3) FSH ↓ more completely; disadvantages: monthly injection (vs 3/6-monthly for agonists), more injection site reactions; chosen when flare contraindicated (e.g. spinal cord metastases, bilateral ureteric obstruction); PBS-listed in Australia.

Oral prodrug of cidofovir (hexadecyloxypropyl-cidofovir - HDP-CDV). MOA: lipid conjugation allows oral bioavailability + intracellular conversion to CDV-PP (cidofovir diphosphate) → inhibits viral DNA polymerase → chain termination; active against orthopoxviruses (smallpox/mpox), adenovirus, CMV, BK virus; lipid conjugate → concentrated intracellularly → ↓nephrotoxicity of parent cidofovir (phosphonate group not present until intracellular conversion). Indications: smallpox (variola virus - US approval under Animal Rule 2021 for bioterrorism preparedness; used compassionately for mpox); adenovirus disease in immunocompromised (investigational/compassionate); CMV (data limited). SE: diarrhoea (most common - dose-limiting), nausea, abdominal pain; ↑LFTs (hepatotoxicity - monitor); less nephrotoxicity than cidofovir (no IV form - eliminates infusion-associated nephrotoxicity). Note: oral formulation (advantage over IV cidofovir); lower nephrotoxicity than parent cidofovir; mpox (monkeypox) - used compassionately alongside tecovirimat; adenovirus - data mainly in paediatric HSCT patients (ADHERE trial - failed primary endpoint but clinically used); available via SAS in Australia.

VP37 (p37) envelope protein inhibitor - first-in-class orthopoxvirus antiviral. MOA: inhibits VP37 - a viral host-range protein required for formation of extracellular enveloped virus (EEV) particles → ↓viral dissemination within host and between cells; no effect on intracellular virus production but blocks spread. Indications: smallpox (US-approved under Animal Rule 2018 - bioterrorism preparedness); mpox (monkeypox - USAID/WHO clinical trials - PALM007 in mpox-endemic regions; used widely during 2022-23 mpox outbreak - compassionate use; US approval for non-variola orthopoxviruses in adults/children). SE: headache, nausea, abdominal pain; drug interactions (CYP2C8 substrate - rifampicin, repaglinide interactions); well tolerated overall. Note: oral formulation (21-day course for mpox; available in 200 mg capsule and 3 mg/kg liquid); international strategic stockpile + Australian NMSs (National Medical Stockpile) include TPOXX; key drug for mpox management in severe/immunocompromised patients; moderate-severe mpox in HIV/immunosuppressed = primary indication for treatment.

NS5A protein inhibitor - component of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (Epclusa) - pangenotypic HCV therapy. MOA: targets HCV NS5A protein (non-enzymatic - essential for viral RNA replication and virion assembly); combined with sofosbuvir (NS5B polymerase inhibitor) → complementary targets → pangenotypic activity with high SVR rates. Indications: as sofosbuvir/velpatasvir combination (Epclusa) - pangenotypic HCV (genotypes 1-6) in adults and paediatric (≥3 yr); compensated and decompensated cirrhosis; NS5A resistance reduces response in GT1a/3 (add voxilaprevir [Vosevi: SOF/VEL/VOX] or switch regimen). SE: headache, fatigue, nausea (well tolerated); drug interactions (amiodarone - bradycardia with sofosbuvir; potent P-gp inducers - rifampicin ↓exposure). Note: sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (Epclusa) - 12-week pangenotypic treatment; previously HCV required genotype-specific regimens; PBS-listed in Australia (pangenotypic - simplified for all genotypes); decompensated cirrhosis use - Child-Pugh B/C tolerated but close monitoring; add ribavirin for decompensated cirrhosis if clinically indicated.

Ileal bile acid transporter (IBAT/ASBT) inhibitor - small molecule. MOA: inhibits IBAT in terminal ileum → ↓enterohepatic bile acid recirculation → ↓intrahepatic bile acid accumulation → ↓pruritus and liver injury in cholestatic disorders. Indications: cholestatic pruritus in Alagille syndrome (ALGS - ICONIC trial: significant ↓pruritus scores; US FDA breakthrough designation; Livmarli 2021); also being studied in PFIC and biliary atresia. SE: diarrhoea (dose-related - bile acid malabsorption in colon → secretory diarrhoea), abdominal pain, liver disease exacerbation (fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption - A, D, E, K - monitor + supplement), fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies. Note: ALGS (Alagille syndrome) - JAG1/NOTCH2 mutation → bile duct paucity → cholestasis and pruritus; maralixibat reduces recirculating bile acids → ↓pruritus; fat-soluble vitamin monitoring essential; oral liquid (2 mg/kg/day in ALGS); compare to odevixibat (same class - PFIC indication).

Ileal bile acid transporter (IBAT) inhibitor - small molecule. MOA: same as maralixibat - inhibits IBAT/ASBT in terminal ileum → ↓enterohepatic bile acid recirculation → ↓intrahepatic bile acid accumulation → ↓cholestasis-associated pruritus and hepatocellular injury. Indications: progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis (PFIC types 1, 2, 3 - PEDFIC-1/2 trials: significant ↓pruritus, ↓serum bile acids, ↓need for liver transplant); Alagille syndrome (investigational - some overlap with maralixibat). SE: diarrhoea, abdominal pain (bile acid malabsorption); fat-soluble vitamin deficiency (A, D, E, K - supplement and monitor); ↑LFTs in some. Note: oral granules/capsules once daily; PFIC-specific first-line medical therapy (before surgical biliary diversion); distinct from maralixibat (ALGS); both are IBAT inhibitors but approved for different cholestatic indications; fat-soluble vitamin monitoring critical; may defer/avoid liver transplantation in responders; TGA approved in Australia.

Pan-PPAR agonist (PPAR-α, PPAR-γ, PPAR-δ/β triple agonist). MOA: activates all three PPAR isoforms → ↓hepatic lipid accumulation (α - fatty acid oxidation ↑), ↓insulin resistance (γ - adipogenesis/glucose metabolism), ↓inflammation + ↑adiponectin (δ - energy expenditure); addresses multiple MASH/NAFLD pathophysiological mechanisms (metabolic, inflammatory, fibrotic). Indications: MASH (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis - formerly NASH) with liver fibrosis (F2-F3 - NATIVE trial: 55% MASH resolution without fibrosis worsening vs 26% placebo; 48.4% fibrosis improvement ≥1 stage vs 23.2%; US-approved June 2024). SE: peripheral oedema (PPAR-γ - fluid retention - class effect; manage with dose reduction), weight gain (fluid + adipogenesis), nausea, diarrhoea; anaemia (PPAR-δ); ↑HDL (expected). CI: pregnancy (teratogenic). Note: first PPAR agonist for MASH (pioglitazone - PPAR-γ only - used off-label; lanifibranor addresses all three pathways); once-daily oral; weight gain + oedema management important; approved for MASH - rapidly evolving field (resmetirom - THRβ agonist - also approved for MASH; obeticholic acid - controversial); TGA registration in Australia - check current status.

Novel calcineurin inhibitor (CNI) - modified ciclosporin analogue. MOA: inhibits calcineurin → ↓NFAT dephosphorylation → ↓IL-2 transcription → ↓T-cell activation; additionally directly stabilises podocyte cytoskeleton (synaptopodin) → ↓proteinuria (mechanism beyond immunosuppression - podocyte protection); 40× more potent than ciclosporin per mg but shorter half-life + predictable PK (no dose monitoring needed). Indications: lupus nephritis (active class III/IV ± V - AURORA-1/2 trials: 49% complete renal response vs 24% with MMF + belimumab; combined with MMF + low-dose corticosteroid). SE: eGFR decline/nephrotoxicity (monitor creatinine 2-weekly initially → monthly; ↑serum Cr >30% from baseline → hold/reduce dose); hypertension, infections, hyperkalaemia; hypertrichosis (less than ciclosporin). Note: requires creatinine monitoring (nephrotoxicity protocol - ↑Cr 30% → dose pause - important safety); does NOT require TDM (therapeutic drug monitoring) unlike standard ciclosporin; oral BD dosing (23.7 mg twice daily); combined with MMF + belimumab (Aurora regimen) for active LN; significant advance for LN remission rates.

First-generation (typical) antipsychotic - dibenzoxazepine class. MOA: D2 receptor antagonism (antipsychotic effect) + D4, 5-HT2A, H1, α1 blockade; Adasuve - inhaled formulation → rapid absorption → therapeutic levels within minutes. Indications: schizophrenia (oral - Loxapac); acute agitation in schizophrenia/bipolar disorder (inhaled Adasuve - 10 mg single dose → ≤2 repeat doses at 2h intervals). SE: extrapyramidal side effects (EPS - oral use; dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism), sedation; Adasuve: bronchospasm (1-2% - serious - inhaled route; CI in active airway disease; requires observation 1h post-dose with rescue β2-agonist). CI: Adasuve - active bronchospasm, COPD, asthma (inhalation bronchospasm risk); severe CNS depression. Note: Adasuve inhaled form - rapid acute agitation treatment (IM/IV alternatives: haloperidol, olanzapine, droperidol); patient-controlled inhaler in monitored setting; bronchospasm monitoring mandatory post-inhalation; oral loxapine less used than newer antipsychotics.

Dual-mechanism intraocular pressure lowering agent - Rho kinase (ROCK) inhibitor + noradrenaline transporter (NET) inhibitor. MOA: (1) ROCK inhibition → ↑trabecular meshwork outflow facility (increased aqueous drainage through conventional trabecular pathway) + ↓ciliary muscle contraction; (2) NET inhibition → ↓sympathetic tone in ciliary body → ↓aqueous production; both pathways ↓IOP. Indications: open-angle glaucoma/ocular hypertension (ROCKET trials - significant ↓IOP; similar to timolol; additive with other agents). SE: conjunctival hyperaemia (most common and striking - red eyes within minutes of instillation - cosmetically significant), cornea verticillata (whorled corneal deposits - reversible on stopping - clinically minor), conjunctival haemorrhage, eye pruritus. Note: once-daily dosing (evening - preferred for 24h IOP control); novel trabecular meshwork mechanism (vs beta-blockers - ↓aqueous production; prostaglandins - ↑uveoscleral outflow; ROCK inhibitors increase conventional outflow - untapped pathway); conjunctival redness warning for patients; available as fixed combo with latanoprost (Rocklatan - netarsudil/latanoprost 0.02%/0.005%).

Bile acid sequestrant (anion exchange resin) - cholesterol-lowering. MOA: non-absorbable anion exchange resin binds bile acids in intestine → ↓enterohepatic bile acid recirculation → liver upregulates CYP7A1 (cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase) → converts cholesterol to bile acids → hepatocellular cholesterol depleted → ↑hepatic LDL-R expression → ↓LDL-C (~15-30%); also ↑HDL slightly; may ↑TG (↑VLDL production - caution in hypertriglyceridaemia). Indications: hypercholesterolaemia (adjunct to diet/statins); biliary pruritus (bile acid sequestration); C.difficile diarrhoea (binds toxin - adjunct); post-bariatric surgery bile reflux. SE: constipation (most common - dose-limiting), bloating, flatulence, nausea; absorption impairment (fat-soluble vitamins A,D,E,K - separate medications by 1-4h; drug interactions - binds many drugs: warfarin, digoxin, thyroid, statins - all must be given 1h before or 4h after colestipol). Note: poor tolerability (GI SE) limits use (vs newer cholestyramine-free agents: colesevelam - better tolerated; ezetimibe; inclisiran); drug-binding interactions - give ALL other medications 1h before or 4h after; powder/tablet forms; not absorbed systemically; ↑TG - avoid in hypertriglyceridaemia.

Anti-FcRn (neonatal Fc receptor) monoclonal antibody fragment (IgG1 Fc fragment - engineered to bind FcRn with high affinity). MOA: binds FcRn → competitive blockade of IgG recycling pathway → ↑IgG catabolism → ↓total IgG (including pathogenic AChR-IgG, MuSK-IgG autoantibodies in MG - but also all IgG subclasses). Indications: generalised myasthenia gravis (gMG) - AChR-antibody positive - ADAPT trial (35% ↓MG-ADL score; rapid response within 1 week); also SC formulation (Vyvgart Hytrulo = efgartigimod + hyaluronidase). Route: IV infusion weekly × 4 (one cycle = 4 weekly infusions) → reassess; repeat cycles as needed. SE: URTI (most common - ↑infection risk due to ↓IgG), headache, nausea; hypersensitivity; ↓all IgG classes (monitor Ig levels - hold if IgG <3 g/L). Note: rapid ↓IgG within 1-2 weeks (clinical improvement mirrors IgG decline); works for AChR-antibody positive gMG (MuSK+ not well studied); repeat cycles based on symptoms; FcRn class now includes rozanolixizumab, nipocalimab, batoclimab; IV or SC options (Hytrulo - SC with hyaluronidase - same efficacy, convenience).

Humanised anti-FcRn (neonatal Fc receptor) monoclonal antibody. MOA: blocks FcRn receptor → ↓IgG recycling → accelerated IgG catabolism → ↓total IgG and pathogenic autoantibodies (AChR-IgG, MuSK-IgG in myasthenia gravis); weekly SC injection. Indications: generalised myasthenia gravis (gMG) - AChR+ and MuSK+ antibody positive - MycarinG trial (significant MG-ADL/QMG improvement; US-approved June 2023). Route: SC infusion (pump) weekly (7 mg/kg via infusion pump for 6 weeks). SE: headache (very common - most frequent AE; migraine-like headaches - can require analgesics), URTI, pyrexia; ↓IgG (infection risk), hypersensitivity; diarrhoea. Note: notable headache SE (more frequent than IV FcRn agents); effective for both AChR+ and MuSK+ MG (broader than complement inhibitors); 6-week treatment cycle then reassess; SC route but requires infusion pump (not simple injection); anti-FcRn class (efgartigimod, nipocalimab, rozanolixizumab) all reduce IgG - similar mechanism, different pharmacokinetics and clinical profiles.

Fully human anti-FcRn (neonatal Fc receptor) monoclonal antibody. MOA: binds FcRn with high affinity → ↓IgG recycling → broad IgG ↓ including pathogenic autoantibodies; designed with extended half-life and broad IgG class reduction. Indications: generalised myasthenia gravis (gMG - AChR+/MuSK+ - Vivacity-MG trial - US-approved 2024); haemolytic disease of the fetus/newborn (HDFN - reduces maternal anti-Rh/Kell IgG crossing placenta); warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (wAIHA - investigational). Route: IV infusion every 2 weeks. SE: URTI, headache; ↓total IgG (infection risk); hypersensitivity. Note: unlike efgartigimod (IV weekly × 4 = cycle) - nipocalimab is continuous biweekly dosing; also unique indication for HDFN (reduction of maternal pathogenic IgG to protect fetus - first therapy for HDFN prevention - significant advance); broader autoimmune indications than other FcRn agents being investigated.

Complement C5 inhibitor (macrocyclic peptide, self-administered SC daily). MOA: binds C5 → blocks C5a and C5b-9 (membrane attack complex) formation → ↓complement-mediated NMJ damage in MG (C5 activation → MAC at NMJ → acetylcholine receptor destruction); SC self-injection (unlike IV eculizumab). Indications: generalised myasthenia gravis (gMG) - AChR-antibody positive (RAISE trial: significant ↓MG-ADL and QMG scores; US-approved 2023). SE: injection site reactions, URTI, headache; risk of encapsulated bacterial infections (Neisseria meningitidis - mandatory meningococcal vaccination before starting - class effect: all C5 inhibitors); haemolysis in PNH not indicated (avoid). CI: unresolved Neisseria meningitidis infection. Note: SC daily self-injection (vs IV eculizumab/ravulizumab - Q2weeks/Q8weeks respectively - zilucoplan avoids clinic visits); meningococcal vaccination MANDATORY (at least 2 weeks before first dose - MenACWY + MenB); prophylactic antibiotics if meningococcal vaccination not completed before urgent start; only for AChR+ gMG (not MuSK+ or seronegative).

Oral plasma kallikrein inhibitor (small molecule) - prophylaxis for HAE. MOA: inhibits plasma kallikrein activity → ↓bradykinin generation → ↓hereditary angioedema attack frequency; same target as berotralstat (both oral plasma kallikrein inhibitors) but different chemical scaffold. Indications: long-term prophylaxis of hereditary angioedema (HAE types I/II - ZENITH-1 trial - significant ↓attack rate; US/EU-approved 2024). SE: GI effects (diarrhoea, nausea - class plasma kallikrein inhibitor SE), headache; drug interactions (CYP3A4). Note: oral twice-daily prophylaxis (similar to berotralstat once-daily); both donidalorsen and berotralstat are oral kallikrein inhibitors - direct competition for market; compare to SC lanadelumab (anti-kallikrein mAb) for prophylaxis; does not replace rescue therapy for acute attacks; KMT - contact prescribing specialist; check TGA approval status in Australia.

Anti-Factor XII (Hageman factor) monoclonal antibody - HAE prophylaxis. MOA: inhibits activated Factor XII (FXIIa) → ↓contact activation pathway → ↓kallikrein-kinin generation → ↓bradykinin production → ↓HAE attacks; targets the contact activation pathway upstream of plasma kallikrein (different site from lanadelumab/berotralstat/donidalorsen which target kallikrein directly). Indications: prophylaxis of HAE attacks (HAE types I/II - VANGUARD trial - significant ↓attack frequency; US-approved 2024; monthly SC injection). SE: injection site reactions, URTI, headache, viral infections; well tolerated overall. Note: once-monthly SC self-injection (convenient vs biweekly lanadelumab or daily/twice-daily oral berotralstat/donidalorsen); upstream target (FXII/Hageman factor) - distinct mechanism from all other HAE prophylaxes; may be preferred for patients needing monthly dosing convenience; check TGA approval status in Australia.

Antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) targeting LPA mRNA - lipoprotein(a) lowering. MOA: GalNAc-conjugated ASO → hepatocyte-targeted delivery → hybridises to LPA mRNA (encodes apolipoprotein[a]) → RNase H cleavage → ↓Lp(a) synthesis; Lp(a) is a genetically determined cardiovascular risk factor (elevated in ~20% of population - associated with ASCVD, aortic stenosis - not modifiable by current therapies). Indications: elevated Lp(a) with established CVD - HORIZON phase 3 trial (cardiovascular outcomes - results awaited; if positive, large unmet need; SC monthly injection → ~80% ↓Lp(a) in phase 2). SE: injection site reactions, flu-like symptoms; thrombocytopenia (class ASO - mild); monitored in trials. Note: investigational pending HORIZON trial results; enormous unmet need (elevated Lp(a) - prevalent genetic CV risk factor with no approved therapy beyond PCSK9i [modest ~25% ↓Lp(a)] and niacin [withdrawn]); small interfering RNA alternative (olpasiran [siRNA] - also targeting Lp[a] - similar profound Lp(a) lowering); not yet TGA/US-approved for Lp(a) lowering.

Serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor (SARI). MOA: potent 5-HT2A/2C receptor antagonism + modest SERT inhibition + H1 antagonism (sedating) + α1 blockade (postural hypotension); sedating properties arise from 5-HT2A + H1 + α1 blockade. Indications: major depression (oral - antidepressant at higher doses 150-400 mg); insomnia (low-dose off-label - 25-100 mg; widely used as sleep aid - non-addictive vs benzodiazepines); also used for agitation in dementia. SE: sedation/somnolence (often beneficial for insomnia indication), orthostatic hypotension, priapism (rare but serious - 1/6000-8000 males - advise patients to seek urgent treatment for prolonged erection), cardiac arrhythmias (rare - avoid with QT-prolonging agents), nausea; less anticholinergic than TCAs. Note: priapism warning - advise all male patients; low-dose widely used for insomnia (non-habit-forming, improves sleep architecture); lower sexual SE than SSRIs (5-HT2C blockade); PBS-listed in Australia.

Reversible inhibitor of MAO-A (RIMA). MOA: selectively and reversibly inhibits monoamine oxidase type A (MAO-A) → ↑synaptic serotonin, noradrenaline, dopamine; reversibility allows displacement by substrates at high concentrations (tyramine - less food interaction risk than irreversible MAOIs). Indications: major depression; social anxiety disorder; dysthymia. SE: insomnia (stimulant - take in morning), headache, nausea, dizziness; serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs; less tyramine interaction risk than irreversible MAOIs (but still avoid high-tyramine foods in excess). Note: reversible (unlike phenelzine/tranylcypromine - irreversible) → much safer tyramine interaction (hypertensive crisis much rarer); allow 1-2 days washout when switching from moclobemide to SSRI (much shorter than 14-day MAOI washout); avoid with SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans, pethidine; widely used in Australia; PBS-listed.

Substituted benzamide antipsychotic - selective D2/D3 receptor antagonist. MOA: selectively blocks dopamine D2 and D3 receptors (predominantly limbic - lower EPS risk than typical antipsychotics at low doses); no significant anticholinergic/antihistamine/adrenergic effects; some debate about weak partial agonism at D2. Indications: schizophrenia (positive and negative symptoms); depression (low-dose off-label - may activate at low doses via presynaptic D2 autoreceptor blockade); Tourette syndrome; gastro-oesophageal reflux (not widely used - off-label antiemetic); anxiety. SE: hyperprolactinaemia (galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, gynaecomastia, sexual dysfunction - prominent), EPS (at high doses - less than chlorpromazine), weight gain, QTc prolongation; few anticholinergic SE. Note: unique biphasic dose-response - low doses (< 300 mg/day): activating/antidepressant (presynaptic D2); high doses (> 400 mg/day): antipsychotic (postsynaptic D2 blockade); hyperprolactinaemia is class-leading concern; PBS-listed in Australia.

Thioxanthene antipsychotic - D1/D2/D3 receptor antagonist. MOA: antagonises dopamine D1 and D2 receptors; also 5-HT2A blockade; at low doses (Fluanxol low-dose tablets) - mild alerting/antidepressant properties (via D1 partial agonism mechanism); depot preparation for schizophrenia maintenance. Formulations: oral (Fluanxol 0.5-3 mg - depression/anxiety); depot IM (Depixol - long-acting - 20-200 mg every 2-4 weeks). Indications: schizophrenia (depot maintenance - Depixol); mild depression/anxiety (oral low-dose Fluanxol). SE: EPS (akathisia - common at antipsychotic doses), hyperprolactinaemia, weight gain, sedation; anticholinergic (dry mouth, constipation); QTc prolongation. Note: unique use at low doses for depression/anxiety (differentiated from other typical antipsychotics - not first-line); depot formulation for adherence-poor schizophrenia; thioxanthene class (also zuclopenthixol - depot for acute agitation and maintenance); PBS-listed in Australia.

Non-selective irreversible MAO inhibitor (MAOI). MOA: irreversibly inhibits both MAO-A (serotonin/noradrenaline) and MAO-B (dopamine) → ↑synaptic monoamines → antidepressant/anxiolytic. Indications: atypical depression (hypersomnia, hyperphagia, mood reactivity, rejection sensitivity - responds better to MAOIs than TCAs), treatment-resistant depression, social phobia, panic disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). SE: TYRAMINE HYPERTENSIVE CRISIS (absolute CI - aged/tyramine-rich foods: aged cheese, fermented meats, Marmite, tap beer, Chianti - abrupt catecholamine release → ↑↑BP → stroke/MI/death - requires strict dietary restriction); serotonin syndrome (with serotonergic drugs); orthostatic hypotension (common - limiting); weight gain, insomnia, sexual dysfunction; hepatotoxicity (rare - phenelzine more than others). CI: pethidine (fatal serotonin syndrome), SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans, sympathomimetics, opioids (many), dextromethorphan. Note: 14-day washout needed after MAOI before starting serotonergic drug; 2-week dietary restriction; reserved for treatment-resistant/atypical cases (significant interaction burden); phenelzine most commonly used irreversible MAOI in Australia.

Selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor (NRI). MOA: inhibits noradrenaline transporter (NET) → ↑synaptic noradrenaline; no significant serotonin/dopamine reuptake inhibition; no significant receptor affinity (unlike TCAs - clean NRI). Indications: major depression; attention-deficit disorder (off-label - Australia). SE: dry mouth, constipation, urinary hesitancy/retention (noradrenergic/anticholinergic-like effects via indirect urinary sympathetic activation), insomnia, tachycardia, sweating, hypotension (paradoxical - posture-related); sexual dysfunction (noradrenaline-mediated). Note: pure NRI (unlike duloxetine - SNRI; unlike TCAs - mixed); meta-analysis questioned efficacy vs placebo in depression (controversial - publication bias debate); approved in Australia/EU; may benefit patients where noradrenergic insufficiency predominates (apathy, fatigue, lack of concentration); urinary retention caution in men/BPH.

Dextrorotatory amfetamine (d-amfetamine) - CNS stimulant. MOA: releases dopamine and noradrenaline from presynaptic terminals + inhibits reuptake → ↑synaptic DA/NA in prefrontal cortex and striatum → ↑attention and ↓hyperactivity; also weak 5-HT release. Indications: ADHD (children and adults - 2nd-line after methylphenidate in Australia - Schedule 8); narcolepsy (excessive daytime sleepiness - Schedule 8); rarely refractory depression (augmentation - specialist use). SE: appetite suppression, weight loss, insomnia, tachycardia, hypertension, growth retardation (long-term in children - monitor height/weight), anxiety, irritability; abuse potential (Schedule 8 in Australia); tics (can unmask/worsen Tourette's). CI: concurrent MAOIs (hypertensive crisis/serotonin syndrome); severe CVD; hyperthyroidism. Note: d-amfetamine only (vs mixed amfetamine salts - Adderall - not available in Australia); lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) is prodrug of dexamfetamine; more potent than methylphenidate with higher abuse potential; supervised prescribing required (Schedule 8).

Reversible acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibitor. MOA: carbamylates AChE → reversible inhibition → ↑acetylcholine at NMJ → ↑muscle fibre activation; does NOT cross BBB (quaternary amine). Indications: myasthenia gravis (MG - first-line symptomatic treatment; ↑NMJ transmission → ↑muscle strength; does not alter disease course but controls symptoms); reversal of non-depolarising NMB (with glycopyrronium - to prevent muscarinic SE); prophylaxis against nerve agent toxicity (Soman - GI absorption reduces exposure window - military use). SE: muscarinic (SLUDGE/DUMBELS): salivation, lacrimation, urinary urgency, diarrhoea, GI cramps, emesis (↑bowel motility/secretions - dose-limiting); bradycardia, bronchospasm; nicotinic effects at high doses (fasciculations, weakness - cholinergic crisis - overdose). Note: muscarinic SE managed with glycopyrronium (not atropine - doesn't penetrate CNS but glycopyrronium is also peripheral); cholinergic crisis with overdose (weakness indistinguishable from MG crisis - distinguish by edrophonium or clinical context); dose titrated to symptom control; 4-6 hourly (shorter duration than neostigmine).

Thyroid hormone receptor β (THRβ) selective agonist. MOA: selectively activates THRβ (hepatic - regulated lipid metabolism) WITHOUT activating THRα (cardiac - avoids tachycardia/arrhythmia of non-selective thyroid hormone agonists) → ↑hepatic fatty acid oxidation + ↓de novo lipogenesis + ↓steatosis + ↓fibrogenic signalling → MASH resolution and fibrosis regression; also ↓LDL-C (↑LDL-R expression - THRβ in liver). Indications: MASH (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis) with liver fibrosis (F2-F4 - MAESTRO-NASH pivotal trial: 25.9% MASH resolution without worsening fibrosis [vs 14.2% placebo]; 24.2% ≥1-stage fibrosis improvement [vs 14.2%] - US-approved March 2024). SE: nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal pain; ↑LDL initially (rebound after initial ↓ - class effect); ↑bile lithogenicity (gallstones/cholelithiasis - US boxed warning in some contexts). Note: first US-approved pharmacotherapy for MASH with fibrosis (landmark - major unmet need addressed); THRβ liver selectivity avoids cardiac toxicity; once-daily oral (80 mg or 100 mg); TGA status in Australia - check current registration; NASH/MASH treatment landscape changing rapidly (resmetirom + lanifibranor both approved 2024).

Anti-Nectin-4 antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) - monomethyl auristatin E (MMAE) payload. MOA: binds Nectin-4 (overexpressed in urothelial cancer cells) → internalisation → MMAE release → microtubule disruption → G2/M arrest → cell death; bystander effect (MMAE also kills adjacent Nectin-4-negative cells). Indications: locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma (EV-301: superior OS vs chemo after platinum + PD-L1/PD-1; EV-302: first-line combined with pembrolizumab - superior PFS + OS vs platinum-based chemo - paradigm-changing). SE: peripheral neuropathy (most common - dose-limiting - cumulative; sensory > motor), hyperglycaemia (MMAE mechanism - even in non-diabetics; monitor BSL), skin reactions (palmoplantar erythrodysaesthesia, maculo-papular rash, SJS/TEN risk), fatigue, alopecia, nausea. Note: EV-302 (enfortumab vedotin + pembrolizumab) - now preferred first-line for eligible patients (superior to platinum/gemcitabine); peripheral neuropathy - dose reduce/pause when grade 2; hyperglycaemia monitoring essential (MMAE-specific mechanism); US FDA/TGA approved; significant advance in bladder cancer.

Selective KIT/PDGFRA inhibitor (type I - binds active conformation). MOA: potent inhibitor of PDGFRA D842V (the most common PDGFRA mutation in GIST - imatinib/sunitinib resistant) and PDGFRA exon 18 mutations; also inhibits KIT D816V (systemic mastocytosis - mast cell disease). Indications: PDGFRA exon 18-mutant GIST (including D842V - NAVIGATOR trial: ORR 88% - unprecedented; first approved therapy for D842V-GIST, previously imatinib-resistant); advanced systemic mastocytosis (KIT D816V - PIONEER/PATHFINDER trials - ORR ~75%; also approved). SE: cognitive effects (memory impairment, confusion - dose-dependent; CNS penetrant - significant); anaemia, periorbital/facial oedema, diarrhoea, nausea, fatigue; intracranial haemorrhage (risk - avoid anticoagulants). Note: PDGFRA D842V testing required before use in GIST; unique CNS penetration → cognitive SE (dose reduce/hold); distinct from imatinib (which fails for D842V GIST - avapritinib ORR 88% vs imatinib 0%); also active in SM (systemic mastocytosis - different from other KIT inhibitors); PBS-listed in Australia for PDGFRA GIST.

Switch-control KIT and PDGFRA kinase inhibitor (dual mechanism - allosteric + ATP-competitive). MOA: unique dual mechanism - occupies allosteric 'switch pocket' (keeps kinase in inactive conformation - prevents activation) + ATP-binding site inhibition → broad spectrum KIT exon 9/11/17/18 + PDGFRA mutations including imatinib/sunitinib/regorafenib-resistant mutations. Indications: advanced GIST (≥4th-line - after imatinib, sunitinib, regorafenib - INVICTUS trial: improved PFS and OS vs placebo; US-approved 2020); first-line GIST (INTRIGUE trial - vs sunitinib - non-inferior; not approved 1st-line but data available). SE: alopecia (most common - dose-dependent - can be severe), palmoplantar erythrodysaesthesia (PPES), myalgia, arthralgia, fatigue, hypertension, nausea. Note: ≥4th-line GIST - very late-stage; switch-control mechanism provides activity against late-onset resistance mutations (that other KIT inhibitors miss); alopecia prominent (warn patients); mutation analysis at progression important; PBS-listed in Australia.

CSF1R (colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor) inhibitor (also KIT/FLT3 inhibition). MOA: inhibits CSF1R → ↓proliferation + survival of monocyte/macrophage lineage cells (tumour-associated macrophages in PVNS/TGCT); same target pathway as sotatercept is NOT - sotatercept is different - pexidartinib targets CSF1R which drives tenosynovial giant cell tumour (PVNS/TGCT) due to CSF1 gene translocation in stromal cells. Indications: symptomatic tenosynovial giant cell tumour (TGCT - previously PVNS - diffuse type or localised unresectable - ENLIVEN trial: 38% overall response rate; US-approved 2019). SE: hepatotoxicity (serious - elevated LFTs - REMS programme - mandatory liver monitoring before each dose; 2 cases of fatal hepatic failure in trials; interrupt/discontinue for severe hepatotoxicity), hair colour depigmentation (greying - melanocyte CSF1R inhibition), fatigue, nausea, abdominal pain; teratogenic. Note: REMS programme mandatory (hepatotoxicity monitoring - ALT/AST/bilirubin before each cycle - hold if significant elevation); 35% response rate for diffuse TGCT (unresectable - surgical synovectomy only alternative); CSF1R inhibition → hair depigmentation (white/grey hair - nearly universal - cosmetic but not serious); PBS-listed in Australia for TGCT/PVNS.

Anti-HER3 antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) - topoisomerase I inhibitor (DXd - deruxtecan) payload. MOA: anti-HER3 (ErbB3) mAb → binds HER3-expressing tumour cells → internalisation → DXd topoisomerase I inhibitor release → DNA SSB → cell death; bystander effect (DXd kills adjacent cells - effective even in heterogeneous HER3 expression). Indications: NSCLC with EGFR mutations (previously treated - including osimertinib-resistant - HER3 expressed in ~80% of NSCLC - HERTHENA-Lung01 trial; US FDA accelerated approval 2024). SE: ILD/pneumonitis (serious - class DXd payload - monitor; hold/stop for grade 2+), nausea, fatigue, alopecia, neutropenia, anaemia; thrombocytopenia. Note: HER3 ADC class (alongside trastuzumab deruxtecan [HER2-DXd] - same payload, different antibody target); ILD is critical safety concern (class effect - DXd payload); EGFR-mutant NSCLC progressing after osimertinib - HER3 ADC active regardless of specific resistance mechanism; monitor O₂ saturation and respiratory symptoms.

Anti-HER2 antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) - maytansine derivative (DM1) payload. MOA: trastuzumab antibody (anti-HER2) conjugated to DM1 (potent microtubule inhibitor) via stable thioether linker → binds HER2 → internalisation → DM1 release → microtubule disruption → cell death; also retains trastuzumab-mediated ADCC. Indications: HER2+ metastatic breast cancer (previously treated - EMILIA trial: superior PFS + OS vs lapatinib + capecitabine; TH3RESA); early HER2+ breast cancer adjuvant (after neoadjuvant therapy with residual disease - KATHERINE trial: 50% ↓recurrence risk vs trastuzumab alone). SE: thrombocytopenia (dose-limiting - typically nadir day 8, recovers by day 15; adjust dose if grade 3/4), peripheral neuropathy (cumulative), hepatotoxicity (↑LFTs, rare portal hypertension - nodular regenerative hyperplasia), infusion reactions, fatigue; teratogenic. Note: thrombocytopenia monitoring essential (platelet count pre-each cycle); do NOT substitute for trastuzumab alone (different drug - ado-trastuzumab emtansine ≠ trastuzumab; different toxicity; different indication); KATHERINE trial - established adjuvant role in HER2+ EBC with residual disease; PBS-listed in Australia.

Steroidal aromatase inhibitor (AI) - type I (irreversible - mechanism-based, 'suicide inhibitor'). MOA: binds aromatase (CYP19A1) active site as false substrate → covalently inactivates enzyme → irreversible inhibition → ↓oestrogen synthesis in peripheral tissues (adipose, muscle, liver - post-menopausal oestrogen source); steroidal structure (unlike non-steroidal letrozole/anastrozole - type II). Indications: postmenopausal HR+ advanced breast cancer (1st-line or after tamoxifen failure); early adjuvant (TEAM trial - non-inferior to tamoxifen → exemestane → switch); breast cancer chemoprevention (high-risk). SE: musculoskeletal symptoms (arthralgia, myalgia, joint stiffness - very common - main tolerability issue), hot flushes, fatigue, osteoporosis (↓oestrogen → ↓bone density → Ca/vitamin D supplementation + DEXA monitoring), vaginal dryness; note: unlike anastrozole/letrozole - mild androgenic activity (androgens generated from steroidal structure - may reduce musculoskeletal SE and osteoporosis). Note: steroidal AI (different class from anastrozole/letrozole - type I irreversible vs type II reversible); mild androgen properties → potentially fewer bone/muscle SE than non-steroidal AIs; once daily oral; commonly used when non-steroidal AI causes intolerable musculoskeletal SE.

Bispecific T-cell engager (BiTE) - anti-DLL3 × anti-CD3. MOA: simultaneously binds DLL3 (delta-like ligand 3 - overexpressed on SCLC, neuroendocrine tumours) and CD3 on T-cells → brings T-cells to DLL3-expressing tumour cells → T-cell-mediated cytotoxicity (tumour cell lysis); DLL3 expressed in >85% of SCLC, minimal normal tissue expression. Indications: extensive-stage SCLC (ES-SCLC) - previously treated (after platinum-based chemotherapy - DeLLphi-301 trial: ORR 40% [10 mg], ORR 32% [100 mg]; US FDA accelerated approval May 2024). SE: CRS (cytokine release syndrome - most common; grade 1-2 - fever, hypotension, tachycardia - hospitalise first 1-2 cycles; stepwise dose escalation protocol), neurological toxicity (ICANS - immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome - confusion, encephalopathy), fatigue, nausea, anaemia; infections. Note: first approved targeted therapy for SCLC (historically only chemotherapy - massive unmet need); IV biweekly after initial weekly doses × 4; CRS management - pre-medicate + hospitalise for first doses; dexamethasone/tocilizumab if grade 2+ CRS; monitoring for ICANS; DLL3 testing recommended but most SCLC expresses DLL3.

Non-steroidal SERM (selective oestrogen receptor modulator) - triphenylethylene derivative (structurally related to tamoxifen). MOA: competitively inhibits oestrogen binding to ERα in breast tissue (antagonist) while partial agonist at bone/uterine/liver ERs; similar mechanism to tamoxifen but slightly different pharmacology (chlorinated side chain). Indications: postmenopausal women with HR+ metastatic breast cancer (first-line or relapsed - IBIS trial; alternative to tamoxifen in postmenopausal metastatic disease); QTc prolongation risk at high doses (off-label prostate cancer). SE: hot flushes, nausea, vaginal discharge/bleeding, endometrial hyperplasia (uterine risk - monitor), thromboembolism (VTE - SERM class - less than high-dose tamoxifen), QTc prolongation (dose-related - unique vs tamoxifen). Note: similar efficacy to tamoxifen for metastatic HR+ breast cancer in postmenopausal women; QTc concern (especially at doses >60 mg/day); not commonly used in Australia (tamoxifen more prevalent); not for premenopausal women (unlike tamoxifen - less data).

GalNAc-conjugated siRNA targeting LPA mRNA - potent Lp(a) lowering. MOA: hepatocyte-targeted GalNAc-siRNA → ASGR receptor uptake → RNAi-mediated cleavage of LPA mRNA → ↓apolipoprotein(a) synthesis → ↓Lp(a) (~80% reduction); Lp(a) is genetically determined and almost invariant with diet/lifestyle; elevated Lp(a) = causal risk factor for ASCVD and aortic stenosis. Indications: elevated Lp(a) in patients with established ASCVD - OCEAN(a)-OUTCOMES phase 3 cardiovascular outcomes trial (ongoing; US-approved November 2024 based on Lp[a]-lowering surrogate endpoint - OCEAN[a]-DOSE: 75 mg or 225 mg SC quarterly → 98% ↓Lp[a]). SE: injection site reactions (mild), URTI; well tolerated. Note: quarterly SC injection (every 3 months - major convenience advantage); 98% Lp(a) lowering (profound - vs pelacarsen [monthly ASO] or PCSK9i [~25%]); US-approved November 2024 for cardiovascular risk reduction; compare to pelacarsen (monthly ASO - HORIZON trial - similar profound Lp[a] lowering); first approved agent specifically targeting Lp(a); TGA status in Australia - check current registration.

IV nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate (2nd generation). MOA: incorporated into osteoclast via phagocytosis → inhibits farnesyl diphosphate synthase → ↓osteoclast function/survival → ↓bone resorption; IV formulation → rapid bone incorporation. Indications: hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM - 90 mg IV single infusion → response within 24-48h - standard treatment); bone metastases (breast cancer, myeloma - monthly infusions; ↓skeletal-related events [SREs]); Paget's disease of bone (single infusion → prolonged remission); osteogenesis imperfecta (paediatric); osteoporosis (when oral bisphosphonates not tolerated). SE: flu-like reaction (acute phase response - fever, myalgia, headache - 24-72h after first infusion; subsequent doses milder); osteonecrosis of jaw (ONJ - especially in cancer/high-dose long-term; dental hygiene critical); renal impairment (infuse slowly - minimum 2-4h - risk of nephrotoxicity); hypocalcaemia + hypophosphataemia; atypical femoral fracture (long-term). Note: ONJ risk - dental assessment before starting and every 6 months; use lowest effective dose/frequency for oncology indications; give after dental procedures heal; hydration important pre/post infusion (renal protection); creatinine monitoring.

Oral aromatic retinoid (vitamin A derivative, 2nd generation). MOA: binds nuclear RAR (retinoic acid receptor) α/γ → alters gene transcription → ↓keratinocyte proliferation + ↑differentiation + ↓inflammation; normalises keratinisation. Indications: severe plaque psoriasis (unresponsive to conventional therapy), pustular psoriasis (generalised - 1st-line), palmoplantar keratoderma, Darier's disease, pityriasis rubra pilaris, ichthyoses, Sézary syndrome (adjunct); lichen planus (off-label). SE: teratogenicity (category X - ABSOLUTE CI in pregnancy or females of childbearing potential within 3 years of stopping - metabolised to etretinate [stored in fat] - prolonged teratogenic risk; strict REMS/pregnancy prevention programme); dyslipidaemia (↑TG, ↑cholesterol, ↓HDL - monitor fasting lipids); hepatotoxicity (↑LFTs - monitor); mucocutaneous - cheilitis, dry lips/mouth (universal - 100%), alopecia, dry eyes, nail changes; skeletal - vertebral DISH (diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis - long-term); pseudotumour cerebri. CI: pregnancy, breastfeeding, hepatic/renal failure, hyperlipidaemia. Note: pregnancy prevention programme mandatory (2 methods of contraception; monthly βhCG tests; 3-year avoidance of pregnancy after stopping); no alcohol (etretinate accumulation → prolonged teratogenicity period extended); PBS-listed in Australia (specialist prescription).

Prostaglandin F2α analogue (FP receptor agonist) - IOP-lowering. MOA: agonises FP (prostaglandin F) receptors in ciliary body → ↑uveoscleral aqueous outflow (primarily) → ↓IOP; most potent IOP-lowering mechanism of all glaucoma drug classes (↓IOP 25-35%). Indications: open-angle glaucoma/ocular hypertension (once-daily evening eye drop - most effective class). SE: conjunctival hyperaemia (red eye - most prominent in first weeks), iris hyperpigmentation (permanent - brown pigmentation - especially hazel irides - warn patients; affects eye with drop - asymmetric if unilateral use), eyelash growth/darkening (hypertrichosis), periorbital fat atrophy (sunken eye appearance - long-term), uveitis (rare). Note: evening dosing (maximum efficacy - prostaglandin circadian timing); iris colour change is permanent (warn before prescribing - especially unilateral use); prostaglandin class = most effective IOP reduction; combined with netarsudil (Rocklatan) for additional IOP lowering; class also includes: latanoprost (original - most studied), bimatoprost, tafluprost (preservative-free).

Direct-acting muscarinic (M3) agonist - miotic + secretagogue. MOA: activates muscarinic M3 receptors → (ophthalmic) pupillary constriction (miosis) + ↑trabecular meshwork outflow → ↓IOP; (systemic oral) stimulates salivary/lacrimal gland secretion → ↑saliva and tears. Indications: (ophthalmic) open-angle glaucoma/OHT (4th-line - superseded by prostaglandins, beta-blockers; pilocarpine used for acute angle-closure - constricts pupil, opens drainage angle); acute angle-closure glaucoma (miotic - pulls iris away from angle - 1% or 2%); angle closure prevention; (oral - Salagen 5 mg TDS) Sjögren's syndrome (dry mouth/eyes), radiation-induced xerostomia (head/neck cancer radiotherapy). SE: ophthalmic - brow ache/headache (ciliary muscle spasm - common - adapts over weeks), blurred vision (near-sightedness increase from accommodation - miosis), retinal detachment risk (extreme myopes - vigorous ciliary muscle contraction); systemic from eye drops: sweating, flushing, increased salivation, nausea; oral - sweating (most common), flushing, urinary frequency, GI distress. Note: ophthalmic - multiple times daily dosing (QDS - inconvenient - limits use); oral for Sjögren's/xerostomia - 5 mg TDS - significant benefit for quality of life; contraindicated with narrow-angle glaucoma for systemic use (paradox - ophthalmic pilocarpine TREATS angle closure; oral pilocarpine not for systemic use in uncontrolled narrow angle).

4-Aminoquinoline antimalarial (related to hydroxychloroquine). MOA: concentrates in parasite's food vacuole → inhibits haem detoxification (haem polymerisation to haemozoin) → toxic haem accumulates → parasite death; also alkalinises lysosomal pH (immune modulation in rheumatic use). Indications: malaria (uncomplicated P.vivax, P.ovale, P.malariae - NOT P.falciparum [widespread resistance]; P.vivax chloroquine resistance emerging in PNG - check local resistance patterns); rheumatoid arthritis, SLE (less commonly used than hydroxychloroquine - hydroxychloroquine preferred due to lower retinal toxicity). SE: retinal toxicity (dose-dependent cumulative - bull's-eye maculopathy - regular ophthalmological review; chloroquine MORE retinotoxic than hydroxychloroquine - prefer HCQ for long-term use); nausea, pruritus (especially in African patients - via histamine release), headache; QTc prolongation; haemolysis (G6PD deficiency - check G6PD before use). Note: G6PD status before prescribing; chloroquine maculopathy more toxic than hydroxychloroquine (higher dose/weight ratio reaches retinal threshold faster - limit dose <2.5 mg/kg/day); for malaria - Vivax/malariae treatment (falciparum now treated with ACT - artemether-lumefantrine); used for P.vivax radical cure + tafenoquine for relapse prevention.

Nucleotide analogue reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NtRTI) - hepatitis B virus (HBV). MOA: adenine nucleotide analogue → phosphorylated intracellularly to adefovir diphosphate → competitive inhibition of HBV DNA polymerase/reverse transcriptase → chain termination → ↓HBV replication; active against lamivudine-resistant HBV (YMDD mutations - tenofovir resistance profile similar to adefovir). Indications: chronic hepatitis B (adults - lamivudine-resistant HBV - now mostly replaced by tenofovir/entecavir which are more potent; still used in some settings). SE: nephrotoxicity (dose-dependent - Fanconi syndrome/proximal tubular dysfunction - monitor creatinine; higher risk at 30 mg/day; 10 mg/day approved dose has lower nephrotoxicity); headache, asthenia, GI discomfort; HBV flare on discontinuation (do NOT stop without suppression). Note: largely replaced by tenofovir (TDF/TAF) and entecavir (more potent, less nephrotoxic) in most guidelines; still used in HBV/HIV-coinfection management; avoid in renal impairment; adefovir resistance develops (rtA181V, rtN236T) - less than lamivudine; monitor renal function/phosphate (Fanconi syndrome risk).

Local anaesthetic (amide class - same class as lignocaine/bupivacaine). MOA: blocks voltage-gated sodium channels → prevents action potential propagation → local anaesthesia; less potent than bupivacaine, similar onset to lignocaine. Indications: topical anaesthesia (EMLA cream - prilocaine 2.5% + lignocaine 2.5% - eutectic mixture; venepuncture, minor procedures, tattoo analgesia); infiltration anaesthesia; regional nerve blocks; IV regional anaesthesia (Bier's block). SE: methaemoglobinaemia (unique to prilocaine - 5-OH prilocaine metabolite oxidises Hb-Fe2+ to MetHb-Fe3+ → impairs O2 delivery → cyanosis - especially in neonates [EMLA use < 3 months], G6PD deficiency, prolonged application); local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST - rare - CNS [perioral tingling, seizures] + CV [QRS widening, arrhythmia] - if injected into blood vessel); allergic reactions (rare - amide class). CI: neonates < 37 weeks gestation (EMLA); G6PD deficiency (methaemoglobinaemia risk). Note: EMLA cream - topical use (45-60 min under occlusion before venepuncture - most common paediatric use); methaemoglobinaemia - resuscitate with methylene blue (1-2 mg/kg IV - reduces MetHb back to Hb); prilocaine preferred over lignocaine for IVRA (Bier's block) in some guidelines (shorter duration → faster washout).

Mast cell stabiliser (and possibly weak TRPV1/sensory nerve modulator). MOA: inhibits degranulation of mast cells (mechanism incompletely understood - possibly inhibits Ca²⁺-dependent mast cell activation) → ↓release of histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins → ↓immediate and delayed hypersensitivity; also inhibits sensory nerve activation (anti-tussive, anti-neurogenic inflammation). Indications: bronchial asthma (inhaled Intal - prophylaxis in mild asthma especially exercise-induced and allergic asthma in children; must use regularly - no acute bronchodilation - no bronchodilator properties; now largely superseded by inhaled corticosteroids); allergic rhinitis (nasal); allergic conjunctivitis (eye drops - Opticrom); food allergy (oral Nalcrom - systemic mastocytosis, food-protein-induced enterocolitis). SE: bronchospasm (paradoxical - with inhaled powder formulation; nebulised preferred); throat irritation; bitter taste; well tolerated overall. Note: NO bronchodilation (must combine with β2 agonist for acute symptoms); requires regular use (4× daily for asthma prophylaxis - adherence challenging); now predominantly used in paediatric asthma (where ICS concerns about growth); oral cromoglicate for systemic mastocytosis/GI food allergy (different indication from inhaled); largely historical first-line replaced by ICS.

SERM (selective oestrogen receptor modulator) - 3rd generation. MOA: agonises ER at bone (↓bone resorption) and liver (↓LDL); antagonises ER at breast (↓proliferation) and uterus (↓endometrial stimulation - protection from oestrogen-induced hyperplasia); unique: combined with conjugated oestrogens (Duavive) - bazedoxifene eliminates need for progestogen in HRT (SERMs + oestrogen without progestogen = TSEC - tissue-selective oestrogen complex). Indications: postmenopausal osteoporosis (Conbriza/Viviant - ↓vertebral fractures); as component of Duavive (conjugated oestrogens + bazedoxifene - menopausal symptoms HRT without progestogen - for postmenopausal women with uterus). SE: hot flushes, muscle spasms, nausea (oral); VTE (class SERM risk); endometrial protection (Duavive - bazedoxifene eliminates need for progestogen); clot risk - avoid if VTE history. Note: Duavive = oestrogen + bazedoxifene without progestogen - advantage of HRT without progesterone SE (breast tenderness, mood changes); bazedoxifene protects uterus while oestrogen relieves vasomotor symptoms; compare to tibolone (synthetic steroid with oestrogen/progestogen/androgen effects); TGA approved in Australia.

Tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) - also antipruritic (topical). MOA: inhibits serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake + potent H1 receptor antagonism (antihistamine) + muscarinic antagonism; H1 antagonism strongest of any TCA → most sedating, most antipruritic; also used topically (Prudoxin 5% cream) for antipruritic effect (systemic absorption minimal). Indications: major depression; anxiety; insomnia (low-dose 3-6 mg - Silenor - approved for sleep maintenance insomnia - much lower than antidepressant dose 75-300 mg); pruritus (topical cream - atopic dermatitis, lichen simplex chronicus); Zonalon - branded topical for itch. SE: sedation (very prominent - H1), anticholinergic (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, cognitive impairment), weight gain, orthostatic hypotension, QTc prolongation (cardiac toxicity - arrhythmia in overdose); topical - systemic absorption (CNS effects, drowsiness). CI: urinary retention, angle-closure glaucoma, acute MI. Note: most sedating TCA (H1 potency); low-dose 3-6 mg for insomnia (distinct from antidepressant doses - much better tolerated); topical - apply to small areas (≤10% BSA) to limit systemic absorption; avoid in elderly (Beers criteria - anticholinergic + falls risk).

Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (CCB) - CNS-selective. MOA: preferentially blocks L-type Ca²⁺ channels in cerebral arteries (lipophilic → crosses BBB; high affinity for cerebrovascular smooth muscle) → ↓cerebral vasospasm following subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH); minimal effect on systemic BP at therapeutic doses (compare to systemic DHP CCBs - amlodipine/nifedipine). Indications: SAH (prevention of delayed cerebral ischaemia/cerebral vasospasm - vasospasm typically peaks days 5-14 post-SAH; NIMODIPINE started within 96h of SAH and continued 21 days - ↓neurological deficits without ↓angiographic vasospasm - paradox); NOT for other types of stroke. SE: hypotension (systemic - dose-limiting; monitor BP), nausea; bradycardia (less than verapamil/diltiazem). Note: enteral administration ONLY (NOT IV in Australia - parenteral solutions not available in some countries; IV nimodipine given in Europe but not licensed IV in Australia - use oral/NG tube); NEVER inject into vein accidentally (catastrophic hypotension + death reported - several fatal errors with IV syringe administration; Nimotop is an oral/NG product in Australia); start within 96h of SAH and continue 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days.

Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (CCB) - 2nd generation, vascular selective. MOA: selective L-type Ca²⁺ channel blocker in vascular smooth muscle (coronary and peripheral arterial) → vasodilation + ↓BP; higher vascular selectivity than nifedipine → less negative inotropic effect; extended-release formulation → smoother plasma levels. Indications: hypertension; stable angina; Raynaud's phenomenon (off-label). SE: ankle oedema (most common - vasodilation → ↑capillary pressure → fluid extravasation - improves with ACEi/ARB combination which reduce capillary pressure), headache, flushing (vasodilation), reflex tachycardia; gingival hyperplasia (CCB class - cyclosporin combination risk); grapefruit juice interaction (CYP3A4 substrate - ↑levels - avoid). Note: grapefruit juice interaction (as with nifedipine/amlodipine - CYP3A4) - advise to avoid grapefruit; ankle oedema more prominent than with systemic CCBs that have less vasoactive effect; extended-release formulation (Plendil - once daily ER); PBS-listed in Australia; effective for HTN + angina.

Thiazide-like diuretic (long-acting) - superior outcome data vs hydrochlorothiazide. MOA: inhibits NaCl cotransporter (NCC/SLC12A3) in distal convoluted tubule → ↓Na/Cl reabsorption → natriuresis + diuresis + ↓plasma volume → ↓BP; longer half-life (~45h vs HCTZ ~10h) → more sustained BP control (better 24h coverage including morning surge). Indications: hypertension (first-line - superior cardiovascular outcomes vs hydrochlorothiazide in ALLHAT and other trials; SHEP trial - isolated systolic HTN in elderly); oedema; diabetes insipidus (nephrogenic - paradoxical - reduces polyuria). SE: hypokalaemia (↓Na/K exchange in DCT → kali-natriuresis), hyponatraemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia (↑Ca reabsorption - side effect that is exploited for nephrolithiasis prevention), hyperglycaemia/new-onset diabetes (↓insulin secretion), hyperuricaemia/gout, dyslipidaemia; impotence. Note: preferred over HCTZ in many guidelines for HTN (ALLHAT - chlorthalidone superior to amlodipine/lisinopril for HF; better 24h BP coverage); longer half-life → more sustained BP lowering; hypokalaemia monitoring; combine with ACEi/ARB for hypokalaemia prevention.

Selective imidazoline I1 receptor agonist (and α2-adrenoceptor agonist) - centrally acting antihypertensive. MOA: selectively activates imidazoline I1 receptors in rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM) → ↓sympathetic outflow → ↓noradrenaline release → ↓peripheral resistance + ↓HR → ↓BP; also weak α2 agonism (less central SE than clonidine which is mainly α2-agonist); not a diuretic. Indications: hypertension (mild-moderate - 2nd or 3rd line - combined with other agents); metabolic syndrome + HTN (improves insulin sensitivity - SONOS trial). SE: dry mouth (most common - less than clonidine), sedation, headache, dizziness; rebound hypertension on abrupt withdrawal (class centrally-acting - taper if stopping); insomnia (less than clonidine). Note: more selective for I1 than α2 (fewer CNS SE than clonidine - less sedation, dry mouth); less rebound hypertension than clonidine on withdrawal; NOT for heart failure (centrally-acting agents - MOXCON trial: excess mortality in HF); oral once-daily (200-400 mcg); PBS-listed in Australia.

Potassium-sparing diuretic (Na⁺ channel blocker). MOA: directly blocks luminal epithelial Na⁺ channels (ENaC) in collecting duct → ↓Na⁺ reabsorption → ↑Na⁺ and water excretion + ↓K⁺ secretion (K-sparing - different from aldosterone antagonists [spironolactone] which work via receptor); effect independent of aldosterone (direct channel block). Indications: oedema (congestive HF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome - combined with thiazide/loop diuretic to prevent hypokalaemia); hypertension (adjunct); hypokalaemia prevention (with kaliuretic diuretics). SE: hyperkalaemia (K-sparing - especially with ACEi/ARB, K-supplements, NSAIDs - avoid combination); hyponatraemia; nephrolithiasis (triamterene crystallises → triamterene stones - risk with concentrated urine); ↑creatinine (↓GFR); folate antagonism (inhibits DHFR - folate deficiency with prolonged use - supplement folate). Note: combine with HCTZ for balanced diuresis (Dyazide - triamterene/HCTZ); K-sparing effect useful when thiazide alone causes hypokalaemia; triamterene stones (distinct from other diuretics - renal stone risk); folate supplementation with prolonged use; CI: renal failure, hyperkalaemia, concurrent K-sparing drugs.

Selective α2A-adrenoceptor agonist - antihypertensive + ADHD (prefrontal). MOA: α2A selective agonism (more selective for α2A vs α2B/α2C than clonidine) → (1) prefrontal cortex: strengthens PFC connections → ↑working memory, attention, impulse control (ADHD mechanism - lower doses, extended release); (2) locus coeruleus + peripheral sympathetic: ↓central noradrenaline output → ↓BP (higher doses). Indications: ADHD (adjunct or monotherapy - Intuniv ER - non-stimulant option; especially ADHD + tic disorders/Tourette's; ADHD + anxiety/autism); hypertension (Tenex - adults; less commonly used vs modern agents). SE: somnolence (most common with ER - dose-dependent - particularly initial weeks; dose before bedtime), ↓HR, hypotension, headache, abdominal pain; rebound hypertension on abrupt discontinuation (class effect - taper). Note: non-stimulant ADHD option (Schedule 4 - no abuse potential unlike stimulants); particularly useful in ADHD + comorbid tics/Tourette's or oppositional defiant disorder; also combined with stimulants for ADHD (complementary mechanism - stimulant vs prefrontal α2A); ER formulation preferred (smoother profile); once-daily dosing; PBS-listed in Australia for ADHD.

Peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonist (PAMORA). MOA: quaternary amine - does not cross BBB → blocks peripheral μ-opioid receptors in GI tract WITHOUT reversing central analgesic effects; GI μ-receptor blockade → reverses opioid-induced constipation (OIC) - ↑bowel motility, ↑secretions, ↑propulsive contractions. Indications: opioid-induced constipation (OIC) in adults with chronic non-cancer pain on opioids (SC injection; oral formulation for advanced illness/palliative care - also SC approved for late-stage illness); also advanced illness/palliative care patients. Route: SC injection or oral. SE: abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhoea, flatulence (GI reactivation - expected effect), diaphoresis, tremor; opioid withdrawal symptoms (rare - hypersensitivity); bowel perforation (rare - caution if known/suspected GI perforation risk). Note: does NOT reverse central analgesia (cannot use for opioid overdose); PAMORA class (compare to naloxegol - oral PAMORA for OIC); SC injection 12mg single dose (need-basis) or oral 450 mg daily; compare to naloxegol (oral) and naldemedine (oral) - all PAMORA class for OIC; PBS-listed in Australia for OIC in cancer pain/advanced illness.

Guanylate cyclase-C (GC-C) receptor agonist. MOA: binds GC-C receptor on intestinal epithelial cells → ↑intracellular cGMP → activates PKG-II → ↑CFTR Cl⁻ secretion + ↓NHE3 Na⁺ absorption → ↑intestinal fluid secretion → ↑bowel movement frequency + ↓stool consistency; also ↑extracellular cGMP → sensitises enteric pain fibres (↓visceral hypersensitivity). Indications: chronic idiopathic constipation (CIC); IBS with constipation (IBS-C) - DISCREPANCY trials. SE: diarrhoea (most common - dose-related - class GC-C agonist; severe diarrhoea reported - pause if develops; take with or without food). CI: children <6 years (boxed warning - GC-C agonist → severe dehydrating diarrhoea in paediatric rat models - do not use; paediatric: avoid entirely under 18 years of age for marketed forms). Note: similar class to linaclotide (GC-C agonist - already present) but different molecular structure (plecanatide is uroguanylin analogue vs linaclotide is guanylin analogue); pH-sensitive (more active in acidic proximal intestine - theoretical advantage for upper GI symptoms); boxed warning for children under 18; take once daily (3 mg) with or without food; limited availability in Australia (check TGA registration).

Sodium-hydrogen exchanger 3 (NHE3) inhibitor. MOA: inhibits NHE3 (intestinal epithelial Na⁺/H⁺ exchanger) → ↓Na⁺ absorption → ↑intraluminal osmotic activity → ↑fluid secretion → softened stool + ↑bowel frequency; also ↓intestinal phosphate absorption (NHE3 participates in paracellular phosphate transport) → ↓serum phosphate in CKD. Indications: IBS-C (irritable bowel syndrome with constipation - T3MPO-1/2 trials - 50 mg BD); hyperphosphataemia in adults with CKD on dialysis (Xphozah - 30 mg BD - ↓intestinal phosphate absorption). SE: diarrhoea (dose-related - limit dose for IBS-C indication; severe diarrhoea - pause/stop), flatulence; abdominal pain. CI: children <6 years (boxed warning - as with linaclotide/plecanatide class). Note: dual indication for two different mechanisms (IBS-C [osmotic laxative effect] and CKD hyperphosphataemia [phosphate absorption blockade]); NHE3 inhibition = novel target for both constipation and phosphate lowering; minimal systemic absorption (local GI action); available in Australia - check TGA status; particularly interesting for dialysis patients who have both constipation and hyperphosphataemia.

Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (CCB) - highly lipophilic, vascular selective, long-acting. MOA: blocks L-type Ca²⁺ channels in vascular smooth muscle → vasodilation → ↓BP; high lipophilicity → membrane partitioning → slow onset + very long effective duration despite moderate half-life (low ankle oedema vs amlodipine - due to balanced vascular compartment distribution). Indications: hypertension (mild-moderate - ELSA trial; PBS-listed in Australia). SE: ankle oedema (LESS than amlodipine - key advantage; lipophilicity → longer tissue distribution → reduced capillary pressure fluctuation), headache, flushing, palpitations (much less than short-acting dihydropyridines). Note: significantly less peripheral oedema than amlodipine in head-to-head trials (ELSA: lercanidipine 4.3% oedema vs amlodipine 8.8%) - preferred when amlodipine oedema is problematic; once-daily oral; CYP3A4 substrate (avoid grapefruit); take 15 min before breakfast (food ↑absorption - take consistently); PBS-listed in Australia.

Tetracyclic antidepressant (TeCA) - selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor. MOA: primarily inhibits noradrenaline reuptake transporter (NET) with minimal SERT inhibition → ↑synaptic noradrenaline; also H1 and α1 blockade (sedation, orthostatic hypotension); structurally tetracyclic (resembles TCA pharmacologically - included in TCA class for practical purposes). Indications: major depression; anxiety with depression; depressive phase of bipolar. SE: sedation (H1 blockade), dry mouth/constipation/urinary retention (anticholinergic - less than amitriptyline), orthostatic hypotension, weight gain; seizure risk (relatively high - lower seizure threshold - particularly at doses >150 mg/day; contraindicated in epilepsy); QTc prolongation (class); skin photosensitivity (rash with sun exposure). CI: epilepsy/seizure history (↑seizure risk), recent MI, QTc prolongation. Note: higher seizure risk than tricyclics (caution; limit dose to ≤150 mg/day in epilepsy risk patients; historically caused more seizures than expected in trials); relatively NE-selective (compare to amitriptyline - balanced SNRI + anticholinergic; maprotiline predominantly NE); now less commonly prescribed than newer antidepressants but available in Australia.

Arterial vasodilator + hair growth stimulant. MOA: (1) oral - opens ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels (KATP) in vascular smooth muscle → hyperpolarisation → vasodilation → ↓afterload → ↓BP; potent vasodilator (3rd-line severe HTN); (2) topical - mechanism in hair growth unclear (KATP opening in dermal papilla → ↑growth factor expression → prolong anagen phase + vessel dilation around follicle). Indications: (oral) severe/resistant hypertension (add-on 3rd-line - requires loop diuretic + beta-blocker to counteract SE - rarely used alone); (topical) androgenetic alopecia (2%/5% solution, 5% foam - applied directly to scalp).
