SE: (oral) sodium/water retention (loop diuretic required), reflex tachycardia (beta-blocker required), hypertrichosis (unwanted hair - reversible - limits use in women - exploited in topical form for hair loss); pericardial effusion/pulmonary hypertension (rare - high doses); (topical) scalp irritation, contact dermatitis, facial hypertrichosis (some absorption). Note: oral minoxidil - always combine with loop diuretic (fluid retention) + beta-blocker (reflex tachycardia) = triple combination for severe HTN; topical minoxidil for hair loss (used indefinitely - hair loss returns if stopped); oral low-dose (2.5-5 mg/day) now emerging for hair loss (off-label - FASTER trial evidence).

Highly selective α1A-adrenoceptor antagonist (alpha-blocker). MOA: selectively blocks α1A-AR (predominantly expressed in prostate, bladder neck, urethra) → ↓smooth muscle tone → ↓urethral resistance → improved urine flow; α1A/α1B selectivity ratio very high (162:1) → minimal vascular α1B effects → less orthostatic hypotension vs tamsulosin/alfuzosin. Indications: symptomatic benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH - lower urinary tract symptoms [LUTS] - significant improvement in Qmax and IPSS scores). SE: retrograde ejaculation (very common - >20% - mechanically caused by α1A relaxation of bladder neck/seminal vesicles → antegrade ejaculation impaired; counsel before prescribing; resolves on cessation - important for men wishing to conceive); dizziness, orthostatic hypotension (less than non-selective alpha-blockers); rhinorrhoea. Note: retrograde ejaculation - high rate (20-30% vs tamsulosin ~11%) - must counsel before starting; for men not concerned about ejaculation (elderly), lower orthostatic hypotension risk may be preferred; intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS) - risk with any alpha-blocker in cataract surgery - inform ophthalmologist prior to cataract surgery; once-daily 8 mg.

Pan-FGFR (fibroblast growth factor receptor 1-4) kinase inhibitor. MOA: inhibits FGFR1-4 → ↓downstream RAS-MAPK and PI3K-Akt signalling → ↓proliferation in FGFR-altered tumours; FGFR3 alterations (mutations + fusions) in ~20-25% of urothelial carcinoma. Indications: locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma (bladder/upper urinary tract) with susceptible FGFR2/FGFR3 alterations (after platinum-based chemotherapy - THOR trial: 35% ORR, improved OS vs chemotherapy; US-approved; also first-line THOR-2 trial data); FGFR testing required. SE: hyperphosphataemia (FGFR1 inhibition in kidney → FGF23 blockade → ↑phosphate reabsorption - monitor serum phosphate; dietary phosphate restriction required); ocular toxicity (central serous retinopathy/CSR - serous retinal detachment - FGFR signalling in RPE - monthly ophthalmology monitoring); stomatitis, palmoplantar erythrodysaesthesia, nail changes, alopecia, diarrhoea; ↑creatinine. Note: FGFR3 mutation/fusion testing required (FISH or NGS); hyperphosphataemia monitoring (dose reduce if P >5.5 mmol/L); monthly eye examinations (CSR risk); FGFR class includes also: pemigatinib (CCA), futibatinib (CCA), infigratinib (CCA) - bladder cancer specific for erdafitinib.

Selective FGFR1/2/3 kinase inhibitor (spares FGFR4). MOA: potently inhibits FGFR1, 2, 3 → ↓downstream signalling in tumours with FGFR2 fusions/rearrangements (cholangiocarcinoma) or FGFR1 mutations (haematological malignancies). Indications: previously treated locally advanced/metastatic intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) with FGFR2 fusion/rearrangement - FIGHT-202 trial: ORR 35%, mPFS 6.9 months (US FDA breakthrough; approved 2020); myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with FGFR1 rearrangement. SE: hyperphosphataemia (FGFR1 inhibition - monitor/restrict phosphate diet), ocular toxicity (CSR - central serous retinopathy - monthly ophthalmic monitoring), stomatitis, diarrhoea, alopecia, palmar-plantar rash; ↑LFTs. Note: FGFR2 fusion testing required (RNA-based NGS preferred - detects all fusion partners vs DNA-based); 2 weeks on/1 week off schedule (21-day cycle - mitigates hyperphosphataemia + ocular toxicity); compare to futibatinib (another FGFR1-4 inhibitor for CCA - less selectivity, similar indications); hyperphosphataemia + ocular monitoring = class FGFR inhibitor monitoring requirements.

Covalent (irreversible) pan-FGFR1-4 inhibitor. MOA: irreversible covalent binding to FGFR1-4 → sustained inhibition (overcomes some FGFR2 resistance mutations that emerge with reversible inhibitors like pemigatinib); targets FGFR2 fusions + secondary resistance mutations (e.g., FGFR2 V565I, N549K). Indications: previously treated locally advanced/metastatic intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA) with FGFR2 rearrangement/fusion - FOENIX-CCA2 trial: ORR 42%, mPFS 9 months (US-approved 2022). SE: hyperphosphataemia (class FGFR inhibitor - monitor phosphate, phosphate-restricted diet), central serous retinopathy (CSR - monthly ophthalmic monitoring), diarrhoea, stomatitis, fatigue, alopecia, hand-foot syndrome, ↑LFTs. Note: once-daily dosing (vs pemigatinib 2 weeks on/1 week off); covalent binding overcomes some secondary resistance mutations (benefit vs pemigatinib for acquired resistance); same monitoring requirements as other FGFR inhibitors (phosphate + ophthalmology); FGFR2 fusion/rearrangement testing required; available in Australia (TGA approved - check PBS status for cholangiocarcinoma).

Dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) inhibitor. MOA: inhibits parasitic DHFR → blocks folate synthesis → ↓thymidylate + purine synthesis → ↓DNA replication in Toxoplasma, Plasmodium; combined with sulfadiazine (synergy - sulfonamide blocks upstream DHPS). Indications: toxoplasmosis (treatment + secondary prophylaxis in HIV - always with sulfadiazine ± folinic acid; preferred for CNS toxoplasmosis); malaria prophylaxis (combined with dapsone as Maloprim - not 1st-line for Australians); Pneumocystis jirovecii (alternative, 2nd line). SE: folate deficiency (megaloblastic anaemia, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia - give folinic acid [leucovorin] concurrently to reduce marrow suppression without rescuing parasite); rash; GI upset; teratogenic (folate antagonist - avoid 1st trimester if possible). Note: always prescribe folinic acid (leucovorin) with pyrimethamine - does NOT reduce antiparasitic efficacy (parasite cannot utilise exogenous folate; human cells can); toxoplasma encephalitis in HIV - treat acute then lifelong secondary prophylaxis (sulfadiazine + pyrimethamine + leucovorin) until CD4 >200 for 6 months.

Biguanide antimalarial (prodrug). MOA: metabolised by CYP2C19 to cycloguanil → inhibits Plasmodium DHFR (antifolate); atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) combination: atovaquone collapses mitochondrial membrane potential → proguanil potentiates (synergy - mechanism distinct from cycloguanil; causal prophylaxis = kills liver-stage parasites). Indications: malaria prophylaxis (Malarone = atovaquone 250 mg/proguanil 100 mg - 1st-line for travellers to P. falciparum regions including sub-Saharan Africa - start 1 day before travel, continue 7 days after); treatment of uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria (Malarone - 3-day course). SE: GI upset (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain - take with food); headache; mouth ulcers (proguanil monotherapy); hepatotoxicity (rare). Note: CYP2C19 poor metabolisers (~20% East Asian - reduced cycloguanil conversion - reduced efficacy for proguanil monotherapy; atovaquone component still active in Malarone - less concern); causal prophylaxis = also covers liver stage (unlike mefloquine/chloroquine - can stop 7 days after return rather than 4 weeks); take with food and water to improve tolerability.

Benzimidazole anthelmintic for liver flukes. MOA: mechanism incompletely understood - metabolised to sulphoxide + sulphone forms → inhibit tubulin polymerisation in Fasciola hepatica → disrupts cytoskeleton + tegument; active against both adult and juvenile/immature flukes (unique - other benzimidazoles mainly adult-active). Indications: fascioliasis (Fasciola hepatica/gigantica - liver fluke - 1st-line WHO treatment; 2 doses of 10 mg/kg 12 hours apart; single dose 10 mg/kg effective in some studies); paragonimiasis (Paragonimus spp - lung fluke; less commonly used vs praziquantel). SE: biliary colic (migration of dead/dying flukes through bile ducts); GI upset; sweating; urticaria; elevated LFTs (transient); dizziness. Note: take with food (fatty meal improves absorption); fascioliasis - common in SE Asia, Middle East, Andean South America, sub-Saharan Africa; zoonosis (sheep/cattle reservoir - contaminated watercress); eosinophilia + RUQ pain + fever suggests acute fascioliasis; chronic: biliary obstruction.

Depolarising neuromuscular blocking agent (anthelmintic). MOA: acts as nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonist → persistent activation of nematode nicotinic AChR → spastic paralysis of worm → expelled by peristalsis; minimally absorbed from GI tract (local luminal action). Indications: enterobiasis (pinworm/threadworm - Enterobius vermicularis - single dose 10 mg/kg; repeat after 2 weeks; treat all household contacts); ascariasis (roundworm - Ascaris lumbricoides); hookworm (Ancylostoma, Necator - less effective than albendazole for heavy infections). SE: mild GI effects (nausea, cramps, diarrhoea - transient); headache; dizziness; rash (rare). Note: no fasting required; single-dose treatment (convenient for children - available OTC in Australia as Combantrin/Early Bird); retreat after 2 weeks (eggs from environment - reinfection common - also re-expose hatched larvae); mebendazole/albendazole preferred for heavy ascariasis/hookworm burden; safe in children >2 years and pregnancy.

Nitrofuran antiprotozoal. MOA: reduced by nitroreductases within Trypanosoma cruzi → generates reactive oxygen/nitrogen species (superoxide, H₂O₂) → oxidative stress → DNA damage + parasite death; T. cruzi deficient in catalase/peroxidase → susceptible. Indications: Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis - T. cruzi - 1st-line with benznidazole; adult 8-10 mg/kg/day in 3-4 divided doses × 60-90 days; paediatric: 15-20 mg/kg/day; most effective in acute phase); human African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness - Trypanosoma brucei gambiense - nifurtimox-eflornithine combination treatment [NECT] - late-stage CNS disease). SE: GI (anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain - frequent - limit compliance); neurological (headache, tremor, seizures, peripheral neuropathy - dose-dependent; reduce dose if neurological SE); rash; weight loss. Note: Chagas disease - early treatment (acute/recent-onset) most effective (cure rate ~80%); chronic phase treatment (established cardiomyopathy) debated - reduces parasite burden but clinical benefit less clear; notify travellers returning from endemic areas (South/Central America).

Nitroimidazole antiprotozoal for Chagas disease. MOA: reduced by type I nitroreductases in T. cruzi → reactive metabolites → covalent modification of parasite macromolecules (DNA, proteins, lipids) → parasite death; mechanism distinct from metronidazole (which works against anaerobes and protozoa via type II nitroreductase-independent mechanism). Indications: Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis - T. cruzi - 1st-line alongside nifurtimox; adult 5-7 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses × 60 days; most effective in acute phase, congenital transmission; US-approved 2017; also used in children for congenital Chagas). SE: dermatitis (rash - most common; pruritic, can be severe - dose-reduce or discontinue if Stevens-Johnson); peripheral neuropathy (dose-dependent, prolonged use); GI (nausea, anorexia); leucopenia; liver enzyme elevation. Note: rash most common SE (~30%); nifurtimox vs benznidazole - similar efficacy; benznidazole generally preferred for better tolerated profile in chronic phase (BENEFIT trial: no improvement in HF outcomes with treatment in chronic cardiomyopathy - but reduces seroconversion); treatment recommended in acute, reactivation, and early chronic phase.

14-membered ring macrolide antibiotic. MOA: binds 23S rRNA of 50S ribosomal subunit → blocks translocation → inhibits bacterial protein synthesis (bacteriostatic); same mechanism as erythromycin but superior pharmacokinetics (longer t½ 10-12 h, OD/BD dosing; better oral bioavailability ~72%; higher tissue concentrations). Indications: community-acquired respiratory tract infections (CAP, bronchitis - Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Legionella cover - PBS-listed in Australia); skin/soft tissue infections (impetigo, cellulitis); atypical pathogens; ENT infections (sinusitis, pharyngitis); genital chlamydia (alternative to azithromycin). SE: GI (nausea, diarrhoea - less than erythromycin; erythromycin motilin effect milder); hepatotoxicity (rare, cholestatic); QT prolongation (less than erythromycin/clarithromycin); drug interactions (CYP3A4 inhibitor - less potent than clarithromycin - caution with statins, warfarin, ciclosporin). Note: widely used in Australia (PBS-listed); 150 mg BD or 300 mg OD; take before food (fasting improves absorption); preferred over erythromycin for better tolerability; drug interactions less extensive than clarithromycin.

Tetracycline antibiotic (prodrug of tetracycline). MOA: binds 30S ribosomal subunit → inhibits aminoacyl-tRNA binding to ribosomal A-site → blocks bacterial protein synthesis (bacteriostatic); active against Propionibacterium acnes and other acne pathogens; prodrug (lymecycline = tetracycline + lysine) → better water solubility → improved GI tolerability. Indications: acne vulgaris (inflammatory acne - reduces P. acnes burden and anti-inflammatory effect; 408 mg OD × 3+ months - equivalent to tetracycline 300 mg BD with better compliance); Chlamydia trachomatis (alternative to doxycycline); respiratory, genital, skin infections. SE: GI (nausea, oesophagitis - less than tetracycline due to prodrug formulation); photosensitivity (sun avoidance, sunscreen); dental staining (avoid in <12 years + pregnant/lactating - binds calcium in developing teeth); ↑BUN (anti-anabolic effect); dizziness; Candida overgrowth; liver toxicity (rare). Note: take on empty stomach (calcium, dairy, antacids, iron chelate → ↓absorption); avoid during pregnancy + children <12 (dental staining + bone effects); OD dosing (vs tetracycline BD-QID) → better compliance for acne; 3-6 month course typical for acne.

Fluorocycline (synthetic tetracycline analogue - 4th generation). MOA: binds 30S ribosomal subunit at primary tetracycline binding site AND secondary site (unique dual binding) → blocks protein synthesis; overcomes both major tetracycline resistance mechanisms: (1) efflux pump (Tet-A, Tet-B - modified C7/C9 substituents reduce efflux); (2) ribosomal protection proteins (Tet-M/O - C7 fluorine + C9 pyrrolidinylacetamido side chain overcome); broad-spectrum including ESKAPE pathogens. Indications: complicated intra-abdominal infections (cIAI - IV; non-inferior to meropenem/ertapenem in IGNITE trials); complicated urinary tract infections (IV; not approved - US FDA rejected - insufficient efficacy in IGNITE4). SE: nausea/vomiting (IV infusion - common → pre-medicate with antiemetics; infusion rate-related); phlebitis; photosensitivity (tetracycline class - avoid sun); ↑LFTs; dizziness; dental/bone effects (tetracycline class - avoid in pregnancy/children). Note: IV-only formulation (no oral); useful for MDR gram-negative coverage (Enterobacteriaceae, Acinetobacter) + MRSA; compare to omadacycline (oral + IV tetracycline for CAP/SSTI); carbapenem-sparing option for cIAI.

Aminocyclitol antibiotic (structurally related to aminoglycosides). MOA: binds 16S rRNA of 30S ribosomal subunit at a site distinct from aminoglycosides → inhibits translocation step of protein synthesis (bacteriostatic, not bactericidal); potent activity against Neisseria gonorrhoeae including PPNG (penicillinase-producing N. gonorrhoeae). Indications: uncomplicated gonorrhoea (IM single dose 2 g) - reserved for cephalosporin-allergic patients or suspected cephalosporin-resistant gonococcal infection; not effective for pharyngeal gonorrhoea; no activity against Chlamydia, Treponema pallidum. SE: injection site pain; nausea; dizziness; urticaria; rarely anaemia/thrombocytopenia. Note: single IM dose (2 g gluteal injection); NOT for pharyngeal gonorrhoea (inadequate penetration → treatment failure); always test for cure (spectinomycin MIC breakpoints less established than ceftriaxone); limited availability - often requires special access in Australia; dual therapy (+ azithromycin) considered for possible chlamydia co-infection.

Morpholine antifungal (topical nail lacquer). MOA: inhibits two enzymes in ergosterol biosynthesis (delta-14-reductase and delta-7-8-isomerase) → accumulation of toxic sterol intermediates (ignosterol, avenasterol) → impaired fungal cell membrane integrity; unique dual-enzyme inhibition within ergosterol pathway (distinct from azoles which target CYP51/lanosterol demethylase). Indications: onychomycosis (fungal nail infection - dermatophytes: Trichophyton rubrum, T. mentagrophytes; some yeasts/moulds; 5% nail lacquer - weekly application; distal/subungual infection where ≤50% nail involved; fingernails 6 months, toenails 9-12 months). SE: local burning, redness, desquamation, nail discoloration (all mild, transient). Note: nail lacquer formulation - file nail surface before application; remove excess with included spatula; nail polish/artificial nails must not be used during treatment; systemic absorption minimal; alternative to oral therapy for mild/moderate onychomycosis; compare to ciclopirox lacquer (also topical antifungal nail lacquer - different MOA); topical-only (no systemic form - unlike terbinafine/itraconazole).

Hydroxypyridinone antifungal (structurally distinct from all other antifungals). MOA: chelates polyvalent cations (Fe³⁺, Al³⁺) → disrupts metal-dependent enzymes (cytochromes, mitochondrial electron transport chain enzymes); also directly disrupts fungal cell membrane integrity → broad-spectrum (dermatophytes, Candida, Malassezia, moulds); mechanism independent of ergosterol pathway (cf. azoles). Indications: topical - dermatophytosis (tinea pedis, corporis, cruris - cream/gel); seborrhoeic dermatitis (1% shampoo - Malassezia-related dandruff); onychomycosis (8% nail lacquer - less effective than oral terbinafine but systemic side-effect-free); Candida skin infections. SE: local irritation, burning, pruritus (mild); nail discoloration (lacquer form). Note: 1% shampoo for seborrhoeic dermatitis/dandruff - apply 2-3× weekly; nail lacquer (8%) - daily application; broad spectrum includes moulds (Aspergillus) + Malassezia - broader than amorolfine; chelates iron - separate from iron supplements in theoretical concern (topical only - minimal systemic absorption); seborrhoeic dermatitis treatment: leave shampoo 3-5 min before rinsing.

Long-acting beta-2 adrenoceptor agonist (LABA) - ultra-long-acting (24-hour duration). MOA: highly selective beta-2 agonist (functional selectivity/biased agonism toward cAMP pathway over beta-arrestin) → smooth muscle relaxation in bronchi and alveoli → bronchodilation; once-daily due to slow receptor dissociation kinetics. Indications: COPD - maintenance bronchodilator (OD via Respimat inhaler - soft mist inhaler); combined with tiotropium (LAMA) in Spiolto Respimat (LAMA+LABA - TONADO trial: superior to either alone for FEV₁ and quality of life). SE: cardiovascular effects (tachycardia, palpitations - less than SABA); muscle cramps; tremor; hypokalaemia (class beta-2 effect - caution with loop diuretics); QT prolongation (minimal). Note: NOT for asthma (LABA + ICS required in asthma - boxed warning for LABA monotherapy in asthma); COPD maintenance only; once-daily Respimat (soft mist) - lower aerosol velocity → better lung deposition than MDI; tiotropium/olodaterol (Spiolto) = first once-daily LAMA/LABA fixed-dose combination in Australia.

Ultra-long-acting beta-2 adrenoceptor agonist (LABA). MOA: highly selective beta-2 agonist → bronchial smooth muscle relaxation → bronchodilation; exceptionally long receptor residency → 24-hour duration (once-daily); used exclusively in fixed-dose combinations (not available as monotherapy - US FDA/TGA requirement given LABA boxed warning). Indications: asthma - fluticasone furoate/vilanterol (Relvar Ellipta - ICS/LABA combination; CONSULT trial; once-daily); COPD - umeclidinium/vilanterol (Anoro Ellipta - LAMA/LABA - once-daily); triple therapy COPD - fluticasone furoate/umeclidinium/vilanterol (Trelegy Ellipta - ICS/LAMA/LABA - IMPACT trial: ↓exacerbations + hospitalisations). SE: typical LABA class effects (tremor, tachycardia, hypokalaemia); hoarseness/dysphonia (ICS component of combination). Note: Ellipta dry-powder inhaler - once-daily; vilanterol never used alone - always in combination; Relvar = only once-daily ICS/LABA (all other ICS/LABAs are BD); Trelegy = first once-daily ICS/LAMA/LABA triple inhaler (PBS-listed Australia for COPD + frequent exacerbations).

Prodrug of terbutaline (LABA). MOA: bis-dimethylcarbamate prodrug → hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase/BuChE) → terbutaline (active form - selective beta-2 agonist → bronchodilation); slow hydrolysis provides sustained terbutaline release → prolonged bronchodilation (~24 h from single dose - once-daily LABA); peak terbutaline at 2-6 hours. Indications: COPD and asthma - maintenance bronchodilation (once-daily oral tablet, 10-20 mg nocte); particularly useful when inhaler technique is poor (oral formulation). SE: tremor, tachycardia, palpitations, headache, muscle cramps (beta-2 class - from released terbutaline); hypokalaemia; insomnia (nocte dosing but terbutaline can cause agitation). Note: prodrug concept - liver + plasma esterases convert bambuterol → terbutaline; caution in plasma cholinesterase deficiency (slow conversion - reduced efficacy + accumulation in theory - also caution with suxamethonium anaesthesia - competes for cholinesterase); oral once-daily alternative to inhaler-based LABAs for patients with poor inhaler technique; terbutaline = mother drug also available as SABA inhaler (Bricanyl).

Alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) inhibitor - antidote. MOA: competitive inhibitor of ADH (Ki ~0.1 µM - very potent, >8,000× more than ethanol) → prevents conversion of methanol → formaldehyde/formic acid; and ethylene glycol → glycolate/oxalate; these toxic metabolites (NOT the parent alcohol) cause toxicity (methanol → optic nerve damage/blindness; ethylene glycol → acute kidney injury via oxalate crystal deposition). Indications: methanol poisoning (confirmed or suspected - fomepizole + haemodialysis ± folate supplementation - folate enhances formate metabolism); ethylene glycol poisoning (fomepizole ± haemodialysis; co-administer thiamine/pyridoxine - cofactors for non-toxic EG metabolism). SE: nausea, headache, dizziness; rash; phlebitis at IV site; mild ↑liver enzymes (rare). Note: ethanol is an alternative ADH inhibitor (cheap but dosing difficult, CNS side-effects - fomepizole preferred if available); haemodialysis removes toxic metabolites AND fomepizole/ethanol (increase dosing frequency during HD session); diagnosis suggested by elevated osmolar gap + elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis + history; methanol - formate causes optic nerve toxicity (blindness possible - irreversible if delayed).

Dithiol chelating agent - heavy metal antidote. MOA: vicinal dithiol groups form stable ring chelates with heavy metals (arsenic, lead, mercury, gold) → forms soluble complexes excreted renally and biliarily; also redistributes metal from enzyme-binding sites (prevents/reverses inhibition of thiol-containing enzymes - e.g., arsenic inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase). Indications: arsenic poisoning (1st-line with DMSA); mercury poisoning (inorganic/elemental - not methyl mercury); lead poisoning (combined with EDTA/CaNa₂EDTA for blood lead >70 µg/dL - encephalopathy; alternates with EDTA); gold toxicity (from gold salt therapy); lewisite (blister agent) antidote. SE: dose-dependent adverse effects (tachycardia, hypertension, nausea, vomiting, headache, burning sensations); alkaline urine recommended (dimercaprol-metal complex dissociates in acid → re-release metal into kidneys); fever; painful IM injection (peanut oil base); contraindicated in hepatic failure (biliary excretion), iron/cadmium/selenium toxicity (dimercaprol-metal complex more toxic than original metal for these). Note: IM injection only (peanut oil vehicle - allergy risk); alkalinise urine with bicarbonate during treatment; modern chelators (DMSA [succimer], DMPS) preferred where available - oral, less toxic; dimercaprol historical but still used where DMSA unavailable.

Thiazine dye with multiple pharmacological actions. MOA: (1) methaemoglobinaemia - provides electrons to methaemoglobin reductase pathway (NADPH-dependent, normally minor) → reduces Fe³⁺ (metHb) → Fe²⁺ (Hb) → restores oxygen-carrying capacity; (2) vasopressor - inhibits NO synthase (NOS) and soluble guanylate cyclase → ↓cGMP → vasoconstriction (vasopressors for refractory shock); (3) serotonin syndrome - MAO-A inhibitor (high doses - caution with serotonergic drugs). Indications: methaemoglobinaemia (acquired - nitrites, dapsone, local anaesthetics, benzocaine - 1-2 mg/kg IV slowly - response within 1 hour); vasoplegic syndrome (post-cardiac surgery/distributive shock refractory to noradrenaline - 1.5-2 mg/kg IV - reduces vasopressor requirements). SE: blue discoloration (skin, urine, stool - transient - reassure; confounds pulse oximetry readings - SpO₂ falsely low - obtain co-oximetry/arterial blood gas); haemolytic anaemia (G6PD deficiency - CONTRAINDICATED - oxidative stress from reduced methylene blue metabolite); serotonin syndrome risk (MAO-A inhibition - avoid with SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs). Note: G6PD deficiency = absolute contraindication; pulse oximetry unreliable during treatment (blue dye absorbs at 660 nm - same wavelength as deoxy-Hb); in G6PD deficiency → ascorbic acid (vitamin C) alternative for methaemoglobinaemia (slower, less effective).

Sulfur donor - cyanide antidote and cisplatin toxicity modifier. MOA: (1) cyanide antidote - sulfur donor substrate for rhodanese (hepatic enzyme - thiocyanate sulfurtransferase) → rhodanese transfers sulfur to cyanide → thiocyanate (non-toxic, renally excreted) - given after hydroxocobalamin or sodium nitrite (which generate metHb) to enhance cyanide detoxification; (2) cisplatin ototoxicity prevention - free thiol groups chelate cisplatin in cochlear perilymph → ↓cisplatin uptake by cochlear hair cells → ↓hearing loss (local injection or IV post-cisplatin in children). Indications: cyanide poisoning (after hydroxocobalamin - IV; dose 12.5 g IV in adults); cisplatin ototoxicity prevention (paediatric patients - SIOPEL/COG protocol - 16 g/m² IV following cisplatin); extravasation antidote for cisplatin/nitrogen mustard (local infiltration - sulphur donation neutralises alkylating agent). SE: GI (nausea, vomiting); hypotension (rapid IV); rash; temporary transient hypotension. Note: in cyanide poisoning - hydroxocobalamin is now 1st-line (superior efficacy, fewer SE); sodium thiosulfate used as adjunct or where hydroxocobalamin unavailable; cisplatin ototoxicity prevention - does NOT reduce antitumour efficacy at recommended doses; thiocyanate renally cleared (accumulates in renal failure → monitor thiocyanate levels if prolonged use).

Oxime - organophosphate (OP) antidote (cholinesterase reactivator). MOA: reactivates acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibited by organophosphates (nerve agents, pesticides) → nucleophilic displacement of phosphoryl group from AChE serine active site → restores esterase activity → reduces acetylcholine accumulation; must be given BEFORE 'ageing' (irreversible conformational change in OP-AChE complex - time-dependent; with some OPs <24-48 hours window). Indications: organophosphate/carbamate insecticide poisoning (with atropine - atropine blocks muscarinic ACh effects; pralidoxime reverses nicotinic + central effects that atropine cannot); nerve agent exposure (sarin, VX, tabun - with atropine; military antidote kits include autoinjector). SE: dizziness, blurred vision, diplopia, headache; nausea; tachycardia (transient - from pralidoxime itself); hypertension; muscle weakness (paradoxical at high doses - own cholinomimetic activity). Note: time-critical - administer as soon as OP poisoning confirmed; oximes do NOT treat carbamate poisoning well (carbamate-AChE complex spontaneously regenerates - pralidoxime has limited benefit and may worsen; use atropine only for carbamates); atropine is given first (life-threatening bradycardia/secretions) - pralidoxime given concurrently or shortly after; WHOPCS recommendation - 1-2 g IV loading then infusion.

Neurokinin 3 (NK3) receptor antagonist - non-hormonal menopause treatment. MOA: blocks NK3 receptor on hypothalamic KNDy neurones (kisspeptin-neurokinin B-dynorphin - thermoregulatory centre) → ↓thermoregulatory set-point oscillation → ↓frequency and severity of vasomotor symptoms (hot flushes/night sweats); mechanism completely independent of oestrogen (first non-hormonal mechanism targeting the KNDy thermostat pathway). Indications: moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms (VMS) associated with menopause (US approval 2023; EMA 2023; suitable for women who cannot/will not use HRT - including hormone-sensitive cancer survivors [breast cancer patients - not yet confirmed safe - pending label]; dose: 45 mg OD). SE: headache; abdominal pain; diarrhoea; hepatotoxicity (↑ALT/AST - monitor LFTs at baseline, 3, 6 months; discontinue if significant elevation); insomnia; back pain. Note: hepatotoxicity signal - contraindicated in moderate/severe hepatic impairment; baseline and periodic LFT monitoring required; first non-hormonal drug approved specifically for menopause VMS (not just off-label); compare to MHT (HRT) - faster onset of action for VMS but no benefits on bone, cardiovascular, or urogenital symptoms; gabapentin/SSRIs also used off-label for VMS but not US-approved for this indication.

Dual SGLT1 and SGLT2 inhibitor. MOA: inhibits both SGLT2 (renal - responsible for ~90% renal glucose reabsorption) AND SGLT1 (gut + renal - responsible for glucose absorption in small intestine and remaining ~10% renal glucose reabsorption) → greater glucosuria + reduced post-prandial glucose rise + osmotic diuresis + natriuresis; SGLT1 inhibition delays carbohydrate absorption in gut → ↓post-prandial glucose spikes + additional cardiovascular benefits (? ↑gut GLP-1 secretion via SGLT1 blockade). Indications: heart failure (SOLOIST-WHF trial: ↓HF hospitalisation/CV death in type 2 DM with HF; US-approved for HF; US-approved across EF spectrum - broader than dapagliflozin/empagliflozin labels); type 1 DM (Zynquista - EU approval adjunct to insulin - withdrawn in some markets due to DKA risk). SE: genital mycotic infections, UTI (class SGLT2 - glucosuria → fungal growth); DKA (higher risk than SGLT2-only inhibitors - particularly in T1DM - due to SGLT1 carb-absorption inhibition + further insulin-suppressed state → euglycaemic DKA); osmotic diuresis (dehydration, hypovolaemia); diarrhoea (SGLT1 GI effects - greater than SGLT2-only inhibitors). Note: euglycaemic DKA - blood glucose may be normal/near-normal despite ketoacidosis - high clinical suspicion needed; HF indication (INPEFA - independent of EF and diabetes status) is differentiated from other SGLT2 inhibitors by broader approved label.

Pancreatic lipase inhibitor (weight management). MOA: reversibly inhibits gastric and pancreatic lipases → prevents hydrolysis of dietary triglycerides → undigested fat not absorbed → faecal fat excretion increases (~30% dietary fat excreted) → reduced caloric absorption from fat; no CNS activity (peripheral only). Indications: obesity management (BMI ≥30, or ≥27 with risk factors - with diet + exercise; 120 mg TID with meals; Alli = 60 mg OTC lower dose); reduces dietary fat absorption → modest weight loss (mean 2-3 kg vs placebo at 1 year with lifestyle modification); may reduce progression from impaired glucose tolerance to T2DM. SE: GI (steatorrhoea, oily spotting, faecal urgency/incontinence - dose-related - proportional to dietary fat intake; take with low-fat diet to minimise); fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption (A, D, E, K - supplement with multivitamin 2+ hours apart from dose); oxalate nephropathy (↑intestinal oxalate absorption → hyperoxaluria → kidney stones - rare but serious - caution in renal disease, history of oxalate stones); rare liver injury (post-marketing). Note: dietary fat restriction essential for tolerability (GI SE proportional to fat intake - incentivises low-fat diet); fat-soluble vitamin supplement required (take 2h before or after orlistat - does not affect absorption if separated); modest weight loss but evidence for cardiometabolic benefit (XENDOS trial: DM prevention); now largely superseded by GLP-1 agonists for obesity.

Muscarinic cholinergic agonist (synthetic choline ester). MOA: directly activates M2/M3 muscarinic receptors on detrusor muscle → ↑detrusor contractility → ↑bladder voiding pressure → facilitated micturition; also activates GI smooth muscle (M3) → ↑GI motility; resistant to cholinesterase hydrolysis (no ester bond accessible to AChE - modified choline ester) → more prolonged action than acetylcholine; selective for muscarinic (weak nicotinic activity). Indications: urinary retention (post-operative, post-partum, neurogenic bladder without outlet obstruction); GI hypomotility (post-operative ileus, GERD - not standard treatment, largely replaced); diagnosis of denervation hypersensitivity (ophthalmic use - pilocarpine alternative). SE: cholinergic (muscarinic) effects - nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhoea; sweating, salivation, lacrimation; bradycardia, hypotension; bronchospasm (M3 bronchial smooth muscle - CONTRAINDICATED in asthma/COPD); urinary urgency. Note: CONTRAINDICATED in bladder outlet obstruction (↑pressure against obstruction → bladder rupture risk); CONTRAINDICATED in asthma/COPD (bronchospasm); do NOT use in GI/urinary obstruction, peptic ulcer; subcutaneous or oral only (IM/IV → severe cholinergic crisis - cardiovascular collapse); largely replaced by alpha-blockers/intermittent catheterisation for urinary retention but still used for post-op urinary retention.

Azo dye urinary analgesic. MOA: mechanism incompletely understood - exerts local topical analgesic action on the mucosa of the urinary tract; exact receptor/molecular mechanism not established (local anaesthetic-like effect on urothelium proposed but not proven); no antibacterial activity. Indications: symptomatic relief of pain, burning, urgency, frequency due to urinary tract infection, instrumentation, or trauma (used as short-term adjunct to antibiotic therapy for UTI; patient comfort while antibiotics take effect - does NOT treat infection). SE: bright orange-red urine/stool (expected - reassure patient - can stain clothing/contact lenses); GI upset; headache; haemolytic anaemia (G6PD deficiency - avoid); methaemoglobinaemia (overdose or G6PD deficiency); hepatotoxicity and renal toxicity (overdose; limit to 2 days maximum). Note: turns urine bright orange-red (normal - counsel patient; may be alarming; stains contact lenses, clothing, toilet); short-term use only (maximum 2 days - not for prolonged use; do NOT delay or replace antibiotic treatment); do not use in G6PD deficiency, renal/hepatic impairment; does not treat infection - antibiotic required; available OTC in USA; prescription in Australia.

N-type voltage-gated calcium channel blocker (VGCC) - intrathecal analgesic. MOA: synthetic analogue of ω-conotoxin MVIIA (cone snail peptide) → selectively blocks N-type (Cav2.2) voltage-gated calcium channels at presynaptic terminals of primary afferent neurones in dorsal horn → ↓calcium-dependent neurotransmitter (substance P, glutamate) release → ↓pain signal transmission; spinal-selective (intrathecal delivery; does not cross blood-brain barrier in significant amounts). Indications: severe chronic pain requiring intrathecal therapy (intractable pain - failed systemic analgesics, intrathecal opioids - cancer pain, failed back surgery syndrome, HIV neuropathy - initiating dose 2.4 µg/day titrated slowly). SE: CNS (dose-limiting - confusion, cognitive impairment, memory loss, psychiatric disturbances [hallucinations, depression, paranoia], dizziness, ataxia - slow titration essential - weeks between dose increases); nausea, vomiting; muscle weakness, gait disturbance; urinary retention. Note: intrathecal only (IV would cause systemic toxicity; no oral bioavailability); no tolerance development (unlike intrathecal opioids - major advantage for chronic use); no respiratory depression, physical dependence; slow titration protocol mandatory (CNS toxicity dose-dependent - months to optimise dose); requires implanted intrathecal pump; NOT compatible with intrathecal opioids in same reservoir (stability concerns).

Selective oestrogen receptor degrader (SERD) - oral. MOA: binds oestrogen receptor-alpha (ERα) → conformational change → ↓ERα transcriptional activity (partial antagonism like tamoxifen) + targets ERα for proteasomal degradation → loss of ER protein (like fulvestrant but oral); active against ERα with ESR1 mutations (L536H, Y537S, D538G) which confer resistance to tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors (structural basis: ESR1 mutations cause constitutive ligand-independent ERα activation → endocrine resistance). Indications: ER+/HER2- metastatic breast cancer with ESR1 mutation (after 1+ lines endocrine therapy; EMERALD trial: ↑PFS vs chemotherapy/fulvestrant in ESR1-mutated cohort; US approval 2023; biomarker testing [circulating tumour DNA ctDNA for ESR1 mutation] required). SE: nausea (most common - 35%), dyspepsia, vomiting; musculoskeletal pain; fatigue; hot flushes; ↑lipids; ↑LFTs (rare). Note: first oral SERD approved for breast cancer; ESR1 mutation testing required (ctDNA assay - blood based - preferred to avoid re-biopsy); compare to fulvestrant (IM injection only - similar MOA but elacestrant oral + active vs ESR1 mutations); ESR1 mutations arise in ~30-40% of ER+ metastatic BC after aromatase inhibitor → targeted therapy.

Pan-AKT (AKT1/2/3) serine-threonine kinase inhibitor. MOA: inhibits all three AKT isoforms (allosteric + ATP-competitive - dual mechanism locks AKT in inactive conformation) → ↓PI3K-AKT-mTOR signalling → ↓cell survival/proliferation; most potent in tumours with PIK3CA/AKT1/PTEN alterations (pathway activation); combined with fulvestrant (ER+ BC) to overcome endocrine resistance driven by PI3K pathway activation. Indications: ER+/HER2- metastatic breast cancer with PIK3CA/AKT1/PTEN alteration (with fulvestrant after prior endocrine therapy ± CDK4/6 inhibitor; CAPItello-291 trial: ↑PFS vs placebo+fulvestrant in biomarker-selected [PIK3CA/AKT1/PTEN-altered] population; US approval 2023; biomarker testing required). SE: diarrhoea (very common - ~72%; manage with anti-diarrhoeal agents; dose reduce if Grade 3+); rash (maculopapular - ~50%; skin toxicity class effect of AKT/PI3K inhibitors); hyperglycaemia (AKT normally promotes GLUT4 expression; AKT inhibition → insulin resistance - monitor FBG, manage with diet/metformin; may require dose reduction); nausea, fatigue; stomatitis. Note: intermittent dosing schedule - 4 days on/3 days off (reduces toxicity vs continuous); PIK3CA/AKT1/PTEN alteration testing required (tissue NGS or ctDNA); hyperglycaemia management important - pre-existing diabetes not contraindication but requires tighter monitoring.

Highly selective PI3Kα (phosphoinositide 3-kinase alpha) inhibitor with additional PIK3CA-mutant protein degradation. MOA: irreversibly inhibits PI3Kα (encoded by PIK3CA) → ↓PIP3 generation → ↓AKT-mTOR activation; uniquely promotes degradation of mutant p110α PIK3CA protein (allosteric mechanism beyond kinase inhibition) → more complete pathway suppression; PIK3CA-activating mutations in ~40% ER+ breast cancer (H1047R, E545K, E542K most common). Indications: ER+/HER2- metastatic breast cancer with PIK3CA mutation (combined with palbociclib + fulvestrant; INAVO120 trial: ↑PFS vs placebo+palbociclib+fulvestrant in PIK3CA-mutant, post-AI therapy; US approval 2024). SE: hyperglycaemia (class PI3K inhibitor - monitor blood glucose - diet, metformin as needed; hold if severe); diarrhoea; stomatitis; nausea; rash; neutropenia (from CDK4/6 inhibitor component); ↑LFTs. Note: compare to alpelisib (other PI3Kα inhibitor - harsher toxicity profile - severe hyperglycaemia, rash; inavolisib more tolerable); PIK3CA mutation testing required; triple combination (PI3Kα + CDK4/6 + endocrine therapy) represents a new therapeutic axis; hyperglycaemia monitoring protocol essential before and during treatment.

Dual IDH1/IDH2 inhibitor - brain-penetrant. MOA: inhibits both mutant IDH1 (R132) and IDH2 (R140, R172) → ↓2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG, oncometabolite) production → 2-HG inhibits TET2 dioxygenases + histone demethylases → hypermethylation/epigenetic silencing → differentiation block; brain-penetrant (crosses BBB - important for CNS tumours - ivosidenib/enasidenib do not adequately cross BBB). Indications: IDH-mutant grade 2 glioma (diffuse astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma - grade 2 per WHO 2021 - after prior surgery - INDIGO trial: ↑PFS vs placebo [28 vs 11 months]; US approval 2024; first systemic therapy approved for grade 2 glioma). SE: ↑ALT/AST (hepatotoxicity - monitor LFTs; withhold/reduce if Grade 3+); nausea; fatigue; headache; seizures (tumour-related - not significantly changed vs placebo); differentiation syndrome (rare - like ivosidenib/enasidenib in AML - monitor for fever, dyspnoea, hypotension). Note: IDH mutation testing required (IDH1/2 by PCR/sequencing - tissue); unlike ivosidenib/enasidenib (AML), vorasidenib specifically designed for CNS penetration; grade 2 glioma typically treated with watch-and-wait after surgery - vorasidenib represents first molecular targeted option; differentiation syndrome monitoring (though less common in glioma vs AML).

Hedgehog pathway inhibitor - smoothened (SMO) antagonist. MOA: binds and inhibits SMO (integral membrane protein in hedgehog pathway) → blocks pathway activation → prevents nuclear translocation of GLI transcription factors → ↓GLI-target gene expression (including BCL-2, BCL-XL, cyclin D, Wnt) → ↓AML stem cell survival and proliferation; hedgehog pathway aberrantly activated in AML leukaemic stem cells → promotes chemo-resistance. Indications: acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) - combined with low-dose cytarabine (LDAC) for newly diagnosed AML in adults ≥75 years or unfit for intensive chemotherapy (BRIGHT AML trial: improved OS vs LDAC alone - 8.8 vs 4.9 months; US 2018). SE: myelosuppression (cytopenia - anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia - combined with LDAC); QT prolongation (monitor ECG, correct electrolytes, avoid QT-prolonging drugs); muscle cramps/spasms; alopecia; nausea; fatigue; peripheral oedema. Note: teratogenic (hedgehog inhibitor class - both males + females must use contraception during + after treatment; males - potential for genitourinary abnormalities in offspring); QT monitoring required (ECG at baseline, periodically); compare to vismodegib/sonidegib (also SMO antagonists but for BCC, not haematological); hedgehog pathway inhibitors show drug class reproductive toxicity.

Hedgehog pathway inhibitor - SMO antagonist (first approved). MOA: first-in-class SMO (smoothened) inhibitor → blocks activation of hedgehog (Hh) pathway → ↓GLI1/2 transcription factor translocation → ↓Hh target gene expression; PTCH1 mutations (most common in BCC - ~90%) or activating SMO mutations lose PTCH1 inhibitory effect on SMO → constitutive Hh pathway activation → abnormal basal cell proliferation. Indications: basal cell carcinoma (BCC) - locally advanced BCC (not amenable to surgery/radiotherapy); metastatic BCC (rare - <1%); 150 mg OD until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity (ERIVANCE trial: ORR 43% aBCC, 30% mBCC). SE: muscle cramps (very common - >70% - PTCH1 expressed in muscle; reduce with electrolyte replacement, stretching, quinine); alopecia (diffuse - reversible on cessation); dysgeusia (taste disturbance - common; ↓food enjoyment → weight loss); amenorrhoea; fatigue; weight loss; nausea. Note: TERATOGENIC (absolute contraindication in pregnancy - Category D; women of childbearing potential → 2 forms contraception or abstinence; verify pregnancy negative before starting; males - do not donate sperm during + 3 months after); muscle cramps most common dose-limiting toxicity - stretching + magnesium supplementation; drug holiday strategy for intolerable side-effects; 150 mg OD oral (convenient once-daily).

SMO (smoothened) inhibitor - 2nd generation hedgehog pathway antagonist. MOA: binds SMO in transmembrane domain → allosteric inhibition → prevents conformational activation → blocks hedgehog pathway signal transduction → ↓GLI transcription factor activity → ↓tumour cell proliferation (same mechanism as vismodegib; structural differences → different binding site on SMO; some vismodegib-resistant SMO mutations retain sonidegib sensitivity). Indications: locally advanced BCC (not amenable to curative surgery or radiotherapy; BOLT trial vs vismodegib: non-inferior ORR; 200 mg OD); recurrent BCC after surgery/radiotherapy. SE: muscle cramps (very common - 50%; class hedgehog inhibitor effect); alopecia, dysgeusia, weight loss, fatigue, nausea (class SE similar to vismodegib); creatine kinase elevation (↑CK - rhabdomyolysis reported - monitor CK at baseline and periodically; check if persistent muscle pain). Note: TERATOGENIC (absolute contraindication pregnancy + lactation; contraception required for women of childbearing potential + males; males - semen contains sonidegib → use contraception during + 8 months after; verify pregnancy test before starting); CK monitoring (unique monitoring requirement vs vismodegib - rhabdomyolysis risk); food effect - take fasted (high-fat meal ↑AUC by 7.4-fold - major food interaction - different from vismodegib which can be taken with/without food).

Anti-CD19 antibody-drug conjugate (ADC). MOA: humanised anti-CD19 IgG1 mAb conjugated (via cleavable linker) to SG3199 (a pyrrolobenzodiazepine [PBD] dimer alkylating warhead) → binds CD19 on B cells → internalisation → lysosomal cleavage of linker → SG3199 crosslinks DNA → DNA double-strand breaks → G2/M cell-cycle arrest → apoptosis; PBD dimers: potent alkylating agents with DNA crosslinking selectivity (minor groove binding). Indications: relapsed/refractory large B-cell lymphoma (diffuse large B-cell lymphoma [DLBCL] and high-grade B-cell lymphoma, after ≥2 prior systemic therapies; LOTIS-2 trial: ORR 48%, CR 24%; US 2021 accelerated approval). SE: myelosuppression (thrombocytopenia - dose-limiting; neutropenia; anaemia - monitor CBC); peripheral oedema (class ADC with PBD warhead - mechanism unclear; Grade ≥3 in ~20%); effusions (pleural, pericardial, ascites - monitor); skin rash; hepatotoxicity (↑LFTs - monitor); photosensitivity. Note: PBD warhead more potent than MMAE/DM1 (other ADC warheads) - theoretically active against chemo-resistant tumours; CD19 expression required (expressed on all B cells); thrombocytopenia monitoring important (pre-medications - dexamethasone reduces oedema/effusion SE); compare to tafasitamab (anti-CD19 non-conjugated mAb + lenalidomide).

Anti-CD19 immunostimulatory antibody (Fc-modified). MOA: humanised anti-CD19 IgG1 mAb with modified Fc region (XmAb technology - two amino acid substitutions S239D/I332E in Fc) → enhanced FcγRIIIa and FcγRIIa binding → ↑ADCC (antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity) + ↑ADCP (phagocytosis) + direct cytotoxicity (apoptosis via CD19 signalling); combined with lenalidomide (immunomodulatory - enhances NK cell activity → synergistic ADCC). Indications: relapsed/refractory DLBCL (tafasitamab + lenalidomide in patients ineligible for autologous stem cell transplant; L-MIND trial: ORR 60%, CR 43%, long durable remission; US 2020 accelerated approval → regular approval 2024). SE: myelosuppression (neutropenia most common - G-CSF prophylaxis often used; thrombocytopenia, anaemia); infusion-related reactions (premedicate); fatigue; diarrhoea; febrile neutropenia; peripheral oedema. Note: CD19 expressed on all B cells (good target in DLBCL - essentially pan-B-cell marker); lenalidomide combination important (synergy - lenalidomide alone modest in DLBCL; combination transforms ORR); not studied after CAR-T (CD19 may be downregulated → CD19-targeting may fail); maintenance tafasitamab monotherapy continues after lenalidomide phase.

Type I interferon - recombinant human IFN-β (non-glycosylated; differs from IFN-β-1a in glycosylation + amino acid at position 17). MOA: binds IFNAR1/IFNAR2 heterodimer → JAK-STAT signalling → ↑expression of multiple interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) → anti-inflammatory (↓IL-2, ↓TNF, ↑IL-10 - shifts Th1→Th2 + Treg induction) + antiviral + antiproliferative effects; in MS - ↓T-cell activation + migration, ↓matrix metalloproteinase expression → ↓BBB permeability → ↓brain inflammation + lesion formation. Indications: relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis (relapsing-remitting MS; CIS [clinically isolated syndrome] - delayed progression to RRMS; secondary progressive MS with ongoing relapses); subcutaneous injection every other day. SE: injection site reactions (erythema, necrosis - rotate sites; most common reason for discontinuation - pre-warm injection to room temperature); influenza-like symptoms (flu-like syndrome - fever, myalgia, chills - first 3 months; manage with paracetamol/NSAIDs + evening dosing; usually subsides); neutralising antibodies (develop in ~30% → may reduce efficacy; check titres 12-24 months); liver toxicity (↑LFTs - monitor); leucopenia; depression. Note: IFN-β-1b vs IFN-β-1a (Avonex, Rebif) - 1b: subcutaneous every-other-day (high frequency); 1a: IM weekly (Avonex) or subcutaneous TW (Rebif); glycosylation differences may affect immunogenicity but clinical significance debated; neutralising antibodies more common with 1b (30%) vs Avonex (5%).

mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) inhibitor - IV rapalog. MOA: binds FKBP12 (FK-binding protein 12) → FKBP12-temsirolimus complex inhibits mTORC1 (mTOR complex 1) → ↓translation of cell-cycle regulators (cyclin D1, HIF-1α, VEGF, c-Myc) → G1 cell-cycle arrest + ↓angiogenesis; semisynthetic rapamycin analogue (more water-soluble → IV formulation); temsirolimus is a prodrug → converted in vivo to sirolimus (active metabolite). Indications: renal cell carcinoma (RCC - advanced - 1st-line for poor-prognosis metastatic RCC, GLOBAL trial: improved OS vs IFN-α; US-approved 2007 - largely superseded by TKIs + IO combinations); mantle cell lymphoma (relapsed/refractory; US-approved). SE: hyperglycaemia (mTOR regulates insulin signalling/glucose metabolism - monitor + manage); hyperlipidaemia (↑TG, ↑cholesterol - statin therapy if needed); myelosuppression (anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia); pneumonitis (class mTOR inhibitor; non-infectious interstitial pneumonitis - 15-35%; cough, dyspnoea, fever; HRCT changes; manage with corticosteroids/dose reduction); wound-healing impairment; stomatitis; infections; ↑creatinine. Note: IV administration (every week - vs oral everolimus); prodrug → sirolimus; pneumonitis monitoring essential (CT if respiratory symptoms); wound-healing impairment - hold perioperatively (4 weeks before major surgery); now largely replaced by sunitinib/pazopanib/IO-based regimens for RCC; mantle cell lymphoma remains an indication.

Non-sedating selective histamine H1 receptor antagonist (2nd generation antihistamine). MOA: selective H1 receptor inverse agonist → blocks histamine-mediated vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, pruritus; does not cross BBB at therapeutic doses (P-glycoprotein substrate → effluxed from CNS) → minimal sedation; not metabolised by CYP450 → low drug interaction potential. Indications: allergic rhinoconjunctivitis (seasonal + perennial - 20 mg OD); urticaria (chronic spontaneous urticaria); PBS-listed in Australia (once-daily). SE: headache, somnolence (rare - less than older antihistamines); fatigue; dry mouth (minimal - less anticholinergic than 1st-gen); no significant QT prolongation. Note: take on empty stomach (food + grapefruit juice ↓absorption via OATP transporter inhibition → bioavailability ↓40% with food - important clinical point - differentiated from loratadine/cetirizine); P-glycoprotein efflux at BBB → CNS-sparing; no CYP450 interactions (unlike ketoconazole + erythromycin interactions with terfenadine/astemizole which caused QT-related withdrawal); 20 mg OD (adult); not recommended <12 years (limited data).

Active primary metabolite of loratadine - selective H1 antihistamine (2nd generation). MOA: direct H1 receptor inverse agonist (more potent than loratadine - lower Ki; H1 selectivity ratio higher); does not cross BBB significantly → non-sedating at therapeutic doses; not a CYP3A4 substrate (unlike loratadine) → fewer drug interactions; also inhibits release of inflammatory mediators from mast cells/basophils. Indications: allergic rhinoconjunctivitis (seasonal + perennial - 5 mg OD); chronic idiopathic urticaria. SE: headache, fatigue (minimal); dry mouth (rare); somnolence (rare); safe in hepatic impairment (unlike loratadine → desloratadine not further metabolised → no accumulation concern). Note: desloratadine vs loratadine - same active metabolite, similar efficacy; desloratadine may have faster onset and slightly better bioavailability; loratadine converted to desloratadine by CYP3A4/2D6 (slow metabolisers → less loratadine effect); available in children ≥2 years (syrup formulation); 5 mg OD (adult); no dose adjustment needed in renal impairment (minor renal excretion).

Active R-enantiomer of cetirizine - selective H1 antihistamine (2nd generation). MOA: R-enantiomer of racemic cetirizine → binds H1 receptor with ~2× greater affinity than racemic mixture; cetirizine is the S+R racemic mix; levocetirizine has higher H1 selectivity → same efficacy at half the dose (5 mg levocetirizine ≈ 10 mg cetirizine for H1 blockade). Indications: allergic rhinoconjunctivitis; chronic idiopathic urticaria (5 mg OD); pruritus from various causes. SE: somnolence (less than cetirizine - due to lower total dose; still more than fexofenadine/bilastine); headache; dry mouth; fatigue; urinary retention (rare - mild anticholinergic). Note: renal dosing - renally excreted → reduce dose in renal impairment (dose interval adjustment); chiral switch drug (levocetirizine from cetirizine - same drug family as esomeprazole from omeprazole, escitalopram from citalopram); minimal food effect; 5 mg OD (adult); available OTC in Australia; children >2 years (oral solution).

First-generation piperazine H1 antihistamine with anticholinergic and anti-emetic properties. MOA: blocks H1 receptors in vomiting centre (chemoreceptor trigger zone [CTZ] and nucleus tractus solitarius) + muscarinic M1 receptors in vestibular apparatus → reduces vestibular input-triggered nausea/vomiting; sedating (crosses BBB - lipophilic). Indications: nausea and vomiting (post-operative, motion sickness, palliative care - preferred in palliative care via SC infusion); vertigo + labyrinthine disorders; morning sickness (pregnancy - but safety limited data); intractable nausea in emergency medicine; postoperative nausea/vomiting (PONV) - alternative when ondansetron/dexamethasone insufficient. SE: sedation (CNS depression - antihistamine + anticholinergic); dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, blurred vision (anticholinergic); tachycardia; extrapyramidal reactions (rare). Note: palliative care gold standard for nausea (commonly given via SC syringe driver - mix with morphine/diamorphine; compatible in most combinations); motion sickness - take 30 minutes before travel (prophylaxis); oral 50 mg TID, parenteral 50 mg IM/IV; available as SC infusion in palliative care; suitable for pregnancy (1st trimester use studied; considered relatively safe vs other antiemetics).

Piperazine antihistamine with calcium channel blocking properties - vestibular suppressant. MOA: blocks H1 receptors + inhibits calcium influx into labyrinthine sensory cells (direct calcium antagonism) → reduces sensitivity of vestibular apparatus to stimuli; also mild alpha-1 antagonist; NOT a traditional voltage-gated calcium channel blocker (different binding site - primarily labyrinthine-specific calcium blocking). Indications: vestibular disorders (vertigo - Menière's disease, labyrinthitis, benign paroxysmal positional vertigo - symptom relief); motion sickness (travel sickness - 15 mg TID + 30 mg 2h before travel); tinnitus (limited evidence); peripheral vascular disorders (historical use - Ca²⁺ channel block in vessels → ↑cerebral + peripheral blood flow - limited evidence). SE: sedation (crosses BBB - antihistamine); dry mouth; weight gain (mild); extrapyramidal effects (Parkinson's-like symptoms) - reported with long-term high-dose use (vestibular calcium blocking + D2-receptor blockade - reversible on cessation; particularly in elderly); nausea. Note: extrapyramidal SE with chronic use - particularly in older patients (drug-induced Parkinsonism - reversible but may mimic degenerative Parkinsonism - be cautious with long-term use in elderly); effective for Menière's/labyrinthine vertigo; 15-30 mg TID; combined with dimenhydrinate in some markets.

First-generation H1 antihistamine with prominent sedative + antiemetic properties. MOA: H1 receptor antagonist + muscarinic antagonist → antiemetic via CTZ blockade + sedation (highly lipophilic → CNS penetration); one of the most sedating antihistamines (used therapeutically as hypnotic). Indications: nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (NVP) - combined with pyridoxine (vitamin B6) as Diclegis/Bonjesta - 1st-line pharmacological treatment for NVP/hyperemesis (Category A in pregnancy - human data confirming safety; endorsed by ACOG/RANZCOG); insomnia (short-term - OTC sleep aid: Restavit 25 mg); antiemetic (post-operative nausea). SE: sedation (prominent - daytime drowsiness common - take only at night for NVP); dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation (anticholinergic); dizziness; rarely paradoxical excitation in children. Note: NVP protocol - Diclegis: doxylamine 10 mg + pyridoxine 10 mg extended-release tablets; start with 2 tablets at night → add morning/afternoon tablets if needed; delay-release formulation helps morning nausea (taken at bedtime); safety in pregnancy established by meta-analyses and decades of use; for insomnia - 25 mg nocte (tolerance may develop with long-term use); lower antihistamine potency vs diphenhydramine but similar sedation.

Piperazine H1 antihistamine - vestibular suppressant and anti-emetic. MOA: blocks H1 receptors in vestibular system + CTZ (chemoreceptor trigger zone) → reduces nausea/vomiting from vestibular stimuli; mechanism includes mild anticholinergic + weak CNS depressant effects; slower onset + longer duration than promethazine (12-24 h effective duration). Indications: motion sickness (OTC - 25-50 mg 1 hour before travel; last 24 hours); vertigo associated with vestibular disease (Menière's, labyrinthitis); nausea and vomiting from labyrinthine disorders. SE: sedation (less than promethazine/cyclizine); dry mouth (anticholinergic - mild); blurred vision; fatigue. Note: OTC availability (most markets) - accessible for self-management of travel sickness; duration 24 hours (once-daily dosing - preferred over dimenhydramine/cyclizine for long journeys); note: Category B in pregnancy - considered safe for NVP (but doxylamine preferred - more evidence); generally used in USA for vertigo (Australia less common - cinnarizine/prochlorperazine more common); 25-50 mg OD for motion sickness prophylaxis.

Intermediate-acting benzodiazepine - hypnotic. MOA: positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A receptors → enhances chloride ion influx → neuronal hyperpolarisation → CNS depression; specifically enhances GABA-A receptor containing α1 subunit → sedation and amnesia (differs from anxiolytic benzodiazepines which preferentially target α2 subunit); intermediate t½ (8-12 h) → minimal next-day hangover vs longer-acting flunitrazepam. Indications: short-term treatment of insomnia (PBS Schedule 8 - controlled drug; difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep; maximum 2-4 weeks use; 10-20 mg nocte). SE: sedation; cognitive impairment (anterograde amnesia - dose-dependent); rebound insomnia (on discontinuation); tolerance + physical dependence (with regular use >2 weeks); withdrawal syndrome (anxiety, tremor, seizures - taper slowly); falls + fractures (elderly - disinhibition + ataxia); respiratory depression (caution COPD/OSA); paradoxical agitation (disinhibition - elderly). Note: Schedule 8 (controlled substance) in Australia - strict prescribing requirements; avoid long-term use (tolerance after 2-4 weeks; dependence risk); taper over weeks if stopping after chronic use (abrupt cessation → withdrawal seizures); CBT-I (cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia) superior long-term; Z-drugs (zopiclone/zolpidem) have similar risks; most widely prescribed hypnotic benzodiazepine in Australia.

Short-to-intermediate acting benzodiazepine - anxiolytic and hypnotic. MOA: GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulator → enhances inhibitory chloride flux → CNS depression; direct conjugation (glucuronidation) - NOT oxidised by CYP450 (unique among benzodiazepines) → active moiety = oxazepam itself; no active metabolites; t½ 6-12 hours. Indications: anxiety disorders (generalised anxiety, acute situational anxiety - PBS-listed); alcohol withdrawal (preferred in hepatic impairment - direct glucuronidation → safe in liver disease; CIWA-Ar guided protocols); insomnia (short-term, mild); elderly patients (preferred benzodiazepine in elderly - LOB mnemonic: Lorazepam/Oxazepam/[te]Mazepam = safe in liver disease, elderly). SE: sedation; cognitive impairment; ataxia; falls (elderly); dependence/withdrawal; rebound anxiety. Note: preferred in hepatic impairment + elderly (glucuronidation intact in cirrhosis/elderly - does not require hepatic oxidation; compare to diazepam → active metabolites accumulate in liver disease/elderly → prolonged/excessive sedation); shorter half-life = less accumulation = better for elderly (LOB rule: Lorazepam, Oxazepam, [te]mazepam - safer in elderly/liver disease); alcohol withdrawal - 15-30 mg QID, taper over 5-7 days.

Long-acting benzodiazepine - hypnotic and antiepileptic. MOA: GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulator → ↑chloride conductance → neuronal hyperpolarisation; long t½ (15-38 h) + active metabolite (7-aminonitrazepam - partial activity) → prolonged effect; anticonvulsant properties in addition to sedation. Indications: childhood epilepsy (infantile spasms, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, myoclonic epilepsy in children - not 1st-line but used in refractory cases; controlled drug); severe insomnia (short-term - adults - 5-10 mg nocte); Schedule 4/8 controlled in Australia. SE: sedation; cognitive impairment; anterograde amnesia; rebound insomnia + withdrawal seizures (on abrupt cessation); next-day hangover (long t½ - especially elderly); respiratory depression (caution in COPD, OSA, elderly); hypotonia (particularly in children - monitoring required - drooling/hypersalivation common in children). Note: use in children (infantile spasms and myoclonic epilepsy) - monitor for hypotonia, respiratory depression, hypersalivation; children dose 0.25-0.5 mg/kg/day in divided doses; adult insomnia 5-10 mg nocte; long t½ → accumulates with repeated dosing (especially elderly - use with caution - prefer short-acting benzodiazepines in elderly); controlled drug in Australia.

Non-benzodiazepine hypnotic (Z-drug) - ultra-short acting. MOA: selective positive allosteric modulator at GABA-A receptor α1 subunit → similar to benzodiazepines mechanistically but selective for α1 subunit (hypnosis/amnesia; less anxiolysis/muscle relaxation than BZDs targeting α2); ultra-short t½ (1 hour) → minimal next-morning sedation; rapid onset (15-30 min). Indications: short-term insomnia (difficulty falling asleep - sleep-onset insomnia; US-approved; 5-10 mg immediately before bed; ultra-short t½ allows middle-of-the-night dosing [if ≥4 hours remain before waking]). SE: sedation; amnesia (dose-dependent - particularly at higher doses); dizziness; rebound insomnia (on cessation - mild); dependence (less than traditional benzodiazepines - short t½ reduces abuse potential vs zolpidem); complex sleep behaviours (sleepwalking, sleep-driving - rare class effect of Z-drugs - boxed warning warning). Note: ultra-short t½ advantage - can be used if waking at 3 AM (if ≥4 h before alarm - unique among Z-drugs); less residual sedation and cognitive impairment than zopiclone/zolpidem; middle-of-the-night dosing (5 mg) for middle-of-night awakening; limited availability in Australia (zopiclone more commonly used); caution with hepatic impairment (reduce dose - CYP3A4/aldehyde oxidase metabolism).

Non-benzodiazepine hypnotic (Z-drug) - S-enantiomer of racemic zopiclone. MOA: selective α1-subunit GABA-A receptor modulator → sedation/hypnosis; active S-enantiomer of zopiclone (chiral switch) → similar efficacy to zopiclone at half the dose; t½ ~6 hours (intermediate - similar to zopiclone); bitter metallic taste (both enantiomers of zopiclone cause this). Indications: insomnia (sleep-onset and sleep-maintenance - US-approved for up to 12 months - longer approved duration than other Z-drugs; 1-3 mg nocte; elderly: 1-2 mg). SE: metallic/bitter taste (very common - distinctive SE of zopiclone/eszopiclone - warn patients; caused by active metabolite [S-desmethylzopiclone] in saliva); sedation; dizziness; rebound insomnia; dependence (Schedule 4 controlled in Australia - caution); complex sleep behaviours (rare - boxed warning warning for all Z-drugs). Note: longer approved use duration (12 months - vs 2-4 weeks for zopiclone/zolpidem - based on ESTORRA trials showing maintained efficacy without tolerance); bitter taste distinguishing SE (ask about it - both zopiclone + eszopiclone); not available in Australia/UK (zopiclone used instead - same drug essentially); primarily USA drug; S-enantiomer chiral switch for patent extension.

Melatonin receptor agonist (MT1 and MT2) - hypnotic. MOA: highly selective agonist at MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors in suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) → promotes sleep-wake cycle regulation; MT1 activation → ↓neuronal firing in SCN → promotes sleep onset; MT2 activation → phase-shifting of circadian rhythm; NO GABA-A activity (not a controlled substance - no abuse potential or dependence). Indications: insomnia characterised by difficulty falling asleep (sleep-onset insomnia - 8 mg before bedtime); not effective for sleep maintenance; circadian rhythm sleep disorders. SE: mild somnolence; dizziness; fatigue; nausea; headache; ↑prolactin (MT1/MT2 expressed in pituitary - rare → amenorrhoea/galactorrhoea); no withdrawal, no rebound insomnia, no dependence. Note: NOT a controlled substance (no dependence/abuse potential - major advantage vs benzodiazepines and Z-drugs); no abuse potential (unscheduled - can be prescribed without controlled drug restrictions); less effective for sleep maintenance than benzodiazepines (does not increase total sleep time significantly); take 30 min before bed; avoid with fluvoxamine (CYP1A2 inhibitor - major - ↑ramelteon AUC 190× - absolute contraindication); US-approved; less widely available outside USA (melatonin OTC serves similar function in many countries including Australia).

Dual melatonin receptor agonist (MT1 + MT2) - circadian rhythm modulator. MOA: binds MT1 (→ sleep promotion) and MT2 (→ circadian phase-shifting) melatonin receptors in suprachiasmatic nucleus → re-entrains non-24-hour sleep-wake rhythm to 24-hour light-dark cycle; more potent MT2 agonist than ramelteon → stronger phase-shifting. Indications: Non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder (Non-24; most common in totally blind patients - absent light entrainment → free-running circadian rhythm → rotating sleep times; SET + RESET trials: ↑entrainment in blind patients; US 2014 orphan drug approval; also approved for paediatric Smith-Magenis syndrome [abnormal melatonin secretion → sleep disturbance]). SE: headache; somnolence; nightmares; upper respiratory tract infection; ↑liver enzymes; ↑prolactin. Note: NOT a controlled substance; requires consistent bedtime dosing at same time each night (circadian re-entrainment requires consistent anchor time); full effect may take weeks to months (gradual circadian re-entrainment); most commonly used in blind patients (light perception absent → cannot entrain to light-dark cycle); available in USA; orphan disease drug - limited international availability; 20 mg nocte (taken before bedtime at same time each night).

Selective muscarinic M1 receptor antagonist - anticholinergic antiparkinsonian drug. MOA: centrally acting antimuscarinic → preferentially blocks M1 over M2 receptors in basal ganglia → ↓excessive cholinergic tone in nigrostriatal pathway (in Parkinson's, dopamine ↓ → cholinergic relative excess → akinesia/tremor) → partial restoration of DA/Ach balance; also peripheral anticholinergic effects. Indications: drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS - acute dystonia [most effective - IV/IM for acute dystonic reaction], akathisia [less effective], Parkinsonism [moderate - helps tremor more than bradykinesia]; most acute dystonia treatment: 5 mg IM/IV - rapid onset); Parkinson's disease (adjunct - rarely 1st-line in modern practice - dementia risk); neuroleptic-induced Parkinsonism. SE: peripheral anticholinergic (dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation, tachycardia); cognitive impairment (↓cholinergic transmission → memory problems - significant in elderly/dementia patients); paradoxical worsening of psychosis; confusion; euphoria (misuse potential - IV biperiden abused in some settings). Note: anticholinergics NOT recommended for akathisia (beta-blockers/propranolol, benzodiazepines, or mirtazapine preferred); IV biperiden for acute dystonia - fastest and most reliable treatment; cognitive SE - avoid in elderly and patients with cognitive impairment; biperiden prophylaxis debated when starting high-potency antipsychotics - adds cognitive/cardiovascular risk - not routinely recommended.

Muscarinic receptor antagonist - antiparkinsonian anticholinergic. MOA: blocks central and peripheral muscarinic receptors → ↓cholinergic overactivity in basal ganglia (nigrostriatal pathway) → ↓tremor + rigidity in Parkinson's disease + drug-induced Parkinsonism; weaker CNS anticholinergic than biperiden; smooth muscle relaxation (peripheral - reduces GI and genitourinary tone). Indications: drug-induced EPS (antipsychotic-induced Parkinsonism, acute dystonia - less used than biperiden for acute dystonia; oral Parkinsonism treatment); Parkinson's disease (adjunct - helps tremor > bradykinesia/rigidity - not 1st-line; used in young patients with tremor-predominant PD where anticholinergic cognitive risk acceptable). SE: dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation, tachycardia (peripheral anticholinergic - dose-dependent); cognitive impairment, memory problems, confusion, hallucinations (central anticholinergic - dose-dependent - major concern in elderly and PD with dementia); xerostomia; euphoria (abuse potential - historical). Note: avoid in PD with cognitive impairment or dementia (worsens cholinergic deficiency → confusion, hallucinations); NOT recommended as prophylaxis for EPS from antipsychotics in most guidelines (risk/benefit unfavourable); benzhexol = trihexyphenidyl (UK/Australian non-proprietary name - same drug); 2-15 mg/day in divided doses; taper slowly to discontinue (withdrawal rebound EPS).

Anticholinergic + antihistamine antiparkinsonian drug. MOA: muscarinic receptor antagonist (particularly M1) + dopamine reuptake inhibitor (mild) + H1 antihistamine → combined anticholinergic + mild dopaminergic action; longest duration of action among anticholinergic antiparkinsonian drugs (t½ ~24 hours → once-daily dosing possible). Indications: acute dystonia (most effective use - IM/IV 1-2 mg - similar to biperiden; reverses antipsychotic-induced dystonia within minutes); drug-induced Parkinsonism (EPS from antipsychotics - 0.5-2 mg BD); Parkinson's disease (adjunct - tremor-predominant PD in younger patients; 0.5-6 mg/day); prophylactic EPS (where antipsychotics known to cause EPS - now less recommended). SE: peripheral anticholinergic (dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, blurred vision, tachycardia); central - cognitive impairment, confusion, hallucinations (anticholinergic delirium - particularly in elderly); heat stroke risk (impairs sweating → hyperthermia - caution in hot weather); CNS effects (sedation - antihistamine component). Note: IM preferred over IV (slower - reduces risk of CNS toxicity); duration: 24 h t½ → OD dosing; primarily used in North America (biperiden/procyclidine used more in Australia/UK); heat-related illness risk in summer (counsel on heat avoidance, adequate hydration - sweating impaired); avoid in closed-angle glaucoma, prostatic hyperplasia, GI obstruction (anticholinergic CI).

Muscarinic anticholinergic - antiparkinsonian drug. MOA: central and peripheral muscarinic receptor antagonist → reduces excessive cholinergic tone in nigrostriatal pathway → antiparkinsonian and anti-EPS effects; similar to biperiden/trihexyphenidyl in mechanism; preferred in some UK/Australian practice patterns. Indications: drug-induced EPS (neuroleptic-induced Parkinsonism, acute dystonia - oral and parenteral; 5-10 mg IM/IV for acute dystonia); Parkinson's disease (adjunct - tremor-predominant; 2.5-5 mg TID); drug-induced tremor (e.g., lithium). SE: peripheral anticholinergic (dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation); central anticholinergic (cognitive impairment, confusion, hallucinations - dose-dependent - elderly susceptible); tachycardia; euphoria (misuse potential - hallucinations sought). Note: commonly used in Australia and UK for EPS management; available as oral liquid (useful for dysphagia, children); typical acute dystonia dose: 5 mg IM; regular oral dose 2.5-5 mg TID; like all anticholinergics - avoid in glaucoma, prostatic hyperplasia, tardive dyskinesia (may worsen TD - anticholinergics paradoxically worsen dyskinesias - only help Parkinsonism + dystonia + tremor); not used for akathisia.

Alkylating oxazaphosphorine chemotherapy agent (analogue of cyclophosphamide). MOA: prodrug - hepatic CYP3A4/2B6 activation → 4-hydroxyifosfamide → aldoifosfamide → isophosphoramide mustard (active alkylating species) → crosslinks DNA (N-7 guanine alkylation, inter/intrastrand crosslinks) → DNA replication block → apoptosis; also produces chloroacetaldehyde (urotoxic metabolite → haemorrhagic cystitis) + acrolein (less than cyclophosphamide). Indications: sarcomas (soft tissue sarcoma, osteosarcoma - 1st-line and salvage; IFO-MAIA regimen); testicular germ cell tumours (relapsed/refractory - VIP, TIP regimens); paediatric cancers (Ewing's sarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma - VAI, VIDE regimens); bladder cancer; lymphoma (salvage regimens). SE: urotoxicity (haemorrhagic cystitis - acrolein + chloroacetaldehyde - ALWAYS co-administer MESNA for uroprotection); nephrotoxicity (renal tubular damage - Fanconi syndrome, diabetes insipidus - aggressive hydration + electrolyte monitoring); encephalopathy (ifosfamide encephalopathy - chloroacetaldehyde metabolite; confusion, somnolence, seizures - potentially severe - methylene blue IV 50 mg as antidote; monitor for CNS SE); myelosuppression; alopecia. Note: MESNA (2-mercaptoethanesulfonate sodium) MANDATORY with ifosfamide (prevents urotoxicity - MESNA inactivates acrolein/urotoxic metabolites in urine); ifosfamide encephalopathy → methylene blue 50 mg IV (unique antidote - inhibits flavin-containing enzymes that produce neurotoxic metabolites from ifosfamide); higher encephalopathy risk than cyclophosphamide (chloroacetaldehyde production - especially in renal impairment, hypoalbuminaemia, prior cisplatin).

Bifunctional alkylating agent with purine analogue properties. MOA: mechlorethamine-like nitrogen mustard alkylating group + benzimidazole ring (structural analogue of purine) → DNA interstrand crosslinks + single-strand breaks → apoptosis via p53-dependent and -independent pathways; activation of DNA damage checkpoints + stress-induced signalling; demonstrates partial non-cross-resistance with other alkylating agents (benzimidazole component → different interaction with DNA from pure alkylators). Indications: chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL - 1st-line for unfit patients; BR [bendamustine-rituximab] regimen; PBS-listed); indolent lymphoma (follicular lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma - BR ± obinutuzumab); mantle cell lymphoma (R-BAC); Waldenström macroglobulinaemia. SE: myelosuppression (neutropenia, thrombocytopenia - Grade 3/4 common - G-CSF prophylaxis often required); infections (immunosuppression - pneumocystis prophylaxis + herpes prophylaxis often given); infusion reactions (chills, fever, pruritus - premedicate with antihistamine + corticosteroid); nausea/vomiting; skin rash; opportunistic infections (lymphopenia persists); secondary malignancies (long-term). Note: BR (bendamustine-rituximab) = standard for unfit CLL + follicular lymphoma (BRIGHT trial); less emetic than CHOP (no vincristine/anthracycline); opportunistic infection prophylaxis important (cotrimoxazole for PCP, aciclovir for herpes - particularly in CLL); available via IV infusion (not oral); compared to fludarabine-based regimens → fewer autoimmune complications but similar efficacy.

Anthracycline antibiotic chemotherapy. MOA: intercalates into DNA base pairs → disrupts topoisomerase II (prevents re-ligation of DNA strand breaks → DNA double-strand breaks → apoptosis); also generates reactive oxygen species (free radical DNA damage) + inhibits DNA/RNA synthesis; 4'-epimer of doxorubicin (same mechanism but epimerisation at C-4' hydroxyl → altered metabolism → reduced cardiotoxicity at equivalent doses). Indications: breast cancer (FEC = 5-FU/epirubicin/cyclophosphamide - adjuvant + neoadjuvant; AC → T regimen; standard breast cancer chemotherapy regimen); gastric/oesophageal cancer (ECF/ECX regimens); bladder cancer (intravesical - post-TURBT adjuvant for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer → ↓recurrence). SE: cardiotoxicity (cumulative dose-dependent - dilated cardiomyopathy - lifetime cumulative dose limit 900-1000 mg/m² [vs doxorubicin 450-550 mg/m²] - less cardiotoxic than doxorubicin at equimolar doses); myelosuppression (neutropenia - G-CSF consideration); nausea/vomiting (moderately emetogenic); alopecia; mucositis; red urine (harmless - metabolite); vesicant (extravasation → severe tissue necrosis). Note: cardiomonitoring - ECHO/MUGA before starting and during treatment (particularly at cumulative dose >550 mg/m²); adriamycin (doxorubicin) vs epirubicin - epirubicin less cardiotoxic → higher lifetime dose permissible; intravesical single instillation within 6 hours of TURBT - reduces bladder cancer recurrence by 40%; red discoloration of urine 24-48 h (harmless - counsel patient).

Anthracycline antibiotic chemotherapy - first anthracycline developed.
