MOA: intercalates into DNA → inhibits topoisomerase II → DNA strand breaks + inhibition of DNA/RNA synthesis; free radical generation → oxidative stress; similar mechanism to doxorubicin/epirubicin but narrow spectrum (mainly haematological malignancies); liposomal formulation (DaunoXome) → ↑tumour delivery, ↓cardiotoxicity. Indications: acute myeloid leukaemia (AML - 7+3 induction regimen: cytarabine × 7 days + daunorubicin × 3 days → standard 1st-line induction; also idarubicin substituted); acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL - induction regimens); Kaposi's sarcoma (liposomal daunorubicin [DaunoXome] - HIV-associated KS). SE: cardiotoxicity (cumulative - dilated cardiomyopathy - lifetime limit ~550 mg/m²; monitor LVEF); myelosuppression (severe - expected during AML induction = aplasia period); nausea/vomiting; mucositis; alopecia; red urine (harmless); vesicant (extravasation injury). Note: 7+3 regimen (cytarabine 100-200 mg/m²/day × 7 days continuous + daunorubicin 60-90 mg/m² days 1-3) = historical gold standard AML induction; idarubicin increasingly preferred over daunorubicin for better CNS penetration + possibly superior efficacy; liposomal (DaunoXome) for KS - ↓cardiotoxicity; cardiac monitoring essential (cumulative dose tracking).

Anthracycline antibiotic chemotherapy - 4-demethoxy daunorubicin (more lipophilic than daunorubicin). MOA: DNA intercalation → topoisomerase II inhibition → double-strand DNA breaks; greater lipophilicity vs daunorubicin → better CNS penetration; oral bioavailability (~30% vs near-zero for doxorubicin - oral formulation possible); metabolised to idarubicinol (active metabolite, t½ ~45 h). Indications: AML induction (1st-line - 7+3 regimen idarubicin + cytarabine; MA [idarubicin + cytarabine] - superior CR rates vs daunorubicin in some studies); ALL; blastic phase CML. SE: myelosuppression (severe - expected; prolonged neutropenia during induction); cardiotoxicity (cumulative - lower cardiotoxicity potential than doxorubicin/daunorubicin due to demethoxy substitution + different metabolic profile; lifetime limit ~150 mg/m² IV); nausea; mucositis; alopecia; red/orange urine; vesicant. Note: AML induction preference - idarubicin (12 mg/m² × 3 days) has largely replaced daunorubicin at many centres (comparable or slightly better response rates; better CNS penetration - ? benefit for CNS disease); oral idarubicin (20-35 mg/m² × 3 days) - available but oral formulation not commonly used clinically; cardiac monitoring (LVEF) required - cumulative dose tracking.

Anthracenedione antineoplastic + multiple sclerosis drug. MOA: intercalates into DNA → topoisomerase II inhibition → DNA strand breaks; also intercalates without covalent binding (similar to anthracyclines but anthracenedione not quinone → less free radical generation → less cardiac oxidative damage than doxorubicin); anti-inflammatory mechanism in MS (reduces T-cell activation + ↓Th1 cytokines). Indications: multiple sclerosis (worsening RRMS, progressive-relapsing MS, SPMS - 2nd-line for severe rapidly progressing disease; IV every 3 months; limited by cardiotoxicity - lifetime cumulative dose 140 mg/m²; largely replaced by better-tolerated DMTs); AML (induction - salvage or ≥65 years); prostate cancer (metastatic hormone-refractory - palliative - mitoxantrone + prednisone: reduces pain/improves QoL but no OS benefit - now superseded by docetaxel/enzalutamide/abiraterone). SE: cardiotoxicity (cumulative cardiomyopathy - monitoring LVEF essential; lifetime limit 140 mg/m²; monitor ECG + ECHO every 3 months in MS patients); myelosuppression; therapy-related AML/leukaemia (topoisomerase II inhibitor class risk); blue-green urine/sclerae/skin discoloration (benign - reassure); nausea; alopecia. Note: LVEF monitoring mandatory (baseline + before each dose in MS; cumulative cardiotoxicity - lower limit than doxorubicin due to anthracenedione metabolic differences but still significant); therapy-related AML (1-2% lifetime risk with MS doses - counsel patients); largely replaced in MS by safer agents (natalizumab, ocrelizumab, alemtuzumab); blue discoloration of urine/veins normal.

Alkylating antibiotic chemotherapy. MOA: prodrug activated by enzymatic reduction (bioreductive alkylation - preferentially in hypoxic tumour cells → activated by NADPH cytochrome P450 reductase) → forms bifunctional alkylating species → interstrand DNA crosslinks (primarily at guanine) → DNA replication block → apoptosis; selective activity in hypoxic tumour microenvironment (advantage in poorly oxygenated solid tumours). Indications: bladder cancer (intravesical - post-TURBT adjuvant for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer - reduces recurrence; instillation within 6 hours of TURBT; also long-term maintenance intravesical); anal cancer (chemoradiation - 5-FU + mitomycin = standard treatment - Nigro protocol); peritoneal carcinomatosis (HIPEC - hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy - colorectal, ovarian, mesothelioma); gastric, colorectal cancer (systemic - historical). SE: myelosuppression (delayed - bone marrow suppression typically nadir 4-6 weeks post-treatment - more delayed than most drugs); haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS - microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia + renal failure - cumulative dose ≥60 mg → 2-10% risk; potentially life-threatening; monitor renal function + blood film); pulmonary toxicity (interstitial pneumonitis); intravesical SE: dysuria, frequency (local bladder irritation), rare systemic absorption. Note: HUS monitoring - cumulative dose risk → beyond 60 mg total; renal function + LDH + blood film monitoring; intravesical use - bladder instillation (40 mg in 40 mL saline × 2 hours); Nigro protocol (anal cancer): 5-FU days 1-4 + mitomycin day 1 + radiotherapy - achieves high local control rates.

Alkylating agent with MAO-inhibiting properties. MOA: prodrug - auto-oxidation + hepatic CYP450 activation → alkylating metabolites → DNA methylation/alkylation → interstrand crosslinks + single-strand breaks; also inhibits MAO (monoamine oxidase - dietary tyramine interactions, drug interactions like pethidine); free radical generation. Indications: Hodgkin's lymphoma (BEACOPP regimen: bleomycin, etoposide, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, procarbazine, prednisone; or older MOPP regimen; advanced Hodgkin's disease); brain tumours (GBM - PCV regimen: procarbazine, lomustine/CCNU, vincristine - for 1p/19q co-deleted oligodendroglioma; IDH-mutant oligodendroglioma); primary CNS lymphoma (MPV/MSKCC regimens). SE: myelosuppression; nausea/vomiting (moderately emetogenic); MAO inhibition (tyramine-containing foods → hypertensive crisis - dietary tyramine restriction required: aged cheese, red wine, cured meats; drug interactions - pethidine, TCAs, SSRIs → serotonin syndrome/hypertensive crisis); CNS effects (fatigue, confusion); teratogenic + mutagenic; secondary AML (long-term); disulfiram-like alcohol reaction. Note: dietary tyramine restriction MANDATORY (MAO inhibition during therapy + 2 weeks after - avoid aged cheese, preserved meats, broad bean pods, alcohol/red wine, yeast extracts); drug interactions - SSRIs/TCAs/pethidine → serotonin syndrome; alcohol → disulfiram-like reaction; PCV regimen uses procarbazine for IDH-mutant oligodendroglioma (6 cycles - EORTC trials show OS benefit).

Progestogenic anti-androgen with potent antigonadotrophic properties. MOA: competitive antagonist at androgen receptors (AR) → blocks testosterone/DHT binding → ↓AR-mediated gene transcription; also potent progestin → activates progesterone receptor → ↓GnRH secretion (negative feedback) → ↓LH/FSH → ↓gonadal androgen production (combined mechanism: peripheral AR block + central ↓testosterone production); anti-androgenic effect stronger than flutamide at gonadotrophin suppression. Indications: prostate cancer (locally advanced/metastatic - adjunct to radiation/chemical castration; control of hot flushes during LHRH agonist therapy [flare prophylaxis]; palliative); acne vulgaris (severe androgenic acne in females - combined with oestrogen as Diane-35/Estelle; PBS-listed); hirsutism (female - PCOS, idiopathic); transgender healthcare (gender-affirming hormone therapy - feminising - + oestrogen). SE: hepatotoxicity (serious - dose-dependent hepatocellular + cholestatic; ↑LFTs → hepatocellular carcinoma with prolonged high-dose use; LFT monitoring essential); cardiovascular (VTE - thrombosis risk - combined with oestrogen → ↑VTE risk vs levonorgestrel pill); adrenocortical insufficiency (glucocorticoid-like activity at high doses); depression; ↓libido; gynaecomastia (males). Note: hepatotoxicity risk - LFT monitoring every 3-6 months (especially at doses >10 mg/day); thrombosis risk - combined contraceptive pills containing cyproterone (Diane-35, Estelle) → higher VTE risk than levonorgestrel pills - not 1st-line OCP; for prostate cancer: now largely replaced by bicalutamide/enzalutamide; low-dose (2 mg) in combination OCP effective for acne/hirsutism.

Selective non-steroidal androgen receptor antagonist. MOA: competitive AR antagonist → blocks testosterone/DHT binding to AR → ↓AR nuclear translocation → ↓androgen-responsive gene transcription; non-steroidal (no progesterone/glucocorticoid cross-reactivity → fewer sex hormone SE vs cyproterone/flutamide); pure anti-androgen (no agonist activity). Indications: prostate cancer (locally advanced - with or without radiotherapy; adjuvant following radical prostatectomy/radiation for node-positive disease; metastatic - combined with LHRH agonist [to prevent testosterone flare]); transgender healthcare (gender-affirming hormone therapy - blocks testosterone effects ± oestrogen in trans women; used for genital feminisation); acne/hirsutism in females (off-label - low dose 25 mg). SE: gynaecomastia + breast pain (most common - peripheral oestrogen activity when testosterone blocked → ↑E:T ratio → breast tissue stimulation - prophylactic breast irradiation or tamoxifen reduces gynecomastia); hot flushes; liver toxicity (↑LFTs - rare but monitor; less hepatotoxic than flutamide); diarrhoea; rarely interstitial pneumonitis. Note: gynecomastia prevention - single-fraction breast irradiation (8 Gy × 1) before starting bicalutamide reduces gynecomastia dramatically (effective prophylaxis); bicalutamide preferred over flutamide (less hepatotoxic) and cyproterone (no glucocorticoid/progestogen activity) for prostate cancer; 150 mg OD monotherapy (for locally advanced); 50 mg OD with LHRH agonist (combined ADT); used in combination with LHRH agonist (prevents 'flare' when LHRH agonist started).

Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) - vaginal oestrogen precursor. MOA: endogenous sex steroid precursor; vaginal suppository formulation → local conversion in vaginal epithelium by endogenous enzymes (steroidogenesis) → oestrogens + androgens (primarily oestrone + testosterone) locally; restores vaginal trophicity without significant systemic oestrogen elevation; acts via both oestrogen receptors (ERα, ERβ) and androgen receptor (AR) in vaginal tissue. Indications: dyspareunia associated with genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM) / vulvovaginal atrophy (VVA) - vaginal insert 6.5 mg/night (US approval 2016; alternative to vaginal oestrogens for postmenopausal women with breast cancer history - minimal systemic oestrogen). SE: vaginal discharge (most common - from restored secretions); vaginal discomfort (initial burning - settles); abnormal pap smear (cervical changes - limited evidence); acne, headache (systemic conversion minimal but possible). Note: minimally elevated serum oestrogen/androgens vs systemic DHEA supplementation (vaginal route + first-pass vaginal metabolism); considered relatively safe in breast cancer survivors (local DHEA with minimal systemic absorption - but data limited - oncologist discussion required); does NOT protect against osteoporosis or systemic menopause symptoms (local action only); compare to ospemifene (oral SERM for dyspareunia - 60 mg OD) and topical vaginal oestrogens; 0.5% cream alternative.

Aromatic diamidine antiprotozoal/antifungal. MOA: mechanism incompletely understood; accumulates in mitochondria and nuclei of parasites → disrupts oxidative phosphorylation; interferes with DNA synthesis (intercalation/binding); disrupts polyamine biosynthesis (selective toxicity); for Pneumocystis - inhibits DHFR + dihydropteroate synthase + thymidylate synthase simultaneously + affects cell membrane. Indications: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) - inhaled (monthly aerosolised - secondary prophylaxis in HIV when cotrimoxazole not tolerated); treatment of moderate-severe PCP (IV pentamidine - 2nd-line after cotrimoxazole); visceral leishmaniasis (alternative to amphotericin, miltefosine); African sleeping sickness (T. brucei gambiense - early stage, before CNS involvement - largely replaced by other agents). SE: inhaled: bronchospasm (pre-treat with salbutamol), cough; injection/IV: hypotension (can be severe → give IV slowly over >60 min with patient lying down), hypoglycaemia (islet cell damage → insulin release → hypoglycaemia; can be delayed days; monitor BGL; followed by hyperglycaemia/diabetes long-term), nephrotoxicity, pancreatitis, cardiac arrhythmias, hypocalcaemia, myelosuppression. Note: severe SE profile (hypotension, hypoglycaemia) → IV pentamidine requires monitoring; hypoglycaemia mechanism (direct β-cell lysis → acute insulin release) followed by β-cell destruction → diabetes mellitus; inhaled prophylaxis - monthly 300 mg via Respirgard II nebuliser; less effective than cotrimoxazole for PCP prophylaxis (peripheral lung distribution issues); reserved for cotrimoxazole intolerance.

Sympathomimetic amine - anti-obesity agent. MOA: releases noradrenaline + dopamine (to lesser extent) from presynaptic terminals → ↑synaptic catecholamines → activates adrenergic receptors in hypothalamic feeding centres → ↓appetite (amfetamine structural analogue - fenethylamine class); indirect sympathomimetic → ↑heart rate, ↑BP, ↑metabolic rate; no direct serotonin release at therapeutic doses. Indications: obesity management (short-term adjunct to diet and exercise - BMI ≥30, or ≥27 with comorbidities; PBS-listed in Australia with authority; 15-40 mg OD in the morning [before 2 PM - stimulant effect prevents sleep]; typically licensed 3-6 months maximum); combined with topiramate (Qsymia - not TGA-approved). SE: cardiovascular (↑HR, ↑BP, palpitations - monitor BP/HR; avoid in cardiovascular disease/uncontrolled hypertension); insomnia (take in morning - stimulant effect); dry mouth; constipation; tolerance (efficacy decreases - use short-term); psychological effects (agitation, euphoria - amfetamine-related - misuse potential); rebound weight gain on cessation; primary pulmonary hypertension (rare class effect - particularly fenfluamine combination [withdrawn] - monitoring recommended). Note: Schedule 8 controlled substance in Australia (Duromine PBS-authority); stimulant effect - morning dosing essential (≤2 PM); cardiovascular contraindications (CAD, uncontrolled HTN, arrhythmias); tolerance develops after weeks - short-term use only; withdrawn/used cautiously given fen-phen pulmonary hypertension history; supervised use with regular BP/HR checks; now increasingly superseded by GLP-1 receptor agonists.

Vitamin D2 - plant-derived vitamin D pro-hormone. MOA: same metabolic pathway as colecalciferol (D3) → hepatic 25-hydroxylation → renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation → active calcitriol → VDR-mediated calcium/phosphate homeostasis; D2 slightly less potent/shorter duration than D3 (25[OH]D₂ t½ shorter than 25[OH]D₃ → less efficient maintenance dosing; D3 preferred for supplementation). Indications: vitamin D deficiency (high-dose prescription treatment of deficiency - 50,000 IU capsules - available as PBS prescription in Australia; not standard OTC like D3); malabsorption syndromes (Crohn's, coeliac - high-dose D2 available); vegan patients (D2 = plant-derived - not from animal sources; preferred for ethical/dietary reasons). SE: same as colecalciferol (hypercalcaemia/hypercalciuria at excessive doses). Note: D3 vs D2 - D3 (colecalciferol) preferred for supplementation (better maintained serum 25[OH]D levels, more potent per IU); D2 (ergocalciferol) - used for high-dose prescription treatment of deficiency; prescription-strength 50,000 IU capsules available in Australia (PBS); efficacy at deficiency-correcting doses (50,000 IU × 8-12 weeks) similar to D3 in most studies; 1,000-2,000 IU D3 equivalence to 400-800 IU ergocalciferol not straightforward (dosing differs between D2 and D3).

1-alpha-hydroxyvitamin D3 - active vitamin D analogue. MOA: prodrug → undergoes rapid 25-hydroxylation in liver → active calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D₃) → binds VDR → ↑intestinal Ca²⁺ + phosphate absorption + renal Ca²⁺ reabsorption + bone mineralisation; bypasses renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation step (impaired in CKD → CKD patients cannot convert colecalciferol/ergocalciferol to active calcitriol). Indications: CKD-associated secondary hyperparathyroidism (↑PTH from ↓calcitriol → bone disease - alfacalcidol suppresses PTH secretion via VDR in parathyroid gland → ↓PTH); renal osteodystrophy; post-thyroid/parathyroid surgery hypocalcaemia; hypoparathyroidism (↑Ca²⁺ absorption in gut compensates for ↓PTH → maintains Ca²⁺); vitamin D-resistant rickets. SE: hypercalcaemia (most important - monitor serum calcium; reduce dose/stop if calcium elevated; more risk than colecalciferol as active vitamin D - frequent Ca²⁺ monitoring required); hypercalciuria; nephrocalcinosis; GI upset; elevated phosphate (if high dose + dietary phosphate not controlled). Note: CKD dosing - start low (250 ng OD) + titrate monitoring Ca/PO4/PTH; hypercalcaemia signal - check Ca before each dose increase; compare to calcitriol (alfacalcidol requires hepatic 25-hydroxylation → calcitriol does not; similar clinical effect - calcitriol slightly preferred in severe hepatic failure); adjust dose based on PTH target + Ca level.

Selective vitamin D receptor activator (SVRA) - synthetic vitamin D2 analogue. MOA: binds VDR with high selectivity → ↓PTH gene transcription in parathyroid glands (PTH suppression) while having less effect on intestinal calcium/phosphate absorption compared to calcitriol → ↓hypercalcaemia + hyperphosphataemia risk; parathyroid-selective (PTH suppression with less hypercalcaemia/hyperphosphataemia than calcitriol). Indications: secondary hyperparathyroidism in CKD (stage 3-5D - all stages including dialysis; oral or IV injection; reduces PTH more selectively with lower hypercalcaemia risk than calcitriol; PBS-listed Australia for dialysis patients); may have additional CV + anti-proteinuric effects in CKD (emerging evidence). SE: hypercalcaemia (less common than calcitriol - monitor Ca²⁺ and phosphate; still occurs - reduce dose if Ca elevated); hyperphosphataemia; GI: nausea, vomiting; allergic reactions. Note: KDIGO guidelines recommend active vitamin D (alfacalcidol, paricalcitol, calcitriol) for elevated PTH in CKD dialysis patients; paricalcitol advantages - less hypercalcaemia/hyperphosphataemia vs calcitriol (parathyroid-selective VDR activation); monitoring: serum Ca, phosphate, PTH every 1-3 months during dose adjustment; target PTH depends on CKD stage (KDIGO 2× to 9× upper normal limit for dialysis).

Gastrointestinal adsorbent - poisoning management. MOA: large surface area (600-1500 m²/g) → adsorbs wide range of drugs/toxins in GI lumen → prevents GI absorption; does NOT adsorb all substances (see Note - ineffective for metals, alcohols, strong acids/bases, caustics); multi-dose activated charcoal (MDAC) → adsorbs drug from enterohepatic recirculation/GI secretion → ↑elimination (useful for carbamazepine, phenobarbitone, theophylline, dapsone, quinine). Indications: acute poisoning/overdose (within 1-2 hours of ingestion of susceptible substances - aspirin, paracetamol [with NAC], tricyclics, benzodiazepines, carbamazepine, digoxin, theophylline, quinine - MOST organic compounds); MDAC (multiple doses q4h × 24h - for severe theophylline, carbamazepine, phenobarbitone, quinine, dapsone - enhances elimination); poisoning first aid (initial GI decontamination - call Poisons Information Centre 13 11 26 in Australia). SE: black stools (harmless - reassure); nausea/vomiting (risk of aspiration → only give if patient conscious + protecting airway - ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION if airway unprotected/drowsy); constipation (sorbitol cathartic sometimes co-formulated to prevent); aspiration pneumonitis (if given to unconscious/drowsy patient). Note: CONTRAINDICATED in corrosive ingestion (burns oropharynx further if aspirated), unprotected airway, bowel obstruction, hydrocarbons (aspiration risk > benefit); NOT effective for: iron, lead, lithium, strong acids/bases, alcohols (methanol/ethanol), cyanide, fluoride; standard dose 50 g (adult) or 1 g/kg (child) in water/soft drink; give within 1-2 hours (most benefit); call Poisons Information Centre first.

Calcium salt - IV/oral calcium replacement and membrane stabiliser. MOA: provides ionised calcium (Ca²⁺) → directly raises serum ionised calcium → physiological effects (membrane potential stabilisation - cardiac, neuromuscular); (1) hypocalcaemia treatment - restores ECF Ca²⁺ → resolves tetany/seizures; (2) hyperkalaemia emergency - Ca²⁺ raises cardiac action potential threshold → stabilises myocardial membrane against hyperkalaemia-induced arrhythmia (does not lower serum K⁺ - membrane-protective effect only); (3) calcium gluconate gel - topical chelation of hydrofluoric acid (HF) burns → converts ionic fluoride to insoluble calcium fluoride → prevents fluoride systemic toxicity. Indications: hypocalcaemia (acute - IV bolus for tetany, seizures, prolonged QTc; symptomatic or ionised Ca < 1.0 mmol/L); hyperkalaemia (severe - cardiac monitoring - 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV over 2-3 min - membrane stabilisation while K-lowering measures take effect); calcium channel blocker overdose (high-dose IV calcium to overcome CCB blockade + high-dose insulin-glucose therapy); HF burns (topical gel); magnesium toxicity (IV Ca²⁺ - antidote for MgSO₄ toxicity). SE: bradycardia (rapid IV injection - inject slowly); hypercalcaemia (over-replacement); tissue necrosis (extravasation - calcium salts cause significant tissue damage - ensure good IV access; calcium gluconate safer than chloride for peripheral IV); ↑digoxin toxicity (hypercalcaemia worsens digoxin toxicity - avoid IV calcium in digoxin toxicity). Note: 10% calcium gluconate = 10 mL ampule contains 2.25 mmol calcium; calcium gluconate safer peripherally than calcium chloride (less sclerosant); hyperkalaemia - calcium does NOT lower K⁺ (give as bridge while waiting for insulin + dextrose, sodium bicarbonate, resonium); digoxin toxicity contraindication.

Amide local anaesthetic - most widely used dental local anaesthetic. MOA: blocks voltage-gated sodium channels (Na⁺) in peripheral nerve axons → stabilises nerve membrane → prevents depolarisation → conduction block (same mechanism as all amide LAs); unique feature: contains thiophene ring (aromatic ring - unlike benzene ring of lidocaine/mepivacaine) → higher lipid solubility + faster tissue diffusion → better spread through bone/hard tissue → improved anaesthesia for maxillary and mandibular blocks with buccal infiltration technique. Indications: dental anaesthesia (most common - buccal/palatal infiltrations, nerve blocks [inferior alveolar, mental, incisive] - 4% concentration with adrenaline 1:100,000 or 1:200,000; can often achieve mandibular anaesthesia with buccal infiltration due to bone penetration); minor oral surgery; periodontal procedures. SE: local toxicity (from excessive dose - tongue/lip biting in children - warn carers that numbness lasts 1-3 h after procedure); CNS/cardiac toxicity (systemic absorption of excessive doses → CNS: perioral tingling, tinnitus, confusion, seizures; Cardiovascular: bradycardia, arrhythmia - always aspirate before injecting); allergic reaction (rare - amide LAs have very low allergy risk - most 'allergy' due to vasovagal or adrenaline/preservative; true amide allergy rare). Note: highest concentration dental LA (4% vs lidocaine 2% - but equivalent safe doses per kg); mandibular buccal infiltration effective (bone permeability of articaine → avoids inferior alveolar nerve block in many cases); adrenaline component: 1:100,000 for longer procedures, 1:200,000 for cardiac patients; maximum safe dose 7 mg/kg (with adrenaline).

Amide local anaesthetic. MOA: sodium channel blocker → reversible nerve conduction block; intermediate duration LA (longer than lidocaine, shorter than bupivacaine); does NOT contain ester linkage (amide - less allergenic than ester LAs); unique: has low vasodilatory activity (unlike most LAs) → can be used plain (without vasopressor) for shorter dental procedures. Indications: dental anaesthesia (inferior alveolar block, infiltrations - 3% mepivacaine plain for shorter procedures where adrenaline contraindicated; 2% mepivacaine + levonordefrin for longer procedures); nerve blocks (plexus, epidural, peripheral); short surgical procedures. SE: same class effects as other amide LAs (CNS: tinnitus, metallic taste, perioral numbness, seizures with overdose; CV: arrhythmia, hypotension); slightly less systemic toxicity than bupivacaine (lower potency); duration 90-150 min (intermediate). Note: advantage over lidocaine - lower vasodilatory effect → mepivacaine plain (no vasopressor) provides effective dental anaesthesia (useful when adrenaline contraindicated - severe uncontrolled hypertension, thyrotoxicosis, phaeochromocytoma); compare to lidocaine (shorter duration, more vasodilation) and bupivacaine (longer duration, higher cardiac toxicity); 3% mepivacaine plain = dental cartridge concentration for vasopressor-free anaesthesia.

Ester local anaesthetic - topical only. MOA: ester LA (para-aminobenzoic acid derivative) → sodium channel blockade → reversible nerve conduction block; used topically only (low systemic absorption from intact mucosa at low doses); hydrolysed by plasma pseudocholinesterase (ester linkage → shorter duration than amide LAs); releases PABA (para-aminobenzoic acid) on hydrolysis (folic acid interference). Indications: topical anaesthesia (oral mucosa - dental pre-injection anaesthesia to reduce needle insertion pain; sore throat sprays/lozenges; rectal anaesthesia for haemorrhoids/fissures; minor skin procedures - aerosol spray - but methaemoglobinaemia risk); minor wound pain; dental procedures (topical gel before injection). SE: methaemoglobinaemia (serious - particularly with oral sprays absorbed on mucosa in infants/neonates - AVOID in infants <2 years; benzocaine converts Hb Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ → metHb - impairs O₂ carriage; presents as cyanosis refractory to O₂ - treat with methylene blue or ascorbic acid; reports in pharyngeal/oral use); contact allergic dermatitis (PABA - avoid in known sulfonamide allergy - cross-reactivity); rarely anaphylaxis. Note: methaemoglobinaemia warning - boxed warning warning for benzocaine gels/sprays in infants (multiple neonatal deaths); ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in infants < 2 years for oral use; adult risk lower but still possible at high doses/mucous membrane application; prefer lidocaine spray for topical anaesthesia in vulnerable populations; PABA metabolite → cross-allergy with sulfonamides, thiazides, PABA-based sunscreens.

Topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (CAI) - eye drops for glaucoma. MOA: inhibits carbonic anhydrase II (CAII) in ciliary epithelium → ↓HCO₃⁻ formation → ↓Na⁺/HCO₃⁻ co-transport → ↓aqueous humour production → ↓IOP; topical CAI = local ocular effect with minimal systemic CA inhibition (cf. oral acetazolamide - systemic); suspension formulation (1% brinzolamide) - less stinging than dorzolamide solution. Indications: open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension (as monotherapy or adjunct to beta-blockers [e.g., timolol] or prostaglandin analogues; 1% BD-TID). SE: blurred vision after instillation (suspension formulation - temporary - tip: look down for 1 min after instilling; main tolerability advantage vs dorzolamide); ocular discomfort, foreign body sensation; bitter taste (nasolacrimal drainage → mouth); headache; systemic CAI effects (rare at topical doses - acidosis, hypokalaemia - caution in severe renal impairment). Note: sulfonamide derivative - contraindicated in sulfonamide allergy; compare to dorzolamide (solution - stings less than acetazolamide IV but more than brinzolamide suspension; similar IOP-lowering); combined brinzolamide/timolol (Azarga) = fixed-dose combination for convenience; apply gentle nasolacrimal pressure after instillation (reduces bitter taste from nasolacrimal drainage); renal impairment caution (accumulates).

Selective beta-1 adrenoceptor antagonist - ophthalmic and systemic. MOA: selective beta-1 blockade (cardioselective) → in eye: ↓sympathetic stimulation of ciliary epithelium → ↓aqueous humour production → ↓IOP (25-30% reduction); systemic (oral) → cardioselective beta-blockade → ↓HR, ↓cardiac output → antihypertensive + antianginal. Indications: glaucoma + ocular hypertension (topical eye drops - 0.25-0.5% solution; less bronchospasm than non-selective timolol → preferred in COPD/asthma - but still some risk); hypertension (oral - 10-20 mg OD - systemic antihypertensive). SE: ophthalmic: local irritation, reduced night vision; systemic absorption → bradycardia, bronchospasm (less than non-selective beta-blockers - but still occurs in severe asthma/COPD → use with caution); cold extremities; depression. Note: beta-1 selectivity advantage - less bronchospasm than timolol (non-selective - beta-1 + beta-2 blockade → beta-2 blockade in bronchi causes bronchoconstriction); but caution still required in asthma/COPD (selectivity lost at higher concentrations); preferred over timolol in patients with reactive airways; IOP reduction ~25-30% (less than prostaglandins ~30-35%, similar to other beta-blockers); avoid bilateral beta-blocker ophthalmic + systemic beta-blocker combination (additive bradycardia).

Alpha-2 adrenoceptor agonist - ophthalmic. MOA: selective alpha-2 agonist → ↓aqueous humour production (ciliary body) + possible ↑uveoscleral outflow → ↓IOP (20-30% reduction); also causes mild eyelid retraction (Müller's muscle stimulation via alpha-1-like effect at sympathomimetic doses - used diagnostically in Horner syndrome). Indications: post-laser trabeculoplasty/laser iridotomy IOP spike prevention (1% solution immediately before and after laser procedure); short-term IOP control (0.5% TID - limited by tachyphylaxis and allergy); Horner syndrome diagnosis - phenylephrine 1% test vs hydroxyamphetamine 1% test - apraclonidine 1% as alternative diagnostic test (apraclonidine causes conjunctival blanching + eyelid elevation in Horner eye due to denervation hypersensitivity - reversal of ptosis/miosis distinguishes Horner from physiological anisocoria). SE: allergic blepharoconjunctivitis (very common with long-term use - up to 30-40% - pruritus, erythema, follicular hyperplasia - limits long-term use); headache; dry mouth; systemic alpha-2 effects (bradycardia, hypotension). Note: tachyphylaxis - efficacy diminishes rapidly (not suitable for chronic use); allergy common (disqualifies long-term use - use brimonidine instead for chronic alpha-2 IOP lowering); Horner test: in postganglionic Horner (3rd-order neuron lesion) → apraclonidine reverses ptosis/miosis due to denervation hypersensitivity; useful for acute IOP spike prevention (peri-laser).

Prostaglandin F2α analogue - preservative-free once-daily eye drop for glaucoma. MOA: FP (prostaglandin F) receptor agonist → ↑uveoscleral outflow (primarily) + ↑trabecular outflow → ↓IOP by 25-35%; preservative-free formulation (no benzalkonium chloride [BAK]) → ↓ocular surface toxicity vs preserved prostaglandin analogues. Indications: open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension (once-daily OD - nocte preferred; preservative-free unit dose - ideal for patients with ocular surface disease, contact lens wearers, or preservative sensitivity; PBS-listed in Australia). SE: conjunctival hyperaemia (red eye - common, often less than latanoprost); increased iris pigmentation (irreversible - accumulation of melanin in iris stromal melanocytes - regulatory safety warning - explain before prescribing; occurs in mixed-colour irides - heterochromia risk; may be noticed by others); periocular skin darkening; hypertrichosis (eyelash growth - lengthening, darkening, increased lashes - cosmetically desired by some patients); ocular surface irritation (preservative-free → less surface toxicity than BAK-preserved drops). Note: preservative-free advantage - patients with dry eye, blepharitis, meibomian gland dysfunction, frequent use → less ocular surface toxicity than BAK-preserved prostaglandins; iris pigmentation warning - document baseline iris colour + photography; latanoprost, bimatoprost, travoprost also prostaglandins - similar efficacy; once-daily nocte (prostaglandins most effective when dosed in evening); unit-dose single-use vials.

Muscarinic antagonist - short-acting mydriatic and cycloplegic. MOA: competitive antagonist at muscarinic M3 receptors → (1) ↓sphincter pupillae (parasympathetic contraction) → mydriasis (pupil dilation); (2) ↓ciliary muscle contraction (accommodation) → cycloplegia (paralysis of accommodation → ↑depth of focus for fundoscopy); short duration (~6 hours) vs longer-acting atropine/homatropine. Indications: fundoscopy and retinal examination (1% solution - pupil dilation for ophthalmoscopy, retinal photography, OCT; most common mydriatic in practice); cycloplegic refraction in children (0.5-1% - less reliable cycloplegia than cyclopentolate - cyclopentolate preferred for refraction); anterior segment examination (iritis - brief cycloplegia). SE: photophobia (dilated pupil → light sensitivity - provide dark glasses; last 6-8 h); blurred near vision (cycloplegia → reading difficulty 4-6 h); local irritation; systemic anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, flushing, tachycardia, urinary retention - mostly with infants/small children via nasolacrimal absorption - more serious risk). Note: apply nasolacrimal pressure after instillation (children - systemic absorption via nasolacrimal duct → risk of anticholinergic effects); warn patients about driving impairment (blurred vision + photophobia - 4-6 h); acute angle-closure glaucoma risk (pupil dilation → narrowing iridocorneal angle - caution in shallow anterior chamber/narrow angle; screen before dilating); tropicamide less effective cycloplegic than cyclopentolate (cyclopentolate preferred for refractions).

Muscarinic antagonist - cycloplegic and mydriatic. MOA: muscarinic M3 receptor antagonist → ↓ciliary muscle contraction (cycloplegia) + ↓sphincter pupillae (mydriasis); stronger + more reliable cycloplegia than tropicamide → preferred for cycloplegic refraction; duration ~24 hours (longer than tropicamide - advise patients). Indications: cycloplegic refraction (children - most common indication - 1-2% solution for refraction assessment under cycloplegia → accurate determination of refractive error not masked by accommodation; removes accommodation to get true refractive status - important in young children + hyperopes where accommodation masks hyperopia); mydriasis (diagnostic examination); treatment of uveitis/iritis (breaks posterior synechiae - prevents adhesion of iris to lens). SE: marked photophobia (mydriasis - 24 h - provide sunglasses); blurred near vision (cycloplegia - 24 h - advise about driving/near work impairment); systemic anticholinergic toxicity (children - especially infants - nasolacrimal absorption → CNS effects: confusion, agitation, hallucinations, tachycardia, flushing, urinary retention - AVOID 2% in neonates/premature infants; 0.5% for infants <1 year; 1% for older children). Note: systemic toxicity risk in children - apply nasolacrimal pressure, 0.5% for infants; cycloplegic refraction gold standard (atropine > cyclopentolate > tropicamide for cycloplegia strength; atropine reserved for very young children with esotropia/high hyperopia); 24-hour duration (warn parents child cannot read at near for 24 h; not to drive if older adolescent).

Ester local anaesthetic - topical ophthalmic. MOA: ester LA (PABA-containing ester linkage) → blocks Na⁺ channels at corneal/conjunctival nerve endings → rapid topical anaesthesia within 30 seconds; very short systemic absorption from ocular surface → minimal systemic effects; hydrolysed locally. Indications: topical ocular anaesthesia (tonometry [contact/applanation], removal of foreign bodies from cornea/conjunctiva, short ocular procedures, minor surgery, examination of painful eye, fitting contact lenses); also used as diagnostic: proxymetacaine → anaesthetises superior oblique muscle - differentiates superior oblique from superior rectus palsies. SE: transient stinging/burning on instillation (brief); allergic contact dermatitis (ester LA allergy - PABA - less common than ester allergy in general due to low systemic absorption); corneal toxicity (prolonged use - repeat doses → disrupts corneal epithelial healing, ↑risk of corneal ulcer - DO NOT prescribe for ongoing home use); no systemic effects (unless excessive volume absorbed). Note: NEVER prescribe topical anaesthetics for home use to treat corneal pain (patient will overuse → corneal toxicity → corneal melting → blindness - this is a well-known serious error; refer instead for treatment of underlying pathology); one-off topical use for procedures is safe; amide alternative: oxybuprocaine (tetracaine/benoxinate) - similar use; PABA derivative - allergy risk in sulfonamide-allergic patients (check allergy history before use in procedures).

Topical ocular corticosteroid - soft steroid. MOA: binds glucocorticoid receptor → anti-inflammatory (↓cytokine production, ↓immune cell recruitment, ↓prostaglandin/leukotriene synthesis) → ↓ocular inflammation; 'soft' corticosteroid - minimal corneal penetration (binds corneal/conjunctival glucocorticoid receptors → surface effect) → less IOP elevation + less cataract compared to dexamethasone/prednisolone (harder steroids). Indications: inflammatory conditions of conjunctiva, cornea, anterior segment (allergic conjunctivitis, seasonal allergic eye disease, contact lens-induced keratoconjunctivitis, episcleritis, pinguecula inflammation, post-operative inflammation where soft steroid sufficient); not for acute serious uveitis (use prednisolone/dexamethasone for more severe inflammation). SE: raised IOP (less than hard steroids - monitor if using > 2 weeks; steroid-induced glaucoma risk - particularly in steroid-responders); posterior subcapsular cataract (prolonged use - less risk than dexamethasone); reactivation of HSV keratitis (corticosteroids → viral reactivation → corneal ulceration - do not use for herpetic keratitis without antiviral cover); infection exacerbation. Note: soft vs hard corticosteroids - fluorometholone/loteprednol (soft - less IOP/cataract risk); prednisolone/dexamethasone (hard - more anti-inflammatory but higher IOP/cataract risk); IOP monitoring at 2 weeks and monthly if longer use; contraindicated in viral keratitis (HSV, VZV), fungal keratitis (worsens infection); drops QID while inflamed → taper.

Soft corticosteroid - designed-to-deactivate topical ocular steroid. MOA: retrometabolic drug design → potent GR-binding corticosteroid locally → corneal/conjunctival GR activation → anti-inflammatory effect; undergoes rapid metabolic conversion to inactive metabolites (Δ1 cortienic acid = inactive) → ↓systemic and intraocular adverse effects (less IOP elevation than dexamethasone/prednisolone); C-20 ester bond → rapid local metabolism → minimal cataract/glaucoma risk. Indications: allergic conjunctivitis (0.2% Alrex for seasonal allergy); post-operative ocular inflammation (0.5% Lotemax); dry eye disease (0.5% - short courses for inflammatory component of DED - evidence supporting pulse use); vernal/atopic keratoconjunctivitis (short courses). SE: IOP elevation (steroid-induced glaucoma - less than hard steroids but monitor if >2 weeks use); posterior subcapsular cataract (minimal risk - safety profile advantage of soft steroids); infection risk (viral/bacterial/fungal - monitor); blurred vision after instillation (gel formulation - temporary). Note: best safety profile among ocular corticosteroids (designed-to-deactivate concept - ester bond cleaved rapidly); preferred for chronic/recurrent ocular surface inflammation where longer steroid courses needed (less IOP risk); dry eye inflammatory component - short pulse course 0.5% QID × 2-4 weeks (reduces inflammatory cycle); monitor IOP even with soft steroids in prolonged use; zylet = loteprednol + tobramycin (antibiotic-steroid combination for bacterial conjunctivitis with inflammation).

Toll-like receptor 7/8 (TLR7/8) agonist - topical immune modifier. MOA: activates TLR7 on plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) + TLR8 on myeloid DCs → innate immune activation → ↑IFN-α, TNF-α, IL-12 production → stimulates Th1 adaptive immune response + NK cell activation → cell-mediated immune clearance of virus-infected/dysplastic cells; no direct antiviral activity - purely immunostimulatory. Indications: actinic keratosis (AK - field treatment - 5% cream 3× weekly × 16 weeks or 3.75% daily × 2 weeks; field-based treatment [treats subclinical lesions] vs lesion-directed cryotherapy); superficial/nodular BCC (basal cell carcinoma - inoperable/cosmetically challenging sites - 5% cream - efficacy lower than surgery/MAL-PDT); external genital warts (condylomata acuminata - HPV 6 + 11 - 5% cream TID × up to 16 weeks; high clearance rate; reduces recurrence). SE: local skin reactions (expected and necessary - erythema, erosion, flaking, oedema, scabbing - indicate immune activation - signpost of response; grade 1-3 reactions; treatment holiday if severe); flu-like symptoms (systemic IFN-α response - fatigue, myalgia, headache - particularly with large field treatment area); pigmentary changes (post-inflammatory hypo/hyperpigmentation). Note: local skin reactions are expected + indicate treatment is working (immune activation → visible inflammatory response at application site is therapeutic); patient education critical (do not stop due to expected reactions - counsel that erythema/erosion = sign of efficacy; BUT hold if ulceration/intolerable - 1-week holiday then resume); cover female genitalia (risk of systemic absorption + potent local inflammatory reaction); avoid contact with eyes.

Antimitotic cytotoxin - topical treatment for external anogenital warts. MOA: plant-derived antimitotic (Podophyllum peltatum extract purified active component) → inhibits tubulin polymerisation → spindle formation failure → mitotic arrest at metaphase → cell death; preferential activity in rapidly dividing cells (HPV-infected keratinocytes proliferate more rapidly → selective cytotoxicity); more potent/selective than crude podophyllin (podophyllotoxin = active purified compound vs podophyllin = crude mixture). Indications: external anogenital warts (condylomata acuminata - HPV 6 + 11; 0.5% solution or 0.15% cream; patient-applied twice daily for 3 days then 4 days rest × up to 4 cycles; can be applied at home by patient - advantage vs cryotherapy which requires clinic visit). SE: local reactions (erythema, burning, stinging, erosion - expected - dose-related; apply only to warts not surrounding skin); systemic toxicity (if large areas treated or mucous membrane absorption - restrict to <10 cm² per session; >10% cream: nausea, dizziness, polyneuropathy, bone marrow suppression - safe small-area use only); TERATOGENIC (absolute contraindication in pregnancy - embryotoxic, anti-mitotic - use cryotherapy instead). Note: patient self-application advantage (home treatment - reduces clinic visits; compliance important - 3 days on/4 days off cycle); maximum treatment area <10 cm² per application (systemic absorption risk with larger areas); circumscribe warts only (avoid surrounding skin); PREGNANCY CONTRAINDICATED - use cryotherapy or trichloroacetic acid for pregnant patients; complete clearance in ~50-70% after 4 cycles; may need additional cycles or alternative treatment.

Photosensitiser prodrug - photodynamic therapy (PDT). MOA: topical 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA) → preferentially taken up by dysplastic/hyperproliferative cells (AK, tumour cells - higher haem biosynthesis activity) → metabolised to protoporphyrin IX (PpIX) via haem pathway → PpIX accumulates selectively in dysplastic tissue (haem synthesis limited → PpIX builds up as haem precursor); illumination with red light (630 nm - MAL/ALA PDT) or blue light (410 nm - ALA-PDT) → PpIX photoexcitation → generates reactive oxygen species (singlet oxygen, ¹O₂) → selective cell death in PpIX-accumulating tissue. Indications: actinic keratosis (AK - field treatment - MAL or nanoemulsion ALA + red light; single-session field treatment - effective for multiple/confluent AKs; better cosmesis than cryotherapy for large areas; repeated cycles); squamous cell carcinoma in situ (Bowen's disease - off-label/some approved indications); bladder cancer fluorescence detection (5-ALA instillation intravesically → PpIX in tumour → blue-light cystoscopy → visualises flat tumours missed on white-light cystoscopy - HAL [hexaminolevulinate] more commonly used for bladder). SE: photosensitivity (APPLICATION SITE ONLY - red light PDT; avoid sun/bright light to treated area × 48 h after PDT; local phototoxic reaction - erythema, burning, stinging, oedema - during and after illumination - expected and necessary = sign of treatment effect); pain during illumination (moderate-severe - NAL score 4-8 - managed with fan/cooling spray/topical anaesthesia). Note: light dose, wavelength, and irradiance determine PDT efficacy; 3-hour incubation under occlusive dressing before illumination (allows PpIX accumulation); daylight PDT (ambulatory PDT) - natural daylight as light source after ALA/MAL application - reduced pain vs conventional PDT (lower irradiance); cosmetic outcomes superior to cryotherapy for large-area AK fields.

Uroprotectant - thiol compound preventing haemorrhagic cystitis. MOA: administered IV → rapidly oxidised in plasma → dimesna (inactive) → filtered at glomerulus → reduced back to mesna (free thiol) in renal tubules → mesna in urine → free thiol groups bind and inactivate acrolein (urotoxic metabolite of cyclophosphamide/ifosfamide) + 4-hydroxy metabolites → forms non-toxic thioether conjugates → prevents acrolein-induced urothelial damage (haemorrhagic cystitis). Indications: prevention of haemorrhagic cystitis (MANDATORY with ifosfamide - dose equivalent to 60-100% of ifosfamide dose in divided doses at 0, 4, 8 hours; also used with high-dose cyclophosphamide [conditioning regimens, HSCT]); NOT used for standard-dose cyclophosphamide (cystitis risk low at standard doses). SE: generally well tolerated; nausea (IV or oral - common with oral form); hypersensitivity reactions (rare); false-positive urine ketone test (interference with urine test strips - artefact from mesna thiol group reducing ketone reagent). Note: MANDATORY with ifosfamide (without mesna, ifosfamide haemorrhagic cystitis 10-30% → mesna reduces to <5%); oral formulation available (BID dosing - more convenient for outpatient ifosfamide regimens - similar efficacy to IV for prevention); adequate hydration also essential (ensure high urine flow → ↑mesna concentration in urine relative to acrolein); mesna only protects lower urinary tract (does not protect against other ifosfamide toxicities: encephalopathy, nephrotoxicity).

Cytoprotective agent - thiol prodrug protecting normal tissues from radiation/chemotherapy. MOA: prodrug - dephosphorylated in tissues by alkaline phosphatase → free thiol WR-1065 (active); preferentially taken up by normal tissues (higher alkaline phosphatase activity vs tumour tissue → differential uptake → selective normal tissue protection); free thiol scavenges reactive oxygen species, alkylating reactive metabolites → ↓DNA damage in normal cells; tumour cells lack alkaline phosphatase or have acidic pH → lower drug activation → differential protection (cytoprotects normal tissue more than tumour). Indications: cisplatin nephrotoxicity prevention (IV 910 mg/m² before cisplatin - ↓cumulative nephropathy in ovarian/lung cancer); radiation-induced xerostomia (post-radiotherapy dry mouth - head and neck cancer - SC 200 mg/m² before each fraction; reduces severe xerostomia); granulocyte reduction (limited evidence). SE: hypotension (most common and clinically significant - BP drops during infusion → patient supine, frequent BP monitoring, IV fluids; temporary - resolves 5-10 min after end of infusion); nausea/vomiting (pre-medicate with antiemetics); flushing, chills; hypocalcaemia (amifostine chelates Ca²⁺ → monitor serum Ca if symptomatic); somnolence. Note: hypotension management - patient recumbent during infusion + BP every 5 min during administration; pause infusion if systolic BP drops >20 mmHg; xerostomia prevention (SC route - better tolerated than IV; ↓mucositis/xerostomia from H+N RT + cisplatin); NOT recommended routinely for other indications (insufficient evidence for most cytoprotective claims); tumour protection concern (theoretical - not proven clinically but some oncologists reluctant to use).

Recombinant keratinocyte growth factor (KGF) - mucositis prophylaxis. MOA: recombinant human KGF-1 (binds KGFR [FGFR2-IIIb]) → ↑proliferation of epithelial cells lining GI mucosa + salivary glands → ↑mucosal thickness + protective mechanisms → ↓chemotherapy/radiotherapy-induced oral mucositis; KGF stimulates goblet cell expansion + mucin secretion → ↑mucous barrier; also upregulates antioxidant enzymes (catalase, superoxide dismutase) in epithelial cells → ↓free-radical damage. Indications: prevention and treatment of severe oral mucositis (grade 3-4) in haematological malignancy patients receiving myelotoxic conditioning for stem cell transplantation (SCHT) - high-dose chemotherapy ± total body irradiation (TBI) → Grade 3-4 mucositis without prevention in 70-90%; palifermin reduces severe mucositis incidence + duration; IV 60 µg/kg/day × 3 days before conditioning + × 3 days after SCT = 6 doses total). SE: skin rash (erythema, oedema - epidermal hyperplasia - common; mild); oedema; arthralgia; dysaesthesia (perioral numbness/altered sensation - unique feature); ↑amylase/lipase; fever; local injection reaction. Note: not given during chemotherapy (potential tumour-protective effect - KGF stimulates tumour growth in KGF-receptor expressing tumours - 24 hours gap minimum between palifermin and chemotherapy/TBI); efficacy = Grade 3-4 mucositis reduced from ~70% to ~40% in SCT setting (≈ 50% relative risk reduction); dysaesthesia (unique SE - perioral tongue/mouth sensation change - temporary - warn patients); must be stored refrigerated.

Neurokinin-1 (NK1) receptor antagonist - antiemetic for CINV. MOA: selective NK1 receptor antagonist → blocks substance P binding in CNS (area postrema, nucleus tractus solitarius, vomiting centre) → ↓delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV); extremely long plasma half-life (180 h - 7 days!) → single-dose pre-chemotherapy covers full CINV-susceptibility window (0-120 h); does NOT inhibit CYP3A4 (key advantage over aprepitant/netupitant which inhibit CYP3A4). Indications: prevention of CINV (delayed nausea/vomiting 24-120 h post-chemotherapy - highly emetogenic chemotherapy [HEC] or moderately emetogenic [MEC]; single oral dose 180 mg before chemotherapy; combined with dexamethasone + 5-HT3 antagonist [triple antiemetic regimen] - EASE/GREATER trials: non-inferior to aprepitant). SE: generally well tolerated; hiccups; constipation; ↑ALT; CNS effects (dizziness, fatigue - uncommon). Note: CYP3A4 advantage - does NOT inhibit CYP3A4 (unlike aprepitant/fosaprepitant → aprepitant interacts with dexamethasone [↑dexamethasone levels → dose reduce], warfarin, chemotherapy - rolapitant avoids these interactions); single pre-chemotherapy dose (convenience - 180 mg PO once per cycle, 1-2 h before); ultra-long t½ → no need for days 2-3 NK1 antagonist (vs aprepitant days 1-3); do NOT repeat more frequently than every 2 weeks (ultra-long t½ - accumulation risk); strong CYP2D6 inhibitor (affects metoprolol, codeine, tricyclics, thioridazine - check interactions).

Nitrosourea alkylating agent - CNS-penetrant. MOA: spontaneously decomposes at physiological pH → chloroethyl diazonium hydroxide (alkylating species) + isocyanate (carbamoylating species) → DNA interstrand crosslinks (guanine O6-alkylation → interstrand crosslinks - prevents DNA replication); lipid-soluble → excellent CNS penetration (crosses BBB - unique advantage for brain tumours); also inhibits DNA repair enzymes (carbamoylation of lysyl residues). Indications: brain tumours (1st-line for IDH-mutant oligodendroglioma/oligoastrocytoma - PCV regimen: procarbazine + lomustine + vincristine - EORTC trials show ↑PFS/OS with PCV post-RT vs RT alone in grade 3 anaplastic oligodendroglioma with 1p/19q co-deletion; also GBM combination + temozolomide [CCNU-TMZ] - CAMELLIA-2 trial improving OS in MGMT-methylated GBM); Hodgkin's lymphoma (salvage - BEACOPP variant). SE: myelosuppression (delayed onset - nadir 4-6 weeks - unusually delayed → ↑cumulative toxicity risk if too-frequent dosing; cycle every 6 weeks minimum); pulmonary toxicity (cumulative - interstitial fibrosis - lifetime dose <1000 mg/m²); hepatotoxicity (↑LFTs); nausea/vomiting (given orally - night dosing with antiemetics); secondary malignancy. Note: once every 6 weeks (delayed myelosuppression nadir 4-6 weeks - monitor CBC at 6 weeks; do NOT dose < every 6 weeks); delayed nadir concept - if CBC checked at standard 2-3 weeks, nadir has not yet occurred - check at 4-6 weeks; cumulative pulmonary fibrosis - limit total lifetime dose; oral capsules (convenient but delayed myelosuppression complicates management).

Polyfunctional alkylating agent - HSCT conditioning and intrathecal use. MOA: trifunctional alkylating agent (aziridine groups) → spontaneously forms reactive ethyleneimine ions → alkylates DNA (guanine N-7, cytosine N-3) → interstrand + intrastrand crosslinks → DNA replication block → apoptosis; polyfunctional (3 reactive alkylating groups per molecule) → irreversible DNA damage; lipid-soluble → CNS penetration (used intrathecally + in high-dose conditioning for CNS tumours). Indications: HSCT conditioning (high-dose regimens - BEAM contains carmustine not thiotepa; TEAM: thiotepa-containing regimens; breast cancer autologous SCT conditioning; brain tumour conditioning); breast cancer (high-dose combination chemotherapy); intrathecal chemotherapy (leptomeningeal metastases - alternative to methotrexate/cytarabine for intrathecal treatment); bladder cancer (intravesical instillation - post-TURBT). SE: myelosuppression (severe - expected with conditioning doses); mucositis; skin hyperpigmentation (unique - thiotepa excreted in sweat → reacts with skin melanocytes → patchy bronzing; daily washing of skin recommended during infusion); CNS toxicity (high-dose → encephalopathy, ataxia, confusion); nausea/vomiting; hepatic veno-occlusive disease (SOS - with conditioning). Note: skin hyperpigmentation - unique and characteristic SE (photosensitisation from thiotepa in sweat → melanocyte activation; frequent washing during infusion); intrathecal thiotepa occasionally preferred over methotrexate (broader CNS distribution); veno-occlusive disease (SOS) risk with conditioning - ursodiol prophylaxis.

Intercalating antineoplastic antibiotic (actinomycin D). MOA: intercalates into DNA double helix (at GpC sequences - minor groove binding) → sterically blocks RNA polymerase → inhibits DNA-dependent RNA synthesis (↓mRNA transcription) AND inhibits topoisomerase II (DNA double-strand breaks) → apoptosis; one of the most potent anticancer agents (low therapeutic index → narrow dose range). Indications: paediatric solid tumours (Wilms' tumour [nephroblastoma] - 1st-line + adjuvant; rhabdomyosarcoma - VAC regimen: vincristine + actinomycin D + cyclophosphamide; Ewing's sarcoma - VAI + VIDE regimens; embryonal tumours); gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD - choriocarcinoma, gestational trophoblastic neoplasia - low-risk: single-agent dactinomycin [pulse dosing] or methotrexate; very high cure rate 100% in low-risk GTD). SE: myelosuppression (dose-limiting - severe neutropenia, thrombocytopenia); hepatic veno-occlusive disease (SOS - dactinomycin associated with higher SOS risk in Wilms' tumour - dactinomycin dose reduction in Wilms' <12 months age); mucositis/stomatitis; nausea/vomiting; alopecia; severe vesicant (tissue necrosis - extravasation → ≥DMSO rescue + plastic surgery); radiation recall (reactivates radiation damage to prior radiation fields - even years later - severe inflammatory reaction at radiation site). Note: radiation recall reaction - dactinomycin can trigger severe inflammatory skin reaction in previously irradiated fields (even years after radiation) - warn patients; Wilms' tumour - VAD or VAC regimen → excellent outcomes (relapse-free survival >85%); GTD - cure rate approaching 100% with methotrexate/dactinomycin ± EMA-CO regimen.

Nitrosourea alkylating agent with unique pancreatic beta-cell tropism. MOA: nitrosourea derivative → alkylates DNA + inhibits glucokinase + disrupts NAD⁺ metabolism → selective pancreatic β-cell toxicity (streptozocin enters β-cells via GLUT2 glucose transporter - high GLUT2 expression in β-cells → selective concentration → β-cell damage → used experimentally for diabetes induction in animals); antineoplastic mechanism: alkylation of tumour DNA + carbamoylation of proteins → neoplastic cell apoptosis. Indications: pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (pNETs - well-differentiated, progressive - streptozocin-based regimens [STZ-5FU, STZ-doxorubicin] - response rate 40-70%; indicated for functioning + non-functioning pNETs; alternative to sunitinib/everolimus in high tumour burden); other NETs (carcinoid tumours - limited evidence); islet cell carcinoma. SE: nephrotoxicity (dose-limiting and cumulative - tubular dysfunction → Fanconi syndrome → proteinuria, aminoaciduria, glycosuria, hypophosphataemia - monitor renal function before each cycle; reduce dose if creatinine elevated; cumulative dose-related - limit total exposure); nausea/vomiting (severe - prophylactic antiemetics essential; acute and delayed; one of most emetogenic agents); myelosuppression (mild - less myelosuppressive than most alkylating agents); hypoglycaemia (insulin release from β-cell damage); hepatotoxicity. Note: nephrotoxicity monitoring - urinalysis + creatinine before each cycle; adequate hydration; avoid nephrotoxic drugs concurrently; pNET treatment algorithms - streptozocin increasingly combined with everolimus (mTOR inhibitor) for advanced pNETs; compare to PRRT (peptide receptor radionuclide therapy) for somatostatin receptor-positive pNETs.

Nitrogen mustard alkylating agent - first anticancer drug and topical MF treatment. MOA: highly reactive bifunctional alkylating agent → spontaneous cyclization → ethyleneimonium ion → alkylates DNA (guanine N-7 interstrand + intrastrand crosslinks) → DNA replication failure → apoptosis; most reactive nitrogen mustard (t½ minutes → must be given rapidly IV or used topically where high local concentration achieved without systemic toxicity). Indications: mycosis fungoides (MF/cutaneous T-cell lymphoma) - topical 0.016-0.02% gel/ointment (Valchlor - US-approved 2013; once-daily application to skin; reduces skin lesion burden; avoids systemic chemotherapy for skin-limited disease); MOPP regimen (nitrogen mustard/Mechlorethamine historical - replaced by ABVD for Hodgkin's); polycythaemia vera (IV - historical - largely replaced). SE: topical: contact dermatitis (common - 20-50%; hypersensitivity skin reaction; continue if not severe - inflammatory reaction indicates response; discontinue for grade 3-4 contact dermatitis); secondary skin malignancy (theoretical - genotoxic - long-term topical exposure); systemic absorption (minimal from skin); if IV: severe local vesicant (extravasation necrosis); intense nausea (within 1-3 hours, antiemetics essential). Note: Valchlor topical - primary use for MF in modern oncology (avoids systemic treatment); contact dermatitis - educate patients (erythema/pruritus is common - distinguish from severe allergic reaction requiring cessation); systemic (IV) = extreme vesicant (healthcare worker PPE - double gloves, eye protection); teratogenic (avoid pregnancy); historical MOPP regimen contains mechlorethamine but largely replaced by ABVD/BEACOPP.

CTLA-4-Ig fusion protein - selective T-cell co-stimulation blocker (kidney transplant). MOA: fusion protein of human IgG1-Fc + extracellular domain of CTLA-4 (high affinity for CD80/CD86 on APCs); binds CD80 (B7-1) and CD86 (B7-2) on antigen-presenting cells → blocks CD28 co-stimulatory signal (CD28-B7 interaction = 2nd signal for T-cell activation) → T-cell anergy/tolerance induction (alloimmune tolerance without calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity); 2nd-generation belatacept vs abatacept: two amino acid substitutions → 10× higher CD86 affinity → adequate immunosuppression. Indications: kidney transplant immunosuppression (prophylaxis of acute rejection - combined with basiliximab induction, mycophenolate, corticosteroids; US/EU-approved; alternative to calcineurin inhibitors [ciclosporin/tacrolimus] - avoids CNI-associated nephrotoxicity → better long-term graft function [eGFR higher at 7 years in BENEFIT trial]). SE: EBV-associated lymphoproliferative disease (post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease [PTLD] - increased risk - particularly in EBV-seronegative recipients → CONTRAINDICATED in EBV-seronegative patients; monitor EBV load); infections (immunosuppression); acute cellular rejection (slightly higher than CNI regimens - particularly in high-risk patients); hypertension; headache; anaemia. Note: CONTRAINDICATED in EBV-seronegative patients (very high PTLD risk - at least 4× increased); PTLD risk monitoring - EBV serology pretransplant (avoid if EBV-naive); long-term eGFR advantage vs CNI (better renal function preservation at 7 years - primary benefit over tacrolimus); monthly IV infusion (inconvenient vs daily oral CNI - compliance barrier).

Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) - recombinant acid beta-glucosidase (glucocerebrosidase) for Gaucher disease. MOA: recombinant human glucocerebrosidase (CHO cell-derived) → catalyses hydrolysis of glucocerebroside (glucosylceramide) to glucose + ceramide; in Gaucher disease - GBA1 gene mutations → glucocerebrosidase deficiency → glucocerebroside accumulates in lysosomes of macrophages (Gaucher cells) → engorges macrophages in reticuloendothelial system (bone marrow, spleen, liver) → organomegaly, bone disease, cytopenias. Indications: type 1 Gaucher disease (non-neuronopathic - most common; visceral disease - hepatosplenomegaly, bone disease, cytopenias; IV infusion every 2 weeks; titrated to response; long-term therapy; PBS-listed in Australia for severe disease); type 3 Gaucher (chronic neuronopathic - ERT treats visceral manifestations but does NOT cross BBB → does not treat neurological disease). SE: infusion reactions (pre-medicate with antihistamine ± corticosteroid; IgG antibody formation → hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis - anti-drug antibodies develop in ~15%; switch to alternative ERT [velaglucerase, taliglucerase] if antibody titre high); flushing, tachycardia (during infusion); headache; nausea. Note: most common lysosomal storage disorder treated with ERT; type 1 = non-neuronopathic (ERT effective for visceral + bone disease); type 2 = infantile neuronopathic (ERT not effective for CNS - lethal in infancy regardless); type 3 = juvenile neuronopathic (ERT partial); alternatives: velaglucerase alfa, taliglucerase alfa; substrate reduction therapy: eliglustat (oral - for ambulatory adults), miglustat; enzyme dose titrated to Hb, platelet count, organomegaly, bone markers.

Substrate reduction therapy (SRT) - oral treatment for Gaucher type 1. MOA: inhibits glucosylceramide synthase (enzyme catalysing first committed step in glucocerebroside synthesis) → ↓glucocerebroside production → substrate reduction → ↓accumulation in macrophage lysosomes (reduces 'overflow' of glucocerebroside even with deficient glucocerebrosidase); oral administration advantage over IV ERT. Indications: type 1 Gaucher disease - adult patients (CYP2D6 extensive, intermediate, or poor metabolisers - NOT for ultrarapid metabolisers; stable on ERT or newly diagnosed adults not appropriate for ERT; ENGAGE trial: non-inferior to ERT for haematological + visceral endpoints; US approval 2014). SE: arthralgia; headache; nausea; fatigue; cardiac conduction (QT prolongation, PR/QRS prolongation - assess cardiac status before starting; ECG monitoring; avoid in pre-existing cardiac conduction abnormalities); diarrhoea. Note: CYP2D6 genotype required before prescribing (CYP2D6 metabolises eliglustat - dosing depends on metaboliser status; ultrarapid metabolisers - insufficient drug exposure → treatment failure - not recommended; poor metabolisers + strong CYP2D6 inhibitors → ↑exposure → cardiac toxicity); cardiac conduction monitoring (ECG before + during); oral once or twice daily (significant compliance advantage vs IV ERT every 2 weeks); compare to miglustat (first oral SRT - less effective, more GI SE); Gaucher disease monitoring: periodic CBC, LFTs, chitotriosidase, spleen volume MRI.

Mono-pegylated interferon alfa-2b - treatment for polycythaemia vera (PV). MOA: activates JAK-STAT signalling via interferon receptor → ↑expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) → anti-proliferative + pro-apoptotic effects specifically targeting JAK2 V617F-mutant haematopoietic stem cells (reduces mutant clone burden - molecular remission possible, unlike hydroxycarbamide); selective reduction of JAK2 V617F allele burden → disease modification (vs symptom control with hydroxycarbamide). Indications: polycythaemia vera (PV) - adults without splenomegaly; SC injection every 2 weeks (PROUD-PV trial: ≥50% reduction in JAK2 V617F allele burden in 22% vs 2% with hydroxycarbamide; superior haematologic + molecular responses; US/EU-approved 2021; TGA approved 2022). SE: influenza-like symptoms (fever, myalgia, fatigue - very common first 3 months - evening injection + paracetamol prophylaxis; subsides); depression (significant - screen and monitor; interferon-class SE - avoid or monitor closely in history of depression); thyroid dysfunction (hyper or hypothyroidism - check TFTs every 3-6 months; transient or permanent); injection site reactions; thrombocytopenia (dose-reduce if platelets <100); liver toxicity (↑LFTs - monitor). Note: disease-modifying (reduces JAK2 V617F allele burden - potential for sustained molecular remission; hydroxycarbamide reduces counts but not mutant clone); long-acting pegylated (every 2 weeks SC - practical vs interferon alfa-2a which was given TW-TID); pregnancy (interferon safe in PV pregnancy - unlike hydroxycarbamide which is teratogenic; PV frequently managed with interferon in pregnancy); compare to ruxolitinib (JAK inhibitor for PV - ruxolitinib for high-risk/resistant PV; ropeginterferon for lower-risk or young patients seeking molecular remission).

Bispecific antibody - haemophilia A coagulation bypass. MOA: humanised bispecific IgG4 antibody that bridges coagulation factors IXa (FIXa) and X (FX) → mimics the cofactor function of FVIIIa → restores thrombin generation in haemophilia A (FVIII deficiency) regardless of FVIII inhibitor status; subcutaneous once-weekly, every-2-weeks, or every-4-weeks; structural analogy to FVIII but not a protein replacement (bispecific antibody - resistant to inhibitor antibodies against FVIII). Indications: haemophilia A - prophylaxis to prevent/reduce bleeding episodes (with or without FVIII inhibitors; approved for all ages; PBS-listed in Australia; HAVEN 1-4 trials: dramatically ↓annualised bleeding rate [ABR] vs no prophylaxis or previous bypassing agents). SE: injection site reactions (very common - erythema, swelling, pain - rotate sites); thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) and thrombosis (when combined with activated prothrombin complex concentrate [aPCC/FEIBA] - serious interaction; aPCC must be avoided or used with extreme caution during emicizumab - use recombinant FVIIa [eptacog alfa] instead for breakthrough bleeding); headache; fatigue. Note: FEIBA/aPCC + emicizumab → TMA risk (thromboembolic events, microangiopathy - use recombinant FVIIa [NovoSeven] for rescue bleeding instead); monitoring: anti-FVIII inhibitor titre (FVIII inhibitor presence does not affect emicizumab efficacy - major advantage); does NOT interfere with lupus anticoagulant assay (can give falsely elevated aPTT - use chromogenic FVIII assay for FVIII monitoring in patients on emicizumab); transformative for haemophilia A management - near-normal life for many patients.

Anti-von Willebrand factor (vWF) nanobody (single-domain antibody). MOA: bivalent nanobody → binds A1 domain of vWF with very high affinity → blocks vWF interaction with platelet GPIb receptor → prevents platelet adhesion to ultra-large vWF multimers (which accumulate in TTP due to ADAMTS13 deficiency) → ↓platelet aggregation + microvascular thrombosis; does NOT affect vWF synthesis or clearance (anti-vWF levels return to normal after cessation); ADAMTS13 replacement by plasma exchange remains essential (caplacizumab reduces thrombosis while waiting for ADAMTS13 to recover). Indications: acquired thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (aTTP - combined with plasma exchange and immunosuppression; HERCULES trial: ↓time to platelet normalisation, ↓aTTP recurrence/deaths, ↓refractory aTTP; US FDA/EMA/TGA approved; 11 mg IV loading then SC OD during + 30 days post-plasma exchange). SE: bleeding (anti-platelet mechanism → ↑bleeding risk - epistaxis, gingival, menorrhagia - serious/fatal bleeding possible if taken without plasma exchange; monitor carefully); injection site reactions; dizziness. Note: does NOT treat underlying ADAMTS13 deficiency (immunosuppression [steroids ± rituximab] + plasma exchange = definitive treatment - caplacizumab bridges treatment); anti-vWF → ↓platelet counts initially may NOT reflect plasma exchange response (platelets recover rapidly when caplacizumab started); extended treatment for 30 days after last PEX (prevents early relapse); ADAMTS13 monitoring to guide immunosuppression + duration.

Recombinant coagulation factor VIIa (rFVIIa). MOA: recombinant activated factor VII → binds tissue factor (TF) at site of vascular injury → TF-FVIIa complex activates FX (extrinsic pathway) → thrombin burst → fibrin clot formation; pharmacological (supraphysiological) doses → TF-independent FXa activation on platelet surface → bypasses intrinsic pathway deficiency (FVIIIa or FIXa deficiency with inhibitors); directly activates FX on activated platelets (FVIII/FIX-independent). Indications: haemophilia A or B with inhibitors (rescue/on-demand bleeding - preferred over aPCC/FEIBA in patients receiving emicizumab prophylaxis due to TMA risk with aPCC; also used for prophylaxis); Glanzmann thrombasthenia (with refractoriness to platelet transfusion); congenital FVII deficiency; acquired haemophilia (FVIII/FIX inhibitors). SE: thromboembolic events (arterial + venous - risk increases with higher doses + atherosclerosis; monitor for MI, PE, stroke - particularly in elderly/cardiovascular risk factors); DIC (rare - with excessive thrombin generation); allergic reactions (recombinant protein - uncommon). Note: NovoSeven for emicizumab-associated bleeding rescue - FEIBA/aPCC contraindicated with emicizumab (TMA); NovoSeven (rFVIIa) is the bypass agent of choice in emicizumab-treated patients; 3-hour half-life → repeat dosing q2-3h for active bleeding; thrombotic risk higher with continuous infusion vs bolus dosing; FVII deficiency - half-life shorter → frequent dosing.

Bispecific T-cell engager (TCE) - GPRC5D × CD3. MOA: binds GPRC5D (G protein-coupled receptor class C group 5 member D - orphan GPCR expressed on myeloma plasma cells and normal skin/tongue epithelium) and CD3ε on T-cells → crosslinks T-cells with myeloma cells → T-cell-mediated cytotoxicity of GPRC5D+ myeloma cells; GPRC5D expressed on myeloma cells and differentiated plasma cells (highly expressed) but also expressed in normal skin/oral mucosa → explains dermatological SE. Indications: relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (≥4 prior lines including IMiD, PI, anti-CD38 mAb - MonumenTAL-1 trial: ORR 73% at 0.4 mg/kg weekly; US-approved 2023; EMA 2023; TGA status - check PBS). SE: cytokine release syndrome (CRS - very common - grade 1-2 in >70%; step-up dosing protocol mandatory; tocilizumab/corticosteroids for high-grade; hospitalisation during initial doses); GPRC5D-related skin toxicity (dysgeusia [bitter/metallic taste, food aversion], xerostomia, nail changes, skin reactions - GPRC5D expressed in oral/skin epithelium → expected on-target SE; oral care + moisturiser + dose modification for severe xerostomia/dysgeusia); infections (immunosuppression); cytopenias. Note: GPRC5D skin/oral SE management - intensive oral hygiene, artificial saliva, taste modifiers for dysgeusia, systemic moisturiser for skin - patient education critical; step-up dosing (3 doses at fraction of target dose before full dose - reduces CRS grade); compare to teclistamab (BCMA × CD3 - same class; talquetamab anti-GPRC5D - alternative target for BCMA-refractory patients); subcutaneous injection.

Bispecific antibody - BCMA × CD3 T-cell engager. MOA: humanised IgG2 bispecific antibody targeting B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA, TNFRSF17) on myeloma cells AND CD3ε on T-cells → T-cell-mediated killing of BCMA+ myeloma cells; BCMA expressed predominantly on plasma cells and myeloma cells → high selectivity; binds two distinct BCMA epitopes + one CD3 epitope → simultaneous engagement. Indications: relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (after ≥4 prior lines including PI, IMiD, anti-CD38 mAb - MagnetisMM-3 trial: ORR 61%; US 2023 accelerated approval; PBS status - check; subcutaneous administration). SE: CRS (cytokine release syndrome - grade 1-2 predominant; step-up dosing reduces severity; IL-6 receptor antagonist [tocilizumab] for grade ≥2); infections (hypogammaglobulinaemia → ↑bacterial/viral/PCP/herpes risk - IVIG replacement, antimicrobial prophylaxis); injection site reactions; cytopenias; immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS - less common than with CAR-T; headache, confusion). Note: step-up dosing protocol (3 doses: 12 mg, 32 mg, then 76 mg OD - 1 week apart - reduces CRS); IVIG replacement for hypogammaglobulinaemia (IgG monitoring monthly); BCMA target - compare to teclistamab (also BCMA × CD3; similar class), talquetamab (GPRC5D × CD3 - different target), and BCMA CAR-T (idecabtagene/ciltacabtagene); elranatamab weekly SC then Q2W after response.

Antibody-drug conjugate - anti-tissue factor (TF). MOA: humanised anti-TF IgG1 mAb conjugated (maleimide linker) to MMAE (monomethyl auristatin E - microtubule disrupting warhead) → binds TF (tissue factor/CD142) on tumour cells → internalised → lysosomal cleavage → MMAE released → inhibits tubulin polymerisation → G2/M cell-cycle arrest → apoptosis; TF highly expressed in cervical cancer + other solid tumours; bystander killing (lipophilic MMAE crosses to adjacent TF-negative cells). Indications: recurrent/metastatic cervical cancer with disease progression on or after chemotherapy (innovaTV 204 trial: ORR 24%; innovaTV 301 trial: ↑PFS vs chemotherapy in 2nd-line [pembrolizumab-pretreated]; US 2021 accelerated approval → 2024 regular approval). SE: ocular toxicity (most distinctive SE - keratopathy: corneal epithelial changes → blurred vision, photophobia, dry eye, discharge - MANDATORY ophthalmology monitoring before each dose; steroid eye drops prophylaxis; hold if significant); peripheral neuropathy (MMAE class - cumulative; sensory > motor; dose-reduce for grade 2+); haemorrhage (anti-TF mechanism - TF is procoagulant → inhibition → ↑bleeding risk; avoid anticoagulants when possible); alopecia; nausea; pneumonitis. Note: ocular monitoring is MANDATORY (ophthalmologist visit before each dose - unique monitoring requirement for this ADC; corticosteroid eye drops prophylaxis + lubricating drops throughout treatment); withhold/reduce for corneal adverse events (Grade 2+ keratopathy → dose hold; Grade 3 → permanent discontinuation); TF expressed in many tumours → trial expansion ongoing (NSCLC, bladder, head/neck).

Selective VEGFR 1/2/3 inhibitor - anti-angiogenic. MOA: orally bioavailable quinazoline - selectively inhibits all three VEGF receptors (VEGFR-1, 2, 3) at low nanomolar concentrations → ↓tumour angiogenesis + lymphangiogenesis; minimal off-target kinase activity compared to other VEGFR TKIs → predicted improved tolerability; VEGF pathway upregulated after prior anti-angiogenic treatment (resistance mechanisms; fruquintinib remains active against regorafenib/TAS-102-refractory CRC). Indications: metastatic colorectal cancer (CRC) - ≥3 prior lines including oxaliplatin + irinotecan ± anti-VEGF ± anti-EGFR (after regorafenib/TAS-102 - FRESCO-2 trial: ↑OS vs placebo in globally recruited patients [including US, EU, Japan] - 7.4 vs 4.8 months; US approval 2023; PBS status - check). SE: hypertension (most common - ↓VEGF → vasoconstriction → monitor BP every 2 weeks; antihypertensive if Grade 2+); palmar-plantar erythrodysaesthesia (hand-foot syndrome - VEGFR class SE - prophylactic skin care); proteinuria (monitor urine protein); haemorrhage (↓VEGF → impaired clotting response - epistaxis, GI bleeding); hepatotoxicity (↑LFTs - monitor); dysphonia; fatigue. Note: 3 weeks on/1 week off cycle (21-day cycle - standard for VEGFR inhibitors); once-daily 5 mg (with or without food); FRESCO-2 global trial is pivotal (global trial population - different from FRESCO-1 which was China-only); potentially active after regorafenib/TAS-102 failure (where limited options exist); dose reduction for Grade 3 HTN/HFSR.

Anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody. MOA: humanised IgG4 anti-PD-1 mAb → blocks PD-1:PD-L1/L2 interaction → restores T-cell cytotoxic activity against tumour cells; humanised IgG4 (minimal Fc effector function - reduces ADCC/complement against T-cells compared to IgG1); similar mechanism to nivolumab/pembrolizumab. Indications: Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC - 1st-line metastatic/recurrent unresectable; POD1UM-201 trial: ORR 52%; US approval 2023); anal canal carcinoma (squamous cell carcinoma of the anus/SCCA - 1st-line metastatic, combined with carboplatin + paclitaxel - POD1UM-303 trial: ↑PFS vs chemotherapy alone; US approval 2023); other PD-L1+ solid tumours (investigational). SE: immune-related adverse events (irAEs - class PD-1 inhibitor; pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis, endocrinopathy, dermatitis - all potential; less reported than pembrolizumab/nivolumab due to smaller patient exposure); fatigue; nausea; musculoskeletal pain. Note: Merkel cell carcinoma - rare but aggressive skin cancer (Merkel cell polyomavirus-associated tumours + UV-induced mutational burden - both PD-L1/immune-responsive); irAE management same as other PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors (corticosteroids for Grade 2+; hold drug; specialist input); Welireg = belzutifan (HIF-2α inhibitor for VHL disease/RCC - different drug, same brand name confusion - retifanlimab = Zynyz brand).
