JAK1/JAK2 and ACVR1 (activin receptor type I/ALK2) inhibitor - myelofibrosis. MOA: inhibits JAK1 + JAK2 (↓JAK-STAT signalling → ↓inflammatory cytokines → ↓spleen volume + constitutional symptoms in MF) PLUS ACVR1 (activin receptor/BMP type I receptor) → ↓hepcidin transcription in liver → ↑iron availability for erythropoiesis → ↑haemoglobin (anaemia benefit unique to momelotinib vs other JAK inhibitors). Indications: myelofibrosis (primary MF, post-PV MF, post-ET MF - intermediate or high risk + anaemia; MOMENTUM trial: ↑transfusion independence + ↑symptom response vs danazol; US-approved 2023; particularly for anaemia-predominant MF where ruxolitinib worsens anaemia). SE: peripheral neuropathy (neuropathy - class effect; monitor - differs from other JAK inhibitors); thrombocytopenia (↓platelet count - monitor CBC); infections (immunosuppression); diarrhoea; nausea; dizziness; hepatotoxicity. Note: anaemia benefit differentiates momelotinib (ACVR1 inhibition → ↓hepcidin → ↑iron utilisation → ↑Hb) from ruxolitinib/fedratinib (which often worsen anaemia - increased transfusion dependence); anaemia-predominant MF = preferred use case; ACVR1 mechanism has been exploited for developing new drugs targeting iron regulation; compare: ruxolitinib (1st-line, high platelet MF), fedratinib (prior ruxolitinib failure), pacritinib (severe thrombocytopenia), momelotinib (anaemia + MF).

JAK2/IRAK1 inhibitor - myelofibrosis with severe thrombocytopenia. MOA: inhibits JAK2 (↓JAK-STAT signalling → ↓splenomegaly + constitutional symptoms) + IRAK1 (interleukin-1 receptor-associated kinase 1 → ↓NF-κB activation → ↓inflammatory cytokines); distinguishing feature: does NOT inhibit JAK1 significantly → less thrombocytopenia vs ruxolitinib (which inhibits JAK1/JAK2 → more myelosuppression) → usable in patients with platelet counts as low as <50 × 10⁹/L (where ruxolitinib is contraindicated/dangerous). Indications: myelofibrosis (intermediate or high risk with platelet count <50 × 10⁹/L - PERSIST-2 + PAC203 trials: ↑symptom response + spleen volume reduction vs BAT [best available therapy]; US approval 2022; only JAK inhibitor approved in severe thrombocytopenia). SE: diarrhoea (most common GI toxicity - manage with antidiarrhoeals; prophylactic loperamide often used); nausea/vomiting; cytopenias (less than ruxolitinib - less thrombocytopenia); cardiac effects (torsades de pointes risk - QT monitoring; avoid QT-prolonging drugs); bleeding (thrombocytopenic patients at baseline risk). Note: severe thrombocytopenia (PLT <50) is the primary indication differentiator (ruxolitinib/fedratinib contraindicated/dangerous when PLT <50 - pacritinib fills this unmet need); QT monitoring required (ECG at baseline + during treatment); avoid with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (↑pacritinib exposure); compare: ruxolitinib (first-line, PLT ≥50), fedratinib (prior ruxolitinib failure, PLT ≥50), pacritinib (PLT <50 - only option).

Iron chelator and topoisomerase II catalytic inhibitor - dual oncology use. MOA: (1) cardioprotection (Cardioxane) - dexrazoxane prodrug → hydrolysed intracellularly to ICRF-198 (open-ring chelating form) → chelates iron in cardiomyocytes → prevents iron-dependent free radical (Fenton reaction) from anthracycline-iron complexes → ↓anthracycline-induced cardiomyopathy; catalytic topoisomerase II inhibitor (not cleaving - prevents anthracycline-DNA adduct-mediated topo II-cleavage complex); (2) extravasation antidote (Savene/Totect) - IV dexrazoxane × 3 days after anthracycline extravasation → chelates anthracycline + reduces free radical damage → prevents tissue necrosis. Indications: prevention of anthracycline-associated cardiomyopathy (Cardioxane - cumulative anthracycline dose - IV 30 min before each doxorubicin dose; recommended when cumulative doxorubicin ≥300 mg/m² - paediatric and adult oncology); anthracycline extravasation treatment (Savene/Totect - anthracycline extravasation within 6 hours - IV 1000 mg/m² days 1-2, 500 mg/m² day 3). SE: myelosuppression (additive to anthracycline-related haematologic toxicity); nausea; injection site reactions; possible ↑secondary malignancy risk (topoisomerase II inhibition - theoretical - concerns have limited widespread use). Note: not recommended for paediatric patients being treated with curative intent (concern about possible reduction in anticancer activity - controversial); used in paediatric leukaemia/solid tumour oncology for cardioprotection; for extravasation - only effective treatment available (vs DMSO topical - dexrazoxane IV superior for vesicant extravasation).

Uricosuric agent + organic acid transport inhibitor. MOA: inhibits urate transporter URAT1 (SLC22A12) in renal proximal tubule → ↓uric acid reabsorption → ↑urinary uric acid excretion → ↓serum uric acid; also inhibits tubular secretion of weak organic acids (penicillins, cephalosporins - probenecid blocks OATP/OAT transporters → ↑antibiotic serum levels - used historically to prolong penicillin action); does NOT affect xanthine oxidase. Indications: gout (hyperuricaemia treatment - 2nd-line to allopurinol/febuxostat; indicated for underexcretors of uric acid [urinary uric acid <600 mg/day - 90% of hyperuricaemic patients]; not for overproducers [risk of uric acid renal stones - avoid if uric acid >800 mg/day]); probenecid-antibiotic combination (historical - prolong penicillin half-life in gonorrhoea; still used with cefazolin for high-dose IV → oral switch strategy). SE: GI (nausea - take with food); uric acid nephrolithiasis (increased urinary uric acid → stone risk - adequate hydration essential + alkalinisation of urine); hypersensitivity rash; gout flares (initial treatment - mobilise urate from tophi → transient ↑serum uric acid → acute gout flare - prophylax with colchicine for 6 months). Note: contraindicated in uric acid overproducers and renal impairment (CrCl <50 → insufficient uricosuria); adequate hydration (2L/day) + alkalinise urine (sodium bicarbonate) to prevent uric acid stones; not started during acute gout attack (mobilises urate → worsens attack - wait 2-4 weeks after acute attack); colchicine prophylaxis when initiating; drug interactions (NSAIDs - probenecid ↑NSAID concentrations via OAT inhibition).

Dicarboxylic acid - topical treatment for acne and rosacea. MOA: multiple mechanisms: (1) antimicrobial - ↓aerobic metabolism of Propionibacterium acnes (Cutibacterium acnes) → bacteriostatic; (2) anti-keratinising - ↓follicular hyperkeratinisation (normalises abnormal follicular cornification); (3) anti-inflammatory - ↓free radical production, ↓IL-1α/TNF-α → anti-inflammatory; (4) tyrosinase inhibition → ↓melanin synthesis → ↓post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (hypopigmenting effect); (5) anti-rosacea - ↓inflammatory mediators + callidin bradykinin pathway → ↓erythema/flushing. Indications: acne vulgaris (mild-moderate - 20% cream or 15% gel; reduces comedonal + inflammatory acne; particularly useful for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation [PIH] in darker skin types - melanocyte-inhibitory + anti-inflammatory); rosacea (15% gel [Finacea] - 1st-line topical - US-approved for papulopustular rosacea; reduces papules/pustules + erythema). SE: local skin irritation (stinging, burning, tingling - common at start - transient, subsides after 2-4 weeks; apply to dry skin after washing); dry skin, pruritus; hypopigmentation (particularly in darker skin - over-bleaching - counsel). Note: takes 4-8 weeks for effect (consistent with retinoids timeline for acne); safe in pregnancy (category B - safer than retinoids which are teratogenic); particularly useful for PIH (post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation) - common in Fitzpatrick skin types IV-VI; non-antibiotic → no antibiotic resistance concerns; available OTC (15% - Azclear/Skinoren in Australia); 2× daily application.

Narrow-spectrum tetracycline antibiotic - acne-specific. MOA: binds 30S ribosomal subunit → blocks aminoacyl-tRNA binding → inhibits bacterial protein synthesis (bacteriostatic); narrow spectrum (selective for gram-positive anaerobes, particularly Cutibacterium acnes [P. acnes] - limited gram-negative and enteric activity compared to other tetracyclines); lower affinity for gram-negative bacteria → ↓disruption of normal gut microbiome compared to doxycycline. Indications: acne vulgaris (moderate-to-severe non-nodular inflammatory acne - once-daily oral 60 mg, 100 mg, or 150 mg (weight-based); US approval 2018; SARe-1/SARe-2 trials: ↑IGA responders vs placebo). SE: GI (nausea - less diarrhoea than doxycycline due to narrow gram-negative spectrum); photosensitivity (less than doxycycline - tetracycline class - still advise sun protection); dental staining (avoid < 12 years, pregnancy/lactation); oesophageal irritation (take with full glass of water, do not lie down after); Candida overgrowth (relatively less - narrow spectrum); pseudotumour cerebri (intracranial hypertension - tetracycline class rare SE - new onset headache + visual changes). Note: narrow-spectrum advantage - less disruption of gut microbiome vs doxycycline/minocycline (potential for better tolerability/less collateral microbiome effects); once-daily dosing; weight-based dosing (60 mg for <55 kg, 100 mg 55-84 kg, 150 mg ≥85 kg); available in USA; not currently TGA-approved but relevant for completeness; compare to doxycycline (broader spectrum, lower cost, more evidence) and minocycline (subantimicrobial dosing for acne, more SE).

Dual-mechanism topical treatment for actinic keratosis. MOA: dual mechanisms - (1) tubulin inhibitor (inhibits tubulin polymerisation → ↓microtubule formation → mitotic arrest) + (2) Src kinase inhibitor (inhibits Src-mediated signalling → ↓cyclin D1 → ↓G1-S cell-cycle progression); both mechanisms selectively target rapidly dividing dysplastic cells (AK) → antiproliferative effects in AK lesions; topical application → minimal systemic absorption. Indications: actinic keratosis on face or scalp (1% ointment - once-daily × 5 consecutive days; non-field treatment - applied to defined area of AK ≤25 cm²; US-approved 2020; EMA 2021; ACNE1/ACNE2 trials: 44% complete clearance vs 5% vehicle at day 57). SE: local skin reactions (erythema, flaking, scaling, erosion - expected and therapeutic - assess after 5 days; Grade 1-2 reactions indicate treatment activity; Grade 3 - consider treatment holiday); periorbital oedema (application near eyes); pain/pruritus at application site; reversible eyelid oedema if applied near orbital rim. Note: once-daily × 5 days (convenient vs imiquimod [3× weekly × 16 weeks] - shorter treatment course; no immune-mediated flu-like symptoms); limited treatment area (≤25 cm² - cannot use for field treatment of large areas - contrast with imiquimod/5-ALA PDT which can treat larger fields); local reactions expected (counsel patients - reassure about expected erythema/scaling); new mechanism (tubulin + Src inhibition) distinct from imiquimod and 5-FU.

Imidazole antifungal - broad-spectrum topical. MOA: inhibits fungal CYP51 (lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase) → ↓ergosterol synthesis → disrupts fungal cell membrane; also inhibits phospholipid biosynthesis + oxidative enzymes; broad spectrum covers dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Epidermophyton, Microsporum), Candida spp, Malassezia, moulds; bacteriostatic activity vs some gram-positive bacteria (streptococci, staphylococci - limited). Indications: dermatomycosis (tinea pedis, cruris, corporis - athlete's foot, ringworm, jock itch - topical cream/powder); vaginal candidiasis (150 mg pessary × 3 nights OR 150 mg × 1 [single dose]; econazole vaginal cream); pityriasis versicolor (Malassezia-related); cutaneous candidiasis; tinea versicolor; seborrhoeic dermatitis (Malassezia-related). SE: local irritation (burning, erythema, pruritus - transient); contact dermatitis (rare); systemic absorption minimal (topical only). Note: broad-spectrum (covers both dermatophytes + Candida → useful when aetiology uncertain); vaginal use - pessary or cream (vs clotrimazole which is also available vaginally - similar efficacy); available as 1% cream + vaginal pessaries in Australia; application 2× daily for skin infections × 2-4 weeks; compare to clotrimazole (similar spectrum + potency), miconazole (also broad-spectrum, available OTC as Daktarin).

Triazole antifungal - topical nail lacquer for onychomycosis. MOA: inhibits CYP51A1 (fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase - triazole target) → ↓ergosterol synthesis → disrupts dermatophyte cell membrane; 5% topical solution - highly lipophilic with low protein binding → penetrates nail plate and subungual space (excellent nail penetration compared to older topical antifungals); active against Trichophyton rubrum and T. mentagrophytes (main onychomycosis pathogens). Indications: onychomycosis (nail fungal infection - toenail - 5% solution QD × 48 weeks; STEPS-1/STEPS-2 trials: complete cure rate 17-18% vs 3-5% vehicle; mycological cure 54-55%; superiority to vehicle but absolute cure rates modest); mild-moderate onychomycosis (nail without matrix involvement preferred). SE: application site reactions (ingrowing toenail, erythema, dermatitis - uncommon); minimal systemic absorption; no significant systemic toxicity. Note: 48-week treatment (very long - poor compliance risk - counsel patients); moderate efficacy (complete cure rate 17-18% - lower than oral terbinafine [complete cure ~35-40%] - but avoids systemic drug interactions/hepatotoxicity); ideal for patients who cannot take oral terbinafine/itraconazole; once-daily application extends to 4 weeks past distal edge of nail; compare to amorolfine (weekly application - less frequent but similar efficacy), tavaborole (different MOA - boro antifungal); topical treatment for mild/moderate disease or systemic antifungal intolerance.

Oxaborole antifungal - topical nail lacquer (novel mechanism). MOA: benzoxaborole compound → inhibits fungal leucyl-tRNA synthetase (LeuRS) - editing site → prevents LeuRS proofreading function → misincorporation of non-cognate amino acids during tRNA aminoacylation → impaired fungal protein synthesis; completely novel antifungal class (boron-containing compound → forms covalent adduct with terminal 2',3'-diol of tRNA) → no cross-resistance with triazoles/polyenes/echinocandins. Indications: toenail onychomycosis (Trichophyton rubrum, T. mentagrophytes - 5% solution QD × 48 weeks; US approval 2014; complete mycological cure + clinical outcome equivalent to efinaconazole). SE: local application site reactions (exfoliation, erythema, ingrown toenail - uncommon); minimal systemic absorption (< 2% of topical dose). Note: novel mechanism (tRNA synthetase inhibitor - LeuRS editing site) → no cross-resistance with azoles or other antifungals (useful if prior azole failure or resistance); 48-week course (same compliance challenge as efinaconazole); absolute cure rates modest (similar to efinaconazole; lower than oral terbinafine); penetrates nail well due to small molecular size; compare to efinaconazole (CYP51 inhibitor - different target; similar efficacy); preferred for confirmed or suspected azole-resistant onychomycosis; alcohol-based solution - allow to dry before wearing socks/shoes.

Triterpenoid antifungal - glucan synthase inhibitor (novel class - oral). MOA: inhibits 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase (same target as echinocandins) → prevents glucan synthesis → ↓fungal cell wall integrity → fungal cell death; triterpenoid (ibrexane-based) vs echinocandins (cyclic hexapeptide) → oral bioavailability (unlike IV-only echinocandins); novel pharmacophore → may be active against echinocandin-resistant Candida (fks mutations may not confer resistance to ibrexafungerp). Indications: vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC - Candida vaginitis - acute uncomplicated: 300 mg BD × 1 day; recurrent VVC prophylaxis: 150 mg BD × 1 day monthly × 6 months - CANDLE trial: ↓VVC recurrence; US 2021 acute VVC + 2022 prophylaxis). SE: GI (nausea, diarrhoea - most common; moderate-severe in ~5%; take with food); abdominal pain; headache; dizziness; embryo-fetal toxicity (avoid in pregnancy - teratogenic in animal studies; REMS program in USA; barrier contraception required). Note: oral glucan synthase inhibitor (first oral drug of this class - echinocandins [caspofungin/anidulafungin/micafungin] are IV only - ibrexafungerp represents oral echinocandin equivalent); REMS program (teratogenicity - reproductive age females require contraception during and for 4 days after treatment); broader spectrum potential than fluconazole (Candida resistance to azoles increasing - ibrexafungerp different target; active against fluconazole-resistant strains); compare to fluconazole (oral - cheaper, established) and nystatin (local - no systemic activity).

Pyruvate kinase R (PKR) activator - oral treatment for haemolytic anaemia. MOA: selectively activates pyruvate kinase R (PKR) isoform → ↑enzymatic activity → ↑ATP production via glycolysis in red blood cells → ↑RBC energy homeostasis → ↓oxidative stress → ↑RBC survival (reduces haemolysis); in PKR-deficiency (hereditary): restores mutant PKR enzyme activity; in thalassaemia (non-PKR deficiency): activates wildtype PKR → improves RBC metabolism in thalassaemic RBCs (secondary PKR dysfunction due to iron/reactive oxygen species). Indications: pyruvate kinase (PKR) deficiency - hereditary haemolytic anaemia (US 2022; EMA 2022; 10-40 mg BD; ACTIVATE/ACTIVATE-T trials: ↑Hb, ↓transfusion requirements); sickle cell disease (phase 2/3 - RISE UP trial exploring Hb F induction + improved RBC metabolism; investigational); alpha-/beta-thalassaemia (phase 3 - ENERGIZE trials ongoing). SE: insomnia (most common - dose-related - morning dosing may help); hyperbilirubinaemia (rapid haemolysis reduction → bilirubin handling changes - transient); ↑uric acid; decreased glucose (PKR activation → ↑glycolysis → ↑glucose utilisation - dose-related hypoglycaemia in fasting state - rare); headache. Note: PKR deficiency - rare autosomal recessive disorder (haemolytic anaemia from birth; mitapivat = first disease-modifying oral therapy; lifelong treatment); splenectomy previously required for severe cases; avoid abrupt discontinuation (acute haemolytic crisis on withdrawal - taper dose); thalassaemia applications under investigation (broader PKR activation in thalassaemia improves RBC quality - phase 3 evidence awaited).

Topical fluoropyrimidine antimetabolite for skin dysplasia and cancer. MOA: same mechanism as IV 5-FU but applied topically → absorbed by dysplastic/rapidly dividing skin cells (AK, superficial BCC) preferentially; 5-fluorouracil → converted intracellularly to fluorodeoxyuridine monophosphate (FdUMP) → inhibits thymidylate synthase (TS) → ↓dTMP synthesis → DNA synthesis inhibition → apoptosis; also incorporates into RNA (FUTP) → disrupts RNA processing. Indications: actinic keratosis (AK - field treatment - 5% cream 2×/day × 2-3 weeks; 0.5% cream once daily × 4 weeks - Carac; highly effective field treatment clearing >80% lesions; cosmetically excellent healing; PBS-listed Australia); superficial basal cell carcinoma (BCC - 5% cream 2×/day × 6 weeks; non-surgical alternative for multiple superficial BCCs in poor surgical candidates); Bowen's disease (5% cream); bowenoid papulosis. SE: local skin reactions (intense - erythema, crusting, erosion, exudation - expected and indicate treatment working; reaches peak at weeks 2-3 → heals weeks 4-6 after cessation; counsel patients BEFORE starting - many stop treatment prematurely); hyperpigmentation post-treatment (transient - fades months); photosensitivity. Note: local skin reaction management - reassure patients before starting (very intense reaction expected + necessary; if treatment stopped early → subclinical AKs not cleared; complete the course); most effective AK field treatment (>80% clearance - better than cryotherapy for field disease; less than PDT for convenience); PBS-listed in Australia (prescription); used for years in dermatology practice; 5% cream (Efudix) most common formulation in Australia.

Polyclonal antibody immunosuppressant. MOA: horse (equine/ATGAM) or rabbit (Thymoglobulin)-derived polyclonal IgG antibodies against human thymocytes/T-cells → multiple mechanisms: (1) complement-mediated lympholysis (anti-T-cell antibodies → CDC of T-cells); (2) Fc receptor-mediated phagocytosis of opsonised T-cells; (3) apoptosis induction; (4) ADCC (NK cell killing of antibody-coated T-cells); Thymoglobulin (rabbit) = more potent, preferred; ATGAM (equine) = less potent but may be used if rabbit allergy. Indications: aplastic anaemia (severe - when no matched sibling donor available or patient ineligible for HSCT; combined with ciclosporin + eltrombopag + horse ATG [rabbit ATG not superior to horse in aplastic anaemia - evidence favours horse ATG + ciclosporin]; PBS-listed); solid organ transplant conditioning (kidney/liver/heart - induction therapy for high-immunological-risk patients; delays acute rejection; steroid-sparing); HSCT conditioning (T-cell depletion - reduces GVHD risk; rabbit ATG preferred for haploidentical HSCT). SE: infusion reactions (fever, chills, rigors, rash, hypotension - very common; pre-medicate with paracetamol + antihistamine + corticosteroid; slow infusion rate); serum sickness (arthralgia, rash, fever, lymphadenopathy - 5-15 days post-infusion; equine ATG > rabbit ATG; manage with corticosteroids); profound lymphopenia/immunosuppression (infection risk - viral reactivation [CMV, EBV, VZV] - monitor + prophylax); thrombocytopenia (acute - during infusion). Note: aplastic anaemia - horse ATG (ATGAM) + ciclosporin preferred over rabbit ATG (RACE trial: horse ATG superior to rabbit ATG for aplastic anaemia - contrary to expectations - mechanism unclear - may relate to Treg induction differences); eltrombopag added to ATG+ciclosporin regimen → improved response rates (NEJM 2017).

Potassium-competitive acid blocker (PCAB) - novel class. MOA: reversibly binds H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump) in a K+-competitive manner (unlike PPIs which require acid-activated prodrug conversion) → immediate and potent acid suppression (does NOT require activation in acidic environment - works at neutral pH → effective for evening dose + between meals); does NOT require conversion from prodrug → faster onset + more consistent acid suppression than PPIs (acid pocket reduction - especially in evening); more potent than PPIs at equivalent doses. Indications: gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD/GORD - healing and maintenance of erosive oesophagitis); H. pylori eradication (component of vonoprazan dual/triple therapy - potent acid suppression improves antibiotic activity; vonoprazan-amoxicillin-clarithromycin or vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual therapy - US-approved 2022; superior H. pylori eradication rates vs PPI-based triple therapy in Japan + now globally; PBS-listed in Australia). SE: nausea, flatulence, diarrhoea (GI - similar to PPIs; generally well tolerated); hypergastrinaemia (class acid-suppression - potent acid suppression → ↑gastrin - theoretical concerns about neuroendocrine tumours with prolonged use); headache; ↑LFTs (uncommon). Note: not a PPI (does not require acid activation - consistent acid suppression regardless of meal timing or CYP2C19 polymorphism - significant advantage over PPIs in CYP2C19 poor metabolisers [who have variable PPI response]); H. pylori eradication - vonoprazan + amoxicillin ± clarithromycin superior eradication rates vs PPI-based regimens (ACID RESOLUTION trial); PBS-listed in Australia (Takecab 10 mg, 20 mg).

Synthetic oestrogen - oral contraceptive component. MOA: potent synthetic oestrogen (17α-ethinyl substitution → oral bioavailability + resistance to first-pass hepatic metabolism; unlike natural oestradiol); binds oestrogen receptors (ERα + ERβ) → genomic effects; in OCP combinations → negative feedback on hypothalamus-pituitary → ↓FSH/LH → ↓ovulation; also ↑cervical mucus viscosity + endometrial atrophy (combined with progestogen); oestrogen component responsible for most cardiovascular SE. Indications: combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs) - paired with various progestins (levonorgestrel, norgestimate, desogestrel, gestodene, drospirenone, dienogest, cyproterone - forming standard 'the pill'); doses range 20-35 µg/day EE (ultra-low 10 µg available in some formulations); emergency contraception (levonorgestrel-only now preferred over 'Yuzpe method' [2×EE+levonorgestrel]); acne (combined with cyproterone → anti-androgenic OCP; combined with desogestrel/gestodene/drospirenone → less androgenic); hormone therapy (historically, now natural oestradiol preferred for HRT). SE: nausea, breast tenderness (oestrogen-related - first few months); venous thromboembolism (VTE - most significant SE; risk proportional to EE dose + progestin type - 3rd/4th gen progestins [desogestrel, gestodene, drospirenone] higher VTE risk than levonorgestrel; pregnancy VTE risk higher than OCP VTE risk); arterial thrombosis (MI, stroke - mainly in smokers ≥35 + migraine with aura); ↑BP; ↑triglycerides; breakthrough bleeding. Note: dose reduction over time (50 µg → 35 µg → 20 µg → 10 µg in ultra-low dose pills); absolute contraindications (WHOMEC Category 4): migraine with aura, smoking ≥35, VTE history, antiphospholipid syndrome, postpartum <6 weeks breastfeeding, breast cancer; COCP failure rate 0.3% perfect use, 9% typical use.

PEGylated anti-TNF-α Fab fragment. MOA: PEGylated Fab fragment (no Fc region - no ADCC or CDC) of humanised anti-TNF-α mAb → high-affinity neutralisation of soluble + membrane-bound TNF-α; lacks Fc region → does NOT cross placenta (FcRn receptor-mediated transport absent) → safe in pregnancy; PEGylation → ↑t½ (SC every 2-4 weeks); TNF neutralisation → ↓NF-κB activation → ↓pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, MMP). Indications: rheumatoid arthritis (RA - moderate-to-severe - monotherapy or combined with MTX; PBS-listed); psoriatic arthritis; axial spondyloarthritis (ankylosing spondylitis + nr-axSpA); Crohn's disease (moderate-to-severe - induction + maintenance); psoriasis (moderate-to-severe - certolizumab approved for plaque psoriasis). SE: infections (most common - URTI, UTI - serious infections including TB/fungal - screen for TB before starting; hold for serious infection); injection site reactions; VTE (↑DVT/PE risk - class anti-TNF); malignancy (lymphoma - anti-TNF class; demyelinating disease [MS-like] - avoid if history of demyelination). Note: pregnancy advantage (Fc-free → does NOT cross placenta via FcRn - negligible transfer to foetus - preferred anti-TNF in pregnancy if biologic required; CRIB/CRADLE studies: certolizumab serum level in cord blood/infant blood negligible); compare to adalimumab/etanercept (Fc-containing → some placental transfer); breastfeeding: certolizumab minimal transfer in breast milk (PEGylated Fab - poor enteric absorption in infant).

Smooth muscle relaxant - antispasmodic for irritable bowel syndrome. MOA: direct action on intestinal smooth muscle → ↓smooth muscle spasm without anticholinergic effects; mechanism incompletely understood - proposed Na+ channel blockade in smooth muscle membranes + inhibition of phosphodiesterase → smooth muscle relaxation → relief of intestinal spasm + colicky pain; selective for GI smooth muscle (unlike antispasmodics with anticholinergic effects - no dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision). Indications: irritable bowel syndrome (IBS - symptom relief - abdominal pain, spasm, colic - 135 mg MR capsule BD or 200 mg TID before meals; PBS-listed in Australia); associated conditions (diverticular disease, functional bowel disorders). SE: very well tolerated (no anticholinergic SE - dry mouth/urinary retention absent - key advantage); headache; dizziness; hypersensitivity reactions (rare - skin rash, urticaria, angioedema - very rare). Note: no anticholinergic SE (differentiates from hyoscine/dicycloverine - mebeverine preferred in elderly or those intolerant of anticholinergic effects); onset of action within 30 min of taking; must take 20 min before meals (modified-release 135 mg twice daily - better compliance than TID dosing); IBS treatment is symptom-based - mebeverine for pain-predominant IBS; evidence: multiple RCTs showing modest benefit vs placebo for abdominal pain in IBS; available OTC in some countries (prescription in Australia); not effective for diarrhoea or constipation predominant IBS - use loperamide or laxatives instead.

Anticholinergic antispasmodic (dicyclomine). MOA: muscarinic receptor antagonist → ↓GI smooth muscle tone and spasm → ↓intestinal colic; also direct smooth muscle relaxant effect (non-anticholinergic component - calcium channel-like effect); quaternary structure (like hyoscine butylbromide) → reduced CNS penetration → less central anticholinergic effects than tertiary amines. Indications: irritable bowel syndrome (IBS - abdominal cramping/spasm - 10-20 mg QID; PBS-listed Australia); infantile colic (historical - but NOT recommended in infants < 6 months - serious respiratory depression risk); functional bowel disorders (spastic colon, diverticular disease spasm). SE: dry mouth (anticholinergic - most common - differentiated from mebeverine which has no anticholinergic SE); blurred vision; urinary retention; constipation; tachycardia; CNS effects (drowsiness, confusion - particularly in elderly); infantile apnoea (contraindicated in infants - case reports of severe respiratory depression + apnoea in infants < 6 months). Note: anticholinergic SE profile (compare to mebeverine which has NO anticholinergic SE - mebeverine preferred in elderly/prostatic hypertrophy/glaucoma patients); CONTRAINDICATED in infants <6 months (respiratory depression risk); anticholinergic contraindications apply (urinary retention, obstructive uropathy, uncontrolled glaucoma, pyloric stenosis, GI obstruction, severe ulcerative colitis); IBS usage largely replaced by mebeverine (fewer SE) but still used; available oral + parenteral; US brand name is dicyclomine (same drug).

Quaternary ammonium anticholinergic antispasmodic (distinct from hyoscine hydrobromide). MOA: quaternary ammonium structure → does NOT cross blood-brain barrier or placenta (highly polar → no CNS anticholinergic effects unlike tertiary hyoscine); blocks muscarinic receptors in GI + urogenital smooth muscle → ↓smooth muscle spasm → relief of colic + cramping; blocks ganglionic nicotinic receptors at GI plexus (additional mechanism). Indications: acute abdominal/pelvic spasm and pain (GI colic - IM/IV 20 mg for acute biliary/renal colic - rapid relief; also for uterine cramping); IBS (oral 10 mg TID-QID - symptom relief for cramping); labour pain (no benefit - not effective for cervical relaxation in labour); end-of-life care (SC infusion - reduces secretions/death rattle in dying patients - combined with morphine/midazolam in syringe driver). SE: peripheral anticholinergic (dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation, tachycardia - milder than tertiary amines; no CNS effects); injection site reactions (IV/IM); hypotension (IV injection). Note: NO CNS effects (quaternary structure → does not cross BBB - no drowsiness/confusion; advantage over hyoscine hydrobromide); palliative care use - SC infusion in syringe driver with other end-of-life medications (compatible with morphine, midazolam, haloperidol); acute colic - IV 20 mg bolus often given with diclofenac (competitive analgesia strategy); OTC oral tablets in most countries for IBS; IV/IM formulation for acute colic.

Second-generation H1 antihistamine - topical nasal and ophthalmic. MOA: selective H1 receptor inverse agonist → blocks histamine-mediated effects; additional anti-inflammatory activity (inhibits release of inflammatory mediators - leukotrienes, PAF, kinins - beyond pure H1 blockade); topical nasal/ocular application → local effect with minimal systemic absorption. Indications: allergic rhinitis (nasal spray - seasonal + perennial - 1-2 sprays per nostril BD; PBS-listed in Australia; faster onset than oral antihistamines [15 min] + intranasal steroids [days]; also effective for vasomotor rhinitis); allergic conjunctivitis (0.05% eye drops - 1 drop per eye BD); combined intranasal formulation (Dymista = azelastine + fluticasone propionate intranasal - superior to each alone for seasonal AR). SE: bitter/metallic taste (characteristic SE - nasal spray drips to pharynx - advise tilting head forward during application; significant cause of poor compliance); somnolence (less than 1st-gen antihistamines - topical route reduces systemic absorption; some sedation from absorbed fraction); nasal irritation/burning; local eye irritation. Note: bitter taste management (most important - instruct patients to tilt head slightly forward + inhale gently - reduces posterior drip + bitter taste; most common reason for discontinuation); onset 15 min (faster than intranasal steroids or oral antihistamines for allergic rhinitis - useful for acute symptom relief + as needed use); combined with intranasal steroid (Dymista) - synergistic for severe seasonal AR.

Selective H1 antihistamine and mast cell stabiliser - ophthalmic and nasal. MOA: dual mechanism - (1) potent selective H1 receptor antagonist → blocks histamine-mediated itch, redness, tearing; (2) mast cell stabiliser → ↓degranulation → ↓release of histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins, thromboxane → both immediate and delayed phase allergic response. Indications: allergic conjunctivitis (eye drops - 0.1% BD, 0.2% OD, 0.7% OD for daily use; Pataday Once Daily - most convenient - OD dosing; quick onset ≤3 min); perennial/seasonal allergic rhinitis (0.6% nasal spray - BD dosing). SE: headache (most common - mild); somnolence (minimal systemic absorption from topical - less than oral antihistamines); mild eye irritation (transient stinging); bitter taste (nasal spray - posterior drip). Note: once-daily formulation advantage (Pataday 0.2% OD - improved compliance vs BD olopatadine or other OD/BD antihistamine eye drops; preservative-free formulations available); dual antihistamine + mast cell stabilising action → effective for both immediate and late-phase allergic response (better than pure antihistamine or pure mast cell stabiliser - synergistic); compare to ketotifen (also dual mechanism eye drops - OTC, cheaper); ophthalmic olopatadine well tolerated long-term (minimal systemic effects from topical ocular route).

H1 antihistamine and mast cell stabiliser - ophthalmic and systemic. MOA: dual mechanism - H1 receptor antagonist + mast cell stabiliser (inhibits mast cell degranulation → ↓histamine/leukotriene release + ↓eosinophil activation); oral form also has anti-PAF (platelet-activating factor) and anti-eosinophil activity; ophthalmic formulation acts locally (minimal systemic effects). Indications: allergic conjunctivitis (ophthalmic 0.025% solution - BD; OTC in many countries - comparable to olopatadine at lower cost); systemic allergic conditions (oral ketotifen - 1 mg BD; allergy prevention; asthma prophylaxis [limited evidence for asthma - replaced by ICS/LABA]; mastocytosis [systemic - 1-2 mg BD - reduces pruritus + flushing in systemic mastocytosis - used off-label]). SE: ophthalmic: mild stinging; headache; oral: sedation (prominent - antihistamine + antihistaminic CNS penetration; fatigue; impaired cognition - limit driving); dry mouth (anticholinergic); weight gain; ↑appetite (antihistamine class - appetite stimulation). Note: mastocytosis use (systemic oral ketotifen - antihistamine + mast cell stabilisation → useful for pruritus + flushing in systemic mast cell disease; also combined with H2 blocker [famotidine/ranitidine] for complete histamine blockade); ophthalmic OTC (affordable effective treatment for allergic conjunctivitis; available as Alaway OTC in Australia); oral form sedating (caution in driving + activities requiring alertness).

Mast cell stabiliser and anti-inflammatory agent. MOA: inhibits mast cell and other immune cell (eosinophil, neutrophil, macrophage) degranulation → prevents release of inflammatory mediators (histamine, leukotrienes, PAF, substance P) upon allergen exposure; also inhibits sensory C-fibre activation → ↓neurogenic inflammation; mechanism not fully elucidated (proposed Cl⁻ channel modulation in mast cells); anti-inflammatory effect independent of bronchodilation. Indications: allergic conjunctivitis (2% ophthalmic solution - Alocril - BD-QID for seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis; symptomatic relief of itching, tearing, redness); mild persistent asthma (inhaler - Tilade 4 mg/puff - prophylaxis; alternative to ICS in mild asthma, particularly paediatric; less effective than ICS but fewer SE; largely replaced by ICS); exercise-induced bronchospasm (inhaler - pre-exercise dose). SE: ophthalmic: mild burning/stinging; headache; bitter taste (systemic absorption via nasolacrimal); inhaled: bitter taste (characteristic - inhaled form has distinctive unpleasant taste; significant non-compliance driver; metallic/bitter taste of nedocromil inhaler → poor acceptance); cough; headache. Note: bitter taste (very distinctive - nedocromil inhaler - many patients stop therapy due to taste; must counsel before prescribing and confirm patient can tolerate taste during follow-up); ophthalmic formulation better tolerated than inhaler; sodium cromoglicate (cromoglycate) = similar drug (mast cell stabiliser class - slightly different formulation - older); largely replaced by modern therapies (dupilumab, antihistamine eye drops with better tolerability) but still used in specific contexts.

IV prodrug of aprepitant - NK1 receptor antagonist for CINV. MOA: phosphate prodrug → rapidly hydrolysed by alkaline phosphatase to aprepitant (active) → selective NK1 receptor antagonist → blocks substance P binding in CNS → ↓delayed CINV; single IV dose (150 mg) replaces 3-day oral aprepitant course (Day 1 only); avoids oral route when patient cannot swallow. Indications: chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV) - prevention of delayed CINV (Day 2-5) from highly emetogenic chemotherapy (HEC - cisplatin, AC regimen) and moderately emetogenic (MEC); combined with 5-HT3 antagonist + dexamethasone (triple antiemetic regimen); IV administration when oral route unavailable or convenient. SE: headache; injection site reactions (phlebitis - infuse over 30 min - do not give as bolus); fatigue; hiccups; constipation. Note: single-dose IV (Day 1) replaces 3-day oral aprepitant (Day 1, 2, 3) - simplifies regimen; CYP3A4 inhibitor (like aprepitant - reduces dexamethasone dose needed when combined - standard in triple regimen: ↓dexamethasone dose by 50% when combined with fosaprepitant/aprepitant); compare to rolapitant (no CYP3A4 interaction - advantage) and netupitant (oral capsule with palonosetron = Akynzeo - similar NK1 mechanism); can infuse over 20-30 minutes via any peripheral vein.

NK1 receptor antagonist - combined with palonosetron for CINV (NEPA). MOA: selective NK1 receptor antagonist → blocks substance P → ↓delayed CINV; combined in fixed-dose capsule with palonosetron (5-HT3 antagonist) → dual-mechanism single capsule antiemetic (NEPA = Netupitant + PAlonosetron - covers both acute [palonosetron - 5-HT3] and delayed [netupitant - NK1] CINV with one tablet); long t½ netupitant (~96 h) → single dose before chemotherapy covers full CINV window. Indications: prevention of CINV - acute and delayed - highly + moderately emetogenic chemotherapy (single capsule [300 mg netupitant/0.5 mg palonosetron] Day 1 of cycle with dexamethasone; PALO-99-007 + NEPA trials: superior to palonosetron alone; US/EU-approved; widely used in oncology). SE: headache; constipation; fatigue; alopecia (underlying cancer/chemo). Note: convenience advantage (one capsule covers both phases of CINV - Day 1 only; no additional Day 2-3 antiemetic needed for most patients); CYP3A4 inhibitor (moderate - reduces dexamethasone metabolism → ↓dexamethasone dose by ~50% in triple regimen → standard dosing: netupitant 300 mg + palonosetron 0.5 mg + dexamethasone 12 mg pre-chemo; Day 2-3 dexamethasone 8 mg); compare to aprepitant/fosaprepitant (also NK1 - separate from 5-HT3 antagonist) and rolapitant (no CYP3A4 interaction - but no fixed-dose combination).

Synthetic cannabinoid - antiemetic. MOA: synthetic analogue of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) → activates cannabinoid receptors CB1 (CNS - reduces emetic reflex) + CB2 (peripheral); CB1 activation in brainstem → ↓vomiting centre activity → antiemetic; also psychoactive effects (CNS CB1). Indications: chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV - refractory to other antiemetics; 1-2 mg BD, starting night before chemotherapy; Schedule 8 in Australia); chronic nausea/vomiting (refractory - difficult GI conditions); anorexia/cachexia (HIV/AIDS, cancer - appetite stimulation via CB1). SE: CNS (very common - drowsiness, dizziness, ataxia, euphoria, dysphoria; impaired driving/mental function); psychosis exacerbation (CB1 activation in limbic system - avoid in history of psychosis/schizophrenia); tachycardia, postural hypotension; dry mouth; perceptual disturbances (cannabis-like intoxication effects); dependence potential; teratogenic. Note: Schedule 8 controlled drug in Australia (due to psychoactive/abuse potential); patient must not drive or operate machinery; psychosis/mania risk - screen history before prescribing; tolerance develops with chronic use (dose escalation may be needed); onset 1-2 hours (not for rescue CINV - use as prophylaxis); taper on cessation (withdrawal symptoms if abrupt stop after prolonged use); compare to dronabinol (THC itself - same class - similar SE profile).

Antiflatulent/defoaming agent. MOA: chemically inert polymer (dimethicone/simethicone) → alters surface tension of gas bubbles in GI tract → coalescence of small gas bubbles → larger bubbles more easily expelled by eructation or flatulence; does NOT affect gas production or absorption (purely physical/mechanical effect - no systemic absorption - chemically inert). Indications: symptomatic relief of intestinal gas (bloating, flatulence, belching after meals - post-prandial bloating; OTC); infant colic (Infacol, Mylicon drops - given before feeds - evidence for infantile colic mixed - Cochrane review: insufficient evidence; widely used despite limited RCT data; safe and well tolerated); endoscopy/ultrasound prep (reduces gas bubbles → clearer images); postoperative gas pain. SE: none significant (chemically inert - not absorbed → no systemic SE; very rarely hypersensitivity). Note: no clinical evidence for infantile colic beyond placebo in RCTs (Cochrane review - no significant benefit vs placebo); widely used due to excellent safety profile + parental reassurance; for adult bloating - may help with post-meal gas; available OTC without prescription; food form (Gas-X in USA) - chewable tablets; not absorbed - safe in pregnancy/lactation; mechanism purely physical (no pharmacology as such).

Faecal softener (stool softener) - surface-active laxative. MOA: anionic surfactant (ionic detergent) → reduces surface tension at oil-water interface in intestinal contents → allows water penetration into faeces → softens stool without stimulating intestinal motility (non-stimulant laxative); also allows incorporation of intestinal fat into stool → lubrication; onset 12-72 hours (slower than stimulant laxatives); minimal systemic absorption. Indications: constipation associated with hard stools (preventing straining - post-surgical, postpartum, haemorrhoids, anal fissure, after MI - avoid straining with Valsalva manoeuvre); chronic constipation (adjunct - often combined with sennosides as combination laxative [Peri-Colace]); rectal/enema formulation (sodium phosphate enema - note: docusate as rectal micro-enema). SE: nausea (oral - mild); diarrhoea (excessive use); abdominal cramps; electrolyte imbalance (with excessive use in elderly); theoretical concern: docusate may enhance absorption of mineral oil → hepatotoxicity (avoid concurrent mineral oil + docusate). Note: stool softener (not stimulant → does not cause colic-type cramping unlike senna/bisacodyl); useful for preventing straining (post-MI, post-op, haemorrhoidal disease - Valsalva manoeuvre contraindicated); limited efficacy compared to stimulant laxatives for established constipation (senna, bisacodyl more effective for functional constipation); overused in palliative care (laxative prophylaxis with opioids - macrogol/senna combination more effective than docusate alone).

Bulk-forming laxative (soluble dietary fibre). MOA: psyllium husk contains mucilaginous polysaccharides (arabinoxylan) → absorbs water → forms viscous gel in GI tract → ↑stool bulk + softness → stimulates normal peristalsis; soluble fibre fermented by colonic bacteria → SCFAs (butyrate) → colonocyte nutrition; also binds bile acids (minor cholesterol-lowering effect). Indications: constipation (prevention and treatment - 3.5-7 g in water 1-3× daily; must take with ≥240 mL water); IBS-constipation (increases stool water content + regularity - NICE recommendation); mild diarrhoea (paradoxically - absorbs water + normalises stool consistency); hypercholesterolaemia (adjunct - modest LDL reduction via bile acid sequestration - 5-10 g/day reduces LDL ~5-10%); diabetes management (reduces postprandial glucose - viscous fibre slows gastric emptying). SE: bloating and flatulence (very common - fermentation of psyllium → gas production; starts with low dose and increases gradually); choking/aspiration if insufficient water (SERIOUS - must take with ≥240 mL water immediately; powder that swells → oesophageal obstruction if swallowed dry or without adequate fluid → regulatory safety warning); hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis (rare - occupational exposures in pharmaceutical workers; IgE-mediated allergy to psyllium protein). Note: adequate hydration essential (≥240 mL water with each dose - oesophageal obstruction without adequate liquid → aspiration risk); start gradually (bloating/flatulence reduce with time as gut microbiome adapts); soluble fibre → bifidogenic effect (↑Bifidobacteria, Lactobacillus); multiple health benefits beyond constipation (cholesterol, glycaemia, colon health).

Bispecific HER2 antibody - dual-epitope anti-HER2. MOA: binds two distinct epitopes on HER2 extracellular domain (domain 2 = trastuzumab binding site + domain 4 = pertuzumab binding site) → dual HER2 blockade simultaneously; unique mechanism (bivalent bridging of HER2 heterodimers → crosslinking → HER2 receptor clustering → enhanced internalisation/degradation - different from trastuzumab+pertuzumab which are separate antibodies); bispecific design (single molecule targeting two HER2 sites) → ↑tumour cell selectivity + ↑Fc-mediated effector functions (ADCC, CDC). Indications: HER2-positive biliary tract cancer (biliary tract carcinoma/BTC - cholangiocarcinoma/gallbladder cancer - 2nd-line after prior platinum-based chemo; US 2024 accelerated approval - HERIZON-BTC-01 trial: ORR 41%, median DoR 12.9 months - first HER2-targeted approval for BTC); HER2-positive gastro-oesophageal adenocarcinoma (GEA - frontline + subsequent lines - HERIZON-GEA trials - investigation ongoing). SE: diarrhoea (most common GI toxicity - grade 1-2 common; manage with loperamide; grade 3 requires dose hold); infusion-related reactions (premedicate with antihistamine + paracetamol; first infusion monitoring); nausea; fatigue; cardiac dysfunction (HER2 inhibition → left ventricular dysfunction - LVEF monitoring); ↑LFTs. Note: HER2 testing required (IHC 3+ or ISH amplification); BTC - HER2 overexpression in 15-20% of intrahepatic CCA + ~30% GBC; first HER2-targeted therapy specifically approved for BTC; LVEF monitoring (baseline + every 12 weeks during treatment); compare to trastuzumab (single HER2 epitope - domain 4) and trastuzumab+pertuzumab (dual domain combination - but as separate drugs).

Anti-CLDN18.2 monoclonal antibody. MOA: chimeric IgG1 mAb → binds CLDN18.2 (claudin 18.2 - tight junction protein - expressed on gastric mucosa; overexpressed in gastric + gastro-oesophageal junction [GEJ] cancer - CLDN18.2 protein becomes accessible on cancer cell surface as tight junction organisation disrupts) → Fc-mediated ADCC + CDC → tumour cell death; CLDN18.2 is highly tumour-selective (normal expression limited to stomach mucosa; cancer cells aberrantly expose surface CLDN18.2). Indications: HER2-negative, CLDN18.2-positive locally advanced/metastatic gastric or GEJ adenocarcinoma - 1st-line combined with FOLFOX or CAPOX (mFOLFOX6) - SPOTLIGHT trial (zanidatamab + FOLFOX: ↑PFS/OS) and GLOW trial (CAPOX: ↑PFS/OS); US-approved 2024; EMA 2024; TGA status - check; CLDN18.2 IHC testing required (≥75% of tumour cells ≥2+ staining). SE: nausea/vomiting (most common - 80%+ of patients - mechanism unclear but CLDN18.2 expressed in gastric mucosa → immune-related mucosal effects; antiemetic prophylaxis mandatory; graded 1-3 events); decreased appetite; peripheral neuropathy (from FOLFOX component - oxaliplatin); fatigue. Note: CLDN18.2 testing mandatory (IHC threshold: ≥75% of tumour cells with moderate-strong [≥2+] staining - high threshold compared to HER2 testing - ~38% of gastric cancers qualify); nausea/vomiting management critical (prophylactic 5-HT3 antagonist + NK1 antagonist + dexamethasone; consider dose reduction if Grade 3); first approved CLDN18.2-targeted therapy; new target class for GI oncology.

Chelating agent and disease-modifying drug - multiple indications. MOA: (1) chelation - forms stable water-soluble complexes with heavy metals (copper, lead, mercury, zinc) → renal excretion; for Wilson's disease: chelates hepatic/CNS copper → urinary copper excretion → ↓copper accumulation; (2) RA mechanism - inhibits T-cell function + macrophage activation (anti-inflammatory + immunomodulatory - mechanism not fully understood); (3) cystinuria - reacts with cystine to form mixed penicillamine-cysteine disulfide (soluble, does not precipitate → ↓cystine kidney stones). Indications: Wilson's disease (hepatolenticular degeneration - copper chelation - 1st-line with trientine as alternatives; 250-500 mg QID; lifelong treatment; monitor 24h urine copper); rheumatoid arthritis (DMARD - 2nd line - pre-biologic era; now rarely used due to adverse effect profile + availability of better tolerated DMARDs); cystinuria (urinary cystine reduction - reduces stone formation + dissolves existing cystine stones). SE: serious toxicity (major limitation): (1) haematological (thrombocytopenia, leucopenia, aplastic anaemia - monitor CBC monthly); (2) renal (proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome - monitor urine protein monthly); (3) autoimmune (penicillamine-induced myasthenia gravis, SLE, pemphigus, polymyositis - unique drug-induced autoimmune syndromes - stop drug if diagnosed); (4) dermatological (elastosis perforans serpiginosa - collagen changes); (5) taste disturbance (metallic taste). Note: penicillin allergy cross-reactivity (rare - penicillamine is a metabolite of penicillin - reports of cross-reactivity but generally not contraindicated in penicillin allergy; use with caution; test dose); monthly monitoring required (CBC + urine protein - toxicity monitoring protocol); Wilson's disease first-line: trientine now preferred (fewer SE); penicillamine alternative in zinc/trientine intolerance.

Copper chelating agent - Wilson's disease treatment. MOA: tetraamine chelator → forms stable ring complexes with copper (Cu²⁺) → ↑urinary copper excretion; selective for copper (less affinity for zinc/iron than penicillamine → less zinc/iron depletion); does NOT form reactive intermediate metabolites (unlike penicillamine - fewer autoimmune SE); less effective overall chelating capacity than penicillamine but similar clinical outcomes with better tolerability. Indications: Wilson's disease (hepatolenticular degeneration - 1st-line alternative to penicillamine; preferred when penicillamine intolerant (autoimmune SE) or in neurological Wilson's (initial penicillamine in neurological Wilson's can paradoxically worsen neurology - trientine safer as initial therapy for neurological Wilson's); 750-1500 mg/day in 3-4 divided doses before meals). SE: iron deficiency anaemia (trientine chelates iron as well as copper → sideroblastic anaemia → monitor iron + supplement separately, separate doses from trientine by several hours); GI: nausea, abdominal pain; proteinuria (less than penicillamine but monitor); rash; headache. Note: neurological Wilson's disease initial therapy - penicillamine can worsen neurological symptoms initially (copper mobilisation → neurological deterioration paradox) - trientine or zinc preferred for neurological presentation; 24h urine copper monitoring (target <100 µg/24h or <200 µg/24h pre-treatment); maintain 1 hour separation from meals + iron supplements (chelation impaired by food/iron); compare to zinc (blocks copper absorption - maintenance therapy; less effective for hepatic disease - adjunct or maintenance, not acute chelation).

4-Hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (HPPD) inhibitor - hereditary tyrosinaemia type 1. MOA: competitively inhibits HPPD → ↓maleylacetoacetate/fumarylacetoacetate production (accumulation of succinylacetone [SA] - toxic metabolite in HT1 - causes DNA damage, Fanconi syndrome, hepatocellular carcinoma risk - SA originates from fumarylacetoacetate accumulation); blocking HPPD upstream redirects tyrosine catabolism → ↑tyrosine + ↑4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate (4-HPPD substrate) accumulation but ↓downstream hepatotoxic metabolites → prevents liver/kidney/neurological damage from SA. Indications: hereditary tyrosinaemia type 1 (HT1 - fumarylacetoacetase deficiency [FAH gene] - fatal liver disease; nitisinone + low-phenylalanine/tyrosine diet - blocks toxic metabolite formation → liver normalisation + ↓HCC risk; dramatically improved outcomes - transforms fatal disease to manageable chronic condition; PBS-listed in Australia; 0.5-1 mg/kg/day). SE: transient thrombocytopenia + leucopenia (early treatment); corneal crystals (tyrosine deposits in cornea - from ↑serum tyrosine; asymptomatic or mild photophobia/reduced vision - reduce with dietary tyrosine restriction; ophthalmological monitoring); liver complications (↑LFTs if doses inadequate - monitor); neurological crisis (rare - crisis can occur even on treatment - porphyria-like). Note: diet essential (nitisinone alone not sufficient - low phenylalanine + tyrosine diet required to prevent corneal crystal deposition and complications from tyrosine accumulation - joint paediatric metabolic dietitian + metabolic physician management); newborn screening (HT1 - tandem mass spectrometry detects ↑tyrosine; early treatment before symptoms prevents most complications); revolutionary drug (pre-nitisinone - liver transplant was only treatment; nitisinone dramatically changed outcomes).

Phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) cofactor - treatment for BH4-responsive phenylketonuria (PKU). MOA: synthetic form of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) - natural cofactor of PAH (phenylalanine hydroxylase) → BH4 stabilises PAH enzyme + increases residual activity in BH4-responsive PAH mutations → ↑conversion of phenylalanine → tyrosine → ↓plasma phenylalanine (Phe); mechanism is pharmacological chaperone + cofactor supplementation; effective only in patients with BH4-responsive PAH mutations (partial loss-of-function mutations - ~30-50% of PKU patients; mild-moderate PKU more likely to respond). Indications: BH4-responsive hyperphenylalaninaemia (HPA) including PKU (phenylketonuria) - reduces blood phenylalanine in responders (typically ≥30% reduction in Phe at 4 weeks = response; dose 10-20 mg/kg/day; used with dietary Phe restriction); BH4 deficiency disorders (separate enzyme defects in pterin metabolism - BH4 biosynthesis defects [GTP cyclohydrolase, 6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin synthase, dihydrobiopterin reductase] → BH4 replacement directly). SE: headache; rhinorrhoea; nausea/GI (mild); ↑blood Phe paradoxically (if diet too liberalised - monitor Phe closely on therapy); haemolysis (rare - G6PD deficiency). Note: response testing (loading test: BH4 20 mg/kg single dose → measure blood Phe at 0, 24, 48h → responders show ≥30% Phe reduction at 24-48h); BH4 responders = can relax dietary protein restriction → ↑quality of life + diet adherence; compare to pegvaliase (enzyme substitution - phenylalanine ammonia lyase → converts Phe to trans-cinnamic acid - more potent Phe reduction but higher SE; for BH4 non-responders); must continue dietary restriction (sapropterin is adjunct - not replacement for PKU diet).

Aminothiol cystine-depleting agent - cystinosis treatment. MOA: free thiol group (–SH) → reacts with cystine (product of CTNS gene dysfunction - defective lysosomal cystine transporter in cystinosis → cystine accumulates in lysosomes → crystalline deposits in all tissues) → mixed disulfide cysteamine-cysteine formed within lysosome → exited via dibasic amino acid transporter (CAT) → ↓lysosomal cystine content; oral systemic form → treats extraocular cystine deposits; ophthalmic eye drops → treats corneal cystine crystals (cannot reach cornea from systemic route). Indications: nephropathic cystinosis (Cystagon/Procysbi - oral - delays/prevents renal failure progression [Fanconi syndrome → chronic kidney disease]; must start early → lifelong; dose titrated to WBC cystine level target <1 nmol half-cystine/mg protein); corneal cystine crystals (Cystadrops - 0.55% ophthalmic gel - QID application - reduces photophobia + blepharospasm from corneal crystals; only topical treatment effective for corneal deposits). SE: foul body odour/breath (characteristic and highly problematic - very unpleasant sulfur-containing metabolites excreted through skin + breath; affects social functioning - most common reason for poor adherence; can use frequent washing + deodorant; Procysbi delayed-release → reduced odour vs immediate release Cystagon); GI (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea - with immediate-release; Procysbi [delayed-release] → ↓GI SE); cutaneous striae/wound healing issues. Note: odour/adherence problem (major clinical challenge; Procysbi [delayed-release formulation] → better odour profile + less frequent dosing [every 12h vs Cystagon every 6h] → better adherence); WBC cystine monitoring (measure leukocyte cystine - target <1 nmol/mg protein at 5.5-6 hours post-dose - optimal control indicator); systemic treatment does NOT reach cornea (separate ophthalmic drops required for corneal crystals).

NNRTI (non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor) - HIV-1 treatment. MOA: binds allosteric site on HIV-1 reverse transcriptase → conformational change → prevents HIV DNA synthesis; 2nd-generation NNRTI → flexible binding mode (DAPY design) → active against many NNRTI-resistant strains (K103N, Y181C). Indications: HIV-1 treatment in treatment-experienced adults with evidence of viral replication + resistance to other ARVs; always used in combination ART. SE: rash (common; rare SJS/TEN - discontinue if severe); nausea; dyslipidaemia; CYP3A4/2C9 drug interactions. Note: must be taken with food (↑ bioavailability); requires resistance testing before use - not first-line; 2nd-gen NNRTI retains activity against K103N (efavirenz resistance mutation).

NNRTI (non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor) - HIV-1 treatment. MOA: binds allosteric site on HIV-1 reverse transcriptase → prevents HIV DNA synthesis; 1st-generation NNRTI - low barrier to resistance (K103N single mutation → complete resistance). Indications: HIV-1 treatment (combination ART); prevention of mother-to-child HIV transmission (single intrapartum dose + newborn dose). SE: hepatotoxicity (serious - first 18 weeks; fatal hepatic necrosis reported - ↑ risk women CD4 >250, men CD4 >400; monitor LFTs); rash (SJS risk - 14-day lead-in period mandatory); fever. CI: initiating in women CD4 >250 or men CD4 >400 (hepatotoxicity risk). Note: 14-day lead-in (200 mg once daily × 2 weeks before 400 mg/day) reduces rash incidence; CYP3A4 inducer - multiple drug interactions; largely superseded by better-tolerated NNRTIs in resource-replete settings.

NNRTI (non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor) - HIV-1 treatment. MOA: novel pyridone NNRTI → binds allosteric site of HIV-1 reverse transcriptase → prevents HIV DNA synthesis; distinct resistance profile from efavirenz/rilpivirine. Indications: HIV-1 treatment (naive or virologically suppressed adults switching regimen); also available as fixed-dose doravirine/lamivudine/tenofovir disoproxil (Delstrigo). SE: generally well tolerated; dizziness; nausea; abnormal dreams; headache; CYP3A4 substrate (rifampicin → contraindicated). Note: neutral lipid profile (advantage vs efavirenz - does not raise triglycerides/LDL); no food requirement; active against K103N + Y181C; once-daily dosing.

HIV protease inhibitor (PI). MOA: binds HIV-1 protease active site → prevents cleavage of Gag-Pol polyprotein → immature non-infectious virions; requires pharmacokinetic boosting (ritonavir or cobicistat). Indications: HIV-1 treatment in combination ART; boosted formulation (Evotaz = atazanavir/cobicistat). SE: hyperbilirubinaemia (indirect - UGT1A1 inhibition → benign jaundice + scleral icterus - not hepatotoxicity); PR interval prolongation (first-degree heart block); nephrolithiasis (atazanavir stones - adequate hydration important); nausea; relatively lipid-friendly vs other PIs. CI: severe hepatic impairment; simvastatin/lovastatin (↑ myopathy risk); PPIs substantially ↓ absorption (avoid high-dose PPIs - H2 blockers preferred; take 10h after H2 blocker). Note: gastric pH-dependent absorption - requires acidic stomach (food + avoid PPI); unboosted only in treatment-naive; CYP3A4 strong inhibitor when boosted.

NRTI (nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor) - HIV; first antiretroviral approved (1987). MOA: thymidine analogue → phosphorylated to AZTTP → incorporated into HIV DNA by reverse transcriptase → chain termination (no 3'-OH → no further elongation). Indications: HIV-1 treatment (combination ART - largely historical in resource-replete settings; still used in resource-limited settings); prevention of mother-to-child HIV transmission (intrapartum IV + neonatal oral prophylaxis - standard regimen globally); post-exposure prophylaxis. SE: bone marrow suppression (macrocytic anaemia, neutropenia - dose-limiting; monitor FBC); myopathy (mitochondrial - proximal - long-term use); nausea; lipoatrophy (mitochondrial toxicity - subcutaneous fat loss). Note: avoid with stavudine (d4T) - phosphorylation antagonism; macrocytosis is an expected on-treatment effect (monitor FBC every 3 months initially); now largely replaced by TAF/TDF/abacavir in high-income settings; historically most widely used NRTI globally.

HIV fusion inhibitor (entry inhibitor). MOA: 36-amino-acid synthetic peptide → binds HR1 domain of HIV gp41 → prevents conformational change required for viral-cell membrane fusion → HIV cannot enter CD4+ T cells. Indications: treatment-experienced HIV-1 in salvage regimens (ongoing viral replication + resistance to other ARVs) - used with other active agents. SE: injection site reactions (painful nodules, induration, erythema - universal - rotate sites; subcutaneous abscesses reported); ↑ bacterial pneumonia risk; hypersensitivity (rare but serious); inconvenient twice-daily SC injections. Note: only approved fusion inhibitor; not oral → twice-daily subcutaneous injections (significantly limits use); no CYP interactions (not hepatically metabolised); expensive; largely replaced by newer salvage options (ibalizumab, fostemsavir) but remains option when all other classes exhausted.

HIV integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI). MOA: chelates Mg2+ cofactors in HIV integrase active site → prevents insertion of HIV DNA into host genome (strand transfer step); requires pharmacokinetic boosting (cobicistat) for adequate exposure. Indications: HIV-1 treatment; available in fixed-dose combinations - elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (Genvoya) and elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil (Stribild). SE: nausea; diarrhoea; headache; ↑ serum creatinine (cobicistat blocks tubular creatinine secretion - not true GFR ↓); numerous CYP3A4 drug interactions (via cobicistat). Note: must be taken with food; lower barrier to resistance vs dolutegravir/bictegravir (Q148H + G140S → resistance); cobicistat pharmacoenhancer has no intrinsic antiviral activity; ↑ creatinine expected early - check baseline eGFR; once-daily as part of STR (single-tablet regimen).

5-HT1B/1D agonist (triptan) - acute migraine treatment. MOA: selective 5-HT1B agonist → cranial vasoconstriction; 5-HT1D on trigeminal nerve terminals → ↓ CGRP + substance P release → ↓ neurogenic inflammation. Indications: acute migraine (with or without aura) in adults. SE: flushing; chest tightness/pressure (non-cardiac); paraesthesia; somnolence; dizziness; nausea. CI: ischaemic heart disease; uncontrolled hypertension; stroke/TIA history; MAOIs; other triptans within 24h; potent CYP3A4 inhibitors. Note: more lipophilic → better CNS penetration than sumatriptan; CYP3A4 substrate (ketoconazole + erythromycin → ↑ levels); onset ~30 min; may repeat after 2h (max 40 mg/dose, 80 mg/day).

5-HT1B/1D agonist (triptan) - acute migraine treatment. MOA: selective 5-HT1B/1D agonist → cranial vasoconstriction + ↓ trigeminal neuropeptide release. Indications: acute migraine in adults; short-term menstrual migraine prophylaxis. SE: flushing; dizziness; nausea; fatigue; chest tightness; paraesthesia. CI: ischaemic heart disease; uncontrolled hypertension; stroke/TIA history; MAOIs; severe hepatic/renal impairment. Note: longer half-life (~6h vs ~2h sumatriptan) → slower onset but lower headache recurrence; used for short-term menstrual migraine prevention (1 mg BD starting 2 days pre-menses); renal elimination → dose reduce in renal impairment.

5-HT1B/1D agonist (triptan) - acute migraine treatment. MOA: selective 5-HT1B/1D agonist → cranial vasoconstriction + ↓ trigeminal neuropeptide release. Indications: acute migraine in adults; short-term menstrual migraine prophylaxis. SE: dizziness; paraesthesia; fatigue; nausea; flushing; somnolence. CI: ischaemic heart disease; uncontrolled hypertension; stroke/TIA; other triptans within 24h. Note: longest half-life of all triptans (~26h) → slowest onset but lowest headache recurrence; preferred for menstrual migraine prevention (2.5 mg BD for 6 days pericatamenially); CYP1A2 substrate.

5-HT1B/1D agonist (triptan) - acute migraine treatment. MOA: selective 5-HT1B/1D agonist → cranial vasoconstriction + ↓ trigeminal neuropeptide release. Indications: acute migraine (with or without aura) in adults and adolescents 12-17 years. SE: paraesthesia; dizziness; nausea; dry mouth; fatigue; chest tightness. CI: ischaemic heart disease; uncontrolled hypertension; stroke/TIA; other triptans within 24h; MAOIs. Note: favourable tolerability profile; dual elimination (renal + hepatic CYP3A4/MAO-A) → dose reduce in severe hepatic/renal impairment; bioavailability ~70%; onset 30-60 min; may repeat after 2h (max 12.5 mg × 2/day).

Recombinant human alpha-L-iduronidase - enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) for MPS I. MOA: lysosomal enzyme replacement → degrades accumulated glycosaminoglycans (dermatan sulfate + heparan sulfate) in lysosomes; in MPS I (Hurler/Hurler-Scheie/Scheie - IDUA gene) → deficient alpha-L-iduronidase → GAG accumulation → corneal clouding, skeletal dysostosis, hepatosplenomegaly, cardiomyopathy, pulmonary disease, intellectual disability (severe Hurler). Indications: mucopolysaccharidosis type I (MPS I) - non-neurological manifestations (does NOT cross BBB); Hurler syndrome ERT given before HSCT (improves transplant outcomes). SE: infusion reactions (flushing, urticaria, pyrexia, rigors - premedicate with antihistamine + paracetamol); antibody formation; anaphylaxis (rare). Note: IV infusion once weekly; does NOT cross BBB → cannot reverse CNS manifestations of severe Hurler (CNS treated by HSCT if done early <18 months); most common mucopolysaccharidosis; neonatal screening allows earlier treatment.

Recombinant human iduronate-2-sulfatase - ERT for MPS II (Hunter syndrome). MOA: lysosomal enzyme replacement → degrades accumulated dermatan sulfate + heparan sulfate; Hunter syndrome (IDS gene - X-linked recessive) → GAG accumulation → coarse facies, joint stiffness, hepatosplenomegaly, cardiac valve disease, obstructive sleep apnoea, hearing loss; CNS involvement in severe form (aggressive behaviour, intellectual disability). Indications: MPS II (Hunter syndrome) - somatic manifestations; almost exclusively males (X-linked). SE: infusion reactions (fever, headache, urticaria, rash, flushing - premedicate); antibody development; anaphylaxis (rare). Note: IV infusion once weekly; does NOT penetrate CNS (intrathecal delivery under investigation for neurological Hunter); life expectancy in severe Hunter: teens-20s without treatment (cardiorespiratory failure); ERT prolongs life + improves somatic features.

Recombinant human acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) - ERT for Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II, acid maltase deficiency). MOA: taken up by lysosomes via mannose-6-phosphate receptor → replaces deficient GAA → degrades lysosomal glycogen in muscle (skeletal, cardiac, smooth) → ↓ glycogen accumulation → ↑ muscle function. Indications: Pompe disease (all forms) - infantile-onset (classic: severe GAA deficiency → hypertrophic cardiomyopathy + profound hypotonia + respiratory failure → death by 1-2 years untreated; ERT dramatically improves survival) + late-onset (proximal muscle weakness + respiratory failure). SE: infusion reactions (urticaria, rash, flushing, fever - premedicate; anaphylaxis risk); antibody formation (CRIM-negative → high antibody titres → ↓ ERT efficacy - immune tolerance induction used). Note: IV every 2 weeks; CRIM (cross-reactive immunological material) status important - CRIM-positive patients have better response; neonatal screening → earlier treatment = dramatically better outcomes; avalglucosidase alfa (Nexviazyme) - newer formulation with improved efficacy.

Recombinant human alpha-galactosidase A - ERT for Fabry disease (Anderson-Fabry disease, GLA gene - X-linked). MOA: lysosomal enzyme replacement → degrades accumulated globotriaosylceramide (Gb3/GL-3) + lyso-Gb3 in vascular endothelium, cardiomyocytes, renal cells → ↓ progressive multiorgan damage. Indications: Fabry disease with confirmed enzyme deficiency - treats renal disease progression, cardiomyopathy, neuropathic pain, cerebrovascular disease. SE: infusion reactions (fever, chills, flushing, urticaria - premedicate); antibody formation; anaphylaxis. Note: agalsidase alfa (Replagal, 0.2 mg/kg fortnightly) vs agalsidase beta (Fabrazyme, 1 mg/kg fortnightly) - both available; comparative efficacy debated; migalastat (Galafold) - oral chaperone → alternative for amenable GLA mutations (~35% of variants); Fabry disease: acroparaesthesias (burning extremity pain), angiokeratomas, corneal verticillata, cardiomyopathy (LVH + arrhythmias), renal failure, CVA; heterozygous females can be significantly affected (X-linked incomplete penetrance).

Recombinant human lysosomal acid lipase (LAL) - ERT for LAL deficiency (LIPA gene). MOA: produced in transgenic chicken egg whites → administered IV → hepatic uptake via mannose receptor + M6P receptor → replaces deficient LAL → hydrolyses lysosomal cholesteryl esters + triglycerides → ↓ lysosomal lipid accumulation + ↑ LDL catabolism. Indications: LAL deficiency - Wolman disease (infantile - near-zero LAL activity → massive hepatic steatosis + cirrhosis → failure to thrive → death by ~6 months untreated; ERT dramatically improves survival) + cholesteryl ester storage disease (CESD - partial LAL deficiency → hypercholesterolaemia + hepatosplenomegaly + liver fibrosis). SE: infusion reactions (fever, urticaria, vomiting, hypertension - anaphylaxis risk); antibody formation; egg protein content → assess egg allergy before use. Note: produced in transgenic chicken eggs - relevant for egg-allergic patients; weekly infusions (Wolman) or fortnightly (CESD); CESD often underdiagnosed (mimics NAFLD/dyslipidaemia - LDL >10 mmol/L typical); LAL deficiency prevalence ~1:300,000 for CESD.

PEGylated recombinant phenylalanine ammonia lyase (PAL) - enzyme substitution for phenylketonuria (PKU). MOA: recombinant PAL from Anabaena variabilis (bacterial enzyme - not the deficient human PAH) → converts phenylalanine → ammonia + trans-cinnamic acid (non-toxic) → ↓ plasma phenylalanine; PEGylation extends half-life + reduces immunogenicity. Indications: PKU (PAH gene mutations) - adults with uncontrolled hyperphenylalaninaemia (plasma Phe >600 µmol/L) despite diet ± sapropterin (BH4 therapy). SE: injection site reactions (very common - bruising, erythema, induration); arthralgia/arthritis (immune-mediated; can be severe); hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis (significant risk - supervised injections required initially; REMS programme in US); fatigue; nausea. Note: subcutaneous injection titrated over months; not oral (unlike sapropterin); anaphylaxis REMS programme; sapropterin (BH4) first-line for BH4-responsive PKU (~35% of variants); pegvaliase for those uncontrolled on other approaches; Phe levels monitored regularly during initiation.

Low-potency topical corticosteroid (class 1/mild - TGA classification). MOA: binds intracellular glucocorticoid receptor → ↓ pro-inflammatory cytokine transcription → anti-inflammatory + antipruritic + vasoconstrictive. Indications: mild-moderate inflammatory dermatoses - atopic dermatitis (eczema) especially face, skin folds, children; seborrhoeic dermatitis; contact dermatitis; nappy dermatitis. SE: skin atrophy (with prolonged use); telangiectasia; perioral dermatitis (paradoxical - if overused on face); hypopigmentation; HPA suppression (rare at standard use but possible with excessive use over large BSA in infants). Note: preferred for facial/intertriginous sites + children (low potency → ↓ atrophy risk vs more potent agents); 0.05% cream/ointment; do not confuse with clobetasol (which is very potent); well-suited for periorbital/perioral and nappy areas; safe for short-to-medium term facial use.

Medium-potency topical corticosteroid (class 3-4 - moderate). MOA: glucocorticoid receptor agonist → ↓ inflammatory cytokines → anti-inflammatory + antipruritic + vasoconstrictive. Indications: psoriasis (stable plaque - body/extremities); eczema (moderate-severe, non-facial); lichen planus; scalp disorders (oil/shampoo formulation); chronic hand eczema. Also: intravitreal implant (Iluvien - sustained-release for diabetic macular oedema + posterior uveitis); otic drops (otitis externa). SE: skin atrophy (localised thinning, striae, telangiectasia - prolonged use/under occlusion); HPA suppression (↓ cortisol - ↑ risk in children over large BSA); perioral dermatitis; folliculitis. Note: 0.025% cream/ointment typical; 0.01% oil for scalp; avoid on face (medium potency → atrophy risk); avoid tight occlusion long-term (greatly ↑ absorption); ophthalmic implant form is entirely different application than topical.

Mild topical corticosteroid (class 2 - mild/moderate; NOT the same potency as clobetasol propionate). MOA: glucocorticoid receptor agonist → ↓ inflammatory mediators → anti-inflammatory + antipruritic. Indications: mild inflammatory dermatoses - atopic eczema (face, flexures, children); seborrhoeic dermatitis; contact dermatitis. SE: mild skin atrophy (prolonged use); telangiectasia; HPA suppression (rare at standard dosing). CI: rosacea; perioral dermatitis; acne; infected skin (without antimicrobial cover). Note: do NOT confuse with clobetasol propionate (Dermovate - class 4, very potent) - clobetasone butyrate (Eumovate) is significantly less potent; suitable for facial use + children; 0.05% cream; use as step-down from more potent agents or for sensitive sites.

Mild-moderate topical corticosteroid (class 2). MOA: glucocorticoid receptor agonist → ↓ inflammatory cytokines → anti-inflammatory + antipruritic. Indications: mild-moderate inflammatory dermatoses - atopic eczema (face, flexures); contact dermatitis; seborrhoeic dermatitis; suitable for children + sensitive areas. SE: skin atrophy; telangiectasia; HPA suppression (rare with appropriate use); perioral dermatitis. Note: 0.05% cream/ointment; mild potency → face + flexures + children; lower risk of atrophy than medium/high-potency agents; good safety profile for maintenance therapy.

Synthetic delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) - oral cannabinoid. MOA: partial agonist at CB1 receptors (CNS - basal ganglia, brainstem emesis centres, hypothalamus) + CB2 receptors → antiemetic (↓ chemoreceptor trigger zone) + appetite stimulation (hypothalamic CB1 → ↑ appetite signalling). Indications: CINV (chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting) - refractory to conventional antiemetics; HIV/AIDS-associated anorexia and weight loss. SE: euphoria/dysphoria; dizziness; somnolence; confusion; anxiety/paranoia; tachycardia; orthostatic hypotension; dry mouth; abuse potential (Schedule 8 in Australia). Note: Schedule 8 controlled drug in Australia (significant psychoactive effects); second/third-line antiemetic (5-HT3 antagonists + NK1 antagonists preferred for CINV); CYP2C9/CYP3A4 substrate; food increases absorption; oral capsule or solution.

Standardised cannabis extract (THC:CBD approximately 1:1) - oromucosal spray. MOA: THC → partial CB1/CB2 agonist → analgesia + antispasmodic; CBD → multiple targets (TRPV1, 5-HT1A) → anti-inflammatory + modulates THC psychoactivity; combined → ↓ spasticity in MS via CNS cannabinoid signalling. Indications: spasticity due to multiple sclerosis - moderate-to-severe, refractory to other antispasticity agents (approved AU, UK, EU, Canada); investigational for neuropathic pain + cancer pain. SE: dizziness; somnolence; nausea; oropharyngeal pain; dysgeusia; euphoria; disorientation; fall risk; abuse potential (Schedule 8 in Australia). Note: oromucosal spray (buccal/sublingual) - NOT inhaled; each spray delivers 2.7 mg THC + 2.5 mg CBD; titrated to max 12 sprays/day; add-on to existing antispasticity therapy (baclofen, tizanidine); controlled drug - monthly prescribing limits.

Ergot alkaloid - acute migraine/cluster headache treatment. MOA: agonist at 5-HT1B/1D (cranial vasoconstriction - primary antimigraine mechanism), alpha-adrenoceptors, dopamine receptors; sustained cranial vasoconstriction → ↓ meningeal vasodilation. Indications: acute migraine (severe/prolonged attacks); cluster headache. SE: nausea/vomiting (often dose-limiting; caffeine co-formulation [Cafergot] reduces this + ↑ absorption); peripheral vasoconstriction (cold extremities, paraesthesia); ergotism (severe vasospasm/ischaemia - risk with overuse or CYP3A4 inhibitors); medication overuse headache (high rebound risk). CI: vascular disease (CAD, PVD, CVD), hypertension, hepatic/renal impairment; macrolide antibiotics + PI antivirals (CYP3A4 inhibitors → ergot toxicity); pregnancy (uterotonic - contraindicated). Note: largely replaced by triptans; limit to ≤2 days/week to avoid ergotism + rebound; caffeine in Cafergot ↑ ergotamine absorption ~40%.

Ergot derivative - acute migraine/cluster headache treatment. MOA: 5-HT1B/1D agonist (cranial vasoconstriction) + alpha-adrenoceptor agonist; less arterial vasoconstriction than ergotamine → more venous; weaker dopamine agonist → less nausea. Indications: moderate-severe acute migraine (IV/IM for status migrainosus in ED; intranasal spray for acute attacks); cluster headache.
