preclinical.summary: Lipid-soluble antioxidant protecting membrane polyunsaturated fats from peroxidation. Deficiency rare but causes haemolysis, ataxia, and neuropathy. Excess can interfere with vitamin K function.

preclinical.name: Michaelis-Menten kinetics
preclinical.summary: Enzyme reaction rate equals Vmax times S divided by (Km plus S). Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax and inversely reflects affinity. Lineweaver-Burk plot linearises this relationship.

preclinical.name: Competitive vs non-competitive inhibition
preclinical.summary: Competitive inhibitors raise Km without changing Vmax (overcome by more substrate). Non-competitive inhibitors lower Vmax without affecting Km. Uncompetitive inhibitors lower both.

preclinical.name: Gram stain
preclinical.summary: Differential stain using crystal violet, iodine, alcohol decoloriser, and safranin counterstain. Gram-positive cells retain crystal violet (purple) due to thick peptidoglycan; gram-negative are stained pink by safranin and have an outer membrane with LPS.

preclinical.name: Peptidoglycan
preclinical.summary: Mesh of N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid cross-linked by peptide bridges, forming the bacterial cell wall. Synthesis is targeted by beta-lactams (transpeptidase inhibition) and vancomycin (binds D-Ala-D-Ala).

preclinical.name: Lipopolysaccharide
preclinical.summary: Outer membrane component of gram-negative bacteria. Lipid A is the toxic moiety, signalling via TLR4 to trigger cytokine release; underpins gram-negative sepsis. Heat-stable, released on bacterial lysis.

preclinical.name: Exotoxin vs endotoxin
preclinical.summary: Exotoxins are secreted proteins (often AB toxins) from both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria; highly potent, antigenic, can be toxoided into vaccines. Endotoxin is LPS from gram-negatives, released on lysis, heat-stable.

preclinical.name: AB toxins
preclinical.summary: Bacterial toxins with two subunits: B binds host receptor, A is the active toxic component. Examples: diphtheria toxin (inhibits EF-2), cholera toxin (activates Gs), pertussis toxin (inactivates Gi), Shiga toxin (cleaves 28S rRNA).

preclinical.name: Superantigens
preclinical.summary: Toxins (e.g., TSST-1 from S. aureus, streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin A) that crosslink MHC II to TCR outside the antigen groove, causing massive non-specific T-cell activation and cytokine storm. Underlie toxic shock syndromes.

preclinical.name: Capsule
preclinical.summary: Polysaccharide layer outside the cell wall that impairs phagocytosis. Major virulence factor of encapsulated organisms: Strep pneumoniae, H. influenzae type b, N. meningitidis, Klebsiella, Salmonella, group B strep. Targeted by opsonising antibodies and conjugate vaccines.

preclinical.name: Biofilm
preclinical.summary: Sessile bacterial community in a self-produced polysaccharide matrix, often on prosthetics or catheters. Highly tolerant to antibiotics and immune clearance. Quorum sensing regulates biofilm formation.

preclinical.name: Quorum sensing
preclinical.summary: Bacterial cell-cell communication via diffusible signal molecules (autoinducers) whose concentration reflects population density. Triggers coordinated expression of virulence factors and biofilm formation above a threshold.

preclinical.name: Beta-lactamase
preclinical.summary: Enzymes that hydrolyse the beta-lactam ring of penicillins, cephalosporins, monobactams, or carbapenems. Categories include penicillinases, ESBLs (cefotaxime resistance), AmpC, and carbapenemases (e.g., NDM, KPC). Inhibited by clavulanate, tazobactam, sulbactam, avibactam.

preclinical.name: MRSA resistance mechanism
preclinical.summary: Methicillin resistance from acquisition of mecA gene encoding PBP2a, which has low affinity for beta-lactams. Treated with vancomycin, linezolid, daptomycin, or ceftaroline.

preclinical.name: Vancomycin resistance
preclinical.summary: Most often in enterococci. vanA and vanB operons replace D-Ala-D-Ala with D-Ala-D-Lac in peptidoglycan precursors, reducing vancomycin affinity 1000-fold. Treated with linezolid or daptomycin.

preclinical.name: Efflux pumps
preclinical.summary: Membrane transporters that actively expel antibiotics, contributing to resistance to tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, and macrolides. Often broad-spectrum, can be plasmid-encoded.

preclinical.name: Plasmid
preclinical.summary: Extrachromosomal, usually circular DNA that replicates independently. Often carries resistance genes (R plasmids) and virulence factors. Transferred between bacteria by conjugation.

preclinical.name: Bacterial conjugation
preclinical.summary: Cell-to-cell transfer of DNA (typically plasmids) via a sex pilus. Major route of resistance gene spread, especially between gram-negatives.

preclinical.name: Transformation
preclinical.summary: Uptake of naked DNA from the environment. Naturally competent species include Strep pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Neisseria. Important for antigenic variation and resistance acquisition.

preclinical.name: Transduction
preclinical.summary: Bacteriophage-mediated transfer of bacterial DNA. Generalised transduction packages random fragments; specialised transduction transfers genes flanking the prophage integration site. Source of some toxin genes (diphtheria, cholera).

preclinical.name: Anaerobic bacteria
preclinical.summary: Cannot grow in normal atmospheric oxygen. Examples include Bacteroides fragilis (gut), Clostridium species, Fusobacterium, Actinomyces. Often cause polymicrobial abscesses; metronidazole and carbapenems have good activity.

preclinical.name: Atypical bacteria
preclinical.summary: Organisms that do not Gram stain reliably or grow on standard media: Mycoplasma (no cell wall), Chlamydia (obligate intracellular), Legionella, Coxiella. Treated with macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones rather than beta-lactams.

preclinical.name: Acid-fast staining
preclinical.summary: Mycolic acid in mycobacterial cell walls retains carbol fuchsin despite acid-alcohol washing. Used for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, atypical mycobacteria, and Nocardia (partially acid-fast).

preclinical.name: Spore-forming bacteria
preclinical.summary: Bacillus and Clostridium species form heat-resistant endospores that survive disinfection. Spores germinate when conditions improve, causing disease (anthrax, tetanus, botulism, C. difficile, gas gangrene).

preclinical.name: Obligate intracellular bacteria
preclinical.summary: Cannot make their own ATP or grow on artificial media. Examples: Chlamydia (uses host ATP), Rickettsia, Coxiella, Ehrlichia. Diagnosed serologically or by PCR.

preclinical.name: Pneumonia pathogens by setting
preclinical.summary: CAP: Strep pneumoniae most common; atypicals (Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydophila) in younger adults. HAP/VAP: Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, Acinetobacter, MRSA. Aspiration: anaerobes plus oral flora.

preclinical.name: UTI pathogens
preclinical.summary: E. coli causes about 80 percent of community UTIs. Others: Staph saprophyticus (young women), Klebsiella, Proteus (struvite stones, urea splitter), Enterococcus, and resistant organisms in healthcare-associated infection.

preclinical.name: Meningitis pathogens by age
preclinical.summary: Neonates: GBS, E. coli, Listeria. Children and young adults: N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae. Older adults: S. pneumoniae, Listeria. Immunocompromised: Cryptococcus, Listeria, gram-negatives.

preclinical.name: GI pathogens with bloody diarrhoea
preclinical.summary: Shigella, EHEC (O157:H7, Shiga toxin, risk of HUS), Salmonella, Campylobacter, Entamoeba histolytica, C. difficile (toxin-mediated colitis). Differs from watery diarrhoea pathogens (Vibrio, ETEC, viruses).

preclinical.name: Sexually transmitted pathogens
preclinical.summary: Bacteria: Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Treponema pallidum, Haemophilus ducreyi. Viruses: HIV, HSV, HPV, hepatitis B. Protozoa: Trichomonas. Parasites: Phthirus pubis.

preclinical.name: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
preclinical.summary: Acid-fast, aerobic, slow-growing rod. Inhaled, contained in granulomas. Latent infection in about a quarter of the world. Treatment: RIPE (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) intensive phase then continuation.

preclinical.name: Candida species
preclinical.summary: Commensal yeast, opportunistic in immunosuppression, diabetes, broad-spectrum antibiotics, indwelling lines. Forms pseudohyphae on tissue. Treated with azoles (mucosal) or echinocandins (invasive).

preclinical.name: Aspergillus species
preclinical.summary: Septate, acute-angle branching mould. Causes invasive aspergillosis in neutropenic patients, ABPA in asthma and cystic fibrosis, and aspergilloma in pre-existing cavities. Treated with voriconazole, isavuconazole, or amphotericin.

preclinical.name: Pneumocystis jirovecii
preclinical.summary: Atypical fungus causing pneumonia in HIV (CD4 below 200) and other immunosuppressed patients. Bilateral interstitial infiltrates and severe hypoxaemia. Treated with high-dose cotrimoxazole, plus steroids if PaO2 below 70 mmHg.

preclinical.name: Plasmodium species
preclinical.summary: Protozoa transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes. P. falciparum causes severe disease; P. vivax and ovale have dormant liver hypnozoites requiring primaquine. Cyclical fevers, haemolytic anaemia, splenomegaly.

preclinical.name: Influenza virus
preclinical.summary: Segmented negative-sense RNA orthomyxovirus. Surface haemagglutinin and neuraminidase drive antigenic drift (point mutation, seasonal) and shift (reassortment, pandemic). Treated with oseltamivir within 48 hours of onset.

preclinical.name: Herpes virus family
preclinical.summary: Double-stranded DNA viruses establishing lifelong latency. Includes HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, EBV, CMV, HHV-6, HHV-8 (Kaposi). Reactivation common in immunosuppression. Aciclovir for HSV/VZV; ganciclovir for CMV.

preclinical.name: HIV virology
preclinical.summary: Retrovirus with two single-stranded RNA copies, reverse transcriptase, integrase, and protease. Binds CD4 plus CCR5 (early) or CXCR4 (late). Treated with combination ART targeting multiple steps in the replication cycle.

preclinical.name: Hepatitis virus comparison
preclinical.summary: HepA, E: faecal-oral, self-limited (E severe in pregnancy). HepB: DNA, blood/sexual/vertical, can be chronic, oncogenic. HepC: RNA, blood, often chronic, curable with direct-acting antivirals. HepD: requires HepB coinfection.

preclinical.name: Sterilisation vs disinfection
preclinical.summary: Sterilisation kills all microbes including spores (autoclave, ethylene oxide, gamma radiation). Disinfection reduces pathogen burden on inanimate surfaces but may not kill spores (bleach, alcohol, glutaraldehyde). Antisepsis applies to living tissue.

preclinical.name: Innate immunity
preclinical.summary: Non-specific, rapid (minutes to hours), no memory. Includes barriers, phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages), NK cells, complement, and pattern recognition receptors. Recognises PAMPs and DAMPs.

preclinical.name: Adaptive immunity
preclinical.summary: Specific, slower (days), with memory. Includes T cells (cellular) and B cells/antibodies (humoral). Diversity from V(D)J recombination. Memory generates faster, larger secondary responses on re-exposure.

preclinical.name: Pattern recognition receptors
preclinical.summary: Recognise conserved microbial patterns. Toll-like receptors are surface or endosomal (e.g., TLR4 binds LPS, TLR3 binds dsRNA). Activation drives cytokine production via NF-kB and IRF pathways.

preclinical.name: MHC class I
preclinical.summary: Expressed on all nucleated cells. Presents endogenous (cytoplasmic) peptides to CD8 T cells via TAP-loaded proteasomal peptides. Down-regulation by tumours or viruses triggers NK cell killing (missing self).

preclinical.name: MHC class II
preclinical.summary: Expressed on professional antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells). Presents exogenous (endosomal) peptides to CD4 T cells. Defects cause bare lymphocyte syndrome.

preclinical.name: T cell subsets
preclinical.summary: CD4 helpers: Th1 (IFN-gamma, intracellular pathogens), Th2 (IL-4/5/13, parasites and allergy), Th17 (IL-17, mucosal bacteria and fungi), Treg (immune tolerance via TGF-beta, IL-10). CD8 cytotoxic: kill infected/transformed cells via perforin and granzyme.

preclinical.name: B cell activation
preclinical.summary: BCR binds antigen, internalises and presents on MHC II to a CD4 T helper, which provides CD40L and cytokines. Drives class switching, somatic hypermutation, and differentiation into plasma cells or memory B cells.

preclinical.name: Immunoglobulin classes
preclinical.summary: IgG (most abundant, crosses placenta, opsonisation), IgM (first responder, pentamer, complement activator), IgA (mucosal, dimer with J chain), IgE (allergy, parasites, mast cell binding), IgD (B cell receptor).

preclinical.name: Complement classical pathway
preclinical.summary: Triggered by antibody-antigen complexes (IgG or IgM) binding C1. Cleaves C4 then C2 to form C3 convertase. Leads to opsonisation (C3b), inflammation (C3a, C5a), and MAC formation (C5b-9).

preclinical.name: Complement alternative pathway
preclinical.summary: Spontaneous C3 hydrolysis on microbial surfaces, amplified in the absence of host regulators. Important early innate defence against gram-negative bacteria.

preclinical.name: Complement lectin pathway
preclinical.summary: Mannose-binding lectin recognises microbial mannose, activates MASP enzymes that cleave C4 and C2, joining the classical pathway. MBL deficiency increases susceptibility to encapsulated organisms.

preclinical.name: Cytokines overview
preclinical.summary: IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha: acute phase, fever. IL-2: T cell growth. IL-4, IL-13: Th2/IgE. IL-5: eosinophils. IL-10: anti-inflammatory. IFN-alpha/beta: antiviral. IFN-gamma: macrophage activation, intracellular pathogens.

preclinical.name: Hypersensitivity type I
preclinical.summary: IgE-mediated mast cell and basophil degranulation. Allergens crosslink surface IgE, releasing histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes. Onset minutes. Anaphylaxis, allergic rhinitis, asthma.

preclinical.name: Hypersensitivity type II
preclinical.summary: IgG or IgM antibodies bind cell-surface antigens, causing complement activation, opsonisation, or ADCC. Examples: autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, transfusion reactions, Goodpasture, myasthenia gravis, Graves.

preclinical.name: Hypersensitivity type III
preclinical.summary: Antibody-antigen complexes deposit in vessels and tissues, activating complement and inflammation. Examples: serum sickness, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, SLE, polyarteritis nodosa.

preclinical.name: Hypersensitivity type IV
preclinical.summary: T cell-mediated, peaks 48 to 72 hours. CD4 (granulomas in TB, contact dermatitis) and CD8 (graft rejection, Stevens-Johnson, drug reactions). No antibody involved.

preclinical.name: Central tolerance
preclinical.summary: Removes self-reactive lymphocytes during development. T cells in thymus undergo positive selection (recognise self MHC) and negative selection (delete strongly self-reactive). AIRE drives ectopic self-antigen expression; defect causes APECED.

preclinical.name: Peripheral tolerance
preclinical.summary: Controls self-reactive lymphocytes that escape thymic selection. Mechanisms: anergy (signal 1 without signal 2), Treg suppression, activation-induced cell death, immune privilege (eye, brain).

preclinical.name: Antigen presentation
preclinical.summary: Dendritic cells take up antigen peripherally, mature, migrate to draining lymph nodes, and present to naive T cells with co-stimulation (CD80/86 to CD28). Without signal 2, T cells become anergic.

preclinical.name: Vaccine types
preclinical.summary: Live attenuated (MMR, varicella, BCG): strong, durable, but contraindicated in pregnancy and severe immunosuppression. Inactivated (rabies, polio Salk). Subunit (HepB, HPV). Toxoid (diphtheria, tetanus). Conjugate (Hib, Men-C). mRNA (COVID-19).

preclinical.name: Natural killer cells
preclinical.summary: Innate lymphocytes that kill virus-infected and tumour cells lacking MHC I (missing self). Release perforin and granzyme; produce IFN-gamma. Regulated by activating and inhibitory KIR receptors.

preclinical.name: Acute phase response
preclinical.summary: Hepatic production of acute phase proteins (CRP, fibrinogen, ferritin, hepcidin) and negative reactants (albumin, transferrin) driven by IL-6, IL-1, and TNF-alpha. Underlies the systemic features of inflammation.

preclinical.name: Cell injury
preclinical.summary: Sequence: reversible (cell swelling, fatty change) progresses to irreversible (membrane damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, lysosomal leak) and cell death. Final common pathways involve ATP depletion, Ca2+ accumulation, ROS, and membrane damage.

preclinical.name: Coagulative necrosis
preclinical.summary: Architecture preserved with ghost outlines for days. Caused by ischaemia in solid organs (heart, kidney, spleen). Denatured proteins resist proteolysis until inflammatory cells clear the debris.

preclinical.name: Liquefactive necrosis
preclinical.summary: Tissue dissolves into viscous fluid. Seen in brain infarction (no dense stroma) and bacterial abscesses (neutrophil enzymes). Forms a cyst-like cavity in the brain.

preclinical.name: Caseous necrosis
preclinical.summary: Cheese-like, amorphous granular debris surrounded by granulomatous inflammation. Classic for tuberculosis but also seen in fungal infections.

preclinical.name: Fat necrosis
preclinical.summary: Lipase from pancreatitis breaks down peri-pancreatic fat; free fatty acids saponify with calcium (chalky white deposits). Traumatic fat necrosis (breast, after trauma) is a non-enzymatic variant.

preclinical.name: Fibrinoid necrosis
preclinical.summary: Bright eosinophilic deposition of fibrin and immune complexes in vessel walls. Seen in malignant hypertension, vasculitis, and pre-eclampsia.

preclinical.name: Gangrenous necrosis
preclinical.summary: Necrosis of a limb. Dry: coagulative, ischaemic. Wet: liquefactive plus infection, foul-smelling. Gas gangrene: Clostridial myonecrosis with gas production.

preclinical.name: Apoptosis
preclinical.summary: Programmed cell death. Intrinsic pathway via mitochondrial cytochrome c release and caspase-9 (response to DNA damage, growth factor withdrawal); extrinsic via Fas/TNF receptors and caspase-8. Cells shrink, nuclei fragment, no inflammation.

preclinical.name: Necroptosis
preclinical.summary: Programmed cell death with necrotic morphology. Mediated by RIP1, RIP3, and MLKL. Important when apoptosis is blocked (e.g., viral infection). Releases DAMPs and triggers inflammation.

preclinical.name: Pyroptosis
preclinical.summary: Inflammasome-mediated cell death driven by caspase-1 cleaving gasdermin D. Releases IL-1 beta and IL-18. Important in defending against intracellular bacteria.

preclinical.name: Ferroptosis
preclinical.summary: Iron-dependent regulated cell death from lipid peroxidation. Inhibited by GPX4 and glutathione. Implicated in neurodegeneration, ischaemia-reperfusion, and cancer therapy responses.

preclinical.name: Acute inflammation
preclinical.summary: Rapid response (minutes to days) with vasodilation, increased permeability, and neutrophil emigration. Cardinal signs: rubor, tumour, calor, dolor, functio laesa. Mediated by histamine, bradykinin, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, chemokines.

preclinical.name: Chronic inflammation
preclinical.summary: Persistent inflammation with macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and tissue destruction plus repair (fibrosis, angiogenesis). Caused by persistent infection, autoimmunity, or chronic exposure to a toxic agent.

preclinical.name: Granuloma
preclinical.summary: Focal collection of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells) with multinucleated giant cells, sometimes lymphocytes and central necrosis. Caseating: TB, fungal. Non-caseating: sarcoidosis, Crohn, foreign body, berylliosis.

preclinical.name: Leukocyte extravasation
preclinical.summary: Steps: margination, rolling (selectins), firm adhesion (integrins binding ICAM/VCAM), transmigration through endothelium, chemotaxis through tissue. LAD I (CD18 deficiency) impairs firm adhesion.

preclinical.name: Resolution of inflammation
preclinical.summary: Outcomes: complete resolution (mild injury, intact stroma), scarring (severe injury, fibrosis), abscess formation, or progression to chronic inflammation. Specialised pro-resolving mediators (lipoxins, resolvins) actively terminate inflammation.

preclinical.name: Wound healing
preclinical.summary: Haemostasis (immediate), inflammation (1 to 3 days), proliferation (granulation tissue, days to weeks), remodelling (weeks to months, type III collagen replaced by type I). Tensile strength reaches about 80 percent by 3 months.

preclinical.name: Hyperplasia
preclinical.summary: Increase in cell number. Physiologic (hormonal: uterus in pregnancy; compensatory: liver after partial hepatectomy) or pathologic (endometrial hyperplasia from unopposed oestrogen). Some pathologic hyperplasias predispose to neoplasia.

preclinical.name: Hypertrophy
preclinical.summary: Increase in cell size, often in tissues with limited proliferative capacity (cardiac, skeletal muscle). Physiologic (exercise) or pathologic (hypertensive heart). Often coexists with hyperplasia in tissues that can divide.

preclinical.name: Atrophy
preclinical.summary: Decrease in cell size or number. Causes: disuse, denervation, loss of hormonal stimulation, reduced blood flow, ageing, pressure, poor nutrition. Involves ubiquitin-proteasome and autophagy pathways.

preclinical.name: Metaplasia
preclinical.summary: Reversible replacement of one differentiated cell type with another. Examples: squamous metaplasia of bronchial epithelium in smokers, columnar metaplasia in Barrett oesophagus. May predispose to dysplasia and cancer.

preclinical.name: Dysplasia
preclinical.summary: Disordered growth with cellular atypia and architectural abnormality, but confined to the epithelium. Reversible early; high-grade dysplasia frequently progresses to invasive cancer.

preclinical.name: Neoplasia
preclinical.summary: Autonomous, clonal cell growth. Benign tumours are well-differentiated, encapsulated, slow-growing, non-invasive. Malignant tumours show anaplasia, invasion, and metastasis. Hallmarks include sustained proliferation, evasion of apoptosis, angiogenesis.

preclinical.name: Hallmarks of cancer
preclinical.summary: Hanahan and Weinberg framework: sustained proliferation, evasion of growth suppressors, resisting cell death, replicative immortality, angiogenesis, invasion and metastasis. Later additions: deregulated metabolism, evading immune destruction, genome instability, tumour-promoting inflammation.

preclinical.name: Tumour markers basics
preclinical.summary: AFP: hepatocellular and yolk sac. CEA: colorectal, monitoring. CA 19-9: pancreatic. CA 125: ovarian. PSA: prostate. hCG: gestational trophoblastic, testicular. Calcitonin: medullary thyroid. Most are imperfectly sensitive or specific; mainly used for monitoring.

preclinical.name: Apoptosis vs necrosis
preclinical.summary: Apoptosis: programmed, ATP-dependent, single cells, intact membranes, no inflammation, cell shrinkage. Necrosis: pathologic, cell swelling, membrane rupture, content release, marked inflammation.

preclinical.name: Reperfusion injury
preclinical.summary: Paradoxical damage when blood flow returns to ischaemic tissue. Reactive oxygen species, calcium overload, mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening, and complement activation worsen injury beyond ischaemia alone.

preclinical.name: Amyloid
preclinical.summary: Misfolded protein aggregates with beta-pleated sheet structure that show apple-green birefringence under polarised light with Congo red. AL (light chain, myeloma), AA (chronic inflammation), ATTR (transthyretin, familial or wild-type cardiac).

preclinical.name: Calcification (dystrophic vs metastatic)
preclinical.summary: Dystrophic: in damaged or necrotic tissue with normal calcium (atherosclerosis, old TB granulomas). Metastatic: in normal tissue due to hypercalcaemia (hyperparathyroidism, chronic kidney disease, vitamin D toxicity).

preclinical.name: Atherosclerosis pathogenesis
preclinical.summary: Endothelial injury, LDL infiltration and oxidation, macrophage uptake forming foam cells, smooth muscle migration, fibrous cap formation. Plaque rupture exposes thrombogenic core, triggering acute thrombotic events.

preclinical.name: Hypoxia vs ischaemia
preclinical.summary: Hypoxia is reduced oxygen delivery to tissue (various causes including anaemia, low PaO2). Ischaemia is reduced blood flow, which also impairs delivery of substrates and removal of waste; tends to cause faster injury than pure hypoxia.

preclinical.name: Free radicals and oxidative stress
preclinical.summary: Reactive oxygen species (superoxide, H2O2, hydroxyl radical) damage lipids, proteins, and DNA. Generated by mitochondria, neutrophils, ionising radiation, reperfusion. Defences: superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione, vitamins C and E.

preclinical.name: Oedema mechanisms
preclinical.summary: Causes per Starling: increased hydrostatic pressure (heart failure, venous obstruction), decreased oncotic pressure (nephrotic syndrome, liver disease, malnutrition), lymphatic obstruction (filariasis, postsurgical), increased capillary permeability (inflammation), sodium retention.

preclinical.name: Shock classification
preclinical.summary: Hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, obstructive (PE, tamponade, tension pneumothorax), distributive (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic). Pre-load, contractility, after-load, and SVR profiles distinguish them and guide management.

preclinical.name: Embolism types
preclinical.summary: Thromboembolic (most common), fat (long bone fracture, 1 to 3 days later), air (line insertion, decompression), amniotic fluid (peripartum, DIC), septic, tumour, foreign body. Site of impact depends on origin and circulation.

preclinical.name: Thrombus vs clot
preclinical.summary: Thrombus forms in flowing blood, laminated (lines of Zahn), attached to vessel wall. Postmortem clot is gelatinous, unlayered, not attached. Distinction useful at autopsy.

preclinical.name: Pharmacokinetics
preclinical.summary: What the body does to the drug: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion. Determines plasma concentration over time. Quantitative parameters include bioavailability, volume of distribution, clearance, and half-life.

preclinical.name: Pharmacodynamics
preclinical.summary: What the drug does to the body: relationship between drug concentration and effect. Includes potency (EC50), efficacy (Emax), receptor binding kinetics, and tolerance.

preclinical.name: Bioavailability
preclinical.summary: Fraction of administered drug reaching systemic circulation in unchanged form. IV is 1.0 by definition; oral is reduced by incomplete absorption and first-pass metabolism. Determined by area under the curve compared to IV.

preclinical.name: First-pass metabolism
preclinical.summary: Metabolism in the gut wall and liver before a drug reaches the systemic circulation. Reduces oral bioavailability (e.g., morphine, propranolol, GTN). Bypassed by IV, sublingual, transdermal, and rectal routes.

preclinical.name: Volume of distribution
preclinical.summary: Apparent volume into which a drug appears to distribute, calculated as dose divided by initial plasma concentration. Low Vd (about 5 L): plasma-bound (warfarin). High Vd: tissue-bound (digoxin, amiodarone). Determines loading dose.

preclinical.name: Drug clearance
preclinical.summary: Volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time. Determined by organ blood flow and extraction ratio. Determines maintenance dose at steady state. Renal clearance combines filtration, secretion, and reabsorption.

preclinical.name: Half-life
preclinical.summary: Time for plasma concentration to fall by half. Equal to 0.693 times Vd divided by clearance. Steady state is reached in about 4 to 5 half-lives.

preclinical.name: Zero vs first-order kinetics
preclinical.summary: First-order: constant fraction eliminated per unit time (most drugs). Zero-order: constant amount eliminated per unit time, occurs when enzymes are saturated (alcohol, high-dose phenytoin, high-dose aspirin).

preclinical.name: Loading dose vs maintenance dose
preclinical.summary: Loading dose equals target concentration times Vd; used to rapidly achieve therapeutic levels. Maintenance dose equals target concentration times clearance; used to balance ongoing elimination.

preclinical.name: Phase I metabolism
preclinical.summary: Functionalisation reactions (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis), mostly by CYP450 enzymes. Adds or unmasks a functional group, often producing an active or toxic metabolite. CYP3A4 metabolises the majority of drugs.

preclinical.name: Phase II metabolism
preclinical.summary: Conjugation reactions (glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, glutathione conjugation) producing polar, water-soluble metabolites for excretion. Usually inactivates the drug; UGT mutations underlie Gilbert's syndrome.

preclinical.name: CYP450 induction and inhibition
preclinical.summary: Inducers (rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, St John's wort, smoking) increase metabolism and lower levels. Inhibitors (grapefruit juice, macrolides, azoles, ritonavir) raise levels. Important source of drug-drug interactions.

preclinical.name: Therapeutic index
preclinical.summary: Ratio of toxic dose 50 to effective dose 50. Narrow therapeutic index drugs (warfarin, digoxin, lithium, theophylline, phenytoin, aminoglycosides) require monitoring. Wider index is safer.

preclinical.name: Agonist vs antagonist
preclinical.summary: Agonist binds and activates receptor (full or partial). Antagonist binds without activating, blocking endogenous ligand. Competitive antagonists shift dose-response right (overcome by more agonist); non-competitive lower maximum effect.

preclinical.name: Partial agonist
preclinical.summary: Binds and activates the receptor but with submaximal efficacy regardless of dose. In the presence of a full agonist, behaves like an antagonist. Examples: buprenorphine (mu opioid), aripiprazole (D2), pindolol (beta).

preclinical.name: Inverse agonist
preclinical.summary: Binds and reduces receptor activity below baseline (suppresses constitutive activity). Distinct from a neutral antagonist, which only blocks an agonist. Examples: some H1 antihistamines, naloxone in some preparations.

preclinical.name: Tachyphylaxis
preclinical.summary: Rapid loss of drug effect with repeated dosing over short intervals, often via receptor desensitisation or transmitter depletion. Examples: nitrates, sympathomimetics, repeated nicotine.

preclinical.name: G protein-coupled receptors
preclinical.summary: Seven-transmembrane receptors coupled to heterotrimeric G proteins. Gs: increases cAMP via adenylate cyclase. Gi: decreases cAMP. Gq: activates phospholipase C, raises IP3 and DAG, Ca2+ release. Most drug targets in clinical use.

preclinical.name: Ion channel receptors
preclinical.summary: Ligand binding directly opens an ion pore. Examples: nicotinic acetylcholine, GABA-A, glycine, NMDA, 5-HT3. Rapid effect (milliseconds), important in neurotransmission.

preclinical.name: Tyrosine kinase receptors
preclinical.summary: Single-transmembrane receptors that dimerise on ligand binding and autophosphorylate. Activate Ras-MAPK and PI3K-Akt pathways. Examples: insulin, EGFR, HER2, VEGFR. Targeted by many oncology drugs ending in -tinib.

preclinical.name: Nuclear receptors
preclinical.summary: Intracellular receptors that bind lipid-soluble ligands (steroids, thyroid hormone, vitamin D, retinoids) and act as transcription factors. Slow onset (hours), durable effects.

preclinical.name: Drug receptor desensitisation
preclinical.summary: Reduction in receptor responsiveness with continued exposure. Mechanisms: receptor phosphorylation (uncoupling), internalisation, down-regulation. Underlies tolerance and tachyphylaxis.

preclinical.name: Therapeutic drug monitoring
preclinical.summary: Measuring drug concentrations to optimise dosing. Useful for narrow-index drugs (vancomycin, gentamicin, digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, tacrolimus). Timing matters: trough levels typically guide dosing.

preclinical.name: Receptor reserve
preclinical.summary: When maximal response occurs with less than full receptor occupancy. Means EC50 is lower than Kd. Provides amplification and resilience to partial receptor loss.

preclinical.name: Steady state concentration
preclinical.summary: Reached when rate of drug input equals rate of elimination, typically after 4 to 5 half-lives. Independent of dosing interval (only depends on average input rate and clearance).

preclinical.name: Renal vs hepatic elimination
preclinical.summary: Drug clearance route influences dosing in organ failure. Renally cleared drugs (aminoglycosides, digoxin, lithium) need adjustment in CKD. Hepatically cleared drugs may need adjustment in liver disease, especially those with high extraction ratio.

preclinical.name: Drug-drug interactions
preclinical.summary: Pharmacokinetic (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion) or pharmacodynamic (additive, synergistic, antagonistic). High-yield mechanisms: CYP3A4 inhibition, P-glycoprotein, protein binding displacement, serotonin syndrome with combined serotonergics.

preclinical.name: Cholinergic receptors
preclinical.summary: Nicotinic (ion channel, autonomic ganglia, NMJ, CNS) and muscarinic (GPCR, M1 to M5). M1 CNS, M2 cardiac (Gi, slows HR), M3 smooth muscle and glands (Gq). Atropine blocks all muscarinic; pancuronium blocks Nm.

preclinical.name: Adrenergic receptors
preclinical.summary: Alpha-1 (Gq, vasoconstriction, pupillary dilation), alpha-2 (Gi, presynaptic inhibition, CNS sedation), beta-1 (Gs, cardiac, renin release), beta-2 (Gs, bronchodilation, vasodilation), beta-3 (Gs, lipolysis, bladder relaxation).

preclinical.name: Loading dose adjustment
preclinical.summary: Loading dose depends on Vd, not on clearance. Therefore not reduced for renal or hepatic failure unless Vd is altered. Maintenance dose, in contrast, is reduced when clearance falls.

preclinical.name: Circle of Willis
preclinical.summary: Anastomotic ring at the base of the brain formed by anterior communicating, anterior cerebral, internal carotid, posterior communicating, and posterior cerebral arteries. Provides collateral flow; site of berry aneurysms (often anterior communicating).

preclinical.name: Brachial plexus
preclinical.summary: C5 to T1 nerve roots forming trunks (upper, middle, lower), divisions, cords (lateral, posterior, medial), and terminal branches (musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median, ulnar). Erb's palsy: upper trunk. Klumpke: lower trunk.

preclinical.name: Lumbosacral plexus
preclinical.summary: Lumbar plexus (L1 to L4): iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, genitofemoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, femoral, obturator. Sacral plexus (L4 to S4): sciatic (tibial and common peroneal), superior and inferior gluteal, pudendal.

preclinical.name: Cranial nerves
preclinical.summary: I olfactory, II optic, III oculomotor, IV trochlear (superior oblique), V trigeminal, VI abducens (lateral rectus), VII facial, VIII vestibulocochlear, IX glossopharyngeal, X vagus, XI accessory (SCM, trapezius), XII hypoglossal (tongue).

preclinical.name: Vagus nerve
preclinical.summary: Mixed nerve with extensive thoracoabdominal distribution. Parasympathetic to heart, lungs, GI to splenic flexure. Sensory to larynx, pharynx, and external auditory canal. Motor to most pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles.

preclinical.name: Hepatic portal vein
preclinical.summary: Drains GI tract, spleen, pancreas, and gallbladder to liver. Formed by union of splenic and superior mesenteric veins. Portal hypertension causes oesophageal varices, caput medusae, anorectal varices via portosystemic anastomoses.

preclinical.name: Coronary artery anatomy
preclinical.summary: Right coronary (RCA): RV, inferior LV (in right-dominant 85 percent), AV node, SA node. Left coronary: LAD (anterior LV, septum, apex), circumflex (lateral LV). Dominance is defined by which artery gives the posterior descending.

preclinical.name: Bronchopulmonary segments
preclinical.summary: Functional and surgical lung subdivisions, each with its own segmental bronchus and artery (vein lies between segments). Right lung has 10 segments, left has 8 to 10.

preclinical.name: Mediastinum
preclinical.summary: Region between the lungs. Superior: thymus, great vessels, trachea, oesophagus. Inferior divided into anterior (thymus), middle (heart, pericardium), posterior (oesophagus, descending aorta, vagi, thoracic duct, azygos).

preclinical.name: Diaphragm openings
preclinical.summary: T8: IVC and right phrenic nerve. T10: oesophagus and vagi. T12: aorta, thoracic duct, azygos vein. Mnemonic: I 8 (ate) 10 EGGS at 12.

preclinical.name: Femoral triangle
preclinical.summary: Boundaries: inguinal ligament (superior), sartorius (lateral), adductor longus (medial). Contents from lateral to medial: femoral nerve, artery, vein, empty space, lymphatics (NAVEL).

preclinical.name: Inguinal canal
preclinical.summary: Oblique passage through the lower abdominal wall. Contains spermatic cord (men) or round ligament (women). Direct hernias: medial to inferior epigastric vessels through Hesselbach's triangle. Indirect hernias: lateral, through deep ring.

preclinical.name: Carpal tunnel
preclinical.summary: Passage on the volar wrist bounded by carpal bones (floor) and flexor retinaculum (roof). Transmits the median nerve and nine flexor tendons (FDS x4, FDP x4, FPL). Compression causes carpal tunnel syndrome.

preclinical.name: Anatomical snuffbox
preclinical.summary: Triangular hollow on the radial wrist bounded by APL/EPB (lateral) and EPL (medial). Contains the radial artery; floor is the scaphoid (tenderness suggests scaphoid fracture).

preclinical.name: Recurrent laryngeal nerves
preclinical.summary: Branches of the vagus that supply intrinsic laryngeal muscles (except cricothyroid). Left hooks around the aortic arch (vulnerable in thoracic surgery, aortic aneurysm, mediastinal disease). Right hooks around the right subclavian.

preclinical.name: Thoracic duct
preclinical.summary: Largest lymphatic channel. Begins at cisterna chyli, ascends through aortic hiatus, drains into the left subclavian-internal jugular junction. Carries most body lymph; injury causes chylothorax.

preclinical.name: Hesselbach's triangle
preclinical.summary: Boundaries: rectus abdominis (medial), inferior epigastric vessels (lateral), inguinal ligament (inferior). Site of direct inguinal hernias.

preclinical.name: Anatomy of the eye
preclinical.summary: Three layers: outer (sclera and cornea), middle uvea (iris, ciliary body, choroid), inner retina. Anterior segment filled with aqueous humour; posterior with vitreous. Optic disc lacks photoreceptors (blind spot).

preclinical.name: Pituitary anatomy
preclinical.summary: Two lobes: anterior (adenohypophysis, from Rathke's pouch, ectoderm) secretes GH, prolactin, ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH; posterior (neurohypophysis, neural origin) stores ADH and oxytocin made in hypothalamus.

preclinical.name: Adrenal anatomy
preclinical.summary: Cortex (mesoderm) three zones: glomerulosa (aldosterone), fasciculata (cortisol), reticularis (androgens). Medulla (neural crest) chromaffin cells make catecholamines. GFR/ACTH+ACTH+ blood supply from three arteries; drained by central vein.

preclinical.name: Spinal cord blood supply
preclinical.summary: Anterior spinal artery supplies anterior two-thirds (motor, spinothalamic); two posterior spinal arteries supply posterior columns. Artery of Adamkiewicz is the dominant feeder to lower cord; vulnerable in aortic surgery.

preclinical.name: Peritoneal cavity
preclinical.summary: Intraperitoneal organs: stomach, jejunum, ileum, transverse colon, sigmoid, spleen, liver. Retroperitoneal (SAD PUCKER): suprarenal, aorta, duodenum (2nd to 4th), pancreas (except tail), ureters, colon (ascending/descending), kidneys, oesophagus (lower), rectum.

preclinical.name: Foregut, midgut, hindgut
preclinical.summary: Foregut (coeliac trunk): oesophagus to mid-duodenum. Midgut (SMA): mid-duodenum to two-thirds of transverse colon. Hindgut (IMA): distal transverse colon to upper anal canal. Pain referral matches embryologic origin.

preclinical.name: Epithelium types
preclinical.summary: Classified by layers (simple, stratified, pseudostratified) and shape (squamous, cuboidal, columnar). Simple squamous: alveoli, endothelium. Pseudostratified columnar ciliated: airway. Stratified squamous: skin, oesophagus.

preclinical.name: Connective tissue overview
preclinical.summary: Cells (fibroblasts, adipocytes, mast cells, macrophages) plus extracellular matrix (collagen, elastin, ground substance). Types: loose, dense regular (tendons), dense irregular (dermis), adipose, cartilage, bone, blood.

preclinical.name: Collagen types
preclinical.summary: Type I: bone, tendon, skin, late wound healing. Type II: cartilage, vitreous, nucleus pulposus. Type III: granulation tissue, reticulin, blood vessels. Type IV: basement membrane. Defects: osteogenesis imperfecta (I), Ehlers-Danlos (III, V).

preclinical.name: Skeletal muscle structure
preclinical.summary: Multinucleated fibres with peripheral nuclei. Sarcomere unit between Z-discs contains thin (actin) and thick (myosin) filaments. Striations from regular thick-thin overlap. T-tubules invaginate to deliver depolarisation to myofibrils.

preclinical.name: Cardiac muscle structure
preclinical.summary: Branched, striated, with central nuclei and intercalated discs containing gap junctions (electrical coupling) and desmosomes (mechanical). Functional syncytium allows coordinated contraction.

preclinical.name: Smooth muscle structure
preclinical.summary: Spindle-shaped, single central nucleus, no striations. Contraction triggered by Ca2+-calmodulin activation of myosin light chain kinase. Found in viscera and vessel walls.

preclinical.name: Goblet cells
preclinical.summary: Mucin-secreting cells of the respiratory and GI epithelium. Decreased in chronic smoke damage of small airways; increased in chronic bronchitis.

preclinical.name: Nephron segments
preclinical.summary: Glomerulus (filtration), PCT (bulk reabsorption, brush border), loop of Henle (countercurrent), DCT (calcium handling, NaCl reabsorption), collecting duct (final water and Na+ handling, principal and intercalated cells).

preclinical.name: Hepatocyte lobule
preclinical.summary: Hexagonal arrangement around a central vein with portal triads (hepatic artery, portal vein, bile duct) at corners. Zone 1 (periportal): O2-rich, gluconeogenesis. Zone 3 (centrilobular): drug metabolism, vulnerable to ischaemia.

preclinical.name: Skin layers
preclinical.summary: Epidermis (stratified squamous): stratum basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum (palms/soles), corneum. Dermis: papillary and reticular. Hypodermis: subcutaneous fat. Adnexal structures: hair follicles, sebaceous, sweat glands.

preclinical.name: Three germ layers
preclinical.summary: Ectoderm: epidermis, nervous system, neural crest. Mesoderm: muscle, bone, connective tissue, kidneys, heart, blood, gonads. Endoderm: gut epithelium, liver, pancreas, lungs, thyroid follicular cells. Gastrulation around week 3.

preclinical.name: Neural crest derivatives
preclinical.summary: Migratory cells derived from neuroectoderm. Give rise to peripheral neurons and glia, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, enteric ganglia, branchial arch cartilage, aorticopulmonary septum, parafollicular C cells, odontoblasts.

preclinical.name: Pharyngeal arches
preclinical.summary: Five arches (1, 2, 3, 4, 6) each with a cartilage, muscle group, nerve, and artery. CN V (1), VII (2), IX (3), X superior laryngeal (4), X recurrent laryngeal (6). Disorders include Treacher Collins (arch 1) and DiGeorge (arches 3 and 4).

preclinical.name: Cardiac embryology
preclinical.summary: Primitive heart tube forms by week 3 and loops by day 23. Septation by week 8 separates atria (foramen ovale closes at birth), ventricles, and aorticopulmonary trunk (spiral septum from neural crest, fails in transposition).

preclinical.name: Fetal circulation
preclinical.summary: Oxygenated blood from placenta via umbilical vein, bypasses liver via ductus venosus, enters right atrium, mostly shunts through foramen ovale (to left heart) or ductus arteriosus (to descending aorta). All shunts close functionally at birth.

preclinical.name: Renal embryology
preclinical.summary: Sequential development: pronephros (regresses), mesonephros (becomes male reproductive tract), metanephros (definitive kidney). Ureteric bud induces metanephric blastema. Failure causes renal agenesis, agenesis with oligohydramnios produces Potter sequence.

preclinical.name: Aortic arch derivatives
preclinical.summary: Arch 1: maxillary artery. Arch 2: stapedial, hyoid arteries. Arch 3: common carotid and proximal internal carotid. Arch 4: aortic arch (left), proximal right subclavian. Arch 6: pulmonary arteries and ductus arteriosus.

preclinical.name: Gut rotation
preclinical.summary: Midgut herniates into the umbilical cord around week 6, rotates 270 degrees counterclockwise around the SMA, returns to abdomen by week 10. Malrotation predisposes to volvulus.

preclinical.name: Teratogenic critical periods
preclinical.summary: Pre-implantation (week 1 to 2): all-or-nothing effect. Embryonic period (week 3 to 8): organogenesis, maximal teratogen sensitivity. Fetal period (week 9 to birth): functional defects and growth restriction.

preclinical.name: Common teratogens
preclinical.summary: Alcohol: fetal alcohol syndrome. Warfarin: chondrodysplasia, fetal warfarin syndrome. ACE inhibitors: renal dysgenesis. Valproate, methotrexate, isotretinoin: multiple anomalies. Rubella, CMV, Zika: infectious teratogens.

preclinical.name: Autosomal dominant inheritance
preclinical.summary: One affected allele sufficient. Vertical transmission, both sexes equally affected, ~50 percent transmission risk per child. Often structural protein or receptor disorders (Marfan, NF1, familial hypercholesterolaemia, HD, ADPKD).

preclinical.name: Autosomal recessive inheritance
preclinical.summary: Two copies needed for disease. Horizontal pedigrees, frequently from consanguinity, often enzyme deficiencies (PKU, Wilson, haemochromatosis, sickle cell, cystic fibrosis). Carriers (heterozygotes) usually asymptomatic.

preclinical.name: X-linked recessive inheritance
preclinical.summary: Affected males predominate, no male-to-male transmission, transmitted through carrier mothers to half their sons. Examples: haemophilia A and B, DMD/BMD, G6PD deficiency, Lesch-Nyhan, colour blindness.

preclinical.name: X-linked dominant inheritance
preclinical.summary: Affected males pass to all daughters and no sons. Heterozygous females affected but more mildly than males. Examples: hypophosphataemic rickets, Rett syndrome, Alport (most cases).

preclinical.name: Mitochondrial inheritance
preclinical.summary: Strictly maternally transmitted. All children of affected females at risk; no transmission from affected males. Heteroplasmy causes variable expression. Examples: MELAS, MERRF, Leber hereditary optic neuropathy.

preclinical.name: Anticipation
preclinical.summary: Disease onset earlier and more severe across generations, typical of trinucleotide repeat expansions. Examples: Huntington (CAG), myotonic dystrophy (CTG), fragile X (CGG), Friedreich's ataxia (GAA).

preclinical.name: Imprinting
preclinical.summary: Expression of only the paternal or maternal copy of a gene due to epigenetic silencing. Loss of imprinted alleles: Prader-Willi (paternal 15q11 loss), Angelman (maternal 15q11 loss).

preclinical.name: Penetrance vs expressivity
preclinical.summary: Penetrance: fraction of carriers who express the phenotype. Expressivity: severity of phenotype among those affected. A gene can have high penetrance but variable expressivity, or vice versa.

preclinical.name: Mosaicism
preclinical.summary: Two or more genetically distinct cell lines in the same individual from a postzygotic mutation. Somatic mosaicism affects tissues unequally; germline mosaicism may produce recurrent affected offspring from unaffected parents.

preclinical.name: Heterozygosity (loss of)
preclinical.summary: Loss of the remaining functional allele at a heterozygous locus, often by deletion, mitotic recombination, or epigenetic silencing. Important in two-hit tumour suppressor inactivation (RB1, TP53, BRCA1/2).

preclinical.name: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
preclinical.summary: Allele frequencies remain constant when assumptions hold (no selection, mutation, migration, drift, random mating). p^2 plus 2pq plus q^2 equals 1. Used to estimate carrier frequencies for recessive disease.

preclinical.name: Lyonisation
preclinical.summary: Random inactivation of one X chromosome in each cell in females early in development. Creates mosaicism for X-linked traits. Explains skewed phenotypes in carriers of X-linked disease.

preclinical.name: Trisomy basics
preclinical.summary: Most arise from meiotic non-disjunction, risk increases with maternal age. Trisomy 21 (Down): commonest viable, intellectual disability, AV septal defect, leukaemia risk. Trisomy 18 (Edwards) and 13 (Patau) usually lethal in infancy.

preclinical.name: Sex chromosome aneuploidies
preclinical.summary: Turner (45,X): short stature, primary ovarian failure, coarctation, lymphoedema. Klinefelter (47,XXY): tall, hypogonadism, infertility, mild learning issues. 47,XYY and 47,XXX often subtle or asymptomatic.

preclinical.name: Microdeletion syndromes
preclinical.summary: Submicroscopic deletions detected by FISH or microarray. DiGeorge (22q11): thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia, cardiac defects. Williams (7q11): supravalvular AS, hypercalcaemia, friendly personality. Cri-du-chat (5p deletion): cat-like cry.

preclinical.name: Sensitivity
preclinical.summary: Proportion of truly diseased correctly identified: TP / (TP plus FN). High sensitivity rules disease out when test is negative (SnNout). Useful for screening.

preclinical.name: Specificity
preclinical.summary: Proportion of truly disease-free correctly identified: TN / (TN plus FP). High specificity rules disease in when test is positive (SpPin). Useful for confirmation.

preclinical.name: Positive predictive value
preclinical.summary: Probability that a positive test reflects true disease: TP / (TP plus FP). Strongly influenced by pretest probability (prevalence): falls in low-prevalence settings.

preclinical.name: Negative predictive value
preclinical.summary: Probability that a negative test reflects true absence: TN / (TN plus FN). Higher in low-prevalence settings; falls when disease is common.

preclinical.name: Likelihood ratio positive
preclinical.summary: Sensitivity / (1 minus specificity). Multiplies pretest odds to give posttest odds. Above 10 strongly rules in; below 1 makes disease less likely.

preclinical.name: Likelihood ratio negative
preclinical.summary: (1 minus sensitivity) / specificity. Below 0.1 strongly rules out; above 1 raises probability. Independent of disease prevalence.

preclinical.name: Pretest and posttest probability
preclinical.summary: Pretest probability is the clinician's estimate before testing (often prevalence or risk-adjusted). Bayes theorem combines pretest odds with a likelihood ratio to give posttest probability.

preclinical.name: Number needed to treat
preclinical.summary: Number of patients who must receive an intervention to prevent one additional bad outcome. Equals 1 / absolute risk reduction. Smaller NNT means more impactful therapy.

preclinical.name: Number needed to harm
preclinical.summary: Number who must receive a treatment to cause one additional harmful event. Equals 1 / absolute risk increase. Used alongside NNT to weigh benefit and harm.

preclinical.name: Absolute vs relative risk reduction
preclinical.summary: ARR is the difference in event rates between groups. RRR is ARR divided by the control event rate. RRR often looks impressive in low-event settings; ARR and NNT give a clinically grounded picture.

preclinical.name: Relative risk vs odds ratio
preclinical.summary: Relative risk is the ratio of event rates; used in cohort studies and trials. Odds ratio is the ratio of odds; used in case-control studies. OR approximates RR when the outcome is rare.

preclinical.name: Confidence interval
preclinical.summary: Range of values within which the true effect is plausibly contained at a stated probability (commonly 95 percent). A CI that crosses the null (1 for ratios, 0 for differences) is statistically non-significant.

preclinical.name: P value
preclinical.summary: Probability of observing data at least as extreme as observed if the null hypothesis is true. Does not measure clinical importance, effect size, or the probability that the hypothesis is correct.

preclinical.name: Type 1 and type 2 error
preclinical.summary: Type 1 (alpha): false positive, rejecting a true null. Type 2 (beta): false negative, failing to reject a false null. Power equals 1 minus beta. Increased with larger samples and larger effects.

preclinical.name: Intention-to-treat analysis
preclinical.summary: Analyses participants in the groups to which they were randomised regardless of adherence or crossover. Preserves the benefits of randomisation and minimises bias from non-random dropout. Per-protocol analysis is more biased but tests efficacy under adherence.

preclinical.name: Selection bias
preclinical.summary: Systematic difference between sampled and unsampled populations, or between treatment groups. Sources include non-random sampling, loss to follow-up, and Berkson's bias in hospital-based studies.

preclinical.name: Confounding
preclinical.summary: A third variable associated with both exposure and outcome distorts the apparent relationship. Addressed by randomisation, restriction, matching, stratification, or multivariable adjustment.

preclinical.name: Lead-time and length-time bias
preclinical.summary: Lead-time bias: earlier detection appears to lengthen survival without changing time of death. Length-time bias: screening preferentially detects slow-progressing disease. Both inflate apparent screening benefit.

psych.name: Circumstantiality
psych.summary: Speech that wanders through excessive, over-inclusive detail but does eventually reach the point. Note: reaching the point is the whole distinction from tangentiality, which never arrives. Common in obsessional personality, anxiety, and hypomania, and not in itself evidence of psychosis.

psych.name: Tangentiality
psych.summary: Replies veer away from the question and never return to it - the answer is related to the question but does not answer it. Note: unlike circumstantiality the goal is never reached, and unlike derailment the drift is a single sustained departure rather than repeated breaks.

psych.name: Derailment
psych.summary: Speech slips between topics with no logical connection between them, the links being obscure to the listener and unremarked by the speaker. A core positive formal thought disorder in schizophrenia. Note: knight's move thinking is the same phenomenon named for the sideways jump; loosening of associations is the older Bleulerian term and is used interchangeably in practice.

psych.name: Flight of ideas
psych.summary: Rapid, continuous speech with abrupt topic changes where the connections *are* discernible - by rhyme, pun, or a distracting stimulus in the room. Note: this is the discriminator from derailment, where no link can be found. Characteristic of mania, and typically accompanied by pressured speech.

psych.name: Thought blocking
psych.summary: Speech stops mid-sentence with the thought experienced as abruptly removed, and the patient cannot recover it. Note: distinguish from ordinary losing one's thread, which the person recognises as their own lapse - thought blocking is often experienced as externally imposed and may be elaborated into thought withdrawal.

psych.name: Word salad
psych.summary: Speech reduced to an unintelligible mixture of words and phrases with no grammatical or semantic structure. The severe end of formal thought disorder.

psych.name: Neologism
psych.summary: A newly coined word, or an ordinary word used with an idiosyncratic private meaning. Note: check it is not simply jargon, slang or a second-language construction before recording it - this is a frequent source of false positives.

psych.name: Clang association
psych.summary: Words chosen for their sound rather than their meaning - rhyme, alliteration, or punning. Most often seen in mania with flight of ideas.

psych.name: Perseveration
psych.summary: Persistent repetition of a word, phrase or response beyond the point at which it is relevant, typically as a reply to subsequent, different questions. Note: strongly suggests an organic cause - frontal lobe damage, dementia or delirium - rather than a primary psychiatric one.

psych.name: Echolalia
psych.summary: Automatic repetition of another person's words or phrases. Seen in catatonia, autism spectrum disorder, frontal syndromes and some dementias.

psych.name: Pressured speech
psych.summary: Rapid, loud, hard-to-interrupt speech reflecting an internal urgency to keep talking. A cardinal sign of mania. Note: describes the delivery, whereas flight of ideas describes the structure; they usually occur together but should be recorded separately.

psych.name: Poverty of speech
psych.summary: Markedly reduced quantity of speech, with brief and unelaborated replies. A negative symptom of schizophrenia. Note: poverty of *content* is different - normal quantity conveying little information - and the two are separately rated.

psych.name: Affect
psych.summary: The observed, moment-to-moment emotional expression - what the examiner sees. Note: mood is the sustained, subjective emotional state - what the patient reports. The conventional shorthand is that mood is the climate and affect the weather, and MSE documentation should record both.

psych.name: Blunted affect
psych.summary: Reduced intensity of emotional expression, with some range preserved. A negative symptom of schizophrenia; also seen in depression and as a medication effect.

psych.name: Flat affect
psych.summary: Near-total absence of emotional expression - immobile face, monotonous voice, no reactivity. The severe end of the same spectrum as blunted affect, and the difference is one of degree rather than kind.

psych.name: Incongruent affect
psych.summary: Emotional expression that does not match the content being discussed - laughing while describing a bereavement. Note: consider cultural expression and anxious laughter before recording this; it is over-called.

psych.name: Labile affect
psych.summary: Rapid, abrupt shifts in emotional expression, often out of proportion to the trigger. Seen in mania, delirium, frontal lobe damage, and pseudobulbar affect after stroke or in motor neurone disease.

psych.name: Euthymic
psych.summary: Normal mood - neither depressed nor elevated. The term for the baseline state, and the target of maintenance treatment in bipolar disorder.

psych.name: Anhedonia
psych.summary: Loss of the capacity to experience pleasure from previously enjoyed activities. Note: one of the two DSM-5-TR gateway criteria for a major depressive episode, alongside depressed mood - at least one must be present, so it is worth asking about explicitly rather than inferring.

psych.name: Avolition
psych.summary: Reduced motivation to initiate and sustain purposeful activity. A negative symptom of schizophrenia. Note: distinguish from anhedonia (pleasure) and from fatigue (capacity) - avolition is about initiation, and the three respond to different interventions.

psych.name: Dysphoria
psych.summary: An unpleasant mood state - irritable, tense or dissatisfied rather than specifically sad. Note: dysphoric mania (a mixed state) carries higher suicide risk than euphoric mania and responds poorly to antidepressants.

psych.name: Psychomotor retardation
psych.summary: Observable slowing of movement, speech and thought. A melancholic feature of depression and one of the few MSE signs that is objectively visible rather than reported.

psych.name: Psychomotor agitation
psych.summary: Purposeless motor activity driven by inner tension - pacing, wringing hands, inability to sit. Note: agitation with depression is a recognised risk-raising combination, since it supplies the volition that severe retardation withholds.

psych.name: Catatonia
psych.summary: A psychomotor syndrome of marked abnormality in movement, volition and responsiveness. Features: stupor, catalepsy, waxy flexibility, mutism, negativism, posturing, mannerisms, stereotypies, agitation, grimacing, echolalia, echopraxia. Note: not specific to schizophrenia - mood disorders are a commoner cause, and general medical causes must be excluded. Lorazepam is first-line and ECT is effective; antipsychotics can worsen it and risk precipitating neuroleptic malignant syndrome, with which it shares considerable overlap.

psych.name: Waxy flexibility
psych.summary: Limbs offer slight, even resistance to repositioning - like bending a candle - and then hold the new posture. A catatonic sign.

psych.name: Negativism
psych.summary: Motiveless resistance to instructions or to attempts at movement, or doing the opposite. A catatonic sign, and not to be read as deliberate refusal.

psych.name: Echopraxia
psych.summary: Automatic imitation of another person's movements. The motor counterpart of echolalia, and likewise a catatonic sign.

psych.name: Stereotypy
psych.summary: Repetitive, purposeless movement performed in a uniform way - rocking, hand-flapping. Note: a mannerism differs in being a purposeful action carried out in an odd or exaggerated manner.

psych.name: Delusion
psych.summary: A fixed false belief held with unshakeable conviction, out of keeping with the person's cultural and educational background, and not amenable to contrary evidence. Note: the cultural qualifier is doing real work - a belief shared by the person's community is not a delusion however implausible it seems to the examiner. Bizarreness is recorded but no longer carries special diagnostic weight in DSM-5-TR.

psych.name: Persecutory delusion
psych.summary: Belief that one is being harmed, harassed, conspired against or surveilled. The commonest delusional theme.

psych.name: Grandiose delusion
psych.summary: Belief in exceptional ability, wealth, identity or mission. Characteristic of mania with psychotic features, and also seen in schizophrenia.

psych.name: Delusion of reference
psych.summary: Belief that neutral events - broadcasts, gestures, headlines - carry personal significance directed at oneself. Note: *ideas* of reference are held with less conviction and some doubt, and sit on a continuum with the delusion rather than being a separate phenomenon.

psych.name: Thought insertion
psych.summary: Experience that thoughts are being placed into one's mind by an external agency and are not one's own. One of the passivity phenomena.

psych.name: Thought withdrawal
psych.summary: Experience that thoughts are being removed from one's mind by an external agency, often elaborated from thought blocking.

psych.name: Thought broadcasting
psych.summary: Experience that one's thoughts are audible to or accessible by others without being spoken.

psych.name: Passivity phenomena
psych.summary: Experiences of one's thoughts, feelings, impulses or actions being controlled by an external force - a disturbance of the sense of agency. Note: these were among Schneider's first-rank symptoms. First-rank symptoms are no longer given diagnostic priority in DSM-5-TR or ICD-11, being neither sensitive nor specific enough, but remain useful descriptive terms.

psych.name: Hallucination
psych.summary: A percept occurring without an external stimulus, experienced as real and located in external space. Note: the modality guides the differential - auditory suggests a primary psychiatric cause; visual, olfactory or tactile hallucinations should prompt a search for an organic one including delirium, substance withdrawal, epilepsy and Lewy body dementia.

psych.name: Illusion
psych.summary: A misperception of a stimulus that is actually there - mistaking a coat on a door for a person. Note: the presence of a real stimulus is the entire distinction from a hallucination. Illusions are common in delirium and in normal people in poor light.

psych.name: Pseudohallucination
psych.summary: A percept experienced in inner subjective space and recognised as not real - a voice heard 'inside the head' and known to be one's own mind. Note: the term is used inconsistently and appears in neither DSM-5-TR nor ICD-11; describe the phenomenon rather than relying on the label.

psych.name: Depersonalisation
psych.summary: Feeling detached from, or an unreal observer of, one's own body, thoughts or actions. Note: reality testing stays intact - the person knows the feeling is a feeling, which separates this from psychosis.

psych.name: Derealisation
psych.summary: Feeling that the surroundings are unreal, dreamlike, flat or visually distorted. The environmental counterpart of depersonalisation, with reality testing likewise intact.

psych.name: Obsession
psych.summary: A recurrent, intrusive thought, image or urge experienced as unwanted and as one's own, causing marked anxiety. Note: recognising the thought as one's own product is what separates an obsession from thought insertion, and resisting it separates obsession from delusion.

psych.name: Compulsion
psych.summary: A repetitive behaviour or mental act the person feels driven to perform to reduce distress or prevent a feared outcome, typically in response to an obsession and recognised as excessive.

psych.name: Rumination
psych.summary: Repetitive, passive dwelling on distressing content and its causes and consequences. Note: unlike an obsession it is usually mood-congruent and not resisted, which is why depressive rumination and obsessional thinking need different treatment approaches.

psych.name: Overvalued idea
psych.summary: A belief held with abnormal intensity and preoccupation that is not frankly delusional and can be conceded as possibly wrong. Note: sits between an obsession and a delusion, and is the usual characterisation of the weight-and-shape beliefs in anorexia nervosa.

psych.name: Insight
psych.summary: The extent to which a person recognises they are unwell, attributes their experiences to illness, and accepts the need for treatment. Note: it is a graded and multidimensional judgement, not a yes or no - record what the patient believes is happening and why, rather than writing 'no insight'.

psych.name: Concrete thinking
psych.summary: Inability to reason abstractly - proverbs and metaphors are interpreted literally. Seen in schizophrenia, intellectual disability and organic brain disease. Note: proverb interpretation is heavily influenced by education and cultural familiarity, so a literal answer is weak evidence on its own.

psych.name: Confabulation
psych.summary: Production of fabricated or distorted memories without intent to deceive, typically filling a genuine memory gap. Note: characteristic of Korsakoff syndrome; the absence of deceptive intent is what separates it from lying.

psych.name: Anosognosia
psych.summary: Inability to recognise one's own deficit, arising from the illness itself rather than from denial. Seen after right-hemisphere stroke, in dementia, and as a substrate of impaired insight in psychosis.

psych.name: Formal thought disorder
psych.summary: Disturbance of the *form* or organisation of thought, inferred from speech. Types: positive - derailment, tangentiality, incoherence, neologisms; negative - poverty of speech and of content. Note: distinct from disorders of thought *content*, which is where delusions sit. Cards and examiners use 'thought disorder' loosely for both, so the distinction is worth keeping explicit.

psych.name: Extrapyramidal side effects
psych.summary: Movement disorders from dopamine D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway. Types: acute dystonia (hours to days), akathisia (days to weeks), parkinsonism (weeks to months), tardive dyskinesia (months to years). Mx: benztropine for dystonia and parkinsonism - it does not help akathisia, for which propranolol is first-line. Reduce the dose or switch to a lower-potency or second-generation agent. Note: anticholinergics can worsen tardive dyskinesia, so correctly identifying which EPSE is present changes the management.

psych.name: Acute dystonia
psych.summary: Sustained involuntary muscle contraction causing abnormal posture - torticollis, oculogyric crisis, trismus, or laryngospasm - typically within hours to days of starting or increasing an antipsychotic. Mx: parenteral benztropine or benzatropine; response is usually rapid. Red flags: laryngeal involvement is an airway emergency. Note: young men on high-potency first-generation agents are at highest risk.

psych.name: Anticholinergic burden
psych.summary: Cumulative muscarinic blockade across a person's whole medication list. Features: dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia; centrally, confusion and delirium. Note: the mnemonic is dry as a bone, blind as a bat, red as a beet, mad as a hatter, hot as a hare. Burden matters more than any single drug, and is a modifiable contributor to falls and to cognitive decline in older people.

rich_summaries.ARDS: Acute respiratory distress syndrome - acute inflammatory lung injury with diffuse alveolar damage, increased capillary permeability and non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Diagnosed by the Berlin criteria - acute onset within 7 days, bilateral opacities on imaging not fully explained by effusion or atelectasis, respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure, and PaO2/FiO2 under 300 on PEEP 5 (mild under 300, moderate under 200, severe under 100). Causes: pulmonary (pneumonia, aspiration, inhalation) or extrapulmonary (sepsis commonest, pancreatitis, TRALI, trauma, burns). Clinical features: rapidly progressive dyspnoea and hypoxia, tachypnoea, diffuse crackles. Ix: ABG shows severe hypoxia; CXR shows bilateral infiltrates; echocardiogram to exclude cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.Mx: treat underlying cause; lung-protective ventilation with low tidal volume (6 mL/kg predicted body weight), plateau pressure under 30, PEEP titration; prone positioning for PaO2/FiO2 under 150 for 16 hours daily; conservative fluid strategy; neuromuscular blockade for severe ARDS; ECMO for refractory hypoxia. Note: mortality 30 to 40%; survivors face long-term cognitive and physical impairment.
rich_summaries.Abruption: Premature separation of a normally sited placenta after 20 weeks, and the obstetric emergency in which the visible blood loss understates the real one. Causes: hypertension and pre-eclampsia, trauma, smoking and cocaine, polyhydramnios with rapid decompression, and previous abruption. Clinical features: constant abdominal pain with a woody, tender uterus, dark vaginal bleeding, and fetal compromise. Concealed abruption bleeds behind the placenta with little or nothing revealed. Ix: this is a clinical diagnosis - ultrasound cannot exclude it. FBC, coagulation profile, fibrinogen, group and hold or crossmatch, Kleihauer, and continuous CTG. Mx: resuscitate, give oxygen and large-bore access, and deliver. Caesarean for fetal compromise or maternal instability; vaginal birth may be appropriate after fetal death. Anti-D for Rh-negative women. Corticosteroids if preterm and the situation allows. Note: a falling fibrinogen is the earliest marker of the consumptive coagulopathy abruption causes, and it falls before the INR moves.
rich_summaries.Acanthosis nigricans: Velvety hyperpigmented hyperkeratotic skin thickening at flexural sites - posterior neck, axillae, groin, antecubital and popliteal fossae. Types: benign (insulin resistance - obesity, T2DM, PCOS, metabolic syndrome; commonest overall) and malignant (paraneoplastic - sudden onset, extensive involvement including palms and mucous membranes, gastric adenocarcinoma in over 60%). Also drug-induced (nicotinic acid, glucocorticoids, OCP, growth hormone) and syndromic (Cushing, acromegaly, familial). Clinical features: symmetrical brown-to-black plaques with thickened rugose texture; often asymptomatic but can itch; skin tags nearby. Sudden widespread onset in a non-obese adult raises occult malignancy. Ix: clinical diagnosis; fasting glucose or HbA1c and lipids in everyone; malignancy workup (gastroscopy, CT) when features are atypical - abrupt, extensive, palmar, or mucosal. Mx: treat the underlying cause - weight loss, metformin and glycaemic control usually improve the benign form. Topical retinoids or keratolytics (salicylic acid, urea) for cosmesis. Note: skin change often precedes T2DM diagnosis by years - screen and act.
rich_summaries.Achalasia: Primary oesophageal motility disorder from loss of inhibitory ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus, giving impaired LOS relaxation and absent peristalsis. Epidemiology: about 1 in 100 000/year, peak 30 to 60; idiopathic loss of nitric oxide inhibitory neurons in most, Chagas disease produces an identical picture in endemic areas. Clinical features: progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the start (distinct from mechanical obstruction), regurgitation of undigested food, chest pain, weight loss; symptoms over months to years. Ix: barium swallow shows dilated oesophagus with a smooth bird-beak taper at the LOS; upper endoscopy first-line to exclude pseudo-achalasia (distal oesophageal or cardia tumour); high-resolution manometry is diagnostic and subtypes it (I aperistalsis, II panoesophageal pressurisation, III spastic). Mx: pneumatic dilatation, laparoscopic Heller myotomy plus partial fundoplication, or per-oral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) - all give lasting relief in about 90%; botulinum toxin for frail patients; CCBs or nitrates if not a procedural candidate. Note: risk of oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma is raised - new dysphagia or bleeding demands re-scoping.
rich_summaries.Acne vulgaris: Chronic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous unit with comedones, papules, pustules and, when severe, nodules and cysts. Epidemiology: begins in early puberty, settling through the 20s-30s. Pathophysiology: androgen-driven sebum, follicular hyperkeratinisation forming the comedone, C. acnes colonisation, then inflammation - each first-line agent hits a different step, which is why combinations beat monotherapy. Clinical features: face, chest, upper back. Mild is comedonal; moderate adds papules and pustules; severe has nodules and scarring. Mx: mild - topical benzoyl peroxide and/or a retinoid (adapalene, tretinoin). Moderate - add oral doxycycline, or the COCP in women. Severe - oral isotretinoin via dermatology. Note: never use an antibiotic without benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid alongside - monotherapy breeds resistance and eTG advises against it. Isotretinoin is highly teratogenic.
rich_summaries.Acoustic neuroma: Benign Schwann-cell tumour of the vestibular division of CN VIII; sporadic and unilateral in over 95%; bilateral tumours are pathognomonic of neurofibromatosis type 2 and the commonest cerebellopontine-angle tumour. Clinical features: unilateral progressive sensorineural hearing loss with tinnitus and impaired speech discrimination out of proportion to the pure-tone loss; vestibular symptoms are usually unsteadiness rather than vertigo because compensation keeps pace; large tumours cause trigeminal numbness, facial weakness, cerebellar signs and eventually raised ICP. Ix: audiogram (asymmetry above 10-15 dB across two adjacent frequencies) then gadolinium MRI of the internal auditory meati (gold standard). Mx: observation with serial MRI for small tumours in older patients (many grow slowly or not at all); stereotactic radiosurgery for small-to-medium tumours with good hearing preservation; microsurgical resection for large tumours or radiosurgery failure; hearing aids or CROS/BAHA once loss stabilises. Note: any adult with asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss or unilateral tinnitus deserves an audiogram - one-sided disease is a schwannoma until MRI proves otherwise.
rich_summaries.Acromegaly: Chronic growth hormone excess in an adult (after growth plate closure); GH excess before closure causes gigantism. Aetiology: over 95% is a pituitary somatotroph adenoma; rarely ectopic GHRH from carcinoid or GH from a pancreatic tumour. Clinical features are insidious over years - enlargement of hands and feet (ring and shoe size increase), coarsening of facial features, frontal bossing, prognathism, macroglossia, carpal tunnel syndrome, deep voice, sweating, and skin tags. Systemic problems include hypertension, insulin resistance and diabetes, obstructive sleep apnoea, cardiomyopathy, and increased colon polyp and cancer risk. Mass effect may give bitemporal hemianopia and hypopituitarism. Ix: IGF-1 is the screening test (elevated for age); confirm with failure of GH suppression on 75 g OGTT (GH stays above 1 microg/L). Pituitary MRI to size and site the tumour; visual fields; anterior pituitary panel. Mx: trans-sphenoidal surgery is first line. Somatostatin analogues (octreotide LAR, lanreotide) for residual disease; cabergoline for mild disease; pegvisomant for resistance. Radiotherapy in refractory disease. Note: cardiovascular disease drives excess mortality.
rich_summaries.Acute angle-closure glaucoma: Sudden obstruction of aqueous outflow at the trabecular meshwork by apposition of the peripheral iris, and a true ophthalmic emergency - vision is lost in hours. Epidemiology: hypermetropic eyes, older patients, women, and East Asian ancestry. Precipitated by dim light, and by anticholinergic, sympathomimetic and some antidepressant drugs. Clinical features: severe unilateral eye pain, blurred vision with haloes around lights, and a red eye. Nausea and vomiting are prominent enough that this is mistaken for an abdominal or neurological problem. The eye is hard, the cornea hazy, and the pupil mid-dilated and unreactive. Ix: tonometry - intraocular pressure is typically well above 40 mmHg. Gonioscopy confirms the closed angle. Mx: discuss with ophthalmology immediately. Lie the patient flat, give topical agents to lower pressure and constrict the pupil, and acetazolamide systemically. Definitive treatment is laser peripheral iridotomy, offered to the fellow eye as well. Red flags: any red painful eye with reduced vision needs a pressure measured before it is called conjunctivitis.
rich_summaries.Acute kidney injury: Rapid decline in renal function defined by KDIGO as a serum creatinine rise of at least 26 micromol/L in 48 hours, a rise to at least 1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours. Causes: pre-renal from volume depletion, sepsis, heart failure or hepatorenal syndrome; intrinsic from acute tubular necrosis (ischaemic or nephrotoxic), acute interstitial nephritis (drug rash and eosinophiluria), or glomerulonephritis (haematuria and proteinuria); post-renal from obstruction at any level. Ix: EUC, FBC, urinalysis and microscopy, FENa if oliguric (under 1% pre-renal, over 2% ATN), renal ultrasound to exclude obstruction and assess size; immunology (ANA, ANCA, complement) and myeloma screen where intrinsic disease is plausible.
