Mx: treat the cause - resuscitate with crystalloid, remove nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, aminoglycosides, contrast where possible), relieve obstruction, treat sepsis. Dialysis for AEIOU - refractory Acidosis, Electrolytes (especially hyperkalaemia), Ingestion, refractory fluid Overload, Uraemic complications. Note: an AKI episode is a risk factor for future CKD, so follow up creatinine after discharge.
rich_summaries.Acute liver failure: Coagulopathy with encephalopathy developing within 26 weeks in someone without pre-existing liver disease. Causes: paracetamol is the commonest in Australia; also hepatitis A and E, idiosyncratic drug reaction, Wilson disease, Budd-Chiari syndrome, ischaemic hepatitis, acute fatty liver of pregnancy. Clinical features: jaundice preceding encephalopathy graded I to IV, asterixis progressing to coma; cerebral oedema in grade III to IV is the leading cause of death. Ix: INR and lactate track severity; paracetamol concentration, viral serology, caeruloplasmin, hepatic vein Doppler; watch glucose, creatinine and cultures for the usual complications. Mx: intensive care; acetylcysteine, which benefits non-paracetamol causes as well; glucose and electrolyte support; early referral to a transplant unit against King's College criteria; avoid sedation. Note: INR is the prognostic marker here, so correcting it without active bleeding discards the best measure of trajectory.
rich_summaries.Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia: Clonal proliferation of lymphoid precursor cells (B-cell 85%, T-cell 15%); the commonest childhood cancer. Bimodal age with peaks at 3 to 5 years and over 50. Philadelphia chromosome (t(9;22), BCR-ABL) is a major adverse prognostic marker. Clinical features: bone marrow failure gives pallor, mucosal bleeding, infection or fever with neutropenia; bone pain, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and testicular or CNS involvement. Mediastinal mass may cause SVC obstruction in T-cell disease. Ix: FBC with blast cells on film, coagulation, tumour lysis screen (EUC, urate, LDH, calcium, phosphate). Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy with flow cytometry, cytogenetics and BCR-ABL. LP for CNS involvement. Mx: risk-stratified multi-agent chemotherapy - induction, consolidation, CNS prophylaxis, maintenance for 2 to 3 years. Add imatinib or dasatinib for Philadelphia-positive disease. CAR-T (tisagenlecleucel) for relapsed or refractory paediatric and young adult disease. Allogeneic transplant in high-risk or relapsed disease. Note: paediatric cure rates now exceed 85% with modern protocols.
rich_summaries.Acute myeloid leukaemia: Clonal proliferation of myeloid blasts with arrested differentiation, causing rapid marrow failure. Epidemiology: median onset around 68; risk raised by prior chemotherapy, radiation, myelodysplasia and Down syndrome. Clinical features: days to weeks of fatigue, infection and bleeding, reflecting anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia; gum hypertrophy and skin infiltration in monocytic subtypes. Ix: blasts on film, often with Auer rods; marrow with 20% or more blasts; flow cytometry, cytogenetics and molecular testing (FLT3, NPM1, CEBPA) drive both prognosis and drug choice; coagulation screen, LDH, urate. Mx: intensive induction chemotherapy then consolidation or allogeneic transplant in fit patients; hypomethylating agents with venetoclax in those unfit for intensive therapy. Note: acute promyelocytic leukaemia is the subtype to recognise immediately - it presents with DIC and life-threatening bleeding, and is treated with all-trans retinoic acid started on suspicion rather than on confirmation. Red flags: fever with neutropenia is a medical emergency; hyperleukocytosis causes leukostasis with hypoxia and confusion.
rich_summaries.Acute pancreatitis: Acute pancreatic inflammation diagnosed on two of three: characteristic pain, lipase above three times the upper limit, or imaging. Causes: gallstones and alcohol account for most; also hypertriglyceridaemia, hypercalcaemia, drugs, post-ERCP and trauma. Clinical features: severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, relieved by sitting forward, with vomiting. Cullen and Grey Turner signs are late and rare. Ix: lipase (more specific than amylase), LFT and lipids to find the cause, calcium, and abdominal ultrasound for gallstones in everyone. CT is for complications, not diagnosis, and is best deferred 72 hours. Mx: aggressive fluid resuscitation with compound sodium lactate, analgesia, and early enteral feeding rather than fasting. Antibiotics only for proven infection. Cholecystectomy during the same admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis. Note: severity is a moving target - reassess rather than scoring once, and persistent organ failure beyond 48 hours defines severe disease.
rich_summaries.Acute psychosis: New-onset psychotic symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganised thought or behaviour) lasting a day or more but not yet meeting criteria for a specific chronic psychotic disorder. Causes: primary psychiatric (first-episode schizophrenia, brief psychotic disorder, bipolar mania, psychotic depression); substance-induced (cannabis, methamphetamine, cocaine, hallucinogens, alcohol withdrawal); medical (delirium, encephalitis including anti-NMDA-receptor, temporal lobe epilepsy, endocrine, steroid-induced, dementia with Lewy bodies). Ix: mental state and risk assessment, collateral history, urine drug screen, FBC, EUC, LFT, TFT, calcium, glucose, B12, folate, HIV and syphilis serology; CT or MRI brain, EEG, LP and autoimmune encephalitis antibodies if atypical, focal signs or age over 40. Mx: acute agitation follows the least-restrictive path - oral olanzapine or risperidone preferred; IM olanzapine or droperidol plus midazolam if sedation needed. Treat the underlying cause. Second-generation antipsychotic if psychiatric. MHA assessment if lacking capacity. Note: duration of untreated psychosis predicts outcome - refer to early psychosis services promptly.
rich_summaries.Acute rheumatic fever: Multisystem inflammatory disease following group A streptococcal pharyngitis (molecular mimicry). Peak age 5 to 15; highest global incidence in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander populations in northern and central Australia. Diagnosis by Jones criteria - 2 major, or 1 major plus 2 minor, plus evidence of recent GAS infection. Sx: carditis with mitral or aortic regurgitation, migratory polyarthritis of large joints, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules; minor - fever, arthralgia, prolonged PR, raised ESR or CRP. Ix: throat swab (often negative by presentation); ASOT and anti-DNase B (rising titre); ECG (PR prolongation); echocardiogram for carditis and valve regurgitation; FBC, CRP, ESR. Mx: single dose IM benzathine penicillin to eradicate GAS; aspirin or naproxen for arthritis; prednisolone for severe carditis; haloperidol or valproate for chorea. Secondary prophylaxis with monthly IM benzathine penicillin for 10 years or until age 21 (longer if carditis or rheumatic heart disease). Note: penicillin for GAS pharyngitis prevents primary attacks in high-risk communities.
rich_summaries.Acute tubular necrosis: The commonest cause of intrinsic acute kidney injury in hospital, from ischaemic or toxic damage to tubular epithelium. Causes: ischaemic, following any sustained prerenal insult such as sepsis, hypovolaemia or cardiac surgery; or toxic, from aminoglycosides, contrast, cisplatin, or myoglobin in rhabdomyolysis. Clinical features: an oliguric phase, then a polyuric recovery phase as tubules regenerate before concentrating ability returns. Ix: urinary sodium above 40 mmol/L and fractional excretion of sodium above 2% distinguish it from prerenal injury, which conserves sodium avidly. Urine microscopy shows muddy brown granular casts and renal tubular epithelial cells. Mx: supportive. Restore perfusion, stop the nephrotoxin, avoid further insults, and dialyse for the usual indications. No agent shortens the course, and loop diuretics do not - they manage fluid, nothing more. Note: watch potassium and volume closely through the polyuric phase, when losses can be litres a day.
rich_summaries.Addison disease: Primary adrenal insufficiency with deficient cortisol and aldosterone. Causes: autoimmune adrenalitis in developed countries; tuberculosis worldwide; adrenal haemorrhage, metastases, and adrenoleukodystrophy. Clinical features: insidious fatigue, anorexia and weight loss; nausea and abdominal pain; salt craving; postural hypotension; hyperpigmentation of palmar creases and buccal mucosa, which distinguishes primary from secondary insufficiency. Ix: hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia is characteristic; early morning cortisol, with a short synacthen test to confirm; ACTH is raised in primary disease and low in secondary; adrenal antibodies; imaging if not autoimmune. Mx: hydrocortisone in divided doses replicating diurnal rhythm, plus fludrocortisone. Sick day rules - double the dose during illness - with a parenteral emergency kit and alert bracelet. Red flags: adrenal crisis presents with hypotension, vomiting and hyponatraemia. Give intravenous hydrocortisone and fluid immediately on suspicion; do not wait for cortisol results, which can be taken first but must not delay treatment.
rich_summaries.Adenomyosis: Presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, causing uterine enlargement and dysfunction. Coexists commonly with endometriosis and fibroids but is a distinct entity. Risk factors: multiparity, previous uterine surgery (caesarean, curettage, myomectomy), age over 40, and tamoxifen use. Clinical features: characteristic secondary dysmenorrhoea worsening progressively over years; heavy menstrual bleeding; chronic pelvic pain; deep dyspareunia; a diffusely enlarged, globular, tender uterus on examination. Ix: transvaginal ultrasound shows asymmetric myometrial thickening, subendometrial cysts, and heterogeneous myometrium; MRI is more sensitive and shows a thickened junctional zone (over 12 mm). Mx: NSAIDs and tranexamic acid for symptom relief. Hormonal suppression with combined oral contraceptive, oral progestogens, depot MPA, or the levonorgestrel intrauterine system (particularly effective). GnRH analogues for refractory disease. Uterine artery embolisation and adenomyomectomy are fertility-sparing options; hysterectomy is definitive. Note: unlike endometriosis, adenomyosis is not particularly associated with infertility on its own.
rich_summaries.Adrenal crisis: Life-threatening acute adrenal insufficiency. Triggers include physiological stress (surgery, infection, trauma, MI) in a patient with known or undiagnosed adrenal insufficiency, abrupt withdrawal of long-term corticosteroids, missed steroid doses in Addison disease, and bilateral adrenal haemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen with meningococcaemia, anticoagulation, antiphospholipid syndrome). Clinical features: hypotension unresponsive to fluids (cardinal), shock, nausea and vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, hypoglycaemia and fever. Hyperpigmentation in undiagnosed primary disease. Ix: do not delay treatment. Random serum cortisol (low) and ACTH (elevated in primary, low in secondary); EUC shows hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia in primary disease; glucose. Formal short Synacthen test after the acute event. Mx: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV stat then 200 mg per 24 hours. Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation with 0.9% saline and 5% dextrose. Treat hyperkalaemia and the trigger. Convert to oral hydrocortisone once stable. Note: patients carry a steroid emergency card, wear a Medic Alert bracelet, and are taught sick-day rules and IM hydrocortisone self-administration.
rich_summaries.Akathisia: Subjective inner restlessness with objective motor restlessness - inability to sit or stand still, shifting weight, rocking, pacing. Caused by dopamine receptor blockade, most often antipsychotics (both first- and second-generation), but also metoclopramide, prochlorperazine and SSRIs. Onset is typically within days to weeks of starting or increasing the offending drug (contrast tardive dyskinesia, which is months to years). Clinical features: patient describes distress, an urge to move, and often distinguishes it clearly from anxiety - they cannot sit through the consultation. Suicide risk rises with untreated akathisia. Ix: clinical diagnosis; Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale grades severity; exclude serotonin syndrome, restless legs, and anxiety. Mx: reduce or switch the offending antipsychotic - move to a lower-affinity or partial agonist (aripiprazole) or clozapine. First-line pharmacological treatment is propranolol 20 to 40 mg BD; second line is a benzodiazepine (short-term) or mirtazapine. Anticholinergics help less than in acute dystonia but are still used. Note: identify and treat urgently - patients discontinue medication and some self-harm to escape the feeling.
rich_summaries.Alcohol use disorder: Problematic pattern of alcohol use causing clinically significant impairment or distress. Diagnosis (DSM-5): two or more of eleven criteria in 12 months across impaired control (using more or longer, cravings, unsuccessful cut-down attempts), social impairment (role failure, interpersonal problems), risky use, and pharmacological (tolerance, withdrawal). Screen with AUDIT or AUDIT-C. Clinical features of withdrawal appear 6 to 24 hours after last drink - tremor, sweating, anxiety, tachycardia; seizures at 24 to 48 hours; delirium tremens (autonomic instability, confusion, hallucinations, high mortality) at 48 to 96 hours. Ix: FBC (macrocytosis, low platelets), LFT (raised GGT, AST over ALT), EUC, magnesium, glucose, coagulation. Mx: withdrawal gets diazepam by symptom-triggered protocol (CIWA-Ar), plus thiamine 300 mg IV before glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Maintenance combines psychosocial support with pharmacotherapy - naltrexone or acamprosate first line (PBS-listed); disulfiram in selected motivated patients. Note: SMART Recovery and AA are complementary options.
rich_summaries.Allergic rhinitis: IgE-mediated nasal mucosal inflammation from inhaled aeroallergens; commonest chronic disease in Australian children and adults. Classification (ARIA): intermittent (under 4 days/week or 4 weeks) versus persistent; mild versus moderate-severe by impact on sleep, activity and school/work. Triggers: seasonal (ryegrass pollen dominant in southern Australia October-December) and perennial (house-dust mite, cat, dog, mould). Clinical features: sneezing, itch, watery rhinorrhoea, blockage; conjunctivitis, asthma or eczema often coexist. Ix: clinical; skin prick or specific IgE where immunotherapy or targeted avoidance would follow. Mx: intranasal corticosteroid (fluticasone, mometasone) first-line for persistent or moderate-severe disease and superior to antihistamine; add non-sedating oral antihistamine for breakthrough; combination intranasal steroid-antihistamine for refractory disease; allergen immunotherapy for confirmed single-allergen disease. Note: PBS-listed intranasal corticosteroids are OTC and cheap - use them regularly, not on demand.
rich_summaries.Alport syndrome: Inherited disorder of type IV collagen affecting kidney, cochlea and eye. X-linked (COL4A5, 80%) is commonest and affects males severely; autosomal recessive (COL4A3 or COL4A4) affects both sexes; autosomal dominant milder. Clinical features: persistent microscopic haematuria from childhood is the earliest sign, episodic macroscopic haematuria after URTI in half, progressive proteinuria and CKD to ESRD by the third to fifth decade in male X-linked cases, hypertension, bilateral high-frequency sensorineural deafness, anterior lenticonus (pathognomonic when present), dot-and-fleck retinopathy, and leiomyomatosis in some. Female X-linked carriers vary from haematuria only to full progression.Ix: urinalysis with dysmorphic red cells; hearing test; ophthalmology; renal biopsy shows characteristic basement membrane splitting on electron microscopy; genetic testing confirms and guides family cascade. Mx: ACE inhibitor or ARB from diagnosis (even in children); BP control; dialysis or transplant for ESRD; hearing aids. Note: post-transplant anti-GBM disease in around 3% of male X-linked recipients.
rich_summaries.Altitude sickness: Hypobaric hypoxic illness on rapid ascent above about 2500 m, spanning acute mountain sickness through life-threatening cerebral or pulmonary oedema. Pathophysiology: hypoxia drives hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and cerebral vasodilation; HAPE - uneven vasoconstriction with endothelial leak, non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema; HACE - vasogenic cerebral oedema. Clinical features: AMS - headache plus nausea, fatigue, dizziness or disturbed sleep, 6 to 12 hours after ascent (Lake Louise score); HAPE - dyspnoea at rest, cough with pink frothy sputum, hypoxia, crackles; HACE - ataxia, altered consciousness, focal signs. Ix: clinical; SpO2 falls below expected for altitude in HAPE and HACE. Mx: mild AMS - halt ascent, analgesia, acetazolamide 250 mg BD; moderate-severe AMS or any HAPE/HACE - immediate descent (definitive), oxygen, hyperbaric bag if descent delayed; add dexamethasone 4 mg 6-hourly for HACE, nifedipine or a PDE-5 inhibitor for HAPE. Prevention: gradual ascent; acetazolamide prophylaxis for rapid ascent or prior AMS. Note: descent trumps every drug - do not wait for evacuation to start losing altitude.
rich_summaries.Amenorrhoea: Absence of menstruation. Primary means no menarche by 15 with secondary sexual characteristics, or by 13 without them; secondary means periods stopping for three cycles or six months. Causes: exclude pregnancy first, every time. Then by compartment - hypothalamic (functional, from energy deficit, excessive exercise or stress), pituitary (prolactinoma, Sheehan), ovarian (PCOS, premature ovarian insufficiency, Turner), or outflow tract (Asherman, imperforate hymen, Mullerian agenesis). Ix: beta-hCG, then FSH, LH, oestradiol, prolactin and TFTs. High FSH points to the ovary, low or normal FSH to the hypothalamus or pituitary. Add testosterone if virilised, karyotype in primary amenorrhoea, and pelvic ultrasound for anatomy. Mx: treat the cause. Restore energy balance in functional disease; oestrogen replacement in premature ovarian insufficiency; dopamine agonist for prolactinoma. Note: hypo-oestrogenism of any cause costs bone, so ask about duration and consider DXA - this is the harm that outlasts the amenorrhoea itself.
rich_summaries.Amniotic fluid embolism: Rare catastrophic obstetric emergency in which amniotic fluid or fetal debris enters the maternal circulation and triggers an anaphylactoid response. Incidence 2 to 8 per 100,000 births; mortality 20 to 60%. Risk factors: advanced maternal age, multiparity, induction of labour, caesarean, instrumental delivery, placenta praevia, abruption, uterine rupture, polyhydramnios, eclampsia. Presents intrapartum or within 30 minutes post-partum in most cases. Clinical features: biphasic - initial acute pulmonary hypertension with sudden hypoxia, cyanosis and cardiovascular collapse (often with seizure), then LV failure and DIC causing massive obstetric haemorrhage. Ix: clinical diagnosis - no confirmatory test in real time. FBC, coagulation and fibrinogen (DIC pattern), cross-match, ABG, ECG, echocardiogram (acute pulmonary hypertension and RV failure). Mx: obstetric emergency call - airway, oxygen, CPR if arrest, IV access, left lateral tilt if antepartum. Massive transfusion protocol with FFP, platelets, cryoprecipitate and tranexamic acid; vasopressors and inotropes; perimortem caesarean within 4 minutes of maternal cardiac arrest. Note: survivors face high rates of neurological injury.
rich_summaries.Amyloidosis: Extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils in tissue, causing progressive organ dysfunction. Types: AL (light-chain, plasma cell dyscrasia) affects cardiac, renal, peripheral nerve and tongue. AA (secondary to chronic inflammation like RA, IBD, chronic infection) affects mostly kidney and GI. ATTR (transthyretin, hereditary or wild-type) causes elderly cardiomyopathy and hereditary neuropathy. Clinical features: cardiac disease gives restrictive cardiomyopathy with low-voltage ECG paradoxical to thick walls on echo and HFpEF; renal gives nephrotic syndrome; neuropathy gives sensorimotor and autonomic features; carpal tunnel precedes cardiac disease in ATTR. Ix: serum and urine electrophoresis with free light chains and immunofixation; affected organ or fat pad biopsy with Congo red and mass spectrometry typing; cardiac MRI and 99mTc-PYP or DPD bone scan (specific for ATTR); NT-proBNP and troponin for staging. Mx: AL gets haematology-led chemotherapy (daratumumab-based). ATTR gets tafamidis or patisiran. AA needs the underlying inflammation controlled. Note: unexplained heart failure with low-voltage ECG and thick walls is amyloid until proven otherwise.
rich_summaries.Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: Progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons, the commonest adult-onset motor neuron disease. Familial in about 10% (SOD1, C9orf72, the latter overlapping with FTD); sporadic otherwise. Clinical features: mixed UMN (spasticity, brisk reflexes, Babinski) and LMN (fasciculations, wasting, flaccid weakness) signs in the same body region, spreading over months. Limb-onset in about 70%, bulbar in about 25% with dysarthria, dysphagia and tongue fasciculations. Sensation and sphincter function are spared; extraocular muscles resist until late. Ix: no confirmatory test - diagnosis by El Escorial or Gold Coast criteria on clinical grounds, supported by EMG (widespread denervation), nerve conduction, MRI brain and spine to exclude mimics, and bloods to exclude thyroid, B12, HIV, syphilis and myeloma. Mx: multidisciplinary clinic. Riluzole modestly prolongs survival; edaravone in selected patients. Non-invasive ventilation improves quality of life and survival when FVC falls. Advance care planning early, PEG when weight loss or unsafe swallow. Note: median survival is 3 to 5 years.
rich_summaries.Anaemia of chronic disease: Anaemia mediated by inflammation, mostly normocytic and normochromic. The commonest anaemia in hospitalised patients. Mechanism: elevated hepcidin (driven by IL-6) traps iron in macrophages and blocks enteral absorption; blunted erythropoietin response and reduced red cell survival compound the picture. Causes: chronic infection, chronic inflammatory disease (RA, IBD, SLE), malignancy, chronic kidney disease. Clinical features: the underlying disease dominates; anaemia is mild (Hb typically 90 to 110) and stable. Ix: FBC, film (normocytic, normochromic), reticulocytes (low or normal), iron studies (low serum iron, low or normal transferrin, low saturation, normal-to-high ferritin - the key discriminator from iron deficiency); soluble transferrin receptor helps identify coexisting iron deficiency. Mx: treat the underlying condition. Iron only if coexisting iron deficiency proven. Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (darbepoetin, epoetin) in CKD or chemotherapy-induced anaemia at Hb below 100, targeting Hb 100 to 115. Note: never give iron on a raised ferritin without clear coexisting iron deficiency.
rich_summaries.Anal fissure: A longitudinal tear in the anoderm distal to the dentate line, over 90% in the posterior midline. Pathophysiology: hard stool tears the anoderm, pain causes internal sphincter spasm, spasm reduces perfusion, and the ischaemia prevents healing. Treatment is aimed at breaking that cycle rather than at the tear. Clinical features: severe tearing pain during defaecation persisting for up to hours afterwards, with bright blood on the paper. A sentinel skin tag marks chronicity. Ix: gentle inspection by parting the buttocks is usually enough. Digital examination is often intolerable acutely. A lateral or multiple fissure suggests Crohn disease, tuberculosis, malignancy or HIV and warrants examination under anaesthetic. Mx: fibre, fluid, stool softeners and warm baths heal most acute fissures. Topical glyceryl trinitrate or diltiazem relaxes the sphincter for chronic ones; headache limits GTN. Botulinum toxin, then lateral internal sphincterotomy. Note: sphincterotomy carries a real risk of incontinence, so counsel explicitly, particularly in women who have given birth.
rich_summaries.Anaphylaxis: Severe, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction, IgE-mediated in most (foods, drugs, insect stings) or non-immune. Diagnosis: acute onset of illness involving skin or mucosal tissue (urticaria, angioedema, flushing) plus respiratory compromise (dyspnoea, wheeze, stridor, hypoxia) or hypotension or persistent GI symptoms - or two or more organ systems after known exposure - or isolated hypotension after known allergen. Ix: clinical - do not delay treatment. Serum mast cell tryptase within 1 to 3 hours supports diagnosis. Specific IgE and skin testing after recovery, referred to a clinical immunologist. Mx: remove the trigger. IM adrenaline into the lateral thigh, 0.01 mg/kg to a maximum of 0.5 mg (500 microg for adults), repeat every 5 minutes as needed. Lie flat with legs elevated. High-flow oxygen. Two large-bore IV cannulae with 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus for hypotension. Nebulised salbutamol for bronchospasm. Antihistamines and steroids are secondary - they do not treat shock. Observe for biphasic reactions for at least 4 to 6 hours. Note: every patient discharges with two adrenaline autoinjectors, an ASCIA action plan, and clinical immunology referral.
rich_summaries.Angioedema: Non-pitting subcutaneous or submucosal swelling from plasma extravasation over face, lips, tongue, larynx, extremities and gut; distinct from urticaria though the two often coexist. Types: mast-cell-mediated (allergic, NSAID, idiopathic; itchy, urticarial, responds to adrenaline/steroid/antihistamine); bradykinin-mediated (hereditary angioedema, ACE-inhibitor, acquired C1-INH deficiency; non-pruritic, no urticaria, poor response to the above). Clinical features: swelling develops over hours, resolves 24-72; laryngeal oedema causes stridor and voice change; abdominal attacks in HAE mimic acute abdomen. Ix: acute is clinical; chronic - C4 (low in HAE and acquired C1-INH deficiency between attacks), C1-INH level and function, C1q (low only in acquired). Mx: airway assessment first; mast-cell-mediated - IM adrenaline for anaphylaxis, antihistamine, steroid; bradykinin-mediated (HAE, ACE-I) - C1-INH concentrate or icatibant; stop ACE inhibitor and never rechallenge; HAE prophylaxis with C1-INH or lanadelumab. Note: adrenaline and steroids do not treat ACE-inhibitor angioedema - stop the drug and get icatibant or C1-INH.
rich_summaries.Ankylosing spondylitis: Chronic inflammatory arthritis of the sacroiliac joints and spine, the radiographic form of axial spondyloarthritis; over 90% carry HLA-B27. Epidemiology: onset before 45 and usually in the twenties, with male predominance. Sx: inflammatory back pain with morning stiffness beyond an hour that eases with movement and worsens with rest; alternating buttock pain; reduced chest expansion; enthesitis at the Achilles and plantar fascia. Extra-articular: acute anterior uveitis, inflammatory bowel disease, psoriasis, aortic regurgitation, conduction block, apical pulmonary fibrosis. Ix: MRI of the sacroiliac joints shows bone marrow oedema years before radiographic sacroiliitis; HLA-B27 and CRP support the diagnosis without making it. Mx: continuous exercise and physiotherapy are the mainstay; NSAIDs first-line; a TNF or IL-17 inhibitor where disease stays active, which on the PBS requires a BASDAI of 4 or more after an adequate NSAID trial. Conventional DMARDs do not work for axial disease.
rich_summaries.Anorexia nervosa: Restriction of intake relative to requirements, with intense fear of weight gain and disturbed experience of body weight or shape. Epidemiology: onset usually in adolescence with female predominance; the highest mortality of any psychiatric disorder, from medical complications and from suicide. Complications: bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, prolonged QT, hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia, amenorrhoea, reduced bone mineral density, dental erosion where there is purging. Ix: ECG, electrolytes, phosphate, magnesium, glucose, liver function, bone densitometry. Mx: medical stabilisation first, with thiamine before nutrition and daily phosphate, potassium and magnesium as intake increases; psychological therapy is definitive - CBT-E, MANTRA or specialist supportive clinical management in adults, family-based treatment in adolescents. Antidepressants do not restore weight. Australian notes: an Eating Disorder Plan funds extended psychological and dietetic sessions under Medicare. Note: DSM-5-TR sets no BMI threshold for diagnosis; BMI grades severity only.
rich_summaries.Antiphospholipid syndrome: Autoimmune hypercoagulable state defined by persistent antiphospholipid antibodies plus thrombosis or pregnancy morbidity. Antibody panel includes lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I, persistent for at least 12 weeks. Primary APS is isolated; secondary APS occurs with SLE or another autoimmune disease. Clinical features: arterial or venous thrombosis (DVT, PE, stroke in a young patient, retinal vein occlusion, Budd-Chiari); recurrent early miscarriage, one or more unexplained fetal deaths at or after 10 weeks, or severe pre-eclampsia; thrombocytopenia, livedo reticularis, cardiac valve vegetations. Catastrophic APS is multi-organ thrombosis over days with high mortality. Ix: lupus anticoagulant assays (dRVVT); anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2GPI ELISA; FBC (thrombocytopenia); coagulation (paradoxically prolonged aPTT that does not correct on mixing); ANA and ENA if secondary suspected. Mx: acute VTE gets warfarin (INR 2 to 3, or 3 to 4 in recurrent). DOACs less effective, especially in triple-positive - avoid. Pregnancy: aspirin plus prophylactic LMWH from positive pregnancy test. Note: catastrophic APS gets steroids, plasma exchange and IVIG in ICU.
rich_summaries.Aortic aneurysm: Permanent dilatation of the aorta to more than 1.5 times its normal diameter, most often infrarenal abdominal. Causes: atherosclerotic degeneration with smoking as the strongest modifiable risk; connective tissue disease (Marfan, vascular Ehlers-Danlos) in younger patients; less often infection or arteritis. Clinical features: usually silent and found incidentally. A pulsatile expansile abdominal mass, back or flank pain, or the triad of pain, hypotension and a pulsatile mass in rupture. Ix: ultrasound for detection and surveillance; CT angiography before repair and in suspected rupture if the patient is stable. Mx: modify risk - stop smoking, treat blood pressure, statin and antiplatelet. Surveillance by size, with elective repair considered at about 55 mm for abdominal aneurysms, or smaller if growing quickly, symptomatic, or in a woman. Endovascular or open repair depending on anatomy and fitness. Red flags: sudden severe back or abdominal pain with haemodynamic compromise is rupture - straight to theatre, not to the scanner.
rich_summaries.Aortic dissection: Intimal tear allowing blood into the aortic media and creating a false lumen. Classification: Stanford A involves the ascending aorta and is surgical; Stanford B is confined distal to the left subclavian artery. Risk factors: hypertension above all, bicuspid aortic valve, Marfan and Ehlers-Danlos syndromes, Turner syndrome, coarctation, cocaine, third trimester pregnancy. Sx: abrupt tearing chest or interscapular pain, maximal at onset; blood pressure differential over 20 mmHg between arms; new aortic regurgitation; stroke, paraplegia or limb ischaemia from branch vessel occlusion. Ix: CT aortography; transoesophageal echocardiography if too unstable to move. A normal chest radiograph excludes nothing. Mx: rate control before pressure control - intravenous esmolol or labetalol to a heart rate under 60, then a vasodilator to systolic 100 to 120 mmHg. Type A goes to theatre immediately; uncomplicated type B is medical; complicated type B gets endovascular repair.
rich_summaries.Aortic regurgitation: Retrograde flow from aorta to left ventricle during diastole. Causes: primary valvular from bicuspid aortic valve, rheumatic disease, infective endocarditis, and calcific degeneration; or aortic root dilation from Marfan syndrome, aortic dissection, syphilis, and idiopathic dilation. Clinical features: acute AR (endocarditis, dissection) presents with sudden pulmonary oedema and cardiogenic shock. Chronic AR is asymptomatic for years before exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, orthopnoea, angina. Signs include early-diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border, wide pulse pressure, water-hammer pulse, head bobbing, displaced hyperdynamic apex, and Austin Flint murmur at the apex. Ix: 12-lead ECG (LVH); CXR; transthoracic echo grades severity by jet width, PHT, LVEF and LV end-systolic dimension; TOE for endocarditis or dissection. Mx: acute severe AR is a surgical emergency. Chronic severe symptomatic AR gets valve replacement; asymptomatic severe AR gets replacement when LVEF drops under 55% or LV end-systolic diameter exceeds 50 mm. Note: no vasodilator evidence outside hypertension - do not treat AR itself with ACE inhibitors.
rich_summaries.Aortic stenosis: Narrowing of the aortic valve outflow. Causes: calcific degeneration in the elderly (commonest); bicuspid aortic valve (40 to 60 years); rheumatic disease (with mitral involvement, still important in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities). Clinical features: crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids; reduced and delayed carotid upstroke; soft or absent S2. Cardinal triad is angina, syncope and heart failure - once symptomatic, median survival without intervention is 2 years. Ix: 12-lead ECG (LVH, LBBB); transthoracic echocardiogram is diagnostic and stages severity (valve area under 1.0 cm2, mean gradient over 40 mmHg, peak velocity over 4 m/s); coronary angiography before intervention. Mx: symptomatic severe AS gets valve replacement - surgical (SAVR) in lower-risk younger patients, transcatheter (TAVI) in higher-risk or older patients and increasingly in low-risk. Asymptomatic severe AS with a positive stress test, LVEF under 50%, or very severe stenosis is offered intervention. Avoid vasodilators. Note: bicuspid AS is associated with aortopathy - image the ascending aorta at diagnosis.
rich_summaries.Aplastic anaemia: Pancytopenia with hypocellular bone marrow, from destruction or suppression of haematopoietic stem cells. Causes: idiopathic and immune-mediated (T-cell attack on stem cells, commonest); drug-induced (chloramphenicol, sulfonamides, carbamazepine, phenytoin, gold, NSAIDs, propylthiouracil); toxin-induced (benzene, insecticides); viral (parvovirus B19, hepatitis viruses, EBV, HIV); radiation; inherited (Fanconi anaemia, dyskeratosis congenita). Clinical features: anaemia, thrombocytopenia (bruising, petechiae, mucosal bleeding), and neutropenia (infection, fever, mouth ulcers). Ix: FBC (all three lineages reduced, low reticulocytes), film (no blasts, no dysplasia), bone marrow biopsy is diagnostic (hypocellular marrow, no fibrosis or infiltration); exclude PNH (flow cytometry) and myelodysplasia. Mx: transfusion support with irradiated leucocyte-depleted products (avoid family donors before transplant); infection prophylaxis and treatment. Severe disease under 40 with a matched sibling gets allogeneic stem cell transplant. Otherwise immunosuppression with anti-thymocyte globulin and ciclosporin, and eltrombopag. Note: overall 5-year survival with modern therapy is 70 to 90%.
rich_summaries.Appendicitis: Acute inflammation of the vermiform appendix, usually from luminal obstruction (faecolith, lymphoid hyperplasia in children, tumour in older adults). Lifetime risk around 7%; peak age 10 to 30; commonest surgical abdomen in the young. Clinical features: initially vague periumbilical pain migrating to McBurney point in the RLQ over 12 to 24 hours, anorexia, nausea, low-grade fever, localised peritonism with rebound and guarding, Rovsing, psoas and obturator signs. Atypical presentation in extremes of age and in pregnancy (displaced cephalad). Ix: clinical diagnosis supported by FBC (leucocytosis), CRP, urine pregnancy test, urinalysis. Contrast CT abdomen (adults), ultrasound (children and pregnancy), MRI in pregnancy if ultrasound inconclusive. Alvarado score aids risk stratification. Mx: laparoscopic appendicectomy with IV antibiotics (gentamicin plus metronidazole per eTG). Non-operative antibiotic-only management is an option for select uncomplicated cases. Percutaneous drainage for large abscess, then interval appendicectomy. Note: perforation risk rises after 24 hours - don't delay.
rich_summaries.Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy: Inherited cardiomyopathy from desmosomal protein mutations (PKP2 commonest), causing fibrofatty replacement of RV myocardium with dilatation, dysfunction and ventricular arrhythmia; LV involvement in half. Autosomal dominant with variable penetrance; presents second to fourth decades. Major cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes - endurance exercise accelerates disease. Clinical features: palpitations, presyncope, syncope, or aborted sudden death; exercise-induced ventricular ectopy or VT with LBBB morphology; later right or biventricular heart failure. Ix: ECG shows epsilon wave in V1-V3, T wave inversion in right precordial leads, prolonged QRS in V1; Holter for ectopy burden; echocardiogram shows RV dilatation and dysfunction; cardiac MRI shows fibrofatty infiltration; genetic testing and first-degree family screening. Mx: exercise restriction (avoid competitive and endurance sport); beta-blockers first line; sotalol or amiodarone for arrhythmia suppression; ICD for aborted SCD, sustained VT, syncope, or severe RV dysfunction; catheter ablation for refractory VT. Note: family screening with ECG and echo saves lives.
rich_summaries.Aspergillosis: Spectrum of disease from Aspergillus (mostly A. fumigatus). Types: allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is a hypersensitivity reaction in asthma or cystic fibrosis with eosinophilia, IgE over 1000, positive Aspergillus IgE and IgG, and central bronchiectasis; aspergilloma is a fungal ball colonising a pre-existing cavity (old TB, sarcoid) causing haemoptysis; chronic pulmonary aspergillosis is progressive cavitary disease; invasive aspergillosis affects the neutropenic or transplant recipient with fever, pleuritic pain, and haemoptysis. Ix: HRCT shows central bronchiectasis in ABPA, fungus ball with air crescent in aspergilloma, halo and reverse-halo signs in invasive disease; serum galactomannan and beta-D-glucan support invasive diagnosis; sputum or BAL culture and PCR. Mx: ABPA gets oral prednisolone with itraconazole as steroid-sparer; aspergilloma is observed if asymptomatic, surgical resection or bronchial artery embolisation for massive haemoptysis; invasive disease gets IV voriconazole first line, with reversal of immunosuppression where possible. Note: invasive disease carries mortality over 50% - early antifungal beats waiting for confirmation.
rich_summaries.Asthma: Chronic inflammatory airway disease with variable, largely reversible airflow obstruction and airway hyperresponsiveness. Clinical features: episodic wheeze, cough, chest tightness and dyspnoea, worse at night and provoked by exercise, cold air, allergens or infection. Variability is the diagnostic hallmark. Ix: spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility - FEV1 rise of 12% and 200 mL; peak flow variability. Normal spirometry between episodes does not exclude asthma. Mx: Australian practice has moved away from short-acting beta agonist monotherapy - adults and adolescents use budesonide-formoterol as anti-inflammatory reliever, as needed or as maintenance-and-reliever therapy. Add LAMA or a biologic in severe disease. Written action plan for everyone. Note: high short-acting reliever use - more than about three canisters a year - independently predicts exacerbation and death, and is the single most useful thing to ask about. Red flags: a silent chest, exhaustion, cyanosis, or a normalising CO2 in acute severe asthma all indicate life-threatening disease - the rising CO2 means the patient is tiring, not improving.
rich_summaries.Atherosclerosis: Chronic inflammatory disease of medium and large arteries with lipid-laden intimal plaques causing luminal narrowing, plaque rupture and thrombosis. Underlies coronary, cerebrovascular and peripheral arterial disease - commonest cause of death worldwide. Risk factors: modifiable - hypertension, dyslipidaemia, diabetes, smoking, obesity, inactivity, poor diet; non-modifiable - age, male sex, family history, CKD. Clinical features depend on vascular bed and range from stable angina, intermittent claudication and TIA at the mild end to acute coronary syndrome, stroke and critical limb ischaemia at the severe. Ix: lipid profile, HbA1c, EUC, eGFR, urinary ACR, ECG, and risk calculation with Australian CVD Risk Calculator (replaced Framingham-based score in 2023).Mx: lifestyle first - Mediterranean diet, exercise, smoking cessation, weight loss. Pharmacological - statin (high-intensity for established disease or high risk), BP control, glycaemic control, antiplatelet for secondary prevention. Revascularisation for symptomatic or unstable disease. Note: LDL targets are lower in secondary prevention (under 1.8 mmol/L, and under 1.4 for very high risk).
rich_summaries.Atrial fibrillation: Supraventricular arrhythmia with disorganised atrial activity and an irregularly irregular ventricular response. Causes: hypertension; ischaemic and valvular heart disease; thyrotoxicosis; alcohol; sepsis; obstructive sleep apnoea. Clinical features: palpitations, dyspnoea, fatigue or syncope - or asymptomatic and found incidentally, which is common. Ix: ECG shows absent P waves, irregularly irregular; TFT, UEC; echocardiography; Holter if paroxysmal. Mx: three separate decisions. Rate control with a beta-blocker or diltiazem suits most; rhythm control - flecainide, amiodarone or cardioversion - where symptoms persist or the AF is new. Anticoagulation is decided independently of rate or rhythm, on CHA2DS2-VASc against HAS-BLED, DOAC preferred except in moderate to severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve. Note: anticoagulation decisions do not change once sinus rhythm is restored - stroke risk tracks the underlying substrate, not the rhythm on the day. Red flags: instability means immediate synchronised cardioversion. A very rapid, broad, irregular complex suggests pre-excited AF in WPW - avoid AV nodal blockers, which can precipitate VF.
rich_summaries.Atrial flutter: Macroreentrant atrial tachyarrhythmia; typical (isthmus-dependent) form travels counterclockwise around the tricuspid annulus at 250-350/min, giving 2:1 AV conduction at 150. Causes: structural heart disease (LV/RV dilation, mitral disease, congenital), COPD, thyrotoxicosis, alcohol, post-cardiac surgery; often coexists with atrial fibrillation. Clinical features: palpitations, dyspnoea, chest discomfort, syncope; regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150/min should raise suspicion. Ix: ECG shows sawtooth flutter waves in II, III, aVF (inverted in typical form) and V1; vagal manoeuvre or IV adenosine unmasks flutter waves; TTE for structure; TFTs, electrolytes. Mx: rate control with beta blocker or non-dihydropyridine CCB (harder than in AF); DC cardioversion (starts 50 J) or ibutilide for rhythm control; cavotricuspid isthmus ablation is first-line for typical flutter (over 90% cure); anticoagulate on the same CHA2DS2-VASc basis as AF. Note: any regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150/min in an older patient is atrial flutter with 2:1 block until an ECG during vagal manoeuvre proves otherwise.
rich_summaries.Atrial septal defect: Congenital left-to-right shunt through the interatrial septum. Types: ostium secundum (about 70%, central, involves fossa ovalis); ostium primum (part of AV septal defect spectrum, associated with Down syndrome, with cleft mitral valve); sinus venosus (superior or inferior); coronary sinus. Clinical features: often asymptomatic in childhood; fixed split second heart sound with pulmonary systolic flow murmur. Adults present with exertional dyspnoea, atrial arrhythmias, or paradoxical embolism. Long-standing shunt drives right heart dilatation and pulmonary hypertension. Ix: transthoracic echo first, TOE for anatomy before closure and for sinus venosus lesions; ECG (right axis and RBBB in secundum, left axis in primum); cardiac MRI or CT for shunt quantification and anomalous veins. Mx: close if Qp:Qs is over 1.5 or symptomatic. Percutaneous device closure for secundum with adequate rims; surgical closure for primum, sinus venosus, or unsuitable anatomy. Note: severe pulmonary hypertension (Eisenmenger) contraindicates closure - shunt reverses and lung transplant becomes the option.
rich_summaries.Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: Neurodevelopmental disorder with persistent inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity. Diagnosis (DSM-5): six or more inattentive OR hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (five if age at least 17), before age 12, in two or more settings, for at least 6 months, with functional impairment. Subtypes: inattentive, hyperactive-impulsive, or combined. Clinical features of the inattentive domain include careless mistakes, distractibility, poor organisation and forgetfulness; the hyperactive-impulsive domain adds fidgeting, restlessness, blurting out and interrupting. Adults have less overt hyperactivity but persistent inattention. Ix: no confirmatory test. Structured interview (Conners, DIVA) with collateral from parents and teachers; exclude hearing and vision problems, sleep disorder, iron deficiency and thyroid disease. Mx: behavioural and parenting support first line under 5. In older children and adults, stimulants (methylphenidate, dexamfetamine, lisdexamfetamine) are first line; atomoxetine or guanfacine for non-response. In Australia, paediatrician or psychiatrist diagnosis and initial prescription. Note: comorbid anxiety, depression, learning disorder and substance use are the rule.
rich_summaries.Autism spectrum disorder: Neurodevelopmental condition with persistent deficits in social communication and interaction, and restricted or repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities, present from early development. Diagnosis: DSM-5 requires both domains, severity graded 1 to 3 by support needed; sensory features (hyper- or hyporeactivity) are part of the criteria. Clinical features: reduced social reciprocity and joint attention, atypical eye contact, difficulty reading nonverbal cues, language delay or unusual patterns, insistence on sameness, stereotyped movements, and intense circumscribed interests. Common comorbidities are intellectual disability, ADHD, anxiety, epilepsy, sleep and feeding problems. Ix: no diagnostic test; multidisciplinary assessment using ADOS-2 and ADI-R in the Australian pathway; hearing test in every child; consider fragile X, chromosomal microarray and MECP2 by phenotype. Mx: early intervention (before age 3 where possible) with a developmental behavioural approach; speech pathology, occupational therapy, and educational supports; NDIS funds the early childhood approach under 9 in Australia. Treat comorbid conditions. Note: no pharmacotherapy for the core features.
rich_summaries.Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia: Immune-mediated red cell destruction by autoantibodies. Types by thermal amplitude: warm AIHA (IgG, active at 37 degrees, extravascular splenic destruction) is commonest - idiopathic in half, secondary to CLL, lymphoma, SLE, or drugs (methyldopa, penicillin, cefotetan); cold agglutinin disease (IgM, complement-mediated intravascular haemolysis) follows Mycoplasma, EBV or lymphoma; paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria (Donath-Landsteiner antibody) follows viral infection in children. Clinical features: anaemia symptoms, jaundice, splenomegaly, dark urine in intravascular haemolysis; cold types show Raynaud-like acrocyanosis. Ix: FBC shows anaemia with high reticulocytes; film shows spherocytes (warm) or agglutination (cold); raised LDH and unconjugated bilirubin, low haptoglobin; direct antiglobulin test (Coombs) positive - IgG in warm, C3d in cold. Investigate cause. Mx: warm AIHA gets prednisolone 1 mg/kg then taper; rituximab second line; splenectomy for steroid-refractory; treat any secondary cause. Cold AIHA - avoid cold, treat underlying lymphoproliferative disorder, rituximab; steroids and splenectomy are ineffective. Transfuse only for life-threatening anaemia.
rich_summaries.Autonomic neuropathy: Disorder of the autonomic nervous system. Causes: diabetes mellitus is by far the commonest; also Parkinson disease and multiple system atrophy, amyloidosis, Guillain-Barre variants, paraneoplastic, alcohol, hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathies, medications, and HIV. Clinical features by system: cardiovascular gives postural hypotension, resting tachycardia, silent MI, sudden cardiac death; GI gives gastroparesis, constipation, faecal incontinence, diarrhoea; genitourinary gives erectile dysfunction, urinary retention, incontinence; sudomotor gives anhidrosis or compensatory sweating. Ix: cardiovascular reflex tests (Valsalva, HRV, tilt-table); gastric emptying scintigraphy for gastroparesis; skin biopsy for small fibre density; investigate cause with HbA1c, B12, TFT, coeliac serology, SPEP, HIV. Mx: treat the cause - glycaemic control in diabetes. Fludrocortisone or midodrine for postural hypotension; metoclopramide or domperidone for gastroparesis; PDE5 inhibitor for erectile dysfunction; intermittent self-catheterisation for retention. Note: silent MI is the diabetic autonomic neuropathy trap.
rich_summaries.Avascular necrosis: Ischaemic death of bone tissue and marrow from disrupted blood supply. Commonest site is femoral head; also humeral head, femoral condyles, talus, scaphoid. Risk factors: corticosteroids (commonest non-traumatic cause), alcohol excess, SLE, sickle cell, antiphospholipid syndrome, hypercoagulability, radiotherapy, Gaucher disease, decompression sickness, trauma (displaced femoral neck fracture disrupts medial femoral circumflex artery). Clinical features: insidious groin or hip pain worse with weight-bearing, reduced hip range of motion (internal rotation lost first), antalgic gait, sudden worsening on collapse, and bilateral hip involvement in up to 80%. Ix: X-ray is insensitive early; MRI is the diagnostic test, detecting early oedema and marrow change; Ficat and ARCO staging.Mx: pre-collapse - reduce risk factors, protected weight-bearing, bisphosphonates, core decompression with or without bone grafting. Collapsed femoral head - total hip replacement. Note: bilateral MRI screening in patients on prolonged high-dose steroids.
rich_summaries.Bacterial tracheitis: Bacterial superinfection of the tracheal mucosa producing thick adherent purulent exudate and airway obstruction; peak age 3-8, usually follows a viral URTI. Aetiology: Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) is commonest; then group A Streptococcus, Moraxella and Haemophilus influenzae. Clinical features: viral prodrome then high fever, brassy cough, biphasic stridor and toxic appearance; no drooling (unlike epiglottitis); poor response to nebulised adrenaline (unlike croup). Ix: primarily clinical; direct laryngoscopy in theatre is diagnostic and therapeutic (pus clearance); CXR may show a 'shaggy trachea' with subglottic narrowing. Mx: keep child calm and transfer to a paediatric centre with theatre and ICU; intubation in theatre by the most experienced clinician for airway control and rigid-bronchoscopic clearance; empirical flucloxacillin plus third-generation cephalosporin, add vancomycin if MRSA risk; ICU ventilation with regular ETT toilet. Red flags: toxic child with biphasic stridor and high fever - involve anaesthetics and ENT immediately.
rich_summaries.Barrett oesophagus: Metaplastic replacement of the distal oesophageal squamous epithelium by intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells; recognised precursor to oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Risk factors: chronic GORD (over 5 years), male, white, central obesity, smoking, age over 50, family history; H. pylori is protective. Clinical features: usually asymptomatic; symptoms are those of underlying GORD; alarm features (dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, iron deficiency, over 55 with new symptoms) mandate urgent gastroscopy. Ix: gastroscopy with Prague C&M classification; Seattle-protocol biopsies (four-quadrant every 2 cm plus visible lesion); pathology confirms intestinal metaplasia and grades dysplasia. Mx: high-dose PPI plus lifestyle measures; surveillance gastroscopy - non-dysplastic 3-5 yearly, low-grade 6-12 monthly or endoscopic eradication, high-grade or intramucosal carcinoma get endoscopic resection plus radiofrequency ablation; oesophagectomy for invasive cancer. Note: PPI reduces reflux symptoms but does not reverse Barrett - cancer risk still needs surveillance.
rich_summaries.Bell palsy: Acute unilateral lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy, presumed HSV-1 reactivation with inflammatory oedema in the narrow facial canal. Clinical features: onset over hours to 3 days, complete unilateral facial weakness including the forehead (distinguishes from upper motor neuron stroke), inability to close the eye, drooping of the corner of the mouth, hyperacusis (stapedius) and altered taste on the anterior two thirds of the tongue (chorda tympani). Postauricular pain is common; hearing loss or vertigo points to Ramsay Hunt or another cause. Ix: clinical diagnosis. No routine imaging or bloods; check for otitis media, cholesteatoma, Lyme disease (in endemic areas), and sarcoidosis if bilateral or atypical. MRI if pattern is not classic. Mx: oral prednisolone 60 mg daily for 5 days then taper over 5 days, started within 72 hours of onset. Add oral valaciclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days in severe cases. Eye care with lubricants and taping at night to protect the exposed cornea. Physiotherapy for facial retraining. Note: most recover fully within 3 to 6 months; House-Brackmann grade at presentation predicts recovery.
rich_summaries.Benign prostatic hyperplasia: Nodular hyperplasia of the periurethral transitional zone of the prostate producing bladder outlet obstruction and lower urinary tract symptoms. Over half of men over 60. Clinical features: obstructive symptoms include hesitancy, poor stream, straining, incomplete emptying and terminal dribbling; irritative symptoms include frequency, urgency, nocturia and urge incontinence. IPSS quantifies severity. Complications include acute urinary retention, recurrent UTI, bladder stones and hydronephrosis. Ix: DRE looks for smooth enlargement (hard, nodular or asymmetric prostate warrants prostate cancer workup). Urinalysis and culture, EUC, PSA after informed decision, post-void bladder scan; renal ultrasound if obstruction suspected. Mx: watchful waiting for mild symptoms. Alpha-1 blocker (tamsulosin, prazosin) gives symptom relief within days. 5-alpha reductase inhibitor (finasteride, dutasteride) shrinks the prostate over 3 to 6 months in prostates over 30 mL. Combination for larger prostates. Surgery is TURP for refractory symptoms; alternatives include HoLEP, Rezum and UroLift. Note: acute retention with bladder over 800 mL - decompress gradually to avoid haemorrhage.
rich_summaries.Binge eating disorder: The most common eating disorder. Diagnosis (DSM-5): recurrent binge eating on average at least once a week for 3 months, with marked distress and no regular compensatory behaviour (distinguishes from bulimia nervosa). Clinical features: binge is objectively excessive food in a discrete time with loss of control, and three or more of eating faster than normal, eating until uncomfortably full, eating without hunger, eating alone from embarrassment, or self-disgust afterwards. Weight is often but not always elevated; comorbid depression, anxiety and metabolic syndrome are common. Ix: no specific test; screen with SCOFF and a direct history. FBC, EUC, glucose, HbA1c, LFT, lipids - metabolic screening is a genuine goal, not a comment on weight. Mx: enhanced CBT for eating disorders (CBT-E) is first-line; interpersonal therapy and guided self-help are alternatives. Lisdexamfetamine is TGA-approved for moderate to severe BED and reduces binge frequency; SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline) reduce binges with smaller effect. Note: weight loss is not the primary goal - binge frequency and psychological distress are.
rich_summaries.Bipolar disorder: Chronic mood disorder with recurrent manic, hypomanic or depressive episodes. Types: bipolar I needs at least one manic episode (7 days, or any duration if hospitalisation or psychosis); bipolar II needs a hypomanic episode (4 or more days) plus a major depressive episode. Cyclothymia is fluctuating subthreshold symptoms for 2 years. Mania is captured by DIGFAST - distractibility, impulsivity, grandiosity, flight of ideas, activity increase, sleep decrease, talkativeness. Ix: no confirmatory test; exclude organic causes with FBC, EUC, TFT, calcium, urine drug screen; collateral history is essential. Mx: lithium is the reference mood stabiliser; sodium valproate (contraindicated in people who could become pregnant) and second-generation antipsychotics are alternatives. Quetiapine or lamotrigine for bipolar depression. Avoid antidepressant monotherapy - risk of mood switch. Note: suicide risk is 15 to 20 times general population; ask at every review.
rich_summaries.Borderline personality disorder: Pervasive pattern of instability across relationships, self-image and affect with marked impulsivity. Onset by early adulthood, diagnosed after age 18. Prevalence around 2%; female predominance in clinical samples. Aetiology combines heritability (~40%) with childhood adversity. Sx (DSM-5 requires 5 of 9): frantic efforts to avoid abandonment; unstable intense relationships alternating idealisation and devaluation; identity disturbance; impulsivity in two self-damaging areas; recurrent suicidal behaviour or self-harm; affective instability; chronic emptiness; inappropriate intense anger; transient stress-related paranoia or dissociation. High comorbidity with depression, PTSD, substance use and eating disorders. Ix: clinical diagnosis; screen comorbidity; assess suicide and self-harm risk at every contact. Mx: structured psychotherapy is first line - dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) has the strongest evidence; mentalisation-based, transference-focused and schema therapies also effective. Pharmacotherapy targets comorbidity or crisis only; avoid polypharmacy and long-term benzodiazepines. Note: prognosis improves with age - remission over 70% at 10 years.
rich_summaries.Bowel obstruction: Mechanical blockage of the intestinal lumen, classified by level and by whether the bowel is strangulated. Causes: adhesions dominate the small bowel, then hernia and malignancy; in the large bowel, malignancy, volvulus and diverticular stricture. Clinical features: colicky pain, vomiting (early in proximal, late in distal), distension and absolute constipation. Bowel sounds are tinkling then absent. Ix: CT abdomen with contrast identifies level, cause and strangulation. Erect chest film if perforation is suspected. EUC and VBG for lactate. Mx: drip and suck - nasogastric decompression, intravenous fluid and correction of electrolytes - is the initial approach for adhesional obstruction, and many settle. Surgery for strangulation, closed loop, perforation, or failure to resolve. Water-soluble contrast is both prognostic and mildly therapeutic. Red flags: constant rather than colicky pain, tachycardia, fever, peritonism or rising lactate mean strangulation and immediate operation.
rich_summaries.Bradycardia: Heart rate under 60/min. Causes: physiological (athletes, sleep, high vagal tone); pathological includes AV block, sick sinus syndrome, hypothyroidism, hypothermia, raised ICP (Cushing reflex), and drugs (beta blockers, non-dihydropyridine CCBs, digoxin, amiodarone, ivabradine, clonidine). Clinical features: often asymptomatic; when symptomatic gives fatigue, presyncope, syncope, dyspnoea, or ischaemic chest pain. Look for haemodynamic instability - hypotension, altered mental state, chest pain, heart failure - which triggers urgent treatment. Ix: 12-lead ECG defines the rhythm; EUC, TFT, troponin, digoxin level if relevant; echo for structural cause; ambulatory monitoring for intermittent symptoms. Mx: stop offending drug and correct electrolytes. Symptomatic bradycardia gets atropine 500 microg IV, repeatable to 3 mg; if inadequate, isoprenaline or adrenaline infusion, or transcutaneous pacing while transvenous pacing is arranged. Permanent pacemaker for symptomatic sinus node dysfunction or high-grade AV block outside reversible causes. Note: Austroads driving rules apply until definitive treatment.
rich_summaries.Breast cancer: The commonest cancer in Australian women; lifetime risk about 1 in 7. Types: invasive ductal (no special type) 75%, invasive lobular (15%, often bilateral), and ductal carcinoma in situ (non-invasive precursor). Molecular subtypes drive treatment - hormone receptor positive (ER, PR), HER2 positive, and triple negative. Risk factors: female sex, age, family history, BRCA1/BRCA2, dense breast tissue, early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, prolonged MHT, alcohol, obesity. Clinical features: painless breast lump, skin changes (peau d'orange, dimpling), nipple retraction or discharge, axillary lymphadenopathy; inflammatory breast cancer presents as diffuse erythema and warmth. Ix: BreastScreen Australia offers 2-yearly mammography 50 to 74 (invited from 40). Triple assessment for any lump - clinical, bilateral mammogram plus targeted ultrasound, and core biopsy. Mx: multidisciplinary. Surgery (breast conserving with radiotherapy, or mastectomy) with sentinel node biopsy. Adjuvant therapy by subtype - endocrine for ER-positive, trastuzumab for HER2-positive, chemotherapy by risk. Note: BRCA testing under CanRisk or eviQ criteria.
rich_summaries.Bronchiectasis: Irreversible bronchial dilatation from chronic airway infection and inflammation. Causes: post-infective is commonest (pertussis, measles, adenovirus, TB in endemic areas), cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, humoral immunodeficiency, ABPA, gastro-oesophageal reflux with aspiration, and foreign body. Clinical features: chronic daily productive cough with purulent sputum, recurrent chest infections, haemoptysis, progressive dyspnoea; coarse crackles and, in severe disease, clubbing. Ix: high-resolution CT is the reference standard (dilated bronchi, signet-ring sign, tram tracks), spirometry (obstructive), sputum culture including atypical mycobacteria and Pseudomonas; work-up for cause with immunoglobulins, aspergillus IgE and IgG, and sweat chloride if young. Mx: daily airway clearance (physiotherapy, ACBT, PEP devices) is the foundation. Treat exacerbations with sputum-directed antibiotics for 10 to 14 days. Long-term azithromycin reduces exacerbations in selected patients. Inhaled colistin for chronic Pseudomonas. Note: eradicate first Pseudomonas isolation - it changes prognosis.
rich_summaries.Bronchiolitis: Acute viral lower respiratory tract infection with inflammation and oedema of the bronchioles in infants under 2 years, peaking at 2 to 6 months. Aetiology: respiratory syncytial virus in most, then rhinovirus, human metapneumovirus, adenovirus, parainfluenza. Clinical features: 2 to 3 day coryzal prodrome, then wheeze, tachypnoea, chest recession and feeding difficulty; fine crackles and wheeze on auscultation; peak severity at day 2 to 3 of respiratory symptoms. Ix: clinical diagnosis. Do not do routine CXR, viral swabs or bloods; oxygen saturation on room air is the practical severity marker. Mx: supportive - minimal handling, small frequent feeds or NG feeds if oral intake is poor, and oxygen for saturations under 90% (RCH guideline). High-flow nasal prongs for moderate work of breathing not responding to low-flow oxygen. Bronchodilators, steroids, adrenaline, antibiotics and chest physiotherapy do not help routine bronchiolitis. Note: admit any infant with apnoea, marked distress, poor feeding, dehydration or SpO2 under 92%; palivizumab prophylaxis is offered to selected high-risk infants.
rich_summaries.Bronchitis: Self-limited inflammation of the tracheobronchial tree, usually viral. Causes: rhinovirus, influenza, RSV, adenovirus, parainfluenza, coronaviruses; bacterial (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Bordetella pertussis) is a minority. Clinical features: cough (productive or dry) lasting under 3 weeks, often preceded by URTI; chest discomfort, wheeze, low-grade fever; auscultation clear or with coarse crackles that clear with coughing. Chronic bronchitis is a distinct COPD phenotype, not this. Ix: clinical diagnosis. CXR only if fever over 38, tachypnoea over 24, tachycardia over 100, focal signs, or duration over 3 weeks - to exclude pneumonia. Consider pertussis PCR in prolonged paroxysmal cough. Mx: symptomatic - fluids, paracetamol, honey for cough in over-1-year-olds. Antibiotics do not shorten viral bronchitis and increase side effects and resistance - reserved for pertussis exposure, severe underlying lung disease, or objective evidence of bacterial infection. Note: acute bronchitis is one of the most over-antibioticised diagnoses in Australian general practice.
rich_summaries.Bronchopulmonary dysplasia: Chronic lung disease of prematurity, defined by need for supplemental oxygen or respiratory support at 36 weeks corrected gestational age; affects around 40% of survivors below 28 weeks. Pathophysiology: arrested alveolarisation and dysmorphic microvasculature after disruption of the canalicular-saccular phase; volutrauma, oxygen toxicity, chorioamnionitis and postnatal infection contribute. Severity (NIH): mild (room air), moderate (under 30% O2), severe (30% or more, or positive pressure) at 36/40. Ix: chest X-ray shows hazy lungs with cystic changes; echo to screen for pulmonary hypertension. Mx: gentle ventilation with permissive hypercapnia and SpO2 target 90-95%, caffeine (reduces BPD), diuretics for symptom relief; low-dose systemic dexamethasone (DART) for ventilator-dependent infants balances neurodevelopmental risk against gain, palivizumab through RSV season, home oxygen and nutritional support as needed. Prevention: antenatal corticosteroids, surfactant, non-invasive ventilation. Note: pulmonary hypertension is the strongest predictor of mortality - screen with echo and refer.
rich_summaries.Brugada syndrome: Inherited channelopathy causing sudden cardiac death in structurally normal hearts. Genetics: autosomal dominant with variable penetrance; SCN5A mutation reduces sodium current in about a quarter. More common in Southeast Asian males, presenting in middle age. Clinical features: often asymptomatic, picked up on family screening or incidental ECG; syncope, nocturnal agonal breathing, or aborted sudden cardiac death from polymorphic VT or VF, often at rest, at night, or with fever. Ix: 12-lead ECG - type 1 pattern is coved ST elevation at least 2 mm in V1 or V2 with a negative T wave, either spontaneous or provoked by a sodium channel blocker challenge (ajmaline, flecainide, procainamide). Types 2 and 3 are less diagnostic. Echocardiogram to confirm structurally normal heart. Genetic testing supports family screening. Mx: avoid triggers - treat fever aggressively with paracetamol; avoid alcohol excess, cocaine, tricyclics, and drugs listed on BrugadaDrugs.org. ICD for survivors of cardiac arrest or symptomatic (syncope with type 1 pattern); quinidine as an adjunct. Family cascade screening. Note: fever is the single most avoidable trigger of arrhythmic events.
rich_summaries.Bulimia nervosa: Eating disorder with recurrent binge eating followed by compensatory behaviour to prevent weight gain, on average at least once a week for 3 months. Clinical features: binge is objectively excessive food in a discrete time with loss of control; compensation is self-induced vomiting, laxative or diuretic misuse, fasting, or excessive exercise. Weight is typically normal or above. Self-evaluation is unduly influenced by shape and weight. Physical signs are parotid enlargement, dental enamel erosion, Russell sign, oedema and menstrual irregularity. Ix: FBC and EUC to detect hypokalaemia and hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis from vomiting; add magnesium, phosphate, LFT and ECG (QT prolongation is the electrolyte hazard to catch). Mx: enhanced CBT for eating disorders is first-line; IPT is an alternative. Fluoxetine 60 mg daily reduces binge and purge frequency and is the only SSRI with evidence in bulimia. Correct electrolytes and arrange dental review. Note: mortality is lower than anorexia but suicide risk is significant.
rich_summaries.CIDP: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy - acquired immune-mediated demyelinating neuropathy, the chronic counterpart of Guillain-Barre. Onset over 8 weeks (GBS is under 4 weeks). Peak age 40 to 60; male predominance. Sx: progressive or relapsing symmetric proximal and distal weakness, large-fibre sensory involvement, areflexia and gait ataxia; autonomic and cranial features are rare (unlike GBS); no respiratory failure. Variants: multifocal motor neuropathy, Lewis-Sumner and distal acquired demyelinating symmetric neuropathy. Ix: nerve conduction studies show demyelination (conduction block, prolonged distal latencies, slowed velocities, temporal dispersion); CSF shows albuminocytological dissociation (raised protein, normal cells); MRI shows nerve root enhancement. Screen for associated MGUS, HIV, hepatitis and lymphoma. Mx: three equivalent first-line options - IV immunoglobulin (usually first for speed), plasma exchange, and corticosteroids. Maintenance with subcutaneous immunoglobulin or steroid-sparing agents. Note: early treatment prevents axonal loss.
rich_summaries.COPD: Progressive airflow limitation that is not fully reversible, from chronic bronchitis and emphysema. Causes: smoking overwhelmingly; biomass exposure; occupational dust; alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency if young or basal-predominant. Clinical features: chronic dyspnoea; productive cough and wheeze; recurrent infection; hyperinflation. Clubbing is not a feature and should prompt a search for cancer or bronchiectasis. Ix: post-bronchodilator spirometry showing FEV1/FVC below 0.7 is required for diagnosis; chest X-ray; alpha-1 antitrypsin if indicated. Mx: smoking cessation is the only intervention that alters progression. Pulmonary rehabilitation and vaccination; inhaled therapy stepped from a reliever through LAMA or LABA to dual therapy, adding an inhaled corticosteroid if exacerbations persist or eosinophils are raised. Long-term oxygen only for chronic hypoxaemia. Note: check inhaler technique before escalating - poor technique is commoner than genuine treatment failure. Target saturations of 88-92% in exacerbation, since over-oxygenation worsens hypercapnia. Red flags: rising CO2 with acidosis needs non-invasive ventilation.
rich_summaries.Candidiasis: Fungal infection with Candida species, most often C. albicans. Mucocutaneous disease covers oral thrush, oesophageal candidiasis, vulvovaginal candidiasis, intertrigo, and chronic paronychia; invasive disease is candidaemia and deep organ candidiasis in the immunocompromised or ICU patient. Risk factors: recent antibiotic use, inhaled or systemic corticosteroids, diabetes, pregnancy, HIV and other immunosuppression, indwelling lines. Clinical features: oral thrush is white plaques on erythematous base that wipe off; oesophageal gives odynophagia (consider HIV if unexplained); vulvovaginal is thick curd-like discharge, itch, dyspareunia. Invasive disease presents as sepsis in a high-risk host. Ix: clinical for uncomplicated disease; wet mount, KOH or culture for atypical; blood cultures and 1,3-beta-D-glucan for invasive disease. Mx: oral thrush gets topical nystatin drops or miconazole gel; refractory or oesophageal disease gets oral fluconazole. Vulvovaginal gets topical clotrimazole or single-dose oral fluconazole. Invasive gets IV echinocandin (caspofungin, anidulafungin) empirically. Note: check HIV in any adult with unexplained oral or oesophageal candidiasis.
rich_summaries.Carbon monoxide poisoning: Toxic exposure to CO, an odourless colourless gas from incomplete combustion (faulty gas heaters, car exhaust in enclosed spaces, house fires, generators, poorly-ventilated cooking). CO binds haemoglobin with 250 times the affinity of oxygen (carboxyhaemoglobin), shifts the dissociation curve left, and binds cytochrome oxidase impairing mitochondrial respiration. Clinical features: mild - headache, nausea, dizziness (often mistaken for flu, especially in winter with faulty heating); moderate - confusion, tachycardia, vomiting; severe - seizures, coma, cardiac ischaemia, arrhythmia, arrest. Cherry-red skin is late and unreliable. Delayed neuropsychiatric syndrome in weeks with cognitive impairment, parkinsonism, personality change. Ix: standard pulse oximetry falsely normal - use co-oximetry or ABG for carboxyhaemoglobin (normal under 3% non-smoker, under 10% smoker); lactate; troponin; ECG. Mx: remove from source; high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather (reduces half-life from 5 hours to 60 minutes); hyperbaric oxygen for severe (LOC, neurological signs, cardiac ischaemia, COHb over 25%, pregnancy). Note: CO alarms are cheap and save lives.
rich_summaries.Carcinoid syndrome: Clinical syndrome from vasoactive peptides (serotonin, tachykinins, histamine, prostaglandins) released by well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumours, predominantly midgut (ileum). Symptoms appear when the portal circulation is bypassed - usually with liver metastases or with primary lung, ovarian or retroperitoneal tumours draining directly into systemic circulation. Clinical features: episodic flushing (face, neck, upper chest), secretory diarrhoea, wheezing and bronchospasm, and right-sided valvular heart disease (tricuspid regurgitation, pulmonary stenosis). Carcinoid crisis (profound flushing, vasomotor collapse) can be precipitated by anaesthesia, biopsy or embolisation. Ix: 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA is the classic biochemical test (avoid tryptophan-rich foods 48 hours before); chromogranin A; localise with CT, MRI, and 68Ga-DOTATATE PET; echocardiogram to assess valves. Mx: octreotide or lanreotide for symptom control and antiproliferative effect. Surgical resection of primary and metastases where feasible. Peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (177Lu-DOTATATE) for progressive disease. Note: cover any procedure with IV octreotide to prevent carcinoid crisis.
rich_summaries.Cardiac tamponade: Life-threatening pericardial effusion raising intrapericardial pressure to a level that impairs cardiac filling. Rate of accumulation matters more than volume - rapid 100 to 200 mL causes tamponade, slow over 1 L may not. Causes: malignancy (commonest non-traumatic - breast, lung, lymphoma), uraemia, infection (viral, TB, purulent), post-cardiac injury (post-MI rupture, post-cardiac surgery, iatrogenic PCI perforation), aortic dissection, connective tissue disease, trauma. Clinical features: Beck triad (hypotension, muffled heart sounds, raised JVP); pulsus paradoxus over 10 mmHg; Kussmaul sign may occur; tachycardia and dyspnoea; shock; PEA arrest. Ix: ECG (low-voltage QRS, electrical alternans); CXR shows enlarged globular heart; TTE is diagnostic and bedside - pericardial fluid with diastolic RV or RA collapse, IVC plethora, respiratory variation. Mx: urgent pericardiocentesis under echo guidance (relief is immediate and diagnostic); surgical pericardial window for recurrent, purulent, or post-cardiac surgery. Fluid resuscitation as a bridge; avoid intubation and positive pressure ventilation. Note: tamponade is a clinical diagnosis - don't delay drainage for imaging.
rich_summaries.Cardiogenic shock: End-organ hypoperfusion from primary cardiac pump failure with adequate volume; commonest cause is acute MI with LV failure; mortality 40-50% despite reperfusion. Aetiology: acute MI with over 40% LV loss (LV pump failure, RV infarct, papillary rupture with acute MR, VSD, free-wall rupture); decompensated cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, valve failure, massive PE, arrhythmia. Clinical features: cool mottled extremities, weak pulses, narrow pulse pressure, hypotension despite adequate filling, oliguria, altered mentation, pulmonary oedema; raised JVP and gallop. Ix: ECG, troponin, ABG plus lactate, portable CXR; urgent echo identifies aetiology (LV function, valve, tamponade, RV strain); central access. Mx: ABC and oxygen; correct arrhythmia; cautious fluid if hypovolaemic; noradrenaline (preferred to dopamine per SOAP-II) plus inotrope (dobutamine, milrinone); early revascularisation for MI-shock (culprit-only PCI per CULPRIT-SHOCK); mechanical support (IABP, Impella, VA-ECMO) as bridge; treat cause. Note: cardiac cause plus a wet lung and cool periphery - the wrong fluid bolus makes it worse.
rich_summaries.Carpal tunnel syndrome: Compression of the median nerve at the wrist as it passes through the carpal tunnel; the commonest peripheral entrapment neuropathy. Risk factors: female sex, pregnancy, obesity, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, acromegaly, amyloidosis, repetitive wrist activity, prior wrist fracture. Clinical features: nocturnal paraesthesia and pain in the median distribution (thumb, index, middle, radial half of ring finger), relieved by shaking the hand (flick sign); weakness of thumb abduction and opposition, thenar wasting in advanced disease. Tinel and Phalen tests are supportive but neither sensitive nor specific enough alone. Ix: clinical diagnosis in typical presentations; nerve conduction studies confirm and grade severity, and are needed before surgery; TFT, HbA1c, rheumatoid screen if underlying cause suspected. Mx: night wrist splints in neutral position; ergonomic modification; NSAIDs for pain; local corticosteroid injection for short-term relief in moderate disease. Carpal tunnel release (open or endoscopic) for persistent symptoms, motor loss, or failed conservative management. Note: pregnancy-related CTS usually resolves postpartum.
rich_summaries.Cataract: Opacification of the crystalline lens; the leading cause of reversible blindness worldwide. Types: nuclear (commonest, central, progressive myopia and second sight); cortical (spoke-like opacities); posterior subcapsular (glare, near-vision loss, faster progression, commoner in steroid use and diabetes); congenital. Risk factors: age, sun exposure, smoking, diabetes, corticosteroids, previous ocular surgery or trauma, uveitis, and myotonic dystrophy. Clinical features: progressive painless visual impairment, glare (particularly with night driving), reduced colour perception, second sight in nuclear sclerosis. Ix: visual acuity, slit-lamp examination, red reflex reduced or absent, fundus obscured. Mx: refer to ophthalmology when visual impairment affects function or the patient is unhappy with the vision - no medical treatment exists. Phacoemulsification with intraocular lens implant is definitive, day-case under topical anaesthesia. Note: congenital cataract needs urgent surgery to prevent amblyopia; check red reflex at every well-child visit.
