rich_summaries.Cauda equina syndrome: Compression of lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus, producing bilateral radicular deficit, saddle anaesthesia and bladder-bowel dysfunction; time-critical spinal emergency. Causes: large central disc herniation (commonest, L4/5 or L5/S1); less often tumour, epidural abscess or haematoma, spinal stenosis or trauma. Clinical features: severe low back pain with bilateral sciatica, saddle and perineal anaesthesia, painless urinary retention with overflow (earliest reliable sign is reduced perianal sensation), loss of anal tone and sexual dysfunction. Ix: post-void bladder scan (retention over 200 mL supports); urgent MRI whole spine within hours; PR for tone; do not delay imaging for other work-up. Mx: urgent (within 24-48 hours from onset) neurosurgical decompression; steroids only for metastatic compression pending radiotherapy; catheterise. Red flags mandating same-day MRI: bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, bladder or bowel change, sexual dysfunction, progressive motor weakness. Note: outcomes correlate with time to decompression - complete cauda equina has worse recovery than incomplete, but delay makes both worse.
rich_summaries.Cavernous sinus syndrome: Compression, thrombosis, inflammation or infiltration of the cavernous sinus, producing dysfunction of the structures it carries - CN III, IV, VI, V1 and V2, internal carotid artery, and sympathetic fibres. Causes: cavernous sinus thrombosis (septic from facial or sinus Staph aureus infection; aseptic from hypercoagulability or dehydration); tumour (nasopharyngeal, meningioma, pituitary macroadenoma, metastasis); carotid-cavernous fistula (post-trauma); inflammatory (Tolosa-Hunt, sarcoid, GPA); infection (mucormycosis in diabetics, aspergillosis, TB). Clinical features: unilateral painful ophthalmoplegia with ptosis, chemosis and proptosis; V1 and V2 sensory loss; Horner syndrome; bilateral eye involvement is specific for cavernous sinus thrombosis. Ix: MRI brain with contrast and MR venography; blood cultures if septic; FBC, coagulation and thrombophilia screen. Mx: septic thrombosis needs IV broad-spectrum antibiotics plus anticoagulation with heparin; corticosteroids for Tolosa-Hunt (dramatic response); treat the underlying cause. Note: mortality 20 to 30% even with treatment.
rich_summaries.Cavernous sinus thrombosis: Thrombosis of the paired cavernous sinuses; septic in most cases. Causes: infection tracks from the face ('danger triangle'), sphenoid or ethmoid sinusitis, dental or middle-ear sepsis, orbital cellulitis; Staphylococcus aureus leads, streptococci and anaerobes for sinus sources. Clinical features: fever, headache, systemic toxicity; painful ophthalmoplegia from CN III, IV or VI palsy (CN VI fails first - it lies free in the sinus lumen); proptosis, chemosis, periorbital oedema; V1 or V2 sensory loss; spread to the contralateral eye through the intercavernous sinuses within 24 to 48 hours is classic. Ix: MRI with contrast plus MR venography - filling defect, sinus expansion, enlarged superior ophthalmic vein; blood cultures; identify the source (CT sinuses, dental review). Mx: IV antibiotics per eTG - vancomycin plus ceftriaxone plus metronidazole for a sinus source; therapeutic heparin unless clearly contraindicated (small trials support it in septic CST); urgent ENT or neurosurgical drainage of the primary focus. Red flags: bilateral eye signs, altered consciousness or meningism suggest ICP rise, meningitis or venous infarction.
rich_summaries.Cellulitis: Acute bacterial infection of deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue, usually Streptococcus pyogenes then Staphylococcus aureus. Clinical features: spreading erythema, warmth, swelling and tenderness with poorly demarcated borders, usually one lower limb, often with fever and an entry point such as tinea pedis. Differential: bilateral presentation is almost never cellulitis - consider venous eczema, lipodermatosclerosis, chronic oedema, DVT. Ix: clinical. Blood cultures only if systemically unwell; mark the erythema border to track progress. Mx: oral flucloxacillin or cefalexin; IV if systemically unwell. Elevate the limb and treat the entry point to reduce recurrence. Note: erythema often appears to extend in the first 24-48 h despite effective treatment, so that alone is not a reason to switch. Red flags: pain out of proportion, crepitus, bullae or necrosis suggest necrotising fasciitis - a surgical emergency.
rich_summaries.Cerebral artery dissection: Intimal tear allowing blood into the arterial wall, forming an intramural haematoma that narrows or occludes the lumen; commonest cause of ischaemic stroke under 45. Types: extracranial internal carotid (commonest) and vertebral arteries; intracranial dissection is rarer and can cause SAH. Causes: trauma (whiplash, chiropractic manipulation, sport, coughing), connective-tissue disease (Ehlers-Danlos IV, Marfan, fibromuscular dysplasia); often spontaneous. Clinical features: unilateral headache or neck pain, partial Horner syndrome (miosis, ptosis, no anhidrosis - carotid), pulsatile tinnitus, lower cranial nerve palsy; ischaemic stroke or TIA hours to days later. Ix: CT or MR angiogram of head and neck (fat-saturated T1 shows crescentic intramural haematoma). Mx: antiplatelet or anticoagulation for stroke prevention (CADISS showed equivalence at 3 months); IV thrombolysis is not contraindicated for acute ischaemic stroke; endovascular stenting for pseudoaneurysm or progressive occlusion. Note: young stroke with neck pain plus Horner is carotid dissection until vascular imaging proves otherwise.
rich_summaries.Cerebral palsy: Non-progressive disorder of movement and posture from injury or malformation of the developing brain (usually before age 2). Prevalence around 2 per 1000 live births in Australia. Risk factors: prematurity (strongest), low birth weight, intrauterine infection, multiple pregnancy, birth asphyxia, neonatal stroke, chorioamnionitis, kernicterus. Types: spastic (commonest, UMN injury - hemi, di, quadriplegic), dyskinetic (basal ganglia - choreoathetosis, dystonia), ataxic (cerebellar), mixed. Clinical features: delayed motor milestones, abnormal tone, persistent primitive reflexes, scissoring gait; associated intellectual disability (50%), epilepsy (30%), visual and hearing impairment, feeding and communication difficulties. GMFCS grades severity. Ix: clinical diagnosis with MRI brain (structural abnormality in 90%); rule out progressive or metabolic disease if atypical; genetic testing if MRI normal. Mx: multidisciplinary - physiotherapy, OT, speech therapy, orthoses; spasticity with oral baclofen or intrathecal pump, botulinum toxin, selective dorsal rhizotomy, orthopaedic surgery. NDIS-funded supports. Note: early intervention before age 2 improves outcomes.
rich_summaries.Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis: Thrombosis of the dural sinuses or cortical veins, causing raised intracranial pressure and venous infarction that does not respect arterial territories. Causes: prothrombotic states, especially pregnancy and the puerperium, combined oral contraceptive, thrombophilia and malignancy; or local causes such as mastoiditis or sinusitis. Clinical features: headache in most, often progressive over days and worse lying flat. Then seizures, focal deficits, papilloedema or encephalopathy. A young patient with a new persistent headache and a seizure is the pattern to recognise. Ix: CT or MR venography. Plain CT is normal in a large minority and a negative D-dimer does not exclude it either. Mx: anticoagulate with heparin even when there is haemorrhagic infarction - the bleeding is venous and secondary to the clot. Then oral anticoagulation for months. Treat seizures and raised pressure; endovascular therapy or decompression for deterioration. Note: investigate for an underlying thrombophilia and review hormonal contraception afterwards.
rich_summaries.Cervical cancer: Malignancy of the uterine cervix, almost always caused by persistent high-risk HPV infection (types 16 and 18 in 70%). Types: squamous cell carcinoma (about 70%) or adenocarcinoma (about 25%). Risk factors: early coitarche, multiple sexual partners, immunosuppression (HIV), smoking, long-term COC use, and non-participation in screening. Clinical features: early disease is asymptomatic and picked up on screening; abnormal vaginal bleeding (post-coital, intermenstrual, postmenopausal), offensive discharge, pelvic or back pain, and lower limb oedema mark locally advanced disease. Ix: Australian Cervical Screening Program - primary HPV test from age 25 every 5 years until 74. Positive result triggers reflex liquid-based cytology and colposcopy with biopsy. Staging with FIGO clinical assessment supplemented by MRI pelvis. Mx: stage-driven - cone excision or radical trachelectomy for early fertility-preserving disease; radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy for stage IB2 to IIA; chemoradiation with cisplatin for locally advanced disease. Note: HPV vaccination on the NIP is the primary prevention.
rich_summaries.Cervical ectropion: Eversion of columnar endocervical epithelium onto the ectocervix, replacing the usual squamous epithelium of the visible cervix. Common and benign in oestrogen-rich states - reproductive years, pregnancy, COCP use. Not premalignant; distinct from CIN. Clinical features: often asymptomatic and noted on speculum as a smooth red circumferential zone around the os; when symptomatic - post-coital or intermenstrual bleeding, watery or mucoid non-purulent discharge, recurrent cervicitis. Ix: infection screen (chlamydia, gonorrhoea, trichomonas, bacterial vaginosis, candida) and cervical screening test per NCSP; colposcopy if screening abnormal or bleeding persists despite treatment. Mx: no treatment if asymptomatic. Stop COCP or switch to non-hormonal contraception if temporally related. Ablative treatment (cryotherapy, electrocautery, silver nitrate) for symptomatic bleeding or discharge after excluding other causes. Note: post-coital bleeding always warrants colposcopy referral even when ectropion is obvious - to rule out cervical cancer.
rich_summaries.Chilblains: Localised inflammatory response of acral skin to cold damp exposure (perniosis); commoner in unheated Australian winters, young women and connective-tissue disease. Pathophysiology: cold-induced small-vessel vasospasm and secondary inflammation, not true frostbite. Clinical features: itchy tender erythematous-violaceous papules over toes, fingers, nose and ears 12-24 hours after cold exposure; blistering or ulceration in severe cases; resolves in 1-3 weeks. Ix: clinical; ANA, complement, cryoglobulins and cold agglutinins if recurrent, unusual sites or systemic features to exclude lupus, cryoglobulinaemia and antiphospholipid syndrome. Mx: warm environment (heating, insulated footwear), keep extremities dry, stop smoking; topical corticosteroid for acute inflammation; nifedipine slow-release for recurrent disease. Note: chilblains persisting into spring or with digital ulceration deserve a connective-tissue-disease screen.
rich_summaries.Chlamydia: Chlamydia trachomatis serovars D to K - the commonest bacterial STI in Australia. Clinical features: asymptomatic in most (about 70% women, 50% men). Women may have discharge, dysuria, intermenstrual or post-coital bleeding, and pelvic pain from ascending PID; men may have urethritis, epididymitis, and rarely reactive arthritis. Rectal, pharyngeal and conjunctival infection occur with matching exposure. Ix: nucleic acid amplification test - first-catch urine in men, self-collected vulvovaginal swab in women, site-specific swabs for rectum, throat and eye. Screen for other STIs at diagnosis. Mx: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days is first line in Australia; azithromycin 1 g stat is an alternative in pregnancy or poor adherence. Doxycycline for 3 weeks in lymphogranuloma venereum or complicated PID. Advise abstinence for 7 days after treatment. Notifiable; partner notification (6 months) and test of cure at 3 months in women under 25 or in pregnancy. Note: undiagnosed chlamydia causes tubal infertility - screen sexually active people under 30.
rich_summaries.Cholangitis: Bacterial infection of the biliary tree, usually from partial or complete CBD obstruction. Causes: choledocholithiasis (commonest), malignant stricture (pancreatic head, cholangiocarcinoma, ampullary), benign stricture, PSC, parasitic infection, post-ERCP. Organisms typically enteric - E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus, and anaerobes. Clinical features: Charcot triad of RUQ pain, fever with rigors, and jaundice (55 to 70% sensitive); Reynolds pentad adds hypotension and altered mental state - marks suppurative cholangitis and impending septic shock. Tokyo Guidelines grade severity. Ix: FBC (leucocytosis), CRP, LFT (cholestatic with raised ALP, GGT and bilirubin), blood cultures x2 before antibiotics, EUC, lactate; ultrasound first line; MRCP or EUS for CBD stones; CT for malignancy. Mx: sepsis management - IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole per eTG). Urgent biliary decompression by ERCP within 24 to 48 hours (or emergently for severe); PTC if ERCP unavailable. Interval cholecystectomy for gallstone-related. Note: delay in decompression is the leading modifiable cause of death.
rich_summaries.Cholecystitis: Inflammation of the gallbladder, in over 90% from a gallstone impacted at the cystic duct (calculous cholecystitis); acalculous cholecystitis occurs in critically ill and fasted patients from gallbladder stasis and carries higher mortality. Clinical features: severe RUQ pain radiating to right shoulder tip, fever, nausea, vomiting; Murphy sign (inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation); distinguish from biliary colic (intermittent, no inflammation) and cholangitis (Charcot triad of pain, fever, jaundice). Ix: FBC, CRP, LFT (mild ALP and bilirubin rise), amylase and lipase, blood cultures if septic; abdominal ultrasound first line - shows gallstones, wall thickening over 3 mm, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy sign; HIDA or CT if equivocal; MRCP if CBD stone suspected.Mx: NBM, IV fluids, IV analgesia, antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate or piperacillin-tazobactam per eTG). Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 72 hours is the reference standard; percutaneous cholecystostomy for unfit patients. Note: acalculous cholecystitis in ICU needs urgent decompression.
rich_summaries.Chronic fatigue syndrome: Also myalgic encephalomyelitis. A disabling multisystem illness defined by post-exertional malaise, not by fatigue alone. Dx: six months or more of substantial reduction in function, with post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep, and either cognitive impairment or orthostatic intolerance. Post-exertional malaise is the required feature and distinguishes this from fatigue of other causes. Ix: there is no confirmatory test. Investigate to exclude mimics - FBC, EUC, LFT, TFT, coeliac serology, CRP, ferritin, glucose, and vitamin D - and stop there rather than searching indefinitely. Mx: symptom-focused and individualised. Activity pacing within an energy envelope; treat sleep, pain and orthostatic intolerance; manage comorbid mood disorder without implying it is the cause. Graded exercise therapy is no longer recommended as a curative treatment and can worsen post-exertional malaise. Note: patients are commonly disbelieved before they are diagnosed, and the therapeutic relationship depends on not repeating that.
rich_summaries.Chronic kidney disease: Sustained eGFR under 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 or albuminuria for at least 3 months. Causes: diabetes and hypertension account for most Australian cases; glomerulonephritis, polycystic kidney disease and reflux nephropathy are the main non-vascular causes. Classification: G1 to G5 by eGFR combined with A1 to A3 by urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (KDIGO heatmap) drives risk. Ix: eGFR, urine ACR on a first-morning sample, urinalysis, renal ultrasound; screen for reversible contributors (obstruction, NSAIDs, dehydration); pursue intrinsic cause when there is haematuria, heavy proteinuria, systemic features or rapid decline. Mx: slow progression - BP under 130/80 with an ACE inhibitor or ARB, glycaemic control targeting HbA1c around 53 mmol/mol, an SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin) if eGFR at least 20 with albuminuria, smoking cessation, lipid control. Treat CKD-MBD, anaemia and acidosis as they emerge. Refer to nephrology at eGFR under 30 or with heavy proteinuria; plan vascular access around eGFR 20. Note: RACGP kidney health check annually in anyone with diabetes, hypertension, CVD, or Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander background.
rich_summaries.Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia: Clonal proliferation of mature but functionally incompetent B lymphocytes; the commonest leukaemia in adults in Australia. Epidemiology: median age around 70; often found incidentally on a routine FBC. Clinical features: frequently asymptomatic; otherwise lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, fatigue, recurrent infection from hypogammaglobulinaemia, and later marrow failure. Ix: persistent lymphocytosis above 5 x 10^9/L with smudge cells on film; flow cytometry showing CD5, CD19, CD23 co-expression is diagnostic; FISH for del(17p) and TP53, which predict poor response to chemoimmunotherapy; direct antiglobulin test. Mx: watch and wait while asymptomatic - early treatment does not prolong survival. Treat for progressive cytopenias, bulky or symptomatic disease, or constitutional symptoms, with targeted agents such as BTK or BCL-2 inhibitors. Complications: autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and immune thrombocytopenia; recurrent infection; Richter transformation to aggressive lymphoma, suggested by rapid nodal growth with fever and a rising LDH.
rich_summaries.Chronic myeloid leukaemia: Myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by the BCR-ABL1 fusion from the Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22). Clinical features: often incidental leukocytosis; otherwise fatigue, weight loss, sweats, and splenomegaly which may be massive and cause early satiety or left upper quadrant pain. Phases: chronic (most at diagnosis), accelerated, and blast crisis resembling acute leukaemia. Ix: marked leukocytosis with the full spectrum of myeloid precursors and basophilia; low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase; BCR-ABL1 by PCR or cytogenetics is diagnostic. Mx: a tyrosine kinase inhibitor - imatinib, or a second-generation agent - with molecular monitoring of BCR-ABL1 transcript levels against defined milestones. Some with sustained deep molecular response can attempt treatment-free remission. Note: CML is the model of targeted therapy - a disease that was uniformly fatal now has near-normal life expectancy on a tablet, and adherence is the main determinant of outcome. Red flags: rising basophils, blasts or a rising transcript level signal progression.
rich_summaries.Chronic pancreatitis: Irreversible fibrosis of the pancreas with progressive loss of exocrine and eventually endocrine function. Causes: alcohol is the commonest in Australia; also smoking, which is independently causative, genetic variants, obstruction, and autoimmune pancreatitis. Clinical features: recurrent or constant epigastric pain radiating to the back, steatorrhoea and weight loss once exocrine reserve falls below about 10%, and diabetes late. Ix: CT or MRCP showing calcification, ductal dilatation and atrophy; endoscopic ultrasound is most sensitive early. Faecal elastase for exocrine insufficiency. Lipase is often normal, which surprises people expecting it to be raised. Mx: stop alcohol and smoking - both change the trajectory. Pancreatic enzyme replacement with fat-soluble vitamins, structured analgesia, and screening for diabetes and osteoporosis. Endoscopic or surgical drainage for obstructing disease. Note: the diabetes here is type 3c - glucagon is lost alongside insulin, so hypoglycaemia is a genuine hazard of treatment.
rich_summaries.Cirrhosis: End-stage chronic liver disease with diffuse fibrosis and regenerative nodule formation. Causes: alcohol, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, chronic hepatitis B and C, haemochromatosis, autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, Wilson disease. Clinical features: compensated disease is often silent; decompensation gives jaundice, ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy and hepatorenal syndrome. Stigmata include spider naevi, palmar erythema and gynaecomastia. Ix: FBC (thrombocytopenia is the earliest portal-hypertension sign), LFT, coagulation, albumin; aetiology screen; abdominal ultrasound with Doppler; FibroScan or biopsy for staging. Score with Child-Pugh or MELD. Mx: treat the cause. Salt restriction and spironolactone plus furosemide for ascites; propranolol or endoscopic ligation for varices; lactulose and rifaximin for encephalopathy; 6-monthly HCC surveillance. Refer for transplant if MELD at least 15. Note: Australians with cirrhosis get influenza and pneumococcal vaccination and avoid NSAIDs, aminoglycosides and paracetamol over 2 g daily.
rich_summaries.Cluster headache: The most severe of the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias, and distinctive enough that the history alone usually makes it. Clinical features: strictly unilateral, excruciating orbital or temporal pain lasting 15 to 180 minutes, once to eight times a day, in bouts of weeks to months. Ipsilateral autonomic features - lacrimation, conjunctival injection, rhinorrhoea, ptosis, miosis. Patients are restless and pace, unlike migraine. Epidemiology: more common in men, often with nocturnal attacks that wake at a consistent hour, and alcohol triggers during a bout only. Ix: clinical, but image with MRI at least once to exclude a pituitary or posterior fossa lesion. Mx (acute attack): high-flow oxygen 12-15 L/min via a non-rebreather, or subcutaneous sumatriptan. Oral triptans are too slow. Prevention: verapamil is first-line, with ECG monitoring as the dose rises; a short prednisolone course or greater occipital nerve block can bridge until it works.
rich_summaries.Coeliac disease: Immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten in HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 carriers, causing villous atrophy and malabsorption. Sx: diarrhoea, steatorrhoea, bloating and weight loss, although the commonest adult presentation is iron deficiency anaemia with no bowel symptoms at all. Extraintestinal: dermatitis herpetiformis, osteoporosis, transaminitis, gluten ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, hyposplenism. Associations: type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease, selective IgA deficiency, Down syndrome. Ix: anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA with a total IgA, taken while still eating gluten; duodenal biopsy showing intraepithelial lymphocytosis, crypt hyperplasia and villous atrophy confirms it in adults. Mx: lifelong gluten-free diet with dietitian input; replace iron, folate, B12, calcium and vitamin D; bone densitometry; pneumococcal vaccination for hyposplenism. Note: serology normalises on a gluten-free diet, so anyone already avoiding gluten needs a formal gluten challenge before testing.
rich_summaries.Colorectal cancer: Adenocarcinoma of the colon or rectum, and the second commonest cause of cancer death in Australia. Screening: the National Bowel Cancer Screening Program offers immunochemical faecal occult blood testing every two years from 45 to 74, with colonoscopy for a positive result. Causes: adenoma-carcinoma sequence through APC, KRAS and TP53; mismatch repair deficiency in Lynch syndrome; the serrated pathway through BRAF. Risk factors: inflammatory bowel disease, family history, processed meat, obesity, alcohol, smoking. Sx: right-sided disease gives iron deficiency anaemia and a mass; left-sided gives altered bowel habit, rectal bleeding, tenesmus and obstruction. Ix: colonoscopy with biopsy; staging CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis; MRI rectum for local staging and circumferential margin. Mx: resection; neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for locally advanced rectal disease; adjuvant oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy for stage III per eviQ.
rich_summaries.Compartment syndrome: Rise in tissue pressure within a closed fascial compartment compromising perfusion; surgical emergency with irreversible necrosis in 4-8 hours. Causes: fracture (tibial shaft most common), crush and reperfusion injury, tight cast or bandage, circumferential burns, prolonged limb ischaemia, bleeding on anticoagulation. Clinical features (six Ps unreliable early): disproportionate pain, pain on passive stretch, tense compartment, paraesthesiae; pulselessness and pallor are late and often absent - a palpable pulse does NOT rule it out. Ix: primarily clinical; intracompartmental pressure if patient unconscious or examination equivocal - delta-P (diastolic minus compartment pressure) under 30 mmHg or absolute over 30 mmHg is diagnostic; CK marks established myonecrosis. Mx: remove all constricting dressings, elevate to heart level (not above), correct hypoxia and hypotension; urgent fasciotomy of all involved compartments; delayed closure with skin grafting; watch for rhabdomyolysis and AKI. Note: opioid requirement rising out of proportion to the injury is the earliest sign - escalate immediately.
rich_summaries.Conjunctivitis: Inflammation of the conjunctiva. Types: bacterial (Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae; also Neisseria gonorrhoeae in neonates and adults with sexual contact, and Chlamydia trachomatis) with purulent discharge and sticky lids; viral (adenovirus commonest) with watery discharge, preauricular lymph node, highly contagious; allergic with bilateral itching and papillae. Clinical features distinguish from red flags - reduced acuity, photophobia, severe pain or fixed pupil point to keratitis, iritis or angle-closure glaucoma, not conjunctivitis. Ix: clinical in typical disease. Swab for hyperacute or copious purulent discharge (gonococcal), or in neonates with any conjunctivitis. Mx: bacterial gets chloramphenicol 0.5% drops 4 times daily with 1% ointment at night for 5 to 7 days (eTG); viral is supportive with cool compresses and hand hygiene; allergic gets antihistamine drop (olopatadine) plus oral antihistamine. Refer neonatal, gonococcal, chlamydial and any red-flag presentation. Note: contact lens wearers with red eye need a slit lamp - Pseudomonas keratitis is sight-threatening.
rich_summaries.Cor pulmonale: Right ventricular dysfunction caused by pulmonary hypertension of pulmonary origin. Causes: COPD is commonest; also interstitial lung disease, chronic pulmonary embolism (CTEPH), pulmonary vasculitis, sleep-disordered breathing, kyphoscoliosis, neuromuscular restriction, and high altitude. Left heart failure with secondary PH is excluded by definition. Clinical features: exertional dyspnoea and fatigue, peripheral oedema, ascites, hepatomegaly with pulsatile liver, raised JVP with prominent v-wave, parasternal heave, loud P2, tricuspid regurgitation murmur, and features of the underlying lung disease. Ix: ECG (right axis, RVH, RBBB, P pulmonale), CXR, ABG, PFT, transthoracic echo (RV size and function, estimated PAP), V/Q scan for CTEPH, polysomnography if OSA suspected; right heart catheterisation confirms. Mx: treat the underlying lung disease. Long-term oxygen for chronic hypoxia (PaO2 under 55, or under 60 with cor pulmonale) improves survival. Cautious diuretics for volume overload. Specific PH therapy only for group 1 or 4 (not group 3). Note: cor pulmonale marks advanced lung disease and warrants palliative care conversation.
rich_summaries.Cord prolapse: Obstetric emergency in which the umbilical cord descends beside or below the presenting part after rupture of membranes, causing cord compression and fetal hypoxia. Risk factors: abnormal fetal lie (transverse or oblique), malpresentation (breech, especially footling), polyhydramnios, high presenting part, multiparity, prematurity, artificial rupture of membranes with a high head, and multiple pregnancy. Clinical features: cord palpable in the vagina or visible at the introitus after spontaneous or artificial rupture of membranes, or an abrupt fetal bradycardia on CTG. Mx: call for help - obstetric team, theatre, paediatric team, anaesthetics. Relieve compression by placing the woman in knee-chest or left lateral head-down (Trendelenburg) position; elevate the presenting part manually per vagina; fill the bladder with 500 mL saline via catheter if delay to delivery is unavoidable. Keep the cord warm and moist; minimise handling. Immediate caesarean unless vaginal delivery is imminent (fully dilated, low station, instrumental feasible). Anti-D if Rh-negative. Note: outcome depends almost entirely on the interval to delivery.
rich_summaries.Crohn disease: Chronic inflammatory bowel disease with transmural, granulomatous inflammation that can affect any part of the GI tract from mouth to anus, characteristically the terminal ileum, with skip lesions. Clinical features: chronic abdominal pain (often right lower quadrant), non-bloody diarrhoea, weight loss, fatigue, and low-grade fever. Perianal disease (fissures, fistulae, abscesses) is distinctive. Extraintestinal features include erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, uveitis, large-joint arthritis, and primary sclerosing cholangitis. Ix: FBC, CRP, ferritin, albumin, LFT, faecal calprotectin (over 250 microg/g); colonoscopy with ileoscopy and biopsies is the reference standard; MR enterography for small bowel; exclude infection. Mx: induction with budesonide (ileocolonic) or oral prednisolone; biologics (infliximab, adalimumab, vedolizumab, ustekinumab, risankizumab) for moderate to severe disease or steroid-dependence. Maintenance with thiopurines, methotrexate or biologics. Surgery for strictures, fistulae, abscesses or refractory disease - not curative. Smoking cessation is essential. Note: annual colonoscopy from 8 years of colonic disease for dysplasia.
rich_summaries.Croup: Viral laryngotracheobronchitis, most often parainfluenza, in children aged 6 months to 6 years. Clinical features: 1 to 2 day viral prodrome, then barking cough, inspiratory stridor and hoarse voice, worse at night and with agitation. Grade clinically as mild (no stridor at rest), moderate (stridor at rest, mild recession), severe (marked recession, distress) or impending failure (exhaustion, cyanosis, drowsiness). Ix: clinical diagnosis; do not distress the child with tests. Steeple sign on neck radiography is neither sensitive nor needed. Mx: keep the child calm on the parent's lap. Oral dexamethasone 0.15 to 0.6 mg/kg (or prednisolone) as a single dose in every child with croup, regardless of severity. Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 for moderate to severe stridor at rest; effect lasts about 2 hours, so observe. Admit any child needing adrenaline or with persistent stridor at rest after steroids. DDx: acute epiglottitis (older, drooling, toxic, no cough - now rare with Hib immunisation), bacterial tracheitis, foreign body, anaphylaxis. Note: humidified air has no evidence of benefit and should not be prescribed.
rich_summaries.Cryptorchidism: Failure of one or both testes to descend into the scrotum by 3 months. Present in 3% of full-term and 30% of preterm males at birth; most descend spontaneously by 3 months. True undescended (along normal path) vs ectopic (aberrant) vs retractile (cremasteric reflex draws into groin but returns manually - not true). Clinical features: empty or hypoplastic hemiscrotum; palpable in the inguinal canal in 80%; impalpable in 20% (intra-abdominal, absent, or vanishing). Complications if untreated: subfertility or infertility (bilateral untreated over 80% infertile), testicular cancer (4 to 10 times risk, especially seminoma, in both testes even after orchidopexy), torsion, inguinal hernia. Ix: examination in warm room with child relaxed; ultrasound is unreliable for impalpable testis; diagnostic laparoscopy for impalpable testis. Mx: refer to paediatric surgery if not descended by 6 months. Orchidopexy between 6 and 12 months (before 18 months) preserves fertility potential and allows cancer surveillance. Bilateral impalpable warrants urgent DSD workup (karyotype, hormones). Note: orchidopexy does not eliminate cancer risk - lifelong self-examination.
rich_summaries.Cushing syndrome: Clinical state of chronic glucocorticoid excess. Causes: exogenous corticosteroid is overwhelmingly the commonest and is often overlooked. Endogenous causes are ACTH-dependent - pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease) or ectopic ACTH from small cell lung cancer - or ACTH-independent adrenal adenoma or carcinoma. Clinical features: central obesity with thin limbs; moon face and interscapular fat pad; hypertension, hyperglycaemia, osteoporosis. The discriminating features are proximal myopathy, wide violaceous striae and easy bruising, since obesity alone produces the rest. Ix: confirm cortisol excess with 24-hour urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol, or overnight dexamethasone suppression. Then ACTH to establish dependence, and image accordingly. Mx: withdraw exogenous steroid gradually where that is the cause; otherwise transsphenoidal surgery, adrenalectomy, or treatment of the ectopic tumour. Note: ectopic ACTH often presents with hypokalaemic alkalosis and pigmentation rather than the classic habitus, because it develops too fast for the phenotype to appear.
rich_summaries.Cystic fibrosis: Autosomal recessive CFTR defect producing thick secretions across exocrine organs, with F508del the commonest Australian variant. Clinical features: recurrent chest infection with bronchiectasis, pancreatic insufficiency with steatorrhoea and failure to thrive, and male infertility from absent vas deferens. Meconium ileus is the neonatal presentation. Ix: newborn screening by immunoreactive trypsinogen then genetic panel; sweat chloride above 60 mmol/L confirms. Mx: multidisciplinary CF centre care - airway clearance physiotherapy, inhaled mucolytics, pancreatic enzyme replacement with fat-soluble vitamins, and aggressive treatment of exacerbations. CFTR modulators (elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor) are PBS-listed for eligible genotypes and have changed the trajectory of the disease. Note: chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonisation marks a step down in prognosis, which is why segregation and early eradication are taken seriously. Red flags: haemoptysis, pneumothorax and distal intestinal obstruction syndrome are the acute presentations.
rich_summaries.Deep vein thrombosis: Thrombus in a deep vein, usually lower limb (calf, popliteal, femoral, iliac); upper limb DVT often catheter-related. Virchow triad - stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability. Risk factors: immobilisation, surgery, trauma, malignancy, pregnancy and post-partum, COCP or HRT, obesity, previous VTE, thrombophilia (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, antiphospholipid syndrome). Clinical features: unilateral leg swelling, warmth, erythema, calf pain, tenderness, dilated superficial veins (Homans sign unreliable); phlegmasia cerulea dolens with massive iliofemoral DVT. Complications include PE, post-thrombotic syndrome, and recurrence.Ix: Wells score - low probability plus negative D-dimer excludes; high probability or positive D-dimer warrants compression ultrasound. Mx: DOAC (rivaroxaban, apixaban) first line for most, LMWH then warfarin for antiphospholipid syndrome, LMWH for pregnancy and cancer-associated. Duration 3 months if provoked, at least 6 months if unprovoked or cancer-related. Thrombolysis for phlegmasia; IVC filter for anticoagulation contraindication.Note: isolated distal calf DVT can be surveilled with serial ultrasound.
rich_summaries.Dehydration: Deficit of total body water, usually with electrolyte loss. Causes: reduced intake, vomiting, diarrhoea, polyuria (DKA, diabetes insipidus, diuretics), sweating, burns, and third-spacing. Clinical features: children are graded by percent body weight lost - mild (under 5%) is thirst and dry mucous membranes; moderate (5 to 10%) adds sunken eyes and fontanelle, reduced skin turgor, tachycardia, delayed capillary refill; severe (over 10%) adds hypotension, lethargy, cold peripheries. Adults compensate longer, so a normal blood pressure does not exclude significant depletion. Ix: EUC, glucose, VBG with lactate, urinalysis; weight if a reliable baseline; urea:creatinine ratio and osmolality by cause. Mx: mild to moderate in a child gets oral rehydration solution (Gastrolyte, Hydralyte) 50 mL/kg over 4 hours plus ongoing losses; NG if oral fails. IV isotonic saline for severe dehydration or persistent vomiting - 20 mL/kg bolus, reassess, then deficit over 24 hours plus maintenance. Note: RCH guideline prefers oral or NG rehydration for acute gastroenteritis - IV is a fallback.
rich_summaries.Delirium: Acute fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness with cognitive change, developing over hours to days and caused by another medical condition. Types: hyperactive (agitated, hallucinating), hypoactive (withdrawn, quiet - the more common and the more missed), or mixed. Causes: PINCH ME - Pain, Infection, Nutrition, Constipation and dehydration, Hypoxia, Medication (anticholinergics, opioids, benzodiazepines, steroids, polypharmacy), Environment change, and Electrolyte or metabolic derangement. Alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal are specific traps. Ix: bedside screen (4AT or CAM), then FBC, EUC, calcium, glucose, LFT, TFT, urinalysis, CXR, ECG, blood cultures if febrile; CT brain and LP only for focal signs, unexplained fever with headache, or no other cause found. Mx: treat the underlying cause. Reorientate, restore sleep-wake, correct sensory impairment, mobilise, and avoid restraint. Antipsychotics (haloperidol or olanzapine) only for severe distress or safety, at the lowest dose and shortest duration; benzodiazepines only in alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal. Note: independently associated with mortality, longer admission and new dementia, so prevention is treatment.
rich_summaries.Delusional disorder: Persistent delusions (fixed false beliefs not amenable to reason and out of keeping with culture) for at least one month, without prominent hallucinations, disorganised thought or mood disturbance sufficient for other psychotic diagnoses; functioning outside the delusional theme often preserved. Prevalence around 0.2%; onset middle to late adulthood; slight female predominance. Subtypes include persecutory (commonest), erotomanic (de Clerambault), grandiose, jealous (Othello), somatic (Ekbom), mixed and unspecified. Content typically non-bizarre. Comorbid depression and anxiety are common. Ix: mental state examination; risk assessment (jealous and persecutory carry violence risk); collateral history essential; screen substance use and medical mimics (Lewy body, temporal lobe epilepsy, endocrine); CT or MRI brain in atypical or late-onset. Mx: therapeutic engagement is the challenge - patients lack insight and rarely present voluntarily. Second-generation antipsychotics offer partial benefit; CBT for delusions; treat comorbid mood or anxiety. MHA if risk to self or others. Note: prognosis better than schizophrenia but relapse on treatment cessation is common.
rich_summaries.Dermatitis herpetiformis: Cutaneous manifestation of coeliac disease - intensely pruritic symmetrical vesicular eruption on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks, scalp) driven by IgA antibodies against epidermal transglutaminase (TG3) deposited at dermal papillary tips. 15 to 25% of coeliac patients have DH; over 90% of DH patients have gluten-sensitive enteropathy on biopsy even when GI symptoms are absent. Adult onset peak in 30s to 40s; male predominance (2:1). HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 associated. Clinical features: grouped tense vesicles usually excoriated (intense itch destroys them before examination); symmetric distribution; burning and stinging preceding lesions. Associated with autoimmune thyroid, T1DM, pernicious anaemia, small bowel lymphoma. Ix: skin biopsy of perilesional skin with direct immunofluorescence shows pathognomonic granular IgA at dermal papillae; anti-tTG and anti-EMA; small bowel biopsy for coeliac. Mx: strict lifelong gluten-free diet is definitive (skin improves over months); dapsone gives dramatic itch relief within days (check G6PD first, monitor for haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia). Note: gluten-free diet also reduces lymphoma risk.
rich_summaries.Dermatomyositis: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy: symmetrical proximal weakness plus characteristic skin changes. Epidemiology: bimodal 5-15 and 40-60 yr; women > men. Pathophysiology: complement-mediated microangiopathy of endomysial capillaries, giving perifascicular atrophy. Clinical features: proximal weakness over weeks to months (deltoids, hip flexors, neck flexors); Gottron papules and heliotrope eruption are pathognomonic; photodistributed poikiloderma (shawl, V and Holster signs); ILD, myocarditis, dysphagia. Ix: CK 2-100x normal; ANA; myositis-specific antibodies (anti-Mi-2 good prognosis, anti-Jo-1 ILD, anti-MDA5 rapidly progressive ILD, anti-TIF1-gamma malignancy); muscle biopsy diagnostic. Mx: prednisolone plus methotrexate or azathioprine; IVIg if refractory. Note: adult disease carries markedly raised malignancy risk, highest in the first 3 years - CT chest, abdomen and pelvis plus age-appropriate screening.
rich_summaries.Developmental dysplasia of the hip: Spectrum of abnormal hip development from dysplasia to frank dislocation, present at birth or evolving in infancy. Risk factors: female sex, firstborn, breech presentation, oligohydramnios, family history, left hip, and swaddling with legs extended. Clinical features: neonatal examination with Ortolani (reduces dislocated hip with abduction) and Barlow (dislocates reducible hip with adduction and posterior pressure); asymmetric skin folds and reduced abduction in older infants; limp or waddling gait at walking age; positive Trendelenburg or Galeazzi (femoral shortening) later. Ix: hip ultrasound before 6 months (routine in Australia for at-risk infants); pelvic radiograph after 6 months (ossification centres visible). Selective ultrasound screening rather than universal in Australia. Mx: under 6 months, Pavlik harness worn continuously for 6 weeks to 3 months; over 6 months, closed reduction with spica cast under anaesthesia; over 18 months or failed closed reduction, open reduction with pelvic osteotomy. Serial follow-up until skeletal maturity. Note: late-diagnosed DDH gives premature osteoarthritis; neonatal screening exists for early detection.
rich_summaries.DiGeorge syndrome: 22q11.2 microdeletion syndrome affecting third and fourth pharyngeal pouch derivatives; 1 in 4000 live births, over 90% de novo; hemizygous TBX1 deletion disrupts neural crest migration into the pharyngeal arches (thymus, parathyroids, aortic arch, craniofacial development). Clinical features (CATCH-22): Cardiac defects (conotruncal - tetralogy of Fallot, interrupted aortic arch, truncus), Abnormal facies (hypertelorism, low-set ears, small chin), Thymic aplasia with T-cell lymphopenia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcaemia from parathyroid hypoplasia; renal anomalies, learning difficulty, higher rates of schizophrenia (about 25%) in adulthood. Ix: FISH or chromosomal microarray; TTE; T-cell subsets; calcium and PTH; renal ultrasound. Mx: cardiac surgery per lesion; calcium and calcitriol; live-vaccine caution and prophylactic antibiotics in complete DiGeorge; thymic transplant for complete phenotype at a specialist centre. Note: conotruncal defect plus neonatal hypocalcaemia deserves microarray - diagnosis changes vaccination and blood-product handling (irradiated CMV-negative).
rich_summaries.Diabetes insipidus: Failure to concentrate urine, from deficient ADH (cranial) or renal resistance to it (nephrogenic), now often called arginine vasopressin deficiency and resistance. Causes: cranial from pituitary surgery, tumour, trauma or infiltration; nephrogenic from lithium, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia or inherited defects. Clinical features: polyuria of more than 3 L a day, nocturia and intense thirst, with hypernatraemia if access to water is restricted. Ix: paired serum and urine osmolality - dilute urine against concentrated plasma is the finding. Water deprivation testing with desmopressin separates the two types; copeptin has largely replaced it where available. MRI pituitary for cranial causes. Mx: desmopressin for cranial disease. Nephrogenic disease needs the cause removed, with a thiazide and a low-solute diet. Note: the danger is not the polyuria but losing access to water - an unconscious or post-operative patient can become profoundly hypernatraemic within hours.
rich_summaries.Diabetes mellitus: Chronic hyperglycaemia from insulin resistance with progressive beta-cell failure. Ix: HbA1c of 6.5% or above, fasting glucose 7.0 or above, or a 2-hour OGTT value of 11.1 or above - confirmed on a second sample unless symptomatic. HbA1c is unreliable in haemoglobinopathy, recent transfusion and chronic kidney disease. Mx: lifestyle plus metformin first-line for most. Then choose by comorbidity rather than by HbA1c alone - an SGLT2 inhibitor for heart failure or chronic kidney disease, a GLP-1 receptor agonist for obesity or established cardiovascular disease. Target HbA1c is around 7% generally, relaxed in the frail or in hypoglycaemia unawareness. Monitoring: HbA1c 3- to 6-monthly; annual retinal screening, urine ACR, eGFR, foot examination with monofilament, and lipids. Note: PBS criteria govern access to SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 agonists in Australia and change periodically - check before prescribing. Metformin needs holding around iodinated contrast and in acute illness. Red flags: rapid weight loss or ketosis suggests type 1 or pancreatic disease, not type 2.
rich_summaries.Diabetic ketoacidosis: Acute hyperglycaemic emergency from absolute insulin deficiency, with ketosis and metabolic acidosis. Criteria: hyperglycaemia (though euglycaemic DKA occurs); ketonaemia 3.0 mmol/L or more; pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 15. Triggers: infection, missed insulin, new-onset type 1 diabetes, myocardial infarction, and SGLT2 inhibitors. Clinical features: polyuria and thirst; vomiting and abdominal pain; Kussmaul respiration; ketotic breath; drowsiness. Mx: fluid first - the deficit is usually 5-7 L. Then fixed-rate insulin at 0.1 units/kg/h. Potassium from the outset unless above 5.5, since total body potassium is depleted however normal the level looks. Add glucose-containing fluid once BGL falls below 14 while continuing insulin, which is clearing ketones, not glucose. Note: euglycaemic DKA on SGLT2 inhibitors is easily missed - check ketones in any unwell patient on one regardless of the glucose. Red flags: cerebral oedema, mainly in children and after rapid osmolar shifts; hypokalaemia is the commonest avoidable cause of death.
rich_summaries.Diabetic nephropathy: Leading cause of end-stage kidney disease worldwide; microvascular complication of type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Pathology: glomerular basement membrane thickening, mesangial expansion, and nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions); progresses from hyperfiltration through microalbuminuria to overt proteinuria and progressive renal decline. Risk factors are duration and severity of hyperglycaemia, hypertension, smoking, family history, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander background. Clinical features: often asymptomatic until advanced; peripheral oedema, hypertension, fatigue, and coexisting diabetic complications (retinopathy supports diabetic renal disease over another cause). Ix: annual urine ACR and eGFR from diagnosis in type 2, or from 5 years post-diagnosis in type 1; renal biopsy only for atypical features. Mx: tight glycaemic control (HbA1c around 53 mmol/mol); BP under 130/80 with ACE inhibitor or ARB titrated to highest tolerated dose; SGLT2 inhibitor; finerenone for residual albuminuria. Refer to nephrology at eGFR under 30 or with heavy proteinuria. Note: RACGP recommends annual kidney health check.
rich_summaries.Dilated cardiomyopathy: Commonest cardiomyopathy; LV or biventricular dilatation with systolic dysfunction not explained by loading or coronary disease. Causes: idiopathic or familial (titin, lamin A/C, desmin mutations - up to 35% have family history), post-viral (coxsackie, parvovirus B19, HIV), toxic (alcohol, cocaine, anthracyclines, trastuzumab), peripartum (last trimester to 5 months post-partum), tachycardia-mediated, and infiltrative (haemochromatosis, sarcoid, amyloid). Clinical features: heart failure with exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea, PND and peripheral oedema, arrhythmia (AF, VT), thromboembolism from dilated chambers, and sudden cardiac death.Ix: ECG (LBBB, AF, poor R wave progression), CXR (cardiomegaly, pulmonary oedema), NT-proBNP, TTE (dilated LV with reduced EF is diagnostic), cardiac MRI for tissue characterisation and fibrosis, coronary angiography to exclude ischaemia; genetic testing and family screening. Mx: HFrEF quadruple therapy - ACEi or ARNI, beta blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor; CRT if QRS over 130 ms with LBBB; ICD for EF under 35% despite optimal therapy; heart transplant for end stage. Note: alcohol cessation and peripartum cases can fully recover LV function.
rich_summaries.Disseminated intravascular coagulation: Systemic activation of coagulation that consumes platelets and clotting factors, producing simultaneous thrombosis and bleeding. Causes: sepsis (commonest); major trauma; obstetric catastrophe including abruption and amniotic fluid embolism; malignancy, especially acute promyelocytic leukaemia. Pathophysiology: massive tissue factor release drives widespread microthrombi, which consume the substrate needed for haemostasis - hence bleeding in a hypercoagulable state. Clinical features: oozing from cannula and venepuncture sites, purpura fulminans, and organ dysfunction from microvascular thrombosis. Ix: thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT and APTT, low fibrinogen, markedly raised D-dimer, schistocytes on film. The trend across serial results is more informative than any single set. Mx: treat the underlying cause, which is the only definitive therapy. Support with platelets, fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate guided by bleeding rather than by numbers alone. Note: fibrinogen falls late and a normal level early does not exclude DIC - it is an acute-phase reactant, so a normal value in a septic patient may already represent a fall.
rich_summaries.Diverticular disease: Herniation of colonic mucosa through the muscular wall at points where vasa recta penetrate, overwhelmingly sigmoid in Western populations. Classification: diverticulosis is the anatomical finding, diverticular disease is symptomatic, and diverticulitis is inflammation of a diverticulum. Clinical features: most diverticulosis is silent. Diverticulitis gives left iliac fossa pain, fever and altered bowel habit. Painless brisk rectal bleeding is the other presentation, from an eroded vas rectum. Ix: CT abdomen with contrast for acute diverticulitis, staging by the Hinchey classification. Colonoscopy is deferred six to eight weeks after an episode to exclude a masked malignancy, and is avoided acutely. Mx: uncomplicated diverticulitis in a well patient is managed without antibiotics in current Australian guidance - analgesia, fluids and review. Antibiotics for systemic upset, immune suppression or comorbidity. Percutaneous drainage for an abscess; surgery for perforation, obstruction or fistula. Note: the old advice to avoid nuts and seeds has been disproven and should not be repeated.
rich_summaries.Diverticulitis: Inflammation, microperforation or macroscopic perforation of a colonic diverticulum; sigmoid in 95% of Western cases. Diverticulosis rises with age (over half of adults by 60) and reflects low-fibre diet and constipation; 10 to 25% develop diverticulitis. Clinical features: constant left lower quadrant pain (left-sided appendicitis), fever, altered bowel habit, nausea; localised peritonism, palpable mass in a phlegmon, tachycardia and rigidity if perforated. Complications: abscess, perforation with faeculent peritonitis, obstruction, colovesical or colovaginal fistula (pneumaturia, faecaluria, recurrent UTI), and bleeding. Ix: FBC, CRP, EUC; contrast CT abdomen and pelvis is the reference standard, Hinchey stages severity. Colonoscopy after 6 to 8 weeks to exclude cancer. Mx: uncomplicated mild - outpatient oral amoxicillin-clavulanate or metronidazole plus ciprofloxacin per eTG. Inpatient IV antibiotics for systemic upset or comorbidity. Percutaneous drainage for abscesses over 4 cm. Emergency surgery (Hartmann) for generalised peritonitis or failure to respond. Note: elective resection is now individualised.
rich_summaries.Down syndrome: Trisomy 21, the commonest chromosomal disorder; risk rises with maternal age. Clinical features: characteristic facies (flat profile, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, small ears, protruding tongue), single palmar crease, sandal gap, and hypotonia. Intellectual disability is universal but variable. Associations include congenital heart disease in about half (AVSD most characteristic, then VSD), duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung disease, hypothyroidism, coeliac disease, hearing and vision impairment, atlantoaxial instability, OSA, early Alzheimer disease, and 20-fold increased risk of acute leukaemia. Ix: antenatal combined first-trimester screening (nuchal translucency plus PAPP-A and beta-hCG) or NIPT; diagnostic CVS or amniocentesis. Postnatal karyotype confirms diagnosis and identifies translocation forms with recurrence implications. Mx: paediatric review including echocardiogram, thyroid at birth and annually, hearing and vision at scheduled intervals, coeliac screen at 2 years. Early intervention with speech and occupational therapy, and NDIS support. Note: parents deserve unbiased non-directive counselling at diagnosis.
rich_summaries.Eating disorders: Serious psychiatric illnesses with the highest mortality of any mental disorder. Types: anorexia nervosa (restriction with significant low weight, intense fear of weight gain, disturbed body image); bulimia nervosa (binges with compensatory behaviour, weekly for at least 3 months); binge-eating disorder (binges without compensation); ARFID (avoidance from sensory or fear features, not body image); OSFED for presentations that do not meet a category. Screening: SCOFF questionnaire; ask about weight preoccupation, binges, purging and compensatory exercise in any young person with weight loss, amenorrhoea, dental erosion or unexplained electrolytes. Ix: FBC, EUC (hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypophosphataemia), magnesium, calcium, LFT, TFT, glucose, ECG (QT prolongation, bradycardia); DXA if amenorrhoea over 6 months. Mx: multidisciplinary care; family-based therapy first line for adolescents with anorexia; CBT-ED and IPT for adults. Admission for medical instability. Refeed cautiously monitoring phosphate, magnesium and potassium daily. Note: BMI is a proxy - normal weight does not exclude a severe eating disorder.
rich_summaries.Eclampsia: New-onset generalised tonic-clonic seizures in a woman with pre-eclampsia, or occasionally as the first sign of pre-eclampsia. Clinical features: seizures may occur antepartum, intrapartum or up to 6 weeks postpartum; often preceded by headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain, hyperreflexia and clonus. Ix: FBC and film, LFT (transaminitis, HELLP), EUC and urate, urinalysis and PCR, coagulation and fibrinogen, group and hold; CTG. Mx: ABC and left lateral; protect the airway. Magnesium sulfate is both anticonvulsant and prevention of further seizures - 4 g IV over 10 to 15 minutes, then 1 g/h for 24 hours after the last seizure or delivery, whichever is later. Monitor for magnesium toxicity (loss of patellar reflexes, respiratory rate under 12, reduced urine output); calcium gluconate 1 g IV is the antidote. Control severe hypertension with IV labetalol, IV hydralazine or oral nifedipine, targeting under 160/110. Deliver once stabilised - route by obstetric indication, not by seizure alone. Note: recurrence risk in a future pregnancy is around 2%; low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks is offered.
rich_summaries.Ectopic pregnancy: Implantation outside the uterine cavity, most often ampullary tubal, and the leading cause of first-trimester maternal death. Causes: anything that damages tubal transport - previous ectopic, pelvic inflammatory disease, tubal surgery, endometriosis, smoking, and pregnancy with an intrauterine device in place. Clinical features: amenorrhoea then unilateral pelvic pain and bleeding at 6-8 weeks. Shoulder tip pain, syncope or peritonism suggest rupture with haemoperitoneum. Ix: urine beta-hCG then transvaginal ultrasound. Above the discriminatory zone of about 1,500 IU/L an empty uterus is ectopic until proven otherwise; below it, serial hCG that fails to double in 48 hours points the same way. Mx: methotrexate for a stable, unruptured, small ectopic with a low hCG and no fetal cardiac activity, with hCG followed to zero. Laparoscopic salpingectomy for rupture, instability, or failed medical management. Anti-D if Rh-negative. Red flags: haemodynamic instability means theatre, not another scan.
rich_summaries.Eczema: Chronic relapsing pruritic inflammatory skin disease, the commonest eczema and part of the atopic triad. Epidemiology: begins in infancy; most improve by adolescence. Pathophysiology: barrier dysfunction first - filaggrin loss-of-function is the strongest genetic risk - allowing allergen entry and Th2 inflammation. That order is why emollients are treatment, not adjunct. Clinical features: itch is obligatory; facial and extensor in infants, flexural in older children and adults, with lichenification and excoriation marking chronicity. Mx: liberal emollients regardless of activity; topical steroid matched to site; calcineurin inhibitors for face and flexures. Note: undertreatment through steroid phobia causes more harm than appropriate steroid use, and is the commonest reason treatment fails. Monomorphic punched-out erosions mean eczema herpeticum - urgent aciclovir.
rich_summaries.Ehlers-Danlos syndrome: Group of inherited connective tissue disorders from collagen defects; 13 subtypes in the 2017 classification. Common features are joint hypermobility, skin hyperextensibility, tissue fragility and atrophic scarring. Subtypes: classical (COL5A1/A2, autosomal dominant, skin and joints prominent); hypermobile (commonest, unknown gene, clinical diagnosis with 2017 criteria); vascular (COL3A1, dangerous - arterial and bowel rupture, translucent skin, characteristic facies, median survival 48 years); kyphoscoliotic. Complications include joint dislocation, chronic pain, dysautonomia (POTS), atrophic scarring, hernia, and pelvic organ prolapse; the vascular subtype adds arterial dissection or rupture, sigmoid perforation and uterine rupture in pregnancy.Ix: clinical diagnosis for hypermobile (Beighton over 5); genetic testing for other subtypes; echocardiogram for aortic root; vascular imaging in vascular EDS. Mx: no cure. Physiotherapy, pain management, psychological support. Vascular EDS - avoid contact sports and arterial catheterisation; celiprolol may reduce arterial events; genetic counselling. Note: pregnancy in vascular EDS is high risk - manage in a tertiary centre.
rich_summaries.Empyema: Pus in the pleural space. Causes: complication of pneumonia (parapneumonic empyema, commonest); lung abscess; oesophageal perforation; haematogenous seeding; post-surgical. Common pathogens are Strep pneumoniae, Strep milleri, Staph aureus (including MRSA), Gram-negatives, and anaerobes. Clinical features: persistent fever after adequate antibiotics for pneumonia, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, weight loss; dullness to percussion, reduced breath sounds. Ix: CXR shows pleural effusion; bedside ultrasound confirms and guides drainage; chest CT for anatomy and abscess. Diagnostic thoracocentesis - empyema is pus, pleural pH under 7.2, glucose under 2.2 mmol/L, LDH over 1000 U/L, or positive Gram stain or culture. Blood cultures. Mx: broad-spectrum IV antibiotics per eTG (amoxicillin plus clavulanate, or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole; add vancomycin if MRSA risk), narrowed by culture, for 4 to 6 weeks. Prompt intercostal chest drain. Intrapleural tPA plus DNase (MIST-2) for loculations. VATS for failed medical management or fibrothorax. Note: delayed drainage is the single biggest predictor of outcome.
rich_summaries.Encephalitis: Inflammation of brain parenchyma, most often infective or autoimmune, distinguished from meningitis by altered mental state and focal features. Causes: herpes simplex is the commonest sporadic viral cause and preferentially affects the temporal lobes; enteroviruses, VZV, EBV, arboviruses (Murray Valley, Japanese, dengue) and rabies also cause disease; autoimmune causes include NMDA receptor and LGI1 antibody encephalitis. Clinical features: fever, headache and altered consciousness with focal neurology - dysphasia, seizures, behavioural change, movement disorder. Ix: CT brain before LP; LP with opening pressure, cell count, protein, glucose, HSV/VZV/enterovirus PCR, autoimmune antibody panel; MRI brain (temporal FLAIR hyperintensity in HSV); EEG. Blood cultures, HIV, arboviral serology. Mx: start IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours empirically on suspicion, before HSV PCR returns. Treat seizures and raised ICP. Autoimmune encephalitis needs IV methylprednisolone, IVIG or plasma exchange, and tumour resection where relevant. Note: notifiable in all Australian jurisdictions.
rich_summaries.Endocarditis: Infection of the endocardium, most often a valve. Causes: Staphylococcus aureus is now the commonest overall (IVDU and healthcare-associated); viridans streptococci for subacute native-valve disease; enterococci from urogenital or GI source; coagulase-negative staphylococci for prosthetic valves; HACEK for culture-negative disease. Clinical features: persistent fever, new or changing murmur, and embolic phenomena (Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, Roth spots, splinter haemorrhages, splenic or cerebral emboli). Ix: three sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics; TTE first, TOE if TTE is negative but suspicion is high or a prosthetic valve is in place. Modified Duke criteria. Mx: empirical IV antibiotics after cultures (flucloxacillin plus benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin, or vancomycin plus gentamicin if MRSA or penicillin allergic), narrowed by susceptibilities and continued for 4 to 6 weeks. Surgery for heart failure from valve destruction, perivalvular abscess, large or embolising vegetations, or uncontrolled infection. Note: dental prophylaxis is reserved for high-risk patients (prosthetic valve, previous endocarditis, unrepaired cyanotic disease) under eTG.
rich_summaries.Endometrial cancer: Malignancy of the uterine endometrium; the commonest gynaecological cancer in Australia. Types: type 1 (endometrioid, oestrogen-driven) is commonest and presents early with postmenopausal bleeding; type 2 (serous, clear cell) is de novo, more aggressive, less oestrogen-dependent. Risk factors for type 1: unopposed oestrogen - obesity, nulliparity, early menarche and late menopause, PCOS, oestrogen-only HRT, tamoxifen; also Lynch syndrome. Clinical features: postmenopausal bleeding (commonest presentation - any warrants investigation), intermenstrual bleeding, menorrhagia. Ix: transvaginal ultrasound measuring endometrial thickness (postmenopausal cut-off 4 mm); endometrial biopsy (Pipelle or hysteroscopy and curettage) is diagnostic. Staging with pelvic MRI and CT chest-abdomen-pelvis. Mx: surgical staging with total hysterectomy plus bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and lymph node assessment. Adjuvant vaginal brachytherapy, external beam radiotherapy or chemotherapy by stage, grade and molecular profile. Fertility-sparing progestogen therapy in selected early-stage disease. Note: any postmenopausal bleeding needs investigation - 10% harbours endometrial cancer.
rich_summaries.Endometriosis: Presence of endometrial-like tissue outside the uterus, hormonally responsive and inflammatory. Common sites are pelvic peritoneum, ovary (endometrioma or chocolate cyst), pouch of Douglas, uterosacral ligaments, bladder and bowel. Clinical features: cyclical pain preceding and during menstruation, deep dyspareunia, dyschezia, dysuria, and subfertility. Severity of symptoms correlates poorly with disease burden. Ix: pelvic examination for tenderness, nodules or fixed retroverted uterus; transvaginal ultrasound for endometrioma and deep infiltrating disease; MRI for bowel or bladder disease. Laparoscopy remains the reference standard for diagnosis and treatment but is not required before empirical medical therapy. Mx: NSAIDs cycle-only for pain, plus combined oral contraceptive or progestogen (norethisterone, dienogest, depot MPA, levonorgestrel IUS) continuously. GnRH analogues with add-back for refractory pain. Laparoscopic excision or ablation for symptoms not controlled medically, endometrioma over 4 cm, or subfertility. Note: average diagnostic delay in Australia is 7 to 12 years; believe the pain and act.
rich_summaries.Enuresis: Involuntary voiding of urine at an age when continence is expected (5 years for nocturnal). Types: nocturnal (bedwetting - by far the commonest) or diurnal; primary means never reliably dry, secondary means recurrence after at least 6 months of dryness. Prevalence is about 15% at age 5, falling by 15% each year. Causes: primary nocturnal enuresis reflects delayed sleep arousal, low nocturnal ADH, or reduced bladder capacity, often familial. Secondary or diurnal enuresis warrants a search for UTI, constipation, diabetes mellitus or insipidus, obstructive sleep apnoea, and psychosocial stressors including abuse. Ix: urinalysis and culture; bladder diary; examine the abdomen, spine and genitals; renal tract ultrasound only for daytime symptoms, UTI or abnormal exam. Mx: reassure the family. Behavioural measures first - fluid before evening, void before bed, avoid punishment. Enuresis alarm is the most effective long-term treatment (60 to 80% success). Desmopressin (short-term or for sleepovers) if the alarm fails or is not feasible. Refer for constipation and daytime symptoms. Note: never punish or shame.
rich_summaries.Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang: ANCA-associated small vessel vasculitis (formerly Churg-Strauss). Three phases - allergic prodrome (rhinitis, nasal polyps, asthma), eosinophilic phase (peripheral eosinophilia and tissue infiltration), and vasculitic phase with systemic small vessel vasculitis. Clinical features: severe adult-onset or worsening asthma is the near-universal feature; mononeuritis multiplex (75%); pulmonary infiltrates that shift; cardiac involvement (myocarditis, coronary arteritis - major cause of death); renal disease milder than GPA or MPA; palpable purpura; sinusitis. Ix: peripheral eosinophilia (over 1.5 x 10^9/L), raised IgE, ANCA positive in 40% (MPO-ANCA); biopsy shows eosinophil-rich necrotising vasculitis with granulomata; CT chest; echocardiogram and cardiac MRI for cardiac involvement. Mx: high-dose prednisolone alone for mild disease; add cyclophosphamide or rituximab for severe organ involvement (Five-Factor Score guides). Mepolizumab (anti-IL-5) is steroid-sparing. Note: leukotriene receptor antagonists were wrongly blamed - vasculitis was already present.
rich_summaries.Epiglottitis: Life-threatening cellulitis of the supraglottic structures. Classically Haemophilus influenzae type b in unvaccinated children; now uncommon in Australia thanks to the NIP, with adults (streptococci, staphylococci) predominating. Clinical features in children: rapid onset high fever, toxic appearance, drooling, tripod position, muffled hot-potato voice, and stridor without cough (distinguishes from croup). Adults present less acutely with severe sore throat, odynophagia, and drooling. Ix: do not distress the child; do not lie them down; do not examine the throat with a spatula. If stable, indirect laryngoscopy or lateral neck radiograph (thumbprint sign) supports the diagnosis. Blood cultures and epiglottic swab after airway secured. Mx: airway comes first - call ENT and anaesthetics immediately for controlled intubation in theatre, with surgical airway backup. IV ceftriaxone plus vancomycin. Adrenaline and steroids are adjuncts. Rifampicin prophylaxis for household contacts of an Hib case. Note: presume epiglottitis in any acutely unwell child with drooling and stridor until proven otherwise.
rich_summaries.Epilepsy: Enduring predisposition to unprovoked seizures - two or more separated by 24 hours, or one with a high recurrence risk. Classification: focal (aware or impaired awareness, with or without progression to bilateral tonic-clonic) or generalised (tonic-clonic, absence, myoclonic, atonic). Classification drives drug choice, so it is not academic. Ix: EEG supports classification but a normal one does not exclude epilepsy; MRI brain for structural cause; BGL, UEC, calcium and toxicology to exclude provoked seizures; ECG, since cardiac syncope is the commonest mimic. Mx: antiseizure medication after a second seizure, or after a first with a structural lesion or epileptiform EEG. Levetiracetam or lamotrigine for both focal and generalised; sodium valproate is effective in generalised epilepsy but contraindicated in people who could become pregnant. Note: driving restrictions under Austroads apply from the first seizure and must be discussed and documented; the patient carries the reporting obligation in most states. Red flags: seizure over 5 minutes is status epilepticus - benzodiazepine, then a second-line agent.
rich_summaries.Epistaxis: Nasal haemorrhage. Anterior epistaxis (about 90%) arises from Kiesselbach plexus on the anterior nasal septum; posterior epistaxis (10%) arises from the sphenopalatine artery, is more severe, and is commoner in older or hypertensive patients. Causes: idiopathic; local (digital trauma, dry mucosa, foreign body, nasal fracture, recent surgery, cocaine, tumour); systemic (anticoagulation, antiplatelets, thrombocytopenia, vWD, haemophilia, HHT, uncontrolled hypertension). Assess sitting forward with blood loss and haemodynamic check. Ix: FBC, group and hold, coagulation if heavy or recurrent; INR if on warfarin. Imaging only for trauma or suspected tumour. Mx: firm pressure on the cartilaginous nose (not bony bridge) for at least 10 minutes, sitting forward. If bleeding continues, topical vasoconstrictor (phenylephrine or cophenylcaine) then silver nitrate cautery of a visible bleeding point on Little area. Anterior nasal packing (Merocel or Rapid Rhino) for uncontrolled anterior bleed; posterior packing plus ENT admission for posterior bleed. Correct coagulopathy. Note: bilateral posterior packing carries risk of toxic shock and hypoxia - inpatient monitoring.
rich_summaries.Erythema multiforme: Acute self-limiting hypersensitivity reaction of skin and mucosa, characterised by target lesions. Types: EM minor (limited skin, minimal mucosal); EM major (skin plus at least one mucosal site, systemic symptoms). Distinct from SJS and TEN (different pathophysiology, more severe, different triggers). Triggers: infection in 90% (HSV commonest by far - recurrent EM often HSV-driven, Mycoplasma pneumoniae in children); drugs (NSAIDs, sulfonamides, penicillins, anticonvulsants); autoimmune; malignancy. Clinical features: sudden eruption of symmetric target lesions (three zones - central duskiness, oedematous ring, erythematous halo) on extensor surfaces, palms and soles; mild systemic symptoms; oral erosions in EM major. Resolves in 2 to 4 weeks. Ix: clinical diagnosis. Investigate trigger - HSV PCR if suggested, Mycoplasma serology or PCR in children, drug history review. Mx: identify and treat trigger; symptomatic - topical steroids and antihistamines, oral hygiene, analgesia; systemic steroids for severe EM major (controversial); prophylactic aciclovir for recurrent HSV-associated EM. Note: EM does not progress to SJS - distinct entities.
rich_summaries.Erythema nodosum: Septal panniculitis presenting as tender erythematous nodules on the anterior shins - the commonest reactive panniculitis. Clinical features: tender poorly demarcated nodules 1-10 cm, bilateral, evolving from red to bruise-like and resolving over 2-8 weeks. They never ulcerate or scar, which distinguishes them from nodular vasculitis. Causes: streptococcal pharyngitis (commonest); sarcoidosis - Lofgren syndrome with hilar adenopathy, arthritis and fever has a good prognosis; tuberculosis; IBD; pregnancy and the COCP; Behcet disease. About half are idiopathic. Ix: clinical; biopsy only if atypical. Seek the cause with ASOT, chest X-ray, ACE and TSH. Mx: treat the cause; NSAIDs, rest and elevation; potassium iodide if refractory. Note: chest X-ray in essentially everyone - sarcoidosis and tuberculosis both present this way and are otherwise missed.
rich_summaries.Febrile neutropenia: Fever in a neutropenic patient - an oncological emergency, since the usual signs of infection are absent when neutrophils are. Definition: single temperature of 38.3 degrees, or 38.0 sustained over an hour, with neutrophils below 0.5 x 10^9/L or expected to fall below it. Clinical features: fever may be the only sign - there is no pus, little erythema, and often no localising feature. Hypotension may be the first indication of sepsis. Ix: blood cultures from peripheral and any central line before antibiotics; FBC, UEC, LFT, lactate; chest X-ray; cultures directed by symptoms. Do not delay treatment for results. Mx: broad-spectrum antipseudomonal beta-lactam - piperacillin-tazobactam or cefepime - within one hour of presentation. Add vancomycin for suspected line infection or haemodynamic instability. G-CSF where prophylaxis is indicated. Note: the one-hour target matters more than antibiotic choice; mortality rises measurably with each hour of delay. Any patient on chemotherapy with a fever needs assessment now, not in the morning.
rich_summaries.Febrile seizures: Seizure with fever (temperature at least 38 C) in a child 6 months to 5 years, without CNS infection or a history of afebrile seizure. Types: simple (generalised tonic-clonic, under 15 minutes, single in 24 hours) is benign; complex (focal, over 15 minutes, or recurrent in 24 hours) carries a small increased epilepsy risk. Clinical features: brief self-limiting seizure at the onset of fever, often the first sign of illness; post-ictal drowsiness is normal but should resolve within an hour. Ix: identify and treat the fever source (viral URTI is commonest); no routine imaging or EEG for simple febrile seizures. Lumbar puncture only for signs of meningitis, persistently altered mental state, or an ill-appearing child under 12 months. Mx: supportive - place safely, do not restrain, time the seizure. Buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam if seizure lasts over 5 minutes. Antipyretics for comfort - they do not prevent recurrence. Parental reassurance is the core. Note: recurrence within the same illness is common; long-term epilepsy risk is 1 to 2% for simple, higher for complex.
rich_summaries.Female infertility: Failure to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse (6 months if over 35). Affects around 1 in 6 Australian couples; causes are female one-third, male one-third, both or unexplained the rest. Causes are ovulatory (PCOS commonest, hypothalamic amenorrhoea, POI, hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disease), tubal (PID especially chlamydia, endometriosis, prior ectopic, tubal ligation), uterine (fibroids, polyps, Asherman adhesions), cervical, and age-related decline in oocyte quality and quantity (marked from 35, steep after 40).Clinical features: menstrual pattern, dysmenorrhoea and dyspareunia (endometriosis), pelvic infection history, weight, hirsutism and acne (PCOS), galactorrhoea. Ix: day-21 progesterone; FSH, LH, oestradiol day 2 to 5; TSH, prolactin, AMH; rubella and varicella serology; transvaginal ultrasound with antral follicle count; HyCoSy or HSG for tubal patency; laparoscopy if endometriosis suspected; semen analysis in the partner. Mx: treat modifiable factors; ovulation induction (letrozole first line for PCOS, clomiphene second); tubal surgery; assisted reproduction (IVF, ICSI, donor). Note: refer early if age over 35 or known factor.
rich_summaries.Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder: Spectrum of lifelong neurodevelopmental disability caused by prenatal alcohol exposure. No safe level of alcohol is established in pregnancy. Diagnostic categories are fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS - all four criteria: growth impairment, characteristic facial features, CNS involvement, prenatal alcohol exposure), partial FAS, and neurodevelopmental disorder associated with prenatal alcohol exposure. Clinical features: characteristic facies (smooth philtrum, thin upper vermilion, short palpebral fissures); pre- and post-natal growth restriction; microcephaly; CNS dysfunction (intellectual disability, ADHD-like features, executive dysfunction, learning problems); congenital heart, renal or skeletal anomalies in FAS. Ix: no confirmatory test. Diagnosis by multidisciplinary assessment against Australian FASD diagnostic criteria with confirmed exposure, growth measurement, dysmorphology examination, and neurodevelopmental assessment. Mx: no cure. Early intervention with speech and occupational therapy, educational support, and behavioural interventions. NDIS funding is available with diagnosis. Note: NHMRC advice is no alcohol in pregnancy or when planning pregnancy.
rich_summaries.Fibromyalgia: Chronic widespread pain with fatigue, unrefreshing sleep and cognitive difficulty, understood as central sensitisation rather than tissue damage. Epidemiology: women > men; often coexists with mood disorders and irritable bowel syndrome. Clinical features: widespread pain over 3 months, fatigue, non-restorative sleep, cognitive fog, hypersensitivity to touch and sound. Ix: inflammatory markers, CK and imaging are all normal - and that normality is the finding. Investigate only what the history suggests; repeated negative testing entrenches illness beliefs. Mx: graded patient-led exercise has the best evidence, with sleep measures, CBT and pain education; amitriptyline or duloxetine may help; opioids do not and cause harm. Note: coexists with inflammatory disease often enough that finding one does not exclude the other.
rich_summaries.Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis: Histological pattern of sclerosis in some glomeruli (focal) and part of the tuft (segmental); commonest cause of primary nephrotic syndrome in adults. Classification: primary (immune-mediated podocyte injury by a circulating factor); genetic (podocin, nephrin, ACTN4 mutations); secondary (adaptive hyperfiltration from reduced nephron mass or obesity; HIV; drug - pamidronate, interferon, heroin). Clinical features: nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria over 3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, hyperlipidaemia) in primary; slowly progressive proteinuria in secondary; hypertension and CKD progression common. Ix: urine ACR or 24-hour protein; renal biopsy is diagnostic (segmental sclerosis on LM; diffuse foot-process effacement on EM in primary, partial in secondary); HIV, hepatitis and autoimmune serology; genetic testing in familial cases. Mx: primary - high-dose prednisolone, calcineurin inhibitor or mycophenolate for steroid-resistant disease; secondary - treat cause plus ACE inhibitor or ARB, SGLT2 inhibitor, statin; anticoagulate high-risk nephrotic patients.
