Note: distinguishing primary from secondary changes everything - immunosuppression treats primary and worsens secondary.
rich_summaries.Folate deficiency: Macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia from folate insufficiency. Causes: inadequate dietary intake (elderly, alcoholism, overcooking of leafy vegetables), malabsorption (coeliac disease, jejunal disease, tropical sprue), increased demand (pregnancy, haemolysis, malignancy, chronic dialysis), and drugs (methotrexate, trimethoprim, phenytoin, sulfasalazine). Clinical features: gradual pallor and fatigue, dyspnoea, glossitis and angular cheilitis; no neurological signs (distinguishes from B12 deficiency). Perinatal folate deficiency causes neural tube defects. Ix: FBC (macrocytic anaemia, hypersegmented neutrophils on film), reticulocytes (low), LDH (raised from ineffective erythropoiesis), serum folate and red cell folate (more stable), always paired with B12. Mx: oral folic acid 5 mg daily for 4 months; treat the cause. Correct any B12 deficiency first - giving folate alone in B12 deficiency can precipitate or worsen subacute combined degeneration of the cord. Note: preconception folate 400 microg daily (5 mg for high risk: previous NTD, diabetes, anticonvulsants, obesity) reduces NTD in Australia.
rich_summaries.Foreign body aspiration: Inhalation of a solid foreign body into the airway. Bimodal - young children (1 to 3 years, commonest; small objects, immature swallowing, no molars) and elderly with reduced airway protection. Common objects include peanuts and other nuts, seeds, coins, small toys, food boluses. Clinical features: witnessed choking event in half; sudden onset cough, wheeze, stridor and cyanosis; complete obstruction gives silent gasping and rapid decompensation. Delayed presentation with focal wheeze, unilateral reduced breath sounds, or persistent pneumonia in the same lobe - right main bronchus most commonly. Ix: chest and lateral neck radiograph (radiolucent objects invisible; unilateral hyperinflation on expiratory or decubitus film supports diagnosis in children); CT for chronic or complicated cases. Bronchoscopy is definitive and therapeutic. Mx: acute complete obstruction gets back blows and chest thrusts in infants under 1, Heimlich manoeuvre over 1, cricothyroidotomy if airway lost. Otherwise urgent rigid bronchoscopy under GA. Note: any child with new focal wheeze or recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe needs bronchoscopy regardless of history.
rich_summaries.Fragile X syndrome: Commonest inherited cause of intellectual disability and commonest single-gene cause of autism. X-linked CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in FMR1 at Xq27.3 - full mutation (over 200 repeats) silences FMR1 and eliminates the FMRP protein. Premutation (55 to 200 repeats) is unstable and carries adult risks - fragile X-associated tremor-ataxia syndrome (FXTAS) in older men, and primary ovarian insufficiency (FXPOI) in women. Males more severely affected. Clinical features: developmental delay, intellectual disability (IQ 40 to 70 in males), autism spectrum, ADHD, anxiety; long face, prominent forehead and jaw, large protruding ears, macro-orchidism post-puberty; joint hypermobility, mitral valve prolapse; seizures in 20%. Ix: targeted FMR1 CGG-repeat sizing and methylation analysis; chromosomal microarray if broader dysmorphology workup; family cascade testing. Mx: no disease-modifying therapy. Multidisciplinary support - early intervention, speech and OT, individualised education; treat comorbid ADHD, anxiety and seizures. Genetic counselling. Note: mothers of affected boys are obligate carriers - offer reproductive counselling.
rich_summaries.G6PD deficiency: X-linked recessive enzyme deficiency reducing NADPH and glutathione, leaving red blood cells vulnerable to oxidative damage. The commonest human enzyme deficiency; prevalent in African, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern and Southeast Asian populations. Clinical features: usually asymptomatic between crises. Acute haemolytic anaemia with pallor, jaundice and dark urine 24 to 72 hours after an oxidative trigger - fava beans (favism), drugs (primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, methylene blue, rasburicase, quinolones), or infection. Neonatal jaundice is common in the Mediterranean variant. Chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia in severe variants. Ix: FBC and film during a crisis (bite cells, blister cells, Heinz bodies on supravital stain); reticulocytes rise; unconjugated bilirubin, LDH, haptoglobin. G6PD enzyme activity assay - measure at least 3 months after a haemolytic episode (false negatives during crisis from young RBC predominance). Mx: withdraw the trigger. Supportive with hydration and transfusion for severe haemolysis. Prevention is education - patient carries a drug avoidance list. Note: screen before prescribing primaquine or tafenoquine for malaria.
rich_summaries.Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease: Symptoms or mucosal injury from retrograde flow of gastric contents into the oesophagus. Pathophysiology: transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxations are the commonest mechanism; reduced tone from a hiatus hernia and raised intragastric pressure from obesity or pregnancy contribute. Clinical features: heartburn and regurgitation are the classic pair; water brash, chronic cough, hoarseness, non-cardiac chest pain and dental erosions are extraoesophageal presentations. Ix: empirical PPI trial is diagnostic in typical disease; endoscopy for alarm features - dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, anaemia, haematemesis or melaena, onset after 55, or failure of 4 to 8 weeks of PPI. Mx: lifestyle first - weight loss, smaller evening meals, no recumbency for 3 hours after eating, elevate the head of the bed, reduce alcohol. Pantoprazole or esomeprazole once daily before breakfast for 4 to 8 weeks, then step down. H2 antagonist at night for nocturnal breakthrough. Fundoplication for objectively confirmed disease refractory to full-dose PPI. Complications: erosive oesophagitis, stricture, Barrett oesophagus and adenocarcinoma.
rich_summaries.Gastroenteritis: Acute infective diarrhoea with or without vomiting. Causes: viruses in about 80% - norovirus (all ages, epidemic, vomiting-predominant), rotavirus (children under 5, now vaccine-preventable on the NIP), adenovirus, sapovirus. Bacterial causes cluster around undercooked meat, poultry, eggs or contaminated water - Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, enterotoxigenic and enterohaemorrhagic E. coli. Consider Giardia and Cryptosporidium in prolonged or travel-related illness; Clostridioides difficile after antibiotics. Clinical features: watery diarrhoea suggests small-bowel; bloody diarrhoea and fever suggests invasive colitic pathogen. Ix: none for mild disease. Stool MCS for bloody or prolonged diarrhoea, after antibiotics, in immunocompromise, or in outbreak; blood cultures if septic. Mx: oral rehydration solution first line. Antibiotics only for severe or invasive disease, immunocompromise, or specific pathogen (azithromycin for shigellosis, metronidazole then vancomycin for C. difficile). Avoid loperamide in bloody diarrhoea, invasive disease and children. Note: Salmonella, Shigella, cholera, STEC and typhoid are notifiable.
rich_summaries.Generalised anxiety disorder: Excessive, persistent and hard-to-control worry about multiple domains most days for at least 6 months, with somatic symptoms causing distress or functional impairment. Lifetime prevalence around 6%; female predominance (2:1); onset in 20s to 30s; commonly comorbid with depression and alcohol use. Sx (DSM-5 requires 3 of 6 for at least 6 months): restlessness, easy fatiguability, difficulty concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance. Screen with GAD-7 (over 10 moderate; over 15 severe). Ix: clinical diagnosis. Screen comorbid depression (PHQ-9), substance use, and medical mimics (hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, cardiac disease, caffeine, steroids, salbutamol, thyroxine). Mx: psychological therapy first line - CBT has strongest evidence; ACT and mindfulness also effective. Pharmacotherapy for moderate to severe - SSRI (sertraline, escitalopram) or SNRI (venlafaxine, duloxetine); pregabalin second line. Avoid benzodiazepines beyond short crisis use. Note: response takes 4 to 6 weeks; warn about initial worsening of anxiety on SSRI start.
rich_summaries.Genitourinary syndrome of menopause: Umbrella term (replacing 'atrophic vaginitis') for chronic genitourinary changes from oestrogen loss. Pathophysiology: falling oestrogen (menopause, oophorectomy, GnRH analogues, aromatase inhibitors, lactation) reduces vaginal glycogen and lactobacilli; pH rises above 5, tissues thin and lose elasticity. Clinical features: vaginal dryness, superficial dyspareunia (the most bothersome symptom), post-coital bleeding, vulvar burning; urinary urgency, frequency, dysuria, recurrent UTIs; unlike vasomotor symptoms it does not resolve spontaneously and worsens over time. Ix: clinical - pale smooth mucosa with loss of rugae, petechiae, friability, vaginal pH above 5; exclude infection and lichen sclerosus. Mx: non-hormonal first - water-based lubricants and hyaluronic acid moisturisers; low-dose vaginal oestrogen is first-line pharmacotherapy (Ovestin cream, Vagifem pessaries, oestriol ring), highly effective with negligible systemic absorption and acceptable after breast cancer in consultation with oncology; systemic MHT if vasomotor symptoms warrant it; ospemifene or vaginal prasterone as alternatives. Note: vaginal dose does not raise serum oestrogen meaningfully.
rich_summaries.Gestational diabetes: Glucose intolerance first recognised in pregnancy, distinct from pre-existing diabetes and resolving after delivery in most. Pathophysiology: placental hormones (human placental lactogen, progesterone, cortisol, growth hormone) drive insulin resistance from mid-pregnancy; GDM is the failure of beta cells to keep up. Risk factors: BMI over 30, previous GDM, previous macrosomia over 4.5 kg, South Asian, Middle Eastern or Aboriginal ethnicity, first-degree relative with type 2 diabetes, PCOS, and maternal age over 40. Ix: universal 75g OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks; diagnostic under ADIPS if fasting is at least 5.1, 1-hour at least 10.0, or 2-hour at least 8.5 mmol/L. Earlier testing in high risk. Mx: dietitian-led carbohydrate management and monitored exercise first; self-monitor fasting and 1-hour post-meal glucose targeting under 5.0 fasting and under 7.4 post-prandial. Add insulin (or metformin where insulin is not acceptable) if targets are not met within one to two weeks. Serial growth ultrasound. Note: repeat OGTT at 6 to 12 weeks postpartum; 50% develop type 2 diabetes within 10 years, so annual glucose review continues indefinitely.
rich_summaries.Gestational trophoblastic disease: Spectrum of tumours from placental trophoblast, from benign hydatidiform mole to malignant gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblastic tumour). Types: complete mole (46XX diploid, all paternal, no fetal tissue, grape-like vesicles, very high hCG); partial mole (69XXY or 69XXX triploid, some fetal tissue, less elevated hCG). Clinical features: first-trimester vaginal bleeding, uterus larger than dates, hyperemesis, early pre-eclampsia under 20 weeks, hyperthyroidism (hCG cross-reacts with TSH receptor), and theca lutein cysts. Ix: quantitative beta-hCG (often over 100,000 IU/L); pelvic ultrasound (snowstorm pattern in complete mole); FBC, EUC, TFT, LFT, coagulation, group and hold; CXR to exclude lung metastases. Mx: suction curettage (misoprostol is avoided). Serial beta-hCG until three consecutive undetectable results then monthly for 6 months. Contraception during monitoring (COCP acceptable). Malignant GTN gets methotrexate (low-risk) or EMA-CO (high-risk) - highly curable. Note: any woman with a prior molar pregnancy needs beta-hCG confirmation of successful surveillance before the next pregnancy.
rich_summaries.Giant cell arteritis: Granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis of the aorta and branches, especially the extracranial carotid branches. Epidemiology: over 50, peak 70-80; women > men; half have polymyalgia rheumatica. Clinical features: new temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, amaurosis fugax or sudden painless visual loss from anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. Ix: ESR and CRP raised; temporal artery ultrasound halo sign; biopsy is the diagnostic standard. Mx: high-dose prednisolone immediately on suspicion - IV methylprednisolone first if visual symptoms; add aspirin and bone protection. Note: biopsy stays positive 1-2 weeks after starting steroids, so treatment never waits for it. Red flags: any visual symptom is an emergency - vision rarely returns and the other eye is at risk within days.
rich_summaries.Glaucoma: Progressive optic neuropathy with characteristic visual field loss, usually with raised intraocular pressure. Types: primary open-angle (commonest, insidious, painless); primary angle-closure (shallow anterior chamber); normal-tension (open-angle, IOP under 22); secondary (uveitis, steroid-induced, traumatic, pseudoexfoliation, pigment dispersion). Clinical features: open-angle is asymptomatic until advanced peripheral visual field loss; acute angle-closure presents with severe unilateral eye pain, blurred vision with haloes, nausea and vomiting, hard red eye and mid-dilated fixed pupil. Ix: IOP (tonometry); gonioscopy; automated visual fields; OCT of retinal nerve fibre layer; dilated fundus examination showing optic disc cupping. Mx: open-angle reduces IOP by 20 to 30% with topical prostaglandin analogues first line (latanoprost, bimatoprost), then beta blockers, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, alpha agonists; selective laser trabeculoplasty; surgery for refractory disease. Acute angle-closure needs immediate acetazolamide, topical agents, and laser peripheral iridotomy. Note: any red painful eye with reduced vision needs pressure measured before it is called conjunctivitis.
rich_summaries.Glioblastoma: The commonest and most aggressive primary brain tumour (WHO grade 4 astrocytoma); peaks 55 to 65 years. Molecularly IDH-wildtype. Median survival with maximal therapy is about 14 to 16 months. Risk factors are largely unknown; prior therapeutic cranial radiation and rare syndromes (Li-Fraumeni, NF1, Turcot) contribute a minority. Clinical features: focal neurological deficits by tumour location (weakness, aphasia, cognitive change), seizures, and raised intracranial pressure - headache worse supine and on waking, morning vomiting, papilloedema. Personality change is common in frontal disease. Ix: MRI brain with gadolinium shows heterogeneously enhancing mass with central necrosis, surrounding vasogenic oedema, and mass effect; often crosses the corpus callosum (butterfly glioma). Stereotactic biopsy or resection provides tissue diagnosis and molecular profile (IDH, MGMT methylation, TERT). Mx: maximal safe surgical resection followed by concurrent temozolomide chemoradiotherapy (Stupp protocol) then adjuvant temozolomide. Bevacizumab for recurrence. Steroids and antiepileptics as needed. Note: MGMT methylation predicts temozolomide response and better prognosis.
rich_summaries.Glomerulonephritis: Inflammation of the glomerulus, presenting as nephritic syndrome (haematuria, hypertension, oliguria, red cell casts, sub-nephrotic proteinuria) or nephrotic syndrome (over 3.5 g protein per day, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, hyperlipidaemia). Causes: nephritic from post-streptococcal, IgA nephropathy, ANCA-associated vasculitis, anti-GBM, lupus or cryoglobulinaemia. Nephrotic from minimal change (children), FSGS, membranous (associated with malignancy in adults), and diabetic nephropathy. Ix: urinalysis with microscopy for casts, urine PCR, EUC, complement (low in post-strep, lupus, cryoglobulinaemia), ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM, ASOT, HIV, HBV, HCV serology, immunoglobulins with SPEP. Renal biopsy defines pathology and drives immunosuppression. Mx: treat the underlying cause; BP control with ACE inhibitor or ARB, sodium restriction, diuretics for oedema; corticosteroids and steroid-sparing agents by biopsy result. Note: rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (halving eGFR over weeks) is an emergency.
rich_summaries.Gonorrhoea: Sexually transmitted infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Gram-negative diplococci); the second commonest bacterial STI in Australia. Antimicrobial resistance is a major public health concern - Australia has documented ceftriaxone-resistant strains. Clinical features: many are asymptomatic (about half of women, a third of men). Men develop urethritis with mucopurulent discharge and dysuria; epididymo-orchitis follows. Women develop cervicitis with discharge, intermenstrual or post-coital bleeding, and pelvic inflammatory disease with tubal infertility. Extragenital involvement includes pharyngeal (usually asymptomatic), rectal (proctitis), and disseminated infection (fever, migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, pustular rash). Neonatal ophthalmia from vertical transmission. Ix: NAAT - first-catch urine in men, self-collected vulvovaginal swab in women, site-specific swabs for rectum, throat and eye. Culture with susceptibility for any confirmed case. Mx: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose plus azithromycin 1 g oral single dose. Test of cure by NAAT at 2 weeks. Contact tracing (2 months); notifiable. Note: suspected pharyngeal infection needs specific pharyngeal test.
rich_summaries.Goodpasture syndrome: Rare autoimmune disease with IgG antibodies against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes, causing rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with pulmonary haemorrhage. Male predominance; bimodal age peaks at 20 to 30 and 60 to 70; HLA-DR15 associated. Triggers: smoking (essential for alveolar involvement), hydrocarbon exposure, infection, cocaine. Clinical features: pulmonary haemorrhage with haemoptysis, dyspnoea, hypoxia and diffuse alveolar infiltrates; renal disease with haematuria, proteinuria, hypertension and rapidly rising creatinine; systemic symptoms are usually absent (unlike ANCA vasculitis). Ix: serum anti-GBM antibody is diagnostic; check ANCA (10 to 40% double-positive, behave worse); urinalysis shows dysmorphic red cells and casts; renal biopsy shows crescentic GN with pathognomonic linear IgG on immunofluorescence. Mx: urgent plasma exchange plus cyclophosphamide and high-dose prednisolone; continue immunosuppression 6 to 12 months. Dialysis for renal failure. Note: creatinine over 500 or dialysis-dependent at presentation rarely recovers renal function; lung haemorrhage is the mortal threat.
rich_summaries.Gout: Inflammatory arthritis from monosodium urate crystal deposition. Epidemiology: men >> premenopausal women; markedly increased in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, Maori and Pacific peoples. Pathophysiology: urate crystals activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, releasing IL-1 beta. Clinical features: abrupt exquisitely painful monoarthritis peaking within 24 h, classically first MTP (podagra); tophi and erosions later. Ix: aspiration shows negatively birefringent needles and excludes sepsis; urate may be normal during an attack - recheck at 2 weeks. Mx: NSAID, colchicine or prednisolone for the attack. Allopurinol for recurrent attacks, tophi or erosions - target urate below 0.36 mmol/L, with colchicine cover. Note: check HLA-B*5801 in high-risk ancestries before allopurinol. Red flags: a hot swollen joint is septic arthritis until aspiration says otherwise - the two can coexist.
rich_summaries.Granulomatosis with polyangiitis: ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis (c-ANCA against PR3). Clinical features: the classic triad involves upper airway (sinusitis, nasal crusting, septum perforation, saddle-nose deformity, otitis media), lower airway (cough, haemoptysis, cavitating nodules), and kidneys (rapidly progressive pauci-immune glomerulonephritis). Also ocular (scleritis, proptosis), cutaneous (palpable purpura, ulcers), neurological (mononeuritis multiplex) and systemic (fever, weight loss, arthralgia). Ix: c-ANCA and PR3 (95% sensitive in generalised disease); urinalysis for red cell casts and proteinuria; EUC, FBC, CRP, ESR, complement, ANA, anti-GBM; chest CT (cavitating nodules); renal biopsy shows necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis with few immune deposits. Mx: life-threatening or organ-threatening disease gets induction with IV methylprednisolone plus rituximab (or cyclophosphamide), plus plasma exchange for severe renal disease or alveolar haemorrhage. Maintenance with rituximab, azathioprine or methotrexate. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis against PJP while immunosuppressed. Note: relapse rate is 30 to 50%; regular urine dipstick and ANCA monitoring guide escalation.
rich_summaries.Graves disease: Commonest cause of hyperthyroidism, caused by TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies (TRAb) driving thyroid hormone overproduction. Epidemiology: peaks 20 to 50, 7 to 8 times more common in women, with familial and HLA associations. Clinical features: general hyperthyroid symptoms (weight loss despite appetite, tremor, heat intolerance, palpitations, AF, anxiety, sweating) plus Graves-specific features - diffuse smooth goitre often with an audible bruit, thyroid eye disease (proptosis, lid retraction, restricted ocular movements, diplopia), pretibial myxoedema, and thyroid acropachy. Ix: TSH (suppressed), free T4 and T3 (elevated), TRAb (positive in over 95%). Radioactive iodine uptake diffusely increased if diagnosis uncertain. Mx: symptomatic control with propranolol. Definitive - carbimazole 15 to 40 mg daily titrated to euthyroid over 12 to 18 months, then trial off; relapse rate 50 to 60%. Radioactive iodine ablation or total thyroidectomy for relapse, severe eye disease, or patient preference. Note: check baseline FBC before carbimazole; agranulocytosis (fever, sore throat) is a medical emergency needing immediate cessation and FBC.
rich_summaries.Group B Streptococcus: Streptococcus agalactiae; commensal in vagina or rectum of 15 to 30% of women. Causes early-onset neonatal sepsis (under 7 days, usually within 24 hours - pneumonia, sepsis, meningitis) through vertical transmission during labour, and late-onset disease (7 to 90 days - meningitis, focal infection). Also causes adult disease - UTI, skin and soft tissue, bacteraemia in diabetes and immunocompromise; postpartum endometritis; endocarditis. Clinical features: neonate with grunting, poor feeding, temperature instability, apnoea, shock; adult per site. Ix: antenatal universal vaginal-rectal swab at 35 to 37 weeks (Australian standard); urine culture; blood cultures; LP for meningitis. Mx: intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis with IV benzylpenicillin at least 4 hours before delivery for GBS-positive women, previous GBS-affected infant, GBS bacteriuria, unknown status with risk factors (preterm labour, ROM over 18 hours, intrapartum fever). Cefazolin for penicillin allergy, clindamycin or vancomycin for anaphylaxis. Neonatal sepsis - IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin. Note: intrapartum prophylaxis has cut early-onset disease by 80% but does not prevent late-onset.
rich_summaries.Guillain-Barré syndrome: Acute immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy causing ascending weakness, typically 1-3 weeks after infection. Causes: Campylobacter jejuni most often, then CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma and influenza. Clinical features: symmetrical ascending flaccid weakness with areflexia, developing over days to 4 weeks; sensory symptoms are usually mild relative to weakness; back and limb pain is common; autonomic instability with arrhythmia and labile blood pressure; facial and bulbar involvement. Miller Fisher variant gives ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia. Ix: nerve conduction studies showing demyelination; CSF with raised protein and normal cell count - albuminocytological dissociation - though this may be normal in the first week. Serial forced vital capacity is the key monitoring test. Mx: intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, equally effective and not combined; supportive care with VTE prophylaxis and cardiac monitoring. Corticosteroids do not work here. Red flags: falling FVC below about 20 mL/kg, bulbar weakness or autonomic instability means ICU. Respiratory failure develops before hypoxia appears on oximetry.
rich_summaries.HELLP syndrome: Severe variant of pre-eclampsia - Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets. Occurs in 0.5 to 0.9% of pregnancies; presents at 27 to 37 weeks in 70% and post-partum in 30% (usually within 48 hours). Hypertension and proteinuria may be mild or absent, delaying diagnosis. Clinical features: right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting, malaise, headache and visual change; hypertension and oedema in most but not all; hepatic tenderness suggests subcapsular haematoma. Complications: DIC, placental abruption, acute kidney injury, hepatic rupture, pulmonary oedema, stroke, fetal death. Ix: FBC (platelets under 100), film (schistocytes), LDH raised, haptoglobin low, AST and ALT often over twice normal, coagulation for DIC, EUC, urate, urinalysis, CTG. Mx: prompt delivery is the only definitive treatment - expedite for gestation over 34 weeks or maternal or fetal compromise at any gestation; corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation if 24 to 34 weeks and delivery can wait 48 hours. Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis; labetalol, hydralazine or nifedipine for severe hypertension; platelets if under 20 or under 50 with bleeding. Note: recurrence risk 3 to 24%.
rich_summaries.HIV: Retroviral infection depleting CD4 T cells; untreated it progresses through acute seroconversion, chronic asymptomatic and AIDS (CD4 under 200 or an AIDS-defining illness). Clinical features: seroconversion 2 to 4 weeks after exposure looks like flu with fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, maculopapular rash and oral ulcers; the chronic phase is asymptomatic for years. Ix: fourth-generation combined HIV antigen and antibody assay is the screen; positives are confirmed with a differentiation assay and quantified with viral load. Baseline CD4, genotype, HBV and HCV serology, syphilis, STI screen and vaccine status. Mx: start antiretroviral therapy at diagnosis regardless of CD4 - integrase inhibitor plus two NRTIs (bictegravir with tenofovir alafenamide and emtricitabine is a standard fixed-dose combination). Target undetectable viral load, which also prevents sexual transmission (U=U). Offer PrEP to HIV-negative people at ongoing risk. Notifiable in every Australian jurisdiction. Note: opportunistic infection prophylaxis follows CD4 - cotrimoxazole under 200 for PCP, azithromycin under 50 for MAC.
rich_summaries.Haemochromatosis: Iron overload, most often hereditary autosomal recessive HFE C282Y homozygous. Pathophysiology: hepcidin deficiency drives excess intestinal iron absorption; iron deposits in liver, pancreas, heart, joints, pituitary and skin. Clinical features: often asymptomatic and picked up on iron studies. When symptomatic - fatigue, arthralgia (second and third MCP joints, hook osteophytes), bronze skin, hepatomegaly with cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus, cardiomyopathy and hypogonadism. Men present earlier; women later because menstruation is protective. Ix: transferrin saturation over 45% or high ferritin triggers HFE genotyping; if C282Y homozygous, confirm with LFT, glucose, ECG, echocardiogram; MRI T2* or biopsy for iron burden if ferritin over 1000 or LFTs abnormal. Mx: therapeutic venesection weekly (450 to 500 mL) until ferritin under 50, then every 3 to 4 months targeting 50 to 100. Avoid iron and vitamin C supplements; limit alcohol; screen for HCC by 6-monthly ultrasound and AFP if cirrhotic. Note: first-degree relatives need genetic and iron-study screening - diagnosis before organ damage is the point.
rich_summaries.Haemolytic disease of fetus and newborn: Maternal IgG alloantibodies cross the placenta and destroy fetal red blood cells expressing the corresponding antigen. Key antibodies are anti-D (RhD, historically the leading cause of severe HDFN), anti-c, anti-K (Kell), anti-E, and ABO (usually mild in type O mothers with type A or B babies). Clinical features: fetal anaemia with hyperdynamic circulation, high-output cardiac failure, hydrops fetalis (skin oedema, ascites, pleural effusion) and intrauterine death. Neonatal features are jaundice within 24 hours, anaemia, hepatosplenomegaly, and kernicterus risk. Ix: antenatal - maternal blood group and antibody screen at booking and 28 weeks; if antibody detected, quantify and titre monthly, monitor MCA peak systolic velocity for anaemia. Neonatal - DAT, FBC, reticulocytes, blood group, bilirubin. Mx: antenatal - refer to maternal-fetal medicine; intrauterine transfusion for severe anaemia. Neonatal - phototherapy, exchange transfusion, IVIG in some cases. Prevention: RhD-negative women get anti-D at 28 and 34 weeks, after any sensitising event, and postpartum if baby is RhD-positive. Note: universal anti-D prophylaxis in Australia has made severe RhD HDFN uncommon.
rich_summaries.Haemolytic uraemic syndrome: Thrombotic microangiopathy - microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury. Types: typical or D+ HUS follows Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (O157:H7) or Shigella, mostly in children after bloody diarrhoea; atypical HUS is complement dysregulation (factor H, factor I, MCP), familial or triggered; secondary causes include malignancy, drugs (calcineurin inhibitors, quinine), pregnancy, and HIV. Clinical features: prodromal bloody diarrhoea in typical HUS, then acute pallor, petechiae, oliguria and hypertension; neurological involvement in atypical. Ix: FBC with schistocytes, LDH high, haptoglobin low, reticulocytosis, coagulation normal (distinguishes from DIC); EUC; stool STEC PCR; ADAMTS13 activity to distinguish from TTP; complement studies for atypical HUS. Mx: supportive in typical HUS - fluid and electrolyte management, dialysis where needed. Avoid platelet transfusions unless bleeding, and avoid antibiotics in STEC (may increase toxin release). Eculizumab for atypical HUS. Note: E. coli O157 is notifiable.
rich_summaries.Haemophilia: X-linked recessive coagulation deficiency. Types: haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency, 80% of cases) and haemophilia B (factor IX deficiency, Christmas disease). Graded as mild (factor 5 to 40%, bleeds with major trauma or surgery), moderate (1 to 5%, bleeds with minor trauma) or severe (under 1%, spontaneous bleeds). Clinical features: haemarthrosis (target joints - knee, elbow, ankle) driving arthropathy; muscle haematoma; intracranial haemorrhage (leading cause of death); mucosal bleeding is less prominent than in platelet or von Willebrand disorders. Ix: prolonged APTT with normal PT, INR, platelets and fibrinogen; correction on mixing studies; specific factor VIII or IX assays confirm diagnosis and grade; vWF to exclude vWD (mimics haemophilia A). Mx: factor concentrate replacement for bleeds and prophylaxis - recombinant factor VIII or IX, or emicizumab for haemophilia A. Desmopressin releases stored factor VIII in mild haemophilia A. Avoid IM injections, NSAIDs and aspirin. Note: inhibitor development complicates management - specialist haemophilia centre.
rich_summaries.Haemorrhoids: Symptomatic enlargement and distal displacement of the normal anal cushions, which are vascular structures contributing to continence rather than varicose veins. Classification: internal haemorrhoids arise above the dentate line and are graded I to IV by prolapse and reducibility; external arise below it and are somatically innervated, which is why they hurt and internal ones usually do not. Clinical features: painless bright rectal bleeding on wiping or coating the stool, pruritus, and a palpable lump. Severe acute pain suggests thrombosis or a fissure instead. Ix: inspection, digital rectal examination and proctoscopy. Investigate the colon in anyone over 45, with iron deficiency, or with a change in bowel habit - attributing bleeding to haemorrhoids without looking is how bowel cancer is missed. Mx: fibre, fluid and avoiding straining are the foundation. Topical preparations give symptom relief only. Rubber band ligation for grades I to III; haemorrhoidectomy for grade IV or failed banding. Note: a thrombosed external haemorrhoid presenting within 72 hours can be excised under local anaesthetic.
rich_summaries.Haemothorax: Blood in the pleural space; usually traumatic but also spontaneous with anticoagulation, malignancy, pulmonary infarction or vascular rupture. Pathophysiology: bleeding source is intercostal or internal mammary artery in most; lung parenchymal bleeding is often self-limiting; great-vessel injury is catastrophic. Clinical features: dyspnoea, pleuritic pain, reduced air entry and dullness to percussion on the affected side; haemodynamic compromise with large volumes; tension develops if air also enters (haemopneumothorax). Ix: eFAST picks up over 100 mL at the bedside; erect CXR shows costophrenic blunting (over 200 mL); CT chest defines volume, source and injuries; cross-match and coagulation. Mx: large-bore (28-32 Fr) intercostal drain; massive haemothorax (over 1500 mL immediately, or over 200 mL/h for 2-4 hours) mandates urgent thoracotomy or VATS; autotransfusion if clean; correct coagulopathy; retained haemothorax over 300 mL at 72 hours needs VATS evacuation to prevent empyema. Note: never clamp the drain of a massive haemothorax to slow output - it worsens tamponade and hides ongoing bleeding.
rich_summaries.Hashimoto thyroiditis: Autoimmune destruction of the thyroid by lymphocytic infiltration with anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies; the commonest cause of primary hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas. Female predominance (7:1); peak age 30 to 50; associated with other autoimmune disease (T1DM, coeliac, vitiligo, pernicious anaemia). Clinical features: insidious fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, menstrual disturbance, depression, cognitive slowing, diffuse rubbery goitre in most; may transiently present with hashitoxicosis; untreated gives myxoedema, pericardial effusion, coma. Rare primary thyroid lymphoma (rapid growth in a Hashimoto goitre warrants biopsy).Ix: TSH raised, free T4 low (or normal in subclinical); anti-TPO antibodies positive in over 90%; anti-thyroglobulin also positive in most; thyroid ultrasound if nodule suspected. Mx: levothyroxine, dosed by weight and titrated to TSH in mid-normal range; recheck TSH at 6 to 8 weeks after any dose change; subclinical hypothyroidism treatment case-by-case (TSH over 10, pregnancy, or symptoms). Note: iron, calcium and PPIs impair thyroxine absorption - separate dosing by 4 hours.
rich_summaries.Heart block: Impaired conduction through the AV node or His-Purkinje system. Classification: first-degree is PR over 200 ms with every P conducted, benign in isolation; Mobitz I (Wenckebach) shows progressive PR ending in a dropped beat, usually AV nodal and benign; Mobitz II shows fixed PR with sudden non-conducted P waves, is infranodal and unstable, and warrants pacing; third-degree has AV dissociation with an escape rhythm whose rate and QRS width predict stability. Causes: idiopathic fibrosis, inferior MI (nodal, often transient), anterior MI (infranodal, ominous), calcific aortic valve disease, cardiac surgery, endocarditis with root abscess, Lyme, sarcoidosis, hyperkalaemia, and drugs (beta blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin, amiodarone). Ix: 12-lead ECG; ambulatory monitoring for intermittent symptoms; EUC, TFT, troponin; echo. Mx: stop offending drug and correct electrolytes. Symptomatic bradycardia gets atropine, then isoprenaline or transcutaneous pacing while a transvenous wire is arranged. Permanent pacemaker for symptomatic AV block, all Mobitz II, and all third-degree outside reversible causes. Note: Austroads driving restrictions apply until pacing is established.
rich_summaries.Heart failure: Clinical syndrome in which cardiac output is inadequate for tissue demand, or is achieved only at raised filling pressures. Classification: HFrEF 40% or below; HFmrEF 41-49%; HFpEF 50% or above. Only HFrEF has therapy that reliably improves mortality. Causes: ischaemic heart disease and hypertension dominate; valvular disease; arrhythmia; alcohol; chemotherapy; cardiomyopathy. Clinical features: exertional dyspnoea and orthopnoea; raised JVP; displaced apex with a third heart sound; bibasal crackles; peripheral oedema. Ix: BNP or NT-proBNP - a normal level essentially excludes it; a normal ECG makes HFrEF unlikely; echocardiography gives the phenotype; UEC, TFT, iron studies. Mx: HFrEF gets the four pillars - ARNI or ACE inhibitor; beta-blocker; mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist; SGLT2 inhibitor - started early at low dose and uptitrated, since each independently reduces mortality. Diuretics relieve congestion without changing survival. In HFpEF, an SGLT2 inhibitor. Note: correct iron deficiency even without anaemia - IV iron improves symptoms and admissions in HFrEF. Red flags: hypotension with cool peripheries and oliguria means cardiogenic shock.
rich_summaries.Henoch-Schönlein purpura: IgA vasculitis, small-vessel, usually following an upper respiratory tract infection in a child under 10. Clinical features: the tetrad of palpable purpura on extensor surfaces and buttocks, arthralgia (usually knee or ankle), colicky abdominal pain, and glomerulonephritis. Purpura and arthralgia come first; renal disease may develop over 6 months and is the long-term prognostic determinant. Ix: FBC, EUC and urate, urinalysis (haematuria, proteinuria) with PCR, LFT, coagulation to exclude thrombocytopenic purpura; abdominal ultrasound if severe pain (intussusception is ileo-ileal in HSP, so barium enema misses it). Renal biopsy if heavy proteinuria or falling function. Mx: supportive, simple analgesia and hydration; most cases resolve within 6 to 8 weeks. Prednisolone for severe abdominal pain, orchitis, or significant nephritis. Immunosuppression (cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate) for crescentic glomerulonephritis. Follow-up: check BP and urinalysis weekly for the first month, then monthly to 6 months. Note: adults with HSP have a worse renal prognosis than children and need specialist follow-up.
rich_summaries.Hepatic encephalopathy: Neuropsychiatric syndrome complicating acute or chronic liver failure; accumulated ammonia and other gut-derived toxins cross the BBB and disturb astrocyte function. Stages: I (subtle cognitive change, altered sleep-wake), II (lethargy, disorientation, asterixis), III (marked confusion, somnolent but rousable), IV (coma). Triggers include GI bleed, infection (SBP), constipation, high protein load, sedatives, diuretics with electrolyte disturbance, dehydration, TIPS, and acute liver injury superimposed on chronic. Clinical features: confusion, sleep reversal, asterixis, constructional apraxia, hyperreflexia, fetor hepaticus. Ix: clinical diagnosis. FBC, EUC, glucose, LFT, CRP, ascitic tap for SBP; exclude other causes of altered consciousness (glucose, ABG, CT head); serum ammonia correlates poorly and is not required. Mx: identify and treat triggers - the acute cause is usually reversible. Lactulose titrated to 2 to 3 soft stools per day; rifaximin 550 mg BD for prevention and recurrence. Nutrition - avoid protein restriction. Liver transplant assessment in recurrent or refractory cases. Note: recurrent HE is a transplant indication.
rich_summaries.Hepatitis A: Picornavirus infection of the liver, faecal-orally transmitted through contaminated food (shellfish, raw produce) and water, or by close contact. Commonest viral hepatitis worldwide; endemic in developing countries. Australia sees imported cases and outbreaks in men who have sex with men and injecting drug users. Incubation 15 to 50 days. Clinical features: prodrome of fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, right upper quadrant pain and dark urine; then icteric phase with jaundice, hepatomegaly, pale stools. Children under 6 are often anicteric. Illness lasts a few weeks and is self-limiting; no chronic carrier state. Fulminant hepatic failure is rare (under 0.5%) but higher in older adults. Ix: LFT with ALT typically over 1000 U/L; anti-HAV IgM diagnostic of acute infection, anti-HAV IgG past infection or vaccination. Mx: supportive - rest, hydration, avoid hepatotoxins including alcohol and paracetamol. Notifiable. Prevention: hepatitis A vaccine on the NIP for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children in NT, Qld, SA and WA, plus travellers and high-risk groups. Post-exposure - vaccine within 2 weeks. Note: no chronic disease and no HCC risk - unlike hepatitis B and C.
rich_summaries.Hepatitis B: Partially double-stranded DNA hepadnavirus, transmitted by blood, sex and perinatal exposure. Clinical features: acute infection is asymptomatic in most; 5 to 10% of adults and up to 90% of perinatally infected infants develop chronic infection (HBsAg persisting over 6 months). Chronic disease progresses through immune tolerant, immune active, inactive carrier and reactivation phases; cirrhosis and HCC are the long-term risks. Ix: serology - HBsAg (active), anti-HBs (immunity), anti-HBc IgM (recent) or IgG (past or chronic), HBeAg and anti-HBe (activity), and HBV DNA. LFT, coexisting HIV, HCV and hepatitis D testing; FibroScan for staging. Mx: acute is supportive. Chronic active disease gets tenofovir alafenamide or entecavir, triggered by ALT, HBV DNA, fibrosis or extrahepatic disease. Notifiable. Prevention: universal infant vaccination on the NIP and birth-dose in high-risk settings. Note: HCC surveillance with 6-monthly ultrasound and AFP for cirrhotics, Asian men over 40, African adults, and family history of HCC.
rich_summaries.Hepatitis C: Blood-borne RNA flavivirus; a leading cause of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma in Australia. Transmission is by shared injecting equipment (over 80% of new infections), unsafe medical procedures, tattoos and piercing with unsterile equipment, needlestick, and rarely sexual or perinatal exposure. Clinical features: acute infection is usually asymptomatic. Around 75% of adults develop chronic infection, which is silent until decompensation - fatigue, arthralgia, then cirrhosis. Ix: anti-HCV screen (positive for life whether or not viraemic), confirmed by HCV RNA. Baseline LFT, HIV, HBV, coagulation, and non-invasive fibrosis assessment (FibroScan or APRI). Mx: direct-acting antiviral therapy for 8 to 12 weeks achieves SVR in over 95% - sofosbuvir with velpatasvir, or glecaprevir with pibrentasvir, are pan-genotypic and PBS-listed. Any GP can prescribe. Treat every diagnosed patient, including those still injecting. HCC surveillance with 6-monthly ultrasound and AFP for cirrhotics continues after cure. Note: cure does not confer immunity - reinfection is possible if exposure risk continues.
rich_summaries.Hepatocellular carcinoma: Primary liver cancer from hepatocytes; commonest primary liver malignancy. Almost always arises on a background of cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis. Risk factors include chronic hepatitis B (integrates into host DNA, can cause HCC without cirrhosis), hepatitis C, alcohol, MAFLD (fastest-growing in Australia), haemochromatosis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, and aflatoxin B1. Male predominance. Clinical features: often asymptomatic and found on surveillance; decompensated liver disease, RUQ pain, weight loss, palpable mass, hepatic bruit, paraneoplastic erythrocytosis or hypercalcaemia. Ix: raised AFP; four-phase contrast CT or MRI liver shows arterial hyperenhancement with venous or delayed washout (LI-RADS diagnostic, biopsy often not needed); FBC, LFT, hepatitis serology; staging CT chest. Mx: BCLC staging guides. Curative - resection for solitary lesion with preserved function, RFA for small lesions, liver transplant within Milan criteria. Locoregional - TACE, SBRT. Systemic - atezolizumab plus bevacizumab first line for advanced disease. Note: 6-monthly ultrasound plus AFP surveillance for all cirrhotic patients.
rich_summaries.Hepatorenal syndrome: Functional renal failure in advanced cirrhosis, driven by splanchnic vasodilation and reflex renal vasoconstriction with intact kidney histology. Types: HRS-AKI (was type 1) is rapid - creatinine at least doubling to over 226 micromol/L in under 2 weeks, often triggered by spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, GI bleed, large-volume paracentesis without albumin, or infection; HRS-NAKI (was type 2) is slower on the background of refractory ascites. Diagnosis is one of exclusion. Clinical features: oliguria, rising creatinine, refractory ascites, low urine sodium (under 10 mmol/L), and bland urinary sediment; no response to volume challenge. Ix: EUC daily, urinalysis and microscopy (bland), urine sodium; septic screen including diagnostic paracentesis; renal ultrasound to exclude obstruction. Mx: withdraw diuretics and nephrotoxins; albumin 1 g/kg on day 1 then 20 to 40 g daily; add terlipressin (or noradrenaline in ICU) targeting a rise in MAP of at least 10 mmHg. Treat precipitant. Liver transplantation is the only definitive therapy. Note: primary prophylaxis of SBP with norfloxacin in high-risk cirrhotics prevents HRS.
rich_summaries.Hereditary spherocytosis: Inherited membrane-cytoskeleton defect producing spherical, less deformable red cells that are trapped and destroyed in the spleen; the commonest inherited haemolytic anaemia in Northern Europeans. Genetics: autosomal dominant in about 75% (ankyrin, band 3, or spectrin) or autosomal recessive (protein 4.2). Clinical features: chronic haemolytic anaemia with jaundice, splenomegaly and pigment gallstones. Severity varies from asymptomatic to transfusion-dependent. Aplastic crisis with parvovirus B19; haemolytic crisis with infection. Ix: FBC with raised MCHC and spherocytes on film, reticulocytes raised, unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, raised LDH, low haptoglobin, direct antiglobulin test negative. Confirmatory eosin-5-maleimide binding test or osmotic fragility. Family screening. Mx: folate; transfusion for severe anaemia. Splenectomy for symptomatic moderate to severe disease (after age 6) - curative for anaemia but not haemolysis, with lifelong sepsis risk. Pre-splenectomy vaccination for encapsulated organisms and lifelong daily penicillin V. Note: cholecystectomy at splenectomy if gallstones concurrent.
rich_summaries.Herpes zoster: Reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus in a sensory ganglion, causing dermatomal pain and rash. Risk factors: increasing age, immunosuppression (HIV, transplantation, biologics, malignancy) and stress. Clinical features: prodromal dermatomal pain, dysaesthesia or itch for 2 to 3 days, then a unilateral vesicular rash respecting the midline in a single dermatome (thoracic in about half). Ophthalmic involvement (Hutchinson sign - tip of nose) risks sight-threatening keratitis. Ramsay Hunt syndrome is facial nerve involvement with ear vesicles, facial palsy and hearing loss. Ix: clinical in typical disease; VZV PCR from a vesicle swab if atypical or immunocompromised. Mx: oral valaciclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days, or famciclovir or aciclovir; start within 72 hours of rash onset to reduce postherpetic neuralgia. Analgesia - paracetamol plus NSAID; gabapentin, pregabalin, amitriptyline or nortriptyline for neuropathic pain. Refer ophthalmology urgently for zoster ophthalmicus. Note: Shingrix recombinant zoster vaccine is on the Australian NIP for adults 65 and over and for immunocompromised adults from 18.
rich_summaries.Hiatal hernia: Herniation of stomach through the diaphragmatic hiatus into the chest. Types: sliding (type I, over 95% - GE junction and cardia herniate up axially, often asymptomatic or causes GORD); paraoesophageal (types II to IV - fundus herniates alongside a normal junction, risk of incarceration, obstruction, volvulus, strangulation). Risk factors: age, obesity, pregnancy, chronic cough or straining, prior gastric or oesophageal surgery. Clinical features: sliding - often asymptomatic, heartburn, regurgitation, dysphagia, iron-deficiency anaemia from Cameron ulcers in the sac. Paraoesophageal - postprandial fullness, chest pain, dysphagia, respiratory symptoms; Borchardt triad in gastric volvulus (chest pain, retching without vomiting, inability to pass NG tube - surgical emergency). Ix: barium swallow for anatomy; endoscopy for mucosal assessment; CT for complications. Mx: sliding - lifestyle (weight loss, small meals, elevate head of bed), PPI for reflux, Nissen fundoplication if refractory. Paraoesophageal - elective repair for symptomatic; urgent for volvulus, obstruction, or strangulation. Note: asymptomatic paraoesophageal in the elderly can often be observed.
rich_summaries.Hirschsprung disease: Congenital absence of ganglion cells in the Auerbach and Meissner plexus of the distal colon, giving functional obstruction with tonically contracted aganglionic segment and proximal dilatation. Rectosigmoid disease predominates (75%). Associations: Down syndrome, MEN2A, NF1, Waardenburg. Boys affected 4 to 1. Clinical features: failure to pass meconium within 48 hours of birth, abdominal distension, bilious vomiting in the neonate; chronic constipation, failure to thrive, and abdominal distension in older children. Digital rectal examination shows a tight anal canal and empty rectum with explosive release of gas and stool. Ix: contrast enema shows transition zone between narrow aganglionic segment and dilated proximal bowel; anorectal manometry shows absent recto-anal inhibitory reflex; rectal suction biopsy is diagnostic (absence of ganglion cells with hypertrophied nerve fibres). Mx: surgical resection of the aganglionic segment with pull-through of ganglionic bowel to the anus (Swenson, Duhamel or Soave). Temporary colostomy in the sick neonate or severe enterocolitis. Note: Hirschsprung enterocolitis (fever, distension, foul-smelling diarrhoea) is the leading cause of death.
rich_summaries.Hodgkin lymphoma: B-cell lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells in a reactive inflammatory background. Epidemiology: bimodal, peaking in the 20s and again after 60; associated with Epstein-Barr virus. Clinical features: painless, rubbery cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy spreading contiguously between nodal groups; mediastinal mass; B symptoms - fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss over 10% in 6 months. Alcohol-induced nodal pain and pruritus are uncommon but characteristic. Ix: excisional node biopsy, not fine-needle aspiration, since architecture is needed; PET-CT for staging; FBC, ESR, LDH, LFT, HIV and hepatitis serology. Mx: ABVD chemotherapy with or without radiotherapy, guided by stage and interim PET response. Cure rates are high, above 80% overall. Note: contiguous spread and a young peak distinguish it clinically from non-Hodgkin lymphoma, which skips nodal groups and is more often extranodal. Complications: long-term survivorship risks matter as much as the disease - secondary malignancy, cardiotoxicity from anthracyclines, bleomycin lung toxicity, and infertility, so counsel on fertility preservation before treatment.
rich_summaries.Horner syndrome: Interruption of the oculosympathetic pathway, producing ipsilateral partial ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis. Causes: first-order, hypothalamus to C8-T2 - lateral medullary infarct, MS, syringomyelia, cord tumour; second-order preganglionic - Pancoast tumour, cervical rib, neck surgery, neuroblastoma in children; third-order postganglionic - carotid dissection, cavernous sinus lesion, cluster headache. Clinical features: partial ptosis from denervation of the superior tarsal muscle, not the complete ptosis of a third nerve palsy; miosis with dilation lag and anisocoria greater in dim light; pupillary light response preserved; iris heterochromia if congenital. Ix: apraclonidine is the test of choice, reversing anisocoria through denervation supersensitivity; hydroxyamphetamine separates third-order from more proximal lesions; imaging follows the level suspected - CT or MR angiography of the neck, CT chest for an apical lesion. Note: anhidrosis localises - hemibody in first-order, face in second-order, absent in third-order. Red flags: painful Horner syndrome is carotid dissection until excluded; new Horner syndrome in a child needs urinary catecholamines for neuroblastoma.
rich_summaries.Hungry bone syndrome: Severe, prolonged hypocalcaemia after parathyroidectomy (or thyroidectomy, hyperthyroidism treatment, or transplant for renal osteodystrophy) as demineralised bone rapidly reincorporates calcium, phosphate and magnesium. Highest risk in longstanding severe hyperparathyroidism with high pre-op PTH, ALP and radiological bone disease (osteitis fibrosa cystica). Clinical features: hypocalcaemia onset within days of surgery and lasting over 4 days; perioral and peripheral paraesthesia, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, carpopedal spasm, laryngospasm, seizures, prolonged QT. Distinguishes from post-op hypoparathyroidism by concomitant hypophosphataemia and hypomagnesaemia (post-op hypoparathyroidism gives high phosphate) and by PTH that is normal or high rather than suppressed. Ix: corrected calcium, phosphate, magnesium, PTH, ALP; ECG for QT. Mx: aggressive IV calcium gluconate for symptomatic or severe hypocalcaemia, then high-dose oral calcium carbonate and calcitriol; replace magnesium; monitor daily until stable. May last weeks. Note: pre-operative bisphosphonate or high-dose vitamin D loading reduces severity.
rich_summaries.Huntington disease: Autosomal dominant neurodegeneration from a CAG trinucleotide expansion in HTT on chromosome 4, with striatal medium spiny neurons lost first. Genetics: 40 or more repeats is fully penetrant; 36 to 39 is reduced penetrance. Anticipation occurs, and is more marked with paternal transmission because expansion happens in spermatogenesis. Clinical features: the triad is movement disorder, cognitive decline and psychiatric illness, and the psychiatric features often come first. Chorea early, giving way to bradykinesia, dystonia and rigidity later. Depression and a substantially raised suicide risk throughout. Ix: genetic testing, which in an asymptomatic person must follow formal predictive testing protocols with counselling before and after. MRI shows caudate atrophy. Mx: no disease-modifying therapy. Treat chorea if it is disabling, treat depression and psychosis actively, and involve a multidisciplinary team early for speech, swallow, nutrition and advance care planning. Note: the psychiatric burden is what most affects quality of life, and it is treatable even though the disease is not.
rich_summaries.Hydrocephalus: Abnormal accumulation of CSF in the cerebral ventricles. Communicating hydrocephalus is impaired CSF reabsorption at the arachnoid granulations (post-meningitis, post-SAH, post-traumatic). Non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus is CSF flow blocked within the ventricular system (aqueduct stenosis, tumour, colloid cyst, Chiari, Dandy-Walker). Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a specific communicating form with the triad of dementia, gait apraxia (magnetic gait), and urinary incontinence - wet, wacky and wobbly. Clinical features: raised ICP with headache worse lying and on waking, morning vomiting, papilloedema, sixth nerve palsy, altered consciousness; infants show head circumference crossing percentiles, bulging fontanelle, sunset eyes, delayed milestones. Ix: CT or MRI brain shows dilated ventricles with or without transependymal CSF flow; identify obstructing lesion. LP with opening pressure - therapeutic tap trial helps select NPH candidates for shunting. Mx: treat the cause where possible. Ventriculoperitoneal shunt is the mainstay; endoscopic third ventriculostomy for aqueduct stenosis. Note: shunt complications drive readmission.
rich_summaries.Hypercalcaemia: Raised serum calcium. Primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy account for about 90% of cases between them - the first dominates in outpatients, the second in inpatients. Mechanism: in malignancy, PTH-related peptide in about 80% - squamous cell, renal and breast; osteolytic metastases in myeloma; rarely tumour calcitriol in lymphoma. Clinical features: the classic bones, stones, groans and psychic moans - polyuria and thirst, nausea, constipation, confusion, weakness. Onset is often rapid, so symptoms appear at lower levels than in primary hyperparathyroidism. Ix: corrected calcium or ionised calcium; PTH is suppressed in malignancy and raised or inappropriately normal in primary hyperparathyroidism; UEC, phosphate. Mx: aggressive intravenous normal saline first - these patients are profoundly volume-deplete from calcium-induced polyuria. Then a bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid), which takes 2-4 days to work, or denosumab in renal impairment. Calcitonin for rapid but transient control. Note: avoid loop diuretics until volume-replete - they were traditionally taught but worsen dehydration and are now reserved for fluid overload.
rich_summaries.Hypereosinophilic syndrome: Sustained peripheral eosinophilia above 1.5 x 10^9/L for over a month with attributable end-organ damage. Classification: primary myeloproliferative (FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion, imatinib-sensitive); lymphocytic variant (clonal T cells driving IL-5); idiopathic; overlap with eosinophilic GPA. Pathophysiology: eosinophils infiltrate tissues and degranulate; endomyocardial fibrosis (Loeffler endocarditis) with mural thrombus and later restrictive cardiomyopathy is the classic and most feared hit; skin, lungs, gut and nerves also affected. Clinical features: cardiac symptoms, rash, wheeze, peripheral neuropathy, hepatosplenomegaly, weight loss. Ix: FBC and film; troponin, ECG, TTE and cardiac MRI to detect myocardial involvement early; exclude secondary causes (strongyloides serology, atopy, drugs, lymphoma, solid tumours) before labelling primary; FIP1L1-PDGFRA screen and T-cell clonality. Mx: FIP1L1-PDGFRA positive - imatinib at low dose (dramatic response); otherwise prednisolone plus a steroid-sparer (hydroxycarbamide, interferon-alpha, mepolizumab); anticoagulate mural thrombus. Note: check strongyloides serology before steroids - masked hyperinfection can be fatal.
rich_summaries.Hyperkalaemia: Potassium above 5.5 mmol/L; life-threatening arrhythmia risk above 6.5. Causes: reduced renal excretion (AKI, CKD, Addison disease, type 4 RTA, ACE inhibitors and ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics, trimethoprim); redistribution from cells (acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, haemolysis, tissue necrosis, insulin deficiency, suxamethonium); and pseudohyperkalaemia (haemolysed sample, tourniquet). Clinical features: often asymptomatic until ECG changes - peaked T waves, PR prolongation, widened QRS, sine wave, then asystole or VF. Ix: repeat sample from free-flowing vein without tourniquet; ECG; EUC, VBG, glucose, digoxin level if relevant. Mx: any ECG change or K over 6.5 gets 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV over 2 minutes to stabilise the myocardium (repeat at 5 minutes if ECG unchanged). Shift K into cells with 10 units short-acting insulin in 50 mL of 50% dextrose IV, plus salbutamol nebuliser. Remove K with sodium zirconium cyclosilicate or patiromer; furosemide if euvolaemic; dialysis for refractory disease. Note: stop all K-retaining drugs and treat the acidosis.
rich_summaries.Hyperlipidaemia: Abnormal blood lipid levels - elevated LDL cholesterol, elevated triglycerides, or reduced HDL - driving atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Primary causes include familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH from LDL receptor mutations), familial combined hyperlipidaemia, and familial hypertriglyceridaemia. Secondary causes include diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis, alcohol, obesity, corticosteroids, thiazides and atypical antipsychotics. Clinical features: usually asymptomatic and detected on lipid screening. FH may show tendon xanthomas, xanthelasma or corneal arcus before age 45. Severe hypertriglyceridaemia (over 10 mmol/L) causes pancreatitis. Ix: fasting lipid profile; TFT, glucose, HbA1c, LFT, EUC. Screen family members if FH suspected. Calculate Australian CVD risk. Mx: lifestyle first - Mediterranean-style diet, weight loss, activity, reduced alcohol. Statin dosed by absolute risk and LDL target; ezetimibe if target not reached; PCSK9 inhibitor for FH or high-risk secondary prevention (PBS-restricted). Fibrates for triglycerides over 10 mmol/L. Note: any adult with LDL over 5 mmol/L or first-degree relative with premature CVD warrants FH screening.
rich_summaries.Hypernatraemia: Serum sodium over 145 mmol/L. Always reflects a water deficit (or rarely, sodium excess). Types: hypovolaemic (renal losses - osmotic diuresis, diuretics; extra-renal - diarrhoea, sweating, burns); euvolaemic (diabetes insipidus - central or nephrogenic; hypodipsia in the frail elderly); hypervolaemic (rare - hypertonic saline, sodium bicarbonate, mineralocorticoid excess). Elderly and infants are highest risk. Clinical features: thirst if intact; lethargy, irritability, muscle weakness, hyperreflexia, seizures and coma; skin turgor and mucosal dryness in hypovolaemia; signs of the underlying cause. Ix: paired serum and urine osmolality; urine sodium; EUC; consider water deprivation test if DI suspected. Mx: correct water deficit slowly to avoid cerebral oedema - reduce sodium no faster than 10 mmol/L per 24 hours (12 if very acute). Oral or NG water first line; 5% dextrose IV if unable. Treat cause - desmopressin for central DI, thiazide plus low-solute diet for nephrogenic. Note: overly rapid correction risks fatal cerebral oedema, especially in chronic hypernatraemia.
rich_summaries.Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state: Severe hyperglycaemia with marked hyperosmolality and profound volume depletion, without significant ketosis - residual insulin is enough to suppress ketogenesis but not gluconeogenesis. Epidemiology: type 2 diabetes, usually older, often precipitated by infection, myocardial infarction or missed medication. Clinical features: days to weeks of polyuria and thirst, then confusion progressing to coma. Focal neurological signs and seizures occur and reverse with treatment. Ix: BGL usually above 30 mmol/L, effective osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg, pH above 7.3 with bicarbonate above 15, minimal ketones. Look for the precipitant. Mx: fluid is the treatment - sodium chloride 0.9%, replacing the deficit over 24-48 hours. Insulin at a lower rate than in DKA, and only once fluids are running. Replace potassium. Thromboprophylaxis, since the thrombotic risk is high. Note: lowering osmolality too fast risks cerebral oedema, so aim for a fall of no more than 3-8 mOsm/kg per hour.
rich_summaries.Hyperparathyroidism: Excess parathyroid hormone secretion. Types: primary is autonomous PTH secretion, most often from a single adenoma (85%), then hyperplasia (10%, sometimes MEN1 or MEN2A) or carcinoma (under 1%); secondary is compensatory PTH rise for chronic hypocalcaemia or vitamin D deficiency, typically in CKD; tertiary is autonomous hyperplasia after long-standing secondary disease. Clinical features: most primary disease is asymptomatic hypercalcaemia on routine bloods - stones, bones, groans, moans (renal calculi, osteoporosis, constipation and pancreatitis, depression and cognitive slowing). Ix: paired calcium and PTH - inappropriately normal or high PTH with hypercalcaemia in primary; 24-hour urinary calcium to exclude familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia; vitamin D, phosphate, EUC, DXA, renal ultrasound. Sestamibi scan and neck ultrasound localise the adenoma. Mx: parathyroidectomy for symptomatic disease, calcium over 2.85, eGFR under 60, urinary calcium over 10 mmol/day, T-score at or below -2.5, age under 50, or fracture. Cinacalcet for those unfit for surgery. Note: post-parathyroidectomy hungry-bone syndrome causes profound hypocalcaemia; monitor for 48 hours.
rich_summaries.Hyperprolactinaemia: Elevated serum prolactin. Causes include physiological states (pregnancy, lactation, stress, sleep, exercise), prolactinoma, stalk effect from any non-secreting pituitary or parasellar lesion, drugs (dopamine antagonists such as antipsychotics and metoclopramide, opioids, oestrogen), primary hypothyroidism, and chronic kidney disease or cirrhosis (reduced clearance). Macroprolactin is a biologically inactive high-molecular-weight complex that reads as high prolactin on assay without clinical effect. Clinical features: in women, amenorrhoea, oligomenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and infertility; in men, reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, gynaecomastia and infertility; both develop reduced bone mineral density from secondary hypogonadism. Ix: repeat prolactin to confirm; beta-hCG, TFT, EUC, LFT; macroprolactin screen (PEG precipitation) if borderline; pituitary MRI if not physiological or drug-induced. Mx: treat the cause. Withdraw offending drug where possible (psychiatry input for antipsychotic switch to aripiprazole). Treat hypothyroidism. Prolactinoma gets dopamine agonist (cabergoline). Note: markedly elevated prolactin with a small adenoma suggests hook effect - dilute the sample.
rich_summaries.Hypertension: Persistently raised arterial pressure - in Australia, clinic readings of 140/90 mmHg or above on repeated occasions. Causes: primary in about 90%; renal parenchymal and renovascular disease; primary aldosteronism; phaeochromocytoma; Cushing syndrome; coarctation; obstructive sleep apnoea; NSAIDs and the COCP. Almost always asymptomatic - detection is by measurement. Ix: confirm with ambulatory or home monitoring. Assess end-organ damage - UEC, urine ACR, fundoscopy, ECG - and calculate absolute cardiovascular risk, since Australian thresholds follow that risk rather than the pressure alone. Mx: lifestyle for all. First-line agents are an ACE inhibitor or ARB, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, or a thiazide-like diuretic; low-dose combination beats maximising one agent. Note: investigate for a secondary cause when hypertension resists three agents, presents before 30, or comes with hypokalaemia. Primary aldosteronism is commoner than traditionally taught and is potentially curable. Red flags: BP above 180/110 with end-organ damage is a hypertensive emergency needing controlled intravenous reduction - dropping it too fast causes watershed infarction.
rich_summaries.Hypertensive emergency: Severe hypertension (usually above 180/120) with acute end-organ damage - hypertensive encephalopathy, ICH or SAH, acute stroke, aortic dissection, ACS, flash pulmonary oedema, AKI, retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema, and microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia. Distinguished from hypertensive urgency (severe BP without end-organ damage), which is managed with oral therapy over hours to days. Ix: 12-lead ECG, troponin, FBC and film (schistocytes), EUC and urate, LDH and haptoglobin, urinalysis, CXR, and targeted imaging - CT head for neurological signs, CT aorta for tearing chest pain, echocardiogram for cardiac features. Mx: admit to a monitored bed. Reduce MAP by no more than 20 to 25% in the first hour, then toward 160/100 over the next 2 to 6 hours. Agent by target organ - IV glyceryl trinitrate for LV failure or ACS, IV labetalol or esmolol plus GTN for dissection (target SBP under 120 quickly), IV hydralazine or labetalol in pregnancy, IV nicardipine in stroke. Note: dissection needs beta blockade before any vasodilator to prevent reflex tachycardia.
rich_summaries.Hypertensive nephropathy: Chronic kidney disease from sustained hypertension driving arteriolosclerosis and ischaemic nephron loss; second-commonest cause of ESKD in Australia after diabetes. Pathophysiology: benign nephrosclerosis (hyaline arteriolosclerosis, glomerulosclerosis, tubulointerstitial fibrosis) from long-standing moderate BP; malignant nephrosclerosis (fibrinoid necrosis, onion-skin hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis) from accelerated hypertension. Clinical features: usually asymptomatic until advanced CKD; long-standing hypertension, LVH, retinopathy; slowly progressive proteinuria (typically under 1 g/day, distinguishing from primary glomerular disease) and rising creatinine. Ix: urine ACR, eGFR trend, renal ultrasound (small, echogenic, symmetrical kidneys); exclude alternative causes (myeloma screen, autoimmune serology, renal artery Doppler if asymmetry). Mx: BP target under 130/80 (KDIGO); ACE inhibitor or ARB first-line even without proteinuria for renoprotection; SGLT2 inhibitor if eGFR above 20 and ACR above 20 mg/mmol; salt below 5 g/day; cardiovascular risk reduction. Note: proteinuria over 1 g/day should prompt reconsideration - consider biopsy for coexisting glomerulopathy.
rich_summaries.Hyperthyroidism: Excess thyroid hormone, most often from Graves disease. Causes: Graves disease (TSH receptor antibodies), toxic multinodular goitre, toxic adenoma, thyroiditis with a transient release phase, amiodarone, and excess levothyroxine. Clinical features: weight loss with preserved appetite; heat intolerance and sweating; tremor and anxiety; palpitations or AF; diarrhoea; goitre. Graves adds orbitopathy and pretibial myxoedema, which no other cause produces. Ix: suppressed TSH with raised free T4 or T3; TSH receptor antibodies for Graves; uptake scan separates Graves and toxic nodules (high) from thyroiditis (low) - which decides whether antithyroid drugs help at all. Mx: carbimazole, or propylthiouracil in the first trimester of pregnancy; beta-blocker for symptom control; then radioiodine or surgery for definitive treatment. Note: warn every patient starting carbimazole to stop and seek an urgent FBC with fever or sore throat - agranulocytosis is rare but can be fatal. Red flags: thyroid storm - fever, agitation, tachyarrhythmia and heart failure - has high mortality and needs ICU.
rich_summaries.Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: Autosomal dominant sarcomere protein disorder (MYH7, MYBPC3 commonest) causing LV hypertrophy without an identifiable secondary cause. Asymmetric septal hypertrophy predominates; LV outflow tract obstruction from systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve occurs in about 70%, worsened by Valsalva, standing and dehydration. Clinical features: often asymptomatic and found on family screening; exertional dyspnoea, chest pain, palpitations, syncope, and sudden cardiac death (often the first presentation, particularly in young athletes). Ix: 12-lead ECG (LVH with strain, deep narrow Q waves, T inversion); transthoracic echocardiogram is diagnostic (wall thickness at least 15 mm, or 13 mm with family history); cardiac MRI quantifies fibrosis; ambulatory monitoring for non-sustained VT; genetic testing. Mx: avoid vasodilators, digoxin, and pure inotropes. Beta blocker or verapamil for symptomatic obstruction. Disopyramide or mavacamten for refractory obstruction. Septal reduction (surgical myectomy or alcohol septal ablation) for drug-refractory LVOT obstruction. ICD for high-risk primary or secondary prevention. Note: cascade family screening from age 10.
rich_summaries.Hypocalcaemia: Corrected serum calcium under 2.1 mmol/L. Causes: hypoparathyroidism (post-thyroidectomy commonest, autoimmune, DiGeorge); vitamin D deficiency; chronic kidney disease; hypomagnesaemia; acute pancreatitis; citrate toxicity in massive transfusion; osteoblastic metastases; drugs (bisphosphonates, denosumab, cinacalcet). Clinical features: neuromuscular includes perioral and digital paraesthesia, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm, laryngospasm, tetany and seizures; Chvostek sign (facial twitch on tapping the facial nerve) and Trousseau sign (carpal spasm within 3 minutes of BP cuff inflated above systolic). Cardiac features include prolonged QT, torsades and heart failure. Ix: corrected calcium, magnesium, phosphate, EUC, PTH, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, ALP; 12-lead ECG. Mx: symptomatic or severe (calcium under 1.9 or QT prolongation) gets 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV over 10 minutes with cardiac monitoring, then infusion. Correct magnesium first if low. Chronic disease needs oral calcium and calcitriol and cause treatment. Note: hungry-bone syndrome after parathyroidectomy is prolonged.
rich_summaries.Hypoglycaemia: Blood glucose under 3.9 mmol/L with Whipple triad - low glucose, consistent symptoms, and resolution with correction. Causes: in diabetes, insulin or sulfonylurea excess relative to intake or activity, or renal failure prolonging drug half-life; without diabetes, alcohol, sepsis, adrenal or pituitary insufficiency, severe liver disease, or insulinoma. Clinical features: autonomic warning (sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger) then neuroglycopenia (confusion, slurred speech, focal deficit, seizure, coma). Hypoglycaemia unawareness develops with recurrent lows and is a major driver of severe episodes. Mx: conscious and able to swallow - 15g fast-acting oral carbohydrate (jelly beans or juice), retest in 15 minutes, repeat if still low, then a longer-acting snack. Impaired consciousness or unable to swallow - IV 10% dextrose 100 mL, or IM glucagon 1 mg if no IV access; recheck at 10 minutes. Investigate a first episode without diabetes with a 72-hour fast measuring paired glucose, insulin, C-peptide and beta-hydroxybutyrate. Note: sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia recurs for many hours, so these patients need admission and an octreotide infusion, not a single dextrose bolus and discharge.
rich_summaries.Hypogonadism: Deficiency of sex steroids. In men, primary (hypergonadotrophic - raised LH and FSH, low testosterone) results from Klinefelter, mumps orchitis, chemotherapy or radiation, undescended testis, or trauma; secondary (hypogonadotrophic - low or inappropriately normal LH and FSH) from hypothalamic-pituitary disease, Kallmann syndrome, opioid or anabolic steroid use, obesity, and functional causes. Female hypogonadism follows the same axis logic. Clinical features: reduced libido, erectile dysfunction and infertility in men; oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea, hot flushes and infertility in women; reduced energy, mood change, muscle mass loss and osteoporosis in both. Ix: morning testosterone (twice on separate days to confirm) with LH and FSH; SHBG and calculated free testosterone if borderline; prolactin, TFT, iron studies (haemochromatosis); pituitary MRI if secondary picture. Semen analysis and DXA. Mx: treat the underlying cause. Testosterone replacement in primary and confirmed secondary hypogonadism, avoiding if fertility desired or prostate cancer present. Oestrogen or MHT for female hypogonadism. Note: opioid- and obesity-related hypogonadism is often reversible.
rich_summaries.Hypokalaemia: Serum potassium below 3.5 mmol/L; below 2.5 mmol/L is life-threatening. Causes: renal loss through diuretics, hyperaldosteronism, Cushing syndrome or renal tubular acidosis; gastrointestinal loss through vomiting or diarrhoea; shift into cells with insulin, beta-2 agonists or alkalosis. Sx: weakness, cramps, ileus, polyuria and palpitations, with rhabdomyolysis when severe. Ix: ECG shows T-wave flattening, U waves, ST depression and a long QU interval; check magnesium, bicarbonate and urinary potassium. Mx: oral potassium chloride if mild; intravenous potassium chloride for severe or symptomatic hypokalaemia, no faster than 10 mmol/hour peripherally and faster only with central access and cardiac monitoring; replace magnesium alongside. Note: potassium will not correct while magnesium is low, because magnesium depletion disinhibits the ROMK channel and drives renal potassium wasting.
rich_summaries.Hypomagnesaemia: Serum magnesium under 0.7 mmol/L. Causes: GI loss (chronic diarrhoea, malabsorption, PPI long-term use), renal loss (loop and thiazide diuretics, Gitelman and Bartter syndromes), poor intake (alcoholism, malnutrition, prolonged parenteral nutrition), redistribution (refeeding, hungry bone, insulin), and drugs (aminoglycosides, amphotericin, cisplatin, foscarnet, calcineurin inhibitors, cetuximab). Clinical features: neuromuscular - tremor, tetany, carpopedal spasm, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, seizures; cardiac - prolonged QT, torsades, ventricular arrhythmias; refractory hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia (magnesium is a cofactor for correcting both). Ix: serum magnesium (over 99% intracellular so serum underestimates deficit); urinary magnesium or fractional excretion; calcium, potassium, phosphate, EUC; ECG. Mx: severe or symptomatic - IV magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 20 minutes, then 40 mmol over 12 hours. Chronic or mild - oral magnesium (glycinate or aspartate better tolerated than oxide). Correct coexisting hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia simultaneously. Note: hypomagnesaemia is the commonest missed cause of refractory hypokalaemia and torsades.
rich_summaries.Hyponatraemia: Serum sodium under 135 mmol/L; the commonest electrolyte disturbance. Assess volume status and serum osmolality first. Causes: hypovolaemic (GI losses, diuretics, Addison disease - urine Na under 20 in extrarenal, over 20 in renal loss); euvolaemic (SIADH, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, primary polydipsia, beer potomania); hypervolaemic (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, CKD). Pseudohyponatraemia in hyperlipidaemia and paraproteinaemia; hyperglycaemia adds a translocational component (correct 2.4 mmol/L per 10 mmol/L glucose above 5.5). Ix: paired serum and urine sodium and osmolality, TFT, morning cortisol, medication review. Mx: severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure, coma) gets 3% saline 150 mL over 10 minutes, repeat to raise sodium 4 to 6 mmol/L, then slow. Otherwise correct the cause - fluid restriction for SIADH, isotonic saline for hypovolaemia. Do not correct faster than 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours (risk of osmotic demyelination). Note: chronic hyponatraemia in the elderly is often iatrogenic - review diuretics and SSRIs first.
rich_summaries.Hypoparathyroidism: Insufficient PTH secretion causing hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia; commonest cause in Australia is post-surgical (thyroidectomy or parathyroidectomy). Causes: post-surgical, autoimmune (isolated or APS-1), congenital (DiGeorge), infiltration (iron overload, Wilson), magnesium depletion (impairs PTH release). Clinical features: perioral and acral paraesthesiae, carpopedal spasm, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, tetany, seizures, laryngo-spasm, prolonged QT with arrhythmia. Ix: low corrected calcium, high phosphate, low or inappropriately normal PTH; magnesium (correct if low); 24-hour urine calcium before starting therapy. Mx: acute - IV calcium gluconate (10 mL of 10% over 10 min, then infusion); chronic - oral calcium and calcitriol titrated to low-normal calcium (avoid nephrocalcinosis); thiazide reduces urine calcium. Note: check and correct magnesium before assuming PTH failure - hypomagnesaemia is a reversible cause.
rich_summaries.Hypothermia: Core temperature under 35 C, from environmental exposure, impaired thermoregulation (elderly, hypothyroid, hypoglycaemia, sepsis, alcohol, drug intoxication) or iatrogenic causes. Classification: mild (32 to 35) is shivering, tachycardia, confusion; moderate (28 to 32) is loss of shivering, bradycardia, arrhythmias, reduced consciousness; severe (under 28) is coma, apnoea, and risk of VF or asystole. Ix: low-reading rectal or oesophageal thermometer; ECG (J or Osborn wave, bradycardia, AF); EUC (potassium over 10 mmol/L in prolonged cardiac arrest predicts non-survival), VBG, glucose, TFT, coagulation, toxicology; look for the precipitant. Mx: handle gently - rough movement can trigger VF. Passive external rewarming for mild cases. Active external rewarming (forced-air warming blanket) for moderate.
