Active internal rewarming (warm IV fluids, warm humidified oxygen, cavity lavage, ECMO) for severe or cardiac arrest. Not dead until warm and dead - continue CPR until core over 32 C. Note: afterdrop and rewarming shock are the traps of unmonitored rewarming.
rich_summaries.Hypothyroidism: Deficiency of thyroid hormone, most often from autoimmune thyroiditis. Causes: Hashimoto thyroiditis is commonest in iodine-replete countries; also post-thyroidectomy, radioiodine, amiodarone, lithium, and central causes from pituitary disease. Clinical features: fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain; constipation and dry skin; menorrhagia; depression and cognitive slowing; bradycardia with delayed reflex relaxation. Onset is insidious and often attributed elsewhere for months. Ix: TSH first - raised with low free T4 in primary disease; raised TSH with normal T4 is subclinical. TPO antibodies confirm autoimmune cause. Low TSH with low T4 means central hypothyroidism. Mx: levothyroxine, starting low in the elderly or those with ischaemic heart disease, retesting TSH after 6-8 weeks. Take on an empty stomach, separated from calcium, iron and proton pump inhibitors. Note: in pregnancy, requirements rise by 25-50% from early in the first trimester and undertreatment affects fetal neurodevelopment - increase the dose promptly and check TSH early.
rich_summaries.Idiopathic intracranial hypertension: Raised intracranial pressure without hydrocephalus, mass or venous obstruction; also called pseudotumour cerebri. Epidemiology: obese women of reproductive age (F:M about 9:1). Pathophysiology: proposed impaired CSF absorption and reduced cerebral venous outflow; obesity is the strongest modifiable driver. Clinical features: daily positional headache (worse lying, on straining or coughing), transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus, diplopia (CN VI palsy is false-localising), progressive field loss; papilloedema is the defining exam finding. Ix: MRI brain plus MR venography to exclude mass, hydrocephalus and dural venous sinus thrombosis (mandatory); LP opening pressure above 25 cm H2O in adults (over 28 in children) with normal CSF composition confirms; formal visual fields and OCT of the optic disc at baseline and serially. Mx: weight loss (7 to 10% body weight can be curative); acetazolamide first-line; topiramate as alternative; large-volume LP as bridge; therapeutic shunt (VP or LP) or optic nerve sheath fenestration when vision is threatened. Note: vision loss is the outcome that matters - urgent involvement if fields deteriorate or papilloedema is severe.
rich_summaries.IgA nephropathy: The commonest primary glomerulonephritis worldwide; IgA immune complexes deposit in the glomerular mesangium and trigger inflammation. Clinical features: synpharyngitic macroscopic haematuria (concurrent with URTI, in contrast to post-streptococcal GN which follows by 1 to 2 weeks), asymptomatic microscopic haematuria and proteinuria on routine screening, or a nephritic picture with hypertension and rising creatinine. Ix: urinalysis with red cell casts, urine PCR and ACR, EUC, complement (normal, distinguishes from post-strep and lupus GN), IgA level (elevated in about half but not diagnostic). Renal biopsy is the reference standard - mesangial IgA deposits with mesangial proliferation. Mx: BP control below 130/80 with ACE inhibitor or ARB titrated to reduce proteinuria under 1 g/day; sodium restriction; SGLT2 inhibitor adds renoprotection. Corticosteroids (or targeted-release budesonide) plus mycophenolate for progressive disease with proteinuria persistently over 1 g/day despite conservative measures. Rapidly progressive disease gets pulse steroids and cyclophosphamide. Note: about a third progress to end-stage kidney disease over decades; MEST-C score at biopsy prognoses.
rich_summaries.Immune thrombocytopenic purpura: Autoimmune platelet destruction and impaired production, with isolated thrombocytopenia and no alternative cause. Clinical features: petechiae, purpura, mucosal bleeding - epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia. Bleeding risk is low above 30 x 10^9/L. Children typically have an abrupt post-viral course that resolves; adults are usually chronic. Ix: a diagnosis of exclusion. Isolated thrombocytopenia on FBC with a normal film apart from large platelets; exclude pseudo-thrombocytopenia from EDTA clumping by repeating in citrate. Test HIV, hepatitis C and Helicobacter pylori. Marrow biopsy only in atypical cases. Mx: treat bleeding or a count below about 20-30 x 10^9/L, not the number alone. Prednisolone or dexamethasone first-line, with IVIg when a rapid rise is needed; then thrombopoietin receptor agonists, rituximab or splenectomy. Note: platelet transfusion is largely ineffective and reserved for life-threatening bleeding, since transfused platelets are destroyed by the same process.
rich_summaries.Impetigo: Superficial bacterial skin infection. Types: non-bullous (commonest, golden honey-crusted erosions, Strep pyogenes with or without Staph aureus) and bullous (large flaccid bullae from Staph aureus exfoliative toxin, commoner in neonates and young children). Highly contagious; peaks in warm humid weather; higher prevalence in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities where post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and rheumatic fever remain endemic. Clinical features: vesicles or pustules on erythematous base progressing to golden crusts, typically around nose, mouth and exposed skin. Bullous form gives flaccid bullae rupturing to a collarette scale. Regional lymphadenopathy. Ix: clinical diagnosis. Swab for culture if refractory, recurrent, MRSA suspected, or outbreak. Mx: hygiene measures. Localised disease gets topical mupirocin 2% three times daily for 5 days. Widespread, bullous, or systemically unwell get oral cephalexin or dicloxacillin for 5 to 7 days (eTG). Add clindamycin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for MRSA. Note: impetigo can trigger PSGN even after eradication - urinalysis 3 to 6 weeks later in the at-risk.
rich_summaries.Infective endocarditis: Infection of the endocardium, usually a valve, and usually one already abnormal - prosthetic, rheumatic, congenital, previously infected - or in the setting of injecting drug use or an intracardiac device. Causes: Staphylococcus aureus commonest overall and in injecting drug use; viridans streptococci after oral bacteraemia; coagulase-negative staphylococci on prosthetic valves; enterococci, HACEK organisms and Coxiella burnetii make up most of the rest. Sx: fever with a new murmur, embolic stroke, or heart failure from acute regurgitation; peripheral stigmata are uncommon but specific. Ix: three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics, then echocardiography, transoesophageal if the transthoracic is unrevealing; modified Duke criteria. Mx: prolonged intravenous antibiotics directed at the organism, empirically flucloxacillin with benzylpenicillin and gentamicin per eTG; surgery for heart failure, uncontrolled infection, abscess or a large mobile vegetation. Note: rheumatic heart disease remains a major substrate in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.
rich_summaries.Influenza: Acute respiratory infection with influenza A or B, seasonal in temperate Australia (June to September). Clinical features: abrupt high fever, rigors, myalgia, headache, dry cough, sore throat and profound malaise; children may vomit. Systemic symptoms last 3 to 5 days, cough up to 2 weeks. Ix: clinical during the season; PCR of a nasopharyngeal or combined nose-and-throat swab confirms and types the virus in high-risk or hospitalised patients. Chest imaging if bacterial pneumonia is suspected. Mx: supportive - fluids, rest, paracetamol. Oseltamivir within 48 hours reduces symptom duration and is indicated for hospitalised patients, pregnant women, children under 5, adults over 65, immunocompromised, chronic disease, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, and severe illness. Post-exposure prophylaxis for high-risk contacts. Complications: primary influenza pneumonitis, secondary bacterial pneumonia (Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae), myocarditis, encephalopathy. Note: annual vaccination on the NIP for over 65, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, pregnant women, chronic disease, and children 6 months to 5 years.
rich_summaries.Insomnia: Difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, or non-restorative sleep, at least 3 nights per week for at least 3 months, with daytime impairment, despite adequate sleep opportunity. Types: primary (idiopathic, psychophysiological, paradoxical) or comorbid (depression, anxiety, pain, restless legs, OSA, drugs, substance misuse, shift work, menopause). Clinical features: prolonged sleep latency, waking through the night, early morning waking, and non-refreshing sleep, with daytime fatigue, mood disturbance, cognitive impairment or impaired function. Ix: history, sleep diary and Epworth; screen for depression, anxiety, substance use, OSA (STOP-BANG) and restless legs; polysomnography only if OSA or another primary sleep disorder is suspected. Mx: CBT for insomnia (CBT-I) is first-line - stimulus control, sleep restriction, sleep hygiene, cognitive restructuring. Short-term hypnotics (temazepam, zopiclone) only for acute stressor, at lowest dose for shortest duration - dependence and tolerance are real. Melatonin for circadian disorders. Note: alcohol worsens sleep architecture and should not be used as a sleep aid.
rich_summaries.Insulinoma: Rare pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour from beta cells secreting insulin autonomously. Incidence 1 to 4 per million per year. 90% are benign, solitary, under 2 cm and sporadic; 10% associated with MEN1 (multiple, often malignant, younger patients - screen for hyperparathyroidism and pituitary tumours). Clinical features present as Whipple triad - symptoms of hypoglycaemia, low measured glucose during symptoms, and relief with glucose. Neuroglycopenic symptoms (confusion, visual change, seizures) often dominate in fasting or exertion; autonomic symptoms may be blunted. Weight gain from frequent eating. Ix: supervised 72-hour fast is the diagnostic test - during hypoglycaemia (glucose under 3.0), inappropriately elevated insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin with negative sulfonylurea screen confirms endogenous hyperinsulinism. Localise with CT or MRI pancreas, endoscopic ultrasound, or Ga-68 DOTATATE PET. Mx: surgical enucleation is curative in over 95% of benign disease. Medical control with diazoxide or octreotide for unresectable disease; everolimus and sunitinib for advanced malignancy. Note: exclude sulfonylurea overdose - it mimics insulinoma biochemistry exactly.
rich_summaries.Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: Failure of ipsilateral eye adduction on conjugate horizontal gaze with contralateral abducting nystagmus, from a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) between the pontine CN VI nucleus and the contralateral CN III nucleus. Convergence is preserved, which separates INO from a third nerve palsy. Causes: bilateral INO in a young adult is essentially MS until proven otherwise; unilateral INO in an older patient is usually a small brainstem lacunar infarct; also brainstem tumour, Wernicke, neurosarcoid. Clinical features: on H-pattern pursuit the adducting eye lags or fails to cross the midline while the abducting eye jerks outward; diplopia on lateral gaze. One-and-a-half syndrome adds an ipsilateral gaze palsy (PPRF plus MLF lesion). Ix: MRI brain focused on the dorsal pontine tegmentum; add contrast, cord imaging and consider CSF (oligoclonal bands, raised IgG index) if MS is suspected. Mx: treat the cause - methylprednisolone for MS relapse, stroke workup for infarct, thiamine for Wernicke; the deficit usually improves as the lesion resolves. Note: bilateral INO in a young woman is an MS presentation until MRI says otherwise.
rich_summaries.Interstitial nephritis: Tubulo-interstitial inflammation of the kidney. Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) is most often drug-induced - NSAIDs, penicillins, cephalosporins, PPIs, allopurinol, sulfonamides, rifampicin, furosemide, thiazides. Other causes include infection (streptococcal, Legionella, Leptospira), autoimmune disease (SLE, Sjogren, sarcoidosis, TINU), and idiopathic. Chronic interstitial nephritis follows analgesic overuse, lithium, chronic obstruction, or reflux. Clinical features: subacute rise in creatinine over days to weeks; the classic drug triad of fever, rash and eosinophilia appears in only about 10% of AIN. Sterile pyuria, mild proteinuria (below 1 g/day) and haematuria. Chronic form is silent until progressive CKD. Ix: EUC, urinalysis and microscopy (white cell casts, pyuria), urine PCR, FBC, immunology screen; renal biopsy is diagnostic - interstitial oedema with lymphocytic infiltrate. Mx: stop the offending drug. Oral prednisolone if creatinine continues to rise 5 to 7 days after drug withdrawal, or with biopsy-proven severe inflammation. Treat infections and underlying autoimmune disease. Note: most drug-induced AIN recovers with prompt drug withdrawal.
rich_summaries.Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy: Cholestatic liver disorder unique to pregnancy, presenting in the second half. Pathophysiology: genetic predisposition (ABCB4, ABCB11, ATP8B1 bile-salt transporter variants) combined with the cholestatic effect of pregnancy oestrogens produces raised serum bile acids. Clinical features: pruritus of the palms and soles worse at night, without a primary rash (secondary excoriations are common), starting in the third trimester. Jaundice is uncommon. Right upper quadrant discomfort and steatorrhoea may occur. Ix: fasting serum bile acids (over 10 micromol/L is diagnostic with typical pruritus; above 40 marks severe disease); LFT (mildly raised ALT and ALP is common); coagulation; ultrasound to exclude other liver disease. Mx: ursodeoxycholic acid 10 to 15 mg/kg/day reduces pruritus and bile acids; sedating antihistamine at night for itch; vitamin K if PT prolonged. Increased fetal surveillance from 34 weeks. Timing of delivery is guided by bile acid peak - deliver by 38 to 39 weeks in mild disease, earlier (35 to 37) if bile acids over 100. Note: recurrence in future pregnancies is 60 to 90%; resolves after delivery.
rich_summaries.Intussusception: Telescoping of proximal bowel into a distal segment, causing wall oedema, venous congestion and eventually ischaemia. Commonest cause of intestinal obstruction between 3 months and 2 years, peaking at 6 to 9 months. Ileocolic predominates. Causes: idiopathic in children (probably lymphoid hyperplasia after viral illness); pathological lead point in older children and adults (Meckel diverticulum, polyp, lymphoma, HSP). Clinical features: episodic severe colicky abdominal pain with drawing up of the legs, vomiting (progressing to bilious), and red-currant jelly stool (late, ominous sign of ischaemia). Between episodes the child appears well or lethargic. Palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant with an empty right iliac fossa (Dance sign). Ix: abdominal ultrasound is the reference standard - target sign in transverse, pseudokidney in longitudinal. Mx: resuscitate with fluids; NG decompression. Air enema reduction under fluoroscopy is first line, successful in 80 to 90%. Surgery for peritonitis, perforation, failed reduction, or an identified lead point. Note: recurrence after successful enema reduction is 10 to 15% and usually early - safety-net advice at discharge.
rich_summaries.Iron deficiency anaemia: Anaemia from depleted iron stores, the commonest anaemia worldwide. Causes: blood loss is the assumption until disproven - menstrual in premenopausal women, gastrointestinal otherwise. Also malabsorption (coeliac disease, atrophic gastritis, bariatric surgery), poor intake, and increased demand in pregnancy and infancy. Clinical features: fatigue, dyspnoea, pallor; angular stomatitis, glossitis, koilonychia and pica when chronic. Ix: microcytic hypochromic film; ferritin is the single best test - low is diagnostic, but it is an acute-phase reactant so a normal level does not exclude deficiency during inflammation. Transferrin saturation below 16% supports it. Mx: oral iron, alternate-day dosing giving better absorption than daily by avoiding a hepcidin rise; intravenous iron for intolerance or malabsorption. Recheck at 2-4 weeks, and continue 3 months past normalisation to refill stores. Note: iron deficiency anaemia in a man of any age, or a postmenopausal woman, mandates gastroscopy and colonoscopy - it is colorectal cancer until proven otherwise. Also test for coeliac disease.
rich_summaries.Irritable bowel syndrome: Functional bowel disorder with no structural pathology. Diagnosis: Rome IV - recurrent abdominal pain at least one day per week for 3 months, related to defaecation or to change in stool form or frequency. Subtypes: IBS-C, IBS-D, IBS-M. Clinical features: cramping abdominal pain relieved by defaecation, bloating, altered bowel habit, mucus per rectum. Ix: exclude organic disease with red flags - age over 50, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, rectal bleeding, iron deficiency anaemia, family history of colorectal cancer or coeliac disease. Minimum workup is FBC, CRP, coeliac serology, TFT, faecal calprotectin (differentiates IBD); stool microscopy and Giardia PCR if diarrhoea predominant. Colonoscopy for red flags. Mx: reassure with a positive diagnosis. Diet - low-FODMAP under an accredited dietitian, regular meals, psyllium fibre for IBS-C. Peppermint oil and antispasmodics for pain. Loperamide for IBS-D; polyethylene glycol or prucalopride for IBS-C. Low-dose tricyclic for pain-predominant disease. CBT and gut-directed hypnotherapy have evidence. Note: red-flag workup is done once, not repeatedly.
rich_summaries.Ischaemic colitis: Colonic ischaemia from hypoperfusion of the watershed areas - splenic flexure (SMA/IMA junction) and rectosigmoid junction. Causes: atherosclerosis, low-flow states (heart failure, sepsis, hypovolaemia), vasospasm (cocaine, amphetamines, ergotamine), embolism, post-aortic surgery, hypercoagulable state, vasculitis. Elderly and vascular-comorbid patients are the typical population. Clinical features: acute onset crampy left-sided abdominal pain followed by bloody diarrhoea or haematochezia; mild to moderate tenderness; usually no peritonism (distinguishes from mesenteric ischaemia). Ix: FBC, EUC, lactate, VBG, coagulation; CT abdomen with IV contrast shows bowel wall thickening, thumbprinting and pericolonic stranding; flexible sigmoidoscopy with cautious biopsy is diagnostic when uncertain. Mx: most (about 80%) resolve with conservative care - bowel rest, IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics for moderate to severe disease, and treatment of the precipitant. Surgery for peritonitis, perforation, gangrene, fulminant colitis, or stricture. Note: high recurrence risk (30%); investigate the vascular and cardiac precipitant.
rich_summaries.Juvenile idiopathic arthritis: Chronic arthritis in at least one joint for at least 6 weeks starting before age 16 - the most common paediatric arthritis. Subtypes (ILAR) include oligoarticular (four or fewer joints, ANA-positive, high uveitis risk), polyarticular RF-negative and RF-positive (the latter resembles adult RA), systemic (Still disease with quotidian fever, salmon-pink rash, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy), enthesitis-related (HLA-B27), psoriatic, and undifferentiated. Clinical features: joint swelling, morning stiffness, limp, altered gait. Uveitis screening is essential and often asymptomatic. Ix: FBC, CRP, ESR, ferritin (very high in systemic JIA and MAS), LFT, ANA, RF, CCP, HLA-B27 by phenotype; exclude septic arthritis and malignancy first. Slit-lamp examination scheduled by subtype. Mx: paediatric rheumatology led - intra-articular steroid for oligoarticular disease, NSAIDs, methotrexate as first-line DMARD, and biologics (etanercept, adalimumab, tocilizumab) for inadequate response. Tocilizumab or anakinra for systemic JIA. Note: macrophage activation syndrome complicates systemic JIA and is life-threatening.
rich_summaries.Kawasaki disease: Acute medium-vessel vasculitis of childhood, almost always under 5 years; the leading cause of acquired heart disease in Australian children. Aetiology unknown. Diagnosis: fever for at least 5 days plus four of five CRASH features - Conjunctivitis (bilateral, non-purulent, limbal sparing), Rash (polymorphous), Adenopathy (cervical, unilateral, over 1.5 cm), Strawberry tongue with lip cracking, and Hands and feet changes (erythema then fingertip desquamation at 2 to 3 weeks). Incomplete Kawasaki (fever plus two or three features) is common under 6 months and needs echo and inflammatory markers to decide. Ix: FBC (neutrophilia, thrombocytosis after week 1), CRP and ESR, LFT, albumin, urinalysis (sterile pyuria); baseline echocardiogram with follow-up at 2 and 6 weeks for coronary aneurysms. Mx: IV immunoglobulin 2 g/kg as a single infusion plus high-dose aspirin, ideally within 10 days of fever onset. Follow-up echocardiography drives long-term antiplatelet or anticoagulation. Complications: coronary aneurysms in about 25% untreated, 5% with timely IVIG. Note: any child with unexplained fever of at least 5 days needs Kawasaki excluded before another diagnosis is closed.
rich_summaries.Kernicterus: Chronic bilirubin encephalopathy from deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in basal ganglia, brainstem and cerebellum; preventable complication of severe neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia. Risk factors: prematurity, haemolysis (Rh/ABO, G6PD, spherocytosis), sepsis, acidosis, hypoalbuminaemia, bilirubin-displacing drugs (sulfonamides, ceftriaxone), delayed feeding, missed jaundice at discharge. Clinical features: acute - lethargy, poor feeding, hypertonia, opisthotonos, high-pitched cry, seizures; chronic - dystonic-athetoid cerebral palsy, sensorineural hearing loss, upward gaze palsy, intellectual disability. Ix: bilirubin plotted on age-in-hours nomogram; FBC, blood group, DAT; MRI shows bilateral globus pallidus T2 hyperintensity. Mx: intensive phototherapy at threshold; exchange transfusion at the exchange line or with acute encephalopathy; treat cause; audiology and neurology follow-up. Note: kernicterus is preventable - a jaundiced newborn missing their day-3 review is the classic presentation.
rich_summaries.Klinefelter syndrome: Male sex chromosome aneuploidy, most commonly 47,XXY; 1 in 500 to 1000 males and often undiagnosed until infertility workup. Pathophysiology: extra X drives progressive testicular hyalinisation from puberty, primary hypogonadism and germ cell loss. Clinical features: tall stature with disproportionately long limbs, small firm testes (under 4 mL post-pubertal), gynaecomastia, incomplete virilisation, azoospermia (commonest identifiable genetic cause of male infertility); verbal and executive weakness, anxiety and ADHD common; reduced bone density; raised risk of breast cancer, mediastinal germ cell tumour, venous thromboembolism, metabolic syndrome. Ix: karyotype; low testosterone with elevated LH and FSH; low inhibin B; semen analysis; DEXA. Mx: testosterone replacement from puberty, titrated to normalise levels and secondary sexual development; microTESE with ICSI can achieve biological fatherhood in a proportion; annual metabolic and bone review. Note: a boy with pubertal delay and small testes deserves a karyotype.
rich_summaries.Lambert-Eaton syndrome: Presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder from antibodies against P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing acetylcholine release. 50 to 60% are paraneoplastic (small cell lung cancer in nearly all - antibodies may precede cancer diagnosis by up to 3 years); the rest are autoimmune. Sx: proximal muscle weakness (legs more than arms) that transiently improves with sustained activity (post-tetanic potentiation, unlike myasthenia which fatigues); depressed or absent tendon reflexes that reappear after exercise; autonomic features (dry mouth, orthostatic hypotension, constipation); mild ptosis, no prominent bulbar signs.Ix: repetitive nerve stimulation shows small CMAPs that increment over 100% with high-frequency stimulation; anti-P/Q VGCC antibodies positive in over 90%; CT chest and PET-CT to hunt SCLC, repeat every 6 months for at least 2 years if initial workup negative. Mx: treat any underlying SCLC. Symptomatic - amifampridine (3,4-DAP) first line, pyridostigmine adjunct. Immunotherapy for non-paraneoplastic - prednisolone, IVIg, plasma exchange, azathioprine, rituximab. Note: unlike MG, cranial and respiratory muscles are largely spared.
rich_summaries.Leptospirosis: Zoonotic infection with Leptospira interrogans; notifiable in Australia. Aetiology: contact with contaminated water or soil - rodent urine leaches into fresh water; occupational (abattoir, farm, cane, dairy) and recreational (freshwater swimming after floods); spirochaetes penetrate skin and mucosa, disseminate, then small-vessel vasculitis drives multi-organ injury. Clinical features: classically biphasic - a septicaemic phase (5 to 7 days of high fever, severe calf myalgia, conjunctival suffusion, headache) then an immune phase; Weil disease is the severe form (jaundice, AKI, haemorrhage, myocarditis, ARDS, meningitis), mortality up to 15%. Ix: microscopic agglutination test (reference standard); PCR in early blood and later urine; LFT, raised CK, thrombocytopenia, AKI. Mx: doxycycline for mild disease; IV benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone for severe; supportive; watch for Jarisch-Herxheimer after first dose. Prevention: cover open wounds around water, rodent control, PPE; doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis. Note: conjunctival suffusion plus severe calf pain earns empirical doxycycline.
rich_summaries.Lithium toxicity: Toxicity from a drug with a therapeutic index narrow enough that the treatment range and the toxic range nearly touch. Causes: dehydration, intercurrent illness, and any drug that cuts renal clearance - thiazides, ACE inhibitors and ARBs, NSAIDs. Acute overdose and chronic accumulation behave differently; chronic is the more dangerous at any given level. Clinical features: coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, vomiting and diarrhoea early; then confusion, myoclonus, seizures and arrhythmia. Neurological signs, not the number, drive urgency. Ix: lithium level (timed 12 hours post-dose), EUC, calcium, TFTs, ECG. Repeat levels - a single value taken early after ingestion understates a rising concentration. Mx: stop lithium, correct volume with sodium chloride 0.9%, and discuss with the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26. Haemodialysis for severe neurotoxicity, renal failure or very high levels. Note: SILENT - persistent cerebellar deficit after apparent recovery - is the reason not to wait and watch.
rich_summaries.Livedoid vasculopathy: Occlusive thrombotic vasculopathy of dermal vessels causing painful lower-leg ulceration with pathognomonic atrophie blanche. Not a true vasculitis - the vessel wall is uninflamed. Epidemiology: young to middle-aged women, summer flares. Causes: about half have a thrombophilia (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, antiphospholipid syndrome, hyperhomocysteinaemia) or connective tissue disease (SLE, Sjögren); the rest idiopathic. Clinical features: recurrent painful punched-out ulcers around the ankles healing to atrophie blanche - porcelain-white stellate scars with telangiectasia, the diagnostic sign; overlying livedo reticularis; disproportionate pain is a discriminator. Ix: skin biopsy showing hyaline fibrin thrombi without leucocytoclastic vasculitis; thrombophilia screen, ANA, antiphospholipid antibodies. Mx: anticoagulation is the mainstay - low-dose aspirin plus a DOAC (rivaroxaban has the best trial evidence); pentoxifylline adjunct; compression. Note: painful stellate white scars separate this from pyoderma gangrenosum (pathergy, neutrophilic on biopsy).
rich_summaries.Long QT syndrome: Inherited ion channel disorder causing prolonged ventricular repolarisation and risk of polymorphic VT (torsades de pointes) and sudden cardiac death. QTc prolongation is over 450 ms in men and over 460 ms in women; over 500 ms is high risk. Types: LQT1 (KCNQ1, loss of IKs, exertion or swimming trigger); LQT2 (KCNH2, loss of IKr, auditory trigger); LQT3 (SCN5A, gain of INa, sleep or rest trigger). Acquired long QT is common - drugs (macrolides, quinolones, antifungals, antipsychotics, methadone, ondansetron), electrolyte disturbance (hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia), and bradycardia. Clinical features: syncope, seizures (often misdiagnosed as epilepsy), or aborted sudden cardiac death; family history of sudden death. Ix: 12-lead ECG with manual QTc calculation (Bazett or Fridericia); ambulatory ECG and exercise test; genetic testing supports family screening. Mx: avoid QT-prolonging drugs (see crediblemeds.org); correct electrolytes. Beta blocker (propranolol, nadolol) for LQT1 and LQT2. ICD for cardiac arrest survivors or high-risk congenital LQTS. Cascade family screening. Note: check any drug against the QT list before every new prescription.
rich_summaries.Lung abscess: Necrotising pulmonary infection with a pus-filled cavity. Causes: aspiration (commonest) with anaerobes in patients with impaired consciousness, alcohol excess, seizures, dysphagia or poor dentition; secondary to pneumonia (Staph aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae); septic emboli from right-sided endocarditis or IVDU; obstruction (tumour, foreign body); haematogenous. Clinical features: subacute or chronic productive cough with foul-smelling sputum, fever, weight loss, night sweats, haemoptysis, and pleuritic chest pain. Consider in any patient with slowly resolving pneumonia. Ix: CXR shows cavitary lesion with air-fluid level, typically in dependent segments; chest CT for anatomy and to exclude tumour; sputum Gram stain and culture (anaerobic if aspiration); blood cultures. Rule out endocarditis with echocardiogram if septic emboli suspected. Mx: prolonged IV then oral antibiotics per eTG (amoxicillin plus clavulanate, or clindamycin, or metronidazole plus benzylpenicillin) until CXR clears (typically 4 to 8 weeks). Percutaneous or surgical drainage for cavities over 6 cm, failure to respond, or complications. Note: bronchoscopy if obstruction or malignancy is suspected.
rich_summaries.Lung cancer: Malignancy arising from bronchial or alveolar epithelium, split for management into non-small cell (about 85%) and small cell (about 15%). Causes: smoking dominates; also asbestos, radon, air pollution and prior thoracic radiotherapy. Adenocarcinoma is the type most often seen in never-smokers. Clinical features: cough, haemoptysis, dyspnoea, weight loss. Local invasion gives hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal palsy, SVC obstruction, or Pancoast syndrome with Horner and T1 wasting. Ix: CT chest and upper abdomen, then PET-CT for staging; tissue by bronchoscopy, EBUS or CT-guided biopsy; molecular testing (EGFR, ALK, ROS1) and PD-L1 on non-small cell. Mx: surgery for early non-small cell with adjuvant chemotherapy, or stereotactic radiotherapy if inoperable. Locally advanced disease gets chemoradiotherapy then durvalumab. Metastatic disease is directed by molecular result - targeted therapy where a driver is present, otherwise immunotherapy with chemotherapy. Small cell is chemotherapy and radiotherapy from the outset. Note: paraneoplastic syndromes point to histology - SIADH and Lambert-Eaton with small cell, PTHrP hypercalcaemia with squamous.
rich_summaries.Lupus nephritis: Renal involvement in SLE, affecting 50 to 60% and driving much of SLE morbidity. Classification (ISN/RPS) runs I to VI, with class IV (diffuse proliferative) the commonest and most aggressive; class V (membranous) presents with nephrotic syndrome; class VI is advanced sclerosing. Clinical features: proteinuria (nephrotic or sub-nephrotic), microscopic haematuria with red cell casts, hypertension, rising creatinine; may be the presenting feature of SLE in young women. Ix: urinalysis with microscopy for casts, urine PCR and ACR, EUC, complement (C3, C4 low in active disease), anti-dsDNA (rises with flare), ANA and ENA panel, anti-phospholipid antibodies. Renal biopsy is essential for any SLE patient with proteinuria over 500 mg/day or unexplained renal impairment. Mx: hydroxychloroquine for all. Class III/IV or membranous with heavy proteinuria - induction with high-dose corticosteroids plus mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide; belimumab or voclosporin as add-on. Maintenance with mycophenolate or azathioprine plus low-dose steroid. ACE inhibitor or ARB and BP control. Note: avoid mycophenolate and cyclophosphamide in pregnancy; time conception for 6 months of quiescent disease.
rich_summaries.Lyme disease: Multisystem infection caused by Borrelia burgdorferi (or B. afzelii, B. garinii) transmitted by Ixodes ticks. Rare in Australia (no established Ixodes-Borrelia cycle) but acquired by travellers to endemic areas - eastern USA, Europe, temperate Asia. Clinical features by stage: early localised (3 to 30 days post-bite) gives erythema migrans (expanding target rash at bite site) and flu-like illness; early disseminated (weeks to months) gives multiple erythema migrans, carditis (AV block), meningitis, cranial neuropathy (bilateral facial palsy is highly suggestive) and radicular pain; late (months to years) gives Lyme arthritis (large joint, usually knee), neuroborreliosis, and acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans. Ix: erythema migrans is a clinical diagnosis; two-tier serology (ELISA screen, positive confirmed by Western blot) for disseminated or late disease. LP if neurological. Mx: early disease gets oral doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days (or amoxicillin if under 8 or pregnant). Neuroborreliosis and carditis with heart block get IV ceftriaxone for 14 to 28 days. Note: chronic Lyme after adequate treatment is not supported by evidence.
rich_summaries.Lynch syndrome: Autosomal dominant germline mutation in a DNA mismatch repair gene (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM) causing microsatellite instability and markedly raised cancer risk. Commonest hereditary colorectal cancer syndrome (2 to 4% of CRC). Raised risks span colorectal (50 to 80% lifetime, right-sided and mucinous, younger age, better stage-for-stage prognosis), endometrial (40 to 60%, commonest gynae cancer in female Lynch), ovarian, gastric, small bowel, urothelial, hepatobiliary, skin (Muir-Torre with sebaceous tumours), and brain (Turcot). Clinical features: family history meeting Amsterdam II or Bethesda guidelines; personal history of early-onset or multiple Lynch cancers. Ix: tumour testing on every new CRC and endometrial cancer - IHC for MMR proteins and MSI testing; germline testing on any MMR-deficient tumour or Amsterdam criteria met. Cascade family testing. Mx: colonoscopic surveillance every 1 to 2 years from age 25 to 30; gynae surveillance and risk-reducing hysterectomy and BSO after childbearing; aspirin 100 mg daily reduces CRC risk (CAPP2). Note: MMR-deficient cancers respond exceptionally well to checkpoint inhibitors.
rich_summaries.Major depressive disorder: Persistent low mood or anhedonia with functional impairment for at least two weeks. Dx: five or more of nine DSM-5 symptoms with mood or anhedonia among them, near-daily for two weeks and causing dysfunction; SIGECAPS covers the rest - sleep, interest, guilt, energy, concentration, appetite, psychomotor and suicidality. Screen with PHQ-9. Ix: no test confirms the diagnosis; investigate to exclude organic mimics with TFT, FBC and ferritin, B12 and folate, EUC, glucose, and a targeted drug and alcohol history. Mx: mild disease responds to CBT, behavioural activation or interpersonal therapy alone; moderate to severe adds an antidepressant, SSRI first line in Australia (sertraline, escitalopram), with SNRI or mirtazapine as second choice. Review at 2 weeks for tolerability and 4 to 6 for response, then switch class or augment if inadequate. ECT for melancholia, psychotic features, catatonia or urgent suicide risk. Note: assess suicide risk at every visit and document specifically, not just at the first; Australian guidance is the RANZCP mood disorders CPG.
rich_summaries.Malaria: Protozoal infection with Plasmodium species transmitted by female Anopheles mosquito. Species are P. falciparum (most severe, no hepatic hypnozoite, sub-Saharan Africa), P. vivax and P. ovale (dormant hypnozoites cause relapse months to years later), P. malariae (quartan fever), and P. knowlesi (zoonotic, Borneo).Incubation 7 days to months. Australia has been malaria-free since 1981; consider in returned travellers from endemic areas. Clinical features: cyclical fever with rigors, sweats, headache, myalgia, nausea, jaundice, and splenomegaly. Severe falciparum brings cerebral malaria (coma or seizures), acidosis, hypoglycaemia, AKI, ARDS, DIC, shock, and parasitaemia over 2%. Ix: thick and thin blood films are the reference standard - repeat every 12 to 24 hours for 3 sets before excluding; rapid antigen tests for triage; FBC (thrombocytopenia is a clue), EUC, LFT, glucose, lactate, VBG. Mx: notifiable. Uncomplicated falciparum gets oral artemether-lumefantrine; vivax and ovale get chloroquine plus primaquine (14 days) to eradicate hypnozoites - check G6PD first (primaquine haemolyses in deficiency). Severe malaria needs IV artesunate.
rich_summaries.Male infertility: Failure to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse (6 months if woman over 35); a male factor contributes in about half. Causes: pre-testicular (hypothalamic-pituitary disease, Kallmann, hyperprolactinaemia, anabolic steroid); testicular (Klinefelter 47,XXY, Y microdeletion, cryptorchidism, mumps orchitis, chemotherapy, radiation, varicocele); post-testicular (obstructive azoospermia from CF CBAVD, vasectomy); lifestyle (smoking, alcohol, obesity, heat). Clinical features: history of undescended testes, mumps, chemotherapy; examine for testicular volume (orchidometer, normal over 15 mL), vas presence, varicocele, gynaecomastia. Ix: two semen analyses per WHO 2021 - count at least 16 million/mL, motility at least 42%, morphology at least 4%; FSH, LH, morning testosterone, prolactin, TFT; karyotype and Y microdeletion if azoospermic. Mx: treat the cause - gonadotrophin therapy for hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, varicocelectomy for symptomatic grade 3, cabergoline for prolactinoma. IVF with intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI); surgical sperm retrieval for obstructive azoospermia. Note: lifestyle modification is cheap and often effective.
rich_summaries.Malignant hyperthermia: Autosomal dominant pharmacogenetic disorder of skeletal-muscle calcium homeostasis triggered by volatile anaesthetics or succinylcholine; life-threatening hypermetabolic crisis. Pathophysiology: mutated RYR1 (or CACNA1S) ryanodine receptor releases sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium uncontrollably on trigger exposure, driving sustained contraction, ATP depletion, heat and metabolic acidosis. Clinical features: rising end-tidal CO2 (earliest), masseter spasm after suxamethonium, tachycardia, mixed acidosis, hyperkalaemia, hyperthermia (late), rhabdomyolysis, DIC. Ix: intraoperative diagnosis; caffeine-halothane contracture test on muscle biopsy for confirmation; RYR1 genetics for family screening. Mx: stop trigger, switch to a clean circuit, hyperventilate with 100% O2 and deepen with propofol; dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV every 5 min to 10 mg/kg (then 1 mg/kg 6-hourly for 24 hours), active cooling, correct hyperkalaemia and acidosis; ICU; refer to the ANZ MH register. Note: rising end-tidal CO2 despite adequate ventilation is the earliest sign - do not wait for temperature to rise.
rich_summaries.Mallory-Weiss tear: Mucosal laceration at the gastro-oesophageal junction from forceful or repeated vomiting, retching, coughing, or any acute rise in intra-abdominal pressure. Risk factors include heavy alcohol use (classic but not exclusive), hyperemesis gravidarum, bulimia, chemotherapy-related vomiting, seizure and forceful cough. Clinical features: small-volume haematemesis (bright red to coffee-ground) following several episodes of non-bloody vomiting; epigastric or retrosternal pain possible; melaena if greater volume swallowed. Usually self-limiting - 90% stop spontaneously. Ix: FBC, coagulation, LFT, EUC, group and hold or crossmatch by severity. Upper GI endoscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic. Mx: supportive with antiemetic, IV fluid resuscitation, IV PPI. Endoscopic haemostasis for active bleeding - adrenaline injection, clips, thermocoagulation. Angiographic embolisation or surgery for refractory. Note: 10% rebleed rate lower than for peptic ulcer; avoid NSAIDs post-episode.
rich_summaries.Marfan syndrome: Autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder from FBN1 mutations coding fibrillin-1; reduced microfibrils cause aberrant TGF-beta signalling and tissue fragility. Clinical features: tall stature with disproportionately long extremities (arachnodactyly, arm span greater than height), pectus excavatum or carinatum, scoliosis, high-arched palate, joint hypermobility. Cardiovascular is the mortality driver - aortic root dilation, aortic dissection, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse. Ocular involvement gives ectopia lentis (upward lens displacement), myopia and retinal detachment. Pneumothorax and dural ectasia. Diagnosis by revised Ghent criteria. Ix: transthoracic echocardiogram for aortic root and valve; slit-lamp for ectopia lentis; genetic testing; cardiac MRI or CT if echo windows poor. Mx: annual echo; beta blocker or losartan slows aortic dilation; elective aortic root replacement at 50 mm (or 45 mm with family history of dissection or rapid growth). Avoid isometric exercise and competitive sport. Genetic counselling. Note: pregnancy in Marfan needs specialist obstetric-cardiology input - dissection risk rises in the third trimester.
rich_summaries.Mastitis: Painful inflammation of breast tissue, usually lactational and bacterial (Staphylococcus aureus via a nipple fissure); non-lactational forms include periductal and granulomatous mastitis. Epidemiology: up to 10% of breastfeeding women, peak in the first 6 weeks. Clinical features: unilateral firm tender erythematous wedge, fever, myalgia and rigors; usually follows milk stasis, cracked nipple, oversupply or missed feed. Ix: clinical; milk culture only for hospital-acquired, recurrent or severe cases; ultrasound if abscess suspected (fluctuance, worsening despite 48 h oral antibiotics). Mx: continue breastfeeding or expressing from the affected side (safe for baby and clears the duct); analgesia, cool packs, correct latch; oral di/flucloxacillin 500 mg QID for 5-7 days (eTG), cefalexin if penicillin allergy, clindamycin if severe allergy or MRSA suspected; ultrasound-guided aspiration for abscess (repeat rather than jump to incision); admit if septic or failing 48 h oral therapy. Red flags: persistent non-lactational inflammatory changes, peau d'orange or nipple change - biopsy to exclude inflammatory breast cancer.
rich_summaries.Measles: Paramyxovirus infection, one of the most contagious diseases known (R0 around 15). Clinical features: 7 to 14 day incubation, then a 2 to 4 day prodrome of high fever with the 3 Cs - cough, coryza and conjunctivitis - and Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa (pathognomonic). A maculopapular rash then appears behind the ears and spreads down, becoming confluent. Infectious from 4 days before to 4 days after rash onset. Ix: measles IgM and IgG, and RNA by PCR on nasopharyngeal swab or urine within the first week; notify public health on suspicion, before results. Mx: supportive; airborne isolation until 4 days after rash onset. Offer MMR to susceptible contacts within 72 hours, or immunoglobulin within 6 days to pregnant women, infants under 6 months and immunocompromised contacts. Complications: otitis media (commonest), pneumonia (the usual cause of death), encephalitis, and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis years later. Note: MMR at 12 and 18 months on the Australian NIP; a single suspected case triggers contact tracing across every shared setting.
rich_summaries.Medication overuse headache: Headache on 15 or more days a month in someone with a pre-existing primary headache who is regularly overusing acute treatment. Dx: the thresholds are 10 days a month or more for triptans, opioids, ergots and combination analgesics, and 15 days a month or more for simple analgesics such as paracetamol and NSAIDs. Clinical features: a headache that has crept from episodic to near-daily, often present on waking, with the original headache type still recognisable underneath. Ix: none beyond excluding a secondary cause if red flags are present. The diagnosis is made on the drug history. Mx: withdraw the overused medication, either abruptly or by taper, with a clear warning that headache worsens for one to two weeks first. Start a preventer at the same time. Review at four to twelve weeks; most improve substantially. Note: opioids and codeine-containing combinations are the worst offenders and the hardest to withdraw, which is a reason not to start them for headache at all.
rich_summaries.Medullary sponge kidney: Congenital cystic dilatation of the medullary collecting ducts producing urinary stasis, nephrocalcinosis and stone disease. Usually sporadic and isolated. Pathophysiology: ectatic precalyceal collecting tubules pool urine, precipitating calcium phosphate then calcium oxalate; incomplete distal renal tubular acidosis is present in about 40% and drives hypercalciuria and hypocitraturia. Clinical features: often incidental; recurrent renal colic, macroscopic or microscopic haematuria, recurrent UTIs; symptoms typically begin in adulthood. Ix: CT urogram is diagnostic - contrast fills the ectatic papillary ducts in a paintbrush or bouquet pattern with medullary microcalcifications; non-contrast CT for acute stones; 24-hour urine for calcium, oxalate, citrate and volume; morning urine pH and serum bicarbonate for RTA. Mx: high fluid intake (2 to 3 L/day); thiazide diuretic for hypercalciuria; potassium citrate for hypocitraturia or RTA; treat stones per eTG. Note: prognosis is generally benign - CKD is uncommon and results from recurrent obstruction or infection, not the malformation itself.
rich_summaries.Melanoma: Malignant tumour of melanocytes, most commonly cutaneous; Australia's incidence is the world's highest (over 55/100 000/year), UV exposure the dominant risk. Risk factors: fair skin, cumulative UV and sunburns, multiple naevi (over 100 or over 5 atypical), family history, immunosuppression, CDKN2A. Clinical features: ABCDE (Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variation, Diameter over 6 mm, Evolution) - 'ugly duckling' is often more useful; four subtypes - superficial spreading (commonest), nodular (rapid vertical growth, worse prognosis), lentigo maligna and acral lentiginous. Ix: dermoscopy then excisional biopsy with 2 mm margin (avoid punch or shave); histology for Breslow, ulceration and mitotic rate; sentinel node biopsy if Breslow above 0.8 mm or ulcerated; staging CT and brain MRI for stage III+; BRAF, NRAS and KIT on advanced disease. Mx: wide local excision with margin dictated by Breslow (5 to 20 mm); adjuvant checkpoint inhibitor for resected stage III; checkpoint inhibitor plus BRAF/MEK combination for metastatic disease. Note: sun-safe behaviour and skin checks are the highest-yield intervention in Australia.
rich_summaries.Meningitis: Inflammation of the meninges, usually infective. Causes: bacterial in adults is most often Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis, with Listeria in the very young, over-50s, pregnant or immunocompromised; viral is commonly enterovirus; consider TB and cryptococcus in chronic or immunocompromised presentations. Clinical features: fever, neck stiffness and altered mental state is the classic triad but is present in only about 40%; headache and photophobia are more sensitive; a non-blanching petechial rash suggests meningococcaemia. Kernig and Brudzinski are specific but not sensitive. Ix: blood cultures then lumbar puncture without delay; CT before LP only if focal deficit, GCS below 12, seizure, immunocompromise, or papilloedema. Mx: give empiric ceftriaxone 2g IV plus dexamethasone 10mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose; add benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin if Listeria risk; add vancomycin if resistant pneumococcus is plausible. Notify public health and offer household contact prophylaxis for meningococcus. Red flags: purpuric rash, shock or reduced GCS - treat before imaging.
rich_summaries.Menopause: Permanent cessation of menstruation, diagnosed retrospectively after 12 months of amenorrhoea; average age at final menstrual period is 51 in Australia. Premature ovarian insufficiency is menopause before 40. Clinical features: vasomotor symptoms in about three quarters, sleep disturbance, mood change, genitourinary syndrome (vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, urinary urgency), and accelerated bone loss. Ix: clinical over 45; FSH is unreliable in perimenopause because of cycle variability. Under 45, measure FSH twice at least a month apart to confirm POI, and exclude pregnancy and thyroid disease. Mx: lifestyle first - exercise, cooling strategies, weight management, reduced alcohol. Menopausal hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms in women under 60 or within 10 years of the final menstrual period, absent contraindications - oestrogen alone if hysterectomised, oestrogen plus progestogen otherwise (RANZCOG). Non-hormonal options include SSRI or SNRI, gabapentin, and CBT. Vaginal oestrogen alone treats genitourinary syndrome with negligible systemic exposure. Note: POI needs oestrogen replacement at least until the average age of menopause.
rich_summaries.Metabolic acidosis: pH under 7.35 with bicarbonate under 22 mmol/L. Compute the anion gap (Na - Cl - HCO3, normal 8 to 12) first; a high gap means added acid, a normal gap means bicarbonate loss. Causes: high anion gap by MUDPILES - methanol, uraemia, DKA, propylene glycol or paracetamol, isoniazid or iron, lactic acidosis, ethylene glycol, salicylates; normal gap by USED CARP - ureteric diversion, small bowel loss, excess saline, diarrhoea, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, Addison, RTA, pancreatic fistula. Ix: VBG or ABG with lactate; EUC, glucose, ketones, salicylate and paracetamol if ingestion possible; osmolar gap for toxic alcohols; urinary anion gap and pH to distinguish RTA from GI loss. Check Winter formula (pCO2 = 1.5 x HCO3 + 8). Mx: treat the cause - fluids and insulin for DKA, source control for sepsis, dialysis for toxic alcohols or severe uraemia or salicylate. Sodium bicarbonate only for pH under 7.1 or specific indications. Note: normal pH does not exclude a mixed disorder.
rich_summaries.Metabolic alkalosis: Acid-base disturbance with pH over 7.45 and bicarbonate over 26 mmol/L. Classification is by urinary chloride: chloride-responsive (urine Cl under 20 mmol/L) - vomiting or nasogastric suction, diuretics after cessation, post-hypercapnia, cystic fibrosis (sweat loss); chloride-resistant (urine Cl over 20 mmol/L) - primary hyperaldosteronism, secondary hyperaldosteronism (Cushing, renal artery stenosis), Liddle syndrome, Bartter and Gitelman syndromes, severe hypokalaemia. Clinical features: often dominated by the underlying cause; alkalosis itself gives paraesthesia, tetany, seizures, confusion, muscle weakness and arrhythmias; reduced ionised calcium contributes to neuromuscular features. Ix: ABG or VBG; EUC (hypokalaemia, hypochloraemia); urine chloride; corrected calcium and magnesium; renin and aldosterone if chloride-resistant. Mx: treat the cause. Chloride-responsive corrects with normal saline and potassium replacement. Chloride-resistant needs cause-specific treatment (spironolactone for aldosteronism). Acetazolamide in refractory contraction alkalosis from diuretics. Note: check for concurrent respiratory acidosis - compensation, not primary problem.
rich_summaries.Metabolic syndrome: Cluster of cardiovascular and metabolic risk factors predicting progression to type 2 diabetes and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Diagnosis (IDF, needs 3 of 5): central obesity (waist over 94 cm men, 80 cm women; ethnicity-specific for South Asian and East Asian); triglycerides over 1.7 mmol/L; HDL under 1.0 (men) or 1.3 (women) mmol/L; BP at least 130/85; fasting glucose at least 5.6 mmol/L or known type 2 diabetes. Clinical features: often asymptomatic and picked up on routine checks; overlap with PCOS, NAFLD, sleep apnoea, gout. Ix: fasting lipids, glucose, HbA1c, LFT (NAFLD), TFT, uric acid; ECG, urine ACR. Calculate 5-year CVD risk. Mx: lifestyle first - structured dietary change (Mediterranean pattern has the evidence), 150 to 300 minutes weekly moderate activity, resistance training, smoking cessation. Treat each component to target - metformin for diabetes or prevention, statin for CV risk, ACE inhibitor or ARB for hypertension. GLP-1 agonists in obesity with cardiovascular indication. Note: metabolic syndrome is a call to action, not a disease - the goal is to prevent the sequelae.
rich_summaries.Microscopic polyangiitis: ANCA-associated pauci-immune necrotising small-vessel vasculitis with p-ANCA against myeloperoxidase (MPO-ANCA). No granulomas and no upper respiratory tract involvement, distinguishing from GPA. Peak age 60 to 70; male predominance. Clinical features: pulmonary-renal syndrome is the hallmark - alveolar haemorrhage (haemoptysis, dyspnoea, drop in haemoglobin) and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (haematuria, proteinuria, oliguria, rising creatinine); systemic upset with fever, weight loss, myalgia and arthralgia; palpable purpura and skin ulcers; mononeuritis multiplex; GI ischaemia. Ix: MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA) positive in over 70%; PR3-ANCA in a minority; urinalysis and urine microscopy; EUC; CXR and HRCT for haemorrhage; renal biopsy shows pauci-immune crescentic GN. Mx: induction with high-dose corticosteroid plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab; plasma exchange for severe alveolar haemorrhage or dialysis-requiring renal failure; maintenance with rituximab, azathioprine or methotrexate for 18 to 24 months at least. Note: MPO-ANCA titres correlate poorly with disease activity - clinical and serial urinalysis matter more.
rich_summaries.Migraine: Primary headache disorder with recurrent moderate to severe headaches. Types: without aura (commonest), with aura (visual or sensory prodrome), chronic migraine (15 or more headache days per month for 3 months), and hemiplegic migraine. Clinical features: unilateral, pulsating, moderate to severe pain lasting 4 to 72 hours, worse with routine activity, with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia. Aura precedes or accompanies the headache, evolves over 5 to 60 minutes, and is fully reversible. Triggers include hormonal change, stress, sleep disturbance, missed meals and alcohol. Ix: clinical diagnosis by ICHD-3 criteria; imaging only for red flags (thunderclap, focal deficit, new after 50, immunocompromise). Mx: acute uses paracetamol or NSAID plus antiemetic; triptan (sumatriptan, rizatriptan, eletriptan) for moderate to severe; gepants (rimegepant, ubrogepant) for triptan failure or contraindication. Preventive when 4 or more per month uses propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate or sodium valproate (not in pregnancy); CGRP antagonists on PBS with prior therapy failures. Note: medication-overuse headache from too-frequent triptan or analgesia is a treatable trap.
rich_summaries.Minimal change disease: Commonest nephrotic syndrome in children (over 80% under 8 years) and 15 to 25% in adults. Effacement of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy with normal light microscopy. T-cell mediated. Often idiopathic; secondary causes include NSAIDs, lithium, Hodgkin lymphoma and viral infection. Clinical features: rapid onset facial and peripheral oedema (periorbital in children), heavy proteinuria (over 3.5 g/day), hypoalbuminaemia, hyperlipidaemia, VTE from urinary antithrombin loss, and infection susceptibility.BP and renal function usually normal (unlike FSGS). Ix: urinalysis dipstick and PCR; serum albumin, lipids, EUC; ANA, complement, hepatitis and HIV for secondary causes; renal biopsy deferred in children (empirical steroid trial) but done in adults or steroid-resistant paediatric cases. Mx: prednisolone 60 mg/m2 daily for 4 to 6 weeks then taper - remission in over 90% of children within 2 to 4 weeks. Steroid-dependent or frequently relapsing cases get cyclophosphamide, ciclosporin, tacrolimus or rituximab. Salt restriction, diuretics, ACE inhibitor for persistent proteinuria, statin, prophylactic anticoagulation if severe. Note: adult MCD remits slower.
rich_summaries.Miscarriage: Loss of pregnancy before 20 weeks, occurring in roughly one in five recognised pregnancies. Types: threatened (bleeding, closed os, viable); inevitable (open os); incomplete; complete; missed (no cardiac activity, closed os); septic. Ix: transvaginal ultrasound; serial beta-hCG where the location is uncertain; blood group and antibody screen. Mx: expectant, medical with misoprostol, or surgical evacuation - choice is largely the woman's, guided by bleeding, sepsis and preference. Give anti-D to Rh-negative women. Offer follow-up and written information; recurrence risk after one loss is not meaningfully raised. Red flags: pain with a positive test and an empty uterus is ectopic until excluded; fever, offensive loss or tenderness suggests septic miscarriage and needs antibiotics and urgent evacuation. Note: investigate for a cause after three consecutive losses, or earlier if there is a second-trimester loss.
rich_summaries.Mitral regurgitation: Retrograde flow from left ventricle to left atrium during systole. Causes: primary (valvular) includes mitral valve prolapse (commonest in developed settings), rheumatic disease, infective endocarditis, and papillary muscle rupture from acute MI; secondary or functional MR arises from LV dilation stretching the annulus. Clinical features: pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla; displaced apex beat, third heart sound. Acute severe MR (papillary muscle rupture) presents with sudden pulmonary oedema and cardiogenic shock; chronic MR is asymptomatic for years before exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, AF and heart failure. Ix: 12-lead ECG (LAE, LVH, AF); CXR; transthoracic echocardiogram grades severity by regurgitant fraction, vena contracta and effective regurgitant orifice area; TOE for anatomy before surgery. Mx: chronic primary severe MR with symptoms, LVEF under 60% or LV end-systolic diameter over 40 mm gets surgery (repair preferred over replacement). MitraClip for high-risk surgical candidates. Secondary MR needs heart failure therapy first. Acute severe MR is a surgical emergency. Note: repair beats replacement wherever anatomy allows.
rich_summaries.Mitral stenosis: Narrowing of the mitral valve orifice, obstructing left atrial emptying. Almost always rheumatic - still important in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. Rarer causes include mitral annular calcification in the elderly, congenital MS, carcinoid, and rare inflammatory disorders. Clinical features: exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea, haemoptysis (rupture of bronchial-pulmonary anastomoses), atrial fibrillation with rapid response and embolic stroke, and pulmonary hypertension with right heart failure. Signs: mid-diastolic rumble at the apex, best heard in left lateral position on expiration; loud S1 and opening snap; malar flush (mitral facies). Ix: ECG (P mitrale, AF); CXR (LA enlargement, splayed carina, pulmonary congestion); transthoracic echo is diagnostic (valve area under 1.5 cm2 is severe). Mx: diuretics for congestion, rate control for AF, anticoagulation with warfarin (DOACs not indicated in rheumatic MS with AF). Percutaneous mitral balloon valvuloplasty for suitable pliable non-calcified valves without significant MR; surgical valve replacement otherwise. Note: severe MS in pregnancy is high risk - cardio-obstetric team review essential.
rich_summaries.Mitral valve prolapse: Billowing of one or both mitral valve leaflets into the left atrium during systole; the commonest valvular abnormality. Aetiology: primary (myxomatous degeneration, familial in Marfan and Ehlers-Danlos) or secondary (rheumatic disease, connective tissue disorders, HCM). Clinical features: most asymptomatic and detected on auscultation - mid-systolic click with or without a late systolic murmur; the click moves earlier with Valsalva and standing. A minority develop chest pain, palpitations, presyncope or arrhythmia. Progression to significant mitral regurgitation occurs in a subset. Ix: transthoracic echo confirms leaflet displacement over 2 mm above the annular plane and characterises leaflet thickness, regurgitation severity and LV function; 12-lead ECG if palpitations; ambulatory monitoring for arrhythmia. Family screening in syndromic cases. Mx: reassure asymptomatic patients - MVP without regurgitation carries near-normal prognosis. Beta blocker for palpitations. Follow with echo every 3 to 5 years. Surgical repair for severe mitral regurgitation. Note: routine endocarditis prophylaxis for dental work is not recommended for MVP under current Australian guidelines.
rich_summaries.Multiple endocrine neoplasia: Group of autosomal dominant syndromes with tumours of multiple endocrine organs. Types: MEN1 - the 3 Ps - Parathyroid hyperplasia in 95%, Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (gastrinoma, insulinoma), Pituitary adenoma (usually prolactinoma); MEN2A (RET) - Medullary Thyroid Cancer in nearly all, Phaeochromocytoma in half, Primary hyperparathyroidism in a third; MEN2B (RET) - MTC that presents earlier and behaves worse, phaeochromocytoma, marfanoid habitus, mucosal neuromas, ganglioneuromatosis; MEN4 (CDKN1B) - MEN1-like. Clinical features depend on individual tumour biology. Ix: genetic testing on any suggestive phenotype and cascade to first-degree relatives. Screen MEN1 with annual calcium, PTH, prolactin, IGF-1, fasting gut hormones; MEN2 with annual calcitonin, plasma metanephrines, calcium; imaging with pituitary MRI, pancreas MRI or EUS, thyroid ultrasound, adrenal CT.Mx: prophylactic thyroidectomy in MEN2 carriers (infancy in MEN2B, before 5 in high-risk MEN2A); tumour-specific surgery. Note: screen for phaeochromocytoma before any adrenal surgery in MEN2.
rich_summaries.Multiple myeloma: Clonal plasma cell malignancy producing monoclonal immunoglobulin and end-organ damage. Epidemiology: median onset around 70; preceded by monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance in essentially all cases. Clinical features: CRAB - hyperCalcaemia, Renal impairment, Anaemia, Bone lesions - with bone pain, fracture and recurrent infection. Ix: serum and urine electrophoresis with immunofixation; serum free light chain ratio; FBC, UEC, calcium, beta-2 microglobulin; whole-body low-dose CT rather than skeletal survey; marrow biopsy for plasma cell percentage and cytogenetics. Mx: induction with a proteasome inhibitor, an immunomodulatory drug and dexamethasone, then autologous stem cell transplant if fit, then maintenance. Bisphosphonates for skeletal protection, plus analgesia and radiotherapy for painful lesions. Note: the rouleaux and raised ESR often come before anything else, and myeloma is a leading cause of an unexplained normocytic anaemia with renal impairment in an older patient. Red flags: back pain with neurological signs is cord compression; hypercalcaemia and hyperviscosity are both emergencies.
rich_summaries.Multiple sclerosis: Immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system, disseminated in time and space. Epidemiology: onset 20-40; women about 3 times more than men; incidence rises with latitude, and Tasmania has among the highest rates in the world. Clinical features: optic neuritis with painful monocular visual loss; internuclear ophthalmoplegia; transverse myelitis; sensory disturbance; Lhermitte sign; Uhthoff phenomenon of transient worsening with heat. Fatigue and bladder dysfunction dominate later disability. Types: relapsing-remitting in about 85% at onset, most evolving to secondary progressive; primary progressive in the rest. Ix: MRI brain and cord with gadolinium showing periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial and spinal lesions; CSF oligoclonal bands; visual evoked potentials. Mx: high-dose methylprednisolone shortens relapses without altering outcome. Disease-modifying therapy is the substance of management and works best started early - from interferons and glatiramer through to natalizumab, ocrelizumab and cladribine. Note: vitamin D deficiency and smoking are modifiable risks for progression.
rich_summaries.Mumps: Acute paramyxovirus infection spread by respiratory droplets. Incubation 12 to 25 days. Australian incidence low since MMR on the NIP, but outbreaks occur in unvaccinated populations and around waning immunity. Clinical features: prodrome of fever, headache, malaise and anorexia; unilateral or bilateral painful parotitis lifting the earlobe (hamster-face) is the hallmark; submandibular and sublingual glands may also swell. Complications include orchitis in post-pubertal males (20 to 30%, usually unilateral, sub-fertility rare), oophoritis, aseptic meningitis or encephalitis, pancreatitis, sensorineural deafness, myocarditis, and first-trimester miscarriage.Ix: clinical diagnosis in typical parotitis. Buccal swab for viral PCR is the reference standard; mumps IgM serology (may be negative early). Amylase raised. Notifiable. Mx: supportive. Isolate for 5 days from parotid swelling onset. Prevention: two doses of MMR at 12 and 18 months on the NIP. Note: post-exposure vaccination does not prevent disease in already-exposed contacts.
rich_summaries.Muscular dystrophy: Group of inherited myopathies with progressive muscle weakness. Duchenne is X-linked recessive with an out-of-frame dystrophin mutation, so dystrophin is absent and boys present at 2 to 5 with Gower sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, waddling gait and delayed motor milestones; loss of ambulation by 12, cardiomyopathy and respiratory failure by the late teens or twenties. Becker is an in-frame mutation with reduced dystrophin, later onset and milder course. Myotonic (DM1) is autosomal dominant CTG expansion in DMPK with distal weakness, myotonia, cataracts, cardiac conduction disease, insulin resistance and frontal balding. Ix: creatine kinase (very high in Duchenne and Becker), genetic testing, ECG and echocardiogram, respiratory function testing; muscle biopsy if genetics inconclusive. Mx: multidisciplinary specialist clinic. Glucocorticoids (deflazacort or prednisolone) delay loss of ambulation in Duchenne; ACE inhibitor for cardiomyopathy; non-invasive ventilation for respiratory failure; ataluren and eteplirsen for selected genotypes. Note: cardiac and respiratory disease are the mortality - surveillance before symptoms.
rich_summaries.Myasthenia gravis: Autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction causing fatigable weakness. Pathophysiology: antibodies against the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor in about 85%, or against MuSK in most of the rest, reducing endplate potential and causing failure with repeated use. Clinical features: fatigable weakness worsening through the day - ptosis and diplopia in most at onset, then bulbar involvement with dysarthria, dysphagia and nasal speech, then proximal limb and respiratory weakness. Ix: acetylcholine receptor and MuSK antibodies; repetitive nerve stimulation showing decrement, or single-fibre EMG; CT chest for thymoma, present in 10-15%; TFT. Mx: pyridostigmine for symptoms; prednisolone with azathioprine or mycophenolate for immunosuppression; thymectomy in thymoma and in younger seropositive patients. Note: many common drugs worsen myasthenia - aminoglycosides, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, beta-blockers, magnesium - so check any new prescription. Red flags: myasthenic crisis with respiratory failure needs monitoring of forced vital capacity, not oximetry, since saturation falls only after decompensation.
rich_summaries.Myocardial infarction: Spectrum of myocardial ischaemia from unstable plaque: unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI. Pathophysiology: plaque rupture with superimposed thrombus. Complete occlusion gives ST elevation; partial occlusion gives NSTEMI or unstable angina. Clinical features: central crushing chest pain radiating to jaw or arm; sweating, nausea, dyspnoea. Frequently atypical in women, older people and diabetes - dyspnoea or collapse without chest pain. Ix: ECG within 10 minutes, repeated if pain continues; high-sensitivity troponin at 0 and 1-3 hours, where the change matters more than a single value. Mx: aspirin 300 mg immediately, a second antiplatelet, anticoagulation and glyceryl trinitrate. STEMI needs reperfusion - primary PCI within 90 minutes, or thrombolysis if PCI is not achievable within 120, the usual constraint outside metro Australia. NSTEMI is risk-stratified with GRACE. Secondary prevention: dual antiplatelet therapy; statin; ACE inhibitor; beta-blocker; cardiac rehabilitation. Note: a normal troponin does not exclude unstable angina; posterior STEMI shows ST depression in V1-V3. Red flags: new murmur, hypotension or pulmonary oedema suggests mechanical complication.
rich_summaries.Myocarditis: Inflammation of the myocardium. Causes are viral in most cases (Coxsackie B, adenovirus, parvovirus B19, HHV-6, SARS-CoV-2), with rarer bacterial (Lyme), fungal, and protozoal (Chagas). Non-infective causes include drug hypersensitivity, toxic drugs (anthracyclines, cocaine, checkpoint inhibitors), and autoimmune disease (giant cell, eosinophilic, sarcoidosis, SLE). Clinical features: chest pain (often pericarditic), dyspnoea, palpitations, syncope, arrhythmia and heart failure. Fulminant myocarditis presents as cardiogenic shock. Ix: 12-lead ECG, troponin (raised), BNP, inflammatory markers, viral serology, and echocardiogram (regional or global dysfunction). Cardiac MRI showing T2 oedema and late gadolinium enhancement in a non-coronary distribution is diagnostic. Endomyocardial biopsy for fulminant or suspected giant cell disease. Mx: supportive heart failure treatment with ACE inhibitor, beta blocker and diuretic; arrhythmia management; activity restriction for 3 to 6 months. Immunosuppression for biopsy-proven giant cell, eosinophilic and autoimmune myocarditis. Mechanical support or transplant for refractory disease. Note: avoid NSAIDs and competitive sport during recovery.
rich_summaries.Myotonic dystrophy: Most common adult muscular dystrophy; autosomal dominant CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the DMPK gene (chromosome 19q13); repeat length correlates with severity and shows anticipation (worsens each generation, more marked with maternal transmission). Types: DM1 (DMPK, commonest); DM2 (ZNF9/CNBP, milder, proximal weakness). Clinical features: distal weakness (hand grip, foot drop), myotonia (delayed muscle relaxation - percussion myotonia on thenar tap, grip myotonia), and characteristic systemic features including frontal balding, ptosis, cataracts, cardiac conduction disease (progressive AV block, sudden death), respiratory muscle weakness, insulin resistance and diabetes, primary gonadal failure, cognitive change. Congenital form is severe hypotonia at birth with maternal transmission. Ix: clinical diagnosis supported by EMG (myotonic discharges); confirmatory genetic testing (triplet repeat sizing); annual ECG, echocardiogram, PFT, slit lamp, HbA1c. Mx: no disease-modifying therapy. Mexiletine for symptomatic myotonia. Pacemaker for conduction disease. Non-invasive ventilation for respiratory failure. Genetic counselling. Note: anaesthetic risk is high.
rich_summaries.Necrotising enterocolitis: Life-threatening intestinal necrosis of the preterm neonate; leading NICU surgical emergency. Incidence 5 to 10% in infants under 1500 g. Pathophysiology combines immature gut motility and immunity, abnormal bacterial colonisation, and ischaemia-reperfusion injury; formula feeding is a major risk factor. Distal ileum and proximal colon most affected. Clinical features: usually second week of life; feeding intolerance, increased gastric aspirates, abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, bloody stools, temperature instability, apnoea, bradycardia, hypotension, shock. Bell staging grades severity. Complications include perforation, peritonitis, sepsis, DIC, short bowel syndrome, and stricture.Ix: abdominal X-ray shows distended bowel loops, thickened wall, pneumatosis intestinalis (pathognomonic), portal venous gas, and free air if perforated; FBC, coagulation, blood cultures, ABG. Mx: NBM and NG decompression, TPN, broad-spectrum antibiotics (ampicillin, gentamicin, metronidazole), fluid resuscitation, ventilatory support, urgent surgery for perforation. Note: prevention with exclusive breast milk feeding, probiotics, and standardised feeding protocols.
rich_summaries.Neonatal jaundice: Visible jaundice in over 50% of term neonates, from immature hepatic bilirubin conjugation and increased red cell turnover. Physiological jaundice peaks day 3 to 5 and resolves by day 10 in term infants; pathological is any within the first 24 hours, beyond 2 weeks in term or 3 weeks in preterm, or conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Pathological aetiologies include haemolytic disease (Rh or ABO, G6PD, spherocytosis), sepsis, TORCH, breast milk jaundice, hypothyroidism, biliary atresia, and Gilbert syndrome. Clinical features: visible jaundice progressing cephalocaudal; kernicterus with hypotonia, lethargy, poor feeding, high-pitched cry, opisthotonus and seizures. Ix: transcutaneous bilirubin as screen; serum total and conjugated bilirubin plotted on the Australian age-in-hours nomogram; FBC, film, blood group and DAT, TFT. Mx: adequate feeding supports enteral bilirubin clearance. Phototherapy per nomogram threshold. Exchange transfusion for very high or rapidly rising bilirubin. Investigate any conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia urgently - biliary atresia needs Kasai portoenterostomy before 8 weeks. Note: any jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathological until proven otherwise.
rich_summaries.Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome: Surfactant deficiency in preterm lungs causing atelectasis, low compliance and hypoxaemia; incidence over 80% below 28 weeks. Pathophysiology: type II pneumocytes produce surfactant from 24-34 weeks; deficiency raises alveolar surface tension and drives collapse plus hyaline-membrane formation. Clinical features: tachypnoea, grunting, nasal flaring, recession, cyanosis, worsening over the first 24 hours. Ix: CXR shows ground-glass opacification with air bronchograms and low volumes; ABG hypoxaemia and respiratory acidosis; exclude sepsis (early GBS mimics RDS). Mx: antenatal corticosteroids for anticipated delivery under 34/40 (halves RDS); delivery-room CPAP; exogenous surfactant via endotracheal tube (INSURE or LISA) for moderate-severe disease; SpO2 target 90-95%; caffeine; nutrition. Note: antenatal steroids at 24-34 weeks give the biggest single reduction in RDS mortality.
rich_summaries.Neonatal sepsis: Systemic bacterial infection in a neonate, split by onset. Early-onset (under 72 hours) reflects vertical transmission - group B streptococcus, E. coli, Listeria, Klebsiella. Late-onset (72 hours to 28 days) is community or healthcare-acquired - coagulase-negative staphylococci, Staphylococcus aureus, Gram-negatives, Candida. Clinical features are non-specific - temperature instability, poor feeding, lethargy, irritability, jaundice, respiratory distress, apnoea, seizures, mottling, shock. Any sick neonate is septic until proven otherwise. Ix: FBC, CRP, blood culture, lumbar puncture (unless clinically unstable), urine culture (SPA in late-onset), CXR if respiratory; consider viral PCR. Mx: empirical antibiotics urgently - benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin for early-onset; flucloxacillin plus gentamicin, or vancomycin plus cefotaxime, for late-onset by local guideline. Add aciclovir if HSV possible. Supportive care with fluid resuscitation, respiratory support, and correction of electrolytes and glucose. Note: intrapartum GBS prophylaxis has reduced early-onset GBS sepsis substantially.
rich_summaries.Nephritic syndrome: Glomerular inflammation presenting with haematuria (dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts - specific for glomerular bleeding), sub-nephrotic proteinuria (usually under 3.5 g/day), hypertension, oedema, and reduced GFR. Causes include post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy (synpharyngitic haematuria), ANCA-associated vasculitis, anti-GBM disease, lupus nephritis, cryoglobulinaemia, and MPGN. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis is a subset with crescents on biopsy and halving of eGFR over weeks. Ix: urinalysis with microscopy for casts, urine PCR, EUC; complement is low in post-strep, lupus and cryoglobulinaemia but normal in IgA and vasculitis; also ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM, ASOT, HIV, HBV, HCV, SPEP. Renal biopsy defines pathology and drives immunosuppression. Mx: treat the underlying cause. BP control with ACE inhibitor or ARB, sodium restriction, and diuretics for oedema. Corticosteroids and steroid-sparing agents by biopsy diagnosis. Note: rapidly progressive disease needs biopsy and immunosuppression within days.
rich_summaries.Nephrolithiasis: Renal or ureteric calculi. Calcium oxalate is commonest (about 75%); other compositions include calcium phosphate, struvite (urease-producing infection - Proteus, Klebsiella), uric acid (radiolucent), and cystine (rare). Risk factors: dehydration, high animal protein and sodium intake, hypercalcaemia, hypercalciuria, hyperuricaemia, hyperoxaluria, renal tubular acidosis, recurrent UTI, family history. Clinical features: severe colicky loin-to-groin pain of sudden onset with restlessness (unlike peritonitis where patients lie still), nausea and vomiting, haematuria, dysuria or frequency if lower ureteric. Ix: urinalysis (microscopic haematuria in over 90%); EUC, calcium, uric acid; pregnancy test. Non-contrast CT KUB is the imaging reference standard. Renal ultrasound for pregnant women and children. Mx: analgesia (IV NSAID first line, add opioid if needed), IV fluids, antiemetic. Stones under 5 mm usually pass spontaneously; medical expulsive therapy with tamsulosin for 5 to 10 mm stones. Urology intervention (ureteroscopy, SWL, PCNL) for larger stones or complications. Note: obstructed infected kidney is an emergency - decompress before treating sepsis.
rich_summaries.Nephrotic syndrome: Proteinuria above 3.5 g a day with hypoalbuminaemia and oedema, from podocyte injury and loss of glomerular charge selectivity. Causes: minimal change disease in children; membranous nephropathy, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and diabetic nephropathy in adults. Secondary causes include SLE, amyloid, hepatitis B and C, and malignancy. Clinical features: periorbital and peripheral oedema, frothy urine, and in severe cases ascites and pleural effusions. Ix: urine protein-creatinine ratio, albumin, lipids, EUC; immunology screen; PLA2R antibody for membranous disease. Renal biopsy in adults, but not usually in children who respond to steroids. Mx: salt restriction and loop diuretics for oedema; ACE inhibitor or ARB to reduce proteinuria; statin; treat the underlying cause. Corticosteroids for minimal change disease. Note: loss of antithrombin III in the urine makes this a prothrombotic state, and renal vein thrombosis is the characteristic complication.
