rich_summaries.Neural tube defect: Failure of neural tube closure at 3 to 4 weeks gestation. Types: anencephaly (absent forebrain, lethal); spina bifida occulta (asymptomatic bony defect, often with skin dimple or sacral hair tuft); meningocele (meninges herniate, cord intact); myelomeningocele (meninges and cord herniate, motor and sensory deficit below the level, neurogenic bladder and bowel, Chiari II with hydrocephalus); encephalocele. Risk factors: folate deficiency (the modifiable one), pre-existing diabetes, maternal obesity, antiepileptic drugs (valproate, carbamazepine), family history. Ix: antenatal - maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (elevated) at 15 to 20 weeks and detailed 18 to 20 week anomaly ultrasound; amniocentesis if uncertain. Postnatally, MRI spine and brain. Mx: multidisciplinary - neurosurgical closure of open lesion within 72 hours; VP shunt for hydrocephalus; intermittent self-catheterisation for neurogenic bladder; bowel management; orthotics and physiotherapy. Note: preconception folate 400 microg daily (5 mg high-risk: previous NTD, diabetes, antiepileptics) reduces NTD by two thirds.
rich_summaries.Neurofibromatosis: Group of autosomal dominant tumour predisposition syndromes with variable expressivity. Types: NF1 (von Recklinghausen, chromosome 17q, neurofibromin loss) is commonest; NF2 (chromosome 22q, merlin loss) is rarer and defined by bilateral vestibular schwannomas; schwannomatosis causes multiple non-vestibular schwannomas. Clinical features of NF1 (2 of 7 criteria): six or more cafe-au-lait macules, axillary or inguinal freckling (Crowe sign), two or more Lisch nodules on iris, two or more neurofibromas or one plexiform, optic pathway glioma, distinctive bone lesion (sphenoid dysplasia, tibial pseudoarthrosis), and a first-degree relative. NF2 presents with hearing loss and vestibular symptoms in adolescence. Ix: clinical diagnosis in NF1; genetic testing where phenotype atypical; MRI brain and orbits for optic glioma; ophthalmology; annual BP. Mx: no cure. Multidisciplinary surveillance - paediatric, neurology, ophthalmology, orthopaedics; treat complications (selumetinib for symptomatic plexiform neurofibroma). Genetic counselling. Note: malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour risk is 8 to 13% lifetime in NF1 - new persistent pain or plexiform growth needs imaging.
rich_summaries.Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: Potentially fatal idiosyncratic reaction to antipsychotics, typical more than atypical, or to dopamine agonist withdrawal; D2 blockade in striatum and hypothalamus. Sx (tetrad): hyperthermia above 38°C, often above 40°C; lead-pipe rigidity; altered consciousness progressing to coma; autonomic instability with diaphoresis, tachycardia, labile BP and tachypnoea. Onset: hours to days after starting or increasing an antipsychotic, or stopping a dopaminergic. Ix: CK often above 1000 and can exceed 100,000; leukocytosis; raised LFTs; metabolic acidosis; myoglobinuria progressing to AKI. Ddx: serotonin syndrome - clonus and hyperreflexia, onset under 24 hours; malignant hyperthermia - inhalational anaesthetic or suxamethonium; anticholinergic toxidrome - dry skin, normal reflexes. Mx: stop the causative drug; IV fluids, active cooling, respiratory support; bromocriptine or dantrolene for rigidity; benzodiazepines for agitation; ECT if refractory or catatonic. Red flags: recovery takes days to weeks; rechallenge with a different antipsychotic no sooner than 2 weeks.
rich_summaries.Non-Hodgkin lymphoma: Heterogeneous group of lymphoid malignancies, mostly B-cell, spanning indolent to highly aggressive behaviour. Classification: aggressive - diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (commonest), Burkitt, mantle cell; indolent - follicular, marginal zone, small lymphocytic. The split determines everything about management. Clinical features: painless lymphadenopathy with non-contiguous spread; extranodal involvement is common - gut, skin, CNS, testis; B symptoms; cytopenias from marrow involvement. Ix: excisional biopsy with immunohistochemistry; PET-CT; bone marrow biopsy; LDH (prognostic); HIV, hepatitis B and C serology before rituximab. Mx: aggressive disease is treated with curative intent - R-CHOP for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Indolent disease is often watched, since treating an asymptomatic follicular lymphoma does not improve survival. Note: the counterintuitive part is that aggressive lymphomas are curable and indolent ones generally are not - fast-growing tumours are more chemosensitive. Red flags: hepatitis B reactivation with rituximab can be fatal, so screen and give antiviral prophylaxis.
rich_summaries.Obesity: BMI at or above 30. Aetiology: chronic positive energy balance with genetic, hormonal, environmental and psychosocial contributors; secondary causes to exclude include hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome, hypothalamic lesions, and drugs (corticosteroids, insulin, sulfonylureas, many antipsychotics, sodium valproate). Complications drive the impact - type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, OSA, NAFLD, GORD, osteoarthritis, colorectal, breast and endometrial cancer, depression, and infertility. Ix: waist circumference (over 94 cm men, over 80 cm women raises risk), BP, lipids, HbA1c, LFT, TFT, uric acid; consider OSA screening. Mx: lifestyle first with structured dietary change (500 to 750 kcal deficit), physical activity, and behavioural support. GLP-1 agonists (liraglutide, semaglutide) and dual GIP-GLP-1 agonists (tirzepatide) are the effective pharmacotherapies; orlistat is second line. Bariatric surgery (sleeve gastrectomy, RYGB) for BMI at or above 40, or 35 with complications. Note: use person-first, non-stigmatising language; weight bias worsens outcomes.
rich_summaries.Obsessive-compulsive disorder: Anxiety disorder with obsessions and compulsions causing distress or functional impairment. Obsessions are recurrent intrusive unwanted thoughts, images or urges (contamination, doubt, symmetry, harm, forbidden themes); compulsions are repetitive behaviours or mental acts (washing, checking, counting, ordering, mental rituals) performed to reduce distress or prevent a feared outcome. Diagnosis (DSM-5): obsessions or compulsions or both, time-consuming (over one hour per day) or causing significant distress or impairment, not attributable to another condition. Ix: no specific test; screen with Y-BOCS; assess for comorbid depression, anxiety, tics and eating disorders. Mx: high-intensity CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP) is first-line psychological therapy. SSRI at higher doses than for depression (fluoxetine 40 to 80 mg, sertraline 100 to 200 mg, escitalopram 20 mg) for 12 weeks before judging response; clomipramine is second line. Combine CBT and SSRI for moderate to severe disease. Note: paediatric-onset OCD may follow group A streptococcal infection (PANDAS) - consider ASO in acute-onset OCD in a child.
rich_summaries.Obstructive sleep apnoea: Repeated upper airway collapse during sleep causing apnoeas, desaturation and arousals. Risk factors: obesity (BMI over 30), male sex, middle age, large neck circumference (over 40 cm), retrognathia and craniofacial abnormalities, tonsillar hypertrophy, evening alcohol. Clinical features: loud snoring with witnessed apnoeas, excessive daytime sleepiness (Epworth over 10), morning headache, nocturia, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive complaints. Ix: STOP-BANG or OSA-50 for screening; laboratory polysomnography is the reference standard and grades severity by apnoea-hypopnoea index (mild 5 to 14, moderate 15 to 29, severe 30 or more). Home sleep studies are acceptable in high pre-test probability with limited comorbidity. Mx: weight loss where relevant, avoid supine sleep and evening alcohol and sedatives. CPAP is first line for moderate to severe disease and for symptomatic mild disease; mandibular advancement splints for mild to moderate or CPAP intolerance. Associations: resistant hypertension, atrial fibrillation, stroke, type 2 diabetes and depression. Note: Austroads rules - excessive sleepiness with a positive study means no commercial driving until treated and controlled.
rich_summaries.Oesophageal cancer: Two main types with distinct risk profiles. Squamous cell carcinoma affects upper and mid oesophagus - smoking, alcohol, hot beverages, achalasia, caustic injury. Adenocarcinoma affects lower third - GORD, Barrett oesophagus, obesity, male sex; now commonest type in Australia. Clinical features: progressive dysphagia solids then liquids, weight loss, odynophagia, retrosternal pain, anaemia from occult bleeding, regurgitation, hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal invasion, supraclavicular lymphadenopathy in advanced disease. Ix: upper endoscopy with biopsy is the reference standard - urgent referral for new dysphagia over 55 or alarm features; CT chest, abdomen and pelvis plus PET-CT for staging; EUS for local T and N; laparoscopy for adenocarcinoma to exclude peritoneal spread. Mx: staged by TNM. Early (T1a) - endoscopic mucosal resection. Localised - neoadjuvant chemoradiation then oesophagectomy (Ivor Lewis for lower, McKeown for upper). Metastatic - palliative chemotherapy, immunotherapy for PD-L1-positive; stenting or radiotherapy for dysphagia relief. Note: 5-year survival remains under 20%.
rich_summaries.Oesophageal varices: Portosystemic collaterals in the lower oesophagus that form when portal pressure rises, and bleed with high mortality. Pathophysiology: a hepatic venous pressure gradient above 12 mmHg is needed for varices to bleed, which is why the gradient rather than the varix size drives risk. Ix: gastroscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic; screen at diagnosis of cirrhosis and periodically thereafter. Mx (acute bleeding): resuscitate with a restrictive transfusion target of about 70 g/L, since over-transfusion raises portal pressure. Give a vasoactive agent (octreotide or terlipressin) and prophylactic antibiotics, then endoscopic band ligation within 12 hours. Balloon tamponade or TIPS if bleeding continues. Prevention: non-selective beta-blocker or band ligation for primary prophylaxis; both after a bleed. Note: antibiotics are not optional - they reduce mortality in variceal bleeding independently of controlling the bleed itself.
rich_summaries.Ophthalmoplegia: Paralysis or paresis of one or more extraocular muscles from CN III, IV or VI dysfunction, or muscle disease. Complete CN III palsy gives ptosis, eye down and out, and mydriasis with impaired accommodation - a mydriatic third nerve palsy is a posterior communicating artery aneurysm until proven otherwise. Pupil-sparing CN III palsy in a diabetic is usually ischaemic. CN IV palsy gives vertical diplopia worse on downgaze and head tilt away from the affected side. CN VI palsy gives horizontal diplopia worse on gaze to the affected side and is the classic false localising sign of raised ICP. Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion) gives impaired adduction with contralateral abduction nystagmus - classic in MS. Ix: clinical examination and cover test; urgent CT and CT angiography for painful third nerve palsy; MRI brain for INO or atypical presentation; TFT for Graves ophthalmopathy; acetylcholine receptor antibodies for fatigable ptosis (myasthenia). Mx: treat the cause. Prisms or eye patching for diplopia. Muscle surgery once deviation is stable. Note: acute painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil is a neurosurgical emergency.
rich_summaries.Opioid use disorder: DSM-5 pattern of opioid use causing clinically significant impairment or distress, with 2 or more of 11 criteria over 12 months (tolerance, withdrawal, escalating use, cravings, functional impairment, continued use despite harm, hazardous use). Australian opioid deaths now exceed road toll; most involve prescription opioids rather than heroin. Clinical features: intoxication - miosis, respiratory depression, sedation, hypotension; withdrawal (peaks 36 to 72 hours for short-acting) - lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, yawning, sweating, mydriasis, piloerection, myalgia, abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, anxiety. Ix: history, urine drug screen, SafeScript check (real-time prescription monitoring), FBC, LFT, BBV screen. Mx: opioid agonist therapy (methadone or buprenorphine-naloxone) via MATOD-authorised prescriber is first line and halves mortality; long-acting injectable buprenorphine improves adherence. Naloxone take-home for overdose reversal. Psychological therapy (CBT, contingency management). Screen and manage comorbid depression and PTSD. Note: MATOD training is free and required for prescribing OAT.
rich_summaries.Optic neuritis: Inflammatory demyelination of the optic nerve producing subacute monocular vision loss; commonest cause is multiple sclerosis, particularly in young women. Aetiology: MS (up to half convert within 15 years), neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (aquaporin-4 antibodies), MOG antibody disease, sarcoidosis, syphilis; toxic and nutritional optic neuropathies are separate entities. Clinical features: unilateral vision loss over hours to days, painful eye movements, dyschromatopsia (red desaturation), central scotoma, RAPD; fundoscopy normal in retrobulbar disease, disc swelling in papillitis. Ix: MRI orbits and brain with gadolinium (enhancing optic nerve; brain white-matter lesions predict MS); AQP4 and MOG antibodies (NMOSD, MOGAD); LP if MS or infection suspected. Mx: high-dose IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3-5 days) speeds recovery without changing final acuity (ONTT); oral prednisolone alone is contraindicated (raises recurrence); MS disease-modifying therapy if brain MRI positive; NMOSD and MOGAD need long-term immunosuppression. Note: NMOSD tends to present with severe bilateral optic neuritis with poor recovery - check AQP4 before defaulting to MS treatment.
rich_summaries.Osteoarthritis: Progressive cartilage wear with subchondral bone remodelling and secondary synovial inflammation; the commonest arthritis. Risk factors: age, female sex, obesity, previous joint injury or surgery, occupational or sporting overuse, family history, joint malalignment. Common sites are knee, hip, hands (DIP with Heberden nodes, PIP with Bouchard nodes, first CMC), cervical and lumbar spine, and first metatarsophalangeal. Clinical features: joint pain worse with activity and relieved by rest, morning stiffness under 30 minutes, crepitus, reduced range of motion, bony enlargement, effusion. Erythema and warmth are absent (distinguishes from inflammatory arthritis). Ix: clinical diagnosis. Radiograph shows joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts (LOSS). Bloods normal - CRP and ESR only raised if another cause. Mx: lifestyle - weight loss, structured exercise, physiotherapy. Paracetamol then topical NSAID (diclofenac gel); oral NSAID in short bursts with PPI. Intra-articular corticosteroid for flares. Joint replacement for refractory pain and functional loss. Note: opioids and glucosamine offer little over placebo.
rich_summaries.Osteomalacia: Defective mineralisation of osteoid in the mature skeleton, producing soft bone with a normal or increased matrix volume. Causes: vitamin D deficiency dominates - inadequate sun exposure, covering dress, dark skin, malabsorption, and chronic kidney or liver disease. Also hypophosphataemia from renal phosphate wasting, and long-term anticonvulsants. Clinical features: diffuse bone pain and proximal myopathy giving a waddling gait and difficulty rising from a chair. Fractures, and pseudofractures (Looser zones) on imaging. Ix: 25-hydroxyvitamin D, calcium, phosphate, ALP and PTH. The characteristic pattern is low or low-normal calcium and phosphate with raised ALP and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Mx: colecalciferol replacement, with calcium if dietary intake is poor, and correction of the underlying cause. Recheck at three months. Phosphate and calcitriol where the defect is renal phosphate wasting. Note: ALP rises before calcium falls, so a normal calcium does not exclude it.
rich_summaries.Osteomyelitis: Infection of bone, haematogenous in children and usually contiguous or secondary to vascular insufficiency in adults. Causes: Staphylococcus aureus dominates. Consider Salmonella in sickle cell disease, Pseudomonas after a penetrating foot injury through footwear, and polymicrobial flora in diabetic foot infection. Clinical features: local pain, warmth and swelling with fever in acute disease; a chronically discharging sinus or a non-healing ulcer in chronic disease. In diabetic foot, a probe reaching bone makes it likely. Ix: MRI is the imaging of choice and is positive early; plain films lag by two weeks. Blood cultures, CRP and ESR for monitoring. Bone biopsy for culture before antibiotics wherever possible - swabs of a sinus mislead. Mx: targeted antibiotics, typically intravenous initially, guided by eTG and culture, with surgical debridement of dead bone or infected hardware. Duration is weeks, not days. Note: culture-directed therapy matters more here than almost anywhere, because the course is long and relapse is common.
rich_summaries.Osteoporosis: Systemic skeletal disease with low bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration, increasing fracture risk. Diagnosis by DXA T-score at least -2.5 at femoral neck, total hip or lumbar spine, or by minimal-trauma fracture at a typical site. Risk factors: age, female sex, postmenopausal oestrogen loss, family history of hip fracture, low body weight, prior fragility fracture, glucocorticoids over 3 months, smoking, excess alcohol, inflammatory disease, hypogonadism. Ix: DXA in anyone with a fragility fracture, on long-term glucocorticoids, or with FRAX 10-year probability at or above 20% major osteoporotic or 3% hip; screen for secondary causes with FBC, EUC, calcium, phosphate, ALP, LFT, TFT, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, PTH, testosterone in men, coeliac serology, consider SPEP. Mx: calcium 1000 to 1300 mg daily from diet and vitamin D 800 to 1000 IU daily; weight-bearing and resistance exercise; fall prevention. Oral bisphosphonate (alendronate or risedronate) is first line, with denosumab or IV zoledronate as alternatives. Teriparatide and romosozumab for severe or refractory disease. Note: PBS in Australia funds bisphosphonate for anyone with a minimal-trauma fracture.
rich_summaries.Osteosarcoma: Malignant bone tumour of osteoid-producing cells; commonest primary bone malignancy in children and young adults. Epidemiology: bimodal - adolescents (growth spurt, distal femur or proximal tibia) and older adults with prior bone disease (Paget, prior radiation); hereditary retinoblastoma, Li-Fraumeni and Rothmund-Thomson raise risk. Clinical features: progressive deep bone pain (worse at night, unrelieved by rest), tender mass, restricted joint movement, pathological fracture. Ix: X-ray shows an aggressive lytic-sclerotic lesion with periosteal reaction (Codman triangle, sunburst spicules); MRI for local extent; chest CT (lung the commonest met site) and whole-body bone scan or PET for staging; ALP and LDH are prognostic; biopsy through a needle track excisable at definitive surgery. Mx: multidisciplinary at a sarcoma centre - neoadjuvant MAP (methotrexate, doxorubicin, cisplatin), limb-salvage surgery, adjuvant chemotherapy tailored to necrosis; pulmonary metastasectomy for resectable disease. Note: 5-year survival is 60 to 70% localised, under 30% with metastasis - refer directly to a sarcoma centre.
rich_summaries.Otitis media: Middle ear infection, most often in children following URTI. Acute otitis media (AOM): Streptococcus pneumoniae, non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis; GAS in older children. Otitis media with effusion (glue ear) is chronic middle-ear fluid without acute infection. Chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM) is high in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and drives conductive hearing loss and speech delay. Clinical features: ear pain (or pulling at ear in preverbal children), fever, irritability, reduced feeding, and conductive hearing loss. Otoscopy shows bulging erythematous tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex and landmarks; perforation with purulent discharge in advanced or CSOM. Ix: clinical diagnosis; audiology and tympanometry for OME or recurrent AOM. Mx: paracetamol and ibuprofen for pain. Observation for 48 to 72 hours in non-severe AOM in children over 2. Amoxicillin 15 mg/kg TDS for 5 days (7 days if severe, under 2, bilateral, or Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander child - per eTG). Grommets for recurrent AOM or persistent OME with hearing loss over 3 months. Note: CSOM needs long-course topical ciprofloxacin plus ENT review.
rich_summaries.Ovarian cancer: The gynaecological cancer with highest mortality - the silent killer; often presenting at advanced stage. Types: epithelial (over 90%, high-grade serous is commonest and most aggressive), germ cell (younger women), sex cord-stromal (granulosa cell). Risk factors include BRCA1/2 (lifetime risk up to 44%), Lynch syndrome, nulliparity, early menarche and late menopause, HRT, and endometriosis. COCP, multiparity, breastfeeding and tubal ligation are protective. Clinical features: vague and insidious - abdominal bloating, early satiety, urinary urgency or frequency, pelvic or abdominal pain, fatigue; ascites, palpable mass, pleural effusion in advanced disease. Ix: pelvic examination; transvaginal ultrasound; CA-125 (raised in 80% but non-specific, so use RMI or IOTA rules); CT chest-abdomen-pelvis for staging. Tissue diagnosis at laparotomy - no biopsy before if malignancy suspected (risk of tumour seeding). Mx: staging laparotomy with TAH, BSO, omentectomy, and cytoreductive debulking. Platinum-taxane chemotherapy adjuvant or neoadjuvant. PARP inhibitors (olaparib, niraparib) for BRCA-mutated or HRD-positive disease. Note: no effective screening in the general population.
rich_summaries.Ovarian cyst: Fluid-filled structure within the ovary. Types: functional (physiological) - follicular cysts, corpus luteum cysts, and theca lutein cysts, which resolve spontaneously in weeks to months; benign neoplasms - mature cystic teratoma (dermoid), serous or mucinous cystadenoma, endometrioma; malignant - epithelial ovarian cancer (usually solid or mixed). Clinical features: often asymptomatic and found incidentally; large cysts cause pelvic pressure, bloating, and frequency; acute pain from rupture, haemorrhage or ovarian torsion (sudden severe pain with nausea and vomiting, more likely with cysts over 5 cm). Ix: pelvic examination; transvaginal ultrasound characterises the cyst; beta-hCG in reproductive-age; CA-125 in postmenopausal cysts or with concerning ultrasound (use RMI or IOTA rules). Mx: simple cysts under 5 cm in premenopause usually resolve - repeat ultrasound at 6 weeks. Larger or persistent cysts get gynaecology review. Suspected torsion is a surgical emergency - laparoscopic detorsion, preserve ovary if viable. Complex or postmenopausal cysts warrant MRI or laparoscopy. Note: any postmenopausal ovarian cyst is malignant until proven otherwise.
rich_summaries.Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome: Iatrogenic complication of controlled ovarian stimulation, usually in IVF. Pathophysiology: exogenous gonadotrophins and hCG trigger supraphysiological VEGF release from the corpus luteum, raising capillary permeability and shifting fluid into the third space. Risk factors: PCOS, young age, low BMI, high antral follicle count, previous OHSS, high oestradiol at trigger, and hCG rather than GnRH agonist trigger. Clinical features: onset within days of hCG (early) or with implantation (late). Mild is distension and nausea; moderate adds ascites and vomiting; severe adds massive ascites, hydrothorax, oliguria, haemoconcentration, VTE, hepatic and renal dysfunction. Ix: FBC (rising haematocrit), EUC, LFT, albumin, coagulation; pelvic ultrasound for enlarged ovaries and free fluid; CT chest if hypoxic. Mx: mild and moderate at home with analgesia, oral fluids and daily review. Severe needs admission - IV crystalloid with human albumin, thromboprophylaxis with LMWH (VTE is the mortality driver), paracentesis for tense ascites. Note: prevention is the point - GnRH antagonist protocol with GnRH agonist trigger and freeze-all in high-risk patients.
rich_summaries.Ovarian mass: Adnexal mass with broad differential by age and menopausal status. Types include functional cysts (follicular or corpus luteum, commonest in reproductive-age women, usually resolve), endometrioma (chocolate cyst), benign neoplasms (dermoid, serous or mucinous cystadenoma, fibroma), malignant (epithelial post-menopausal, germ cell in younger women, sex cord-stromal), and metastatic (Krukenberg from gastric or colon).Complications: torsion (sudden severe pelvic pain and vomiting - surgical emergency), rupture with haemoperitoneum, infection. Clinical features: often incidental; pelvic pain or pressure, bloating, urinary or bowel symptoms, dyspareunia, abnormal bleeding; acute abdomen if torsion or rupture. Ix: urine pregnancy test in reproductive-age; transvaginal ultrasound with IOTA or RMI; tumour markers (CA-125 for epithelial, AFP, beta-hCG, LDH for germ cell); CT or MRI for staging when malignancy suspected. Mx: simple cyst under 5 cm in premenopausal - observe over 1 to 2 cycles. Persistent, complex or symptomatic - laparoscopic cystectomy or oophorectomy. Suspected malignancy - refer to gynae-oncology. Note: torsion needs same-day imaging and surgery to salvage the ovary.
rich_summaries.Ovarian torsion: Twisting of the ovary and often fallopian tube on its pedicle, occluding blood supply and causing ischaemia and infarction. Gynaecological emergency. Risk factors: ovarian mass over 5 cm (mature cystic teratoma is commonest; ovarian hyperstimulation with theca lutein cysts), pregnancy, tubal ligation, and long utero-ovarian ligament. Rarely occurs with malignant tumours (they adhere). Clinical features: sudden severe unilateral lower abdominal or pelvic pain, often waking from sleep, with nausea and vomiting; pain may be colicky if intermittent. Pelvic examination reveals tender adnexal mass. Fever and leucocytosis develop late as infarction sets in. Ix: pregnancy test in every reproductive-age woman; FBC, CRP; transvaginal ultrasound with Doppler is first-line - enlarged ovary, whirlpool sign, reduced or absent flow (present flow does not exclude - dual blood supply). Mx: urgent laparoscopy for detorsion; preserve the ovary if any viability; cystectomy for the underlying mass; oophoropexy in recurrent torsion. Note: normal Doppler does NOT exclude torsion - clinical picture and surgical exploration decide.
rich_summaries.Pancreatitis: Inflammation of the pancreas, acute or chronic. Acute diagnosis needs two of three - characteristic pain, lipase over three times upper limit, or imaging changes. Causes: gallstones and alcohol dominate acute; also hypertriglyceridaemia, hypercalcaemia, drugs, post-ERCP, trauma, tumour. Clinical features of acute: severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, relieved by sitting forward, with vomiting; Cullen and Grey Turner signs are late and rare. Chronic pancreatitis presents with recurrent pain, exocrine insufficiency (steatorrhoea, weight loss) and endocrine insufficiency (type 3c diabetes); alcohol is the leading cause. Ix: lipase (more specific than amylase), LFT, lipids and calcium to find cause, abdominal ultrasound for gallstones; CT for complications after 72 hours in severe disease. Mx: aggressive fluid resuscitation with compound sodium lactate, analgesia, early enteral feeding. Antibiotics only for proven infection. Cholecystectomy during the same admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis. Alcohol cessation, pancreatic enzyme replacement, drainage for chronic disease. Note: organ failure beyond 48 hours defines severe disease.
rich_summaries.Panic disorder: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks plus persistent concern about future attacks or maladaptive behavioural change (typically avoidance, sometimes agoraphobia). Diagnosis (DSM-5): at least one attack followed by 1 month of worry about further attacks or significant avoidance. Clinical features: panic attack is an abrupt surge of intense fear peaking within minutes, with at least four of thirteen symptoms - palpitations, sweating, tremor, shortness of breath, choking, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, chills or heat, paraesthesia, derealisation, fear of losing control, fear of dying. Attacks may wake the patient from sleep. Frequent ED presentations with suspected ACS are common. Ix: clinical diagnosis. Exclude thyrotoxicosis, phaeochromocytoma, hypoglycaemia and substance withdrawal - TFT, ECG, urine drug screen, glucose. Mx: CBT with interoceptive exposure is first-line psychological therapy. SSRI (sertraline, escitalopram, paroxetine) or SNRI (venlafaxine) first line pharmacological - start low, warn about early activation, uptitrate. Avoid long-term benzodiazepines. Note: educate patient that panic attacks are not dangerous and peak within minutes.
rich_summaries.Papilloedema: Optic disc swelling from raised intracranial pressure; always bilateral. Causes include any raised ICP - brain tumour, hydrocephalus, idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, encephalitis, malignant hypertension, subdural haematoma, and CO2 retention. Clinical features: often asymptomatic in early disease; transient visual obscurations lasting seconds with posture change, enlarged blind spot on perimetry, and progressive visual field loss with sustained ICP; headache worse on lying flat and on Valsalva, morning nausea and vomiting, sixth nerve palsy (false localising sign). Ix: fundoscopy shows blurred disc margins, disc elevation, absent venous pulsations, Paton lines, disc haemorrhages; OCT quantifies peripapillary nerve fibre layer thickening; urgent CT or MRI brain to exclude mass and hydrocephalus; MR venogram for sinus thrombosis; LP with opening pressure if imaging normal. Mx: treat the underlying cause. IIH responds to weight loss, acetazolamide, and surgical CSF diversion or optic nerve sheath fenestration for progressive vision loss. Note: unilateral disc swelling is not papilloedema.
rich_summaries.Paracetamol overdose: Australia's commonest deliberate self-poisoning, and one where the antidote works reliably if given early enough. Pathophysiology: therapeutic doses are conjugated; in overdose these pathways saturate and NAPQI accumulates, depleting glutathione and causing centrilobular hepatic necrosis. Clinical features: asymptomatic or nausea for the first 24 hours, then right upper quadrant pain and rising transaminases at 24-72 hours, then encephalopathy and coagulopathy. The well-looking patient at presentation is the trap. Ix: paracetamol level at 4 hours or later post-ingestion plotted on the Australian nomogram; ALT, INR, EUC, BGL, VBG. Mx: activated charcoal within 2 hours of a significant ingestion. Acetylcysteine by the guideline regimen, started without waiting for a level if presentation is late, staggered, or the time is unknown. Discuss with the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26. Note: refer for transplant assessment using the King's College criteria - acidosis, or the triad of INR above 6.5, creatinine above 300 micromol/L and grade III-IV encephalopathy.
rich_summaries.Parkinson disease: Neurodegenerative disease from dopaminergic neurone loss in the substantia nigra with alpha-synuclein Lewy body deposition. Clinical features: bradykinesia is obligatory, plus rest tremor at 4-6 Hz, rigidity, or both. Asymmetry at onset is characteristic. Non-motor features precede motor ones by years - REM sleep behaviour disorder, hyposmia, constipation, depression. DDx: drug-induced parkinsonism (antipsychotics, metoclopramide - symmetrical and reversible), progressive supranuclear palsy (early falls, vertical gaze palsy), multiple system atrophy (autonomic failure), vascular parkinsonism (lower body predominant), essential tremor (postural not rest, improves with alcohol). Mx: levodopa with carbidopa is the most effective symptomatic therapy; dopamine agonists and MAO-B inhibitors are alternatives in younger patients to defer motor complications. Physiotherapy, speech therapy and exercise all have evidence. Note: never stop Parkinson medication abruptly in hospital, and never withhold it for fasting - missed doses cause severe akinesia and can precipitate a neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome.
rich_summaries.Patent ductus arteriosus: Failure of the ductus arteriosus to close after birth. Physiologically the ductus closes in the first 72 hours as PGE2 falls and oxygen tension rises. Persistence gives a left-to-right shunt (aorta to pulmonary artery) with pulmonary overcirculation and LV volume overload. Risk factors: prematurity (main), congenital rubella, high altitude, female sex. Clinical features: continuous machinery murmur best heard at the left infraclavicular region; bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure. In preterm infants, difficulty weaning from ventilation, heart failure, and necrotising enterocolitis; older children may be asymptomatic or have exertional dyspnoea and growth failure. Ix: echocardiogram is diagnostic and quantifies shunt size; ECG (LVH in large shunts); CXR (cardiomegaly, pulmonary plethora). Mx: preterm - indomethacin, ibuprofen or paracetamol to constrict the ductus; surgical or catheter closure if medical fails. Term infants and children - percutaneous device closure for haemodynamically significant PDA or to prevent endocarditis. Note: severe pulmonary hypertension (Eisenmenger) contraindicates closure - the shunt has already reversed.
rich_summaries.Pelvic inflammatory disease: Ascending infection of the female upper genital tract - endometrium, fallopian tubes, ovaries, and pelvic peritoneum. Causes: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are the classic pathogens; Mycoplasma genitalium is increasingly recognised; polymicrobial with anaerobes and endogenous flora in complicated cases. Clinical features: pelvic or lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia, abnormal vaginal discharge, intermenstrual or post-coital bleeding, fever, and cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness on examination. Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome adds perihepatitis with right upper quadrant pain. Ix: endocervical NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, consider Mycoplasma genitalium; HVS; pregnancy test (ectopic mimics); FBC, CRP, STI screen; pelvic ultrasound for tubo-ovarian abscess. Mx: low threshold to treat empirically. Outpatient regimen is ceftriaxone 500 mg IM stat plus doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days plus metronidazole 400 mg BD for 14 days. Inpatient IV for severe disease, pregnancy, TOA, or failed outpatient. Contact tracing and abstinence. Note: PID is a leading preventable cause of tubal infertility and chronic pelvic pain in Australia.
rich_summaries.Pelvic organ prolapse: Descent of one or more pelvic organs through the vaginal walls beyond their normal position. Types: cystocele (anterior, bladder), rectocele (posterior, rectum), enterocele (apical, small bowel), uterine, and vaginal vault after hysterectomy; staged 0 to IV by POP-Q. Risk factors: vaginal parity, age, menopause, obesity, chronic cough, constipation and heavy lifting. Clinical features: vaginal bulge sensation, pelvic pressure, splinting to void or defaecate, obstructive urinary symptoms, urinary or faecal incontinence, and dyspareunia. Ix: clinical examination supine and standing with Valsalva; urodynamics if considering surgery with urinary symptoms. Mx: lifestyle first - weight loss, treat cough and constipation, pelvic floor muscle training for stage 1 or 2. Pessary (ring or Gellhorn) for symptom relief in any stage. Surgery (native tissue repair, sacrocolpopexy, colpocleisis) for pessary failure. Note: vaginal mesh for prolapse has been withdrawn or restricted in Australia.
rich_summaries.Peptic ulcer disease: Mucosal break extending through the muscularis mucosae of the stomach or duodenum. Causes: Helicobacter pylori and NSAIDs account for nearly all of it, the latter by suppressing mucosal prostaglandins; gastrinoma is rare. Sx: epigastric burning pain. Duodenal ulcer eases with food and wakes the patient at night; gastric ulcer is provoked by eating and comes with weight loss. Complications: bleeding with haematemesis or melaena, perforation, gastric outlet obstruction, penetration into the pancreas. Ix: gastroscopy is definitive and every gastric ulcer is biopsied to exclude malignancy; urea breath test or faecal antigen for H. pylori, off proton pump inhibitor for two weeks. Mx: eradication where H. pylori is present, esomeprazole with amoxycillin and clarithromycin for seven days per eTG; stop the NSAID; endoscopic haemostasis for bleeding; surgery for perforation. Note: serology cannot separate current from past infection and must not be used to confirm eradication.
rich_summaries.Pericarditis: Inflammation of the pericardium. Causes: viral (Coxsackie, echovirus, adenovirus) is commonest; post-MI Dressler syndrome; uraemic; autoimmune (SLE, RA); bacterial (rare, including TB in endemic settings); malignant; and post-cardiac-surgery. Clinical features: sharp pleuritic retrosternal chest pain worse lying flat and relieved by sitting forward; friction rub is highly specific but intermittent. Look for pulsus paradoxus and raised JVP suggestive of tamponade. Ix: ECG evolves - stage 1 shows widespread concave ST-elevation with PR depression (PR elevation in aVR); troponin (raised in myopericarditis); FBC, CRP, EUC, creatinine, and echocardiogram (effusion, tamponade physiology); consider TFT, autoimmune screen, TB workup by phenotype. Mx: high-dose NSAID (ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily) or aspirin plus colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily for 3 months reduces recurrence. Treat the cause. Pericardiocentesis for tamponade or purulent pericarditis. Note: refractory or recurrent disease may need corticosteroids or IL-1 antagonists.
rich_summaries.Peripheral arterial disease: Atherosclerotic narrowing of the limb arteries, and a marker of systemic vascular risk as much as a limb problem. Clinical features: intermittent claudication, reproducible at a fixed distance and relieved by rest. Progression gives rest pain relieved by hanging the leg down, then ulceration and gangrene. Signs are absent pulses, hair loss, cool shiny skin and delayed capillary return. Ix: ankle-brachial index - below 0.9 is diagnostic, above 1.4 suggests incompressible calcified vessels and is unreliable, typically in diabetes or chronic kidney disease. Duplex ultrasound, then CT or MR angiography before intervention. Mx: supervised exercise therapy is first-line for claudication and outperforms most expectations. Stop smoking, antiplatelet, high-intensity statin, and tight glycaemic and blood pressure control. Revascularisation for chronic limb-threatening ischaemia or lifestyle-limiting symptoms that fail conservative care. Note: beta-blockers are not contraindicated, despite the persistent belief that they are.
rich_summaries.Peripheral artery disease: Atherosclerotic narrowing of arteries supplying the limbs (lower more than upper). Prevalence rises with age; shares risk factors with CAD - smoking (dominant), diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, CKD, age, male sex. Marker of systemic atherosclerosis - 5-year cardiovascular mortality around 20%. Clinical features: asymptomatic in half, intermittent claudication (reproducible calf, thigh or buttock pain on walking, relieved by rest), rest pain in critical limb ischaemia (worse lying, relieved by dependency), tissue loss, 6 Ps of acute limb ischaemia (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia), and Leriche syndrome (aortoiliac).Ix: ABPI under 0.9 diagnostic; over 1.4 suggests incompressible vessels (diabetes, CKD). Duplex ultrasound for anatomy; CTA or MRA before intervention. Mx: risk factor modification is transformative - smoking cessation, statin, clopidogrel, BP and glycaemic control; supervised exercise programme (best evidence for claudication); cilostazol for refractory claudication. Revascularisation for critical limb ischaemia or lifestyle-limiting claudication despite optimal therapy. Note: acute limb ischaemia is a surgical emergency.
rich_summaries.Peripheral neuropathy: Damage to peripheral nerves. Patterns are polyneuropathy (distal glove-and-stocking, most commonly diabetic), mononeuropathy (single nerve like median in CTS or common peroneal at the fibular head), mononeuritis multiplex (patchy involvement of multiple nerves in vasculitis, diabetes, HIV), and radiculopathy. Large-fibre involvement gives weakness and loss of proprioception with absent reflexes; small-fibre gives pain and autonomic features with preserved reflexes. Causes: diabetes is by far the commonest; also alcohol, B12 deficiency, thyroid disease, chronic kidney disease, monoclonal gammopathy, chemotherapy, amiodarone, HIV, hepatitis C, Guillain-Barre and CIDP, and hereditary (CMT). Clinical features: symmetrical distal paraesthesia, burning pain, numbness, weakness starting in toes and ascending; reduced ankle jerks and vibration sense early. Ix: HbA1c, FBC, EUC, LFT, TFT, B12, SPEP with free light chains, HIV, hepatitis C, ANA; nerve conduction studies and EMG. Mx: treat the cause. Neuropathic pain gets amitriptyline, gabapentin, pregabalin, or duloxetine (PBS-listed for diabetic neuropathy). Note: any rapid or asymmetric pattern warrants urgent neurology workup.
rich_summaries.Peritonitis: Inflammation of the peritoneum. Primary (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, SBP) occurs in ascites, usually cirrhotic - single-organism translocation, typically E. coli or Klebsiella. Secondary peritonitis follows loss of GI luminal integrity - perforated peptic ulcer, appendix, diverticulum, bowel or gallbladder; anastomotic leak; ischaemic bowel; abdominal trauma; PID. Tertiary is persistent inflammation after adequate treatment. Clinical features: severe generalised abdominal pain, systemic sepsis, guarding, rebound tenderness, silent abdomen, later shock. SBP presents insidiously in cirrhotics with worsening ascites, encephalopathy, subtle fever. Ix: FBC, EUC, LFT, lactate, coagulation, amylase or lipase, blood cultures; erect CXR for free gas; CT abdomen with IV contrast identifies source. Diagnostic paracentesis in ascites - SBP is neutrophils over 250/mm3. Mx: sepsis bundle with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. SBP gets ceftriaxone or piperacillin-tazobactam plus albumin. Secondary needs urgent surgical source control plus antibiotics. Note: cirrhotic patients with ascites and any deterioration need diagnostic paracentesis to exclude SBP.
rich_summaries.Peritonsillar abscess: Suppurative collection in the peritonsillar space between the tonsil capsule and the superior pharyngeal constrictor; the commonest deep neck space infection and usually a complication of acute tonsillitis. Aetiology: polymicrobial - group A Streptococcus plus oral anaerobes (Fusobacterium necrophorum, Prevotella). Clinical features: severe unilateral sore throat, odynophagia, trismus, muffled 'hot potato' voice, drooling, ipsilateral ear pain; uvular deviation away from the swelling with medial displacement of the tonsil. Ix: clinical diagnosis; intraoral ultrasound or CT with contrast if uncertain or if parapharyngeal extension suspected. Mx: drainage (needle aspiration or incision and drainage) is the definitive treatment plus IV antibiotics - benzylpenicillin plus metronidazole, or amoxicillin-clavulanate; single dose of dexamethasone reduces pain and trismus; analgesia and hydration; consider interval tonsillectomy for recurrent disease. Red flags: stridor, drooling with airway compromise, extension into parapharyngeal space or Lemierre syndrome (jugular thrombophlebitis, septic pulmonary emboli) mandate ENT and airway team involvement.
rich_summaries.Pernicious anaemia: Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells reducing intrinsic factor and causing cobalamin (B12) malabsorption; commonest cause of B12 deficiency in Australia. Epidemiology: peak 60-70, F>M, associated with autoimmune thyroid disease, vitiligo, T1DM and Addison. Clinical features: insidious fatigue, glossitis, lemon-tinge pallor; subacute combined degeneration of the cord (posterior column loss, spastic paraparesis) and peripheral neuropathy; cognitive impairment; long-standing disease raises gastric adenocarcinoma and carcinoid risk. Ix: macrocytic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils, low reticulocytes, raised LDH and bilirubin; low serum B12; anti-intrinsic-factor antibodies (specific, 60% sensitive) plus anti-parietal-cell antibodies (sensitive); gastroscopy if diagnosis unclear. Mx: IM hydroxocobalamin 1 mg alternate days for two weeks (or until neurological improvement plateaus), then 3-monthly for life; correct iron and folate; screen for other autoimmune disease. Note: never give folate alone in unexplained macrocytic anaemia - it can precipitate or worsen subacute combined degeneration.
rich_summaries.Pertussis: Bordetella pertussis infection (whooping cough), highly contagious, with disproportionate risk to young infants. Clinical features: three phases - catarrhal (1 to 2 weeks) is coryza and mild cough, the most infectious phase; paroxysmal (2 to 6 weeks) is characterised by paroxysmal coughing fits with inspiratory whoop, post-tussive vomiting and cyanosis; convalescent (weeks to months) is a lingering cough. Infants under 6 months may present with apnoea rather than whoop, and pneumonia and pulmonary hypertension carry the mortality. Ix: nasopharyngeal swab for pertussis PCR is the reference test; serology (anti-PT IgG) supports later diagnosis. Lymphocytosis on FBC. Mx: azithromycin (or clarithromycin) for 5 days is first line - reduces infectivity but has limited effect on symptoms once paroxysms are established. Post-exposure prophylaxis for household contacts of a young infant, pregnant women in third trimester, and healthcare workers with infant contact. Notifiable urgently. Note: dTpa in pregnancy (20 to 32 weeks) plus the NIP infant schedule keep infants protected.
rich_summaries.Peutz-Jeghers syndrome: Autosomal dominant STK11 (LKB1) mutation causing hamartomatous GI polyps and mucocutaneous pigmentation. Polyps commonest in small bowel; not premalignant themselves but syndrome carries markedly raised risk of multiple cancers. Clinical features: mucocutaneous melanotic macules on lips, buccal mucosa, fingers and toes in infancy (fade in adulthood except buccal); recurrent abdominal pain and intussusception from small-bowel polyps (commonest presentation); GI bleeding and iron deficiency anaemia; small-bowel obstruction. Raised cancer risk across GI (colon, small bowel, stomach, pancreas), breast (up to 45% lifetime), gynae (ovarian SCTAT, cervical adenoma malignum), testicular Sertoli cell in prepubertal boys. Ix: clinical diagnosis; genetic testing confirms and guides family cascade. Mx: polyp surveillance and removal from age 8 - capsule endoscopy plus upper endoscopy and colonoscopy every 2 to 3 years; cancer surveillance (annual breast MRI from 25, pancreatic MRI or EUS annually, cervical cytology, testicular examination). Note: consider PJS in a young patient with unexplained intussusception.
rich_summaries.Phaeochromocytoma: Catecholamine-secreting tumour of adrenal chromaffin cells; the extra-adrenal counterpart is a paraganglioma. Epidemiology: up to 40% are germline, so all patients are offered genetic testing - SDHx, VHL, RET and NF1. Clinical features: the classic triad is episodic headache, sweating and palpitations on a background of hypertension, though presentation is often just resistant or paroxysmal hypertension. Ix: plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary metanephrines, taken supine after 30 minutes rest. Locate with CT or MRI once biochemistry is positive, then functional imaging. Mx: alpha blockade with phenoxybenzamine or prazosin for 10-14 days first, adding a beta-blocker only afterwards, then surgical resection with an experienced anaesthetic team. Note: beta blockade before alpha blockade leaves unopposed alpha stimulation and can precipitate hypertensive crisis - the sequence is the exam point and the clinical one. Red flags: crisis can be triggered by anaesthesia, contrast or abdominal palpation.
rich_summaries.Pharyngitis: Inflammation of the pharynx and tonsils. Causes: viral in most (rhinovirus, adenovirus, EBV, influenza, coxsackievirus); group A streptococcus in 15 to 30% of paediatric cases and 5 to 10% of adults; less commonly gonorrhoea, Fusobacterium necrophorum (Lemierre syndrome), diphtheria. Clinical features: sore throat, fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, absence of cough; scarlatiniform rash or strawberry tongue in scarlet fever. Ix: use Centor or McIsaac score to risk-stratify - fever over 38, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, absence of cough, age 3 to 14. Score 4 or 5 warrants throat swab for GAS. In Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities with rheumatic fever risk, treat empirically without waiting. Mx: symptomatic with paracetamol and ibuprofen. GAS in Australia gets phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg BD for 10 days (or azithromycin for penicillin allergy) - the point is preventing rheumatic fever. Admit for peritonsillar abscess, airway compromise, or systemic illness. Note: EBV mononucleosis mimics strep - amoxicillin causes a rash in EBV, avoid.
rich_summaries.Pheochromocytoma: Catecholamine-secreting tumour of adrenal medulla chromaffin cells (extra-adrenal sympathetic paraganglia give paraganglioma). Rule of 10s: 10% extra-adrenal, 10% bilateral, 10% malignant, 10% familial, 10% in children - though familial fraction is now around 40% with expanded testing (MEN2, VHL, NF1, SDHx mutations). Clinical features: classic triad of episodic headache, palpitations and sweating; hypertension (paroxysmal or sustained); pallor, tremor, anxiety, sense of impending doom; triggers include beta-blockers alone, anaesthesia and abdominal palpation. Ix: 24-hour urinary or plasma fractionated metanephrines (higher sensitivity than catecholamines); CT or MRI adrenals to localise; MIBG or Ga-68 DOTATATE PET for extra-adrenal or metastatic disease; genetic testing in everyone. Mx: laparoscopic adrenalectomy is curative. Pre-op alpha blockade (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) for 10 to 14 days, then beta-blocker only after alpha block is established, plus liberal salt and fluid for volume expansion. Note: hypertensive crisis needs phentolamine or sodium nitroprusside - never beta-blocker alone.
rich_summaries.Pituitary adenoma: Benign monoclonal tumour of the anterior pituitary. Classification: functional (secretory) or non-functional; microadenoma (under 10 mm) or macroadenoma. Functional types include prolactinoma (commonest), GH (acromegaly), ACTH (Cushing disease), TSH (rare central hyperthyroidism), and gonadotrophinoma (usually silent). Clinical features reflect hormone excess by cell type - galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea and infertility in prolactinoma; coarse features, sweating, prognathism and carpal tunnel in acromegaly; central obesity, striae, hypertension and diabetes in Cushing. Mass effect gives bitemporal hemianopia, headache and hypopituitarism. Ix: pituitary MRI with dynamic contrast; hormone panel - prolactin (dilute if very high), morning cortisol and dexamethasone suppression, IGF-1 and OGTT for GH, TFT and gonadotrophins; formal visual fields. Mx: prolactinoma responds to dopamine agonist (cabergoline) - medical is first line even for macroprolactinoma. Trans-sphenoidal surgery for other functional adenomas and for compressive lesions. Radiotherapy for residual or refractory disease. Note: apoplexy - sudden headache, ophthalmoplegia and visual loss - is an emergency.
rich_summaries.Placenta accreta: Abnormal placental invasion into the myometrium; spectrum of accreta (into decidua basalis), increta (into myometrium), percreta (through to serosa or adjacent organs). Risk factors: previous caesarean (risk rises steeply with each), placenta praevia over a previous scar (classic high-risk pattern), previous uterine surgery (myomectomy, Asherman), advanced maternal age, multiparity, IVF. Clinical features: usually asymptomatic antenatally; suspected on imaging in high-risk pregnancy; catastrophic postpartum haemorrhage at delivery if unrecognised, with failed placental separation. Ix: greyscale and colour Doppler ultrasound at 20 weeks in any praevia over a scar - loss of retroplacental clear zone, placental lacunae, bladder-uterine interface abnormality. MRI for posterior placenta or uncertain ultrasound. Mx: refer to tertiary centre with obstetric, gynae-oncology, urology, IR, anaesthetics, haematology and neonatology capability. Planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34 to 36 weeks with placenta left in situ is standard. Ureteric stents, cross-matched blood, cell salvage. Note: unplanned delivery is the single biggest avoidable driver of morbidity.
rich_summaries.Placenta praevia: Placenta implanted in the lower uterine segment, covering or reaching the internal cervical os. Classification: placenta praevia covers the os; low-lying is within 2 cm but not covering. Risk factors: previous caesarean (risk rises with each), previous praevia, previous uterine surgery, multiple pregnancy, advanced maternal age, smoking, and assisted reproduction. Clinical features: painless bright-red vaginal bleeding in the second or third trimester, often without warning; uterus soft and non-tender, fetus usually stable; malpresentation is common. Ix: transvaginal ultrasound is safe and the reference standard; low-lying placentae at the 18 to 20 week scan are re-imaged at 32 weeks. Never perform a digital vaginal examination until praevia is excluded. Mx: expectant if stable and preterm; admit for significant bleeds, corticosteroids between 24 and 34 weeks, anti-D if Rh-negative, group and hold or crossmatch on presentation. Elective caesarean at 36 to 37 weeks for persistent praevia. Note: consider placenta accreta spectrum in any praevia over a previous caesarean scar - MRI and multidisciplinary planning.
rich_summaries.Placenta previa: Placenta implanted in the lower uterine segment, covering or reaching the internal cervical os. Classification: placenta previa covers the os; low-lying is within 2 cm but not covering. Risk factors: previous caesarean (risk rises with each), previous previa, previous uterine surgery, multiple pregnancy, advanced maternal age, smoking, and assisted reproduction. Clinical features: painless bright-red vaginal bleeding in the second or third trimester, often without warning; uterus soft and non-tender, fetus usually stable; malpresentation is common. Ix: transvaginal ultrasound is safe and the reference standard; low-lying placentae at the 18 to 20 week scan are re-imaged at 32 weeks. Never perform a digital vaginal examination until previa is excluded. Mx: expectant if stable and preterm; admit for significant bleeds, corticosteroids between 24 and 34 weeks, anti-D if Rh-negative, group and hold or crossmatch on presentation. Elective caesarean at 36 to 37 weeks for persistent previa. Note: consider placenta accreta spectrum in any previa over a previous caesarean scar - MRI and multidisciplinary planning.
rich_summaries.Placental abruption: Premature separation of a normally implanted placenta from the uterine wall, after 20 weeks. Risk factors: hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (commonest), abdominal trauma (MVA, intimate partner violence), cocaine and methamphetamine, smoking, previous abruption (recurrence 10 to 15%), polyhydramnios with rapid decompression, multiple pregnancy, and thrombophilia. Clinical features: painful vaginal bleeding, tender rigid uterus, fetal distress or demise; the uterus is often hypercontractile with high resting tone. Bleeding may be concealed - normal external loss does not exclude major abruption. Ix: FBC, coagulation and fibrinogen (falls early in DIC), group and crossmatch, Kleihauer if Rh-negative; continuous CTG; ultrasound has poor sensitivity. Mx: resuscitate - two large-bore IV lines, warmed crystalloid then blood products via massive-transfusion protocol; call obstetric team early. Deliver by caesarean for compromise; expedited vaginal delivery if labour is advanced and both stable. Anti-D if Rh-negative. Note: any pregnant woman with abdominal trauma needs at least 4 hours of CTG - abruption may present late.
rich_summaries.Pleural effusion: Fluid in the pleural space, separated into transudate and exudate by Light criteria. Criteria: exudate if pleural to serum protein exceeds 0.5, pleural to serum LDH exceeds 0.6, or pleural LDH exceeds two thirds the upper limit of normal serum LDH. Causes: transudate - heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypothyroidism; exudate - parapneumonic, malignancy, tuberculosis, pulmonary embolism, connective tissue disease, oesophageal rupture. Sx: dyspnoea and pleuritic pain, with a stony dull percussion note, reduced breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance at the base. Ix: erect chest radiograph blunts the costophrenic angle beyond about 200 mL; ultrasound-guided aspiration for protein, LDH, glucose, pH, cytology, MCS and adenosine deaminase. Mx: treat the cause; intercostal drain for a complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema; indwelling pleural catheter or talc pleurodesis for recurrent malignant effusion. Note: pleural pH below 7.2 in a parapneumonic effusion means it needs drainage, not more antibiotics.
rich_summaries.Pneumocystis pneumonia: Opportunistic fungal pneumonia caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii, an AIDS-defining illness. Affects the immunocompromised - HIV with CD4 under 200, organ or stem cell transplant recipients, high-dose prolonged steroids or biologics, haematological malignancy, primary immunodeficiency. Clinical features: insidious onset over weeks in HIV (more acute in non-HIV), progressive exertional dyspnoea and dry cough, low-grade fever, chest examination often normal despite hypoxia, desaturation on exertion is a key clue. Complications: respiratory failure, pneumothorax. Ix: CXR shows bilateral perihilar interstitial infiltrates (may be normal early); HRCT shows ground-glass opacification; ABG or exertional SpO2 shows hypoxia; raised LDH; sputum or BAL for PCR (most sensitive) or silver stain; HIV test in newly-diagnosed. Mx: high-dose IV or oral cotrimoxazole for 21 days; add corticosteroids (prednisolone 40 mg BD tapered) if PaO2 under 70 mmHg or A-a gradient over 35. Second-line - pentamidine, clindamycin plus primaquine, atovaquone. Prophylaxis with cotrimoxazole in HIV with CD4 under 200. Note: negative PCR essentially excludes.
rich_summaries.Pneumonia: Acute lower respiratory tract infection acquired outside hospital, with consolidation on imaging. Causes: Streptococcus pneumoniae most commonly; Haemophilus influenzae; Mycoplasma; Legionella; respiratory viruses. Clinical features: fever, productive cough, pleuritic pain, dyspnoea; bronchial breathing, focal crackles, dullness to percussion. Older patients may present only with confusion or a fall. Ix: chest X-ray; FBC, UEC, CRP; blood and sputum cultures if moderate to severe. Severity is scored with CORB or SMART-COP in Australia rather than CURB-65. Mx: per eTG - amoxicillin for mild disease, adding doxycycline for atypical cover; IV benzylpenicillin with doxycycline for moderate; ceftriaxone with azithromycin for severe. Review at 48 hours. Note: tropical northern Australia is the exception that changes management - Burkholderia pseudomallei (melioidosis) and Acinetobacter require meropenem-based cover in severe disease, so ask about location and wet-season exposure. Red flags: failure to improve by 48-72 hours suggests empyema, abscess, resistant organism or an obstructing lesion.
rich_summaries.Pneumothorax: Air in the pleural space. Types: primary spontaneous (tall thin young men, smoking, apical blebs); secondary spontaneous (COPD, asthma, cystic fibrosis, TB); traumatic; iatrogenic (central line, transbronchial biopsy, positive-pressure ventilation); and tension. Clinical features: sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea; reduced breath sounds, hyperresonance and reduced expansion on the affected side. Tension adds tracheal deviation, raised JVP, tachycardia and hypotension. Ix: erect chest radiograph confirms most; CT for occult pneumothorax after trauma or if plain film is equivocal; bedside ultrasound (absent lung sliding). Do not delay treatment for imaging in suspected tension. Mx: tension is a clinical diagnosis - immediate needle thoracostomy (second space midclavicular or fifth space anterior axillary), then intercostal catheter. Primary spontaneous under 2 cm and asymptomatic is observed with oxygen; larger or symptomatic gets needle aspiration or intercostal catheter. Secondary almost always needs a catheter. Note: no flying for at least 1 week after resolution; no diving ever after a pneumothorax.
rich_summaries.Polyarteritis nodosa: Necrotising vasculitis of medium-sized muscular arteries with no glomerulonephritis and no ANCA (distinguishes from ANCA-associated vasculitis). Associated with hepatitis B in around 30% - vaccination has cut incidence. Middle-aged adults; male predominance. Clinical features: systemic fever, weight loss and myalgia; skin (livedo reticularis, purpura, nodules, ulcers, digital infarcts); mononeuritis multiplex; renovascular hypertension; mesenteric ischaemia with post-prandial pain; cardiac ischaemia; orchitis. Lungs are spared. Ix: FBC (anaemia, leucocytosis), ESR and CRP raised, hepatitis B serology, ANCA (negative), urinalysis. Biopsy of clinically affected tissue (sural nerve, skin, muscle) is diagnostic. Mesenteric or renal angiography shows characteristic microaneurysms and beading. Mx: high-dose prednisolone plus cyclophosphamide for severe disease; methotrexate or azathioprine for maintenance. Hepatitis B-associated PAN gets antiviral therapy plus plasma exchange plus shorter steroid course. Note: untreated 5-year survival is under 15%.
rich_summaries.Polycystic ovary syndrome: Common endocrine disorder of hyperandrogenism and ovulatory dysfunction, diagnosed on the Rotterdam criteria - two of three: oligo-ovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovarian morphology. Pathophysiology: insulin resistance drives ovarian androgen production and lowers SHBG, raising free testosterone. Clinical features: oligomenorrhoea, hirsutism, acne, subfertility, acanthosis nigricans. Ix: testosterone and SHBG with free androgen index, LH and FSH, prolactin and TFTs to exclude mimics; 17-hydroxyprogesterone if androgens are markedly raised; oral glucose tolerance test. Ultrasound is not required if the other two criteria are met, and is not used within 8 years of menarche. Mx: weight management is first-line and improves every domain. Combined oral contraceptive for cycle control and hyperandrogenism; metformin for metabolic features; letrozole first-line for ovulation induction. Note: anovulatory cycles leave unopposed oestrogen, so endometrial protection matters - investigate cycles longer than 90 days.
rich_summaries.Polycythaemia vera: Myeloproliferative neoplasm with clonal expansion of erythroid, myeloid and megakaryocytic lineages. JAK2 V617F mutation in over 95%, JAK2 exon 12 in the rest. Peak age 60; slight male predominance. Clinical features: often asymptomatic and found on FBC; hyperviscosity (headache, dizziness, visual disturbance, tinnitus), aquagenic pruritus after warm shower, erythromelalgia, plethora and conjunctival suffusion, splenomegaly, arterial and venous thrombosis (including splanchnic and cerebral veins), haemorrhage from platelet dysfunction, and secondary gout.Ix: FBC (Hb over 165 male or 160 female, or Hct over 0.49 male or 0.48 female); JAK2 mutation testing; low erythropoietin (distinguishes from secondary polycythaemia); bone marrow biopsy for WHO criteria. Rule out secondary causes (smoking, sleep apnoea, high altitude, EPO-secreting tumour). Mx: aspirin 100 mg daily plus therapeutic venesection to target Hct under 0.45; cytoreduction with hydroxyurea for high-risk (age over 60 or prior thrombosis); ruxolitinib second line. Note: transformation to myelofibrosis or AML in around 10% at 15 years.
rich_summaries.Polymyalgia rheumatica: Inflammatory condition causing aching and morning stiffness of the shoulder and hip girdles and neck, without true weakness. Epidemiology: age over 50, peak 70s; women 3x more than men. Pathophysiology: inflames peri-articular structures, not muscle - hence normal CK and preserved strength. Clinical features: bilateral girdle ache, morning stiffness over 45 min; constitutional symptoms. Ix: raised ESR/CRP, normocytic anaemia; CK normal; RF and anti-CCP negative. Mx: prednisolone 12.5-25 mg daily, tapered over 12-24 months on symptoms not ESR; bone protection. Note: steroid response is dramatic and near-diagnostic - no substantial improvement within a week means another diagnosis. Red flags: headache, jaw claudication or visual symptoms mean giant cell arteritis - high-dose steroids same day.
rich_summaries.Polymyositis: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy causing symmetrical proximal weakness without the skin changes of dermatomyositis. Epidemiology: peak 30-60 yr, rare in children; women > men. Pathophysiology: CD8 T-cell cytotoxicity with endomysial inflammation - cell-mediated, unlike dermatomyositis. Clinical features: insidious proximal weakness of shoulder and hip girdles; dysphagia; no rash. Ix: CK markedly raised; ANA and anti-Jo-1; muscle biopsy shows endomysial infiltrate invading non-necrotic fibres. Differential: inclusion body myositis (older, asymmetric, distal - finger flexors and quadriceps - and steroid-unresponsive); immune-mediated necrotising myopathy including statin-associated anti-HMGCR; hypothyroid and drug-induced myopathy. Note: a diagnosis of exclusion, and diagnosed far more often than it occurs - asymmetric, distal or steroid-unresponsive weakness should prompt reconsideration.
rich_summaries.Portal hypertension: A hepatic venous pressure gradient above 5 mmHg, becoming clinically significant above 10 and the threshold for variceal bleeding above 12. Causes: classified by site. Prehepatic is portal vein thrombosis; hepatic is cirrhosis in most Australian practice, also schistosomiasis and nodular regenerative hyperplasia; posthepatic is Budd-Chiari or constrictive pericarditis. Clinical features: the consequences rather than the pressure - varices, ascites, splenomegaly with thrombocytopenia, caput medusae, and hepatic encephalopathy from portosystemic shunting. Ix: ultrasound with Doppler for flow direction and portal vein patency; gastroscopy for varices; ascitic tap with a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 11 g/L or more confirming portal origin. Mx: treat the cause, non-selective beta-blockade to lower the gradient, and manage each complication on its own terms. TIPS for refractory ascites or bleeding. Note: thrombocytopenia here reflects splenic sequestration, not marrow failure, and does not need treating on its own.
rich_summaries.Post-operative ileus: Transient inhibition of GI motility after surgery; near-universal after abdominal procedures and also after non-abdominal surgery. Pathophysiology: neurogenic (sympathetic inhibition), inflammatory (bowel handling releases cytokines), pharmacological (opioids), and metabolic (hypokalaemia). Normal recovery is small bowel by 24 hours, stomach by 48, colon by 72. Prolonged ileus persists past day 3 to 5 and delays discharge. Clinical features: abdominal distension, absent bowel sounds, nausea and vomiting, failure to pass flatus, intolerance of oral intake. Distinguish from mechanical obstruction (high-pitched sounds, colicky pain, imaging transition point). Ix: clinical diagnosis. EUC, FBC and CRP for sepsis or anastomotic leak; erect and supine abdominal X-ray shows dilated small and large bowel without transition point; CT abdomen if obstruction suspected or peritonism. Mx: NBM until bowel activity returns, IV fluids and electrolyte replacement, NG decompression if vomiting, minimise opioids (multimodal analgesia, TAP block, paracetamol, NSAIDs). Early mobilisation. Alvimopan shortens duration after bowel resection. Note: ERAS protocols cut incidence.
rich_summaries.Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis: Immune-complex nephritic syndrome following group A streptococcal infection - 1 to 3 weeks after pharyngitis or 3 to 6 weeks after skin infection (impetigo). Type III hypersensitivity depositing immune complexes in the glomerulus. Predominantly affects children; still important in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities where streptococcal skin disease is endemic. Clinical features: abrupt nephritic syndrome - haematuria (cola-coloured urine), hypertension, oliguria, peripheral and periorbital oedema, mild proteinuria. Ix: urinalysis with red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells; EUC; complement C3 low with C4 normal or slightly low (distinguishes from lupus and MPGN); ASO and anti-DNase B titres (anti-DNase B is more sensitive for skin infection). Renal biopsy only for atypical features or failure to resolve. Mx: supportive - salt and fluid restriction, loop diuretic for oedema, antihypertensive (calcium channel blocker or hydralazine). Penicillin for residual carriage. Prognosis is excellent in children (over 95% full recovery). Note: C3 normalises within 8 weeks - persistent low C3 warrants biopsy.
rich_summaries.Post-traumatic stress disorder: Persistent disturbance following exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence - experienced directly, witnessed, learned about happening to a close person, or repeated occupational exposure. Diagnosis: symptoms for at least one month across four DSM-5 clusters - intrusion (flashbacks, nightmares, memories); avoidance (of reminders, thoughts, feelings); negative alteration in cognition and mood (persistent negative beliefs, distorted blame, detachment, anhedonia); alteration in arousal (hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, irritability, sleep disturbance, reckless behaviour). Symptoms under one month are acute stress disorder. Ix: no confirmatory test; PCL-5 and CAPS-5 are structured tools; screen for depression, substance use, TBI and chronic pain. Mx: trauma-focused CBT and EMDR are first-line psychological therapies. Pharmacotherapy with SSRI (sertraline or paroxetine) or SNRI (venlafaxine) if therapy is unavailable, declined or inadequate. Prazosin for trauma-related nightmares. Avoid benzodiazepines - they worsen the course and impair therapy. Note: complex PTSD (from prolonged interpersonal trauma) needs longer phase-based therapy.
rich_summaries.Postpartum depression: Depressive episode arising within 12 months of delivery; onset within 4 weeks meets DSM-5 peripartum specifier. Distinct from baby blues (transient tearfulness days 2 to 5, self-limiting) and postpartum psychosis (florid psychotic features within weeks, psychiatric emergency). Risk factors: prior depression or PPD, prior anxiety, poor social support, adverse life events, obstetric complications, unplanned pregnancy, adolescent or advanced maternal age, gestational diabetes. Clinical features: standard depressive syndrome with peripartum-specific themes - intrusive thoughts of harm to the infant, difficulty bonding, feelings of failure. Ix: screen with Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) at antenatal visits and 6 to 12 weeks postnatal; PHQ-9 for severity. Assess suicide and infanticidal risk directly. Exclude thyroid dysfunction and anaemia. Mx: mild disease responds to psychological therapy (CBT, IPT); moderate to severe adds SSRI (sertraline preferred if breastfeeding). Admit for significant self-harm risk or psychosis; mother-and-baby unit preserves attachment. Note: PPD is the leading cause of maternal death in the first postnatal year in Australia - screen actively.
rich_summaries.Postpartum haemorrhage: Blood loss of at least 500 mL from the genital tract within 24 hours of birth (primary), or between 24 hours and 12 weeks postpartum (secondary). Major primary PPH is 1000 mL or more, or any loss with haemodynamic compromise. Causes: 4 Ts - Tone (uterine atony, 70 to 80%), Trauma (perineal, vaginal or cervical laceration, rupture), Tissue (retained placenta or membranes), Thrombin (coagulopathy). Secondary PPH is usually endometritis or retained products. Ix: FBC, coagulation, fibrinogen, group and crossmatch, VBG with lactate; ultrasound for retained products. Mx: bimanual uterine massage; two large-bore IV lines, warmed crystalloid then blood products via massive-transfusion protocol; empty the bladder; then uterotonics in sequence - IV oxytocin (bolus then infusion), IM ergometrine (avoid in hypertension), IM carboprost (avoid in asthma), misoprostol per rectum. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours reduces mortality. Escalate to intrauterine balloon tamponade, uterine artery embolisation, compression sutures or hysterectomy if bleeding continues. Note: active third-stage management with prophylactic oxytocin 10 units IM is the single most effective prevention.
rich_summaries.Pre-eclampsia: New hypertension after 20 weeks with evidence of maternal organ dysfunction or uteroplacental insufficiency. Proteinuria is supportive but no longer required. Pathophysiology: failed spiral artery remodelling gives placental ischaemia and release of antiangiogenic factors, producing systemic endothelial dysfunction. Clinical features: headache, visual disturbance, epigastric or right upper quadrant pain, oedema, hyperreflexia. Ix: BP, urine protein-creatinine ratio, FBC, EUC, LFT, urate, and fetal assessment with CTG and growth ultrasound. Mx: the only cure is delivery. Treat severe hypertension with labetalol, nifedipine or hydralazine; magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis and treatment; corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity before 34 weeks. Timing of birth balances maternal deterioration against prematurity. Note: aspirin from 12 weeks reduces recurrence in women at high risk, and calcium supplementation helps where dietary intake is low. Red flags: HELLP, eclampsia, abruption and pulmonary oedema.
rich_summaries.Preeclampsia: New hypertension after 20 weeks gestation with proteinuria or other end-organ involvement. Diagnosis: BP at least 140/90 on two occasions plus proteinuria (urinary PCR at least 30 mg/mmol) or maternal organ dysfunction (renal, hepatic, haematological, neurological) or uteroplacental dysfunction (IUGR). Risk factors are primiparity, previous pre-eclampsia, chronic hypertension, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, autoimmune disease, obesity, multiple pregnancy, assisted reproduction, and family history. Clinical features: often asymptomatic and picked up on routine antenatal BP. Severe disease is defined by BP at least 160/110, creatinine rise, transaminases at least twice normal, platelets under 100, pulmonary oedema, or neurological symptoms. Ix: FBC and film, EUC and urate, LFT, coagulation, urine PCR; CTG and fetal growth ultrasound. Mx: labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa for BP; magnesium sulfate for severe disease or eclampsia prevention; deliver at 37 weeks (or earlier if severe or fetal compromise). Note: low-dose aspirin from 12 to 16 weeks in women at moderate to high risk reduces recurrence.
rich_summaries.Preterm labor: Labour with regular uterine contractions and cervical change between 20 and 37 weeks gestation. Risk factors: previous preterm birth (the strongest predictor), short cervix on ultrasound, infection (bacterial vaginosis, UTI, chorioamnionitis), multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios, uterine anomaly, cervical surgery, smoking, and low socioeconomic status. Clinical features: regular painful contractions with cervical dilatation or effacement; spontaneous rupture of membranes may precede or accompany. Ix: sterile speculum for rupture (pooling, ferning); fetal fibronectin swab between 22 and 34 weeks helps rule out (negative FFN has strong NPV); transvaginal cervical length; MSU, HVS, CTG. Mx: transfer to a unit with appropriate neonatal capacity. Antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone 11.4 mg IM two doses 24 hours apart) between 24 and 34+6 weeks; tocolysis with nifedipine to buy time for steroids and transfer; magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection under 30 weeks; group B strep intrapartum prophylaxis. Note: progesterone or cervical cerclage for prevention in selected women with a previous preterm birth or short cervix.
rich_summaries.Primary biliary cholangitis: Autoimmune destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts (renamed from primary biliary cirrhosis in 2015). Middle-aged women (10:1). Associations: Sjogren, autoimmune thyroid, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis. Clinical features: often asymptomatic and picked up on cholestatic LFTs; fatigue and pruritus are the commonest symptoms; xanthelasma, hepatomegaly, jaundice in advanced disease; portal hypertension and cirrhosis in the later course; HCC risk once cirrhotic. Ix: cholestatic pattern (ALP and GGT raised disproportionate to ALT and AST); anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA-M2) positive in 95% and highly specific; raised IgM; liver biopsy only if diagnosis uncertain; ultrasound to exclude extrahepatic obstruction; MRCP if PSC is a differential. Mx: ursodeoxycholic acid 13 to 15 mg/kg first line, improves survival; obeticholic acid or fibrates for inadequate response; cholestyramine or rifampicin for pruritus; fat-soluble vitamin replacement; liver transplant for end-stage. Note: recurs in graft in around 25% but graft failure is uncommon.
rich_summaries.Primary hyperaldosteronism: Excess autonomous aldosterone secretion, the commonest cause of secondary hypertension. Types: bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (about 60%); aldosterone-producing adrenal adenoma (Conn syndrome, about 35%); rare familial and adrenal carcinoma. Clinical features: hypertension (often resistant to three or more agents), spontaneous or easily provoked hypokalaemia (about a quarter), and metabolic alkalosis; often asymptomatic. Cardiovascular risk exceeds matched essential hypertension. Ix: screen with morning aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) after correcting potassium and stopping interfering drugs (MRAs off 4 to 6 weeks; ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta blockers, diuretics off 2 weeks; verapamil OK). Confirm elevated ARR by non-suppression on saline infusion. Adrenal CT locates a nodule; adrenal venous sampling lateralises before surgery. Mx: laparoscopic unilateral adrenalectomy for adenoma. Bilateral hyperplasia and non-surgical candidates get mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone or eplerenone). Note: screen anyone with resistant hypertension, hypokalaemia on a diuretic, or an adrenal incidentaloma.
rich_summaries.Prolactinoma: The commonest functional pituitary adenoma; benign monoclonal tumour of lactotroph cells producing prolactin. Classification: microprolactinoma (under 10 mm) or macroprolactinoma (10 mm or more). Clinical features in women include amenorrhoea, oligomenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, and infertility (recognised earlier so smaller at diagnosis). In men there is reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, infertility, and gynaecomastia (recognised later). Macroprolactinoma adds mass effect - bitemporal hemianopia, headache, hypopituitarism from stalk compression. Both sexes develop reduced bone mineral density from secondary hypogonadism. Ix: fasting serum prolactin (usually well over 250 microg/L in prolactinoma; macroprolactinoma may need dilution to exclude hook effect); TFT and beta-hCG; pituitary MRI; formal visual fields. Anterior pituitary panel and DXA.
