Mx: dopamine agonist (cabergoline first line, bromocriptine alternative) - medical therapy is first line even in macroprolactinoma and often normalises prolactin and shrinks the tumour. Trans-sphenoidal surgery for medical failure or intolerance. Note: rule out drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia before prolactinoma workup.
rich_summaries.Prostate cancer: Adenocarcinoma of the prostate, usually peripheral zone, with a natural history slow enough that overtreatment is a real harm. Epidemiology: the commonest cancer in Australian men. Risk rises with age, family history and African ancestry. Clinical features: usually asymptomatic when localised. Lower urinary tract symptoms more often reflect benign hyperplasia. Bone pain suggests metastatic disease, which is characteristically sclerotic. Ix: PSA with digital rectal examination, then multiparametric MRI before biopsy, then transperineal biopsy. Grade with the ISUP grade group. Stage with PSMA PET where indicated. Mx: active surveillance for low-risk disease, which is the default rather than a compromise. Radical prostatectomy or radiotherapy for intermediate and high risk. Androgen deprivation for advanced disease, with an androgen receptor pathway inhibitor or docetaxel added up front in metastatic disease. Note: population PSA screening is not recommended in Australia; the discussion is individual and should cover overdiagnosis explicitly.
rich_summaries.Prosthetic valve disease: Complications of prosthetic heart valves. Types: mechanical (bileaflet St Jude commonest) are durable but need lifelong warfarin; bioprosthetic (bovine, porcine, or transcatheter) last 10 to 15 years but avoid long-term anticoagulation. Complications include valve thrombosis (mechanical on inadequate anticoagulation, new heart failure with muffled clicks), structural deterioration (bioprosthetic), prosthetic valve endocarditis (early under 60 days usually Staph, late resembles native IE), paravalvular leak, haemolysis, embolism and stroke, and anticoagulation bleeding.Ix: history and examination (muffled clicks are ominous); TTE with TOE if thrombosis or endocarditis suspected; fluoroscopy for mechanical leaflet motion; blood cultures x3 before antibiotics; FBC and haptoglobin; INR review. Mx: mechanical valves need lifelong warfarin (INR 2.5 to 3.5 mitral, 2.0 to 3.0 aortic). Thrombolysis or urgent surgery for valve thrombosis. Prosthetic IE needs prolonged IV antibiotics and often surgery. Note: DOACs are contraindicated with mechanical valves - only warfarin.
rich_summaries.Pseudogout: Arthropathy from calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition, formerly pseudogout. Epidemiology: strongly age-related, uncommon under 60. Clinical features: acute severe pain with overlying erythema, reduced range of movement, swelling and warmth. Differential: distinguished from acute gout by the joints involved - knee and wrist rather than first MTP - a longer duration of attacks, and more frequent systemic symptoms. Ix: aspiration shows positively birefringent rhomboid crystals, the mirror image of gout; chondrocalcinosis on X-ray is common with age and not diagnostic alone. Mx: NSAIDs, colchicine or intra-articular steroid. No equivalent of urate-lowering therapy exists. Note: look for a secondary cause if young or polyarticular - check ferritin, calcium, PTH and magnesium for haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism and hypomagnesaemia.
rich_summaries.Pseudohypoparathyroidism: PTH resistance rather than PTH deficiency; GNAS mutation with genomic imprinting so phenotype depends on parental origin. Types: PHP Ia (maternal GNAS - Albright hereditary osteodystrophy features plus multi-hormone resistance to PTH, TSH, gonadotropins, GHRH); PHP Ib (isolated PTH resistance, no AHO); PHP II (rare); pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism (paternal - AHO features, normal biochemistry). Biochemistry matches hypoparathyroidism (low calcium, high phosphate) but PTH is high. Clinical features: hypocalcaemia (paraesthesia, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, tetany, seizures); AHO phenotype in Ia - short stature, round facies, brachydactyly of 4th and 5th metacarpals, obesity, subcutaneous calcifications. Ix: corrected calcium, phosphate, PTH, 25-OH vitamin D, magnesium; TSH, LH, FSH, sex hormones to catch other resistances; genetic testing confirms. Mx: oral calcium and calcitriol to normalise calcium; treat coexisting hormone resistances. Note: PTH over-suppression is not a concern unlike in true hypoparathyroidism.
rich_summaries.Psoriasis: Chronic immune-mediated disease of accelerated keratinocyte turnover producing well-demarcated scaly plaques. Epidemiology: bimodal onset in the 20s and 50s; strongly genetic. Pathophysiology: an IL-23/Th17 axis shortens epidermal transit from about a month to days, giving parakeratosis and thick silvery scale. Clinical features: plaques on extensor surfaces, scalp and sacrum; Auspitz and Koebner signs; nail pitting. Variants: guttate, flexural, pustular, erythrodermic. Associations: psoriatic arthritis in up to 30%; metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease. Mx: topical corticosteroid with calcipotriol; phototherapy if extensive; methotrexate or acitretin; biologics per PBS. Note: ask about joints at every review - psoriatic arthritis is erosive and skin usually precedes it by years. Avoid systemic steroids, which risk pustular rebound on withdrawal.
rich_summaries.Puerperal sepsis: Sepsis from the genital tract within 42 days of childbirth, miscarriage or abortion; a leading cause of maternal mortality. Common pathogens are group A streptococcus (most virulent), E. coli, group B streptococcus, anaerobes, Staph aureus, and polymicrobial infection. Sources are endometritis (commonest), wound infection, mastitis, UTI, and retained products of conception. Risk factors include prolonged rupture of membranes, prolonged labour, multiple vaginal examinations, caesarean, retained products, obesity, diabetes, and anaemia. Clinical features: fever, tachycardia, offensive lochia, uterine tenderness, wound erythema, hypotension. GAS may present with minimal local signs but profound shock. Ix: FBC, CRP, EUC, LFT, lactate, coagulation; blood cultures and high-vaginal swab; pelvic ultrasound for retained products or abscess. Mx: hour-1 sepsis bundle. Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics per eTG (amoxicillin plus clavulanate plus gentamicin, or piperacillin-tazobactam); add clindamycin if GAS suspected. Evacuate retained products. Surgical debridement or hysterectomy for necrotising infection. Note: postpartum women compensate well until they crash.
rich_summaries.Pulmonary embolism: Occlusion of pulmonary arteries by thrombus, usually embolised from a deep vein thrombosis of the lower limb or pelvis. Clinical features: dyspnoea and pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, tachypnoea, hypoxaemia; haemoptysis, syncope, or signs of DVT. Presentation is frequently non-specific, which is why a structured probability assessment matters more than clinical impression. Ix: apply Wells or revised Geneva first. Low probability with a negative D-dimer excludes PE; otherwise CT pulmonary angiography, or V/Q in pregnancy or renal impairment. ECG usually shows sinus tachycardia, S1Q3T3 being uncommon. Mx: anticoagulate on suspicion where imaging is delayed. A DOAC is first-line; low molecular weight heparin in pregnancy and cancer. Thrombolysis for massive PE. Duration 3 months if provoked, longer if unprovoked or recurrent. Note: D-dimer is useful only to rule out, and only when pretest probability is low - ordering it in a high-probability patient cannot change management and delays imaging. Red flags: hypotension or arrest means massive PE - consider immediate thrombolysis.
rich_summaries.Pulmonary hypertension: Mean pulmonary arterial pressure at least 20 mmHg at rest on right heart catheter. Five WHO groups by aetiology: group 1 pulmonary arterial hypertension (idiopathic, heritable, drug-induced, connective tissue disease, HIV, portal hypertension, congenital heart disease); group 2 left heart disease (commonest); group 3 lung disease or hypoxia (COPD, ILD, sleep apnoea); group 4 chronic thromboembolic PH; group 5 multifactorial. Clinical features: exertional dyspnoea and fatigue, syncope, chest pain, and features of right heart failure - raised JVP, right ventricular heave, loud P2, tricuspid regurgitation, hepatomegaly, ascites and peripheral oedema. Ix: 12-lead ECG (right axis, RV strain), CXR, BNP, transthoracic echo (estimates PAP), 6-minute walk, V/Q scan (to screen for CTEPH), and PFT. Right heart catheterisation confirms. Mx: treat the cause. Group 2 and 3 - optimise underlying disease. Group 1 gets targeted therapy (endothelin receptor antagonists, PDE5 inhibitors, prostanoids, riociguat), by risk stratification. Group 4 - pulmonary endarterectomy is potentially curative. Note: any new PAH diagnosis needs specialist PH-centre care.
rich_summaries.Pulmonary oedema: Accumulation of fluid in the pulmonary interstitium and alveoli. Types: cardiogenic from raised pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (LV dysfunction, valvular disease, ACS, arrhythmia, hypertensive crisis, volume overload) or non-cardiogenic from increased permeability (ARDS, TRALI, aspiration, neurogenic). Clinical features: severe dyspnoea, orthopnoea, pink frothy sputum in cardiogenic; bilateral fine crackles, raised JVP and third heart sound support cardiogenic. Ix: ECG for ischaemia or arrhythmia, CXR (bilateral perihilar infiltrates, Kerley B lines, cardiomegaly in cardiogenic), BNP or NT-proBNP, troponin, EUC, ABG, bedside echo. Mx: cardiogenic gets upright positioning, high-flow oxygen, non-invasive ventilation if hypoxic, IV furosemide 40 to 80 mg, and nitrates if BP allows. Treat the precipitant and avoid morphine (raises mortality). Non-cardiogenic disease needs treatment of the underlying cause and lung-protective ventilation. Note: monitor for hypokalaemia after aggressive diuresis.
rich_summaries.Pulmonary stenosis: Obstruction to right ventricular outflow at subvalvular, valvular or supravalvular level. Valvular is commonest and usually congenital - isolated in most, syndromic in Noonan, Williams, congenital rubella, or Alagille syndromes; also part of tetralogy of Fallot. Acquired causes are rheumatic and carcinoid. Clinical features: mild is asymptomatic; moderate to severe gives exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, chest pain, and syncope; right heart failure and cyanosis in critical cases; ejection systolic murmur at left upper sternal edge that radiates to the back, with an ejection click that softens on inspiration (unlike aortic click); wide split S2 with soft P2. Ix: ECG shows RVH and right axis; CXR shows prominent pulmonary artery from post-stenotic dilatation; echocardiogram is diagnostic and grades gradient. Mx: mild stenosis (gradient under 40 mmHg) is observed. Moderate to severe (gradient over 40 mmHg) or symptomatic gets balloon valvuloplasty (first line for valvular stenosis, success over 90%). Surgical valvotomy or replacement for dysplastic valves and subvalvular or supravalvular disease. Note: neonatal critical PS is duct-dependent - start prostaglandin E1.
rich_summaries.Pyelonephritis: Upper urinary tract infection involving renal parenchyma. Most cases are ascending from the lower tract - E. coli in 80%, then Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterococcus, Staph saprophyticus in young women. Risk factors: female sex, sexual activity, pregnancy, urinary obstruction (stones, BPH), diabetes, immunosuppression, vesicoureteric reflux, recent instrumentation. Clinical features: fever, rigors, flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, nausea and vomiting, plus lower tract symptoms (dysuria, frequency, urgency). Systemic upset distinguishes from cystitis. Ix: urinalysis, mid-stream urine culture before antibiotics; FBC, EUC, CRP, blood cultures; renal ultrasound or non-contrast CT KUB for obstruction or abscess. Mx: outpatient for mild - amoxicillin plus clavulanate 875/125 mg BD for 10 to 14 days per eTG. Inpatient IV for sepsis, pregnancy, vomiting, or urinary obstruction - IV gentamicin plus amoxicillin, or ceftriaxone. Percutaneous nephrostomy or ureteric stenting for obstructed infected kidney. Note: repeat imaging after severe or recurrent pyelonephritis to exclude structural cause.
rich_summaries.Pyloric stenosis: Hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle causing gastric outlet obstruction; the commonest surgical cause of vomiting in infants. Epidemiology: 4 to 1 male to female, first-born males, positive family history, presents at 2 to 8 weeks (peak 4 to 6 weeks). Clinical features: projectile non-bilious vomiting immediately after feeds; the infant remains hungry and feeds vigorously between vomits; visible peristalsis across the epigastrium; palpable olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. Weight loss, dehydration and failure to thrive follow. Ix: VBG classically shows hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (from HCl loss in vomit); paradoxical aciduria late. Abdominal ultrasound is definitive - pyloric muscle thickness at least 3 mm and length at least 15 mm. Mx: correct fluid and electrolyte deficit first - 0.9% saline with added potassium once urine output is established, targeting normal chloride, bicarbonate and potassium before surgery. Definitive treatment is Ramstedt pyloromyotomy (open or laparoscopic). Feeding resumes within 6 hours postoperatively. Note: never operate on the alkalosis - anaesthesia in an unresuscitated infant risks apnoea.
rich_summaries.Pyoderma gangrenosum: Neutrophilic dermatosis of rapidly expanding painful ulcers with violaceous undermined edges; diagnosis of exclusion after infection, malignancy and vasculitis. Associations: inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn and UC), rheumatoid arthritis, haematological malignancy (AML, MDS, myeloma) and monoclonal gammopathy; a third are idiopathic. Clinical features: tender papule or pustule breaks down into a deep ulcer with violaceous overhanging border and purulent base (commonest on shins); pathergy - worsening after trauma or surgery - is the discriminator; variants include bullous (haematological), pustular (IBD) and peristomal. Ix: edge biopsy shows neutrophil-rich infiltrate without vasculitis; swab and screening bloods exclude mimics; look for an associated condition. Mx: potent topical corticosteroid or tacrolimus for small lesions, systemic prednisolone (0.5-1 mg/kg/day) or ciclosporin for extensive disease; TNF-alpha inhibitor (infliximab, adalimumab) if refractory or IBD coexists, plus non-adherent dressings and analgesia - avoid debridement (pathergy). Note: an enlarging leg ulcer with a violaceous overhanging edge and disproportionate pain deserves biopsy before debridement.
rich_summaries.Q fever: Zoonotic infection with Coxiella burnetii, an intracellular gram-negative bacterium. Reservoir in cattle, sheep, goats and kangaroos (Australia has unusually high wildlife reservoir). Transmission by inhalation of aerosolised bacteria from birth products, urine, faeces, contaminated wool or hides. Occupational risk in abattoir workers, farmers, shearers, vets. Clinical features: asymptomatic in half; acute Q fever gives a flu-like illness with high fever, retro-orbital headache, myalgia, atypical pneumonia, or granulomatous hepatitis; chronic Q fever (under 5%) presents months to years later with culture-negative endocarditis (aortic valve, prior valvulopathy), osteomyelitis, or vascular graft infection; post-Q fever fatigue syndrome in 10 to 20%. Ix: serology is standard - phase II antibodies rise in acute, phase I in chronic; PCR positive early; blood cultures negative; echocardiogram if endocarditis suspected. Notifiable. Mx: acute - doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days; chronic Q fever endocarditis needs doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine for at least 18 months. Prevention - Q-VAX vaccine for at-risk workers (screen first). Note: vegetations often too small for TTE - TOE needed.
rich_summaries.Ramsay Hunt syndrome: Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve, giving zoster in the ear with facial nerve palsy. Clinical features: the classic triad is severe unilateral otalgia, a vesicular rash in the external auditory canal or on the pinna (Hunt sign), and lower motor neuron facial palsy. Additional cranial nerve involvement gives sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo (CN VIII), and altered taste (chorda tympani). Severity of facial palsy is worse than Bell palsy and prognosis less complete. Ix: clinical in typical disease; VZV PCR of a vesicle swab if diagnosis uncertain or the patient is immunocompromised; pure-tone audiometry for hearing loss. Mx: oral valaciclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 to 10 days plus prednisolone 60 mg tapered over 2 weeks, both started within 72 hours of onset for the best chance of recovery. Eye care with lubricants and taping at night to protect the exposed cornea. Analgesia. ENT and audiology referral. Note: partial recovery of facial function is the rule; complete recovery in around half if treated early, fewer if treated late.
rich_summaries.Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis: Nephritic syndrome with rapid loss of renal function over days to weeks and crescents on renal biopsy. Types by immunofluorescence: type I anti-GBM (Goodpasture; linear IgG); type II immune complex (post-infectious GN, lupus nephritis, IgA nephropathy, cryoglobulinaemia, endocarditis; granular deposits); type III pauci-immune (ANCA-associated vasculitis - GPA, MPA, EGPA; commonest type in adults). Clinical features: haematuria with dysmorphic red cells and casts, sub-nephrotic proteinuria, hypertension, oliguria, rising creatinine over days to weeks; systemic features by cause (haemoptysis in anti-GBM, sinusitis and lung nodules in GPA, malar rash in lupus). Ix: urinalysis and urine microscopy; EUC; serology (ANA, anti-dsDNA, complement, ANCA, anti-GBM, cryoglobulins, hepatitis serology, blood cultures); urgent renal biopsy is essential. Mx: high-dose corticosteroids plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab; plasma exchange for anti-GBM and severe ANCA vasculitis; treat any underlying infection. Note: delay of days changes outcome - biopsy on the day of admission.
rich_summaries.Raynaud phenomenon: Vasospasm of digital arterioles in response to cold or emotional stress, giving triphasic colour change - white (vasospasm), blue (deoxygenation), red (reactive hyperaemia). Primary Raynaud is idiopathic (younger women, symmetrical, no underlying disease, benign). Secondary Raynaud reflects an underlying disorder - systemic sclerosis, SLE, mixed connective tissue disease, Sjogren, dermatomyositis, cryoglobulinaemia, vibration white finger, hypothyroidism, drugs (beta blockers, ergot, cocaine). Clinical features: episodic pallor and cyanosis of fingers, sometimes toes, ears, nose; pain and paraesthesia during attack. Nailfold capillary changes and digital ulcers or gangrene point to secondary disease. Ix: ANA, ENA panel including anti-centromere and anti-Scl-70; nailfold capillaroscopy; TFT. Mx: general - warm hands and body, avoid vasoconstrictor drugs and nicotine. Nifedipine (or amlodipine) first line pharmacological; second line sildenafil or losartan; iloprost infusion for critical digital ischaemia. Treat the underlying disease in secondary. Note: digital ulcers and asymmetric onset warrant prompt rheumatology referral.
rich_summaries.Reactive arthritis: Aseptic arthritis triggered by a remote infection, typically 1 to 4 weeks after a GI or genitourinary infection. Triggers: post-enteric (Salmonella, Campylobacter, Yersinia, Shigella) or post-venereal (Chlamydia trachomatis, the commonest STI trigger). HLA-B27 positive in up to 80% and predicts severity. Clinical features: asymmetric oligoarthritis of lower limb large joints (knee, ankle), enthesitis (Achilles, plantar fasciitis), dactylitis. Extra-articular features are conjunctivitis or anterior uveitis, sterile urethritis, circinate balanitis, keratoderma blennorrhagicum, and oral ulcers. The arthritis-urethritis-conjunctivitis triad (historically Reiter) captures the pattern. Ix: FBC, CRP, ESR; joint aspirate (sterile, distinguishes from septic arthritis); stool MCS, chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT, HIV and syphilis screen; HLA-B27; ANA and RF (negative). Mx: treat the triggering infection if still present (doxycycline for chlamydia). NSAIDs first line; intra-articular corticosteroid for flare. Sulfasalazine or methotrexate for persistent arthritis over 6 months; anti-TNF for refractory. Note: most resolve within 6 to 12 months; 20% become chronic.
rich_summaries.Refeeding syndrome: Metabolic collapse from reintroducing carbohydrate to a chronically undernourished patient; insulin surge drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium intracellularly, precipitating arrhythmia, cardiac failure and neurological compromise. High risk (NICE): BMI under 16, weight loss over 15% in 3-6 months, negligible intake over 10 days, or prefeeding low phosphate, potassium or magnesium; anorexia nervosa, alcohol use disorder and prolonged postoperative starvation are the recurring settings. Clinical features: within 72 hours of feeding - arrhythmia, cardiac failure, weakness, rhabdomyolysis, seizures, delirium, Wernicke encephalopathy, oedema. Mx: parenteral thiamine 200-300 mg daily for 3 days plus vitamin B complex before any calories; start 5-10 kcal/kg/day (high risk) or 10-20 (moderate) and advance over 4-7 days; replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium proactively; restrict fluid; daily bloods and cardiac monitoring in high risk. Note: thiamine before glucose - loading carbohydrate into a thiamine-deficient patient precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy.
rich_summaries.Renal cell carcinoma: Renal tubular epithelial malignancy; 3% of adult cancers, M>F, peak 60-70; clear cell is the commonest histology (75%). Risk factors: smoking, obesity, hypertension and ESKD with acquired cystic disease; hereditary syndromes include VHL, hereditary papillary RCC and tuberous sclerosis. Clinical features: increasingly picked up incidentally; classical triad of haematuria, flank pain and palpable mass in under 10% implies advanced disease; left varicocele from renal-vein occlusion; paraneoplastic (polycythaemia, hypercalcaemia, Stauffer hepatic dysfunction); lung, bone, liver and brain mets. Ix: contrast CT of abdomen and pelvis characterises and stages (look for renal-vein and IVC tumour thrombus); CT chest; biopsy for small masses or systemic-therapy candidates. Mx: partial nephrectomy for T1a (under 7 cm) or solitary kidney; radical nephrectomy for larger localised disease; active surveillance for small masses in older patients; targeted therapy (sunitinib) plus checkpoint inhibitor for metastatic disease; RCC is chemo- and radioresistant. Note: RCC often has no urinary symptoms - an incidental renal mass over 4 cm needs urology referral.
rich_summaries.Respiratory failure: Inadequate gas exchange. Type 1 (hypoxaemic) is PaO2 under 60 mmHg with normal or low PaCO2. Causes include V/Q mismatch (pneumonia, PE, ARDS, pulmonary oedema, asthma), shunt (ASD, hepatopulmonary syndrome, pulmonary AVM), and diffusion limitation (interstitial lung disease). Type 2 (hypercapnic) is PaO2 under 60 mmHg with PaCO2 over 45 mmHg. Causes are anything reducing minute ventilation - COPD, neuromuscular disease (Guillain-Barre, myasthenia, MND), chest wall (kyphoscoliosis, obesity hypoventilation), CNS depression, severe asthma. Clinical features: dyspnoea, tachypnoea, accessory muscle use, cyanosis, altered mental state; asterixis, bounding pulse, headache and papilloedema in hypercapnia. Ix: ABG confirms type and severity; CXR and imaging by cause; ECG, troponin, D-dimer for cardiac and thromboembolic workup. Mx: address the cause. Oxygen to target SpO2 94 to 98% (or 88 to 92% with COPD or hypercapnic risk). BiPAP for type 2 with acidosis, CPAP for cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Invasive ventilation for NIV failure, reduced GCS, or exhaustion. Note: rising CO2 in an asthma exacerbation on treatment is peri-arrest.
rich_summaries.Retinopathy of prematurity: Proliferative retinal vasculopathy of preterm infants from disordered postnatal retinal angiogenesis; leading preventable cause of childhood blindness. Risk factors: gestational age under 32 weeks or birthweight under 1500 g; prolonged supplemental oxygen with fluctuating SpO2, sepsis and poor postnatal growth. Pathophysiology: phase 1 vaso-obliteration from relative hyperoxia, then phase 2 VEGF-driven neovascularisation as the maturing retina outstrips its blood supply. Classification: staged 1-5 (demarcation line to total retinal detachment) and zoned I-III (posterior to peripheral); 'plus disease' - dilated tortuous posterior vessels - is a treatment threshold. Screening: dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy from 4-6 weeks (or 31 weeks corrected) for infants under 31 weeks or 1250 g, repeated 1-2 weekly until vascularisation completes. Mx: laser photocoagulation of avascular retina is standard; intravitreal anti-VEGF for zone I or aggressive posterior disease, with longer follow-up for late reactivation; vitrectomy for detachment. Note: SpO2 target 90-95%, not higher - SUPPORT and BOOST-II show lower targets reduce severe ROP without harming survival.
rich_summaries.Retropharyngeal abscess: Suppurative collection in the retropharyngeal space. Epidemiology: children under 5 predominantly - retropharyngeal nodes regress by that age, infection tracks from URTI or otitis-related lymphadenitis; in adults follows penetrating trauma or extension from vertebral osteomyelitis. Group A Streptococcus, Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) and oral anaerobes; often polymicrobial. Clinical features: fever, neck pain and stiffness, dysphagia and drooling, muffled 'hot potato' voice, torticollis with extended neck, trismus; stridor is late and signals impending airway loss. Complications: extension via the 'danger space' to the mediastinum (descending necrotising mediastinitis), Lemierre syndrome. Ix: lateral neck X-ray shows prevertebral widening (over 7 mm at C2, over 14 mm at C6 in adults); CT neck with contrast is gold standard. Mx: airway takes priority (senior anaesthetic input, ready to intubate or tracheostomy); IV antibiotics per eTG - amoxicillin-clavulanate, or clindamycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin if severe, plus vancomycin for MRSA risk; ENT-led drainage. Red flags: stridor, tripod posture or drooling mandate airway control before imaging.
rich_summaries.Rhabdomyolysis: Skeletal muscle breakdown releasing myoglobin, potassium, phosphate and creatine kinase into the circulation. Causes: crush injury, a long lie after a fall, seizures, extreme exertion, statins, alcohol, psychostimulants, heat stroke, neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Sx: myalgia, weakness and dark cola-coloured urine, though the full triad appears in a minority. Ix: creatine kinase above five times the upper limit confirms it; urine dipstick positive for blood with no red cells on microscopy; follow potassium, phosphate, calcium, urate and creatinine. Mx: early high-volume 0.9% sodium chloride titrated to urine output above 1 to 2 mL/kg/hour; treat hyperkalaemia; dialysis for refractory acidosis, hyperkalaemia or oliguric acute kidney injury. Note: early hypocalcaemia reflects calcium deposition in damaged muscle and rebounds during recovery, so leave it alone unless symptomatic.
rich_summaries.Rheumatic fever: Immune-mediated sequela of group A streptococcal pharyngitis, still endemic in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities in northern Australia. Diagnosis: revised Jones criteria - evidence of preceding GAS infection (throat swab, ASO or anti-DNase B) plus two major criteria, or one major and two minor. Major criteria are carditis (pancarditis, mitral regurgitation commonest), polyarthritis (large joint, migratory), Sydenham chorea, subcutaneous nodules and erythema marginatum. Minor criteria are fever, arthralgia, raised CRP or ESR, and prolonged PR interval. Ix: throat swab and ASO or anti-DNase B; FBC, CRP, ESR; ECG; echocardiogram is mandatory to detect subclinical carditis in every suspected case. Mx: benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units IM stat to eradicate residual GAS. Aspirin or naproxen for arthritis; prednisolone for severe carditis; carbamazepine or valproate for chorea. Secondary prophylaxis with monthly benzathine benzylpenicillin IM for at least 10 years, longer with carditis or valve disease. Notifiable in Australian jurisdictions running control programs. Note: RHD Australia coordinates registry and prophylaxis.
rich_summaries.Rheumatic heart disease: Chronic valve damage following acute rheumatic fever, and in Australia a disease of profound inequity - rates among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are among the highest reported anywhere. Pathophysiology: molecular mimicry between group A streptococcal M protein and cardiac tissue drives autoimmune valvulitis. Clinical features: the mitral valve is affected most often, then aortic. Mitral stenosis gives exertional dyspnoea, atrial fibrillation and haemoptysis; regurgitation gives volume overload and heart failure. Ix: echocardiography defines and grades it, and detects subclinical disease in screening programs. ECG, and ASOT or anti-DNase B if acute rheumatic fever is suspected. Mx: secondary prophylaxis with benzathine benzylpenicillin G every 28 days is the single most important intervention and continues for years. Manage the valve lesion medically, then repair or replace. Register the patient with the state RHD control program. Note: acute rheumatic fever is notifiable, and diagnosis uses the Australian criteria, which differ from Jones in high-risk groups.
rich_summaries.Rheumatoid arthritis: Chronic symmetrical inflammatory polyarthritis of small joints with an erosive synovitis and systemic features. Epidemiology: onset 30-50 yr; women 3x more than men; smoking is the strongest modifiable risk. Pathophysiology: citrullinated self-proteins drive anti-CCP; synovial pannus releases proteases and RANKL, eroding bone. Clinical features: symmetrical MCP, PIP, wrist and MTP swelling; morning stiffness over an hour, easing with use; DIPs spared. Extra-articular: nodules, ILD, scleritis. Ix: anti-CCP (more specific, predicts erosions), RF, raised ESR/CRP; X-ray periarticular osteopenia and marginal erosions. Mx: methotrexate within weeks of diagnosis, treat-to-target to remission; escalate to biologic or JAK inhibitor per PBS; steroids only to bridge. Note: the window to prevent erosions is months - suspected inflammatory arthritis needs urgent referral, not a trial of NSAIDs.
rich_summaries.Rickets: The childhood counterpart of osteomalacia: defective mineralisation at the growth plate, so the deformity is of growing bone rather than only of bone strength. Causes: nutritional vitamin D deficiency is commonest, particularly in exclusively breastfed infants without supplementation, with dark skin or limited sun exposure. Also X-linked hypophosphataemic and vitamin D-dependent forms. Clinical features: frontal bossing, rachitic rosary, wrist and ankle widening, bowing of the legs once weight-bearing, and delayed milestones. Hypocalcaemic seizures in infancy. Ix: wrist radiograph showing metaphyseal cupping, splaying and fraying, with the same biochemistry as osteomalacia. Mx: colecalciferol with adequate dietary calcium, treating the mother too if the infant is breastfed. Phosphate and calcitriol for hypophosphataemic forms, or burosumab in selected cases. Note: deformity in a young child largely remodels once biochemistry is corrected.
rich_summaries.Rosacea: Chronic inflammatory facial skin condition of unknown aetiology, peaks 30 to 50 years, commoner in fair skin (Fitzpatrick I-II). Subtypes: erythematotelangiectatic (persistent central facial erythema with flushing and telangiectasia), papulopustular (acne-like papules and pustules without comedones), phymatous (skin thickening and nodularity, rhinophyma), and ocular (dry eyes, blepharitis, conjunctivitis, keratitis). Triggers: heat, sunlight, alcohol, spicy food, hot drinks, stress, wind, cosmetics. Ix: clinical diagnosis. Exclude lupus, seborrhoeic dermatitis, steroid-induced rosacea. Mx: identify and avoid triggers; daily broad-spectrum sunscreen; gentle skin care. Erythematotelangiectatic gets topical brimonidine or oxymetazoline for flushing, pulsed dye laser or IPL for telangiectasia. Papulopustular gets topical metronidazole, ivermectin or azelaic acid; oral doxycycline 40 to 100 mg daily for moderate to severe or refractory disease. Phymatous - isotretinoin, laser resurfacing or surgery. Ocular - lid hygiene, artificial tears, ophthalmology referral. Note: topical corticosteroids exacerbate rosacea - do not use.
rich_summaries.Rotavirus: Double-stranded RNA virus of the Reoviridae family; leading cause of severe dehydrating gastroenteritis in children worldwide (before vaccination, responsible for half a million deaths a year). Australian burden dramatically reduced since RV1 (Rotarix) added to the NIP in 2007. Peaks in winter and spring. Faecal-oral transmission with very low infectious dose; incubation 1 to 3 days. Clinical features: sudden-onset fever, vomiting (24 to 48 hours), then profuse watery non-bloody diarrhoea for 5 to 8 days; dehydration is the main danger, especially under 2 years. Extraintestinal features rare (seizures, transaminitis). Ix: clinical diagnosis in typical cases; stool antigen or PCR when confirmation matters (outbreaks, hospitalised, immunocompromised). Notifiable in most states. Mx: oral rehydration solution (hydralyte, gastrolyte) is first line - small frequent sips; nasogastric fluid if oral fails; IV fluid for severe dehydration or shock. Ondansetron single dose in ED reduces admissions. Continue breastfeeding. No antibiotics. Note: vaccine must be given by 6 months (first dose) and 24 weeks (second) - live vaccine with small intussusception risk.
rich_summaries.Rubella: Togavirus infection, usually a mild childhood exanthem; matters because of congenital rubella syndrome. Clinical features: prodrome of low-grade fever with tender posterior cervical and suboccipital lymphadenopathy, then a fine pink maculopapular rash starting on the face and spreading down over 24 hours, fading in the same order. Arthralgia is common in adults, particularly women. Up to half of infections are subclinical. Ix: rubella IgM and rising IgG, or PCR of throat or urine within the first week of rash; confirm on serology in pregnancy rather than clinically. Mx: supportive; isolate for 7 days after rash onset and keep away from pregnant women. Notifiable urgently. Complications: congenital rubella syndrome after first-trimester maternal infection - sensorineural deafness, cataracts, patent ductus arteriosus, microcephaly and intellectual disability. Note: MMR at 12 and 18 months on the Australian NIP is why local infections are now almost all imported; check rubella immunity pre-pregnancy and vaccinate postpartum if non-immune (MMR is contraindicated in pregnancy).
rich_summaries.Sarcoidosis: Multisystem granulomatous disease with non-caseating granulomas, most often affecting the lungs and intrathoracic lymph nodes. Epidemiology: onset 20 to 40, higher incidence and severity in people of African ancestry. Clinical features: half are asymptomatic bihilar lymphadenopathy, and pulmonary disease gives dry cough and dyspnoea. Cutaneous involvement gives erythema nodosum or lupus pernio. Ocular gives uveitis. Cardiac gives arrhythmia, conduction block or cardiomyopathy, and neurological favours cranial nerves, particularly facial. Lofgren syndrome (fever, bihilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum, arthritis) has excellent prognosis. Ix: chest imaging (staging 0 to IV), calcium (hypercalcaemia from vitamin D activation), LFT, ACE (supportive not diagnostic), ECG, and tissue biopsy of the most accessible affected site showing non-caseating granulomas. Exclude TB before steroids. Mx: observation if asymptomatic. Oral corticosteroids for symptomatic pulmonary, cardiac, neurological, ocular, hypercalcaemia or progressive systemic disease. Methotrexate as steroid-sparing. Note: cardiac and neurological involvement carry the mortality.
rich_summaries.Scabies: Skin infestation by Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis; spread by prolonged skin-to-skin contact; endemic in remote Aboriginal communities where crusted disease drives GAS pyoderma and downstream ARF and APSGN. Clinical features: intensely itchy papular rash worse at night in finger webs, wrists, axillae, waist, genitals and feet; pathognomonic burrows on lateral fingers; symptoms lag infestation by 4-6 weeks in a first episode. Crusted (Norwegian) scabies: hyperkeratotic scaly plaques with millions of mites in immunocompromised or elderly; highly infectious. Ix: clinical; dermoscopy shows the mite; scrapings for microscopy if unclear. Mx: topical permethrin 5% neck-down for 8-12 hours, repeated at day 7; oral ivermectin 200 microgram/kg on days 1 and 8 for widespread, crusted or institutional outbreaks; treat all household contacts simultaneously; wash bedding at 60 degrees or seal for 72 hours; itch may persist 2-4 weeks post-treatment. Note: NT and remote-community outbreaks follow the Healthy Skin Guideline - treat contacts even if asymptomatic to break the cycle.
rich_summaries.Schizoaffective disorder: Chronic psychotic disorder with concurrent substantial mood episodes. Diagnosis (DSM-5): uninterrupted illness during which a major mood episode is concurrent with schizophrenia criterion A symptoms; delusions or hallucinations for at least 2 weeks in the absence of a major mood episode during the illness; mood symptoms present for the majority of the total illness duration; not attributable to substance or medical condition. Subtypes: bipolar (manic episodes) or depressive. Clinical features: mixed psychotic and mood presentation. Ix: no confirmatory test; exclude substance-induced and organic causes (FBC, EUC, TFT, calcium, urine drug screen, HIV, syphilis, MRI brain if atypical). Longitudinal history is essential. Mx: second-generation antipsychotic plus a mood stabiliser or antidepressant by subtype. Paliperidone is the only agent with a specific TGA indication in schizoaffective disorder. Combine with CBT, family intervention, vocational and social support. Metabolic monitoring from the first script. Note: suicide risk is similar to schizophrenia.
rich_summaries.Schizophrenia: Chronic psychotic disorder with continuous illness for at least six months and active-phase symptoms for at least one month. Dx: two or more of delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour, and negative symptoms - at least one from the first three. Onset typically late teens to mid twenties in males, later in females. Ix: no confirmatory test; exclude organic causes with FBC, EUC, LFT, TFT, calcium, B12, urine drug screen, HIV and syphilis serology, and MRI brain in atypical or late-onset presentation. Mx: second-generation antipsychotic first line - risperidone, olanzapine, aripiprazole, paliperidone; long-acting injectables improve adherence and are offered early rather than after multiple relapses. Clozapine for treatment resistance (inadequate response to two adequate trials), with mandatory neutrophil monitoring and clinical review for myocarditis. CBT for psychosis, family intervention and vocational support are core, not optional. Note: physical health mortality gap is about 15 years, largely cardiometabolic, so metabolic monitoring is part of the treatment plan from the first script.
rich_summaries.Scleroderma: Systemic sclerosis - autoimmune fibrosis with vasculopathy affecting skin and internal organs. Types: limited cutaneous (about 70%, skin distal to elbows and knees plus face, anti-centromere antibody, gives CREST - Calcinosis, Raynaud, oesophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia); diffuse cutaneous (proximal skin, anti-Scl-70, higher risk of ILD and scleroderma renal crisis); systemic sclerosis sine scleroderma. Clinical features: Raynaud phenomenon (often the first sign years before), sclerodactyly and digital ulcers, skin thickening, oesophageal dysmotility with reflux, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary arterial hypertension, and scleroderma renal crisis. Ix: ANA (positive in over 90%), anti-centromere, anti-Scl-70, anti-RNA polymerase III (renal crisis risk); HRCT chest for ILD; echocardiogram and right heart catheter for PAH; annual PFT and echo. Mx: no cure. Raynaud with nifedipine, sildenafil or iloprost. ILD with mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide, nintedanib for progressive fibrosis. PAH with endothelin antagonists and PDE5 inhibitors. Renal crisis with ACE inhibitor even at raised creatinine. Note: ACE inhibitor treats renal crisis, not causes it.
rich_summaries.Sepsis: Life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response to infection. Septic shock is sepsis with lactate over 2 mmol/L and vasopressor need to keep MAP at least 65 mmHg despite fluid resuscitation. Ix: lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics where possible, FBC, EUC, LFT, coagulation, VBG, urinalysis and cultures from any plausible source (urine, sputum, wound, line, CSF); imaging directed by source. Mx: Hour-1 sepsis bundle - measure lactate, take cultures, give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, start 30 mL/kg crystalloid if hypotensive or lactate over 4, and start vasopressors (noradrenaline first line) if MAP stays under 65 after fluids. Source control - drain, remove or debride - within hours where relevant. Reassess fluid status dynamically after the initial bolus rather than repeating it blindly. DDx: pancreatitis, major trauma or burns can mimic SIRS without infection; anaphylaxis and adrenal crisis look septic briefly. Red flags: lactate over 4, GCS drop, oliguria, mottling or a rising vasopressor requirement mean escalate now, not after the next set of bloods.
rich_summaries.Septic arthritis: Bacterial infection of a joint. Cartilage is destroyed within days, so this is a same-day emergency. Causes: Staphylococcus aureus most often; streptococci; Neisseria gonorrhoeae in young sexually active adults; Gram-negative bacilli in the elderly and immunosuppressed. Risk factors: prosthetic joint, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, injecting drug use, immunosuppression, overlying skin infection. Sx: a single hot swollen joint, severe pain on any movement, inability to weight-bear, fever. Ix: urgent joint aspiration before antibiotics for synovial white cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystal microscopy; blood cultures; CRP. Mx: flucloxacillin intravenously as empirical cover per eTG, vancomycin where MRSA is likely, ceftriaxone for gonococcal disease; joint washout or repeated aspiration alongside. Note: a synovial white cell count under 50 x 10^9/L does not exclude it, particularly in a prosthetic joint, and crystals do not exclude it either.
rich_summaries.Septic shock: Subset of sepsis with persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP at least 65 mmHg AND lactate over 2 mmol/L despite adequate volume resuscitation. Mortality over 40%. Pathophysiology: dysregulated host response drives distributive shock with profound vasodilation, endothelial dysfunction, capillary leak, and cardiac depression; warm-hyperdynamic phase early, cold-hypodynamic phase late. Ix: hour-1 sepsis bundle needs lactate, blood cultures from two peripheral sites before antibiotics, FBC, EUC, LFT, coagulation with fibrinogen, VBG, procalcitonin, and cultures from any plausible source. Mx: give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour (piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem plus vancomycin for local eTG cover), start 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid if hypotensive or lactate over 4. Vasopressors (noradrenaline first line; add vasopressin for refractory) targeting MAP 65 mmHg through a central line. Source control within 6 to 12 hours. Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day for vasopressor-refractory shock. Note: escalate to ICU early; delay in antibiotics or source control drives mortality.
rich_summaries.Septicaemia: Historical term for bacteria in the bloodstream causing clinical illness; modern practice uses bacteraemia (bacteria in blood) and sepsis (life-threatening organ dysfunction from dysregulated host response to infection). Bacteraemia may be transient (procedures, gum brushing), intermittent, or continuous (endovascular infection, endocarditis, line infection). Septic shock is sepsis with lactate over 2 mmol/L and vasopressor need to keep MAP at least 65 mmHg despite fluid resuscitation. Ix: lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics where possible, FBC, EUC, LFT, coagulation, VBG, urinalysis and cultures from any plausible source; imaging by source. Mx: Hour-1 sepsis bundle - measure lactate, take cultures, give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, start 30 mL/kg crystalloid if hypotensive or lactate over 4, start vasopressors (noradrenaline first line) if MAP stays under 65 after fluids. Source control within hours. DDx: SIRS from pancreatitis, trauma or burns; anaphylaxis; adrenal crisis. Note: septicaemia and sepsis are used interchangeably in older Australian documentation.
rich_summaries.Serotonin syndrome: Excess serotonergic activity, usually from a drug combination, developing within hours rather than days. Causes: an SSRI or SNRI with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor is the most dangerous pairing; also tramadol, pethidine, fentanyl, linezolid, triptans, lithium, St John's wort, MDMA and cocaine. Sx: neuromuscular excitation with clonus, hyperreflexia and tremor, greatest in the lower limbs; autonomic instability with hyperthermia, tachycardia and diaphoresis; agitation and delirium. Criteria: Hunter criteria require a serotonergic agent plus spontaneous clonus, or inducible or ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or tremor with hyperreflexia, or hypertonia with temperature above 38.5 C and clonus. Differential: neuroleptic malignant syndrome evolves over days with lead-pipe rigidity and hyporeflexia. Mx: stop the offending drugs; benzodiazepines for agitation and rigidity; active cooling; oral cyproheptadine; intubation and paralysis if hyperthermia is uncontrolled.
rich_summaries.Shoulder dystocia: Obstetric emergency where the fetal head has delivered but the anterior shoulder is impacted behind the maternal symphysis pubis. Risk factors: fetal macrosomia (most predictive but only half of cases occur in large babies), gestational diabetes, previous shoulder dystocia, prolonged second stage, instrumental delivery, and maternal obesity. Clinical features: turtle sign (head retracts against the perineum), failure of restitution, no descent with routine traction. Mx: call for help and start HELPERR - Help, Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts hyperflexion), external suprapubic Pressure, internal rotational manoeuvres (Rubin, Woods screw, reverse Woods), Remove the posterior arm, and Roll onto all fours (Gaskin). Never apply fundal pressure. Cleidotomy, Zavanelli or symphysiotomy are last-resort. Document times and manoeuvres carefully. Complications: neonatal brachial plexus injury (Erb palsy), clavicular or humeral fracture, hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, maternal postpartum haemorrhage and perineal trauma. Note: rehearsed team simulation reduces morbidity - Australian units drill this.
rich_summaries.Sickle cell disease: Autosomal recessive haemoglobinopathy in which HbS polymerises when deoxygenated, deforming red cells and causing vaso-occlusion and haemolysis. Clinical features: painful vaso-occlusive crises, dactylitis in infants, and functional asplenia from repeated infarction. Chronic haemolysis gives anaemia, gallstones and leg ulcers. Ix: haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC; film shows sickle cells and Howell-Jolly bodies. Mx: hydroxycarbamide raises HbF and reduces crises and mortality. Penicillin prophylaxis and full vaccination against encapsulated organisms. Crises need prompt analgesia including opioids, hydration, oxygen and a search for infection. Transfusion or exchange for stroke, acute chest syndrome or priapism. Note: fever in a functionally asplenic patient is a medical emergency, not a symptom to observe. Red flags: acute chest syndrome, stroke, splenic sequestration and aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19.
rich_summaries.Sinusitis: Inflammation of the paranasal sinuses. Acute (under 4 weeks) is almost always viral; bacterial sinusitis is suggested by symptoms over 10 days, double-worsening, or severe onset with high fever and purulent discharge (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis). Chronic sinusitis lasts over 12 weeks and is often polymicrobial with nasal polyposis or allergy as background. Clinical features: facial pain worse on leaning forward, purulent nasal discharge, congestion, hyposmia and cough. Ix: clinical in typical acute disease. CT of the paranasal sinuses for chronic, complicated or refractory disease; nasal endoscopy in specialist review. Mx: acute viral gets saline irrigation, intranasal steroid, decongestant, analgesia. Bacterial gets amoxicillin (or amoxicillin plus clavulanate if severe) for 5 to 7 days per eTG. Chronic disease uses long-term intranasal steroid, saline rinses, allergy management, and ENT referral. Red flags: orbital cellulitis (proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, reduced acuity) or intracranial extension (severe headache, focal signs, meningism) need urgent imaging and IV antibiotics. Note: antibiotics are over-prescribed for acute sinusitis in Australia.
rich_summaries.Sjögren syndrome: Autoimmune exocrinopathy - lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands causing keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes) and xerostomia (dry mouth). Primary isolated or secondary to another connective tissue disease (RA, SLE, systemic sclerosis). Female predominance (9:1); peak age 40 to 60. Clinical features: dry gritty eyes, corneal abrasion, dry mouth with dental caries and oral candidiasis, parotid enlargement, dry skin and vagina, arthralgia, Raynaud, and fatigue; extraglandular disease includes ILD, renal tubular acidosis, small-fibre neuropathy and cytopenias.Non-Hodgkin lymphoma risk is markedly elevated (especially parotid MALT - suspect persistent unilateral parotid swelling). Ix: Schirmer under 5 mm in 5 min; ocular staining score; unstimulated whole salivary flow; anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB); ANA and RF often positive; minor salivary gland biopsy when diagnosis uncertain. Mx: symptomatic - artificial tears and saliva, pilocarpine for xerostomia, dental prevention. Hydroxychloroquine for arthralgia and fatigue; immunosuppression for extraglandular disease. Note: pregnant women with anti-Ro face fetal cardiac block risk - fetal echocardiogram surveillance.
rich_summaries.Social anxiety disorder: Persistent marked fear or anxiety about one or more social situations in which the person is exposed to possible scrutiny. Diagnosis (DSM-5): situations almost always provoke fear or anxiety, are avoided or endured with intense distress, are out of proportion to actual threat, last at least 6 months, and cause clinically significant impairment. Types: generalised (most social situations) or performance only (public speaking, musical performance). Clinical features include fear of embarrassment or humiliation, anticipatory anxiety for days before an event, autonomic symptoms during (sweating, tachycardia, tremor, blushing), and avoidance that shrinks the person's world over time. Comorbid depression and alcohol use disorder are common. Ix: clinical diagnosis; screen with Liebowitz or Mini-SPIN; exclude thyrotoxicosis and substance-related presentations. Mx: CBT with exposure is first-line psychological therapy. SSRI (sertraline, escitalopram, paroxetine) or SNRI (venlafaxine) first line pharmacological; beta blockers for performance-only subtype. Avoid long-term benzodiazepines. Note: average delay to diagnosis in Australia is over a decade; ask directly.
rich_summaries.Somatic symptom disorder: One or more distressing somatic symptoms plus excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviours related to the symptoms - persisting for at least 6 months. Diagnosis (DSM-5): one or more somatic symptoms causing significant distress or disruption; excessive time and energy devoted to the symptoms; symptoms may or may not have a medical explanation - the disorder is about the response, not the presence or absence of pathology. Related conditions include illness anxiety disorder, functional neurological (conversion) disorder, factitious disorder (deliberate deception), and malingering (deliberate for external gain, not a disorder). Clinical features: recurrent presentations, multiple specialist referrals, repeated negative investigations, extensive doctor-shopping. Ix: carefully exclude organic disease with targeted workup; avoid repeat investigation. Mx: continuity with a single trusted GP; regular scheduled visits (not symptom-driven); CBT with graded acceptance and behavioural activation; treat comorbid depression and anxiety. SSRI has some evidence. Note: acknowledge the reality of symptoms without conceding fictitious pathology.
rich_summaries.Spinal cord compression: Compression of the cord or cauda equina by tumour, most often from vertebral metastasis. Causes: breast, lung and prostate primaries account for most; also myeloma, renal and lymphoma. Clinical features: back pain first, typically for weeks and often worse lying flat or on coughing, then neurological signs - limb weakness, sensory level, and finally bladder and bowel dysfunction. Ix: whole-spine MRI within 24 hours, and sooner with neurological signs. Whole spine, because multiple levels are involved in about a third and imaging only the painful level misses them. Mx: dexamethasone 16 mg immediately on suspicion, before imaging confirms it, with proton pump cover and glucose monitoring. Then urgent radiotherapy or surgical decompression depending on stability, prognosis and tissue diagnosis. Note: pretreatment ambulatory status is the strongest predictor of walking afterwards, so the window for useful intervention closes with the loss of power, not with the onset of pain. Red flags: new back pain in anyone with known malignancy is cord compression until imaging says otherwise.
rich_summaries.Squamous cell carcinoma: Cutaneous SCC is the second commonest skin cancer, arising from keratinocytes; can metastasise (2 to 5%). Risk factors: cumulative ultraviolet exposure, actinic keratoses (premalignant precursor), fair skin, chronic immunosuppression (transplant recipients have 65-fold risk), HPV, chronic wounds or scars (Marjolin ulcer), and arsenic exposure. Clinical features: enlarging firm keratotic or ulcerated papule or plaque on sun-exposed skin - scalp, face, ears, dorsum of hands, lips. In situ disease (Bowen) is a scaly erythematous patch; keratoacanthoma is a rapidly growing crateriform nodule that may regress. Ix: dermoscopy; excisional or punch biopsy is definitive. Stage with clinical examination, lymph node examination, and imaging for high-risk lesions (perineural invasion, over 4 mm depth, immunosuppressed, ear or lip). Mx: excise with 4 to 6 mm margins for low-risk lesions, wider or Mohs for high-risk sites. Radiotherapy for inoperable disease. Cemiplimab (PD-1 inhibitor) for advanced or metastatic disease. Reduce ongoing UV exposure and photoprotect. Note: 6-monthly full skin check after a first SCC; annually after 2 years without a new lesion.
rich_summaries.Status epilepticus: Seizure lasting at least 5 minutes, or two or more seizures without recovery between. Time is neuron - prolonged activity drives neuronal injury. Causes include poor antiepileptic drug adherence (commonest in known epilepsy), alcohol withdrawal, CNS infection, stroke, tumour, metabolic derangement, drug toxicity and eclampsia. Clinical features: generalised tonic-clonic is classic; focal or non-convulsive status may present as prolonged confusion, aphasia or behavioural change. Ix: check glucose immediately, then FBC, EUC, calcium, magnesium, LFT, VBG, AED levels and toxicology; CT head and LP if new-onset or CNS infection suspected; EEG for non-convulsive status. Mx: ABC first, IV access, glucose if hypoglycaemic, thiamine before glucose in the malnourished. First line at 0 minutes is IV midazolam 10 mg (or IM 5 to 10 mg). Second line at 5 to 10 minutes is levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4.5 g) IV, or sodium valproate 40 mg/kg IV, or phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV. Refractory disease needs intubation and continuous EEG-guided propofol, midazolam or thiopentone infusion in ICU. Note: post-ictal state must not delay second-line therapy.
rich_summaries.Stroke: Acute neurological deficit from cerebral infarction (about 85%) or haemorrhage (about 15%). Clinical features: sudden focal deficit fitting a vascular territory - anterior circulation gives hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, dysphasia or neglect; posterior gives ataxia, diplopia, vertigo and crossed signs. Ix: non-contrast CT immediately to exclude haemorrhage, then CT angiography and perfusion; BGL, since hypoglycaemia mimics stroke; ECG and prolonged monitoring for AF; carotid imaging. Mx: thrombolysis within 4.5 hours with BP below 185/110; thrombectomy up to 24 hours for large vessel occlusion with favourable imaging. Admit to a stroke unit - this alone improves outcomes as much as any drug. Haemorrhagic stroke needs BP lowering and anticoagulation reversal. Secondary prevention: antiplatelet or anticoagulation for AF, statin, BP control, carotid endarterectomy where indicated. DDx: Todd paralysis after seizure; hypoglycaemia; migraine with aura; subdural haematoma; hypertensive encephalopathy; tumour. Note: time is brain - the target is door-to-needle under 60 minutes, so investigation and treatment run in parallel.
rich_summaries.Subarachnoid haemorrhage: Bleeding into the subarachnoid space, usually from a ruptured berry aneurysm. Risk factors: hypertension, smoking, family history, polycystic kidney disease, Ehlers-Danlos and Marfan syndromes. Clinical features: thunderclap headache reaching maximum intensity within a minute, classically the worst of the patient's life; vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia, reduced consciousness, seizure. A sentinel bleed may precede it by days to weeks. Ix: non-contrast CT within 6 hours is close to 100% sensitive; beyond that, lumbar puncture at 12 hours looking for xanthochromia. CT angiography to define the aneurysm. Mx: neurosurgical referral; endovascular coiling or surgical clipping; nimodipine to reduce delayed cerebral ischaemia; blood pressure and analgesia control. Complications: rebleeding, delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm at days 4-14, hydrocephalus, hyponatraemia from cerebral salt wasting or SIADH. Red flags: any thunderclap headache needs imaging, regardless of how well the patient looks by the time they are seen.
rich_summaries.Subdural haematoma: Bleeding between dura and arachnoid from torn bridging veins, crossing suture lines and appearing crescentic on CT. Epidemiology: acute after significant trauma; chronic in older people, those on anticoagulants, and those with alcohol-related brain atrophy, where the causative injury may be trivial or not recalled. Clinical features: acute disease presents with impaired consciousness after trauma. Chronic disease presents insidiously with headache, confusion, gait disturbance or focal weakness, and is a reversible mimic of dementia. Ix: non-contrast CT head. Acute blood is hyperdense, chronic is hypodense, and subacute can be isodense to brain - look for midline shift and effaced sulci rather than the collection itself. Mx: reverse anticoagulation urgently and discuss with neurosurgery. Surgical evacuation by burr hole for symptomatic chronic collections, craniotomy for acute ones. Small asymptomatic collections may be observed. Red flags: falling GCS, anisocoria or a rising blood pressure with bradycardia mean herniation and immediate escalation.
rich_summaries.Substance use disorder: Problematic pattern of use of any psychoactive substance causing clinically significant impairment or distress. Diagnosis (DSM-5): two or more of eleven criteria within 12 months across impaired control, social impairment, risky use, and pharmacological (tolerance, withdrawal). Substance-specific presentations: opioid (miosis, respiratory depression); stimulant (mydriasis, tachycardia, psychosis); benzodiazepine (sedation with intact pupils); cannabis (conjunctival injection, appetite, psychosis); ketamine (dissociation, cystitis). Ix: no specific test. Structured history and urine drug screen (know its false negatives and windows); FBC, EUC, LFT, glucose, HIV, HBV, HCV in injecting use. Mx: withdrawal - buprenorphine or methadone for opioids, diazepam for alcohol and benzodiazepines. Maintenance - opioid substitution with buprenorphine or methadone; naltrexone for alcohol and opioid; acamprosate for alcohol. Motivational interviewing and psychosocial support throughout. Harm reduction with needle exchange and take-home naloxone. Note: co-occurring mental illness is the rule, not the exception; treat both together.
rich_summaries.Sudden infant death syndrome: Sudden unexpected death of an infant under 1 year, unexplained after post-mortem, scene examination and history review. Epidemiology: peak 2-4 months, over 90% before 6 months; Australian incidence fell 85% after the 1991 Back to Sleep campaign but remains higher in Aboriginal infants. Risk factors: prematurity, prone or side sleeping, soft bedding and overheating, maternal smoking and antenatal alcohol, bed-sharing (especially with a smoker, sedated adult or on a couch), formula feeding; the Triple Risk model explains convergence of vulnerable infant, developmental window and exogenous stressor. Prevention: back to sleep; face and head uncovered; smoke-free pregnancy and household; safe sleep environment (firm flat mattress, cot in parents' room for 6-12 months); breastfeed if possible; dummy for sleep once breastfeeding is established. Note: bed-sharing is the strongest modifiable risk factor in Australian data - room-sharing on a separate surface for the first 6-12 months is what to advise.
rich_summaries.Superior vena cava syndrome: Obstruction of the superior vena cava impairing venous return from head, neck and upper limbs. Causes: malignancy in about 60% - lung cancer (particularly small cell) commonest, then non-Hodgkin lymphoma and metastatic disease; benign causes include thrombosis from central venous catheters or pacemaker leads, fibrosing mediastinitis, and aortic aneurysm. Clinical features: gradual or acute onset facial and neck swelling, plethora and cyanosis, dilated upper limb and chest wall veins, headache and dizziness worse on bending forward, dyspnoea, cough, hoarseness, and Pemberton sign (facial plethora and stridor when arms raised). Airway compromise, cerebral oedema and reduced conscious level mark severe disease. Ix: urgent contrast-enhanced CT chest defines level and cause; tissue diagnosis by bronchoscopic biopsy, EBUS, or CT-guided percutaneous biopsy before treatment. Mx: head elevation and oxygen. Dexamethasone reduces oedema. Endovascular SVC stenting gives rapid relief and is first line for severe symptoms. Cause-specific chemotherapy or radiotherapy for small cell lung cancer and lymphoma. Anticoagulation for thrombotic cause. Note: SVCS is rarely emergent.
rich_summaries.Supraventricular tachycardia: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia originating at or above the AV node. Types: AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT) is commonest, from dual AV nodal pathways; AV re-entrant tachycardia (AVRT) uses an accessory pathway such as WPW; atrial tachycardia arises from an ectopic atrial focus. Clinical features: abrupt-onset regular palpitations at 150 to 220/min with chest tightness, dyspnoea, presyncope and polyuria; often stopped by Valsalva. Ix: 12-lead ECG in tachycardia and after conversion; EUC, TFT, magnesium; ambulatory monitoring for infrequent episodes; look for delta wave on resting ECG for WPW. Mx: stable - vagal manoeuvres first (modified Valsalva has higher yield), then IV adenosine 6 mg then 12 mg via a large-bore proximal cannula with continuous rhythm strip. Second line is IV verapamil or a beta blocker (avoid verapamil if WPW or wide QRS). Unstable patients get synchronised DC cardioversion. Catheter ablation is curative in over 95% of AVNRT and AVRT and is offered early for recurrent or symptomatic disease. Note: adenosine may briefly provoke atrial fibrillation, which is dangerous in WPW - avoid AV nodal blockers in known pre-excited AF.
rich_summaries.Syncope: Transient loss of consciousness from global cerebral hypoperfusion, with spontaneous complete recovery. Types: reflex or vasovagal is commonest (prodrome of nausea, sweating and warmth, triggered by prolonged standing, pain or emotion); orthostatic (drop of at least 20/10 mmHg on standing, from volume depletion, autonomic failure or drugs); and cardiac (arrhythmia or structural such as aortic stenosis, HCM or pulmonary embolism). Cardiac syncope has no or brief prodrome, often on exertion or supine, and carries the mortality. Ix: 12-lead ECG on everyone; lying and standing blood pressure; echo if murmur, exertional syncope or abnormal ECG; ambulatory monitoring or an implantable loop recorder for recurrent unexplained events. Bloods only where the history suggests cause. Mx: reassure and educate for reflex syncope - trigger avoidance, counter-pressure manoeuvres, adequate salt and fluid; treat the cause for orthostatic and cardiac; admit any cardiac or high-risk presentation. Note: driving restrictions under Austroads apply and depend on the type - a single reflex event is not the same as cardiac or recurrent, and the patient carries the reporting obligation.
rich_summaries.Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic h: Euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia from unsuppressed ADH. Causes: malignancy especially small cell lung cancer; CNS disease including stroke, haemorrhage and meningitis; pulmonary disease; and drugs - SSRIs, carbamazepine, and thiazides among others. Criteria: hyponatraemia with low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine above 100 mOsm/kg, urinary sodium above 30 mmol/L, clinical euvolaemia, and normal thyroid, adrenal and renal function. Clinical features: often asymptomatic when chronic; nausea, headache, confusion, and seizure or coma when severe or rapid. Rate of fall matters more than the absolute level. Mx: treat the cause; fluid restriction first-line; salt tablets or tolvaptan in resistant cases. Hypertonic saline only for severe symptoms. Note: correct no faster than 8-10 mmol/L in 24 hours - overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia causes osmotic demyelination syndrome, which is irreversible. Volume status is what separates SIADH from hypovolaemic and hypervolaemic hyponatraemia, so assess it before treating.
rich_summaries.Syphilis: Sexually transmitted infection caused by the spirochaete Treponema pallidum; notifiable in every Australian jurisdiction and resurgent. Clinical features: primary, 9-90 days - painless indurated chancre at the inoculation site with regional lymphadenopathy, heals spontaneously; secondary, 6-12 weeks - maculopapular rash involving palms and soles, condylomata lata, alopecia, hepatitis, uveitis; latent - asymptomatic with positive serology; tertiary, 10-30 years - gummas, aortitis with aortic regurgitation, neurosyphilis. Ix: dark-field microscopy or PCR of a lesion swab; treponemal EIA or TPHA screens and stays positive for life; RPR or VDRL titres track activity and response. Mx: benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g IM single dose for primary, secondary and early latent; three weekly doses for late latent and tertiary; benzylpenicillin IV for 15 days in neurosyphilis. Note: tabes dorsalis gives a wide-based gait, lancinating pains and Argyll Robertson pupils, which accommodate but do not react to light. Red flags: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction within 24 hours of the first dose - fever, rigors, hypotension; screen every pregnancy for congenital syphilis.
rich_summaries.Syringomyelia: Fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) within spinal cord parenchyma, usually cervical, expanding over years. Causes: Chiari malformation type I (commonest, from cerebellar tonsil descent obstructing CSF flow); post-traumatic (months to years after SCI); post-inflammatory (meningitis, arachnoiditis); tumour (haemangioblastoma, ependymoma); idiopathic. Clinical features reflect central cord expanding outward - suspended cape-distribution loss of pain and temperature with preserved vibration and proprioception (dissociated sensory loss from crossing spinothalamic fibres); LMN weakness and wasting of hand intrinsics; UMN signs in legs from lateral corticospinal involvement; Horner if cervicothoracic; painless neuropathic arthropathy (Charcot joints). Ix: MRI whole neuraxis is diagnostic - defines syrinx extent, tonsillar descent and any tumour. Mx: asymptomatic small syrinx is observed. Progressive symptoms drive surgery - posterior fossa decompression for Chiari-associated; shunt for post-traumatic; resect any obstructing tumour. Note: early surgery preserves function - established deficits rarely reverse.
rich_summaries.Systemic lupus erythematosus: Multisystem autoimmune disease from immune complex deposition, relapsing and remitting. Epidemiology: women 9x more than men, reproductive years; more common and more severe in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. Clinical features: malar rash sparing nasolabial folds, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, alopecia; non-erosive arthritis; serositis; lupus nephritis; cytopenias. Ix: ANA screens (a negative makes lupus very unlikely); anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm are specific, dsDNA titre tracks activity; low C3/C4 in flares; urinalysis with ACR at every visit. Mx: hydroxychloroquine for nearly everyone - reduces flares, damage and mortality; mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide for organ-threatening disease. Note: lupus nephritis is usually asymptomatic until advanced, so routine urinalysis is what detects it.
rich_summaries.Systemic sclerosis: Autoimmune connective tissue disease with vasculopathy, fibrosis and immune activation. Female predominance (4:1); onset 30 to 50. Subtypes are limited cutaneous (CREST - Calcinosis, Raynaud, oEsophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia, distal to elbows, anti-centromere, PAH risk), diffuse cutaneous (widespread skin, anti-Scl-70, ILD and renal crisis), and sine scleroderma. Clinical features: Raynaud phenomenon often years before other features, skin thickening starting distally, telangiectasia and calcinosis, digital ulcers, GORD and dysphagia, ILD and pulmonary hypertension, and scleroderma renal crisis (accelerated hypertension and AKI).Ix: ANA positive in over 90%; anti-centromere, anti-Scl-70, anti-RNA polymerase III (renal crisis marker); nailfold capillaroscopy; PFT and HRCT for ILD; echocardiogram for PAH; EUC and BP. Mx: no disease-modifying drug. Immunosuppression (mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide, rituximab) for skin and ILD; nifedipine and iloprost for Raynaud; PPI for GORD; bosentan and sildenafil for PAH; ACE inhibitor for renal crisis. Note: ACE inhibitor for renal crisis even in AKI - transforms mortality.
rich_summaries.TORCH infections: Congenital and perinatal infections sharing IUGR, microcephaly, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, thrombocytopenia and rash. Causes are captured by TORCH - toxoplasmosis, other (syphilis, varicella, parvovirus B19, HIV, Zika, listeria), rubella, CMV (the commonest congenital infection), and herpes simplex. Pathogen-specific features: toxoplasmosis gives chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications; rubella gives sensorineural deafness, cataracts, patent ductus arteriosus; CMV gives sensorineural deafness (commonest cause of non-genetic deafness), periventricular calcifications, microcephaly; congenital syphilis gives snuffles, rhagades, saber shins, Hutchinson teeth; neonatal HSV gives skin-eye-mouth, encephalitis or disseminated disease. Ix: TORCH serology in mother and infant; head ultrasound or MRI; hearing screen; ophthalmology. CMV urine or saliva PCR in the first 3 weeks confirms congenital disease. Mx: pathogen-specific - benzylpenicillin for syphilis, valganciclovir for symptomatic congenital CMV, aciclovir for neonatal HSV. Note: prevention includes rubella and varicella immunity checks preconception, and screening for syphilis and HIV in every pregnancy.
rich_summaries.Takayasu arteritis: Chronic granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis of the aorta and its major branches. Epidemiology: young women (15 to 40, F:M about 8:1), higher prevalence in East and South Asian populations. Pathophysiology: transmural inflammation drives concentric wall thickening then stenosis, occlusion or aneurysm; subclavian arteries most commonly affected. Clinical features: two phases classically - a pre-pulseless systemic phase (fever, weight loss, arthralgia, night sweats), then a pulseless phase (limb claudication, absent or unequal pulses, bruits, arm-to-arm BP difference over 10 mmHg, renovascular hypertension, angina, TIA). Ix: ESR and CRP elevated but often normal in burnt-out disease; MRA of aorta and branches is diagnostic; PET-CT for activity when MRA is equivocal. Mx: high-dose prednisolone (1 mg/kg) with early steroid-sparing (methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate); tocilizumab for refractory disease; treat hypertension and cardiovascular risk; revascularisation only in the quiescent phase - active-disease intervention restenoses rapidly. Note: normal inflammatory markers do not exclude active disease - wall enhancement on imaging is more reliable.
rich_summaries.Tardive dyskinesia: Involuntary repetitive movements caused by prolonged dopamine D2 receptor blockade, most often from antipsychotics but also from metoclopramide and prochlorperazine. Risk factors: older age, female sex, African ancestry, first-generation and higher-potency antipsychotics, longer exposure and cumulative dose, diabetes, and prior movement disorder. Clinical features: predominantly orofacial - lip smacking, tongue protrusion, chewing, grimacing; limb and trunk choreoathetoid movements; respiratory dyskinesia; typically emerges after months to years and may worsen paradoxically when the offending drug is stopped. Ix: clinical diagnosis; use the AIMS scale for baseline and monitoring. Mx: review the antipsychotic - switch to a lower-affinity or partial-agonist agent (aripiprazole) or clozapine where feasible. Add a VMAT2 inhibitor (valbenazine or deutetrabenazine) - the only class with strong evidence in TD. Anticholinergics do NOT help TD (they help acute dystonia and drug-induced parkinsonism) and may worsen it. Note: prevention through minimum-effective-dose antipsychotic and regular AIMS screening every 6 months is core practice.
rich_summaries.Tension headache: The commonest primary headache, and the one most often over-investigated and under-managed. Clinical features: bilateral, pressing or tightening, mild to moderate, not aggravated by routine activity, without vomiting. Photophobia or phonophobia may occur but not both. Pericranial tenderness is common. Classification: episodic if fewer than 15 days a month, chronic if 15 or more for over three months. Ix: none if the history is typical and examination normal. Mx: simple analgesia for infrequent attacks, limited to fewer than 15 days a month. Amitriptyline is the best-supported preventer for chronic tension headache. Address sleep, posture, stress and neck pain, since these do more work than the medication does. Note: the single most useful question in a frequent headache is how many days a month analgesia is taken - medication overuse converts episodic headache into chronic daily headache and no preventer works until it is withdrawn.
rich_summaries.Tetanus: Neurotoxin-mediated illness from Clostridium tetani spores contaminating a wound; rare in Australia thanks to universal vaccination, risk highest in older adults with waning immunity and the unimmunised. Pathophysiology: spores germinate in anaerobic tissue; tetanospasmin travels retrograde along peripheral nerves to spinal inhibitory interneurons, blocks GABA and glycine release, produces uninhibited motor firing. Clinical features: trismus (lockjaw, first sign), risus sardonicus, opisthotonos, painful reflex spasms triggered by stimulus, dysautonomia; neonatal tetanus follows unhygienic cord care. Ix: clinical; spatula test (posterior pharynx triggers spasm rather than gag) supports. Mx: quiet dark environment; wound debridement; HTIG IM at a site distant from vaccine; metronidazole; benzodiazepines for spasm; intubation and neuromuscular blockade with magnesium for severe disease. Prevention: ADT booster every 10 years or 5 for a tetanus-prone wound; HTIG plus vaccine if under 3 previous doses. Note: antitoxin does not reverse fixed toxin.
rich_summaries.Tetralogy of Fallot: Commonest cyanotic congenital heart disease beyond the neonatal period. Four components (VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction from pulmonary stenosis, and RV hypertrophy). Associated with 22q11 deletion (DiGeorge). Clinical features are cyanosis appearing in the first year (may not be present at birth), hypercyanotic (tet) spells precipitated by crying, feeding or waking (the baby squats to increase systemic vascular resistance and reduce right-to-left shunt), failure to thrive, harsh ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border, and single S2. Ix: pre-ductal oximetry low; CXR shows boot-shaped heart with concave pulmonary artery segment; ECG shows right axis and RVH; echocardiogram is diagnostic. Mx: spell management with knee-to-chest position, oxygen, morphine, IV fluid, beta-blocker, phenylephrine. Definitive surgical repair (VSD closure and RVOT widening) at 3 to 6 months. Modified Blalock-Taussig shunt palliates neonates too small for repair. Note: even after repair, pulmonary regurgitation and arrhythmia are life-long risks.
rich_summaries.Thalassaemia: Inherited disorder of globin chain synthesis producing microcytic hypochromic anaemia, ineffective erythropoiesis and iron overload. Types: alpha-thalassaemia by number of affected genes (1 silent, 2 trait, 3 HbH disease, 4 Bart hydrops fetalis - lethal); beta-thalassaemia as minor (heterozygous, asymptomatic), intermedia, or major (homozygous, transfusion-dependent from infancy). Clinical features: minor is often picked up on FBC with disproportionate microcytosis; intermedia and major present with anaemia, growth failure, hepatosplenomegaly, skeletal changes from marrow expansion and endocrine failure. Ix: FBC (very low MCV, near-normal RBC count), reticulocytes, iron studies (to exclude coexisting iron deficiency), haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC (elevated HbA2 or HbF in beta; normal in alpha), and molecular testing for alpha. Mx: minor needs no treatment - do not give iron unless proven deficient. Transfusion-dependent disease gets regular red cell transfusion targeting pre-transfusion Hb 90 to 100, iron chelation (deferasirox or deferoxamine), and allogeneic stem cell transplant for cure. Note: preconception carrier screening is offered to at-risk populations in Australia.
rich_summaries.Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura: Thrombotic microangiopathy caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency (activity under 10%). ADAMTS13 cleaves ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers; deficiency leaves them uncleaved, causing platelet microthrombi with haemolysis and thrombocytopenia. Acquired form (commonest) is an autoantibody against ADAMTS13, triggered by infection, pregnancy, drugs or autoimmune disease; congenital (Upshaw-Schulman) is rare.
