Clinical features: pentad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, neurological signs and acute kidney injury - full pentad is uncommon; MAHA plus thrombocytopenia without another cause should trigger TTP workup. Ix: FBC with schistocytes on film, low platelets, high LDH, low haptoglobin, high indirect bilirubin, reticulocytosis; DAT negative; coagulation normal; ADAMTS13 activity confirmatory but do not wait. Mx: urgent plasma exchange with fresh frozen plasma starts before ADAMTS13 result. High-dose corticosteroids. Rituximab. Caplacizumab (anti-vWF nanobody) shortens time to platelet recovery. Never transfuse platelets unless severe bleeding. Note: untreated mortality exceeds 90%; treated survival over 80%.
rich_summaries.Torsades de pointes: Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with QRS complexes twisting around the isoelectric baseline; occurs on a background of prolonged QT and often triggered by a bradycardia-dependent pause. Can degenerate to VF and sudden death. Causes: congenital long QT syndrome; acquired long QT from drugs (methadone, sotalol, amiodarone, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, ondansetron, haloperidol, quetiapine, tricyclics, domperidone), electrolyte disturbance (hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia), bradyarrhythmia, and starvation. Clinical features: sudden syncope, palpitations, or cardiac arrest. Ix: ECG shows characteristic twisting QRS polarity; EUC, magnesium, calcium; drug review; family history and 12-lead in relatives if congenital. Mx: unstable - unsynchronised DC shock. Stable - IV magnesium sulfate 2 g bolus even with normal levels, correct potassium to 4.5 to 5.0, stop QT-prolonging drugs; overdrive pacing or isoprenaline to increase heart rate above 90 bpm and shorten QT. Long-term beta-blocker for congenital long QT; ICD for survivors or high-risk congenital cases. Note: check a QTc on every ECG when starting a QT-prolonging drug.
rich_summaries.Toxic shock syndrome: Systemic illness from bacterial superantigen (TSST-1, streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin) that non-specifically activates T cells and drives a cytokine storm. Aetiology: Staphylococcus aureus (menstrual with retained tampon; non-menstrual with skin, wound or postsurgical focus); group A Streptococcus (often with necrotising fasciitis). Clinical features: fever over 38.9, hypotension, diffuse sunburn-like macular erythroderma followed by palmar-plantar desquamation 1-2 weeks later, plus involvement of three or more organ systems. Ix: blood cultures (positive in over 60% of streptococcal, under 5% of staphylococcal); vaginal or wound swab; FBC, U&E, LFT, CK, coagulation, lactate. Mx: aggressive fluid resuscitation and vasopressor; source control (remove tampon, drain, debride); empirical vancomycin plus clindamycin (suppresses toxin production) plus a beta-lactam active on the organism; consider IVIG for severe or streptococcal cases; ICU. Note: erythroderma plus hypotension plus a retained tampon or surgical wound is TSS until proved otherwise.
rich_summaries.Toxoplasmosis: Intracellular protozoal infection with Toxoplasma gondii; cats are definitive host. Global seroprevalence around 30%. Acquired by ingesting oocysts (cat faeces, contaminated soil) or tissue cysts (undercooked meat). Types: immunocompetent acquired infection is asymptomatic in 90%, otherwise a self-limited mononucleosis-like illness with cervical lymphadenopathy; reactivation in HIV or transplant recipients causes cerebral toxoplasmosis with ring-enhancing lesions, chorioretinitis, or pneumonitis; congenital infection from primary maternal infection gives the classic tetrad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications and seizures. Ix: serology (IgM plus IgG, avidity for gestational timing); PCR of blood, CSF or amniotic fluid; MRI brain in immunocompromised. Mx: immunocompetent adults need no treatment. Immunocompromised or sight-threatening ocular disease gets pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine and folinic acid for 6 weeks. Pregnancy: spiramycin if fetal transmission not confirmed, escalate to pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine after 18 weeks if confirmed. Note: HIV patients with CD4 under 100 and positive Toxoplasma serology need primary prophylaxis with cotrimoxazole.
rich_summaries.Transient ischaemic attack: Transient focal neurological deficit from ischaemia without infarction - now defined on tissue rather than the old 24-hour clock, so imaging matters. Clinical features: sudden onset, resolving typically within an hour; amaurosis fugax, hemiparesis, dysphasia. Ix: urgent MRI with diffusion weighting is preferred - it reclassifies many TIAs as minor stroke; carotid imaging, ECG and prolonged rhythm monitoring, glucose, lipids. Mx: dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel for 21 days then single agent, started immediately in high-risk TIA; anticoagulate if AF; high-intensity statin; BP control; carotid endarterectomy within 2 weeks for symptomatic stenosis of 70-99%. Note: the risk of completed stroke is highest in the first 48 hours, so a TIA is an emergency, not a reassuring event. Australian guidance is for specialist assessment within 24 hours in high-risk patients. Advise not to drive and notify licensing requirements. Red flags: crescendo TIAs, or symptoms with a known critical stenosis, warrant admission.
rich_summaries.Transient tachypnea of the newborn: Delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid causing transient respiratory distress in the newborn; the commonest cause of neonatal respiratory distress. Risk factors: elective caesarean without labour, late preterm, macrosomia, maternal diabetes, maternal asthma, precipitous delivery. Clinical features: tachypnoea (over 60/min), grunting, nasal flaring, mild recession and mild cyanosis within hours of birth; resolves within 24 to 72 hours. Infant otherwise appears well. Ix: clinical diagnosis of exclusion. Pulse oximetry, CXR shows perihilar streaking and fluid in fissures with hyperinflation. Exclude neonatal sepsis, meconium aspiration, RDS, pneumonia and congenital heart disease. Mx: supportive - warm environment, minimal handling, small frequent feeds or NG if tachypnoea limits oral intake, oxygen for saturation over 90%. CPAP for moderate to severe distress. Empirical antibiotics until infection excluded. Note: TTN by definition resolves within 72 hours - persistent distress means another diagnosis.
rich_summaries.Transposition of great arteries: Ventriculoarterial discordance - the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle, creating parallel circulations incompatible with life unless mixing occurs (ASD, VSD, or patent ductus). Second commonest cyanotic congenital heart disease after tetralogy of Fallot; male predominance; associated with maternal diabetes. Clinical features: severe cyanosis within hours of birth, worsening as the ductus closes; single loud S2; usually no murmur unless VSD present; tachypnoea without respiratory distress. Ix: pre-ductal and post-ductal pulse oximetry (both low); hyperoxia test fails to raise PaO2 above 100 mmHg (rules out parenchymal lung disease); CXR shows egg-on-a-string silhouette with narrow mediastinum and increased pulmonary vascularity; ECG shows right axis and RVH; echocardiogram is diagnostic and defines mixing lesions. Mx: start prostaglandin E1 infusion immediately to keep the ductus open; emergency Rashkind balloon atrial septostomy if inadequate mixing; arterial switch (Jatene) within the first 2 weeks is the definitive repair. Note: excellent long-term survival (over 90%) after switch but lifelong cardiology follow-up.
rich_summaries.Tricuspid regurgitation: Retrograde flow from RV to right atrium in systole. Most is functional from annular dilatation in pulmonary hypertension, RV dysfunction, or left heart disease; primary causes include endocarditis (IV drug use with Staph aureus, classic right-sided IE), rheumatic (usually with mitral), carcinoid, Ebstein anomaly, pacemaker lead trauma. Clinical features: often asymptomatic in mild disease; fatigue and reduced cardiac output; right heart failure with raised JVP with prominent v-wave, pulsatile hepatomegaly, ascites, peripheral oedema; holosystolic murmur at left lower sternal edge that increases on inspiration (Carvallo sign); AF is common. Ix: ECG (right strain, AF); TTE quantifies severity - vena contracta, effective regurgitant orifice area; TOE for endocarditis; blood cultures if IE suspected. Mx: treat underlying cause and diuretics for congestion. Antibiotics for IE. Surgical repair or replacement for severe symptomatic TR; transcatheter interventions increasingly used. Note: bioprosthetic valve preferred in the tricuspid position - mechanical valves thrombose readily in low-pressure circulation.
rich_summaries.Tricuspid stenosis: Rare valvular lesion - obstruction of the tricuspid orifice raises right atrial pressure. Almost always rheumatic and coexists with mitral stenosis. Rare non-rheumatic causes include carcinoid, endocarditis (IV drug use), congenital atresia, SLE, and pacemaker lead-related.Clinical features: fatigue and low cardiac output; right-sided congestion with raised JVP (prominent a-wave), hepatomegaly, ascites, peripheral oedema; coexisting mitral stenosis often dominates. Low-pitched mid-diastolic murmur at left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration (Carvallo sign); opening snap; may be masked by MS. Ix: ECG shows tall peaked P waves; CXR shows right atrial enlargement without pulmonary congestion; TTE quantifies gradient. Mx: diuretics and salt restriction for congestion. Percutaneous balloon valvuloplasty for isolated rheumatic TS; surgical repair or replacement usually combined with mitral valve surgery. Note: bioprosthetic valves preferred in tricuspid position - mechanical valves thrombose readily in low-pressure circulation.
rich_summaries.Tricyclic antidepressant overdose: Highly dangerous overdose from tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline, nortriptyline, dothiepin, clomipramine, imipramine); narrow therapeutic-to-toxic margin. Mechanisms: sodium channel blockade (cardiac arrhythmia, QRS widening, seizures), anticholinergic effects, alpha-1 blockade (hypotension), CNS depression. Clinical features: onset within 6 hours. Anticholinergic toxidrome (dry, hot, red, mad, blind, tachycardic, urinary retention, ileus), reduced consciousness, seizures, hypotension, and cardiac toxicity - sinus tachycardia, wide QRS, prominent R wave in aVR, torsades. Ix: 12-lead ECG (QRS over 100 ms predicts seizures, over 160 ms predicts arrhythmia; R wave in aVR over 3 mm), VBG for acidosis, EUC, paracetamol level. Mx: contact Poisons Information Centre (13 11 26). Activated charcoal within 1 hour if airway protected. Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV bolus for QRS over 100 ms, hypotension or arrhythmia - target arterial pH 7.5. IV fluids and noradrenaline for hypotension. Benzodiazepine for seizures. Intralipid for cardiac arrest. Note: flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdose.
rich_summaries.Trigeminal neuralgia: Recurrent brief paroxysms of severe unilateral facial pain in one or more trigeminal divisions (V2 and V3 most common), usually from neurovascular compression of the trigeminal root by an aberrant artery. Epidemiology: peak 50-70, F:M 1.7:1; onset under 40 raises suspicion of secondary cause. Clinical features: electric shock-like pain lasting seconds, triggered by light touch, chewing, cold air or toothbrushing; pain-free between attacks; no sensory deficit in classical TN. Red flags for secondary cause (MS plaque, CP-angle tumour): bilateral, V1 alone, sensory loss, other cranial nerve signs, age under 40. Ix: MRI brain with dedicated trigeminal sequences. Mx: carbamazepine first-line (start 100 mg BD, titrate; check sodium and FBC), oxcarbazepine alternative; add-on lamotrigine, baclofen or gabapentin; microvascular decompression (Jannetta) gives the most durable relief in fit patients; percutaneous rhizotomy or gamma knife for those unsuited to open surgery. Note: response to carbamazepine is itself a diagnostic feature - poor response should prompt review of the diagnosis.
rich_summaries.Tuberculosis: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection by respiratory droplet nuclei, as latent infection (positive IGRA or TST, no symptoms, not infectious) or active disease. Clinical features: pulmonary TB with cough over 3 weeks, haemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss and low-grade fever; extrapulmonary sites include lymph node, pleural, spinal (Pott disease), meningeal, miliary and genitourinary. Ix: three sputum samples for AFB smear, mycobacterial culture and Xpert MTB/RIF; chest imaging (apical cavitating infiltrate in reactivation, hilar lymphadenopathy in primary); HIV test on every new diagnosis. IGRA is preferred over TST in the BCG-vaccinated. Mx: active pulmonary TB gets RIPE (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for 2 months, then rifampicin and isoniazid for 4 months, under a specialist TB service with directly observed therapy in Australia. Add pyridoxine; check baseline LFTs and visual acuity. For latent TB, isoniazid for 6 to 9 months, or rifampicin for 4 months, if at risk of reactivation. Notifiable. Note: multidrug resistance changes both regimen and duration - never start empirical retreatment without susceptibility results.
rich_summaries.Tumour lysis syndrome: Metabolic emergency from massive tumour cell breakdown releasing intracellular contents. Risk factors: bulky, rapidly proliferating, chemosensitive disease - Burkitt lymphoma, ALL, AML with high white count - plus pre-existing renal impairment or volume depletion. Usually within 72 hours of starting treatment, occasionally spontaneous. Clinical features: from the electrolyte derangement - arrhythmia, tetany, seizures, and acute kidney injury from urate and calcium phosphate deposition. Ix: hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia and consequent hypocalcaemia, with rising creatinine. Monitor 6- to 12-hourly in high-risk patients. Mx: prevention is the whole game - vigorous intravenous hydration, with allopurinol for moderate risk and rasburicase for high risk or established disease. Treat hyperkalaemia urgently; dialysis for refractory derangement or oliguric renal failure. Note: do not give calcium for asymptomatic hypocalcaemia - it precipitates with the high phosphate and worsens renal injury. Rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.
rich_summaries.Turner syndrome: Complete or partial monosomy of X (45,X or 45,X mosaic) in females; 1 in 2500 live female births and the commonest chromosomal abnormality lethal in utero. Clinical features: short stature (SHOX haploinsufficiency, adult height 143 cm untreated), primary amenorrhoea with streak gonads, webbed neck, low posterior hairline, cubitus valgus, widely-spaced nipples, neonatal lymphoedema; associations include bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation (up to 40%, drives dissection risk), horseshoe kidney, hypothyroidism, coeliac disease, sensorineural deafness; normal intelligence with non-verbal learning difficulty. Ix: karyotype from lymphocytes (skin biopsy if mosaicism suspected); TTE and cardiac MRI at diagnosis and periodically for aortopathy; renal ultrasound; TFTs, coeliac serology and glucose annually. Mx: growth hormone from age 4 to 6; oestrogen from age 11 to 12 for pubertal induction and bone protection, transitioning to combined HRT to natural menopause; oocyte donation for fertility. Note: aortic dissection risk is lifelong - warn about pregnancy (high mortality if aortic root over 25 mm/m^2).
rich_summaries.Ulcerative colitis: Chronic inflammatory bowel disease with continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum extending proximally. Classification: proctitis (rectum only), left-sided (distal to splenic flexure), or extensive/pancolitis. Clinical features: bloody diarrhoea, urgency, tenesmus, abdominal cramping, and rectal bleeding; extraintestinal features overlap Crohn - PSC (more common in UC), arthritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum. Ix: FBC, CRP, faecal calprotectin, exclude infective colitis (stool MCS, C. difficile); flexible sigmoidoscopy in acute severe UC to avoid perforation risk of colonoscopy, then full colonoscopy when settled. Truelove-Witts criteria grade severity. Mx: mild to moderate - topical mesalazine then oral; add steroids for flare. Moderate to severe gets oral prednisolone; steroid-refractory or dependent disease goes to biologics (infliximab, vedolizumab, ustekinumab, tofacitinib). Acute severe UC needs admission, IV hydrocortisone, VTE prophylaxis, and day-3 rescue with infliximab or ciclosporin; colectomy if failing. Note: annual surveillance colonoscopy from 8 years of extensive disease for dysplasia.
rich_summaries.Urinary incontinence: Involuntary loss of urine, classified by mechanism because treatment differs entirely between the types. Types: stress, from urethral sphincter weakness; urgency, from detrusor overactivity; mixed; overflow, from chronic retention; and functional, where continence fails for reasons outside the urinary tract. Ix: bladder diary, urinalysis to exclude infection, post-void residual, and examination for prolapse or atrophy. Urodynamics only before surgery or when the picture is unclear. Mx: pelvic floor muscle training for at least three months is first-line for stress incontinence. Bladder training for urgency, then an antimuscarinic or mirabegron - prefer mirabegron in older patients, since antimuscarinic anticholinergic load is associated with cognitive decline. Topical oestrogen for genitourinary syndrome of menopause. Surgery for stress incontinence that fails conservative care. Note: treat constipation, review diuretics and caffeine, and check for retention before escalating - reversible contributors are common and easily missed.
rich_summaries.Urinary tract infection: Bacterial infection of the urinary tract; over 80% from Escherichia coli. Classification: uncomplicated (non-pregnant premenopausal woman, normal tract) or complicated (pregnancy, male, catheter, structural abnormality, immunocompromise, recent instrumentation, healthcare-associated). Clinical features: cystitis with dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain and cloudy urine; pyelonephritis adds fever, rigors, flank pain and CVA tenderness with systemic upset. Ix: urinalysis and mid-stream urine culture before antibiotics; renal ultrasound for recurrent UTI, suspected obstruction, or failure to respond. Mx: uncomplicated cystitis in Australia gets trimethoprim 300 mg at night for 3 days, or nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days (eTG). Pyelonephritis needs oral amoxicillin plus clavulanate or IV gentamicin plus amoxicillin for 10 to 14 days. Pregnancy: treat asymptomatic bacteriuria; avoid trimethoprim in the first trimester and nitrofurantoin at term. Men and children warrant imaging and specialist review. Note: recurrent uncomplicated UTI in women is three in 12 months and benefits from behavioural measures and post-coital voiding.
rich_summaries.Urticaria: Transient pruritic wheals from mast cell degranulation, with or without angioedema. Clinical features: individual wheals resolve within 24 h leaving no mark, though the eruption may persist far longer. Acute is under 6 weeks, chronic beyond. Causes: acute - viral infection (commonest), drugs, food, stings. Chronic spontaneous urticaria is usually autoimmune. Ix: none in typical acute disease; FBC and ESR/CRP if chronic. Extensive allergy testing has poor yield. Mx: a second-generation antihistamine (cetirizine, fexofenadine), up-titrated to four times standard dose if needed; omalizumab if refractory. Note: a single lesion lasting beyond 24 h, or leaving bruising, is urticarial vasculitis and needs biopsy. Red flags: wheals with airway or GI symptoms or hypotension are anaphylaxis - IM adrenaline, not an antihistamine.
rich_summaries.Uterine fibroids: Benign monoclonal smooth muscle tumours of the myometrium, oestrogen and progesterone dependent; the commonest pelvic tumour in women. Classification: intramural (commonest), submucosal (heaviest bleeding, most fertility impact), subserosal (bulk symptoms), pedunculated, and cervical. Clinical features: many are asymptomatic; heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding is the classic presentation, along with dysmenorrhoea, pelvic pressure, urinary frequency, constipation, dyspareunia and subfertility. Ix: FBC and ferritin for iron-deficiency anaemia; pelvic ultrasound is first line; saline-infusion sonography or MRI define submucosal disease and map before intervention. Mx: expectant if asymptomatic. For heavy bleeding, tranexamic acid or NSAIDs cycle-only, then hormonal options - combined oral contraceptive, oral or depot progestogen, or the levonorgestrel intrauterine system. GnRH analogues shrink fibroids before surgery. Uterine artery embolisation, myomectomy (fertility-sparing) and hysterectomy are the procedural options. Note: rapid growth or growth after menopause raises suspicion of leiomyosarcoma and warrants specialist referral.
rich_summaries.Uveitis: Inflammation of the uveal tract, classified anatomically because the site predicts both the associations and the risk. Types: anterior (iritis) is commonest; intermediate, posterior and panuveitis carry more risk to vision. Causes: about half are idiopathic. Otherwise HLA-B27-associated disease, sarcoidosis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, or infection with herpes viruses, toxoplasma or syphilis. Clinical features: anterior disease gives a painful red eye with photophobia, blurred vision and a small irregular pupil, with circumcorneal injection. Posterior disease is painless with floaters and visual loss. Ix: slit lamp examination showing cells and flare in the anterior chamber, with targeted serology guided by the pattern. Mx: ophthalmology review. Topical corticosteroid with a cycloplegic to relieve spasm and prevent synechiae; systemic immunosuppression for severe or posterior disease. Note: JIA-associated uveitis is typically asymptomatic and white, which is why those children are screened rather than waiting.
rich_summaries.Varicella: Primary infection with varicella-zoster virus. Clinical features: 10 to 21 day incubation, then a brief prodrome of fever and malaise before successive crops of pruritic vesicles at different stages (macule, papule, vesicle, crust), starting centrally and spreading to include the scalp and mucous membranes. Infectious from 1 to 2 days before rash until every lesion has crusted. Ix: clinical in typical disease; VZV PCR from a vesicle swab if atypical or high-risk. Mx: supportive with paracetamol and antihistamine or calamine; avoid NSAIDs (necrotising fasciitis) and aspirin in children (Reye syndrome). Oral aciclovir within 24 hours of rash onset in adolescents, adults, pregnant women and household contacts; IV aciclovir in the immunocompromised and in severe disease. Offer VZIG to non-immune pregnant contacts, neonates and the immunocompromised within 96 hours of exposure. Complications: bacterial superinfection, varicella pneumonia (adults and pregnant women), encephalitis, cerebellar ataxia, and congenital varicella syndrome from first- or second-trimester maternal infection. Note: MMRV at 18 months on the Australian NIP; school exclusion until all lesions have crusted.
rich_summaries.Vasculitis: Inflammation of blood vessel walls, classified by the size of vessel predominantly involved. Classification: large vessel - giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis; medium vessel - polyarteritis nodosa, Kawasaki disease; small vessel ANCA-associated - granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis; small vessel immune complex - IgA vasculitis, cryoglobulinaemic, anti-GBM. Clinical features: constitutional illness with multi-organ involvement - palpable purpura, glomerulonephritis, alveolar haemorrhage, mononeuritis multiplex, and sinusitis with saddle-nose deformity in GPA. Ix: ANCA with PR3 specificity in GPA and MPO in MPA and EGPA; anti-GBM, complement, cryoglobulins; urinalysis for red cell casts; biopsy of the affected organ confirms. Mx: induction with rituximab or cyclophosphamide plus high-dose prednisolone; maintenance with rituximab or azathioprine; plasma exchange for anti-GBM disease or severe alveolar haemorrhage. Note: the emergency is a rising creatinine with an active sediment, not the rash.
rich_summaries.Ventricular septal defect: Congenital left-to-right shunt across the interventricular septum; the commonest congenital heart defect. Types: perimembranous (about 80%, near tricuspid valve), muscular (may be multiple - Swiss cheese septum), outlet (supracristal, high in septum near pulmonary valve, at risk of aortic regurgitation), and inlet (AV septal defect spectrum, associated with Down syndrome). Clinical features: harsh pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, louder with smaller defects (Roger murmur); small VSDs are asymptomatic; large VSDs cause failure to thrive, sweating with feeds, tachypnoea and recurrent chest infections, progressing to Eisenmenger syndrome if uncorrected. Ix: transthoracic echocardiogram is diagnostic and quantifies shunt; ECG (LVH in significant shunt), CXR (cardiomegaly, pulmonary plethora in large VSD). Mx: small VSDs are observed - many close spontaneously in the first year. Medical management of heart failure (diuretic, ACE inhibitor) for symptomatic infants awaiting closure. Surgical or percutaneous device closure for large shunts (Qp:Qs over 1.5), symptomatic heart failure, or endocarditis prevention. Note: Eisenmenger contraindicates closure.
rich_summaries.Ventricular tachycardia: Wide-complex tachycardia (QRS over 120 ms) originating below the AV node. Types: monomorphic VT usually arises from a scar (post-MI, dilated or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, ARVC, sarcoid); polymorphic VT includes torsades de pointes on the background of a long QT (congenital or acquired). Clinical features: sustained VT gives palpitations, chest pain, presyncope, syncope or cardiac arrest. AV dissociation, capture and fusion beats favour VT over SVT with aberrancy. Ix: 12-lead ECG in and out of the arrhythmia; EUC, magnesium, troponin, digoxin level; echocardiogram; cardiac MRI for scar substrate. Mx: pulseless VT and VF get defibrillation and CPR under ALS. Unstable VT with a pulse gets synchronised DC cardioversion. Stable monomorphic VT gets IV amiodarone 300 mg then infusion; correct potassium and magnesium. Torsades gets IV magnesium sulfate 2 g, overdrive pacing, removal of QT-prolonging drugs. ICD for secondary prevention or high-risk primary prevention; catheter ablation for recurrent scar-mediated VT. Note: any wide-complex tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise.
rich_summaries.Vitamin B12 deficiency: Deficiency causing megaloblastic anaemia and, independently, neurological disease. Causes: pernicious anaemia (autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor); gastrectomy or ileal resection; Crohn disease; metformin and long-term proton pump inhibitors; strict vegan diet. Clinical features: fatigue and pallor; glossitis; and neurological features - symmetrical paraesthesiae, loss of proprioception and vibration from subacute combined degeneration of the cord, ataxia, and cognitive or mood change. Ix: macrocytic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils; low serum B12; raised methylmalonic acid and homocysteine confirm functional deficiency when B12 is borderline. Intrinsic factor antibodies are specific but insensitive for pernicious anaemia. Mx: intramuscular hydroxocobalamin, loading then maintenance; lifelong if the cause is not reversible. High-dose oral is adequate in dietary deficiency. Note: neurological disease occurs without anaemia and can be irreversible if treatment is delayed - do not wait for a low haemoglobin. Never replace folate alone in combined deficiency; it corrects the anaemia while the cord degeneration progresses.
rich_summaries.Vitamin D deficiency: Serum 25-OH vitamin D under 50 nmol/L (severe under 30). Very common in Australia despite sunny climate - up to 30% deficient, higher in dark-skinned, veiled, institutionalised, elderly, and malabsorption populations. Causes: inadequate sun exposure (main source), poor dietary intake, malabsorption (coeliac, cystic fibrosis, bariatric surgery, IBD), CKD, liver disease, medications (anticonvulsants, corticosteroids, rifampicin). Clinical features: often asymptomatic; muscle weakness (proximal myopathy), bone pain and tenderness, fatigue, secondary hyperparathyroidism with hypocalcaemia and hypophosphataemia, rickets in children (bowed legs, rachitic rosary, delayed fontanelle closure), and osteomalacia in adults with pseudofractures.Ix: 25-OH vitamin D; corrected calcium, phosphate, PTH, ALP; renal and liver function. Screen high-risk groups per RACGP. Mx: cholecalciferol - 1000 to 2000 IU daily for mild deficiency, high-dose loading (3000 to 5000 IU daily for 6 to 12 weeks) for moderate to severe, then maintenance. Ensure adequate calcium intake. Treat underlying cause. Note: routine screening of asymptomatic adults not recommended.
rich_summaries.Vitiligo: Autoimmune destruction of epidermal melanocytes producing sharply demarcated depigmented macules and patches. Classification: non-segmental (commonest, symmetrical, generalised or focal, progressive) or segmental (unilateral, dermatomal, usually stable and early-onset). Clinical features: milky-white macules with clearly demarcated edges, often on face (periorificial), hands, elbows, knees, and genitalia; Koebner phenomenon; hair depigmentation (poliosis). Wood lamp accentuates lesions. Associated autoimmune conditions in about a quarter - thyroid disease commonest, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anaemia, Addison disease, alopecia areata. Ix: clinical with Wood lamp; skin biopsy if uncertain; screen for autoimmunity (TFT, glucose, B12, morning cortisol by phenotype). Mx: education and psychological support; sun protection and cosmetic camouflage. Topical corticosteroids and calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus) first line. Narrowband UVB phototherapy for widespread disease. Ruxolitinib topical for non-segmental facial disease. Depigmentation of remaining skin in extensive stable disease. Note: repigmentation is slow and incomplete.
rich_summaries.Volvulus: Bowel twist on its mesenteric axis producing closed-loop obstruction and ischaemia. Sigmoid volvulus is commonest in Western adults (institutionalised elderly, chronic constipation, neuropsychiatric disease); caecal volvulus in younger patients (congenital malrotation or long mesentery, pregnancy, prior surgery); gastric is rare; midgut volvulus in neonates with malrotation. Clinical features: acute onset cramping abdominal pain, distension, obstipation, vomiting (early in caecal, late in sigmoid). Sigmoid typically indolent; caecal presents more acutely with signs of small-bowel obstruction. Ix: abdominal radiograph - coffee-bean sign for sigmoid (large dilated loop pointing to right upper quadrant), embryo sign for caecal; CT with contrast shows whirl sign and confirms vascular compromise. Mx: sigmoid without peritonitis gets flexible sigmoidoscopy detorsion with rectal tube, then elective sigmoidectomy (recurrence over 40% without surgery). Caecal is always operative (right hemicolectomy or caecopexy). Peritonitis, perforation or gangrene at any site needs emergency laparotomy. Note: any child with bilious vomiting has midgut volvulus until proven otherwise.
rich_summaries.Vulvodynia: Chronic vulvar pain of at least three months without an identifiable cause; multifactorial. Types: localised provoked vestibulodynia (commonest - burning at the vestibule on touch, tampon or intercourse); generalised unprovoked (constant burning). Pathophysiology: peripheral and central sensitisation, pelvic floor hypertonicity, psychosocial contributors. Clinical features: dyspareunia, tampon intolerance, sitting discomfort; external examination often normal. Ix: diagnosis of exclusion - swab for candida, HSV and STIs, examine for dermatoses (lichen sclerosus, lichen planus) and biopsy any lesion; cotton-swab (Q-tip) test maps allodynia. Mx: multidisciplinary and stepwise - validation and irritant avoidance, pelvic-floor physiotherapy (first-line for hypertonicity), topical lidocaine 5% for provoked pain, low-dose amitriptyline or duloxetine for constant pain, gabapentin as add-on; psychosexual and CBT input; topical oestrogen if postmenopausal atrophy contributes; vestibulectomy for refractory provoked cases with proven allodynia. Note: frequently misdiagnosed as recurrent candidiasis - absence of hyphae on microscopy should redirect.
rich_summaries.Wernicke encephalopathy: Acute thiamine (B1) deficiency with a characteristic clinical triad - ophthalmoplegia (lateral gaze palsy, nystagmus), ataxia (wide-based gait), and encephalopathy (confusion, reduced consciousness). Only a minority present with the complete triad. Causes: alcohol use disorder (commonest in Australia), hyperemesis gravidarum, prolonged parenteral nutrition without thiamine, bariatric surgery, gastrointestinal malignancy, refeeding after starvation, post-glucose loading in the thiamine-deplete. Untreated, progresses to Korsakoff syndrome (anterograde amnesia, confabulation, apathy). Ix: clinical diagnosis - do not delay treatment. Serum thiamine if available but not needed. MRI (mammillary body and periventricular T2 hyperintensity) supports diagnosis; FBC, LFT, glucose, EUC and magnesium. Mx: parenteral thiamine before or with glucose - Pabrinal (high-dose vitamin B and C) 2 pairs of ampoules IV over 30 minutes three times daily for 2 to 3 days, then oral thiamine 100 mg TDS. Correct magnesium (thiamine cofactor). Treat the underlying cause. Note: any at-risk patient presenting to ED gets IV thiamine before IV glucose - the reverse can precipitate Wernicke.
rich_summaries.Wilson disease: Autosomal recessive ATP7B mutation causing defective hepatic copper excretion into bile, with accumulation in liver, brain, cornea, kidney and heart. Prevalence 1 in 30,000. Presents 5 to 35 years. Clinical features: hepatic (acute or chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, fulminant failure often with Coombs-negative haemolysis and low ALP relative to bilirubin); neurological (dysarthria, tremor, dystonia, parkinsonism, wing-beating tremor); psychiatric (personality change, depression, psychosis); Kayser-Fleischer corneal rings (virtually all neurological cases, half of hepatic); Fanconi syndrome; haemolytic anaemia. Ix: serum caeruloplasmin low (under 0.2 g/L); 24-hour urinary copper raised (over 1.6 micromol/day); slit-lamp for Kayser-Fleischer rings; liver biopsy for hepatic copper (most reliable); genetic testing confirms. Screen first-degree relatives. Mx: copper chelation with penicillamine or trientine; zinc acetate blocks intestinal absorption (maintenance); low-copper diet (avoid shellfish, liver, nuts, chocolate); liver transplant for fulminant failure. Note: lifelong treatment essential; discontinuation causes rapid relapse and fatal decompensation.
rich_summaries.Wolff-Parkinson-White: Congenital accessory pathway between atrium and ventricle that bypasses the AV node, giving ventricular pre-excitation. Clinical features: WPW pattern is short PR (under 120 ms), delta wave and widened QRS on resting ECG. WPW syndrome adds a tachyarrhythmia. Two dangers dominate - AV re-entrant tachycardia (AVRT, orthodromic in over 90%, narrow regular) and, more dangerously, atrial fibrillation with rapid conduction down the accessory pathway - an irregular, wide, very fast rhythm that can degenerate to VF. Ix: 12-lead ECG in and out of the arrhythmia; ambulatory monitoring; electrophysiology study for pathway localisation and risk (shortest pre-excited RR interval in AF). Mx: stable orthodromic AVRT gets vagal manoeuvres then IV adenosine. Pre-excited AF or unstable disease gets synchronised DC cardioversion or IV procainamide. AV nodal blockers (adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin, IV amiodarone) are contraindicated in pre-excited AF - they accelerate the pathway. Definitive treatment is catheter ablation, curative in over 95%. Note: any wide, irregular, fast tachycardia is pre-excited AF until proven otherwise.
rich_summaries.von Willebrand disease: Commonest inherited bleeding disorder (prevalence around 1%). Deficiency or dysfunction of von Willebrand factor impairs platelet adhesion and reduces factor VIII (which vWF chaperones). Types: type 1 (partial quantitative deficiency, autosomal dominant, mild, 70 to 80%); type 2 (qualitative defect - 2A, 2B, 2M, 2N); type 3 (near-complete deficiency, autosomal recessive, severe). Acquired vWD occurs with aortic stenosis (Heyde), lymphoproliferative disorders and hypothyroidism. Clinical features: mucocutaneous bleeding - epistaxis, easy bruising, heavy menstrual bleeding, prolonged bleeding after dental extraction or minor surgery; deep tissue and joint bleeding are uncommon (unlike haemophilia). Ix: FBC, APTT (may be prolonged), PT and fibrinogen normal; vWF antigen, vWF activity (ristocetin cofactor), factor VIII activity; multimer analysis to subtype. Mx: desmopressin (DDAVP) releases endogenous vWF - test dose confirms response, avoid in type 2B and type 3. vWF-containing factor VIII concentrate for severe bleeding. Tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeding. Avoid antiplatelets and NSAIDs. Note: combined OCP or tranexamic acid for heavy menstrual bleeding.

signs.name: Dyspnoea
signs.summary: Subjective awareness of uncomfortable breathing. A symptom, so it is reported rather than measured. Note: quantify it by function - flights of stairs, metres on the flat - because that is what changes with treatment and what the patient can report reliably at follow-up.

signs.name: Orthopnoea
signs.summary: Breathlessness on lying flat, relieved by sitting up. Mechanism: recumbency redistributes splanchnic and lower limb blood into the thorax, raising preload beyond what a failing left ventricle can handle, and the abdominal contents push the diaphragm up. Note: quantify it in pillows, and ask whether the number has changed - the trend carries the information. Also occurs in large pleural effusion, massive ascites and diaphragmatic weakness, so it is not specific to heart failure.

signs.name: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea
signs.summary: Waking abruptly from sleep gasping for breath, typically one to two hours in, and needing to sit or stand for relief that takes several minutes. Note: more specific for heart failure than orthopnoea. The delay before relief distinguishes it from the near-instant relief of simple orthopnoea, and the distress is often described as frightening rather than merely uncomfortable.

signs.name: Tachypnoea
signs.summary: Raised respiratory rate, above about 20 breaths per minute in an adult. Note: the most frequently omitted and most predictive single observation in deteriorating patients - it moves earlier than blood pressure or conscious level, and is weighted accordingly in most early-warning scores.

signs.name: Stridor
signs.summary: Harsh, monophonic sound from turbulent flow through a narrowed upper airway - loudest over the neck, not the chest. Note: inspiratory suggests extrathoracic obstruction, expiratory intrathoracic, biphasic a fixed lesion. Red flags: new stridor in an adult is an airway emergency until proven otherwise.

signs.name: Wheeze
signs.summary: Continuous musical sound from airflow through narrowed intrathoracic airways, typically expiratory and polyphonic. Note: a quiet chest in acute asthma is worse than a loud one - it means too little air is moving to generate sound. Fixed monophonic wheeze suggests a single obstructed airway, so consider tumour or foreign body.

signs.name: Crackles
signs.summary: Discontinuous popping sounds from small airways or alveoli opening. Types: fine and late-inspiratory in pulmonary fibrosis and pulmonary oedema; coarse and early-inspiratory in bronchiectasis and secretions, and these often clear with coughing.

signs.name: Pleural rub
signs.summary: Creaking sound from inflamed pleural surfaces moving over one another, heard in both inspiration and expiration and unchanged by coughing. Suggests pleurisy, pulmonary infarction or pneumonia reaching the pleura.

signs.name: Haemoptysis
signs.summary: Coughing up blood from the respiratory tract. Causes: bronchitis and bronchiectasis, malignancy, tuberculosis, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, anticoagulation, and pulmonary-renal syndromes. Note: confirm it is not haematemesis or a nasopharyngeal source before working it up; massive haemoptysis kills by asphyxiation rather than exsanguination, so positioning the bleeding side down matters.

signs.name: Clubbing
signs.summary: Bulbous swelling of the distal digit with loss of the normal nail-fold angle, increased nail bed fluctuance and a positive Schamroth window sign. Causes: lung cancer, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, pulmonary fibrosis, empyema; cyanotic congenital heart disease and infective endocarditis; inflammatory bowel disease, coeliac disease and cirrhosis. Note: uncomplicated COPD and asthma do not cause it, so clubbing in a COPD patient is a reason to look for cancer.

signs.name: Cyanosis
signs.summary: Blue discolouration from an absolute concentration of deoxygenated haemoglobin above roughly 50 g/L. Types: central, affecting tongue and mucous membranes, from arterial desaturation or an abnormal haemoglobin; peripheral, affecting extremities only, from poor local flow. Note: because the threshold is absolute rather than a percentage, anaemia can mask profound hypoxaemia and polycythaemia makes cyanosis appear early. It is an unreliable sign either way - use the saturation.

signs.name: Murmur
signs.summary: Sound produced by turbulent blood flow within the heart or great vessels. Features: describe timing, site of maximal intensity, radiation, character, pitch, grade out of six, and the effect of respiration and posture. Red flags: any diastolic murmur, any murmur with symptoms, a thrill (grade 4 or above), or a murmur with an abnormal ECG or a displaced apex needs an echocardiogram. Isolated soft mid-systolic murmurs in asymptomatic young people are usually innocent.

signs.name: Thrill
signs.summary: A palpable murmur - vibration felt over the praecordium. Note: its presence makes the murmur at least grade 4 of 6 by definition, and effectively excludes an innocent murmur.

signs.name: Parasternal heave
signs.summary: Sustained outward thrust felt with the heel of the hand at the left sternal edge, indicating right ventricular hypertrophy or volume overload - so look for pulmonary hypertension, mitral stenosis or an atrial septal defect.

signs.name: Jugular venous pressure
signs.summary: Height of the internal jugular pulsation above the sternal angle, a bedside estimate of right atrial pressure; normal is 3 cm or less at 45 degrees. Note: distinguished from the carotid by being biphasic, impalpable, obliterable by light pressure and varying with posture and respiration. A raised JVP with clear lungs points to right-sided causes - pulmonary embolism, tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, cor pulmonale.

signs.name: Pulsus paradoxus
signs.summary: Exaggeration of the normal inspiratory fall in systolic pressure, beyond 10 mmHg. Note: not actually paradoxical - the direction is normal and only the magnitude is abnormal. Suggests cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, or severe acute asthma and COPD, where large negative intrathoracic pressures do the same thing.

signs.name: Tachycardia
signs.summary: Heart rate above 100 beats per minute in an adult. Note: narrow versus broad complex is the first branch point, and regularity the second; treat the patient's haemodynamic state, not the number.

signs.name: Palpitations
signs.summary: Unpleasant awareness of one's own heartbeat. Note: the discriminating questions are onset and offset - abrupt start and stop suggests a re-entrant tachycardia, gradual suggests sinus tachycardia from anxiety, anaemia or thyrotoxicosis. Palpitations with syncope, exertional onset or a family history of sudden death need urgent assessment.

signs.name: Presyncope
signs.summary: The sensation of impending faint without loss of consciousness. Carries broadly the same differential and the same significance as syncope, and should not be dismissed as the milder complaint.

signs.name: Claudication
signs.summary: Reproducible muscle pain brought on by walking a predictable distance and relieved within minutes by rest, from peripheral arterial disease. Note: distinguish from neurogenic claudication in spinal stenosis, where relief needs flexion rather than merely stopping - so walking uphill or leaning on a trolley is easier, which is the reverse of the vascular pattern. Red flags: rest pain or tissue loss means critical limb ischaemia.

signs.name: Oedema
signs.summary: Excess interstitial fluid, clinically detectable once several litres have accumulated. Note: pitting versus non-pitting is the useful split - pitting suggests raised hydrostatic pressure or low oncotic pressure; non-pitting suggests lymphoedema or myxoedema. Symmetry matters as much - unilateral leg oedema raises deep vein thrombosis, while bilateral oedema points to a systemic cause.

signs.name: Jaundice
signs.summary: Yellow discolouration of skin and sclerae from hyperbilirubinaemia, usually visible above about 50 micromol/L. Types: prehepatic (unconjugated, from haemolysis or Gilbert syndrome), hepatic, and post-hepatic or obstructive (conjugated, with pale stool and dark urine). Note: check the sclerae in natural light - carotenaemia yellows skin but spares them.

signs.name: Ascites
signs.summary: Free fluid in the peritoneal cavity, detected by shifting dullness or a fluid thrill once roughly 1.5 L is present. Ix: diagnostic paracentesis with a serum-ascites albumin gradient - 11 g/L or above indicates portal hypertension, below suggests malignancy, tuberculosis or pancreatic causes. Note: send a cell count on every tap; over 250 neutrophils per microlitre is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis regardless of symptoms.

signs.name: Hepatomegaly
signs.summary: Palpable liver enlargement, measured as span in the midclavicular line rather than as centimetres below the costal margin, since hyperinflation displaces a normal liver downward. Note: a pulsatile liver suggests tricuspid regurgitation; a hard craggy edge suggests malignancy; tenderness suggests acute congestion, hepatitis or abscess.

signs.name: Splenomegaly
signs.summary: Palpable spleen, which implies at least a doubling in size. Enlarges towards the right iliac fossa, moves with respiration, has a notch and no palpable upper border, and is not ballotable - the features that separate it from a kidney. Causes: portal hypertension, haematological malignancy, haemolysis, infection including malaria and infectious mononucleosis, and infiltrative disease.

signs.name: Dysphagia
signs.summary: Difficulty swallowing. Note: solids progressing to liquids suggests a mechanical obstruction; solids and liquids together from the outset suggests a motility disorder such as achalasia. Red flags: new dysphagia at any age warrants urgent endoscopy, particularly with weight loss or anaemia.

signs.name: Odynophagia
signs.summary: Pain on swallowing, indicating mucosal injury or inflammation rather than obstruction - oesophagitis, candidiasis, herpes or CMV in the immunocompromised, or pill-induced ulceration.

signs.name: Steatorrhoea
signs.summary: Pale, bulky, offensive, difficult-to-flush stool from fat malabsorption. Suggests pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, coeliac disease, bile salt deficiency or bacterial overgrowth.

signs.name: Tenesmus
signs.summary: Persistent sensation of incomplete evacuation with an urge to defaecate despite an empty rectum. Suggests a rectal mass, proctitis or inflammatory bowel disease.

signs.name: Paraesthesia
signs.summary: Abnormal spontaneous sensation - tingling or pins and needles - without a stimulus. Note: the distribution carries the diagnosis - glove-and-stocking suggests polyneuropathy, dermatomal a root, and a peripheral nerve territory an entrapment.

signs.name: Allodynia
signs.summary: Pain provoked by a stimulus that is not normally painful, such as light touch or bedsheets. A hallmark of neuropathic pain and of central sensitisation.

signs.name: Hyperalgesia
signs.summary: Exaggerated pain from a stimulus that is normally painful. Note: distinct from allodynia, where the stimulus is not normally painful at all, and the pair are usually rated separately in neuropathic pain assessment.

signs.name: Ataxia
signs.summary: Incoordination of movement not explained by weakness. Types: cerebellar, with past-pointing, dysdiadochokinesis and a wide-based gait unaffected by closing the eyes; and sensory, from proprioceptive loss, where closing the eyes makes it markedly worse - a positive Romberg test.

signs.name: Dysarthria
signs.summary: Impaired articulation from weakness or incoordination of the speech muscles. Note: language itself is intact - comprehension, naming and writing are normal, which separates it from dysphasia and matters because the lesions are in different places.

signs.name: Dysphasia
signs.summary: Impairment of language itself - production, comprehension, or both. Types: expressive or Broca (non-fluent, comprehension relatively preserved, insight retained and frustration common); receptive or Wernicke (fluent but empty speech, impaired comprehension, often unaware); conduction (repetition disproportionately affected); global.

signs.name: Nystagmus
signs.summary: Involuntary rhythmic eye oscillation, named by the direction of the fast phase. Note: peripheral vestibular nystagmus is unidirectional, horizontal-torsional and suppressed by visual fixation; central nystagmus may be vertical, direction-changing, or unsuppressed by fixation, and that combination is the worrying one.

signs.name: Ptosis
signs.summary: Drooping of the upper eyelid. Causes: third nerve palsy (with a down-and-out eye and often a dilated pupil); Horner syndrome (partial ptosis with miosis and anhidrosis); myasthenia gravis (fatigable and variable); myotonic dystrophy. Red flags: painful ptosis with a dilated pupil suggests a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.

signs.name: Diplopia
signs.summary: Double vision. Note: establish first whether it resolves on covering either eye - binocular diplopia implies ocular misalignment and a neurological or orbital cause, whereas monocular diplopia persisting with one eye covered is almost always ocular, usually refractive or cataract.

signs.name: Hyperreflexia
signs.summary: Exaggerated tendon reflexes, an upper motor neurone sign - so expect spasticity, clonus and an extensor plantar response with it.

signs.name: Clonus
signs.summary: Rhythmic involuntary contractions provoked by sustained stretch, most often tested at the ankle. Note: more than about four beats is pathological and indicates an upper motor neurone lesion; sustained clonus in a patient on serotonergic drugs is a key feature of serotonin syndrome.

signs.name: Fasciculation
signs.summary: Visible irregular twitching of a muscle fascicle at rest, from spontaneous discharge of a motor unit. Note: benign fasciculation is common, particularly in calves and eyelids; fasciculation *with wasting and weakness* is the combination that suggests motor neurone disease.

signs.name: Spasticity
signs.summary: Velocity-dependent increase in tone with a catch and give - the clasp-knife phenomenon. An upper motor neurone sign. Note: contrast rigidity, which is constant through the range and independent of velocity, and is extrapyramidal.

signs.name: Rigidity
signs.summary: Increased tone throughout the range of movement and independent of velocity. Types: lead-pipe, uniform; cogwheel, ratcheting, being lead-pipe rigidity with superimposed tremor. An extrapyramidal sign of parkinsonism.

signs.name: Bradykinesia
signs.summary: Slowness of movement with progressive reduction in amplitude and speed on repetition - watch finger-tapping decrement. Note: the obligatory feature for a clinical diagnosis of parkinsonism; tremor and rigidity are not sufficient without it.

signs.name: Chorea
signs.summary: Brief, irregular, non-repetitive involuntary movements flowing from one body part to another, often incorporated into apparently purposeful actions. Causes: Huntington disease, Sydenham chorea, systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid syndrome, thyrotoxicosis, levodopa and other drugs, pregnancy.

signs.name: Myoclonus
signs.summary: Sudden, brief, shock-like involuntary muscle jerk. Note: asterixis is negative myoclonus - a brief lapse of tone rather than a contraction - and points to metabolic encephalopathy, hepatic, uraemic or hypercapnic.

signs.name: Oliguria
signs.summary: Urine output below about 0.5 mL/kg/hour, or under 400 mL per day in an adult. A defining criterion in acute kidney injury staging and often the earliest sign of it.

signs.name: Polyuria
signs.summary: Urine output above about 3 L per day. Causes: osmotic diuresis in hyperglycaemia, diabetes insipidus, hypercalcaemia, resolving acute kidney injury, diuretics, and primary polydipsia. Note: distinguish from frequency, which is passing normal total volumes more often - the two are routinely conflated in histories.

signs.name: Nocturia
signs.summary: Waking from sleep to pass urine. Causes: benign prostatic hyperplasia, overactive bladder, heart failure and peripheral oedema redistributing at night, obstructive sleep apnoea, diabetes, and evening diuretic timing.

signs.name: Haematuria
signs.summary: Blood in the urine. Types: visible or macroscopic, and non-visible detected on dipstick or microscopy. Note: visible painless haematuria is malignancy until proven otherwise and needs urgent urological referral. Dysmorphic red cells or red cell casts point to a glomerular source instead; beetroot, rifampicin and myoglobin are the classic mimics.

signs.name: Proteinuria
signs.summary: Abnormal protein loss in urine, quantified by albumin-creatinine ratio on a first-void sample rather than by dipstick. Note: above 3.5 g per day with hypoalbuminaemia and oedema defines nephrotic syndrome. Dipstick detects albumin poorly at low levels and misses light chains entirely.

signs.name: Dysuria
signs.summary: Pain or burning on passing urine. Usually urinary tract infection, but consider urethritis, vaginitis, prostatitis and stones, particularly when the urine is repeatedly clear on culture.

signs.name: Uraemia
signs.summary: The clinical syndrome of accumulated nitrogenous waste in advanced kidney failure - nausea, anorexia, pruritus, fatigue, a metallic taste, and later encephalopathy, asterixis, pericarditis and bleeding from platelet dysfunction. Note: uraemic pericarditis and encephalopathy are indications for urgent dialysis, and the urea level itself correlates poorly with symptoms.

signs.name: Cachexia
signs.summary: Loss of muscle mass, with or without fat loss, driven by an underlying illness and its inflammatory mediators - not reversed by nutritional support alone. Seen in malignancy, advanced heart failure, COPD, chronic kidney disease and chronic infection.

signs.name: Sarcopenia
signs.summary: Progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength and function, primarily age-related. Note: distinguished from cachexia by the absence of a driving inflammatory illness, and unlike cachexia it does respond to resistance training and protein intake. A core component of physical frailty.

signs.name: Lymphadenopathy
signs.summary: Enlarged lymph nodes. Note: the worrying features are size above 2 cm, hard or fixed texture, supraclavicular site, painlessness, and persistence beyond four to six weeks - particularly with constitutional symptoms. Tender mobile nodes in a drainage territory are usually reactive.
